t-e-lawrence: Thomas Edward Lawrence was born on 16 August 1888 in Tremadog, Wales, the illegitimate son of Sir Thomas Chapman, an Anglo-Irish landowner, and Sarah Lawrence, a governess in Chapman's household. His parents did not marry but lived together under the name Lawrence. In 1896 the family moved to Oxford, where he attended the City of Oxford High School for Boys and read history at Jesus College from 1907 to 1910. Before the war he worked as an archaeologist for the British Museum, chiefly at Carchemish in Ottoman Syria.

After the outbreak of war in 1914 he was commissioned in October and sent to the Arab Bureau, a military intelligence unit in Cairo, arriving on 15 December. The Arab Revolt began in June 1916, and in October he was sent to the Hejaz, where he interviewed the sons of Sharif Hussein and concluded that Faisal was the best candidate to lead it. With Faisal he developed a strategy of avoiding the capture of Medina and extending northwards towards Damascus. In 1917 he proposed a joint attack on Aqaba, led by Sharif Nasir of Medina.

Lawrence arrived in Damascus around 9 am on 1 October 1918, several hours after it had fallen, and helped establish a provisional Arab government under Faisal. After the war he joined the Foreign Office and attended the Paris Peace Conference as a member of Faisal's delegation. In 1922 he withdrew from public life and served as an enlisted man in the Army and the Royal Air Force until 1935. King George V offered him a knighthood in October 1918, but he declined, because he thought British policy had betrayed the Arab cause.

His major work is Seven Pillars of Wisdom, his account of the Arab Revolt, which he rewrote three times and published in 1926. An abridged version, Revolt in the Desert, appeared in March 1927 and was a best-seller. He also translated Homer's Odyssey and wrote The Mint, on his service in the RAF, which was published after his death. Some alleged embellishments in Seven Pillars have been disproved, but his own notebooks refute his claim to have crossed Sinai from Aqaba to the Suez Canal in 49 hours without sleep; the ride lasted more than 70 hours. Richard Aldington attacked his veracity in 1955. Lawrence died in 1935 at the age of 46 after a motorcycle crash in Dorset.
t-s-eliot: Thomas Stearns Eliot was born into a Boston Brahmin family. His paternal grandfather, William Greenleaf Eliot, had moved from New Bedford, Massachusetts, to St. Louis to establish a Unitarian church there, and his father, Henry Ware Eliot, was president and treasurer of the Hydraulic-Press Brick Company. His mother, Charlotte Champe Stearns, wrote poetry and was a social worker, then a new profession in the United States.

Eliot moved to the United Kingdom in 1914, at the age of 25, and married Vivienne Haigh-Wood at Hampstead Register Office on 26 June 1915. He taught French and Latin at Highgate School, where John Betjeman was among his students, and in 1917 took a position at Lloyds Bank in London. On 29 June 1927 he converted from Unitarianism to Anglicanism, and in November he took British citizenship, describing himself as "classicist in literature, royalist in politics, and anglo-catholic in religion".

In 1915 Ezra Pound recommended "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" to Harriet Monroe of Poetry magazine. Eliot wrote most of it at 22, and its opening lines, comparing the evening sky to "a patient etherised upon a table", were considered shocking at a time when Georgian Poetry was admired. The Waste Land appeared in The Criterion in October 1922, with a dedication to Pound, "il miglior fabbro", for his editing of a longer manuscript. "Ash-Wednesday" (1930), his first long poem after his conversion, was less ironic and concerned with spiritual matters.

Eliot regarded Four Quartets as his masterpiece. Its four poems, "Burnt Norton" (1936), "East Coker" (1940), "The Dry Salvages" (1941) and "Little Gidding" (1942), meditate on time and are each associated with one of the four elements. Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats (1939) was the basis of the musical Cats, first produced in the West End in 1981. His criticism strongly influenced New Criticism, and critics led by Anthony Julius have accused him of antisemitism for the depiction of Jews in poems such as "Gerontion".

From 1932 Eliot lived apart from Vivienne, who was committed to a mental hospital in 1938 and died in 1947. He died of emphysema at his home in Kensington on 4 January 1965 and was cremated at Golders Green. As he wished, his ashes were taken to St Michael and All Angels' Church in East Coker, Somerset, the village from which his ancestors had emigrated to America, where a plaque carries lines from East Coker: "In my beginning is my end. In my end is my beginning."
ta-prohm: Ta Prohm is the modern name, meaning "Ancestor Brahma", of a temple about one kilometre east of Angkor Thom and on the southern edge of the East Baray, near Siem Reap. It was built in the Bayon style, largely in the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries, and was originally called Rajavihara, the "Royal Monastery". Jayavarman VII founded it as a Mahayana Buddhist monastery and centre of learning, one of the first temples of his great building programme.

Its main image, of Prajnaparamita, the personification of wisdom, was modelled on the king's mother. The northern and southern satellite temples were dedicated to the king's guru, Jayamangalartha, and to his elder brother. The foundation stele records that more than 12,500 people lived at the site, among them 18 high priests and 615 dancers, with a further 80,000 in surrounding villages providing services and supplies, and that the temple amassed gold, pearls and silks.

Ta Prohm is a flat Khmer temple, not a temple-mountain. Five rectangular walls enclose a central sanctuary, and the temple faces east, so that the sanctuary lies to the west along a long east-west axis. The three inner enclosures are galleried. Face towers like those of the Bayon were added to the gateways in the thirteenth century, and building went on as late as the reign of Srindravarman at the end of that century.

There are few narrative reliefs compared with Angkor Wat or Angkor Thom, but a badly eroded one shows the Great Departure of Siddhartha, the future Buddha, and others show devatas, meditating ascetics and temple guardians. The temple was built without mortar. After it was abandoned, trees took root in the loosened stones.

The temple was abandoned after the fall of the Khmer Empire in the fifteenth century. When conservation of the Angkor temples began in the early twentieth century, the École française d'Extrême-Orient chose to leave Ta Prohm largely as it was found, as a concession to the general taste for the picturesque. Much work has since gone into stabilising the ruins and keeping their look of neglect.

Two kinds of tree dominate the ruins, though sources disagree on their identification: the larger is either the silk-cotton tree or Tetrameles nudiflora, the smaller either a strangler fig or the gold apple. UNESCO inscribed Ta Prohm on the World Heritage List in 1992. The Archaeological Survey of India and the APSARA Authority carry out its conservation.
tabare-vazquez: Tabaré Ramón Vázquez Rosas was born in the La Teja neighbourhood of Montevideo on 17 January 1940, the fourth child of Héctor Vázquez, a worker of the state company ANCAP, and Elena Rosas. His grandparents came from Ourense and Santiago de Compostela in Galicia. He studied medicine at the Medical School of the Universidad de la República and graduated as an oncologist in 1972. In 1976 a grant from the French government let him train further at the Gustave Roussy Institute in Paris. He was president of the football club Club Progreso from 1979 to 1989.

From 1990 Vázquez was the first Intendant of Montevideo from the Frente Amplio coalition, carrying out the functions of both mayor of the city and governor of the department. In 1994 he ran for president and received the most votes of any candidate, but under the Ley de Lemas system the election went to Julio María Sanguinetti of the Colorado Party, the highest-finishing candidate of the party with the most votes. In 1996 he replaced the coalition's historic leader, Líber Seregni, as its leader. In 1999, in the first election after the Ley de Lemas was scrapped, he led the first round with 40.1 percent but lost the runoff to Jorge Batlle.

Vázquez won the presidency in the first round of the 2004 election, with 50.45 percent of valid votes, and took office on 1 March 2005. He was the first president from a left-wing party and the first since the 1830s who was not a member of the National or Colorado parties. His first term was marked by a conflict with Argentina over pulp mills on the Uruguay River and by closer relations with Brazil and Argentina. He did not sign the Free Trade Area of the Americas proposed by George W. Bush. He strengthened the unions and improved social services; between 2005 and 2008 the minimum wage rose from 1,350 to 4,150 pesos. The constitution barred immediate re-election, and José Mujica succeeded him in 2010.

He was elected again in the runoff of 30 November 2014, defeating Luis Lacalle Pou, and took office on 1 March 2015. He devoted much of his second term to fighting non-communicable diseases. The World Health Organization gave him its Director-General's Award in 2006 for his tobacco-control leadership.

Vázquez left office in March 2020. He died of lung cancer in Montevideo on 6 December 2020, aged 80, and Uruguay declared three days of national mourning. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic his funeral was held in intimacy, and he was buried at the Cementerio de La Teja beside his wife, María Auxiliadora Delgado, whom he had married in 1964.
tabaristan: Tabaristan, also written Tabarestan, was a mountainous region on the Caspian coast of northern Iran. It corresponds to the present-day province of Mazandaran, which became the usual name of the area from the 11th century onwards. It took its name from the Tapurians, who had been deported there from Parthia by the Parthian king Phraates I. Its local language, Mazandarani or Tabari, is first attested in the works of early Muslim geographers and has about the same distribution today.

At the rise of the Sasanians the region belonged, with Gilan and Daylam, to the kingdom of Padishkhwargar under Gushnasp, who submitted to Ardashir I on condition of keeping his kingdom. His line ruled until Kavad I removed it, and under the Sasanians the region enjoyed considerable autonomy. In the 640s the Dabuyid prince Gil Gavbara conquered Daylam and Gilan, and Yazdegerd III acknowledged him as ruler, giving him the title Padashwārgarshāh. Gil Gavbara kept his realm independent during the Muslim conquest of Iran. His son Baduspan I received Ruyan in 665, founding the Baduspanid dynasty, and the Qarinvandids and Bavandids held the mountains as Dabuyid vassals.

Farrukhan the Great contained a large Umayyad invasion in 716. The last Dabuyid, Khurshid, was defeated in 760 by the Abbasid general Abu al-Khaṣīb Marzuq. Tabaristan then became a province of the caliphate, ruled from Amul by an Arab governor, while the Bavandids, Qarinvandids, Zarmihrids and Baduspanids stayed largely autonomous in the interior as tributary vassals. In 783 Wandad Hurmuzd and Sharwin I rebelled; local accounts say the Muslim inhabitants were massacred in one day, though Wilferd Madelung thinks this exaggerated. The caliph al-Mahdi's forces defeated the rebels in the following year, and Wandad Hurmuzd was captured and pardoned.

Amul became the leading town and the main producer of silk fabrics; the commentator and historian Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, who died in 923, bore its name. Zaydi Shi'ism established Islam properly there in the 9th and 10th centuries. The Bavandids used Pahlavi legends on their coins as late as the early 11th century, and dynasties such as the Bavandids and Ziyarids went on commemorating their pre-Islamic past with festivals such as Nowruz and Mehregan. The oldest known work in Tabari, the Marzban-nama, survives only in Persian translation.
tabasco: Tabasco, officially the Free and Sovereign State of Tabasco, is one of the 32 federal entities of Mexico. It covers 24,731 square kilometres and is divided into seventeen municipalities. It borders Campeche to the northeast, Veracruz to the west and Chiapas to the south, and the Petén department of Guatemala lies to the southeast. The northwest lies on the coastal plain of the Gulf of Mexico. Rain falls plentifully all year, and most of the state is covered in rainforest. Since 1994 it has been divided for documentation into two regions named after the Grijalva and Usumacinta rivers.

The Olmec civilisation dominated much of what is now Tabasco about 3,000 years ago, and its main site there is La Venta, surrounded by swamps and marshes about 15 km from the Gulf. The Maya began to dominate part of the state around 300 CE; their sites include Comalcalco, Pomoná, El Tortuguero and Jonuta. At Comalcalco they built in adobe brick because the area lacked building stone, using clay and lime extracted from shells.

The first Spanish contact came in 1518, when Juan de Grijalva landed at the mouth of the river that now bears his name. Hernán Cortés came the next year and fought the natives at the Battle of Centla; among the twenty female slaves he received as conqueror was La Malinche. The territory was never fully subjugated because of its climate, terrain and lack of minerals, and the Franciscans who arrived in the 16th century did not stay. European diseases decimated the local population, and the Spanish brought African slaves to work plantations. Significant agricultural production, chiefly cacao and cattle, came only in the 18th century.

Tabasco became one of the first fourteen states under the 1824 Constitution. During the Mexican–American War troops under Matthew C. Perry took the port of Frontera in 1846 and later Villahermosa, but guerrilla groups and the climate forced the United States to withdraw. Its forces returned in 1847 and occupied the capital for thirty-five days, causing great destruction.

Villahermosa is the capital. The state produces petroleum and natural gas, and its farming includes cacao, coconut, bananas, sugar cane and cattle. Most speakers of indigenous languages use the Tabascan dialect of Chontal Maya. The Parque Museo de La Venta in Villahermosa, created in the 1950s by the writer Carlos Pellicer, shelters major pieces from La Venta, and Comalcalco is the Maya site open to the public. The state seal was granted in 1598 by Philip II of Spain to the town of Villahermosa, then called San Juan Bautista.
tabennisi: Tabenna, Tabennisi or Tabennesi is a Coptic name, and its form and the monastery's location were long uncertain. Greek manuscripts of the Lausiac History of Palladios give several spellings, and one manuscript of Sozomene splits the name into two words, one of them the Greek for island. This misreading seems to lie behind the phrase of the 14th-century writer Nikephoros Kallistos Xanthopoulos, "in a certain island called Tabenne", and so behind the tradition that the monastery stood on an island, which no ancient document supports. Recent archaeological work places the monastery on the edge of the modern village of Faw Qibli.

According to tradition, Pachomius was collecting wood at the abandoned village when a vision told him to build a monastery there. The monks first built a church for the village and then one for themselves. The community grew so fast that a sprawling village formed beside it. It was too remote to draw many pilgrims, but it did not escape the authorities: records of its taxation, dated 367, come from the Hermopolite nome, although Tabenna lay within the Tentyrite nome.

In the autumn of 329 Athanasius of Alexandria visited the monks and ordained Pachomius a priest. A second house was soon founded at Pbow, also an abandoned village; Pachomius settled there around 336-37, and it became the largest house, with 600 monks by 346. Further monasteries followed between Esna and Akhmim after 340. The whole formed an order under a superior general, who moved between the houses and appointed their superiors, and all the monks gathered at the mother house of Tabenna twice a year, at Easter and on 13 August, when the superiors reported on their management to the general bursar.

After Pachomius died on 9 May 346, Petronius succeeded him but died three months later. Orsisius followed, until a monastery's revolt in 351 led Theodorus of Tabennese, an early disciple, to take charge as Orsisius's vicar until his death in 368, by which time there were twelve houses for men and three for women. In 390 Archbishop Theophilus I of Alexandria helped the order found the monastery of Metanoia at Canopus, whose Latin monks spread its rule in the West. Palladios put the Pachomians at about 7,000 around 400. The order accepted the Council of Chalcedon, and divisions over it came only in the 6th century.
tabernacle: The Hebrew word mishkan means a residence or dwelling place, and the English word comes from the Latin tabernaculum, meaning tent or hut. The Septuagint renders it with the Greek skene, itself a Semitic loanword for tent. The biblical scholar Michael B. Hundley argues that the Priestly source uses the terms tabernacle and tent of meeting together to stress the tent's double function as a divine dwelling on earth and a place where the god meets his people.

In Exodus the Tabernacle was a rectangular enclosure with a fence of fabric, poles and staked cords, set up whenever the tribes camped and oriented to the east. Inside stood a sanctuary draped with goat-hair curtains, roofed with rams' skins. Its inner room, the cube-shaped Holy of Holies, held the Ark of the Covenant, which contained the two stone tablets of Moses, a golden urn of manna and Aaron's rod. Bezalel, son of Uri, of the tribe of Judah, was the main builder, assisted by Oholiab and skilled artisans. Priests burned incense twice a day, and only they could enter the innermost room, once a year on Yom Kippur.

According to the Hebrew Bible, after the conquest of Canaan the main camp was at Gilgal and the Tabernacle was moved to Shiloh in Ephraimite territory, where it stayed through most of the rule of the Judges. After the Philistines captured the Ark its history is separate from the Ark's. Under King Saul it was moved to Nob and, after Saul massacred the priests there, to the hill-shrine at Gibeon. David placed the Ark in a tent in Jerusalem, while the Tabernacle remained at Gibeon, until Solomon brought the structure and its furnishings to the Temple. The Tanakh does not mention it after the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in about 587 BCE.

Traditional scholars hold that the description reflects a real tabernacle, pointing to parallels with structures from ancient Egypt in the Late Bronze Age. Mark S. Smith and William G. Dever, among others, derive it from tent shrines in Canaan, Babylonia and Egypt, such as the Midianite tent shrine of Hathor in the Timna Valley.

Liane Feldman sees contrasting descriptions in the Pentateuch, a large ornate tent in the Priestly source and a smaller one for Moses in another strand. Some scholars believe the Tabernacle as described may never have existed but reflects the cultic objects and imagery of Jerusalem. Synagogues are said to follow its outlines, with an ark at the front for the Torah scrolls, a lamp that is always lit and a raised bimah.
tabinshwehti: Tabinshwehti was born at Toungoo Palace on 16 April 1516 to King Mingyi Nyo and his concubine Khin Oo, a village chief's daughter. His name means Unitary Golden Umbrella, the golden umbrella being the symbol of Burmese kings. He was trained in martial arts, horse and elephant riding and strategy alongside Ye Htut, the son of his wet nurse, who became his right-hand man. He came to the throne aged 14 when his father died on 24 November 1530.

About April 1534 Ye Htut's affair with the king's half-sister Thakin Gyi, treason under Burmese law, was discovered; Tabinshwehti gave him the princess in marriage and a princely title, winning lasting loyalty. Late that year he attacked the Hanthawaddy kingdom, probably urged on by older ministers. After raids failed, misinformation led King Takayutpi to execute his own loyal ministers, and Pegu fell without a shot. After a victory at Naungyo, Ye Htut was given the title Bayinnaung, King's Elder Brother.

Martaban, defended by Portuguese mercenaries, fell in May 1541 after a seven-month siege; Tabinshwehti had the viceroy, his family and the defenders executed for refusing amnesty. Prome surrendered on 19 May 1542 after Bayinnaung destroyed an Arakanese relief army, and Toungoo forces reached Pagan. Tabinshwehti was crowned there in the manner of the Pagan kings and again at Pegu in 1545 in the Hanthawaddy tradition, wearing his hair in the Mon style and naming a Mon, Khay Ma Naw, chief queen.

His invasion of Arakan ended when Min Bin flooded the besiegers out of Mrauk-U by opening the city's reservoirs, and a truce followed on 30 January 1547. On 14 October 1548 he led 12,000 men into Siam through the Three Pagodas Pass, but Siamese counterattacks broke the siege of Ayutthaya in January 1549.

Introduced to wine by a young Portuguese mercenary, he became an alcoholic and handed day-to-day government to Bayinnaung. On 30 April 1550, his 34th birthday, swordsmen sent by Smim Sawhtut, governor of Sittaung, beheaded him in his tent during a hunting trip. Each major governor then declared himself independent. The historian Victor Lieberman called his death "one of the great turning points of mainland [Southeast Asia] history", and the Tabinshwehti nat is one of the 37 spirits worshipped in Myanmar.
table-bay: Table Bay lies on the Atlantic Ocean at the northern end of the Cape Peninsula, which runs south to the Cape of Good Hope. It takes its name from the flat-topped Table Mountain that dominates it. The bay is relatively shallow, covering about 100 square kilometres and sloping gently from east to west to a maximum depth of 35 metres at the centre of its mouth. Its bedrock is shale, slate and sandstone of the Malmesbury group, like the rocks of Robben Island and Mouille Point, and the seabed is partly bare rock and patches of sand. Whale Rock and Green Point are hazards where several ships were wrecked or grounded.

Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488. The first European to anchor in the bay was the Portuguese navigator António de Saldanha in 1503, who also made the first recorded ascent of Table Mountain. The bay was first called Aguada de Saldanha, the watering-place of Saldanha, until the Dutch navigator Joris van Spilbergen renamed it Table Bay in 1601.

The bay is a poor natural harbour, exposed to north-westerly storm waves, and many sailing ships sheltering there in the 17th and 18th centuries were driven ashore by winter storms. The Dutch nevertheless persisted, since good harbours are scarce on this coast, and Saldanha Bay lacked fresh water while Simon's Bay and Hout Bay had their own drawbacks. On 6 April 1652 Jan van Riebeeck established a refreshment station for the Dutch East India Company, and a small fort, the Fort of Good Hope, was built on the shore. The settlement grew into Cape Town.

A modern harbour was built by land reclamation and breakwaters. Work on the first breakwater began in 1860, when Prince Alfred ceremonially tipped the first load of rocks. It protected the Alfred Basin, now part of the Victoria & Alfred Waterfront, and the deeper Duncan Dock came later. Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela was imprisoned for decades, lies in the bay. In November 1953 the Dutch tanker Sliedrecht had an accident that oiled the bay's beaches.
table-of-ranks: The Table of Ranks (Russian: Tabel' o rangakh) was a formal list of positions and ranks in the military, government and court of Imperial Russia. Peter the Great introduced it in 1722 while he was engaged in a struggle with the existing hereditary nobility, the boyars. It reorganised the foundations of the feudal Russian nobility, which had rested on the system of mestnichestvo, by recognising service in the army, the civil administration and at court as the basis of an aristocrat's standing in society.

The table divided ranks into 14 grades. In theory all nobles, whatever their birth or wealth, began at the bottom and rose through their service (sluzhba) to the tsar. All grades were open by merit, but promotion required qualification for the next rank, and grades 1 to 5 required the personal approval of the tsar. Achieving a level in the table automatically granted a level of nobility. A civil servant promoted to the 14th grade gained personal nobility (dvoryanstvo), and holding an office in the 8th grade conferred hereditary nobility. Nicholas I raised this threshold to the 5th grade in 1845, and in 1856 it was set at the 4th grade for the civil service and the 6th for military service.

Peter I also laid down rules of precedence. Princes related to him or married to his princesses took precedence, and a naval officer outranked an army officer at sea, while on land the army officer was superior. Fines of two months' salary were set against those who falsely claimed a higher rank, and women advanced in rank with their husbands.

Many noblemen at first resisted the system, shunning the life of the civil servant, but its eventual effect was to create an educated class of noble bureaucrats. Later tsars weakened Peter's intention of a nobility bound to him by personal service. In 1762 Peter III abolished the compulsory 25-year military or civilian service for nobles, and in 1767 Catherine the Great made promotion through the 14 ranks automatic after seven years, regardless of position or merit.

In practice, non-noble civil servants were often passed over for promotion to the 8th grade. This created a class of eternal titular councillors who held the same position for life and were satirised by writers such as Nikolai Gogol and Fyodor Dostoevsky. With occasional revisions the table remained in effect until the Russian Revolution of 1917, and the Bolshevik government formally abolished it on 11 November 1917.
tables-of-heraclea: Heraclea became a municipium after accepting Roman citizenship in 89 BCE, and the long Latin inscription on two of the bronze tablets concerns the municipal regulations of the town. It is a major authority for the municipal law of ancient Italy and for the study of Roman law. On the back of these tablets is an earlier inscription in Doric Greek defining the boundaries of lands that belonged to temples.

Scholars traditionally identified the Latin text with the Lex Iulia Municipalis, a law issued in 45 BCE to regulate the institutions of towns throughout Italy. It is now widely believed that the tablets do not record one law but bring together material from several pieces of legislation. The origin of the municipal regulations is still debated: they may have formed part of the Lex Iulia Municipalis, though some scholars argue that they go back to the earlier lex Iulia de civitate.

The tablets were found separately, in the bed of the Cavone river a short way from the site of Heraclea in the direction of Metapontum, and the major one was in two fragments. One fragment was bought by Francesco Ficoroni and taken to England, where it was sold to Brian Fairfax the younger; after Fairfax's death in 1749 Philip Carteret Webb bought it, and it was returned to Naples in 1752.

Michel Maittaire first published the Latin inscription in 1735. Alessio Simmaco Mazzocchi published both inscriptions with commentaries in two volumes at Naples in 1754 and 1755, and Heinrich Eduard Dirksen and Friedrich Carl von Savigny later wrote legal commentaries on the Latin text.
tablet-of-shamash: The tablet came to light during Hormuzd Rassam's excavations of 1878 to 1883, inside a terracotta coffer sealed beneath an asphalt temple floor. It was broken into two large and six small pieces; by the time of King Nabopolassar, between 625 and 605 BCE, it had already broken into four parts and been repaired. The coffer also held two clay impressions of the presentation scene, and it has been suggested that it contained a second tablet and a third impression, now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums.

The stone was kept in a clay cast, or squeeze, laid over its face to protect it, which suggests it was an object of reverence, perhaps put away as traditions changed. Its edges are serrated like a saw. The relief at the top shows Shamash seated beneath symbols of the sun, moon and star, wearing a horned headdress and holding the rod-and-ring symbol in his right hand. Before him a large sun disk on an altar hangs from above, held by two figures. Of three figures on the left, the central one, dressed like the god, is taken to be Nabu-apla-iddina receiving the symbols of the deity.

Short captions name the image of Shamash, the great lord who dwells in the Ebabbara at Sippar, place Sin, Shamash and Ishtar over against the heavenly ocean, and label the god's headdress and rod. The cuneiform text below runs to fifteen passages mixing prose, poetry and rhetoric in the manner of Mesopotamian royal inscriptions. It tells how Sippar and the Ebabbar temple fell into disrepair after the god's statue was lost, how a solar disk stood in for it, and how a new figure of the god found east of the Euphrates let the king make a new statue of lapis lazuli and gold. The rest records the royal grant, much like a kudurru, and the temple's practices, priestly rules and dress.
tabora: Tabora is the capital of Tanzania's Tabora Region and the administrative seat of Tabora Urban District, which had a population of 226,999 at the 2012 census. It has a tropical savanna climate with two seasons of about equal length, a wet season from November to April and a dry season from May to October. Its people rely mainly on agriculture, as subsistence farmers or small-scale tobacco growers. The streets are lined with century-old mango trees planted by Omani traders, and the town is known as the fruit capital of western Tanzania.

Coastal traders settled in the region to take advantage of the ivory and slave caravan trade, and Swahili and Omani traders established Kazeh near present-day Tabora. By 1870 the town had between 5,000 and 10,000 inhabitants living in roughly fifty large square houses. Each held up to several hundred people and had inner courtyards, garden plots, store rooms, servant quarters and outbuildings for slaves. Nyamwezi villages surrounded it, and their people provided produce and caravan labour. The Sultan of Zanzibar appointed a representative there, the town was part of the Kingdom of Unyanyembe, and traders came from as far north as the Kingdom of Buganda. In August 1871 the forces of the Nyamwezi ruler Mirambo sacked it and burned a quarter of the town.

German East Africa was proclaimed a protectorate over the region in 1885, but as late as 1891 travellers reported Tabora to be a lawless town, and the German administration gained control of it only later that year. As a major station on the Central Line it became the most important administrative centre of central German East Africa. In 1916 the colonial garrison struck an emergency coinage there, mostly crude copper and brass rupie coins marked T. During the Tabora Offensive of the East African Campaign, Belgian Congo colonial forces, the Force Publique under General Charles Tombeur, captured the town on 19 September 1916 after ten days and nights of heavy fighting.

Tabora is a junction on the Central railway line, which runs east to Dar es Salaam, west to Kigoma on Lake Tanganyika and north to Mwanza on Lake Victoria. Roads lead to Singida, Kigoma, Mbeya and Mwanza, though salt flats to the west prevent a direct road to Kigoma. The town is also known for two schools. Tabora Boys Secondary School was founded in 1922 to educate the sons of African chiefs and was called the Eton of Tanganyika, and Julius Nyerere studied there. Tabora Girls Secondary School was established in 1928.
tabqa-dam: A dam on the Euphrates near the Syria-Turkey border was first proposed in 1927, when Syria was a French mandate. After independence in 1946 its feasibility was studied and shelved. In 1957 the Syrian government reached an agreement with the Soviet Union, in 1960 it signed a financing agreement with West Germany as part of the United Arab Republic, and in 1965, after Syria left the union, a new agreement was reached with the Soviet Union.

The dam was built between 1968 and 1973 and the power station was finished on 8 March 1978. The cost was US$340 million, of which US$100 million was a Soviet loan, and up to 12,000 Syrians and 900 Russian technicians worked on it. About 4,000 Arab families from the flooded valley were resettled.

5 kilometres long and 60 metres high, with a power station of eight Kaplan turbines at its southern end. Euphrates Lake behind it is about 80 kilometres long and on average 8 kilometres wide. It was planned to generate 880 MW and to irrigate 640,000 hectares, but the irrigation scheme suffered from gypsum-rich soils, salinisation and collapsing canals, and by 2000 about 124,000 hectares were irrigated.

Filling the lake in 1974, together with the filling of Turkey's Keban reservoir and a drought, cut the flow to Iraq and brought the two states close to conflict until Saudi Arabia and the Soviet Union mediated in 1975. The lake also supplies drinking water to Aleppo.

The upper Syrian Euphrates valley had been intensively occupied since at least the Late Natufian period. Before the flooding, an archaeological rescue programme excavated more than 25 sites. Between 1965 and 1970 foreign missions worked at Mureybet, Tell Qannas, Mumbaqat, Selenkahiye and Emar, and in 1971, with support from UNESCO, Syria appealed for wider help and changed its antiquities law so that foreign missions could claim part of their finds. The minarets of Mureybet and Meskene were moved to higher ground, and the castle of Qal'at Ja'bar, turned into an island by the lake, was reinforced. Many finds are displayed in the National Museum of Aleppo.
tabriz: Tabriz lies in the valley of the Quru River in Iran's historic Azerbaijan region, between the Sahand and Eynali mountains, at an elevation of between 1,350 and 1,600 metres. The valley opens into a plain that slopes gently down to the eastern shore of Lake Urmia, 60 kilometres to the west. The area is prone to earthquakes, and the city has been devastated and rebuilt several times; earthquakes are recorded in 858, 1041 and 1721. According to some sources the name derives from tap-riz, meaning flowing hot, in reference to the area's thermal springs.

Early history is poorly documented. An Iron Age graveyard of the first millennium BCE was found beside the Blue Mosque, and the city appears as Tarui or Tauris in an inscription of the Assyrian king Sargon II dated 714 BCE. After the Muslim conquest the Azd tribe from Yemen settled there. In 791 Zubaidah, wife of the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, rebuilt the city after a devastating earthquake and beautified it so much that she was credited as its founder.

Tabriz was the capital of the Ilkhanate from 1265, and under Ghazan Khan, who came to power in 1295, it reached its highest splendour. It was again a capital under the Qara Qoyunlu from 1375 to 1468 and the Aq Qoyunlu from 1468 to 1500. Ismail I was crowned there in 1501 and announced Twelver Shia Islam as the official religion of the Safavid Empire, and the largely Sunni population was forced to convert. After the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 Selim I sacked the city, and in 1555 Tahmasp I moved the capital to Qazvin to escape the growing Ottoman threat.

Its closeness to the West made Tabriz the centre of the Iranian Constitutional Revolution between 1905 and 1911, led locally by Sattar Khan and Bagher Khan. Russian forces occupied it in 1909 and again from December 1911, executing about 1,200 residents, and held it until 1917.

Tabriz is the capital of East Azerbaijan province and the largest economic centre of north-western Iran, with a population of over 1.7 million in 2016. Most of its people speak Iranian Azerbaijani as their first language and Persian as their second. Its Bazaar is a World Heritage Site, and most preserved monuments date from the Ilkhanid, Safavid and Qajar periods. The city is known for hand-woven carpets, and the University of Tabriz was established in 1947.
tabula-cortonensis: The tablet was handed to the police in October 1992 by a man who claimed to have found it at a construction site the month before. It was then in seven fragments, with its bottom right corner missing; investigators found that it had been broken in antiquity, so the lost piece may have been separated centuries ago. The finder proved to have lied about where he found it and was tried for mishandling artefacts, but was found innocent. Local researchers believe it came from another building site and was hidden so that construction would not be delayed by archaeological work, and its real origin remains unknown.

The bronze measures just over 8 inches by about 11 and is between 2 and 3 millimetres thick. Its two-sided inscription of 40 lines is the third longest known in Etruscan, after the Liber Linteus Zagrabiensis and the Tabula Capuana, and the longest discovered in the 20th century. It contains thirty-four known Etruscan words and as many that had never been recorded, and a new letter, a reversed epsilon, which appears only in the dialect of Cortona and seems to mark a sound different from E.

Scholars such as Larissa Bonfante and Nancy de Grummond read the text as a notarised record of the division of an inheritance or a sale of real estate. It mentions a vineyard, cultivated land and an estate in the territory of Lake Trasimeno, and concerns the aristocratic Cusu family and Petru Scevas and his wife. Two groups of witnesses and Larth Cucrina Lausisa, a chief magistrate of the territory of Cortona, certified it, and it ends by dating itself by the two magistrates in office that year.

Readings differ on the direction of the transaction: Wylin has Petru obtaining land from the Cusu, while van der Meer, following Maggiani, has Petru ceding it to them. Rex Wallace notes that in third- and second-century Tuscany large plots were divided among individual families, and the tablet may record such an allocation. The missing piece is believed to hold only names.
tabula-rogeriana: Its full Arabic title is Nuzhat al-mushtāq fī ikhtirāq al-āfāq, "The Excursion of One Eager to Penetrate the Distant Horizons". Around 1138 the Norman King Roger II invited the Muslim geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi to his court in Palermo. After al-Idrisi described his own travels in North Africa and Western Europe, Roger commissioned an atlas from him. Al-Idrisi interviewed experienced travellers, keeping only what they agreed on and seemed credible, and Roger sometimes took part. He also sent agents to check the information. His sources were largely works of the Abbasid age, above all Arabic translations of Ptolemy's Geography and the Balkhi school of geography. The work took some fifteen years and was completed in 1154, a few weeks before the king's death.

The book, in Arabic, is divided into seven climatic zones in the Ptolemaic manner, each divided into ten sections, and each section has a two-page map, seventy in all. The maps put south at the top and Mecca in the middle, and each is followed by commentary on the physical, cultural, political and economic conditions of the region. Areas near Roger's kingdom, in North Africa and Europe, are more accurate, while distant ones such as Southeast Asia are less detailed.

Al-Idrisi also produced a silver disc of 140 kilograms engraved with the combined world map, made to his calculation of the earth's circumference of 37,000 kilometres, an error of less than ten percent. The original atlas and disc were destroyed in a rebellion led by Matthew Bonnellus in 1160.

Because al-Idrisi left several drafts, surviving manuscripts differ. Ten copies survive, five of them complete in text. The oldest, from about 1325, is in the Bibliothèque nationale de France (MS Arabe 2221), and a copy made in Cairo in 1553 is in the Bodleian Library. The most complete manuscript is in Istanbul. Al-Idrisi also made a shorter version for Roger's son William II, the "Little Idrisi". Gabriel Sionita translated the work into Latin in Paris in 1619. Many contemporary scholars hailed it as the best work of geography of the period. It treated mapmaking as a scientific task, unlike earlier Christian maps based on the Bible. Orientalists reprinted sections in the 19th century.
tacfarinas: His name is the Latinised form of the Berber Tikfarin or Takfarin. He came from Thagaste, today Souk Ahras in Algeria, and was apparently not of royal or noble birth. He grew up amid long conflict over the central Tunisian plateau, the summer grazing ground of the Musulamii and Gaetuli, which Rome under Augustus was fencing off for wheat. His personal motives are unknown, but the Roman occupation of those pastures was probably the deciding factor. He served for some years in an auxiliary regiment before deserting.

Tacfarinas organised his raiders into regular units on the Roman model, and the Musulamii clans accepted him as their paramount leader. A leader named Mazippa brought over many of the Mauri, and the Cinithii of southern Tunisia joined him. In 17 CE the proconsul Marcus Furius Camillus routed his army in a pitched battle. Tacfarinas returned to raiding, and the high grain prices at Rome, with riots in 19 CE, were probably due to his insurgency. Under Lucius Apronius he besieged a fort on the river Pagyda, after which Apronius had the cohort that fled decimated, and failed against the veterans of Thala.

He then offered peace in return for land, which the emperor Tiberius rejected with outrage. Quintus Junius Blaesus, given a second legion, offered amnesty to his allies, built many small forts garrisoned all year and captured his brother in 22 CE. Tiberius declared the war won and withdrew the extra legion. Tacfarinas now presented himself as the leader of a war to free Numidia, and Mauri, Libyphoenician peasants and warriors of the Garamantes joined him.

Driven from the siege of Thubursicum, he camped near the ruined fort of Auzea, where Roman light infantry and Numidian cavalry surprised him at dawn. His bodyguards were killed and his son captured, and he threw himself on the spears of his attackers. The proconsul Publius Cornelius Dolabella then had the whole plateau registered for land tax, a survey completed in 29 or 30 CE, and the Musulamii were probably shut out of their old pastures for good. Tiberius refused Dolabella the triumphal honours his three predecessors had received.
tachira: Táchira is one of the three Venezuelan Andean states, with Mérida and Trujillo. It covers 11,100 square kilometres and had 1,168,908 inhabitants at the 2011 census. It borders Zulia to the north, Barinas and Mérida to the east, Apure and Barinas to the south, and the Colombian department of Norte de Santander to the west. Its mountains are the southern continuation of the Mérida range, and its highest point, the Páramo El Pulpito, is about 3,995 m above sea level. The Andes of Táchira rose during the Eocene, when the Nazca and Caribbean plates began to slide under the South American plate.

The territory was inhabited by Timote, Cuica and Chibcha groups such as the Machirí, Umuquena and Táriba, and was colonised extensively in the 16th century. Captain Juan Maldonado Ordoñez y Villaquirán founded San Cristóbal in 1561 and Francisco de Cáceres founded La Grita in 1576, which began the farming of the area. La Grita was the capital of its province until European trading companies arrived and settled mainly in the more accessible San Cristóbal. The Dominican Friar Alonso de Andrada said the first mass in the territory on 25 July 1558.

For over two hundred years Táchira was Venezuela's main coffee producer. Important European trading houses arrived in the 19th century, but the region stayed relatively isolated from the rest of the country, and received more cultural influence from Colombia. At the end of the 19th century the national oil industry was born at the place now called La Petrolia, where Venezuela's first oil wells were drilled. Táchira became a state in 1863 and in 1864 joined the United States of Venezuela as an independent state. In 1881 it joined Guzmán (Mérida) and Trujillo in the Great State of Los Andes, and when that was dissolved in 1899 it recovered its status as a separate state.

The capital, San Cristóbal, lies at 825 metres above sea level on a succession of river terraces and is one of the oldest cities in Venezuela. Its position on the border with Colombia makes it a commercial city. Táchira's economy rests on coffee, pineapple, cattle and food processing, and the state is connected to Colombia by three international bridges. Its protected areas include El Tamá National Park, Chorro El Indio National Park and the Páramo El Zumbador.
tacitus: Little is known of the personal life of Tacitus. What is known comes from scattered hints in his own works, the letters of his friend Pliny the Younger and an inscription found at Mylasa in Caria. He was born in 56 or 57 into an equestrian family. His place of birth and his first name are not known: the letters of Sidonius Apollinaris call him Gaius, and the major manuscript of his work gives Publius. His marriage to the daughter of a senator from Gallia Narbonensis suggests that he came from that province. He owed his rank to the Flavian emperors, as he says himself.

Tacitus studied rhetoric in Rome to prepare for a career in law and politics. In 77 or 78 he married Julia Agricola, daughter of the general Gnaeus Julius Agricola. He entered political life as a quaestor in 81 or 82 under Titus, became praetor in 88 and served in the provinces from about 89 to about 93. He gained acclaim as an orator, which sits ironically with his cognomen, Tacitus, meaning silent.

He and his property survived the reign of Domitian, but the experience left him jaded and perhaps ashamed of his own complicity, and instilled in him the hatred of tyranny evident in his works. In 97, under Nerva, he became suffect consul, the first of his family to do so. In 100 he and Pliny prosecuted Marius Priscus, proconsul of Africa, for corruption. In 112 to 113 he held the governorship of the province of Asia.

Five works ascribed to Tacitus survive, with gaps. The Life of Agricola and the Germania date to about 98. The Germania is an ethnographic work on the Germanic tribes outside the empire. The Dialogue on Oratory followed about 102, the Histories about 105 and the Annals about 117. The Histories and the Annals were meant to form a single work of thirty books, a continuous narrative from the death of Augustus in 14 to the death of Domitian in 96.

Of the Histories only the first four books and part of the fifth survive, covering the year 69 and part of 70. Of the Annals, books 7 to 10 and parts of others are missing. The first half survives in a single manuscript from Corvey Abbey and the second half in one from Monte Cassino.
tackys-revolt: Jamaica had been under British rule since the invasion of 1655, and its plantation economy depended on the forced labour of Africans brought by the Atlantic slave trade. Tacky, a Fante, had been a paramount chief in Eguaafo, in present-day Ghana, and had himself sold prisoners of war into slavery before a rival state and the Dutch defeated his army near Elmina and sold him in turn. He and his lieutenants planned to take Jamaica from the British and found a free state, inspired by the resistance of the Maroons under Queen Nanny in the First Maroon War. The plot was an island-wide conspiracy run by a secret network of Coromantee.

Before daybreak on Easter Monday, 7 April 1760, Tacky's men took the Frontier and Trinity plantations, killing some of the white overseers, then seized gunpowder and about 40 firearms from the storeroom at Fort Haldane near Port Maria. Hundreds joined them. Lieutenant Governor Sir Henry Moore sent militia, who were joined by Maroons from Moore Town, Charles Town and Scott's Hall. When the militia killed a captured Obeahman who had claimed he could not be killed, many rebels lost heart and went back to their plantations. On 14 April Maroons routed Tacky's remaining men in Rocky Valley, and the Maroon marksman Davy shot Tacky and cut off his head.

On 25 May a second rising began in Westmoreland under Apongo. The rebels repelled the militia on 29 May, but on 1 and 2 June regulars, militia and Accompong Maroons stormed their barricade, and many rebels, among them women and children, were killed or driven over a precipice. Apongo was captured on 3 July and died in a cage. Under a leader named Simon, rebels held out in the Cockpit Country into 1761, and small bands fought on through the decade.

Over 60 white colonists, a similar number of free people of colour and some 400 rebels died; captives were burned alive or starved in iron cages, and more than 500 were sold to British Honduras. The damage cost the colony over £100,000. The Assembly passed harsh laws on the black population and banned Obeah. The revolt inspired further risings in 1765 and 1766, and historian Trevor Burnard wrote that only the American Revolution surpassed its shock to the imperial system in the 18th century. A monument to Tacky stands in Port Maria.
tacna: Tacna, officially San Pedro de Tacna, lies in the Caplina River valley in southern Peru, about 35 km north of the border with Chile, and is the capital of the department of Tacna. The surrounding area is generally desert, with a few fertile spots near the mountains. The name is derived from the Quechua words taka, meaning to hit, and na, meaning place. At the time of the Spanish conquest the region was multiethnic, with local sedentary populations making up about 66% of the people, settlers from the Altiplano about 25% and fishing people known as Camanchacos about 9%. The encomienda system was established there in 1540.

In 1811 the royal accountant Francisco Antonio de Zela started the push for Peruvian independence from Spain at Tacna, and in 1828 President José de La Mar declared it the Heroic City. It was the capital of the short-lived Peru–Bolivian Confederation from 1836 to 1839. Sodium nitrate and other resources brought prosperity and a wave of Italian immigrants. The War of the Pacific ended this: a large Peruvian and Bolivian army was quartered in the city in poor sanitary conditions, which cost it much of its population to infectious diseases, and Chile captured it in May 1880 after defeating the allied army outside the city under General Manuel Baquedano.

Under the Treaty of Ancón of 1883, Chile was to administer the provinces of Tacna and Arica for ten years, after which a plebiscite would decide their sovereignty. When the ten years ended, the two sides could not agree whether to include a large number of imported Chilean labourers in the vote. Chilean authorities pursued a campaign of Chilenization, which Peruvian nationalists defeated, and the plebiscite was never held. Peruvian historiography calls the period the cautiverio. Tacna's patriotic Paseo de la Bandera began in 1901 when a group of its people defied a Chilean ban on showing Peruvian flags.

The Treaty of Lima of 1929 gave Chile Arica, while Peru recovered Tacna and received an indemnity of 6 million dollars and other concessions; the treaty took effect on 28 August 1929. Each year on 28 August a large Peruvian flag is carried through the city in the Paseo de la Bandera, which celebrates the return of Tacna to Peru. Tacna is a commercial city, with trade based on links with northern Chile, and it has monuments commemorating Peruvian independence and the War of the Pacific, among them the arch of the Alto de la Alianza complex and the Tacna Parabolic Arch. The Toquepala caves nearby have yielded some of the oldest human remains in Peru.
tadeusz-kosciuszko: Tadeusz Kościuszko was born in February 1746 on the Mereczowszczyzna estate in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, now in Belarus; his exact birthdate is unknown. He was the youngest son of Ludwik Tadeusz Kościuszko, an officer and member of the szlachta, whose family held modest lands worked by 31 peasant families. After graduating from the Corps of Cadets in Warsaw, he went to Paris in 1769 on a royal scholarship. As a foreigner he could not enter the French military academies, so he enrolled in the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture, studied architecture privately, and audited military lectures for five years. The French Enlightenment and the economic theory of physiocracy left a strong impression on him.

In 1776 Kościuszko sailed for America and, with Benjamin Franklin's recommendation, was commissioned a colonel of engineers in the Continental Army. He built fortifications including those at West Point, and as chief engineer to General Nathanael Greene he helped the Continental Army cross the rivers in the Race to the Dan in 1781. In 1783 the Continental Congress promoted him to brigadier general.

He returned to Poland in 1784 and became a major general in the Commonwealth army in 1789. In the Polish-Russian War of 1792 he commanded a division, and although he lost no battle, the king capitulated and the Second Partition followed. In March 1794, in Kraków's Main Square, he announced an uprising and took the title Naczelnik. He won at Racławice on 4 April by leading a charge of peasant volunteers armed with scythes, and at Połaniec he issued a proclamation granting serfs civil rights and reducing their labour obligations. He was captured at the Battle of Maciejowice in October 1794, and the uprising's defeat in November led to the Third Partition of 1795.

After Catherine II died, Tsar Paul I pardoned Kościuszko in 1796 and he left for the United States. A friend of Thomas Jefferson, he wrote a will in 1798 dedicating his American assets to the education and freedom of enslaved people in the United States, but its execution proved difficult and the funds were never used as he intended. He eventually returned to Europe and lived in Switzerland until his death on 15 October 1817. He is a national hero in Poland, the United States, Lithuania and Belarus.
tadhg-mor-ua-cellaig: Tadhg Mór Ua Cellaigh was the 36th King of Uí Maine and the first Chief of the Name. He was the first king of Uí Maine to bear the surname Ua Cellaigh, which came from his grandfather Ceallach mac Finnachta, a sixth-generation descendant of Eoghan Finn, himself descended from the first king, Maine Mór. He succeeded Muirgus mac Domnaill, who was killed in battle in 986.

Tadhg seems to have been present at the battles of Lough Ree in 987 and at the hosting to Tara in 999. He allied himself with Brian Boru against Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill, King of Mide, and against two Kings of Connacht, Cathal mac Conchobar mac Taidg and Tadg in Eich Gil. He secured marriage alliances with Brian, as one of his sisters is said to have become one of Brian's many wives, and his position was strengthened when Brian became High King in 1002. In 1014 he accompanied Brian to Dublin, where he fought and died at the Battle of Clontarf.

John O'Donovan recorded a tradition, current among the O'Kellys of Hy-Many in the early 19th century, that they bore an enfield as their crest from the time of Tadhg Mór, because of a belief that this fabulous animal came out of the sea at Clontarf to guard his body from the Danes until his followers rescued it. O'Donovan also noted the annals' record that Tadhg was chief of Hy-Many in 1003 and was slain at Clontarf fighting for Brian, which is why pedigrees often call him Tadhg Catha Bhriain, Tadhg of the Battle of Brian.
All but one of the later kings of Uí Maine descended from him or bore the surname Ua or Ó Cellaigh, until Feardorcha Ó Cellaigh resigned the title in the late 16th century.
tadodaho: In Haudenosaunee oral tradition Tadodaho was a warrior and the primary chief of the Onondaga, said to have a twisted body and to kill his enemies from a distance without seeing them. His people believed him a sorcerer, and he led the Onondaga in raids against the Cayuga and the Seneca. The name appears in many forms, among them Adodarhoh, Atartaho and Tatotarho; The Iroquois Book of Rites, edited by Horatio Hale in 1883, takes Atartaho to mean entangled.

In the story Tadodaho broke up three attempts by Hiawatha to bring the nations to council, and the deaths of Hiawatha's three daughters were ascribed to his powers. Deganawidah, of the Huron, and Hiawatha then walked with the chiefs of the Cayuga, Mohawk, Oneida and Onondaga to Canandaigua Lake singing the Peace Hymn and won over the Seneca. Advised by Jigonhsasee, the Mother of Nations, they healed Tadodaho with a holy medicine ceremony: Hiawatha combed the mats from his hair and Deganawidah smoothed the seven crooks of his body with herbs and wampum. Tadodaho became firekeeper and chairman of the council, and the last steps toward peace were taken at Onondaga Lake.

The name passed to the Onondaga chief who presides over the Grand Council, seen as the spiritual successor of the first Tadodaho. He is chosen for life by the 49 other chiefs, who are themselves selected by the Clan Mothers, and the post is also called the Head Chief of All the Six Nations. The Great Council Fire is still kept on the Onondaga reservation in present-day New York.

In 1968 the Tadodaho George A. Thomas demanded the return of 25 wampum belts held by the New York State Museum, a dispute an anthropologist called the great wampum war. Leon Shenandoah, a custodian at Syracuse University, was chosen on 7 December 1968 and served for over 25 years until his death in 1996, opposing gambling enterprises among the Haudenosaunee. Sidney Hill, chosen in 2002, led a group of Onondaga in 2005 in filing a claim in federal court to some 4,000 square miles of Upstate New York.
tadukhipa: Tadukhipa, in Hurrian Tadu-Hepa, was a princess of Mitanni, the daughter of King Tushratta and his queen Juni, and the niece of Artashumara. Almost nothing is known of her early years. Her aunt Gilukhipa, Tushratta's sister, had married Pharaoh Amenhotep III in the tenth year of his reign, and Tadukhipa was to marry him more than two decades later. Tushratta sent her to Egypt around 1355 BCE, in the thirty-sixth year of Amenhotep's reign, to marry the pharaoh, who was a close ally.

Tushratta sent her with many gifts: a gold-plated chariot inlaid with precious stones, a pair of horses, a litter adorned with gold and precious stones, clothes, a horse saddle adorned with gold eagles, jewellery such as bracelets and armlets, and a large chest to hold them. Amenhotep had offered golden statues in return as part of the marriage agreement, but no evidence exists that they were ever sent. Tushratta had asked that his daughter become Great Royal Wife, a position already held by Queen Tiye. Tadukhipa appears in seven of Tushratta's 13 letters among the Amarna letters, which are the main evidence for her, and after Amenhotep's death Tushratta wrote to complain that the statues had not arrived.

Amenhotep III died soon after she arrived, and his son Amenhotep IV became pharaoh. It is speculated that she then married him. Tushratta wrote to him repeatedly and in one letter sent greetings to Tadu-Ḫeba, his daughter and the pharaoh's wife, together with the pharaoh's other wives, sons, chariots, horses and troops.

Some scholars tentatively identify her with Kiya, a known wife of Amenhotep IV, who lived at Amarna with her own sunshade and was shown with the pharaoh and at least one daughter. Petrie, Drioton and Vandier proposed instead that she took a new name and became Queen Nefertiti, whose name, "the beautiful one has come", might point to foreign origin. Seele, Meyer and others reply that Tey, wife of Ay, was Nefertiti's nurse, which argues against this, since a mature princess would need no nurse, and that Nefertiti is a quintessentially Egyptian name linked to Hathor.
tadun: Tadun was a younger relative of the Wuhuan chieftain Qiuliju and was known among the Wuhuan for his wisdom, skill in command, strength and ferocity. When Qiuliju died, sometime in the early 190s, his son Louban was too young to rule, so Tadun succeeded him as leader. Besides the Wuhuan of Liaoxi Commandery, around present-day Lulong County in Hebei, he ruled those of Youbeiping, Yuyang and Shanggu commanderies, around present-day Tangshan, Miyun and Yanqing.

Throughout the 190s Tadun supported the warlord Yuan Shao in his struggle against Gongsun Zan for supremacy in northern China. In return Yuan Shao granted imperial seals and honours to Tadun and the other Wuhuan chieftains in the name of Emperor Xian, the figurehead emperor of the Eastern Han. When Louban had grown up, Tadun handed the leadership to him but remained in charge of the Wuhuan of Liaoxi; the other chieftains, among them Nanlou, Supuyan and Wuyan, pledged their allegiance to Louban.

After Yuan Shao died in 202, his son and successor Yuan Shang kept up the friendship with the Wuhuan. When Cao Cao defeated Yuan Shang and drove him north, he took shelter with Tadun, who tried without success to help him regain his lands in northern China.

In 207 Cao Cao personally led a campaign against Yuan Shang and the Wuhuan. By the time the Wuhuan realised that he was coming it was too late, though they still mustered thousands of horsemen. The two sides met at the Battle of White Wolf Mountain near Liucheng, southwest of present-day Chaoyang in Liaoning. During the battle Tadun was captured by the Tiger and Leopard Cavalry, led by Cao Cao's cousin Cao Chun, and was afterwards executed by Zhang Liao, one of Cao Cao's generals.
taedong-river: The Taedong River rises in the Rangrim Mountains in the north of North Korea and flows south-west into Korea Bay at Nampo, passing through the capital, Pyongyang, on the way. It is the second-longest river in North Korea and the fifth-longest on the Korean peninsula, and it is generally deep. Pyongyang lies about 110 km upstream from the mouth, Sunchon 192 km and Taehung 414 km. Large ships can navigate it up to 65 km inland, although most commercial traffic stops at Songrim, so the river is widely used for transport.

The kingdom of Koguryo was founded on its banks. Many archaeological sites from the Neolithic and the Bronze Age have been found along the river, together with relics and ruins from Koguryo. It was once also known as the Pae River.

A bridge over the Taedong was partly destroyed during the Korean War, yet several hundred Koreans used it to cross and flee south. Max Desfor's photograph of the scene, Flight of Refugees Across Wrecked Bridge in Korea, won the 1951 Pulitzer Prize in Photography. In 1986 the 8-km-long West Sea Barrage, with three locks and 36 sluices, was completed at the river's mouth near Nampo; it controls floodwater and irrigates land newly reclaimed from the Korea Gulf. Other dams, such as the Nyongwon Power Station, provide energy, and Pyongyang has six bridges over the river, among them the Ongryu, Rungra and Taedong bridges.
taejo-of-goryeo: Wang Kŏn was born in 877 to a powerful maritime merchant family of Goguryeo descent based in Songak, modern Kaesong, the eldest son of Wang Ryung. A work of the late twelfth century, the Pyeonnyeon tongnok, made his grandfather Chakchegon a son of Emperor Suzong of Tang who met a dragon king on a sea voyage.

The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture and the Doosan Encyclopedia call this story hagiographical, and the Joseon compilers of the Goryeosa dismissed it. Modern historians hold that his ancestors were influential Goguryeo lords who traded by sea with China for generations. Songak became the original capital of Later Goguryeo in 901.

In 895 Kung Ye led his forces into the north-western part of Silla, where Wang Ryung and many local clans quickly surrendered, and Wang Kŏn followed his father into Kung Ye's service. Kung Ye promoted him to general and regarded him as his brother.

In 900 he led a successful campaign against local clans and the army of Later Baekje in the Chungju area, and in 903 a naval campaign against the south-western coast of Later Baekje. In 913 he became prime minister of the renamed Taebong. Its king, Kung Ye, began to call himself the Buddha, executed many monks and later his own wife and two sons, and the public turned away from him.

On the night of 24 July 918 four top-ranked generals, Hong Yu, Pae Hyŏn-gyŏng, Sin Sung-gyŏm and Pok Chigyŏm, agreed to overthrow Kung Ye and crown Wang Kŏn, who at first opposed the plan. Kung Ye was killed near the capital, Cheorwon, and the generals installed Wang Kŏn at sunrise. He renamed the kingdom Goryeo and the next year moved the capital to Gaegyeong. He promoted Buddhism as the national religion, had the ruined Pyongyang repopulated and made it the Western Capital, and sought alliances with local clans rather than conquering them.

In 927 Kyŏn Hwŏn of Later Baekje captured Gyeongju, and Taejo, striking at his army with 5,000 cavalry, was heavily defeated at the Battle of Gongsan, losing most of his army and the general Sin Sung-gyŏm. In 935 Silla's last king, Gyeongsun, surrendered his land and was given the title of prince. In 936 Taejo's final campaign against Sin-gŏm of Later Baekje ended in Sin-gŏm's surrender. Taejo gave titles and land to nobles of the states he had defeated and welcomed Balhae refugees after the Khitans destroyed Balhae in 926. He died of disease in 943.
taejo-of-joseon: Taejo, born Yi Sŏnggye on 4 November 1335 in Ssangseong Prefecture on the frontier of the Yuan dynasty, was the son of Yi Chach'un, an ethnic Korean official serving the Mongol-led Yuan. By the late fourteenth century Goryeo, 400 years old, was tottering from years of war and de facto occupation by the disintegrating Mongol Empire. Its court was divided between scholar-officials, old aristocratic families and generals who fought off the Japanese pirates and the Red Turbans, among them Yi Sŏnggye and his rival Ch'oe Yŏng.

Yi began his career as an officer in 1360, helped to recapture the capital, Gaegyeong, from the Red Turbans in 1361 and defeated the Yuan general Naghachu in 1362. He gained prestige in the 1370s and 1380s by repelling the Japanese pirates.

In 1388 a Ming messenger demanded the return of part of Goryeo's northern territory, and Ch'oe Yŏng argued for an invasion of the Liaodong Peninsula. Yi opposed it but was chosen to lead it, and at Wihwa Island on the Amnok River he turned his army back. He marched into the capital, defeated Ch'oe and deposed King U in a coup. He placed U's young son on the throne, had both put to death after a failed attempt to restore U, and made Wang Yo, King Gongyang, the new ruler. In 1392 Yi forced Gongyang to abdicate and took the throne, ending 475 years of Goryeo rule.

In 1393 he named the dynasty Joseon, and in 1394 he established the new capital at Hanseong, today Seoul. He improved relations with Ming China. No new institutions were created, and no massive purges occurred in his reign. In 1398 his son Yi Pang-wŏn revolted and killed the minister Chŏng To-jŏn and two sons of the late Queen Sindeok, in the First Strife of Princes. Taejo named his second son, Yi Pang-gwa, his successor and abdicated.

Taejo retired to the Hamhung Royal Villa and kept his distance from Yi Pang-wŏn, who took the throne in 1400 as King Taejong. A tradition said he executed the emissaries his son sent, but recent studies have found that those men died in revolts that happened in the region. He died on 27 June 1408 at Changdeokgung. Many regard him as a decisive ruler who eliminated a crippled governing system and saved the country from foreign forces, though some scholars, particularly in North Korea, view him as a traitor to the old regime.
taejong-of-joseon: Yi Pangwŏn was born on 21 June 1367, the fifth son of the future King Taejo and his first wife, Lady Han. He qualified as an official in 1382, studied under Confucian scholars and helped found Joseon by assassinating powerful officials who stayed loyal to Goryeo, most prominently Chŏng Mongju.

He expected to be named heir, but Taejo and Chŏng Tojŏn favoured Yi Pangsŏk, a son of Taejo's second wife. Chŏng Tojŏn saw Joseon as a kingdom led by its ministers by virtue of the king's appointment, whereas Yi Pangwŏn wanted direct rule through an absolute monarchy. When his father fell ill, he launched the First Strife of the Princes and had both sons of the second wife, including the crown prince, murdered. Taejo abdicated in favour of Yi Panggwa, later King Jeongjong. Early in 1400 their brother Yi Panggan failed in a coup, and Jeongjong then abdicated in favour of Yi Pangwŏn.

Taejong abolished the privilege of aristocrats and senior officials to keep private armies, which removed their means of raising large revolts and enlarged the national army. He revised the land tax, and the discovery of hidden land doubled national wealth. Decisions of the State Council took effect only with the king's approval, which ended the custom of ministers deciding among themselves. He also created the Sinmun Office to hear complaints from subjects who felt wronged by officials or aristocrats.

He promoted Confucianism as the state ideology, closed many Buddhist temples and added their possessions to the national treasury. He set up hopae, tags recording the bearer's name and residence, to control movement, and in 1403 ordered 100,000 pieces of metal type. He attacked the Jurchens on the northern border and Japanese pirates in the south, and began the Ōei Invasion of Tsushima in 1419.

To limit the influence of in-laws and powerful clans, he executed or exiled some of the supporters who had helped him to the throne, among them the four brothers of his wife Queen Wŏngyŏng and Sim On, Sejong's father-in-law. He died four years after his abdication, at Suganggung, and was buried at Heolleung in Seoul. He remains a controversial figure, since he eliminated many rivals yet ruled effectively and laid a solid foundation for Sejong's reign.
tafari-benti: Tafari Benti, of Oromo descent, joined the Ethiopian Army at the age of 20, graduated from the Holetta Military Academy and served in the Second, Third and Fourth Divisions. In 1967 he was military attaché in Washington, D.C., where he and other Ethiopian colleagues met racial discrimination. He was a brigadier general with the Fourth Division in Asmara when Lieutenant General Aman Mikael Andom, the first chairman of the Derg, was killed at his home on 23 November 1974; after Mengistu Haile Mariam's interim chairmanship, the Derg appointed Tafari in his place.

As chairman of the Provisional Military Administrative Council, Tafari delivered the junta's public announcements, among them that of 11 September 1975 that the Derg would create a political party aligned with the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. The monarchy was formally abolished in March 1975. The Ottaways judged him a neutral and powerless figure, too colourless to front the revolution, but René Lafort saw signs that he leaned towards Mengistu's opponents: in July 1975 he proposed a united front with the civilian left, including the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Party (EPRP) and MEISON, a strategy Mengistu opposed.

In 1976 the Derg split over Mengistu's growing power, and a committee under Captain Mogus Wolde Mikael reformed its structure. On 29 December 1976 Tafari announced the restructuring, which limited Mengistu's powers and sent his supporters to posts in the countryside. Flanked by Mogus and Captain Alemayehu Haile, he also criticised the lack of a vanguard party, words Lafort read as calling the bloody conflict between MEISON and the EPRP unjustifiable.

Mengistu, with his ally Lieutenant Colonel Daniel Asfaw, moved against them. At a routine meeting on 3 February 1977 soldiers arrested Tafari and the members suspected of conspiring with the EPRP, who were killed the same day, among them Mogus and Alemayehu. Radio Ethiopia then broadcast Mengistu's charge that they had been secret EPRP supporters, and he claimed to have found a 47-page plan in Tafari's possession. Fidel Castro held that Tafari's nationalism was one reason for his fall.
tafilalt: Tafilalt, also written Tafilet and historically called Sijilmasa, is a traditional region of Morocco centred on its largest oasis, and it largely corresponds to Errachidia Province. The name is a Berber word meaning a jug, specifically a pottery jar used to store water. The oasis lies entirely along the Ziz River and is known for its dates. Before mechanised transport it was ten days' journey south of Fez and Meknes, across the Atlas Mountains.

Settlements existed in the area before Islam, especially in the Roman period, but the first continuously inhabited town after the spread of Islam was Sijilmasa, founded by the Midrarid dynasty. It stood on the direct caravan route from the Niger River to Tangier and became prosperous. The traveller Ibn Battuta wrote of visiting it in the fourteenth century on his journey from Fez to Mali. The Aït Atta destroyed Sijilmasa in 1818, and its ruins include two gateways.

In the 17th century the Alawi dynasty of Morocco first achieved political ascendancy in Tafilalt. In 1606 Sultan Zidan Abu Maali hid there, profited from gold mined in the area, built an army and eventually took Marrakesh. A few years later, in 1610, Ahmed ibn Abi Mahalli also raised an army in the region and took Marrakesh, but lost control after Sidi Yahya ben Younes liberated the city for Zidan.

A revolutionary movement arose against the sultan about a decade afterwards and was repressed after four months of skirmishes. Tafilalt was later a major centre of the Dila'ites, and in 1648 sultans of Morocco began sending sons and daughters who would not inherit titles or power to live there. The first European to visit in the modern era was René Caillié in 1828, followed by Gerhard Rohlfs in 1864. Rabbi Israel Abuhatzeira, known as Baba Sali, was born there in 1889.
taga-castle: Taga Castle was a jōsaku-style castle, more a fortified city than a military stronghold, on a plateau 10 kilometres north-east of Sendai near the Pacific coast, close to the natural port of Shiogama and protected by marsh and rivers. A square enclosure some 3.4 kilometres round was formed by a 5-metre earthen rampart topped by a wooden palisade, with a dry moat outside. From the south gate a road over 20 metres wide led to an inner walled square of 100 metres, which held the higher government offices, workshops and storehouses.

The court of the Ritsuryō state sent expeditions north to bring the Emishi under its rule, and a great Emishi rising in 709 destroyed many of its earlier administrative centres. The inscription found at the site names Ono Azumahito as the founder of the castle as the provisional capital of Mutsu Province. With Akita Castle and Okachi Fort in Dewa Province it was one of the main bases of the Yamato advance into northern Honshu, and its commander, the Chinjufu-shōgun, was the northern counterpart of the commander of Dazaifu in Kyushu. It was renovated in 762.

The Emishi sacked and burned the castle in 780, and it was rebuilt. After the campaigns of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro moved the frontier north from 802, it kept administrative tasks while military work passed to strongholds further north. The Jōgan tsunami of 869 damaged it badly, and it fell into ruin from the 10th century as the old administration collapsed and Hiraizumi rose under the Northern Fujiwara. During the Nanboku-chō period Kitabatake Chikafusa and his son Kitabatake Akiie briefly held the site for the Southern Court.

The site, excavated from 1955, is an archaeological park, with the Tōhoku History Museum in its grounds and the ruins of the temple Tagajō Haiji to the south-east. The stele, discovered in the Edo period and visited by Matsuo Bashō in 1689, who wrote of it in Oku no Hosomichi, became a National Treasure in 2024.
tagalog-language: Tagalog is a Central Philippine language within the Austronesian family, and so related to Malagasy, Javanese, Indonesian, Malay and Tetum. It is closely related to the languages of the Bicol Region and the Visayas, including Waray, Hiligaynon and Cebuano. It differs from them in its treatment of the Proto-Philippine schwa vowel, which merged with one vowel in most Bikol and Visayan languages and with another in Tagalog. The word Tagalog is possibly derived from taga-ilog, meaning river dweller. The linguists David Zorc and Robert Blust speculate that the Tagalogs and other Central Philippine groups originated in northeastern Mindanao or the Eastern Visayas.

Before the Spanish arrived in 1521 and began colonisation in 1565, Tagalog was written in an abugida called Baybayin, with symbols for three vowels and 14 consonants. It belongs to the Brahmic family of scripts and is believed to descend from the script used by the Bugis in Sulawesi. It gradually gave way to the Latin alphabet taught by the Spaniards. Until the first half of the 20th century Tagalog was written in various ways based on Spanish orthography, in a 32-letter alphabet called the abecedario. In 1940 the grammarian Lope K. Santos introduced a 20-letter alphabet called the Abakada, and in 1971 the alphabet was expanded to make room for loans, especially Spanish and English family names.

Tagalog was declared the official language by the first revolutionary constitution of the Philippines, the Constitution of Biak-na-Bato, in 1897. The selection of a Tagalog-based national language in 1937 caused controversy, with speakers of Cebuano and Ilocano mainly regarding it as a cultural imposition. President Manuel L. Quezon signed Executive Order No. 263 in 1939, designating the language the Wikang Pambansâ, and on 12 April 1940 the teaching of the national language was ordered in all public and private schools. The first Tagalog Bible, Ang Biblia, was published in 1905.

Tagalog is spoken as a first language by the ethnic Tagalog people, a quarter of the population of the Philippines, and as a second language by the majority. Its standardised form, Filipino, is the national language and one of the two official languages with English. The Tagalog homeland, Katagalugan, covers much of central and southern Luzon, and Tagalog is also spoken natively on Marinduque and Mindoro.

The language commonly uses verb-subject-object order and is agglutinative, with verbs that take many prefixes, infixes and suffixes. Its vocabulary is mostly native Austronesian, with many Spanish and English loanwords and, from the precolonial use of Trade Malay, many Malay words. Words from Sanskrit, Tamil, Hokkien and other Chinese languages, Japanese, Arabic and Persian also appear. The polite particles pô and hô express respect to elders and others.
tages: Tages is known only from Latin authors of the late Roman Republic and the Empire, whose accounts of him are quasimythical. Versions of his birth vary: he is sometimes the grandson of Jove, and in Ovid's telling a Tyrrhenian ploughman saw a clod turn into a man who spoke of things destined to happen and of how the Etruscans could learn the future. Since the Etruscan alphabet had no G, the name is most likely a Latin form of an Etruscan word.
