Ghiyath prevailed and became ruler of Firuzkuh. Yildiz took Ghazni from the Ghurid rulers of Bamiyan and soon recognised Ghiyath's authority, ruling the city in fact while acknowledging Ghurid rule.

Uneasy at Yildiz's hold on Ghazni, Ghiyath asked the Khwarazmian ruler Muhammad II for help, but Muhammad instead invaded his lands and took Balkh and Termez. In 1208 Qutb-ud-din Aibak, the semi-independent Ghurid governor of India, occupied Ghazni, but Yildiz defeated him forty days later. In 1214 Yildiz killed Ala al-Din Atsiz and set Atsiz's cousin Ala al-Din Ali on the Ghurid throne as his puppet.

A year later Muhammad II conquered Firuzkuh, captured Ala al-Din Ali and decisively defeated Yildiz at Ghazni. Yildiz fled to Punjab, took Lahore from Nasir ad-Din Qabacha and claimed the throne of Delhi as heir to Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad. The Delhi Sultan Iltutmish rejected the claim, answering that the dominion of the world belonged to whoever was strongest and that destiny had long ago abolished hereditary succession. Their armies met at Tarain in January 1216. Yildiz was taken prisoner, led through the streets of Delhi and sent to Budaun, where he was put to death that year. Qabacha then occupied Lahore again.
taj-al-muluk-buri: Buri, a Turkoman, served with his father Toghtekin as an officer in the army of Duqaq, the Seljuk ruler of Damascus. He is first mentioned in 1099, when Duqaq sent him to take Jableh, a town between Antioch and Tripoli that had rebelled against Fakhr al-Mulk ibn 'Ammar, qadi of Tripoli. Buri governed despotically, the people appealed to Fakhr al-Mulk, who captured him, but he was treated well and sent back to Damascus. After Duqaq's death in 1104 power passed to Toghtekin, and Buri acted as regent.

In 1108 he went with Fakhr al-Mulk to Baghdad to seek help from the caliph al-Mustazhir; on their return they learned that Tripoli had fallen to the Crusaders. In 1110 the domain around Baalbek was given to him after the eunuch al-Taj Gümüshtegin was deposed for intriguing against his father. In 1119 he led an army against King Baldwin II of Jerusalem, who had raided Adra'at and held a hill against his attack until Buri was crushed. On 25 January 1126 he fought beside his father at the Battle of Marj al-Saffar, where Baldwin II defeated them, though the Franks lost so heavily that they could not march on Damascus.

He succeeded Toghtekin, uncontested, in February 1128. In 1129 his vizier uncovered an alleged plot by the Assassins to deliver Damascus to the Crusaders, and Buri had the pro-Nizari vizier Abu Ali Tahir ibn Sa'id al-Mazadaqani killed; in the disorders that followed, 6,000 or 10,000 Assassins were slain by the militia and the mob. Baldwin II, unaware that the plot had been discovered, besieged Damascus until 5 December 1129, when heavy rains turned the land around the city into marsh and forced his retreat.

On 7 May 1131 two Assassins of his own guard, probably sent from Alamut, wounded him severely. He hurried his recovery despite the care of the city's best physicians, and after riding a horse his wound reopened, causing his death on 6 June 1132. He was married to Zumurrud Khatun. His three sons, Shams al-Mulk Isma'il, Shihab ed-Din Mahmud and Jamal ad-Din Muhammad, succeeded him and fought one another over the inheritance. The Burid dynasty of Damascus was named after him.
taj-mahal: Shah Jahan, the fifth Mughal emperor, commissioned the Taj Mahal in 1631 as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died on 17 June that year giving birth to their 14th child. Court historians record that he avoided royal affairs for a week in his grief and for two years gave up music and lavish dress. He chose land south of Agra on which stood a mansion of Raja Jai Singh I, who agreed to give it in exchange for a large palace in the centre of the city.

Construction began in 1632. The mausoleum was completed in 1648 and the rest of the complex in 1653. More than 20,000 workers and artisans took part under a board of architects led by the court architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori. The white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, and 28 kinds of precious and semi-precious stone, from China, Tibet, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Arabia among other places, were inlaid in it.

The mausoleum stands on the right bank of the Yamuna at the centre of a complex of 17 hectares, with a mosque, a guest house and formal gardens enclosed by a crenellated red sandstone wall on three sides. It draws on Timurid and Mughal models, including the Gur-e Amir in Samarkand, the tomb of Timur, and Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, which inspired its charbagh garden.

The marble building stands on a square plinth with four identical sides, each with an iwan, a vaulted arched doorway, and is topped by an onion-shaped marble dome 23 metres high with a gilded finial. Shah Jahan himself was later buried beside his wife. The plan is symmetrical and aligned north to south, and the marble appears to change colour with the hour and the weather.

Shah Jahan, deposed by his son Aurangzeb in 1658, was held at Agra Fort, from where he could see the Taj Mahal, and died in 1666. By the late 19th century parts were in disrepair, and Lord Curzon ordered a restoration completed in 1908. The Archaeological Survey of India has maintained it since 1947.

UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1983 as the jewel of Muslim art in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage. A longstanding story that he planned a black marble twin across the river comes from the writings of the traveller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, and excavations in the 1990s showed that the blackened stones at Mehtab Bagh had been white.
taj-ul-masajid: The name means Crown of Mosques. Nawab Shah Jahan Begum of Bhopal began the building in Shahjahanabad, a newly built walled suburb of the city. The year is uncertain: one estimate gives 1871, while Aarif Aziz, a Bhopal journalist and the author of Masajid-e-Bhopal, gives 1887. The mosque was planned among three water bodies, the Munshi Hussain Talab, the Noor Mahal Talab and the Motia Talab, and Hamidullah Khan helped build one of its gates on Shah Jahan Begum's suggestion.

The later work was led by the Islamic scholar Imran Khan Nadwi, while his brother Salman Khan Nadwi supervised the construction, which cost 20 million Indian rupees. The entrance was afterwards renovated with motifs from 13th-century Syrian mosques, donated by the Emir of Kuwait in memory of his late wife.

The Taj-ul-Masajid is a Sunni mosque affiliated with the Tablighi Jamaat, part of the Deobandi movement, and holds about 26,000 worshippers. Its design draws largely on Mughal architecture. Two octagonal minarets 18 storeys high, topped with marble domes, rise above the facade, and the main hall, with its pillars and marble floor, recalls the Jama Masjid in Delhi and the Badshahi Mosque of Lahore. A courtyard with a large ablution tank at its centre lies before the prayer hall.

A double-storeyed gateway has four recessed archways, and the main prayer hall has nine cusped multifold openings. Its massive pillars carry 27 ceilings on squinted arches, 16 of them decorated with petalled designs. The mosque also has a zenana, a space for women, which was rare at the time of its building, when women usually prayed at home.

From 1948 to 2001 the mosque hosted the Bhopal Tablighi Ijtema, the annual three-day congregation of the Tablighi Jamaat, until a shortage of space moved the gathering to Intkhedi, outside the city. During the COVID-19 pandemic the building served as a vaccination centre.
tajikistan: Tajikistan is landlocked and is the smallest country in Central Asia by area. It borders Afghanistan to the south, Uzbekistan to the west, Kyrgyzstan to the north and China to the east, and the Wakhan Corridor of Afghanistan separates it narrowly from Pakistan. Mountains of the Pamir range cover more than 90 percent of the country, and most of it lies more than 3,000 metres above sea level. The lower land is in the north, part of the Fergana Valley, and in the southern valleys of the Kofarnihon and Vakhsh rivers, which form the Amu Darya. The Amu Darya and the Panj mark the border with Afghanistan.

Cultures in the region date back to at least the fourth millennium BCE, among them the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, the Andronovo culture and the pre-urban site of Sarazm, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Samanid Empire (819–999) began with four brothers, each ruling territory under Abbasid Caliphate suzerainty. In 892 Ismail Samani united the state under a single ruler, and it became independent. The Samanids developed Samarkand and Bukhara as cultural centres of the Iranian world. The area came under the Khanate of Bukhara in the 16th century.

Between 1864 and 1885 Russia took control of all of Russian Turkestan, including the parts of present-day Tajikistan held by Bukhara and Kokand. In February 1990 riots and strikes in Dushanbe over housing and unemployment drew in the nationalist and democratic opposition and Islamists, and Soviet Internal Troops were brought in. After independence the country fell into civil war between factions marked by clan and regional loyalties. Gharm and Gorno-Badakhshan groups, led by liberal reformers and Islamists who became the United Tajik Opposition, rose against the government of President Rahmon Nabiyev, in which people from Khujand and Kulob predominated. Foreign states supported different factions. All but 25,000 of more than 400,000 ethnic Russians left, and a peace agreement ended the war by 1997.

Dushanbe is the capital and largest city, with over 1.2 million people. Tajikistan is a presidential republic of four administrative divisions: the provinces of Sughd and Khatlon, the autonomous province of Gorno-Badakhshan and the Regions of Republican Subordination. Tajik is the state language and Russian the language of inter-ethnic communication. The Yaghnobi language, spoken by about 25,000 people in the north, is the only direct descendant of Sogdian. Sarazm is on the World Heritage List, and the country is a member of the United Nations and the CIS and the OSCE.
tajiks: The Tajiks are a group of Persianate Eastern Iranian peoples native to Central Asia, living mainly in Afghanistan and Tajikistan, with substantial minorities in Pakistan and Uzbekistan. They are of mixed origin, and descend chiefly from Bactrians, Sogdians and Scythians, but also from Persians, Greeks and Turkic peoples. They are therefore mainly Eastern Iranian in ancestry while speaking a form of Persian, a Western Iranian language, which they likely adopted in the seventh century CE after the Islamic conquest of Persia, when Persian spread east and the Bactrian and Sogdian languages gradually died out. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes them as direct descendants of Iranian peoples attested in Central Asia from the middle of the 1st millennium BCE.

Before the Arab conquest the ancient Tajiks were chiefly farmers. After the conquest Islamization brought rapid urbanisation to Khorasan and Transoxiana, which lasted until the Mongol invasion. Samarkand, Bukhara, Khujand and Termez are surviving ancient urban centres of the Tajik people.

The word Tajik is most plausibly traced to the Middle Persian tāzīk, meaning Arab. In the 8th century Turks of Central Asia used a variant for their Muslim adversaries in general, and by the 11th century the Qarakhanid Turks applied it to the Persian Muslims of the Oxus basin and Khorasan. Persian writers of the Ghaznavid and Seljuq periods took the word over, and Iranians soon accepted it as a name for themselves. The terms Fārsīwān, Persian speaker, and Dīhgān, settled villager, were also used. The Tajik term was once used with a pejorative sense for eastern Persians, but it has become acceptable in recent decades.

The language of the Tajiks is an eastern variety of Persian called Dari, from darbārī, of the royal courts. In Tajikistan, where it is written in Cyrillic, it is called Tajiki; in Afghanistan it is written in the Perso-Arabic script. The Soviet Union introduced the Latin script in 1928 and later Cyrillic, and the Persian of Tajikistan came to be treated as a separate Tajik language. Many Tajik authors have lamented this separation.

Zoroastrian and Buddhist heritage is recorded among the Tajiks, and fire temples have been found at Balkh and in Bactria. Today the great majority are Sunni Muslims, with small Twelver and Ismaili Shia minorities. Their culture is predominantly Persianate but contains strong elements of Turkic cultures and is infused with Islamic traditions. The Tajiks are the largest ethnic group in Tajikistan, and the term does not refer to a cohesive transnational ethnic group.
tajlu-khanum: Her ancestry is uncertain. The Italian writer Angiolello and the Iranian historian Manuchihr Parsaʹdust make her a granddaughter, through a daughter, of the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Yaqub (r. 1478–1490); John Woods proposed Mihmad Beg as her father and Amir Hamza as her grandfather, and Jean Aubin proposed Bakr Beg Mawsillu as her maternal grandfather. She had a sister, Beksi Khanum. Accounts of her marriage also differ: Angiolello and Ramusio place it after Ismail's victory over Murad ibn Ya'qub, while Safavid historians such as Budaq Monshi Qazvini say she had been the wife of the Afrasiyabid ruler Kiya Husayn II and entered Ismail's harem after he ended Kiya Husayn's rule.

Ismail composed poetry for her and took her riding and to archery practice; she was described as the only one of his wives skilled with the sword, riding with him to his battles. She bore him two sons, Tahmasp Mirza and Bahram Mirza Safavi, and two daughters, Pari Khan Khanum and Mahinbanu Khanum. Ottoman sources claim she was captured at the Battle of Chaldiran, while Safavid sources say she was lost and found by Mirza Shah Hossein; the historian Roger Savory held that the captured wife was Behruzeh Khanum. The chronicle Javāher al-Akhbār says the appointment and dismissal of amirs and ministers followed her will.

As queen mother she bore the title Navab ‘Alayh and stood between the shah and his courtiers. She saved Qazi Jahan when Montasha Sultan meant to kill him, advised the leaders of the Teklu, Rumlu and Ostajlu tribes in their disputes, and backed Chuhah Sultan in the killing of Div Sultan Rumlu. In 941 AH she sent Sayyid Abdullah Laleh to negotiate peace with Ibrahim Pasha, governor of Baghdad.

Qizilbash leaders who feared her influence spread the rumour that she meant to depose Tahmasp in favour of Bahram Mirza. Tahmasp confiscated her estates and sent her to Shiraz, where she fell ill and died a few months after arriving. In 1519 she had paid for work at the Fatima Masumeh Shrine in Qom, commissioning the Golden Iwan with its muqarnas ceiling, dedicated to Ismail, and rebuilding the Golden Dome. After 1524 she built Ismail's tomb at Ardabil beside that of the Safavid ancestor Shayk Safi.
takamatsu: Takamatsu is the capital of Kagawa Prefecture, on the island of Shikoku. It lies on the Takamatsu Plain, part of the Sanuki Plain, and its northern part faces the Seto Inland Sea, forming a semicircular urban area centred on Takamatsu Port and Takamatsu New Port. The western part of the city is an alluvial fan formed by the Koto River, and the eastern part is a flood plain of the Kasuga and Shinkawa rivers.

In the north-east, Yashima is a table-shaped plateau protruding into the sea, the site of the Battle of Yashima in the Genpei War, and Cape Takei is the northernmost tip of the main island of Shikoku. Parts of the city lie within the Setonaikai National Park, and it includes a number of small inhabited islands.

The area belonged to the ancient Sanuki Province. During the Heian and Kamakura periods it was the closest port to Honshu from Shikoku, a transportation centre and a gateway for pilgrims to the Kotohira Shrine. In the Sengoku period Ikoma Chikamasa built the first Takamatsu Castle in 1588.

In 1642 Matsudaira Yorishige, the son of Tokugawa Yorifusa of Mito Domain and a grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu, was awarded the Takamatsu Domain, assessed at 120,000 koku, which his descendants ruled until the Meiji restoration.

The city was created on 15 February 1890, when the modern municipal system was established, and the castle tower that had been its symbol was destroyed during the Meiji period. In World War II the XXI Bomber Command of the United States chose Takamatsu as a target because it was a focal point of Shikoku's rail and road transport and held some industry vital to the war effort.

On 3 July 1945, 128 B-29 bombers dropped over 800 tons of incendiary bombs, destroying 78 percent of the built-up area and killing 1,359 people. The city recovered quickly after the war and was designated a core city with greater local autonomy on 1 April 1999. In 2005 and 2006 it absorbed several neighbouring towns.

Takamatsu is the largest municipality in Shikoku. It holds most of the national government's branch offices for the island and many companies' regional offices, and it is the home of the Shikoku Railway Company. The Seto-Ōhashi Bridge links its rail line to Okayama on Honshu. Kagawa University and Takamatsu University are in the city. The 2020 census counted 417,496 people.
takano-choei: Takano Chōei was born Gotō Kyōsai on 12 June 1804, the third son of Gotō Sōsuke, a middle-ranking samurai of Mizusawa Domain in Mutsu Province, in present-day Iwate Prefecture. As a boy he was adopted by his uncle Takano Gensai, who had studied medicine under Sugita Genpaku and led him to the same profession. In 1820 he went to Edo to study medicine, paying his way with money won in a lottery. He studied under Sugita Hakugen and then Yoshida Chōshuku, who gave him the name Chōei, and after Yoshida's death in 1824 he took over some of the teaching.

A year later he went to Nagasaki, where he paid for his studies under Philipp Franz von Siebold by writing papers on Japanese life and culture, gathering plants and translating Dutch books. Watanabe Kazan was a fellow student. When the school was shut and Siebold expelled in 1828, Chōei had to flee. He settled in Edo in 1830, wrote his Fundamentals of Western Medicine, and with Watanabe Kazan joined the Shōshikai, a study group of intellectuals interested in foreign affairs. He also wrote treatises on famine relief and on contagious diseases in 1836.

In 1838 he married and published Yumemonogatari (The Tale of a Dream), which criticised the shogunate's handling of the Morrison Incident of 1837. Treated harshly because of his samurai status, he was sentenced to life and spent five years in the commoners' section of the Kodenmachō prison, where he wrote Bansha Sōyaku Shōki, a history of Western knowledge in Japan from the Sengoku period to the 1830s. In 1844 he had a fire started in the prison and escaped, living afterwards under various aliases; he is said to have poured acid on his face to disguise himself.

In March 1850 he returned to Edo and practised medicine under a false name in Aoyama Hyakunin-cho. An informant betrayed him, and the Edo Machi-bugyō sent men to arrest him; he died in the struggle, though what happened is uncertain. A stone monument marks his hiding place, and his grave at Zenko-ji in Kita-Aoyama bears an inscription by Katsu Kaishū. His family house in Ōshū was designated a National Historic Site on 13 April 1933.
takasugi-shinsaku: Takasugi was born on 27 September 1839 in Hagi, the castle town of the Chōshū Domain, the first son of Takasugi Kochūta, a middle-ranked samurai. He became a favourite student at Yoshida Shōin's private school, the Shōka Sonjuku, and in 1858 entered the Shōheikō at Edo. He visited his teacher in jail after his arrest in the Ansei Purge, and Shōin was executed on 21 November 1859. In January 1860 he married Inoue Masa in a match arranged by his parents.

Takasugi was among the most extreme advocates in Chōshū of expelling foreigners. In 1862 the domain sent him secretly to Shanghai, where the effects of European imperialism during the Taiping Rebellion convinced him that Japan must strengthen itself or share the fate of the Qing Empire. He was implicated in the attack on the British legation in Edo on 31 January 1863. His Kiheitai of June 1863 had 300 soldiers, about half of them samurai, but he was dismissed as its leader about two months later after a deadly clash with another unit.

After the Western powers attacked Shimonoseki in September 1864, the domain made him Director of Military Affairs and, at 25, entrusted him with negotiating peace. He concluded that Japan must learn from the West, rearmed the Kiheitai with modern rifles and turned the movement to expel the barbarians and revere the Emperor against the shogunate itself. When conservatives took power after the shogunate's expedition of 1864, he gathered about a dozen followers, among them Yamagata Aritomo, Itō Hirobumi and Inoue Kaoru, and won the civil war that began on 13 January 1865. On 7 June 1866 Chōshū defeated the Second Chōshū expedition on four fronts.

His tuberculosis worsened in October 1866. Nursed by his mistress O-Uno, later the nun Tani Baisho, and the poet Nomura Bōtō, he died on 17 May 1867, aged 28, and was buried near the Kiheitai's camp at Mount Kiyomizu in Yoshida. The Meiji Restoration followed a year later. In 1884 his comrades raised funds for the hermitage Tōgyō-an beside his grave, which became a National Historic Monument in 1934. Many of his friends and followers joined the genrō, the senior statesmen of the Meiji era, and Hagi remembers him for his reforms.
take-me-out-to-the-ball-game: The verses tell of Katie Casey, a young woman mad about baseball. When her beau calls to ask her out to a show, she agrees to go only if he takes her to the ball game instead, and in the second verse she knows the players by their first names and leads the crowd in the song. In a later form of the song the heroine is called Nelly, and Jack Norworth wrote an alternative version of the words in 1927. Most people know only the chorus, perhaps because the verses are written in the third person.

The song was first sung by Norworth's wife, Nora Bayes, with whom he also wrote Shine On, Harvest Moon, and it was taken up by many vaudeville acts. Sales of records, sheet music and piano rolls made it one of the most popular hits of 1908. The first recorded version was by Edward Meeker, and the Haydn Quartet, led by the tenor Harry MacDonough, made a successful recording for Victor Records; the best-known recording was credited to Billy Murray and the Haydn Quartet, though Murray did not sing on it. Norworth and Albert Von Tilzer saw their first Major League Baseball games 32 and 20 years later.

The song was first played at a ballpark in 1934, at a high school game in Los Angeles, and later that year at the fourth game of the 1934 World Series. Its chorus is now traditionally sung during the seventh-inning stretch, often with the home team's name in place of the words home team. The custom spread after Harry Caray, the announcer of the Chicago White Sox, began singing it in 1976 and kept it up with the Chicago Cubs from 1982, when their games were broadcast nationally.

Meeker's recording was added to the National Recording Registry of the Library of Congress in 2010, and the song received the Towering Song Award of the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2008. The music and the 1908 words are in the public domain in the United States, and the 1927 words followed on 1 January 2023.
takechi-hanpeita: Takechi, also known as Takechi Zuizan, was born on 24 October 1829 in Fukii Village in Tosa Province, now part of Kōchi City, the son of an upper-class samurai. Five generations earlier his lower-ranking family had grown rich through farming and won a change of status. In 1841 he took up the Nakanishi-ha Ittō-ryū school of swordsmanship. His parents died in 1849, and that year he married the eldest daughter of Shimamura Genjirō to support his elderly grandmother. He opened his own dōjō in 1854 and by 1855 had over 120 disciples, among them Nakaoka Shintarō and Okada Izō. Sent to Edo to reform the domain's dōjō there, he met Sakamoto Ryōma.

The house arrest of the daimyō Yamauchi Yōdō by the tairō Ii Naosuke in 1859 angered many Tosa samurai, and the sonnō jōi movement spread quickly in the domain. A tour of Kyushu in 1860 brought Takechi the works of the kokugaku scholar Hirata Atsutane. In Edo in 1861 he met samurai of Chōshū, Satsuma and Mito, including Katsura Kogōrō, Kusaka Genzui and Takasugi Shinsaku, and they agreed to press their domains to expel the foreigners and the court to issue edicts against the unequal treaties. In August he secretly formed the Tosa Kinnō-tō, with 192 members, mostly lower-ranking samurai and some ronin.

The domain was then run by Yoshida Tōyō, who favoured opening the country to trade and uniting court and shogunate, and who dismissed Takechi's petitions as unrealistic. After three members of the party killed Yoshida, Takechi took action to seize the Tosa government. Party members acted as a death squad in Kyoto, killing political opponents. Takechi drafted petitions for imperial rule over the five Kinai provinces and a national army answering to the emperor, and was received as an imperial envoy by Shogun Tokugawa Iemochi.

Yamauchi Yōdō turned against the party, and three members confessed to Yoshida's murder under interrogation. Takechi refused to flee and was arrested; he denied any part in the killing. On 3 July 1865, after 1 year 8 months and 20 days in prison, he was ordered to commit seppuku while four other leaders were sentenced to decapitation. Survivors such as Nakaoka Shintarō carried on against the shogunate. Takechi was pardoned in 1877 and raised to Senior Fourth Court rank in 1891. His former residence and grave in Kōchi became a National Historic Site in 1936, and the Zuizan Shrine is dedicated to his deified spirit.
takeda-clan: The Takeda were descended from Emperor Seiwa and were a branch of the Minamoto clan, through Minamoto no Yoshimitsu. Yoshimitsu's son Minamoto no Yoshikiyo was the first to take the name Takeda, from the Takeda domain in Hitachi Province that his father granted him. By the end of the Heian period the family controlled Kai Province.

The Takeda supported their cousin Minamoto no Yoritomo against the Taira clan in the Genpei War, and after Yoritomo's defeat at Ishibashiyama in 1181 they sent an army of 25,000. Takeda Nobumitsu became governor of Kai, helped the Hōjō during the Jōkyū War and received the governorship of Aki in 1221. The family later held Wakasa from 1440 as well, and its rivalry with the Uesugi clan began after a reprisal in 1415 and lasted roughly 150 years.

Takeda Harunobu, born in 1521, succeeded his father Nobutora in 1540 and took the name Shingen in 1559. He fought the Hōjō clan and, to the north, Uesugi Kenshin in the Battles of Kawanakajima, which began in 1553; the severest was fought on 10 September 1561. Shingen is credited with turning samurai from archers into lancers, and his cavalry gave the Takeda army the name Kiba Gundan, "mounted army", although some historians argue his tactics were neither impressive nor revolutionary.

He died of illness on 13 May 1573, aged 53. His son Takeda Katsuyori continued the expansion south and west and briefly extended the clan's rule to its widest extent, but Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated him at Nagashino in 1575. In 1582 two of his relatives defected and Nobunaga destroyed the clan, most of whose followers abandoned Katsuyori.

Three major cadet branches, the Aki, Wakasa and Kazusa Takeda, spread the name across Japan. The family's code of law, the Kōshū Hatto, dates from the 15th century, and the Kōyō Gunkan, written largely by Kōsaka Masanobu in the mid-16th century, records the family's history and Shingen's tactics. Descendants of the clan took prominent positions in the Tokugawa shogunate, and in 1868 several daimyo families, among them the Matsumae of Hokkaidō's only fief, were of Takeda descent.
takeda-nobutora: Nobutora was the son of Takeda Nobutsuna (1471–1507) and had several sons, among them Nobushige and Nobukado. He controlled the Province of Kai as a daimyō in the Sengoku period. He defeated Imagawa Ujichika at the Battle of Iidagawara in 1521, Hōjō Ujitsuna at the Battle of Nashinokidaira in 1526 and Suwa Yorishige at the Battle of Shiokawa no gawara in 1531. In 1536 he fought Hiraga Genshin at the Battle of Un no Kuchi; when Nobutora was forced to retreat, his son Harunobu, later known as Takeda Shingen, turned the fight around, defeated Hiraga and took the castle.

Of his daughters, Joukei-in (1519–1550) married Imagawa Yoshimoto, Nanshou-in married Anayama Nobutomo, and Nene married Suwa Yorishige. To secure the alliance with Yoshimoto he gave him the katana Soza Samonji, which after Yoshimoto's death at Okehazama passed to Oda Nobunaga, then to Toyotomi Hideyoshi and from him to Tokugawa Ieyasu; it is now one of the Cultural Properties of Japan.

Nobutora wished to leave his domain to another son, Nobushige, rather than to Harunobu, and it was Harunobu who overthrew him and sent him away to Suruga. He came back to Kai only after Shingen's death in 1573, at the invitation of his grandson Katsuyori, when he was in his eighties; some reported that even as an old man he still struck fear into those around him. He died on 27 March 1574, a year after his son, and was buried at the Daisenji temple in Kōfu. The Kōyō Gunkan, completed in the Edo period, portrays him as a coarse and arrogant samurai.
takeda-shingen: Takeda Shingen was born on 1 December 1521, the first son of Takeda Nobutora, daimyo of Kai Province. After his coming-of-age ceremony he took the formal name Harunobu, with a character from the name of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshiharu. He was a poet in his youth and in 1536 helped his father win the Battle of Un no Kuchi. In 1540 he took control of the clan. Accounts of the change are not entirely clear, but Nobutora is thought to have planned to name Shingen's brother Takeda Nobushige as heir, and he was sent into custody in Suruga under the Imagawa clan. In February 1559 Harunobu became a Buddhist novice and received the name Shingen.

Kai was a poor province with little arable land and no coast, yet Shingen became one of the leading daimyo of the late Sengoku period. He set out to conquer Shinano Province, taking castle after castle from 1543, until Murakami Yoshikiyo fled to Echigo and appealed to Uesugi Kenshin. Their rivalry produced five encounters at Kawanakajima. In the fourth, according to a well-known tale, Kenshin fought Shingen in single combat, Kenshin with a sword and Shingen with an iron war fan, and Shingen lost two leading generals.

After Imagawa Yoshimoto died in 1560, Shingen allied with the Oda and Tokugawa clans and by 1567 was ready to invade Suruga. This angered Hōjō Ujiyasu, and Shingen broke with the Hōjō in 1568 and besieged Odawara in 1569. In 1573, urged by the shogun Ashikaga Yoshiaki, he marched towards Kyoto and defeated the Oda–Tokugawa forces at the Battle of Mikatagahara.

Shingen besieged Noda Castle in Mikawa Province and died on 13 May 1573, aged 51. Accounts differ: an old war wound, a sniper's bullet or pneumonia. His son Takeda Katsuyori succeeded him, and Oda Nobunaga's matchlock-armed infantry destroyed the Takeda cavalry at the Battle of Nagashino. The historian Kazuto Hongō argued that Shingen never built a war economy: his lands yielded at most 600,000 koku of rice a year, enough for 20,000 soldiers, about half what Nobunaga could raise. Tokugawa Ieyasu later took in many former Takeda retainers and borrowed from Shingen's government and military arrangements.
takelot-ii: Takelot II, with the throne name Hedjkheperre Setepenre and the epithet Si-Ese, was a pharaoh in Middle and Upper Egypt. He has been identified as the High Priest of Amun Takelot F, son of the High Priest of Amun Nimlot C at Thebes, and so a grandson of King Osorkon II. Takelot F served for a time as High Priest under Osorkon II, and the reliefs of Temple J at Karnak, which he dedicated in that office, show Osorkon II as the king. He proclaimed himself king in the last three regnal years of Osorkon II.

Most Egyptologists accept David Aston's hypothesis of 1989 that Shoshenq III, not Takelot II, was Osorkon II's actual successor at Tanis. On this view Takelot II ruled a separate kingdom that embraced Middle and Upper Egypt, while the kings at Tanis controlled only Lower Egypt. All documents naming him and his son Osorkon B come from Middle or Upper Egypt. He added the epithet Si-Ese, Son of Isis, to his titulary to link himself with Thebes and to distinguish his name from that of Takelot I.

In year 11 of Takelot II an insurrection began at Thebes under Pedubast I, whose followers challenged the king's authority. Takelot sent his son, the Crown Prince Osorkon B, southwards by river to put it down. Osorkon kept control of the city and proclaimed himself High Priest of Amun. He had some of the rebels' bodies deliberately burned, to deny their souls any hope of an afterlife.

In year 15 a second major revolt broke out, and Pedubast I expelled Osorkon's forces from Thebes. A long struggle followed in Upper Egypt between the faction of Takelot II and Osorkon B and that of Pedubast I and Shoshenq VI. Osorkon recorded his campaigns in the Chronicle of Prince Osorkon, carved on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak, dating them by the years of Takelot II and later by those of Shoshenq III. He finally won back Thebes and afterwards took the kingship as Osorkon III.

A donation stela made by Osorkon as High Priest, shortly before Takelot died, attests the king's brief 25th year and grants 35 aurourae of land to Takelot's daughter Karomama E. No tomb or final resting place for him had been found by 2008. Osorkon B did not succeed his father at once, and the throne passed possibly to another son, Iuput I. Takelot II married his sister, the Great Royal Wife Karomama Merymut II. Their children included Osorkon B and Bakenptah B, a general of Herakleopolis.
takelot-iii: Takelot III, whose full name was Usermaatre Setepenamun Takelot Si-Ese, was the eldest son and successor of Osorkon III. He had earlier served as High Priest of Amun at Thebes. Quay Text No. 13 equates year 28 of Osorkon III with year 5 of Takelot III, which shows that he ruled the first five years of his reign in a coregency with his father. He succeeded as sole king the following year.

Several documents attest him. A donation stela from Gurob calls him "The First Prophet of Amun-Re, General and Commander Takelot", and a stone block from Herakleopolis calls him the Chief of Pi-Sekhemkheperre and king's son by Tentsai. Quay Text No. 4 records his year 6, and a graffito on the roof of the Temple of Khonsu records his year 7, long believed to be his highest date.

In February 2005 a Columbia University expedition found a hieratic stela at Amheida in the Dakhla Oasis dated to year 13 of Takelot III. It records a land donation to the temple of Thoth by the local governor Nes-Djehuti, chief of the Shamin Libyans, and ends with a list of eleven priests who benefited. Olaf Kaper and Robert Demarée published it in 2006. The same chief appears in a stela of year 24 of the Nubian king Piye, which suggests that the two kings were near contemporaries.

Scholars have debated whether his rule was longer. A graffito at Wadi Gasus naming years 12 and 19 was once read as linking Takelot III to the Nubian king Shabaka, but Claus Jurman's 2006 study redated it to the Nubian period, so year 19 cannot be assigned to Takelot III. Frédéric Payraudeau argued that Papyrus Berlin 3048, dated to year 14 of a king Takelot, belonged to him, but later assigned it to Takelot II, because the papyrus names a fourth prophet of Amun, Harsiese, known from that reign. His highest date therefore remains year 13.

Takelot III was the husband of Irtiubast, named as a king's daughter on the coffin of their son Osorkon G. He was succeeded at Thebes not by any of his three known sons, Osorkon F, Ihtesamun and Djedptahefankh D, but by his younger brother Rudamun, another son of Osorkon III. Since custom required a king's son to succeed him, this suggests that Takelot III reached an advanced age and outlived his sons.

Rudamun was in turn succeeded at Thebes by King Ini, who ruled there for at least five years before the city fell permanently under Kushite control in the reign of Piye. Piye conquered Egypt in his 20th year, by which time Takelot III and Rudamun had both died.
takeno-joo: His father, Nobuhisa, took the family name Takeno and, after wandering the country, settled in the port city of Sakai, where he built up a thriving trade in leather goods used by warriors. His mother was the daughter of a priest of the Kōfukuji temple in Yamato Province. Known in his youth by the common name Shingorō, Jō'ō carried on the family business while serving as an attendant at the Hongan-ji temple at Yamashina, in Yamashiro Province.

In 1532 he took the tonsure and became known as Jō'ō. Until about the age of thirty-five he hoped to become a teacher of renga, linked verse composed in groups. In Kyoto he learned the secrets of waka poetry from the aristocratic master Sanjōnishi Sanetaka, and his wealth allowed him to gather a large collection of classical works on the art.

Chanoyu, the tea ceremony, had risen quickly in prominence in Kyoto during the Sengoku period, and Jō'ō set out to develop a style suited to the customs of Sakai rather than the capital. Sanjōnishi Sanetaka and his renga circle shaped this work, as did his own Zen training. Following Murata Jukō, he became an early proponent of wabi-cha, the restrained style of tea.

He came to be regarded as the foremost tea master of Sakai. Among his pupils were the wealthy merchant Imai Sōkyū, who married his daughter, and Sen no Rikyū, through whom his teaching passed into later Japanese tea culture. When Jō'ō died in 1555, his legitimate son, Takeno Shingorō, also called Takeno Sōga, was only six years old. Imai Sōkyū became the boy's guardian, and the son inherited the estate and in time became a tea master himself.
takht-e-soleyman: Takht-e Soleymān, Persian for Throne of Solomon, lies midway between Urmia and Hamadan, very near the present-day town of Takab and 400 km west of Tehran. The fortified site stands on a hill created by the outflow of a calcium-rich spring pond. It appears on the Peutinger Map. The biblical name came after the Muslim conquest of Persia in the 7th century. Folk legend says King Solomon imprisoned monsters in a nearby crater about 100 m deep, called Zendan-e Soleyman, the Prison of Solomon, and that he created the flowing pond.

Excavations have revealed traces of an occupation of the 5th century BCE in the Achaemenid era and later Parthian settlements in the citadel. Coins of the Sasanian shahs and of the Byzantine emperor Theodosius II have also been found. The citadel holds the remains of Adur Gushnasp, a Zoroastrian fire temple of the Sasanian era. It housed one of the three Great Fires, or Royal Fires, before which Sasanian rulers humbled themselves in order to take the throne, and was dedicated to the warrior class.

The Ilkhanid ruler Abaqa (r. 1265-82), a son of Hülagü, chose the site for a summer and hunting palace, partly because of the large ruins of the old temple and palace, whose layout he could use. Building probably began in 1271 and was completed by his son Arghun. The choice also helped the Ilkhanids, who had not been Muslim at first, to present themselves as part of Iran's history. The palace stood within an oval fortified wall, around a courtyard with an artificial lake, with four iwans and polygonal chambers. An audience hall with a large dome stood on the site of the fire temple.

The Ilkhanid complex is the only surviving secular structure of that period. Its walls carried painted stucco and lustre tiles in the lajvardina technique. Tiles show dragons and phoenixes alongside scenes from the Shahnameh, such as Fereydun defeating Zahhak, and quotations from the Qur'an. A stucco plate found in the southern octagonal chamber, now in the National Museum of Iran, carries a 42 cm muqarnas plan, one of the earliest known Islamic architectural plans of its kind.
The British explorers Theodore and Mabel Bent dug at the site in early May 1889. Takht-e Soleymān was recognised as a World Heritage Site in July 2003, and a small museum shows finds from it.
takht-i-bahi: Takht-i-Bahi stands about 15 kilometres from Mardan in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, on a small hill about 150 metres high, with a small fortified city of the same era nearby. The origin of the name is uncertain. A local belief ties it to two wells or springs on the hill, and others suggest meanings such as throne of the water spring or throne of origin.

The buildings are of local stone mortared with lime and mud and fall into four main areas: the Stupa Court, the monastic chambers with cells, assembly halls and a dining area, a later temple complex of stupas, and a Tantric complex of small, dark cells with low openings that may have been used for certain forms of meditation.

Archaeologists distinguish several building periods. An inscription bearing the name of Gondophares (20-46 CE) has been found at the site, and after him the area came under Kujula Kadphises, the first Kushan king; the first period, lasting to the 2nd century, is linked with Kanishka and other Kushan kings. The Stupa Court and assembly hall belong to the 3rd and 4th centuries, and a third phase, associated with the Kidara Kushana rulers, to the 4th and 5th.

In the middle of the 5th century the Huns subjugated the region and ended Kushan rule. Their rulers Toramana and his son Mihirakula are said to have killed many inhabitants and destroyed most Buddhist monasteries, and evidence suggests Takht-i-Bahi was damaged then, though the complex appears to have been in use until the 7th century.

A French officer made the first modern reference to the ruins in 1836, and excavations began in 1864. Many objects are in the British Museum, among them a stair-riser showing devotees in Hellenistic costume. The site was restored on a large scale in the 1920s and listed as a World Heritage Site in 1980, when UNESCO called it exceptionally well preserved. Once remote and little visited, it now has a road and car park below the ruins and is popular with visitors.
takhtsinhji: Takhtsinhji Jaswantsinhji was born on 6 January 1858, a Rajput chief of the Gohil clan, and succeeded to the throne of Bhavnagar on the death of his father, Jaswantsinhji, in 1870. He was the first student of the Rajkumar College at Rajkot and later studied under an English officer. During his minority, which ended on 5 April 1878, the state was administered jointly by E. H. Percival of the Indian Civil Service and Gaurishankar Udayshankar, who had served Bhavnagar in various capacities since 1822. He attended the Delhi Durbar in 1877.

At twenty he took charge of a territory of nearly 3,000 square miles. His first public act was to sanction a railway linking the state with one of the main trunk lines, the first enterprise of its kind by a raja in western India, and the commerce and development that followed confirmed his policy of progressive administration. In 1886 he introduced a system of constitutional rule, placing several departments in the hands of a council of state of four members under his own presidency.

The reform, supported by Lord Reay, the governor of Bombay, provoked a virulent attack on him. He brought his defamers to trial at the High Court of Bombay, and the punishment of the ringleaders broke up a system of blackmail to which rajas were regularly exposed. He also reformed the revenue department and built water works, modern docks, a port, bridges and roads. Knighted KCSI in 1881 and made GCSI in 1886, he visited England in 1893 at the opening of the Imperial Institute to pay homage to Queen Victoria, and the University of Cambridge awarded him the degree of LL.D.

Takhtsinhji became the chief patron and benefactor of the Rajkumar College and supported Gujarat College, Fergusson College, the Wadhwan Girassia School and several schools for girls and women. He named the Samaldas Arts College, founded in 1885, after Samaldas Mehta, later diwan of the state. He died at the Moti Bagh Palace on 29 January 1896, at the age of 38, and was succeeded by his eldest son, Bhavsinhji II.
taksin: Taksin was born on 17 April 1734 at Ayutthaya. His father, Yong Saetae, a tax-collector, was of Teochew descent from Chenghai District in Guangdong, and his mother, Nokiang, was of Mon-Tai descent. As a boy he was adopted by Chaophraya Chakri, the Grand Chancellor of Civil Affairs in the reign of King Boromakot, who gave him the Thai name Sin, meaning money or treasure. After about three years as a Buddhist monk he entered the service of King Ekkathat and became governor of Tak, which gave him the name Phraya Tak. In 1765 he took part in the defence of Ayutthaya against the Burmese.

On 3 January 1767, three months before Ayutthaya fell, Taksin left the besieged city with about 500 followers and went to Rayong on the Gulf of Thailand, where he raised a small army. The country then split into six parts, with Taksin controlling the east coast. He made his capital at Thonburi, which lay closer to the sea, was hard to invade by land and could be held by his limited forces, and was crowned king there on 28 December 1767. From 1768 to 1771 he subdued rival lords at Phimai, Phitsanulok, Fang and Nakhon Si Thammarat, so that Thonburi became the new centre of power.

His reign was filled with war. He is recorded as waging nine campaigns against Burma, the first ending with a Burmese army routed at Bang Kung in 1767, and he also fought to subjugate the northern Thai kingdom of Lanna, the Laotian principalities and Cambodia. In 1777 his general Chao Phraya Chakri conquered Champasak. Taksin also paid high prices for rice to induce foreign traders to bring in food, distributed rice and clothing, and had roads built and canals dug. China recognised him as the legitimate ruler of Siam in 1772.

In 1781 Taksin showed increasing signs of mental trouble, according to Thai historians. He came to believe himself a future Buddha and required the monkhood to recognise him as a stream-winner, and monks who refused were demoted or flogged. Famine, looting and unrest added to the strain. He was taken in a coup and killed in 1782, and his friend Chakri took the throne, founding the Rattanakosin Kingdom and the Chakri dynasty. Under the Chakri kings Taksin was not highly honoured, but after the revolution of 1932 he came to be regarded as a national hero, and he later received the title Maharat, the Great.
taksony: Taksony, also called Taxis or Tocsun, was according to the Gesta Hungarorum, written around 1200, the son of Zoltán and of an unnamed daughter of Menumorut, a local ruler defeated by the conquering Hungarians shortly before 907. Whether Menumorut was an actual person is debated. The same source says Zoltán abdicated in his favour three years before his own death.

Modern historians challenge this account of his youth. Liudprand of Cremona, a nearly contemporaneous writer, reports that Taxis came to Italy with a large army in 947, which suggests that he was born considerably earlier than the date the Gesta gives. Around 950 the Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus wrote that Fajsz, Taksony's cousin, was then grand prince of the Hungarians.

A later writer, Johannes Aventinus, says Taksony fought at the Battle of Lechfeld on 10 August 955, where Otto I routed an army of 8,000 Hungarians. If so, he was one of the few Hungarian leaders to survive. Historians including Zoltán Kordé and Gyula Kristó suggest that Fajsz abdicated in his favour around that time. After the battle the Hungarian raids in Western Europe stopped and the Hungarians had to retreat from the lands between the Enns and Traisen rivers, though they continued their incursions into the Byzantine Empire until the 970s.

The Gesta Hungarorum records that a great host of Muslims arrived from the land of Bular under Taksony, and that Pechenegs came too, to whom he granted land from the region of Kemej as far as the Tisza. The contemporary Ibrahim ibn Yaqub recorded Muslim merchants from Hungary in Prague in 965. Liudprand writes that Pope John XII consecrated a bishop, Zacheus, in 963 and sent him to the Hungarians to preach that they should attack the Germans, but there is no evidence that Zacheus ever arrived.

Taksony died in the early 970s, after arranging the marriage of his elder son Géza to Sarolt, daughter of Gyula of Transylvania. The names of two of his sons, Géza and Michael, are preserved. His own wife is said in the Gesta to have come from the land of the Cumans, an anachronism; historians think it preserves a memory of a Turkic origin, Khazar, Pecheneg or Volga Bulgarian.
takua-pa: The district lies on the Andaman Sea coast, with Si Phang Nga National Park to the north and Khao Lak-Lam Ru National Park, which includes the beach resorts of Khao Lak, in the south. Its neighbours are Khura Buri to the north, Phanom of Surat Thani province and Kapong to the east, and Thai Mueang to the south.

The town was first named Takola and was also known by the Tamil name Takkolam, a word for piper cubeba; it may have abounded in such spices, been settled from the place of the same name in the Tamil country, or both. It is said to have been the finest harbour on the west coast of the peninsula for trade between Srivijaya and the Tamil kingdoms of the Cholas and Pallavas.

Finds at Ban Thung Tuek resemble the Tang ceramics, pottery from India and glassware from Persia found at Laem Pho across the isthmus, suggesting an overland route by which traders could avoid piracy in the Strait of Malacca. A Vishnu temple stood there, for which the merchant body Kodumbalur Manigramam built a tank, recording the work in Tamil.

The later name Takua Pa comes from takua, the Thai word for lead, though tin was the most important ore found nearby. Long administered by Nakhon Si Thammarat, the town became a province in 1892, part of Monthon Phuket. The province was merged into Phang Nga Province on 1 April 1932, and the district of Talat Yai was renamed Takua Pa. In the first half of the 20th century it was an important tin-dredging area, worked by the English Siamese Tin Syndicate and the Australian Satupulo No Liability Co. with narrow-gauge tramways along the rivers; Thai firms had taken over by the early 1980s.

By 2008 rubber plantations covered the former dredged land, and the public library in Takua Pa town displays photographs of the dredging of the 1920s and 1930s. The centre for identifying the bodies found after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, which devastated Khao Lak, is in the district, with a cemetery for unidentified foreign victims. The district is divided into eight sub-districts and 51 villages.
tala-al-badru-alayna: The song's second line greets the moon rising from the Thaniyāt al-Wadāʿ. Some readers take this for a pass north of Medina and so judge the Hijra story geographically unlikely, since Muhammad is said to have arrived first at Qubāʾ, south of the city. Classical geographers, however, knew more than one place of the name. The medieval geographer Yāqūt al-Ḥamawī described Thaniyat al-Wadāʿ as a pass used by travellers heading for Mecca, and other early writers mention a similar pass on the Meccan side of Medina.

Ibn Hajar al-ʽAsqalani recorded that many authorities placed a Thaniyat al-Wadāʿ on the Mecca road while acknowledging another on the Syrian side, and reports cited by the historian al-Samḥūdī have Muhammad coming from Qubāʾ and passing near such a place before entering the city. Some scholars also read the plural Thaniyāt as pointing to several passes, and a number of historians therefore regard the objection as inconclusive. Ibn Hajar al-ʽAsqalani is the main voice for the other view, that the song welcomed Muhammad back to Medina after the Battle of Tabuk.

The nasheed has been recorded many times, among others by Oum Kalthoum, Mishary Rashid Alafasy, Sami Yusuf, Yusuf Islam, Native Deen, Maher Zain and Junaid Jamshed. It accompanies the scene of the Hijra in the 1976 film The Message, directed by Moustapha Akkad. Olivia Newton-John sang it as an interlude on her album Grace and Gratitude (2006), and Maryem Tollar performed it over the closing credits of the Canadian sitcom Little Mosque on the Prairie.

The Syrian German composer Malek Jandali used it in a piece for piano and orchestra, The Moonlight, and the Brazilian composer Marcus Viana arranged it for his 2003 album Poemas Místicos do Oriente. In December 2015, when Syrian refugees first began arriving in Canada, a children's choir in Ottawa sang an arrangement by Laura Hawley at a holiday concert.
talagunda-inscription: The pillar stands in front of the ruined and partly restored Pranavalingeshwara temple, a Shiva temple of the 5th century, northwest of the village of Talagunda in Shikaripur taluk. B. L. Rice, then Director of Archaeological Researches in Mysore, found the inscription in 1894 and gave a photograph to the Indologist Buhler, who published it in 1895. Rice printed a prose translation in 1902 in volume 7 of Epigraphia Carnatica, and the Sanskrit scholar F. Kielhorn a fuller verse-by-verse reading in Epigraphia Indica in 1906.

The text is cut into an octagonal pillar of hard grey granite, 1.635 metres high, that narrows slightly as it rises. On seven faces it runs in two vertical lines from the foot of the pillar, and on the eighth in one short line. It is generally dated to between 455 and 470 CE.

The inscription opens with Siddham and an invocation to Shiva and consists of 34 verses in classical Sanskrit, written in the Kadamba script in a mix of metres; its first 24 verses are the earliest known use of the matrasamaka metre. It traces the Kadamba family to a Brahmin line that tended a kadamba tree by its house, and tells how Mayurasharma went with his preceptor Virasarman to study at the ghatika of the Pallava city, took up the sword, defeated the Pallava frontier guards and was at last given a territory reaching the western sea.

It then names his successors, Kangavarman, Bhagiratha, Raghu and Kakustha, praises Kakusthavarman for marrying his daughters into the Gupta and other royal families, and records that he had a great water tank made at the temple. The last verse says that Kubja wrote the poem on the stone at the command of the king's son Shantivarma.

The Sanskrit scholar Sheldon Pollock calls its language wonderful literary Sanskrit, and the pillar shows that classical Sanskrit had spread into South India by about 455 to 470 CE. It attests to Kanchipuram as a centre of advanced study, and it is the earliest epigraphic evidence in Karnataka of a Shiva temple, a temple tank and the worship of the Shiva Linga. The historian Hampa Nagarajaiha argues that its Brahmin identity reflects a Jain usage rather than a Vedic caste.
talakad: Talakadu lies on the left bank of the Kaveri, 45 km from Mysore and 133 km from Bangalore, at a point where the eastward-flowing river changes course and the sand on its banks spreads over a wide area. The town once had more than 30 temples. The old city lies buried beneath sand for nearly a mile, with only the tops of two gopuras visible; the sand hills used to advance 9 or 10 feet a year, mainly during the south-west monsoon, forcing people to abandon their houses and move inland.

One tradition derives the name from two Kirāta twin brothers, Tala and Kādu, who cut down a tree that wild elephants worshipped and found in it an image of Shiva; the Sanskrit form of the name is Dalavana-pura. Its earliest authentic mention is with the Ganga kings. According to an old chronicle, Harivarma, assigned to 247–266 CE, was installed at Skandapura but lived at Dalavanapura, and later kings of the line were crowned there. The Cholas renamed the captured town Rājarājapura. After Vishnuvardhana took it, Talakadu was made up of seven towns and five mathas, and it stayed with the Hoysalas until the mid-fourteenth century before passing to a feudatory of the Vijayanagar rulers.

In 1610 Rāja Wodeyar of Mysore took Talakadu. According to the story told of it, Rāni Alamelamma, wife of the Vijayanagar representative Tirumala-Rāja, refused him her jewels, threw them into the Kaveri and drowned herself opposite Mālangi, cursing that Talakadu should become sand, Mālangi a whirlpool and the Mysore kings be without heirs.

The surviving group of temples is a popular Hindu pilgrimage site, and the town has grown with the wet cultivation watered by the Mādhavamantri anicut. The Kírti Nārāyana temple has been excavated, the Vydyanatheshwara temple is the most imposing left uncovered, and the Ānandēsvara and Gaurisankara temples were unearthed in the early nineteenth century; an inscription dates the Gaurisankara to the reign of Chikka-Dēva-Rāja-Wodeyar (1672–1704).
talal-of-jordan: Talal was born in Mecca on 26 February 1909, the eldest son of Abdullah bin Hussein and Musbah bint Nasser. Abdullah, a son of Hussein bin Ali, Sharif of Mecca, founded the Emirate of Transjordan in 1921. Talal was educated privately in Amman, graduated from the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, in 1929 and was commissioned in the cavalry of the Arab Legion. He became aide to his grandfather, the ousted King of the Hejaz, in exile in Cyprus, and by 1948 he was a general. In November 1934 he married Zein al-Sharaf bint Jamil, and their son Hussein was born in 1935.

Transjordan became the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan after it sought independence in 1946, and Talal became crown prince. On 20 July 1951 Abdullah I was assassinated at the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem by a Palestinian, amid rumours that he planned a peace treaty with Israel. Prince Hussein, aged fifteen and at his grandfather's side, survived. Talal became king.

His main achievement was the constitution ratified on 1 January 1952, which made the government collectively, and the ministers individually, responsible to the Jordanian Parliament. He is also judged to have eased relations with Egypt and Saudi Arabia. Historians differ on his attitude to Britain. A British resident called him deeply anti-British at heart, while Avi Shlaim argues that his resentment of British interference was genuine. A set of stamps issued for his accession was withdrawn and burned after he left the throne.

In 1952 the British resident, Queen Zein al-Sharaf and Prime Minister Tawfik Abu al-Huda reported that Talal was mentally ill, and he was flown to Paris for treatment. Abu al-Huda summoned both houses of parliament, which on 11 August 1952 unanimously deposed him on medical grounds, citing schizophrenia. Abu al-Huda governed until Hussein came of age on 2 May 1953. Talal had wished to live in the Hejaz but was sent to a sanatorium in Istanbul, where he died on 7 July 1972.
talamone: Talamone stands on a rocky promontory on the southern edge of the Maremma nature reserve, in the province of Grosseto, about 25 kilometres from Grosseto and 10 kilometres from Orbetello. It overlooks the whole stretch of coast as far as Mount Argentario. The country around it is Mediterranean scrub with long sandy beaches lined with pines. Diodorus Siculus wrote that the Argonauts named the town after the hero Telamon, an etymology now regarded as a mythological invention.

The town was already a flourishing place in the Etruscan period. In 225 BCE the Celts who had overrun Etruria and killed 6,000 Romans at Faesulae were marching on Rome under the Gaesatae kings Concolitanus and Aneroëstes when the Romans met them nearby; 40,000 Celts were killed, ending the Celtic threat to Rome and opening northern Italy to Roman influence. Sulla later razed Talamone for the support its citizens had given Marius, and the emperor Trajan developed its port and had a villa connected to it.

The late Middle Ages left few marks on the town, which passed from the Aldobrandeschi, among others, to the Republic of Siena, until in 1559 the territory was ceded to Spain. The port was a stage of Admiral Horatio Nelson's expedition to Egypt in 1798, and in 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi stopped there with the Expedition of the Thousand to take on water and weapons.

Talamone is a frazione of the comune of Orbetello, in the Tuscan Maremma. Its monuments include a Roman cistern and villa, the Church of Santa Maria Assunta, the town walls, the Rocca Aldobrandesca and several coastal towers, and the southern entrance to the Maremma Natural Park is on its outskirts.
talatal-ghar: Rudra Singha moved the Ahom capital from Garhgaon to Rangpur, then called Tengabari, in 1707. He began the palace in semi-permanent materials and brought an architect from Cooch Behar, Ghanashyam, to design the new capital. His successor Rajeswar Singha (Surempha) rebuilt it with major additions in brick, including the three floors below ground that give the building its name. The wooden chambers of the upper floor were burnt during the Moamaria rebellion, the Burmese invasions and by the British.

The palace had seven storeys, four above ground and three below, which were sealed and filled during the British era. It was built of brick and an indigenous cement made from a mixture including bora chaul, a sticky rice, and swan's eggs. Two tunnels were used as escape routes: one, about 3 kilometres long, ran to the Dikhow River and the other, 16 kilometres long, to the Garhgaon Palace. Several rooms run from east to west along a long corridor, with many smaller wings from north to south.

Of the royal apartments on the upper storey only a few rooms remain, near an octagonal room in the northern wing that served as a prayer house. Around them stood the Mantranaghar, or conference room, the Barcharā assembly hall of bamboo and wood, the royal archives, and the halls of the chief justice and of the secret assembly; isolated rooms to the south were probably the queen's lying-in room and the royal kitchen. Reliefs of hunting scenes, flowers, gods and goddesses once covered the walls, and few survive. A brick wall and an earthen fort with water-filled dikes surrounded the palace, and a Gola Ghar nearby stored gunpowder and ammunition.

Excavations in 2000–2001 uncovered buried structures on the north-western and north-eastern sides of the complex: a brick platform, a pathway, long walls, a drain of terracotta pipes, and vases, vessels, dishes and bowls. In early April 2015 IIT Kanpur and the Guwahati circle of the Archaeological Survey of India carried out a five-day ground-penetrating radar survey at the Talatal Ghar and the Kareng Ghar, the first in the north-east, which found no sign of a secret tunnel.
tale-of-aqhat: The Tale of Aqhat is one of the three longest texts found at Ugarit, with the Legend of Keret and the Baal Cycle, which were recorded by the same hand. The story survives on three clay tablets, found in 1930 and 1931, which lack its beginning and end. According to David Wright about 650 poetic lines remain, most of them concerned with ritual performances or their contexts. Gaps in the tablets leave several points uncertain, and scholars read them differently.

Danel, a righteous ruler who gives justice to widows and orphans, has no son. For six days he makes offerings at a temple, and on the seventh the god Baal asks the high god El to grant him one. After Aqhat's birth Danel holds a feast for the Kotharat, goddesses of childbearing, and the craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis gives him a bow in thanks for his hospitality. Fontenrose reads the gift as coming while Aqhat is an infant, Wright after he has grown up.

At a feast attended by gods, Anat offers Aqhat gold and silver, then immortality, for the bow. He refuses, telling her to get a bow of her own from Kothar-wa-Hasis, that women have no business with such weapons, and that all humans must die. Anat complains to El and, after threatening him, wins his reluctant leave. Her follower Yatpan, turned into an eagle, attacks and kills Aqhat, and the bow is broken in the attack. Anat mourns him and the bow, and foresees that the crops will fail.

Unaware of his son's death, Danel goes on judging in the city gate, while his daughter Pugat sees drought setting in and birds of prey circling. Two young men bring the news. Danel asks Baal to bring down the vultures overhead, and in the mother of the vultures he finds Aqhat's bone and fat, which he buries by the Kinneret, the Sea of Galilee. Pugat sets out to avenge her brother by killing Yatpan.
tale-of-sinuhe: The story is known by several names, among them the Story of Sanehat. It was likely composed at the beginning of the Twelfth Dynasty, after the death of Amenemhat I and the accession of Senusret I as sole pharaoh.

The oldest known copy dates from the reign of Amenemhat III, and the work was so popular within Egypt that newer copies have been found ranging up to 750 years after the original. It is known from more primary sources than any other ancient Egyptian literary narrative, at least five papyri and 30 ostraca, spanning the Middle Kingdom and the New Kingdom. Most other such narratives are known from a single period.

The text opens in the style of the autobiographical inscriptions common in Middle Kingdom tombs, listing the titles and services of Sinuhe, a follower of the royal family. It then turns to his receiving news of the king's sudden death, apparently by assassination, while he is on an expedition in Libya with the king's eldest son. Fearing that he may be implicated in a conspiracy, Sinuhe flees, crosses Lake Maaty and nearly dies of thirst before a leader who once visited Egypt recognises him and gives him water and boiled milk.

He meets Amunenshi, ruler of upper Retjenu, who entrusts him with command of his armies. He defeats a challenger, yet longs for home, and prays to be buried in the land where he was born. Senusret I sends for him, and a long exchange of letters follows. The king offers him burial in Egypt, and Sinuhe returns to court, where he is cleansed and restored to his Egyptian identity. The story closes in the form of a tomb inscription addressed to visitors.

Modern readers have offered several reasons for his flight. The more common view, called by Meltzer the impulsive school, holds that he fled in a sudden fear of the disorder that followed the king's death. Others suggest that he was involved in the killing, or took the chance to escape the monarchy, and John Baines notes an interpretation in which guilt at abandoning his homeland drives his exile.

The name Sinuhe derives from the Egyptian for son of the sycamore, a tree associated with Hathor. The tale has been compared with the biblical story of Joseph, and its challenger with Goliath. It inspired the novel Sinuhe the Egyptian (1945) by Mika Waltari, which was made into a film.
tale-of-the-shipwrecked-sailor: The tale opens with a frame. A retainer comforts his master, who is returning from an apparently failed expedition and fears how the king will receive him, repeating the proverb that the mouth of a man saves him. To encourage him, he tells of an earlier voyage to the King's mines. A sudden wind raised waves eight cubits high, his ship and its crew of 120 were lost, and he alone was washed up on an island where there was nothing that was not there.

As he made a burnt offering to the gods he heard thunder, felt the earth shake and saw a giant serpent approach. The serpent asked him three times who had brought him there, carried him to its home and told him not to fear: after four months sailors he knew would rescue him.

The serpent related its own tragedy, how a fallen star had burned its 74 kin; in some translations its daughter survived. Laughing at the sailor's promise of incense, it called itself Lord of Punt and said the island would become water. It sent him home with spices, incense, elephants' tusks, greyhounds and baboons, and the king made him an attendant. The master's reply closes the tale: why give water to a goose at dawn before its slaughter?

Vladimir Golenishchev found the papyrus, known as P. Leningrad 1115, in the Imperial Hermitage of St Petersburg; according to Gaston Maspero, he discovered it in 1880 and presented it to scholars at the 5th International Congress of Orientalists in Berlin in 1881. He published a French translation in 1881 and a full photographic edition in 1913. The scribe, Amenaa, called himself excellent of fingers despite a few slips, and in 1987 The Guinness Book of Records named his signature the oldest surviving one on papyrus.

Some read the tale as a story of inspiration or reassurance for noble listeners, perhaps a courtly piece. Others see a spiritual quest in which the traveller journeys through the cosmos to meet a primordial god. Richard Mathews calls it the oldest fantasy text, with the genre's archetypal narrative, and sees in its serpent the prototype of the dragon. Its language is colourful, with rhythmical prose and alliteration.
taleh: Taleh lies in the eastern Sool province, in the Nugaal Valley in the centre of the lands of the Dhulbahante clan. According to the Dervish veteran Ciise Faarax Fikad, it was chosen as the Dervish capital because the Dhulbahante insisted on the Nugaal, because it lay far from the colonial administrative centres, and because it kept its distance from groups hostile to the movement: the Somali signatories of British treaties, the Majeerteen, the followers of Mohamoud Ali Shire and most of the Ogaden.

Although the name Taleh is used for the whole Dervish complex, it strictly applies to one structure of a four-part compound with Falat, Silsilad and Dar Ilaalo. The main fortress, Silsilad, measured about 350 by 300 feet, and the look-out tower of Dar Ilaalo, on a hillock behind it, stood some 50 feet high. The main fort was built around older Dervish tombs, the earliest those of Sultan Nur Ahmed Aman and Carro Seed Magan, the mother of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan. Silsilad also held a horse stable that features widely in Somali poetry.

After the Royal Air Force bombed the town on 4 February 1920, it was taken days later. The Dervish commander at Taleh, Ismail Mire, and Artan Boos were among the dead. In an April 1920 letter to the governor of Italian Somalia, the Dervish leader wrote that the British had come with six airplanes and that most of the Dhulbahante had surrendered, handing over twenty-seven garesas full of rifles, ammunition and money. Mohammed Abdullah Hassan escaped to the Ogaden.

Taleh has about 4,374 inhabitants. Control of the district was contested between Somaliland, Puntland and local clan administrations after the Somali civil war; in January 2012 the Dhulbahante proclaimed Khatumo State with Taleh as its capital, a claim not recognised by its neighbours, and in July 2025 SSC-Khatumo was announced as the core of the federal member state of Waqooyi Bari, in which the town now lies.
tales-of-the-alhambra: Irving travelled from Madrid to Granada in 1828, shortly after completing a biography of Christopher Columbus, to continue research for A Chronicle of the Conquest of Granada, a history of the years 1478–1492. Because of his celebrity, the governor of the Alhambra and the archbishop of Granada gave him access to the palace, and with a 17-year-old guide, Mateo Ximenes, he gathered its legends before moving on. The following year he returned and lived in an apartment in the Alhambra for about three months, with access to its archives. His travels in Spain ended when he was appointed secretary of legation at the United States Embassy in London, where he arrived by late September 1829.

The book combines description, myth and narratives of real events, reaching as far as the destruction of some of the palace's towers by the French under Count Sebastiani in 1812 and the further damage done by an earthquake in 1821. Among its stories are the Legend of the Moor's Legacy, the Legend of the Three Beautiful Princesses, the Legend of Prince Ahmed Al Kamel and The Arab Astrologer. It was published in May 1832 in the United States by Lea & Carey and at the same time in England by Henry Colburn, under the name Geoffrey Crayon, and was called his Spanish Sketch Book. In 1851 Irving wrote an Author's Revised Edition titled The Alhambra.

Alexander Pushkin based his 1834 verse tale The Tale of the Golden Cockerel on two chapters of the book, and Pushkin's poem in turn inspired Vladimir Belsky's libretto for Nikolay Rimsky-Korsakov's opera The Golden Cockerel. Dudley Buck set part of the Don Munio chapter in his 1874 oratorio The Legend of Don Munio, Taslimuddin Ahmad translated the book into Bengali in the 19th century, and it was the basis of the 1950 Spanish film Tales of the Alhambra. The city of Alhambra, California, is named after the book: in 1874 the daughter of Benjamin Wilson, who was reading it, urged him to use the name for his new development. A plaque marks the rooms where Irving stayed.
talha-ibn-ubayd-allah: Talha was born around 594 into the Taym clan of the Quraysh in Mecca, the son of Ubayd Allah ibn Uthman and al-Sa'ba bint Abd Allah of the Hadram tribe. He is said to have been among the first eight converts to Islam, after Abu Bakr urged his associates to follow him. During the persecution of the Muslims in 614 to 616, Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid tied Talha to Abu Bakr and left them bound together, and since nobody from the Taym clan came to help, they became known as the Two Tied Together. In 622 he settled in Medina.

Talha missed the Battle of Badr because Muhammad had sent him to scout Abu Sufyan's caravan, but he was awarded a share of the plunder as if he had fought. At the Battle of Uhud he stayed close to Muhammad while most of the army fled, and took an arrow aimed at Muhammad's face with his hand, losing two fingers. He was said to have suffered 39 or 75 wounds and was called the living martyr. He fought at the Battle of the Trench, and was given the name Talha al-Fayyad after paying for the expedition of Dhu Qarad.

In July 632 Abu Bakr appointed him, with Ali ibn Abi Talib and Zubayr, to command a third of the guard units formed to defend Medina against Tulayha. Under the caliph Umar he sat on the consultative council, and in 635 to 636 he joined advisers who urged Umar to stay in the capital instead of leading the army at Qadisiyyah. He was a successful cloth merchant who left an estate estimated at 30 million dirhams.

Talha was killed at the Battle of the Camel on 10 December 656. Accounts differ on how: in one, Marwan ibn al-Hakam, fighting on the same side as Aisha, shot him in the thigh; in another, Ali's supporters killed him as he retreated. He rode from the field and bled to death. In Sunni Islam he is counted among the ten to whom Paradise was promised and was called the Generous by Muhammad, while in Shia Islam he is viewed critically because of his part in the First Fitna.
talhae-of-silla: According to the Samguk sagi, Talhae was born in a small kingdom 1000 li northeast of Wa, which that history calls Dapana-guk and the Samguk yusa names variously Ryongseong-guk, Jeongmyeong-guk, Wanha-guk or Hwaha-guk. His father, King Hamdalpa, took his birth as an egg for an ill omen and had it boxed and floated out to sea. It came ashore east of Gyerim, near present-day Gyeongju, where an old woman raised him as a fisherman, and his family is said to have taken over a high official's house by claiming to be metalsmiths.

In 8 CE he married the daughter, or younger sister, of King Namhae of Silla, and he was probably an old man when he took the throne. Offered the succession to Namhae, he let the older Yuri reign first, and Yuri in turn named Talhae his successor.

In 64 the rival kingdom of Baekje attacked Silla several times, and in 77 Silla fought the Gaya confederacy. In legend, the retainer Hogong found the infant Kim Alji, ancestor of the Gyeongju Kim family, in a golden box in the royal Gyerim forest in 65, and Talhae then named his kingdom Gyerim; the name Silla was officially adopted much later. The Garakguk-gi, quoted in the Samguk yusa, tells how Talhae arrived by sea and demanded the throne of King Suro of Gaya, lost a contest of magic in which each turned into birds, and fled into the land of Gyerim.

Talhae founded the Gyeongju Seok clan, one of the noble clans that shared the Silla throne in the early Common Era. Some scholars place his homeland in the Japanese archipelago; Kenichi Kamigaito held that he was a king of Tanba province who made jade there and reached Silla along a trade route, and argued that the Seok clan traded with Japan. Another view takes Ryongseong-guk for a nation of the Ainu. A tomb believed to be his stands in northern Gyeongju, and the Gyeongju National Museum occupies the site where he built a palace.
taliesin: Details of Taliesin's life are sparse. The first mention of him is in the Saxon genealogies appended to four manuscripts of the Historia Brittonum from 828, which name five poets of the time of Ida of Bernicia, Taliesin among them. This is considered fairly credible, since another of the five, Aneirin, mentions him; Aneirin is known as the author of Y Gododdin, elegies to the men of Gododdin who died fighting the Angles at the Battle of Catraeth around 600. In 1960 Ifor Williams identified eleven medieval poems ascribed to him as possibly composed as early as the sixth century.

Most of these praise King Urien of Rheged and his son Owain mab Urien, and they refer to Urien's victories at Argoed Llwyfain, the Ford of Clyde and Gwen Ystrad and to an enemy leader, Fflamddwyn, identified as Ida or his son Theodric. Other poems show him serving as court bard to Brochfael Ysgithrog of Powys and his successor Cynan Garwyn.

The works ascribed to him survive in the Middle Welsh Book of Taliesin. John T. Koch argues that the description of Easter in the poem Yspeil Taliesin indicates that Urien and Taliesin were Christians who kept the Latin rather than the Insular Easter, and that Taliesin linked Latin Christian literature with the court poets of the Heroic Age. From the twelfth century Welsh court bards adopted his persona to claim prophetic inspiration, or awen, so that much scholarly work tries to separate the poems of the original bard from those of later poets who took up his name.

In legend he is Taliesin Ben Beirdd, chief of bards. The tale of his boyhood, first recorded in full in the sixteenth century by Elis Gruffydd, makes him Gwion Bach, a servant of Cerridwen who tasted her potion of inspiration, was reborn from her and was cast into the sea in a leather bag. Elffin, son of Gwyddno Garanhir, found him and named him Taliesin. At 13 he is said to have correctly prophesied the manner and imminence of the death of Maelgwn Gwynedd.

Later tradition placed him at the court of King Arthur, as in the tale of Culhwch and Olwen, but the historical poet's career belongs to the last half of the sixth century, well after the dates given for Arthur's victories. The architect Frank Lloyd Wright named his Wisconsin home and studio Taliesin.
talimali-band-of-apalachee: The historical Apalachee were a people who spoke a Muskogean language and lived on the border of Florida and Georgia north of the Gulf of Mexico until the beginning of the 18th century. English and Native slaving raids from the Carolina province between 1702 and 1704 drove refugees west from the Spanish missions, and some settled near the Mobilians at Mobile with the Tawasa and Chato.
