A yellow fever epidemic soon struck the newcomers. They were devout Catholics, and the governor of Louisiana, Le Moyne de Bienville, noted both their religious zeal and their skill as workers.

The Apalachee later asked to move into Louisiana, and Director General Jean-Jacques Blaise d'Abbadie judged them good farmers and hunters who could help supply New Orleans. Roughly 80 survivors reached New Orleans in late September 1763 and went to settle on the Red River under their newly elected chief, Martin. In the 19th century their land there was sold away or taken; the planter Isaac Baldwin destroyed their homes and crops and used his slaves to drive them out. An appeal to Congress for reparations in 1834 failed, and they moved to Emmanuel and Bayou Cypre.

Through the 20th century the community faced harassment from the Ku Klux Klan and the racism of the Jim Crow South, and many hid their Indigenous heritage. Only in the 1980s did the band's leaders feel secure enough in central Louisiana to assert their identity in public, and in 1996 the Talimali Band of Apalachee Indians organised as a nonprofit based in Pineville, Louisiana.

The band, formerly called the Apalachee Indians of Louisiana, has about 300 members and remains Catholic, and it took part in the Native American Mass at St. Francis Xavier Cathedral with other Louisiana tribes. It is neither federally nor state recognised. It submitted a letter of intent to petition for federal recognition in 1996 and an application on 26 August 1997, but no completed petition. Authorities in Leon County, Florida, have recognised it as descended from the 18th-century Apalachee of Florida, and Louisiana admits its members to the scholarship programme of the state's Office of Indian Affairs without granting tribal recognition.
talivaldis: Known in Latin as Thalibaldus de Tolowa, Tālivaldis was a Latgalian elder whose date of birth is unknown. His home district was the area around Trikāta, where he had his castle. He first appears in 1208, fighting against the Saccalians and Ugandians as an ally of the Latgalian dukes Rūsiņš and Varidots, at a time when he was a vassal of the Pskov Republic.

When the Northern Crusades began, Tālava lay within the spheres of influence of both Bishop Albert of Riga and Pskov. Tālivaldis chose Albert, hoping that the Germans would help the Tālavians resist pressure from the Russians, and as Albert's vassal he joined the crusaders' wars against the Estonian tribes. In 1211 the Estonians raided Tālava in revenge and pillaged the country around Trikāta. In 1212 he gave no support to the Autīne revolt, a joint Latgalian and Livonian revolt against the crusaders. In 1213 invading Lithuanians captured him in his castle at Trikāta, but he escaped while being taken back to Lithuania as a prisoner.

Bishop Albert and the crusaders had no interest in keeping an independent Latgalian state, and the war of attrition between the Tālavians and the Estonians served the German occupiers. In 1215 Tālivaldis was killed by Estonian raiders, who according to the Livonian Chronicle of Henry burnt him alive. His sons Rameka and Drivinalds soon took revenge with a raid that plundered the raiders' land severely. After his death his lands were divided between the crusaders and Albert of Riga, and his sons became vassals of Albert and adopted Roman Catholicism.
tallahassee: Indigenous peoples occupied the Tallahassee area for thousands of years before European contact. Around 1200 the large and complex Mississippian culture built earthwork mounds near Lake Jackson, which survive today and are preserved in the Lake Jackson Archaeological State Park. The city covers 254.3 square kilometres, of which 247.9 are land, and lies in a humid subtropical climate with long summers and short, mild winters.

Florida became an American territory in September 1821, in accordance with the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819, and Tallahassee became its capital in 1824. According to the city's heritage account, most of its original founders were settlers from North Carolina, descended from Scots or from Scots Presbyterians from County Down and County Antrim. Florida State University, founded in 1851, stands on the oldest continuous site of higher education in the state. Frenchtown is the oldest historically black neighbourhood in Florida.

Until the Second World War Tallahassee remained a small Southern town, with virtually the whole population within one mile of the Capitol. Its main economic drivers were the colleges and state government. The first plan to consolidate government buildings in one downtown area was the Taylor Plan of 1947, and in 1974 the Capitol Center Planning Commission produced a plan for expanding the centre, projecting 2.3 million square feet of new government facilities. In the Jim Crow period, laws passed by Democrats in Florida disenfranchised most African Americans until the late 1960s, which kept the Republican Party uncompetitive in the area for decades.

Tallahassee is the capital of Florida, the county seat of Leon County and its only incorporated municipality, with 196,169 residents at the 2020 census. It holds the Florida State Capitol, the Supreme Court of Florida and the Governor's Mansion, and is a college town, home to Florida State University, Florida A&M University and Tallahassee State College. Its museums include the Museum of Florida History, the Old Capitol Museum, the Knott House Museum and Mission San Luis de Apalachee.
tallapoosa-river: The Tallapoosa runs 265 miles (426 km) from the southern end of the Appalachian Mountains in Georgia south and west into the Appalachian foothills of Alabama. It is formed where McClendon Creek and Mud Creek meet in Paulding County, Georgia, and it joins the Coosa River about 10 miles (16 km) north-east of Montgomery, near Wetumpka in Elmore County, to form the Alabama River. Towns along it include Tallapoosa, Georgia, which is named after the river, Wadley, Alexander City, Dadeville and Tallassee.

The river, and above all its lower course, was a major population centre of the Creek Indians before the early 19th century. Its name comes from the Creek words Talwa posa, meaning Grandmother Town, and the Creek regard their Tallapoosa branch as one of the oldest. Horseshoe Bend National Military Park, managed by the National Park Service, lies on its banks just upstream of Lake Martin and preserves a battle site of the Creek War.

The first hydroelectric dam in Alabama was built on the river in 1902 by Henry C. Jones, an electrical engineer of Auburn University, at the site of the present Yates Dam. Destroyed in the flood of 1919, it was rebuilt, and it later belonged to the Montgomery Light & Water Power Company. In 1928 it was replaced by the Yates Dam.

Four hydroelectric dams stand on the river, Yates, Thurlow, Martin and R. L. Harris, which generate electricity for Alabama Power, a unit of the Southern Company. Lake Martin at Dadeville, formed by a dam on the river, is a large water recreation area, and below Thurlow Dam there is a short run of Class II to IV whitewater. The river is a major source of drinking water for Montgomery, about 60 per cent of the city's supply.
talmud: Talmudic tradition emerged and was compiled between the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE and the Arab conquest in the early seventh century. In antiquity the two major centres of Jewish scholarship were the academies of Syria Palaestina and of Babylonia, and each produced a Talmud. The earlier, the Jerusalem Talmud, was compiled in Galilee between the late fourth century and the first half of the fifth. It is also called the Palestinian Talmud, which is more accurate, since it was not compiled in Jerusalem, and it draws on the teachings of rabbis at Tiberias, Sepphoris and Caesarea.

The Babylonian Talmud consists of documents compiled over late antiquity, from the 3rd to the 6th centuries. Babylonian centres of learning included Nehardea, Nisibis, Mahoza, Pumbedita and the Sura Academy. Tradition holds that Rav Ashi and Ravina II compiled it around 500 CE, but it is more likely to have been compiled in the middle of the sixth century.

The Talmud follows the structure of the Mishnah, a compilation of legal opinions and debates by the Tannaim, rabbis of the second century CE. It is divided into six orders, abbreviated as Shas, and 63 tractates, with 517 chapters in all. The Gemara is a commentary on the Mishnah, produced by the Amoraim, rabbis of the third to fifth centuries, through a process of debate called shakla v'tarya, or taking and throwing. It also comments on baraitot, traditions of the Oral Torah that are not in the Mishnah. Short later treatises, the minor tractates, are printed at the end of the order of damages.

The Babylonian Talmud is much longer, at about 2.5 million words, and a third of its material is non-legal Aggadah, against a sixth in the Jerusalem Talmud. It is written mostly in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, with quotations of the Mishnah, baraitot and Hebrew scripture in Hebrew. The Jerusalem Talmud is written in a Western Aramaic dialect and is more fragmentary because its redaction was incomplete.

The only complete manuscript of the Talmud, Munich Codex Hebraica 95, dates from 1342. The earliest manuscript fragments, from the Cairo Genizah, date from the late seventh or eighth century, and Ms. Oxford 2673, with much of tractate Keritot, is the earliest manuscript with a known date, 1123.

Until the Haskalah of the 18th and 19th centuries the Talmud was the centrepiece of Jewish culture in nearly all communities and served as the guide for daily life. The word Talmud means study or learning, from the Semitic root lmd. When used without qualification it refers to the Babylonian Talmud, which has received far more attention from commentators and is held to be the more authoritative.
talos: Talos is a man of bronze who protected Crete from pirates and invaders, also spelled Talus or Talon. The sources vary widely on his role and genealogy. In the Argonautica of Apollonius of Rhodes, written in the first half of the 3rd century BCE, he is a descendant of the bronze race that sprang from ash-trees, bronze and invulnerable except for a vein in his ankle protected by only a thin layer of skin. Zeus gave him to Europa to guard Crete, which he did by running around the island three times.

When the Argo approached Crete on its return voyage he kept it at bay by hurling boulders. Medea declared that she alone could defeat him, and by magic, summoning the keres, caused him to graze his ankle, so that the ichor drained from his body. Apollonius compares his fall to that of a felled pine tree, which has been taken to imply a size larger than human, though no ancient source states explicitly that he was a giant.

Pseudo-Apollodorus collected several traditions. Talos either belonged to the Race of Bronze or had been given to Minos by Hephaestus, and he was either a bull or a bronze man. He guarded Crete by running round it three times daily and had a single vein from neck to ankles, stopped by a bronze nail. In one version Medea drove him mad with drugs, in another she promised immortality and pulled the nail, and in a third the Argonaut Poeas shot him in the ankle.

Pausanias reports from Cinaethon of Sparta that he was the son of Cres, the personification of Crete, and from Ion of Chios that he was a son of Oenopion. Simonides told that Talos seized people of Sardinia who refused to go to King Minos and leaped into flames holding them, a story given to explain the phrase sardonic laugh. The dialogue Minos, attributed to Plato in antiquity, rationalises him as a man who carried the laws of Crete, written on bronze tablets, round the villages three times a year.

Artistic sources linking Talos with the Argonauts predate Apollonius. Three kraters from around 400 BCE show his death. On the vase now in the Jatta National Archaeological Museum, the name vase of the Talos Painter, he falls backwards, painted white, into the arms of the Dioskouroi, while Medea holds a bowl and Poseidon and Amphitrite look on.

A vase from Caudium and a fragment from Spina show similar scenes, with a small winged figure, probably Thanatos, at his ankle. He also appears on three coins of Phaistos of the Classical and early Hellenistic periods, as a naked winged figure throwing a stone, the wings read by Richard Buxton as a sign of his speed.
tama-people: Many Tama are subsistence farmers living in permanent settlements, where they grow millet, beans, cucumbers, gumbo and sesame; some are traders, and they also keep cattle, camels and goats. Most are Muslims, though some animistic beliefs persist. Their traditional home is Dar Tama. They include several subgroups: the Abu Sharib, Gimr, Kibet, Marari, Mileri and the Tama proper. All live in Chad except the Gimr and the Mileri, who live near Saref Omra and Kebkabiya in Sudan.

For centuries the Tama were governed by sultans, many of whom were believed to be of Dadjo origin. At various times they were subject to the sultans of Wadai to the west and of Darfur to the east, but they always kept a sultan of their own. In the 1800s they were known as a warlike people who fought with the spear and had kept their independence for two centuries, resisting invasions on at least two occasions. They were part of the Sultanate of Darfur in the early 1800s, Turkish-Egyptian Sudan governed the area later in the century, and under French colonial rule, which reached little beyond southern Chad, a figurehead sultan was installed.

During the Sahelian drought of the 1980s Zaghawa herders moved into Dar Tama and displaced some of the Tama. Armed horsemen raided Tama livestock, and the situation worsened after Idriss Déby, a Zaghawa, came to power and favoured his own group in government and police posts in Dar Tama. These grievances led to the founding in 1994 of the National Resistance Alliance (ANR), from which the largely Tama rebel United Front for Democratic Change (FUC) later split.

In 2006 a robbery of a Tama man and the gunfight that followed left 20 dead, and Zaghawa raids on Tama villages killed dozens and displaced thousands that year. In August 2006 3,300 Tama civilians fled to Sudan, and that October another 1,800 refugees reached the UN-sponsored camps of Mile and Kounoungo. Human Rights Watch could not corroborate allegations of Tama attacks on Zaghawa civilians.
tamale: Tamale lies in the Tamale Metropolitan District, which covers about 647 km2. The district borders the Sagnarigu District to the west and north, the Mion District to the east, the East Gonja District to the south and the Central Gonja District to the southwest. The city stands within the Kingdom of Dagbon, and is traditionally inhabited by the Dagombas. Gonja, Mamprusi, Nanumba, Konkomba and Akan people also live there.

The climate is tropical savanna (Köppen Aw), with a single rainy season each year. Mean monthly rainfall is about 89 mm, spread over some 95 days of showers, and mean monthly temperatures are around 34 °C, with minimums near 23 °C. Humidity is lowest between December and March, at about 30 percent, and highest around August, at about 70 percent.

The area of Tamale once consisted of small villages under the Kingdom of Dagbon, and it was a popular destination of cattle trails in the region. In 1907 the British decided to establish administrative headquarters there, with help from the Dakpema, after German officials had taken over Yendi. A road added in 1920, nicknamed the Great North Road, helped make Tamale an important centre of business in the Northern Territories.

Through the 20th century the population grew rapidly, as people looked for water and electricity, and land taken for infrastructure threatened residents' ability to farm. A series of disputes between the Gulkpe Na and the Dakpema over power in the town arose in part because British indirect rule created an imbalance between the chiefs. Local councils were later introduced and indirect rule was discontinued, but tension between the chiefs has continued. In 1960 Tamale became the capital of the Northern Region, after the region had separated from the rest of the north.

Tamale is the capital of the Northern Region and Ghana's third largest city, with 374,744 people at the 2021 census. Its economy rests on agriculture, trading, teaching and manufacturing. The first educational institution was a teacher training college of 1944, followed by a secondary school in 1951; British wishes to keep the Northern Territories agricultural and pastoral held education back, but the city has since become the educational hub of northern Ghana. It has the Tamale Teaching Hospital and Tamale International Airport, about 11 km from the centre.

Most residents are Muslim: 90.5 percent at the 2010 census. Annual festivals include the Damba festival, Bugum chugu, Eid ul-Fitr and Eid Adha, and the Dagbamba perform dances such as the Baamaya and Tora. The Aliu Mahama Sports Stadium hosted some matches of the 2008 African Cup of Nations.
tamanrasset: Tamanrasset, also known as Tamanghasset or Tamenghest, stands in the Ahaggar Mountains at an altitude of 1,320 metres. It is an oasis, where citrus fruits, apricots, dates, almonds, cereals, corn and figs are grown despite the difficult climate. The climate is a hot desert one with very little rain, although the altitude moderates the summer heat. The name is said to derive from Imanrassaten, a noble tribe now associated with the Ajjers, which reportedly once lived in the wadi region or used it to mark the boundaries of its grazing lands.

The place originated as the centre of a network of camel caravan routes that ran from Kano, Lake Chad, Gao, Agades and Zinder. Under French rule in Algeria the Catholic priest Charles de Foucauld built his hermitage here in 1905, and the fort was established by 1915. Foucauld was shot to death outside his compound on 1 December 1916 by Sermi ag Thora, acting under the command of El Madani ag Soba.

As a military post the settlement was named Fort Laperrine, after General François-Henry Laperrine, who died in the desert nearby in 1922. On 1 May 1962, near Ecker, 150 km north of Tamanrasset, a French underground nuclear test was accidentally vented. The shaft had been improperly sealed, a flame burst through the concrete cap, and radioactive gases and dust rose in a plume up to 2,600 metres high. Radiation was detected hundreds of kilometres away. About a hundred French soldiers and officials, including two ministers, were irradiated; the number of Algerians contaminated is unknown.

Tamanrasset is the capital of Tamanrasset Province and the chief city of the Algerian Tuareg. Its population was 92,635 at the 2008 census, up from 72,741 in 1998. It is a centre of trade across the Sahara and into neighbouring countries, and it is served by Tamanrasset Airport and the Trans-Sahara Highway. The Museum of the Hoggar holds exhibits on Tuareg life and culture, and the commune includes the locality of Assekrem among its fourteen.
tamar-of-georgia: Tamar belonged to the Bagrationi dynasty and was the daughter of George III of Georgia and his consort Burdukhan, a daughter of the king of Alania. Her name is of Hebrew origin, and like other biblical names it was favoured by the Bagrationi, who claimed descent from David, the second king of Israel. Her father proclaimed her heir and co-ruler in 1178. Medieval Georgian sources gave her the title mepe, meaning king, which stressed that she was the first woman to rule Georgia in her own right.

Tamar was crowned a second time at Gelati cathedral near Kutaisi after her father's death in 1184. Part of the aristocracy questioned the legitimacy of a woman ruler, and others tried to use her youth to gain autonomy, so that she needed the support of her aunt Rusudan and the Catholicos-Patriarch Michael IV and had to make him chancellor. She married Yury Bogolyubsky, son of Andrey Bogolyubsky of Vladimir-Suzdal, in 1185, but divorced him and expelled him two years later, and she defeated his later coup attempts. In 1191 she married the Alan prince David Soslan, with whom she had two children, George and Rusudan, who both became monarchs.

Tamar then revived Georgia's expansion. In the 1190s Georgia reduced Shirvan to a tributary state, and David Soslan defeated the Eldiguzid atabeg Abu Bakr at the Battle of Shamkor. Armenian generals, Zakare and Ivane Mkhargrdzeli, took fortresses towards the Ararat Plain. In 1204 Alexios I Megas Komnenos and his brother David, her nephews, founded the Empire of Trebizond with Georgian troops. By the end of her reign Georgia stretched from the crest of the Greater Caucasus to Erzurum and near Ganja, and Tamar issued coins with Georgian and Arabic inscriptions.

Tamar crowned her son Lasha-Giorgi coregent and became ill while discussing state affairs at the Nacharmagevi castle near Gori. She was taken to Tbilisi and then to the castle of Agarani, where she died, and she was buried at Gelati. Her reign saw a flowering of Georgian culture, with domed cathedrals and Shota Rustaveli's epic The Knight in the Panther's Skin, revered in Georgia as the finest achievement of its native literature. Medieval chroniclers called her a protector of the widowed, and the Georgian Orthodox Church later canonised her, commemorating her on 14 May (1 May in the Julian calendar). The Georgian state she left collapsed under Mongol attacks within two decades.
tamaudun: Tamaudun is one of three royal mausoleums of the Second Shō dynasty of the Ryukyu Kingdom, beside Urasoe yōdore at Urasoe Castle and Izena Tamaudun near Izena Castle. It lies a short distance from Shuri Castle. King Shō Shin, the third king of the line, who reigned from 1477 to 1527, had it built for his father, King Shō En. The site covers 2,442 square metres and consists of two stone-walled enclosures and the north-facing tomb, backed by a natural cliff to the south.

The tomb has three compartments laid out from east to west. Kings and queens lie in the eastern one, princes and other members of the royal family in the western. The central chamber served the Ryukyuan custom of senkotsu: the dead were kept there for a limited time to decompose, after which the bones were washed and placed in urns in the eastern or western chamber according to rank. A stone stele in the outer enclosure records the completion of the work and names Shō Shin with eight others involved in the building. Stone lions, shisa, guard the tomb, and a courtyard paved with coral fragments lies before it.

Seventeen of the 19 kings of the Second Shō dynasty, which ruled from 1470 to 1879, are buried here with queens and royal children. Shō En died in 1476, so his remains waited about 25 years before they were placed in the finished tomb. Shō Sen'i was never reburied here, and Shō Nei chose burial at Urasoe yōdore after the Invasion of Ryukyu. The last burials were those of Shō Ten, Prince of Nakagusuku and son of the last king, Shō Tai, in 1920 with traditional royal rites, and of his wife in 1931. Some of the dead remain unidentified.

Standing near the Japanese Supreme Commander's office in 1945, the mausoleum was caught in the artillery bombardment that also struck Shuri Castle. Its east and west chambers were destroyed and the ruins looted, though the tombs and royal remains survived. In 1992 Hiroshi Shō, great-grandson of Shō Tai, gave Tamaudun and the gardens of Shikina-en to the City of Naha. It was named a National Historic Site in 1972, inscribed by UNESCO on 2 December 2000 among the Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu, and declared a National Treasure in 2018.
tamaulipas: Tamaulipas, officially the Free and Sovereign State of Tamaulipas, is one of the 32 federated entities of Mexico and is divided into 43 municipalities. It borders Nuevo León, San Luis Potosí and Veracruz, and has a 370 km stretch of the border with Texas along the Río Bravo, known in the United States as the Rio Grande. Its largest cities include Reynosa, Matamoros, Nuevo Laredo, Tampico and Mante. The name derives from Tamaholipa, a Huastec term whose prefix tam- means place where; the meaning of holipa is not agreed, though high hills is a common interpretation.

The area has been inhabited for at least 8,000 years, originally by the nomadic Chichimec and the sedentary Huastec, together with hunter-gatherer and fishing peoples. Spain subjugated its inhabitants only gradually; the first permanent Spanish settlement was Tampico in 1554. Franciscan missionaries and widespread ranching followed, forcing native peoples from their lands. In the mid-18th century the region became a separate province of New Spain called Nuevo Santander, and towns along the Rio Grande, among them Laredo, Mier, Camargo and Reynosa, were founded under Escandón as a defensive line.

In 1824 Tamaulipas was one of the 19 founder states of the United Mexican States. The Republic of Texas, created in 1836, claimed northern Tamaulipas, and after the Mexican–American War the state lost more than a quarter of its territory in 1848 through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Its capital, Aguayo, was renamed Ciudad Victoria in honour of Guadalupe Victoria, the first president of Mexico. The last French soldiers left the state in 1866, before the fall of Emperor Maximilian's empire in 1867. Growth followed, especially after the railroad reached Tampico.

Ciudad Victoria is the capital and a significant educational centre. In the north the economy shares much with that of Texas and includes many maquiladoras, while the south rests on petrochemical industries around Altamira and Ciudad Madero and on the ports of Tampico and Altamira. The Tropic of Cancer crosses the southern part of the municipality of Victoria. The state anthem, Himno a Tamaulipas, was composed in 1926.
tambor-de-mina: Tambor means drum in Portuguese, after the place of rhythm in worship. Mina comes from the castle of São Jorge da Mina in present-day Ghana and was a name given to enslaved African people in Brazil, covering different peoples over time and place. Slavery in Maranhão was concentrated in the Itapecuru Valley, the Baixada Maranhense and São Luís. The religion is practised mainly in Maranhão, Piauí, Pará and the Amazon region, and has two main models in Maranhão, Jeje and Nagô.

The Casa das Minas, or Querebentã de Tói Zomadônu, was probably founded in São Luís in the 1840s by Maria Jesuina, an African woman brought to Brazil as a slave, whom Pierre Verger identified as Queen Nã Agontimé, wife of King Agonglô of Dahomey and mother of King Guezô. The Casa de Nagô, almost as old and in the same neighbourhood, was founded by Josefa and Maria Joana Travassos, African women of the Yoruba tradition.

Believers worship voduns, gods of the Fon or Jeje people who are forces of nature and deified ancestors, as well as orixás and spirits called encantados. The voduns form five families, among them the Davice, the Dahomean royal family, and the Quevioçô, or Nagô voduns; each family has its own part of the house and its own songs. The Casa das Minas counts about 45 voduns and 15 tobossis, child-like female deities. The encantados are held to be people who did not die but vanished and live in a magical kingdom, the Encantaria; they include gentis, European kings such as King Sebastian of Portugal, and caboclos of native or Moorish origin.

In the Casa das Minas the songs are in the Jeje language and only women, the vodunsis, lead ceremonies, while men play the drums. No full initiations took place there after 1914, and its last vodunsi, Dona Deni, died in 2015. Temples also hold popular festivals such as the Feast of the Divine Holy Spirit, Bumba-meu-boi and Tambor de Crioula, said to be requested by the spirits. Hundreds of temples exist, and the Terecô of Codó derives from the tradition.
tambov-rebellion: Alexander Antonov was sentenced in 1904 to twenty years in prison for blowing up a train, was amnestied after the February Revolution and returned to his native Tambov, where he joined the Left Socialist-Revolutionaries. Tambov's peasants largely supported the October Revolution because the Decree on Land legalised expropriation, but the Bolsheviks had hardly any rural supporters, and in March 1918 their delegates were thrown out of the local soviets after the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. War communism meant compulsory grain requisition without payment. The quotas rested on rough pre-war estimates, when Tambov had produced about a million tonnes of grain a year, and ignored the devastation of the war. Peasants answered by sowing less.

In the summer of 1919 Antonov fled to the forest and formed a band that killed several Bolshevik activists. The first guerrillas were Red Army deserters, Socialist-Revolutionaries and peasants who resisted the searches. They killed more than 200 grain collectors, and their numbers grew from 150 to 6,000 by early summer 1920.

On 19 August 1920 a revolt broke out at Khitrovo after a requisitioning detachment took everything it could. Neighbouring villages joined, and the rebels, armed partly with pitchforks and clubs, repelled the Red Army. Their attack on Tambov was scattered by machine guns, and Antonov led the movement into guerrilla war. Its political body was the Union of Working Peasants, which demanded free trade, an end to requisitioning and the dissolution of the Cheka and the Soviet administration. By October 1920 the Bolsheviks held only Tambov itself and a few small towns, and the rebels had killed around 1,000 Communist Party members. Between October 1920 and January 1921 they mobilised 50,000 partisans.

On 2 February 1921 the Soviet leadership announced the end of requisitioning and its replacement by a tax in kind, and on 20 March an amnesty was offered. In May the Union proclaimed the Provisional Democratic Republic of the Tambov Partisan Region.

In May 1921 Lenin ordered Mikhail Tukhachevsky to suppress the uprising with up to 100,000 soldiers, armoured vehicles, heavy artillery and Cheka units. On 12 June he received permission to use chemical weapons, with orders to clear the forests with poison gas. The rebels were practically defeated by the end of June. About 6,000 fighters who surrendered were shot or deported, and between 50,000 and 100,000 villagers, including about 1,000 children, were held in camps in July 1921, where epidemics of cholera and typhus killed many. About 100,000 people were arrested and about 15,000 killed. The uprising is seen as one factor that prompted Lenin's New Economic Policy.
tamesna: The name is written Tamesna in Berber and Tāmasnā in Arabic. The 16th-century Andalusian author Leo Africanus, in his Description of Africa, counted Temesna among the provinces of Fez and placed it between the river Ommirabih in the west and the Buragrag in the east, with the Atlas to the south and the ocean to the north. He described it as a plain about fourscore miles long and threescore broad, once the chief of the seven provinces, with forty great towns and three hundred castles.

Its indigenous people were the Barghwata. Leo tells that in the year 323 of the Hegeira a man he calls Chemim, son of Mennal, a self-proclaimed prophet, freed the province from tribute and made a pact with the king of Fez that left him Temesna, which he ruled for about thirty-five years and his successors for nearly a century more.

In Leo's account the Lamtuna king who had built Maroco then sent religious teachers to win the province over; its people had them murdered and raised an army of fifty thousand men. The king crossed the Ommirabih, put the inhabitants to the sword and razed their towns in eight days, while the king of Fez cut off those who had fled north near the Buragrag, so that only a small remnant survived and the land was left to wild beasts.

About 150 years later, Leo writes, King Mansor brought Arabs from Tunis and settled them there; they held it for fifty years before the Lamtuna drove them out. The Marinid dynasty then granted Tamasna to the Zenata and Hawwara confederations, who came to dominate the province and, in Leo's day, could field sixty thousand horsemen and held two hundred castles.
tamil-brahmi: Tamil-Brahmi, also called Tamili or Damili, differs in small but telling ways from the Brahmi of the Edicts of Ashoka. It adds diacritics to several letters for sounds not found in Prakrit, and in many inscriptions a consonant written without a sign stands for the bare consonant, a change suited to Tamil words, which often end in consonants. Among early Indian scripts it shares this only with the Bhattiprolu script of Andhra Pradesh. The epigraphist Iravatham Mahadevan divided its history into three stages, and from the 5th century CE Tamil was written in Vatteluttu, Grantha or the Tamil script.

Jaina texts already name a script called Damili among eighteen in use in India. Mahadevan's view, generally accepted and favoured by Richard Salomon, is that northern Brahmi reached the south through the southern inscriptions of Ashoka; R. Nagaswamy proposed instead a common indigenous source for both. Kamil Zvelebil placed the earliest inscriptions, such as those of Netunceliyan at Mangulam, around 250 BCE.

Since the 1990s earlier dates have been claimed. Potsherds from Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka led Coningham and colleagues to propose a pre-Ashokan Brahmi there, and K. Rajan and Yatheeskumar argued from radiocarbon dates of about 520–490 BCE at Porunthal and Kodumanal that the script existed by 490 BCE. The scholar Harry Falk rejected both, citing errors in calibration and in reading Megalithic graffiti as letters, and called the claims regional chauvinism; the linguist David Shulman shares the doubt but urges an open mind.

According to Zvelebil the script began with Jains and Buddhists but was soon used by kings, chiefs, potters and other ordinary people. Cave and rock-bed inscriptions near Madurai record gifts of resting places to monks, while coins and other inscriptions name merchants in gold, sugar, iron, salt and textiles, and some name kings and heroes known from the Sangam poems, which helps date Tamil literature.

Finds reach far beyond Tamil Nadu: potsherds at Poonagari in Jaffna, a gold bar at Thenur near Madurai, an inscription of about 50 CE in Oman, sherds at Quseir al-Qadim and Berenice Troglodytica on the Red Sea, and a goldsmith's touchstone of the 3rd century CE at Wat Klong Thom in Thailand, which suggests that Tamil goldsmiths worked in Southeast Asia.
tamil-nadu: Tamil Nadu covers 130,058 square kilometres on the southeastern coast of the Indian peninsula. The Western Ghats and the Deccan Plateau lie to the west, the Eastern Ghats to the north and the Bay of Bengal to the east, with the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait to the southeast and the Laccadive Sea at the southern cape. The river Kaveri crosses the state. The name means the land of the Tamils.

Excavations at Keezhadi have revealed a large urban settlement, with the earliest artefact dated to 580 BCE. Inscriptions at Adichanallur use Tamil Brahmi, dated to the 5th century BCE. In the Sangam period, from about 500 BCE to 300 CE, Tamilakam was ruled by three monarchical states: the Cheras in the west, the Pandyas in the south and the Cholas in the Kaveri delta. Their kings patronised the Vedic religion, Buddhism and Jainism and sponsored some of the earliest Tamil literature. The oldest surviving work is the Tolkāppiyam, a Tamil grammar.

The Pallavas, with Kanchipuram as their capital, were noted for their patronage of architecture, and the gopuram, the tower at the entrance of a temple, originated with them. They built the rock-cut monuments of Mahabalipuram and temples at Kanchipuram, and were in constant conflict with the Cholas and Pandyas until the Chola prince Aditya I defeated them in the 9th century. The Vijayanagara kingdom, founded in 1336, conquered the entire Tamil country by about 1370 and ruled for almost two centuries, until its defeat at the Battle of Talikota in 1565. Its military governors, the Nayaks of Madurai and Thanjavur, then took control and rebuilt temples such as the Meenakshi Temple at Madurai.

European colonisation began with trading ports in the 17th century, and the British controlled much of the state as part of the Madras Presidency for two centuries. After 1947 it became Madras State, which lost Andhra in 1953 and took its present shape when states were redrawn on linguistic lines in 1956. It was renamed Tamil Nadu on 14 January 1969.

Tamil Nadu is the southernmost state of India, with its capital at Chennai, and 72.1 million people at the census of 2011. Tamil, the first language recognised as classical in India, is its official language, and 87.6 per cent of its people follow Hinduism. It has four World Heritage Sites and is known for its great temples and its classical Tamil literature.
tamilakam: The name joins Tamiḻ and the suffix -akam and means roughly home of Tamil; Kamil Zvelebil considered it the most ancient term for Tamil territory. A later preface to the Tolkāppiyam places the land where Tamil is the mother tongue between the northern Venkata hill and the southern Kumari, and the Silappadikaram (c. 2nd century CE) runs it from the hills of Vishnu at Tirupati to the cape, naming four great cities: Madurai, Uraiyur, Kanchi and Puhar. Scholars assume the seas formed its eastern and western limits, so it included ancient Kerala but not north-eastern Sri Lanka.

The earliest datable references to the Tamil kingdoms are inscriptions of the 3rd century BCE. Ashoka's edicts mention independent states beyond his southern frontier, and Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription tells of the destruction of a "confederacy of Tamil powers". The Cholas held the Kaveri valley, the Pandyas the Vaigai valley, ruling first from the port of Korkai and later from Madurai, and the Cheras western Tamil Nadu and Kerala, beside minor chieftains called Velirs. Tondai Nadu, once under the Cholas, emerged as the independent Pallava country by the 6th century CE. The region mostly stayed unconquered by northern powers such as the Maurya and Gupta empires.

Paddy was the chief crop and served as a medium of exchange in inland trade. Madurai and Urayur made cotton and silk cloth in great demand, and Korkai's pearls were sought in northern India and in Rome. Muziris, a Chera port on the Malabar Coast, was a major centre of Indo-Roman trade. Tamil settlers reached the Maldives, Sri Lanka and a few coastal places of Southeastern Asia, and in 145 BCE Elara, a Chola general or prince, took the throne at Anuradhapura and ruled for forty-four years until Dutugamunu defeated him.

The lands of Tamilakam now lie in the Indian states of Tamil Nadu and Kerala, the union territories of Puducherry and Lakshadweep, and the southern parts of Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Roman coins and amphorae found in Kerala and Tamil Nadu attest its ancient trade with Rome. In modern Indian usage the name often refers to Tamil Nadu alone.
tamils: The Tamils are a Dravidian ethnic group who natively speak Tamil and trace their ancestry mainly to the south of the Indian subcontinent. Archaeological evidence from Tamil Nadu indicates continuous human occupation for more than 3,800 years. Megalithic urn burials at Adichanallur date back to 1500 BCE, and excavations at Keezhadi have revealed a large urban settlement, with its earliest artefact dated to 580 BCE. Inscriptions and potsherds from these sites use Tamil Brahmi, a rudimentary script dated to the 6th century BCE. The meaning of the name Tamil is unclear, and scholars have proposed several derivations, among them 'self-speak' or 'our own speech'.

In the Sangam period, between about 300 BCE and 300 CE, the Tamil country, Tamilakam, was ruled by the three crowned kings, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, with smaller Velir chieftains beside them. Coastal towns grew with trade across the Indian Ocean, and excavated artefacts indicate early trade with the Romans. The Pallavas later ruled from the 3rd to the 9th century CE, and the Vijayanagara Empire from the 14th to the 17th century.

In the 10th century the Cholas established their influence across Sri Lanka and parts of Southeast Asia, and scripts carried by Tamil traders, such as Grantha and Pallava, shaped the development of many Southeast Asian scripts. The Jaffna Kingdom controlled the Tamil territory in the north of Sri Lanka from the 13th to the 17th century. European colonisation began in the 17th century.

Tamils have migrated worldwide since the 19th century. Many went as indentured labourers or traders to British territories such as Malaya, Burma, South Africa, Fiji and Mauritius, and a large emigration of Sri Lankan Tamils began in the 1980s.

In India Tamils form about 5.7 per cent of the population and the majority in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, and they are a significant share of the populations of Sri Lanka, Malaysia and Singapore. Sri Lanka's government counts Sri Lankan Tamils, descended from the old Jaffna Kingdom and the eastern Vannimai chiefdoms, separately from Indian Origin Tamils, descendants of 19th-century plantation labourers in the central highlands.

Tamil literature has an antiquity of more than two thousand years, beginning with the Sangam anthologies. Hinduism is the major religion, with smaller numbers of Christians and Muslims. Pongal, a harvest festival in January, and Puthandu, the new year in April, are major festivals, and Bharatanatyam is among the classical performing arts.
tampere: Tampere lies in the Finnish Lakeland, between Lake Näsijärvi and Lake Pyhäjärvi, which differ in water level by 18 m. The Tammerkoski rapids that connect them have been an important source of power throughout history, most recently for generating electricity. The Pyynikki Ridge, a large esker formed from moraine during the Weichselian glaciation, rises 160 m above sea level. The name derives from the rapids, and the explanation most accepted traces it to a Proto-Samic phrase for a deep, slow part of a stream followed by the word for rapids.

The earliest known permanent settlements around Tammerkoski date from the 7th century, when settlers from the west began to farm land in an area largely inhabited by Tavastian tribes. The population stayed small for centuries, and in 1638 Governor-General Per Brahe the Younger ordered two markets a year at Tammerkoski. The first industries in the 17th century were watermills and sawmills.

The neighbouring parish of Pirkkala had been the most important parish in the area through the Middle Ages. In 1771 and 1772 the pastor Erik Edner proposed a town on the banks of the rapids, Gustav III of Sweden made it a market town, and on 1 October 1779 Tampere received full town rights. Farming was forbidden within the city limits, so its inhabitants lived mainly by trade and crafts, and when the Grand Duchy of Finland was formed in 1809 the town still had fewer than a thousand inhabitants.

Tampere became known as the Manchester of the North for its past as a centre of Finnish industry, and the red-brick factories along the Tammerkoski, such as Finlayson and Tampella, shaped the city. It was also the scene of political events in the early 20th century. In 1905 the conference of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, led by Vladimir Lenin, met in the Tampere Workers' Hall and decided to launch an armed insurrection. On 1 November 1905, during the General Strike, the Red Declaration was proclaimed in Keskustori.

Tampere is the regional capital of Pirkanmaa and the most populous inland city in the Nordic countries, with about 263,000 inhabitants. Finnish is the first language of most of them. Its buildings range from the Old Stone Church of Messukylä, the only medieval one, to Tampere Cathedral. Pispala, a ridge between the two lakes, housed much of the industrial labour in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and joined the city in 1937.
tampico: Tampico lies on the north bank of the Pánuco River, about 10 kilometres inland from the Gulf of Mexico, in the south-east of the state of Tamaulipas and directly north of Veracruz. The name comes from the Huastec tam-piko, meaning place of otters or water dogs, a reference to the otters that lived in the rivers and lagoons of the Pánuco delta. The area had several Huastec settlements, among them the important site at Las Flores, which flourished between 1000 and 1250 CE.

In 1532 the Franciscan priest Andrés de Olmos established a mission and monastery over a former Huastec village, and at his request Spanish officials founded San Luis de Tampico in 1554. That site was abandoned in 1684 because of frequent pirate attacks, and the area stayed empty for nearly 150 years. The present city was founded on 13 April 1823, after Mexican independence. It lived at first from exporting silver and from trade as a market town for an agricultural region. In 1829 Spain sent troops from Cuba to regain the region, but General Antonio López de Santa Anna forced them to surrender in September.

The first oil well in Mexico was drilled near Tampico, at Ébano, in 1901 by the Californian Edward Doheny, who founded the Mexican Petroleum Company. American investment and a large American community followed, and the Chijol Canal, begun in 1901, carried oil 120 km south through the fields to Tuxpan. The city became the chief oil-exporting port of the Americas and the second busiest in the world. On 9 April 1914, during the Mexican Revolution, a confrontation between Mexican soldiers and sailors of the USS Dolphin, the Tampico Affair, led the United States to occupy Veracruz for seven months and helped bring down General Victoriano Huerta. Mexico nationalised its oil industry in 1938.

The oil boom paid for the grand buildings of the downtown, often compared with those of Venice and New Orleans. Wrought-iron balconies, some bearing the plaques of the Derbyshire forge of Andrew Handyside and Company, line the Plaza de la Libertad, and the neoclassical Town Hall and the English redbrick Customs House stand nearby. The cathedral on the Plaza de Armas dates from the late 19th century, and Doheny gave large sums for its construction after 1902. In 1895 snow was reported to have fallen in Tampico, the farthest south at a coastal location in North America.
tamsui: Tamsui is a seaside district of New Taipei City, Taiwan, beside the Tamsui River and overlooking the Taiwan Strait. Its name means "fresh water" in Chinese. The Ketagalan aborigines called the place Hoba, "stream's mouth", which gave the Hokkien Hobe. The Spanish called the region Casidor and the river Kimalon, and Dutch records give Tamsuy and Tampsui. George Leslie Mackay popularised the spelling Tamsui in his 1895 book From Far Formosa. The term was historically ambiguous and could mean the harbour, the river, the village of Hobe, Twatutia, Banka or the whole district.

The Spanish arrived in the early 17th century and established the town and mission of Santo Domingo, aiming to secure their trade routes from coastal Fujian to the Philippines against the Dutch, British and Portuguese. They abandoned the settlement in 1638 and were expelled from Taiwan by the Dutch in 1642. The Dutch built a new fort over the ruins and named it Fort Antonio, after Governor-General Antonio van Diemen; it is now known as the Red Castle. They also encouraged Han Chinese settlement. Koxinga drove them out in 1662 and continued that policy until his grandson Zheng Keshuang surrendered to the Qing in 1683.

Tamsui became a major fishing and trade port, and the Qing established a naval outpost there in 1808. In 1862 it was opened to foreign trade under the Treaty of Tientsin, exporting tea, camphor, sulfur, coal, opium and dyes, and by the mid-19th century it was the largest port in Taiwan, with a British consulate at Fort Santo Domingo. George Leslie Mackay arrived on 9 March 1872 and founded Taiwan's first hospitals in Western medicine and Oxford College, now part of Aletheia University.

In 1884, during the Sino-French War, Admiral Amédée Courbet blockaded the harbour. The French were defeated at the Battle of Tamsui, which traditional accounts credit to the goddess Mazu. When Taiwan passed to Japan in 1895, silt was already reducing the port, and its trade moved to Keelung; public works under Japanese rule made it a local administrative and cultural centre.

After 1945 Tamsui was a small fishing town of Taipei County, and from 2010 it has been a district of New Taipei City. The Taipei Metro's Tamsui Line, opened in 1997, brought a sharp rise in visitors. The district has 205,706 residents and several universities, among them Aletheia, St. John's and Tamkang, and its sites include Fort Santo Domingo and the Red Castle.
tanagra-figurine: Although named after Tanagra, the figurines were made in many places, among them Alexandria, Tarentum in Magna Graecia, Centuripe in Sicily and Myrina in Mysia, and were exported across the Greek world. They were coated with a liquid white slip before firing and sometimes afterwards tinted with watercolours, as in the Lady in Blue in the Louvre. Typically 10 to 20 centimetres high, they show women, and some men and boys, in elegant everyday dress with hats, wreaths or fans; some may represent stock characters of Menander's New Comedy. Their modellers took particular care with the himation drawn over the head and shoulders above a chiton.

Most seem to have been decorative rather than religious, and although they were placed in their owners' tombs, they do not appear to have been made specially for burial or meant to serve the dead in the afterlife.

Col. W. M. Leake described the ruins of Tanagra after a visit in 1806, and in 1852 the French General Staff published a map showing the first six graves found there. From the end of the 1860s ploughmen of Vratsi in Boeotia began to uncover tombs, and in 1870 a wave of grave robbing ruined many of them and broke most of the vases. After illegal digging permits were confiscated in 1873, the Archeological Society of Athens sent Panagiotis Stamatakis to excavate the intact graves in 1874-1879. Villagers went on digging at night for lack of guards, and the number of figurines found was never published.

The figurines suited the 19th-century middle-class taste for realism. Jean-Léon Gérôme made a polychrome sculpture of the spirit of Tanagra, and one French critic called the women they portray the parisienne of the ancient world. Oscar Wilde compared characters to them in The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891) and An Ideal Husband (1895), and the novelist Paul Bourget collected them. Demand from collectors in the late 19th century led to forgeries.
tanah-datar: The name means Flat Land. The landlocked regency lies in the middle of West Sumatra province, between Mount Marapi and Mount Singgalang, at an average altitude of 400 to 1,000 metres. Its land is mostly hilly and takes in two thirds of Lake Singkarak. The climate is moderate, with temperatures between 12 °C and 25 °C and more than 3,000 millimetres of rain a year, most of it falling from September to February, which supports extensive farming.

Many relics of Minangkabau tradition survive in the regency, both as objects and as customary institutions. Among its historic sites are the Pagaruyung Palace, or Istano Basa Pagaruyuang, with its museum, the Adityawarman Inscription and other stone inscriptions in Sanskrit and Malay from the 14th century, several sites with standing megaliths known as batu tagak, the Batu Basurek and Batu Batikam stones, and Fort van der Capellen.

The old village of Pariangan, the Balimbing tower house, the Lubuk Bauk surau and the village of Pandai Sikek, where the traditional songket cloth called kain balapak is woven, are also among its historic places, as are the Balai Ruang Sari and the Istano Rajo. The pledge Adat Basandi Syarak, Syarak Basandi Kitabullah, also known as the Satie Oath, came from Bukit Marapalam at Puncak Pato, in the North Lintau Buo district.

Tanah Datar covers 1,337.1 square kilometres and is divided into fourteen districts; its seat is the town of Batusangkar. The city of Padang Panjang lies within it but is a municipality of its own. The regency had 371,704 inhabitants at the 2020 Census.

It is an agricultural area: more than 70% of its people work in food crops, plantations, fisheries and animal husbandry, and tourism and small industry also rest on farming. The traditional bull race pacu jawi is held in the regency.
tanaro: The Tanaro is a river of 276 kilometres in north-western Italy, called Tanarus in Latin. It begins in the Ligurian Alps, near the border with France, where two smaller streams, the Tanarello and the Negrone, meet at the boundary between Piedmont and Liguria. The main source of the Tanarello lies on the slopes of Monte Saccarello above Monesi, a village in the commune of Triora. The mountain marks the meeting point of three drainage basins: the Tanaro itself, the Roya, which rises in France and reaches the sea at Ventimiglia, and the Argentina, which flows into the Ligurian Sea at Taggia.

From there the river flows through Ormea, Garessio, Ceva, Alba, Asti and Alessandria and enters the Po near Bassignana. Its main tributaries are the Stura di Demonte, the Pesio, the Ellero and the Borbore from the left and the Bormida and the Belbo from the right. It is the most significant right-bank tributary of the Po in length, size of drainage basin and discharge, and at the confluence it is about 50 kilometres longer than the upper Po.

The river's flow varies greatly with the seasons. The Ligurian Alps are too low and too close to the sea to hold snow fields or glaciers large enough to feed it through the summer, so its regime resembles an Apennine stream: a maximum discharge that can reach 1,700 cubic metres per second in spring and autumn, and very little water in summer.

The river is also prone to flooding. Between 1801 and 2001 sections of its basin were flooded on 136 occasions, and the whole valley was affected in November 1994. The left bank of the Tanaro near Asti was the scene of the Battle of Pollentia on 6 April 402.
tancred-king-of-sicily: Tancred was born in Lecce, the illegitimate son of Roger III, Duke of Apulia, the eldest son of King Roger II, and of Emma, a daughter of Achard II, Count of Lecce. After Duke Roger's death, King Roger II kept Tancred and his brother William in close custody at Palermo. On 9 March 1161 Tancred joined his uncle Simon, Prince of Taranto, in invading the palace and detaining King William I and Queen Margaret.

The rising failed, and Tancred took pardon on condition of exile to Constantinople. He returned in 1166 under his cousin William II, was granted Montescaglioso before the end of 1168, and built it into the county of Lecce. He also served as constable and chief justiciar of Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro.

In 1174 Tancred led a Sicilian fleet to Egypt, which briefly besieged Alexandria, and in June 1185 a fleet of 300 ships to Durazzo, after which Thessaloniki was looted. When William II died in 1189, Tancred, though he had sworn fealty to Constance, seized the island and was crowned early in 1190. The vice chancellor Matthew d'Ajello and the official class backed him, and Pope Clement III was persuaded to support him, while most nobles favoured Constance and her husband Henry VI. Critics mocked his short stature as that of "The Monkey King".

Richard I of England arrived in 1190 on crusade, and demanded the release of his sister Joan, William II's widow, whom Tancred had imprisoned. Richard took Messina on 4 October 1190, and in March 1191 Tancred agreed to a treaty, by which Joan was freed and Richard and Philip recognised Tancred as king. In 1191 Henry and Constance, crowned emperor and empress in April, invaded, but disease broke their army at the siege of Naples. Tancred then held Constance captive, until Pope Celestine III secured her release in 1192 in exchange for recognition of Tancred as king.

Tancred won campaigns against the Apulian barons in 1192 and 1193. He died at Palermo on 20 February 1194, two months after his son and co-king, Roger III. His widow Sibylla of Acerra governed for their young son William III. Henry VI returned that year with an army financed by the ransom of Richard I, and Naples surrendered in May. The people of Palermo admitted the emperor on 20 November 1194. Tancred's family fell into Henry's hands, and William III seems to have died in Germany in 1198. Henry had Tancred's body taken from its grave. His death opened the way for Hohenstaufen rule in Sicily.
tancred-prince-of-galilee: Tancred was most likely born in southern Italy to Odo, called the Good Marquis, and Emma of Hauteville, a daughter of Robert Guiscard. Most medieval authors, including William of Tyre, make him a nephew of Bohemond I of Antioch through his mother, though Ralph of Caen and Orderic Vitalis mistook Emma for Guiscard's sister. His link to the House of Hauteville came only through Emma. Some modern scholars place his father's family among the Aleramids, a ruling house of northern Italy.

In 1096 he joined Bohemond on the First Crusade. At Constantinople he refused to swear the oath to Emperor Alexios I Komnenos that the other leaders took, and the surrender of Nicaea to Alexios's army deepened his distrust of the Byzantines. In 1097 he took Tarsus, Adana and Mopsuestia in Cilicia. He claimed, with Gaston IV of Béarn, to have been the first crusader to enter Jerusalem on 15 July 1099. During the sack he gave his banner to citizens sheltering on the roof of the Temple of Solomon, but other crusaders massacred them.

After the Kingdom of Jerusalem was established, Godfrey of Bouillon enfeoffed Tancred with Tiberias, and he held the nucleus of the Principality of Galilee. When Bohemond was captured at the Battle of Melitene in August 1100, Tancred took over the regency of Antioch by March 1101. On his coinage he called himself servant of God or grand emir, not prince. With Genoese help he took Lattakiah in April or May 1103 after a siege of 18 months, and in 1105 he defeated Ridwan of Aleppo near Artah.

After the crusaders' defeat at Harran in 1104, Tancred also governed Edessa, but in 1108 he had to give it back to Baldwin of Le Bourcq. Bohemond left for Italy, and Tancred ruled Antioch as he wished. Between 1109 and 1111 he conquered the whole of Cilicia, and in 1110 he brought Krak des Chevaliers under his control. King Baldwin I of Jerusalem restored Galilee to him in 1109 on condition that he became the king's vassal.

Tancred remained regent of Antioch for Bohemond II until his death in 1112 during a typhoid epidemic. He had married Cecile of France and died childless, and was buried in the porch of the cathedral of St Peter at Antioch. His first biography, the Gesta Tancredi, was written about 1120 by Ralph of Caen, who served under him. It depicts a pious but violent and opportunistic warrior who was troubled by the sinfulness of the knightly profession. Torquato Tasso made him an epic hero in Jerusalem Delivered in 1581, and later works by Monteverdi, Voltaire and Rossini drew on his story.
tancredo-neves: Tancredo de Almeida Neves was born on 4 March 1910 in São João del-Rei, Minas Gerais, of mostly Portuguese descent. After his schooling in his home town he moved to Belo Horizonte, took a law degree at the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais in 1932 and served as a public prosecutor in 1933. He sympathised with the Liberal Alliance that brought Getúlio Vargas to power in 1930.

He was elected city councilman of São João del-Rei in 1935 and became president of the council. After the New State was instituted in November 1937 he returned to law, acted for his city's railway union and for a time worked in the textile business.

In 1947 he was elected to the Minas Gerais state legislature for the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and was one of the spokesmen for the state constitution. He became a federal deputy in 1950, and on 26 June 1953 President Vargas appointed him Minister of Justice, a post he held until Vargas's suicide in 1954.

On 25 August 1961 he announced the installation of parliamentarism, which let João Goulart take the presidency after the resignation of Jânio Quadros and so avoided a military coup. Congress approved the amendment on 2 September, and Goulart named him President of the Council of Ministers on 8 September. After the military coup of 1964 he was among the few who saw Goulart off into exile, and he did not vote for Castelo Branco.

A moderate critic of the regime, he joined the Brazilian Democratic Movement, was re-elected deputy several times and became a senator in 1978. He founded the Popular Party in 1980 and in 1982 was elected governor of Minas Gerais, serving from 1983.

When the Dante de Oliveira amendment for direct presidential elections was defeated in 1984, after the Diretas Já campaign, Neves became the candidate of the Democratic Alliance of opposition parties. He was elected by the electoral college on 15 January 1985. Suffering abdominal pain, he delayed announcing his illness until the heads of state had arrived, since he feared that military hardliners would refuse to hand power to the vice-president. He was taken to hospital during the inauguration events and died on 21 April 1985. The official explanation was diverticulitis, but twenty years later doctors at the Hospital da Base in Brasília said it had been a benign tumour.
José Sarney took office as president. Law 7.465 of 21 April 1986 placed Neves among the former presidents of Brazil. The Tancredo Neves Memorial opened in São João del-Rei in 1990.
tanegashima: Tanegashima is the easternmost and the second largest of the Ōsumi Islands, after Yakushima. It lies roughly 43 kilometres south of the southern tip of the Ōsumi Peninsula in southern Kyushu, and 115 kilometres south of Kagoshima. The island is of volcanic origin but flat in appearance, with its highest point only 282 metres above sea level. It is 57 kilometres long and between 5 and 10 kilometres wide, with a humid subtropical climate.

Burials at the Yokomine and Hirota sites show a well-developed culture on the island by the end of the 4th century CE. The Nihonshoki records that the imperial court gave a banquet for the islanders in 677 and sent missions in 679, 683 and 695. Tane Province was set up there in 702 and lasted until 824, when it was merged into Ōsumi Province. About 1140 the island became part of the Shimazu Estate. A branch of the Higo clan later became autonomous there and took the name Tanegashima, and the clan ruled the island until the Meiji restoration.

The island is traditionally known as the place where European firearms reached Japan in 1543, and until modern times firearms were colloquially called tanegashima. Two Portuguese traders, António Mota and Francisco Zeimoto, are credited with bringing them; Fernão Mendes Pinto's claim in his memoirs of 1614 to have been in the first landing party has been discredited. During the Muromachi period the island was a relay station on a Chinese trade route linking Sakai and Ningbo, and the clan's ties with the Hosokawa clan and the Honnō-ji Temple in Kyoto explain the rapid spread of firearms to central Japan.

Tanegashima is part of Kagoshima Prefecture and is divided into the city of Nishinoomote and the towns of Nakatane and Minamitane. Its knives and scissors are traditional handicrafts, made with techniques said to date from about 1185, when the exiled Taira clan brought craftsmen from Kyoto, and the island is also a centre of iron sand production. The Tanegashima Space Center, established in 1969 and run by JAXA, is Japan's largest space development centre.
tang-campaign-against-the-eastern-turks: After the fall of the Sui dynasty, the Eastern Turkic Khaganate under Shibi Qaghan backed rival rebels to keep China divided, giving the future Tang founder Li Yuan 2,000 horses in 617 while taking tribute from him. Once the Tang had won, the Turks raided its lands from 623 to 626, and in 626 Illig Qaghan reached the Wei River opposite Chang'an. Emperor Taizong rode out to parley and the Turks withdrew, probably for a payment. Taizong then trained new units of mounted archers himself and drilled his generals in steppe warfare.

A volcanic eruption in 626 cooled the climate of Mongolia and northern China, and heavy snow in 627 killed much of the nomads' livestock. When Illig demanded more from his subject tribes, they revolted by the summer of 628, the Xueyantuo north of the Gobi most dangerously. Illig's nephew Ashina Shibobi, flogged for failing to crush the uprisings, fled to the Tang.

Li Jing was named commander-in-chief on 11 September and opened the offensive on 13 December 629, with six columns advancing along a front of 1,200 km. With 3,000 light cavalry he attacked Illig's camp at Dingxiang by night, driving him north to Iron Mountain, where Li Shiji's forces joined the pursuit. Illig sued for peace, but while talks were under way Li Jing struck on 27 March 630 with 10,000 cavalry, while Li Shiji blocked the way north. Some 10,000 Turks were killed. Illig escaped, but Turks who had surrendered caught him and handed him over on 12 May 630.

Illig died a prisoner in China. More than a hundred Turks became Tang generals or officials above the fifth rank, and several thousand Turkic families settled in Chang'an. The rest were settled on the borderlands as a buffer against the Xueyantuo, under Qilibi Khan as a puppet ruler. Attempts to revive the khaganate under Ashina Hubo, Ashina Nishufu and Ashina Funian failed, until Illig's grandson Qutlugh, named Ilterish Qaghan in 680, founded the Second Turkic Khaganate.
tang-code: The Tang Code grew out of the code of the Northern Zhou of 564, which was itself based on the earlier codes of the Cao-Wei and the Western Jin of 268. It was drawn up in 624 at the request of Emperor Gaozu of Tang, with the aim of smoothing the earlier laws and reducing physical punishments such as mutilation, so as to ease social tensions in the newly pacified Tang territories. It was revised in 627 and 637 under the influence of Emperor Taizong and promulgated in 652, under Emperor Gaozong, with 502 articles in 12 sections, before the commentary was added.

The code combined Legalist and Confucian views of law and was supplemented by civil statutes and regulations. Each offence was tied to a fixed penalty, which was then raised or lowered according to the relation between offender and victim. Within the family this was measured by the kind and length of mourning owed to each degree of kinship; outside it, by rank in a hierarchy headed by the emperor, in which officials stood above ordinary men and they above people of servile status. A slave who harmed his master was punished more severely than a commoner who did the same, and a master who harmed his slave less severely.

The magistrate's task was to fix the offence as the code defined it and set the penalty. If evidence and testimony did not decide a case, he could ask higher officials for permission to use judicial torture: no more than 200 blows with a prescribed interrogation stick, in up to three sessions at least twenty days apart. If the accused confessed nothing, the accuser was tortured in turn. Penalties ranged from beating with a rattan or a bamboo stick through penal labour and exile to death by strangulation or decapitation. Private households found with the Luoshu Square or the Yellow River Map, used in divination, faced two years of forced labour.

The Tang Code is the earliest Chinese code to survive complete, and it became the basis for later dynastic codes in China and elsewhere in East Asia. The sinologist Jacques Gernet called it "an admirable composition of faultless logic", and Wallace Johnson and Denis Twitchett described it as "a very rational system of justice".
tang-dynasty: The Tang dynasty was founded by Emperor Gaozu, born Li Yuan, who had been Duke of Tang and governor of Taiyuan during the collapse of the Sui dynasty. The Li family were of ethnic Han origin and belonged to the north-western military aristocracy; Gaozu's mother was part Xianbei. Official Tang records trace the family's descent from Laozi, and Li Yuan used the claim to attract a following. The Tang took advantage of Sui decline and precipitated its final collapse in 618, and the first half of the dynasty was a period of progress and stability. The territory won by the military campaigns of its early rulers surpassed that of the Han dynasty.

The dynasty was formally interrupted from 690 to 705, when Empress Wu Zetian seized the throne and proclaimed the Wu Zhou dynasty, becoming the only legitimate Chinese female emperor. Emperor Xuanzong, who reigned from 712 to 756, ruled when the dynasty was at the height of its power.

The An Lushan rebellion of 755–763 ended its prosperity: An Lushan, a Tang commander, rebelled in Hebei with more than 100,000 troops, took Luoyang and named himself emperor of a new Yan state, and the court fled Chang'an. The Uyghur Khaganate helped recapture the capital, but demanded an enormous tribute in silk, and the Tang were never again able to reconquer Central Asia.

Regional military governors, the jiedushi, rose in the ninth century and weakened civil order. In the 840s Emperor Wuzong suppressed Buddhism. The rebellion of Huang Chao from 874 to 884 devastated northern and southern China and sacked both Chang'an and Luoyang; the Tang never recovered, and the dynasty ended in 907. It was followed by the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

The dynasty kept a civil service recruited by examinations and recommendations. Emperor Taizong issued a legal code that later Chinese dynasties and neighbouring polities in Vietnam, Korea and Japan took as a model; the earliest surviving code, of 653, has 500 articles. Candidates sat the mingjing, on the Confucian classics, or the jinshi, which tested essays and poetry. An official census of 609 counted about 50 million people.

By 742 the armies had about 500,000 men, and in 668 Tang and Silla forces destroyed the kingdom of Goguryeo. Chang'an, the capital, was laid out in 108 walled wards, and its checkerboard plan was copied in Heian-kyō. Over 48,900 Tang poems by more than 2,200 authors survive, among them those of Li Bai and Du Fu, and woodblock printing produced the Diamond Sutra of 868, the first full-length book printed at regular size.
tang-jingsong: In 1882 the Qing government sent Tang to Vietnam to judge whether the Vietnamese could resist French expansion in Tonkin. There he persuaded Liu Yongfu to take the field against the French with the Black Flag Army, and Liu's intervention led to the French defeat at the Battle of Paper Bridge on 19 May 1883, in which Henri Rivière was killed. Tang was the only senior Chinese commander in the Sơn Tây Campaign of December 1883, and his loyalty to Liu there was never forgotten by the Black Flag leader.

In September 1884 Tang led the Yunnan Army down the Red River from Lào Cai to threaten the French post of Tuyên Quang, with Liu Yongfu serving under him. Although the post was never taken, his methodical conduct of the Siege of Tuyên Quang was praised by Zhang Zhidong, the Viceroy of Liangguang, and Cen Yuying, the Viceroy of Yun-Gui. Captain Jean-François-Alphonse Lecomte of the Tonkin Expeditionary Corps wrote that the mandarins had directed the attack in a very intelligent manner.

Tang succeeded Shao Youlian as governor of Taiwan in 1894 and, when the First Sino-Japanese War broke out, invited Liu Yongfu to command the Qing forces in southern Taiwan. After the island was ceded to Japan in April 1895, officials who resolved to resist proclaimed the Republic of Formosa. The Japanese landed in northern Taiwan on 29 May and defeated the Chinese forces at Keelung on 3 June. When the news reached Taipei on 4 June, Tang fled that night to Tamsui, where disorder delayed his departure, and sailed for the mainland on the evening of 6 June aboard the steamship Arthur.

Resistance continued under Liu Yongfu, but the republic collapsed when the Japanese occupied Tainan on 21 October 1895, and Liu too fled to the mainland. Tang died in 1903 at his home in Guilin, aged 63. His most important contribution to the Qing war effort had come in Tonkin, where he brought the Black Flag Army under Chinese command.
tang-of-shang: Tang was born Zi Lü and is named Da Yi or Tai Yi on oracle bones, where the character yi marks the day on which sacrifices were made to him. Cheng Tang is a posthumous title. He was said to descend from Xie, and so from Emperor Ku and the Yellow Emperor. Because his time precedes the Late Shang, records of his life are limited to oracle bone inscriptions and works written after his death.

Tang succeeded Shi Gui as ruler of the Predynastic Shang, one of many kingdoms under the suzerainty of the Xia. His minister Yi Yin is said to have won his confidence through cooking, advising on the balance of the five flavours before giving political advice. Yi Yin spent about three years as an envoy at the Xia capital and came back critical of Xia politics. He urged war but held that allies must first be won and Xia's vassals weakened.

In the 21st year of Jie's reign Tang took the Youluo and forced the Jing to surrender. The next year Jie imprisoned him at Xiatai but later released him, and many neighbouring clans came to revere Shang. Tang is said to have won the support of as many as 40 smaller kingdoms by pointing to Jie's mistreatment of his people, telling them that he must follow the Mandate of Heaven. The Book of Documents contains a speech attributed to him after the Battle of Mingtiao, though its authenticity is disputed.

The Shang army defeated Jie's forces at Mingtiao in a heavy thunderstorm. Jie fled to Sanzong, was pursued to Cheng by the Shang general Wuzi, and was captured at Jiaomen and deposed. Tang succeeded him as paramount king. According to the Bamboo Annals, when drought struck in the first five years of his reign he had golden coins made so that poor families could buy back children sold in the famine.

In oracle bone inscriptions Tang appears about 350 times as Da Yi, and sacrifices to him were particularly grand, with banquets, drums to announce the rite and offerings of oxen. In the classical canon he is usually named with Emperor Yao, Emperor Shun and King Wu of Zhou as a good ruler, in contrast to Jie and Di Xin, and the Three Character Classic of the Song dynasty pairs him with Yu the Great and King Wu as the Three Kings.
tanganyika-territory: Before the First World War the area formed part of German East Africa, which Germany had declared a protectorate in 1885 under Carl Peters. The Germans repressed the Maji Maji Rebellion of 1905 brutally and developed the colony around cash crops such as sisal, cotton, coffee and cocoa; in 1913 sisal made up 30% of exports, and the Central Line railway linked much of the country to Dar es Salaam.

British Empire and Belgian Congo forces gradually occupied it during the East Africa Campaign, although German resistance continued until 1918. Under the Treaty of Versailles the territory went to Britain, apart from Ruanda-Urundi, assigned to Belgium, and the Kionga Triangle, assigned to Portuguese Mozambique. The British needed a new name and took it from Lake Tanganyika, rejecting among others Smutsland, Windsorland and Kilimanjaro.

The mandate was formalised on 20 July 1922, and on 22 March 1921 Belgium had ceded the Kigoma District to the territory. The British wanted a 'Black man's country' like Nigeria and adopted indirect rule. Under the governor Sir Horace Bryatt, whose anti-German policy expelled Germans and halved the European population, ex-German plantations were sold to European companies. The Asian population rose from 8,698 in 1912 to 25,144 in 1931.

In 1927 Tanganyika joined the customs union of Kenya and Uganda, and cooperation grew through the East African High Commission, which lasted from 1948 to 1961. The Tanganyika African National Union, founded in 1954 under Julius Nyerere, won every seat in the 1958 election, and internal self-government followed in 1960. A party of British settlers, the United Tanganyikan Party, founded in 1956, was ineffective.

Tanganyika became independent on 9 December 1961, after Nyerere had met a British government representative to arrange the steps. He had become prime minister in 1960 under British rule and became president when it was declared a republic in 1962. Independence came peacefully, but the country was short of money and infrastructure, and refugees from the Congo, Burundi and Rwanda arrived. After the Zanzibar Revolution of 1964, Tanganyika merged with Zanzibar into the United Republic of Tanganyika and Zanzibar, which became the United Republic of Tanzania on 26 April 1964.
tangata-manu: In Rapa Nui mythology the god Makemake was the chief deity of the bird-man cult. Three others were linked with it: Hawa-tuu-take-take, the male Chief of the eggs, his wife Vie Hoa, and the goddess Vie Kenatea, each with a servant god of their own. Contestants chanted the names of all eight in the rituals that preceded the egg hunt.

Priests called ivi-attua, who could be men or women, revealed in prophecies which men of importance would compete. Each appointed one or two hopu, men of lesser status, who swam to Motu Nui with provisions in a bundle of reeds called a pora and waited for the sooty terns, while their sponsors waited at Orongo on the south-western tip of the island. Many hopu died from sharks, drowning or falls from the cliffs.

The finder of the first egg called from the highest point of Motu Nui to tell his patron to shave his head, and the cry was passed up the cliffs to Orongo. He then fasted alone on the islet before swimming back with the egg in a reed basket tied to his forehead and climbing the cliffs of Rano Kau. His patron, head shaved and painted white or red, became the new tangata manu and led a procession to Anakena or Rano Raraku, depending on whether his clan was of the west or the east.

He received food and tribute, his clan alone could gather that season's eggs and fledglings on Motu Nui, and he spent a year in seclusion in a ceremonial house, tapu for five months, with long nails and a headdress of human hair.

Christian missionaries ended the cult in the 1860s. During the Mana Expedition of 1913-15 the archaeologist and anthropologist Katherine Routledge collected the names of 86 bird men. The 1994 film Rapa Nui depicts a version of the race to Motu Nui.
tangaxuan-ii: Tzimtzincha-Tangaxuan II ruled the Purépecha Empire from 1520. After hearing of the fall of the Aztec Empire, he sent emissaries to the Spanish victors, and a few Spaniards came back with them to his capital, Tzintzuntzan, where gifts were exchanged. They returned with samples of gold, which awakened the interest of Hernán Cortés in the Purépecha state.

In 1522 a Spanish force under Cristóbal de Olid reached Tzintzuntzan within days. The Purépecha army numbered many thousands, perhaps as many as 100,000, but at the decisive moment it chose not to fight. Tangaxuan submitted to Spanish rule and was baptised Francisco when his realm made peace with Cortés. In return for his cooperation he kept a large degree of autonomy, and for some years both he and Cortés regarded themselves as rulers of Michoacán, with the people paying tribute to both.

Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán, president of the first Audiencia, set out to conquer northwestern Mexico with a force of 5,000 to 8,000 men.
