In 51 BCE he warned Cicero, then proconsul of Cilicia, that the Parthian crown prince Pacorus had crossed the Euphrates into Syria; Cicero told the Senate he was the most loyal ally beyond the Taurus. Cicero's campaign against the tribes of southern Amanus that followed probably extended Tarcondimotus's reach. In the civil war of 49 BCE he backed Pompey, sending ships to his fleet, but after Pharsalus Julius Caesar pardoned and confirmed him, perhaps also granting him Roman citizenship.

After Caesar's murder he allied with Cassius, then turned to Mark Antony after Philippi in 42 BCE. When Pacorus and Quintus Labienus occupied Syria in 40 BCE he refused to submit, and Antony made him king about 38 BCE. Strabo says the Romans named him king for his manly virtues, and he struck bronze coins with the epithet Philantonios.

In his late sixties or early seventies he led his own squadron under Antony's admiral Gaius Sosius off western Greece. Just before the main battle at Actium, Sosius routed the fleet of Octavian's admiral Tarius but was then beaten by Marcus Agrippa, and Tarcondimotus died fighting, the only eastern client king to fall. His son Philopator I lost the royal title within a year. Augustus restored it in 20 BCE to Tarcondimotus II, who refounded Anazarbus as Caesarea; the line ended with Philopator II in 17 CE, when Tiberius brought the land under direct Roman rule.
tarfaya: Tarfaya is a coastal town in western Morocco, at the level of Cape Juby on the Atlantic, about 890 kilometres southwest of Rabat and around 100 kilometres from both Laayoune and Lanzarote in the Canary Islands. It is the capital of Tarfaya Province and had 8,027 inhabitants at the 2014 census. Sebkha Tah, the lowest point in Morocco at 55 metres below sea level, lies in the province, and the Khenifiss National Park, on UNESCO's Tentative list, shelters migratory birds, with more than 20,000 birds of 211 species breeding, nesting and feeding there regularly.

In 1882 the Scottish trader Donald McKenzie founded a trading post here, called Casa del Mar or Port Victoria. Sahrawi tribes asked Sultan Hassan I to intervene, and he negotiated the British withdrawal by the Treaty of Cape Juby in 1895. In 1912 the territory, then called Cape Juby, was part of Spanish territory, and the town was a Spanish colony known as Villa Bens. It was united with Morocco in 1958, at the end of the Ifni War.

In 1927 the airmail company Aéropostale, founded by Pierre-Georges Latécoère to link France to its colonies in Africa, made the Cape Juby airfield a refuelling and stopover station. The writer and aviator Antoine de Saint-Exupéry was its station manager for 18 months and sometimes negotiated with rebellious Moorish tribes for the release of imprisoned pilots, as he described in his first novel, Southern Mail.

A museum in honour of Aéropostale, Saint-Exupéry and its pilots opened on 28 September 2004. The town has a desert climate and an airport with the IATA code TFY. It has symbolic importance in Moroccan history in connection with the Green March of November 1975, and the Tarfaya Wind Farm, the largest in Africa, was commissioned in December 2014.
targowica-confederation: The Targowica Confederation was established by Polish and Lithuanian magnates on 27 April 1792 in Saint Petersburg, with the backing of the Russian Empress Catherine II. It opposed the Constitution of 3 May 1791, adopted by the Great Sejm, especially the provisions that limited the privileges of the nobility. The text of its founding act was drafted by the Russian general Vasili Stepanovich Popov, chief of staff of Prince Grigori Alexandrovich Potemkin. Its founding act declared that the wishes of the Empress, an ally of the Commonwealth, were only to use her armies to return freedoms, security and happiness to its citizens.

The confederation's purpose was proclaimed on 14 May 1792 in the small town of Targowica, on the Potocki estate, now in Ukraine. Four days later two Russian armies invaded the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth without a formal declaration of war. The forces of the confederation inflicted some defeats on the armies of the Commonwealth, the Sejm and King Stanisław August Poniatowski in the Polish–Russian War of 1792, and as a result the king formally joined the confederation. Its leader, as marshal, was Stanisław Szczęsny Potocki, who had written that every true Pole not blinded by the Prussian and royalist cabal was convinced that the fatherland could be saved only by Russia.

The confederation's victory precipitated the Second Partition of Poland and made possible the Third Partition and the final dissolution of the Commonwealth in 1795. This surprised most of the confederates, who had wished only to restore the earlier order and had expected that overthrowing the Constitution of 3 May would do so.

Several leading members were condemned during the Kościuszko Uprising of 1794: Szymon Marcin Kossakowski was hanged at Vilnius on 25 April 1794, Józef Kazimierz Kossakowski and others were sentenced on 9 May, and Potocki and Franciszek Ksawery Branicki were sentenced to death but never apprehended; Potocki's portrait was hanged on 29 September 1794. In 1795 Catherine rewarded Potocki with the Order of Alexander Nevsky. In Polish, targowiczanin became a synonym for traitor, and Targowica for treason.
tarhunazi: Tarhunazi, written Tarḫunazi in transliteration, ruled the Iron Age state of Kammanu, whose centre was the city of Melid. His name comes from Tarḫunz, the chief Luwian storm god, a common element in Neo-Hittite names. By the 8th century BCE the kings of Melid no longer set up hieroglyphic Luwian inscriptions, so everything known of his reign comes from Assyrian accounts, above all the annals of Sargon II, who dealt with the Neo-Hittite states of the region both in war and by diplomacy.

In 719 BCE, the third year of Sargon II, the Assyrians deposed King Gunzinanu of Kammanu. Tarhunazi, possibly his son, quickly took the throne, and the same year Sargon recognised him as a vassal. He swore an oath of loyalty and became a tributary of the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

Resenting his dependence, Tarhunazi rebelled around 713 BCE. He corresponded with Mita, ruler of Mushki and an enemy of Assyria, who may have pressed him to join the Mushki sphere of influence in Anatolia, as he had done with Ambaris, king of neighbouring Tabal. News of the broken oath reached Nineveh.

In 712 BCE, the tenth year of his reign, Sargon set out to punish him. He overran Kammanu with a mercenary army of Suteans and laid siege to Melid. Tarhunazi left the city in haste and fled to the fortress of Til Garimmu near the border with Tabal, which had once been the Hittite fortress of Tegarama. He was taken in there, but Sargon captured the fortress and carried Tarhunazi and his family to Nineveh, where he probably suffered punishment for defying the Assyrian king.
tarhunt: The name goes back to a Proto-Anatolian *Tṛḫu-ent-, "conquering", from an Indo-European root meaning to cross over or overcome, the root of Latin trans- and English through. Nearly every Anatolian language used it: Hittite Tarḫunna-, Luwian Tarḫunt-, Carian Trquδ- and Lycian Trqqas. Norbert Oettinger argued that the god's functions come from the Indo-European thunder god *Perkʷūnos, under a new epithet that sounded like the name of the Hattian storm god Taru. The oldest personal name built on it, Tarḫuan, appears in a 19th-century BCE text from Kültepe, and the Hittite city of Tarḫuntašša was named after the god.

Among the Luwians the weather god was linked less with the bull than with the horse: a ritual from Arzawa against horse-plague feeds his horses and oils his chariot. His epithets call him powerful, helpful and stern. He ran ahead of the king in battle, ruled the mountains and the heavens, and as the god of the thunderbolt, piḫaššaššiš, gave his name, it is held, to the Greek winged horse Pegasus. The Hittite Great King Muwatalli II chose the weather god of the thunderbolt as his protector and said the god had raised him and made him king.

A Luwian innovation was the weather god of the vineyard, first called upon in a 16th-century BCE ritual to make the royal vineyard thrive. In the 8th century BCE King Warpalawas II of Tuwana had him carved on the rock at İvriz holding grapes and ears of wheat. Aleppo was a great city of the weather god from the early Bronze Age.

More than sixty Iron Age reliefs and statues show him: bearded and helmeted with axe and thunderbolt, standing on a bull as the weather god of Aleppo, or carrying grain and grapes as in Tabal. The bull-borne image returned in Roman times as Jupiter Dolichenus, worshipped from Doliche as far as central Europe. A relief from Arslantepe shows him fighting a serpent-like water creature, a myth that may have passed through Cilicia into the Greek story of Zeus and Typhon.
tarikh-al-fattash: The chronicle gives an account of the Songhai Empire from the reign of Sunni Ali (ruled 1464-1492) to 1599, with a few references to events of the following century, and it also mentions the earlier Mali Empire. Together with the Tarikh al-Sudan, it is known as one of the Timbuktu Chronicles.

The French journalist Félix Dubois learnt of the chronicle in Timbuktu in 1895 but could not obtain a copy: most copies had been destroyed early in the 19th century on the order of the Fula leader Seku Amadu. In 1911 an old manuscript lacking its first pages was found in Timbuktu (Manuscript A), and a copy of it was sent to the Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris (Manuscript B). A year later a seemingly complete manuscript naming Mahmud Kati as author was found in Kayes; this Manuscript C has an opening chapter and other additions and deletions.

In September 1913 Albert Bonnel de Mézières acquired in Timbuktu an anonymous 24-page text, written at the request of Askiya Dawud b. Harun, who reigned in Timbuktu between 1657 and 1669. Octave Houdas and Maurice Delafosse published the Arabic text with a French translation in 1913, adding the unique parts of the 24-page text in French only, as Appendix 2. Its Arabic manuscript has since disappeared.

The published text raised problems. Manuscript C has Mahmud Kati born in 1468, while the Tarikh al-Sudan gives the death of him, or of a namesake, in 1593, which would make him 125 years old. Its first chapter also contains a prophecy of the last of twelve caliphs, Ahmad of the Sangare tribe in Massina, the tribe of Seku Amadu. In 1971 Nehemia Levtzion argued that Manuscript C was a forgery of Seku Amadu's time, in the first quarter of the 19th century, and that the chronicle was probably written soon after 1664.

In 2015 Mauro Nobili and Mohamed Shahid Mathee, drawing on manuscripts not studied before and on the rediscovered Manuscript A, argued that the edition conflates two works: the Tarikh Ibn al-Mukhtar, and a rewriting of it by Nūḥ b. al-Ṭāhir with a different ideological aim, whose attribution to Mahmud Kati is an invention. Their view is widely accepted among historians of West Africa, though its effect on accounts of the period is still debated.
tarikh-al-sudan: The author, Abderrahmane al-Sa'di, was born on 28 May 1594 and died at an unknown date after 1655-56, the last date his chronicle mentions. He spent most of his life working for the Moroccan Arma bureaucracy, first in the administration of Djenné and the Massina region of the Inland Niger Delta, and from 1646 as chief secretary to the Arma administration of Timbuktu. Together with the Tarikh al-fattash, another 17th-century history of Songhay, his work is known as one of the Timbuktu Chronicles.

The opening sections give short histories of earlier Songhay dynasties, of the Mali Empire and of the Tuareg, and biographies of the scholars and holy men of Timbuktu and Djenné. The main part covers the Songhai from the middle of the 15th century to the Moroccan invasion of 1591, and then Timbuktu under Moroccan rule. Al-Sa'di seldom names his sources; for the earlier period he presumably relied on oral tradition, and from around 1610 he wrote from first-hand knowledge. He also recorded the tradition that a ruler named Kaya-Magha founded the first kingdom in the region, with its capital at Ghana, and that forty-four kings reigned before the people of Mali took over.

In 1853 the German scholar Heinrich Barth, visiting Timbuktu for the British government, consulted a copy at Gwandu in present-day northwest Nigeria, but believed the author to be the Timbuktu scholar Ahmed Baba. Forty years later the French journalist Félix Dubois, in Timbuctoo the Mysterious, pointed out that the chronicle records Ahmed Baba's death and so could not be his work.

After the French occupation of Mali in the 1890s, the Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris acquired two copies: one sent by Louis Archinard and one made for Dubois at Djenné in 1895. The Arabic scholar Octave Houdas studied these and a third, better copy dated 1792, sent by the linguist René Basset, and published the Arabic text in 1898 and a French translation in 1900. A century later John Hunwick published a partial English translation and listed four further manuscripts, which differ mainly in the spelling of names.
tarim-basin: The Tarim Basin is an endorheic basin of about 888,000 square kilometres, bounded by the Tian Shan to the north and the Kunlun Mountains to the south. The Taklamakan Desert fills much of it and is too dry for permanent habitation. The Yarkand, Kashgar and Aksu rivers join to form the Tarim River, which runs along the north side and ends at Lop Nur, a marshy saline depression.

Meltwater from the mountains feeds the oases along which the Silk Road routes ran: one route north of the desert, one south, and a shorter middle route across the Lop Nur region, which became uninhabitable in the 4th century and has been deserted since the 6th. The historical Uyghur name for the basin is Altishahr, meaning six cities.

Bronze appeared in the basin from about 2000 BCE, in six cultural zones. Mummies found at Loulan, the Xiaohe tomb complex and Qäwrighul were once suggested to be Tocharian, but recent evidence points to a distinct population. The Han dynasty came to influence the basin in the reign of Emperor Wu, and General Ban Chao (32–102 CE) wrested control from the Xiongnu at the end of the 1st century. The Chinese administered it as the Protectorate of the Western Regions.

The Kushans expanded into it in the 1st and 2nd centuries and established a kingdom at Kashgar. Kingdoms such as Kucha and Khotan passed Buddhism and other influences between India, Central Asia and China; the monk Kumārajīva came from Kucha.

Under Emperor Taizong the Tang dynasty campaigned against the oasis states, then vassals of the Western Turkic Khaganate: Gaochang was annexed in 640, Karasahr taken in 644 and Kucha conquered in 649. From the late 8th to 9th centuries the region changed hands between the Tang and the Tibetan Empire. Satuq Bughra Khan of the Kara-Khanid Khanate converted to Islam in 966, and Khotan fell to the Kara-Khanid Khanate around 1006; the basin became Islamic over the following centuries. In the early 14th century its eastern parts belonged to the Chagatai Khanate, and the Dughlat tribe held the western basin and raised Tughlugh Timur to the throne in 1347.

The basin lies in the Xinjiang region of north-western China, and Uyghurs form the majority in cities such as Kashgar and Hotan. Xinjiang as a single province dates from 1884, after the Qing conquest of 1759, when the Tarim Basin and Dzungaria had been governed separately. Excavations have found wooden tablets in the Kharosthi script of the 3rd and 4th centuries at Niya, and Buddhist murals at Miran that show links with Central Asia and northern India.
tarim-yemen: Tarim lies in the Hadhramaut valley of southern Yemen, about 180 kilometres inland from the coast and 35 kilometres north-east of Seiyun, whose airport is the nearest. The Hadhramaut spans about 90,000 square kilometres, with a narrow arid coastal plain below a plateau averaging around 1,400 metres in altitude, cut by deep wadis. Tarim has a hot desert climate with very little rain, though a few times a year heavy rainfall brings flooding. It is described as the theological, juridical and academic centre of Wadi Hadhramaut, and as home to a very high concentration of Sayyids, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad. Imam al-Haddad was among its scholars.

Tradition holds that the citizens of Tarim converted to Islam when a delegation from Hadhramaut met the Prophet Muhammad in Medina in 631, and that Abu Bakr prayed for more scholars and water for the town because its people stood with him in the Ridda wars of 632 to 633. A Wahhabi invasion in 1809 destroyed valuable books and documents from the Robat at Tarim and ravaged the economy, which increased emigration, above all to Hyderabad in India.

There Umar bin Awadh al-Qu'aiti made a fortune and founded the Qu'aiti dynasty, which signed a treaty with the British in 1888 and created a unified sultanate in 1902, within the Aden Protectorate. Tarim stayed under Kathiri rule, as a pocket of Kathiri territory in the country of the Tamim, who owed allegiance to the Qu'aiti sultanate.

In February 1937 the Qu'aiti and Kathiri sultanates made peace, known as Ingrams' Peace after Harold Ingrams, the first political officer in Hadhramaut, and Sayyid Abu Bakr al-Kaf, whose family fortune, made in Singapore, paid for it. The British withdrew from South Yemen in November 1967, the National Liberation Front took power, and Tarim became part of the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen until South and North Yemen unified in 1990.

The town is said to contain up to 365 mosques, one of which, the Sirjis Mosque, dates to the seventh century. The Al-Muhdhar Mosque has a mud minaret of about 53 metres, completed in 1914. The Al-Kaf Library holds more than 5,000 manuscripts, and about thirty mansions were built between the 1870s and 1930s in styles taken from British India and Southeast Asia.
tariq-ibn-ziyad: Medieval Arabic historians give contradictory accounts of Tariq's origins and ethnicity, and details of his personality are uncertain. Many modern scholars hold that he was a Berber mawla, a freedman client, of Musa ibn Nusayr, the Umayyad governor of Ifriqiya. According to David Nicolle he came from a Berber tribe native to the Tafna in what is now Algeria, and he first appears in the record as governor of Tangier. Ibn Abd al-Hakam (803–871) says Musa appointed him governor of Tangier after its conquest in 710–711.

An unconquered Visigothic outpost remained at Ceuta, held by a nobleman named Julian, Count of Ceuta. In the story told by Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Julian was enraged because King Roderic had raped his daughter, Florinda la Cava, at the Visigothic court, and so he made a treaty with Tariq and used his merchant ships to carry the Muslim army across the straits. Tariq's army, which landed on or about 26 April 711, consisted of about 7,000 soldiers, largely of Berber stock but with Arab troops, and it gathered at the mountain that became known as Jabal Tariq, or Gibraltar.

Roderic assembled an army said to number 100,000, though the real figure may have been much lower. Most of it was commanded by the sons of Wittiza, whom Roderic had deposed, and it was defeated at the Battle of Guadalete on 19 July, where Roderic was killed. Tariq then divided his army into four. One division took Córdoba under Mughith al-Rumi, others took Granada and further places, and Tariq's own took Toledo before he advanced north to Guadalajara and Astorga. He was de facto governor until Musa arrived a year later, and within a few years the two had taken two-thirds of the peninsula.

In 714 the caliph al-Walid I ordered both Tariq and Musa back to Damascus, where they spent the rest of their lives. Arabic sources differ on their relationship: some tell of Musa's anger and envy at a freedman's conquest, while al-Baladhuri says only that Musa wrote him a severe letter and the two were later reconciled. The historians Ibn Khallikan, in 1274, and al-Maqqari, in the 16th century, attribute to him a long speech to his troops before Guadalete. He also appears in a story of the One Thousand and One Nights.
tarki: Tarki, called Tarğu in Kumyk and formerly also spelled Tarkou or Tarku, stands on the Tarki-tau mountain, Tarğu-taw in Kumyk, in the Republic of Dagestan in Russia. It was the capital of the historical Kumyk states until Russia abolished them. According to some scholars, the town occupies the site of Samandar, the capital of Khazaria until the early 8th century. Tarki is named in Armenian chronicles of the 7th and 8th centuries, in the Catalan Atlas of 1375 and by Timurid historians.

In 1396 Timur passed through Tarki during the Tokhtamysh–Timur war. The Shamkhalate took shape in the Middle Ages and later became the Shamkhalate of Tarki, whose rulers submitted to Russian authority more than once, the first time early in the 17th century. In 1668 Cossacks under Stepan Razin sacked the town. The shamkhals were obliged to accept Russian suzerainty again during Peter the Great's Persian Expedition of 1722 and during Catherine the Great's Persian Expedition of 1796.

Tarki finally came under Russian control by the terms of the Treaty of Gulistan in 1813. Eight years later the Russians built Burnaya Fortress there. It was succeeded by Fort-Petrovsk, raised on the grounds of the Kumyk town of Andzhi-kala, or Anji, which is now Makhachkala.

On 12 April 1944 the Kumyks of Tarki and of the neighbouring villages of Kyakhulay and Alborukent were rounded up and deported on the orders of the communist authorities of Dagestan. They were moved onto land of the Chechen, Karachay, Balkar and Crimean Tatar populations, who had themselves been deported to Central Asia on Stalin's orders two months earlier. The reason given was that the area would serve the farming needs of highland peoples resettled in Tarki. The Kumyks lost their traditional capital for years, and part of their cultural inheritance was destroyed.

Tarki was granted the status of an urban-type settlement in 1958. It falls under Sovetsky City District of the City of Makhachkala and, as a municipality, is part of Makhachkala Urban Okrug; the census of 2010 counted 15,356 inhabitants. In 2017 the Dagestan government announced that it had built 3,000 houses for Laks on land in Tarki that had belonged to Kumyks, and the Kumyk community set up a protest camp seeking restitution for the deportation of 1944, which the Russian government had not acknowledged.
tarkwa: Tarkwa lies in the Western Region of Ghana and is known locally as the Golden City. The area around it holds a number of Fante communities, among them Efuanta, Tamso, Aboso, Akoon, Nzemaline, Bogrekrom and Kwabedu. The gold occurs in several low-grade conglomeratic reefs of mid-Proterozoic age, called Tarkwaian after the town, and the area is also mined for manganese.

The Tarkwa Goldfield was found a few years before the Witwatersrand Goldfield in South Africa, and in the late 19th century a number of mining companies clustered between the villages of Aboso and Tamso. Tarkwa became a junction on the railway and is served by a station of the Ghana Railway Corporation. Mining has brought accidents as well as wealth: on 23 September 2023 a pit caved in and killed 7 people. Some land, such as the Ndumfri forest reserve, is closed to mining, and in September 2023 three people were jailed for mining in a restricted area.

Tarkwa is the capital of the Tarkwa-Nsuaem Municipal District and had 218,664 inhabitants in 2021. The Tarkwa mine, a large open-cast gold mine northwest of the town, is one of the largest gold mines in the country, producing about 24 tons of gold a year by moving 100 million tons of earth. The Nsuta manganese mine lies east of the town and the Iduapriem Gold Mine 10 kilometres to the south. The town is home to the University of Mines and Technology and to Tarkwa Senior High School, Tarkwa Technical Institute and Fiaseman Senior High School, and it is the main seat of the Tarkwa-Nsuaem Municipal Assembly.
tarlac-city: Tarlac City is the capital of the province of Tarlac in the Philippines, 124 kilometres north of Manila and 126 kilometres from Baguio. It lies at the centre of the province along the Tarlac River, at 24 to 50 metres above sea level. Parts of it are said to be among the few portions of land in the province not created by ancient eruptions of Mount Pinatubo. It stands where Kapampangan and Pangasinan languages and cultures meet, and both are widely spoken, along with Ilocano and Tagalog; most residents are Kapampangans.

The first settlers came from Bacolor in Pampanga and founded their settlement in 1788, clearing the land and fertilising the soil. The name derives from tarlak, an Aeta word for a weed called talahib, and the area was described as matarlak, meaning abundant with tarlak grass. The community grew quickly as settlers arrived from Bataan, Pampanga and Zambales, and Kapampangan became its native language. When the province of Tarlac was founded in 1872, the town became its capital.

The town became a city in stages. A law of 1969 converted it into a city, but its plebiscite rejected cityhood. In 1990 thirteen barangays were separated to form part of San Jose, leaving an area of 274.66 square kilometres. Republic Act No. 8593 of 12 March 1998 made it a component city, and its residents approved the change in April 1998.

The 2024 census counted 401,892 people, the most in the province, in 76 barangays. Most residents are Christians, mainly Roman Catholics. The city is the educational centre of the province and has the main campus of Tarlac State University. MacArthur Highway runs through it, and it is a bus stop for travellers between the south and the Ilocos Region.
tarnovo-constitution: The constitution was adopted by the Constituent National Assembly at Veliko Tarnovo as part of the establishment of the Principality of Bulgaria. It was based on the Belgian charter of 1831 and was considered advanced for its time. Because the Treaty of Berlin of 1878 restricted Bulgaria's independence and made it a de facto vassal state of Turkey, the monarch bore the title of Prince rather than tsar, as it had been during the First and the Second Bulgarian Empire.

The constitution made Bulgaria a constitutional, hereditary monarchy with a parliament elected by the people, and divided power between executive, legislative and judicial branches. The prince had to be male and Orthodox, although a legal exception allowed the election of the Lutheran Alexander of Battenberg. Ministers took responsibility for the acts they signed, deputies had immunity, and the prince's signature was needed for a bill to become law. Eastern Orthodoxy was the official religion, but followers of other faiths were held equal. Aristocratic titles and censorship were banned, property was declared sacrosanct, all male citizens, the monarch included, had to serve in the army, and citizens could form parties and companies. Article 61 freed any slave who set foot on Bulgarian territory.

The constitution was often set aside. The ban on censorship was suspended in the 1880s by a law of the Russian general Sobolev, which restricted the press to seven newspapers and magazines, and the whole constitution was suspended in 1881 by a Grand National Assembly that Alexander manipulated. Amendments in 1893 and 1911 strengthened royal power, and after Prince Ferdinand proclaimed independence in 1908 the text was amended to name the country the Kingdom of Bulgaria and to replace Prince with tzar.

It was suspended again after the coups of 1934, led by Kimon Georgiev, and of 1944, organised by the Bulgarian Communist Party; in 1945 the People's Tribunal, which had not the status of a court, passed more than 10,000 sentences. The referendum of 1946, held under Soviet occupation, ended the monarchy, though the constitution made no provision for such a change, and on 4 December 1947 the Dimitrov Constitution replaced it.
tarnowskie-gory: Tarnowskie Góry, in German Tarnowitz, lies in Silesia in the Silesian Highlands near Katowice. Its name comes from Tarnowice, a local village, and góry, which in Old Polish meant mines. The German name was introduced in the late 18th century, after the Third Silesian War. In the Middle Ages the region was inhabited by Lechitic Polish tribes, and in the 10th century it became part of the emerging Polish state under Mieszko I.

An outbreak of plague in 1676-77 decimated the population. The Prussian army entered the town on 16 December 1740 during the first of the Silesian Wars, and in 1742 Austrian rule ended and Tarnowskie Góry fell under Prussia. Around 1780 Friedrich Wilhelm von Reden opened a government-controlled mine and a silver and lead foundry. Salomon Isaac, a Jewish trade agent and mining entrepreneur, contributed greatly to Silesian mining and metallurgy, although Jews were restricted or banned from the area.

In 1788 a Newcomen atmospheric engine was imported from Wales to drain the mines, and eventually eight steam engines were used. Drainage tunnels were later cut to replace them, and a 600-metre part of the Fryderyk adit is now a tourist route, the Black Trout Adit. A school of mining was begun in 1803, and the Upper-Silesian Brotherhood Cooperative, an insurance society for miners, had its headquarters in the town. The first railway, to Opole, arrived in 1857, and by the end of the century the town was becoming one of the largest marshalling yards in Europe.

Early in the 20th century the silver ore ran out and mining stopped. After the plebiscite that followed three Silesian uprisings of 1919-1921, the Tarnowitz district voted 61.7 percent to join Poland, although the city itself voted 82 percent for Germany, and in 1922 the town was returned to Poland.

The town, with 61,842 inhabitants in 2021, is in the Silesian Voivodeship. The Historic Silver Mine of Tarnowskie Góry is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Black Trout Adit has been a national Historic Monument since 2004, and the town has a museum opened in 1958 and the 16th-century Gwareks' bell-tower, named for the old Polish word for miners. The Gwarki Tarnogórskie festival has marked mining culture each September since 1957.
tarom: Tarom is a region and county of Zanjan province in Iran, with its capital at the city of Ab Bar. Historically it was divided into Upper Tarom and Lower Tarom, and medieval Arabic geographers wrote the name as at-Tarumayn, "the two Taroms". The mountainous Upper Tarom was counted as part of Daylam. The name was applied to a right-bank tributary of the Sefid Rud, and the region comprised the river and its own tributaries.

The chief place of Lower Tarom was the castle and town of Semiran, on the main highway to Sarab. The castle crowned a rocky mount above the lower town and had triple walls. Ibn Muhalhal, visiting about 943, called it one of the main strongholds of the Daylamite kings and said it had about 2,850 houses. The Buyid amir Fakhr al-Dawla took it in 989 from the Vahsudan dynasty, and Al-Muqaddasi wrote at about the same time of lions of gold and the sun and moon on its walls.

Nasir-i Khusraw, who passed in 1046 on his pilgrimage to Mecca, called Semiran the capital of Tarom and said a thousand men garrisoned the fortress, which had an underground conduit for water. By the early 1200s, when Yaqut al-Hamawi visited, the Nizaris had slighted it, though he still called it "a mother of castles". Yaqut also mentioned Qilat, a mountain fortress on the Daylam frontier that had belonged to the Nizaris of Alamut, with a town of markets and a many-arched masonry bridge below it.

The 14th-century author Hamdallah Mustawfi described the two Taroms in his Nuzhat al-Qulub as fertile, supplying most of the fruit of the city of Soltaniyeh, and populated mostly by Shafi'i Sunnis. Firuzabad had been the capital but was "a complete ruin", and Andar in Upper Tarom had replaced it. He divided the region into five districts, the largest around the Crown Castle (Qal'ah Taj) with about 100 villages, and gave their combined revenue as 64,000 dinars.

In 2019 Gilvan District was formed from the Central District, and the village of Gilvan became a city in 2024. The county had 46,641 people at the 2016 census. Tarom belongs to the Tarom-Hashtjin Metallogenic Province, an important epithermal region of Iran with lead, zinc, copper, iron and manganese, and gold deposits at Khalifeloo, Abbasabad and Chargar.
taromai: Taromai, whose name is also read Tarumoi and Tarumī, is known chiefly from Chinese records, which gave him the title of King of Sannan. He first sent to the Chinese emperor in 1415, presenting himself as heir to King Ōōso without saying clearly how he was related to him. By his report, Ōōso had been killed by his elder brother Tabuchi, who was in turn killed by local chiefs in favour of Crown Prince Taromai.

The account was unusual, since Okinawan rulers routinely led the Chinese to believe that the throne passed from father to son, and the historian Dana Masayuki has suggested it may have covered an illegitimate seizure of power. His last recorded contact with the Chinese court was in 1429. His name is also unusual in the Chinese records, as it seems to be a genuine Okinawan given name, Taru-mi: Tarū was a common name, and -mi a suffix used by the ruling elite.

Later Okinawan histories knew the King of Sannan as the Aji, or local ruler, of Ōzato, but did not know how many men had held the title. The Chūzan Seikan of 1650 tells of an unnamed King of Sannan who lost the support of his people and was overthrown by Shō Hashi, then Aji of Sashiki, and Sai Taku's edition of the Chūzan Seifu of 1701 largely followed it.

Sai On's edition of the Chūzan Seifu of 1725 changed the story. Drawing on Chinese diplomatic records, he added the tribute missions sent in Taromai's name, named Taromai as the last King of Sannan and placed the fall of Sannan in 1429, after the last mission. To fit this to the older narrative he had to divide Ōzato in two, treating Shō Hashi's early conquest as that of the Aji of Shimasoe-Ōzato and the King of Sannan as the Aji of Shimajiri-Ōzato. Diplomatic documents of Taromai are preserved in the Rekidai Hōan.
tarot: Early European playing cards were probably based on the Egyptian Mamluk deck, and the first records of them in Europe date to 1367 in Bern. The first documented tarot decks were recorded between 1440 and 1450 in Milan, Ferrara, Florence and Bologna, when additional trump cards with allegorical illustrations were added to the four-suit pack. The earliest documentation of the trionfi is a statement in the Florence court records of 1440 about the transfer of two decks to Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta. The oldest surviving cards are the Visconti-Sforza Tarot, painted in the mid-15th century for the rulers of the Duchy of Milan. The name tarocchi first appeared in Brescia around 1502.

A tarot pack has four suits of 14 cards each, with a separate 21-card trump suit and the Fool. Italian decks use swords, batons, coins and cups, and French-suited ones clubs, diamonds, hearts and spades. Trump order varied by region, perhaps from the 1440s. In Florence a larger deck of 97 cards, Minchiate, added astrological symbols and the four elements. Tarot spread to France and Switzerland during the Italian Wars, and the oldest Marseille deck is Philippe Vachier's of 1639.

Tarot was first a card game, and the earliest complete description of the rules of a French variant dates to 1637. The earliest evidence of divination is an anonymous manuscript from around 1750. In the 1780s Antoine Court and Jean-Baptiste Alliette, called Etteilla, popularised esoteric tarot in Paris. French occultists claimed links to ancient Egypt and Kabbalah, claims for which scholars find no historical evidence. Michael Dummett called them the subject of the most successful propaganda campaign ever launched.
tarquinius-priscus: According to Livy, Tarquinius came from the Etruscan city of Tarquinii and was first named Lucumo. Modern scholars note that lucumo was a title of political rank among the Etruscans, meaning king, so the tradition may have mistaken a title for a personal name. His father Demaratus was a Greek merchant from Corinth, who according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus belonged to the Bacchiadae and left the city when Cypselus overthrew them.

After inheriting his father's fortune, Lucumo was denied office at Tarquinii because his father was Greek-born. His wife Tanaquil, gifted in prophecy, persuaded him to move to Rome, where foreigners were said to be readily made citizens. Tradition tells that an eagle took his cap on the Janiculum and replaced it, an omen she read as a sign of kingship. In Rome he took the name Lucius Tarquinius and became the trusted adviser of King Ancus Marcius.

When Ancus died his sons were still boys. Tarquinius sent them off on a hunting trip and then won the Comitia Curiata with a speech, becoming the first king in Roman history to canvass for the throne. He is said to have fought the Latins, the Sabines and the Etruscans, held Rome's first triumph in Etruscan style, and added a hundred men from lesser noble families to the Senate, bringing it to two hundred.

The sources also credit him with building. He is said to have laid permanent seating for the Circus Maximus and to have built the Cloaca Maxima to drain the low ground for the Forum. He began the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill and a stone wall around the city, though neither was finished in his reign; the temple was dedicated under Tarquinius Superbus in 509 BCE. Tradition also gives Rome the fasces, the curule chair and the toga praetexta from him.

According to tradition, assassins organised by the sons of Ancus Marcius killed him with a blow of an axe to the head, and Tanaquil is said to have managed the transfer of power so that Servius Tullius took the throne. Modern historians treat most of the account as foundation legend shaped in a later age; Livy and Dionysius wrote about five hundred years after the events, relying on annalists who survive only in fragments. The 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica noted that the story of his Corinthian origins is chronologically impossible. Excavations beneath the Forum have found channels thought to belong to an early Cloaca Maxima.
tarquinius-superbus: Ancient accounts of the regal period mingle history and legend. Tarquin was said to be the son or grandson of Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of Rome. The oldest sources make him Priscus's son, but modern historians think that impossible under the traditional chronology. His mother was supposedly Tanaquil, who placed Servius Tullius on the throne after the sons of Ancus Marcius had Priscus assassinated.

Servius married his daughters to Tarquin and his brother Arruns. According to the tradition, the ambitious Tullia Minor and Tarquin conspired to bring about the deaths of her sister and of Arruns, and then married. Tarquin courted the patrician senators with presents, seated himself on the throne in the senate house, denounced Servius, and threw the aged king down the steps; Servius was murdered in the street by Tarquin's assassins.

Tarquin began by refusing to bury Servius and putting to death senators he suspected of loyalty to him. By not replacing them and not consulting the senate he reduced its size and authority. He made an ally of Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum, one of the most eminent Latin chiefs, by betrothing his daughter to him, and persuaded the Latins to renew their treaty with Rome.

He took the wealthy town of Suessa Pometia and with its spoils began the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill. When he could not take Gabii by arms, his son Sextus fled there, pretending to have been beaten, won command of its troops and, on a sign from his father, killed or banished its leading men. Tarquin is said to have ordered the excavation of the cloaca maxima, and, by one story, to have bought three of nine Sibylline Books from the Cumaean Sibyl after she burned the others.

In 509 BCE the pace and burden of his building had angered the Roman populace, and Tarquin marched against the Rutuli to besiege Ardea. In the story, his son Sextus Tarquinius raped Lucretia, the wife of Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, and she stabbed herself after telling her husband and father. Lucius Junius Brutus persuaded the comitia to revoke the king's imperium and send him into exile, and two consuls were elected in his place.

Tarquin sought help from Etruscan cities and from Lars Porsena of Clusium. In 499 or 496 BCE he joined Octavius Mamilius's Latin army, which Rome defeated. He then went to the court of Aristodemus at Cumae, where he died in 495 BCE. The expression tall poppy syndrome takes its name from Livy's tale of Gabii.
tarraco: The area was inhabited from the 5th century BCE by Iberians, who had commercial contacts with the Greeks and Phoenicians settled on the coast. Tarraco is first mentioned after Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus arrived at Empúries in 218 BCE at the start of the Second Punic War, which began the Roman conquest of Hispania. In 217 BCE reinforcements arrived under Publius Scipio, and the two brothers are credited with strengthening the fortifications and establishing a military port.

The Roman wall was probably built on top of an older Iberian one. Scipio Africanus used Tarraco as his winter base in 211 and 210 BCE, and the fishermen of the city served with their boats at the siege of Carthago Nova. The conquest of the peninsula took over 200 years, and Tarraco stayed a supply and winter base in the wars against the Celtiberians. Strabo says the governors of Hispania Citerior also resided there.

Julius Caesar probably made it a colonia around 45 BCE, as Colonia Iulia Urbs Triumphalis Tarraco. In 27 BCE Augustus replaced Hispania Citerior with the larger province of Hispania Tarraconensis, named for its capital, and spent time at Tarraco while directing the campaigns in Cantabria. The old Via Herculea became the Via Augusta, and the city flourished, with Pomponius Mela calling it the richest port on that coast. Galba lived there for eight years before being proclaimed emperor in 68 CE.

The amphitheatre and the provincial forum were probably built after Vespasian's reorganisation of the province, and Hadrian is thought to have held a conventus there in the winter of 122 to 123. Economic difficulties set in at the end of the 2nd century. Diocletian's reforms left Tarraco the capital of a much smaller province. The Visigoths under King Euric occupied it in 476, apparently without much destruction, and the Muslims arrived in 713 or 714, ending its ancient history.

Tarraco is the ancient name of the present city of Tarragona in Catalonia, and the oldest Roman settlement on the Iberian Peninsula. Its archaeological ensemble is one of the largest sites of Roman Hispania preserved in Spain, and UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 2000, citing its importance in Roman planning and urban design and its testimony to the Mediterranean world in antiquity.

The amphitheatre stands near the shore with large parts of its structure surviving. The Roman aqueduct of Les Ferreres, called the Devil's Bridge, crosses a valley about 4 kilometres from the city, and the Tower of the Scipios, a Roman tomb, lies 1.5 kilometres to the north-west.
tarrafal-camp: The camp stood in the village of Chão Bom, in the Municipality of Tarrafal, and was founded by Decree 26:539 of 23 April 1936, under the control of the secret police, the PVDE. Its official name was the Cape Verde Penal Colony, later the Chão Bom Work Camp. The site was chosen because it was remote, so that testimony would not reach the public, and because its climate was unhealthy, with little drinking water and many mosquitoes in the rainy season. Historian Fernando Rosas called it the peak of repression in Portugal.

The first 157 prisoners arrived from Lisbon on 29 October 1936, among them strikers of Marinha Grande and men of the Sailors' Revolt of 1936. They lived in canvas tents behind barbed wire and a deep ditch, and were made to work for 45 days in great heat building the walls and roads. Malaria and other diseases followed, and the doctor who came in 1937 had no medicine and only signed death certificates. In 1944, of 226 prisoners, 72 had never been tried and 55 had served out their sentences. The worst punishment was the Frigideira, the frying pan, a concrete block where temperatures reached 50 to 60 degrees Celsius and prisoners were given bread and water every other day.

Of the 340 Portuguese held in the first phase, 34 died, among them Bento Gonçalves, leader of the Portuguese Communist Party, in 1942, and Mário Castelhano of the General Confederation of Labor. Communist prisoners kept up political study in secret despite lacking paper and pencils. From 14 April 1961 the camp held militants of the liberation movements of Angola, Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde, about 230 in all, among them the writer Luandino Vieira from 1964 to 1972; a new punishment cell, the Holandinha, replaced the Frigideira. The camp was closed on 1 May 1974, a week after the Carnation Revolution.

After serving as a recruitment centre and barracks between 1975 and 1985, the camp became the Museum of Resistance in 2009. On 14 August 2016 the government of Cape Verde declared it a National Heritage Site, and 29 October, the day the first prisoners arrived, is kept as Antifascist Resistance Day.
tarragona: Tarragona stands on the Costa Daurada on the Mediterranean shore, around the mouth of the river Francolí. The Romans developed it on a coastal hill, some 75 to 90 metres above sea level, near an earlier Iberian settlement. Its position atop a high rock gave it the epithet arce potens Tarraco. The real founding date is unknown. One Catalan legend says it was named for Tarraho, eldest son of Tubal, and another attributes the name to Tearcon the Ethiopian, a pharaoh of the seventh century BCE.

During the Second Punic War the brothers Publius Cornelius Scipio and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus fortified Tarraco and made it a fortress and arsenal against the Carthaginians. It became the capital of Hispania Citerior and then of Hispania Tarraconensis, and also a bishopric seat. Augustus wintered there after his Cantabrian campaign and gave the city honorary titles. Its Jewish community, established in the Roman era, is among the oldest in Spain.

After the end of the Western Roman Empire the Vandals and the Visigoths took the city, and Visigothic rule ended with the Umayyad conquest of Hispania in 714. It was an important border city of the Caliphate of Córdoba between 750 and 1013. The County of Barcelona took it in 1117, and from 1129 to 1173 it was the capital of the short-lived Principality of Tarragona. It later belonged to the Principality of Catalonia within the Crown of Aragon until 1714.

In the Peninsular War the army of Louis-Gabriel Suchet besieged it from 5 May to 29 June 1811 and stormed the defences, killing or capturing almost all the Spanish garrison. In the Spanish Civil War it stayed with the Republic until Nationalist troops captured it on 15 January 1939.

The Archaeological Complex of Tàrraco is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The remains include parts of the Roman walls, the circus, the second-century amphitheatre and Les Ferreres Aqueduct, 217 metres long. Tarragona Cathedral dates from the 12th and 13th centuries and combines Romanesque and Gothic elements. The Santa Tecla Festival, held from 15 to 24 September, has been held since 1321, and the castells, human towers, are a living tradition there.
tartu: Tartu lies about 186 kilometres southeast of Tallinn on the Emajõgi river, which connects Lake Võrtsjärv with Lake Peipus. Archaeological evidence of permanent settlement on the site dates to as early as the 5th century CE. By the 7th century local inhabitants had built a wooden fortification on the east side of Toome Hill, and around the 9th and 10th centuries the settlement became an inland trading centre. The name is thought to derive from the Estonian word for aurochs, tarvas.

From the 13th century until the end of the 19th, the town was known in most of the world by variants of Dorpat. In 1262 the army of Prince Dmitri of Pereslavl captured and destroyed it but could not take the bishop's fortress on Toome Hill. In the 1280s Dorpat joined the Hanseatic League. In 1558 Tsar Ivan the Terrible began the Livonian War by besieging it, and the local bishop was imprisoned in Moscow, which ended local self-government. The city then passed between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and Sweden, which held it for good from 1625.

In 1708 Russian forces blew up the remaining fortifications and houses and deported the citizens to Russia, and with the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 the city became part of the Russian Empire. The Great Fire of 1775 destroyed most of the buildings in the centre, and the town hall was built between 1782 and 1789. In the second half of the 19th century Tartu was the cultural centre of the Estonians: it hosted the first song festival in 1869, the founding of the Vanemuine theatre in 1870 and of the Society of Estonian Literati in 1872. Much of the city was destroyed in the Second World War, and under Soviet rule the population almost doubled from 57,000 to over 100,000 between 1944 and 1991.

Tartu is often called the intellectual capital of Estonia. It is the seat of the Supreme Court of Estonia, the Estonian National Museum, whose new main building opened in 2016, and the Vanemuine theatre, the oldest Estonian-language theatre, and it is the birthplace of the Estonian Song Festivals. After independence was regained in 1991 the old town was renovated and St. John's Church, in ruins since the war, was restored.
tartus: Tartus lies on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean, on a coastal plain bordered to the east by the Syrian Coastal Mountain Range, whose limestone hills in places give way to basalt. Arwad, the only inhabited island on the Syrian coast, lies a few kilometres off the shore. The name derives from the Ancient Greek Antaradus, meaning the town facing Aradus, which became Tortosa in Latin and Ṭarṭūs in Arabic. It has a Mediterranean climate with mild, wet winters and hot, humid summers. The city was governed from Latakia until the 1970s, when Tartus Governorate was created.

Tartus was founded as a Phoenician colony of Aradus, the larger settlement on the island, and was called Antaradus. Little remains of it. In the Greco-Roman and Byzantine periods it had its own bishops, and bishops of Antaradus and of Aradus appear at councils from Chalcedon in 451 onward. The first chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary is said to have been built there in the 3rd century, and the city was favoured by Constantine for its devotion to her cult. Caliphate armies under Ubadah ibn al-Samit conquered it in 636, and Mu'awiya I built an amsar complex there.

Frankish forces captured the city in 1099 during the First Crusade. Raymond of Saint-Gilles recaptured it in February 1102 after a two-week siege, and in 1123 the Crusaders built the semi-fortified Cathedral of Our Lady of Tortosa over a Byzantine church popular with pilgrims.

In 1152 Tortosa was handed to the Knights Templar, who made it a military headquarters and about 1165 built a castle with a large chapel, an elaborate keep and thick double concentric walls. Nur ad-Din Zangi held it briefly. Saladin recaptured it in 1188, but some Templars kept the keep for another hundred years until it fell in 1291, the last Templar outpost on the Syrian mainland. They then held the island of Arwad for another decade. Under the Mamluks the city lost its prestige, which it regained under Ottoman rule through trade with Cyprus and Europe.

Muhammad Ali Pasha of Egypt conquered Tartus in 1832. The Ottomans regained it in 1839, and in 1840 British frigates and marines attacked the citadel without capturing it. Ottoman rule lasted until 1918.

Tartus is a major port and the second largest port city in Syria after Latakia, with a 2023 population estimated at 458,327. The historic centre is built on and inside the walls of the Templar fortress, whose moat still separates the old town from the modern city. The former cathedral, the Romanesque-Gothic Notre-Dame of Tartus of the 12th century, has housed the National Museum of Tartus since 1956.
taruga: Taruga lies in the Middle Belt of Nigeria and is one of many sites in the centre of the country where objects of the Nok culture have been excavated. Since 1945 similar figurines and pottery have been found across the area, often uncovered by chance by tin miners, with dates from before 500 BCE to 200 CE. The region was probably moister and more heavily wooded then than it is today, though still north of the zone of dense forest, and its people would have lived by farming and raising cattle.

As the climate slowly became drier, the people of the Nok culture may have moved south. On this view they could be among the ancestors of peoples such as the Igala, Nupe, Yoruba and Ibo, whose art shows likenesses to the earlier Nok works.

The early terracotta figurines of Taruga are decorated with bands of oblique comb stamping, parallel grooves, false relief chevrons and incised hatched triangles, designs that appear to have influenced the later traditions of Ife. Later styles resemble finds from Rim in Upper Volta, with twisted and carved roulettes. Many of the heads and busts may once have belonged to whole figures, which probably represented heroes and ancestors and were kept in shrines in village compounds. Pots were covered with raised dots made by a carved roulette, often joined by grooved lines in a net-like pattern. Both figurines and pottery were fired at low temperature and are fragile.

The furnaces bear on an open question. It has been suggested that iron smelting reached the region from North Africa, perhaps by way of Meroe, but it may equally have grown locally out of copper smelting, in which iron ore was used as a flux. The beehive and cylindrical furnaces of West Africa differ in form from those of North Africa and Mesopotamia, and the iron workers of Taruga seem to have pre-heated the air entering the furnace to reach higher temperatures.

A short blade of around the 4th century BCE was probably made by piling: smelted fragments were wrapped in clay, heated to 1200 °C, taken from the fire and forged into a single piece, a method that limited oxidation during the long heating. Its metal is unusually free of impurities.
tarut-island: The island covers 20.3 square kilometres and lies 6 km off the coast in Qatif Governorate, joined to the mainland by three causeways. Its two traditional harbours were Sanabes in the north-east and Darin in the south, and in early times its only source of water was a spring known as the Tarout Bath. The ancient Arabic name was apparently Ishtarut; Ptolemy's Geographia calls it Tharrō, and in the Middle Ages it was often called Dairin or Daryn after one of its towns.

The island linked Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley Civilisation and the Arabian Peninsula. Danish archaeologists excavated pottery there in 1968, and many steatite vessels from the hill of Tell Rafī'ah are carved with cats, nude men and motifs of the sea and fishing; the stone came from south-western Persia, but the carving seems to have been local. A dark grey statue of a naked man, 94 cm high and almost certainly Sumerian, was found by a ploughman in the 1950s. Villagers who linked it with jinn cut it in half and beheaded it, but it was restored.

In 676 CE a synod held at Darin by Patriarch George I of the Church of the East first required that a marriage be blessed by a priest to be valid. The foundations of the present castle date from the Uyunid dynasty, and the Portuguese built a military fort there between 1515 and 1521, during their control of trade through the Persian Gulf. They were forced to hand it over in 1559 and withdrew to Bahrain. The Treaty of Darin between Ibn Saud and the United Kingdom was signed on the island in 1915.

Tarout Castle stands on a small hill at the centre of the island, overlooking Al Deyrah, the oldest quarter, with its stone and mud buildings and narrow streets. Statues, copper and pottery vessels and weapons found on the island are displayed in Riyadh, the restored Sumerian statue in the National Museum there.
tasciovanus: Tasciovanus, also found as Tasciovantis, is known only from coins. He appears to have become king of the Catuvellauni around 20 BCE, ruling from Verlamion, and he is believed to have moved the tribal capital there from an earlier settlement near present-day Wheathampstead. Recent excavations on the southern plateau of the Ver valley found mid-first-century Roman pottery and Roman republican denarii minted between 100 and 80 BCE, evidence of a settlement there from the early 1st century BCE.

For a short time, around 15 to 10 BCE, he issued coins from Camulodunum, present-day Colchester, apparently displacing Addedomarus of the Trinovantes. He then struck coins again at Verlamion. The legend RICON stands for Rigonos, a Common Brittonic word for a great, divine or legitimate king. Other abbreviated names on his coins, such as DIAS, SEGO and ANDOCO, are usually read as the names of co-rulers or subordinate kings, though they may be mint-marks. He was succeeded by Cunobeline, who ruled mainly from Camulodunum, while Epaticcus, another son, extended his power westward into the lands of the Atrebates.

A genealogy in the medieval Welsh manuscript British Library Harley MS 3859 has the line Caratauc map Cinbelin map Teuhant, that is Caratacus, son of Cunobelinus, son of Tasciovanus. The three are in the right order though in the wrong historical setting, and the change in their names suggests a long oral tradition. Teuhant would be Techwant or Teichwant in modern Welsh.

Geoffrey of Monmouth's fictional Historia Regum Britanniae of 1136 turned him into Tenvantius, son of Lud. In this story he and his brother Androgeus were minors when their father died, so the throne passed to their uncle Cassibelanus. Tenvantius became Duke of Cornwall, fought against Julius Caesar and succeeded his uncle, and his son Kimbelinus had been raised at the court of Augustus. Middle Welsh versions name him Teneufan and Trahayant, and as Tenewan ap Lludd he is claimed as an ancestor of the Mathrafal dynasty in the Mostyn manuscript 117.
tasgetius: Tasgetius, in Gaulish Tasgetios or Tasgiitios, ruled the Carnutes, whose land corresponded roughly to the French departments of Eure-et-Loir, Loiret and Loir-et-Cher and was held to be the sacred centre of Gaul, where the druids met each year. The Carnutes, like several larger Gallic peoples, had once had kings but seem to have moved to an oligarchic or proto-republican government. Rome often found a single king easier to deal with than a fractious council, and Caesar presented the appointment of Tasgetius as a restoration of his family's former rank. His name comes from the Gaulish tasgos, badger.

His reign probably began late in 57 BCE, after Caesar's campaign against the Belgic peoples. According to Caesar, the killers acted openly and many Carnutes were among the instigators. Fearing that the whole people would defect, Caesar sent Lucius Plancus with a legion from the Belgian lands to winter among the Carnutes, find the men responsible and send them to him under arrest. Caesar blamed an anti-Roman faction; some modern scholars argue that ordinary Gallic politics were at work, and that Caesar exploited them and presented them as signs of a coming revolt.

Caesar praises Tasgetius for his goodwill, benevolentia, and for virtus, a quality he grants to only six people in his commentaries; the only other man of free Gaul so praised is Commius of the Atrebates, also made king by Caesar. Bronze coins inscribed Tasgiitios, showing a crowned head with an ivy leaf and the name Elkesovix and a winged horse on the reverse, are assumed to be his. A hoard found in 1956, thought to have been buried in 51 BCE, included them.

The overthrow of a king Caesar had appointed was one of the events that led to the great Gallic rising of 52 BCE under the Arvernian leader Vercingetorix. Caesar also records that the Carnutes were placed as clients under the Remi, Rome's most loyal Belgic ally, which the scholar George Long thought probably followed from the murder.
tashkent: Tashkent is in northeastern Uzbekistan, on a well-watered plain on the road between Samarkand and Shymkent, just across the border in Kazakhstan. It sits at the confluence of the Chirchiq River and several of its tributaries and is built on deep alluvial deposits up to 15 m deep. The city lies in an active tectonic area and suffers numerous tremors and occasional earthquakes. Its climate is Mediterranean with some humid continental influences: winters are cold and often snowy, and summers are long, hot and dry.

Abu Rayhan Biruni wrote that the name comes from the Turkic tash and the Persian kent, Stone City or City of Stones. The older name Chach has been traced by Ilya Gershevitch to an Old Iranian word for an area of water or lake, though Ünal criticises that derivation as based on too many assumptions and derives Čač from a Proto-Turkic word for stone.

Tashkent's history stretches back centuries as part of the ancient Silk Road. Before the influence of Islam in the mid-8th century, Sogdian and Turkic culture was predominant. Genghis Khan destroyed the city in 1219, after which it was rebuilt and profited from its place on the Silk Road. From the 18th to the 19th centuries it was an independent city-state, before being re-conquered by the Khanate of Kokand. The Russian Empire took Tashkent in 1865, and it became the capital of Russian Turkestan. In 1868 the Samarkand Kufic Quran was taken as a war trophy from Samarkand to Saint Petersburg, and the Bolsheviks returned it to Tashkent in 1923.

In Soviet times the city grew greatly and its population changed because of forced deportations from throughout the Soviet Union. Thousands of Pontic Greeks were displaced in the early 1940s, and about 11,000 refugees of the Greek Civil War were sent to Tashkent after 1949. Its population was 1,902,000 in 1983 and about 2,136,600 in 1991. The 1966 earthquake destroyed much of the city, which was rebuilt as a model Soviet city and was then the fourth-largest in the Soviet Union, after Moscow, Leningrad and Kiev. The Tashkent Metro, the first in Central Asia, opened in 1977.

Tashkent is the most populous city in Central Asia. Ethnic Uzbeks form the majority, and Uzbek is the main language, with Russian used as a lingua franca. Most of the ancient city was destroyed in the 1917 revolution and the 1966 earthquake. Surviving landmarks include the Kukeldash Madrasah, dating from the reign of Abdullah Khan II (1557-1598), Chorsu Bazaar, the Hazrati Imam Complex and the mausoleum of Qaffol Shoshi, built in 1542. The city marked 2,200 years of written history in 2009.
tashkent-declaration: Peace after the Indo-Pakistani War of 1965 was achieved on 23 September through interventions by the Soviet Union and the United States, both of which pushed the two countries towards a ceasefire to avoid an escalation that could draw in other powers. The Soviet Union then hosted a meeting in the city of Tashkent in Uzbekistan from 4 to 10 January 1966, hoping to create a more permanent settlement. The Soviet politician Aleksei Kosygin moderated between the Indian prime minister Lal Bahadur Shastri and the Pakistani president Muhammad Ayub Khan.

The declaration, signed on 10 January 1966, was hoped to be a framework for lasting peace. The Indian and Pakistani armies were to pull back to their pre-conflict positions, the pre-August lines, no later than 25 February 1966. Neither country would interfere in the internal affairs of the other. Economic and diplomatic relations were to be restored, prisoners of war were to be transferred in an orderly way, and both leaders were to work towards better bilateral relations.

Ministerial talks followed on 1 and 2 March 1966 as the declaration required, and though unproductive, diplomatic exchange continued through the spring and summer. Sharp differences over Kashmir left bilateral discussions without a resolution. The treaty was heavily criticised in both countries, where people had expected more concessions to their own side. In India it was faulted for containing no no-war pact and no renunciation of guerrilla warfare across Kashmir. Shastri died suddenly in Tashkent after it was signed, in circumstances described as mysterious, and conspiracy theories arose that he had been poisoned.

The Indian government has refused to declassify a report on his death, saying that it would harm India's foreign relations, cause disruption in the country and breach parliamentary privileges. In Pakistan the agreement caused widespread distress, and demonstrations and riots broke out while Ayub Khan was in seclusion. He addressed the nation on 14 January 1966 to explain it and was eventually able to quell the unrest, but the declaration greatly damaged his image and was one of the factors in his downfall in 1969.
tashkent-soviet: The Tashkent Soviet was founded on 2 March 1917, during the Russian Revolution, at an inaugural meeting of thirty-five workers from the Central Asian Railway. It was headed by a technician, I. I. Bel'kov. The next day a meeting in the local Duma set up an Executive Committee of Public Organisations to manage what it called the sociopolitical and economic life of the city.

Only two Central Asians, the lawyers Fayzulla Khodzhayev and Tashpolad Narbutabekov, sat on that committee. Tashkent was a divided city: the predominantly Muslim Central Asians generally lived in the Old City, while Russians and other Europeans lived in the New City, where the railway had been built. The Soviet set up its own provisions commission to fight what it called trader-marauders, a term soon applied to Central Asians alone, and it did not welcome a Muslim branch of the Social Democratic Party formed by Central Asian workers.

Many Central Asians nonetheless had high hopes of the post-tsarist era. The poet Sirajiddin Makhdum Sidqi wrote popular verse in support of the revolution, and veterans of the Jadid resistance to the draft of 1916, among them Munawar Qari, organised the Tashkand Muslim Council.

Before the revolution the Bolsheviks had little influence in Tashkent and no organisation of their own, so they worked with the Mensheviks. A Regional Soviet was formed by the first Regional Congress of workers' and soldiers' deputies between 7 and 15 April 1917, while the Executive Committee of the Tashkent Soviet, dominated by Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries, held sway in the city. The Turkestan Committee appointed in Petrograd refused to recognise the Soviets, and the Soviets in turn questioned the legitimacy of its every attempt to assert authority.

After the July Days in Petrograd many in Tashkent turned to the Bolsheviks, and on 21 July the Tashkent Social Democratic organisation adopted the call for all power to the Soviet. With food shortages critical in September and distrust of the Provisional Government growing, a crowd of thousands elected a presidium headed by a Bolshevik. When the Provisional Government fell, power passed to the Soviets.
tasker-h-bliss: Tasker Howard Bliss was born on 31 December 1853 in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, to George Ripley Bliss and Mary Ann Bliss. After a year at Bucknell, then Lewisburg University, he entered the United States Military Academy at West Point, where he excelled in languages, mathematics and tactics and graduated eighth in his class on 16 June 1875. Commissioned in the 1st Artillery, he returned to West Point in 1876 to teach French until 1882, and on 24 May 1882 he married Eleanora Emma Anderson. Their daughter Eleanora became one of the first women to gain a doctorate in geology, at Bryn Mawr College.

In 1885 Bliss taught at the Naval War College, which sent him to England, Germany and France to study their military schools, and from 1888 he was aide-de-camp to the Commanding General, John M. Schofield. In 1897 he went to Spain as military attaché, returning when war broke out in 1898. He was chief of staff of the 1st Division, I Army Corps, in Puerto Rico, and from December 1898 Collector of Customs for Cuba and the Port of Havana, later negotiating the ratification of the Cuban tariff treaty.

Made a brigadier general by Act of Congress, he became President of the Army War College in 1903. In the Philippine Islands he took over Moro Province after General Leonard Wood resigned over the First Battle of Bud Dajo.

Bliss became Assistant Chief of Staff in 1915 and Chief of Staff on 22 September 1917, and from November 1917 he was also the American Permanent Military Representative on the Supreme War Council. Retired for age on 31 December 1917, he was recalled by President Woodrow Wilson the next day and sent to Versailles. As a plenipotentiary at the Paris Peace Conference he signed the Treaty of Versailles for the United States.

From 1920 to 1927 Bliss was governor of the U.S. Soldiers Home in Washington, and in 1930 he was promoted to full general on the retired list. He died on 9 November 1930 and is buried in Arlington National Cemetery. Two Navy transports were named after him. Fort Bliss in Texas, often thought to honour him, is named after Lieutenant Colonel William Wallace Smith Bliss, a veteran of the Mexican War.
tasmola-culture: Everything known of the culture comes from the barrows, or kurgans, in which it buried its dead. A cemetery usually pairs a large barrow with a smaller one beside it, and the mounds stand in clusters of 10 to 15, often with a central passage, or dromos, leading to the burial. Early kurgans were large, 30 to 50 m across and 3 to 5 m high; later ones measured 15 to 25 m across and 0.5 to 1.5 m high. Characteristic finds are bronze arrowheads, daggers and belt ornaments, and the bronze and gold work shows the influence of the preceding Begazy–Dandybai culture.

Around 600 BCE groups from the Tasmola culture are thought to have settled in the southern Urals, where they contributed to the rise of the Sauromatian culture. In central Kazakhstan the Tasmola culture was followed by the Korgantas culture, to which the later kurgans belong. The Tasmola people may correspond to the Issedones of ancient Greek writers.

A genetic study published in Nature in May 2018 examined eight Sakas buried on the central steppe between about 900 and 500 BCE, most of them assigned to the Tasmola culture. It found about 56 per cent Western Steppe Herder ancestry and 44 per cent southern Siberian hunter-gatherer ancestry, more of the latter than in other peoples of the Scythian cultures. Its authors suggested that the central steppe Sakas were a major source of western Eurasian ancestry among the Xiongnu, and that the Huns emerged when the Xiongnu conquered Sakas.

A study of 2021 modelled them as roughly 50 per cent Khövsgöl Late Bronze Age, 45 per cent Western Steppe Herder and 5 per cent BMAC-like ancestry. Three outliers from Birlik carried about 70 per cent more Ancient Northeast Asian ancestry, suggesting recent migrants from the east, an ancestry also found among later Huns. The male lines were dominated by the R-M417 and Q-M242 lineages.
taspar-qaghan: Taspar, whose personal name was Ashina Açu, was the third son of Bumin Qaghan and of princess Wei Changle, and he became the fourth khagan of the First Turkic Khaganate. A passage in Sogdian on the Bugut stele has been read as a chain of his titles and epithets, including the steppe rank čor, the personal name Aču and the regnal name Tatpar Qaɣan. Scholars treat this reading as tentative, since damage to the stone and the Sogdian spelling allow several alternatives.

Taspar appointed his nephews Ashina Shetu and Börü as lesser khagans in the east and the west. He shifted his alliance from the Northern Zhou to the Northern Qi, sent a horse as a gift in 572 and gave asylum to the defeated Qi prince Gao Shaoyi, placing former Qi subjects who had fled or been captured under his command. He still kept good relations with the Zhou, sending them another horse in 574. Around the new year of 578 Gao Shaoyi declared himself emperor with Turkic military help.

Taspar attacked the Zhou repeatedly until the spring of 579, when he sought peace. Emperor Xuan of Northern Zhou offered him Princess Qianjin in marriage if he would surrender Gao Shaoyi, and Taspar refused. In 580, after Xuan's death, the regent Yang Jian sent the princess anyway and then had the official Heruo Yi bribe Taspar. Taspar invited Gao Shaoyi to a hunt, where Heruo Yi seized him; the prince was taken to Chang'an and exiled to what is now Sichuan.

Taspar died of illness in 581. He was converted to Buddhism by the Qi monk Huilin, for whom he built a pagoda. In his reign Sogdian Manichean refugees from Persia and Buddhist refugees from Qi and Zhou arrived in numbers, and these Sogdians devised the Göktürk runes to write Turkic, translating sutras such as the Nirvana Sutra in 575.

He left the throne to Talopien, son of his elder brother Muqan Qaghan, against the custom that it pass to the son of the eldest brother, Ishbara Qaghan. The council rejected the will, saying Talopien's mother was not of Turkic origin, and chose Amrak instead. Talopien's faction refused to accept him, and the dispute led to the civil war of 581 to 603, which greatly weakened the khaganate and began its long decline.
tassili-najjer: Tassili n'Ajjer, meaning plateau of rivers, is a mountain range and plateau in south-eastern Algeria at the borders of Libya and Niger, covering more than 72,000 square kilometres. Its highest point is Adrar Afao, at 2,158 metres, and the nearest towns are Djanet and Illizi. The range is mostly sandstone stained by desert varnish, and erosion has formed rock forests resembling a lunar landscape, nearly 300 natural rock arches in the south-east, deep gorges and permanent pools in the north.

Because of its height and the water-retaining sandstone, vegetation is more lush than in the surrounding desert, with open woodland of endangered Saharan cypress and Saharan myrtle. It is a national park and Biosphere Reserve and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1982.

The highlands show occupation from 5500 to 1500 BCE, mainly by transhumant pastoralists of the Neolithic who camped there in the dry season, while hearths and stone tumuli in the lowlands date between 6000 and 4000 BCE. Hunter-gatherers lived in the region between about 10,000 and 7500 years ago, and after 7500 years ago people organised into pastoral groups in response to an increasingly unpredictable climate.
Cattle were herded across wide areas as early as 3000 to 2000 BCE, followed by horses before 1000 BCE and then camels, whose arrival reflects the growth of trans-Saharan trade.

European study of Algerian rock art began in 1863. Westerners were widely introduced to Tassili through sketches by French legionnaires, particularly Lieutenant Charles Brenans in the 1930s, who brought the archaeologist Henri Lhote. Lhote returned several times between 1956 and 1970. His expeditions have been heavily criticised, his team being accused of faking images and of damaging paintings by brightening them for tracing and photography.

The rock art, first reported in 1910, includes about 15,000 engravings so far identified. The earliest pieces are presumed to be around 12,000 years old, although sources vary considerably, and most date to between 9,000 and 10,000 years ago or later. The subjects are large wild animals such as antelopes and crocodiles, cattle herds, and humans hunting and dancing. The art falls into five traditions: Archaic, Round Head, Bovidian or Pastoral, Horse and Camel. The Round Head paintings include some of the oldest and largest exposed rock paintings in Africa, with figures over five metres tall, and their concentration in particular places suggests ritual centres.

The Horse period shows chariots and riders beside Libyan-Berber inscriptions that remain undeciphered. The Camel period coincides with caravan routes that carried salt, goods and enslaved people across the Sahara.
tassilo-iii-of-bavaria: Tassilo was the son of Duke Odilo of Bavaria and Hitrud, a daughter of Charles Martel. When Odilo died in 748, Tassilo was still a child, and Pepin the Short's half-brother Grifo tried to seize the duchy. Pepin, then Mayor of the Palace, removed Grifo and installed Tassilo as duke under Frankish overlordship, acting as his guardian. According to the Royal Frankish Annals, Tassilo became Pepin's vassal in 757 at an assembly at Compiègne and swore numerous oaths. One scholar, K. L. Roper Pearson, suggests that the annalist reworked the account to stress Charlemagne's overlordship.

Around 760 Tassilo married Liutperga, a daughter of the Lombard king Desiderius, continuing a tradition of Lombardo-Bavarian connections. He travelled several times to Italy to see his father-in-law and to build relations with the pope. When his cousins Charles and Carloman took power among the Franks in 768, he was reportedly regarded as a kingly ruler. That year he founded Gars Abbey on the Inn, and in 769 he issued the foundation charter of Innichen Abbey at Bolzano. He also founded Kremsmünster Abbey. Historians agree that he acted as a sovereign but did not intend to become king himself.

In 772 he sent his son Theodo to Italy to be baptised by Pope Adrian I in Rome on 19 May. In 773 an embassy he sent to the pope was blocked by Charles, who distrusted his alliances with Saxons, Wends and Avars. Tassilo could not protect the pope against Lombard expansion, which may explain why Rome later gave him no support against Charlemagne.

In 788 the Franks accused Tassilo of defaulting on his military duty to Pepin by leaving the campaign in Aquitaine in 763. The Royal Frankish Annals say he "brushed aside his oaths and all his promises and sneaked away on a wicked pretext". Roper Pearson suggests this began a campaign to portray him as an oath-breaker unfit to rule, and Stuart Airlie argues that Charlemagne removed him because of his greater power and independence. At a diet at Ingelheim in 788 Tassilo was deposed and entered a monastery. In 794 the Synod of Frankfurt compelled him to renounce his and his family's claims to Bavaria. He reportedly died at Lorsch Abbey. His daughters Cotani and Rotrud were forced to become nuns in 788.
tata-steel: The Tata Iron and Steel Company, known as TISCO, was founded by Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata and established by Sir Dorabji Tata on 26 August 1907 in Jamshedpur. It began pig iron production in 1911 and steel production in 1912. During the First World War it kept operating by supplying steel for the war effort in India. In 1920 TISCO and Burmah Shell formed the Tinplate Company of India as a joint venture, to meet the demand for tinplate that arose after the war. By 1939 TISCO operated the largest steel plant in the British Empire.

The company launched a modernisation and expansion programme in 1951, which was scaled up in 1958 to reach a capacity of two million metric tonnes a year. By 1970 it employed about 40,000 people in Jamshedpur and 20,000 in neighbouring coal mines.
