Two attempts were made to nationalise it: Prime Minister Indira Gandhi tried in 1971, and Prime Minister Morarji Desai in 1979, encouraged by Industry Minister George Fernandes and Steel Minister Biju Patnaik. Both failed, the second halted after protests from labour unions. The company was renamed Tata Steel in 2005.

After 2004 it grew by acquisition. It bought the steel-making operations of Singapore's NatSteel in 2004 and a majority stake in Thailand's Millennium Steel in 2005. In 2006 it bid for the Anglo-Dutch company Corus against a counteroffer from Brazil's Companhia Siderúrgica Nacional, and secured it on 31 January 2007 with a final bid of 608 pence per share, valuing Corus at £6.7 billion. Corus then produced four times more steel a year than Tata Steel. Later, in 2017, it acquired Bhushan Steel through insolvency proceedings, and in 2022 the Tata Group merged seven of its metal companies into Tata Steel.

Tata Steel introduced labour policies early. It adopted an eight-hour working day in 1912, free medical care in 1915 and schools for employees' children in 1917. Paid leave, a provident fund and accident compensation followed in 1920, vocational training in 1921, maternity benefits in 1928, profit-sharing bonuses in 1934 and a retirement gratuity in 1937.

The European business came under strain after the Corus purchase, from oversupply, labour unions, cheap Chinese imports and pressure to decarbonise. Tata Steel sold its long products division in Scunthorpe in April 2016, and in October 2021 it split its European business into Tata Steel Netherlands and Tata Steel UK. On 11 September 2024 Tata Steel UK announced that 2,500 jobs would be lost at Port Talbot. Its Dhamra Port in Odisha drew criticism from Greenpeace and others for harm to local ecology, and the company said it was working with the IUCN on standards.
tatar-assr: The resolution creating the republic was signed on 27 May 1920 and it was proclaimed on 25 June 1920, with Kazan as its capital. Its territory had before the October Revolution of 1917 belonged to the Kazan, Simbirsk and Ufa governorates of Imperial Russia. In 1921 the republic, like the neighbouring Volga region, was struck by a drought that caused mass famine, and in 1921–22 it received more than 8 million poods of seeds and 6 million poods of food supplies from other regions.

During the 1920s and 1930s the republic changed from a mainly agrarian economy to an agrarian-industrial one, and its industry grew faster than the average of the Russian Soviet republic and of the Soviet Union. The largest machine-building, chemical and light-industry plants of the autonomy were built under the first Five-Year Plans.

The number of Tatar workers, technicians and engineers at large enterprises rose from 3,100 in 1921 to 16,400 in 1932. Kazan was the only industrial hub apart from two plants, and in 1932 construction began there of the aviation complex Kazmash. Agriculture was collectivised, with the first Machine Tractor Station founded in 1930, and the republic was awarded the Order of Lenin on 3 January 1934.

During the Second World War factories and engineers from Moscow and the east of the country were evacuated to the republic, among them Moscow Aviation Plant No. 22, moved to Kazan in the autumn of 1941. After the war the oil and gas industry grew rapidly with the development of the Romashkino oil field.

9 million tons in 1970, and from 1956 the republic led the Soviet Union in oil production for a long period. The Druzhba pipelines carried oil to the COMECON countries, and plants were built at Nizhnekamsk, Bugulma and Almetyevsk, with the Kama Automobile Plant near Naberezhnye Chelny begun in the 1970s.

The republic received the Order of the October Revolution on 24 June 1970, for the 50th anniversary of its founding, and the Order of Friendship of Peoples on 29 December 1972. On 30 August 1990 it was renamed the Tatar Soviet Socialist Republic, and it later became the Republic of Tatarstan.
tatars: The name Tatar possibly referred first to the Tatar confederation, which Genghis Khan incorporated into the Mongol Empire. Western cartographers later applied the term, often spelled Tartar, to anyone from the northern and central Asian landmass then known as Tartary. The name became that of populations of the former Golden Horde in Europe, such as those of the Kazan, Crimean, Astrakhan, Qasim and Siberian Khanates. The Persian word is first recorded in the 13th century in reference to the hordes of Genghis Khan. Studies of ancestry suggest that the three main groups, the Volga, Crimean and Siberian Tatars, formed independently of one another.

The Volga Tatars descend from Kipchaks of the Golden Horde or from Volga Bulgars who survived the Mongol conquest of 1236 to 1237. About 40 thousand Tatars arrived with Khan Uluk-Muhammad in 1438 to 1445 when the Kazan Khanate was formed. Its conquest by Ivan IV in 1552 followed a six-month siege.

The Crimean Tatars formed between the 13th and 17th centuries, mainly from Kipchaks and Ottoman Turks. Crimea passed to the Giray dynasty, founded by Hacı Giray after an embassy invited him from Lithuania in 1441.

In 1502 the Crimean Khanate defeated the Great Horde, and it was among the strongest powers in Eastern Europe until the early 18th century, formally a vassal of the Ottoman Empire. A major source of income was frequent raids into Eastern Europe and the Caucasus for slaves.

Russia annexed it in 1783, and at least 800 thousand Tatars left Crimea by the early 20th century. In May 1944 the Soviet State Defense Committee ordered the deportation of all Crimean Tatars to Central Asia, and 46 per cent of them are said to have died during the deportation and the first years of exile.

Tatars settled in the Polish-Lithuanian lands between the 13th and 17th centuries. The Lipka Tatars first settled in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania at the beginning of the 14th century, and Grand Duke Vytautas invited a further, Muslim wave towards the end of it. The grand dukes encouraged the migrations because of the Tatars' reputation as skilled warriors, and the settlers were granted szlachta (noble) status. Estimates for the 17th century put their number at about 15,000, in about 60 villages with mosques.

They kept their religion and culture through royal privileges and internal autonomy, and were allowed to marry Christians, which was uncommon in Europe at the time. By the 18th century they had adopted the local language. The May Constitution of 1791 gave them a seat in the Sejm. Henryk Sienkiewicz's historical novels made their role well known in Poland.
tatarstan: Tatarstan lies in the centre of the East European Plain, about 800 kilometres east of Moscow, between the Volga and the Kama rivers. It covers 68,000 square kilometres and borders Kirov, Ulyanovsk, Samara and Orenburg oblasts and the republics of Mari El, Udmurtia, Chuvashia and Bashkortostan. Its capital and largest city is Kazan. Oil, natural gas and gypsum are its main natural resources.

The earliest known organised state within its present boundaries was Volga Bulgaria (c. 700 to 1238), a mercantile state with trade contacts across Inner Eurasia, the Middle East and the Baltic. Islam was introduced by missionaries from Baghdad around the time of Ibn Fadlan's journey in 922. The Golden Horde and the Khanate of Kazan followed, until Russia conquered the khanate in 1552. In the 19th century the region became a centre of Jadidism, an Islamic movement that preached tolerance of other religions.

During the Civil War of 1918 to 1920 Tatar nationalists tried to found an independent Idel-Ural State with the neighbouring Bashkirs. The Bolsheviks, who had at first supported it, arrested members of its parliament in March 1918. The Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was established on 27 May 1920, with boundaries that did not include a majority of the Volga Tatars. On 30 August 1990 Tatarstan declared its sovereignty. A constitution approved by about 62 per cent of voters in 1992 defined it as a sovereign state, but the Russian Constitutional Court declared the referendum and constitution unconstitutional. Since the 2002 text, the constitution defines Tatarstan as part of the Russian Federation.

Tatarstan is a republic of the Russian Federation. Its two state languages are Tatar and Russian, and the official script is Cyrillic. The 2021 census counted 4,004,809 inhabitants, among them about 2 million Tatars and 1.5 million Russians, with Chuvash, Mari and Udmurts in smaller numbers. Most Tatars are Sunni Muslims, and a minority, the Keräşen Tatars, are Orthodox Christians. Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the republic: the Kazan Kremlin, the Bulgarian State Museum-Reserve, and the Assumption Cathedral and Monastery of the town-island of Sviyazhsk.
tatev-monastery: The Tatev plateau was in use before Christianity, when it held a pagan temple, replaced by a modest church after the Christianization of Armenia in the 4th century. Tradition derives the name from Eustateus, a disciple of Thaddeus the Apostle who preached and was martyred in the region. A folk legend instead has a builder falling into the gorge and calling "Ta Tev", Armenian for "give me wings". The historian Stepanos Orbelian describes a new church built beside the old one in 848 with the help of Prince Philip of Syunik, and Bishop Hovhannes later won the support of Prince Ashot of Syunik for a larger monastery.

Tatev became a feudal institution. Peasants of Tsouraberd and other villages rejected its authority, and their protests twice grew into uprisings that lasted, with interruptions, until 990, when King Vasak of Syunik razed Tsouraberd. The bishopric owned 47 villages and received tithes from 677 others. In 940–950 Bishop Hakob tried to secede from Etchmiadzin and was anathematised by Catholicos Anania Mokatsi.

The fortified complex has three churches, a library, a refectory, a bell tower and a mausoleum. The church of Saints Paul and Peter, the oldest surviving building, was built between 895 and 906 as a domed basilica, with bas-relief portraits of Ashot and Princess Shushan on its eastern façade.

Frescoes added in 930 were painted by artists invited from Constantinople working with Armenian painters, and little survives. The Holy Mother of God Church was added in 1087, and Saint Gregory the Illuminator's was replaced in 1295 under Bishop Stepanos Orbelian. Outside the walls stands an olive press, one of the best preserved in Armenia, and near the cathedral stands the Gavazan, a column about eight meters tall crowned by a khachkar-type cross, which sways without falling.

A university operated at Tatev between 1390 and 1434. In the early 1340s Hovhan Vorotnetsi came from Gladzor and, with the patronage of the Orbelian princes, organised it in three departments: scriptures and the humanities, the arts of the book including miniature painting, and music. After his death in 1388 Grigor Tatevatsi became abbot, and teaching extended to the Old and New Testaments, the church fathers, Plato, Aristotle and Porphyry.

Its scholars opposed the Fratres Unitores, an Armenian branch of the Dominican order, and helped persuade the authorities to return the supreme patriarchal throne from Sis to Etchmiadzin, achieved in 1441. The university ceased to function after the invasions of Shah Rukh in 1434.
tatiana-proskouriakoff: Tatiana Avenirovna Proskouriakoff was born in Tomsk, in the Tomsk Governorate of the Russian Empire, the daughter of a chemist and a physician. During the First World War the family went to the United States, where Tsar Nicholas II had asked her father to oversee the production of munitions, and the Russian Revolution kept them there. They lived in Ohio and then in Lansdowne, Pennsylvania, where she graduated as valedictorian of her class. She took American citizenship in 1924.

In 1926 she enrolled at the Pennsylvania State College School of Architecture, graduating in 1930 as the only woman in her class. As a graduate student at the University of Pennsylvania she drew archaeological illustrations as a volunteer at the University Museum, and through its assistant curator Linton Satterthwaite she joined its excavations at Piedras Negras, in the Usumacinta region, in 1936–37, first to draw the ruined buildings.

Her reconstruction drawing of the Piedras Negras acropolis caught the attention of Sylvanus Morley. Unable to persuade the Carnegie Institution of Washington to hire her, he raised funds for her to travel to Copán and Yucatán in 1939, and in the early 1940s she became a research associate there. Her analysis of 1942 established that the ruins of Takalik Abaj in Guatemala were in part Maya. From 1950 to 1955 she worked at the excavations of Mayapan.

While tracing how the style of Maya sculpture changed over time, she found that the dates on the stelae marked events in the lives of rulers, and from their pattern she showed a sequence of seven rulers over two hundred years. In 1958 she moved to the Peabody Museum at Harvard University, as honorary curator of Maya art, and worked there until she retired in 1977. In 1967 she wrote the preface to the English translation of a monograph by Yuri Knorozov on Maya writing.

She received the Alfred V. Kidder Medal in 1962 and was elected to the American Philosophical Society in 1981. In her last years she had Alzheimer's disease, and she died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 30 August 1985. Her history of the Maya, on which she had worked for over twenty years, was published after her death. On Easter Sunday 1998 her colleague David Stuart carried her ashes to Piedras Negras, where they were interred at the summit of the Acropolis she had once drawn.
tatmadaw: The name Tatmadaw literally means Royal Armed Forces in Burmese. The same name is applied to the army of the Burmese monarchy from the 9th to the 19th centuries, which covers the forces of the Pagan dynasty, the Ava Kingdom, the Toungoo dynasty and the Konbaung dynasty.

That army had a small standing force of a few thousand men to defend the capital and palace, and a much larger conscript army raised in wartime under the ahmudan system. It was defeated by the British over a span of six decades in the 19th century. Under British rule the colonial government mistrusted the Burmese and kept them out of its forces until it lifted the ban on recruits in 1937.

At independence in 1948 the Tatmadaw was weak, small and disunited, with the most serious tension between Karen officers from the British Burma Army and Burmese officers from the Patriotic Burmese Force. Since then it has faced ethnic insurgencies, especially in Chin, Kachin, Kayin, Kayah and Shan states. In February 1953 it fought Kuomintang troops under General Li Mi, who had invaded Burma from the frontier, in Operation Naga Naing, which ended in a defeat for the Tatmadaw. General Ne Win took control in a coup in 1962 and tried to build an autarkic society called the Burmese Way to Socialism.

After the violent repression of nationwide protests in 1988 the military formed the State Law and Order Restoration Council, held elections in 1990, ignored the victory of the National League for Democracy and imprisoned its leader Aung San Suu Kyi. The Tatmadaw rewrote the constitution in 2008, and the pro-military Union Solidarity and Development Party won the 2010 elections, which most opposition groups boycotted.

The National League for Democracy won in 2015. After the USDP lost another election in 2020, the Tatmadaw annulled the result and deposed the civilian government, and a renewed civil war followed. In Rakhine State the conflict between Buddhists and Rohingya Muslims escalated, and the Rohingya minority has faced oppression and, from 2017, what has been called genocide.

Officially called the Defence Services, the Tatmadaw comprises the army, navy and air force, with the army by far the largest and the one that has fought most of the 40 or more insurgent groups since 1948. Under the 2008 constitution the Commander-in-Chief of Defence Services leads the Tatmadaw, certain actions need the approval of the eleven-member National Defence and Security Council, and the president has no command role. A quarter of the seats in both houses of the legislature, the Pyidaungsu Hluttaw, are reserved for military appointees.
tattooed-serpent: Tattooed Serpent, Obalalkabiche in Natchez and Serpent Piqué in French, was war chief of the Natchez of the Grand Village, near present-day Natchez. The name went with the office, which was always held by the younger brother of the paramount ruler, whose title was Yak-stalchil, the Great Sun. The Tattooed Serpent who died in 1725 had been preceded by his own maternal uncle, who died in 1700 and bore the same name while in office. As the emblem of his office he wore an elaborate tattoo of a serpent circling his body from his foot to his mouth.

With his brother the Great Sun he allied the Natchez with the French colonists, and he was a friend of the colonist and chronicler Antoine-Simon Le Page du Pratz. In 1723 he helped the French negotiate the peace that ended the Second Natchez War, in which the Natchez of the White Apple Village had attacked them. According to the chronicle of Dumont de Montigny, his sister, called La Glorieuse by the French, said that he was like a Frenchman.

When he died in 1725 the Great Sun was so stricken that he wanted to follow him in death, and Le Page du Pratz prevented him. Following Natchez custom, a number of commoner servants were put to death by garrotting. According to Le Page du Pratz, two of his wives, his sister La Glorieuse, his first warrior, his doctor, his head servant and the servant's wife, his nurse, a maker of war clubs and several old women chose to die and be buried with him, and an infant was strangled by its parents. The retainers' faces were painted red and they were drugged with large doses of nicotine or Jimson weed.

His body was carried on a litter of cane matting and cedar poles to the temple on a low platform mound, where the retainers were strangled. He was buried in a trench in the temple floor and they in other places on the mound; months later the bones were cleaned and kept as bundle burials in the temple. His successor was his sister's second eldest son, and both he and the Great Sun were followed by much younger men. As the pro-British White Apple village gained influence the alliance with the French weakened, leading to the Natchez Massacre of 1729.
tatya-tope: Tatya Tope was born Ramachandra Panduranga Yewalkar into a Marathi Deshastha Brahmin family at Yeola, near Nasik. An official statement names his father as Panduranga Yewalkar and his mother as Rukhma Bai. He was a personal adherent of Nana Saheb of Bithoor. A witness at his trial described him as a man of middling stature, with a wheat complexion, who always wore a white turban. British letters were confused about him, calling him minister of Baroda in one and the same person as Nana Saheb in another.

After the rebellion at Kanpur broke out on 5 June 1857, Nana Saheb became its leader and was declared Peshwa in late June, after the British at Cawnpore had surrendered on 25 June. Tope acted in Nana's name from Bithur. He was one of the leaders involved in the killing on 27 June 1857 of 180 women and children after the British agreed to surrender. He held a defensive position until driven out on 16 July 1857, and was defeated again in the Second Battle of Cawnpore, which began on 19 November 1857 and lasted seventeen days, when Sir Colin Campbell counterattacked. He then took shelter with the Rani of Jhansi.

He helped Rani Lakshmibai escape the British assault on Jhansi. Together with Rao Saheb, a nephew of Nana Saheb, they took Gwalior Fort and proclaimed Hindavi Swaraj, or Hindu self-rule, in the name of Nana Saheb Peshwa. After losing Gwalior, Tope and Rao Saheb fled to Rajputana, where he persuaded the army of Tonk to join him.

Tope continued resistance as a guerrilla in the jungles after the revolt was put down. He won the Siege of Charkhari against Ratan Singh and replaced artillery lost at the Banas River, then moved towards Indore with the British under General John Michel in pursuit. He and Rao Saheb divided their forces, joined again in October and were defeated at Chhota Udaipur.

At his trial Tope admitted the charges but said he could be held accountable only to his master, the Peshwa. He was executed on 18 April 1859 at Sipri. Every year the state government and local people pay tribute to him on that day at a Shaheed Mela. Some writers, among them Srinivas Balaji Herdikar in his book The 1857, have claimed that Tope was not hanged and that another man, Narayan Rao Bhagvat, was hanged in his place.
tau-american-samoa: Taʻū is the largest inhabited island of the Manuʻa Islands and the easternmost volcanic island of the Samoan Islands. In the early 19th century it was sometimes called Opoun. It is the eroded remnant of a hotspot shield volcano with a caldera complex on its south face. Lata Mountain, at 931 metres, is the highest point in American Samoa, and the south coast has sea cliffs rising to 3,000 feet. The island has a land area of 44.31 square kilometres and had 790 people at the 2010 census.

On its western coast the adjoining villages of Lumā and Siufaga are together called Taʻū village, named capital of the Manuʻa Islands. The south-eastern half of the island is part of the National Park of American Samoa, which includes the ancient sacred site of Saua, considered the birthplace of the Polynesian people.

In ancient times the three islands of the Manuʻa Group formed one polity, and Taʻū was its main centre of authority, home of the Tui Manuʻa paramount chieftaincy. In 1986 researchers found ceramic-bearing sites in Taʻū village, including a sherd of Polynesian Plain Ware, and test excavations reached deeper layers of the Ancestral Polynesian period.

On 13 June 1722 Jacob Roggeveen of the Dutch West India Company sighted the island. The people placed offerings of food along the beach for what they called the Sailing Gods, and several men paddled out in outrigger canoes and climbed aboard to trade coconuts for metal nails. After barely two hours Roggeveen sailed west.

On 11 March 1900 Commander Benjamin Franklin Tilley anchored off Taʻū village and asked the Tui Manuʻa to join the chiefs of Tutuila in signing a Deed of Cession to the United States. At a meeting the next day, Tui Manuʻa Elisala questioned the right of foreign powers to interfere in what he considered a sovereign state. He acknowledged American sovereignty in general terms and accepted its protection, but refused to cede his own lands on Taʻū. The island was where Margaret Mead, then aged 23, carried out the research in the 1920s that she published in 1928 as Coming of Age in Samoa. A hurricane in early 1987 destroyed nearly all the homes on the island.

Taʻū forms part of the Manuʻa District of American Samoa with Ofu and Olosega, and is divided into three counties: Faleāsao, Fitiʻuta and Taʻū. The Taʻū unit of the national park covers about 2,025 hectares and is the park's largest section. Since 2016 the island has drawn almost all its electricity from a solar array with battery storage.
tauke-khan: Tauke Khan, in full Tawakkul Muhammad Bahadur Qazi Khan, was born in 1635, a son of Jahangir Khan of the Kazakh Khanate. After Jahangir Khan died in 1652, Erdeni Batyr, ruler of the Jungars, sharply increased his military pressure on the khanate in an attempt to conquer it. Erdeni Batyr died in 1670 and was followed by Galdan Boshugtu Khan and later by Tsewang Rabtan, so that the Jungar threat lasted through the whole of Tauke's life.
During these invasions a weak ruler named Bahadur Khan had taken the Kazakh throne. The Kazakhs soon deposed him, which opened the way for Tauke Muhammad, who began to rule in 1680.

From 1698 the Kazakhs divided their khanate into juzes, and keeping them united became a hard task. Tauke remained khan of all three and held the Kazakhs together, earning, like his father before him, the honorific title Shah-i-Turan, Persian for King of Turan. In 1692 he had made contact with Peter I of Russia, and the Russian Empire afterwards lowered its trade taxes, known as the bazh tax.

In 1710 he united the three juzes at Kuntobe, near the city of Tashkent, and fought the Jungars at a place named Augyr, where he won a victory over them. He is also known for refining the Kazakh code of laws and issuing it again under the title Jetı Jarğı, the Seven Charters.

After Tauke's death the Great juz, the Middle juz and the Little juz were no longer able to follow a single policy. Abu'l Khair Khan of the Little juz was in name the senior khan of the whole Kazakh Khanate, but in practice each juz was ruled on its own by its own khan, and Tauke is remembered as the last ruler to keep the three together.
taunggyi: Taunggyi lies at an elevation of 1,436 metres on a high basin among the mountains of eastern Myanmar, and unlike many towns it is built along the mountain ridges rather than on a valley floor. Its name means big mountain in Burmese and refers to a ridge on its east, part of the Shan Hills, whose high point is called Taung-chun, the Spur. The city has a humid subtropical climate with a dry winter from December to March and a wet summer from April to November, and it is known as a cool hill station. It is 635 kilometres from Yangon by road.

Before the town was founded, villages such as Mon Che, Hum Bwa and Oo See stood in the area under the Nyaungshwe sawbwas. After the British annexation of Upper Burma in 1885 the colonial administration first put its headquarters for the Shan States at Maing Thauk (Fort Stedman) on Inle Lake, but malaria and the damp, low ground made it unsuitable. In 1894 the offices moved to the higher plateau where the village of Taunggyi stood, and the town was planned as a hill station on a grid of streets. By 1906 it housed about 1,000 buildings and was the residence of the British Superintendent of the Southern Shan States.

After independence in 1948 Taunggyi remained the capital of Shan State. Its position on the road to Kengtung and the Thai border made it a junction for trade, and migration brought a mixed population of Pa-O, Shan, Intha and Burmese-Chinese communities.

Taunggyi is the capital of Shan State and its administrative, commercial and educational centre, with several universities. National Highway 4 links it with Meiktila to the west and Kengtung and the Thai border to the east, while the nearest airport is at Heho. The city has Buddhist monasteries, the cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Taunggyi, a Baptist church, mosques and Chinese temples, and a Shan State Cultural Museum. The Tazaungdaing festival, which marks the end of the rainy season, is marked by the Taunggyi Hot Air Balloon Festival. Inle Lake and the Kekku Pagodas, with hundreds of stupas dating from the 16th century, lie nearby.
taunus: The Taunus is the southeastern part of the Rhenish Slate Mountains. This low mountain range is about 75 kilometres long from south-west to north-east and about 35 kilometres wide, and covers some 2,700 square kilometres. The Rhine and the valley of the Lahn bound it on the west and north, the Main and the Rheingau on the south, and the plain of the Wetterau on the east. It is divided into the Vordertaunus, the Hohe Taunus, the Hintertaunus and the Idstein Depression. The highest parts, in the Feldberg massif, are wooded, colder and wetter than the lowlands around them.

Its rocks are mostly slates, phyllites and sandstones laid down in the Ordovician to Devonian periods. Taunus quartzite, a very weather-resistant rock, forms many summits, among them the Altkönig and the Kleiner Feldberg. Iron ore, silver ore and roofing slate were mined in the Lahn area from the 17th to the 20th century, and between Idstein and Usingen pits were worked from the late Middle Ages. The last active lead and silver mine, at Heftrich, closed around 1924.

The Roman frontier, the Limes, was built across the Taunus, and the Saalburg, a restored Roman fort, now houses a museum. After the fall of the Limes in 259 or 260 CE the Alamanni settled in the range, and Alemannic cemeteries survive in its southern foothills. Around 500 CE, after the Battle of Tolbiac, the area passed to the Frankish confederation. The Celtic ring walls on the Altkönig are built of Taunus quartzite.

Until the late 18th century the range was known simply as die Höhe, the height, a name kept in Bad Homburg vor der Höhe and Rosbach vor der Höhe. The name Taunus comes from the Annals of Tacitus, which mention a fort in monte Tauno, probably near present-day Friedberg. In past centuries the Taunus became known among aristocrats for its hot springs.

Several spa towns lie in the Taunus. Bad Schwalbach is mentioned in documents from the 16th century, and Bad Ems has been one of the most reputed therapeutic spas in Germany since the 17th century. By the 19th century the best-known spa towns were Wiesbaden, Bad Homburg vor der Höhe, Bad Nauheim and Bad Soden am Taunus. Groundwater from the quartzite, pumped through four tunnels, contributes much to the water supply of Wiesbaden. The Ford Taunus car line is named after the range.
taurus-mountains: The Taurus Mountains are a mountain complex in southern Turkey, extending in a curve from Lake Eğirdir in the west to the upper reaches of the Euphrates and Tigris rivers in the east. They form part of the Alpide belt of Eurasia and were known in antiquity also as Mons Masius. They are divided into three chains. The Western Taurus arcs around the Gulf of Antalya, with peaks above 3,000 metres; the highest is Kizlarsivrisi, at 3,086 metres, in the Bey Mountains. The Central Taurus includes Mount Demirkazık, at 3,756 metres, and the Bolkar and Aladağlar ranges. The Southeastern Taurus forms the northern boundary of the Southeastern Anatolia Region and North Mesopotamia.

The mountains were formed by the collision of the African and Eurasian tectonic plates and rest mainly on limestone. In the Aladağlar and Bolkar ranges the eroded limestone has formed karst landscapes with waterfalls, underground rivers and some of the largest caves in Asia. The climate is Mediterranean, and at lower elevations evergreen oak and Turkish pine grow, with black pine, Lebanon cedar and Taurus fir above 1,200 metres.

The name appears in the Histories of Polybius as Taûros. According to the scholar Heinrich Kiepert, it was borrowed into Greek from an Old Aramaic root meaning mountain. The bull was a common symbol of the storm gods of the ancient Near East, and the mountains held many storm-god temples. The ancient Syrians held that the thunderstorms of these mountains were the work of the storm god Adad, who made the Tigris and Euphrates rise and flood and so fertilise their land. Modern scholars place the Hurrians, probably the originators of the various storm gods, in the Taurus at their probable earliest origins. At Kestel there is a Bronze Age site where early evidence of tin mining has been found.

The Cilician Gates, or Gülek Pass, crossed the range north of Tarsus and has been the principal route through it since ancient times, linking the coastal plain of Cilicia with central Anatolia. In the Amanus range, a natural frontier with Cilicia to the west and Syria to the east, the passes such as the Amanian Gate were of great strategic importance. In 333 BCE Alexander the Great defeated Darius III at the Battle of Issus in the foothills between two of them. In World War I, the German and Turkish railway through the Taurus was a major objective of the Allies.
tausret: Tausret's birth date is unknown. She did not hold the title of King's Daughter, so her later claim to kingship came only through her marriage to Seti II. No children of the couple are known, unless tomb KV56 in the Valley of the Kings, where Theodore Davis found jewellery bearing their names, holds the burial of a child. Aldred thought it the tomb of a daughter, while Maspero thought the objects belonged to Tausret's own burial. After Seti II's death she acted as regent for his heir Siptah, probably her stepson, together with the chancellor Bay, a man of West Asian origin.

A hieratic ostracon published by Pierre Grandet records that Bay was killed on the order of Siptah in the fifth year of that king, on the 27th day of the third month of Shemu. Aidan Dodson believes the initiative was Tausret's, so that she no longer had to share power with her rival. When Siptah died she took the throne herself, with the title Daughter of Re, and counted his years as her own, which explains why Manetho gives her seven years as Thuoris. Papyrus Harris I claims that during these years Egyptian territory in Canaan fell effectively under a man called Irsu, who allied himself with her.

Her highest known date, year 8, comes from a foundation block of her mortuary temple at Gournah, found in 2011 by the University of Arizona Egyptian Expedition. Since the temple was largely completed, with walls, plaster and a roof, she probably ruled for a ninth year, which would give her about three years of sole rule. Her name appears at Abydos, Hermopolis, Memphis and in Nubia. A pair statue in Munich shows Siptah seated on her lap, and her name is linked with the turquoise mines at Serabit el Khadim and Timna.

Her reign ended in a civil war, described on the Elephantine stela of Setnakhte, founder of the Twentieth Dynasty. Most likely he overthrew her, though it is not known whether she was deposed or died in office. Setnakhte took over her tomb KV14, replacing her images with his own, and reburied Seti II in KV15. Her mortuary temple was dismantled and its blocks were reused at Medinet Habu early in the reign of Ramesses III, whose list of kings there leaves out Amenmesse, Siptah and Tausret. Her mummy has not been found; some scholars think the woman known as Unknown Woman D, from KV35, may be Tausret, but the only support is that the mummification fits the period.
tavira: Tavira lies in the east of the Algarve on the south coast of Portugal, 28 kilometres east of Faro and 75 kilometres west of Huelva across the Guadiana into Spain. The Gilão River meets the Atlantic here. The municipality had 26,167 inhabitants in 2011 and covers 606.97 square kilometres. Tavira is the Portuguese representative community for the inscription of the Mediterranean Diet as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity of UNESCO.

The settlement's origins go back to the late Bronze Age. In the 8th century BCE it became one of the first Phoenician settlements in the west of Iberia, with massive walls, at least one sanctuary, two harbours and a regular urban plan, which lasted until the end of the 6th century BCE. Excavations on the hill of Santa Maria found part of a casemate fortification wall and ritual deposits. The site was later revived in the so-called Tartessian period and abandoned again by the end of the 4th century BCE. Under Caesar the Romans built a new port about 7 kilometres from modern Tavira, which prospered and declined with the empire.

The Moorish period, from the 8th to the 13th century, shaped the area's agriculture, culture and architecture, with whitewashed buildings and Moorish style doors. The Moors built Tavira Castle, two mosques and palaces, and the seven-arched bridge once thought Roman proves to be a 12th-century Moorish work. The area stayed mostly rural until the 11th century, when the town grew rapidly into one of the important settlements of the Gharb al-Andalus. In 1242 Dom Paio Peres Correia retook Tavira after seven of his principal knights were killed during a truce. His troops killed most of the population, and the few survivors were confined to a small quarter known as the Mouraria.

In the 18th century the river port shipped salt, dried fish and wine, but the earthquake of 1755 destroyed almost all the town's buildings. It was rebuilt with many 18th-century buildings and has 37 churches. The church of Santa Maria do Castelo, built on the ruins of a mosque and dating to the 13th century, holds the tombs of Paio Peres Correia, who died in Tavira in 1275, and his knights. Fishing was once the main industry but declined, partly because of the changing migration of tuna and the silting of the Gilão. The sand-bar island of Ilha de Tavira forms part of the Ria Formosa wetlands.
tavole-palatine: The temple belonged to a countryside sanctuary near the river Bradano, standing on the last of the Givoni, ancient sandbanks by the river's right bank, about three kilometres from the city of Metapontum. It was built over the remains of a Neolithic village on the prehistoric road from Siris-Heraclea. Remains of the wall of the temenos, the sacred enclosure, and of a very ancient altar can still be seen. The temple was dedicated to Hera and to Apollo.

It was at first attributed to the cult of Athena, but a fragment of a vase found during the excavations of 1926 proved to be a votive offering to Hera, showing that she was the patron of the sanctuary.

The building was a hexastyle peripteral temple: a central naos with a pronaos in front and an adyton at the rear, surrounded by a colonnade of six columns on each short side and twelve on each long side, thirty-two in all. The surviving columns have twenty flutes and Doric capitals. The stylobate measured 34.29 by 13.66 metres and the naos 17.79 by 8.68 metres. Built of a local limestone called mazzarro, the temple has decayed a great deal.

In the 5th century BCE it had a tiled roof with multi-coloured decoration in the Ionic tradition, with lion-head protomes and gargoyles. Terracotta decoration, statuettes, pottery and smaller fragments of columns found near the temple in 1926 are kept in the Museo archeologico nazionale di Metaponto. The temple was restored in 1961.

The ruins have carried several names. Until the 19th century they were also known locally as the Mensole Palatine, the Palatine Shelves, or the Colonne Palatine, probably recalling the struggles of the French paladins against the Saracens. They were called the Scuola di Pitagora, the School of Pythagoras, in memory of the philosopher Pythagoras, and in the Middle Ages the Mensae Imperatoris, the Tables of the Emperor, probably after the Holy Roman Emperor Otto II, who camped at Metapontum during his expedition against the Saracens in 982.
tavoliere-delle-puglie: The plain, whose name means the table of the Apulias, covers about 3,000 square kilometres and takes up nearly half of the traditional region of Capitanata. It was once a sea bottom. It is bounded by the Daunian Pre-Apennines to the west, the Gargano Promontory and the Adriatic Sea to the east, the Fortore river to the north and the Ofanto river to the south. In winter the two rivers sometimes flood it, while drought is frequent in summer.

Neolithic farmers lived on the plain more than 7,000 years ago and practised ritual defleshing of their dead, as light cut marks on the bones show, sometimes up to a year after death. They placed the bones in Scaloria Cave, mixed with animal bones, broken pottery and stone tools.

In the Middle Ages the older practices of farming and river control were lost, and the land became largely marshy and unhealthy. The plain was given over mostly to sheep, which moved along cattle-tracks across it to the pastures of the Apennines. The name Tavoliere itself comes from the Medieval Latin Tabularium, the table on which officials of the transhumance classified the land set aside for sheep farming.

After extensive drainage works the plain is highly cultivated, with wheat, beet and tomatoes, especially around Foggia, and olives and vines that give oils and wines of quality. Its main centres, from north to south, are San Severo, Lucera, Foggia and Cerignola. More than thirty communes lie on the plain, among them Troia, Manfredonia, Ascoli Satriano, Torremaggiore and Ordona, the site of ancient Herdonia.
tawagalawa-letter: The text, catalogued as CTH 181, was written around 1250 BCE or earlier. Its author is generally identified as Hattusili III, though some scholars have argued for Muwatalli II; the fragmentary state of the tablet leaves the author uncertain and says nothing about who the addressee was. The Hittite king sought help against anti-Hittite activity in western Anatolia, above all that of the warlord Piyamaradu, who had fled to territory under Ahhiyawa after a failed rebellion in Lukka.

The king offered three courses: to hand Piyamaradu over, to expel him, or to give him asylum on condition that he attempt no further revolt. No reply survives, but Ahhiyawan control in western Anatolia grew in the following decades, which suggests the appeal was rejected. Though the king rebukes his counterpart for earlier support of Piyamaradu, the tone is respectful, and the form of address my brother, otherwise used for the rulers of Egypt and Babylonia, has been taken as a sign that Ahhiyawa was seen as a rising power.

The letter is named after a brief mention of Tawagalawa, brother of the Ahhiyawan king, whose name has been proposed as a Hittite form of the Greek Eteocles, attested in Mycenean Greek as E-te-wo-ke-le-we, perhaps passed on through Luwian. Early studies thought the opening of the letter concerned him; after the work of Itamar Singer and Suzanne Heinhold-Krahmer in 1983 most scholars read it as concerning Piyamaradu, though there are difficulties with that reading. More recent research tends to see Tawagalawa as the king's predecessor, the passages about him as flashbacks. Piyamaradu also appears in the Manapa-Tarhunta letter and the Milawata letter, which likewise names Millawanda and its dependent city Atriya.

The letter refers to an earlier quarrel between the Hittites and the Ahhiyawans over the land of Wilusa, now settled in peace. Since most scholars identify Wilusa with Troy, the passage has been said to give a striking background to the Homeric tradition of an Achaean attack on Ilios. The verb used, however, could describe anything from an exchange of sharply worded tablets to open war.
tawergha: Tawergha, whose name means the green island in the Berber language, lies 38 kilometres from Misrata and falls under that city's administration. It stands on the road from Sirte to Misrata, and in Roman times its position on the route linking Sirte, along the Mediterranean coast, to Egypt helped the Romans control Libya. The town was known for its palm trees and dates, among them the Bersiel date, used in making ropes, and later for raising cattle and chickens.

In pre-colonial times tens of thousands of black slaves worked on its plantations, making Tawergha the only town on the Libyan coast with a black majority. Under colonial rule they were nominally freed but stayed poor; in the Gaddafi period they received full education, and many reached high posts in the army and civil service.

During the Libyan Civil War of 2011 the town served as a base for operations against Misrata, which had risen against Muammar Gaddafi in February. Misratans accused Tawerghans of leading the two-month siege of their city and of atrocities against its people. Anti-Gaddafi forces claimed to have captured Tawergha on 12 August 2011. The British journalist Andrew Gilligan found it almost empty in September of a population of around 30,000, and reported a campaign of ethnic cleansing by the Misrata Brigade, with slogans aimed at the residents' dark skin.

Amnesty International reported in February 2012 that militiamen were burning homes to prevent any return, and in May 2012 a commission of inquiry of the UN Human Rights Council described killings, arbitrary arrests and torture of Tawerghans across Libya as a war crime. Human Rights Watch put the number displaced at about 40,000.

A return agreed by the United Nations-backed Libyan government in December 2017 was blocked by a militia in February 2018. After a peace agreement between the Tawergha Local Council and the Mayor of Misrata in June 2018, displaced people began to resettle the town, and by August 2022 the United Nations Development Program reported that 45% had returned.
tawhiao: He was the son of Te Wherowhero and his senior wife Whakaawi, a member of the Ngati Mahuta hapū, and was raised by his mother's parents. He was named Tūkaroto to commemorate his father's stand against Ngāpuhi at the siege of Mātakitaki pā in 1822. The Anglican missionary Robert Burrows baptised him Matutaera (Methuselah), a name he repudiated in 1867. In 1858 his father was installed as the first Māori King to promote Māori unity against Pākehā encroachment; the Ngāti Maniapoto chief Tanirau supported a hereditary succession, and Matutaera was elected king on his father's death in 1860.

Unlike his father, he embraced the kingship. After the invasion of the Waikato in 1863 he was baptised into the Pai Mārire faith by its founder, Te Ua Haumēne, at Te Namu pā in Ōpunake, taking the name Tāwhiao, meaning encircle the world. After the defeats at Rangiriri and Ōrākau the Kīngitanga lost between about 500 and 2,000 killed and wounded, by the estimates cited by the historian Vincent O'Malley, and about a million acres of its land was confiscated. Tāwhiao led his people into the land of Ngāti Maniapoto, where he governed Te Rohe Pōtae, the King Country, as an independent state, warning Europeans that they risked death if they crossed its border. It also sheltered Te Kooti from 1872.

On 11 July 1881 Tāwhiao rode into Pirongia with five or six hundred men and laid down his gun at the feet of Major William Mair, the Government Native Officer; seventy-seven guns were laid beside it. The opening of the North Island Main Trunk railway ended the King Country's independence. In London in 1884, with the Member of Parliament Wiremu Te Wheoro, he asked for full and separate Māori self-government under Section 71 of the New Zealand Constitution Act 1852.

His Kīngitanga parliament at Maungakawa, set up in 1892 and later renamed Te Whakakitenga, drew mainly the Waikato, Maniapoto and Hauraki peoples, and its recommendations were ignored by the national Parliament. Tāwhiao died suddenly on 26 August 1894 and, as is Tainui custom, was buried in an unmarked grave on Mount Taupiri; his son Mahuta Tāwhiao succeeded him. He is credited with founding the annual Poukai and the Bank of Aotearoa, and with building the Kīngitanga into a lasting institution. His sayings, which counselled peace between Māori and Pākehā, are handed down as prophecies, and some Māori joined the Mormon church in the belief that he had foretold its missionaries, though there is little contemporary evidence that he converted.
tawhid: The word tawhid, an assertion or declaration of oneness, comes from the Arabic verb wahhada, which can mean to make one or to consider to be one. In Islam it holds that God is indivisibly one and single. The first part of the declaration of faith, the shahada, is the declaration of belief in the oneness of God, and Muslims believe that the whole of Islamic teaching rests on it. Chapter 112 of the Quran, al-Ikhlas, states that God is One, never had offspring and was not born, and has no equal. The Quran uses 99 terms, the Excellent Names of God, to express the complexity of the divine nature.

Its opposite is shirk, associating partners with God, a term usually translated as polytheism but understood to be more complex. It is classed as greater shirk, open and apparent, and hidden shirk, such as performing rituals for social recognition. The Quran says that God does not forgive associating others with Him but forgives anything else of whoever He wills.

Muslim theologians have argued for the oneness of God by reason. Against the polytheism of pre-Islamic Arabia, the Quran argues that God as creator of everything excludes lesser gods, who would themselves have to be created, and that the order of the universe shows a single administrator. Verse 21:22 says that had there been gods besides God in the heavens and earth, both would have been ruined. Later theologians reasoned that two gods would sooner or later have conflicting wills, and one would be powerless, which is incompatible with being God. Avicenna (965–1037) proposed an ontological argument in the Metaphysics of The Book of Healing, distinguishing essence from existence.

Scholars have understood tawhid in different ways. Some theologians use it for the whole discussion of God and his attributes, and sometimes for the whole of kalam, Islamic theology. Philosophers such as al-Farabi, al-Razi and Avicenna interpreted it by reason, under the influence of Plotinus's emphasis on divine simplicity. In Sufism it is both an affirmation in speech and a practical realisation of God's unity, through purification from worldliness.

Tawhid shaped Muslim culture widely. Early Muslims understood religion to cover the state, law and society, since God's rule extends to all creatures and to all aspects of life. A single raised index finger is used as a symbol of tawhid. The wish to preserve God's transcendence led to the prohibition of visual depictions of God and of any prophet, and the dominant forms of Islamic art became calligraphy and arabesque. The medieval scholar al-Ghazali held that a believer who thinks himself better than another through wealth or colour adopts the hierarchical principle of Iblis and so falls into shirk.
tawi-tawi: Tawi-Tawi is the southernmost province of the Philippines, part of the Sulu Archipelago between the Sulu Sea in the north and the Celebes Sea in the south. It shares sea borders with the Malaysian state of Sabah and the Indonesian province of North Kalimantan, both on Borneo. It consists of Tawitawi Island and 106 surrounding islands and islets with a land area of 1,087.4 square kilometres, and the main island accounts for 580.5 of them. The name is the Sinama form of jawi-jawi, Malay for the banyan tree, which grows abundantly there. The capital is Bongao, and the island supports several endemic species, among them the Tawitawi brown dove and the Sulu hornbill.

Carbon dating of bones, jars and shells from the Bolobok Rock Shelter places human presence there between 6,810 BCE and 3,190 BCE, among the earliest evidence in Southeast Asia. For centuries the area was a centre of Sama culture, and some islands hold old burial grounds with Sama okil carvings of ancestors. The first mosque in the Philippines, the Sheik Karimol Makhdum Mosque, was established in 1380 by the Arab trader and missionary Makhdum Karim. The area was heavily converted to Islam, especially after the founding of the Sultanate of Sulu, although many Sama kept part of their older animist religions.

Later centuries brought foreign claims. The sultan of Sulu made agreements with Alexander Dalrymple of the British East India Company in 1761 and 1762, and in 1878 Baron von Overbeck leased the sultan's land in Borneo for the British North Borneo Company. The Spanish built a naval base at Tata'an and garrisons at Bongao and Siasi. American forces occupied Jolo in 1899, and by the Treaty of Washington in 1900 Spain ceded Sibutu and Cagayan de Sulu to the United States for US$100,000. The Imperial Japanese Navy used the waters as a fleet anchorage during World War II.

The municipalities of Tawi-Tawi were part of Sulu until 11 September 1973, when Presidential Decree No. 302 made it a province, with Romulo Espaldon as its first governor. Its seat was at first Bato-Bato, in the municipality of Balimbing, and moved to Bongao in 1979. The province lies in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and has 11 municipalities.
tawusi-melek: In Yazidi creation stories God assigned all the world's affairs to the seven Divine Beings, who are also called the Seven Angels or heft sirr, the Seven Mysteries. According to religious tradition, nature, with all its phenomena of light and darkness, emanates from a single source, which is Tawûsî Melek. Passages of the qewls, the Yazidi sacred texts, stress his power on the earth, in the sky and sea and on the mountains. Yazidis hold that he was entrusted with the care of the world after he passed a test and created the cosmos from the cosmic egg. They describe him as eternal and as an eternal light.

Yazidi accounts of creation differ greatly from those of Judaism, Christianity and Islam, because they derive from ancient Mesopotamian and Indo-Iranian traditions. Their cosmogony is therefore closer to those of the ancient Iranian religions, Vedic Hinduism, Yarsanism and Zoroastrianism. In Yarsanism, which shares many similarities with Yazidism, a figure called Malak Tawus is held to be pure and sinless. In the Yarsani doctrine of cycles, he is labelled Shaitan in the age of Islamic law and called Dawud in the age of Truth, so Yarsanis do not curse Satan.

In Yazidi mythology, when Tawûsî Melek descended to the earth, the seven colours of the rainbow became a seven-coloured bird, the peacock, which flew around the earth to bless it and came to rest at Lalish. The peacock is his symbol, and its colours stand for the diversity of the world. It is a sacred bird that Yazidis may not hunt, eat, curse or ill-treat, and images of it decorate Lalish, other shrines and many homes.

The first Wednesday of Nîsan, in Eastern April, is believed to be the day he descended as light, and it is the holy day on which Sersal, the Yazidi New Year, is marked. On the eve of the feast 365 or 366 lamps are lit, matching the number of days in the year.

Muslims and followers of other Abrahamic religions have mistakenly identified the Peacock Angel with Satan, a misconception that led to centuries of violent persecution of Yazidis as devil-worshippers. Some also claimed that he was Ahriman, the evil figure of Zoroastrianism. Yazidis avoid the Arabic word Shaitan and words that sound like it. Mentioning the names other faiths give the evil spirit is considered sinful, since it would imply evil as an independent entity and diminish God's omnipotence. Outsiders mistook their avoidance of gatherings where such figures were cursed for veneration.
taxila: Taxila, known in Sanskrit as Takṣaśilā, lies on the Pothohar Plateau in Punjab, Pakistan, about 25 kilometres north-west of the Islamabad and Rawalpindi area, near the Indus. The Sanskrit name is translated as City of Cut Stone or Rock of Taksha. According to the Ramayana the city was founded by Bharata, brother of Rama, and named for his son Taksha. The modern name derives from the Greek rendering recorded in Ptolemy's Geography.

Settlement in the Taxila valley goes back to the late 4th or early 3rd millennium BCE at Sarai Khola, and the first major settlement, on the Hathial mound, was established around 1000 BCE. Taxila was a capital of the Gandhara kingdom, together with Puṣkalāvatī, though at times it formed its own district or city-state. It may have grown considerably by the time of the Achaemenid conquest of the 6th century BCE. In 326 BCE its king Taxiles, called Āmbhi, surrendered to Alexander the Great without a battle; Greek historians described the city as wealthy, prosperous and well governed, and Alexander kept Taxiles as satrap.

Within about a decade of Alexander's departure Chandragupta Maurya captured the city. Buddhist texts say Chanakya came from Taxila, and under Ashoka, the grandson of Chandragupta, it became a great seat of Buddhist learning. It lay on the ancient Grand Trunk Road linking Pataliputra to Central Asia. In the 2nd century BCE the Indo-Greeks built a new capital, Sirkap, across the river, and Maues overthrew the last Greek king of Taxila around 90 BCE. Inscriptions of 76 CE show Kushan rule, and Kanishka later founded Sirsukh, the latest of the ancient settlements, when the city was known for trade in silk, sandalwood, horses, cotton, pearls and spices.

The invading Hunas devastated Taxila in the 5th century, and by the time the monk Xuanzang described it in the 7th century it was in decline. Its ruins were rediscovered in the mid-19th century by Alexander Cunningham and extensively excavated by Sir John Marshall. UNESCO designated Taxila a World Heritage Site in 1980. Some scholars regard the so-called university of ancient Taxila as one of the earliest centres of education in Asia.
tay-son-dynasty: In the 18th century the Lê dynasty reigned in name, while the Trịnh lords ruled the north from Thăng Long and the Nguyễn lords the south from Huế. Land gathered in the hands of a few landlords, officials grew corrupt, and examination degrees were at one point sold. When Siam under Taksin forced the Nguyễn to give up conquests such as Hà Tiên, and the regent Trương Phúc Loan held power after the death of Lord Nguyễn Phúc Khoát in 1765, heavy taxes and corruption drove three brothers of Tây Sơn, Nguyễn Nhạc, Nguyễn Huệ and Nguyễn Lữ, to rise in 1771.

No relation of the Nguyễn lords, they promised to remove corrupt officials and redistribute land, and won support from poor farmers, some highland peoples and, after taking Qui Nhơn in 1773, its merchants.

While the Trịnh seized Phú Xuân from the north, the Tây Sơn took the last Nguyễn stronghold of Gia Định in 1776 and massacred its Chinese population; of the Nguyễn family only Nguyễn Ánh escaped, to Siam. A Siamese army sent on his behalf in 1780 could not defeat them. In 1788 a Qing army sent by the Qianlong Emperor to restore the fugitive Lê Chiêu Thống took Thăng Long, but Nguyễn Huệ attacked during the Lunar New Year celebrations and won at Ngọc Hồi-Đống Đa. He then sought peace with the Qing, and in 1789 the Qianlong Emperor named him King of Annam; Chinese and Vietnamese sources agree that he sent an impostor to Beijing in his place.

Quang Trung built warships and gave posts and noble ranks to Chinese pirates such as Chen Tien-pao and Cheng I, but his plans died with him in 1792. Under his young son Nguyễn Quang Toản, Emperor Cảnh Thịnh, real power lay with his uncle Bui Dac Tuyen, whose purge executed many who had served Quang Trung and drove others away. Nguyễn Ánh, aided by French adventurers enlisted by Bishop Pigneau de Behaine, took Quy Nhơn in 1800, Phú Xuân in 1801 and Thăng Long in 1802, when Nguyễn Quang Toản was captured and executed. The dynasty had ended the long war between the Trịnh and Nguyễn and united the country for the first time in 200 years.
tayang-khan: According to The Secret History of the Mongols, Tayang was so weak at birth that his father, Inanch Bilge, did not expect him to reach adulthood, and he was therefore also called Torluq Tayang, Weak Tayang. His brother Buyruq Khan was older. On succeeding his father he married his stepmother Gürbesu in a levirate marriage, and his horde lived along the shores of the Black Irtysh.

In 1200 Tayang took in Jaqa Gambu, a Kerait prince and brother of Toghrul, who had fled to him. After Genghis Khan defeated Toghrul in 1203, Toghrul himself escaped into Naiman lands, where a Naiman patrol failed to recognise him and killed him. When Toghrul's head was brought to Tayang, he stepped on it and crushed it. Seeing so powerful a ruler fall, he resolved to strike at Genghis first, against the counsel of Gürbesu and his general Sabraq, and sought an alliance with Alaqush Tegin of the Ongud, a fellow Nestorian, who warned Genghis instead.

The armies first met on 17 May 1204 in the Khangai Mountains, where Naiman patrols beat Genghis's vanguard. Genghis, with a much smaller force, had each man light five campfires, and when Tayang heard of the many fires he proposed a retreat and a war of raids. His son Kuchlug called him a coward, and the angered Tayang crossed the Orkhon River, joined by Jamukha, Toktoqa, chief of the Merkids, and Quduqa of the Oirats.

Faced with Genghis's commanders Jebe, Subutai, Khubilai and Jelme, Tayang fell back again, and Jamukha, seeing him hesitate, left the Naimans. The weakened Naiman army was ambushed at night, and Tayang was killed trying to escape. Genghis took Gürbesu as his own wife, while Kuchlug fled to his uncle Buyruq.
taygetus: The Taygetus massif is about 100 kilometres long, running from the centre of the Peloponnese to Cape Matapan, its southernmost point. It overlooks Sparta and Kalamata and lies within the prefectures of Arcadia, Laconia and Messenia. The Eurotas has some of its headwaters in the northern part of the range, and the slopes are heavily forested, mainly with Greek fir and black pine.

The name is one of the oldest recorded in Europe, appearing in the Odyssey, and in myth it came from the nymph Taygete. In Byzantine times and until the 19th century the mountain was also called Pentadaktylos, Greek for five-fingered. Its highest summit, Profitis Ilias, is probably the classical Mount Taleton mentioned by Pausanias. Geologically the range is a limestone horst beside the Eurotas rift valley, and the Sparta fault below its eastern face caused the earthquake of 464 BCE that levelled Sparta.

The slopes have been inhabited since at least Mycenean times, and near the village of Arna the site of Arkina has three beehive tombs. The mountain was one of Sparta's natural defences. The Spartans threw criminals into a chasm called Ceadas, and remains of adults found there by the University of Athens appear to confirm it as a place of punishment for criminals, traitors and captives.

Plutarch wrote that Spartan elders judged newborn babies and left those thought unfit at the foot of Taygetus. No other ancient source says this, and the bones found at the site belonged to adolescents and adults, not infants. In the age of the barbarian invasions the mountain sheltered the native population, and many villages on its slopes date from then. In Medieval times the citadel and monastery of Mystras was built on its steep slopes and became a centre of Byzantine civilisation and the capital of the Despotate of the Morea.

Mystras is occupied by a tiny religious community, its buildings are well preserved, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In antiquity the peak of Taleton was dedicated to Helios, to whom horses were sacrificed, and to Zeus. Today the summit is linked to the Prophet Elias, and each 20 July, his feast day in the Greek Orthodox calendar, a festival with a large bonfire is held at the chapel on the peak. Profitis Ilias is a popular hiking destination, and the European walking route E4 runs along the lower slopes.
tayichiud: The Tayichiud were a subclan of the Kiyat Borjigin and one of the three core tribes of the Khamag Mongol confederation. They first appear in the record under Ambaghai Khan in 1148, but the clan was founded by his grandfather Chirhya Lynhua, son of Khaidu Khan, founder of the Kiyat clan. They lived in the south of present-day Zabaykalsky Krai and in Mongolia's Dornod Province. Though the Borjigids and the Tayichiud shared an ancestor in Bodonchar Munkhag, they were at times bitter rivals for the leadership of the Khamag Mongol.

Khabul Khan of the Borjigin had seven sons but named Ambaghai, son of Sengum Bilge of the Tayichiud, as his successor, and Ambaghai became the second khan of the Khamag Mongol. Rule then passed back and forth between the two lines until it came to Genghis Khan. The Secret History of the Mongols portrays the Tayichiud as his bitter enemies, allied at times with Jamukha.

Genghis destroyed the ruling clan, but descendants who had surrendered rose high in the Mongol Empire. Jebe, born Jurgaadai, of the Besud clan of the Tayichiud, struck the final blow to the Jurchens in the conquest of the Jin dynasty in 1219 and defeated the Kypchaks and their allies at the Battle of Kalka in 1223. Baiju, commander of the Tammachi in Persia, was also a Besud. Chilaun, one of Genghis Khan's four close companions, came from the Suldus subclan; his descendant Chupan was named chief commander of all Mongol khanates by the Yuan court in 1327. Buyan Suldus overthrew the Qara'unas in Transoxiana in 1359 and was executed in 1362 by Tughluq Temur.

Under Timur the tribe was led by Amir Musa, who clashed with Timur several times yet was bound to the dynasty by marriage. His daughter Tuman Agha and his niece Saray Mulk Khanum both married Timur, the latter becoming his chief consort, and his son Muhammad Beg married Timur's daughter Aka Begim. Their son Sultan Husayn Tayichiud held high posts in the army and was the last of the clan's line, ending in 1405. People with the clan name Taichiud or Taijiud are found today in Mongolia, Inner Mongolia and Kalmykia.
tayma: Tayma, also spelled Tema, is a city and governorate in Tabuk Province, north-western Saudi Arabia, and a major oasis. It lies where the trade route between Medina and Dumah begins to cross the western Nafud desert, about 264 km south-east of Tabuk and 400 km north of Medina. It is one of the largest archaeological sites in Saudi Arabia, and its constant water supply made it a stopover even though it was not on the Frankincense Road.

The earliest evidence of settled life is from the early 4th millennium BCE. In the mid-2nd millennium BCE the settlement expanded and was enclosed by a massive wall of mudbrick and sandstone, and the domestication of the dromedary helped it become an economic centre. In the early Iron Age Egypt's influence is shown by the Pharaonic Tayma inscription, found in 2010 about 60 km to the north-west, the first hieroglyphic inscription found in Saudi Arabia, in the name of Ramesses III. A building held Egyptian votive figurines and scarabs.

From the 8th century BCE Tayma had close ties with Mesopotamia and was under Assyrian control without formal annexation. Assyrian governors raided caravans affiliated with it, and a gate inscription of Sennacherib at Nineveh records gifts from the people of Sumu'il and Tema. Nabonidus, the last Babylonian king, used Tayma as the base for his campaigns in north-western Arabia, and inscriptions in cuneiform and Taymanitic name him king of Babylon. After the Achaemenid empire fell, Tayma declined and came under the hegemony of the Lihyanite dynasty of Dedan; in the Hellenistic period it became a focus of the Nabataean Kingdom. Tayma appears in the Hebrew Bible, where Tema is a son of Ishmael and Jeremiah lists it among rich cities.

Arabic tradition describes a Jewish population in late antiquity, and pre-Islamic poetry associates Tayma with the poet Samaw'al ibn 'Adiya. Tradition says the Jews were exiled under the caliph Umar. Medieval geographers praised its spring, wells and palm groves, and it later became a rest stop on the pilgrimage route between Syria and the holy cities.

The city walls described by al-Bakri are still visible and give the ruin its characteristic profile, and the oasis is known for its dates. Charles M. Doughty first mapped the site in 1877, and the Tayma stele found by Charles Huber in 1883, which lists the gods of Tayma in the 6th century BCE, is in the Louvre. Its monuments include Qasr Al-Ablaq, built in the 6th century by Samaw'al ibn 'Adiya and his grandfather 'Adiya.
tayy: Early Arab genealogists traced the Tayy to Julhumah ibn Udad, called Tayy, a descendant of Kahlan ibn Saba and so of Qahtan, held to be the common ancestor of the southern Arab tribes; a tradition cited by al-Tabari derived his name from a word meaning to plaster, since he was said to have been the first to plaster the walls of a well. In the late 2nd century CE the tribe settled among the ranges of Aja and Salma, with Khaybar as its chief oasis, displacing part of the Banu Assad, and the mountains came to be called Jabal Tayy, later Jabal Shammar. Its two main branches were the Al al-Ghawth and the Al Jadila.

The Tayy were so widespread in the Syrian Desert that Syriac writers used their name, Ṭayyāy, for Arab tribesmen in general and even for Muslims, and through Syriac it passed into Middle Persian as Tāzīg, meaning Arab. In the late 6th century the Fasad War split the tribe, and members of the Jadila converted to Christianity and became allies of the Ghassanids.

Adi ibn Hatim and Zayd al-Khayr converted to Islam with much of the tribe in 629–630. Accounts of the Tayy's part in the Ridda Wars differ widely, but Adi kept many of its clans from fighting the Muslims and sent Caliph Abu Bakr the 300 camels of tribute in dispute. Tayy fought in the conquest of Persia, and Christian Tayy tribesmen on the Sasanian side changed sides at the Battle of the Bridge in 634.

In the First Fitna the Tayy of Arabia and Iraq backed Ali while those of Syria backed Mu'awiya, and a Tayyid commander killed Raja Dahir in the conquest of Sindh in 712. Qahtaba ibn Shabib led the Abbasid movement in Khurasan, and the poets Abu Tammam and al-Buhturi rose under the Abbasids.

After 861 the Tayy dominated the southern Syrian Desert. Their Jarrahid chief Mufarrij ibn Daghfal handed the rebel Alptakin to the Fatimids, became governor of Ramla and commanded the routes between Egypt, Syria, Iraq and Arabia. Driven out in 981–82, the Jarrahids sacked a pilgrim caravan and destroyed a Fatimid army at Ayla, but had regained their place in Palestine by Mufarrij's death in 1013.

Mufarrij's descendants later served the Burids of Damascus and their Zengid successors, and at times fought beside the Crusaders. By the end of the 11th century, according to the historian Mustafa A. Hiyari, the Banu Rabi'ah branch of the Tayy and the Mazyadid branch of the Banu Assad were the last influential Arab tribes in Syria and Iraq. Jabal Shammar remains the tribe's traditional homeland.
tazeroualt: Tazerwalt lies in the Anti-Atlas mountains of southern Morocco, and its name is also spelled Tazeroualt. Sidi Ahmed Ou Moussa, a marabout from the Souss, settled in the area and founded a zawiya there, where hundreds of followers came to hear his teaching. He kept close relations with the ruling Saadian dynasty and used his religious standing to carve out an enclave of power within the Saadian state. After his death his grave became a place of pilgrimage, and his descendants inherited much of his wealth and status.

The death of the Saadian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur in 1603 threw Morocco into instability, and Sidi Ahmed Ou Moussa's grandson Sidi Ali Bou Dmia turned the family's religious standing into political power. Calling himself amir of Tazerwalt, he founded his capital at Iligh and bound the region to him through his religious following and tribal alliances. Holding overland trade routes and ports such as Agadir, he raised a sizable army, mainly of slaves, and pushed his borders east. By the mid-17th century he ruled a wide stretch of the Sahara and of Morocco south of the Atlas, including the trading centres of the Draa valley, Sijilmasa, Touat and Taghaza, and at its height the state reached from the Atlantic to Touat.

The rise of the Alaouite dynasty in Tafilalt undid this. In the late 1650s the Alaouites took Sijilmasa and cut away much of Tazerwalt's economic power. Sidi Ali Bou Dmia died in 1659 and was briefly followed by his son Muhammad, and in 1670 the Alaouites razed Iligh, ending the state's independence.

The family kept wealth and prestige as the House of Iligh through its descent from the saint. Without ever challenging Alaouite rule directly, it regained much political and even military power in the 18th and 19th centuries, controlling much of the Souss and dealing in trade and diplomacy with both the Alaouite sultans and European powers. Sidi Ahmed Ou Moussa's zawiya is still a place of pilgrimage, in the village that bears his name.
tbilisi: Tbilisi stands on the banks of the Kura River. Its name comes from the Old Georgian tpili, meaning warm, because of the area's numerous sulfuric hot springs. Until 1936 the name in English and most other languages followed the Persian pronunciation, Tiflis. On 17 August 1936, by order of the Soviet leadership, the official Russian names of various cities were changed to match the local language, and the Georgian form was modernised from Ṭpilisi to Tbilisi on the proposal of Georgian linguists. Some languages, among them Turkish, Persian, Greek, Spanish and German, have kept a form of Tiflis. Its position at the crossroads between Europe and Asia, near the Silk Road, made it a point of contention among powers.

Archaeologists found evidence of continuous habitation of the suburb of Dighomi since the early Bronze Age, and stone artifacts from the Paleolithic. In the late Bronze Age and early Iron Age it was the largest settlement in the Caucasus. According to legend the site was covered by forest as late as 458. One widely accepted variant of the foundation myth says that King Vakhtang I of Iberia (r. c. 447/49 - 502/22) went hunting with a falcon, which caught or injured a pheasant, and both birds fell into a hot spring and died of burns. The king was so impressed by the springs that he had the forest cleared and built a city there.

King Dachi of Iberia (r. 522-534), Vakhtang's successor, moved the capital of Iberia from Mtskheta to Tbilisi and began building the fortress wall that marked the city's new boundaries. From the sixth century Tbilisi grew steadily because of its strategic position on trade and travel routes between Europe and Asia. It served as the capital of various Georgian kingdoms and republics.

Between 1801 and 1917, as part of the Russian Empire, it was the seat of the Caucasus Viceroyalty, which governed both the northern and southern sides of the Caucasus. Its population has always been diverse in culture, ethnicity and religion, though overwhelmingly Eastern Orthodox Christian.

Tbilisi is the capital and largest city of Georgia, with more than 1.3 million inhabitants, almost one third of the country's population. Its architecture mixes medieval, neoclassical, Beaux Arts, Art Nouveau, Stalinist and modern buildings. Among its landmarks are the Sameba and Sioni cathedrals, the medieval Narikala Fortress and the Georgian National Museum.
tbilisi-state-university: Tbilisi State University was established in 1918, when Georgia had declared itself an independent national democratic state, through the leadership of the historian Ivane Javakhishvili and a group of followers. Among the co-founders were the scientists Giorgi Akhvlediani, Shalva Nutsubidze, Dimitri Uznadze, Grigol Tsereteli, Akaki Shanidze and Andrea Razmadze, and Elizabeth Orbeliani became the first woman to teach there. The chemist Petre Melikishvili was the first rector. Excluding academies and theological seminaries, which had worked in Georgia for centuries, it was the first university in Georgia and the Caucasus, and at the time the only institution of its kind in the region.

The university is housed in the former Georgian Nobility Gymnasium, built by the architect Simon Kldiashvili from 1899 to 1906. Niko Tskhvedadze, a founder of the Society for the Spreading of Literacy among Georgians, oversaw its construction. The university opened on the day of remembrance of the Georgian king David the Builder, with a single faculty, that of philosophy, and Javakhishvili gave the first lecture. At the start of 1918 it had 18 professors and lecturers, 369 students and 89 free listeners.

Georgia had a tradition of education, in the School of Philosophy and Rhetoric of Phazisi in Colchis in the fourth century and the Gelati and Iqalto academies of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, but as a colony of Russia it had no national institution of higher education for centuries. Through the Bolshevik and Communist period, despite forced ideology and fierce censorship, the university kept schools in mathematics, psychology, philosophy, linguistics and historiography, and it encouraged the foundation of the Academy of Science of Georgia. In 1989 it was named after Javakhishvili.

The university has no central campus, and its buildings are spread through the city; the oldest, building number 1, houses the administration. Its yard holds the Pantheon of Tbilisi State University, where its founders are buried. A printing press was set up in 1923, a publishing house in 1933 and the university archive in 1933, and its scholarly Proceedings have appeared since 1919. Medical education was restored in 1994. It now has seven faculties, among them humanities, law, economics and business, and medicine, and branches in cities such as Sokhumi, Poti and Zugdidi.
te-deum: The Te Deum is a Latin Christian hymn, named from its incipit Te Deum laudamus, Thee, God, we praise. Its authorship is traditionally ascribed to Saint Ambrose, who died in 397, or to Saint Augustine, who died in 430, and it is sometimes known as the Ambrosian Hymn, though authorship by Ambrose is unlikely. Nineteenth-century scholarship proposed Saint Hilary of Poitiers and Saint Nicetas of Remesiana, whose name appears with the hymn in manuscripts from the 10th century onward. Hymnologists of the 20th century, especially Ernst Kähler in 1958, showed the link with Nicetas to be spurious. The hymn almost certainly dates to the 4th century, and its authorship is considered uncertain.

The Te Deum has structural similarities with a eucharistic prayer, and it has been proposed that it was originally composed as part of one. It was written on a Gregorian chant melody. It follows the outline of the Apostles' Creed, mixing a poetic vision of the heavenly liturgy with a declaration of faith. The petitions at its end, beginning Salvum fac populum tuum, are a selection of verses from the Psalms added later.

The hymn was part of the Old Hymnal when it was introduced to the Benedictine order in the 6th century and was kept in the Frankish Hymnal of the 8th century. It was removed from the New Hymnal that became prevalent in the 10th century and restored in the 12th century in hymnals that sought to recover the praiseful intent of the Rule of Saint Benedict. In the traditional office it is sung at the end of Matins on days when the Gloria is said at Mass. It is also used in Morning Prayer in the Anglican Book of Common Prayer, as an option in Matins for Lutherans, and in many Reformed churches.
A Te Deum service is a short service of thanksgiving, often held at short notice, to celebrate good news such as a military victory, the signing of a peace treaty or the birth of a royal child.

The text has been set to music by many composers, among them Handel, Haydn, Mozart, Berlioz, Verdi, Bruckner, Dvořák and Britten. The prelude to Marc-Antoine Charpentier's setting is well known in Europe as the theme music of Eurovision broadcasts. William Walton wrote a Coronation Te Deum for the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in 1953, and Puccini's opera Tosca features the opening of the hymn at the end of Act I. The 18th-century German hymn Großer Gott, wir loben dich is a free translation of it.
teaching-for-merikare: The work is a sebayt, or teaching, written in Middle Egyptian, the classical phase of the language. Its author has a king of the First Intermediate Period, possibly named Kheti, address his son, the future king Merykara, on how to be a good king and avoid evil. Merykara was a king of the 9th or 10th Dynasty, which ruled northern Egypt while the country was divided. Setting the work in such a time may have given the author more freedom to describe the limits of royal authority than writing of a king of a united Egypt would have allowed. Like later royal testaments, it may also have served to legitimise the reigning king.

The first section, mostly lost, deals with putting down rebellion, and the second with the treatment of the king's subjects. The third advises on running the army and religious services, and the fourth describes the king's achievements and how to emulate them.

The king is told to quarry new stone rather than reuse old monuments, an ideal set against the acknowledged practice of reuse.
