The destruction of a sacred territory at Abydos is recorded, and the king expresses remorse, as if accepting responsibility for sacrilege committed in his name and subject to divine judgement of the dead. The duty to uphold Maat, the right order of the world, is stressed, and the text ends with a hymn to an unnamed creator god and a call to heed the instructions.

The teaching is the first known treatise on kingship in the form of a royal testament, a genre later found in the Hellenistic and Islamic worlds and paralleled by the speculum regum of medieval Europe. Its contrast between the real and the ideal makes it a reflection on power without parallel in ancient Egyptian writing. It is known from three fragmentary papyri of the late 18th Dynasty, Papyrus Hermitage 1116A, Papyrus Moscow 4658 in the Pushkin Museum of Fine Arts and Papyrus Carlsberg 6, which only partly complement one another. The most complete, the Leningrad papyrus, has the most scribal errors and omissions.
teanum-sidicinum: Teano, the ancient Teanum Sidicinum, is a town in the province of Caserta in Campania, about 30 kilometres northwest of Caserta on the main railway line from Naples to Rome. It stands at the southeast foot of an extinct volcano, Rocca Monfina. Strabo calls Teanum the most important town on the Via Latina, joined by a branch road from Suessa.

Teanum Sidicinum was the capital of the Oscan tribe of the Sidicini, who drove the Aurunci from Roccamonfina. They probably submitted to Rome in 334 BCE, and their troops were grouped with those of Campania in the Roman army. Like Cales, Teanum kept the right of coinage, and like Suessa and Cales it remained faithful to Rome in both the Hannibalic and the Social wars. It was apparently made a colony by Claudius, not by Augustus.

In the 4th century Teano became the seat of a diocese, and it was later an important Lombard county, part of the Duchy of Benevento. Monks from Montecassino took refuge there when their abbey was destroyed in 883, and one of the first documents in the vernacular Italian was issued there in 963. On 26 October 1860 Teano was the site of the Handshake of Teano, when Giuseppe Garibaldi, having wrested the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies from the Neapolitan Bourbons, shook hands with Victor Emanuel II, King of Sardinia, and hailed him as King of Italy.

Roman remains include a theatre of the 2nd century BCE, rebuilt in the 2nd century CE, once one of the largest in Italy at 85 metres in diameter, and extensive baths known as Le Caldarelle. The cathedral of St Clement, begun around 1050 and finished in 1116, uses Corinthian columns taken from the ancient town. The castle, built by the dukes of Sessa in the 15th century on a fortress of the 4th century BCE, served as a prison in the Bourbon era. The cathedral is the see of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Teano-Calvi.
teatro-allantica: The name means theatre in the style of the ancients. Duke Vespasiano I Gonzaga commissioned it as part of his effort to turn his small ducal seat into an idealised classical city. Its place on the town's principal street, the Via Giulia, and its separate building show the standing theatre had come to hold as a mark of the civilised society the duke was trying to create. The prestigious site was cramped and narrow, however, and its conversion into a theatre demanded considerable ingenuity from Scamozzi. It is the second-oldest surviving indoor theatre in the world, after the Teatro Olimpico in Vicenza, and with that theatre and the Teatro Farnese in Parma one of only three Renaissance theatres still standing.

Scamozzi had overseen the completion of the Teatro Olimpico after the death of Andrea Palladio, and had designed the perspective scenery on its stage. Its influence shows in the colonnade behind the seating and in the set. The building at Sabbioneta, however, is about three times as long as it is wide, where the Olimpico's space is nearly square. Palladio had been forced to stretch the ideal semicircle of a Roman theatre into an ellipse; Scamozzi was forced the other way, and his seating became a horseshoe.

Scamozzi also gave up the elaborate classical scaenae frons that defines the Olimpico and had obliged him to build seven separate street scenes there. Instead he built a single trompe-l'œil view of one street. The false-front buildings shrink rapidly over a short distance, the floor rises steeply and the two sides of the street close in, giving the illusion of great depth. With so narrow an auditorium, one perspective served every seat.

In the 17th century the original scenery was removed and replaced by a system of sliding wings. Scamozzi's plans, which show the perspective street in their upper right corner, were kept in the archives of the Uffizi in Florence, and in the twentieth century new scenery was built from them and set in the theatre.
teatro-di-san-carlo: The Teatro di San Carlo stands next to the Royal Palace in Naples and the Piazza del Plebiscito. The Bourbon king Charles VII of Naples commissioned it to replace the old, dilapidated and too small Teatro San Bartolomeo of 1621. It was designed by Giovanni Antonio de Medrano, a Sicilian nobleman and royal architect, with Angelo Carasale, the former director of the San Bartolomeo, responsible for the furnishings. The horseshoe-shaped auditorium was built for 75,000 ducats and had 184 boxes in six orders and a royal box for ten people. Blue and gold, the Bourbon colours, dominated the decoration.

The theatre was inaugurated on 4 November 1737, the king's name day, with Domenico Sarro's opera Achille in Sciro, to a libretto by Metastasio. The first seasons showed the royal preference for dance and featured castrati. Gluck was called to Naples to direct his Clemenza di Tito in 1752. Domenico Barbaia became manager of the royal opera houses in 1809. On 13 February 1816 a fire broke out during a dress rehearsal for a ballet and destroyed part of the building. On the orders of King Ferdinand IV, Barbaia rebuilt it within ten months with the architect Antonio Niccolini, and it reopened on 12 January 1817 with Johann Simon Mayr's Il sogno di Partenope.

Gioachino Rossini was house composer and artistic director of the royal opera houses from 1815 to 1822 and wrote ten operas in this period, among them Otello and Mosè in Egitto. Gaetano Donizetti followed from 1822 until 1838 and composed sixteen operas for the theatre, including Lucia di Lammermoor in 1835. Verdi wrote Alzira and Luisa Miller for it. After the unification of Italy in 1861 Naples lost its status as the musical centre of Italy, and by 1874 falling income closed the house for a year. Bombs damaged it in the Second World War, and its first opera performance after the liberation of Naples in 1943 was La bohème on 26 December.

The San Carlo is the oldest continuously active opera venue in the world, opened decades before Milan's La Scala or Venice's La Fenice. Its opera season runs from late November to July, and its ballet season from December to early June. The seating, once 3,285, has been reduced to 1,386. Since the 1844 redecoration under Niccolini the interior has been red and gold. A renovation costing 67 million euros, carried out in 2008 and 2009, was meant to return the house to its condition after the rebuilding of 1816, and it reopened on 27 January 2010.
teatro-regio-parma: The theatre was built as the Nuovo Teatro Ducale, the New Ducal Theatre, to replace a small and narrow ducal theatre of 1688 in the Palazzo di Riserva, which had become obsolete as a growing middle class wished to see opera; it closed after a performance of Rossini's Zelmira in 1828 and was demolished. Construction began in 1821 on the site of the former Monastery of St. Alexander, next to the Ducal Palace. Marie Louise, Duchess of Parma, Napoleon I's divorced second wife, oversaw the work, which she financed, and asked for interiors in the sobriety of neoclassicism, in white and light blue.

Rossini was first invited to compose for the opening on 16 May 1829 but was too busy, so the task fell to Bellini, whose Zaira received a frosty reception. Between 1849 and 1860 the house was called the Teatro Reale, and with the unification of Italy in 1861 it took its present name.

The auditorium seats 1,400, with four tiers of boxes topped by a gallery. The neoclassical façade, unchanged since it was built, has a colonnade of ten Ionic granite columns supporting five windows, with bas-reliefs by Tommaso Bandini of two muses. In 1853, under the Bourbon Duke Carlo III, the interior was redecorated with red velvet and gold ornament. Giovan Battista Borghesi painted the ceiling with frescoes of playwrights, and a chandelier made in Paris, 4.5 metres high and weighing 1,100 kg, was installed in 1854 when gas lighting came in. The stage was lit by electricity by 1907.

Verdi, born about 20 miles from Parma, directed his Nabucco there on 17 April 1843, and since then the Regio has staged every one of his operas; between 1829 and 1979 his Aida was given 177 times. Since 2003 the company has held a Verdi Festival each October, with a concert called Buon Compleanno Maestro Verdi on 10 October. The audience has a reputation for being demanding: in the early years of the old Ducale the tenor Alberico Curioni was whistled and booed, shouted obscenities back and was arrested, and in the 19th century protests more than once brought the curtain down.
teatro-san-cassiano: A theatre of the Tron family for spoken comedies stood on the site by 1581, in the parish of San Cassiano in the Santa Croce district, not far from the Rialto. Letters of that year already mention its boxes, later a key feature of the Italian opera house, and the Council of Ten began to demand that such theatres be strong and safe so that no collapse could happen. The Council closed it in 1585, together with the Michiel family's theatre; it probably reopened after 1607, and fires destroyed it in 1629 and 1633.

In 1636 the brothers Ettore and Francesco Tron told the authorities that they meant to open a theatre for music. It opened in 1637 with L'Andromeda, with music by Francesco Manelli and a libretto by Benedetto Ferrari, and it was the first opera house where each spectator bought a ticket. No image of the building survives, but a notary's document of 1658 and later surveys point to 153 boxes in five tiers.

From 1639 Francesco Cavalli became the theatre's leading composer. His Le nozze di Teti e di Peleo of that year is the first fully surviving opera written for the house, and works such as La Didone, L'Egisto, L'Ormindo and Giasone followed. Pietro Andrea Ziani, Marc'Antonio Ziani, Antonio Gianettini and Tomaso Albinoni also worked there, and in the 18th century Albinoni's long collaboration kept opera going, with works by Antonio Lotti and Baldassare Galuppi among others.

The old theatre was small: its proscenium was a little over 8 metres wide and its stage about 6.5 metres deep. A new theatre designed by Francesco Bognolo opened in 1763 with La morte di Dimone by Antonio Tozzi, its stage made about 3 metres deeper by demolishing two small houses behind it. In 1776 Giacomo Casanova described its fifth-tier boxes as a place of vice. The last known season was that of 1798, and in 1805 the French closed it.

After its demolition in 1812 its site became the Albrizzi garden. A project to reconstruct the theatre of 1637 in Venice, conceived and financed by the English entrepreneur and musicologist Paul Atkin, was launched in June 2019 with a conference, an exhibition and a concert, with period stage machinery and moving sets planned and the formal support of the Comune of Venice.
tebessa: Tébessa is a city in north-eastern Algeria near the border with Tunisia, the capital of Tébessa Province. Its classical name was Theveste, the Latin form of the Greek Thebeste, and the ancient Greeks also knew it as Hekatompyle, meaning Hundred Gates. It is known for the wall around the city and its gates and for traditional Algerian carpets. The surrounding province has many phosphate mines, among them the Djebel Onk mine, and the city is linked by road and rail with Tunisia and the rest of Algeria.

Once the empire was established, the 3rd Augustan Legion was based at Theveste before it moved to Lambaesis. The town later became a colony, probably under Trajan in the early 2nd century, when it was flourishing with about 30,000 inhabitants.

It became a Christian centre: its bishop Lucius attended the council of Carthage in 256 and died a martyr two years later, Maximilianus was martyred on 12 March 295 and Crispina on 5 December 304. Donatists held a council there, and in the 4th and 5th centuries the city was a hotbed of Manichaeism. A Latin Manichaean codex was found in a cave near the city in June 1918 and is now kept in Cologne.

The Byzantine patrician Solomon rebuilt Theveste and incorporated it into Byzantine North Africa early in the reign of Justinian I. The Muslim conquest in the 7th century reduced its importance without destroying it, and in the 11th century the Banu Hilal settled in the region. In the 16th century the Ottoman Empire placed a small garrison of Janissaries there, and the French occupied the town in 1851. After Algerian independence it became the capital of its own province.

The ruins are rich in ancient monuments. They include the Arch of Caracalla, a triumphal arch of 214, a Roman theatre, the Temple of Minerva of the early 3rd century with mosaics, a 4th-century amphitheatre, and the remains of the basilica of St Crispina, one of the largest in Africa, rebuilt in 535 by Solomon. The Byzantine walls of the 6th century, popularly called Solomon's Walls, are flanked by thirteen square towers, and Solomon also built his own tomb in the town. The city has an archaeological museum.
technical-university-of-darmstadt: The university grew from the Höhere Gewerbeschule, a higher trade school founded in 1836, which received its own building near the Altes Pädagog on Kapellplatz in 1844. It was followed by the Technische Schule in 1864 and the Grand Ducal Hessian Polytechnic in 1868. In political circles there was heated debate over whether a poor state such as the Grand Duchy of Hesse could afford a polytechnic at all. On 10 October 1877 Louis IV, Grand Duke of Hesse, raised the school to the Technische Hochschule zu Darmstadt, and the Abitur became a requirement for admission.

Student numbers stayed so low after 1877 that in 1881 and 1882 there were public debates about closing the institution. The local government and the university chose instead to set up the first chair of electrical engineering in the world, in 1882, held by Erasmus Kittler. The first faculty of the subject followed in 1883, along with the first degree course in it, and student numbers rose steadily afterwards. New buildings, including the Altes Hauptgebäude, opened on Hochschulstrasse in 1895, and the right to award doctorates came in 1899. A chair of aeronautics and flight mechanics was set up in 1913.

After 1933 the university lost scholars under the Nazi regime. The chemist Gerhard Herzberg, later Nobel laureate of 1971, was dismissed in 1934 because his wife was Jewish and emigrated to Canada. In 1947 the university hosted the first International Congress on Engineering Education, where participants discussed the moral responsibility of engineers and scientists. A chair of scientific policy was created in 1951 under Eugen Kogon. Reforms of the 1970s gave it a presidential statute and departments, and on 1 October 1997 it took the name Technische Universität Darmstadt, in part because Technische Hochschule had been misread in English-speaking countries as technical high school. In 2005 it became the first German public university with administrative autonomy.

Ten of the university's 13 departments are in engineering, natural sciences and mathematics, and three in the social sciences and humanities. It is concentrated on three campuses in Darmstadt, Inner City, Lichtwiese and the Botanical Garden, and with the universities of Mainz and Frankfurt it forms the Rhine-Main-Universities. Nobel laureates linked with it include the physicist Peter Grünberg, the chemist Hermann Staudinger and Herzberg. Chaim Weizmann, the first president of Israel, is among its alumni.
tecumseh: Tecumseh was born in Shawnee territory in what is now Ohio, probably at the town of Chillicothe on the Scioto River, into the Panther clan of the Kispoko division. His father, the war chief Puckeshinwau, was killed in the 1774 Battle of Point Pleasant, after which the Shawnees ceded Kentucky to the colonists. His older brother Cheeseekau, a noted war chief, taught him.

At the age of fifteen Tecumseh attended an intertribal conference at Lower Sandusky, where speakers such as Joseph Brant argued that Indian lands were held in common and that no more should be ceded without the consent of all the tribes. As a young war leader he joined Chief Blue Jacket's armed struggle, which ended in defeat at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794 and the loss of most of Ohio in the 1795 Treaty of Greenville.

In 1805 his younger brother Lalawéthika, later known as Tenskwatawa, began preaching that Native Americans should reject European influences, stop drinking alcohol and return to a traditional way of life. Tecumseh followed his teachings. In 1808 the brothers established Prophetstown in present-day Indiana, which grew into a large multi-tribal community.

After the Treaty of Fort Wayne Tecumseh became prominent and tried to build a confederacy from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico. In August 1810 he met William Henry Harrison at Vincennes and demanded that the treaty be rescinded, saying that otherwise they would have to fight it out. In 1811, while he was in the South seeking allies, Harrison defeated Tenskwatawa at the Battle of Tippecanoe and destroyed Prophetstown.

In June 1812 Tecumseh joined the British at Fort Malden. He took part in the Siege of Detroit under Major-General Isaac Brock, where he led about 530 warriors, and General William Hull surrendered on 16 August 1812. At Fort Meigs in 1813 he is said to have stopped the killing of American prisoners.

After the American naval victory in the Battle of Lake Erie on 10 September 1813, General Henry Procter decided to retreat from Amherstburg. Tecumseh reluctantly agreed and retreated with him up the Thames River. At the Battle of the Thames on 5 October he held the right with about 500 warriors while Procter's left collapsed, and he was killed in the fighting led by Colonel Richard Mentor Johnson. His confederacy collapsed after his death.

He was admired even by Americans who had fought him, and Harrison called him one of those uncommon geniuses who produce revolutions. He became a folk hero in American, Indigenous and Canadian history.
tecumsehs-war: The Treaty of Greenville, which ended the Northwest Indian War after the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794, ceded much of present-day Ohio, and chiefs such as Black Hoof of the Shawnee and Little Turtle of the Miami urged accommodation with the United States. The death of the Lenape chief Buckongahelas in May 1805 set off a witch-hunt, from which Tenskwatawa emerged as leader of a nativist revival that rejected liquor, European clothing and firearms and forbade further land sales. Pressed by settlers and the Wapakoneta Shawnee, he and Tecumseh founded Prophetstown near the meeting of the Wabash and Tippecanoe Rivers in 1808, which drew followers from many nations.

In the Treaty of Fort Wayne, signed on 30 September 1809, Governor William Henry Harrison of the Indiana Territory bought over 3,000,000 acres along the Wabash River after persuading the Miami and later the Wea and Kickapoo. Tecumseh revived the idea of Blue Jacket and Joseph Brant that Native land belonged in common to all tribes and could not be sold without the agreement of all. In August 1810 he came to Vincennes with 400 armed warriors; at Grouseland he demanded that the treaty be annulled, the meeting nearly ended in violence, and he warned that otherwise he would ally with the British.

In 1811, while Tecumseh travelled south seeking allies, finding most southern nations unwilling but winning the Red Stick faction of the Creeks, Harrison marched up the Wabash with more than 1,000 men. On 6 November 1811 his army reached Prophetstown. Before dawn the next day about 500 warriors sent by Tenskwatawa attacked the camp; Harrison's men held, and they burned the town afterwards in what became known as the Battle of Tippecanoe.

Tenskwatawa lost prestige and his brother's confidence, but Tecumseh quietly rebuilt the alliance. Americans blamed the British for arming the tribes, and Tippecanoe fed the tension that led to war with Britain a few months later. Tecumseh joined the British in Canada and fought on until he died in 1813 against Harrison's Army of the Northwest at the Battle of the Thames, near present-day Chatham, Ontario, after which his confederacy broke apart. Harrison, nicknamed Tippecanoe, later became President largely on the memory of the victory. Some historians treat the war as the last phase of a Sixty Years' War for the Great Lakes region.
tecun-uman: At the time of the Spanish conquest the K'iche' were ruled by four lords, as the Popol Vuh, Bartolomé de las Casas and the Título de Totonicapán record. The first-born son of the Keeper of the Mat, the most powerful of them, was expected to prove himself by leading the K'iche' army and bore the title nima rajpop achij, which the Título K'oyoi gives to Tecun Uman. The genealogies in the Popol Vuh and the Título de Totonicapán call the son of the Keeper of the Mat Tecum at the time of Alvarado's arrival.
Uman may not be part of his name: in the Título C'oyoi, the earliest document to name him, umam seems to mean grandson of, so that he is Tecum, grandson of the K'iche' king Don K'iq'ab'.

Hernán Cortés sent Pedro de Alvarado against the K'iche' and Kaqchikel after hearing that they were harassing Spain's allies, with 180 cavalry, 300 infantry, 4 cannons and thousands of allied warriors from central Mexico. A K'iche' army failed to stop his crossing of the Samalá River, and on 8 February 1524 his forces stormed Xetulul. On the approach to the valley of Quetzaltenango, K'iche' warriors ambushed and drove back the Mexican allies, but a Spanish cavalry charge, a shock to warriors who had never seen horses, scattered them. In his letter to Cortés of 11 April 1524, Alvarado wrote only that one of the four chiefs of Utatlán, the captain general of all the country, was killed, without naming him.

Local tradition places his death on the Llanos de Urbina near the village of Cantel. In the legend he wore quetzal feathers and was accompanied by his nahual, a quetzal; he killed Alvarado's horse and was then speared through the heart, and the grieving bird, landing on his chest, gave all male quetzals their red breast. Other versions have him turn into a quetzal or an eagle, or fall to one of Alvarado's soldiers, Argueta, whose descendants keep a lance said to bear his blood. He is commemorated each year on 20 February, though some Maya cultural activists see his status as a national hero as ironic, given the long mistreatment of Guatemala's native population.
teesta-river: The Teesta rises at the Teesta Khangtse Glacier, above 5,400 metres, in the eastern Himalayas and flows south through gorges and rapids in Sikkim. Streams from Tso Lhamo Lake, Gurudongmar Lake and the Thangu and Yumthang valleys feed it, and the Rangeet River, its largest tributary, joins it before it turns south into West Bengal. It reaches the plains at Sevoke, about 22 kilometres north-east of Siliguri, where the Coronation Bridge and a railway bridge link the north-eastern states to the rest of India.

Of its 414 kilometres, 305 lie in India and 109 in Bangladesh, and it drains 12,540 square kilometres. It passes Jalpaiguri and Mekhliganj, enters Bangladesh at Dahagram in Rangpur Division and joins the Brahmaputra, there called the Jamuna, near Gaibandha. Tropical deciduous trees cover the lower hills along its route and alpine vegetation the upper ones. During the monsoon landslides often dam parts of the river, and it has caused severe flooding in Bangladesh.

The Teesta once flowed south from Jalpaiguri in three channels, the Punarbhaba, the Atrai and the Karatoya. The flood of 1787 changed its course: it turned south-east and became part of the Brahmaputra system.

Its water has long been disputed between India and Bangladesh. Negotiations began in 1983, when a temporary arrangement gave Bangladesh 36 per cent and India 39 per cent, with the remainder unallocated. A water-sharing treaty signed by both countries in 1996, following the Ganges water dispute, dealt with sharing in general terms, and the sharing of the Teesta itself remains unsettled.

Dams and barrages control the river in both countries. In Sikkim they include the Teesta V Dam, rated at 510 megawatts, while the Teesta Barrage stands at Gajoldoba in Jalpaiguri district and the Barakhata Teesta Barrage in Nilphamari District in Bangladesh. The river area lies in the seismically active Zone V. It is the largest river of Sikkim and the second largest of West Bengal after the Ganges.
tefnakht: Tefnakht began his career as Great Chief of the West and prince of Sais, and was a late contemporary of Shoshenq V, the last ruler of the 22nd Dynasty. According to Kenneth Kitchen he was the second ruler of Sais, after Osorkon C. He set up two donation stelas in years 36 and 38 of Shoshenq V. The stela of year 38, from Buto, gives him the boastful epithet Great Chief of the entire land and lists his titles as prophet of Neith, Edjo and the Lady of Imay. These titles show that he controlled Sais, Buto and Kom el-Hish before the 22nd Dynasty ended, which reflects a political base in the western Delta.

Tefnakht made Sais his capital and allied with other minor kings of the Delta to conquer Middle and Upper Egypt, then under the Nubian king Piye. He captured and united many Delta cities, which made him more powerful than any of his predecessors in the 22nd or 23rd dynasties. He took Memphis and besieged Herakleopolis, an ally of Piye, and Nimlot, the ruler of Hermopolis, defected to his side.

Two naval engagements checked his coalition's advance, and Piye recaptured Memphis. After further campaigns Tefnakht's allies surrendered and he found himself isolated. He sent a letter formally submitting and swearing loyalty to Piye, but he was the only Lower Egyptian prince who avoided seeing Piye face to face. These events are told on Piye's Great Victory stela, set up on New Year's Day of his twenty-first regnal year. Soon afterwards Piye returned to Nubia and never came back to Lower Egypt.

Tefnakht was left alone as prince of Sais and over time restored his control in the Delta. He is generally thought to have proclaimed himself king as Shepsesre Tefnakht I after Piye left, and he is thought to have reigned from roughly 726 to 718 BCE. Bakenranef succeeded him at Sais.

Kitchen and most scholars identify him with the king of the Athens donation stela of year 8, although Olivier Perdu has argued for a later Tefnakht II. Tefnakht is absent from Manetho's tradition, perhaps because the Aegyptiaca survives only in abbreviated form or because he was considered a usurper. Diodorus Siculus and Plutarch say he dishonoured the memory of Menes, and Diodorus adds that on a campaign in Arabia he ran out of supplies, lived humbly and came to denounce luxury.
tegal: The city developed from a small village called Tetegual. Its modernisation began in the early 1530s, and it became part of the Pekalongan Regency, which acknowledged the Pajang Empire, successor of the Sultanate of Demak. Ki Gede Sebayu is named as the founder. Together with the local people he sought to expand agriculture on the fertile soil, and his coronation as leader was held together with a harvest festival. By district ordinance, 28 July is the anniversary of the city.

The colonial sugar industry of the Dutch East Indies originated in Tegal and Pekalongan, and Tegal Regency remained a major sugar centre until the mid-twentieth century. In the 1920s Tegal was a centre of activism for the Communist Party of Indonesia, whose local leaders were among the instigators of the 1926 rebellion. On 8 October 1945 the Three Regions Movement was founded in Tegal, Pekalongan and Brebes to replace the aristocratic regents with ordinary people, accusing them of cooperating with the Japanese in World War II. The republic's government in Yogyakarta declared it illegal, and Indonesian forces defeated the rebels on 21 December 1945.

Tegal lies on the north coast road of Central Java, 329 kilometres east of Jakarta, and covers 39.14 square kilometres. It is administratively separate from Tegal Regency, which borders it to the south and east. It had 273,825 inhabitants at the 2020 census, and its built-up area, which stretches well beyond the city boundary, had 1,602,546. Trade and services are the main sectors of the economy. The city is known for its warung, called warteg, and for tea products, and its language, Bahasa Tegal, resembles the speech of Banyumas in its vocabulary.
tegbesu: Oral traditions hold that Tegbesu, also known as Bossa Ahadee, was the son of Agaja and Hwanjile, a woman said to have brought Vodun to the kingdom. He was not Agaja's eldest son. Agaja had greatly enlarged Dahomey, conquering Allada in 1724 and Whydah in 1727, which brought opposition from the royal families of both, who held fortified islands off the coast, and semi-regular war with the Oyo Empire. One tradition tells that Agaja had to send a son to Oyo as part of Dahomey's tribute, that only Hwanjile was willing to let hers go, and that this sacrifice won Tegbesu his father's favour, though his brother Zinga remained the official heir.

According to one oral history, when Agaja died Tegbesu's brothers surrounded his house to stop him reaching the palace, but he escaped, reached it, and was appointed king by the Great Council. The historian Edna Bay notes that the oral histories disagree on exactly who appointed him.

Tegbesu came to power when Dahomey needed its rule accepted by the peoples it had recently conquered, and he is credited with a number of administrative changes to that end. Having spent much of his youth in Oyo, he modelled the palace complex and several offices on those of that empire. He moved the capital back from Allada to Abomey and set up a puppet king to rule in Allada, and he took more wives to build family ties across the kingdom. In Ouidah he had several officials opposed to him put to death and replaced with loyal men, and in 1745 he created the Yevogan, a single official to deal with all European trade in place of separate officers for each European power.

His reign saw the first prominent kpojito, or mother of the leopard: Hwanjile, who is said to have changed Dahomey's religious practice by creating two new deities and tying worship more closely to the king. The slave trade grew considerably under him and became the largest part of the king's income, reportedly bringing him £250,000 a year.
tegernsee-abbey: The early history of the abbey, officially St. Quirinus Abbey, is obscure, since the Magyar incursions of the early 10th century and a fire in about 970 destroyed earlier evidence. The community was founded in 746 beside an existing Church of Our Saviour by the brothers Otkar and Adalbert of the Huosi, one of the five old ruling clans of Bavaria. It was consecrated in 754 and settled by monks from St. Gall. The founders obtained relics of the Roman martyr Quirinus from Pope Paul I. A later tradition, which cannot be verified, held that the brothers withdrew from the world after a son of Pippin the Younger killed Otkar's son with a chessboard.

After the fall of Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria the abbey became a Carolingian royal monastery, but Hungarian raids and the confiscations of Arnulf, Duke of Bavaria, weakened it. Emperor Otto II refounded it as an Imperial Abbey in 978 with monks from St. Maximin's Abbey, Trier. Under the monk Froumund and Abbot Ellinger it became a centre of literature, manuscript production and learning; its workshops made stained glass for Bishop Gottschalk of Freising and cast the doors of Mainz Cathedral in 1014. This golden age lasted almost to the end of the 12th century and produced, besides the Ruodlieb, the Play about the Antichrist and the Tegernsee love letters.

From 1189, when Manegold of Berg was made abbot through the intrigues of the Counts of Andechs, noble families came to dominate the house, and it declined in the 13th and 14th centuries; it burned down in 1410. A visitation in 1426 began a revival, and with the support of Cardinal Nikolaus von Kues the abbey became a centre of the Melk reform, opening the house to a wider range of social classes. Its scribes compiled the Liber illuministarum around 1500, it had its own printing press from 1573, and it survived a raid by Swedish soldiers in the Thirty Years' War.

The abbey was dissolved on 17 March 1803. King Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria acquired the buildings in 1817, and as Schloss Tegernsee they passed to the Dukes in Bavaria, a branch of the Wittelsbach family, who still own them. The former abbey church is the parish church of St. Quirinus, and the site also houses a grammar school and the Ducal Bavarian Brewery of Tegernsee.
tegin-shah: Tegin Shah, also called Shahi Tegin or Sri Shahi, and known to the Chinese as Wusan Teqin Sa, the Tegin Shah of Khorasan, succeeded Barha Tegin on the throne of the Turk Shahis. The dynasty was of Western Turk or mixed Western Turk-Hephthalite origin and ruled from Kabul and Kapisa to Gandhara, with Kabulistan as its heartland. It was in constant conflict with the eastward expansion of the Umayyad Caliphate. The Arabs took Sistan about 650 CE and captured Kabul in 665 CE, but the Turk Shahis struck back and recovered Kabul, Zabulistan around Ghazni and Arachosia as far as Kandahar. In 697–698 CE the Arabs again failed to take Kabul and Zabulistan, and their general Yazid ibn Ziyad was killed.

With the Iltäbär of Zabulistan, Tegin Shah sent a joint embassy to the Tang emperor at Xi'an to have their thrones confirmed. According to the Old Book of Tang, the envoys offered an astrological text, secret medical recipes and foreign medicines, and an imperial edict gave the king the title Geluodazhi Tele. Geluodazhi is thought to render the name of the Khalaj, making him Tegin of the Khalaj, and his coins in Gupta script name him hitivira kharalāča, probably Iltäbär of the Khalaj. The ruler of Zabulistan received a similar title, and it seems the Turk Shahi rulers were Khalaj Turks.

In the 27th year of the Kaiyuan era, 739 CE, the Old Book of Tang records that the king asked, because of his old age, that his son should succeed him. The emperor agreed and sent an envoy to confer the royal title on Fromo Kesaro by imperial edict.
tegucigalpa: Tegucigalpa lies in the southern-central highlands of Honduras, in a valley ringed by mountains, in the department of Francisco Morazán, of which it is also the departmental capital. The city stands on a chain of mountains, at elevations of 975 metres at its lowest points and 1,463 metres in its highest suburbs, and is hilly with few flat areas. The Choluteca River separates it from its sister city Comayagüela. The surrounding country was open woodland of pine and oak, and the climate is a tropical savanna one, tempered by the altitude, with a rainy and a dry season.

The Spaniards claimed the site on 29 September 1578 and founded it as the Real de Minas de San Miguel de Tegucigalpa, on the site of an existing settlement of the Lenca and the Tolupans. Juan de la Cueva became its first mayor in 1579. Among its first important buildings were the Dolores Church (1735), the San Miguel Cathedral (1765), the Casa de la Moneda (1780) and the Immaculate Conception Church (1788). The origin of the name is uncertain: the most widely accepted version derives it from a Nahuatl phrase meaning 'hills of silver', although the local people are said to have been unaware of the mineral deposits, and other proposals include 'painted rocks'.

On 30 October 1880 President Marco Aurelio Soto moved the seat of government from Comayagua to Tegucigalpa. The constitution of 1936 made Tegucigalpa and Comayagüela a single Central District, formed on 30 January 1937, and the constitution of 1982 keeps that arrangement as the permanent national capital. In late October and early November 1998 Hurricane Mitch stayed over Honduras for five days; on saturated ground and deforested slopes the rain caused catastrophic flooding, especially in Tegucigalpa, and destroyed parts of the city along the banks of the Choluteca.

Tegucigalpa is the largest city of Honduras and its political and administrative centre, seat of the national government and of the National Autonomous University of Honduras, founded in 1847. Legally the capital is the Municipality of the Central District, though nearly all government institutions stand on the Tegucigalpa side of the river, while Comayagüela on the western bank is largely made up of lower-income neighbourhoods. The census of 2013 counted 1,157,509 people in the Central District. Roman Catholicism has been the leading religion since the Mercedarian missions of about 1548, and the Diocese of Comayagua was moved to the city and renamed the Diocese of Tegucigalpa by 1916.
tehran: Tehran is bounded in the north by the southern end of the Alborz range, whose highest point near the city is Tochal Peak at 3,963 metres. The northern districts begin at about 1,800 metres, with houses and streets on steep slopes, while Rey at the southern end lies at about 1,100 metres beside the single mountain of Raga. Fertile meadows and villages, fed by the Karaj and Jajrud rivers, lie to the west and south-west. Mount Damavand, Iran's highest peak, stands near the city and figures in Ferdowsi's Šāhnāme as the homeland of Keyumars and the place where King Fereydun bound the dragon fiend Zahhak.

The origin of the name is disputed. The city's own account derives it from the Persian words for 'bottom' and 'slope', the foot of the mountain, while the linguist Zana Kamrani proposes that it means 'the warm place', in contrast to Shemiran, 'the cool place'.

Archaeological remains from the ancient city of Ray suggest that settlement in the area is more than 6,000 years old. In the Median period part of present-day Tehran was a suburb of the prominent city of Rhages, which appears in the Avesta and in Old Persian inscriptions as a province; from there Darius I sent reinforcements to his father Hystaspes in Parthia. In 641 the last Sasanian king, Yazdgerd III, issued his final appeal to the nation from Rhages before fleeing to Khorasan. Because the city resisted the Muslim invasion, the Arabs ordered it destroyed and rebuilt by the aristocrat Farrukhzad.

In the ninth century Tehran was a well-known village, though less so than the flourishing Rhages nearby. Agha Mohammad Khan of the Qajar dynasty first chose it as the capital of Iran in 1786, because of its closeness to Iran's contested territories in the Caucasus and to avoid the rival factions of earlier dynasties. Under Reza Shah the city gained Iran's first institute of higher learning, bank, railway line and museum. Large-scale construction began in the 1920s, and Tehran became a destination for mass migration from all over Iran, especially in the 20th century.

Tehran is the capital and largest city of Iran, with 8,693,706 inhabitants at the 2016 census. Persians are the majority, with Azeris the second-largest ethnic group at about 10 to 15 per cent. Its historical sites include the Golestan Palace of the Qajar dynasty, a World Heritage Site, and the Sa'dabad and Niavaran palace complexes; the Azadi Tower was built in 1971 to mark 2,500 years of the Persian Empire.
teia: Little is known of Teia's early life except that he was the elder brother of Aligernus. He served as a military officer under Totila, who revived Gothic resistance in the Gothic War against the Byzantine Empire and within a decade recovered much of the Italian peninsula. The historian Procopius mentions Teia in the later stages of the war, when Justinian I sent his chamberlain Narses with an army to end it. Totila sent Teia with 2,000 cavalry to guard the River Po, but Narses crossed the river without fighting and marched towards Rome. Totila recalled Teia, whose reinforcements arrived just as the armies met at the Battle of Taginae in July 552, where the Goths were defeated and Totila was mortally wounded.

Teia gathered the remaining Gothic forces at Ticinum (Pavia), where they chose him king, and took possession of the treasury there. He urged the Franks to move against the Byzantines, but they preferred to let the two sides wear each other down. When Narses took Rome with little resistance, Teia ordered the killing of all the Roman senators and their families held as hostages in Campania, and of 300 children of prominent Italian families whom Totila had collected.

Narses then besieged Cumae, where Totila's war chest was held and Teia's brother commanded the garrison. Teia marched south, making lengthy detours that took nearly thirty days, but Narses intercepted him near Mount Vesuvius. The Goths camped near Pompeii facing the Byzantines across the Sarno River, and a two-month stalemate followed. It ended when the Gothic admiral defected, cutting off supplies, and Teia withdrew to Mount Lactarius.

In October the Goths attacked there; the sources disagree on whether the date was 1 or 30 October. Both armies fought on foot, and Teia led repeated assaults until a spear killed him. The Byzantines displayed his head on a spear, yet the Goths fought on for two more days. Procopius wrote that the battle showed a heroism inferior to that of none of the heroes of legend, and the survivors negotiated a withdrawal, on terms that differ between Procopius and Agathias. By 554 the Ostrogothic kingdom had faded, and silver coins minted in Teia's name had circulated from Pavia along the Alpine trade routes.
teimuraz-i-of-kakheti: Teimuraz was the eldest son of David I of Kakheti and Ketevan, and a grandson of Alexander II, whom his own son Constantine I had killed in an Iranian-sponsored coup. When Christian Kakhetians rallied by Ketevan overthrew Constantine, the nobles asked Shah Abbas I to confirm Teimuraz, and the shah, at war with the Ottoman Empire, agreed. Later, having refused a summons to Isfahan, Teimuraz sent his mother and his sons Levan and Alexander to the shah as hostages, but in 1614 Abbas, aided by the defector Giorgi Saakadze, drove him into Imereti.

On 15 September 1615 Kakhetian nobles under David Jandieri rose against the shah's appointee Isa Khan and proposed Teimuraz as king of all eastern Georgia. His forces routed an Iranian army at Tsitsamuri, but Abbas came in person in 1616; towns such as Gremi and Zagem shrank to villages, and the descendants of the more than one hundred thousand peasants deported make up the bulk of the ethnic Georgian population of Iran. In 1625 Saakadze turned against Iran, won the Battle of Martkopi and restored Teimuraz as king of Kartli and Kakheti, and in 1626 Teimuraz defeated Saakadze at Bazaleti.

His embassy to Philip IV of Spain and Pope Urban VIII produced only the first printed Georgian book, a Georgian-Italian dictionary (Rome, 1629). Sheltering Daud Khan cost him both kingdoms in 1633 to Shah Safi's favourite Rostom. Pardoned and restored to Kakheti in 1638, he swore allegiance to Tsar Michael in 1639, but in 1648 Rostom routed him at Magharo, where his last surviving son David fell.

Educated at the Safavid court, Teimuraz wrote a Georgian full of Persian imagery and loanwords. In 1629–34 he translated and adapted Persian romances, among them Layla and Majnun, Yusuf and Zulaikha, The Rose and the Nightingale and The Candle and the Moth. His first poem, The Book and Passion of Queen Ketevan (1625), drew on the Augustinian missionaries who witnessed her death; Donald Rayfield wrote that whatever Georgia lost in the king, it gained in the poet. In exile in 1649–56 he mourned his kingdom and cursed the bloodthirsty king of Persia.

After failing to win Russian help, though he visited Tsar Alexis in June 1658, Teimuraz retired to a monastery in 1661. Vakhtang V sent him to Isfahan, where Abbas II received him with honour but imprisoned him after his grandson Heraclius tried to take Kakheti. He died in captivity at the fortress of Astarabad, and his remains were buried at the Alaverdi Monastery.
teimuraz-ii-of-kakheti: Teimuraz II of the Bagrationi dynasty was a son of Heraclius I and Princess Ana Cholokashvili. With his mother he ruled as regent for his absent brother David II from 1709 to 1715. In 1732 the Turks killed another brother, King Constantine, and took control of his kingdom, and Teimuraz, his successor, fled to the mountains of Pshavi and fought the occupiers from there. He was also a lyric poet, who translated from Persian and composed his poems, as the sources put it, virtually on horseback.

In July 1735 the Persian ruler Nader Shah Afshar invaded Kakheti and forced the Turks out of most of eastern Georgia. He summoned Teimuraz to his headquarters at Erivan and, when Teimuraz refused to convert to Islam, had him detained. Teimuraz escaped in October 1735 and stirred unrest, but was captured by the close of 1736. In 1738 the shah released him to counter a Georgian rebellion and made him governor of Kakheti, while his son Heraclius II campaigned with Nader Shah in India. Teimuraz, aided by Erekle II, crushed the rebels led by Givi Amilakhvari, and in return the shah abolished in 1742 a heavy tribute on Kakheti and helped him subdue the duchies of the Aragvi and the Ksani.

In 1744 the shah confirmed him as king of Kartli and gave his son a Kakhetian crown, laying the ground for later reunion. They were the first Christian kings recognised since 1632, and both were crowned at Svetitskhoveli Cathedral at Mtskheta on 1 October 1745. When their influence grew they withdrew their loyalty, and Nader Shah sent 30,000 troops under the converted Georgian Amilakhvari, but the shah was murdered in 1747. The rulers expelled the Persian garrisons, checked pretenders in 1749 and 1750, and made the khanates of Yerevan, Ganja and Nakhichevan tributaries. They fought Dagestani raiders without complete success.

Teimuraz hoped Russia would protect the Christians of the Caucasus. He sent an embassy to Saint Petersburg in 1752 without result, and in 1760 he visited the Russian court himself with a plan for a Georgian expedition to put a Russian candidate on the Persian throne. Russia, occupied with the Seven Years' War, did not take it up. He died suddenly in the Russian capital on 8 January 1762 and was buried next to his father-in-law Vakhtang VI at Astrakhan. Heraclius succeeded him as king of Kartli, joining the two kingdoms in the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. In July 2013 Georgia raised the possibility of reburial of his remains.
teispids: Anshan, in the southern Zagros, had been part of the Elamite Kingdom in the second millennium BCE. In the Neo-Elamite period the kingdom weakened, its kings could no longer assert their authority over Anshan, and many Iranians moved into the region. After the Neo-Assyrian Empire sacked the Elamite capital Susa in 646 BCE, the Elamite Kingdom disappeared, and at some time in the 7th century BCE Anshan became an independent kingdom under Teispes. The historian Pierre Briant places the formation of the kingdom in this setting and dates Teispes' accession to around 635 BCE.

The oldest genealogy of the kings of Anshan is in the Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian text, in which Cyrus II gives himself and his forebears the title King of Anshan in keeping with Elamite tradition. It sets out the line as Teispes, Cyrus I, Cambyses I and Cyrus II, and shows that before Cyrus the Great their whole domain was Anshan, now identified with the plain near Marvdasht in Fars province. Cyrus II then conquered a vast area of southwestern Asia, and the line continued with his son Cambyses II and with Bardiya.

The Teispid line ended in 522 BCE, when Darius I seized the throne after killing its last members. According to Maria Brosius and Bruce Lincoln, Darius sought to legitimate his rule by claiming a common ancestry with the Teispid kings and giving the impression that they were Achaemenids. In inscriptions at Pasargadae dating from around 510 BCE, Cyrus II is made to say "I am Cyrus the King, an Achaemenian". In the Behistun Inscription Darius presented a double line of kings descended from Teispes and from an ancestor named Achaemenes, whom he called the father of Teispes and the first King of Anshan. The Cyrus Cylinder makes no mention of Achaemenes.
tejeros-convention: The leaders of the revolution met at a friar estate in Tejeros, in San Francisco de Malabon (now General Trias), at first to discuss the defence of Cavite, much of which Governor General Camilo de Polavieja had retaken. The meeting turned instead to the question of who should lead the revolution. Andrés Bonifacio, the Supremo of the Katipunan, had come to Cavite months earlier to mediate between the factions and had sided with the Magdiwang; he and his allies held that the Katipunan already functioned as a government, while the Magdalo and some Magdiwang sympathisers wanted a new one. Filipino historians regard the convention as the first presidential and vice-presidential election in Philippine history, though only members of the Katipunan took part.

After a day of heated debate Bonifacio took the chair and obtained the assembly's agreement that its decisions would be respected. Emilio Aguinaldo, absent at the front at Pasong Santol, was elected president; Mariano Trias became vice president, Artemio Ricarte captain-general and Emiliano Riego de Dios director of war. Bonifacio was elected director of the interior, but Daniel Tirona objected that the post needed a man with a lawyer's diploma. Bonifacio demanded an apology, drew a pistol on Tirona until Ricarte stopped him, declared the day's proceedings null and void as supreme president of the Katipunan, and left. Santiago Álvarez and Gregoria de Jesús later wrote in their memoirs that many ballots had been filled in before they were handed out.

Aguinaldo and the other officers, except Bonifacio, took their oaths at Santa Cruz de Malabon, while Aguinaldo's brother Crispulo was killed in the Battle of Pasong Santol on 24 March 1897. Bonifacio and 45 followers drew up the Acta de Tejeros on 28 March rejecting the result, and at Naik on 19 April a further document repudiating the new government. Aguinaldo openly assumed the presidency on 24 April 1897. Acting on complaints from Severino de las Alas and Jose Coronel, he ordered Bonifacio's arrest; at Limbon, Indang, Bonifacio was wounded and his brother Ciriaco killed, and Andrés and his brother Procopio were tried for treason by Aguinaldo's war council. The Tejeros government lasted until 1 November 1897, when the Republic of Biak-na-Bato replaced it.
tekle-haymanot-of-gojjam: Born Adal Tesema, he was the son of Tesema Goshu and grandson of Ras Goshu Zewde. His father died while he was a minor, and a rival prince of the house, Ras Desta Tadla, took control of Gojjam and imprisoned him. Adal escaped to the lowlands, raised an army, defeated Desta and submitted to Emperor Tekle Giyorgis, who confirmed him as Shum of Gojjam and Dejazmach and let him marry his sister, Laqetch Gebre Mehdin.

In 1871 Kassay Mercha, the future Yohannes IV, defeated Tekle Giyorgis and restored Desta, but after Kassay left Gojjam Adal returned, killed Desta and united the province. He submitted to Yohannes in 1874 as Ras Tekle Haymanot. On 20 January 1881 at Debre Tabor Yohannes made him negus of Gojjam and of Kaffa, the latter only if he could conquer it, and gave him 8,000 rifles. Menelik of Shewa also wanted Kaffa, and after Embabo Yohannes let Menelik keep it.

In January 1887 Tekle Haymanot defeated the Mahdists at Madana, between Gederaf and Gallabat. The next year a Mahdist army under Abu Anga defeated him at Sar Weha on 18 January 1888 and went on to sack and burn Gondar, where, according to the missionary Joseph Ohrwalder, priests were killed and hundreds of women and children taken into slavery. When Abu Anga invaded again in July, Tekle Haymanot crushed his army. In September 1888 he refused to send troops to Yohannes, who suspected a plot with Menelik and laid waste to much of Gojjam until he submitted.

After Yohannes died at Gallabat in 1889, Tekle Haymanot pledged allegiance to Menelik II, who reinstated him as Shum of Gojjam and named him an advisor. At Adwa he commanded 8,000 riflemen, 15,000 spearmen and 700 cavalry. He died on 10 January 1901. Menelik, judging Gojjam too valuable for one man, then divided it into three parts under different men, one of them from Shewa. Of his three sons, Bezabah, Hailu and Balaw, Ras Hailu later ruled as Hailu II of Gojjam.
tekle-haymanot-saint: Tekle Haymanot was born in Zorare, a district of Selale on the eastern edge of Shewa, into an Amhara family of the long-established Christian population of northern Shewa. His hagiographical tradition traces his ancestors' migration south from the old Aksumite lands through Bete Amhara, a movement the historian Taddesse Tamrat places within the wider southward spread of Christian settlers after Aksum's decline. He was the son of the priest Tsega Zeab and his wife Egzi'e Haraya, also called Sarah, who according to tradition had pledged their firstborn to God.

In his youth Shewa suffered raids by Motolomi Sato, the pagan king of Damot beyond the Jamma River, and several traditions tell of his dealings with that king. His father gave him his first religious teaching; he was made a deacon at fifteen and was later ordained a priest by Pope Cyril III of Alexandria.

At about thirty he went north to study, spending nine years under Iyasus Mo'a at the island monastery of Lake Hayq and then staying at Debre Damo under Abbot Yohannes after visiting Axum. Tradition holds that he received the full monastic habit on his return journey at Lake Hayq; Taddesse Tamrat reads this account as a later attempt to assert that monastery's seniority over his followers.

Back in Shewa he settled between Selale and Grarya, where in 1284 he founded the monastery of Debre Atsbo, renamed Debre Libanos in the 15th century. Its abbot, the Ichege, came to rank second only to the Abuna. Emperor Zara Yaqob promoted the saint's veneration and the monastery's standing.

He lived 29 years after the foundation and was first buried in the cave where he had lived as a hermit; almost 60 years later he was reburied at Debre Libanos, where Emperor Haile Selassie built a new church over the tomb in the 1950s. He is often shown as an old man with wings and one visible leg, after stories of his standing in prayer until a leg broke. Historians such as Taddesse Tamrat and G.W.B. Huntingford regard his role in the Solomonic restoration as a later invention, since older traditions credit Iyasus Mo'a. His feast falls on 30 August, and hagiographies of him were written from the 15th century onward.
tel-dan-stele: The stele is a fragmentary stele with an Old Aramaic inscription in the Phoenician script. Fragment A was found in July 1993 by Gila Cook, a member of the team led by Avraham Biran, among the rubble of a wall at Tel Dan; fragments B1 and B2 followed in June 1994. They were found not in their original setting but reused, and Biran and his colleague Joseph Naveh published them in 1993 and 1995. The stele is now in the Israel Museum.

There is widespread agreement that the three fragments belong to one inscription and that B1 and B2 fit together, but less on how A fits with them. The earliest possible date is about 870 BCE, and Lawrence J. Mykytiuk thinks it could hardly be later than 750 BCE. A few scholars, Niels Peter Lemche, Thomas L. Thompson and F. H. Cryer, have proposed later dates, and Cryer and Lemche argued that it was a modern forgery, a view most scholars have rejected because the fragments came from controlled excavations.

Most scholars identify the author, who is not named, as Hazael of Aram-Damascus, an important regional power in the late ninth century BCE. In the reconstructed text the author tells how the king of Israel invaded his father's land, how the god Hadad made him king and went before him, and how he defeated kings with their chariots and horsemen. Biran and Naveh read the names of two victims as Joram, son of Ahab, king of Israel, and Ahaziah, son of Joram, of the House of David, though scholars are evenly divided on these identifications.
Biran's translation has the author kill seventy kings. André Lemaire argues that the reading rests on a very small part of a letter and that the text speaks of two kings and two thousand chariots.

The stele is the earliest widely accepted reference outside the Hebrew Bible to the name David as founder of a Judahite polity, and one of only four known inscriptions from about 1200 to 800 BCE that name Israel, the others being the Merneptah Stele, the Mesha Stele and the Kurkh Monoliths. A minority of scholars dispute the reading bytdwd as "House of David", since no word divider separates byt and dwd; they suggest a place name, a divine epithet or other words. The stele is generally accepted as genuine.
tela: The Spanish conquistador Cristóbal de Olid founded the town on 3 May 1524 near Tehuacán, an indigenous town ruled by a cacique named Cucumba, and called it Triunfo de la Cruz after the feast of that day; the name survives on a promontory in the bay. Some historians derive the name Tela from Tetela, Nahuat for land of hills and craggy mountains. Spanish presence on this coast was light, and English privateers, later buccaneers, used the bay to attack Spanish ships. Garifuna people, exiled by the English from St Vincent to Roatán in 1797, settled at Tela in 1808 and founded communities at Triunfo de la Cruz and San Juan.

Tela became a municipality in 1876, joined the department of Atlántida in 1902 and was made a city in March 1927. It grew as a port from 1914, when the Tela Railroad Company of the United Fruit Company made it its Honduran headquarters, which stayed there until 1970. The company brought in many workers of African descent from the English-speaking Caribbean, above all Jamaica and Belize, who introduced English and Methodist and Anglican churches. Its planned town, Tela Nueva, was segregated by race, with the best houses in a zone kept for Euro-American employees.

Mestizo workers resented the West Indians, the government took an anti-West Indian line, immigration laws were hardened in 1929 and 1934, and hundreds of Caribbean people were deported in the 1930s. Floods ruined the banana industry in 1930. Tela was the centre of the 1954 General Strike, which won major concessions for workers; many English-speaking residents, who had been lukewarm or hostile towards it, then faced retaliation and left the region.

The town had a population of 39,920 in a calculation of 2023. Garifuna villages such as Triunfo de la Cruz, San Juan and Tornabé lie along the beaches on either side. Passenger trains run from Tela to Puerto Cortés, and the town's patron saint, San Antonio, is honoured with a festival every June.
telaga-batu-inscription: The stone was found around the 1950s at Sabokingking, in the 3 Ilir quarter of Ilir Timur II in Palembang, South Sumatra, and is now shown in the National Museum of Indonesia in Jakarta under inventory number D.155. It is carved on andesite, 118 cm tall and 148 cm wide, in Pallava letters. Around thirty Siddhayatra inscriptions had been found earlier in southern Sumatra, all concerning the Siddhayatra journey of Dapunta Hyang Sri Jayanasa, which the Kedukan Bukit inscription places around 605 Saka, or 683 CE. All of them are kept in the same museum.

Much of the long text is eroded and hard to read, probably because the stone was used in the ritual it describes. Water was likely poured over the inscribed face, gathered at the foot of the stone and channelled through the spout, to be drunk by those who swore loyalty to the king. Most of the text lays curses on anyone who commits or has committed treason against the kadatuan of Srivijaya or disobeys the orders of the datu.

The readable lines address princes (rājaputra), ministers, regional rulers (bhūpati), generals (senāpati), judges (dandanayaka), inspectors of workers, smiths and weapon makers (vāsīkarana), soldiers, officials, clerks (kāyastha), artisans, ship captains, traders (vaniyāga), and the king's servants and slaves, and tell them that they will be killed by the spells of their oath if they are not loyal.

According to Casparis, the groups named were those thought likely to revolt against Srivijayan rule, which is why the ruler had them pledge their loyalty under the threat of a curse. The inscription preserves one of the most complete surviving lists of state officials.

Because these titles are so many and so finely graded, some historians have argued that they existed only in the capital, and so that the court of Srivijaya lay at Palembang. Soekmono disagreed: since the stone threatens those who commit treason against the kadatuan, he held that it need not have stood at the centre of the court, and he placed the capital at Minanga, named in the Kedukan Bukit inscription and assumed to lie near Candi Muara Takus.
telangana: Telangana lies on the Deccan Plateau, in the central stretch of the eastern seaboard of the Indian Peninsula, and covers 112,077 square kilometres. It borders Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh to the north and Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka to the south. The Godavari and Krishna rivers drain it, along with smaller rivers such as the Bhima, the Manjira and the Musi, but most of the land is arid. The name comes from Telinga, and was used to set the predominantly Telugu region of the old Hyderabad State apart from Marathwada and Kalyana-Karnataka.

One of the earliest known political formations here was the Aśmaka Mahajanapada, which flourished roughly between 700 and 400 BCE and was the only southern kingdom among the sixteen great Mahajanapadas. Its capital, Podana, is identified by most scholars with present-day Bodhan. The region later belonged to many empires, among them the Maurya, Satavahana, Chalukya, Chola, Rashtrakuta, Delhi Sultanate, Bahmani Sultanate and Golconda Sultanate. The region experienced a golden age under the Kakatiya dynasty, which ruled most of present-day Andhra Pradesh and Telangana from 1083 to 1323; Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra II were prominent rulers. It weakened after the attack of Malik Kafur in 1309 and was dissolved when Muhammad bin Tughluq's forces defeated Prataparudra in 1323.

From the seventeenth to the nineteenth century the Mughals and the Nizams of Hyderabad ruled the region. In 1823 the Nizams ceded the Northern Circars and the Ceded Districts to British India, which left Hyderabad a landlocked princely state. When India became independent in 1947 the Nizam wished to stay independent, and the Government of India annexed Hyderabad State on 17 September 1948 in a military operation called Operation Polo. After decades of protest by the Telangana movement, the state of Telangana was created in 2014 from the Telugu regions of the former Hyderabad State.

Telangana has Hyderabad as its capital. Telugu is the primary official language and Urdu the second; about 75 per cent of people speak Telugu and 12 per cent Urdu. Before 1948 Urdu was the official language of Hyderabad State and the language of the educated elite. At the 2011 census Hindus formed 85.1 per cent of the population and Muslims 12.7 per cent. Warangal Fort, the Kakatiya capital, has the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, which appears on the state emblem, and the Ramappa Temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The state is divided into 33 districts.
telavi: Telavi is the main city and administrative centre of the province of Kakheti. It lies on the foothills of the Tsiv-Gombori Range, 500 to 800 m above sea level, facing the range to the south and south-west and bordering the Alazani Valley to the north and east. The Greater Caucasus Mountain Range, which runs to the north of the valley, can be seen from most of the city.

The first archaeological finds from Telavi date from the Bronze Age. In the 2nd century CE the Greek geographer Claudius Ptolemaeus mentions a name, Teleda, that refers to it. From the 8th century it grew into a fairly important political and administrative centre. The Arab geographer Al-Muqaddasi in the 10th century listed it beside Tbilisi, Ganja, Shamkhor, Shemakha and Shirvan, and noted that most of its population was Christian.

From the 10th to the 12th centuries Telavi was the capital of the Kingdom of Kakheti and later of Kakheti-Hereti. During the Georgian state's 12th and 13th centuries it became one of its most important political and economic centres. After the united Georgian Kingdom disintegrated in the 15th century its role declined and it became an ordinary town of trade and crafts. It regained importance in the 17th century as the capital of the Kingdom of Kakheti, and by 1762 it was the second capital, after Tbilisi, of the united eastern Georgian Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti.

King Erekle II, who was born and died in Telavi, reigned from 1744 to 1798, and the period was a special epoch for the town. He founded a theological seminary and a theatre there, and Georgians remember him affectionately as Patara Kakhi, the Little Kakhetian. In 1801 Kartli-Kakheti was annexed by the Russian Empire and Telavi lost its status as a capital. In the 19th century it was the centre of the Telavi uezd in the Tiflis Governorate, with small industries such as pottery, leather painting and wine-making. About 12,000 people lived there at the end of the century, around 9,000 of them Armenians and 2,000 Georgians.

Telavi has about 16,800 inhabitants. It keeps four fortification monuments from four periods, which leads scholars to call it the most medieval city in Georgia. They include Batonis Tsikhe, a 17th-century fortress that is one of the few well-preserved medieval royal palaces in the country, and Dzveli Galavani, the fortress of the first Kakhetian kings. Nearby are the 11th-century Alaverdi Cathedral, the Ikalto Academy, where Shota Rustaveli studied, the ruins of Gremi and the Tsinandali Gardens. The Armenian churches of the old town were mostly closed in 1923.
telegraph: Signalling over distance is ancient. The signal towers of the Great Wall of China are among the oldest examples, and by 400 BCE signals could be sent by beacon fires or drum beats. These ancient systems, including Chinese ones, could send only predetermined messages and so were not true telegraphs. The first true telegraph in widespread use was the optical telegraph of Claude Chappe, which operated in France from 1793; its stations signalled to each other with shutters or paddles. The word telegraph, from the Greek for writing at a distance, was coined by Chappe himself.

Early electric telegraphs were electrostatic, with a system over a substantial distance by Ronalds in 1816, which the British Admiralty rejected as unnecessary because its optical telegraph to Portsmouth seemed adequate. Electromagnetic systems replaced the electrostatic ones. The first operative electric telegraph, by Gauss and Weber in 1833, linked Göttingen Observatory to the Institute of Physics about a kilometre away.

Cooke and Wheatstone received a patent for an electric telegraph on 12 June 1837, and the world's first permanent railway telegraph, between London Paddington and West Drayton, was completed in July 1839. Railway companies installed lines first in Germany and Britain, and private companies then offered a public service along them. Samuel Morse developed a rival system in the United States, and the Morse system was adopted as the international standard in 1865, using a modified code developed in Germany in 1848.

Ocean cables needed a flexible insulator that resisted seawater. Gutta-percha, a natural rubber sent to London from Singapore by William Montgomerie in 1843, proved suitable, and a cable between Dover and Calais was laid in 1850, though a French fishing vessel severed it almost at once. It was relaid the next year, and connections to Ireland and the Low Countries followed. Telegrams became popular once prices fell, and at their peak in 1929 an estimated 200 million were sent.

The electric telegraph freed communication from the time constraints of the postal service and revolutionised society and the global economy. Earlier optical lines had been installed by governments, often for military purposes, and reserved for official use. By the end of the 19th century the telegraph was increasingly common among ordinary people. Some feared that it would erode public discourse by carrying irrelevant, context-free news; Henry David Thoreau imagined that the first news over the Atlantic cable would be that Princess Adelaide had the whooping cough.

Use began to decline around 1920 with the growth of the telephone, which grew out of work on the harmonic telegraph. Teleprinters, punched tape and the Baudot code automated transmission, and telex, a switched network of teleprinters, became operational in Germany in 1933.
telemark: Telemark lies in south-eastern Norway, extending from the Hardangervidda mountain plateau in the north to the Skagerrak coast in the south. Its landscape includes a rugged coastline, valleys, lakes, hills and mountain plateaus. The name means the mark of the Thelir, the ancient North Germanic tribe that inhabited what is now Upper Telemark in the Migration Period and the Viking Age. The Norse form was Þelamǫrk, whose last element means woodland or borderland. Traditional Telemark, now called Upper Telemark, lies inland and makes up more than two thirds of the county by its traditional definition. The south, Grenland, is flatter, closer to the coast and more urban.

Upper Telemark had more self-owning farmers than any other region of Norway, in the Middle Ages and later. It kept Norse culture to a greater degree, in its more egalitarian society, religion, values and language, and the people were often described as the most violent in Norway. Its farmers held on to aspects of Old Norse religion and later of Catholicism longer than other regions and often defied the central authorities of Denmark-Norway. Its dialects are the closest to Old Norse, and it has more buildings from medieval times than any other Norwegian region. Upper Telemark traditionally lacks cities entirely.

Grenland and the Skien fjord were marked by cities, seafaring, trade and industry, with more contact with continental Europe. Skien was in the early modern period one of Norway's most important cities, ahead of Christiania, though its importance declined after the Napoleonic Wars. The playwright Henrik Ibsen was born there. During the union with Denmark the two regions became the fief of Bratsberg, named after the farm where the governor had his seat. With the introduction of absolute monarchy in 1662 it became a county, and it was renamed Telemark in 1919.

Kviteseid in Upper Telemark is known as the birthplace of skiing as a modern sport. The Telemark style of skiing, invented by Sondre Norheim, and the Telemark landing of ski jumping are named after it. Telemark has also been a major industrial region for centuries, with paper mills in Grenland and heavy water and fertiliser production by Norsk Hydro in Upper Telemark.

Telemark merged with Vestfold in 2020, and on 1 January 2024 the county of Telemark was re-established. Its largest population centres are Skien, Porsgrunn, Notodden, Rjukan and Kragerø. The international road E134, the fastest route between Oslo and Bergen, runs through its inland municipalities. The Gea Norvegica Geopark, established in 2006 in the south, is the first UNESCO Global Geopark in Scandinavia.
telerig: Telerig first appears in Byzantine sources in 774, but he is considered the immediate successor of Pagan, who was murdered in 768. In May 774 Emperor Constantine V launched a major expedition against Bulgaria, leading his field army by land and sending a fleet of 2,000 ships carrying horsemen towards the Danube Delta. The fleet landed near Varna, yet Constantine did not press his advantage and withdrew, and soon afterwards the two sides agreed a truce.

The truce did not last. In October 774 Telerig sent an army of 12,000 men to raid Berzitia in Macedonia and carry its population off to Bulgaria. Constantine gathered 80,000 troops, surprised the Bulgarians and won a decisive victory, but his attack on Bulgaria itself failed when the imperial fleet met contrary winds in the Black Sea. After Telerig's trick over the Byzantine agents, the expected Byzantine retaliation never came, because Constantine died in 775.

Despite this success, Telerig found it necessary to flee in 777 to the new emperor, Leo IV the Khazar. The Byzantine government granted him asylum and the title of patrikios. He converted to Christianity under the name Theophylaktos and married a cousin of Empress Irene of Athens.

The Ja'far Tarikh, a Volga Bulgar compilation of the 17th century whose authenticity is disputed, calls him Dilyarek and makes him the son of an earlier ruler, Teles or Telets. Telerig Nunatak, on Greenwich Island in the South Shetland Islands of Antarctica, is named after him. As Telerikh he is a major character of Harry Turtledove's alternate-history story Islands in the Sea of 1989, first published in Alternatives, edited by Robert Adams.
telescope: The word telescope was coined in 1611 by the Greek mathematician Giovanni Demisiani for one of Galileo Galilei's instruments, presented at a banquet of the Accademia dei Lincei. In the Starry Messenger Galileo had used the Latin term perspicillum. The Greek roots are tele, far, and skopein, to look or see, giving teleskopos, far-seeing. The first practical instruments were refracting telescopes with glass lenses, used both on land and for astronomy. Word of the invention spread through Europe, and Galileo heard of it before building his own version.

Originally the telescope was an optical instrument that used lenses, curved mirrors or both to observe distant objects. The word now covers a wide range of instruments that detect different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. There are three main optical types: the refracting telescope, which forms an image with lenses; the reflecting telescope, which uses mirrors; and the catadioptric telescope, which combines mirrors with lenses. A place holding one or more telescopes or other instruments is called an observatory.

Radio telescopes are directional antennas that usually employ a large dish. By correlating the signals received by several dishes, astronomers compute high-resolution images, a technique called aperture synthesis. X-rays are harder to focus, and X-ray telescopes use ring-shaped mirrors of heavy metals that reflect the rays at a glancing angle; Hans Wolter outlined three ways of building such a telescope in 1952. Because the atmosphere is opaque to most of the spectrum, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray instruments are carried on balloons or satellites.

The idea that the light-gathering element could be a mirror instead of a lens was investigated soon after the refracting telescope appeared. Parabolic mirrors promised less spherical aberration and no chromatic aberration. In 1668 Isaac Newton built the first practical reflecting telescope, of the design now called the Newtonian reflector. The achromatic lens of 1733 partly corrected the colour fringes of simple lenses and allowed shorter, more useful refractors.

Reflectors were long hampered by mirrors of speculum metal, which tarnished quickly in the 18th and early 19th centuries. Silver-coated glass mirrors, introduced in 1857, and aluminised mirrors, from 1932, eased the problem. Refractors cannot grow beyond about one metre across, so most large research telescopes built since the turn of the 20th century are reflectors. John Dobson invented the Dobsonian telescope in 1956. The first purpose-built radio telescope began operating in 1937, and infrared telescopes followed in the 1960s.
tell-afis: Tell Afis lies in the Idlib Governorate, 11 kilometers north of the ancient site of Ebla. The tell covers 28 hectares, about 570 by 500 meters, with an extensive lower town and an acropolis at its northern edge. The Stele of Zakkur, with an Aramaic dedication to the gods Iluwer and Baalshamin, was found at the top of the acropolis in 1903 by the French consul Henri Pognon and is now in the Louvre. The stele calls the city Hazrach, and the Bible names it Hadrach in Zechariah 9.

Occupation began in the Late Chalcolithic (4000-3200 BCE), when a megalithic stone wall and a moat surrounded the foot of the acropolis and the people herded mostly sheep. In the Middle Bronze Age the region came under the Kingdom of Yamhad, centred on Aleppo, and both the lower town and the acropolis were walled. Levels of the 13th century BCE, the time of the Hittite ruler Hattusili III, held nine cuneiform tablets and fragments, two of them in Hittite.

After a small settlement in Iron Age I, the town grew large in Iron Age II (950-750 BCE) as part of the Kingdom of Hamath. On the western acropolis excavators found a temple rebuilt over several periods, the later phases a stone building of 38 meters by 32 meters with a vestibule, long hall and rear room, and a cultic area beside it. The Neo-Assyrian empire under Tiglath-Pileser III occupied the site around 738 BCE, and in 720 BCE Sargon II defeated the Kingdom of Hamath. Under the Assyrians the city was called Hatarikka.

William F. Albright collected Iron Age pottery from the surface in 1932, Paolo Matthiae excavated in the 1970s, and a joint team of the universities of Rome, Pisa and Bologna under Stefania Mazzoni and Serena Maria Cecchini dug from 1986 until 2010. Local quarrying had already damaged the site, which was reportedly harmed again by encampments during the Syrian civil war.
tell-al-rimah: The mound lies in Nineveh Governorate, roughly 80 kilometres west of Mosul in the Sinjar region and 15 kilometres south of Tal Afar. The site covers about 25 hectares inside a polygonal city wall, with low mounds within it and a central mound 30 metres high and 100 metres across. Its ancient name is uncertain: Karana, Qattara and Razama have all been proposed for the 2nd millennium BCE, with archaeologists now leaning towards Qattara, and Zamaḫâ for the 1st millennium.

The city was at its largest and most prominent in the 2nd millennium BCE, in the Old Babylonian age of Zimri-Lim of Mari, Hammurabi of Babylon and Shamshi-Adad I. Samu-Addu ruled Karana in the last years of Shamshi-Adad; after Shamshi-Adad's death Hatnu-rapi, an ally of Zimri-Lim, took power; Ashkur-Addu, son of Samu-Addu, deposed him; and Aqba-hammu, husband of Samu-Addu's daughter Iltani, deposed Ashkur-Addu and became a vassal of Hammurabi. The site was later destroyed and abandoned, then reoccupied in the Late Bronze Age, when Karana appears often in tablets from Nuzi. After another abandonment it was lightly settled in Neo-Assyrian times.

Seton Lloyd surveyed the region in 1938.
