The British School of Archaeology in Iraq team that dug the site from 1964 to 1971 was joined for the first three years by the Penn Museum and Theresa Howard Carter. Only 12 rooms of the palace were excavated because of its depth. Its Old Babylonian tablets, mostly from the time of Aqba-hammu, are largely records of loans of grain or tin and show a thriving wine industry. The site also has a third-millennium example of brick vaulting.

Iltani's archive of about 200 tablets covers some four years; her sister Amat-Shamash, a priestess at Sippar, once sent her a gift of shrimp. The Abu-tab archive of about 100 tablets dates mostly to the reign of Shalmaneser I. The stela of Adad-nirari III records the tribute of Ia'asu the Samaritan and contains the first cuneiform mention of Samaria by that name.
tell-el-farkha: Tell el-Farkha, Chicken Hill, lies in the eastern Nile Delta about 120 kilometres north-east of Cairo. It is made up of three mounds, the Western, Central and Eastern Kom, covering about 400 by 110 metres, just over 4 hectares, and rising about 5 metres above the plain. The site lay on a major trade route, and throughout its occupation it traded widely with the ancient Near East and Upper Egypt. It was first noted in 1987 by an Italian mission of the Centro Studi e Ricerche Ligabue of Venice, which excavated its Old Kingdom remains between 1988 and 1990.

Occupation began in the Lower Egyptian culture around 3700 BCE, passed into the Naqada culture, which is thought to have come from the south, and peaked in Dynasties 0 and 1 around 3000 BCE before ending in the early Fourth Dynasty, about 2600 BCE. A catastrophic fire destroyed most of the settlement around 3350 BCE. A large warehouse served trade with the southern Levant until that trade vanished. An administrative-cultic centre grew up on the Western Kom, a residential and business quarter on the Central Kom and a necropolis on the Eastern Kom, where 150 graves and a large building that the excavators see as an early form of mastaba tomb have been found.

The work of 1998 onwards, led by Marek Chłodnicki and Krzysztof Ciałowicz for the Jagiellonian University in Kraków and Warsaw University, has produced the site's best-known finds. A brewery on the Western Kom, dated to about 3500 BCE, had thirteen large brick vats; residues show a mash mainly of emmer wheat with some barley, and deliberate malting. Vessels bear pot marks, sometimes seen as forerunners of hieroglyphs, and the names of Iry-Hor and of Narmer. Two statuettes of nude men, about 60 and 30 cm tall, of gold sheet fastened with 140 gold rivets over a lost wooden core, with lapis lazuli eyes, probably show a Predynastic ruler and his son.
tell-halaf: Tell Halaf lies in Al-Hasakah in north-eastern Syria, a few kilometres from Ras al-Ayn, in the fertile valley of the Khabur River. It was the first site excavated of the Neolithic culture later named for it, and it flourished from about 6100 to 5400 BCE. The Halaf culture was succeeded in northern Mesopotamia by the Ubaid culture, and the site was then abandoned for a long period. The Mitanni Empire controlled the region from the 15th century BCE until about 1345 BCE, when Suppiluliuma I of Hatti conquered Carchemish and Tell Halaf became a Hittite city under the viceroy of Carchemish.

In the 10th century BCE the rulers of the small Aramaean kingdom of Bit Bahiani took their seat at the site, refounded as Guzana or Gozan. King Kapara built the hilani, a palace in Neo-Hittite style decorated with statues and relief orthostats. In 894 BCE Adad-nirari II recorded it as a tributary Aramaean city-state, and in 808 BCE the city and its surroundings became a province of the Assyrian Empire, with the governor's seat in a palace on the eastern part of the citadel mound. Guzana survived the collapse of Assyria and remained inhabited until the Roman-Parthian period. The lower town extended 600 metres north to south and 1,000 metres east to west.

On 19 November 1899 the German diplomat Max von Oppenheim, travelling for Deutsche Bank on the route of the Bagdad Railway, found the site after local tales of stone idols buried in the sand. Several statues were uncovered within three days, among them a "Sitting Goddess", and a test pit reached the entrance to the Western Palace. Having no permit, he reburied them. He began a full campaign on 5 August 1911 with five archaeologists and five hundred local workers, financed by his father's banking fortune, at a cost of around 750,000 marks. Locals had meanwhile damaged some finds, partly from superstition and partly to obtain building material.

The dig found the large statues and reliefs of Kapara's palace, a cult room and tombs, and Neolithic pottery, then, with the finds of Samarra, the oldest painted pottery known. After the First World War Oppenheim sold some pieces to museums, returned to the site in 1927 and resumed digging in 1929. His finds were divided with the French authorities: about 80, two thirds, went to Berlin, and 35 to Aleppo, forming the core of the National Museum of Aleppo. He opened a private Tell Halaf Museum in Berlin-Charlottenburg in July 1930. In November 1943 a British phosphorus bomb burned it completely; the basalt pieces were shattered by thermal shock when the fire was fought, and many statues burst into dozens of pieces.
tell-harmal: The mound lies within modern Baghdad, about 600 metres from Tell Muhammad, which may be ancient Diniktum, and about 2 kilometres from Tell al-Dhiba'i, thought to be the town of Uzarzalulu. Eshnunna itself stood some 30 miles to the south-west, and Tell Ishchali and Khafajah lay a few miles away on the left bank of the Diyala River. The name Shaduppum means the treasury. Its tutelary deity was Bēl-gašer, and the goddess Ninkarrak and the local goddess Arhanitum were also worshipped there.

The site was occupied from at least the Akkadian period, but little is known of it outside Old Babylonian times. Excavators distinguished five layers. Layer III saw the building of the fortification wall under rulers such as Ipiq-Adad II and Naram-Suen of Eshnunna. Layer II, from the reigns of Dadusha (c. 1800–1779 BCE) and Ibal-pi-el II (c. 1779–1765 BCE), held most of the tablets; it was destroyed by fire, thought to have been set by Hammurabi when he took the town in his 31st year. The uppermost layer is thought to be Kassite.

The town was an irregular rectangle of about 147 by 133 metres, enclosed by a wall 5.6 metres thick with a towered gateway in the north-east. Inside stood a large temple of 28 by 18 metres, where the Harmal Lions were found, a smaller double shrine and an administrative building of 23 by 23 metres. Taha Baqir and Sayid Muhammed Ali Mustafa dug the site from 1945 to 1949, prompted by planned housing and illegal digging, and found about 3,000 tablets, only about a third of them published. Besides the laws and mathematics they include two tablets of the Epic of Gilgamesh, texts on creation and the flood, and the longest list of geographical names yet known.

In 1962 the Iraqi authorities fenced the wall circuit, the main temple and the archive building, rebuilt the walls to just above ground level and set up terracotta copies of the Harmal Lions. The two small temples by the eastern wall were reconstructed as visitor museums. A team from Baghdad University and the German Archaeological Institute under Peter Miglus and Laith Hussein worked there in 1997 and 1998, though ground water 2 metres below the surface kept them from digging below Level IV.
tell-leilan: Tell Leilan lies near the Wadi Jarrah in the Khabur River basin in Al-Hasakah Governorate, north-eastern Syria. It was occupied from the 5th millennium BCE and began as a small farming village about 5000 BCE. In the late third millennium it was known as Shekhna. Other flourishing cities stood nearby: Hamoukar about 50 km to the south-east, Tell Brak about 50 km to the south-west and Tell Mozan, ancient Urkesh, about 50 km to the west. Leilan, Brak and Urkesh were particularly prominent in the Akkadian period.

The city grew large about 2600 BCE, three hundred years before the Akkadian Empire, and had a large wall by that time. Under the Akkadian Empire it was an administrative centre. A layer of sediment about a metre thick, containing no evidence of human habitation, offered clues to the end of the Akkadian imperial city; analysis indicated that about 2200 BCE a drought was severe enough to affect agriculture and settlement. The period from about 2350 to 2000 BCE saw climate change in northern Mesopotamia, which became drier.

The Amorite warlord Shamshi-Adad I of Ekallatum (1813-1781 BCE) conquered the region and revived the abandoned site. He valued its rich agricultural production, made it the capital of his empire and renamed it Shubat-Enlil, "the residence of the god Enlil". The city had a royal palace, a temple acropolis reached by a straight paved street from the city gate, a planned residential area and a surrounding wall. It covered about 90 hectares and may have had 20,000 people at its peak.

After Shamshi-Adad's death the city became the capital of Apum and prospered until Samsu-iluna of Babylon sacked it in 1726 BCE. Minor kings ruled there, among them Turum-natki, Zuzu and Haja-Abum, and Qarni-Lim of nearby Andarig kept a large palace. Later rulers of Andarig, Atamrum and Himdiya, held it after it was sacked by Elamites. Shubat-Enlil was abandoned about 1700 BCE.

A Yale University team led by Harvey Weiss excavated the mound from 1979 until 2008. Among the finds is an archive of 1,100 cuneiform clay tablets kept by the city's rulers, dating to the 18th century BCE, which record dealings with other Mesopotamian states and how the city administration worked. Finds are displayed in the Deir ez-Zor Museum. Tell Mohammed Diyab, 7 km to the south-east, covers about 50 hectares and has yielded significant remains from the Amorite period, including the time of Shamshi-Adad I.
tell-tayinat: The low tell lies on the east bank at a bend of the Orontes River, about 25 kilometres southeast of Antakya, ancient Antioch, and near Tell Atchana, the site of Alalakh. It has an upper mound of about 20 hectares and a lower mound now buried under the floodplain. Besides the Iron Age capital, it has been proposed as Alalaḫu, a place named in the Palace G archive of Ebla in the late 3rd millennium BCE, and as Calneh, a city of the Hebrew Bible.

The site was a major town in two phases. In the Early Bronze Age it covered around 25 hectares and was the largest settlement of the Amuq Plain in Early Bronze IVB; finds of that time include Khirbet Kerak ware, thought to reflect the Kura-Araxes culture, 17 figurines, two wheels, a cylinder seal and clay sealings. After the fall of the Hittite Empire it became the capital of the kingdom of Walistin or Palistin, later Patina, whose rulers still bore royal Hittite names in the 8th century BCE.

From the 9th century BCE its kings paid tribute to Assyria: Ashurnasirpal II lists silver, gold, 100 talents of tin, 100 talents of iron, 1000 oxen and 10,000 sheep from its ruler Labarna. Tiglath-pileser III forced King Tutammu to submit, and Assyrian control lasted until the reign of Ashurbanipal. A raised citadel, reached through a monumental gate complex, overlooked the lower city.

The Oriental Institute in Chicago excavated the site from 1935 to 1938 under Robert Braidwood, finding bit-hilani palaces and a temple whose plan recalls Solomon's Temple. A University of Toronto team has dug there since 2004. In a temple's inner sanctum it found cuneiform tablets, most of them the menologium Iqqur Ipuš. In 2012 it found the head and torso of a statue of King Suppiluliuma with a Hieroglyphic Luwian inscription on its back, and in 2017 a female statue in the citadel gate. A farmer's paving stone proved to belong to a stele of Sargon II. An earthquake in 2023 damaged the expedition house and the store of finds.
telugu-cholas: The Telugu Chodas ruled parts of present-day Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and southern Odisha, first as samantas, or vassals, of the Pallavas and later of the Imperial Cholas. They were divided into many branches, among them the Renati, Pottapi, Velanati, Konidena, Nannuru, Nellore and Kunduru Chodas, and all claimed descent from Karikala Chola, a Tamil king of the Sangam age. Several used the title lord of the city of Urayur. Little is known of some lines: the Nannuru Chodas of Pakanadu, to whom the Telugu poet Nanne Choda belonged, are believed to have been subordinates of Vikramaditya VI of the Kalyani Chalukyas.

The Velanati Chodas ruled Velanadu, in the modern Guntur district, at first from Chandolu and later from Vengi and Pithpuram. They rose among the vassals of the Chalukyas of Vengi under Kulothunga Chola I, who backed them to hold Vengi against the Kalyani Chalukyas. Rajendra Choda II took the title Durjayakulaprakasa, claiming descent from Durjaya, an Andhra chieftain of tradition. Their rulers ran from Gonka I (1076–1108) to Pruthviswara (1186–1207), after which the Kakatiyas overran their country.

The Konidena Chodas, a branch of the Pottapi line, ruled Kammanadu from Konidena near Narasaraopeta. Their early kings were independent, but Tribhuvana Malla Choda served Gonka II, and after the fall of Velanadu they submitted to Ganapatideva of the Kakatiyas. The Kunduru Chodas held parts of Telangana from 1080 to 1260 under the Western Chalukyas and the Kakatiyas, and Eruva Cholas ruled Eruvanadu.

The Nellore Chodas were the strongest branch, ruling south Andhra from 1100 to 1350 through twelve rulers, from Bijjana and Manumasiddharasa I to Viragandagopala. The Chola emperors and later the Kakatiyas held supremacy over them, but in practice they were largely independent, and at times their power reached into the Hoysala and Chola kingdoms.
telugu-language: Telugu descends from Proto-Dravidian, which linguistic reconstruction places around the fourth millennium BCE. It belongs to the South Dravidian-II, or South-Central Dravidian, subgroup, with Gondi, Kuvi, Koya, Pengo, Konda and Manda. The philologist Mikhail S. Andronov places its separation from Proto-Dravidian at about 1000 BCE. The name is explained as a form of Tenugu, from the Proto-Dravidian word for south, meaning the people who lived to the south of the speakers of Sanskrit and Prakrit; Telugu results from an alternation of n and l.

Its history is divided into phases. Telugu words appear early in Prakrit inscriptions, and one early word, nāgabu, found at the Amaravati Stupa, is dated to about 200 BCE. The first long inscription entirely in Telugu, dated to 575 CE, is attributed to the Renati Choda king Dhanunjaya and was found in the Kadapa district. Titles of Mahendravarman I in Telugu, from about 600 CE, are inscribed in caves in Tamil Nadu. About 10,000 pre-colonial inscriptions survive in Telugu.

Telugu is a Dravidian language native to the Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, where it is the official language, and is also official in the Yanam district of Puducherry. It is spoken by about 100 million people and is the most widely spoken member of its family. Words generally end in vowels. Its grammar has suffixes only, with three noun classes, seven cases and a basic subject-object-verb order. Most of its vocabulary is inherited from Proto-Dravidian, with many borrowings from Sanskrit. There are Telangana, Rayalaseema, Coastal Andhra and North Andhra dialects, and standard Telugu is based on the speech of educated speakers of the central dialect.

Telugu has an unbroken literary tradition of over a thousand years. The Vijayanagara Empire dominated from 1336 to the late 17th century, and Telugu literature had what is considered its Golden Age in the 16th century under Krishnadevaraya. The Venetian explorer Niccolò de' Conti, visiting in the 15th century, noted that its words end in vowels, as in Italian, and called it the Italian of the East. In the precolonial era it became the language of high culture throughout South India, which Vijaya Ramaswamy compared to the dominance of French in Europe. Telugu also predominates in Carnatic music.

Persian and Arabic influence produced a distinct variant around Hyderabad, beginning with the Delhi Sultanate in the 14th century. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries English influence and the printing press, especially in the Madras Presidency, shaped writers such as Kandukuri Veeresalingam and Gurajada Apparao. The Andhra Pradesh Official Language Act of 1966 declared Telugu the official language of the state, later divided into Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
tem-baiteke: Tem Baiteke belonged to the Tuangaona family, whose founder, Tetabo, is remembered in oral tradition for uniting Abemama against invaders from the north in the 18th century. He was announced as the firstborn son of the high chief (uea) Tawaia by Tea, a wife of Tawaia's father Karotu; R. G. Roberts held that Karotu was his real father, while H. E. Maude thought the truth could not be known. His birth name is forgotten: he became known as Tem Baiteke for his sharpshooting. He succeeded Tawaia, who died about 1850 after a reign Maude called brief and uneventful.

In the 1840s beachcombers, whalers and coconut-oil traders, among them ships of Richard Randell's firm, had been encroaching on the islands. In January 1851 Tem Baiteke ordered all nine foreigners on Abemama killed, and the 25 on Kuria and Aranuka were executed some months later. Randell defended the killings, saying the beachcombers had abused the islanders; Maude noted that Randell then held a near monopoly of the islands' trade. Tem Baiteke confined visiting ships to a single port on the isolated islet of Abatiku, where he could watch everything that came in and out, guns included.

In 1863 the people of Kuria refused their annual tribute of virgins, and a punitive expedition under Binatake, another son of Tea and a warrior reputed merciless, sailed in a ship of Smith, Randell, and Fairclough. The rebels, who had a few guns and powder but no shot, relied on the spells of their chief priest, Tenu, and fled once he was shot. Each island had held over 1,000 people; afterwards each held about 100, and his rule went unchallenged.

Maude judged that no earlier ruler in the Gilbert Islands had held such power. Tem Baiteke took over the village meeting houses (maneaba), where the old men (unimane) had decided matters in council, and became the sole lawmaker. He divided the people into hereditary classes: the uea's family, the minor chiefs (toka or inaomata), who owed their land and status to him alone, the lesser landed aomata, the landless rang and the enslaved toro. Maude called this a social revolution that replaced a slave-owning but otherwise egalitarian community with a feudal one. In late 1878 he abdicated in favour of his eldest son, Binoka.
tem-binoka: Tem Binoka was born about 1840, the first son of Tem Baiteke, uea (high chief) of Abemama, Kuria and Aranuka. According to oral tradition, his family, the utu of Tuangaona, owed its rise to Tetabo, who united Abemama against invaders in the 18th century; Tetabo's grandson Karotu was recognised as the first uea of the three atolls. In 1851 Baiteke executed every beachcomber on his islands, confined visiting ships to the islet of Abatiku and took control of the import of firearms. Binoka grew up in privilege and learned reading, writing, arithmetic and geography from a mission teacher sent by Hiram Bingham in 1873.

One of his first acts as uea was to make the copra trade with Europeans a royal monopoly: copra was the most valuable commodity of the Gilbert Islands, and Abemama their largest producer. He owned stores and trading ships, but could not compete with the foreign firms, and his commercial ventures ended with the loss of his ship, the Coronet. In December 1883 he occupied Nonouti, hoping to conquer the whole archipelago, but the warship HMS Dart expelled his garrison the following month. After defeating the last recorded rebellion against him in 1885 he ruled quietly.

He allowed no outsiders a permanent presence and deported the missionary Tuppoti for trying to set up a copra business. The Scotsman George McGhee Murdoch organised production on his lands. How far the stories of his despotism are exaggerated is hard to judge; Murdoch is said to have kept Binoka's murderous habits from his later visitors.

Robert Louis Stevenson spent two months on Abemama in 1889 and portrayed Binoka in In the South Seas (1896), spelling his name Tembinok', as a sympathetic despot of a bygone era and, in Stevenson's words, the last tyrant. Binoka died of an infected abscess on 10 November 1891 and was succeeded by his adopted son Bauro, with his brother Timon as regent. The following year Captain Edward Davis moored at Abemama to proclaim the Gilbert Islands a British protectorate, and Murdoch became District Agent and Tax Collector.
temasek: The name is usually derived from the Malay word tasik, meaning lake or sea, and may mean a place surrounded by the sea. It appears as Tumasik in the Nagarakretagama, an Old Javanese eulogy of 1365, and in the Malay Annals and the Pararaton. Yuan and Ming Chinese documents wrote it as Danmaxi. Two settlements were recorded there: Long Ya Men, thought to be the entrance of Keppel Harbour, and Ban Zu, on a hill thought to be today's Fort Canning Hill.

Archaeology points to an urbanised settlement by the 14th century, with a large earthen wall and moat and buildings on stone and brick foundations. Pottery, coins and jewellery imported from China, India, Sri Lanka and Indonesia have been found, and in 1928 gold ornaments of the mid-14th century were dug up at Fort Canning Hill. Yuan envoys came to Long Ya Men in 1320 to obtain tame elephants, and its people sent a tribute and trade mission to China in 1325.

The Chinese traveller Wang Dayuan visited around 1330. He wrote that lakawood and tin were traded with merchants from Quanzhou, that pirates in two to three hundred boats attacked returning junks, and that a few years earlier the city had resisted a Siamese attack of about 70 ships for a month. As the Majapahit and Ayutthaya kingdoms both claimed the island, Portuguese sources say that late in the 14th century Parameswara of Palembang killed its ruler, ruled it as Singapura for five years and then moved on to found the Sultanate of Malacca. The Portuguese burnt a settlement there in 1613.

Sometime in the 14th century the name Singapura replaced Temasek, which had fallen out of use by 1500. It was revived in colonial and modern times, and the Republic of Singapore uses it for its two highest national honours, the Bintang Temasek and the Darjah Utama Temasek, and for institutions such as Temasek Holdings and Temasek Polytechnic.
temenggong-abdul-rahman: Abdul Rahman was born in the Johor Sultanate in 1755, the son of Tun Abdul Hamid. In 1802 Sultan Mahmud Ri'ayat Shah installed his father as temenggong after the death of his grandfather, Temenggong Abdul Jamal, but his father died the next year. The sultan then named his uncle Engku Muda Muhammad, who wanted instead the post of Yang di-Pertuan Muda. After that uncle's death, the sultan installed Abdul Rahman as temenggong at Lingga in 1806.

When Sir Stamford Raffles arrived on 29 January 1819, the temenggong lived near the Singapore River with some 400 to 500 residents. British records show that he had paid for Teochew Chinese settlers to open gambier plantations on what became Pearl's Hill and had advanced money to some cultivators against repayment in produce. A brother-in-law and supporter of Tengku Hussein, he helped Raffles bring the exiled prince from Penyengat Island in the Riau Islands to Singapore, so that Hussein could be recognised as sultan of Johor.

Under the treaty of 6 February 1819 the sultan received 5,000 Spanish dollars a year and the temenggong 3,000, and the British granted him the hereditary style of His Highness. In 1823 he and his followers moved to 200 acres at Teluk Belanga, at the foot of present-day Mount Faber, land allotted by Raffles. On 2 August 1824 he and Sultan Hussein signed the Treaty of Friendship and Alliance with John Crawfurd, the second Resident of Singapore. The temenggong received a lump sum of 26,800 Spanish dollars and a monthly stipend of 700, agreed to keep free trade in his possessions and undertook not to correspond with foreign powers without the East India Company's permission.

Abdul Rahman died on 8 December 1825 at his house, Istana Bukit Aur, at Teluk Belanga, and was buried at the nearby royal cemetery, Makam Diraja Teluk Blangah. His son Tun Haji Abdullah succeeded him informally. He is remembered above all for his part in the Treaty of Singapore of 1819, which opened the island to the British East India Company.
temenggong-daeng-ibrahim: Daeng Ibrahim was born on 8 December 1810 at Pulau Bulang, in Kepulauan Riau, the second son of Temenggong Abdul Rahman and Inche Yah Moffar; he was also known as Daeng Ronggek, Tengku Chik and Daeng Kechil. In 1811 the family moved to Singapore Island and settled by the Singapore River. In 1823 his father took the household and its followers to 200 acres at Teluk Belanga granted by Stamford Raffles, where the palace of Istana Bukit Aur was finished in 1824. After his father's death in 1825, his elder brother Tun Haji Abdullah served informally as temenggong.

Daeng Ibrahim took over from his brother as the de facto temenggong in 1833 and introduced the kangchu system to develop the growing of black pepper and gambir. His appointment was made official only on 19 August 1841, at New Harbour, before George Bonham, the Governor of the Straits Settlements, and Tun Ali, Raja Bendahara of Pahang.

On 10 March 1855 he and Ali Iskandar signed a treaty with the British in Singapore, officiated by Governor William John Butterworth. Ali was crowned Sultan of Johor and received 5,000 Spanish dollars and an allowance of 500 a month, but kept only Kesang in Muar, and his title could not pass to his heirs; all other power over Johor went to Daeng Ibrahim, who governed it from Teluk Belanga. After the Dutch deposed Sultan Mahmud Muzaffar Shah of Riau-Lingga in 1857, Daeng Ibrahim signed a treaty in 1861 with Tun Mutahir, Raja Bendahara of Pahang, recognising each other's states and his descendants' right to rule Johor, so that the remnants of the old empire became two independent states.

He died of a high fever at Istana Temenggong in Teluk Belanga on 31 January 1862 and was buried beside his father at the royal burial ground of Teluk Blangah. His eldest son, Abu Bakar, succeeded him. Temenggong Road in Singapore and the Masjid Temenggong Daeng Ibrahim are named after him.
temes-county: The county lay in the Banat, bounded by the Danube in the south and the Mureș in the north, and it shared borders with the Kingdom of Serbia and the Hungarian counties of Torontál, Arad and Krassó-Szörény. The Bega, Timiș, Bârzava and Caraș flowed through it, and in 1910 it covered 7,433 km2. Its seat Temesvár, meaning Temes Castle, was also the capital of the Kingdom of Hungary between 1315 and 1323.

The county was formed in the 12th century, after Hungarian rule was established in the region, and was named after the Temes river; it is first mentioned in 1212. In 1070 the Pechenegs, allied with the Byzantines, devastated the area before King Géza I routed them, and King Ladislaus I repelled later Cuman and Byzantine raids. By the reign of King Béla III much of the land was settled by Slavic and Turkic groups. After the Ottoman conquest the territory belonged to the Temeşvar Eyalet, and in 1594-1595 the local Christians, mainly Serbs and Romanians, rose in the Banat uprising.

The Habsburg monarchy took the region in the war of 1716-1718 and, under the Treaty of Passarowitz, made it the province of the Banat of Temeswar. Between 1849 and 1860 the area belonged to the Voivodeship of Serbia and Temes Banat, an Austrian crownland; the county was recreated in January 1861 and enlarged in 1873 with parts of the former Banat Military Frontier, Fehértemplom among them. In the autumn of 1918 a short-lived Banat Republic was proclaimed at Temesvár. Hungary, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and Romania all claimed the county until the Paris Peace Conference divided it.

The Romanian part of the old county now lies in Timiș County, except for a strip about 10 km wide along the Mureș, which is in Arad County. The south-western third, given to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, belongs to the Serbian autonomous region of Vojvodina, with the towns of Vršac, Bela Crkva and Kovin.
temne-people: Oral tradition places the Temne homeland in the Fouta Djallon highlands of present-day Guinea. Bankole Taylor dates their migration as far back as the 11th or 12th century, after the fall of the Jallonkadu Empire, and Fulani dominance in the 15th century drove them further south. In Sierra Leone they forced the Limba northeast and the Bullom southwards and settled along the Rokel River down to the Sierra Leone River and Port Loko Creek. In the mid-16th century the Mane, a Mandé army from the east, conquered their lands, and the general Farma Tami ruled the Temne from Robaga, near present-day Freetown.

Portuguese records give the earliest mention of the Temne: Pacheco Pereira, writing between 1505 and 1508, noted their words for gold, water and rice, and in 1594 André Álvares de Almada described village courts where advocates in masks pleaded before the chief. The Futa Jallon Jihad of the early 18th century brought slave raids, the sale of war captives into the Atlantic trade and an influx of Susu and Yalunka.

King Naimbana of Koya, hostile to the slave trade until his death in 1793, signed the treaty of 1788 giving the colonists the land his sub-chief Tom had ceded, and gave land and labour to the Black Nova Scotians who founded Freetown. Koya fought Loko, Mende and Susu rulers between 1807 and 1888, and in 1889 the Temne lands fell to Britain. A hut tax due from 1 January 1898 set off the Hut Tax War of that year, in which the chief Bai Bureh took a leading part.

The Temne language is related to the Baga language of Guinea. The Temne are traditionally farmers of rice, cassava, millet and kola nut. Society is patrilineal and was organised in numerous independent chiefdoms of villages, whose headmen usually inherited the post from the founder; in contemporary Sierra Leone chiefs are elected. A chief carries a sacred force, and the chiefdom spirit is represented by a mask whose wearer, the Sanko, appears with the chief throughout his life. Some clans had endogamous castes of artisans and musicians, and enslaved people formed the lowest stratum.

Bankole Taylor estimates that 90% to 95% of the Temne are Muslims, while in the southeastern parts many have joined Islam with older beliefs in spirits and divination. Traditional religion centres on a Supreme Being, Kuru Masaba, approached through patrilineal ancestral spirits, and chiefdoms take part in secret societies such as the men's Poro and Ragbenle and the women's Bondo.
tempio-malatestiano: Two churches stood on the site before it: the 9th-century church of Santa Maria in Trivio and the 13th-century Gothic church of the Franciscans, a single nave ending in three apses, the central one probably frescoed by Giotto, to whom the crucifix now in the second chapel on the right is also attributed. Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta asked Leon Battista Alberti, in his first church commission, to turn the building into a mausoleum for himself and Isotta degli Atti. The work was carried out by the Veronese Matteo di Andrea de' Pasti, and marble was taken from Roman ruins at Sant'Apollinare in Classe and Fano and from headstones of the surrounding cemetery.

The dome shown on Matteo's foundation medal of 1450, modelled on the Pantheon, was never built, and the façade's upper part was left unfinished: Sigismondo's fortunes fell steeply after his excommunication in 1460, and at his death in 1466 the building stood as it does now. Officially it is the Cathedral Basilica of Santa Colomba, named for Columba of Sens.

Alberti drew on Roman triumphal arches, above all the Arch of Constantine, and, as Rudolf Wittkower noted, took details from the Arch of Augustus; the side arcades recall Roman aqueducts, with a sarcophagus in each blind arch. Inside, chapels hold the tombs of Sigismondo, Isotta and his earlier wives Ginevra d'Este and Polissena Sforza, and that of the philosopher Gemistus Pletho, whose remains Sigismondo brought back from the Balkans. Agostino di Duccio carved the reliefs of the Chapel of the Planets, whose Cancer panel shows Rimini in the 15th century, and the dancing angels of the Chapel of Childhood Games; the SI monogram recurs throughout.

Some contemporaries saw the church as a glorification of paganism, and Pope Pius II, Sigismondo's bitter enemy, called it full of pagan gods and profane things. The building was heavily damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt from pieces recovered from the rubble by men of the Allies-affiliated Monuments, Fine Arts, and Archives unit.
temple: The word comes from Ancient Rome, where a templum was a sacred precinct defined by a priest, or augur. It shares a root with the word template, a plan marked out on the ground before building. English applies it by convention to the places of worship of most extinct ancient religions and of Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism and Taoism, but not usually to Christian churches, mosques or synagogues.

Mesopotamian temples developed from the cults of Sumerian, Akkadian, Assyrian and Babylonian gods. Their commonest form was the ziggurat, a terraced pyramid of sun-baked brick with a shrine on its flat top. Göbekli Tepe in southern Turkey, built between the 10th and 8th millennium BCE, has T-shaped stone pillars carved with animals and pictograms.

A temple is often regarded by believers as the house of one or more deities. Offerings are made, clergy maintain it, and the building may be open only to them in whole or part. Egyptian temples were called ḥwt-nṯr, mansion of a god, and their rituals were held to sustain the god and so maintain maat, the order of nature. They also stored grain and came to own large parts of the arable land.

Greek and Roman temples began as wood and mud brick and grew to monumental stone and marble. They faced east and had altars in front for sacrifice. In Greek temples the cella holding the cult statue stood at the centre, and in Roman ones at the back. A Hindu temple centres on the garbhagriha, the inner sanctuary housing the murti of a deity, and a Buddhist stupa first sheltered relics of Gautama Buddha.

In Judaism the Temple Mount in Jerusalem was the site of the First Temple of Solomon and the Second Temple, with the Holy of Holies at the centre, which only the High Priest could enter. The Dome of the Rock, built about 690 CE, stands there now. From the 18th century Jews in Western and Central Europe began calling synagogues temples. In the Eastern Orthodox tradition the word temple is used for church buildings, and some Protestant churches adopted it after the Enlightenment. In 1832 Joseph Smith received a revelation to restore temple worship among Latter Day Saints, and the Kirtland Temple was the first they built.
temple-entry-proclamation: The proclamation grew out of a campaign for social reform in Travancore inspired by the teachings of Narayana Guru and others. A deputation of six leaders appointed by the Harijan Sevak Sangh toured the princely state to win support among caste Hindus for letting the backward castes into state-run temples. The historian Romila Thapar counts the Vaikom Satyagraha of 1924-25, against the ban on Dalits using a public road near a temple at Vaikom, as a significant precursor; its demands widened from access to the roads to entry into the temples themselves.

The regent Maharani Sethu Lakshmi Bayi, after meeting Mahatma Gandhi, released those imprisoned under Moolam Thirunal for joining the Vaikom protests and opened the north, south and west roads to the Vaikom Mahadeva Temple, but not the eastern road used by Brahmins, saying that as regent she lacked the power. Gandhi then put the question to the twelve-year-old prince, who promised that it would happen in his reign. In 1932 Chithira Thirunal appointed a committee to examine temple entry, and he signed the proclamation on the eve of his 24th birthday.

C. P. Ramaswami Iyer presented the decision as the ruler's free act rather than the result of agitation. In an open letter Gandhi told the Maharaja that the proclamation had made him a mahatma and hoped other Hindu princes would follow. The Universities of Andhra and Annamalai gave him D.Litt. degrees, and life-size statues of him were put up in Trivandrum and Madras. Critics argued that the measure was meant to stop lower-caste Hindus converting in large numbers to Christianity, and sociologists hold that it struck at caste discrimination while uniting Hindus against further conversions.

The proclamation had little effect in Cochin or British Malabar, whose rulers opposed temple entry for Dalits; the Zamorin argued that the temples were private property and that no ruler could decide the question. Cochin issued its own proclamation on 22 December 1947, in force from 14 April 1948, exempting the royal family's temple, and Malabar gained the right under the Madras proclamation of 12 June 1947. The Government of Kerala observes Temple Entry Proclamation Day as a social reformation day.
temple-in-jerusalem: According to the Hebrew Bible, the First Temple was built by King Solomon in the 10th century BCE, completed in 957 BCE. As the sole place of Israelite sacrifice, according to Deuteronomy, it replaced the Tabernacle built in the Sinai under Moses. The Bible says it was sacked a few decades later by Shishak, identified as the pharaoh Shoshenq I. It was destroyed c. 587 BCE in the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem. Archaeological excavations have not found remnants of it.

According to the Book of Ezra, Cyrus the Great called for the Second Temple to be built, and work began in 538 BCE. Some 19th-century calculations place completion on 21 February 515 BCE, though some modern researchers consider these dates unreliable. The governor Zerubbabel dedicated the new temple, and Herod the Great later renovated it.

The First Temple had an outer court where people assembled, an inner court of the priests and the temple building, with the larger Holy Place and the smaller inner sanctum, the Holy of Holies. The Herodian Temple was the most elaborate, with a wide precinct including the Court of the Gentiles, the Court of the Women and the Court of the Israelites for ritually pure Jewish men. Two surviving pieces of Herod's expansion are the Temple Warning inscriptions, which forbade pagans to enter the courtyard, and the Trumpeting Place inscription.

Daily morning and afternoon offerings were made there, with special offerings on festivals, while Levites recited Psalms. The daily service included the Shema and the Priestly Blessing, which still form the basis of the traditional morning service.

The destruction of the Temple is mourned on the fast day of Tisha B'Av, and weddings traditionally end with the groom breaking a glass in remembrance. Daily prayer contains petitions for its rebuilding. In the Middle Ages the Temple appeared in illuminated manuscripts, marriage contracts and wedding rings.

For Muslims the site is the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, or Haram al-Sharif, regarded as the third-holiest site in Islam and the destination of Muhammad's Night Journey. According to tradition, Umar cleared the site after the Muslim conquest, and the Dome of the Rock was built on the mount under Abd al-Malik. In Christianity, Matthew 24:2 records Jesus predicting the destruction of the Second Temple.
temple-of-aphaia: The temple stands on a peak of about 160 m on the eastern side of Aegina, some 13 km by road east of the main port. Aphaia was worshipped only at this sanctuary, and the building was long known as the Temple of Jupiter Panhellenius. Large numbers of Late Bronze Age figurines, many of them female, suggest an open-air sanctuary to a fertility and farming deity, perhaps in continuous use from the 14th century BCE, which some take as a sign of a Minoan connection.

An altar of about 700 BCE marks the first known building phase, and an inscription of the mid-7th century BCE records a house built for Aphaia by a priest. A first stone temple, dated before 570 BCE, had a cella with two levels of columns and a back room, or adyton. It burned, with much of the sanctuary, around 510 BCE, and its remains were packed into the fill of a new terrace, where they kept traces of paint.

The new temple is a Doric building with a colonnade of six by twelve columns on a platform of 15.5 by 30.5 m, and all but three of its outer columns are monolithic. Inside, two rows of five columns carried a second level reaching the roof. Sphinxes stood at the corners of the roof, whose tiles and antefixes were of marble. Proposed dates run from 510 to 470 BCE.

Each pediment had Athena at its centre among combatants, fallen warriors and arms, celebrating the heroes of Aegina. The western pediment, in Archaic style, showed the Trojan War told by Homer, with Ajax, son of Telamon, prominent. The eastern, thought to be later and closer to Classical work, showed the earlier war of Heracles against King Laomedon of Troy, with Telamon at his side.

Pausanias mentioned the site briefly in the 2nd century CE, and the Antiquities of Ionia made the temple known in Western Europe in 1797. In 1811 the English architect Charles Robert Cockerell and Baron Otto Magnus von Stackelberg took the fallen pediment figures. In Munich the Danish sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen restored them, and they shaped the Neoclassicism of Leo von Klenze. The German School in Athens excavated the site in the 20th century, first under Adolf Furtwängler, and a campaign under Dieter Ohly from 1966 found substantial remains of the older temple in 1969.
temple-of-artemis: The temple stood near the ancient city of Ephesus, near modern Selçuk in Turkey. The sacred site was older than the temple itself: excavations in 1987–1988 confirmed that it was occupied as early as the Bronze Age, and a peripteral temple with a floor of hard-packed clay was built in the second half of the 8th century BCE, perhaps the earliest Greek temple surrounded by colonnades anywhere. In the 7th century BCE a flood destroyed it. The ancient accounts differ on the older history: Pausanias believed the temple pre-dated the Amazons, while Callimachus attributed the first sanctuary to them.

The second temple was sponsored at least in part by Croesus, who founded Lydia's empire and was overlord of Ephesus. Designed from around 550 BCE by the Cretan architect Chersiphron and his son Metagenes, it was 115 metres long and 46 metres wide and supposedly the first Greek temple built of marble. A rich foundation deposit yielded more than a thousand items, including what may be the earliest coins of electrum. The temple attracted merchants, kings and sightseers.

In 356 BCE it burned down. Ancient sources describe an arson by Herostratus, who sought fame; the Ephesians sentenced him to death and forbade anyone to mention his name. Modern scholars have questioned his part. Alexander the Great offered to pay for the rebuilding, but the Ephesians refused, saying it would be improper for one god to build a temple to another, and after his death they rebuilt it at their own expense from 323 BCE. The third temple measured 137 by 69 metres, with more than 127 columns. The cult of Artemis was closely tied to the civic identity of Ephesus, and large crowds came each year for the main procession.

According to Jordanes, a raid by the Goths in the 3rd century CE set fire to the temple, though the extent of the damage is unknown, and Christian authors refer to its closure in the 5th century. Some of its stone was reused in other buildings. The site was rediscovered in 1869 by an expedition led by John Turtle Wood and sponsored by the British Museum, after six years of searching; excavations continued until 1874, and David George Hogarth excavated in 1904–1906. Sculpted fragments are displayed in the British Museum. Today a single column built from fragments marks the site.
temple-of-athena-alea: The cult joined the Olympian goddess Athena with Alea, a local deity of Tegea, and the sanctuary served as a marker of Tegean identity. Finds there show contact with the Argolid and Laconia. The Greek travel writer Pausanias reported that the temple was said to have been built by the local hero Aleus, son of Apheidas, whose name may have been worked back from the goddess's once her own traditions were half forgotten. The first temple probably dates to the early Archaic period, and Herodotus wrote that it held chains from a failed Spartan attack on Tegea in the 6th century BCE.

The second temple was of the Doric order. Pausanias described rows of Doric, Corinthian and Ionic columns, the Calydonian boar hunt on the east pediment and the local hero Telephos fighting Achilles on the plain of the Caycus. The boar hunt tied Tegea to the heroine Atalanta, and Telephos was the son of Heracles and Auge, in myth the first priestess of Athena Alea. The ivory cult statue by Endoeus, together with the boar's tusks, was carried to Rome by Augustus for the Forum of Augustus. Statues of Asclepius and Hygieia by Scopas flanked the cult image.

The temple was an old and respected place of asylum, where the Spartan Leotychides and the Spartan general Pausanias, among others, sought refuge. Two festivals were held there: the Aleaia for the goddess and the Halotia for a victory over the Spartans. According to Pausanias, the priest was a boy who served only until puberty.

The Irish painter and author Edward Dodwell identified the site in 1806 with the help of Pausanias's text. A German team made the first excavations in the 1870s and published them in 1880; French missions followed in the early 1900s, and Greek teams dug in 1908 and in 1976 and 1977. Since the 1990s the Norwegian Institute at Athens has worked there, after the Norwegian archaeologist Erik Østby found remains of the earlier sanctuary that French publications had taken for an Early Christian or Byzantine church.
temple-of-athena-lindia: The sanctuary stood on the acropolis of Lindos, then the capital of Rhodes, above a natural cave in the cliff that may have been an earlier cult place; before the temple was founded the site seems to have served the cult of a local goddess. The first temple is dated to the 6th century BCE and was probably built by Cleobulus. Its cult statue, reconstructed from votive statuettes, showed Athena seated and wearing a polos crown.

Ancient writers gave the temple a mythical founding. Pseudo-Apollodorus says that Danaus dedicated a statue of Athena Lindia there in gratitude for her help in building the ship on which he fled with his daughters, while Strabo credited the founding to the Danaïdes themselves. According to Callimachus, the image set up by Danaus was a xoanon that was later replaced by a statue. Rhodes also figured in the myth of Athena's birth, when gold was said to have rained on the island.

After a fire the temple was replaced in the late 4th century BCE by a new Doric building measuring 7.75 by 21.65 metres. Its new cult statue showed a standing Athena carrying a shield and wearing a polos rather than a helmet; since it was fastened to the wall of the cella, it may have been larger than life. The sanctuary was excavated by the Italian archaeologists Maiuri and Jacopi between 1910 and 1932, and also by the Danish archaeologists K.F. Kinch and Chr. Blinkenberg.

The shrine was a significant Pan-Hellenic sanctuary of Athena and probably the regional centre of her cult. In Pindar's telling, in the 5th century BCE, the sons of Helios founded a precinct on the city's height but brought no fire with them, and Philostratus the Elder later set the fireless sacrifices of the Rhodians against the burnt offerings of the Athenians. Alexander the Great and many of his successors sacrificed at Lindos and dedicated weapons there after their victories, and the Temple Chronicle listed many of its votive gifts, among them works by Boethus and by the painter Parrhasios of Ephesus.
temple-of-edfu: Edfu was one of several temples built under the Ptolemaic Kingdom, among them those at Dendera, Esna, Kom Ombo and Philae, and its size reflects the prosperity of the time. The present temple was begun on 23 August 237 BCE and at first consisted of a pillared hall, two transverse halls and a barque sanctuary surrounded by chapels.

Work started under Ptolemy III Euergetes and was completed in 57 BCE under Ptolemy XII Auletes. It stands on the site of an earlier, smaller temple of Horus, which was oriented east-west rather than north-south, and inscriptions on a ruined pylon to the east point to building under Ramesses I, Seti I and Ramesses II.

The inscribed walls give details of the temple's construction and preserve the mythical reading of it, and of all temples, as the Island of Creation. According to the creation myth on the inner face of the perimeter wall, the world was at first covered by water. Reeds grew where the land neared the surface, and Horus landed there as a falcon, which began the cult of Edfu. The serpent Apophis tried to impede creation but was defeated, and a falcon formed the sky dome. The gods Thoth and Seshat then planned the first temple, built at first of reed, and sixty gods formed a living wall to protect it.

The temple was the largest dedicated to Horus and Hathor of Dendera, and it was the centre of several festivals sacred to Horus. Each year Hathor travelled south from Dendera to visit Horus at Edfu, an event marking their sacred marriage and the occasion of a great festival and pilgrimage. The walls also carry scenes of the Sacred Drama, the age-old conflict between Horus and Seth.

Over the centuries the temple was buried to a depth of 12 metres beneath drifting sand and silt left by the Nile, and local people built houses over its grounds. By 1798, when a French expedition identified it, only the tops of the pylons showed. In 1860 the French Egyptologist Auguste Mariette began to free it from the sands. It is nearly intact and a good example of an ancient Egyptian temple, and a naos of Nectanebo II from an earlier building survives in its inner sanctuary. Its columns were copied in the frontage of the Temple Works in Holbeck, Leeds.
temple-of-hibis: The temple stands about 2 kilometres north of Kharga and was once surrounded by the town of Hibis, in Egyptian Hebet, the plough, whose remains now lie under the fields. Archaeological evidence suggests an older temple of the New Kingdom on the same spot. Building began in the 26th Dynasty, most likely under Pharaoh Psamtik II, or possibly as early as the 25th Dynasty, and Darius I is credited with the decoration of the walls. Hakor of the 29th Dynasty, Nectanebo I and Nectanebo II, possibly Ptolemy IV and at least one Roman emperor added to it later.

It was devoted to two local forms of Amun, Amun of Hibis and Amun-Ra of Karnak who dwells in Hibis, though some hold it was dedicated to Amun and Osiris. An avenue of sphinxes passes through a series of pylons to the temple proper, which was once surrounded by a lake. The walls of the hypostyle hall are shaped like huge papyrus rolls and carry hymns to Amun, many known from earlier times, and a scene of Seth defeating Apep that some art historians see as a forerunner of Saint George and the Dragon.

The walls are given to Theban theology and the roof to Osiris. The naos is divided into nine registers holding almost 700 figures of gods and kings, each register opening with the king performing a ritual, and the provinces of Egypt appear in Osirian form, while the inscriptions beside them are brief or absent. The temple follows Theban temples of the New Kingdom and Ptolemaic period in plan and texts, but its decoration is bolder in style.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art of New York led a first excavation that began in 1909, and a newer campaign led by Eugene Cruz-Uribe began in 1985. The temple's seclusion probably accounts for its good condition, but for several decades rising groundwater has been damaging its foundations, and the Egyptian Antiquities Service considered taking the whole temple apart and moving it.
temple-of-jupiter-optimus-maximus: Much of what is known of the first temple comes from later Roman tradition. King Lucius Tarquinius Priscus vowed it while fighting the Sabines, and according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Livy, the foundations and most of the superstructure were completed by Lucius Tarquinius Superbus. Livy records that when the augurs sought permission to remove other shrines from the site, only Terminus and Juventas were believed to have refused, so their shrines were built into the new temple. Workmen digging the foundations also found a man's head, which the augurs said meant that Rome would be head of a great empire.

Each member of the triad had a separate cella, with Juno Regina on the left, Minerva on the right and Jupiter Optimus Maximus in the middle. The first temple was decorated with terracotta sculpture, of which a quadriga of Jupiter on the roof and the cult statue were said to be the work of the Etruscan artisan Vulca of Veii. The temple was surrounded by the Area Capitolina, which held shrines, altars, statues and trophies.

The temple was destroyed four times. The first burned in 83 BCE, during the civil wars under Sulla, together with the Sibylline Books. The second, dedicated by Quintus Lutatius Catulus, burned in fighting in December 69 CE. Vespasian rebuilt it, and it burned again in 80 CE. Domitian then built a fourth, with a roof of gilded bronze tiles, finished in 82 CE.

The fourth temple is thought to have stood largely intact for over three hundred years, until pagan temples were closed by Emperor Theodosius I in 392. Procopius says the Vandals stripped half its gilded bronze tiles in 455. Ruins were still well preserved when Poggio Bracciolini visited in 1447, and they were destroyed in the 16th century when a palace was built on the site. Portions of the podium and foundations can be seen today behind the Palazzo dei Conservatori. The size of the first temple remains disputed. In 2014 the original terracotta decoration was discovered, allowing the first reconstruction of its earliest appearance.
temple-of-literature-hanoi: The Temple of Literature, Văn Miếu in Vietnamese, stands in Hanoi to the south of the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long. It was founded and first built in 1070, in the reign of Emperor Lý Thánh Tông. According to the record of that year, statues of Confucius, his four best disciples, Yan Hui, Zengzi, Zisi and Mencius, and the Duke of Zhou were carved, and 72 other statues of Confucian scholars were painted. Ceremonies were held to them in each season.

In 1076, under Lý Nhân Tông, the Imperial Academy (Quốc Tử Giám), Vietnam's first university, was established within the temple to educate bureaucrats, nobles, royalty and other members of the elite. It remained open until 1779. In the early 19th century the Nguyễn monarchs moved the academy to their new capital at Huế, and the Hanoi academy became a school of the Hoài Đức District. The Trần dynasty and later dynasties reconstructed the temple.

The layout resembles that of the temple at Qufu, Confucius' birthplace, and covers over 54,000 square metres, with the Văn lake, the Giám park and five courtyards inside a brick wall. The Great Gate opens onto three paths, the centre one reserved for the monarch, the left for administrative mandarins and the right for military mandarins. The Khuê Văn pavilion, built in 1805, stands in the second courtyard, and the fourth courtyard is the ceremonial heart of the complex.

Students, most of whom had passed the regional examination, studied at the academy for three to seven years. They learned Chinese, Chinese philosophy and history, and read the Four Books and the Five Classics. Success in the Hội examination led to the royal Đình examination at court, where the monarch himself posed the questions and ranked those who passed.

In 1484 Emperor Lê Thánh Tông began the construction of the stone stelae of doctors, ordering 116 stelae resting on carved blue stone turtles, to honour talent and encourage study. The turtle symbolises longevity and wisdom. 82 stelae remain. They record the names and birthplaces of 1,307 graduates of 82 triennial royal examinations. Between 1442 and 1779 the Lê dynasty held eighty-one of these examinations and the Mạc dynasty one. The stelae were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2011.

The French protectorate registered the temple as a Monument historique in 1906. Parts of it were demolished between 1945 and 1954 to make room for a hospital, and the fifth courtyard was destroyed in 1946 during the First Indochina War. It was rebuilt in 2000, and major restorations also took place in 1920 and 1954.
temple-of-olympian-zeus-agrigento: The temple stands in the Valle dei Templi among several other Greek temples. Its history is unclear, but it was probably founded to commemorate the Battle of Himera, in which Akragas and Syracuse defeated the Carthaginians under Hamilcar. According to the historian Diodorus Siculus it was built with Carthaginian slave labour, presumably soldiers captured in the battle, and it remained unfinished when the Carthaginians took the city in the Siege of Akragas; its roof was already missing then. Polybius, describing Akragas in the 2nd century BCE, called it unfinished but second to none in Greece in design and dimensions.

The temple measured 112.7 by 56.3 metres at the stylobate and stood some 20 metres high, built of small stone blocks. Its front had seven half-columns, an archaic feature that left no room for a central door, and each long side fourteen. Instead of a free-standing colonnade, the columns were engaged in a continuous curtain wall that carried the immense entablature; Diodorus wrote that a man could fit in their grooves. Between them stood atlases some 7.5 metres high, nude, alternately bearded and clean-shaven, generally thought to have stood on a recessed ledge with their hands raised to bear the upper part of the building.

The interior, inspired by Phoenician-Carthaginian architecture, was a triple-aisled hall of pillars whose middle lay open to the sky. According to Diodorus the eastern pediment showed a Gigantomachy and the western the fall of Troy. Before the eastern front stood the pilastered base of a huge high altar.

Earthquakes eventually brought the temple down, and in the 18th century it was quarried heavily for building stone for Agrigento and Porto Empedocle, so that only a broad platform heaped with fallen pillars and blocks survives. One atlas has been reassembled in the nearby archaeological museum, with a replica among the ruins. Some interpret the figures as a symbol of the Greek enslavement of the Carthaginian invaders, others see Egyptian influence, and Joseph Rykwert took the temple's size as confirming the reputed extravagance of the Akragans.
temple-of-the-feathered-serpent: The pyramid stands at the southern end of the Avenue of the Dead, Teotihuacan's main thoroughfare, inside the Ciudadela, a high-walled enclosure whose courtyard could have held the city's entire adult population. Two mansions north and south of it are thought to have housed powerful families, and the Adosada platform, built in the 4th century, stands in front of it to the west. It is a six-level step pyramid in the talud-tablero style. In antiquity it was painted, with a blue background decorated with carved sea shells, and the eyes of the heads held obsidian that would glimmer in the light.

Scholars differ on what the heads that alternate with the feathered serpents show: some identify them as Tlaloc, Mary Ellen Miller and Karl Taube as a war serpent, and Michael D. Coe as a fire serpent wearing a headdress with the Teotihuacan symbol for war. The carvings are among the earliest known representations of the feathered serpent, often identified with the much later Aztec god Quetzalcoatl.

The pyramid is thought to carry two hundred and sixty feathered serpent heads, each with an opening in its mouth large enough for a marker, and it is believed that the people of Teotihuacan moved a marker around the building to follow the ritual calendar. Excavations led by Cowgill in 1988 and 1989 showed that the pyramid was burned in a hot fire and that its debris went into the Adosada platform, which some read as a political change, perhaps a rejection of autocratic rule in favour of a collective leadership.

The sacrificial burials, found in the 1980s, hold more men than women. Many of the men were buried with weapons, military dress and necklaces of human teeth, and researchers have taken them for warriors, probably in Teotihuacan's own service. Sugiyama argues that their careful arrangement was tied to the calendar and to the symbolism of creation.

In late 2003 Sergio Gómez Chávez and Julie Gazzola of the National Institute of Anthropology and History found a tunnel after heavy rain opened a sinkhole near the pyramid. After years of planning and survey by ground-penetrating radar, digging was allowed in 2009. A shaft 14 metres deep leads to a corridor nearly 100 metres long that ends in galleries in the rock. By 2015 nearly 75,000 fragments of objects had been found, among them greenstone figures, jaguar bones, wooden masks inlaid with jade and quartz, hundreds of metallised spheres and pools of liquid mercury.
temple-of-the-inscriptions: Its Classic Maya name was Bʼolon Yej Teʼ Naah, the House of the Nine Sharpened Spears. It is the largest stepped pyramid at Palenque and stands at a right angle to the south-east of the palace. A temple sits on an eight-stepped pyramid, making nine levels in all. Its five front entrances are framed by six piers, labelled A to F, with stucco reliefs and texts. Piers B to E show figures holding an infant-like God K with a serpent for one leg, whose six-toed foot is thought to refer to Kan Bahlam II.

The standing figure on Pier C may be Pakal's mother, Lady Zac-Kuk, and the one on Pier E is most likely Kan Bahlam I, the great-great-grandfather of Kan Bahlam II, who stressed his descent through these images. The piers were once painted red, yellow and blue, blue for the heavens and the gods and yellow for Xibalba, the underworld. The three tablets record events of Pakal's life and, in their last two columns, his death and his heir.

To bear the weight of the pyramid, the chamber was built with cross vaulting and recessed buttresses. The sarcophagus lid shows Pakal lying on the earth monster above the open jaws of a jaguar, which stand for Xibalba, while the Celestial Bird perches on the Cosmic Tree above him, so that he lies between the heavens and the underworld. His ancestors are carved along the sarcophagus, six generations back. The jade mask has eyes of shell, mother of pearl and obsidian; smaller jade heads lay in the sarcophagus and a stucco portrait of the king beneath it.

Palenque had been visited and studied for more than two hundred years before the tomb was found. Alberto Ruz Lhuillier lifted a slab of the temple floor and found a stairway filled with rubble, which led to the crypt once cleared. Five skeletons of men and women, sacrificial victims meant to follow Pakal into Xibalba, lay at its entrance. Merle Greene Robertson, suspended from the ceiling, is the only person to have photographed the lid; the tomb was then resealed and has not been opened since.
temple-of-the-obelisks: The temple stands on the remains of an older sanctuary that Maurice Dunand called the L-shaped Temple, after the arrangement of its two rooms and courtyard. That building was put up around 2600 BCE, about two centuries after the Temple of Baalat Gebal some 100 metres to the west, and had well-built walls. It was dedicated to the male tutelary god of the city and is thought to have burned down at the end of the Early Bronze Age. The later temple kept its general outline but was built with irregular walls, and it remained in use from the Middle Bronze Age until the Iron Age or later.

It was an open-air sanctuary, its obelisks and standing stones set in a court around the cella. Unlike its predecessor it had no single god to worship and probably followed the tradition of the Syro-Palestinian cult. It was one of seven main cult buildings around the central spring and artificial lake of Byblos, each perhaps the heart of a neighbourhood. While the neighbouring Temple of Lady Byblos yielded many Egyptian goods, this temple and the L-shaped Temple show designs inspired by Syria, which suggests that parts of the city dealt with different regions. A jeweller's workshop and the mass of finds point to trade or other economic activity there.

Its best-known monument is the Abishemu Obelisk, a limestone obelisk of around 1800 BCE commemorating King Abishemu I of Byblos. Its Egyptian hieroglyphic inscription is read as a dedication to Heryshaf, widely though not universally taken here as the Egyptian form of the Canaanite war god Resheph.

Dunand identified the temple and excavated it over several decades from 1924. Most of the obelisks still stood upright in their original places, and a few lay buried in a favissa, a pit for votive deposits. To reach the L-shaped Temple he dismantled the upper building and set it up again 40 metres to the east. Almost all the finds are in the National Museum of Beirut. The poor excavation record and Dunand's unfinished publications have made later study of Byblos harder.
temple-of-the-tooth: According to legend, the tooth relic was kept at Kalinga after the Buddha's death, and when that kingdom was attacked, Princess Hemamali and her brother Prince Dantha brought it to the island on the instructions of their father, King Guhasiva. Hemamali is said to have hidden it in her hair. They landed during the reign of Sirimeghavanna of Anuradhapura (301 to 328), and the king enshrined it at the Meghagiri Vihara. Guarding the relic became the monarch's duty and the custodianship came to symbolise the right to rule the island, so kings built tooth temples close to their palaces at Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa and Dambadeniya. Under the Kingdom of Gampola the relic was kept at Niyamgampaya Vihara.

During the reign of Dharmapala of Kotte the relic was hidden in a grinding stone at Delgamuwa Vihara in Ratnapura, and it was later brought to Kandy. King Vimaladharmasuriya I built a two-storey building for it. In 1603, when the Portuguese invaded Kandy, it was carried to Meda Mahanuwara in Dumbara, and it was recovered under Rajasinha II. The present temple was built by Vira Narendra Sinha, and the octagonal Paththirippuwa and the moat were added under Sri Vikrama Rajasinha.

The Sri Dalada Maligawa stands in the royal palace complex of the former Kingdom of Kandy and is a World Heritage Site. Monks of the Malwathu and Asgiri chapters conduct worship in the inner chamber three times daily, at dawn, at noon and in the evening. On Wednesdays the relic is bathed symbolically with a herbal preparation, and the water is distributed among those present. The relic is encased in seven golden caskets inlaid with gems, which represent a stupa. The golden canopy and fence were built in 1987.

The annual Kandy Esala Perahera pays homage to the relic. Beside the temple stands the royal palace and the audience hall, built in 1783, where the Kandyan Convention was read out on 2 March 1815. The temple was attacked in 1989 by the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna, which meant to capture the relic, and in 1998 by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, whose bomb destroyed the main entrance gate and damaged the palace front. A public exposition in April 2025 drew about 450,000 devotees in one day and caused four deaths from heat exhaustion and fatigue.
templo-mayor: The Mexica began the Templo Mayor, called Huēyi Teōcalli in Nahuatl, sometime after 1325 and rebuilt it six times, each new structure covering the one before it. The first temple, of earth and wood, is known only from records because the high water table prevents excavation. The second was built between 1375 and 1427 under Acamapichtli, Huitzilihuitl and Chimalpopoca, and the third, with a staircase of eight stone standard-bearers, under Itzcoatl. The largest known expansion was carried out in 1454 under Moctezuma I, and the fourth temple holds the richest sculpture. The fifth was built under Tizoc.

The sixth temple belongs to the reign of Ahuizotl, who finished Tizoc's work and walled off the Sacred Precinct with a wall of serpent heads. A carved stone shows two rulers celebrating the opening of the temple on 19 December 1487. The seventh and last temple was first mentioned by the conquistadors in 1519 and was altered for the last time in 1520. Fray Bernardino de Sahagún reported that the precinct held 78 buildings, with the Templo Mayor towering above them all.

The pyramid had four sloped terraces and two stairways leading to twin shrines, Tlaloc on the left and Huitzilopochtli on the right. It was a symbolic Hill of Coatepec, where according to Mexica myth Huitzilopochtli was born and defeated his sister Coyolxauhqui. The great stone disk of her dismembered body lay at the foot of his side, and the northern half represented Tonacatepetl, the mountain home of Tlaloc. Cortés and his men admired the number and magnificence of the temples but disliked the Mexica beliefs and human sacrifice. After 1521 the temples were sacked and demolished, and a church, later the cathedral, was built on the western half of the precinct.

The temple's exact location was forgotten, and early excavations by Leopoldo Batres, Manuel Gamio and others found only parts of it. On 21 February 1978 electricity workers struck a stone disk over 3.25 metres across and weighing 8.5 tonnes, which was later identified as the relief of Coyolxauhqui and dated to the end of the 15th century. Excavation directed by Eduardo Matos Moctezuma followed from 1978 to 1982, and more than 7,000 objects were found, mostly offerings, now in the Templo Mayor Museum, built in 1987. The site is part of the Historic Center of Mexico City, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
temporary-provisions-against-the-communi: The Republic of China adopted its constitution in 1947, in the middle of the Chinese Civil War. In March 1948 the National Assembly chose to amend it through Article 174 to give the state emergency powers to fight the war, and the Temporary Provisions were adopted on 10 May 1948. They were meant to lapse after three years, but in 1954, after the government's defeat and retreat to Taiwan, the National Assembly extended them indefinitely. Of their four amendments, the one of 1966 allowed supplementary elections to the National Assembly from the Taiwan Area, and another followed in 1972, after the People's Republic of China replaced the Republic of China in the United Nations in 1971.

The Provisions allowed the creation of the Taiwan Garrison Command and the National Security Council, both to enforce martial law, and exempted the president and vice president from the limit of two terms. During the Period of Communist Rebellion the president could adopt emergency measures through a resolution of a cabinet meeting of the Executive Yuan, free of the regular procedures of Articles 39 and 43 of the constitution.

These wide powers turned the Republic of China into a de facto presidential system, with the president also chairman of the Kuomintang, although the constitution had laid out a parliamentary system. In effect the Provisions set the constitution aside, and civil and political freedoms on Taiwan were curtailed under martial law.

With the end of the Kuomintang's single-party system and at the end of the Cold War, the National Assembly decided on 22 April 1991 to repeal the Provisions. On 30 April President Lee Teng-hui announced that their measures would end the next day, and on 1 May the Additional Articles of the Constitution of the Republic of China came into force.

The repeal left some ambiguity in relations across the Taiwan Strait and over the political status of Taiwan. It raised questions such as whether the Communist rebellion had in a sense succeeded, so that the government of the People's Republic was now recognised as legitimate, and whether the Communist Party could now lawfully operate in Taiwan.
ten-commandments: The phrase Ten Commandments comes from Exodus 34:28, Deuteronomy 4:13 and Deuteronomy 10:4, and in each case can be translated as the ten words, sayings or matters. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, rendered it as dekalogos, which became Latin decalogus and English Decalogue.

In the biblical narrative the revelation begins in Exodus 19, when the Israelites reach Mount Sinai, also called Horeb. On the third morning there are thunders, lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain, and in Exodus 20 God speaks the words of the covenant to all the people. Scholars have proposed three main datings: early Mosaic authorship, a pre-exilic monarchic origin, or a postexilic composition. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman argue for the seventh century BCE, and David H. Aaron for a date after 586 BCE.

The seventeen verses of Exodus 20:1 to 17 and Deuteronomy 5:4 to 21 are divided into ten commandments in different ways, although they contain more than ten imperatives. One approach separates the prohibition of other gods from that of images, as in the Septuagint and among Eastern Orthodox and Reformed Christians following Calvin. Another joins them, as Augustine did in the 4th century, dividing the prohibition on coveting into two. The Samaritan Pentateuch adds an instruction to sacrifice to Yahweh, which Samaritans count as the tenth.

Exodus 34:28 itself names the passage of Exodus 34:11 to 27 as the Ten Commandments, and since it concerns proper worship rather than murder or theft, some scholars call it the Ritual Decalogue and the better known text the Ethical Decalogue.

In Judaism the commandments are the foundation of rabbinic law, held to state God's universal and timeless standard, unlike the rest of the 613 commandments the tradition finds in the Torah. Most Christian traditions hold that they remain valid and divinely authoritative. In the New Testament, Jesus refers to the prohibitions of murder and adultery in the Sermon on the Mount and repeats five of them in Matthew 19. In Islam the receiving of the tablets by Moses is described in Surah A'raf, and Surah An'am 6:151 to 153 is widely taken as a reinstatement of the commandments.

After the Reformation, European Protestants replaced some visual art in churches with plaques of the Ten Commandments. In England such Decalogue boards also represented the monarch's emphasis on royal law within the churches. In 1980 the United States Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional a Kentucky statute requiring a copy in every public classroom. Hundreds of monuments were placed as publicity for Cecil B. DeMille's 1956 film The Ten Commandments.
ten-days-campaign: The Congress of Vienna in 1815 had joined the former Austrian Netherlands and Liège to the Dutch Republic as the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. The southern provinces rose in August 1830, and by November, when a cease-fire was agreed, Dutch forces had been driven from most of present-day Belgium. Many Belgian conscripts deserted, and much of the Dutch army was overseas fighting the Java War. William I saw the failure to crush the revolt as a humiliation and hoped a victory would strengthen his hand in negotiations.

When the National Congress offered the crown to Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, William prepared to invade. A Dutch force of 50,000 under the Prince of Orange, the future William II, gathered in North Brabant. Across the border stood just 24,000 Belgians, many of them poorly trained militia of the Garde Civique, divided into the Army of the Meuse in Limburg and the Army of the Scheldt around the Dutch-held citadel of Antwerp, too far apart to support each other.

The Dutch crossed the border near Poppel on 2 August 1831, days after Leopold's coronation, drove the Belgians back at Ravels and routed them at Turnhout the next day. The army then split up, winning at Houthalen and defeating the Army of the Meuse near Hasselt on 8 August, the Army of the Scheldt's advance guard near Boutersem on 11 August and the Belgians near Leuven on 12 August. Leopold appealed for help on 8 August, and France sent Marshal Étienne Gérard's army across the border without informing the other Great Powers. After the intervention of the British diplomat Robert Adair, a ceasefire was signed on 12 August, and the last Dutch troops were home around 20 August.

Belgium's weakness led the London Conference to impose harsher terms in the Treaty of XXIV Articles, which gave parts of Limburg and Luxembourg to the Netherlands. When General David Hendrik Chassé bombarded Antwerp from its citadel, Gérard returned on 15 November 1832, and Chassé surrendered on 23 December. Henri Pirenne wrote that the Dutch advance almost resembled a military parade, but that no revival of Orangism followed.
ten-great-campaigns: In 1752 Dawachi and the Khoit-Oirat prince Amursana competed for the title of Khan of the Dzungars. Beaten, Amursana fled to the Qing court, and the Qianlong Emperor backed him once he accepted Qing authority. In 1755 the Manchu general Zhaohui, aided by Amursana and the Khoja brothers Burhān al-Dīn and Khwāja-i Jahān, advanced along the Ili and forced Dawachi to surrender. Amursana, made only one of four equal khans, revolted in 1756 and after defeats in 1758 fled to Russia, where he died. The Khoja brothers then rose in Altishahr, were defeated in 1759 and were handed over by Sultan Shah of Badakhshan.

The other campaigns were more in the nature of police actions on frontiers already established. The second war against the Gyalrong of Jinchuan, in western Sichuan, became a protracted war of attrition against tribes holding stone towers in steep mountains; it cost the treasury several times as much as the conquest of the Dzungars and Xinjiang, and the Qing generals were ruthless in annihilating the local Gyalrong. Four invasions of Burma between 1765 and 1769 claimed the lives of over 70,000 Qing soldiers and ended in a truce in December 1769, with the Qing forces encircled.

In Taiwan the general Fuk'anggan put down the rising of Lin Shuangwen and the Tiandihui (Heaven and Earth Society) and executed its leader. A Qing army sent into Vietnam to restore Lê Chiêu Thống was defeated by the Tây Sơn, and Qianlong then recognised Nguyễn Huệ (Quang Trung) as ruler. After Gurkha incursions into southern Tibet in 1788, an army of 10,000 under Fuk'anggan crossed the passes in the winter of 1791–92 and pushed the Gurkhas back, and a peace signed at Betrawati obliged Nepal to send tribute every five years.

In his later years Qianlong styled himself Old Man of the Ten Completed [Great Campaigns], and in 1792 he wrote the Record of Ten Completions enumerating the victories. The campaigns cost more than 151 million silver taels, and their results were modest.
