The Jinchuan tribes, fewer than 30,000 households, took five years to pacify; Burma settled into continued tributary status, and when relations resumed in 1790 the Burmese held them to be on equal terms while Qianlong claimed victory. The destruction of the Dzungars, by contrast, secured the northern and western boundaries of Xinjiang and removed any rival influence in Mongolia and over the Dalai Lama.
ten-lost-tribes: The Ten Lost Tribes were those of the Twelve Tribes of Israel said to have been exiled from the Kingdom of Israel after it was conquered by the Neo-Assyrian Empire. They were Reuben, Simeon, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Manasseh and Ephraim, which is to say all but Judah and Benjamin, based in the neighbouring Kingdom of Judah, which survived until the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem in 587 BCE.

The exile, known as the Assyrian captivity, was an instance of the long-standing Assyrian policy of resettling subjugated populations. The scriptural basis is 2 Kings 17:6, which says that the king of Assyria took Samaria and placed the Israelites in Halah, in Habor on the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.

Many Israelites survived the conquest and remained in Samaria, and the Samaritans, a distinct religious community with their own Torah and holy mountain at Mount Gerizim, trace their ancestry to ancient Israel. The New Standard Jewish Encyclopedia states that some members of the tribes stayed in the land, some were assimilated and others were presumably absorbed by the last Judean exiles, and that the deported Israelites soon assimilated. Josephus wrote that the ten tribes were beyond the Euphrates, an immense multitude.

In the 7th and 8th centuries CE their return was linked to the coming of the Messiah. The Talmud records a disagreement: Rabbi Akiva held that they would not return, Rabbi Eliezer that they would, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda said it depended on whether their deeds improved. The apocryphal Second Esdras, written before the end of the first century CE, describes their journey to a land called Arzareth.

From the 17th century, tales of the lost tribes multiplied. Menasseh's argument rested on a verse of Isaiah, an old Jewish community found in China by Matteo Ricci and Antonio Montezinos's reported meeting with the tribes in South America. The historian Tudor Parfitt argues that the myth was a vital feature of colonial discourse, and that, with Prester John, it guided exploration and contact with indigenous peoples in the Age of Discovery. In 1650 the minister Thomas Thorowgood argued that the native peoples of North America descended from the tribes.

Many groups have claimed descent from the tribes. Kurdish Jews and the Pashtuns hold such traditions, as do the Lemba and the Igbo Jews of Nigeria. In 2005 the chief rabbi of Israel ruled that the Bnei Menashe of Mizoram and Manipur descend from a lost tribe, and in 2021 4,500 of them had emigrated to Israel. British Israelism has been widely rejected by historians, and archaeologists consider the nineteenth-century theory linking the earthworks of the Mississippian culture to the tribes pseudo-scientific.
ten-thousand: The Ten Thousand were a force of mercenary units, mainly Greek, employed by Cyrus the Younger to take the Persian throne from his brother Artaxerxes II. According to Xenophon, who led them and recorded their march in the Anabasis, they numbered about 10,400 when they set out in 401 BCE.

They came in contingents under commanders such as Clearchus of Sparta, Proxenus of Boeotia, Menon and the Spartan Cheirisophus, and were backed by Persian troops under Ariaeus, whom Xenophon puts at 100,000 but most modern historians put at about 20,000. At the Battle of Cunaxa, Xenophon states, the Greek heavy troops routed their opponents twice at the cost of one wounded man, and only afterwards learned that Cyrus had been killed.

Stranded far from home without food, employer or reliable allies, the Greeks refused the demand of the satrap Tissaphernes for surrender. He instead fed them and led them north, then invited their senior officers to a feast, where they were taken prisoner and executed. The army elected new officers, among them Xenophon, Timasion, Xanthicles, Cleanor and Philesius, and marched north through Corduene and Armenia, fighting the Carduchians in the mountains, crossing the Centrites River and enduring winter without suitable clothing. From the heights of Mount Theches they saw the sea and shouted "Thalatta! Thalatta!", "The sea! The sea!"

After reaching Trapezus they continued west to Bithynia and Byzantium, where a dispute with the Spartan admiral Anaxibius led to a fight and a proclamation that Cyrus's soldiers in Byzantium be sold as slaves. Now about 8,000 strong, they served the Thracian Seuthes in a campaign against the Thynians, and then the Spartan general Thibron in a war against Tissaphernes in Ionia. By the time Xenophon left them, they numbered just under 6,000.

Xenophon's conduct of the retreat led the American historian Theodore Ayrault Dodge to rank him first among the generals before Alexander the Great, and Dodge singled out his reserve behind the phalanx and his use of devastation to hold back pursuers. The march has inspired modern writers and artists: the 1965 novel The Warriors, which became a 1979 film, Iris Murdoch's novel The Sea, the Sea, a video game campaign and several novels, as well as Shane Brennan's account of retracing the route on foot in 2000.
ten-years-war: The uprising was led by Cuban-born planters and other wealthy natives. Lax enforcement of the ban on the slave trade had brought an estimated 90,000 enslaved Africans to Cuba from 1856 to 1860, although a strong abolitionist movement existed on the island, and planters in the east faced rising costs. In May 1865 Cuban criollo elites asked the Spanish Parliament for tariff reform, political representation and judicial equality for all Spaniards. Instead the colonial government raised taxes by six per cent and silenced political opposition and the press. Discontent was strongest among the planters of eastern Cuba, and in July 1867 the Revolutionary Committee of Bayamo was founded under Francisco Vicente Aguilera.

Carlos Manuel de Céspedes, who owned the sugar mill of La Demajagua, had planned the rising for 14 October 1868, but the Spaniards discovered the plan and he moved it forward. On 10 October he issued the 10th of October Manifesto at La Demajagua, freed his slaves and asked them to join the struggle. The manifesto aimed at abolishing slavery with compensation, freedom of assembly and of the press, and a free and independent nation. By the end of the month some 12,000 volunteers had enlisted. The rebels took Bayamo, where Perucho Figueredo composed the anthem La Bayamesa, but Spain retook it on 12 January, after fighting had burned it down.

On 10 April 1869 an assembly at Guáimaro separated civil government from military command, and Céspedes became the first president of the Republic in Arms. The Spanish relied on the Voluntary Corps, which grew to more than 70,000 men and executed eight students of the University of Havana on 27 November 1871. Ignacio Agramonte was killed on 11 May 1873, and Céspedes was deposed and killed on 27 February 1874. After the Third Carlist War ended in 1876, Spain had more than 250,000 troops in Cuba.

Tomás Estrada Palma was captured on 19 October 1877. The rebel government dissolved on 8 February 1878, and General Arsenio Martínez Campos persuaded most rebels to accept the Pact of Zanjón, signed on 10 February 1878. Antonio Maceo protested at Baraguá on 15 March, and the war ended on 28 May 1878. The pact promised reforms and freed the slaves who had fought for Spain, and Spain abolished slavery in Cuba in 1880 in a gradual form that required freed people to keep working for their masters.

About 190,000 people died, among them 100,000 Cubans and 90,000 Spaniards, mostly of disease. The Little War of 1879 to 1880 followed, and veterans such as the Maceo brothers, Gómez and Calixto García led the Cuban War of Independence from 1895. The war also devastated the coffee industry.
tenagino-probus: Nothing is known for certain of Probus's origins or early career. His family name, Tenagino, is rare: its only other recorded bearers appear in two inscriptions from northeast Italy, which may point to that region without proving it. The name does show that his family held Roman citizenship before the Constitutio Antoniniana of 212, and so may have been people of substance. Some evidence suggests long military service, and he was probably one of the professional soldiers who gained governorships and commands once reserved for senators.

His first known post was as praeses of Numidia, commanding the Legio III Augusta at Lambaesis, the only significant Roman force in north Africa. An inscription from Lambaesis of 267-268, under Gallienus, is generally taken to refer to him, and he may have been the province's first equestrian governor. Inscriptions from Thamugadi and Thuburbo Maius name him as governor under Claudius II. Stories in the Historia Augusta of his suppressing an insurrection in Carthago and killing one Aradio in single combat are generally rejected.

Claudius II then made him prefect of Egypt, a post of the highest trust, and sent him into Creta et Cyrenaica against the Marmaritae, nomads of the Marmarica; a Greek inscription from Cyrene, then called Claudiopolis, celebrates the victory. He next led a naval campaign against Gothic pirates raiding the islands and the southern coast of Asia Minor, probably in concert with a force under Lucius Aurelius Marcianus.

The fullest account of his end is by Zosimus. A pro-Palmyrene faction led by one Timagenes encouraged the invasion, and Zenobia's general Septiminus Zabdas entered Egypt with 70,000 men, defeated 50,000 loyalists and left a garrison of 5,000. Probus returned, expelled the garrison and beat Zabdas again with local forces and soldiers from Africa. Following Timagenes to the fortress of Babylon, his army was surprised by 2,000 men who had seized a nearby height; captured, he killed himself. The Historia Augusta calls him Probatus, and some of his deeds were credited by it to the future emperor Probus.
tenali: Tenali lies in the southern deltaic region of the Krishna River, at an average height of 13 metres above sea level, in the Western Delta system. Three canals from the Krishna flow through the town, the East canal, the Nizampatnam canal and the West canal. They make it part of the rice bowl of Andhra Pradesh, and they led to its affectionate name Andhra Paris, after the canals of Paris. Local lore says the name Tenali is a corruption of Tella Naali, the white Naali tree, a pale-barked Indian elm that grows plentifully around the town. The soils are mainly red and black, and paddy is the major crop.

The Andhra Satavahana dynasty ruled the region around the present town from 225 BCE to 225 CE. Excavations near Tenali have turned up relics that show the existence of Jainism, and the Ramalingeswara temple holds an inscription of the 16th century. Tenali Rama, one of the eight poets and jesters at the court of the early 16th-century Vijayanagara ruler Krishnadevaraya, came from the town.

The Tenali municipality was constituted in 1909. During the Quit India Movement the people of Tenali answered Mahatma Gandhi's call with a general strike on 12 August 1942. British police opened fire at Morrispeta and seven people were killed on the spot. The place was later renamed Ranarang Chowk, where seven pillars and a statue of Mother India stand in memory of the seven martyrs. The town was also a home of the Rationalist movement of 1940 and the Radical Humanist Movement of 1950, associated with M. N. Roy.

Tenali is known for drama, fine arts, literature and poetry. In 1929 it hosted the formation of the Andhra Nataka Kala Parishad, and it staged the play Kanyasulkam. Modern writers from Tenali include Gudipati Venkata Chalam, Kodavatiganti Kutumbarao and Tripuraneni Ramaswamy, and Chakrapani, the founder of Chandamama, also came from there. Several early stars of Telugu cinema were born in or near the town, among them Govindarajula Subba Rao, the first Telugu cinema hero, and Kanchanamala, the first heroine. The Yalavarthy Veda Pathashala, one of the oldest Vedic schools, was founded in 1894. Tenali is also known for jalebi made with jaggery instead of sugar.
tenant-farmer: In tenant farming the landowner contributes the land and often some operating capital and management, while the tenant contributes labour and varying amounts of capital and management. In the United States tenants typically bring their own tools and animals, which sets them apart from sharecroppers, who usually provide little besides their family's labour and pay with a portion of the crop, often half, the landlord furnishing working stock, tools, seed and housing. In most developed countries in the 21st century the landlord's right to evict a tenant is restricted at least to some degree.

In England rural society had three tiers: landowners, tenant farmers and farmworkers. Many tenants became affluent, employing labourers and managing more than one farm. The tenanted share of farmland fell to around 60% in 1950 and 35% in 1994, as high inheritance taxes broke up estates. The Agricultural Holdings Act 1948 gave tenants lifetime security, while the Agricultural Tenancies Act 1995 introduced the easily ended Farm Business Tenancies.

In Ireland, where 50% of the country belonged to only 750 families, the abuse of tenants drove emigration and fed the Home Rule Movement and the Land War. After the Land League of 1879 and a series of Land Acts, the Irish Land Act 1903 let the state finance tenants to buy out their landlords, and over 316,000 tenants bought 11,500,000 acres before independence. The Irish Land Commission, reconstituted in 1923, was dissolved in March 1999.

Norway's husmenn numbered 65,060 at their height in 1855, worked mostly for their landlords and could not vote; many emigrated to Canada and the United States, Marcus Thrane took up their cause after 1848, and by 1910 they were under 5% of society. In Sweden and Finland the crofters, torpare, often paid their lease in labour, and the yearly-contracted farm labourers, statare, were abolished in 1918 in Finland and 1945 in Sweden.

In Meiji Japan about 30% of land was held by tenants, until the Farm Land Reform Law of 1946 banned absentee landlordism and by the 1950s had virtually ended the relationship. In the Black Belt of the American South until the mid-20th century, white landowners divided old plantations into small farms for African-American tenants, who bought on credit through the year and handed over the cotton at harvest. The racially integrated Southern Tenant Farmers Union won gains for sharecroppers in the 1930s.
tendai: Teachings of the Chinese Tiantai school had reached Japan as early as 754 with Jianzhen, but took root in an organised school only when Saichō joined the Japanese mission to China in 804 and founded Enryaku-ji. Seven days after his death the court allowed Tendai its own bodhisattva precept ordination, separate from the powerful schools in Nara, and Gishin, the first head of the order, presided over the first ordinations in 827. Ryōgen, the 18th abbot of Enryaku-ji, was close to the Fujiwara clan, and through him Tendai became dominant at the court in Kyoto.

He is said to have hired an army to protect Mount Hiei, though some scholars attribute the rise of warrior monks to the decline of the imperial bureaucracy and the growth of temple estates. Tendai monks attacked the Hongan-ji in 1465, and the school took part in the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185. In the Edo period Tendai was folded into the Tokugawa temple registration system, and Enryaku-ji was rebuilt with shogunal support.

Philosophically Tendai kept the beliefs of Chinese Tiantai, founded on the doctrines of Zhiyi and Zhanran, such as the infinite lifespan of the Buddha, the buddha-nature of all beings and the 'three thousand realms in a single thought moment'. Saichō also brought Zen, Pure Land, esoteric and Vinaya elements from China, and his heirs Ennin, Enchin and Annen promoted esoteric practice.

Senior teachers train in the Four Integrated Schools of perfect teaching, esotericism, meditation and precepts. The school ordains with the bodhisattva precepts drawn from the Brahmajala Sutra, with no monastic Pratimokṣa, which Saichō defended in his Kenkairon, and which did not distinguish monastics from laypersons. Its esoteric branch is called Taimitsu, against Shingon's Tōmitsu.

Tendai held that all beings have buddha-nature, which brought Saichō into debate with the Hossō scholar Tokuitsu, whose school held that some beings lack the seeds of buddhahood. The medieval school was where the doctrine of hongaku, innate enlightenment, developed, and the theory of honji suijaku, which treated the kami as traces of buddhas, helped join native Japanese religion to Buddhism. Hōnen, Eisai, Shinran, Dōgen and Nichiren were all trained at Mount Hiei before founding schools of their own in the Kamakura period. The Meiji government's separation of Shinto from Buddhism led to the confiscation of temple lands and a decline in patronage.
tenes: Ténès is a town on the coast of Algeria, around 200 kilometres west of the capital Algiers. Its name comes from the Berber TNS, meaning camping. In antiquity the local tribes were known, according to Ptolemy, as the Bakoyta. Its harbour served for centuries as an outlet for the fruit and grain of the fertile land around it.

Ténès was founded as a Phoenician port in or before the 8th century BCE. Like other Phoenician harbours it fell under the hegemony of Carthage around the 6th century BCE and of the Romans after the Punic Wars. Its Punic name became Cartenna or Cartennae, a plural that suggests a separate Berber settlement nearby. It rose to colony status under the empire. The Vandals sacked it during their conquest of Roman North Africa. It was then reconquered by the Byzantines and taken by the Umayyad Caliphate, after which it disappeared except for a mostly ruined fortification.

Medieval Ténès was founded by Spaniards in the 9th century, and al-Bakri dates it to 875 or 876 (262 AH). They set up their base 3.2 kilometres from the former settlement and invited settlers from Elvira and Murcia, but many left because of outbreaks of fever. Berbers from Suk Ibrahim on the Chelif replaced them, and the city prospered despite its unhealthy climate. A local dynasty claiming descent from Ali ruled for a time. After the 10th century it passed in turn under Fatimid, Sanhaja, Maghrawa, Almoravid, Almohad and Ziyanid control. In the later 15th century it prospered amid the exodus of Moors after the War of Granada.

Oruç Reis sacked Ténès in 1517, and his brother Hayreddin Barbarossa conquered it for the Ottoman Empire a few years later. It received a garrison, but its economic life gradually collapsed, and its European grain trade was gone by the 18th century. Following the French invasion of Algiers in 1830 the town came under the Emir Abdelkader, who tried to revive its port, and the locals surrendered to the French without a fight in 1843.

Modern Ténès was established by the French in 1847 on the ruins of the Phoenician and Roman colony. French writers had at first assumed that ancient Cartennae lay at Mostaganem, until engravings found by archaeologists settled the identification. The harbour, about 1.5 kilometres away, first served as a port for goods from the Chelif and declined after the Algiers–Oran railway was built. The town has Phoenician and Roman tombs, prehistoric caves at Sidi Merouane, the Great Mosque of Sidi Ahmed Boumaza and a lighthouse.
tengrism: The name Tengri is first recorded in Chinese chronicles, in the 4th century BCE, as the sky god of the Xiongnu. Tengrism formed from Turkic and Mongolic folk religions that had many deities, spirits and gods and resembled the religious traditions of Siberia, Central Asia and Northeast Asia; ancestor worship played an important part. The cult of Heaven-Tengri is fixed in the Old Turkic script of the Göktürks in inscriptions of the 8th to 10th centuries. The word Tengrism itself is recent: it was brought into scholarly use in 1956 by the French scholar Jean-Paul Roux.

Tengrism is an animistic belief system that includes medicine, reverence of nature and ancestor worship. It centres on the sky god Gök Tengri, who stays abstract and is never shown in human or animal form, while other deities are often personified. Itugen, an earth or fertility deity, often accompanies Tengri; Umay is the goddess of children, and Kayra and Ülgen are other gods. Its cosmology divides the world into the heavens, the Earth and an underworld, joined by a world tree, and a shaman, called a kam, can communicate with the spirits of these worlds. People and animals are believed to have several souls.

Old Turkic inscriptions describe humans as the product of Heaven above and Earth beneath, so that mankind is part of nature and holds no special rank over it. Scholars disagree on its character: many hold it to have been mainly polytheistic and shamanistic, first touched by monotheism in the imperial period, while the Turkish historian Ahmet Taşağıl argues that it had a distinct theological structure around an abstract deity in heaven.

Tengrism was the prevailing religion of the Göktürk, Hun, Xiongnu, Bulgar and Mongolic peoples and the state religion of several medieval states, among them the First Turkic Khaganate, Khazaria and the Mongol Empire. The Orkhon inscriptions say that Tengri had a large part in the choice of the khagan and in guiding his acts, many of which were done because Heaven so ordained. The Secret History of the Mongols, written in 1240, traces Genghis Khan's ancestry to Borte Chino, the Blue Wolf, born with destiny from Tengri. Khans also held religious debates, whose outcomes were viewed as guided by heavenly support.

Tengrism was assimilated into Mongolian Buddhism, surviving unassimilated only in far-northern Mongolia, and Turkic and Mongolic peoples in Central Asia largely converted to Islam during the 14th century, often through Sufism, in which both Gök Tengri and Allah appear as names of God. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 a revival has taken place in Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Mongolia and parts of Russia such as Buryatia and Sakha. Related movements include Altaian Burkhanism and the Chuvash Vattisen Yaly.
tengzhou: Tengzhou lies on the Huanghuai Plain in the south of the warm temperate zone. Taiyi Mountain borders it on the east and Weishan Lake on the west, and its elevation ranges from 33.5 to 596.6 metres. The average annual temperature is 13.6 °C, and the average rainfall is 773.1 millimetres. The county-level city administers 21 township-level divisions, five subdistricts and sixteen towns. Besides the Han Chinese majority, thirty ethnic minorities live there, the largest of which is the Hui.

The settlement is said to date back to the Yellow Emperor. After the collapse of the Shang dynasty the area became the centre of the independent state of Teng, a feudal vassal state of the Spring and Autumn period, which was eventually conquered. It was then incorporated as Teng County, and the county kept that name until the Jin dynasty, when it became the Tengyang Prefecture. The prefecture was abolished at the start of the Ming dynasty. From 1945 to 1953 the county's administration changed many times before it again became Teng County, and on 7 March 1988 it became the county-level city of Tengzhou.

Tengzhou was probably the birthplace of the philosopher Mozi, and the master carpenter Lu Ban is also counted among its natives. Others from ancient times include Teng Wengong, Xi Zhong, Shusun Tong and Gongsun Hong.

The city has a Mozi Memorial Hall, which shows his biography and his scientific and technological achievements, and a Lu Ban Memorial Hall with halls on woodworking tools, weapons, architecture and boats and bridges. The old town of the Teng state preserves an ancient city wall and the Wengong Ancient Platform, one of the Eight Scenic Spots of Ancient Teng. The Weishan Lake wetland holds a large red lotus scenic area. Major industries include chemicals, minerals, petroleum, coal, food processing, Chinese medicine, electronic components and cement. The Beijing-Shanghai railway and National Highway 104 run through the city, and its two ports connect to the Grand Canal.
tennes: Tennes, called Tabnit II in Phoenician, ruled the Phoenician city-state of Sidon as a subject of the Achaemenid Empire. His predecessor was Abdashtart I, known in Greek as Straton I, the son of Baalshillem II. Soon after the failure of Artaxerxes III's campaign against Egypt, the Phoenicians declared their independence from Persian rule, and rulers in Anatolia and Cyprus followed. Artaxerxes ordered Belesys II, satrap of Syria, and Mazaeus, satrap of Cilicia, to invade and hold the Phoenicians in check. Tennes, aided by 4,000 Greek mercenaries whom the Egyptian pharaoh Nectanebo II sent under Mentor of Rhodes, defeated both satraps and drove the Persian forces out of Phoenicia.

Artaxerxes then led an army himself, given as 300,000 foot soldiers and 30,000 cavalry, with 300 triremes and 500 transports. Refused by Athens and Sparta, he gained a thousand Theban hoplites under Lacrates, three thousand Argives under Nicostratus and six thousand Greeks from the Greek cities of Anatolia. These, with the mercenaries from Egypt who later went over to him, were the troops on whom he chiefly relied.

As the king approached, Tennes tried to buy his own pardon by handing over 100 leading citizens of Sidon and then admitting Artaxerxes within the defences. Artaxerxes had the 100 transfixed with javelins, and 500 more who came out to beg for mercy met the same fate. Forty thousand people are said to have died when the city burned, and Artaxerxes sold the ruins to speculators hoping to dig treasure from the ashes. Tennes himself was put to death, and Jews who had supported the revolt were later sent to Hyrcania on the Caspian Sea.
tennessee: Tennessee is a landlocked state that borders eight others: Kentucky and Virginia to the north, North Carolina to the east, Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi to the south, and Arkansas and Missouri to the west. It is divided into three Grand Divisions, East, Middle and West Tennessee. The Blue Ridge Mountains along the eastern border reach some of the highest elevations in eastern North America, the Cumberland Plateau has scenic valleys and waterfalls, and West Tennessee has level, fertile plains. The Tennessee River crosses the state twice and the Mississippi River forms its western border.

The first inhabitants were Paleo-Indians who arrived about 12,000 years ago, at the end of the Last Glacial Period. Archaeologists name the Archaic (8000–1000 BCE), Woodland (1000 BCE–1000 CE) and Mississippian (1000–1600 CE) periods. Squash, corn, gourds and sunflowers were first grown in Tennessee during the Woodland period, when the first mounds were built, and Mississippian peoples developed organised chiefdoms and built many ceremonial structures. The state's name comes most directly from the Cherokee town of Tanasi. A Spanish party under Juan Pardo met a village called Tanasqui in 1567, and Governor James Glen of South Carolina is credited with the modern spelling in the 1750s.

The Watauga Association of 1772, a frontier pact, is generally regarded as the first constitutional government west of the Appalachian Mountains. The area was first part of North Carolina and then of the Southwest Territory, and it became the 16th state on 1 June 1796. Its constitutions date from 1796, 1834 and 1870. The capital moved among Knoxville, Nashville and Murfreesboro before Nashville became the permanent capital in 1843. The nickname The Volunteer State reflects a strong tradition of military service.

Tennessee was a slave state until the Civil War and was politically divided: most of the west and middle supported the Confederacy, while the east was largely pro-Union. It was the last state to secede and the first former Confederate state readmitted to the Union. In the 20th century it moved from an agrarian society to a more diversified economy, helped by the Tennessee Valley Authority and by Oak Ridge, established in the Second World War to house the Manhattan Project's uranium enrichment facilities.

Nashville is the capital and largest city; Memphis, Knoxville, Chattanooga and Clarksville follow. The state has 95 counties and about 7.2 million people. Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the most visited national park in the United States, lies in the east. Tennessee has done much to develop country, blues, rock and roll, soul and gospel music, and the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville has broadcast continuously since 1925.
tenochtitlan: Tenochtitlan, also called Mexico-Tenochtitlan, was a Mexica altepetl, or city-state, on an island in Lake Texcoco. The exact date of its founding is unclear; 13 March 1325 was chosen in 1925 to mark the 600th anniversary. Tradition held that the Mexica were to settle where an eagle with a snake in its beak perched on a cactus, and they saw this vision on a small swampy island. The city covered an estimated 8 to 13.5 square kilometres and was linked to the mainland by causeways to the north, south and west, broken by bridges that could be pulled away. Canals ran through it, so that every part could be reached on foot or by canoe.

Lake Texcoco was brackish. The levee of Nezahualcoyotl, reputedly designed by him and completed around 1453, kept fresh spring water around the city. Two double aqueducts of terracotta, each more than 4 kilometres long, brought water from the springs at Chapultepec. The city was divided into four zones, each of 20 districts called calpullis.

Using the chinampa system, the Mexica built up and expanded the island, and Tenochtitlan became the capital of the expanding Aztec Empire in the 15th century. After a flood of the lake the city was rebuilt under Ahuitzotl, who ruled between 1486 and 1502. Its population has been estimated at between 200,000 and 400,000, and one academic survey arrived at 212,500 people on 13.5 square kilometres. In the ceremonial centre, a walled square 500 metres to a side, stood about 45 public buildings, among them the Templo Mayor, dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc. The marketplace of its sister city Tlatelolco drew, by Hernán Cortés's estimate, about 60,000 people daily.

Cortés arrived on 8 November 1519, and the ruler Moctezuma II received him as an ambassador. Cortés later besieged the city, causing famine, while disease spread among its people. Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521. Cortés then directed its systematic destruction and founded Mexico City on its ruins, with a Spanish zone, the traza, at the centre. Indigenous people were settled in San Juan Tenochtitlan and Santiago Tlatelolco, each with its own council.

The ruins lie in the historic centre of Mexico City. The Templo Mayor was dismantled and built over by the Spanish, and its site was rediscovered in the early 20th century; major excavations took place from 1978 to 1982 after workers found a stone disc of the goddess Coyolxauhqui, 3.25 metres across. Mexico City's Zócalo stands on the original central plaza, and many of the old causeways correspond to modern streets. The World Heritage Site of Xochimilco contains what remains of the Mexica capital's waters, boats and floating gardens.
tensho-embassy: The embassy takes its name from the Tenshō era. It was led by Mancio Itō (1570–1612), chosen as spokesman of the group sent by Ōtomo Sōrin, daimyō of Bungo Province on Kyūshū and a close relative of Mancio's father. With him went three other young noblemen, Miguel Chijiwa, Julião Nakaura and Martinho Hara, two servants and their tutor and interpreter Diogo de Mesquita. Valignano travelled with them only as far as Goa in Portuguese India, where he was to take up new duties, and the party visited Macau, Kochi and Goa on the way to Lisbon.

The envoys reached Lisbon in August 1584 and went on through Évora and Toledo, where Archbishop Gaspar de Quiroga received them, to Madrid, where Philip II, king of Spain and Portugal, received them on 14 November 1584. They saw El Escorial and the king's Indian rhinoceros, then travelled by way of Alcalá de Henares, Murcia and Alicante to Livorno, Pisa and Florence, meeting Francesco I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany.

On 22 March 1585 they arrived in Rome, and the next day Pope Gregory XIII embraced them at a consistory in the Sala Regia; they gave the papacy a pair of folding screens, now lost, showing Azuchi, the site of Nobunaga's castle. Gregory died on 10 April, and his successor Sixtus V made them knights of the Order of the Golden Spur, while Mancio Itō became an honorary citizen of Rome. The envoys then visited Venice, Mantua, Milan, Genoa and Barcelona before sailing from Lisbon on 8 April 1586, and reached Japan on 21 July 1590.

The envoys' notes became the basis of De Missione Legatorum Iaponensium ad Romanam Curiam by the Jesuit Duarte de Sande, published at Macau in 1590; the historian Derek Massarella judges that it had no long-term effect on Japanese views of Europe. Valignano ordained the four as the first Japanese Jesuit fathers. Mancio Itō died in Nagasaki in 1612. The Tokugawa shogunate banished Martinho Hara in 1614, and he died in Macau in 1629. Miguel Chijiwa left the Society of Jesus before 1601. Julião Nakaura was tortured to death as a martyr in Nagasaki in 1633 and beatified on 24 November 2008.
tenskwatawa: Born Lalawethika, He Makes a Loud Noise, in early 1775, he was one of triplets born to Puckeshinwa and Methoataske in a Shawnee village on the Mad River in western Ohio. His father, a leader of the Kispokotha division, had been killed at the Battle of Point Pleasant, and the children were raised by their older sister Tecumpeas. Overshadowed by Tecumseh, he failed as a hunter and warrior, lost the sight of his right eye to his own arrow and drank heavily. He was at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794 and later trained as a medicine man under the healer Penagashea.

After the Treaty of Greenville of 1795, Governor William Henry Harrison pressed pro-accommodation chiefs to cede more land, often for far less than its market price, while settlers moved in and sold alcohol. In May 1805, reviving as his body was being prepared for burial, Lalawethika told of a vision of two worlds and took the name Tenskwatawa, Open Door. He forbade marriage with whites and Euro-American food, clothing and goods, and accused opponents, including Christian converts, of witchcraft. When Harrison challenged him to perform a miracle, he correctly predicted the eclipse of 16 June 1806.

Prophetstown, founded with Tecumseh in 1808 where the Wabash and Tippecanoe Rivers meet, drew some 3,000 people from an estimated 14 tribal groups, most of them Shawnee, Delaware and Potawatomi. The brothers denounced the Treaty of Fort Wayne of 1809. With Tecumseh away in the South, Tenskwatawa's 600 to 700 men attacked Harrison's camp of about 1,000 before dawn on 7 November 1811, assured that his spells would protect them; he stayed out of range. After the defeat some wanted to kill him, and he went to Canada, where he fled the Battle of the Thames in October 1813.

In 1824, at the request of Lewis Cass, governor of Michigan Territory, he returned to help with the removal of the Shawnee west of the Mississippi, reaching their reservation in Kansas on 14 May 1828 and founding another Prophetstown there. George Catlin painted his portrait. He died in his cabin in November 1836; the White Feather Spring marker of 1978 shows the approximate place of his grave. Historians have disagreed over whether he or Tecumseh led the movement, but he gave the resistance before the War of 1812 its spiritual foundation.
tenterfield-oration: The north of New South Wales lay far from the colonial capital, Sydney, yet close to commercial centres across the border in Queensland, and Queensland's border import tariffs frustrated many in the neighbouring districts, who strongly favoured free trade. The six Australian colonies were then self-governing but remained under the authority of the British Colonial Secretary. Parkes had a personal tie to the town: he had been elected Member for Tenterfield within a few hours of his defeat in East Sydney in 1884.

Parkes spoke of the Federal Council, which had sat in Tasmania without New South Wales. Appointed by the colonial governments and without executive power, it could not, he argued, set up or control an Australian army, yet carrying out the recommendations of General Edwards on military matters required a central authority to bring the colonies' forces into one army. He also called for a uniform railway gauge across the roughly two thousand miles of line from South Australia to Queensland.

Comparing Australia's population of three and a half millions with that of the Americans when they formed the United States, he declared that what the Americans had done by war, Australians could bring about in peace. He proposed a convention of delegates appointed by the colonial parliaments to devise a constitution for a federal parliament of two houses, and closed with lines from The Dominion by the Queensland poet James Brunton Stephens.

The speech was widely published in Australian newspapers. The colonies agreed to send delegates to a conference in Melbourne in 1890, which began the drafting and adoption of the Commonwealth Constitution over the 1890s and led to the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901. Parkes's later efforts earned him the title of Father of Federation. The Governor-General formally commemorated the site in 1946, and in 1999 Bob Carr, Premier of New South Wales, compared the speech's significance to that of Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address.
tenzing-norgay: Accounts of Tenzing's early life conflict. In his autobiography he wrote that he was a Sherpa born and raised at Tengboche in Khumbu, in north-eastern Nepal; many later accounts say he was born in Tibet, in the Kama Valley, and grew up at Thame. He was born Namgyal Wangdi, and his name was changed on the advice of the head lama of Rongbuk Monastery. His exact date of birth is unknown, but the Tibetan calendar year and Hunt's statement that he was 39 in 1953 make 1914 likely. After the ascent of Everest he decided to celebrate his birthday on 29 May.

As a teenager he ran away from home twice, to Kathmandu and then to Darjeeling, where he settled among the Sherpas and eventually acquired Indian citizenship. He once went to Tengboche Monastery to become a monk, but decided that was not for him and left.

At 20 he joined Eric Shipton's 1935 British reconnaissance expedition to Everest, and he went on three official British attempts from the Tibetan side in the 1930s as a high-altitude porter. In 1952 he took part in the two Swiss expeditions, the first serious attempts from the Nepalese side; on 28 May he and Raymond Lambert reached about 8,595 metres on the south-east ridge, a new altitude record.

In 1953 he joined John Hunt's expedition of over 400 people. After Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans turned back from the South Summit on 26 May, Hunt directed Tenzing and Edmund Hillary to go for the summit. They reached the summit at 11:30 on 29 May and stayed about 15 minutes. Journalists asked which of them was first; Hunt answered that they reached it together, as a team, and in his 1955 autobiography Tenzing wrote that Hillary stepped on top first. Hillary and Hunt were knighted, while Tenzing, who was not a British subject, received the George Medal.

In 1954 Tenzing became the first Director of Field Training of the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute in Darjeeling. In 1959 the Government of India awarded him the Padma Bhushan. He died of a cerebral haemorrhage in Darjeeling on 9 May 1986, at the age of 71, and was cremated at the Institute. In 2003 the Indian government renamed its highest adventure sports award after him, and in 2008 Lukla Airport became Tenzing–Hillary Airport.
teodoro-de-croix: Teodoro de Croix was born on 20 June 1730 at Prévoté Castle near Lille, the third son of Alexandre-Maximilien-François de Croix, Marquis of Heuchin, and Isabelle-Claire-Eugène de Houchin. He entered the Spanish army at 17 and went to Italy as an ensign of grenadiers of the Royal Guard. In 1750 he moved to the Walloon Guards, bodyguards of the Bourbon kings of Spain, becoming a lieutenant and a knight of the Teutonic Order in 1756 and a colonel in 1760.

In 1766 he came to New Spain as a captain in the guard of Viceroy Carlos Francisco de Croix, marqués de Croix, and served as commandant of the fortress of Acapulco and inspector of all the viceroyalty's troops until 1770. When the viceroy's term ended in 1771, both men returned to Spain together with the visitador José de Gálvez.

The new Commandancy General joined seven provinces, from the Californias and Sonora y Sinaloa to Coahuila, Nuevo León and Spanish Texas, in answer to attacks by Apaches, Seris, Comanches and others and to fear of other European powers; its seat was to be Arizpe, Sonora. Named by King Charles III on 16 May 1776, Croix replaced Hugo Oconór, took office on 1 January 1777 and set out to inspect the territory that August.

Independent of the viceroy in most of it, he answered directly to José de Gálvez, now minister of the Indies. He took Juan Agustín Morfi as chaplain, who became the leading chronicler of the New Philippines, and he raised the strongest military force the frontier from Texas to Sonora had seen.

Named lieutenant general and viceroy of Peru on 13 February 1783, he handed the frontier command to Felipe de Neve. In Lima he divided the government among seven intendancies, built the anatomical amphitheatre, began the Botanical Garden, strengthened the coastal fortifications and helped create the Junta Superior de Comercio and the Tribunal de Minería in 1786.

He took rigorous measures against the ideas of the Encyclopedists and of the revolutionaries of the United States and France, and he sent the naval officer José de Moraleda y Montero to chart the Chiloé Archipelago. The people of Lima called him el Flamenco, the Fleming. Back in Spain he became a colonel of the king's bodyguard and a commander of the Teutonic Order in 1791, and he died in Madrid the following year.
teofilo-braga: Joaquim Teófilo Fernandes Braga was born in São José, Ponta Delgada, in the Azores, the youngest of seven children, three of whom died in infancy. His mother died when he was three, and his father, a former artillery lieutenant who taught at the local secondary school, married a woman who treated the boy badly. He took refuge in books and at fifteen, in 1859, published a book of verse, Folhas Verdes. He arrived at the University of Coimbra in April 1861 and joined its Faculty of Law, living austerely.

At Coimbra Braga took part, on the edge of the group, in the Coimbra Question of about 1865, a quarrel between the older writer António Feliciano de Castilho and young dissenters including Antero de Quental. His reply to Castilho was As Teocracias Literárias, and he later wrote that the controversy left him shunned by critics and publishers and turned him from poetry to scholarship. In 1872, the year he took his law degree, he won a chair in modern literature in a public competition.

Under the influence of Auguste Comte he became a positivist, writing Traços Gerais de Filosofia Positiva and Sistema de Sociologia. His other works include the História da Literatura Portuguesa, studies of popular poetry and folklore, and the four-volume História da Universidade de Coimbra. Critics accused him of omitting citations, and Sílvio Romero called him the Father of Charlatans. In politics he stood for deputy in 1878 as an independent federalist republican and wrote the História das Ideias Republicanas em Portugal in 1880.

Braga joined the Political Directorate of the Republican Party on 1 January 1910. The revolution began on the morning of 4 October 1910 and lasted until the next day, and he was acclaimed President of the Provisional Government. In May 1915, after Manuel de Arriaga resigned following the dictatorship of General Pimenta de Castro, the assembly elected Braga to the presidency.

A widower who lived austerely, he walked about even as president with an umbrella or cane, and he lost his sight late in life. He asked in his will for a civil burial without ceremony and died on 28 January 1924, aged 80. He was buried in the Jerónimos Monastery in Belém, Lisbon.
tepanecs: The Tepanecs arrived in the Valley of Mexico in the late 12th or early 13th century. They were a sister people of the Mexica and the Acolhua, speaking Nahuatl and sharing the same general pantheon, though some authors suspect partly Otomi or Matlatzinca origins. Their patron god was Ototontecuhtli, also called Cuecuex, a major deity among the Otomi, Matlatzinca and Mazahua as well. Their name comes from their mythical city of origin, Tepanohuayan or Tepano, drawn as a stone, and their lands were called Tepanecapan.

Tradition compiled by several historians counts them among the seven tribes that set out from Chicomoztoc, the Seven Caves, whose location is uncertain. Mid-20th-century opinion placed it at La Quemada; later investigators look north of the Valley of Mexico, towards ancient Tula, or to the hill of Chiconauhtla south of Teotihuacan.

According to tradition the Chichimec ruler Xolotl welcomed them to the valley, and they settled on the west shore of Lake Texcoco, where under their tlatoani Acolnahuacatl they took Azcapotzalco from its earlier inhabitants. Under Tezozomoc they controlled nearly all of the valley and parts of the Toluca and Morelos valleys; native sources say he lived past 100.

After his death his sons Tayatzin and Maxtla came to the throne, and Maxtla most likely poisoned his brother. In 1428 Maxtla was overthrown by the new Triple Alliance of the Mexica of Tenochtitlan, the Acolhua of Texcoco and his fellow Tepanecs of Tlacopan, which became the leading Tepanec city, though smaller and less prestigious than its two partners. When the Spaniard conquistadores arrived, the Tepanecs were subject to the alliance and no longer an independent people; they are known from accounts drawn from the codex traditions and compiled by novohispanic historians.
tepehuan-revolt: The Tepehuán lived on the eastern slopes and valleys of the Sierra Madre Occidental, mostly in what became the state of Durango. They spoke a Uto-Aztecan language and lived chiefly by farming, unlike the nomadic Chichimeca to the east. Spanish settlers arrived from the 1570s to mine silver and raise cattle, and the Jesuits founded missions from 1596 at Santiago Papasquiaro, Santa Catarina de Tepehuanes and later El Zape. Epidemics in 1594, 1601-1602, 1606-1607, 1610 and 1616-1617 may have reduced the Tepehuán and their neighbours from more than 100,000 people to fewer than 20,000.

In 1616 a baptised Tepehuán named Quautlatas began preaching through the mountains under the sign of a broken cross. Calling himself a bishop, he taught that the old gods were angry, that all Spaniards had to be killed or driven out, and that those killed by the Spanish would rise again after seven days. Many Tepehuán linked baptism with the disease and death that followed it; the Jesuits blamed the devil.

On 16 November 1616 the Tepehuán attacked a wagon train outside Santa Catarina de Tepehuanes, and coordinated attacks under six war chiefs, the best known Francisco Gogoxito, followed across the region. About 100 people were killed in the church at El Zape and as many at Santiago Papasquiaro, and only one Jesuit in Tepehuán territory survived the first attacks. Governor Gaspar de Alvear had 75 local Indigenous leaders executed and in December rescued 400 Spaniards and allies. The Spanish abandoned their policy of peace by purchase for a war of fire and blood, and killed Gogoxito, the last war chief, in March 1618.

More than 200 Spaniards, 10 missionaries, an unknown number of their allies and perhaps 4,000 Tepehuán died, many of hunger and disease, and property worth as much as a million pesos was destroyed. The missionaries returned in 1618, though raids went on, and the revolt was declared over in 1620. The region took half a century to recover, and missions were afterwards better protected by soldiers. Three Tepehuán groups survive, in Chihuahua and southern Durango.
tepelene: Tepelenë is a town and municipality in Gjirokastër County in southern Albania. It lies on the left bank of the Vjosa River, on a plateau about three kilometres downstream from the river's union with the Drino. North of the town the Bënça flows into the Vjosa. Its location at the confluence of two valleys has made it an important traffic hub in southern Albania. A ruined citadel stands on a point 300 metres above the river.

The name has been explained in three ways: from the Turkish word Tepedelen, meaning head-piercing; from Tepe e Lenes, the hill of Lenes; or, the version regarded as most convincing, from an Illyrian word Antibylyne, meaning in front of the Bylynes.

The Byzantines built a defensive tower there, which was developed under the Ottoman Empire in the 15th century and again by Ali Pasha in the early 19th century. Tepelenë and Ioannina were Ali Pasha's headquarters. The British writer Edward Lear visited in 1847 and noted devastated buildings. In July 1833 the inhabitants rose in revolt against Emin Pasha, and in February 1909 the Young Turk revolutionaries met there to try to persuade Albanian nationalists to join them.

An earthquake in 1920 severely damaged the town, which was rebuilt completely. Italian forces landed in Albania on 7 April 1939 and took Tepelenë. After the failed Italian invasion of Greece in 1940 the Greek army advanced towards the town but could not take it, and withdrew in late April 1941 after the German invasion of Yugoslavia. After the war the socialist government turned the Italian army camp into a labour camp, where influential Albanian families of earlier governments were held. The camp closed in 1954. In March 1997 a people's committee took charge of the town during the unrest and released the opposition politician Fatos Nano from the local prison.

The municipality was formed in the 2015 local government reform by merging Kurvelesh, Lopës, Qendër Tepelenë and Tepelenë. Until districts were abolished in 2000 the town was the seat of Tepelenë District. The municipality had 8,949 inhabitants at the 2011 census, on an area of 431.50 square kilometres. The National Road 4 from Fier to Gjirokastër runs through it, and a mineral water plant is an important local enterprise.
tepeticpac: The name comes from Nahuatl and means at the top of the hill. The settlement spread over the hills of Cuauhtzi, Tenextepetl, Coyotepetl and El Fuerte, between about 2,350 and 2,540 metres above sea level, in what is now the village of Santiago Tepeticpac in the municipality of Totolac. Deep ravines, walls, ditches, narrow passages and watchtowers up to seven metres tall made it a stronghold and the last refuge of the Tlaxcaltecan lords in an invasion; a ditch more than 350 metres long, the Gran Zanja, blocked the approach from the north. Instead of large pyramids it had open plazas flanked by low platforms on at least 169 terraces, which archaeologists link to Tlaxcallan's collective government.

Excavation shows an earlier Epiclassic occupation of the hills, followed by abandonment, before the Late Postclassic town. Tradition holds that Teochichimec migrants, led by their god Camaxtli, drove out the Olmeca-Xicallancas with bow and arrow, and that their leader Culhuatecuhtli Quanex founded Tepeticpac and gave land to his brother Teyohualminqui, founder of Ocotelolco. Colonial sources disagree on the dates. The principal deity seems to have been Tezcatlipoca, and the warriors fought under a wolf standard. Great questions of war and foreign policy were decided by a council of the lords of the four head towns.

In 1519 Tepeticpac was ruled by Tlehuexolotzin, who joined the other three lords in the alliance with the Spanish forces of Cortés and sent warriors to the conquest of the Aztec Empire. A chapel built on El Fuerte was wrecked by a storm in 1552 and pulled down in 1553. Some years before, around 1545, several Tlaxcaltecan nobles had been executed for idolatry, among them Don Francisco Tecpanécatl, a lord of Tepeticpac. On 9 June 1591 a caravan of 228 people from Tepeticpac left with the Tlaxcaltecan colonists bound for the northern frontier, settling near San Miguel Mexquitic in present-day San Luis Potosí.

The archaeological zone lies about five kilometres north of the city of Tlaxcala. The National Institute of Anthropology and History has excavated, mapped and consolidated it, and a protected core of 98 hectares has been marked out. Among the finds is the skeleton of a gomphothere discovered in 2014.
tequesta: The Tequesta lived in southeastern Florida for roughly 2,000 years, from about the 3rd century BCE. Their lands ran along Biscayne Bay in present-day Miami-Dade County and north through Broward County at least as far as Pompano Beach, and at times took in the Florida Keys. Their main town, which the Spaniards named Tequesta after its chief, stood on the north bank of the Miami River, a site settled for at least 2,000 years. The Glades culture of the region shows a continuous native pottery tradition from about 700 BCE. Most anthropologists now doubt an old idea that the Tequesta were related to the Taino of the Antilles. The linguist Julian Granberry holds that they probably spoke the same language as the Calusa.

The Tequesta did not farm. Most of their food came from the sea: fish, turtles, manatees, sharks and porpoises, with venison and many wild fruits, berries and roots. Hernando de Escalante Fontaneda, who lived among the peoples of southern Florida for seventeen years in the 16th century, wrote that the monk seal was reserved for the upper classes. During the worst of the mosquito season most people of the main village moved to the barrier islands or the Keys. Estimates of their number at first contact range from 800 to 10,000. Spanish accounts describe the bones of chiefs kept as objects of reverence, a belief that each person has three souls, and, in claims resting mainly on one missionary, human sacrifice.

Juan Ponce de León stopped in 1513 at a bay he called Chequesta, apparently Biscayne Bay. In 1565 Pedro Menéndez de Avilés was well received there, and the chief's brother went with him to Spain and converted. The mission Menéndez founded in March 1567, with thirty soldiers and the Jesuit brother Francisco Villareal, suffered when the soldiers executed an uncle of the chief and was abandoned in 1570. From 1704 Spain resettled Florida Native Americans in Cuba, where many soon died; of 280 taken in 1710, almost 200 died. A second mission in 1743 lasted less than three months. When Spain ceded Florida to Britain in 1763 the remaining Tequesta were evacuated to Cuba, and in the 1770s Bernard Romans saw only abandoned villages.
terai: The Terai lies south of the Sivalik Hills and north of the Indo-Gangetic Plain. It is a land of tall grasslands, scrub savannah, sal forest and clay-rich swamps. Nepal's Terai covers about 23.1 per cent of the country's land at an elevation between 67 and 300 metres, and in India the region spreads eastward from the Yamuna across Haryana, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal. Large rivers such as the Ganges, Karnali, Narayani and Kosi have built alluvial fans across it. The name comes from a word meaning low, marshy ground at the foot of a watershed.

The Inner Terai consists of five elongated valleys between the lower Himalayan range and the Sivalik Hills, among them the Dang and Chitwan valleys. They were agriculturally productive but extremely malarial, and under the Rana dynasty some stretches were kept forested by decree as a defensive belt called Char Kose Jhadi.

After the Muslim invasion of northern India in the 14th century, Rajput nobles and their entourage migrated to the Himalayan foothills and gained control from Kashmir to the eastern Terai over the following three centuries. By the 16th century the rulers of Palpa and Makwanpur controlled the mid-western Terai, and by the 17th the eastern Terai too. The Shah dynasty conquered the eastern Nepal Terai in the 1770s, and Bahadur Shah conquered the Tulsipur State in 1785. From at least 1786 the Shah rulers appointed officers there to levy taxes and hunt game; at the end of the 18th century 200 to 300 elephants were caught each year.

After Nepal lost the Anglo-Nepalese War, the British annexed the western Terai when the Sugauli Treaty was ratified. They returned part of it, today's Kanchanpur, Kailali, Banke and Bardiya districts, in 1860, as a reward for Nepal's aid in the Indian Rebellion of 1857. The Indian Terai remained largely uninhabited until the end of the 19th century because of its marshes, jungle and malaria, and heavy logging of its sal forest began in the 1920s.

Malaria was eradicated with DDT in the mid-1950s, after which people from the hills moved onto the plains, and about 16,000 Tibetan refugees settled in the Nepal Terai in 1959 and 1960. The Tharu and Dhimal are its indigenous peoples, and more than 120 ethnic groups and castes live there. The Terai is the most productive region of Nepal, with rice, wheat and sugar cane among its crops. Chitwan National Park was established in 1973, and tea has been grown in Jhapa District since 1960.
teraupoo: Teraupoʻo was born around 1855 at Avera, a village on the east coast of Raiatea in the Leeward Islands of the Society Islands, under the name Hapaitahaa a Etau. He was counted a chief of a minor lineage. A decade before his birth the neighbouring Kingdom of Tahiti had been made a French protectorate in the Franco-Tahitian War, while the Leeward kingdoms, Raiatea-Tahaa among them, had their independence guaranteed by France and Great Britain in the Jarnac Convention of 1847. The French historian Auguste Charles Eugène Caillot wrote that he came to resent the French after a French officer kicked him.

In 1880 King Tahitoe of Raiatea accepted a provisional French protectorate and was deposed by his subjects for it. When King Tamatoa VI ordered submission to the French, Teraupoʻo refused, built up a resistance force in 1887 and set up a government at Avera under Tuarii, a younger daughter of Tahitoe, as queen. France annexed Raiatea and Tahaa on 16 March 1888, after Britain agreed to set the 1847 convention aside. The French held the old capital of Uturoa, but guerrilla warfare kept them out of the countryside. His followers, the Teraupiste, were put at 800 men, though the historian Newbury counted hardly more than 359 under arms.

Teraupoʻo believed that Great Britain would intervene, but the Raiateans appealed in vain to Robert Teesdale Simons, the British consul in Tahiti, and in 1895 the British Resident Frederick Moss refused to meet Queen Tuarii. In 1896 Governor Gustave Gallet brought two warships and two hundred soldiers from New Caledonia. The rebel government and 1700 rebels surrendered by his deadline of 1 January 1897, but Teraupoʻo fought on and hid with his wife and daughter in a cave on Faneuhi mountain until the light of a fire betrayed them on the night of 15–16 February 1897. The six-week campaign cost nearly fifty lives, mostly Raiatean.

The Chamber of Deputies in Paris ratified the annexation on 19 November 1897. The resistance leaders were deported to Nouméa in New Caledonia and their followers to Ua Huka in the Marquesas Islands, while others were put to forced labour on Raiatea's roads. Teraupoʻo, his wife and his brother Hupe, who had served as his general-in-chief, remained in exile until 1905. Allowed to return, he lived as a recluse and died at Vaiaau on 23 December 1918, during the Spanish flu epidemic. The next indigenous leader to call for resistance to French rule was Pouvanaa a Oopa in 1958.
tercan: Tercan, formerly Mama Hatun and, in the Byzantine era, Derzene, is the seat of Tercan District in Erzincan Province in Eastern Anatolia. It lies on the north bank of the Tuzla Su, a tributary of the Euphrates, and had a population of 4,846 in 2021. It is notable above all for the 12th-century complex built by the Saltukid ruler Melike Mama Hatun, which comprises her tomb, a mosque, a hammam and a caravanserai that was heavily restored in recent years.

The main town of the region of Derzene was originally Pekeriç, which Tercan superseded perhaps in the early Ottoman period. In the Middle Ages and the early Ottoman period two routes met at Tercan: one linking Erzurum with Erzincan and Sivas, the other coming from the upper Kelkit basin by the Pekeriç plain. The 17th-century Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi visited in 1647, called the place Mamahatun, wrote about the Saltukid complex and described the town as a Muslim village of two hundred houses.

The caravanserai, just east of the town centre, is a roughly square building around a central courtyard. Two rows of five separate rooms on the north and south sides were for better-off travellers, and long rooms beside them served as stables and sleeping quarters for most guests. The monumental east entrance is flanked by raised recesses where guards were posted, and rooms beside the entrance hall stored merchandise. At the west end are three tall iwans that sit awkwardly in the design and may have been copied from another building, such as a medrese. The building was changed significantly in the early Ottoman period, when the porticos on the courtyard were lost and two rooms at each west end became iwans.

The türbe stands in the middle of a circular courtyard enclosed by a thick wall with a walkway and parapet along its top. The richly decorated entrance portal on the south-west is framed by a muqarnas. Wide arched niches inside the wall were designed to hold tombs of family members, and one has since become a fountain. The windowless main tower has a staircase leading to a burial chamber that lies partly below ground. Other sights nearby include the Kötür bridge, Pekeriç fortress and the Abrenk church.
terceira: Terceira lies 1,181 kilometres due west of Lisbon and covers 396.75 square kilometres. It consists of four overlapping stratovolcanoes built over the Terceira Rift, a triple junction between the Eurasian, African and North American tectonic plates, and rising from more than 1,500 metres of ocean depth. The oldest, the Cinco Picos complex, finished its main activity some 370,000 years ago, and its caldera has largely been refilled to form a fertile plain. The only historical eruptions were in 1761, along a fissure on the Santa Bárbara volcano, and in 1867 and 1998 to 2000 from vents off the west coast.

The island first appears on the Venetian map of Andrea Bianco in 1436 as the Insula de Brasil. It may have been discovered on 1 January 1445 by Vicente de Lagos, pilot of Gonçalo Velho Cabral, and was first called the Island of Jesus Christ before the colloquial Terceira, meaning third, took over. Colonisation began by decree of Henry the Navigator on 21 March 1450, with the Fleming Jácome de Bruges as administrator. After he disappeared in 1474 the island was divided into the captaincies of Angra and Praia. Settlers from Madeira, enslaved people, New Christians and Jews developed wheat, sugar-cane and woad.

In the Portuguese succession crisis of 1580 the Azores were the only part of the Portuguese overseas empire to resist the Spanish, until the summer of 1583. The Azores welcomed the restoration of Portuguese independence under John IV in 1640. In the 1820s constitutionalists on Terceira set up a Junta Provisória in the name of Queen Maria II in 1828, and hostilities broke out at the Battle of Praia da Vitória in 1829. On 15 March 1830 the constitutionalist forces named Angra the Portuguese capital, and in 1832 Pedro I arrived to form a government in opposition to the absolutist regime in Lisbon.

Terceira has a population of 53,311. Its main town, Angra do Heroísmo, is the oldest city of the Azores, the historical capital of the archipelago and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is also the seat of the archipelago's Supreme Court. The island has two main seaports, at Angra do Heroísmo and Praia da Vitória, and the Lajes air base, which Portugal opened to the United States by an agreement signed in 1944. Portuguese bullfighting is popular, including the street version called tourada à corda.
tercio: The tercio served the Spanish Army under the Catholic Monarchs and Habsburg Spain. Its organisation and tactics grew out of the innovations of Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, called El Gran Capitán, during the Granada War (1482–1491) and the Italian Wars, which united the pike with the arquebus. The term at first denoted not a combat unit but an administrative one, commanding garrisons in Italy. The first official tercio, that of Lombardy, was created in 1534, and the tercios of Naples and Sicily followed in 1536.

The origin of the word is doubtful. Some historians link it to a Roman legion of Hispania, or to the threefold division of the Spanish forces in Italy, or to three types of fighters. Others derive it from the three thousand men mustered in the first units.

A tercio was commanded by a maestre de campo appointed by the king. Each originally had ten companies of 300 men, eight of pikemen and two of arquebusiers; the companies were later cut to 250 and the share of gunmen rose steadily. The core were Spanish subjects admired for discipline, but the army was supplemented by troops of many nations: in 1621 only seven of its 47 units were of Spanish origin.

In battle the pikemen formed a hollow square holding swordsmen, with groups of arquebusiers at the corners. Tercios fought at Bicocca in 1522, Pavia in 1525, and Mühlberg in 1547, where they helped Charles V defeat a league of Protestant princes. When pay ran out they could mutiny: in April 1576 unpaid tercios occupied Antwerp and sacked it for three days.

The first real challenge on the open battlefield came at Nieuwpoort in 1600, where Maurice of Orange's shallower linear formations brought more guns to bear. In the Thirty Years' War Gustavus Adolphus defeated tercio-style formations, though the tercios played a decisive part in defeating the Swedish army at Nördlingen in 1634. Their reputation of invincibility in open battle was shattered at Rocroi in 1643. In 1704 the Spanish tercios were turned into regiments and the pikeman was dropped. From 1920 the units of the Spanish Legion bore the name tercio as an honorary title.
terek-river: The Terek rises in the Mtskheta-Mtianeti region of Georgia, near the juncture of the Greater Caucasus range and the Khokh Range, south-west of Mount Kazbek. It winds north in a white torrent between the town of Stepantsminda and the village of Gergeti toward North Ossetia and Vladikavkaz, then turns east through Chechnya and Dagestan. Below Kizlyar it divides into two branches and forms a swampy delta about 100 kilometres wide where it enters the Caspian Sea. The Terek drains most of the north-eastern Caucasus, as its sister river the Kuban drains the north-western Caucasus into the Black Sea.

Its tributaries include the Malka, Ardon, Sunzha and, from the Darial Pass, the Kistinka and Armkhi. The main cities on the river are Vladikavkaz, Mozdok and Kizlyar, and small hydroelectric stations on its upper course provide power as well as irrigation.

In the Georgian Royal Annals the river is called Lomeki, from the Ingush name for its upper reaches, meaning mountain water. The Khazar capital Samandar may have stood on its banks. In 1262 the army of Hulagu, khan of the Ilkhanate, was defeated on the Terek by the army of Berke, khan of the Golden Horde, led by Berke's nephew Nogai Khan, in the Berke-Hulagu war, the first civil war of the Mongol Empire. In 1395 Timur defeated Tokhtamysh on the river.

The Terek Cossack Host, which existed from 1577 to 1832 and again from 1860, had its base in the Terek basin, and during the Russian conquest of the Caucasus it was part of the North Caucasus Line. Leo Tolstoy's novel The Cossacks is set on the river among its Cossacks. In late August 1942 German forces reached the Terek near Mozdok, the furthest extent of their conquests in the Soviet Union, but were unable to advance beyond a small bridgehead toward the Baku oil fields.
terence: Ancient authors say that Terence was born in Carthage and came to Rome as a slave in the household of an otherwise unknown senator, P. Terentius Lucanus, who educated and freed him, after which he took the name Terentius. He is said to have become a member of the Scipionic Circle. This biography derives from the Vita Terenti preserved in the commentary of Aelius Donatus and attributed to Suetonius, and it is often construed as conjecture based on the plays and their production notices. His cognomen Afer, meaning the African, may be the source of the report of African birth, since such names did not necessarily denote origin.

Terence wrote six comedies based on Greek originals by Menander or Apollodorus of Carystus, and all six survive complete. According to the production notices, each was staged by the company of Lucius Ambivius Turpio, with music by a tibicen named Flaccus. Andria was produced in 166 BCE, Heauton timorumenos in 163, Eunuchus and Phormio in 161, and Adelphoe and Hecyra in 160, the last after two abortive productions. Rome had no permanent theatre before 55 BCE, so the plays were staged on temporary wooden stages for audiences of fewer than 2,000.

Unlike Plautus, Terence favoured simple, conversational Latin over visual humour. Five of the six plays centre on a pair of young men in love. In his prologues he abandoned the traditional explanation of the plot and instead answered criticism, aimed at an old and spiteful poet whom Donatus identified as Luscius Lanuvinus.

According to tradition, Terence sailed east around the age of 25 and died either of disease in Greece or in a shipwreck on the return. His plays quickly became school texts, and by the end of the 2nd century BCE he was a literary classic. By the late 4th century CE he was one of four canonical school authors, with Cicero, Sallust and Vergil, and he kept a central place in the European curriculum until the 19th century, influencing William Shakespeare and Molière. The Codex Bembinus, kept in the Vatican library, dates to the 4th or early 5th century.
terengganu-inscription-stone: The stele is 89 cm high and 53 cm wide at the top and weighs 214.8 kg. All four of its faces carry inscriptions in Classical Malay, written from right to left in Jawi, the Arabic script adapted to Malay as Islam spread through Southeast Asia from the 10th or 11th century. It records a proclamation by a ruler of Terengganu called Seri Paduka Tuan, urging his subjects to extend and uphold Islam and giving them 10 basic Sharia laws. It also contains a number of Sanskrit terms, a trace of the region's Hindu past, and alludes to the maritime trade that grew around Kuala Berang during the Islamisation of the area.

Most dots of the Arabic-derived and native Jawi letters cannot be seen. Its spelling already shows features of modern Jawi, such as keeping tāʼ marbūṭah in the Arabic loanword Jumaat and using qāf for glottal stops in closed final syllables. Its letter nya, written with three dots above, is the oldest known example of that Jawi letter.

Villagers found the stone in 1887 on a steep bank of the Tersat river at Kampung Buluh in Hulu Terengganu, and it was later used at the village surau as a step before the prayer hall. In 1902 the nobleman Pengiran Anum Engku Abdul Kadir bin Engku Besar and his tin-prospector friend Syed Husin bin Ghulam Al-Bokhari noticed its inscriptions and had it carried by raft to Kuala Terengganu, where Sultan Zainal Abidin III placed it on Bukit Puteri near the palace.

In July 1922 the Deputy British adviser, Major H.S Peterson, had the Japanese photographer N. Suzuki photograph it for study by C.O. Blagden, who first deciphered it. From 1923 it was lent to the Raffles Museum in Singapore, and in 1960 it moved to the National Museum of Malaysia. Terengganu lobbied for its return from 1979, and in 1991 the Federal Cabinet agreed; it is now in the Terengganu State Museum.

In 2009 a meeting in Barbados of UNESCO's International Advisory Committee placed the stone on the Memory of the World International Register. It was the fourth such recognition for Malaysia, after the Hikayat Hang Tuah, the Sejarah Melayu and the correspondence of Sultan Abdul Hamid.
terentii-shtykov: Terentii Fomich Shtykov was born on 13 March 1907 into a farming family in eastern Belarus. He joined the Soviet Communist Party in Leningrad in 1929 and was active in the Komsomol. In 1938 he became Second Secretary of the Leningrad Regional Committee and the protégé of its First Secretary, Andrei Zhdanov, whose support allowed him to rise quickly. In the Second World War he served as a political commissar on fronts near Leningrad, and as commissar of the Far Eastern Front he helped Marshal Kirill Meretskov accept the Japanese surrender in northern Korea on 19 August 1945.

In January 1946 Shtykov replaced Ivan Chistyakov as the senior Soviet officer in charge of northern Korea. He chose the staff of the Soviet Civil Administration, reported directly to Zhdanov and Joseph Stalin, and backed Kim Il Sung, a support that was decisive in Kim's rise. He headed the Soviet delegation to the Joint Soviet-American Commission, which failed to agree on a unified Korean government. He was the main instigator of the land reform of March 1946, which confiscated land from landowners and Japanese collaborators and gave it to poor and landless peasants without compensation. In December 1946 he and two other Soviet generals fixed the composition of the provisional assembly, and the 1948 constitution was drafted chiefly by Stalin and Shtykov in Moscow.

As ambassador, Shtykov helped Kim persuade a reluctant Stalin to allow an attack on the South, predicting that it would not draw in the West. After the Battle of Inchon reversed the war, he was removed from military affairs on 22 November 1950 and recalled, never to return to Korea.

Demoted to major general on 3 February 1951, he held posts in Kaluga, Novgorod and Primorskiy oblasts, and served as ambassador to Hungary from 1959 until 1960, when his hardline Stalinism clashed with the policies of János Kádár. He died on holiday on 25 October 1964. The historian Andrei Lankov calls him "the actual architect of the North Korean state as it emerged in 1945–50", though official North Korean media credit his policies to Kim.
teresa-countess-of-portugal: Teresa was born around 1080, the illegitimate daughter of King Alfonso VI of León by Jimena Muñoz. In 1093 her father married her to a French nobleman, Henry of Burgundy, a nephew of Queen Constance who was giving the king military help against the Muslims on the Portuguese march. Alfonso VI entrusted the county of Portugal to Teresa and Henry in 1096. After the king's death in 1109 they went on governing the lands south of the Minho as far as the Mondego, and by December 1111 they also governed Zamora.

Henry died in 1112, leaving Teresa to deal with the political and military situation. She took on the government herself, first occupying herself mainly with her southern lands, recently reconquered from the Muslims as far as the Mondego. Pope Paschal II, recognising her defence of Coimbra, called her queen in a bull of 18 June 1116, and she is explicitly called queen in a document of 1117, which leads some to call her the first monarch of Portugal. She fought her half-sister Queen Urraca in 1116 and 1120, and allied herself with Fernando Pérez, Count of Traba, the most powerful Galician nobleman, who had rejected his first wife to marry her openly.

In 1121 Teresa was besieged and captured at Lanhoso. The Treaty of Lanhoso, arranged with help from the archbishops of Santiago de Compostela and Braga, freed her on condition that she hold the County of Portugal as a vassal of the Kingdom of León, though she kept her royal title.

By 1128 the Archbishop of Braga and the main Portuguese nobles were tired of her Galician alliance. They rebelled, and her son Afonso Henriques defeated her troops at the Battle of São Mamede near Guimarães. He sent her, with the Count of Traba and their children, into exile in Galicia, near the Portuguese border, where she died on 11 November 1130. Afonso Henriques succeeded her and eventually led Portugal to full independence as a kingdom. With Fernando Pérez she had two daughters, Teresa and Sancha, and with Henry four children, among them Afonso Henriques, who was born in 1109.
teresa-of-avila: Teresa Sánchez de Cepeda Dávila y Ahumada was born on 28 March 1515, either in Ávila or in Gotarrendura. Her paternal grandfather, Juan Sánchez de Toledo, was a converso, a Jew forced to convert to Christianity or emigrate; the Spanish Inquisition condemned him for allegedly returning to Judaism, but he later assumed a Catholic identity. Her father, Alonso Sánchez de Cepeda, was a successful wool merchant and one of the wealthiest men in Ávila.

Her mother raised her as a dedicated Christian. Fascinated by accounts of the lives of the saints, she ran away at seven with her brother Rodrigo to seek martyrdom in the fight against the Moors, until an uncle brought them home. After first resisting a religious vocation, she entered the Carmelite Convent of the Incarnation in 1534, at the age of 20, to the disappointment of her father.

Teresa wrote her autobiography, The Life of Teresa of Jesus, at Ávila between 1562 and 1565, as a defence of her ecstatic experiences; it was published after her death. The Way of Perfection appeared in 1566 and taught her nuns how to progress through prayer. The Interior Castle, written in 1577 and published in 1588, compares the soul to a castle with seven successive mansions, the innermost holding God, and treats the journey of faith as a passage through them to union with God.

In the autobiography she describes four stages of prayer, using the image of watering a garden: mental prayer and meditation, a prayer of quiet, absorption in God, and an ecstatic state. Commentators note that she wrote from her own experience and did not compose a systematic theology of prayer. Her other writings include poems and 342 surviving letters.

Teresa fell ill on a journey from Burgos to Alba de Tormes and died in 1582, just as Catholic Europe changed from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar and the dates of 5 to 14 October were removed. She died either before midnight on 4 October or early on 15 October, which is her feast day. She was buried at the Convento de la Anunciación in Alba de Tormes. Her body was moved to Ávila in 1585 and returned to Alba de Tormes in 1586, when Pope Sixtus V ordered that it remain there on pain of excommunication.
teresa-teng: Teresa Teng was the only daughter among five children of waishengren parents who had fled to Taiwan after the communist takeover of mainland China in 1949. Her father was a soldier in the Republic of China Armed Forces, and the family lived in military dependents' villages, first in Yunlin and then in Pingtung.
