Her father retired in 1957 and sold cakes to make ends meet. He loved Peking opera and her mother Huangmei opera, and both took her to theatres. At six she began voice lessons through an acquaintance of her father who instructed an Air Force band, and her first mentor introduced her to singing before military audiences, a practice she kept up throughout her life.

Her professional career began in 1967, when she hosted the television programme One Star a Day. At fourteen she left school to focus on music and signed with Yeu Jow Records, releasing albums of dance tunes, Western covers and folk tunes. She sang in nightclubs and set a record at Paris Night in Taipei with 70 consecutive days of 90-minute shows. In Hong Kong she worked with Polydor from 1975, and her album Island Love Songs: Goodbye My Love won the Ten-Star Prize. Her first Cantonese album, in 1980, was the year's best-seller.

She entered the Japanese market in 1973. Her first Japanese single, released on 1 March 1974, sold about 30,000 copies, but her second, Airport, released on 1 July 1974, sold 700,000. In 1979 she was caught entering Japan with a fake Indonesian passport and barred for a year. In 1983 she signed with Taurus Records and released Light Exquisite Feeling, which set twelve Tang and Song poems to music and was her first album of entirely new songs. In Taiwan her songs were also used in the Kuomintang's psychological war against the Chinese Communist Party, and were blasted from speakers on Kinmen Island towards the mainland.

Teng died on 8 May 1995, at the age of 42, while on holiday in Chiang Mai, Thailand. Several sources reported a severe asthma attack, while Thai doctors attributed her death to heart failure. No autopsy was performed, because the families of Teng and of her fiancé Paul Quilery declined it, and the police closed the case for lack of evidence.

She is credited as the first pop superstar of the Far East and a pioneer of modern Chinese popular music. Her songs were recorded in Mandarin, Hokkien, Cantonese, Shanghainese, Japanese, Indonesian, English and Italian. In 2007 she was inducted into the Popular Music Hall of Fame at the Koga Masao Museum of Music in Tokyo, the only non-Japanese person so honoured.
teriitaria-ii: Teriitaria was born around 1790, the eldest child of Tamatoa III, king of Raiatea, and of Tura'iari'i Ehevahine, a daughter of Queen Tehaʻapapa I of Huahine. The Tamatoa line was counted among the highest-ranking chiefly families of the Society Islands, but after Puni of Faanui on Bora Bora conquered Raiatea and Tahaa in 1768, it lived on Huahine. Titles passed through first-born daughters, so her place as eldest daughter gave her special status.

Around 1809 her father married her and her younger sister Teriʻitoʻoterai Teremoemoe to Pōmare II of Tahiti, then in exile on Moorea and in need of allies. He preferred the younger sister, but Teriitaria received the rank of queen and the title Pōmare Vahine. She had no children; her sister bore the future Pōmare III and Pōmare IV.

Teriitaria took the Christian side and led warriors herself in the wars that restored Pōmare II. On 11 November 1815 she stood at the head of the Christian warriors beside Mahine, king of Huahine and Maiao, at the Battle of Te Feipī, which restored Pōmare rule over Tahiti. After Pōmare II died in 1821 she sat on the regency council for the young Pōmare III, heading it from 1823, and in 1826 she signed a commercial treaty with Commodore Thomas ap Catesby Jones of the United States.

She remained regent for Pōmare IV after 1827, but her attempts to monopolise the pearl trade and to fix prices and wages led to her replacement by Tati in April 1828. In February 1832 she helped to put down the Taiarapu rebellion, commanding her warriors with sabre and pistol.

For decades she ruled Huahine from Tahiti. When France seized the Tahitian throne she went with Pōmare IV into exile on Raiatea from 1844 to 1847. On 17 January 1846 Commandant Louis Adolphe Bonard landed 400 soldiers and marines at Fare; at the Battle of Maeva her forces held them off for two days, killing 18 and wounding 43, and the French withdrew.

The people of Huahine later accused her of seizing land, punishing without regard to her own laws and oppressing foreigners, and replaced her with Ari'imate Teurura'i. Her supporters were defeated in a civil war on 18 March 1854, and she was taken to Tahiti. She died at the royal palace in Papeete in 1858.
termez: Old Termez, a few kilometres west of the modern city on the Amu Darya, was founded sometime before the 3rd century BCE, making it one of the oldest towns of Central Asia. Most recent scholarship holds that it is the site of Alexander the Great's Alexandria on the Oxus, though some identify that city with Ai-Khanoum. After Seleucid rule it became part of the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom. Under the Kushan Empire Greek gave way to Bactrian in administration, and Termez, called Ta-li-mi in Chinese sources, became an important centre of Mahāsāṃghika Buddhism. In the 7th century the monk Xuanzang reported about ten monasteries with about a thousand monks.

The Umayyad Caliphate conquered the city in 676. It again became a religious centre under the Abbasid and Samanid empires, and produced the hadith scholar al-Tirmidhi and the Sufi theologian al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi. From the 11th to the 13th centuries it passed through the hands of the Ghaznavid, Seljuk, Karakhanid and Khorezmshah kingdoms. After a two-day siege in 1220 Genghis Khan's troops destroyed it, and one account says that the people were driven onto the plain and killed. Ibn Battuta found a new town, built two miles from the river. It later came under the Timurids and the Emirate of Bukhara, but by the second half of the 18th century it was again abandoned.

A village called Pattakesar stood near the ruins. The Russian Empire stationed a river fleet on the Amu Darya from 1887, and in 1900 the Emirate of Bukhara gave it over 9,000 acres. In 1928, under Soviet rule, Pattakesar was renamed Termez, and it became a town in 1929. During the Soviet–Afghan War of 1979 to 1989 over 100,000 Soviet troops were stationed there, and the Afghanistan–Uzbekistan Friendship Bridge was built. Soviet forces withdrew across it in 1989.

Termez is the capital of Surxondaryo Region in southern Uzbekistan and has about 182,800 inhabitants. The bridge at Hairatan, about 12 km east, is the only border crossing between Uzbekistan and Afghanistan. Its Archaeological Museum, opened in 2002, holds about 27,000 items, many of them Buddhist. Surviving sites include the Zurmala Stupa of the 1st to 2nd centuries, Fayaz Tepe, Kara Tepe and the Sultan Saodat necropolis of the Termez Sayyids, built between the 10th and 17th centuries.
ternopil: Ternopil, known until 1944 mostly as Tarnopol, stands on the banks of the Seret River in western Ukraine and belongs to the historical regions of Galicia and Podolia. Its Polish name, Tarnopol, means Tarnowski's city. The city began as a military stronghold and castle protecting the eastern borders of the Polish kingdom from Tatar raids. On 15 April 1540 King Sigismund I the Old, in Kraków, gave Jan Amor Tarnowski permission to establish it near Sopilche.

In 1570 the city passed to the Ostrogski family and in 1623 to the Zamoyski family. Turkish forces under Ibrahim Shishman Pasha almost completely destroyed it in 1675, during the Polish–Ottoman War, and Aleksander Koniecpolski rebuilt it. After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 it came under Austrian rule; it was under Russian rule from 1809 and returned to Austria in 1815. A railway linked it with Lemberg in 1870, and a Ukrainian gymnasium opened in 1898. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries it was the only urban locality in Galicia where ethnic Ukrainians outnumbered Poles.

It was proclaimed part of the West Ukrainian People's Republic on 11 November 1918 and became its temporary capital after Polish forces captured Lwów. Polish forces took it on 15 July 1919, and in the interwar period it was the capital of the Tarnopol Voivodeship. Soviet troops entered on 17 September 1939, and the city was incorporated into the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. After German occupation began on 2 July 1941, 10,000 Jews were killed in the city by July 1943 and another 6,000 were sent to the Belzec extermination camp. The Soviet offensive of 1944 almost completely destroyed it, and it was rebuilt in a Soviet style.

Ternopil is the administrative centre of Ternopil Oblast and has been part of independent Ukraine since 1991. It is an important railway hub, and its light, food, electronics and construction industries grew under Soviet rule. Its universities include the West Ukrainian National University and the Ternopil Ivan Pul'uj National Technical University.
terp: A terp is also called a wierde, woerd, warf, warft, werf, werve or værft, the names of the different languages and dialects of northern Europe. Such mounds are found on the North European Plain wherever people needed safe ground against storm surges, high tides and floods from sea or river before dykes were built. Besides Friesland, Groningen and Zeeland in the Netherlands, they occur in southern Denmark and north-western Germany, above all in East Frisia and Nordfriesland.

Further examples stand in the Rhine and Meuse plains of the central Netherlands, at Avendorp near Schagen, beneath Den Helder, at Kampereiland at the mouth of the IJssel, on the former island of Schokland, and at Bredene and Leffinge near Oostende in Belgium. On the Halligen islands of Nordfriesland people still live on terps without the protection of dykes.

In Friesland the mound is called a terp, plural terpen, a word that means village in Old Frisian and is related to English thorp, German Dorf and Dutch dorp. Frisian settlements were raised on terpen up to 15 metres high, and the mounds formed a network that redirected large floods. The first period of building dates to 500 BCE and the second to 200–50 BCE. In Groningen, where the mound is called a wierde, the first was also built around 500 BCE or perhaps earlier.

In the mid-3rd century the sea rose so sharply that the clay district was deserted, and settlers returned only around 400. A third period of building began around 700, in Old Frisian times, and ended with the coming of the dike somewhere around 1200.

Over the centuries the rubbish and waste of their inhabitants made the mounds fertile, and in the 18th and 19th centuries many were dug away to spread their soil on farm fields. Some 1,200 terpen are recorded in Groningen and Friesland alone, from abandoned sites and single farms to villages and old towns such as Leeuwarden, Dokkum and Bolsward. Place names ending in -werd or -ward recall a village built on a mound, though most terp villages have names ending in -um, from a word for a farmyard. Names ending in -terp, such as Ureterp, refer only to the Old Frisian word for village.
terqa: Terqa was an ancient city at the site of Tell Ashara on the middle Euphrates in the Deir ez-Zor Governorate of Syria, about 80 km from the modern border with Iraq and 64 km north of Mari. By Neo-Assyrian times its name had become Sirqu. It stood near the mouth of the Khabur, a trade hub on the Euphrates and Khabur rivers, with Mari to the south and Tuttul (Tell Bi'a) to the north. It ruled a larger hinterland, but because the valley could hold only one main political centre it was always second to Mari. Its principal god was Dagan.

Little is known of its early history, though it was already sizable in the Early Dynastic period. In the Early Bronze Age Ebla and Mari competed for hegemony on the Euphrates and Terqa was contested between them; the Akkadian Empire later took control. It was an urban centre with a massive defensive wall, yet a provincial city under Mari. Yahdun-Lim of Mari commemorated building the walls of Mari and Terqa in a year-name, and the city then came under Shamshi-Adad of the Amorite Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia. Zimri-Lim named a year for offering a great throne to Dagan of Terqa, and it was governed for him by Kibri-Dagan.

When Hammurabi of Babylon attacked his former ally Zimri-Lim and destroyed Mari, power in the middle Euphrates shifted to Terqa, which became the leading city of the kingdom of Hana after the decline of Babylon. About the middle of the 15th century BCE it came under the Mitanni kingdom, and the kings Sinia and Qiš-Addu ruled in that time. Later Terqa fell within the sphere of the Kassite dynasty of Babylon and then the Neo-Assyrian Empire; a stele of Tukulti-Ninurta II was found nearby.

Ernst Herzfeld briefly excavated the site in 1910, and François Thureau-Dangin and P. Dhorme worked there for five days in 1923. A team from the International Institute for Mesopotamian Area Studies, led by Giorgio Buccellati and Marilyn Kelly-Buccellati, excavated for ten seasons from 1974 to 1986, and a French team under Olivier Rouault continued until about 2010. Two thirds of the remains lie under the modern town of Ashara, and about half the original site has been eroded by the Euphrates.

The finds include a city wall of three concentric masonry walls, built about 2900, 2800 and 2700 BCE and in use until at least 2000 BCE; a temple of the healing goddess Ninkarrak, with beads of agate, carnelian and lapis lazuli and bronze figurines of dogs, her sacred animals; and the House of Puzurum, which held an archive of contracts from the time of the kingdom of Hana. The Deir ez-Zor Museum keeps 550 cuneiform tablets from Terqa.
terracina: Terracina lies on the coast 56 km (35 mi) southeast of Rome, on the Via Appia, and the site has been occupied continuously since antiquity. It had strategic importance because the Volscian Hills reach the sea there, leaving no space for passage between them and the coast. The site also commands the Pontine Marshes, which Livy called a city surrounded by marshes, and it possessed a small harbour. The ancient sources give two names: the Latin Tarracina and the Volscian Anxur, the latter being the name of Jupiter as a youth, the tutelary god of the city.

Terracina joined the Etruscan League of twelve cities during the 600s BCE, and by 509 BCE it was under Roman supremacy, as the first treaty between Rome and Carthage reports. It was re-occupied by the Volsci, recaptured by the Romans in 406 BCE, lost in 402, recovered in 400 and finally secured by a colony of Roman citizens in 329 BCE. The Via Appia, built in 312 BCE, added to its importance. Under Trajan a cut was made in the rocks of the promontory to carry the road, and the port was built under Trajan and Antoninus Pius. The emperor Galba was born there in 3 BCE.

Terracina is mentioned in the Gothic War, and Theodoric is said to have had a palace there. It was sacked in 409 and 595, and later remained a Byzantine stronghold and became part of the Duchy of Naples. In 872 Pope John VIII brought it under the Holy See. In 1088 it was the seat of the first conclave held outside Rome, and in the 11th and 12th centuries it grew and became a free commune.

Malaria and raids by pirates from North Africa eroded the town in the 16th century. Pope Pius VI later began draining the marshes. The Concordat of 1818 between Pope Pius VII and Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies set its position on the border of the Papal States and the Kingdom of Naples. In 1934 it passed from the province of Rome to that of Latina. It suffered heavy damage in World War II, and afterwards a large new quarter, Borgo Marino, grew along the coast.
terracotta-army: Work on the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang began in 246 BCE, soon after he succeeded his father as King of Qin at the age of 13. The historian Sima Qian (145–90 BCE), writing about a century after the mausoleum was completed, said that the project eventually involved 700,000 conscripted workers. He described a burial with palaces, towers, officials and valuable objects, with the rivers of China simulated in mercury and the heavens on the ceiling. His account does not mention the terracotta figures. High levels of mercury later found in the soil of the tomb mound have lent support to it.

Later accounts say that the complex was looted by Xiang Yu, a contender for the throne after the emperor's death. Fire damage on figures in two of the pits, burnt roof rafters and the missing weapons have been taken as evidence of this looting and of a fire that brought the roof down on the figures.

The figures stand about 1.75 to 2 metres tall, the officers being taller, and differ in uniform and hairstyle according to rank. Scholars have identified ten base face forms, which were developed further so that each face looks different. Heads, arms, legs and torsos were made separately in workshops by government labourers and local craftsmen, then joined. The figures were painted with pigments including cinnabar, malachite and azurite, but the lacquer and colour flake off within minutes of exposure to dry air.

Pit 1, 230 metres long and 62 metres wide, holds the main army of more than 3,000 figures in eleven parallel corridors. Cavalry, infantry and chariots fill Pit 2, and Pit 3 is a command post with high-ranking officers. Perhaps left unfinished, Pit 4 is empty.

The army was found on 29 March 1974 by farmers digging a well about 1.5 kilometres east of the tomb mound: Yang Zhifa, his five brothers and a neighbour, Wang Puzhi. Archaeologists including Zhao Kangmin then investigated the site. Estimates from 2007 put the three main pits' contents at more than 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots with 520 horses, and 150 cavalry horses. The army is part of a necropolis covering about 98 square kilometres. The emperor's tomb itself appears to be a sealed space about 100 by 75 metres and remains unopened.

The naturalism of the figures has prompted debate. The art historian German Hafner suggested in 1986 a link with Hellenistic sculpture, while the site's chief archaeologist Zhang Weixing has said there is no substantial evidence for one. Few earlier figurines are known.
tertullian: Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus was a prolific author of the Roman province of Africa. Little reliable evidence about his life survives, and most of it comes from passing references in his own writings. He was well educated, and wrote at least three books in Koine Greek, none of which survives. Some sources describe him as Berber, and the linguist René Braun suggested a Punic origin. He called himself Poenicum inter Romanos, Punic among Romans. Jerome and Eusebius described him as a lawyer and a priest, but in his surviving writings he never calls himself ordained. His conversion to Christianity perhaps took place about 197 or 198, and he wrote that Christians are made, not born.

Thirty-one of his works survive, together with fragments of more, covering apologetics against paganism and Judaism, polemic, church discipline and morals. His Apologeticus, addressed to the Roman magistrates, defends Christians against pagan reproaches and demands a fair trial for them before they are condemned. In it he wrote that the blood of the Christians is seed. His five books against Marcion, written in 207 or 208, are the most comprehensive of his polemical works and are invaluable for understanding the early Christian view of Gnosticism.

In his treatise against Praxeas he used the words trinity, economy, persons and substance, though he did not state the later doctrine of the immanent Trinity, and his teaching that the Son is subordinate to the Father was later rejected by the Catholic Church. He attacked the use of Greek philosophy in Christian theology, asking what Athens has to do with Jerusalem, and urged Christians to avoid the theatre and the amphitheatre.

Around 207 Tertullian was attracted to the New Prophecy of Montanism. Most scholars today reject the claim that he left the mainstream church or was excommunicated, and the extent of his involvement is disputed. In the time of Augustine a group of Tertullianists still had a basilica in Carthage. Jerome says that Tertullian lived to old age, and Cyprian highly regarded him. Through his doctrinal works he became the teacher of Cyprian and the predecessor of Augustine, and he has been called the father of Latin Christianity. He was never canonised.
teruel: Teruel stands 915 metres above sea level in a remote, mountainous part of Aragon. Its climate is harsh, with wide daily variation in temperature, and its surroundings contain archaeological sites and rock outcrops with some of the oldest dinosaur remains of the Iberian Peninsula. The city is known for its cured ham and its pottery. Its isolation gave rise in 1999 to a campaign group with the slogan Teruel existe, Teruel exists, which pressed for greater recognition and investment in the town and the province.

The area was populated in the time of the Celtiberians, who called it Turboleta, and was later occupied by the Romans. Some authors hold that the site, specifically its Jewish quarter, was called Tirwal, from an Arabic word for tower. On 1 October 1171 King Alfonso II of Aragon captured Tirwal, threatened by the Almohad capture of Valencia and wanting to strengthen the southern border of his kingdom. That year he founded Teruel and granted it fueros and privileges to encourage settlement. A legend tells that the town's wise men found a favourable omen in a bull on a high place beneath a star, which explains the bull and star on the city's arms.

Teruel took part in the conquest of Valencia and in the War of the Two Peters against Castile, and in 1347 Pedro IV of Aragon granted it the title of city for its support at the Battle of Épila. Its Jewish and Mudéjar communities became important in the city's economic life. Many members of the Jewish community were killed in the persecutions of 1391, and others accepted Christianity to save their lives.

In the Spanish Civil War much of the city was destroyed. The Battle of Teruel, from December 1937 to February 1938, was one of the bloodiest of the war. The town changed hands several times, first falling to the Republicans and then being retaken by the Nationalists, after heavy artillery and aerial bombardment. The two sides suffered up to 140,000 casualties between them, and the Nationalists won a decisive victory.

Teruel is regarded as the town of Mudéjar because of its many buildings in that style, all part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Mudéjar Architecture of Aragon. Four churches belong to it, notably the cathedral. Other landmarks include the Torre de El Salvador, the Torre de San Martín, and El Torico, a small bull on a tall column in the main square. The church of San Pedro holds the mausoleum of Isabel de Segura and Diego de Marcilla, whose tragic love has inspired writers and an opera.
tervel: Tervel is first mentioned in Byzantine sources in 704, when the deposed and exiled emperor Justinian II approached him. Justinian secured his support for a restoration in exchange for friendship, gifts and his daughter in marriage. With 15,000 horsemen provided by Tervel, Justinian entered Constantinople in 705 and executed the emperors Leontius and Tiberius III. Tervel received gifts, the title of kaisar, which made him second only to the emperor and the first foreign ruler to hold it, and a concession in northeastern Thrace called Zagora. Whether Justinian's daughter Anastasia was in fact married to Tervel is unknown.

Three years later Justinian broke the arrangement and moved to recover the area, but Tervel routed the Byzantines at the Battle of Anchialus in 708. In 711 Justinian asked again for help and received only 3,000 men; he was captured and executed, and Tervel raided Thrace in 712, plundering as far as the neighbourhood of Constantinople.

When the Arabs under Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik besieged Constantinople in 717, the new emperor Leo III the Isaurian appealed to Tervel on the strength of a treaty of 716. The Bulgars attacked the Arab rear and, in the early summer of 718, defeated them in battle; Theophanes the Confessor says they killed some 22,000. Shortly afterwards the Arabs raised the siege.

The Nominalia of the Bulgarian khans places Tervel in the Dulo clan and gives him a reign of 21 years. Most researchers think the Madara Rider relief was made in his time to commemorate victories over the Byzantines and to honour Asparukh. A later cult of a St Trivelius rests on Paisius of Hilendar's History of 1762, which identified him with a monk shown in an engraving of 1741; the engraving in fact depicted Stefan Dragutin of Serbia as Saint Theoctistus. Tervel Peak on Livingston Island in Antarctica is named after him.
tervuren: Tervuren is a municipality in the province of Flemish Brabant, in Flanders, made up of the villages of Duisburg, Tervuren proper, Vossem and Moorsel. Its official language is Dutch, and the presence of expatriate workers in and around Brussels has given it many foreign residents. It adjoins the Brussels-Capital Region at the Sonian Forest and is linked to Brussels by the processional avenue Tervurenlaan, which Leopold II had built for the Universal Exhibition of 1897. It runs through the forest and the neighbourhoods of Woluwe-Saint-Pierre as far as Cinquantenaire Park, and a tramline runs alongside it.

For centuries people took Tervuren to be the Fura where Saint Hubert died in 727, but there is no historical proof, and recent scholarship places Fura in Voeren. A document of 1213 proves the presence of Henry I, Duke of Brabant, possibly in a wooden fortification, which grew into Tervuren castle, the residence of the dukes of Brabant in the 14th and 15th centuries.

The castle was demolished in 1782 under Joseph II, who also demolished the Chateau Charles, the short-lived summer retreat of Charles of Lorraine. After 1815 the park was granted to William, the prince of Orange and son of the King of the United Netherlands, who built the Pavilion of Tervuren, which burned down in 1879.

Tervuren is the home of the Royal Museum for Central Africa, which has called itself the AfricaMuseum since 2018. Tram 44, between Brussels and the museum, exists because Leopold II wanted to bring visitors from around the world to his 1897 exhibition of the Congo Free State.

The museum is an ethnographical and natural history museum that focuses on the Congo, a former Belgian colony, and it was originally intended as a colonial museum; from 1960 it has concentrated more on ethnography and anthropology. It stands among gardens and a park with lakes, and St Hubert Chapel is at the west end of the park. The British School of Brussels has been in Tervuren since 1970.
teshub: Teshub was one of the oldest Hurrian deities and is considered a pan-Hurrian god, worshipped wherever Hurrians lived, from south-eastern Anatolia to the Zagros Mountains. He is first attested in Hurrian personal names of the Ur III period, the oldest being Teššop-šelag from the seventh year of Shu-Sin's reign, and probably in an inscription of Tish-atal of Urkesh. His high standing reflects the importance of weather gods in northern Mesopotamia and nearby areas, where, unlike in the south, farming relied on rainfall rather than irrigation. In Hurrian religion Teshub was king of the gods, with authority over mortals and gods on earth and in heaven, though not over the sea or the underworld.

As a weather god he was both destructive and protective. Winds, lightning, thunder and rain were his weapons, and he sent the rain that made vegetation grow and created rivers and springs. Depictions are rare. He was typically shown as an armed, bearded figure, sometimes holding a bundle of lightning, as at Yazılıkaya, and he was believed to ride in a chariot drawn by two bulls.

According to the Song of Emergence, Teshub was born from the split skull of Kumarbi, after Kumarbi bit off the genitals of Anu in a battle over kingship in heaven. His wife was Ḫepat, originally a goddess of Aleppo, and their children were Šarruma, Allanzu and Kunzišalli. Teshub was equated with the Mesopotamian Adad and the Ugaritic Baal and influenced the Hittite Tarḫunna and the Luwian Tarḫunz, though all of these were also worshipped separately.

His main cult centre was Kumme, a city not yet securely located, probably east of the Tigris in the valley of the Eastern Khabur. His other great sanctuary was Arrapha, near modern Kirkuk. In the kingdom of Mitanni he was worshipped at Kaḫat, and King Tushratta called him his lord in letters to the Egyptian pharaohs Amenhotep III and Amenhotep IV. At Aleppo, under growing Hurrian influence in the fifteenth and fourteenth centuries BCE, he was placed over the older god Adad, and in the second half of the second millennium BCE he was the deity most often named in Hurrian personal names, as in texts from Nuzi.

He was worshipped at Ugarit in the thirteenth century BCE, where Hurrian and local deities appear together in offering lists. The Hittites worshipped him, probably from the time of Šuppiluliuma I, and in southern Anatolia he came to head many local pantheons. His myths include the Kumarbi Cycle, which tells of his rise to kingship and the challenges he faced from Kumarbi, and the Song of Release, known from bilingual Hurrian and Hittite editions made about 1400 BCE.
tetela-people: The peoples of the Kasai Basin up to Maniema understood themselves as descendants of AnKutshu Membele, and many accepted the label Tetela, imposed in colonial times, only in the 20th century. Batetela did not exist as a clan or tribe: it first appears in journals and books between 1885 and 1887, apparently from Watetera, the name for bilingual communities of the Barua lands in Maniema whom Arab slave traders called Utotera. Emil Torday, who studied the peoples of the Congo in 1908 and 1909, was told by a group bearing the Luba title Sungu that the Arabs had given them the name, and he found it not in general use.

In 1869-70 Watetera groups came into contact with Tippu Tip, a slave trader from Zanzibar, and the chieftain Gongo Lutete began working with him and the Arabs, leading slave raids on the left bank of the Lomami River. In the Congo Arab war of 1892-1894 the Watetera went over to the Belgians. The Belgians executed Gongo Lutete in 1893, which has been reported as the cause of the first of the Batetela Rebellions in 1895; uprisings went on until 1908.

Patrice Lumumba, the first Prime Minister of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, assassinated in 1961, was a Tetela. The researcher Ludo De Witte suggested that the scattering of the Batetela across several provinces helped shape the nationalism of figures such as Lumumba. In 1975 many Batetela were purged from the military.

Today the Batetela live between Lusambo and the Upper Congo River, in the provinces of Sankuru and Maniema, by hunting and gathering, fishing and farming cassava, bananas and kola nuts; many count as subgroups of the larger Mongo group. Most speak the Tetela language; the Methodist Episcopal Church South founded a mission at Wembo-Nyama in 1910, and from 1914 Daniel and Edith Mumpower recorded the Otetela language. They have a large set of proverbs and use three drums: the ngomo for dancing, the six-toned lukumbi slit drum, used for poetry and messages, and the small ekuli, once a signal of victory.
tetouan: Tétouan lies in the Martil Valley on the northern slope of a fertile valley, a few miles south of the Strait of Gibraltar and about 60 kilometres east-south-east of Tangier. It is one of the two major Moroccan ports on the Mediterranean, with its harbour at Martil, at the river's mouth. Mountains rise to the south and west, and the city sits in a belt of orchards growing oranges, almonds and pomegranates. A few miles outside it lies the ancient town of Tamuda, where Mauretanian settlements date to the 3rd century BCE and Phoenician and Roman artefacts have been found.

The Marinids built a casbah and mosque at Tétouan in the late 13th century, and in 1305 the sultan Abu Thabit Amir expanded and fortified the settlement as a base for attacks on Ceuta. The Castilians destroyed it in retaliation for piracy, and in 1436 the Portuguese commander of Ceuta sent a raiding party against it while it was recovering. The modern city dates from the late 15th century, when Ali al-Mandri, who had emigrated from Granada, rebuilt and fortified it. Muslim and Jewish refugees from Andalusia settled in northern Morocco, and Tétouan became a major centre of Andalusian civilisation. It is nicknamed the Daughter of Granada, and many families still keep keys to their old homes there.

From the 1530s Tétouan became one of the main centres of piracy in the western Mediterranean. In the 17th century the wealthy al-Naksis family governed it, until the Alaouite sultan Moulay Ismail took it at the end of the century. Spain took the city on 4 February 1860 under General Leopoldo O'Donnell, later made Duke of Tetuán, and evacuated it in May 1862. In 1913 it became the capital of the Spanish protectorate, governed by a Khalifa and a Spanish high commissioner, and remained so until 1956. The Spanish built new districts, the Ensanche, around a large circular plaza. During the protectorate Tétouan became a centre of Moroccan publishing and of the nationalist movement led by Abdelkhalek Torres, Abdessalam Bennuna and Mohammed Daoud.

The medina of Tétouan has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997, and since 2017 the city has belonged to the UNESCO Creative Cities Network for crafts and folk art. Its architecture is largely Andalusian, with carved and painted ceilings, tilework and houses with fountains. The city has seven gates and many Sufi zawiyas. A Sephardic Jewish community that spoke the Judaeo-Spanish known as Haketia once lived there. Most residents speak Arabic, and Spanish and French are also widely used.
tetrapolitan-confession: The confession is also called the Strasbourg Confession or Swabian Confession, and its Latin name, Confessio Tetrapolitana, means confession of the four cities. Martin Bucer and Wolfgang Capito were called to the Diet of Augsburg by the envoys of Strasbourg, who knew that Philipp Melanchthon was preparing a Saxon confession setting out the Lutheran position. It was handed to the Emperor Charles V on 9 July 1530.

Since 1524 the north German Lutherans and the south Germans and Swiss had disagreed over the Lord's Supper: the Lutherans held to sacramental union, the physical presence of Christ's body, the Zwinglians to memorialism, the sacrament as a spiritual memorial. The quarrel had peaked at the Marburg Colloquy between Zwingli and Luther in 1529. The confession was meant to prevent a schism within Protestantism.

The text rests on an early draft of the Augsburg Confession, which Bucer and Capito had secretly obtained, revised in a Zwinglian direction. Its 23 chapters open with the rule that nothing should be taught but what Scripture explicitly states, a statement absent from the Augsburg Confession. The first version held, probably in Capito's words, that Christ truly gives his body and blood in the Supper, but especially to the spirit, through faith. Even this offended the Lutherans, and at the insistence of the Strasbourg envoys Jakob Sturm and Matthis Pfarrer it was softened further.

For political reasons the confession was set aside in practice within a year, when the four cities joined the Schmalkaldic League, and in 1536 the theologians of Strasbourg signed the Wittenberg Concord, which brought the Lutheran and Reformed churches into line. It nonetheless remained Strasbourg's formal confession until 1598. Girolamo Zanchi and Conrad Hubert appealed to it, though after the 1560s it was seen as little more than a general statement of Protestant belief. It is the oldest confession of the Reformed tradition written in Germany, and Bucer himself stayed true to it, reciting it even on his deathbed.
tetrarchy: The first phase, sometimes called the diarchy, began when Diocletian made the general Maximian caesar in 285 and promoted him to augustus in 286. Diocletian took care of the east and Maximian of the west. In 293, thinking that civic and military problems needed more attention, Diocletian expanded the imperial college with Maximian's consent by appointing two caesares, one responsible to each augustus: Galerius and Constantius I.

The word tetrarchy, from the Greek for leadership of four people, was never applied in antiquity to Diocletian's college. It described independent portions of a kingdom, such as the tetrarchy of Judaea after the death of Herod the Great. Diocletian's arrangement was a college led by one supreme leader. The term entered scholarship in 1887 and became current only after Otto Seeck used it in 1897.

Diocletian and Maximian abdicated on 1 May 305, and Galerius and Constantius became augusti, with Valerius Severus and Maximinus Daza as new caesares. The system broke down quickly. When Constantius died in 306, his army proclaimed his son Constantine augustus. Maxentius, the son of Maximian, rebelled and defeated Severus, who was murdered in 307, and Maxentius and Maximian both declared themselves augusti. A conference at Carnuntum in 308 made Licinius augustus in the west, but Constantine and Maximinus refused to accept a superior, and both were recognised as augusti in 309.

Constantine forced Maximian's suicide in 310. Galerius died naturally in 311, Maxentius was defeated by Constantine at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312 and killed, and Maximinus killed himself at Tarsus in 313. Two rulers remained until Constantine defeated Licinius in 324 and became sole augustus. The fourfold division survived in the praetorian prefectures, and the idea of sharing imperial power recurred repeatedly.

The four tetrarchs based themselves in cities closer to the frontiers rather than in Rome, which stayed the nominal capital. Nicomedia was the capital of Diocletian, Sirmium of Galerius, Mediolanum (Milan) of Maximian and Augusta Treverorum (Trier) of Constantius. There was no precise regional division, and the Roman state was never split into four sub-empires. Each emperor was often in the field, delegating most administration to a praetorian prefect.

The public image of the four was carefully managed to suggest a united empire, and official portraits and coins show them with identical features. The system was meant to solve the problem of the third century, when an emperor could command on only one front. Under it Galerius crushed the Persian king Narseh in 298 and gained a treaty that kept peace for a generation, and Constantius defeated the British usurper Allectus.
tetricus-i: Gaius Pius Esuvius Tetricus was born in Gaul, on an unknown date, to a noble family of Gallic origin. By 271 he was a senator and governor of Gallia Aquitania. The Gallic Empire had broken away from Rome in the Crisis of the Third Century. In early 271 its emperor Victorinus was murdered by an officer, Attitianus, allegedly because he had seduced the officer's wife. According to the historian John F. Drinkwater, Victorinus's mother Victoria, who could not take the throne herself as a woman, chose Tetricus and secured the army's support with large bribes. The army proclaimed him emperor in spring 271 at Burdigala, now Bordeaux, though he was not present.

Tetricus was recognised by all of Gaul except Gallia Narbonensis, and by Britannia, but not by Hispania. In late 271 he moved the capital from Colonia to Augusta Treverorum, now Trier, to guard against Germanic raiders. He fought them with some success and held a triumph, but later withdrew troops and abandoned forts, and one raid reached the Loire. While Aurelian was occupied with the Palmyrene Empire, Tetricus recovered Gallia Narbonensis, and he put down a revolt by Faustinus. He made his son Tetricus II caesar in 273. Roman writers cast him as a civilian unfit for an emergency, but Drinkwater argues this may reflect Aurelian's propaganda and that Tetricus proved an able commander against the Germans.

Aurelian marched into northern Gaul in early 274, and the armies met in February or March at the Battle of Châlons. Tetricus was captured, his army was defeated and the Gallic Empire rejoined the Roman Empire. Several Roman writers say that he had already agreed to surrender, quoting Virgil's words "pluck me out, O undefeated one, from these troubles"; modern historians regard this as imperial propaganda, which suited Aurelian because it made Tetricus a traitor to his own army.

Tetricus and his son were paraded in Aurelian's triumph at Rome wearing Gallic trousers rather than chains, and were pardoned. Tetricus became a senator and governor, of Lucania and Bruttium or of all Italy, as the sources disagree. He died of natural causes in Italy several years later.
tetum-language: In the fifteenth century, before the Portuguese arrived, Tetun spread through central and eastern Timor as a contact language under the Belunese-speaking Kingdom of Wehali, then the most powerful kingdom on the island. The Portuguese, present from about 1556, settled mostly in the west, and only in 1769, when the capital moved from Lifau to Dili, did they begin to promote Tetun as an inter-regional language. Timor was one of the few Portuguese colonies where a local language, not a form of Portuguese, became the lingua franca, because Portuguese rule was indirect, exercised through local kings who embraced Catholicism and became vassals of the King of Portugal.

After the Carnation Revolution in Portugal in 1974, Indonesia invaded East Timor and banned Portuguese, making Indonesian the sole official language. The Roman Catholic Church adopted Tetun as its liturgical language, making it a focus of cultural and national identity. When the United Nations Transitional Administration in East Timor took over in 1999, Tetun Dili was proclaimed the official language, and on independence in 2002 Tetun and Portuguese were both declared official.

Tetun is an Austronesian language, spoken in Timor-Leste and in Belu Regency and Malaka Regency in Indonesian West Timor. The linguist Geoffrey Hull distinguishes four dialects: Tetun Dili or Tetun Prasa, spoken in the capital and its surroundings; Tetun Terik, spoken on the south and southwestern coasts; Tetun Belu, spoken in a central strip of the island and split between Timor-Leste and West Timor, where it has no official status; and Nana'ek, spoken in the village of Metinaro.

Tetun Dili developed during colonial rule, with simpler grammar than other varieties and a heavily Portuguese vocabulary. Ethnologue and some researchers classify it as a Tetun-based creole, a position that is disputed. Without previous contact it is not immediately mutually intelligible with Tetun Terik.

Native words include liafuan, word, from lia, voice, and fuan, fruit, and Timór Lorosa'e, Timor of the rising sun, from loro, sun, and sa'e, to rise. Many words come from Portuguese, such as eskola, school, governu, government, and obrigadu, thanks, and others from Malay, such as uma, house, from rumah. Hybrid words add the Portuguese suffix -dór to a Tetun verb: han, to eat, gives handór, a glutton.

Plurals are not normally marked on nouns, and the word sira, they, can express them. Like other Austronesian languages, Tetun has two forms of we: ami, which excludes the person addressed, and ita, which includes them. Nouns of agents are formed with the suffix -na'in, so that hakerek, to write, gives hakerek-na'in, writer.
teucer: In Greek mythology Teucer was the son of King Telamon of Salamis Island and his second wife Hesione, daughter of King Laomedon of Troy. Through his mother he was the nephew of King Priam and the cousin of Hector and Paris, all of whom he fought against in the Trojan War, alongside his half-brother Ajax the Great.

At Troy Teucer shot his arrows from behind Ajax's giant shield. When Hector was driving the Achaeans back towards their ships, Teucer killed many of the charging Trojans, among them Hector's charioteer Archeptolemus, son of Iphitos, but Apollo foiled every shot he aimed at Hector himself. Hector wounded him with a huge rock, and after Zeus broke his bow he fought on with a spear. He was one of those who entered the Trojan Horse, and in all he killed thirty Trojans and wounded Glaucus, son of Hippolochus.

After Ajax's suicide Teucer guarded the body to make sure it was buried, insulting Menelaus and Agamemnon when they tried to stop the burial, until Odysseus persuaded Agamemnon to allow it. Tried before his father, he was found guilty of negligence for bringing back neither his half-brother's body nor his arms, and was disowned. He then joined King Belus of Tyre in a campaign against Cyprus, received the island as his reward, founded Salamis there and married Eune, daughter of King Cinyras, who bore him a daughter, Asteria.

The Roman poet Horace gave Teucer's parting words to his companions in the seventh ode of his first book of Odes: "nil desperandum", do not despair. The Lindos Chronicle records that he dedicated a quiver and a bow at the temple of Athena at Lindos. Local legends of Pontevedra in Galicia make him the city's founder, and it is sometimes called the City of Teucer; some versions say he drowned trying to reach a sea nymph called Leucoina. His name is believed to be related to that of the Hittite storm god Tarku.
teuku-umar: Umar joined the Acehnese guerrilla forces in 1873, at the age of 19. He first fought around Meulaboh and later extended his operations to other parts of West Aceh. At about the age of 20 he married Nyak Sofia, and not long afterwards he took Nyak Malighai as a second wife. In 1880 he married his cousin Cut Nyak Dhien, who later joined him in the guerrilla campaign.

After a peace agreement between the Dutch colonial government and the Acehnese fighters, Umar entered Dutch service as an undercover operative, over Cut Nyak Dhien's objections, and rose through the ranks of the colonial army. When fighting resumed he worked against the Acehnese struggle. On 1 January 1894 the Dutch rewarded him with the title Johan Pahlawan and command of a legion of 250 fully armed soldiers, later adding 120 more troops and 17 lieutenants.

On 30 March 1896 Umar and his men deserted, taking with them 800 weapons, 25,000 bullets, 500 kilograms of ammunition and 18,000 dollars. Joined by 400 soldiers under Teuku Panglima Polem Muhammad Daud, they attacked the Dutch forces, killing 25 and wounding 190. The Dutch governor responded by sending troops in large numbers to capture or kill him, and on 11 February 1899 he died in a surprise attack by Dutch troops at Meulaboh. He was buried in the Mugo area, and Cut Nyak Dhien went on leading the guerrillas after his death.

In the 1930s Sukarno named Teuku Umar as one of the pahlawan tiga-sekawan, the three heroic friends, together with Diponegoro and Imam Bonjol. Umar has since been officially designated a National Hero of Indonesia. Many streets across the country carry his name, among them a main thoroughfare in the Menteng suburb of Jakarta, and a field in Meulaboh is also named after him.
teungku-chik-di-tiro: He was born in 1836 in Tiro, in Pedir in the Aceh Sultanate, to Tengku Syekh Abdullah and Siti Aisyah. He studied with his father until he was 15, then with his uncle Teungku Chik Dayah Cut di Tiro and several other teachers, and spent two years in Aceh Besar, studying Islam by day and joining friends in the fight against the Dutch by night. Called home to teach with his uncle, he later went on the hajj to Mecca, where talks with Islamic leaders and revolutionaries from Sumatra, Java and Borneo deepened his resolve to fight the Dutch.

In 1880 a band of guerrillas passing through Tiro sought an ulama to lead them, and di Tiro joined them at their base on Mount Miram. He travelled across Aceh preaching holy war in the mosques and wrote to other ulama, determined to drive the Dutch out by 1883. With some 6,000 fighters and the support of the Sultan of Aceh, his forces cut communications between Dutch forts and set up a base at Mureu.

In May 1881 they took the Dutch fortress at Indrapuri, then those at Krueng Jreu and Gle Kameng, and the Dutch reinforced Lambaro, Aneuk Galong and Samahani. In early 1883 his men attacked Kutaraja, now Banda Aceh, failing to take it but killing the Dutch controller; at the height of the war the Dutch held only 4 square kilometres.

In 1884, when the sultan was told that di Tiro had become the people's leader, the sultan declared that he was still sultan, and in August di Tiro stated that he had no wish to take the throne. In 1885 he offered the Assistant Resident Van Langen peace if the Dutch converted to Islam, and he wrote again in 1888 without reply.

On 21 January 1891 he was served poisoned food by the son of the leader of Sagi, to whom the Dutch had offered a leadership post for killing him, and he died soon after being taken to the Aneuk Galong fortress for treatment. He was buried in the family graveyard at Meureu in Aceh Besar. Teuku Umar, Cut Nyak Dhien, Cut Nyak Meutia and his own family carried on the struggle. President Suharto declared him a National Hero of Indonesia on 6 November 1973, and streets bear his name, among them one in Menteng in Jakarta. He was the great-grandfather of Hasan di Tiro, founder of the Free Aceh Movement.
teuta: Her name is attested in Greek and Latin as Teuta, a form of the Illyrian *Teuta(na), "queen", literally "mistress of the people". After the death of her husband Agron, king of the Ardiaei, in 231 BCE she acted as regent for her stepson Pinnes. The kingdom stretched along the Adriatic coast from central Albania to the Neretva river and probably controlled most of the Illyrian interior. The ancient sources, written by Greeks and Romans who were generally hostile to the Illyrians, bias what is known of her.

According to Polybius, Teuta told her commanders to treat all neighbouring states as enemies and supported the piratical raids of her subjects. In 231 BCE her armies attacked Elis and Messenia and then captured the Epirote city of Phoenice, which was soon freed against a fee and freeborn prisoners. Illyrian pirates looted so many Italian merchant ships that the Roman Senate sent ambassadors to Scodra. Polybius says Teuta told them piracy was a traditional custom she could not end, and that one envoy answered insolently and was murdered on the voyage home, allegedly on her order. In Appian's account two envoys were killed by Illyrian lemboi while Agron was still alive, so the interview may not have taken place.

In 229 BCE Rome declared war and for the first time sent armies across the Adriatic, about 20,000 troops and 200 ships under Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus and Lucius Postumius Albinus. Her governor Demetrius surrendered Corcyra to them, and the Romans besieged Scodra while Teuta withdrew to Rhizon. Polybius reports that in early spring 228 BCE she agreed to pay an annual tribute, to rule only north of Lissus, now Lezhë, and not to sail beyond it with more than two unarmed ships. According to Cassius Dio she abdicated in 227 BCE.

Appian says that after the defeat Teuta sent an embassy to Rome to return captives and to apologise for what happened under Agron, not under her. Marjeta Šašel Kos considers Appian's the most objective portrait, and Peter Derow finds his story of the murder of the envoys more plausible than that of Polybius, whose narrative was written almost a century later and probably rests on Fabius Pictor. A legend rooted in Risan holds that she ended her life in grief by throwing herself from the Orjen mountains at Lipci. Teuta is a common given name among Albanian women, and the club Teuta Durrës was named after her in 1930.
teutberga: Teutberga, also spelled Theutberga, belonged to the Bosonid dynasty, a family of great influence in Frankish politics. She was the daughter of Boso the Elder, Count of Turin and Valois, and of Engeltrude. Her brother Hucbert was Count of Valois and lay abbot of Saint Maurice's Abbey. Her marriage to Lothair II, a great-grandson of Charlemagne, was probably arranged to bind the noble houses more closely to the royal Carolingian line.

The marriage was politically useful but strained. Lothair had a long relationship with his concubine Waldrada, with whom he had children, and by 857 he was seeking to annul his marriage, charging Teutberga with misconduct that included incest and abortion. Most scholars regard the accusations as politically motivated. Her brother Hucbert opposed Lothair and led an armed revolt in her support, and in 858 she underwent an ordeal by boiling water to prove her innocence, which she survived.

Several synods tried to dissolve the marriage, but the Church's opposition grew. In 863 Pope Nicholas I declared the annulment invalid and ordered Lothair to restore Teutberga as queen. Lothair complied for a time but went on seeking an annulment until his death. The struggle made her the central figure in one of the most politically charged marriage disputes of the 9th century.

After Lothair died, Teutberga retired to a monastery, where she died in 875. Her case became a precedent in debates on royal marriage and papal intervention. Her resistance helped to affirm the Church's authority over marriage law in the Carolingian Empire, influenced church teaching on the indissolubility of marriage and showed how politically vulnerable queens were in the early medieval period.
teutoburg-forest: The Teutoburg Forest is a long, narrow range of low forested hills of three ridges, in the German states of Lower Saxony and North Rhine-Westphalia. It forms the northern edge of the German Central Uplands and extends from the eastern surroundings of Paderborn in the south to the western surroundings of Osnabrück in the north-west. South of Bielefeld a gap called the Bielefeld Pass divides it into the Northern Teutoburg Forest, two thirds of the range, and the Southern Teutoburg Forest, one third.

The oldest ridge, in the north-east, is Triassic limestone. Deciduous forest covers most of the ridges, and cereals are grown in parts of the valleys. The highest points are the Velmerstot (468 m) in the south and the Dörenberg (331 m) in the north. The river Ems rises at the western base of the southernmost part, and the range divides the Ems basin from the Weser basin. A hiking trail, the Hermannsweg, runs 156 km along it from Rheine to Leopoldstal.

Until the 17th century the hill ridge was officially called the Osning. It was first renamed the Teutoburg Forest in 1616, by the historian and geographer Philipp Clüver, in memory of the battle of 9 CE, and the name became common after Ferdinand of Fürstenberg used it in his history and had it printed on maps. The Roman historian Tacitus named the battle's location as the saltus Teutoburgiensis, a forest valley. Its exact site is disputed, and recent excavations suggest that at least the final stages took place further north-west, at Kalkriese, north of Osnabrück.

After the Napoleonic wars, in a period of national renaissance, German people came to see Arminius, also called Hermann the Cherusker, as an early figure of resistance to foreign rule and a symbol of national unity. The monumental statue known as the Hermannsdenkmal was raised on the hill of Grotenburg near Detmold, close to where the most popular theory of the time placed the battle. Emperor William I dedicated it in 1875. The old name Osning survived among local people, and the part of the ridge around the Ebberg near Bielefeld is still called by it.

Apart from a short area south of Osnabrück, the whole range lies in North Rhine-Westphalia. It is made up of two nature parks, the TERRA.vita Nature Park in the north-west and the Teutoburg Forest / Egge Hills Nature Park between Bielefeld and the river Diemel. Fighting took place in the forest at the very end of the Second World War. The composer Johannes Brahms liked to walk there while he stayed in Detmold.
teutones: The name Teutones derives from a Proto-Indo-European stem meaning people or tribe, with an ending common to both Celtic and Germanic tribal names. It can be read as Celtic or as pre-Germanic, and the personal names of their rulers show strong Celtic influence. The earliest classical writers counted the Teutones as Celts. Julius Caesar apparently was the first to draw a line between Celts and Germanic peoples, and later Strabo and Velleius Paterculus called them Germanic. Pliny placed them among the Ingaevones, related to the Cimbri and the Chauci.

Where they came from was uncertain even in antiquity. Plutarch wrote that nobody could tell what people they were or whence they had set out. Pytheas, as reported by Pliny, described the Teutones as neighbours of the island of Abalus, where amber washed ashore and was traded by them. Pomponius Mela placed them on the island of Codannovia in the Codanus Bay, usually read as Scandinavia in the Baltic. Stefan Zimmer notes that the Teutones and the Cimbri left traces in place names in Jutland.

The Teutones are known above all from the Cimbrian War against the Roman Republic. The Cimbri and Teutones won decisive victories over Roman armies at Noreia and, in 105 BCE, at Arausio, then divided their forces. Gaius Marius defeated them separately: the Teutones in 102 BCE at the Battle of Aquae Sextiae, near present-day Aix-en-Provence, and the Cimbri in 101 BCE. This ended the war.

Valerius Maximus and Florus report that the king of the Teutones, Teutobod, was taken in irons. They also say the surrender terms required three hundred married women to be handed over to the Romans as concubines and slaves. When the women learned of this, they begged to serve in the temples of Ceres and Venus instead. Refused, they killed their own children and then strangled one another during the night. Some surviving captives are said to have joined the rebelling gladiators in the Third Servile War of 73 to 71 BCE.

The tale of the Teutonic women passed into Roman legend as an example of Teutonic fury. In ninth-century monastic Latin texts the word Teuton began to refer to speakers of West Germanic languages, used as a learned alternative to the term theodiscus, meaning of the people. The adjective Teutonic has often been used since to mean Germanic.
teutonic-order: The fraternity that preceded the Order was formed by German merchants from Bremen and Lübeck during the siege of Acre, in the Third Crusade. In 1191 they took over a hospital in the city to care for the sick and began to call themselves the Hospital of St. Mary of the German House in Jerusalem. Pope Clement III approved it, and the Order came to play an important part in Outremer, controlling the port tolls of Acre.

In 1211 King Andrew II of Hungary granted the Order the district of Burzenland in Transylvania, to defend his south-eastern border against the Cumans. By 1220 the knights had built five castles, but the Hungarian nobility grew suspicious, and in 1225 Andrew expelled the Order.

In 1226 Duke Konrad I of Masovia asked the knights to subdue the pagan Old Prussians and gave them Chełmno Land as a base. Emperor Frederick II issued the Golden Bull of Rimini, granting the Order the conquest and possession of Prussia. After the fall of Acre in 1291 the Order moved its headquarters briefly to Venice, then to Marienburg, and turned its campaigns against the pagan Grand Duchy of Lithuania, joined each season by knights from England and France. It won victories at Strėva in 1348 and Rudau in 1370. In 1398 it conquered Gotland and drove out the Victual Brothers.

The Lithuanian ruler Jogaila was baptised in 1386, married Queen Jadwiga of Poland and became King of Poland. At Grunwald in 1410 Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen and 50 of the Order's 60 higher dignitaries died. Heinrich von Plauen held Marienburg, and the First Peace of Thorn in 1411 left the Order nearly all its land, though its reputation for invincibility was gone.

The Grand Master, elected by the general chapter, was the highest officer and until 1466 sovereign prince of Prussia, though in practice a first among equals. The Order had three national chapters, Prussia, Livonia and the Holy Roman Empire, each under a Landmeister. The smallest unit was the commandry, ruled by a Komtur, where knight-brothers, priest-brothers, sergeant-brothers and half-brothers, who worked in the economy and in healthcare, lived together as in a monastery. The knights wore a white surcoat with a black cross, granted by Pope Innocent III in 1205.
tevaram: The three poet-saints lived, by the dating of Peterson and Prentiss, between the 6th and 8th centuries CE, or by Champakalakshmi's in the 7th to 9th; Appar and Sambandar probably overlapped between 570 and 670, and Sundarar lived in the late 7th or early 8th century. In the Pallava period they travelled across the Tamil country, singing in temples and public places at a time when Hindus, Jains and Buddhists competed for royal and urban patronage. Their lives are known mainly from later hagiographies, chiefly the Periya Puranam, full of miracles and of Jain persecutors, which has made their reliability and even their centuries a matter of controversy.

The hymns long passed on mainly by word of mouth. Champakalakshmi sees three stages: composition by the saints, adoption in temple ritual by patikam singers, and deliberate arrangement into a canon, which monastic pontiffs folded into the Shaiva Siddhanta canon in the 13th century.

Volumes I to III hold the 383 or 384 hymns of Sambandar, IV to VI the 313 of Appar, and VII the 100 of Sundarar. Most hymns, or patikams, have ten or eleven verses, each a four-line stanza with a refrain, and the last verse often carries the poet's signature. They are set to 23 of the 103 pan modes of ancient Tamil music, to be sung with a stringed instrument such as the yal. The scholar Zvelebil quotes a Tamil saying: my Appar sang of me, Sambandar sang of himself, Sundarar sang of women. The hymns show that the Nataraja image and the Shiva linga were already established, and they name the temples later counted as the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams.

Tradition holds that Raja Raja Chola I (985–1013), hearing excerpts at court, sent the priest Nambiyandar Nambi to recover the hymns, which were found as palm leaves half eaten by white ants in a chamber of the Chidambaram Nataraja temple, and that the king overcame the opposition of the temple's Dikshitars, earning the name Tirumurai Kanda Cholan. The Madras Tamil Lexicon calls the collection a Tamil Veda. Inscriptions from the 8th century record hymn singers in Shiva temples; Rajaraja maintained 48 of them, called pidarars, and from the 13th century the odhuvars took over the singing, as they still do after the daily rituals in the temples of Tamil Nadu.
tevfik-esenc: Tevfik Esenç was an Ubykh Circassian citizen of Turkey. He was fluent in Ubykh, Adyghe and Turkish. For a time he was raised by Ubykh-speaking grandparents in the village of Hacıosman, called Lek'uaşüa in Ubykh and Hundjahabl in Adyghe. He served a term as the muhtar, or mayor, of that village before he received a post in the civil service of Istanbul.

In Istanbul Esenç worked at length with the French linguist Georges Dumézil and his associate Georges Charachidzé to record his language, although not all of Charachidzé's writings have been published. Other scholars who met him and wrote on Ubykh include the Norwegian Hans Vogt, the British linguist George Hewitt, who made recordings with him in Istanbul, the Abkhazian Viacheslav Chirikba, who has written on Ubykh settlements and surnames, and the Turkish linguist A. Sumru Özsoy.

Esenç had an excellent memory and understood quickly what Dumézil and the other visiting linguists wanted. He was a primary source for the Ubykh language and also for the mythology, cultural history and customs of the Ubykh people. His command of Turkish, Ubykh and Adyghe, a West Circassian language, allowed some comparative work between Ubykh and Adyghe, two members of the Northwest Caucasian family. He was a purist, and Dumézil considered his idiolect the closest thing to a standard literary Ubykh that existed.

Esenç closed his work on Ubykh with a speech addressed to Charachidzé. He asked forgiveness for any mistakes and said that if he found someone who knew more Ubykh than he did, he would speak with that person too. He told Charachidzé that from that day he was the Ubykh language, the one who would explain and speak it, and ended: This is where Ubykh comes to an end.

Esenç died on the night of 7 October 1992, at the age of 88. He was buried in the village cemetery of Hacıosman, his birthplace, beside his wife Emine, and was survived by three sons and two daughters. After his death the Ubykh language went extinct, despite the efforts of many linguists. The knowledge of Ubykh language and culture that exists today rests largely on his work. In 1994 A. Sumru Özsoy organised the international Conference on Northwest Caucasian Linguistics at Boğaziçi University in memory of Dumézil and Esenç.
tewa: Tewa oral history tells of an emergence from inside the earth at Sip’opheh, identified with San Luis Lake at the Great Sand Dunes in present-day Colorado, after which the Winter Moiety travelled south along the east side of a river and the Summer Moiety along the west, until they joined in the Tewa Basin. The ancient northern homeland is called Tewayógeh, great Tewa place.

The archaeologist Scott Ortman argues that the Tewa descend from the Ancestral Puebloan inhabitants of Mesa Verde who left it in the 13th century, when the basin's population quadrupled between 1200 and 1350 and newcomers brought farming that relied on rainfall, the keeping of turkeys and carbon-painted pottery. Michael Schillaci contests this, reading the evidence as a wider diaspora from Mesa Verde.

After 1300 the settlements of the Pajarito Plateau drew together into towns with central plazas, and Tewa villages spread to Ojo Caliente and the Galisteo Basin. In 1598 the conquistador Juan de Oñate set the capital of Spanish New Mexico at Yúngéh, across the river from Ohkay Owingeh, before it moved to Santa Fe in 1609. The Spanish forced Catholicism on the Pueblos and built missions in every one.

In 1680 the Tewa and other Pueblos killed their priests, destroyed the churches and drove the Spanish to El Paso del Norte. Diego de Vargas retook Santa Fe in 1694, and a second revolt in 1696 was crushed. The Tewa of the Galisteo Basin, the Tano, moved to the Hopi at First Mesa that year.

In 1912 the Pueblo of San Juan sued to secure its status as American Indians, and in 1920 the Pueblo Lands Board was set up to settle disputed land claims. The Tewa won full citizenship while keeping their rights to land, water and religious practice.

Every Tewa belongs to one of two moieties, the Summer People and the Winter People. The Summer Chief leads farming and the prayers for rain, the Winter Chief hunting and the winter ceremonies. Four sacred mountains bound their world: Lake Peak, Sandia Peak, Chicoma Mountain and San Antonio Mountain. Each pueblo is held to lie at the centre of the world, marked by an upright stone in its plaza, and many religious matters are not shared with outsiders. The Tewa were farmers of maize, beans and squash, and pottery remains their chief art. Most Tewa pueblos now run programmes teaching children to read and write Tewa, and Ohkay Owingeh has published a dictionary.
tewodros-ii: Tewodros II was baptised Kassa and was born in Qwara, west of Gondar. His father, Hailegiorgis Woldegiorgis, was an Amhara nobleman of the Qwara district. Chronicles make his mother a noblewoman of Gondar, though Hormuzd Rassam says she came from Amhara Sayint. He claimed that his father descended from Emperor Fasilides through a daughter. He grew up in the Zemene Mesafint, the Age of the Princes, when regional lords made and unmade puppet emperors at Gondar.

He began as a shifta, or outlaw, and after gathering a large following he took back his father's fief of Qwara and all of Dembiya, sharing captured grain and money with the peasants. Empress Menen Liben Amede arranged his marriage to her granddaughter Tewabech Ali.

Kassa served first in the army of his relative Kenfu Haile Giorgis. In 1837 he led an attack on Ottoman forces at Gallabat, and in March 1848 he suffered a defeat at Dabarki against Egyptian-controlled Sudan, after which he began to modernise his army with firearm drills and artillery. He occupied Gondar in January 1847 and took Empress Menen prisoner before releasing her.

Becoming emperor in 1855, he brought Shewa and Gojjam back under imperial rule, crushed the lords of Wollo and Tigray, and moved his capital from Gondar to Debre Tabor and later to Magdala. He held the Shewan prince Sahle Maryam, the future Menelik II, whom he brought up as his own son and married to his daughter Alitash.

He sought to make governors and judges salaried appointees, set up a standing army, a library, tax codes and administrative districts. His attempt to tax church lands brought him enemies in the church. Rebellions drew him away on campaign almost constantly. After the death of his wife Tewabech his behaviour grew more erratic and vengeful. After a rebel, Tedla Gwalu, was defeated in February 1863, Tewodros ordered the killing of 7,000 prisoners.

Tewodros had imprisoned European captives, among them the members of Hormuzd Rassam's mission, which led Britain to send an expedition under Robert Napier in 1868. The British defeated his army at Arogye on 10 April 1868. Tewodros released the Europeans, but ordered 300 Ethiopian prisoners thrown over a cliff. On 15 April 1868, as British troops stormed Magdala, he killed himself rather than surrender. His son Alemayehu was taken to England and died there in 1879, aged 19. A modern commentator holds that his suicide made possible his own resurrection as a symbol of defiant Ethiopian independence.
texan-santa-fe-expedition: The expedition belonged to Mirabeau B. Lamar's plan to make the young Republic of Texas a continental power, which he believed had to happen quickly to stave off the growing movement for annexation to the United States. His administration had already courted the New Mexicans by sending a commissioner in 1840, and many Texans believed New Mexico would welcome joining the republic. The venture was meant to compete with the trade of the Santa Fe Trail.

The party left Kenney's Fort, in present-day Round Rock near Austin, on 19 June 1841, with 21 ox-drawn wagons of goods valued at about 200,000 dollars. It carried the commissioners William G. Cooke, Richard F. Brenham, José Antonio Navarro and George Van Ness and a military escort of some 240 men under Hugh McLeod; the journalist George Wilkins Kendall and the English jurist Thomas Falconer later wrote accounts of it. Poor preparation, raids, wasted water and the loss of its Mexican guide left it lost on the plains, and McLeod sent an advance guard ahead.

That guard, led by Cooke and John S. Sutton, reached the Pecos Valley in mid-September 1841. At the village of Anton Chico it met a force of about 1500 men, many of them Puebloan recruits, sent by Governor Manuel Armijo. Promised safe conduct, the exhausted Texans gave up their arms. The next morning Armijo had them bound and put their execution to a vote of his officers, which spared them by one vote. They were held over the winter at the Perote Prison in Veracruz until United States diplomacy won their release on 13 June 1842.

Texans blamed Captain William G. Lewis, who had vouched for the safe conduct, as a traitor, and Lamar's presidency was further tarnished. The failure showed that Texas lacked the resources to hold its western claims, and many voters turned to Sam Houston, who favoured annexation; Texas joined the Union in 1845. The border dispute then passed to the United States and fed the tensions that led to the Mexican–American War. Under the Compromise of 1850 Texas gave up the Santa Fe region that Lamar had sought.
texas: Texas lies in the south-central United States. The Rio Grande forms its border with the Mexican states of Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas, the Red River borders Oklahoma and Arkansas, and the Sabine River borders Louisiana. One classification divides the state, from south-east to west, into the Gulf Coastal Plains, the Interior Lowlands, the Great Plains and the Basin and Range Province of Far West Texas, which holds desert valleys and wooded mountain slopes.

The name comes from the Caddo word táy:shaʼ, meaning friend, which the Spanish applied, as Tejas or Texas, to the Caddo themselves, specifically the Hasinai Confederacy. In the 18th century Spanish rule called the area Nuevas Filipinas, or the province of the Tejas, and later the province of Texas. An alternative etymology advanced in the late 19th century connected the name with the Spanish teja, roof tile.

Before European contact Texas lay between the Southwestern and Plains cultural spheres, with the Ancestral Puebloans to the west, the Mississippian culture to the east and the civilisations of Mesoamerica to the south. The languages spoken included Caddoan, Atakapan, Athabaskan, Coahuiltecan and Uto-Aztecan, besides isolates such as Tonkawa. The agricultural, mound-building Caddo controlled much of the north-east, the Karankawa lived along the central coast, and Apache peoples lived throughout the interior. No one culture dominated the whole territory.

Spain was the first European country to claim and control Texas, followed by a brief French colonisation. The territory became part of Mexico after its independence from Spain in 1821. Rising tensions between settlers and the Mexican government led to the Texas Revolution, which included the Battle of the Alamo, and to the independent Republic of Texas in 1836. In 1845 Texas joined the United States as the 28th state, which helped spark the Mexican-American War.

Texas remained a slave state until the American Civil War, in which it seceded from the Union and joined the Confederate States. After the war and the restoration of its representation in the federal government, it went through a long period of economic stagnation before substantial growth in the 20th century. The current Texas Constitution was adopted in 1876.

Austin is the state capital, and the largest metropolitan areas are the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex and Greater Houston. At the 2020 census Texas had 29,145,505 residents, the second-largest population of any state after California; it is also the second largest in area, after Alaska. Its nickname, the Lone Star State, refers to the single star on the flag of the Republic of Texas.
texas-revolution: The revolution followed a decade of political and cultural clashes between the Mexican government and the large and growing population of Anglo-American settlers in Texas, then part of the Mexican state of Coahuila y Tejas. The Mexican government had become more centralised and had stripped Texas of its autonomy, and curbed immigration from the United States and the holding of slaves as property. Mexico had abolished slavery in 1829 but made an exemption for Texas that was never written into the constitution. Slavery is not mentioned in the Texas Declaration of Independence, but the ownership of enslaved people mattered greatly to many settlers.

The uprising was part of a larger revolt in several provinces against the regime of President Miguel Barragán and General Santa Anna. The Mexican Congress passed the Tornel Decree, which declared that foreigners fighting Mexican troops would be treated as pirates.

Fighting began on 2 October 1835 at Gonzales, over a small cannon the army had lent the town. On 10 October about 125 volunteers, thirty of them Tejanos, stormed the presidio at Goliad, and Texian forces laid siege to Béxar. By mid-December the small Mexican garrisons had been defeated. The Consultation, meeting on 3 November, set up a provisional government under the Constitution of 1824 but did not declare independence, and its infighting left Texas with little effective government. A convention at Washington-on-the-Brazos declared independence on 2 March 1836.

Santa Anna entered Texas in mid-February 1836 with his Army of Operations. His troops defeated the garrison at the Alamo on 6 March and killed almost all its defenders. General José de Urrea won on the coast and executed most of those who surrendered at Goliad. Sam Houston, now commander of the army, withdrew while terrified civilians fled in the Runaway Scrape. On 21 April his army of about 900 men surprised Santa Anna's force of about 700 at the Battle of San Jacinto and routed it. Many Mexican soldiers who tried to surrender were killed.

Santa Anna was captured the next day. To save his life he ordered the remaining Mexican troops to retreat south of the Rio Grande, and he signed the Treaty of Velasco, which gave Texas its independence. Mexico refused to recognise the republic, because Santa Anna had signed as a prisoner, and intermittent conflict continued into the 1840s. The Republic of Texas was annexed by the United States in 1845 as the 28th state, which led directly to the Mexican–American War.
tezpur: Tezpur lay under the Koch dynasty and in the sixteenth century became part of the Ahom kingdom, whose rulers are known for their administration and patronage of art and culture. The city saw several battles in the medieval period. At Da Parbatia, a village close to the west of the city, excavations in 1924 uncovered a stone door frame with extensive carvings from a sixth-century temple, over which a brick Shiva temple of the Ahom period was later built. A large artificial lake, the Harjara Pukhuri, was excavated in the early ninth century and is named after Harjara Varmana of the Mleccha dynasty, and the Bamuni Hills hold ruins with sculpture of the ninth and tenth centuries.

Local tradition ties many places to the legend of Banasura, a king of the asuras. His daughter Usha is said to have worshipped at the Bhairabi Temple, and the hillock called Agnigarh, the hill of fire, is held to be where she was kept, surrounded by fire, in her romance with Aniruddha, grandson of Krishna. At the Rudrapada Temple on the bank of the Brahmaputra, tradition holds that Shiva left the print of his left foot on a stone.

Tezpur stands on the north bank of the Brahmaputra in Sonitpur district, 175 kilometres north-east of Guwahati, and is the largest of the cities on the north bank. The population of the municipal area was 102,505 at the 2011 census. It is an educational centre, with Tezpur University and several colleges. At Bhomoraguri a stone inscription records the plan of the Ahom general Kalia Bhomora Borphukan to bridge the Brahmaputra; almost two centuries later a bridge of 3.015 km, named after him, joins Tezpur to Silghat.
thaba-bosiu: Thaba Bosiu is a plateau of about 2 square kilometres, 1,804 metres above sea level, between the Orange and Caledon Rivers in the Maseru District, 24 km east of Maseru, in the valley of the Phuthiatsana River. It rises about 106 metres above the valley, and its summit is ringed by sheer cliffs some 12 metres high on average. It has eight springs and six passes, the main one being the Khubelu pass, and there is San rock art nearby. Many Basotho believe the mountain has magical properties: earth taken from it, it is said, returns there overnight.

Moshoeshoe I and his people came from Butha-Buthe in July 1824, escaping the Difaqane or Mfecane wars. The name is loosely translated as mountain at night, since they arrived after dark, and Moshoeshoe spread word that the mountain grew larger at night to frighten his enemies.
