The plateau could hold livestock and stores for a long siege, and he gave cattle and protection to refugees, many of whom stayed under his rule. In 1837 Private David Webber of the 72nd Seaforth Highlanders, given refuge there, built him a stone house of two rooms. Mzilikazi attacked the mountain without success.

The Boers of the Orange Free State began a siege on 18 August 1865. Louw Wepener led the assault behind an artillery bombardment, but only about 100 of his men were still with him by 5 pm, and he was shot at the top of the Khubelu pass, since also called Wepener's pass: the only enemy ever to reach the summit. The siege lasted until January 1866. Starving, the Basotho signed a treaty in April 1866 giving up three thousand cattle and more than two-thirds of their arable land. After the Third Free State–Basotho War, Moshoeshoe sought British protection, granted in March 1868 on the eve of a new Boer attack.

On 27 December 1966 King Moshoeshoe II, who contested the legitimacy of Prime Minister Leabua Jonathan's government and his own lack of executive power, held protest meetings that ended in a prayer meeting on the mountain. Jonathan banned it as a promotion of insurrection. Clashes with the security forces left 10 dead, opposition leaders were arrested, and the king, under house arrest, had to promise not to address public gatherings without the government's consent.

Lesotho declared the mountain a national monument in 1967, and in the 1990s the government began, with international development support, a programme to preserve and present it. Moshoeshoe II was buried on the summit beside Moshoeshoe I in 1996. A cultural village, a conference centre and lodgings stand at its foot, below the historic site on the plateau.
thado-minbya: He was born Rahula on 7 December 1345, the son of Princess Soe Min Kodawgyi of Sagaing and Viceroy Thado Hsinhtein of Tagaung; through his mother he was a grandson of King Saw Yun, founder of the Sagaing Kingdom. Since 1315 central Burma had been split between Sagaing and Pinya, and from 1359 both suffered heavy raids from the Shan state of Maw. His stepfather, King Thihapate of Sagaing, made him governor of Tagaung, 200 km to the north, with the title Thado Minbya. When the Maw took the fort, the prince escaped to Sagaing on a single war elephant, only to be imprisoned by Thihapate.

In April 1364 the Maw overran Sagaing. Thihapate fled downriver to Kya-Khat-Wa-Ya, where Thado Minbya, who had escaped, had him executed and in May declared himself king. He won over the Sagaing court, rebuilt its army and in August or September crossed the Irrawaddy, took Pinya and had its ruler Uzana II executed. Over the next six months he drained the swamps at the meeting of the Irrawaddy and Myitnge, beside the Kyaukse granary, and built a fortified island capital, proclaimed as Ava on 25 February 1365; its brick walls were finished on 6 July 1365.

He then tried to bring the south under his rule. He took Pagan without a fight in 1365 but failed before Sagu. In 1365–66 he captured Nganwegon, where he killed its leader Baya Kyawthu himself and ate a meal on the corpse's chest, horrifying his own staff; in 1366–67 Taungdwin submitted. He was harsh with corrupt monks, beheading one who had stolen a widow's gold, while supporting orthodox clergy and learning. In September 1367, besieging Sagu again, he caught smallpox and died at Swegyo near Pagan.

The king, only 21, left no heir. His queen Saw Omma and Nga Nu, commander of the palace guard, seized power and proclaimed themselves rulers at Sagaing, but the ministers gave the throne to Swa Saw Ke, who became king on 5 September 1367. Ava, chosen for its defensible site, remained the capital of successive Burmese kingdoms for most of the next five centuries. The royal chronicles do not agree on his dates of birth, death and reign.
thado-minsaw-of-prome: He was born Min Ba Saw, the seventh of the eight children of Narapati I of Ava and his chief queen, Atula Thiri Maha Yaza Dewi. He married his first cousin Myat Hpone Pyo, youngest daughter of his maternal uncle Saw Shwe Khet, a governor of Prome and later of Tharrawaddy. They had three sons and three daughters, and she died at Tharrawaddy before he became king. His Tai name was Hso Ming Hpa.

He grew up at Ava until 1460, when his father made him governor of Tharrawaddy, the southernmost town on the border with the Hanthawaddy kingdom. His eldest brother, Thihathura I, confirmed him in the post on coming to the throne in 1468. In late 1472 or early 1473 he and another brother, Mingyi Swa, viceroy of Prome, plotted a rebellion against the king, counting on help from King Dhammazedi of Hanthawaddy that never came. Both submitted in February 1473, and Thihathura pardoned them and restored them to their posts.

After Thihathura's death in 1480 his son Minkhaung II faced a major revolt by his brother Minye Kyawswa of Yamethin. When Mingyi Swa died in 1482, Thado Minsaw seized Prome, declared himself independent and took his late brother's chief wife, Saw Myat Lay, as his chief queen. An army from Ava withdrew after a month under fire from fire arrows, cannon and newly acquired muskets, and Ava, worn down by the Yamethin revolt and the rebellions of Mohnyin and Kale, sent no other. His kingdom reached from Tharrawaddy in the south to Myede in the north.

For decades he kept out of the wars of Upper Burma and stayed at peace with Hanthawaddy, the strongest kingdom of the region. In the 1520s, with Ava failing under the attacks of the Confederation of Shan States, he joined its leader Sawlon. On 22 March 1525 their armies sacked Ava, though its king, Shwenankyawshin, his grandnephew, escaped. The Prome forces brought back the poet monk Shin Maha Rattathara. His son Bayin Htwe succeeded him.
thaenae: Thaenae lay in or near Thyna, now a suburb of Sfax on the Mediterranean coast of south-eastern Tunisia. Its founders gave it the Punic name tʿynt, which Barclay V. Head transcribed as Thainath. Greek writers rendered it Thaína and Thenae, and Latin ones Thenae, Thaena and Thaenae. Strabo called the town Thena, and Ptolemy gave it both as Thaina and Theaenae. In a later period it became a Roman colony with the name Aelia Augusta Mercurialis.

The town began as a Phoenician colony and, with the rest of ancient Tunisia, passed under Carthaginian and then Roman control in the time of the Punic Wars. Around the time of Julius Caesar and Augustus it struck its own bronze coins, showing a female head, taken to be either Serapis or Astarte, and on the reverse a temple of four columns, with the town's name in Punic letters. The surviving ruins include a bath house, a wealthy townhouse, city walls, housing of poorer people and an early Christian basilica.

In late antiquity Thenae was the seat of a bishop, and a life of St Fulgentius records a council held there. Six bishops are known. Eucrazio attended the council of 256 in Carthage called by St Cyprian. A Catholic bishop, Latonio, and a Donatist rival, Securo, both appeared at the council of 411 in Carthage. Pascasio took part in the synod of 484 summoned by the Vandal king Huneric and was afterwards exiled. Pontian spoke at the council of 525, and Felix attended the antimonotelite council of 646.

The ruins of the ancient town stand at Thyna, on the edge of Sfax. Thenae survives as a titular see of the Roman Catholic Church, whose holders since 1906 have included Andrzej Maria Deskur and Marian Duś, a former auxiliary bishop of Warsaw.
thagaste: Thagaste, also written Tagaste, lay in the north-eastern highlands of Numidia, around 60 miles from Hippo Regius, modern Annaba, 20 miles southwest of Thubursicum and about 150 miles from Carthage. The region was densely forested, and in antiquity its mountains served as a natural citadel against invaders, among them the Romans, the Vandals, the Byzantines and the Umayyads. Researchers in the Canary Islands have linked the name to Tegueste, which they derive from a Guanche word of Berber origin meaning humid.

Thagaste began as a small Numidian village of a Berber tribe. It became a Roman municipium in the first century of Roman rule and is mentioned by Pliny the Elder; a few Italian settlers lived there, but most inhabitants were romanised Berbers. Trade grew, and the town flourished above all under Septimius Severus. Augustine's mother, Saint Monica, was a Christian, and his father, Patricius, was a pagan who later became a Christian.

The town had a basilica and a diocese, the most important in Byzantine Numidia; three of its bishops are known, Saint Firminus, Saint Alypius, Augustine's friend, and Saint Gennarus. The wealthy gens Valeria, later under Saint Melania, held an estate nearby so large that it included two episcopal sees, one Catholic and one Donatist. The Byzantines fortified Thagaste with walls, and it fell to the Umayyad Caliphate towards the end of the seventh century.

After centuries of neglect French colonists rebuilt the town, now called Souk Ahras. By tradition Augustine meditated under an olive tree on a hill of the town; the tree still stands and is a meeting place for followers of Augustinian spirituality.
thai-national-anthem: About five days after the coup of June 1932, Luang Nithetkolakit revealed that he belonged to the People's Party and regretted that the party had no proper song for its success. He asked Phra Chenduriyang again, and this time the request came from the new power in Siam, so the musician reluctantly agreed. He completed the anthem on 6 July 1932 during a tram ride from Tha Tien to Bang Khun Phrom, arranging it for the Royal Siamese Navy Orchestra, and asked that his name not be revealed.

When the orchestra first played it at the Ananta Samakhom Throne Hall the following week, the newspaper Srikrung named him as composer. His commander, the Minister of the Palace, reprimanded him for making a national anthem on his own authority, and in October 1932 he was laid off from his post and re-entered it at half his former salary.

The conspirators of Khana Ratsadon asked Khun Wichitmatra to write words. His Phleng Chat Sayam had two stanzas of eight verses and had been printed by 29 August 1932. It was popular but never declared official, and it was banned because some lines spoke of seizing power. In 1934 the government held a competition for official lyrics. For a Western-style anthem the committee recommended Phra Chenduriyang's melody, with a revised version of Khun Wichitmatra's words and a second set by the runner-up, Chan Khamwilai. The Cabinet approved these on 20 August 1934.

The two sets made thirty-two lines in all, and most Thais preferred to sing only Khun Wichitmatra's. In 1939, when Siam became Thailand, a competition produced new lyrics by Luang Saranupraphan, cut from sixteen lines to eight and naming the new country. They were adopted on 10 December 1939.

Regulations of 1935 provided a full-length and a shortened performance of the anthem. Prime Minister Plaek Phibunsongkhram ordered the anthem played every day at 08:00 and 18:00 and told the public to stand in respect. Under his rule people who did not stand in silence could be fined up to 2,000 baht or jailed for up to a year; the law has since been abolished.

Today the morning and evening playings match the raising and lowering of the national flag at schools, workplaces and public buildings, and radio and television broadcast it twice a day. Pupils sing it at assembly each school day.
thailand: Thailand shares land borders with Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and Malaysia and has coasts on the Gulf of Thailand and the Andaman Sea. It covers about 513,120 square kilometres, and the Gulf of Thailand covers 320,000 square kilometres. The north is the mountainous Thai highlands, where Doi Inthanon rises to 2,565 metres. The northeast, Isan, is the Khorat Plateau, bordered on the east by the Mekong. The centre is dominated by the flat Chao Phraya River valley, which runs into the Gulf of Thailand, and the south is the narrow Kra Isthmus widening into the Malay Peninsula.

The Chao Phraya and the Mekong are the indispensable watercourses of rural Thailand, and both are used for industrial-scale production of crops. The climate is shaped by the southwest and northeast monsoons, and most of the country has a tropical savanna climate.

Rice cultivation began around 2000 BCE, and the Ban Chiang site in the northeast is the earliest known centre of copper and bronze production in Southeast Asia, dating between 2000 and 1000 BCE. By the 6th century early multiethnic kingdoms had emerged, including the Mon principalities of Dvaravati and Hariphunchai, and in the 9th century the Khmer people established the Khmer Empire, centred in Angkor. Historians suggest the ancestors of the Thai people migrated from southern China and northern Vietnam between the 6th and 11th centuries, intermixing with Mon and Khmer populations.

King Ramkhamhaeng's reign (1279 to 1298) marked the inception of a unified Thai identity. After the destruction of Ayutthaya in 1767, King Taksin established the Thonburi Kingdom, and Rama I moved the capital to Bangkok in 1782. Siam was the only country in Southeast Asia to avoid European colonisation, though it ceded territory and trade rights through unequal treaties. The People's Party carried out a bloodless revolution on 24 June 1932, and the country was officially renamed Thailand on 24 June 1939.

Thailand has had 20 constitutions and charters since 1932, and all state that politics operate within a constitutional monarchy. The National Assembly has a 200-member Senate and a 500-member House of Representatives. The population is about 66 million, and Theravada Buddhism is central to modern Thai identity.
thaj: Thaj lies about 90 kilometres west of Jubail, on the edge of a small village called Sabkha, and about 95 km from the coast of the Arabian Gulf. It is a rich oasis with ancient palm groves and more than twenty old wells, twelve of which are still in use, among ruins of buildings of black mud brick. Surveys in the 1960s found many burial mounds to the west, south and east of the town, some ring-shaped and up to 50 metres across, others marked by capstones or stone cists.

Excavations since the mid-20th century have traced the town's long life. A Danish mission under Geoffrey Bibby dug a small area in 1968, finding Seleucid pottery and Bronze Age arrowheads. A joint Harvard-Saudi team in 1977 confirmed trade links in the Hellenistic, Parthian and Sassanian periods, and a Saudi-UK excavation of 1983 found graveyards, tombstones with Hasaitic inscriptions, clay animal figures and 36 coins, concluding that settlement may have run from 300 BCE to 300 CE. Work between 2000 and 2006 under Abdulhameed al-Hashash showed that salt from the surrounding marshes was exported.

Two inscribed amphoras from burials outside the city carry one text in Aramaic, probably taken over from Achaemenid administration, and one in South Arabian cursive, or zabur, the first attestation of that script in the core region of Hasaitic writing. Both scripts were thus used side by side in Eastern Arabia, and the spread of the South Arabian one is thought to reflect trade between Gerrha and South Arabia around 300 BCE.

Thaj remained known after antiquity. A castle was built there in the late 6th century by Rashid ibn Shihab al-Yashkuri, and the Umayyad poets Dhu al-Rummah and al-Farazdaq named it. Arab geographers of the 10th and 11th centuries, al-Hamdani and al-Bakri, described it as a watering place and village of al-Bahrayn, and it served as a caravan stop. The first European to visit it was W. H. Shakespeare, who found two South Arabian grave inscriptions, the first of their kind known in northern Arabia.
thalassocracy: A thalassocracy, also called a maritime empire, is a state whose realms are primarily maritime. Traditional thalassocracies seldom dominate interiors, even in their home territories, and so differ from empires whose territories extend into mainland interiors, a land-based hegemony known as a tellurocracy. The term can also simply mean naval supremacy. The ancient Greeks first used the word for the government of the Minoan civilization, whose power depended on its navy.

The modern use revives a word from a list in the Chronicon of Eusebius, a bishop of Caesarea Maritima in the early 4th century, which the scholar John Linton Myres called the List of Thalassocracies. It names a succession of powers with exclusive control of the sea, beginning with the Lydians after the fall of Troy and ending with Aegina. Because it omits Aegina's submission to Athens, it was probably compiled before the Delian League was consolidated.

In the Mediterranean, the Phoenician states of Tyre, Sidon and Carthage and the Delian League of Athens were seaborne powers. The medieval maritime republics, among them Venice, Genoa and Pisa, controlled trade and territory for centuries and were essential to the Crusades. From the 12th to the 15th century Genoa held a monopoly of Western Mediterranean trade. The Crown of Aragon acted as a thalassocracy in the 14th and 15th centuries, and the Swedish Empire of the 17th century rested on control of most of the Baltic coast.

In Southeast Asia the first thalassocracies arose from about the 2nd century CE as trading ports on the routes between Funan and India through the Malacca Strait. Srivijaya emerged by the 7th century by subjugating neighbouring thalassocracies such as Melayu, Kedah, Tarumanagara and Mataram, and it controlled the sea lanes and the spice trade. Singhasari subjugated it around 1275, and Majapahit (1293 to 1527) absorbed it. In the Age of Exploration the Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch and British empires held overseas possessions together through naval supremacy.
thales-of-miletus: Thales came from Miletus, a mercantile city at the mouth of the Maeander River in Ionia. The main source for the details of his life is the third-century CE writer Diogenes Laërtius, who wrote some eight centuries after Thales's death and drew on sources that often contained unreliable or even fabricated information. Herodotus called him a Phoenician by remote descent, and Diogenes names his parents as Examyas and Cleobulina, but other writers represent him as a genuine Milesian of distinguished family.

Later writers said that he visited Egypt, where he learned geometry, or Babylonia. Scholars dispute this, since such journeys were a commonplace attribution to philosophers by later writers explaining the origin of their mathematical knowledge.

Thales is counted among the Seven Sages of Greece, semi-traditional statesmen and founding figures, and Diogenes calls him the first of them. The Delphic maxim know thyself was attributed to him. Diogenes also tells of a gold tripod or bowl to be given to the wisest man, which passed round the sages and returned to Thales, who dedicated it to Apollo. According to Diogenes he advised the Milesians not to join the Lydians in a symmachia, a fighting together; when King Croesus was defeated by Cyrus the Great, Miletus was spared because it had taken no action.

Herodotus reported that Thales predicted a solar eclipse in 585 BCE. He also tells that Thales got the army of Croesus across the river Halys by digging a diversion upstream, though he himself finds the story doubtful.

Thales sought to explain natural phenomena by rational hypotheses that referred to natural processes, not to the will of gods and heroes. His best-known thesis, reported by Aristotle in the Metaphysics, is that the originating principle of nature, the arche, is a single material substance, water. Aristotle did not hold the view himself, though the attribution to Thales is generally accepted. Thales thought the Earth floats on water, and explained earthquakes as the Earth being rocked by waves.

Aristotle regarded him as the first natural philosopher, a view that most other writers did not adopt until eighteenth-century historians made it prominent. According to Aristotle he held that all things are full of gods, reasoning that lodestones and amber have souls because they cause movement. Thales is the namesake of Thales's theorem in geometry, and he was said to have calculated the heights of the pyramids and the distance of ships from the shore.
thamal-al-dulafi: Thamal was a eunuch who, as his nisba al-Dulafi shows, began as a slave soldier (ghulam) of the Dulafid dynasty of Jibal, which the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tadid suppressed in 896. He first appears in 917/8, when the caliph gave him command of a naval expedition against the Byzantine Empire. He returned with prisoners and booty, while the governor of Tarsus, Bishr al-Afshini, led that year's raid by land.

In 920 he took 25 ships to Egypt against a Fatimid invasion. He kept the Fatimid fleet out of the Rosetta branch of the Nile and on 12 March, near Abukir, routed it, most of its crews being killed or captured. In spring 921 his fleet retook the harbour of Alexandria, and he then joined the Abbasid commander-in-chief Mu'nis al-Muzaffar in blockading the Fayyum Oasis until the Fatimid forces burned their equipment and withdrew west across the desert.

In 923 his sea raid reportedly took 1,000 prisoners and over 28,000 animals, and by then he seems to have been governor of Tarsus. According to al-Mas'udi, in 924 he sailed close to Constantinople and agreed with the Bulgarians on joint action in Tsar Simeon's war against the Byzantines, though nothing is known to have come of it. From 924 to 926 he fought the Qarmatians in Iraq while his lieutenant Bushra held Tarsus.

Back on the frontier, he defeated a Byzantine army in 927 and the renegade Kurdish leader Ibn al-Dahhak on his return. In 931, by Ibn al-Athir's account, a spring raid through deep snow killed 600 Byzantine soldiers and captured 3,000, and the summer expedition plundered Amorium, abandoned by its garrison, and reached Ancyra. The women and children taken were said to have sold for 136,000 gold dinars.

After a raid in 932 successful enough for letters announcing victories on land and sea to be read in the mosques of Baghdad, Thamal disappears from the sources. A raider called al-Thamali in 941/2 was most likely one of his retainers. His men stayed powerful in Tarsus: Bushra succeeded him as governor and then Nasr al-Thamali, the Thamaliyya faction killed their rival Tarif in 938, and his ghilman are attested there as late as the mid-960s.
thane: Thane emerged as an urban area under the Shilahara dynasty, which ruled the North Konkan between 800 and 1265 CE. Its names in inscriptions include Srī-sthānaka, Sthānaka and Srī-sthāna. A Chinchani inscription of 1053 CE, issued by Vija-ranaka of the Modha family, states that brahmanas from Srī-sthāna settled at Samyana in his territory. A Shilahara inscription of 1094 CE calls Srī-sthānaka a velakula, a harbour that was an important centre for import and export. Early medieval Arab sources give the name as Thāna, and Ibn Battuta and Abulfeda knew it as Kukin Tana.

A Marathi chronicle, the Mahikavatichi Bakhar, written between the 15th and 17th centuries and of doubtful accuracy, tells that in the 12th century a general named Balkrishn-rao Somvanshi captured Thane from the Shilahara king Yashwant-rao. In the 13th century, according to the same text, Nagar-shah, the ruler of Gandevi, took the area, and it later passed to the Yadavas of Devagiri and back to Nagar-shah as a vassal of the Delhi Sultanate. It was then ruled in turn by local families, the Muzaffarids of Gujarat and the Portuguese.

In the 17th century the Thane area was contested between the Portuguese, the Mughals and the Marathas, and Shivaji captured it from the Mughals in 1675. The Portuguese regained control and began building a fort in 1734, but the Marathas captured the place in 1737. At the start of the First Anglo-Maratha War the East India Company occupied Salsette Island and Thana Fort; the island was recaptured by the forces of Haripant Phadke and Tukoji Holkar, but after the Treaty of Salbai of 1782 both the fort and Salsette were under British control.

Thane, spelled Thana until 1996, is a city in the state of Maharashtra in western India. It lies in the north-east of Salsette Island, neighbours Mumbai and belongs to the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. It is the headquarters of Thane district, and the 2011 census counted 1,886,941 inhabitants. Marathi is the main language, with Hindi widely understood, and some East Indian families in the Khatri ward still speak Portuguese. About 1,800 of India's Jews live in the city.

On 16 April 1853 a passenger train service was inaugurated between Bori Bunder in Bombay and Thane, a distance of 34 km, hauled by three locomotives named Sahib, Sindh and Sultan. When the line was extended to Kalyan in May 1854, the Thane viaducts, the first railway bridges, were built over Thane creek.
thanh-thai: Thành Thái was born Nguyễn Phúc Bửu Lân on 14 March 1879, the son of the emperor Dục Đức and Empress Dowager Từ Minh. While the emperor Tự Đức was alive, Prince Quang Thái, as he then was, was placed under house arrest with his family for his connections with opponents of the emperor. When the emperor Đồng Khánh died, the French colonial authorities and the high-ranking mandarins decided that Quang Thái was the ideal successor and enthroned him.

He reigned for 18 years, from 1889 to 1907. At ten he was already recognised as very intelligent, and realised that palace spies were keeping watch over him for the French. Where Đồng Khánh had tried to be friendly with the French, Thành Thái took a course of passive resistance, refraining from open rebellion, which would have been political suicide, but making his feelings clear through symbolic gestures and biting remarks. He is said to have slipped out of the palace dressed as a commoner to talk with his people.

He was the first Vietnamese monarch to cut his hair in the French style and to learn to drive a car. As the palace filled with French spies, he is said to have feigned insanity to escape their scrutiny, and so to have pressed for Vietnamese autonomy. He was on his way to join a resistance movement in China when French forces arrested him, declared him insane and forced him to abdicate in 1907. His young son was installed as Emperor Duy Tân.

Thành Thái was exiled first to Vũng Tàu. When Duy Tân rebelled against the French, both were exiled to Réunion in 1916. Their lives there were hard, and they could not even pay rent. In 1925 the emperor Khải Định learned of his situation and sent him 1,000 piastres, and later gave him money occasionally.

In May 1947 he was allowed to return home, but was kept under house arrest in Vũng Tàu. He died in Saigon in 1954 at the age of 75 and was buried at An Lang, the tomb of Dục Đức, in Thừa Thiên Huế Province. Vietnamese tradition counts him, with Hàm Nghi and Duy Tân, as one of three patriotic emperors for their stand against French colonial rule, and roads in Vietnam bear his name.
thanjavur: Thanjavur lies in the Cauvery delta, 340 km south-west of Chennai and 56 km east of Tiruchirappalli. The tributaries of the Cauvery, among them the Grand Anaicut canal, the Vadavaaru and the Vennaaru, flow through it. The plains beside the river have been cultivated from time immemorial, but most of the city and its surroundings lie in the New Delta, a dry upland tract that was brought under irrigation in the early 19th century. The district is known as the rice bowl of Tamil Nadu. Several explanations of the name are given, among them a Tamil phrase meaning the town where refugees entered and a legend of an Asura named Tanjan, slain on the site by Neelamegha Perumal, an incarnation of Vishnu.

Sangam-period Tamil records do not mention Thanjavur, though some scholars think the city existed then. The region was conquered by the Mutharayars in the sixth century, who ruled it until 849. The Cholas returned to prominence under Vijayalaya in about 850; he took Thanjavur from the Mutharayar king Elango Mutharayar and built a temple to the goddess Nisumbhasudani, and his son Aditya I consolidated the hold on the city. Thanjavur became the most important city of the Chola Empire and remained its capital until Gangaikonda Cholapuram emerged in about 1025. Rajaraja I, who reigned from 985 to 1014, built the Brihadeeswarar Temple there.

After the Cholas the city was ruled by the Mutharayars, the Pandyas, the Vijayanagar Empire, the Madurai Nayaks, the Thanjavur Nayaks and the Thanjavur Marathas. The Bhonsle family ruled the Thanjavur region from 1674 to 1855, and most of the Maratha kingdom was annexed by the British Empire in 1799. The Maratha palace, begun by the Nayaks, stayed in the family's hands. Thanjavur has been part of independent India since 1947.

Thanjavur is an important centre of religion, art and architecture in southern India. The Brihadeeswarar Temple, dedicated to Shiva and covered inside with wall paintings of the Chola and Nayak periods, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, and the Great Living Chola Temples around the city share that status. The historian Percy Brown called its construction a landmark in the evolution of building art in South India. The city is also the home of Tanjore painting, a style unique to the region, and the Saraswati Mahal Library dates from the end of the 16th century. Tamil is the widely spoken language, and Thanjavur Marathi and Saurashtra are also spoken.
thanksgiving: Prayers of thanks after harvests are common among most religions. The North American holiday is rooted in English traditions of the Reformation, when Puritans wished to replace church holidays with specially called Days of Fasting and Days of Thanksgiving in response to events seen as acts of providence. Days of Thanksgiving were called after the victory over the Spanish Armada in 1588, and an annual one began in 1606 after the Gunpowder Plot failed. The charter of the English settlers who landed at Berkeley Hundred in Virginia on 4 December 1619 required the day of their arrival to be kept yearly as a day of thanksgiving.

The more familiar account, centred on the Pilgrims, is historically inaccurate as an origin. A multi-day festival at Plymouth Colony in 1621 followed a good harvest, though it was not then called a thanksgiving. The Wampanoag, who had a mutual defence treaty with the colonists, were alarmed by ceremonial gunfire and were welcomed to join the feast. The festival was largely forgotten for hundreds of years and was termed the first Thanksgiving only in a footnote to an 1841 book by Alexander Young. George Washington proclaimed a nationwide thanksgiving for 26 November 1789, and Abraham Lincoln set a national Thanksgiving for the final Thursday of November in 1863.

On 26 December 1941 Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the resolution setting the fourth Thursday of November from 1942, after he had moved the holiday a week earlier in 1939, which some called Franksgiving. In Canada the first official Thanksgiving was held on 15 April 1872 for the recovery of the Prince of Wales, and Parliament moved the holiday in 1957 to the second Monday of October. Liberia observes it under a statute of 1883. Other days of similar name have different origins: Japan's Labor Thanksgiving Day on 23 November has roots in the Shinto harvest ceremony Niiname-sai, and Grenada's marks the 1983 invasion of the island.
thar-desert: The Thar Desert lies in the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent, across the border between India and Pakistan. About two thirds of it is in India, mostly in Rajasthan, with parts in Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab, and the remainder in the provinces of Sindh and Punjab in Pakistan. It is bordered by the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the north, west and northeast, by the Rann of Kutch to the south and by the Aravalli Range to the east. Sandy plains broken by low eroded hills rise to about 325 metres towards the Aravallis, and much of the desert is covered by sand dunes.

Most rain falls in the southwest monsoon from June to September. The Luni is the longest river of the desert. The 649-kilometre Indira Gandhi Canal, which carries water from the Indus system, is a major source of irrigation and drinking water, and rain is stored in reservoirs known as tobas, johads and taankas.

The region grew arid over a long time. During the Last Glacial Maximum, an ice sheet on the Tibetan Plateau meant that there was no monsoon over the subcontinent. Later the rise of the Aravallis changed the hydrography, and the Ghaggar-Hakra river system, which fed the region, no longer reached the sea. Beginning about 4,500 to 5,000 years ago the monsoons that fed it diminished further. The Indus Valley Civilisation had prospered along the river system, and as the Hakra dried to an intermittent river the urban Harappan civilisation declined into smaller agricultural communities.

Parts of the desert came under the Mauryan Empire by the third century BCE and the Gupta Empire in the 5th century CE. Mahmud of Ghazni annexed the region in the 11th century. Rajput states began to form in the late 7th century and later rose to prominence, and they resisted the Mughal Empire, which began with Babur's invasion, for over 200 years. The Marathas controlled most of the region in the 18th century, and in the 19th it came under British suzerainty as a number of princely states. The partition of India split the desert between India and Pakistan, with large-scale conflicts and mass migration across the new borders.

The Thari people, who speak a language of the Rajasthani family, are the natives of the region, and most live in small villages, many of them nomadic. Herding, limited agriculture and handicrafts support the economy. Desert National Park in Rajasthan covers 3,162 square kilometres, and Lal Suhanra in Pakistan is a UNESCO biosphere reserve. Natural gas was discovered in the Jaisalmer basin in 1988.
tharangambadi: Tharangambadi, formerly Tranquebar, lies on the Coromandel Coast in the Mayiladuthurai district of Tamil Nadu, 15 kilometres north of Karaikal and near the mouth of the Uppanar, a distributary of the Kaveri River. Its name means place of the singing waves, while the old name Trankebar remains current in modern Danish. The place dates back to the 14th century, and the Masilamani Nathar temple to Shiva, built in 1306 on land given by Maravarman Kulasekara Pandyan I, is its oldest monument. Until 1620 it belonged to the Thanjavur Nayak kingdom.

The town was established on 19 November 1620 as the first Danish trading post in India. King Christian IV sent his envoy Ove Gjedde, who made a deal with Raghunatha Nayak of Thanjavur and built Fort Dansborg. The Danes paid an annual tribute to the Rajah of Tanjore. A Jesuit congregation of Tamil fishermen converted by Portuguese missionaries already existed there, and the Catholic church was probably demolished to build the fort, which was the residence and headquarters of the governor and officials for about 150 years.

Dansborg was besieged in 1644 without result. In 1648 the Tranquebar Rebellion, which may have begun as a response to the inspector Willem Leyel's treaty with the Mughals against Danish piracy, ended in a show trial that sent him back to Denmark. Frederick III abolished the company two years later, but a garrison unaware of this held the colony, and the commoner Eskild Anderson Kongsbakke kept the fort until May 1669, when the frigate Færø arrived.

Tranquebar was the base of two German Lutheran missionaries, Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Pluetschau, among the first Protestant missionaries in India. Ziegenbalg translated the Old and New Testaments into Tamil, imported a printing press and printed the Tamil New Testament in 1714. The press printed 300 books in Tamil within a hundred years.

The New Jerusalem Church was built in 1718. The British occupied Tranquebar in February 1808 during the Napoleonic Wars, and it returned to Denmark under the Treaty of Kiel in 1814. Denmark sold it to the British in 1845, together with Serampore in Bengal. It was then still a busy port, but it lost importance after a railway opened to Nagapattinam.

Fort Dansborg, the second largest Danish fort ever built after Kronborg at Helsingør, is now a museum of colonial-era objects, with a moat that has disappeared and rooms that are partly ruined. The Tranquebar Museum displays porcelain, Danish manuscripts, Chinese tea jars and objects from the Vijayanagara and Thanjavur Nayak periods. The New Jerusalem Church holds services every Sunday; it was damaged in the tsunami of 2004 and re-consecrated in 2006. The Zion Church, consecrated in 1701, is the oldest Protestant church in India.
tharros: The city, also called Tharras and Tarrhae in ancient sources, lies on the southern shore of the Sinis peninsula, which forms the northern cape of the Bay of Oristano, by the cape of San Marco, near the village of San Giovanni di Sinis in the municipality of Cabras. Ptolemy and the Itineraries mention it, and it seems to have been one of the most important places on the island. A village built by the Nuragic peoples stood near the hill of Su Muru Mannu.

On top of Su Muru Mannu archaeologists found a tophet, an open-air sacred place common to Phoenician settlements in the western Mediterranean, seen as a first sign of colonisation and urbanisation. The city was inhabited by Phoenicians, then by Punic people and then by Romans. An inscription records the repair of the road from Tharras to Cornus as late as the reign of the emperor Philip, and the Antonine Itinerary places it 18 miles from Cornus and 12 from Othoca, but most of its Roman history is unknown.

A bishopric was founded around 400, with one probable bishop, Johannes, recorded about 500. In 1000 it was raised to a metropolitan archdiocese to match the prestige of the Giudice of Arborea, who resided there. After Orzocorre I of Arborea moved to Oristano in 1070 under pressure of Saracen raiders, the town was effectively abandoned and later used for centuries as a quarry. The diocese was suppressed in 1093 and its territory given to the new archdiocese of Oristano.

Tharros is an open-air museum with active excavations, where the tophet, the baths, temple foundations and houses and artisans' workshops can be seen. Most of its finds are held in the Archaeological Museum at Cagliari, the Antiquarium Arborense, the museum at Cabras and the British Museum. A 2021 study of ancient DNA found people from North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula among 14 individuals buried in its southern necropolis of the Punic Age.
tharu-people: The Tharu are recognised as an official ethnicity by the Government of Nepal and as a scheduled tribe by the Government of India. The origin of the name is uncertain. It may come from sthavir, a follower of Theravada Buddhism, and Tharu in the central Nepali Terai see themselves as the original people of the land and descendants of Gautama Buddha. The Rana Tharu of western Nepal connect the name to the Thar Desert and claim descent from Rajputs who moved to the forests in the 16th century, a claim some scholars reject. According to Alberuni, Tharu people had lived in the eastern Terai since at least the 10th century. In 2011 Nepal counted 1,737,470 Tharu, 6.6% of its population.

After the unification of Nepal in the late 18th century, members of the ruling families received land grants in the Terai and the right to collect revenue from the cultivators. The Tharu became bonded labourers in a system called Kamaiya. In 1854 Jung Bahadur Rana enforced the Muluki Ain, a general code that classed the Tharu among the touchable, enslavable, alcohol-drinking groups. In the late 1950s the World Health Organization helped the Nepalese government eradicate malaria in the forests of the central Terai, and after the programme with DDT in the 1960s many people from the hills and elsewhere settled there. Many Tharu families in the western Terai lost their land and were forced to work as Kamaiya.

When Chitwan's first protected areas were set up, Tharu communities were made to leave their lands, and when Chitwan National Park was designated, soldiers destroyed villages inside it. They were denied any right to own land, and so were left landless and poor.

In July 2000 Nepal abolished bonded labour under the Kamaiya system and declared the loan papers illegal. The families were freed from their debts but were left homeless and jobless. During the Nepalese Civil War the Tharu endured intense violence, and after the peace accord of 2006 Tharu organisations called for an autonomous Tharu state within a federal Nepal.

The Tharu consider themselves a people of the forest. In Chitwan they have lived in the forests for hundreds of years, practising short-fallow shifting cultivation of rice, wheat, mustard, maize and lentils and gathering forest products. They show resistance to malaria that research has linked to genes for thalassemia, although the immunity is limited, not complete, and many Tharu, especially babies, died of the disease. Different groups speak different languages, including variants of Bhojpuri in the centre and Maithili in the east. Their art includes Mokha wall painting, Ashtimki painting and Sikki grass crafts, and festivals include Maghe Sankranti and Jur Sital. Rana Tharu traditionally live in longhouses called Badaghar, with families of up to 31 members under a Mukhiya.
thatbyinnyu-temple: The temple stands just inside the south-eastern corner of the old city wall of Pagan. King Sithu I founded it in 1144/45, and according to the royal chronicles it was his second great temple after the Shwegugyi, the king being said to have given boatloads of rubies to both. It was built in a period of rededication to Theravada Buddhism and religious scholarship and completed in 1150/51. Work on the terraces was never finished: indentations there were meant to hold a series of over 500 ceramic plaques showing the jataka stories, which apparently were never set in place.

The brick temple, covered in white stucco with stone-paved terraces, is crowned by a sikhara tower with a hti at its pinnacle, and its style is somewhat similar to that of the nearby Ananda Temple. It rises from a platform about 58 m on each side, with an entry hall projecting on the east and smaller projections on the other three sides. Seen from outside it resembles stacked cubes separated by receding terraces, their corners set with stupa obelisks, and its architectural height is 61.3 metres. The taller Shwesandaw Pagoda, at least 100 m, is a stupa rather than a temple.

The building served as a monastery and library as well as a place of worship, housing monks, images, books and relics. Inside are pointed arches in the wide halls, barrel vaults elsewhere and two tiers of windows to each floor; murals once covered the ceilings, and the Buddha's footprints survive on the ceiling of the western porch. The scholar Paul Strachan calls it an expression of the self-confident Burmese spirit of nationhood.

The earthquake of 1975 damaged the finial, the main Buddha statue and the corner stupas and opened cracks up to 23 cm wide; repairs were finished by 1979 and the structure strengthened in the early 1990s. The magnitude 6.8 earthquake of 24 August 2016 left it among the 36 worst-hit structures. It was reinforced with Chinese help in 2017, and in April 2019 a Chinese archaeological team began a nine-year restoration. The temple is Monument #1597 of the Bagan Archaeological Area, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 6 July 2019.
thatta: Thatta is a city in the Pakistani province of Sindh. Its name refers to riverside settlements, and an 18th-century scholar, Ḳāni, offered two derivations, one from a word for migration to the city and one from the Sindhi thatt, a place of gathering. Thatta may stand on the site of ancient Patala, the main port on the Indus in the time of Alexander the Great, though the site of Patala has long been debated. It has also been identified by some historians with the seaport of Debal named by the Arab conquerors, while others place that port at modern Karachi.

The Sumra dynasty ruled from Thatta from 1051 for about three hundred years. In 1351 the Samma dynasty seized the city and made it their capital, and the Makli Necropolis rose to prominence as a burial ground in their time. Muhammad bin Tughluq died in 1351 on a campaign to capture Thatta, and Firuz Shah Tughlaq failed twice to subdue it, in 1361 and 1365. In 1520 Shah Beg of the Arghun-Tarkhun dynasty defeated the Samma ruler Jam Feroz. When Mirza Isa Khan I sought Portuguese aid in 1555, about 700 Portuguese soldiers arrived in 28 ships to find the conflict already won; when they were refused payment they plundered the town and killed many inhabitants in the Sack of Thatta of 1557.

From 1592 Thatta was governed by the Mughal Empire. Shah Jahan took refuge there as a prince, and in his reign Thatta Subah was created with its capital in the city. A storm nearly destroyed the city in 1637, and the Shah Jahan Mosque was given to it in 1647 as part of its rebuilding, though it was not completed until 1659. The Dutch East India Company kept a trading post there from 1652 to 1660, and in the 1650s the city had 2,000 looms.

Then the Indus silted up and shifted its course east during the second half of the 17th century, and the port was abandoned. The Kalhora dynasty took Thatta in 1736 and the Talpur dynasty later seized it. In the early 19th century its population had fallen to about 20,000 from a high of 200,000 a century before. Sindh passed to the British in 1843, and in 1847 Thatta was administered as part of the Bombay Presidency.

The Makli Necropolis, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is one of the world's largest cemeteries, with monumental tombs built between the 14th and 18th centuries in a syncretic funerary style characteristic of lower Sindh. The Shah Jahan Mosque is richly embellished with decorative tiles and is considered to have the most elaborate display of tile work in South Asia.
thaya: The Thaya (Czech Dyje) is a right tributary of the Morava River. It is formed by the confluence of the German Thaya and the Moravian Thaya at Raabs an der Thaya, and flows through Lower Austria and the South Moravian Region. Together with the German Thaya, its main source, it is 311 km long; counted from the confluence, it is 235.4 km. The German Thaya rises in the territory of Schweiggers at 658 m, and the river enters the Morava at Lanžhot at 151 m, the southernmost and lowest point of Moravia. The drainage basin covers 13,419 square kilometres and the river has 573 tributaries.

Both names, Thaya and Dyje, come from the Illyrian word duja, which can be translated as rushing river. The first written mention is from 985, when the name was written Taja. Part of the course forms the Austrian-Czech border. The most populated settlements on the river are the towns of Znojmo and Břeclav. For water management the Thaya and the German Thaya count as two different rivers with separate numbering of river kilometres. The largest reservoirs, the three Nové Mlýny reservoirs, are built directly on the river, with others at Znojmo and Vranov.

The river flows through the Podyjí and Thayatal national parks, where protected species include the European crayfish and the brown trout, and the common kingfisher nests along it. The confluence area with the Morava, with its pools, oxbow lakes and channels, is the most valuable ichthyological site in the Czech Republic: about 80 per cent of native Czech fish species live there, 15 per cent of them found only there. Since 2024 it has been protected as the Soutok protected landscape area. About 209 km of the river is navigable, and it passes through the Lednice–Valtice Cultural Landscape, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
the-anarchy: The war began as a succession crisis. Henry I intended his lands to pass to his only legitimate son, William Adelin, who drowned in the White Ship disaster of 1120. Henry then sought to leave the English throne to his daughter, Empress Matilda, but only partly persuaded the nobility to support her. On his death in 1135 his nephew Stephen of Blois seized the throne with the help of his brother Henry of Blois, bishop of Winchester.

Stephen and Matilda were first cousins. David I of Scotland invaded the north at once, and Stephen came to terms with him at Durham. In 1138 Robert of Gloucester, an illegitimate son of Henry I, renounced his fealty and declared for Matilda, triggering a rebellion in Kent and the south-west, while Geoffrey Plantagenet, Matilda's husband, invaded Normandy.

Matilda invaded in 1139 with Robert, landing at Arundel. Castles were easily defended, so fighting was mostly attrition: sieges, raiding and skirmishing, with armies of knights, infantry and many mercenaries. Matilda came to control the south-west and much of the Thames Valley, Stephen the south-east, and barons who supported neither held much of the country.

At the Battle of Lincoln on 2 February 1141 Stephen was captured, and his authority collapsed over most of the country. Matilda was driven out of London by hostile crowds before she could be crowned, and Stephen's wife Matilda of Boulogne captured Robert at the rout of Winchester, so the two sides exchanged their captives. Stephen almost captured Matilda at the Siege of Oxford in 1142, but she escaped across the frozen Thames.

Geoffrey conquered Normandy in her name in 1143 and was recognised as duke after taking Rouen in 1144. By the mid-1140s the war was stalemated. Rebel barons in the north and in East Anglia grew powerful, and regions of heavy fighting were widely devastated. Robert of Gloucester died in 1147, and Matilda returned to Normandy in 1148, leaving her eldest son Henry FitzEmpress to continue. In 1152 the Church refused to recognise Stephen's son Eustace as the next king.

Henry invaded in 1153, and the armies faced each other at the siege of Wallingford Castle, but the Church brokered a truce. During the negotiations Eustace died, and the Treaty of Wallingford let Stephen keep the throne while recognising Henry as his successor. Stephen died of a stomach disorder on 25 October 1154, and Henry became the first Angevin king of England. A chronicler of Peterborough wrote that men said openly that Christ and his saints were asleep. The name the Anarchy was coined by Victorian historians, though modern historians question whether it is accurate.
the-ballad-of-the-green-berets: Sadler began writing the song while he was training to be a Special Forces medic, and after earning his Parachutist Badge he knew that one line would mention "silver wings upon their chests". The words were written in part in honour of U.S. Army Specialist 5 James Gabriel Jr., a Special Forces operator and the first native Hawaiian to die in Vietnam, killed by Viet Cong gunfire on a training mission with the South Vietnamese Army on 8 April 1962. A verse naming Gabriel was not used in the recorded version.

A demonstration tape was made in a rudimentary recording studio at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, with the help of Gerry Gitell and Lieutenant General William P. Yarborough. Sadler then recorded the song and eleven others with Sid Bass at RCA's 24th Street Studios in New York City, and the single came out together with the album Ballads of the Green Berets.

In the United States the single shipped two million copies in its first five weeks, then the fastest-selling single in RCA's history. It topped the Billboard Hot 100 in March 1966 and stayed at number one for five weeks, and it also reached number one on Billboard's Easy Listening chart and number two on its Country survey. Billboard's year-end chart of December 1966 placed it tenth, but a later revision ranked it first for the year; on Cash Box's year-end chart it tied for first with "California Dreamin'" by the Mamas and the Papas. The single sold more than nine million copies.

Sadler sang it on The Ed Sullivan Show on 30 January 1966 and on The Hollywood Palace and The Jimmy Dean Show. It was one of the few popular songs of the Vietnam War years to cast the military in a positive light, dwelling on the soldiers rather than on battle, and the musicologist R. Serge Denisoff called it the most successful topical song of the Vietnam War era in sales and chart activity.

The song was used in the 1968 John Wayne film The Green Berets, based on Robin Moore's book. Wayne asked for it as his theme, while the film's composer, Miklós Rózsa, feared it would sound old-fashioned. Rózsa still made two arrangements of it for the opening and closing credits; he thought them "corny" but judged that Wayne could "get away" with the song.
the-battle-of-algiers-film: The film was inspired by Souvenirs de la Bataille d'Alger, a 1962 book by the FLN commander Saadi Yacef, who wrote it while a prisoner of the French. After independence Yacef was released and became a leader in the new government, and the Algerian government backed the adaptation of his memoir. Salash Baazi, an FLN leader exiled by the French, approached the Italian director Gillo Pontecorvo and the screenwriter Franco Solinas with the project. The film uses composite characters: Colonel Mathieu is a composite of several French counterinsurgency officers, especially Jacques Massu, although Yacef said he was based more on Marcel Bigeard.

The Battle of Algiers is an Italian-Algerian film of 1966 about the Algerian War. Pontecorvo and the cinematographer Marcello Gatti shot it in black and white, in the style of a newsreel, and American releases carried a notice that not one foot of newsreel was used.

Pontecorvo cast non-professional Algerians, many of whom had lived through the real battle; the only professional actor was Jean Martin, who played Mathieu, and Yacef himself plays El-Hadi Jafar. The story follows Ali La Pointe and the organisation of FLN cells in the Casbah, and the French paratroopers sent to defeat them. Both sides are shown committing atrocities against civilians. Pontecorvo wrote the music with Ennio Morricone.

The film won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival and was nominated for three Academy Awards. In France it caused political controversy: the French journalists at Venice left the festival when it won, and the government banned it for a year. No private distributor would take it, and it was released only in 1971, after bomb threats from the far-right Organisation Armee Secrete.

In the United States the response was more positive from the start. Insurgent groups and state authorities have both treated it as a commentary on urban guerrilla warfare, and Pontecorvo replied that it champions everyone deprived of his rights. Filmmakers such as Stanley Kubrick and Costa-Gavras praised or drew on it.
the-beatles: In November 1956 the 16-year-old John Lennon formed a skiffle group with friends from Quarry Bank High School for Boys in Liverpool, named the Quarrymen after the school song. Paul McCartney met Lennon on 6 July 1957 and joined shortly after, and in 1958 George Harrison, then 15, was enlisted as lead guitarist after playing Raunchy for Lennon on the upper deck of a Liverpool bus. Stuart Sutcliffe joined on bass in January 1960 and suggested the name Beatals, in tribute to Buddy Holly and the Crickets. By mid-August 1960 they were simply the Beatles.

The Beatles built their reputation playing clubs in Liverpool and in Hamburg, West Germany, from 1960. Ringo Starr officially joined in 1962. Manager Brian Epstein shaped them into a professional act, and the producer George Martin developed their recordings. After signing with EMI they had their first hit, Love Me Do, in late 1962. By early 1964 they were international stars, leading the British Invasion of the American pop market. They retired from live performance in 1966 and made more sophisticated albums, among them Revolver (1966) and Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967). In 1968 they founded Apple Corps. The band broke up in 1970.

Their arrival in the United States in 1964 is credited with beginning the album era. Young adults abroad name them among the people they most associate with British culture. In 1965 Queen Elizabeth II appointed the four members Members of the Order of the British Empire, and they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1988, their first year of eligibility.
the-blitz: Before the war, writers on air power such as Giulio Douhet and Billy Mitchell held that bombers could not be stopped and that bombing civilians would collapse morale. From July to September 1940 the Luftwaffe attacked Fighter Command and its airfields to gain air superiority as a prelude to invasion. With the Royal Air Force still fighting, Adolf Hitler and Reichsmarschall Hermann Göring ordered a new policy of mass attacks on British cities on 6 September 1940, beginning with London.

Britain had prepared. London held nine million people, a fifth of the population, and the Auxiliary Fire Service had 138,000 personnel by July 1939. Civilians had been issued 50 million respirators. Night defences were weak, however: in July 1940 only 1,200 heavy and 549 light anti-aircraft guns stood in the whole country.

The first raids, from 7 September 1940, were aimed chiefly at the Port of London. The Luftwaffe relied on radio beams such as Knickebein to find targets at night, and the British, alerted by R. V. Jones, learned to jam and bend them. After October the campaign was fought at night. From November 1940 it turned to industrial cities, above all in the West Midlands. The raid on Coventry on the night of 14 November destroyed most of the city centre and its cathedral, damaged about 21 factories seriously and caused a brief 20 percent dip in aircraft production.

A large raid on London on 29 December 1940 produced a firestorm known as the Second Great Fire of London. In 1941 Hitler, prompted by Erich Raeder of the Kriegsmarine, ordered attacks on British ports and shipping to support the submarine war. The campaign ended with a large raid on the night of 10–11 May 1941; the last date given for it is 16 May.

The Luftwaffe dropped around 40,000 long tons of bombs, but British production rose steadily; the chief effect was to force the dispersal of aircraft and component manufacture. Most severely hit cities took 10 to 15 days to recover, Birmingham three months. The German command lacked a method for destroying British industry, and its effort was spread across many targets. Between June 1940 and March 1941 it recorded the loss of 2,265 aircraft.

The image of national solidarity, the Blitz spirit, was questioned by Angus Calder in The Myth of the Blitz (1991), who pointed to divisions of class and anti-social behaviour. After the raids, 750,000 tons of London rubble went by rail to make runways on airfields in East Anglia.
the-bonnie-banks-o-loch-lomond: In the best-known words the singer recalls the banks where he and his true love walked, and the chorus answers: "O ye'll tak' the high road, and I'll tak' the low road, And I'll be in Scotland afore ye", for the lovers will never meet again. One reading ties the song to December 1745, when Bonnie Prince Charlie retreated to Scotland, and hears a soldier rueing his sacrifice for the king; in Celtic mythology the low road was a fairy route by which a soldier killed abroad returned home in spirit.

The other reading makes the chorus the last words of a Jacobite rebel before his execution, perhaps at Carlisle, where dozens of rebels were executed: he sees his lover at the gallows and tells her they will meet again in Scotland by different routes. The song later became, despite these Jacobite readings, one of a handful of folk signifiers of British unity as the empire grew.

One of the earliest printings of the music was made in 1840 by Paterson and Sons in Edinburgh, titled "Bonnie Loch Loman" and credited to "a lady", with arrangements by Finlay Dunn and John Thomson. Lady John Scott was often named as the composer, but she only wrote down the tune and words after hearing a boy sing them in the streets of Edinburgh. Precedents for the tune have been found in the Danish and Faroese "Dankonning lod gribe en havfrue fin" and in "Godesses", a tune in John Playford's 1651 collection The Dancing Master.

Both the 1840 printing and Lady John Scott's words differ markedly from the common form of today, while an 1849 broadside, "Flora's Lament for Her Charlie", largely parallels it. The song is often wrongly credited to the poet Andrew Lang, who in 1876 wrote his own poem "The Bonnie Banks o' Loch Lomond, 1746". The Irish song "Red Is the Rose", popularised by Tommy Makem, is sung to the same melody with similar themes.

Ralph Vaughan Williams arranged the song for baritone and male choir in 1921, and Charles Ives quoted it in "The Alcotts" movement of his Concord Sonata. The jazz singer Maxine Sullivan recorded it on 6 August 1937 in an arrangement by Claude Thornhill, and her swing version led other acts to swing folk songs. The Scottish band Runrig released it as their first single in 1982 and recorded it again in 2007 with 50,000 supporters of the Scotland national football team for the BBC's Children in Need appeal.
the-bonnie-blue-flag: Harry McCarthy first sang the song at a concert in Jackson, Mississippi, and performed it again in September 1861 at the New Orleans Academy of Music for the First Texas Volunteer Infantry regiment as it mustered in. The New Orleans music publishing house of A. E. Blackmar issued six editions between 1861 and 1864, with three further arrangements. When Major General Benjamin Butler captured New Orleans, he is said to have arrested Blackmar, fined him $500, destroyed the copies of the music and ordered a fine of $25 for anyone caught singing or whistling it.

The first line, "We are a band of brothers, and native to the soil", recalls the St Crispin's Day speech in William Shakespeare's Henry V. The Library of Congress copy of 1861 continues "Fighting for our liberty with treasure, blood, and toil", while another 1861 version has "fighting for the property we gained by honest toil". Eleven further editions were published with different words, and the Confederate widow Annie Chambers Ketchum published new verses as "The Gathering Song".

The full song names the seceding states verse by verse, from South Carolina to Tennessee, ending with the single star of the flag grown to eleven. For the sake of the metre the third verse changes the order of secession: Alabama is said to take South Carolina by the hand, though Mississippi and Florida left the Union before it. Another verse hails Davis as "our loved President" and Stephens as a "statesman rare".

As with many songs of the American Civil War, the tune also served the Union. J. L. Geddes, a British-born colonel, wrote "The Bonnie Flag With the Stripes and Stars" in 1863, singing of the Union and equal rights, and a Mrs C. Sterett published another Union version in New York. The "Song of the Irish Volunteers", sung by the 69th New York regiment of the Irish Brigade, used the same melody.

The song has been heard in many films, among them Gone with the Wind of 1939, where Rhett Butler names his daughter Bonnie Blue Butler, The Searchers, The Horse Soldiers, The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, Glory and Gettysburg.
the-book-of-the-courtier: Castiglione worked on the book for twenty years, beginning in 1508, drawing on his own years as a courtier in the Duchy of Urbino and, later, on the Spanish court he knew as Ambassador of the Holy See from 1524 to 1529. It was printed by the Aldine Press just before his death. The work portrays the small courts of the High Renaissance that were vanishing in the Italian Wars and pays tribute to the friends of his youth, above all Duchess Elisabetta Gonzaga of Urbino, who died in 1526.

The book takes the form of conversations held over four nights among the courtiers of Urbino; Castiglione, though then a member of the court, is not one of the speakers. They debate whether the courtier needs noble rank, physical prowess, modesty and a pleasing physique, and along the way discuss nobility, humour, women and love. The ideal that emerges joins a warrior spirit and athletic skill to a good knowledge of the humanities, the classics and the fine arts, with a good voice and proper bearing.

Much of the discussion concerns speech. Count Ludovico, echoing Cicero and Quintilian on delivery, asks for a voice that is sonorous, clear and sweet, and makes sprezzatura, a studied nonchalance that conceals art, the source of grace (grazia). Castiglione chose not to imitate Boccaccio's Tuscan, writing instead in the Italian of his native Lombardy; the Count argues that old Tuscan words would be an affectation and that style, authority and grace matter more than the dialect chosen.

The book quickly became popular and was read as a courtesy book or book of manners, alongside later works such as Giovanni Della Casa's Il Galateo (1558) and Stefano Guazzo's The Civil Conversation (1574), though it is at once a drama, an open-ended philosophical discussion and an essay, and has also been read as a veiled political allegory. Editions appeared in six languages and in twenty European centres. Thomas Hoby's English translation of 1561 shaped the English upper class's idea of the gentleman, especially in Elizabethan England.
the-british-grenadiers: The melody came into Britain as a military march during the reign of William III, from 1689 to 1702, and resembles a march written for Prince John William of Friesland. Henry Grattan Flood proposed another source, the 1672 Dutch march Wilhelmus van Nassouwe. The song is said to commemorate an assault by 700 British grenadiers on the French-held fortress of Namur in August 1695, during the Nine Years' War. A Granadeer's March was named in a London publication of 1706, though it may not be the same tune, and Francis Grose quoted two lines of the words in his Military Antiquities of 1786 as part of a song he already thought old.

The song honours grenadiers in general, not the Grenadier Guards alone, and every Fusilier unit was entitled to it. It is the regimental quick march of the Royal Artillery and the Honourable Artillery Company since 1716, the Corps of Royal Engineers since 1787, and the Grenadier Guards and the Royal Regiment of Fusiliers since 1763, and an authorised march of artillery and grenadier regiments in Australia, Canada and Gibraltar. Its standard band orchestration was approved in 1762. The words speak of storming palisades and throwing grenades from the glacis, of fusees, the short muskets of grenadier officers, and of the caps, pouches and looped coats that marked these troops. It is heard each year at Trooping the Colour.

The tune was popular in Britain and North America through the 18th and 19th centuries and was set to many other texts, church hymns among them. Joseph Warren wrote the parody Free America to it in 1774, and the Irish poet Edward Lysaght used it for a ballad dedicated to Henry Grattan. Ignaz Moscheles used it in the finale of his Piano Concerto No. 4 of 1823, and Charles Ives in Three Places in New England. Students of Girton College set new words to it in 1871 in honour of the first three women to pass the Cambridge tripos. Film and television use it to signal a British setting.
the-brus: Written in octosyllabic lines, the poem gives a historical and chivalric account of Robert the Bruce and Sir James Douglas from the events leading up to the English invasion of 1296 to Scotland's restored position between the Treaty of 1328 and the death of Thomas Randolph, Earl of Moray, in 1332. At its centre, in placement as well as weight, stands a long account of the Battle of Bannockburn of 1314, often judged the finest part of the work.

Bruce overshadows all his companions: of Edward Bruce's victories in Galloway Barbour says only that he might have rivalled any of his contemporaries except his brother. The king is drawn as a hero of the chivalric romance, freedom is to be won at all costs, and the best-known passage begins "A! fredome is a noble thing". The poem opens with a proem in which Barbour says he will tell a true story so that the deeds of brave men are not forgotten.

Barbour wrote the poem in about 1375, in the words of one critic, to throw behind the new king, Robert II, who gave Barbour a pension, the weight of his grandfather's achievements and reputation. It is a romance based on a lost life of Douglas and on one or more chronicles of King Robert's times. At the start Barbour conflates three Bruces into the single figure of his hero, probably on purpose; the historian Archie Duncan notes his fondness for exaggerated army sizes, and the order of events is sometimes changed.

No one has doubted Barbour's authorship, but it has been argued that the surviving text is an edited copy, perhaps by John Ramsay, a Perth scribe who wrote out both extant manuscripts, one in the Advocates Library in Edinburgh and the other at St John's College, Cambridge.

Despite its errors of fact, the poem has more historical truth than is usual in verse chronicles such as Blind Harry's Wallace of the following century, and it has long been treated as a trustworthy source for the period. Its account of these events became a keystone of Scotland's national story, and its influence can be seen in Robert Burns's Scots Wha Hae and in Walter Scott's The Lord of the Isles and Castle Dangerous.
the-bund: The term bund was borrowed into English from Hindustani, where it meant a dyke or embankment; in the Chinese treaty ports it was applied to an embanked quay. The Chinese name means outer bank, distinguishing this riverfront from the inner bank next to the old walled city of Shanghai. The Bund stretches one mile (1.6 km) along the Huangpu River, traditionally from Yan'an Road in the south to the Waibaidu Bridge over Suzhou Creek in the north. It faces the skyscrapers of Lujiazui in Pudong and centres on a stretch of Zhongshan Road, named after Sun Yat-sen.

The area lies north of the old walled city. It began as a British settlement, and the British and American settlements were combined in the International Settlement in 1863. From the 1860s to the 1930s it was the centre of the foreign establishment in Shanghai, a legally protected treaty port, with banks and trading houses from Britain, France, the United States, Japan and other countries, the British consulate, the Shanghai Club and a newspaper. By the 1940s it housed the headquarters of many major financial institutions in China.

After the Communist victory in the Chinese Civil War many institutions moved to Hong Kong in the 1950s, and statues of colonial figures were removed. From the late 1970s buildings returned to their former uses. After typhoon floods a tall levee was built, and in the 1990s Zhongshan Road was widened to ten lanes, which removed most of the parkland. From 2008 traffic was reorganised, with six lanes put into a tunnel and the promenade widened; the Bund reopened on 28 March 2010, before the World Expo. On 31 December 2014 a stampede in a crowd estimated at 300,000 killed at least 36 people and injured 47.

Some 52 buildings in Western classical and modern styles, among them Neo-Classical, Gothic Revival and Art Deco, line the west side of the road. They include the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation's building of 1923, the Customs House of 1927 with a clock modelled on Big Ben, and Sassoon House with the Cathay Hotel, now part of the Peace Hotel. At the northern end, Huangpu Park holds the Shanghai People's Heroes Memorial Tower, built in 1993.
the-californias: The Baja California Peninsula is bounded by water on three sides, the Pacific Ocean to the south and west and the Gulf of California to the east, while Alta California had the Pacific on the west and deserts on the east. The Peninsular Ranges, the eastern Transverse Ranges and the Sierra Nevada, with the Colorado, Mojave and Great Basin deserts in their rain shadows, kept Spanish settlement near the coast. The eastern border of upper Las Californias was never officially defined under Spanish or Mexican rule; a northern boundary was set by the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819.

The plural name goes back to a time when the land was thought to be one or several islands. The first Spanish attempt at occupation, the Jesuit Eusebio Kino's Misión San Bruno of 1683, failed. In 1697 Juan María de Salvatierra founded Misión de Nuestra Señora de Loreto Conchó, the nucleus of Loreto, the first permanent settlement and first administrative centre of the province. The Jesuits went on to found 18 missions in the lower two-thirds of the peninsula before their expulsion in 1767, when Franciscans took over under Governor Gaspar de Portolá.

A dispatch of 28 January 1768 from Viceroy de Croix and the visitador José de Gálvez established the province name Las Californias. Expeditions led by Portolá in 1769, Pedro Fages in 1770 and Juan Bautista de Anza in 1774–76 carried settlement north to the San Francisco Bay Area, and in 1804 the province was divided into Alta California, with its capital at Monterey, and Baja California. Independent Mexico made both territories; a single department of Las Californias existed from 1836 under the Siete Leyes until their repeal in 1847.

Under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 2 February 1848 most of Alta California passed to the United States, and the new border ran slightly north of the old Alta-Baja line. In 1853 William Walker tried to seize Baja California and Sonora for a Republic of Sonora but was defeated by Mexican forces under Antonio Meléndrez.

Seven American states were formed wholly or partly from the old Californias, beginning with California in 1850. Baja California became a state of Mexico in 1952 and Baja California Sur in 1974. The Commission of the Californias is a forum for cooperation between the three state governments.
the-canon-of-medicine: The English title comes from the medieval Latin Canon Medicinae, a translation of the Arabic al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, in which canon, often rendered as law or legal code, suggests an ordered system or a complete, universal encyclopedia. The medical traditions of Galen, and through him Hippocrates, had dominated Islamic medicine from its beginnings, and Avicenna sought to fit them into Aristotle's natural philosophy. He began the work in Gorganj, continued it in Rey and finished it in Hamadan in 1025. The result has been called a clear and ordered summa of the medical knowledge of his time, and a more concise reference than Galen's twenty volumes.

The first of the five books treats basic medical and physiological principles, anatomy, regimen and general therapy. It sets out the four causes of illness on Aristotelian lines, the four elements, the temperaments and the humours, and holds that the body cannot be restored to health unless the causes of health and disease are known. Book 2 is a materia medica that lists alphabetically about 800 simple substances of plant, mineral and animal origin, with the properties of each, and gives seven rules for testing new drugs, partly taken from Galen.

Book 3 describes the diseases of each part of the body from head to foot, with cause, symptoms, diagnosis, prognosis and treatment; its chapters on the nervous system and on strokes are noted for their detail. Conditions of the whole body, such as fevers, poisons, wounds and fractures, are covered in Book 4, which closes with a treatise on personal hygiene. Book 5 is a formulary of 650 compound drugs drawn from Arabic, Indian and Greek sources, with Avicenna's comments on the differences between recipes and on which remedies proved effective.

The work was translated from Arabic into Latin as Canon medicinae, and its systematic arrangement and its combination of Galen's medicine with Aristotle's philosophy helped it enter European scholastic medicine. Medical scholars began to use it in the thirteenth century, and university courses took it up from the fourteenth. Its influence declined in the sixteenth century as humanists preferred ancient Greek and Roman authorities to Arabic ones, though others defended Avicenna's innovations. The earliest printed Latin edition appeared in 1472, and covered book three only. Eleven complete incunables followed, then fourteen more Latin editions until 1608. The Canon remains an important text in Unani medicine in India.
the-canterbury-tales: The Canterbury Tales is an anthology of twenty-four stories, mostly in verse, written in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer between 1387 and 1400. They are presented as part of a fictional storytelling contest among pilgrims travelling from London to the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral. The General Prologue introduces some 30 pilgrims, and Chaucer's stated plan was four stories from each, two on the way to Canterbury and two on the way back, about 120 in all. Most scholars think the work was incomplete at the end of his life. Chaucer began it during the years when he was Controller of Customs and Justice of the Peace from 1386 and Clerk of the King's Works from 1389.

Frame tales were an established genre, but Chaucer's collection differs from most in its intense variation. Most collections kept to a theme, usually a religious one, and even in the Decameron the storytellers stuck to the theme of the day. A pilgrimage brought together a diverse company, and the contest invites the reader to compare tales in many genres, from the Knight's Tale of chivalry to others in lower styles. Two tales, Sir Topas and The Tale of Melibee, are told by Chaucer himself, who travels with the pilgrims in his own story.

The tales reflect the controversies of the late 14th century: the Western Schism, Lollardy under John Wycliffe, the abuse of indulgences by pardoners, and the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. They are among the first English literary works to mention paper. Several characters are religious figures, so religion is a major theme, and the Knight's Tale examines chivalry, which was in decline in Chaucer's day, though scholars dispute whether it was meant to show its flaws.

No manuscript exists in Chaucer's own hand. There are 84 manuscripts and four incunabula editions, more than for any other vernacular English text except the Prick of Conscience. They vary in minor and major ways, and there is no agreement on a complete version or on Chaucer's intended order. Most modern editions divide the tales into ten Fragments, following the Ellesmere order, while Victorian editors used the nine Groups of F. J. Furnivall.

In the 15th century John Lydgate and Thomas Occleve praised Chaucer as the best English poet, and the Knight's Tale was the most respected. The incompleteness led medieval authors to add tales, such as the Tale of Beryn, to some manuscripts. The work may have helped popularise the English vernacular in literature, as against French or Latin. Shakespeare and John Fletcher based The Two Noble Kinsmen on the Knight's Tale, first performed in 1613 or 1614.
the-communist-manifesto: In spring 1847 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels joined the League of the Just, which became the League of Communists. At its first congress, held from 2 to 9 June, the League asked Engels to draft a statement of its programme. He wrote the Draft of a Communist Confession of Faith, a catechism of 22 questions, and in October produced the Principles of Communism, a longer one of 25 questions. Several scholars see the kernel of the Manifesto in this second text.

Marx delayed the work while lecturing on political economy and writing for the Deutsche-Brüsseler-Zeitung.
