In late January 1848 the League's Central Committee sent him an ultimatum demanding the manuscript by 1 February. The Manifesto was written over six to seven weeks, and only one page of draft is known to survive. Engels is credited as co-author, but the final text was penned by Marx; Engels wrote in 1883 that its basic thought belonged solely to Marx.

The Manifesto has a preamble and four sections. The preamble opens with the line about a spectre haunting Europe and urges communists to state their views openly. The first section, Bourgeois and Proletarians, sets out historical materialism: all earlier societies were marked by an exploiting minority and an exploited majority, and under capitalism the industrial working class, the proletariat, stands against the owners of the means of production, the bourgeoisie.

The authors argue that the bourgeoisie, by constantly revolutionising production, displaced feudal powers, and that in doing so it creates its own grave-diggers. In their view the proletariat will become conscious of its power and overthrow it, leading to a classless society. They also proposed ten measures for a society moving towards communism, which their 1872 preface called dated.

The pamphlet was published anonymously in late February 1848 in London, as a 23-page German text issued by the Communist Workers' Educational Association. Marx was expelled by the Belgian police on 4 March. The first English version, translated by Helen Macfarlane, appeared in November 1850 in George Julian Harney's Chartist paper The Red Republican, which also named the authors for the first time.

After years of obscurity the text revived in the early 1870s, through Marx's role in the First International, his support for the Paris Commune of 1871 and the treason trial of German Social Democratic leaders, where prosecutors read it into the record. A new German edition of 1872 first used the short title The Communist Manifesto. After the October Revolution of 1917 it became required reading for Leninist parties, and by its centenary in 1948 general publishers were printing it widely.
the-consolation-of-philosophy: Boethius wrote the work during a one-year imprisonment, awaiting trial and eventual execution for alleged treason under the Ostrogothic King Theodoric the Great. He had stood at the height of power in Rome as magister officiorum and was brought down by treachery. The book is a conversation between himself and a female personification of philosophy, Lady Philosophy, who discusses the transitory nature of wealth, fame and power and calls the things of the mind the one true good. In Book I Boethius laments his imprisonment; Book II uses the wheel of Fortune; Book III turns to the divine source of wisdom; Book IV treats good and evil; and Book V argues that Chance is guided by Providence and takes up free will.

The work is prosimetrical, written in alternating sections of prose and metered verse, in which Boethius shows a virtuosic command of the forms of Latin poetry. It is classified as a Menippean satire, a fusion of allegorical tale, Platonic dialogue and lyrical poetry, and is heavily influenced by Plato. Boethius answers religious questions without reference to Christianity, relying on natural philosophy and the Classical Greek tradition. Henry Chadwick called it the work of a Platonist who is also a Christian.

From the Carolingian epoch to the end of the Middle Ages and beyond it was one of the most popular philosophical works, read by statesmen, poets, historians, philosophers and theologians, and through Boethius much of the thought of the Classical period reached the medieval West. Close to four hundred manuscripts survive. King Alfred translated it into Old English, Notker Labeo into Old High German, Jean de Meun into Old French and Geoffrey Chaucer into Middle English as Boece; Queen Elizabeth I also made a translation. Its themes echo in Dante, Milton and Chaucer's Knight's Tale, and the wheel of Fortune was popular throughout the Middle Ages.
the-crystal-palace: The commission in charge of the Great Exhibition was established in January 1850, and the project was to be funded by public subscription. An executive building committee that included Isambard Kingdom Brunel and Robert Stephenson, chaired by William Cubitt, invited designs on 15 March 1850. The building had to be temporary, simple, cheap and quick to build, since the exhibition was already scheduled to open on 1 May 1851. The name may come from a piece by Douglas Jerrold in the satirical magazine Punch in July 1850, which spoke of a palace of very crystal.

Joseph Paxton's modular design was scaled around the size of the glass panes made by Chance Brothers of Smethwick, the largest then available, at 10 inches by 49 inches. Nearly the whole surface could therefore be glazed with identical panes, which cut cost and building time. More than 1,000 iron columns carried 2,224 trellis girders. Fox, Henderson and Co took possession of the site in July 1850, and more than 5,000 navvies worked on it. It was completed in thirty-nine weeks, with 293,000 panes of glass.

The Great Exhibition ran from 1 May to 15 October 1851, and Queen Victoria opened it. Its objects ranged from the Koh-i-Noor diamond to a hydraulic press and a fire engine. Prices were reduced so that working people could attend from 26 May. Over six million admissions were counted, and the surplus of £186,000 helped found the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Science Museum and the Natural History Museum in South Kensington.

A consortium of eight businessmen moved the building to Penge Place, at the top of Sydenham Hill, and rebuilt it from 1852 in a quite different, enlarged form. It stood there from June 1854. Its courts told the history of art, and the park held models of dinosaurs made by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins. The site also hosted the FA Cup Final from 1895 to 1914. In the First World War more than 125,000 men were trained there for the navy. The move cost far more than the original building, and the company never repaid its debt.

On the evening of 30 November 1936 an explosion in the women's cloakroom started a fire, and the Penge fire brigade was called. Eighty-nine fire engines and over 400 firemen attended, but within hours the Palace was destroyed. The fire spread quickly in high winds, helped by dry timber flooring and a large quantity of flammable material, and its glow was visible across eight counties.
the-deluge: In a wider sense the term covers the period from the Khmelnytsky Uprising of 1648 to the Truce of Andrusovo in 1667. Bohdan Khmelnytsky led Zaporozhian Cossacks and Ukrainian peasants against Polish and Lithuanian magnates, and the revolt sharpened the rivalry between Russia and the Commonwealth over Ukraine. In June 1654 the forces of Tsar Alexis invaded the eastern half of the Commonwealth and took Smolensk on 3 October 1654.

Sweden had a large army and little money to pay it, and the Commonwealth, weakened by war with the Cossacks and Russia, seemed easy prey. King John II Casimir lacked support among the nobility, and some nobles favoured Charles X Gustav of Sweden. Two Lithuanian princes, Janusz Radziwiłł and Bogusław Radziwiłł, signed the Treaty of Kėdainiai in 1655, which would have placed two duchies carved from Lithuania under Swedish protection.

In July 1655 two Swedish armies entered Greater Poland, which had not seen war for centuries. The noble levy gathered near Ujście lacked gunpowder, cannon and food, and two magnates quarrelled over whether to fight. The Swedes occupied the remaining half of the country. John Casimir returned from exile and reached Lwów on 10 February 1656. Polish guerrilla warfare harassed the Swedes, and Charles Gustav abandoned the siege of Zamość and began to retreat on 3 March 1656.

George II Rákóczi of Transylvania, once Poland's ally, joined the Swedish side, and the Treaty of Radnot of December 1656 proposed to divide the Commonwealth among Charles X Gustav, Bogusław Radziwiłł, Frederick William of Brandenburg, Khmelnytsky and Rákóczi. In 1658 Polish and Austrian forces besieged Toruń, which capitulated on 30 December. The Treaty of Oliva ended the war with Sweden on 3 May 1660.

By the Treaty of Oliva Poland gave up most of Livonia, John II Casimir renounced his claim to the Swedish throne while keeping the title of king of Sweden for life, and Sweden pledged freedom of trade in the Baltic. The war with Russia ended with the Truce of Andrusovo in 1667, which gave Russia Left-bank Ukraine.

The Commonwealth lost approximately one third of its population and its status as a great power. Of Warsaw's pre-war population of 20,000 only 2,000 remained, and by Polish estimates 188 cities and towns, 136 churches, 89 palaces and 81 castles were completely destroyed. Swedish troops took thousands of works of art, books and valuables, most of them never returned. Robert I. Frost argued that the Deluge began a period of decline, while Timothy Snyder and Andrew Wilson stressed the failure of the Treaty of Hadiach of 1658 to keep Ukraine within the Commonwealth.
the-dream-of-the-rood: The poem is written in alliterative verse and falls into three parts by speaker. In the first (lines 1–27) the dreamer sees the Cross covered with gems and feels his own wretchedness beside it, until he notices that amid the stones it is stained with blood. In the second (lines 28–121) the Cross tells its story: enemies cut it down and carried it away, and it learnt that it was to bear not a criminal but Christ. Pierced with nails and mocked as he was, it stands with him as a victor, is raised and adorned with gold and silver, and charges the dreamer to tell others. In the third (lines 122–156) the dreamer praises God and hopes for eternal life.

The Vercelli Book, a manuscript now in the Italian city of Vercelli, holds the poem among twenty-three homilies and six religious poems, among them Andreas, The Fates of the Apostles and Elene. Runic passages on the narrow side panels of the Ruthwell Cross give part of its crucifixion narrative in an early Northumbrian dialect. It is unclear whether a whole poem existed when the cross was erected, and recent scholarship tends to see the runes as a later addition to the monument. The eleventh-century Brussels Cross bears a distich that was probably inspired by the poem.

The author is unknown. Nineteenth-century scholars such as Daniel H. Haigh and George Stephens credited it to Cædmon, and Franz Dietrich to Cynewulf, whose signed Elene stands in the same manuscript; neither attribution is accepted now. Leonard Neidorf has argued from metre, vocabulary and syntax that at least two poets contributed to it.

Scholars read the poem as a meeting of the Germanic heroic tradition and Christian doctrine. Christ appears as a warrior who unclothes himself and leaps onto the Cross, and the Cross as a loyal retainer forced to take part in his lord's execution; Bruce Mitchell called the poem the central literary document for understanding that resolution of competing cultures. Richard North has argued that its image of Christ's death draws on an Anglian ideology of the world tree, while others see an Anglo-Saxon re-imagining of Christianity. Rebecca Hinton has compared the dream to early medieval Irish sacramental penance.
the-emergency-india: Between 1967 and 1971 Indira Gandhi gained near-absolute control of the government and the Indian National Congress by concentrating power in the Prime Minister's Secretariat. When the Supreme Court held in the Golaknath case of 1967 that Parliament could not amend fundamental rights, Parliament passed the 24th Amendment in 1971 to nullify it, and the 26th Amendment likewise reversed a ruling on the princes' privy purses. Unrest followed, notably the Nav Nirman movement in Gujarat from December 1973 to March 1974, which forced the state's chief minister to resign, and the assassination of the railway minister Lalit Narayan Mishra by a bomb. Raj Narain, whom she had defeated in 1971, brought charges of election fraud against her in the Allahabad High Court.

President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed issued the proclamation under Article 352 of the Constitution because of a prevailing "Internal Disturbance", and the Emergency took effect on 25 June 1975. The government cited threats to national security, a recent war with Pakistan, drought, the 1973 oil crisis and strikes that it said had paralysed administration. Siddhartha Shankar Ray, chief minister of West Bengal, had proposed the step. The order let the prime minister rule by decree, elections were postponed and civil liberties were suspended. More than 100,000 opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned, among them Jayaprakash Narayan, Morarji Desai and Atal Bihari Vajpayee, and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and Jamaat-e-Islami were banned. The press was censored: the Indian Express published a blank editorial on 28 June.

The 42nd Amendment made extensive changes to the Constitution. In September 1976 Sanjay Gandhi began a mass sterilisation programme, and 8.3 million sterilisations were recorded in 1976-1977, most of them forced, against 2.7 million the year before. Demolitions in Delhi displaced 700,000 people. Opposition continued: the Akali Dal's Democracy Bachao Morcha, launched in Amritsar on 9 July, led over 40,000 people to court arrest. Others supported the Emergency, among them Vinoba Bhave, J. R. D. Tata and Khushwant Singh.

On 18 January 1977 Gandhi called elections for March and released several opposition leaders, though others stayed in prison. The Emergency officially ended on 21 March 1977, after the Janata movement campaigned on a choice between "democracy and dictatorship". The Janata administration's attempts to try officials and Congress politicians for abuses were largely unsuccessful, and only a few low-level officials were convicted. The Emergency's legacy remains controversial, and it is the subject of novels and films, several of which were banned, among them Gulzar's Aandhi and Amrit Nahata's Kissa Kursi Ka.
the-exodus: The Exodus is told across Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. In Genesis the Israelites had come to live in the Land of Goshen in Egypt during a famine, under the protection of Joseph, a high official at the pharaoh's court. Exodus begins with a new pharaoh who did not know Joseph and who, alarmed by the number and strength of the Israelites, enslaves them and has them build the store cities of Pithom and Rameses. One child is hidden in a basket on the Nile and adopted by the pharaoh's daughter, who names him Moses. As a young man he kills an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave and takes refuge in Midian, where he marries Tzipporah.

The narrative describes the plagues of Egypt, the departure of the Israelites through a passage in the Red Sea under Moses, the revelations at Mount Sinai and the wanderings in the wilderness up to the borders of Canaan, over forty years in all. At Sinai Yahweh makes a covenant with the Israelites, who will keep his laws and worship only him, and he will protect them as his chosen people. The covenant is told in stages, from the people's agreement to the book of the covenant to the Ten Commandments written on stone tablets, and the laws are set out in several codes, among them the Book of the Covenant, the Holiness Code of Leviticus and the Deuteronomic Code.

Modern scholars hold that the Pentateuch does not give an accurate account of Israelite origins; the Israelites appear to have emerged in the central highlands of Canaan in the late second millennium BCE from the indigenous Canaanite culture. No non-biblical text or archaeological find directly supports the people or events, and most scholars omit them from histories of Israel.

Many think a small group of Egyptian origin may have joined the early Israelites and contributed its own story. The earliest traces are in the 8th-century BCE prophets Amos and Hosea, and most scholars date the composition of the Pentateuch to the Achaemenid period.

The Exodus is central in Judaism, recalled in daily prayers and at Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. Early Christians read it as a prefiguration of salvation by Jesus, and the Quran tells it as part of the life of Moses, who is mentioned 136 times. It has also inspired settlers in America, African Americans seeking freedom and liberation theology.
the-federalist-papers: The Federal Convention sent the proposed Constitution to the Confederation Congress, which submitted it to the states at the end of September 1787. Critics soon appeared in the New York press: Cato on 27 September and Brutus on 18 October, writings later grouped as the Anti-Federalist Papers. Alexander Hamilton decided to launch a defence and explanation of the Constitution for the people of the state of New York. He recruited John Jay, who wrote Nos. 2 to 5 and No. 64, and James Madison, who became his main collaborator. The series appeared under the name Publius, after Publius Valerius, a founder of the ancient republic of Rome.

The authors tried to hide their identities because Hamilton and Madison had attended the convention. The essays were written in haste, sometimes three or four in a week. Publisher J. & A. McLean released the first 36 essays as a bound volume on 22 March 1788, and a second volume on 28 May contained Nos. 37 to 85.

In No. 1 Hamilton listed six topics: the usefulness of the Union, the weakness of the Confederation, the need for an energetic government, the conformity of the Constitution to republican principles, its likeness to the state constitutions, and the security it would give to liberty. Madison's No. 10 discusses preventing rule by a majority faction and advocates a large commercial republic, and No. 51 gives the argument for checks and balances. Hamilton's No. 70 argues for a single chief executive and No. 78 lays the groundwork for judicial review of federal acts by federal courts. In No. 84 he opposes adding a bill of rights, fearing that a written list would be read as the only rights people had.

The Constitution was ratified on 21 June 1788 by the nine states required. Historians doubt how much the essays contributed: they were not reliably reprinted outside New York, ten states had ratified before New York did on 26 July, and John Kaminski suggests that their effect on citizens of New York was negligible. Authorship was long uncertain. Hamilton's list, made before his duel with Aaron Burr, credited him with 63 essays, while Madison's list of 1818 claimed 29. Modern scholars generally credit Hamilton with 51, Madison with 29 and Jay with 5, with 12 disputed. Federal judges have used the essays as a contemporary account of the framers' intentions since Calder v. Bull in 1798.
the-feminine-mystique: In 1957 Betty Friedan was asked to survey her former Smith College classmates for their fifteenth reunion. Many of them proved unhappy as housewives, and the results led her to research psychology, media and advertising and to interview other suburban housewives. She had meant to write an article, but no magazine would publish it, and so it became a book, published by W. W. Norton on 19 February 1963. It sold over a million copies at first. Her chapter on Freud was inspired by Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex of 1949.

The book opens with what Friedan called the problem that has no name, the widespread unhappiness of women in the 1950s and early 1960s, even among wives and mothers living in material comfort. She argues that women misread this as a private failing. Women's magazines, whose editorial decisions she says were made mostly by men, advertisers and the education system promoted the image of the happy housewife, and Friedan holds that this led many women to lose their own identities.

She criticises Sigmund Freud, whose ideas were very influential in the United States, for treating women as destined to be housewives, and criticises functionalism and the changes in women's education from the 1940s. She also draws on Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs, arguing that women need meaningful work, as men do, to reach self-actualisation. The last chapter proposes a new life plan: not treating housework as a career, not seeking total fulfilment through marriage and motherhood alone, and finding work that uses a woman's full mind.

Many women reacted angrily, feeling that the book implied wives and mothers could never be fulfilled. Joanne Meyerowitz argues that many magazines of the period did not place women solely in the home, as Friedan stated. Daniel Horowitz points out that although Friedan presented herself as a typical suburban housewife, she had been involved in radical politics and labour journalism in her youth. Critics including bell hooks, Kirsten Fermaglich and Lisa Fine note that she wrote almost entirely of white, middle-class women, and she has also been criticised for prejudice against homosexuality.

The book is widely credited with sparking second-wave feminism in the United States. Friedan received hundreds of letters from unhappy housewives, and she helped found and became the first president of the National Organization for Women, organised in 1966 with 30 women. By 2000 the book had sold over 3 million copies and had been translated into many languages. A fiftieth-anniversary edition appeared in February 2013 with a new introduction by Gail Collins.
the-fens: The Fens cover nearly 1,500 square miles (3,900 square kilometres) in south-east Lincolnshire, most of Cambridgeshire and the westernmost parts of Norfolk and Suffolk. Most of the land lies within a few metres of sea level, and drainage and the shrinking of the peat mean that many parts now lie below it. A few hills stood dry as islands when the fens around them flooded. The largest, the 23-square-mile Kimmeridge Clay island, carries the cathedral city of Ely.

The Great Level, the largest region of fen, covers about 500 square miles around the lower Nene and the Great Ouse and is also called the Bedford Level, after Francis Russell, 4th Earl of Bedford, who headed the investors in the 17th-century drainage. Today the Fens produce grain and vegetables and contain around half of the grade 1 agricultural land in England.

People settled the fen edges and islands from the Mesolithic to hunt and fish, and Flag Fen and the Must Farm quarry are internationally important Bronze Age sites. The Romans built the Fen Causeway between Denver and Peterborough and probably the Car Dyke on the western edge, and exported salt, beef and leather from the region. After Roman Britain ended, some Iceni may have moved into the Fens to avoid the Angles, since the marshes were easily defended. The Fens were later called the Holy Land of the English for the monasteries of Crowland, Ely, Peterborough, Ramsey and Thorney.

Drainage began in earnest in the 1630s, when investors had contracts with Charles I; the Earl of Bedford led one syndicate, and the engineer Cornelius Vermuyden was involved in the second phase of construction in the 1650s. The scheme met huge opposition from locals who lost their living from fishing and wildfowling. The Fen Tigers tried to sabotage the work. Most of the draining came in the late 18th and early 19th century, again against rioting and sabotage. In the 1820s coal-powered steam engines such as Stretham Old Engine replaced windpumps, and after the Second World War small electric stations took over. Once drained, the peat began to oxidise and shrink, so the land continued to sink and the banks had to be raised.

The Great Fen Project, begun in 2003, returns parts of the Fens to a pre-agricultural state, flooding some farmland to make nature reserves. About 4,000 farms work the Fens, and more than 70 per cent of the area lies in environmental stewardship schemes. Towns include Boston, King's Lynn, Spalding, Wisbech, March and Ely.
the-first-nowell: "The First Nowell" is listed as number 682 in the Roud Folk Song Index. The word nowell, an early modern English synonym of "Christmas", comes from the French Noël and ultimately from the Latin natalis, "of birth". It was regularly used in the burden of carols in the Middle Ages and into the early modern period, with 15th-century examples including "Nowell sing we now all and some" and "Nowel – out of youre slepe arise and wake", and it came to mean a Christmas song or carol.

The current form was first published in Carols Ancient and Modern (1823) and Gilbert and Sandys Carols (1833), both edited by William Sandys and arranged by Davies Gilbert, who also wrote extra lyrics. Writing in 1915, Anne Gilchrist noted that the carol was not recorded before Sandys's publication.

The melody is unusual among English folk tunes: it consists of one phrase repeated twice, followed by a refrain that varies it, and all three phrases end on the third of the scale. Gilchrist guessed, from church gallery parts found in Westmorland, that the tune began as a treble part to another carol, "Hark, hark what news the angels bring", passed down orally and later remembered as the melody. A conjectural reconstruction of that earlier version appears in The New Oxford Book of Carols.

The lyrics vary from book to book. They draw on the annunciation to the shepherds and the adoration of the shepherds from the second chapter of Luke, while the Star of Bethlehem comes from the story of the Magi in Matthew and does not appear in the shepherds' story.

Today the carol is usually sung in a four-part arrangement by John Stainer, first published in his Carols, New and Old in 1871. Victor Hely-Hutchinson used variations of its theme in his Carol Symphony. In the early 1930s the American folklorist James Madison Carpenter made audio recordings of several traditional versions in Cornwall, which can be heard online through the Vaughan Williams Memorial Library.
the-fountain-of-bakhchisaray: Pushkin began the poem in the spring of 1821, after visiting the Fountain of Tears at the Bakhchysarai Palace in 1820. The bulk of it was written during 1822, the draft was finished in spring 1823, and in the autumn of 1823 he made his final changes and prepared it for printing. The first edition appeared on 10 March 1824. The poem has 578 lines of freely rhymed iambic tetrameter.

In the harem of the Crimean khan Giray, the Georgian concubine Zarema is sad because the khan has fallen out of love with her. His mind is on Maria, a Polish nobleman's daughter kidnapped during a Tatar raid. Maria is inconsolable, spends her time in prayer to the Virgin Mary and prefers death to the fate of a non-believer's concubine. At night Zarema goes to Maria's room and tries with threats to make her reject the khan, so that he will love Zarema again. Soon after, Maria dies, and the guards of the harem drown Zarema.

The khan goes to war to forget his troubles but remains tormented. On his return he orders a fountain built in the palace in memory of Maria, which the young maidens of Crimea, learning of the sad legend, call the fountain of tears. In an epilogue the narrator wanders through the abandoned palace, sees a woman's ghost and wonders whether it is Maria's or Zarema's, recalls a love for whom he yearns, and wishes to return to Crimea.

The Pushkin scholar Sergei Bondi writes that the poem most closely resembles the canon of Romantic poems in its fragmentary form, its deliberate incoherence and ambiguity, as in the fate of Zarema and Maria, its lyricism and the musicality of its verse. He thinks Khan Giray underdeveloped, but sees Zarema as an improvement on the Circassian heroine of The Prisoner of the Caucasus, and calls the exchange between the two women unusually diverse in feeling, tone and content.

Pushkin himself spoke almost only negatively of it. In October 1823 he wrote to Pyotr Vyazemsky that it was, between them, rubbish, though its epigraph, a quotation from the Persian poet Saadi, was charming; he did think the exchange between Zarema and Maria had dramatic merit.

The poem inspired many works: Alexander von Zemlinsky's opera Sarema in 1897, Anton Arensky's cantata in 1899, a short film by Yakov Protazanov in 1909 and 1910, Alexander Ilyinsky's opera in 1911, and Boris Asafyev's ballet in 1934. In the 1840s Karl Briullov painted a picture on the subject.
the-fronde: The Fronde arose from the financial strain of French involvement in the Thirty Years' War, which ended in 1648, and of the continuing Franco-Spanish War, which began in 1635. Paying for the wars forced the government of Cardinal Mazarin to raise taxes, most of which fell on the bourgeoisie, whose power base lay in the regional Parlements.

The most important, the Parlement of Paris, refused to register the new decrees as an assault on established rights. Louis XIV had become king in 1643 at the age of five, so France was ruled by a regency dominated by his mother, Anne of Austria, and Mazarin. Nobles who had lost influence under Cardinal Richelieu at first supported the Parlements.

The first phase, the Fronde of the Parlements, began in May 1648, when a tax on judicial officers led the Parlement of Paris to demand constitutional reforms. After Prince Louis II de Condé's victory at Lens in August, Mazarin arrested the leaders of the Parlement, and Paris rose and barricaded its streets. The court fled the city on the night of 22 October. The Peace of Westphalia then freed the army, Condé besieged Paris, and the Peace of Rueil of 11 March 1649 ended this phase after little bloodshed.

The second phase, the Fronde of the Princes, lasted from 1650 to 1653 and was a scramble for power among discontented nobles, among them Gaston, Duke of Orleans, Condé, his brother the Prince of Conti and the Viscount of Turenne. Mazarin arrested Condé, Conti and Longueville on 14 January 1650, and Turenne led a rebellion against the court, which ended with his defeat at Rethel in December 1650. When Mazarin returned in December 1651 the war began again, with Turenne and Condé on opposite sides. The royal army trapped Condé's forces in the Faubourg St. Antoine on 2 July 1652, and the king entered Paris on 21 October 1652.

Mazarin returned unopposed in February 1653. Tired of the turmoil and disgusted with the princes, the country came to look to the king and his party as the representatives of order, and the Fronde is thought to have prepared the absolutism of Louis XIV. Condé entered the service of the king of Spain, and the war with Spain continued in Flanders, Catalonia and Italy until the Peace of the Pyrenees on 5 November 1659. On 27 January 1660 Condé obtained the forgiveness of Louis XIV, and the later careers of Turenne and Condé were as obedient subjects of their king.
the-gambia: The Gambia is the smallest country on the African mainland. Its borders mirror the meandering Gambia River, which flows through the middle of the country, and Senegal surrounds it on all sides except the 80 kilometres of Atlantic coastline in the west. It is less than 50 kilometres wide at its widest point, with an area of 11,295 square kilometres. The present boundaries were defined in 1889 after an agreement between the United Kingdom and France, though fixing the final borders took nearly 15 years. The river, known locally as the River, is navigable deep into the continent.

The name derives from the Mandinka term Kambra or Kambaa, meaning the Gambia River. Portuguese explorers adopted a variation of it, which was later anglicised. In 1964 Prime Minister Dawda Jawara asked that the name keep the definite article, in part to reduce confusion with the newly independent Zambia.

Arab traders gave the first written accounts of the area in the ninth and tenth centuries. Muslim merchants and scholars established communities in West African commercial centres and carried out trans-Saharan trade, exporting gold, ivory and people taken captive in raids and sold as slaves. At the beginning of the 14th century most of the present Gambia was part of the Mali Empire. The Portuguese reached the area by sea in the mid-15th century and began to dominate overseas trade.

In 1588 António, Prior of Crato, a claimant to the Portuguese throne, sold exclusive trade rights on the river to English merchants, and in 1618 King James I granted a charter to an English company. Between 1651 and 1661 parts of the Gambia, including St. Andrew's Island and Fort Jakob, were ruled by the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia under Prince Jacob Kettler, before being ceded to England in 1664.

Britain and France struggled for supremacy on the Senegal and Gambia rivers through the 18th century. The 1783 Treaty of Versailles gave Britain the Gambia River, but France kept an enclave at Albreda until it was ceded in 1856. The British established the military post of Bathurst, now Banjul, in 1816, and the Gambia gained independence on 18 February 1965.

The Gambia is the Republic of The Gambia, a republic since 1970, and its capital is Banjul, an island city once called Bathurst. English is the sole official language, and Mandinka is spoken as a first language by 38 per cent of the population. The Mandinka are the most numerous ethnic group. The river and its slave-trade history are the setting of Alex Haley's Roots.
the-golden-ass: The date of composition is uncertain. Scholars have considered it a youthful work that came before Apuleius' Apology of 158–159, or the climax of his literary career, and perhaps as late as the 170s or 180s. Apuleius adapted the story from a Greek original whose author is said to be an otherwise unknown Lucius of Patrae, who shares the name of the lead character and narrator.

That Greek text is lost. A similar tale of disputed authorship, Lucius or the Ass, is traditionally attributed to the writer Lucian, a contemporary of Apuleius, and appears to be an abridgement of the lost work.

The narrator Lucius, a Greek who is revealed at the end to come from Madaurus, the hometown of Apuleius, travels to Thessaly, regarded as the birthplace of magic. His curiosity and desire to see magic lead him to try a spell to turn himself into a bird. It goes wrong and he becomes an ass, and the cure is to eat a fresh rose. Thieves then carry him off, and he passes from owner to owner, among them bandits, a band of priests of Cybele, a baker and a cook.

The story is filled with inset tales told by the characters he meets. The longest is Cupid and Psyche, which an old woman tells to a kidnapped young woman, Charite, over Books Four to Six. In this guise Lucius, a member of the Roman country aristocracy, shares the miseries of slaves and poor freemen who are reduced to little more than beasts of burden by wealthy landowners.

In the last book the tone abruptly changes. Lucius prays to the Queen of Heaven, who is revealed as Isis. She tells him to eat the crown of roses carried by one of her priests in a procession. He is restored to human form, is initiated into her cult, and later into that of Osiris at Rome.

Apuleius' style is innovative, mannered, baroque and exuberant. The work is regarded as a precursor of the episodic picaresque novel, a genre later taken up by writers such as Francisco de Quevedo, François Rabelais, Miguel de Cervantes, Voltaire and Daniel Defoe. Augustine of Hippo called it The Golden Ass, and the confessional tone of its suffering is thought to have influenced his Confessions, though he refers to Apuleius derisively in The City of God.

Giovanni Boccaccio based two tales of The Decameron on it, the Fuller's Wife and the Wife's Tub. William Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, from about 1595, has Bottom's head changed to an ass's. In 1517 Niccolò Machiavelli wrote his own version as a poem in terza rima, left unfinished at his death.
the-great-game: Britain feared that Russian expansion to the south would threaten India, while Russia feared the spread of British interests into Central Asia. On one major view the rivalry began on 12 January 1830, when Lord Ellenborough, president of the Board of Control for India, told the governor-general, Lord William Bentinck, to open a trade route to the Emirate of Bukhara. Britain hoped to make Afghanistan a protectorate and to use the Ottoman Empire, Persia, Khiva and Bukhara as buffer states. The term Great Game was coined in 1840 by the British intelligence officer Captain Arthur Conolly and was popularised by Rudyard Kipling's novel Kim of 1901.

Britain annexed Sind in 1843 and fought the two Anglo-Sikh Wars, in 1845–1846 and 1848–1849, which brought the Punjab and the later North-West Frontier Province under its rule. After the Crimean War ended in 1856 with Russia's defeat, Alexander II of Russia waited some years and then expanded in two campaigns. Russia occupied Chimkent in 1864, Tashkent in 1865, Khokhand and Bukhara in 1866 and Samarkand in 1868, and Khiva in 1873.

Afghanistan was the main point of contact. In 1878 Russia sent a mission to Kabul uninvited; when Sher Ali Khan refused a British mission and turned back its envoy, the Second Anglo-Afghan War began, and 40,000 men invaded from British India in November 1878. The Treaty of Gandamak of 1879 and the accession of Abdur Rahman Khan left Afghanistan under British control of its foreign policy, with internal sovereignty, as a buffer. Persia was another field: Britain and Persia fought in 1856–1857 after a Persian assault on Herat.

The two powers never fought each other directly in the Great Game, and they also cooperated. Their agreement of 21 January 1873 treated Badakhshan and the Wakhan Corridor as Afghan, and the Afghan Boundary Commission followed the protocol of 10 September 1885. A frontier defined by the Pamir Boundary Commission in 1895 is the date many historians give for the end of the game. The Anglo-Russian Convention of August 1907 placed Afghanistan and southern Iran in the British sphere and Central Asia and northern Iran in the Russian sphere, and treated Tibet as neutral.

Historians do not agree on the dating. Edward Ingram places the beginning in 1832–1834 and the end in 1842, with the British withdrawal from Afghanistan, while Konstantin Penzev dates its start to Russia's victory over Persia. David X. Noack sees a later contest between Britain and the Soviet Union from 1919 to 1933.
the-hague: The Hague, in Dutch Den Haag, short for 's-Gravenhage, is the capital of the province of South Holland. It lies on the west coast facing the North Sea, and its coastal area includes the seaside resort of Scheveningen. The name comes from the Middle Dutch word hag(h)e, meaning hedge, enclosure or hunting ground, and first appeared in 1242. The fuller 's-Gravenhage, the count's enclosure, appeared in 1347 and refers to the Count of Holland. The municipal government adopted the shorter name in 1990.

The area belonged to the Roman province of Germania Inferior. Little is known of the city's origin, since no contemporary documents describe it, but it was founded by the last counts of the House of Holland. Floris IV presumably bought a court by the present Hofvijver in 1229 but died in a tournament in 1234. His son William II lived there, and after he was elected King of the Romans in 1248 he had builders turn the court into a royal palace, later called the Binnenhof. The Ridderzaal, or Knights' Hall, was completed under his son Floris V and still stands. From the 13th century the counts of Holland used The Hague as their administrative centre and residence.

In 1806, when the Kingdom of Holland was a puppet state of the First French Empire, Louis Bonaparte granted the settlement city rights. After Belgium separated in 1830, Amsterdam stayed the capital while the government remained in The Hague. When government grew more prominent after 1850 the city expanded quickly, with streets built for civil servants and for Dutchmen retiring from the administration of the Netherlands East Indies.

The Hague is the seat of the Dutch government, the States General, the Supreme Court and the Council of State, while Amsterdam is the official capital. The Ridderzaal is still used for political events such as the annual speech from the throne. Most foreign embassies in the Netherlands are in the city. It is home to the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court and the Permanent Court of Arbitration, and the Royal Library of the Netherlands is also there.
the-holly-and-the-ivy: The words of the carol occur in three broadsides printed in Birmingham in the early 19th century. William Hone's Ancient Mysteries Described of 1823 lists "The holly and the ivy, now are both well grown" among the Christmas carols then printed every year. The complete words appear in a book review of 1849, whose anonymous writer proposed them in place of a reading in the book under review. Sylvester's 1861 collection A Garland of Christmas Carols says it came from an old broadside printed a century and a half earlier, around 1711, and Husk's Songs of the Nativity of 1864 repeats this. The early 19th-century sources give no music.

Many variants were collected from traditional singers. The most popular traditional one seems to have been "The Holly Bears a Berry", while the "Sans Day Carol" is considered a variant with a different tune. The words were sung to countless folk melodies, three more of them collected in Gloucestershire alone, and some late 19th-century collections set them to an "old French carol" in D minor.

The melody now used was first published in Cecil Sharp's English Folk-Carols in 1911. Sharp heard it from Mrs Mary Clayton at Chipping Campden in Gloucestershire, and his transcription of her third verse is dated 13 January 1909. The melody keeps to the notes of a hexachord.

Holly has carried Christian symbolism since medieval times, and in the carol the holly represents Jesus and the ivy his mother, the Virgin Mary. Holly and ivy have been a mainstay of British church decorations at Advent and Christmas since at least the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, when churchwardens' accounts mention them regularly. The carol is related to an older piece that Sharp called The Contest of the Ivy and the Holly, a contest between the traditional emblems of woman and man.

A British Museum manuscript quoted by Hone begins "Nay, my nay, hyt shal not be I wys", with holly standing in the hall and ivy outside the door, and Henry VIII wrote a love song, Green Groweth the Holly. Sir Henry Walford Davies wrote a choral arrangement often performed at the Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols and by choirs elsewhere, and the Trans-Siberian Orchestra's "The Prince of Peace" is set to the same music.
the-internationale: The title comes from the First International, the alliance of workers that held a congress in 1864. Pottier intended his text to be sung to the tune of La Marseillaise, and it was reputedly sung to that tune at his burial in November 1887. An earlier version, written in September 1870, marked the Third Republic declared after Prussia's defeat of the Second French Empire and honoured the First International. The text that endures is the one Pottier authorised for his Chants Révolutionnaires, published by his fellow Communard Jean Allemane in April 1887.

The melody was composed in 1888 by Pierre De Geyter for the choir La Lyre des Travailleurs of the French Workers' Party in his hometown of Lille. He had been commissioned by Gustave Delory, the future mayor of Lille, who had received the text from a young socialist teacher, Charles Gros. Pottier's lyrics contain one-liners that became slogans, and others such as Ni Dieu, ni César, ni tribun, meaning neither God, nor Caesar, nor tribune, were already familiar in the workers' movement.

The Second International adopted the song as its official anthem, and it became a standard of the socialist movement from the late nineteenth century. The first English version has been attributed to Pottier himself, and the first US translation was made by Charles Hope Kerr, who heard it in Lille in 1894. By the time of the International Socialist Congress in Copenhagen in 1910 versions existed in 18 languages. Arkady Kots made the first Russian translation in 1902, and after the Bolshevik Revolution its future tenses were rewritten in the present. Qu Qiubai made a new Chinese translation in 1923, and the song was played at the close of the Chinese Communist Party's third National Congress that year.

In the Soviet Union it was the national anthem until it was replaced by the State Anthem of the USSR; Arturo Toscanini's orchestration of it was broadcast in 1943 for the anniversary of the October Revolution. In South Africa communists, unionists and activists of all races sang it until the Communist Party was suppressed from 1950.

Pierre De Geyter's authorship was obscured. To protect his job as a woodcarver, the first leaflets gave only the French form of his name, Degeyter, and a second edition named his brother Adolphe as the composer. Pierre lost a lawsuit over this in 1914 and was legally recognised as the author only in 1922. Adolphe died in 1916, leaving a note explaining the fraud. Pierre De Geyter died in 1932, and the music is now in the public domain.
the-knight-in-the-panthers-skin: The poem was written during the Golden Age of the Kingdom of Georgia, in the reign of Queen Tamar, who had been enthroned by her father, King George III of Georgia. Tamar expanded the kingdom to its historical maximum, repulsed invasions and set up protectorates over many Muslim and Christian lands. Georgian trading caravans reached Ayyubid Egypt, the Kievan Rus and the Byzantine Empire.

Shota Rustaveli, born in the Meskhetian village of Rustavi, was close to the queen and possibly served as her treasurer. In the prologue he says he wrote the poem to praise Tamar, whom he calls a king. The historian Stephen H. Rapp sees it as an expression of the Iranian epic tradition rather than of Byzantine literature, and Rustaveli calls it a Persian tale translated into Georgian. It runs to over 1,600 quatrains in the shairi verse form.

The story is set in the invented lands of Arabia and India. Avtandil, commander of the armies of King Rostevan of Arabia, is asked by the king's daughter Tinatin to find a mysterious knight in a panther's skin within three years. After two years and nine months he finds Tariel, son of King Saridan, living in a cave. Tariel had fallen in love with Nestan-Darejan, daughter of King Pharsadan, who was promised to another suitor. At her request he killed the suitor, and she was set adrift on the sea.

Avtandil swears friendship to Tariel and sets out again to find Nestan-Darejan. In the city of Gulansharo, Patman tells him that Nestan was abducted by Kaji, the demon king. Avtandil, Tariel and Nuradin-Phridon go to the land of Kaji with three hundred men and free her. Avtandil marries Tinatin in Arabia, Tariel marries Nestan in India, and the three friends reign in their own realms.

The poem celebrates friendship, loyalty and courtly love, and condemns forced marriage and slavery. Readers see Nestan-Darejan as an allegory of Tamar and the settings as colourful stand-ins for the Georgian kingdom.

Until the early 20th century a copy of the poem was part of the dowry of every bride. Its moral framework is Christian, though the poem contains no prayers and no references to Christ, and it refers to the Quran to show that most characters are Muslim. Because Rustaveli presents God as a universal force, the Georgian Orthodox Church in the past destroyed copies, believing him to be a Muslim.

Interest abroad began in 1802 with a Russian translation of the first stanza. Marie-Félicité Brosset made a partial French translation in 1828, and Marjory Wardrop published the first English translation in 1912. The poem has been translated into dozens of languages, and Lyn Coffin's English version of 2015 keeps the shairi form.
the-last-judgment-memling: The triptych shows the Last Judgment at the second coming of Christ. In the central panel Jesus sits in judgment over the world while St Michael the Archangel weighs souls and sends the damned towards Hell; the sinner in the right-hand pan of his scales is a donor portrait of Tommaso Portinari. The left-hand panel shows the saved being led into heaven by St Peter and the angels. Angelo Tani ordered the work for the Chapel of St Michael at the Badia Fiesolana.

Paul Beneke gave the painting to his patrons, lay brothers of the Brotherhood of Saint George, who donated it to their church. A long lawsuit against the Hanseatic League sought its return to Italy, and Duke Charles the Bold of Burgundy, Emperor Rudolf II and Tsar Peter I of Russia all tried to buy or remove it, but it stayed in the church until 1807.

Looted in the Napoleonic Wars, it hung for eight years in the Musée Napoléon in Paris under inventory number 563, wrongly labelled as a work of Jan van Eyck. The German artists Ferdinand and Heinrich Olivier wrote of seeing it there, Ferdinand weeping with joy, and German newspapers praised how well it held up beside the works around it. Despite the objections of Vivant Denon it was taken to Berlin in 1815 and then sent home.

In 1942 Willi Drost, curator of the National Museum, moved it out of the city ahead of expected Allied bombing, and it was hidden in several places. The Red Army found it in 1946 and sent it to the Hermitage Museum in Leningrad, where it stayed for ten years. In 1956 it went to Warsaw for extensive restoration and then back to Gdańsk.
the-last-supper-leonardo: The painting measures 460 by 880 centimetres and covers an end wall of the dining hall of the convent. Ludovico Sforza planned to remodel the church as a family mausoleum and commissioned the work to decorate its wall; the lunettes above it carry Sforza coats of arms. On the opposite wall is the Crucifixion fresco by Giovanni Donato da Montorfano, to which Leonardo added figures of the Sforza family in tempera. These have deteriorated in much the same way.

Leonardo did not work continuously, and the start date is uncertain because the convent's archives for the period were destroyed. A document of 1497 indicates that the painting was nearly complete. A prior who complained about the delay was told, according to the report, that if Leonardo could not find the right face for Judas he would use the prior's features.

The scene follows the Gospel of John, at the moment after Jesus announces that one of the apostles will betray him. The twelve react in four groups of three, with Jesus at the centre. Judas, in shadow, clutches a small bag and tips over a salt cellar, and Peter holds a knife. Leonardo seats all the diners on one side of the table, so that none has his back to the viewer, and leaves Judas among them rather than apart. The perspective lines meet at Jesus's turned right cheek.

The apostles were named from an unsigned mid-sixteenth-century fresco copy; before that only Judas, Peter, John and Jesus had been identified with certainty. Two early copies attributed to Leonardo's assistants survive, one by Giampietrino in London and one by Cesare da Sesto in Ponte Capriasca, Switzerland.

The damage began early. By 1556 Giorgio Vasari described the work as a muddle of blots, and in 1652 a doorway was cut through its lower centre and later bricked up. Restorations were attempted by Michelangelo Bellotti in 1726 and Giuseppe Mazza in 1770, and Stefano Barezzi damaged the central section in 1821 when he tried to remove it from the wall. In 1796 French troops used the refectory as an armoury and stable, and on 15 August 1943 Allied bombing struck the room, though sandbags protected the wall.

From 1978 to 1999 Pinin Brambilla Barcilon led a major restoration, and the painting was returned to display on 28 May 1999 in a sealed, climate-controlled room. Its changes of colour and tone drew criticism, notably from the art historian James Beck. Since Dan Brown's novel The Da Vinci Code (2003), some writers have claimed that the figure beside Jesus is Mary Magdalene, but art historians hold that it is John.
the-lion-sleeps-tonight: "Mbube" was written and composed by Solomon Linda in 1939. It was first published in South Africa and reached the United States a decade later. It is sung in a call and response format in four-part harmony, over three chords in a progression borrowed from the marabi harmonic cycle common in twentieth-century South African music. The Zulu lyrics are said to document an episode of Linda's childhood when he chased a lion while herding cattle. In the closing seconds Linda breaks into a brief howl, which Rian Malan describes as a haunting skein of fifteen notes.

Gallo sent records to Decca in the United States, where Alan Lomax salvaged them from being discarded and handed the box to Pete Seeger of the Weavers. Seeger transcribed the song word for word but misheard the chorus as "wimoweh". The Weavers recorded it as "Wimoweh" in 1951 at the Village Vanguard, with Seeger singing falsetto, and Gordon Jenkins added a brass accompaniment that stressed Linda's howl. Malan wrote that it was faithful to the Zulu original in almost every respect except for the finger-popping rhythm.

In 1961 the Brooklyn doo-wop group the Tokens, who had heard the Weavers live, recorded their own version for RCA. They changed the melody and added English lyrics, and it topped the US charts. By the mid-2000s over 150 artists had recorded the song. Robert John took it to No. 3 in the United States in 1971, and Tight Fit topped the British charts in 1982. The song was featured in Disney's The Lion King in 1994.

Disputes over credit began about 1951, when Seeger protested that Linda, as the true author, should be paid, and at one point sent him a cheque of $1,000 himself. In 1971 The Richmond Organization acknowledged that the song was based on "Mbube", and from then on Linda's family received 12.5 percent of the earnings of "Wimoweh". The Tokens' writers, Hugo Peretti, Luigi Creatore and George David Weiss, wrongly thought the tune traditional and credited their version to themselves.

Malan's essay in Rolling Stone in 2000 estimated that the song had earned some $15 million in royalties, and François Verster's documentary A Lion's Trail, two years later, drew further attention. In July 2004 Linda's family sued Disney for 10 million rand over The Lion King, with the support of the South African government. Within two years they reached an out-of-court settlement with Abilene Music for past royalties and a share of future revenue. The case had legal effects, including on British copyright law. Some writers call "Mbube" the most widely known melody born in Africa.
the-merchant-of-venice: The play is believed to have been written between 1596 and 1598. Francis Meres mentioned it in 1598, and its first edition of 1600 says it had been performed divers times. A reference to the ship the Andrew is thought to allude to the Spanish ship St. Andrew, captured by the English at Cádiz in 1596. James Roberts entered it in the Register of the Stationers Company on 22 July 1598, and Thomas Heyes published the first quarto in 1600. That edition is regarded as accurate and is the basis of the text in the 1623 First Folio.

A merchant forfeiting a deadly bond after standing surety for a friend was a common tale in late 16th-century England. The test of the suitors, the rescue from the pound of flesh by the friend's new wife disguised as a lawyer, and her demand for a betrothal ring appear in Il Pecorone by Giovanni Fiorentino, published in Milan in 1558. The story of the three caskets is in the Gesta Romanorum, probably compiled at the end of the 13th century.

Bassanio, a young Venetian who has squandered his estate, wishes to woo Portia, the wealthy heiress of Belmont, and needs 3,000 ducats. His friend Antonio, a merchant, has no ready cash because his ships are at sea, so Bassanio turns to the Jewish moneylender Shylock, and Antonio guarantees the loan. Though the First Folio classes the play as a comedy, it is remembered mostly for its dramatic scenes and for Shylock's demand for a pound of flesh. It holds two well-known speeches: Shylock's Hath not a Jew eyes? and Portia's on the quality of mercy.

Critics disagree over whether the play is antisemitic. Harold Bloom argued in 1998 that it is deeply so, and others point to Shylock's plea for the rights of all who suffer discrimination. English Jews had been expelled under Edward I in 1290 and could not return until 1656, and in Venice Jews had to live in a ghetto and wear a coloured hat in public.

The earliest recorded performance was at the court of King James in the spring of 1605. In 1701 George Granville's adaptation, The Jew of Venice, played the role of Shylock comically and was acted for about forty years. Charles Macklin returned to the original text in 1741. According to the actor Jacob Adler, the tradition of a sympathetic Shylock began with Edmund Kean in the first half of the 19th century, and Henry Irving's proud Shylock of 1879 was called the summit of his career. Adler himself played the part in Yiddish in New York. Operas based on the play include Reynaldo Hahn's Le marchand de Venise, first performed in Paris on 25 March 1935.
the-minstrel-boy: Charles Villiers Stanford named a source for the tune in a restored collection of Irish songs in 1895, but the scholars Veronica Ní Chinnéide and Una Hunt judge that he did not research it properly, and several of his attributions were corrected in Alfred Moffatt's Minstrelsy of Ireland in 1898. Hunt also found that Aloys Fleischmann cited as sources works that postdate Moore, and that Moore had better access to manuscripts and printed sources than earlier researchers believed. The air appears under Moore's title in George Thomson's collection of Scottish and Irish airs in 1816, which has led to the unproven suspicion that Thomson sent it to Moore.

The song has two verses. A young minstrel goes to war with his father's sword and his harp; he falls, and rather than let the harp sound in slavery under the foe's chain, he tears its strings apart. Like several of the Irish Melodies it is melancholy and nostalgic, and its harp, a romantic symbol of Ireland, is broken with no promise of restoration. Matthew Campbell has called its symbolism overdone and its tone histrionic beside The Last Rose of Summer, while George Bernard Shaw called the words visionary. Early American audiences took up its themes of freedom and passed over its references to slavery, though Moore, after travelling there, had written with disappointment of American slavery in 1806.

It became one of the best-known songs of a collection that was immensely popular in Ireland and Great Britain, and Moore himself came to be nicknamed the Minstrel Boy. A third verse by an unknown author was added during the American Civil War. Rafael María de Mendive's Spanish version of 1863, El trovador, kept the references to slaves at a time when slavery still stood in Cuba.

Composers and writers returned to it often: Stanford quoted it at the head of his Fourth Irish Rhapsody, John Philip Sousa worked it into his Mother Hubbard March of 1885, Benjamin Britten used distorted forms of it in his opera Owen Wingrave, and James Joyce parodied it in Finnegans Wake and quoted it in Ulysses. Singers who recorded it include John McCormack, Paul Robeson and Joe Strummer, whose version was used in the film Black Hawk Down. It was played at the opening of the memorial at the World Trade Center site on 11 September 2011.
the-moon-represents-my-heart: Weng Ching-hsi thought little of the tune and considered throwing it away; the lyricist Sun Yi found it in a pile of works meant for disposal and judged it a good song. After Sun wrote the words, the two sold it to Li Ge Records in 1972. Chen Fen-lan sang it first, on her album Dreamland in May 1973, and Liu Guan-lin recorded it in November of the same year. Teresa Teng recorded it for her Mandarin album Love Songs of the Island, Vol. 4: Love in Hong Kong, released by Polydor Hong Kong on 19 December 1977, and her version made it known across the Chinese-speaking world.

Teng's recording lasts three minutes and 27 seconds and has been described as a love song with a waltz-like lilt. The anthropologist Kevin Latham called it a relatively simple love ballad, like most gangtai songs of the time, the popular music of Hong Kong and Taiwan. The linguist Adrian Tien, in The Semantics of Chinese Music, notes that the moon has long served in Chinese culture to express sorrow over lost love or hope of reunion, and cites the song as a modern example of that image.

Foreign music had been kept out of mainland China for decades, and romantic songs were condemned there as bourgeois and decadent. From the late 1970s Teng's songs, soft and restrained against the officially sanctioned revolutionary songs, spread widely, and this one became among the first popular gangtai songs in the country while the leaders of the People's Republic tried to suppress her music. The film director Jia Zhangke recalled it as something completely new, a personal world after a time when everything had been collective.

The song has been covered by many singers, among them Nana Mouskouri, Faye Wong, Leslie Cheung, Andy Lau, Siti Nurhaliza and Kenny G, and in 2019 the Museum of Chinese in America in New York staged an exhibition inspired by it. In 2026 it was played at the state dinner of Xi Jinping's state visit to the United States. Sun Yi sued Li Ge Records over the rights and lost, so the company holds the copyright.
the-mountain-wreath: Njegoš wrote the work in Cetinje during 1846 and had it printed the next year at an Armenian monastery in Vienna. It is a modern epic in verse written as a play, so combining three of the major modes of literary expression. It is built around an allegedly historical event of Metropolitan Danilo's rule, the mass execution at Christmas of Montenegrins who had converted to Islam, known as the Inquisition of the Turkicized (Istraga Poturica). A recent History of Montenegro holds that such an event occurred in 1707 but was highly localised, confined to the Ćeklići clan, and some Balkan historians doubt the massacre happened at all.

The poem follows Njegoš's ancestor Metropolitan Danilo I Petrović-Njegoš as he tries to regulate relations among the warring tribes. It opens with Danilo's vision of the spread of Turkish power in Europe; torn by inner conflict, he sees that the struggle is inevitable but dreads its outcome. In scenes of dialogue and monologue the drama widens into pictures of Montenegrin feasts, gatherings, customs and beliefs, and two assemblies of chieftains, one on the eve of Pentecost and one on the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, resolve to drive out the Turks.

Its 2,819 verses set three opposing civilisations side by side: patriarchal Montenegro, the Ottoman Empire and Venice. Written in the decasyllabic metre and language of Serbian epic folk poetry, it gave many lines that became proverbs, such as "When things go well 'tis easy to be good, / In suffering one learns who is the hero!"

The historian Srđa Pavlović notes that each generation of South Slav historians and politicians has drawn on the poem to support opposing views. Michael Sells, a professor of Islamic history and literature, points out that it was required reading in all the schools of pre-war Yugoslavia and was memorised and quoted by radical Serb nationalists of the 1990s, and the journalist Tim Judah called it "a paean to ethnic cleansing". Pavlović proposes reading it instead as a tale of a long-gone tribal society, set in the context of Njegoš's own time and his efforts to advance pan-Slavism and the Illyrian Movement.
the-mounth: The name is of Pictish origin, from a word meaning mountain, related to the Welsh mynydd, and it is always called the Mounth and pronounced munth. The upland lies between the Highland Boundary and the River Dee. At its western end a high, rolling plateau cut by deep glacial troughs such as Glen Isla, Glen Callater, Glen Muick and Glen Clova rises to Glas Maol, 1,068 metres, with the granite mass of Lochnagar, 1,155 metres, and the White Mounth around it.

Eastward the plateau broadens into lower moorland cut by valleys such as Glen Esk and Glen Tanar, falling gently to the North Sea cliffs between Stonehaven and Aberdeen. This is the best-preserved expanse of the ancient Highland pre-glacial upland surface. The Mounth takes in eastern Highland Perthshire, the Angus Glens and southern Aberdeenshire, and its higher parts lie within the Cairngorms National Park. The ranges to the north-west, the Monadh Liath and the Monadh Ruadh, carry the same name: the Grey Mounth and the Red Mounth.

The Mounth was long a strong barrier that to some extent cut the northeast off from the rest of the Scottish Lowlands, physically and culturally. In the Middle Ages the Causey Mounth, a raised road on a rock causeway, was built across the boggy eastern end to link Stonehaven with Aberdeen, by way of Cowie Castle, Muchalls Castle, Portlethen Moss and the Bridge of Dee. The Earl Marischal and the Marquess of Montrose took this road in 1639 with a Covenanter army of 9,000 men in the first battle of the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.

Many other old routes cross the range. The Elsick Mounth ran from Stonehaven to Drum and the Slug Road from Stonehaven to Durris; the Cairn o' Mounth led from Fettercairn to Kincardine o' Neill; the Firmounth linked Glen Esk with Glen Tanar; the Capel Mounth ran from Glen Clova to Glen Muick; and the Tolmounth, or Jock's Road, from Glen Doll to Glen Callater. Several are now followed by modern roads, among them the Cairnwell Road over the Devil's Elbow, now the A93.
the-nutcracker: After the success of The Sleeping Beauty in 1890, Ivan Vsevolozhsky, the director of the Imperial Theatres, commissioned Tchaikovsky to compose a double bill of an opera and a ballet, with Marius Petipa again as collaborator. The opera was Iolanta. Hoffmann's tale contains a long flashback explaining how the Prince was turned into the Nutcracker, and this was cut. Petipa began the choreography in August 1892, but illness removed him and his assistant of seven years, Lev Ivanov, was brought in. Some contemporary accounts credit Petipa, though Ivanov is often named as choreographer.

The story opens on Christmas Eve in Nuremberg in the 1820s, where the Stahlbaum family decorates a tree. Drosselmeyer, a toymaker and Clara's godfather, brings dancing dolls and a wooden nutcracker, which Clara's brother Fritz breaks and Drosselmeyer mends. In the second act Clara and the Prince travel to the Land of Sweets, ruled in his absence by the Sugar Plum Fairy. A celebration follows with dances for chocolate, coffee, tea and candy canes, a waltz of flowers and a final dance by the Sugar Plum Fairy and her Cavalier. The score uses a celesta, which Tchaikovsky had employed already in The Voyevoda in 1891.

Tchaikovsky made eight numbers into The Nutcracker Suite, first performed under his direction on 19 March 1892. It was instantly popular, while the complete ballet did not reach great popularity until George Balanchine's staging became a hit in New York City. In 1919 Alexander Gorsky gave the Sugar Plum Fairy's dances to Clara and the Prince, played by adults, and Vasili Vainonen's version of 1934 did likewise. Major American ballet companies earn around 40% of their annual ticket revenue from the work. Critics in the United States have objected since the 2010s to the stereotyped Chinese and Arabian dances.
the-pillow-book: The book is a collection of essays, anecdotes, poems and descriptive passages with little connection to one another, except that they express the ideas and whims of Sei Shōnagon, prompted by moments of her daily life. Translator Meredith McKinney calls it a genre-bending miscellany of short, largely unrelated pieces. Its writing falls into three kinds: narratives of events she witnessed at court, her own thoughts and opinions on various matters, and the lists, of which there are 164, with headings such as hateful things, things of beauty and things that make the heart grow fonder.

Its paragraphs are brief and easy to read even for modern Japanese speakers. Shōnagon observes everyday life and the four seasons, and the word okashi, lovely, recurs in place of the pathos of things found in The Tale of Genji. Her feelings are mixed with subtle sentiment reflecting the downfall of Fujiwara no Michitaka, the father of Empress Teishi, and the misfortunes of the emperor and empress.

Shōnagon meant her writing to be private, as a way to express thoughts she could not state publicly because of her lower status at court. Part of it was accidentally revealed during her life: she left it on a cushion put out for a visiting guest, who carried it off despite her pleas.

In the late 10th and early 11th centuries Japanese men typically wrote in Chinese characters, while women wrote in hiragana, a syllabary derived from them, and the book is written entirely in Japanese. According to Matthew Penney, the only Chinese terms are in place-names and personal titles. Most of it was probably written while she served at court, though some later entries seem to be drawn from memory.

The book circulated at court and for several hundred years existed in handwritten manuscripts, with scribes changing the order of entries and adding or removing passages. Four main variants are known, of which the Sankanbon and Nōinbon are held the most complete and accurate. It was first printed in the 17th century. Six passages were first translated into English in 1889 by T.

A. Purcell and W. G. Aston, followed by Arthur Waley's partial translation in 1928, Ivan Morris's complete one in 1967 and Meredith McKinney's in 2006. It influenced the zuihitsu genre, whose other major works include Kamo no Chōmei's Hōjōki and Yoshida Kenkō's Tsurezuregusa, and which found a wide audience among the merchant classes of the Edo period.
the-prince: Machiavelli's letters show that a version, with the Latin title De Principatibus, Of Principalities, was being written in 1513, the year after the Medici regained control of Florence and a few months after Machiavelli's arrest, torture and banishment by the incoming Medici regime. He discussed it for a long time with his friend Francesco Vettori, whom he wanted to commend it to the Medici. It was originally intended for Giuliano di Lorenzo de' Medici, and after Giuliano died in 1516 it was dedicated to Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici. William Connell views its writing as a lengthy process of revision from 1513 to 1515. No manuscript in Machiavelli's own hand survives.

Machiavelli says that the book holds the knowledge of the actions of great men, drawn from his own political experience as well as from reading. It begins by describing the kinds of state, using the word stato for all forms of supreme political power, whether republican or princely. It treats new princedoms, either wholly new or added to an older state, and ecclesiastical principalities, using the Borgia family as a nearly successful example. He argues that the two essential foundations of any state are sound laws and strong military forces, and that a prince should have his own arms and avoid mercenaries.

Machiavelli holds that a prince should make war his chief study, since being disarmed makes you despised, and that it is wiser to take a side than to be neutral. In the last chapters he argues that fortune governs only half of our actions, and that the princes who rise highest take risks and adapt to changing circumstances.

The printed version appeared in 1532, five years after Machiavelli's death, with the permission of the Medici pope Clement VII, although controversy had surrounded his writings since the work first circulated in manuscript. About fifteen editions of The Prince and nineteen of the Discourses on Livy were in circulation before Paul IV placed them on the Index in 1559. Interpreters differ: some read it as satire, as Garrett Mattingly did, and Rousseau held that Machiavelli, by choosing Cesare Borgia as his hero, aimed to expose tyranny. The treatise gave rise to the word Machiavellian.
the-red-army-is-the-strongest: The song answers the last Crimean offensive of Pyotr Wrangel's troops in July 1920. Its second verse echoes the call for a final effort in the Crimea that the Revolutionary Military Council published in Pravda on 10 July. Black Baron was a nickname of Wrangel's, from his alleged liking for black uniforms, in which he also dressed some of his elite units. The offensive was halted, and on 14 November 1920 Wrangel and the remains of his army were evacuated from Crimea to Constantinople.

The first verse tells how the White Army and the Black Baron are preparing to restore the Tsar's throne, but from the taiga to the British seas the Red Army is the strongest of all. That claim returns in every verse and became the conventional title, although the song has a separate refrain. In oral transmission between 1920 and 1925 the words varied; Gorinshtein later recalled that his original text had four or five verses. The melody may draw on Eastern European Jewish folk music, since one passage is also heard in the Yiddish song Dus Zekele mit Koilen.

The song was sung in 1923 at a rally in Leningrad against Lord Curzon's ultimatum, and Nadezhda Krupskaya, the wife of Vladimir Lenin, named it among her favourite songs beside The Internationale. It appeared under several titles until the present one settled in 1937, and it was printed without its authors' names until the musicologist A. Shilov established them in the 1950s.

Abroad, the Chapaev Battalion of the International Brigades adopted it in the Spanish Civil War, and the Czech communist Julius Fučík is said to have sung it in a Nazi torture chamber. German communists sang a free translation in the Weimar Republic, and in 1927 Fritz Brügel set Die Arbeiter von Wien to the tune, later sung by the Republikanischer Schutzbund in the Austrian Civil War of February 1934. That version passed into Turkish as Avusturya İşçi Marşı, and the Corsican song Borgu uses the same melody.
the-red-flag: The song opens "The people's flag is deepest red, It shrouded oft our martyred dead", and its chorus ends "We'll keep the red flag flying here." Connell wanted it sung to "The White Cockade", a pro-Jacobite anthem by Robert Burns, but it is normally sung to the tune of "Lauriger Horatius", better known as the German carol "O Tannenbaum". The British socialist writer Adolphe Smith Headingley popularised that tune in the 1890s; Connell disapproved of it as church music, conservative by nature.

The song became the anthem of the British Labour Party from its founding, and of the Irish Labour Party and the Northern Irish Social Democratic and Labour Party; the New Zealand Labour Party used it until the late 1940s. It is traditionally sung at the close of each party's national conference, at Labour's together with Jerusalem. Translated versions are sung by the Japanese Communist Party and the Korean People's Army.

In the United States it was the first song in the first edition of the Little Red Songbook of the Industrial Workers of the World in 1909, which printed five of the six stanzas. In 1913 the IWW songwriter Joe Hill, recalling the Magonista rebellion of 1911, proposed singing "The Workers' flag is deepest red" instead, since he held "the people" to be middle class.

"The Red Flag" was first sung in the House of Commons on 1 August 1945, when Parliament met after Clement Attlee's Labour Party had defeated Winston Churchill's Conservatives. Labour members sang it again on 28 March 1979, when a motion of no confidence brought down the Labour government, in February 2006 for the centenary of the party's founding, and in September 2019 in protest at the prorogation of Parliament.

Billy Bragg recorded the song in 1990 with the Scottish folk singer Dick Gaughan, singing it to Connell's chosen tune of "The White Cockade", and in 1982 Robert Wyatt included it in his collection of socialist and resistance songs. Leon Rosselson parodied it as "The People's Flag Is Palest Pink", mocking a perceived lack of socialist principle in the Labour Party, and football supporters of Manchester United, Sunderland, Chelsea and other clubs sing chants to its tune.
the-satire-of-the-trades: The text is a long speech in which Kheti tells his son that he has seen "a man seized for his labor" and commoners suffering "violent beatings", fates Pepi can avoid by directing his heart to writing. Most of the work describes other lines of work in hyperbolic terms. Of the builder of walls it says: "His apron is mere rags and the rest-house far behind him. His arms are dead from wielding the chisel, and every measurement is wrong; He eats his food with his fingers and washes once a day."

Kheti then advises his son on conduct at the scribal school: to be serious, to avoid places of ill fame and to study many things. Before closing he praises the scribe's duties once more and celebrates the career Pepi has begun. The same Kheti may have composed the Instructions of Amenemhat, though this is uncertain.

As a schoolboy text, the work taught young scribes the values and tasks of the profession, and pupils were expected to memorise passages and write them out. A surviving ostracon of the Satire in two hands, one skilled and one amateurish, shows how this worked: an experienced scribe wrote one section and the start of the next, and the pupil completed the unfinished verse, a test of both memory and writing.

Although the whole text is preserved on the Papyrus Sallier II, that copy is badly corrupted, and fragments are kept in the British Museum, the Louvre, the Morgan Library & Museum and other collections. The instruction is echoed by Ben Sira in the Book of Sirach at 38:24 to 39:11.

Gaston Maspero named the work the Satire des Métiers, and it has usually been read as a satire since. Miriam Lichtheim points to its exaggeration and lightness of tone, and argues that a serious reading would show a scribal disdain for labourers out of keeping with Ptahhotep's instruction and The Loyalist Teaching, which demand respect for manual workers. Wolfgang Helk agrees with Chris Rollston that it is not satire, and William K. Simpson places it outside the tradition of satire, though it has elements of one.
the-second-sex: Volume One, Facts and Myths, asks what a woman is. Beauvoir compares the physiology of men and women and concludes that values cannot be based on physiology, so that the facts of biology must be read in their ontological, economic and social context. She rejects the views of Sigmund Freud, Alfred Adler and Friedrich Engels, and traces the history of women's condition from ancient Greece and Rome through Christianity, courtly love, the Napoleonic Code and the Industrial Revolution to trade unions, birth control and women's suffrage. She argues that women's historical insignificance, not an inferiority, has doomed them to inferiority, and she examines the myths about women in writers such as Henry de Montherlant, D. H. Lawrence, Paul Claudel, André Breton and Stendhal.

Volume Two, Lived Experience, follows a woman's life. A girl is taught to be a woman, her feminine destiny is imposed on her by society, and she has no innate maternal instinct. Beauvoir then describes puberty, sexual relations, marriage, motherhood, the work of married women, prostitution and old age. She calls marriage an institution that almost always destroys woman and argues that abortion is not an issue of morality. She concludes that women must work for their own liberation and looks to a future of equality in which men and women affirm their brotherhood.
