The book was condemned by the Vatican and remained on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum until the Index itself was abolished in 1966. A Spanish translation printed in Argentina was banned in Francoist Spain in 1955, and Spanish feminists smuggled in copies. Beauvoir recalled in a 1974 interview that Camus was furious and that professors threw the book across the room, partly because she had spoken about female sexuality. The sex researcher Alfred Kinsey thought it interesting as literature but of no value to science.

Its attack on psychoanalysis helped inspire later feminist arguments, including Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique, Kate Millett's Sexual Politics and Germaine Greer's The Female Eunuch. Camille Paglia calls it the supreme work of modern feminism. Judith Butler reads the line One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman as separating sex from gender, a reading contested by Toril Moi and Nancy Bauer. Critics have also charged Beauvoir with an unconscious misogyny and with writing from a middle-class standpoint.

The 1953 English translation by H. M. Parshley, which cut great swaths of the text and mistranslated its philosophical vocabulary, was widely judged poor. Beauvoir asked for a more faithful one in a 1985 interview, and a complete translation by Constance Borde and Sheila Malovany-Chevallier appeared in November 2009.
the-skye-boat-song: The tune was noted down in the 1870s by Anne Campbell MacLeod, later Lady Wilson. According to the folk music collector Andrew Kuntz, she was being rowed across Loch Coruisk on Skye when the rowers broke into the Gaelic rowing song Cuachag nan Craobh, and she wrote down what she remembered of the air. Sir Harold Boulton, 2nd Baronet, gave it new English words with Jacobite associations, and the two published it in London in 1884 in Songs of the North, which ran to at least twenty editions. Later editions dropped MacLeod's name and called it an old Highland rowing measure arranged by Malcolm Lawson.
The song appears in no older book of Scottish songs. Kuntz observed that it succeeded perhaps too well, as people soon began to remember learning it as children from old Gaelic lines.

Boulton's words tell how Prince Charles Edward Stuart, disguised as a serving maid, escaped by boat with the help of Flora MacDonald after the defeat at the Battle of Culloden in 1746, crossing from Benbecula to the Isle of Skye. Written nearly a century and a half after the event, the song draws on the motifs of Jacobitism. Robert Louis Stevenson, judging the Jacobite words unworthy of the plaintive tune, wrote his own verses, probably in 1885, which give the boat's course past Mull, Rum and Eigg, a route that is unhistorical for a voyage from Benbecula. It is set in the style of an iorram, a Gaelic rowing song, and is often sung as a slow lullaby in 6/8 time.

Tom Bryce made the first recording on 29 April 1899, and the song became a standard of Scottish folk and dance musicians. Michael Tippett arranged it for unaccompanied chorus in 1957; Paul Robeson, Tom Jones, Rod Stewart, Tori Amos and many others recorded it, and Roger Whittaker's duet with Des O'Connor reached the UK top ten in 1986. Bear McCreary adapted it, with Stevenson's words, for the opening titles of the series Outlander in 2014. Pipers played it as the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II went up the Long Walk to Windsor Castle on 19 September 2022, and the line Over the Sea to Skye is central to tourism on the island.
the-social-contract: The Social Contract, originally published as On the Social Contract; or, Principles of Political Right, was written in French by the Genevan philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau and published in 1762. It takes up the problems of commercial society that Rousseau had already identified in his Discourse on Inequality of 1755. Its epigraph, from Virgil's Aeneid, reads foederis aequas dicamus leges, Let us set equal terms for the truce.

Rousseau asks whether there can be a legitimate political authority, since people's dealings in his time seemed to leave them in a state far worse than the state of nature. He concludes in the first book that force does not create right, and that people are obliged to obey only legitimate powers. Legitimate authority must be compatible with individual freedom and therefore be consented to, so there must be a social contract. Unlike Grotius, Hobbes and Pufendorf, he holds that the right to freedom is inalienable, so the people cannot obligate themselves to anyone but themselves. The only legitimate contract establishes the people themselves as rulers, through the general will, which may legislate only general laws that apply equally to all.

He separates the sovereign from the government, which is his term for the executive power, because the sovereign cannot deal with particular matters without damaging the generality of law. When the government exceeds the limits set by the people, the people should abolish it and begin anew. He argues that equality is essential for the attainment of liberty. He thought small city-states like his native Geneva best suited to freedom, an elected aristocracy preferable for states of that size, and a benevolent monarch for very large ones.

On publication the book was prohibited in France, and Rousseau fled the country to avoid imprisonment, though it was mainly his chapter on civil religion that caused the controversy. It was also banned in Paris, burned in Geneva and listed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum. Voltaire, who often mocked Rousseau, said that to burn a book of argument is to say that one lacks the wit to reply to it. The Jesuit Alfonso Muzzarelli published a refutation in Italy in 1794.

Immanuel Kant acknowledged his debt to Rousseau's political philosophy, of which the book is perhaps the closest to a complete statement. Noah Webster borrowed heavily from it for Sketches of American Policy in 1785. Maximilien Robespierre wrote in his diary during the Estates General of 1789 of how Rousseau had taught him to know himself.
the-solent: The Solent is about 20 miles (32 kilometres) long and between 4 and 8 kilometres wide. Hurst Spit projects into it and narrows the sea crossing between Hurst Castle and Colwell Bay to just over 1 mile (1.6 kilometres). The Isle of Wight shelters the strait, which has a complex tidal pattern. It has a double high tide that lengthens the period in which deep-draught ships can be handled at Southampton. Spithead, off Gilkicker Point near Gosport, is traditionally where the monarch reviews the Royal Navy.

The name predates Old English and is first recorded in 731 as Soluente, by Bede. This spelling suggests a derivation from a Brittonic element, -uente, found also in Venta Belgarum, the Roman city, and in the name of Winchester.

The Solent was originally a river valley. The River Frome was the source of the River Solent, and the Avon, Hamble, Itchen and Test were its tributaries. When the Ice Age ended, melt water carved the estuary deeper and the south of England sank slowly. The estuary flooded, and the Isle of Wight became separated from the mainland as the chalk ridge between The Needles and Old Harry Rocks eroded, about 7,500 years ago. Divers have found, off Bouldnor on the Isle of Wight, the submerged remains of a wooden building made around 6000 BCE.

In the early 16th century Henry VIII built coastal defences at each end of the Solent, part of his Device Forts. In 1545 English and French fleets fought an inconclusive battle there. The only significant loss was Henry's flagship, the Mary Rose, which foundered while making a sharp turn. Of a crew of over 400, fewer than 35 survived. The wreck was found in 1971 and raised in 1982, and its hull and many objects are in the Mary Rose Museum at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard. More forts, the Palmerston Forts, were built in the 19th century.

The Solent is a major shipping lane for passenger, freight and military vessels and a recreational area for water sports, notably yachting. It hosts the Cowes Week sailing event every year, and it was one of two sites for the sailing events at the 1908 Summer Olympics. In April 1912 the liner Titanic departed from it. Much of its coastline is a Special Area of Conservation, and it borders protected landscapes including the New Forest National Park.
the-song-of-australia: On 20 October 1859 the judges awarded the prize for the words to Mrs C. J. Carleton of Adelaide, the English-born poet Caroline Carleton, and the Gawler Institute offered a second prize of ten guineas for music to her text. The air was to be written in the G clef within a set range, with any chorus for three or four voices and an optional pianoforte part. On Friday 4 November the four judges, Francis S. Dutton, A. Ewing, George W. Chinner and William Holden, examined twenty-three settings and unanimously chose the one under the motto One of the Quantity. It proved to be by Carl Linger (1810–1862), a German-born musician prominent among the Australian Forty-Eighters.

The poem, printed in the South Australian Register on 21 October 1859, has five stanzas, each opening with There is a land and closing on the word Australia. They pass from summer skies and forest heights to corn, vines and wine, hidden gold and rubies, homesteads and children's voices, and end with a flag waving over a land where no shackled slave can breathe the air, fairest of Britain's daughters. Critics at once found it pleasant but too tame: one complained it could as well describe California, another that it did not mention sheep. The Advertiser of 24 October defended the judges and the poem.

The Adelaide Liedertafel under Linger sang it at a South Australian Institute soirée at White's Rooms in Adelaide on 14 December 1859, and it was a feature of the opening of the Adelaide Jubilee International Exhibition in 1887. The baritone Peter Dawson called it the finest national anthem ever written and recorded it in 1932. In 1924 George Edwin Yates, member for Adelaide, proposed it in federal parliament as the national anthem and sang the first verse over his colleagues' objections.

It was one of four songs in the national plebiscite of 1977, with Waltzing Matilda, God Save the Queen and Advance Australia Fair. It came last nationally but first in South Australia, a result put down to its being taught in schools there and, to a lesser extent, in Western Australia and Tasmania, while Advance Australia Fair was sung by schoolchildren in the more populous states.
the-sorrows-of-young-werther: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, aged 24, wrote the novel in five and a half weeks between January and March 1774, and it appeared anonymously; a revised edition followed in 1787. It drew on real triangular relationships. In the summer of 1772 Goethe fell in love at Wetzlar with Charlotte Buff, who was engaged to Christian Kestner, and then with Maximiliane von La Roche, who married Peter Anton Brentano in January 1774. A further source was Karl Wilhelm Jerusalem, a 25-year-old lawyer known to Goethe's circle, who suffered a similar impossible love for an engaged countess and killed himself on the night of 29 or 30 October 1772 with a pistol borrowed from Kestner.

The book is presented as letters written by Werther, a sensitive young artist, mostly to his friend Wilhelm, with some details supplied by an unidentified editor. He stays in the fictional village of Wahlheim, based on Garbenheim near Wetzlar, and meets Charlotte, who cares for her siblings after their mother's death. He loves her although he knew before meeting her that she was engaged to Albert, eleven years her senior. He befriends them both, leaves for Weimar, where he is turned away from a gathering of the aristocracy because he is not a nobleman, and returns to find them married.

Charlotte tells him to visit less often and suggests that it is only the impossibility of possessing her that makes his desire so strong. Werther, who had made pessimistic remarks about life even before meeting her, resolves to take his own life. He asks Albert for his pistols on the pretext of a journey, and Charlotte hands them over at Albert's command. The novel ends with Werther's death and burial.

The Sorrows of Young Werther was an immediate international bestseller, perhaps the first in literary history. It gave rise to Werther Fever: young men across Europe dressed as Werther does in the novel, and prints, decorated Meissen porcelain and a perfume were sold. Napoleon Bonaparte admired it and carried it on his campaign in Egypt. It is a main novel of the Sturm und Drang period and influenced later Romanticism. Some readers were reported to have copied Werther's suicide, which is known as the Werther effect, though the biographer Rüdiger Safranski calls this a persistent rumour. Leipzig banned the novel in 1775, and Denmark and Italy banned it too.

Goethe later distanced himself from the book and regretted the fame it brought him. Friedrich Nicolai wrote a satire with a happy ending, and Goethe attacked him for it in verse. Jules Massenet adapted the novel as the opera Werther in 1892.
the-spectator-1711: The first number appeared on 1 March 1711, and the original run of 555 numbers, each about 2,500 words long, was collected into seven volumes. The paper was revived without Steele in 1714, appearing three times a week for six months, and those numbers formed an eighth volume. Eustace Budgell, a cousin of Addison's, and the poet John Hughes also wrote for it. In Number 10 Mr. Spectator set out its aim: "to enliven morality with wit, and to temper wit with morality".

The letters and essays claimed to be the observations of a spectator of the London coffee-house scene, and ranged over politics, foreign affairs, the theatre, the arts, poetry and love, often with a humorous tone. Women were a target audience, and readers were urged to treat the paper as part of the tea-equipage and read it each morning. The paper sought to give its readers topics for well-reasoned discussion and to equip them for polite conversation.

In Number 11, of 13 March 1711, Steele told the story of Inkle and Yarico, drawn from Richard Ligon's A True and Exact History of the Island of Barbadoes of 1647: a young London trader saved and hidden by an Indian woman sells her to a merchant once they reach the English colony, even after she tells him she is pregnant. Seven decades later George Colman turned the tale into a comic opera.

The daily circulation was only about 3,000 copies, but Addison estimated that each number was read by about a tenth of London's population, a claim scholars find reasonable, since most readers saw it in subscribing coffee houses. It catered to the emerging middle class of merchants and traders and, though it declared itself neutral, was widely seen as promoting Whig values. In the American colonies James Madison read it avidly as a teenager, and it shaped Benjamin Franklin's style in his Silence Dogood letters. Jürgen Habermas sees it as instrumental in forming the public sphere in 18th-century England. The standard edition is Donald F. Bond's of 1965.
the-spirit-of-the-laws: Montesquieu spent about ten years and a lifetime of thought on De l'esprit des lois, a work covering law, social life and anthropology. It was published anonymously in 1748, as was the norm, and its influence outside France was aided by rapid translation into other languages. Thomas Nugent published an English translation in 1750, which has been revised and reprinted many times.

The treatise runs to thirty-one books in six parts. Montesquieu classifies political systems as republican, monarchical or despotic. A monarchy is restrained by a fixed set of laws; a despotism is not. Each kind has a principle that drives its citizens' behaviour: the love of virtue in democratic republics, the love of honour in monarchies and the fear of the ruler in despotisms. A system cannot last long without its principle, and he claims that the English failed to establish a republic after the Civil War because their society lacked the love of virtue.

He also treats political liberty, by which he means personal security under dependable and moderate laws. Building on John Locke's Second Treatise of Government, he argues that executive, legislative and judicial functions should be assigned to different bodies, so that each can restrain the others, and he studies the English political system at length. He argues for fair trials, the presumption of innocence, proportionate punishment, freedom of thought, speech and assembly, and against slavery. The bulk of the work examines how geography and climate interact with cultures to produce the spirit of a people, which inclines it toward certain institutions.

In 1751 the Roman Catholic Church placed the book on its Index Librorum Prohibitorum. It influenced Catherine the Great, who wrote her Nakaz (Instruction) under its influence, the Founding Fathers of the United States Constitution, and Alexis de Tocqueville, who applied Montesquieu's methods to American society in Democracy in America. In his 1827 essay on Machiavelli, Macaulay wrote that Montesquieu enjoyed perhaps a wider celebrity than any political writer of modern Europe.

Montesquieu is often credited with more or less inventing political sociology. Many of his specific claims lack rigour to modern readers, and later writers caricatured his theory as explaining legal variation by a community's distance from the equator. His naturalistic approach to politics nevertheless inspired the modern fields of political science, sociology and anthropology.
the-star-spangled-banner: The words come from a poem called the Defence of Fort M'Henry, which Francis Scott Key wrote after he witnessed the British Royal Navy's bombardment of Fort McHenry during the Battle of Baltimore in the War of 1812. He was inspired by the large American flag, with 15 stars and 15 stripes, that flew over the fort after the battle. Key gave the poem to his brother-in-law Joseph H. Nicholson, who saw that the words fit a popular melody, The Anacreontic Song, by the English composer John Stafford Smith, written for the Anacreontic Society, a gentlemen's club of amateur musicians in London.

Nicholson took the poem to a printer in Baltimore, who anonymously made the first known broadside on 17 September; two copies survive. On 20 September the Baltimore Patriot and The American both printed it with the note Tune: Anacreon in Heaven, and it was in the end printed in 17 newspapers from Georgia to New Hampshire. Thomas Carr of Baltimore then published words and music together as The Star Spangled Banner; his arrangement introduced the raised fourth that became the standard departure from the earlier tune. The first public performance came in October, when the actor Ferdinand Durang sang it at Captain McCauley's tavern.

Bands played the song at public events such as Independence Day celebrations through the 19th century. The United States Navy adopted it officially in 1889, and in 1916 President Woodrow Wilson ordered it played at military and other appropriate occasions. Congress passed a joint resolution making it the national anthem on 3 March 1931, which President Herbert Hoover signed into law.

Although the poem has four stanzas, usually only the first is performed. The melody has a range of a twelfth, which makes it difficult for nonprofessional singers. Most performances follow a 1918 arrangement by Walter Damrosch and John Philip Sousa. Translations appeared as immigrant communities grew, among them a German version in 1861, probably to encourage German-American service in the Union forces, and later Hebrew, Yiddish, Irish, Navajo, Cherokee and Samoan versions. At the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City the athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos each raised a black-gloved fist while the anthem played at their medal ceremony, a gesture Smith described as a human rights salute.
the-tale-of-genji: The tale is said to have been written by the noblewoman and lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu at the peak of the Heian period. She lived when the Fujiwara clan was at the height of its power and Fujiwara no Michinaga was regent in all but name, and she is believed to have shaped the character of Genji partly on her experience of him. The tale may have been written chapter by chapter and delivered to aristocratic women of the court. How much of it Murasaki wrote has been debated for centuries. Her own diary mentions the tale in 1008, and the author of the Sarashina Nikki recorded in 1021 her joy at acquiring a complete copy of more than fifty chapters.

The first section, chapters 1 to 33, follows the early life and love affairs of Hikaru Genji, son of an emperor and a low-ranking concubine, whom the emperor removes from the succession for political reasons by giving him the surname Minamoto. The second, chapters 34 to 41, tells of his old age and death, and the last, chapters 42 to 54, turns to his grandson Niou and supposed son Kaoru. Of some four hundred characters, almost none is named. They are called by function, rank or relation, such as Minister of the Left, which court manners made necessary.

The language is Heian court Japanese, in kana rather than the kanji used for more prestigious writing, and it needs specialised study. The tale ends abruptly. Arthur Waley thought it finished, Ivan Morris thought later chapters were lost, and Edward Seidensticker thought Murasaki simply wrote as long as she could.

The original manuscript no longer exists, but about 300 later copies differ from one another. In the thirteenth century Minamoto no Chikayuki and Fujiwara Teika each edited and revised the text, and Teika's more conservative version is thought to represent the original better. A twelfth-century picture scroll, the Genji Monogatari Emaki, is the earliest surviving Japanese picture scroll, though only about 15 per cent of it remains. Tosa Mitsuoki painted scenes in Heian style in the seventeenth century, and ukiyo-e prints of the Edo period also took the tale as a subject.

A century after its completion it was already hard to read without notes. The poet Akiko Yosano turned it into modern Japanese in the early twentieth century. Suematsu Kencho made the first, incomplete English translation in 1882, and Arthur Waley's version appeared from 1925 to 1933.
the-tale-of-igors-campaign: The poem describes the failed raid of 1185 by Igor Svyatoslavich, Prince of Novgorod-Seversk, on the Polovtsians, the name Rus' sources give to the Cumans, who lived along the lower Don. Other figures of the Rus' world appear, among them the bard Boyan and the princes Vseslav of Polotsk, Yaroslav Osmomysl of Halych and Vsevolod the Big Nest of Suzdal. The author appeals to the warring princes of the Rus' to unite against the constant threat from the Turkic East. Igor's campaign is also recorded in the Kievan Chronicle of about 1200.

The text shows Christianity and the old Slavic religion side by side. Igor's wife Yaroslavna calls on the forces of nature from the walls of Putyvl, and Christian motifs stand beside depersonalised pagan gods. Its main themes are patriotism, the power of nature and the homeland. Scholars have compared it with the Song of Roland and the Song of the Nibelungs, but it differs from these in its many vivid descriptions of nature.

The only manuscript, claimed to date from the 15th century, was found in 1795 in the library of the Transfiguration Monastery in Yaroslavl. Its superior, Joel Bykovsky, sold it to the landowner Aleksei Musin-Pushkin as part of a collection of ten texts. Musin-Pushkin made a transcription for Catherine the Great in 1795 or 1796 and published the poem in 1800 with the paleographers Alexei Malinovsky and Nikolai Bantysh-Kamensky. The manuscript was reported to have burned in the Moscow fire of 1812 with Musin-Pushkin's library. Vladimir Nabokov translated it into English in 1960, and Dmitry Likhachev prepared the standard Soviet edition.

After the manuscript was lost, doubts arose about its authenticity, partly because contemporary fabrications such as the Songs of Ossian were known. The current scholarly consensus holds it to be a work of the late 12th century, perhaps composed orally and written down in the 13th. Edward L. Keenan has argued that Josef Dobrovský forged it, but Andrey Zaliznyak concluded in 2004 that forgery is virtually impossible, noting that birch bark documents found in Novgorod showed that puzzling words of the poem were common speech in the 12th century.

The publication caused a stir in Russian literary circles because the poem was the earliest Slavonic writing without any element of Church Slavonic. Alexander Borodin adapted the story as the opera Prince Igor, first performed in 1890, which became one of the classics of Russian theatre. The poem also became a subject of politics: in the Soviet Union, attempts to question its authenticity were condemned.
the-tale-of-kieu: The poem's original title is Đoạn Trường Tân Thanh, A New Cry From a Broken Heart. Nguyễn Du took his plot from a seventeenth-century Chinese novel, Jīn Yún Qiào, a straightforward romance by an unknown writer who used the pseudonym Qīngxīn Cáirén, and used it to convey the upheavals of late 18th-century Vietnam. Loyal to the Lê dynasty, he reluctantly joined the government of Emperor Gia Long after the Nguyễn conquest of 1802, a position of divided loyalty partly mirrored in Kiều, who submits to circumstances while her heart longs for her first love.

In 3,254 verses, the story is set in Ming China under the Jiajing Emperor. Kiều pledges herself to the young scholar Kim Trọng, but when a silk dealer's slander leaves her father and brother facing prison she sells herself to Scholar Mã, who proves to be a pimp, rapes her and takes her to Madam Tú's brothel. Bought out and married by Student Thúc, she is enslaved by his jealous first wife, Lady Hoạn, flees to a Buddhist temple and is tricked into another brothel.

There she meets Từ Hải, leader of a rebel army, and they reign together over a short-lived kingdom for five years, until Hồ Tôn Hiến tricks her into persuading her husband to surrender, which leads to his death. Married off to a local official, Kiều throws herself into the Qiantang River but is saved by the nun Giác Duyên. Kim Trọng, now an official, finds her at last, and she marries him but refuses a physical relationship with him.

Đào Duy Anh, the first to compare the poem with its source, judged that Nguyễn Du kept the Chinese story but rearranged it to be more coherent; Nguyễn Hữu Sơn finds it more emotional than the original. Some post-colonial writers read it as an allegory of the rise of the Nguyễn dynasty. It has been translated into 20 languages, in English by Huỳnh Sanh Thông in 1983 and Timothy Allen in 2019, among others. Kim Vân Kiều (1924), the first theatrical film made in Vietnam, followed its plot, and Phạm Duy adapted it as a song cycle in 1997.
the-three-ravens: After the birds find the slain knight guarded, a "fallow doe" comes to his body, "as great with young as she might go", a figure for the knight's pregnant lover or mistress. She lifts his bloody head, kisses his wounds, carries him away on her back and buries him before the prime, and she herself is dead before evensong, leaving the ravens without a meal. The ballad closes: "God send euery gentleman, Such haukes, such hounds, and such a Leman."

The 1611 text can be sung straight through in stanzas of four lines, or in stanzas of two lines with the first repeated three times, which appears the more canonical form. Each stanza carries the refrains "downe a downe, hay downe" and "With a downe, derrie, derrie, derrie, downe, downe". Newer versions with different music were recorded into the 19th century, and Francis James Child gathered several in his collection of ballads as number 26.

"The Twa Corbies", a darker Scots ballad whose words clearly derive from "The Three Ravens", was first published in Walter Scott's Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border in 1803. Charles Kirkpatrick Sharpe wrote to Scott on 8 August 1802 that a Miss Erskine of Alva had given it to him from an old woman's recitation. Here two birds find that the hawk and hound have gone hunting and the lady has taken another mate, so they will pick out the knight's eyes and line their nest with his hair, while "The wind sall blaw for evermair" over his bones.

Both ballads have been translated into many languages, among them German by Theodor Fontane, Danish by Svend Grundtvig, Hebrew by Nathan Alterman and Yaakov Shabtai, and Basque by Jon Mirande. Aleksandr Pushkin published a partial Russian version of "The Twa Corbies" in 1828, which became well known among Russian speakers. In fiction, the Lady Mevrian sings the song in mourning for her brother in E. R. Eddison's 1922 novel The Worm Ouroboros, and Dorothy L. Sayers quotes the ballad's last two lines in Clouds of Witness.
the-troubles: The roots of the conflict lie in the Plantation of Ulster of 1609, when Scottish and English settlers were given land taken from the native Irish, and in later conflicts between Catholics and Protestants. As Home Rule drew near in 1912, unionists led by Edward Carson signed the Ulster Covenant and formed the Ulster Volunteer Force. Unionists and loyalists, mostly Ulster Protestants, wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom, while nationalists and republicans, mostly Catholics, wanted a united Ireland. It was not a religious war, though the division ran along those lines.

Writers disagree on the start of the Troubles, proposing the formation of the modern Ulster Volunteer Force in 1966, the civil rights march in Derry on 5 October 1968, or the deployment of British troops on 14 August 1969. Tensions grew during a campaign by the Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association against discrimination against the Catholic minority. The government tried to suppress the protests, the Royal Ulster Constabulary was criticised for sectarianism and brutality, and loyalists opposed the campaign. The riots of August 1969 brought British troops, in what became the Army's longest operation, and peace walls were built to separate communities.

Catholic support for the Army fell after Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972, when British paratroopers shot dead thirteen unarmed men at an anti-internment rally in Derry. The violence included bombings and shootings by the Provisional IRA, the INLA and loyalist groups such as the UVF and UDA, as well as killings by state forces, collusion, riots and the creation of no-go areas. In 1981 ten republican prisoners died on hunger strike, and the first, Bobby Sands, had been elected to Parliament. Republican and loyalist ceasefires were declared in 1994, and the IRA ended its own with the Docklands bombing in London on 9 February 1996.

Talks between the main parties led to the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, which restored self-government to Northern Ireland on the basis of power-sharing and provided for consent, civil and political rights, police reform, paramilitary disarmament and the early release of prisoners. An executive with the four main parties, Sinn Féin among them, was formed in 1999, and the Royal Ulster Constabulary became the Police Service of Northern Ireland.

More than 3,500 people died. About 52% were civilians, 32% members of the British security forces and 16% members of paramilitary groups. Republican paramilitaries were responsible for about 60% of deaths, loyalists for 30% and the security forces for 10%.
the-weald: The Weald is the eroded remains of an anticline, a dome of layered Lower Cretaceous rocks worn down to expose sandstone ridges and clay valleys. Its hard central sandstones form the High Weald, the softer sandstones and clays of its edges the gentler Low Weald, and the Greensand Ridge to the north and west holds its highest points. It stretches about 85 miles from west to east and 30 miles from north to south, and its streams feed the Mole, Medway, Stour, Rother, Cuckmere, Ouse, Adur and Arun. The name comes from the Old English weald, forest.

Wealden sandstones contain ironstone, and with timber for charcoal the area became the centre of the Wealden iron industry; of the 33 iron mines listed on the Ordnance Survey Map of Roman Britain, 67% lie in the Weald. By the later 16th century as many as one hundred furnaces and forges were at work. The 9th-century Anglo-Saxon Chronicle gives the forest a length of 120 miles or more and tells how in 477 Ælle drove the Britons into the wood called Andred'sley.

Population grew between 800 and 1300 as woodland was cleared into small irregular fields, and seasonal pasture settlements, the folds of Sussex and the dens of Kent, became permanent by the end of the 12th century. In 1216 archers of the Weald under William of Cassingham ambushed the French army of Prince Louis near Lewes. In 1264 Wealden archers harried the army of King Henry III of England, who ordered captured archers executed and beheaded 300 after a local man shot his cook.

Woodland still covers 23% of the Weald, one of the highest shares in England. Parts lie in the South Downs National Park and the Surrey Hills and High Weald Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and Ashdown Forest, a Norman royal hunting forest, is said to be the largest remaining part of Andredesweald. The largest towns include Horsham, Tunbridge Wells and Tonbridge.
the-wealth-of-nations: The Wealth of Nations was published in two volumes on 9 March 1776, during the Scottish Enlightenment. It was the product of seventeen years of notes and earlier studies, and took Smith some ten years to write. It drew on the conversation of economists of the time, such as Nicholas Magens, about conditions at the beginning of the Industrial Revolution. In the 18th century much of the world economy was dominated by European feudal and mercantilist institutions, with hereditary privilege, guilds, colonial trading monopolies and protective tariffs. Smith offered a reformed economic theory to replace the mercantilist and physiocratic theories.

Book I holds that the division of labour caused a greater increase in production than any other factor, and that it arises from humans' propensity to barter and is limited by the extent of the market. Book II treats stock and capital, and Book III the different progress of opulence in different nations, in which Smith argues that capital is directed first to agriculture, then to manufactures and last to foreign commerce.

Book IV attacks mercantilism, in particular protectionist tariffs and the idea that large reserves of precious metals are necessary for a country's success. Smith rejected the view that wealth came from zero-sum competition between states. He argued that individuals pursuing their own interest often promote that of society, using the metaphor of an invisible hand, which appears only once in the book. He also criticised slavery, rent-seeking by landlords, primogeniture, public debt and military spending for imperial purposes, and favoured public education, a judiciary and a standing army. Book V sets out four maxims of taxation: proportionality, transparency, convenience and efficiency, and Smith called a land value tax most reasonable.

The first edition sold out in six months. The printer William Strahan wrote that Hume thought it required too much thought to be as popular as Edward Gibbon's history, and Gibbon praised it as an extensive science in a single book. In 1791 James Madison cited it in Congress against a national bank, and Thomas Jefferson called it the best book on money and commerce, unless Say's Political Economy could be had. It was translated into French, German and Spanish in the late 18th century, and the Spanish Inquisition banned the French translation.

The book did not at once transform policy, but it became one of the most influential of modern times. Karl Marx called it the true Bible of the classical political economy of the 18th century, and Marxian economics developed as a critique of the tradition it established. Modern scholars stress that Smith used the invisible hand sparingly, acknowledged the dangers of monopolies and supported some state intervention.
the-wearing-of-the-green: The song is set to an old Irish air. Halliday Sparling's Irish Minstrelsy (1888) prints an anonymous Green upon the Cape dated to 1798, a longer poem in which a croppy from Belfast travels into exile and is questioned in Paris by Napoleon Bonaparte. In an 1802 version published in Dundalk, Green on my Cape, the narrator meets Robert Emmet at Brest, and versions of the 1840s and 1850s again feature Napoleon. The tune was first published in The Citizen, or Dublin Monthly Magazine in 1841, and a variant followed as Up! For the Green in James Duffy's The Spirit of the Nation (1845).

In the usual form the narrator is a rebel who has left Ireland and meets a public figure, in most versions Napper Tandy, who asks for news from home and hears that those wearing green are persecuted. The best-known version is by Dion Boucicault, written for his 1864 play Arragh na Pogue, or the Wicklow Wedding, set in County Wicklow during the 1798 rebellion. Boucicault said he based it on a half-remembered Dublin street ballad. His added third and last verses advise emigration to America rather than defiance at home. Henry Grattan Curran, son of John Philpot Curran, wrote a version of his own and claimed the original came from County Tipperary.

John McCormack recorded the song in 1904 and again in 1912, and Judy Garland in 1940. Wellington Guernsey made a version for voice and piano in 1866, and Charles Villiers Stanford arranged the melody to new words by Alfred Perceval Graves in 1900. The air carries other songs, among them The Rising of the Moon, about the same rising, and The Orange and the Green, about a marriage across the Protestant and Catholic divide. The Wearing of the Grey, a lament for the Confederate States Army, was published to it in 1865. Gerald O'Hara sings it in Margaret Mitchell's Gone with the Wind.
the-wild-colonial-boy: Versions of the ballad name the bushranger Jack, with surnames such as Dolan, Doolan, Duggan and Donahue, and it is unclear whether it first referred to a real person. One candidate is Jack Donahue, also spelled Donohoe, an Irish convict sent to Australia in the 1820s who became a bushranger and was killed by police. Another is John Doolan, a juvenile convict of the 1860s born in Castlemaine, Victoria, who also took to bushranging; he was not shot but captured and sentenced to a further convict term. The stories of the two may have blended over time, or the name of Donahue may have been changed to hide the song's origins.

The song was already in circulation by 1880. According to a report in The Argus in November of that year, Ann Jones, keeper of the Glenrowan Hotel, asked her son to sing it while the Kelly Gang were at her hotel that June.

In a common version the hero is Jack Doolan, born of poor but honest parents in Castlemaine, who leaves home at scarcely sixteen to roam as a bushranger, robbing wealthy squatters. In sixty-one he holds up the Beechworth mail coach and robs Judge MacEvoy. Three mounted troopers, Kelly, Davis and FitzRoy, try to take him; refusing to surrender, he shoots Kelly, is mortally wounded by Davis and keeps firing at FitzRoy as he falls. The chorus calls on his companions to roam the mountains and scorn to live in slavery bound down with iron chains.

The song is sung in John Ford's 1952 film The Quiet Man, in the scene where John Wayne's character first enters the bar at Innisfree. The American band Dr. Hook performed it on Australian television in early 1981 and released a studio recording that reached No. 4 on the Australian charts in April 1981. The Pogues and The Dubliners used its tune for Jack's Heroes, a 1990 single celebrating the Republic of Ireland national football team.
the-wrekin: The hill stands about three miles (4.8 km) south-west of Wellington, on the border between Shropshire and Telford and Wrekin. Its crest and north-western slopes are formed of Precambrian volcanic rocks of the Uriconian series, rhyolites, tuffs and agglomerates laid down about 680 million years ago in a volcanic island arc. Dolerite dykes were intruded around 563 million years ago, and the south-eastern side is mostly Cambrian sandstone and shale, including the Wrekin Quartzite.

Together with the neighbouring Ercall, the hill forms part of the Church Stretton Complex, where the Cymru and Wrekin terranes meet along a fault running north-north-east. Despite a common belief, it was never a volcano itself: it is made mainly of volcanic rock, and its volcano-like profile was shaped by other natural processes.

The name first appears, as Wreocensetun, in a charter of 855 copied into a late 11th-century Worcester cartulary; it probably passed into English through Mercian from the British Celtic Wrikon-, and the early Welsh poems of Canu Heledd name Dinlle Wrecon, the fort of Wrecon. The summit hillfort, almost 8 ha in size, is the place to which the name Uriconio first referred. In 47 CE, it is thought, Roman invaders stormed and burned the fort and moved the defeated Cornovii to Wroxeter, Viroconium Cornoviorum. A warning beacon stood on the hill from the Second World War until 1960.

The summit carries the Wrekin transmitting station, whose red beacon was installed in 2000 to mark the millennium. The hill is owned by the Raby Estate and gives its name to the wider district around Telford and Wellington and to a parliamentary constituency. In local speech going all around the Wrekin means taking the long way round, and A. E. Housman named the hill in A Shropshire Lad.
the-wretched-of-the-earth: Some readers take the French title from the opening line of The Internationale, but Fanon's biographer Adam Shatz traced it to Sales nègres, a poem by the Haitian poet Jacques Roumain. The first section, On Violence, starts from the premise that decolonisation is always violent: the colonial world is two societies that exclude each other, and the settlers deny the natives' humanity. Fanon divides the colonised into workers valued for their labour, colonised intellectuals recruited to speak for the settlers' views, and the lumpenproletariat, whom Marxists dismissed but whom he expected to turn to violence first.

He warns that offers of non-violence and compromise blunt a movement, citing Léon M'ba of Gabon, who said after independence in 1960 that between Gabon and France nothing had changed. In On National Culture he argues that a national culture cannot be recovered from a romanticised precolonial past, but is made in the present struggle against colonial rule, as when Algerian storytellers reshaped their tales, and that it is a stage towards international solidarity.

Sartre's preface supported Fanon's case for violence as necessary for the mental health and liberation of the colonised. After Sartre backed Israel in the Six-Day War of 1967, Fanon's widow, Josie Fanon, had the preface removed from new editions. Homi K. Bhabha, in the foreword to the 2004 edition, criticised the preface for narrowing the book to its call for violent resistance. Robert J. C. Young credits Fanon in part for the interest of postcolonial writing in how experience and cultural identity are produced, and some scholars compare his idea of national culture with Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak's strategic essentialism.

Critics have questioned his reliance on the nation. Christopher L. Miller argued that he overlooked the borders imposed on Africa in the Scramble for Africa, and Neil Lazarus that the unified peasant consciousness he described did not match Algeria after independence in 1962. Part of On National Culture began as a speech of 1959 to the Second Congress of Black Writers and Artists in Rome, and it criticised the Négritude movement founded in part by his teacher Aimé Césaire. Constance Farrington's English translation appeared in 1963 and Richard Philcox's in 2004.
theagenes-of-megara: Everything known of Theagenes comes from anecdotes recorded by authors writing several centuries after his death, and their reliability is uncertain. Aristotle gives two accounts of his rise: in one Theagenes persuaded the Megarians to grant him a bodyguard, which he then used to seize the city; in the other he came to power by slaughtering the flocks of the rich beside a river.

Modern historians treat both stories with caution. The bodyguard is a stock element in ancient accounts of how tyrants took power, and the meaning of the slaughtered flocks is disputed. Aristotle saw the episode as a tyrant siding with the poor masses against the rich aristocracy, but recent scholarship has suggested this reading may be anachronistic and has questioned whether such a conflict existed in archaic Megara. Greg Anderson sees the act as part of Theagenes' effort to assert his dominance over the Megarian aristocracy, while Thomas Figueira has proposed that it reflects a religious dispute over the ownership of sacred flocks.

Thucydides records that Theagenes married his daughter to Cylon of Athens, an Olympic victor, and supplied the force with which Cylon, after consulting the Delphic Oracle, seized the Acropolis during the Olympic Games. Cylon and his followers were besieged and killed. Some scholars link this failure with Theagenes' own fall. Plutarch says only that he was overthrown and exiled, without explaining how, and that Megara was afterwards ruled by an oligarchy.

The geographer Pausanias credited Theagenes with a fountain in Megara and the long underground aqueduct that fed it, which he called worth seeing for its size, ornament and number of columns. Archaeologists have uncovered this fountain, but the surviving building dates to the early fifth century BCE and cannot be his work, although an earlier structure may have stood on the same site.

Although very little is known of his life, Theagenes is counted among the archetypal early Greek tyrants. He is also mentioned in Aristophanes' comedy Peace, where the chorus persuades Trygaeus not to sacrifice a fat swine, lest they be associated with the swinishness of Theagenes.
theatre: Modern Western theatre comes in large measure from the theatre of ancient Greece, from which it takes technical terms, classification into genres and many themes, stock characters and plot elements. Western theatre originated in the city-state of Athens, as part of a wider culture of performance that included festivals, religious rituals, law, athletics, music and poetry. Attendance at the City Dionysia was an important part of citizenship. The Greeks also developed dramatic criticism and theatre architecture.

According to Aristotle, the first theoretician of theatre, its origins lie in festivals honouring Dionysus. Greek drama consisted of tragedy, comedy and the satyr play. Athenian tragedy emerged in the sixth century BCE and flowered in the fifth. Playwrights at the City Dionysia presented a tetralogy, usually three tragedies and one satyr play. Official records begin in 501 BCE, when the satyr play was introduced. Of more than a thousand tragedies performed in the fifth century BCE only 32 survive, with complete texts by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides.

Theatre is a collaborative art that uses live performers, usually actors, to present a real or imagined event before a live audience in a specific place, often a stage. The word comes from the Ancient Greek théatron, a place for viewing. Greek performances took place in semi-circular auditoria cut into hillsides, seating 10,000 to 20,000 people, with a dancing floor called the orchestra and a scene building called the skene. The actors, always men, wore masks and each might play several parts. Modern musical theatre emerged from comic opera, variety, vaudeville and music hall in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Theatre has been part of human culture for more than 2,500 years and has produced many theories. Aristotle's Poetics, from about 335 BCE, is the earliest surviving example and has influenced theories ever since. He held that tragedy has six parts, in order of importance plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle. Konstantin Stanislavski treated theatre as an art autonomous from literature, and his system of actor training spread across Europe and the United States.
thebaid: The Thebaid, or Thebais, took its name from Thebes, modern Luxor, and comprised the 13 southernmost nomes of Upper Egypt. Under the dynasties of the pharaohs the region was dominated by Thebes and by the priesthood of the temple of Amun at Karnak. The region stretched along the Nile from Abydos in the north to Aswan in the south, and its ancient name was Thēbaïs in Greek.

In Ptolemaic Egypt the Thebaid formed a single administrative district under the Epistrategos of Thebes, who was also responsible for overseeing navigation in the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. Its capital was Ptolemais Hermiou, a Hellenistic colony on the Nile that served as the centre of royal political and economic control in Upper Egypt.

Under the Roman Empire, Diocletian created the province of Thebais, guarded by the legions I Maximiana Thebanorum and II Flavia Constantia. It was later divided into Upper Thebaid, Thebais Superior, the southern half with its capital at Thebes, and Lower or Nearer Thebaid, Thebais Inferior, the northern half with its capital at Ptolemais.

Around the 5th century the desert of the Thebaid became a place of retreat for a number of Christian hermits, and it was the birthplace of Pachomius. Christian art came to represent the Thebaid as a landscape filled with monks, and Anatole France's novel Thaïs opens among an ascetic community along the Nile there.

The ancient bishoprics of the region are listed in the Annuario Pontificio as Catholic titular sees. Those of Thebais Prima include Antinoöpolis, the metropolitan see, with Hermopolis Magna, Panopolis (Akhmim), Cusae and the Kharga Oasis. Those of Thebais Secunda include Ptolemais Hermiou, its metropolitan see, with Syene (Aswan), Philae, Coptus (Qift), Tentyris (Dendera), Latopolis (Esna), Apollonopolis Magna (Edfu), Hermonthis and Thinis.
thebes-greece: Excavations in and around Thebes have revealed a Mycenaean settlement, cist graves holding weapons and ivory, and clay tablets in Linear B, which show its importance in the Bronze Age. The Cadmea, the central citadel, shows signs of destruction towards the end of the Mycenaean era, and much of the site was abandoned. Thebes was the setting of myths about Cadmus, Oedipus, Dionysus and Heracles, and the Iliad calls it Seven-Gated Thebes to distinguish it from the city in Egypt. In 480 to 479 BCE a contingent of 400 Thebans stood at Thermopylae, but the governing aristocracy then joined Xerxes I and fought for him at Plataea, and the victorious Greeks took away the city's presidency of the Boeotian League.

Thebes was a firm ally of Sparta in the Peloponnesian War, but it broke with Sparta afterwards. A Spartan force seized the Cadmea in 382 BCE; three years later the garrison was expelled and a democratic constitution replaced the oligarchy. The army trained and led by Epaminondas and Pelopidas, which included the Sacred Band of Thebes, defeated the Spartans at Leuctra in 371 BCE. Thebes then led a large coalition into Peloponnesus and crippled Sparta, partly by freeing many helots. Its predominance was short, and after Epaminondas died at Mantinea in 362 BCE it fell back to a secondary power.

Thebes and Athens lost the Battle of Chaeronea to Philip II of Macedon in 338 BCE. After an unsuccessful revolt in 335 BCE, Alexander the Great and his Greek allies destroyed the city, except, according to tradition, the house of Pindar and the temples, divided its territory among other Boeotian cities and sold its people into slavery. Ancient writers treat this as excessive. Cassander re-established Thebes in 315 BCE, but it never regained its prominence, and Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged it in 293 and 292 BCE.

Thebes came under Roman rule after the Boeotian League was dissolved in 146 BCE, and in the late 7th century Justinian II made it the capital of the Theme of Hellas. By the middle of the 12th century it was the biggest producer of silks in the Byzantine Empire, until the Normans of Sicily plundered it in 1147 and took craftsmen to Palermo. The city conquered by the Fourth Crusade in 1205 is today the largest city of Boeotia in Central Greece. It has an archaeological museum, remains of the Cadmea and the church of Luke the Evangelist, which holds the saint's tomb and relics.
thembu: According to Xhosa oral tradition, the Hala clan migrated along the east coast of southern Africa before settling in KwaZulu-Natal. The earliest known Thembu ancestor is Chief Mbulali Ka-Nanzinzaba, whose grandson Mthembu led his people from KwaZulu-Natal to Dedesi in the present-day Eastern Cape. The Thembu became a single political entity under Nxeko, who settled at Dedesi and was granted a chieftainship by King Togu, who later let him form a new Xhosa state. Nxeko built his kingdom by drawing in fragments of other peoples, among them the amaBomvana, amaVundle, amaMpondomise and amaMfengu.

Tradition also tells of a branch that stayed behind in KwaZulu-Natal, around Qhudeni and Msinga, descended from Mvelase, a son of Mthembu, and drawn into the Zulu Kingdom during its expansion under King Shaka in the 19th century. Its people, often counted as Zulu today, kept their name as the AbaThembu bakwaMvelase.

In the 19th century Europeans often called the Thembu Tamboekie or Tambookie, a Khoisan term at first used only for the followers of Chief Maphasa, who moved west of the Great Kei River in the 1820s. The Thembu had an independent kingdom until the British conquest. King Ngubengcuka repelled a cattle raid by King Moshoeshoe I of the Basotho, his men driving the raiders from a forest with clubs cut from its trees, after which the forest was named Nduku, stick; Moshoeshoe's brother Magabane died of his wounds. After the conquest the Thembu came under the Cape Colony as part of Transkei, a Bantustan under apartheid regarded with Ciskei as the homeland of the Xhosa people.

The kingdom has two royal houses. The great house, the Eastern Thembu, is at the Bumbane Great Palace in Mthatha; the right-hand house, the Western Thembu, is at the Qamata Great Palace in Cofimvaba and long enjoyed autonomy. The Xhosa clan name of the Thembu kings is Ntlazi aNkosiyane, and recent kings, among them Sabata Jonguhlanga Dalindyebo, have taken the surname Dalindyebo after a 19th-century king. Descendants of Nxeko include Nelson Mandela, whose father was a nobleman of a junior branch of the AmaMadiba royal clan, and Walter Sisulu.
themis: The name Themis means divine law, as distinct from human ordinance, and literally that which is put in place, from the Greek verb títhēmi, to put. To the ancient Greeks she was originally the organiser of the communal affairs of humans, particularly assemblies. The historian Moses Finley called themis, as Homer used the word, untranslatable: sometimes it means right custom, proper procedure or social order, and sometimes merely the will of the gods, with little of the idea of right.

In Hesiod's Theogony she is one of the twelve Titan children of Gaia and Uranus and the second wife of her nephew Zeus. A fragment of Pindar instead makes her the first wife of Zeus, brought to Olympus by the Moirai. Hyginus makes her a daughter of Aether and Terra, and in Prometheus Bound, traditionally attributed to Aeschylus, she is the mother of Prometheus.

Hesiod's Theogony gives the first recorded appearance of Justice as a divine person. Their daughter Dike, who represents temporal justice, carried out with her mother the final decisions of the Moirai. Judges were often called themistopóloi, servants of Themis. She was an earth goddess much like her mother Gaia, and in some stories the two are hard to tell apart; in Prometheus Bound Prometheus says she is called by many names, including Gaia. Classical sources describe her as a sober-looking woman holding scales, and some depictions show her with a sword. She is not wrathful.

When Nemesis brings retribution on those who disregard Themis, the two shared a small temple at Rhamnous. Her myths are oracular. According to one legend, she received the oracle at Delphi from Gaia and later gave it to Phoebe, who gave it to her grandson Apollo as a birthday gift. Ovid has her warn Zeus and Poseidon not to marry Thetis, since Thetis's son would be more powerful than his father, and tell Deucalion to throw the bones of his mother over his shoulder after the deluge. In the Iliad Zeus tasks her with calling the gods to council.

Themis had temples at Dodona, at Tanagra, in Athens near the Acropolis, at Rhamnous beside the temple of Nemesis, and in Phthiotis. Pausanias describes her sanctuary at Thebes, which held a white marble image and stood beside a sanctuary of the Moirai, and an altar to her stood at Olympia. At Epidauros she shared a sanctuary with Aphrodite. Modern depictions often call her Lady Justice, and statues of the figure stand outside many courthouses.
themistocles: Themistocles was born in the Attic deme of Phrearrhii, the son of Neocles, whom Plutarch calls no very conspicuous man at Athens. His mother's name was either Euterpe or Abrotonum, and her origin is given variously as Halicarnassus, Thrace or Acarnania. Plutarch indicates that because of her background he was something of an outsider. He grew up after Cleisthenes had set up the Athenian democracy, which opened power to men like him. He moved to the Ceramicus, a down-market part of Athens, and courted the poor, and he was the first in Athens to practise law as a preparation for public life.

Elected Archon Eponymous in 493 BCE, he began the building of a new port at Piraeus, which had three natural harbours and could be easily fortified. Naval power depended on the common citizens as rowers, so the policy also strengthened ordinary Athenians. In 483 BCE he persuaded the Athenians to build a fleet of 200 triremes. At the congress of Greek states in 481 BCE the other naval powers refused to let Athens command the fleet, and the Spartan Eurybiades took the command, although Herodotus is clear that Themistocles commanded in all but name.

Later he grew arrogant and made enemies. The Spartans promoted Cimon, son of Miltiades, as a rival, and he lost favour by building a sanctuary of Artemis Aristoboulē, meaning of good counsel, near his home. In 472 or 471 BCE he was ostracised. The Spartans then tried to implicate him in the treason of their general Pausanias. He fled, found sanctuary with Alexander I of Macedon at Pydna, and sailed to Asia Minor.

Thucydides has his ship land at Ephesus, while Plutarch has it dock at Cyme. Themistocles sought service with Artaxerxes I and became governor of Magnesia, perhaps the first ruler to issue coins with his own portrait. According to Thucydides he died at Magnesia in 459 BCE, aged 65, of natural causes, although rumour held that he poisoned himself rather than make war on Athens.

He died with his reputation in tatters, but Pericles rehabilitated it in the 450s BCE, and by the time of Herodotus he was again seen as a hero. Plutarch calls him the man most instrumental in achieving the salvation of Greece. His naval policy lay behind the Delian League and the later Athenian Empire.
themistokli-germenji: Gërmenji was born in Korçë in 1871 into a family from the village of Gërmenj, in present-day Kolonjë near the border with Greece; his grandfather Demetrius had moved to Korçë in 1860 and taken Gërmenji as the family name. For economic reasons his father Atanas left, first for Egypt and then for Bucharest and Istanbul, while his mother Konstandina and the other children stayed in Korçë.

His Liria (Freedom) Hotel in Korçë became a centre of the Albanian National Awakening, where the Congress of Monastir and the Albanian revolts of 1909 to 1912 were planned. He favoured cooperation with the Bulgarians. In 1911 he travelled to Italy and Greece in search of support, but Greece declared him persona non grata after he refused to give up nationalist propaganda south of Vlora as a condition of working with the Greek authorities against the Ottoman Empire.

He led a guerrilla band of men of different religions and social classes against the Ottoman Empire, and was captured and imprisoned in Ioannina while trying to seize Ottoman military supplies between Saranda and Gjirokastra. In the first stages of the conflict between the Principality of Albania and the Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus he fought in the defence of his native Korçë, which Albanian forces failed to hold against the pro-Greek Northern Epirus movement.

French officers met Gërmenji on 24 November 1916, five days before the French army occupied Korçë. On 10 December a commission he led signed a protocol with Colonel Descoins creating an autonomous province of Korçë, Bilishti, Kolonja, Opar and Gora, with the commission's 14 members as its administrative council; the declaration was approved by Maurice Sarrail. The new authorities formed a police force and gendarmerie, set up a postal service and issued stamps, and Gërmenji received the Croix de Guerre for taking part with the Korçë battalion in the French capture of Pogradec.

He was executed in Thessaloniki on 7 November 1917. It later became clear that the tribunal had made a grave judicial error, misled by Greek informers who wanted a powerful Albanian leader removed. A statue of Gërmenji as a freedom fighter stands in a main square of Korçë.
themistoklis-sofoulis: Sofoulis was born on 24 November 1860 in Vathy, on Samos, then an autonomous principality under Ottoman suzerainty; his father, Panagiotis Sofoulis, had fought for the island's autonomy. He studied philosophy at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and archaeology in Germany, and took part in excavations around Greece.

In 1900 he left archaeology and was elected a deputy for Samos, soon heading the Progressives, who wanted reform and union with the Kingdom of Greece. In 1902 he became president of the Samian parliament. Riots in May 1908, after the Prince, Andreas Kopasis Omoudopoulos, called in Turkish troops, forced him to flee to Greece. In the First Balkan War he landed with exiled Samians, and on 11/24 November 1912 the island's parliament declared union with Greece.

Sofoulis served as Governor General of Macedonia from April 1914, Interior Minister of Eleftherios Venizelos's National Defence government in Thessaloniki during the National Schism, and Speaker of Parliament until 1920. He became leader of the Liberal Party after Venizelos left Greece and was prime minister from 25 July to 27 November 1924. He was again Speaker from 1926 to 1928, Minister of Military Affairs until 1930 and Speaker until 1933, and once more in 1936, when he signed the Sofoulis-Sklavainas Pact with the KKE.

During the Axis occupation he kept contacts with the Allies but refused to cooperate with the National Liberation Front (EAM), which he accused of planning a Communist seizure of power. On 19 May 1944 the Germans imprisoned him in the Haidari concentration camp until the liberation. After his defeat in the elections of 1946 he tried to prevent the Greek Civil War by offering the Communists an amnesty. As prime minister again from 7 September 1947 he negotiated with the KKE, but under strong US pressure the proposals were dropped.

Sofoulis died in Kifissia on 24 June 1949, aged 88, before the civil war ended. Though a centrist, he led the government and the royal army through the war and persuaded General Alexandros Papagos to return to active service. He was admired for his clarity and courage in old age, and his career is remembered for his ability to balance between rival camps.
theo-van-gogh-film-director: Theodoor van Gogh was born on 23 July 1957 in The Hague to Anneke and Johan van Gogh. His father served in the Dutch secret service. He was named after his paternal uncle Theo, who was captured and executed as a resistance fighter during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands during World War II. After dropping out of law school at the University of Amsterdam, he became a stage manager.

Van Gogh made his debut as a director with the film Luger in 1981. He won a Gouden Kalf for Blind Date (1996) and another for In het belang van de staat (1997), the second of which also earned a Certificate of Merit at the San Francisco International Film Festival. He made numerous films, many on political themes, and from the 1990s he also worked in television. His last completed film, 06/05, a fictional treatment of the assassination of the politician Pim Fortuyn, was released in December 2004.

From the 1980s he was also a newspaper columnist and used his columns to attack politicians, actors, writers and others he saw as part of the establishment. He took pleasure in provocation and often criticised Islamic cultures; on his website De Gezonde Roker he harshly criticised multicultural society. His last book, Allah weet het beter (2003), strongly condemned Islam. He supported the nomination of Ayaan Hirsi Ali for the Dutch parliament, and from her script he made the ten-minute film Submission, which tells the stories of four abused Muslim women.

After the broadcast of Submission, Van Gogh and Hirsi Ali received death threats, and he refused protection. At about 9 a.m. on 2 November 2004 he was shot and his throat was cut as he cycled to work in Amsterdam. His killer, Mohammed Bouyeri, a 26-year-old Dutch-Moroccan, pinned a note with a knife to his body, threatening Hirsi Ali. Bouyeri was convicted on 26 July 2005 and sentenced to life imprisonment without parole.

The murder widened and polarised the debate in the Netherlands about the position of its more than one million Muslim residents. In the following weeks mosques and Islamic schools were attacked, and churches were targets in turn. A sculpture, De Schreeuw, was unveiled in Amsterdam's Oosterpark on 18 March 2007.
theobald-bourke-1st-viscount-mayo: Tibbot belonged to the MacWilliam Íochtar, the Lower MacWilliam Burkes of County Mayo, a Hiberno-Norman lineage descended from William de Burgh, who had been granted the overlordship of Connacht in 1215. Tradition says he was born just before his mother's fleet fought Barbary pirates. By 1585 Gráinne O'Malley was ruling the lordship with him, and that year the lord deputy, Sir John Perrott, took him hostage to secure her compliance with the Composition of Connaught; as a prisoner he learnt English, and he married Maeve O'Conor Sligo.

Freed by Richard Bingham in 1586, Tibbot joined a rebellion, sought a truce in 1587, rose again in 1589 and made peace in March 1590, by then the recognised chief of his clan. In 1592 he raised Mayo for Red Hugh O'Donnell, but was left without support when O'Donnell sought peace, and was pardoned. In May 1593 he was arrested for promising to raise an army in support of Brian Óg O'Rourke; his mother visited Queen Elizabeth in London in June and obtained his release, and on a second visit in April 1594 she secured favourable terms of surrender and regrant for him.

In 1595 O'Donnell had a cousin, Tibbot MacWalter Kittagh Bourke, made chief in his place, and Tibbot would not join O'Donnell and Hugh O'Neill in the Nine Years' War. He first helped the English commander Clifford, then took a less active part. Knighted the year after James I succeeded Elizabeth in 1603, he was arrested in 1608 on a charge of plotting to help the earls who had fled Ireland, which proved unfounded, and in 1610 he was again suspected and pardoned. He came to hold most of the lands of the smaller clans he represented in their dealings with Dublin.

In 1613–15 he sat as one of the two members for Mayo in the Parliament of Ireland, voting as a Catholic against new boroughs for Protestant members. Cleared with his son Miles of plotting a Spanish-supported Catholic revolt during the Anglo-Spanish War, he was made viscount in June 1627, and in 1628 joined other Catholic nobles in petitioning for the reforms known as the Graces. He died on 18 June 1629 and was buried at Ballintubber Abbey. Miles, raised as an Anglican and educated at Oxford, succeeded him, and the air Lord Mayo is said to have been composed by David Murphy to win back his favour.
theobald-i-of-blois: Theobald was the son of Theobald the Elder, Viscount of Tours from 908, and of Richildis, whose origins are debated. His French nickname, le Tricheur, means cheater. He rose with a new generation of counts on the Robertian lands after Hugh the Great became Duke of the Franks in 936 and delegated part of his holdings to his vassals, among them Fulk the Good at Angers. Theobald is considered the duke's best lieutenant, and his power in Neustria counterbalanced that of the Norman count William Longsword.

A sister or daughter of Theobald married Alan II, Duke of Brittany, and after Alan's death Theobald and Fulk II of Anjou divided a regency there, based on Rennes and Nantes. About 943–44 Theobald married Luitgarde, widow of William I of Normandy, whose dower around Évreux tightened his grip on Normandy. When King Louis IV was captured by a Norman faction at Easter 945, Hugh placed him in Theobald's custody; to win his freedom about a year later Louis gave Laon to Hugh, who handed it to Theobald, but it was lost in 949.

After Hugh the Great died on 16 June 956, Theobald held something close to a regency in Neustria for the young Hugh Capet. He went to war with Richard I of Normandy, attacking Évreux in 961 and failing before Rouen in 962, after which the Normans burned Chartres and killed his eldest son, also called Theobald. Hugh Capet, now duke and Richard's brother-in-law, disapproved of these policies, beginning a distrust between the House of Blois and their Capetian overlords, and Theobald turned to the Carolingian king Lothair.

By the time of his death Theobald had built vast power on the Loire, dominating central France. His son Odo succeeded him as Count of Blois, another son, Hugh, became Archbishop of Bourges, and his daughter Emma married William IV of Aquitaine. After a war with Odalric, Archbishop of Reims, over the castle of Coucy, one of his sons held the castle from the archbishop.
theobald-i-of-navarre: Theobald was born in Troyes on 30 May 1201, the son of Theobald III of Champagne and Blanche of Navarre, youngest daughter of Sancho VI of Navarre. His father died less than a week before his birth, and Blanche ruled Champagne as regent until he turned twenty-one in 1222. His uncle, Count Henry II, had left large debts, and Theobald's right to the succession was challenged by Henry's daughter Philippa and her husband Erard I of Brienne, in the Champagne War of Succession from 1215. In 1222 he bought out their rights, and in 1234 he paid off Philippa's elder sister Alice as well. He became a notable trouvère, and many of his songs have survived, some with music.

As count, Theobald refused to enforce Louis VIII's measures against Jewish moneylenders in 1223, having an agreement that guaranteed Jews safety in return for taxes. At the siege of Avignon in 1226 he served only the minimum forty days and went home; when Louis died soon after, rumours accused him of poison. Rival lords invaded Champagne in 1229 and 1230, and he repulsed them at a cost that forced him to sell his overlordship of Blois, Sancerre and Châteaudun.

In 1234 he succeeded his uncle Sancho VII as king of Navarre and immediately affirmed the fueros of the realm. He made pacts with Castile, Aragon and England and began the codification of the law in the Cartulario Magno and the Fuero General. In 1239 he led the Barons' Crusade. It was not glorious militarily, but by treaty with the Ayyubids of Damascus the Kingdom of Jerusalem regained Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Nazareth and most of Galilee. He returned late in 1240, bringing a piece of the True Cross and the Provins rose from Damascus.

Theobald spent his last years travelling between Navarre and Champagne. The bishop of Pamplona held a synod in 1250 to excommunicate him, but Pope Innocent IV granted that only the Holy See could do so. He died at Pamplona on 8 July 1253 and was buried in its cathedral. He was the first Frenchman to rule Navarre. His elder son Theobald II succeeded him, and then his younger son Henry I.
theobald-ii-count-of-champagne: Theobald was the son of Count Stephen of Blois and Adela of Normandy, a daughter of William the Conqueror, and the elder brother of King Stephen of England. Although he was the second son, he was appointed above his older brother William. He accompanied his mother throughout their domain on hundreds of occasions, and after she retired to the convent at Marcigney in 1125 he administered the family properties with great skill. Adela died there on 8 March 1137, the year after her son Stephen was crowned king of England. Theobald held Auxerre, Maligny, Ervy, Troyes and Châteauvillain as fiefs from Odo II, Duke of Burgundy.

King Louis VII of France came into conflict with Theobald when he allowed Count Raoul I of Vermandois, the seneschal of France, to repudiate his wife Eleanor, a sister of Theobald and of King Stephen, so that Raoul could marry Petronilla of Aquitaine, sister of Louis's own queen. The war lasted two years, from 1142 to 1144, and the royal army occupied Champagne and took Vitry-le-François, where 1,500 people died when Louis deliberately burned the church. The scholar Pierre Abélard, famed for his love affair with and marriage to his student Héloïse d'Argenteuil, sought asylum in Champagne during Theobald's time.

In 1123 Theobald married Matilda, daughter of Duke Engelbert of Carinthia, and they had many children. Henry I succeeded him in Champagne, and Theobald V became count of Blois and seneschal of France. Their daughter Adela became queen of France as the wife of Louis VII. William White Hands became archbishop of Reims in 1176 and a cardinal in 1179, and Stephen of Sancerre died as a crusader at the siege of Acre. Theobald also had an illegitimate son, Hugh, abbot of Lagny near Paris.
theobald-walter: Theobald was a son of Hervey Walter and Matilda de Valoignes, a daughter of Theobald de Valoignes; his brothers were Hubert, Bartholomew, Roger and Hamon. He and Hubert were brought up by their uncle Ranulf de Glanvill, the justiciar of King Henry II of England, who had married their mother's sister Bertha. His father had held the hereditary office of butler of England, and Theobald himself is also recorded as Chief Butler of England. He was the first of the Butler family of Ireland to use the surname.

Prince John landed at Waterford on 25 April 1185 as Lord of Ireland and granted Theobald the hereditary butlership, by which he and his heirs were to serve the kings of England the first cup of wine at their coronation. Henry II later added the prisage of wines, two tuns from every ship laden with twenty tons of wine that broke bulk in an Irish port. Theobald went with John through Munster and Leinster and received five and a half cantreds in the north-east of the Kingdom of Limerick, lands that now make up baronies in the counties of Clare, Offaly, Tipperary and Limerick.

In 1185, in the war that followed Rory O'Connor's attempt to regain his throne, Theobald's men were involved in the death of Donal Mor McCarthy during a parley near Cork. In 1194 he backed his brother Hubert against Prince John, received the surrender of John's supporters at Lancaster and was made sheriff there, holding the post until Christmas 1198 and again after John became king in 1199. In early 1200 John stripped him of his offices and lands for irregularities as sheriff, and they were not restored until January 1202; a grant of 1201 by William de Braose, 4th Lord of Bramber, appears to mark his restoration.

Theobald founded the Abbey of Woney near Murroe in County Limerick around 1200, as well as Cockersand Abbey in Lancaster, the abbey of Nenagh in County Tipperary and a religious house at Arklow in County Wicklow. He married Maud le Vavasour, heiress of the Yorkshire baron Robert le Vavasour, and their children were Theobald le Botiller, 2nd Chief Butler of Ireland, and Maud. He died at Arklow Castle on 4 February 1206 and was buried at Wotheney Abbey.
theobald-wolfe-tone: Tone was born on 20 June 1763. His father, Peter Tone, was a prosperous coach-maker with a farm near Sallins, County Kildare, and a member of the established Anglican church. His mother, Margaret Lamport, was the daughter of a sea captain and a Catholic, and she converted to her husband's church, according to the early biographer R. R. Madden, when Tone was eight. He was baptised a Protestant and named Theobald Wolfe after his godfather, Theobald Wolfe of Blackhall.

In October 1791 Tone addressed a small reform club in Belfast, whose Presbyterian members had invited him as author of An Argument on behalf of the Catholics of Ireland. The tract, with a print-run of 16,000, argued that Catholic emancipation was the key to reform. At his suggestion the club took the name Society of the United Irishmen. In 1792 he became assistant secretary to the Catholic Committee, and in January 1793 he was among the delegation received by George III at Windsor. In May 1794 evidence against him helped the government justify proscribing the Society.

In August 1795 Tone settled in Philadelphia, but he was disillusioned by America and sailed for France on New Year's Day 1796. In Paris his memorials reached Lazare Carnot of the Directory. On 15 December 1796 an expedition under Hoche, of 44 ships carrying between 12,000 and 25,000 troops, sailed from Brest with Tone as a chef de brigade, and reached Bantry Bay on 22 December. Storms prevented a landing, and Tone remarked that England had had its luckiest escape since the Armada. In May 1798 Bonaparte sailed for Egypt instead of Ireland.

At his court-martial in Dublin on 8 November 1798 Tone said he had sought to separate Ireland from Great Britain in fair and open war, and that he neither asked for pardon nor complained. He died on 19 November 1798.

His name has been invoked by different factions of Irish republicanism, and each holds its own commemoration at his grave at Bodenstown. Thomas Davis organised the first memorial there in 1843, and Patrick Pearse called the site the holiest place in Ireland in 1913. After 1922 some writers dismissed him as not Irish enough, while others stressed his work for the Catholic Committee. His son William, raised in France, served in Napoleon's army and received the Legion of Honour.
theocritus: Little is known of Theocritus beyond what can be inferred from his writings. He calls Polyphemus, the Cyclops of the Odyssey, his countryman, which points to Sicily. An anonymous epigram has him say that he is one of the great populace of Syracuse, the son of Praxagoras and Philinna, and allusions in the Idylls appear to support this.

The information about his parentage bears the stamp of authenticity and disposes of a rival theory, based on a misreading of Idyll 7, that made him the son of one Simichus. Idylls 4 and 5 are set near Croton, from which scholars infer that he knew Magna Graecia personally. He probably lived for a time in Alexandria, where he wrote about everyday life, and it is speculated that he lived on Kos and in Egypt during the time of Ptolemy II.

Two collections of his poems were made at an early date, one of doubtful authorship forming a corpus of bucolic poetry, the other a strict collection of the works held to be his.
