The Suda says he wrote the so-called bucolic poems in the Doric dialect. The Idylls divide into bucolics, set in the country, and mimes, set in a town. In Idyll 1, Thyrsis sings of the mythical herdsman Daphnis, who defies Aphrodite and dies rather than yield to the passion she inflicts on him.

In Idyll 11 Polyphemus loves the sea-nymph Galatea and finds solace in song, and in Idyll 6 he is cured of his passion. Idyll 7, the Harvest Feast, is set on Kos, with the poet speaking as Simichidas. Several other bucolics are singing-matches, in which the second singer varies the theme chosen by the first. The three mimes are Idylls 2, 14 and 15. In 2, Simaetha, deserted by Delphis, tells the story of her love to the moon; in 15, Gorgo and Praxinoë go to the festival of Adonis.

The only poems that can be dated are 16, which praises Hiero II of Syracuse, and 17, which celebrates the marriage of Ptolemy Philadelphus and his sister Arsinoë, held to have taken place in 277 BCE. Arsinoë died in 270 BCE, so Idylls 15 and 17 must fall within that period. Several poems once attributed to him, among them Idylls 19 to 21, 23 and 25, are now generally considered spurious. 48.
theodelinda: Theodelinda was the daughter of Duke Garibald I of Bavaria and Waldrada. Through her mother she was descended, according to tradition, from the Lombard king Waco, whose family had ruled seven generations earlier. Her first husband was Authari, king of the Lombards and son of King Cleph, but he died in 590 after a brief marriage. Pope Gregory I may have had an interest in the match, since it joined a Catholic Bavarian with the Arian Lombards, as he had earlier promoted the marriage of the Frankish princess Bertha to Æthelberht of Kent.

According to Paul the Deacon, Theodelinda was so highly esteemed that after Authari's death she was asked to remain in power and choose a successor. Roger Collins doubts this, and thinks political bargaining or force more likely lay behind her choice. Two months after Authari died she married Agilulf. He remained an Arian but allowed their son to be baptised a Catholic, and his dukes worried that he had committed himself to the faith of the conquered. Agilulf did not let her faith shape his policy towards the Byzantines.

Theodelinda corresponded with Pope Gregory I, and some of the letters, which touched on her husband's conversion, are recorded by Paul the Deacon. She welcomed Catholic missionaries across her realm. Gregory sent her silver ampullae, a gospel casket and a gem-encrusted golden cross from Byzantium. Shortly before Agilulf's death in 616 he named her co-regent for their son Adaloald, and after Adaloald came of age she remained co-ruler. She was queen for some thirty-five years and her influence reached across much of Italy between the Apennines and the Alps.

Theodelinda built a Catholic cathedral dedicated to St John the Baptist at Monza, near Milan, and endowed it richly. According to Paul the Deacon she also founded monasteries, among them one at Bobbio and later one at Pedona. The treasure of the cathedral at Monza includes a gilded silver sculpture of a hen with her chicks, which was probably another gift from Gregory. Her work helped restore Nicene Christianity to primacy in Italy against its rival, Arian Christianity.
theodemir-visigoth: Theodemir, also written Theudimer, was a comes, or count, prominent in the south-east of the province of Carthaginensis, around Murcia, during the last decades of the Visigothic kingdom. Probably during the joint reign of Egica and Wittiza he drove off a Byzantine fleet that had raided the coasts of southern Iberia. The date is disputed: it may have belonged to Leontios's expedition to relieve Carthage in 697, or have come around 702 or late in Wittiza's reign. Most historians see it as an isolated incident, not an attempt to recover the province of Spania lost in the 620s.

After King Roderic was defeated at the Battle of Guadalete, Theodemir resisted the Arab invaders until he was beaten in a pitched battle and made peace. The treaty, kept in at least three sources and preserved by the Andalusian historian Ibn Adarí in the 13th century, named seven cities: Orihuela, Valentila, perhaps Valencia, Alicante, Mula, Bigastro, Eyya, probably Ojós, and Lorca. Christians who submitted kept their lives, families, customs and churches, but each paid a yearly tribute of one dinar with measures of wheat, barley, grape juice, vinegar, honey and oil, half as much for slaves, and they had to hand over the conquerors' enemies.

Theodemir kept his land and local authority, and he later travelled to Damascus to have the treaty confirmed by the Umayyad caliph. How long it held in practice, whether until his death or not, is unknown.

His death is recorded in the Chronicle of 754, which describes his son Athanagild as very wealthy. Scholars debate whether Athanagild succeeded him; if he did, it was around 740, and his fate is unknown. Tudmir had lost its independence by the 780s. Later Gothic nobles of the region tried to claim descent from Theodemir, a sign of his standing, and the novel Amaya o los vascos en el siglo VIII of 1879 names him among those who resisted Islamic rule.
theodor-herzl: Theodor Herzl was born on 2 May 1860 on Dohány utca in the Jewish quarter of Pest, then in the Kingdom of Hungary, to Jeanette and Jakob Herzl, German-speaking, assimilated Jews of the Neolog tradition. His father was a highly successful businessman. After a brief legal career in Vienna he became the Paris correspondent of the Viennese newspaper Neue Freie Presse. He also wrote comedies and dramas, among them Das Neue Ghetto of 1898, his only play with Jewish characters. On 25 June 1889 he married Julie Naschauer; the marriage was unhappy, although three children were born to it.

In Paris Herzl followed the Dreyfus affair, in which the Jewish army captain Alfred Dreyfus was falsely convicted of spying for Germany. Herzl said that the case turned him into a Zionist, though some modern scholars think he may have exaggerated its influence. Convinced that anti-Jewish sentiment made assimilation impossible, he published the pamphlet Der Judenstaat on 14 February 1896 in Leipzig and Vienna.

In 1897 Herzl founded the Zionist newspaper Die Welt in Vienna and convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel, where he was elected president of the Zionist Organization, a position he held until his death. He met Wilhelm II on 29 October 1898 near Mikveh Israel and again in Jerusalem, and proposed to Abdul Hamid II that Zionism could improve the sultan's reputation and finances in exchange for Jewish settlement in Palestine. Through Joseph Chamberlain he negotiated for a charter at Al 'Arish in Sinai, which the Earl of Cromer blocked as impractical. At the Sixth Zionist Congress in 1903 he presented the Uganda Scheme, which met strong opposition and was rejected.

Herzl died of cardiac sclerosis on 3 July 1904 at Edlach in Reichenau an der Rax, Lower Austria, at the age of 44. His will asked for the poorest-class funeral without speeches, yet some six thousand people followed the hearse. He was first buried in the Döbling district of Vienna, and in 1949 his remains were taken to Israel and buried on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem, which is named after him. He is mentioned in the Israeli Declaration of Independence and is known in Hebrew as Chozeh HaMedinah, the Visionary of the State. Herzl Day is an Israeli national holiday.
theodor-mommsen: Mommsen grew up in Bad Oldesloe in Holstein, where his father was a Lutheran minister, and studied largely at home. Unable to afford Göttingen, he enrolled at the University of Kiel, where he studied jurisprudence from 1838 to 1843 and took the degree of Doctor of Roman Law. He shared rooms with the future poet Theodor Storm, and the two published a collection of poems with his brother Tycho. A royal Danish grant then allowed him to travel to France and Italy to study preserved Roman inscriptions. In 1848 he worked as a war correspondent in Rendsburg, supporting German annexation of Schleswig-Holstein, and the Danes forced him to leave.

He became professor of law at Leipzig in 1848 but had to resign in 1851 after protesting against the new constitution of Saxony. After a professorship in Roman law at Zurich, he moved to Breslau in 1854 and became a research professor at the Berlin Academy of Sciences in 1857. From 1861 he was professor of Roman History at Berlin, lecturing until 1887. As secretary of the Historical-Philological Class of the Academy from 1874 to 1895 he organised many editions of original sources. The Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum eventually ran to seventeen volumes; fifteen appeared in his lifetime and he prepared five himself. Its method required every transcription to be checked against the original inscription. He also edited the Corpus Iuris Civilis and the Codex Theodosianus.

Mommsen sat in the Prussian House of Representatives from 1863 to 1866 and from 1873 to 1879, and in the Reichstag from 1881 to 1884. He opposed Otto von Bismarck's social policies in 1881 so sharply that he narrowly avoided prosecution. When Heinrich von Treitschke began a campaign against Jews in 1879, Mommsen denounced it in a pamphlet, and in 1890 he co-founded the Association for Combating Antisemitism. He was nevertheless a vehement German nationalist, and in an 1897 letter he called Czechs apostles of barbarism and advocated blows against them.

On 7 July 1880 a fire in his Berlin workroom destroyed several old manuscripts, some on loan from libraries, while he tried to save his papers. He had sixteen children with his wife Marie, and his grandson Theodor Ernst Mommsen and great-grandsons Hans and Wolfgang Mommsen became historians. He died on 1 November 1903. Bernard Shaw cited Mommsen's view of Julius Caesar as an inspiration for Caesar and Cleopatra, and Alfred Thayer Mahan formed the thesis of The Influence of Sea Power upon History while reading his History of Rome.
theodora-porphyrogenita: Theodora was the third and youngest daughter of Emperor Constantine VIII and Helena, daughter of Alypius. Porphyrogenita, born into the purple, was the title of a child born in the capital to a reigning emperor. Basil II prevented his nieces from marrying into the Byzantine nobility, since a husband would gain a claim on the throne, and Theodora lived in obscurity in the women's quarters of the palace.

She refused to marry Romanos Argyros, whom her father had chosen as successor, saying that he was already married and that as third cousins they were too closely related. Zoë married him instead. Accused in 1031 of plotting with Constantine Diogenes, the Archon of Sirmium, she was confined in the monastery of Petrion and forced to take the monastic habit, and she stayed there for eleven years.

Michael V, adopted by Zoë, banished her to the Princes' Islands. A popular uprising began on 19 April 1042, in support of both sisters. Theodora at first refused to leave Petrion, but both sisters were crowned on 21 April and Michael V escaped to a monastery. Theodora ordered him blinded and made a monk. She was officially the junior empress but in practice the driving force of the joint administration, which sought to curb the sale of public offices and to improve the administration of justice.

After two months of acrimony Zoë married Constantine IX on 11 June 1042, and power passed to him. After Zoë's death in 1050 Theodora seems to have retired to a convent. When Constantine IX lay dying in January 1055, his councillors favoured Nikephoros Proteuon, but her supporters persuaded Theodora to assert her right. She was brought to the Great Palace and the imperial guard proclaimed her emperor. She purged senior officials, controlled the nobles and presided in person in the Senate, and her coins and seals called her Theodora, Augusta and porphyrogenita.

Contemporary judgements varied. Michael Psellus called the joint reign a failure, while John Scylitzes held that the sisters conscientiously rectified the abuses of earlier reigns. Of her sole rule it is said that she damaged her reputation by excessive severity toward private enemies and by relying on menials as advisors.

At seventy-six she refused all suggestions of marriage and would not name an heir. She fell gravely ill in late August 1056, and on 31 August her advisers chose Michael Bringas as successor, taking a nod from the speechless empress as assent. He was crowned as Michael VI, and Theodora died a few hours later, ending the 189-year rule of the Macedonian dynasty.
theodora-wife-of-justinian-i: Much of Theodora's early life, including the date and place of her birth, is uncertain, and later sources propose Syria, Cyprus, Paphlagonia and Alexandria; modern scholars think she was most likely raised in Constantinople. Her father, Acacius, kept bears for the Green faction of the Hippodrome. After his death her mother remarried, and when the Greens refused to give the family his post, the Blue faction gave it to them. She worked as an actress, and later travelled to North Africa as the concubine of Hecebolus, governor of the Libyan Pentapolis.

The chief source for this period is the Secret History of Procopius, which some modern scholars regard as slanderous and exaggerated, though David Potter writes that behind its inventions there lies the semblance of fact. Justinian could not marry an actress under the law of Constantine's time; after the death of Empress Euphemia in 524, Emperor Justin issued an edict allowing it.

Theodora was crowned augusta when Justinian became emperor in 527. Justinian called her his partner in his deliberations in a law of 535, and the Secret History says she sat in state councils. She helped bring down the praetorian prefect John the Cappadocian in 541, and Procopius alleges that she ordered the murder of the Ostrogothic queen Amalasuintha, a claim that a surviving letter of King Theodahad appears to support. In 528 the couple ordered the brothels closed, and she founded a convent called the Metanoia for former prostitutes, though Procopius describes the women as confined there.

During the Nika riots of January 532 the rioters proclaimed Hypatius, nephew of Emperor Anastasius I, as emperor, and Justinian's officials prepared to flee. According to Procopius, Theodora told the council that flight was wrong and that royal purple was the noblest shroud. Scholars such as J. A. S. Evans think the speech is dramatised and reflects palace discussions rather than her literal words. Justinian's troops attacked the crowd in the Hippodrome and killed over 30,000 rebels.

Theodora supported the Miaphysites against her husband's Chalcedonian position, though Procopius and Evagrius Scholasticus suggested that the two only pretended to disagree. She founded a monastery at Sykae and sheltered Miaphysite leaders in the palace. Her opposition to Pope Silverius ended with his exile and starvation, and Vigilius was appointed in his place. She died on 28 June 548, probably of cancer, and was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles. Mosaics in the Basilica of San Vitale at Ravenna, completed in 547, show her in imperial dress, and the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox Churches commemorate her as a saint on 14 November.
theodora-wife-of-theophilos: Theodora was born about 815 at Ebissa in Paphlagonia, the daughter of the droungarios and tourmarches Marinos and of Theoktiste Phlorina. Her family is generally believed to have been of Armenian descent, although no contemporary source calls her Armenian. In 830 Euphrosyne, stepmother of the emperor Theophilos, held a bride-show for him, and he chose Theodora by giving her a golden apple. She was crowned on 5 June 830. They had seven children, including the future emperor Michael III. Theophilos was an iconoclast, but Theodora secretly venerated icons, and none of their children grew up to be iconoclasts. Theophilos died on 20 January 842 and named Theodora regent for the two-year-old Michael, with advisers including the eunuch Theoktistos.

In March 843 Theodora restored the veneration of icons, ending the second Iconoclasm, at an assembly that met at Theoktistos's house and accepted the Second Council of Nicaea. The iconoclast patriarch John VII was replaced by Methodios I, and on 11 March 843 the restoration was marked by a procession in the Hagia Sophia, remembered since as the Feast of Orthodoxy. Shortly afterwards she ordered the army to convert or execute the Paulicians of the empire; some converted, thousands were killed, and many fled across the border.

Expeditions to Sicily in 848 and Crete in 853 failed, but the empire gained the upper hand over Bulgaria and the Abbasid Caliphate. Historians debate whether Theodora or Theoktistos held the real power. In November 855 Michael and Theodora's brother Bardas had Theoktistos killed, and on 15 March 856 Michael declared himself sole emperor and deposed her. She accepted this without a struggle.

Theodora lived in the palace until 857 or 858, when she was confined to the convent at Gastria. She may have been released about 863 and given a ceremonial role. She died some time after Basil I murdered Michael in 867. The Orthodox Church recognises her as a saint.
theodore-i-laskaris: Theodore Laskaris was born to a noble but not particularly prominent Byzantine family. His mother belonged to a branch of the imperial Komnenos family, and he proudly took her surname. The Laskaris held estates in western Asia Minor. Late in 1200 the emperor Alexios III Angelos, who had no sons, married his younger daughter Anna to Theodore, and before 1203 Theodore received the title of despot, which showed his right to succeed his father-in-law.

When the Fourth Crusade reached Constantinople in 1203, Alexios III fled, and Theodore, who had been imprisoned, escaped across the Bosporus into Asia Minor. After the crusaders took the city on 12 April 1204, a group of aristocrats offered the crown to Theodore's brother Constantine, who refused it. Theodore organised the Greeks' resistance to the Latins in Bithynia, at first in the name of Alexios III.

The defeat of the Latins by Tzar Kaloyan of Bulgaria at the Battle of Adrianople on 14 April 1205 secured Theodore's position. He drove the Latin garrisons from most Anatolian fortresses, moved his capital from Bursa to Nicaea, and took the title of emperor in 1205. In 1208 a Church council at Nicaea elected Michael Autoreianos patriarch, and on Easter Sunday, 6 April 1208, the patriarch crowned him emperor and autocrat of the Romans. Some of his opponents argued that the council was not a properly convoked synod.

In 1211 Sultan Kaykhusraw I and Alexios III invaded his lands, and the armies met at Antioch on the Maeander. Theodore killed Kaykhusraw in single combat and took Alexios III prisoner. It was a costly victory, for his best troops, Latin mercenaries, died there, and the Latin emperor Henry of Flanders defeated him on the Rhyndakos River in October. The peace that followed acknowledged his empire in practice. Around 1214 he and Sultan Kaykaus I invaded the Empire of Trebizond, and western Paphlagonia came under his control. In 1220 he failed to take Constantinople by force.

Theodore died in November 1221 and was buried at the monastery of Saint Hyakinthos in Nicaea. His son-in-law John Doukas Vatatzes won a struggle for the throne against his brothers. Theodore had built a functioning successor state from next to nothing, in the judgement of the historian Warren Treadgold. He revived the Ecumenical Patriarchate, issued his own coinage and levied regular taxes from 1216 at the latest. His successors expelled the Latins from Constantinople and revived the Byzantine Empire in 1261.
theodore-i-palaiologos: Theodore was the youngest surviving son of Emperor John V Palaiologos and Helena Kantakouzene, and a grandson of the former Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos. In 1376, already named despotēs, he was charged with governing Thessalonica, but before he could take it his eldest brother Andronikos IV Palaiologos imprisoned him, with their father and his brother Manuel, in the Prison of Anemas in Constantinople until 1379. After John V's restoration Manuel received Thessalonica, and Theodore became the first member of his dynasty appointed Despot of the Morea, after the final defeat of the Kantakouzenos clan.

The Morea was then divided among many powers: the fragments of the Principality of Achaea, Nerio I Acciaioli at Corinth, Venice at Coron and Modon, the Knights Hospitaller, and Navarrese mercenaries who under Pedro de San Superano seized Achaia and raided Byzantine lands. Theodore spent his first five years fighting local landlords and survived an assassination plot. He called in the Ottomans, whose army under Evrenos arrived in September 1387 and won the campaign with him, though the land they seized was returned only after Theodore met Murad I.

He bought Corinth between September 1395 and January 1396 but, unable to rebuild and defend its fortifications, sold it to the Knights Hospitaller in 1397. In 1395 Evrenos and the Navarrese raided the despotate and took Akova Castle, and in June 1397 an Ottoman army under Yakub Pasa took Argos and enslaved at least 14,000 people. After further Ottoman attacks in 1399 and 1400 Theodore sold the whole despotate to the Knights Hospitaller, regaining it in 1404.

Theodore married Bartolomea Acciaioli, a daughter of Duke Nerio I Acciaioli of Athens, but is not known to have had children with her. His illegitimate daughter Theodora married Süleyman Çelebi, the Ottoman ruler at Edirne, in 1404. Shortly before his death on 24 June 1407 he took monastic orders as Theodoret, and he was buried at the Brontochion Monastery. He was succeeded by Theodore II Palaiologos, a son of Emperor Manuel II.
theodore-ii-laskaris: Theodore was born in the imperial palace at Nicaea, the only child of Emperor John III Doukas Vatatzes and Irene Laskarina, eldest daughter of Theodore I Laskaris, who had founded the Empire of Nicaea after the crusaders captured Constantinople in 1204. He adopted his mother's family name. He studied under two leading scholars, Nikephoros Blemmydes and George Akropolites, learning grammar, poetry, rhetoric, logic, mathematics, astronomy, geometry and music, and he began writing treatises on theological, historical and philosophical themes in his youth.

In 1235 he married Elena Asenina to secure an alliance with her father, Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria, against the Latin Empire of Constantinople. From 1241 he acted as his father's lieutenant in Asia Minor, and from about 1242 he was a co-ruler though never crowned. He formed a close circle of young intellectuals, above all George Mouzalon, a page of low birth, while his relations with aristocrats such as Theodore Philes and Michael Palaiologos grew tense.

Theodore succeeded his father on 4 November 1254 and was crowned by Patriarch Arsenios Autoreianos on Christmas 1254. He dismissed many high officials and army commanders of aristocratic origin and replaced them with loyal friends, some of low birth. He allied defensively with the Seljuk Sultan of Rum, Kaykaus II, against the Mongols, and reformed the army by recruiting more soldiers from the peasantry of Asia Minor.

The Bulgarian tsar Michael II Asen invaded Thrace and Macedonia in the winter of 1254 to 1255, and Theodore led the counter-attack himself, forcing the invaders out of Thrace. He later made peace, and in 1256 he forced Michael II Komnenos Doukas of Epirus to cede Servia and Dyrrachium, securing control of the Via Egnatia. Michael II then allied with Stefan Uroš I of Serbia and Manfred of Sicily against him. His newly appointed generals could not resist their joint invasion in 1257. Negotiations with a papal legate on church union proved fruitless.

Theodore fell seriously ill in November 1257. George Pachymeres diagnosed epilepsy, while Akropolites noticed extreme weight loss and Blemmydes called it a strange disease. Modern historians of medicine have not agreed on a diagnosis. He died on 16 August 1258, of either chronic epilepsy or cancer, having appointed George Mouzalon regent for his underage son John IV.

Within ten days Mouzalon fell victim to an aristocratic plot, and Michael Palaiologos assumed the regency, soon usurping the throne. The patriarchal appointment of Arsenios, whom hostile sources called Theodore's sole nominee, later gave rise to the Arsenite Schism, which lasted from 1265 to 1310.
theodore-komnenos-doukas: Theodore was the son of the sebastokrator John Doukas and Zoe Doukaina, and a great-grandson of the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos through his paternal grandmother Theodora. The emperors Isaac II Angelos and Alexios III Angelos were his first cousins. He preferred the surname Doukas or Komnenos Doukas to Angelos, and the hostile later historians Nikephoros Gregoras and Theodore Skoutariotes were the only medieval writers to call him Angelos.

Nothing is known of his life before the capture of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade in 1204, after which he served Theodore I Laskaris of Nicaea for some years before being called to Epirus, where his half-brother Michael I Komnenos Doukas had founded a principality.

Michael was assassinated in late 1214 or 1215, and Theodore sidelined Michael's young illegitimate son Michael II and took over Epirus. He allied himself with the Serbian prince Stefan II Nemanjić, expanded into Macedonia, and captured the Latin Emperor Peter II of Courtenay in 1217. Thessalonica fell to him in 1224.

He claimed the imperial title, and since the Metropolitan of Thessalonica refused to crown him, because the Patriarch at Nicaea was regarded as legitimate, a council of bishops at Arta in March 1225 recognised only him as emperor and Archbishop Demetrios Chomatianos of Ohrid crowned him. That year he took Chalcidice and Mount Athos, advanced through western Thrace and blockaded Adrianople. His attack on Constantinople was delayed until 1230, when he marched against Bulgaria instead and was defeated and captured by John Asen II at the Battle of Klokotnitsa in April.

Theodore was freed in 1237, when his daughter Irene married John Asen II. He re-entered Thessalonica disguised as a beggar and ousted his brother Manuel. Having been blinded, he could not hold the throne, so he installed his son John, and ruled in his name. In 1241 John III Doukas Vatatzes invited him to Nicaea, and Theodore was in effect detained there.

Vatatzes annexed Thessalonica in 1246, and in 1252 forced Theodore's nephew Michael II to terms and took Theodore prisoner. He died in exile around 1253. The biographer Konstantinos Varzos judged that his ambition to recover Constantinople and his rivalry with Nicaea delayed the restoration of the Byzantine Empire by several decades.
theodore-roosevelt: Theodore Roosevelt Jr. was born at 28 East 20th Street in Manhattan on 27 October 1858, the son of the businessman Theodore Roosevelt Sr. and Martha Stewart Bulloch. A sickly child with debilitating asthma, he overcame his health problems through vigorous exercise, which he called the strenuous life. He was homeschooled, solid in geography and bright in history, biology, French and German, but weak in mathematics and the classical languages. He entered Harvard University in September 1876, and his father's sudden death in 1878 devastated him. His book The Naval War of 1812, published in 1882, remains a standard study of the war.

In 1881 Roosevelt won election to the New York State Assembly. He lost the 1886 race for mayor of New York City, finishing third, and served on the United States Civil Service Commission from 1889 to 1895, fighting the spoilsmen. Appointed Assistant Secretary of the Navy in 1897, he called for a build-up of naval strength. When the Spanish–American War began in 1898 he resigned to form the Rough Riders with Colonel Leonard Wood, and returning a war hero he won the New York governorship by just 1 per cent.

Chosen as William McKinley's running mate in 1900, he became president when McKinley, shot by the anarchist Leon Czolgosz, died on 14 September 1901. He was elected to a full term in 1904 and, keeping his pledge not to run again, secured the 1908 nomination for William Howard Taft. After failing to win the Republican nomination in 1912 he founded the Bull Moose Party, and the split let the Democrat Woodrow Wilson win. He then led an expedition to the Amazon basin, where he nearly died of tropical disease. His offer to lead volunteers to France in the First World War was rejected, and he died on 6 January 1919.

Roosevelt's Square Deal had three main goals: conservation of natural resources, control of corporations and consumer protection. In 1902 he opposed the merger that created the Northern Securities Company, challenging the banker J. P. Morgan. He sought a larger regulatory role for the federal government in place of 19th-century laissez-faire. Henry Kissinger's analysis holds that he was the first president to hold that the United States had a duty to make its power felt globally. His Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine held that the United States had to police the Western Hemisphere, lest European powers intervene there. He also made the White House the daily centre of news, and is credited with inventing the presidential press briefing.
theodore-rshtuni: Theodore, or Theodoros, Rshtuni was a nakharar, a magnate, and is equated with Pasagnathes, the patrikios of the Armenians in the chronicle of Theophanes the Confessor. Before the Arab invasions he was appointed sparapet, commander-in-chief of the Armenian forces in the Armenian Marzpanate, and in 634 marzban of Armenia. After the nakharars overthrew the prince David Saharuni in 638 or 640, Theodore became the leading prince of Byzantine Armenia with the title Prince of Armenia, ishkhan hayots'.

The chronology of the Arab invasion is unclear, since Arab and Armenian sources contradict each other. With the Byzantine general Procopius, Theodore met the first Arab attack in 640, but a failed manoeuvre let the Arabs plunder the capital, Dvin, and carry off 35,000 inhabitants into slavery. In 641 Emperor Constans II, on the advice of Catholicos Nerses III, made him commander of the Armenian troops and a patrikios. He won a victory over the Arabs and was recognised as ruler of Armenia by Constans in 643, but the Byzantines blamed him for a severe defeat that Procopius suffered.

Constans wintered at Dvin in 652–653, and his attempt to impose Chalcedonian doctrines such as Monotheletism offended the Armenian clergy and nobles. When the Muslims defeated the remaining Byzantine troops in 653, Theodore helped push the Byzantines out. According to the Soviet Armenian Encyclopedia, Constans then deposed him, he took refuge on the island of Akhtamar, and he was restored in 654 after the Byzantine commander Maurianus was driven into the Caucasus.

Judging him untrustworthy, the Arabs sent him to Damascus, where he died in captivity. His son-in-law Hamazasp IV Mamikonian succeeded him as prince, and his body was buried in the tomb of his forefathers in his home district of Rshtunik. Manuk Abeghian and other scholars see his popularity in the figure of Keri Toros in the epic of David of Sasun, and the writer Tserents made him the subject of a historical novel, Theodoros Rshtuni.
theodore-svetoslav: Theodore Svetoslav was the son of George Terter I by his first wife, Maria. His birth date is unknown. Soon after Ivan Asen III took the throne in 1279, his father divorced Maria to marry the new emperor's sister, and Maria and her son were sent as hostages to the Byzantine Empire and settled in Nicaea. He remained a hostage until 1285, when the Patriarch of Bulgaria, Joakim III, arranged his release.

His father later associated him as co-emperor and issued coins showing the two side by side. He was then sent to the Golden Horde, where his sister married Chaka, a son of Nogai. Poor during part of his exile, he married the rich Euphrosyne.

Theodore Svetoslav emerged from obscurity in 1298 or 1299 when he accompanied his brother-in-law Chaka in an invasion of Bulgaria, and helped persuade the nobility to accept Chaka. When the army of the khan Toqta entered Bulgaria in pursuit of Chaka, he plotted against Chaka and had him strangled in prison in 1300, sending the severed head to Toqta, who withdrew his armies. His reign saw the stabilisation of the country, the end of Mongol control of Tarnovo and the recovery of parts of Thrace.

He punished those who stood in his way, including his former benefactor, Patriarch Joachim III, who was accused of treason and executed. Rivals backed by Andronikos II failed: Radoslav Voisil was captured about 1301, and Michael Asen II advanced with a Byzantine army about 1302 without success. In 1304 Theodore Svetoslav took the fortresses of Mesembria, Anchialos, Sozopolis and Agathopolis. The Byzantine counterattack failed at the battle of Skafida near Poros, where the co-emperor Michael IX Palaiologos fled. The war continued with mutual pillaging and ended with a treaty in 1307, sealed by his marriage to Theodora, a daughter of Michael IX.

He remained at peace thereafter. He probably reasserted central control over provinces such as Vidin peacefully, and recovered the banate of Severin from Hungary. During the Byzantine civil war he sent military support to Andronikos III Palaiologos.

Theodore Svetoslav died in early 1322 and was succeeded by his son George Terter II, whom he had by Euphrosyne. It is not known whether he had children by Theodora Palaiologina. Terter Peak on Greenwich Island in the South Shetland Islands is named for him, and his seal appears on the reverse of the Bulgarian 2 lev banknote issued in 1999 and 2005.
theodore-von-neuhoff: Theodor Stephan von Neuhoff was born in Cologne, the son of the Westphalian nobleman Leopold Wilhelm Freiherr von Neuhoff zu Pungelscheid and his wife, Amélie Collin. Educated at the French court, he served in the French army and then in that of Sweden. Georg Heinrich von Görtz, minister to Charles XII, saw his gift for intrigue and sent him to England and to Spain to negotiate with Cardinal Alberoni.

After that mission failed he served Alberoni in Spain until the cardinal's exile, and then Baron Ripperda; he was made a colonel and married one of the queen's ladies-in-waiting, Catalina Sarsfield, whom he soon deserted. In France he became caught up in John Law's finances and the Mississippi Company boom, and he then wandered through Portugal, the Netherlands and Italy.

At Genoa he met Corsican rebels and exiles and persuaded them that he could free their island from Genoese rule if they made him king. With the help of the Bey of Tunis he landed in Corsica in March 1736 with military aid. As King Theodore I he issued edicts, founded an order of knighthood and made war on the Genoese, at first with some success, but quarrels among the rebels soon led to defeat. The Genoese put a price on his head and published an account of his past, and in November 1736 he left, saying he would seek foreign help.

He was arrested for debt in Amsterdam. Once free, he sent his nephew to Corsica with arms and returned himself in 1738, 1739 and 1743, but Genoese and French forces continued to hold the island. He lived for some years at the manor of 't Velde near Zutphen, still planning his return.

In 1749 he went to England to seek support, fell into debt and was confined in a debtors' prison in London until 1755, when he declared himself bankrupt and made over his kingdom to his creditors. He lived on the charity of Horace Walpole and other friends until his death in London in 1756, and was buried at St Anne's Church, Soho, under an epitaph by Walpole. He is the subject of Giovanni Paisiello's opera Il re Teodoro in Venezia of 1784 and one of the six kings in Venice in Voltaire's Candide.
theodoric-i: Theodoric succeeded King Wallia in 418. The Romans had ordered Wallia to move his people from Iberia to Gaul, and Theodoric completed their settlement in Gallia Aquitania II, Novempopulana and Gallia Narbonensis, then used the declining power of the Roman Empire to extend his territory southwards. After the death of Emperor Honorius and the usurpation of Joannes in 423, he tried to take the road junction of Arelate, but the general Aëtius, assisted by the Huns, saved the city. The Visigoths made a treaty and received Gallic noblemen as hostages. The later Emperor Avitus visited Theodoric, lived at his court and taught his sons.

In 436 the Franks were plundering Cologne and Trier, and Theodoric saw a chance to take Narbo Martius and reach the Mediterranean. The commander Litorius, with the help of the Huns, drove the Visigoths back to Tolosa, but Theodoric won the decisive battle there, and Litorius died of his injuries in Gothic captivity. Avitus then offered a peace treaty, which Theodoric accepted, and the Romans perhaps recognised the sovereignty of the Visigothic state at this time.

Relations with the Vandals turned hostile after Huneric, son of the Vandal ruler Geiseric, accused Theodoric's daughter, his wife, of plotting to kill him and in 444 had her mutilated and sent home. Theodoric then married another daughter to the Suevic king Rechiar in February 449, and Rechiar, with Visigothic troops, devastated the country around Caesaraugusta and took Ilerda by guile.

When Attila invaded Gaul, Avitus arranged an alliance between Theodoric and his long-standing enemy Aëtius. Theodoric joined with his whole army and his sons Thorismund and Theodoric. The allies relieved the city of Aurelianorum in June 451 and followed the Huns to the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains near Troyes, where Theodoric commanded the right wing. His forces contributed decisively to the Roman victory, but he was killed. Jordanes gives two accounts: that he was thrown from his horse and trampled, or that the Ostrogoth Andag killed him with a spear. His body was found the next day, and according to Gothic tradition his warriors buried him on the field. Thorismund was elected king at once.
Three of his sons ruled in turn and died violently: Thorismund was murdered in 453 by Theodoric II, who was murdered in 466 by Euric. Euric ruled until his death in 484.
theodoric-ii: Theodoric succeeded his brother Thorismund in 453 after a brief reign of which little is known; it is only known that Theodoric had killed him. He began as a faithful ally of Rome. After the murder of Flavius Aetius in 454, the assassination of Valentinian III on 16 March 455 and the Vandal sack of Rome on 22 May, the Roman senator Avitus, who was at Theodoric's court in Toulouse and had been his mentor in youth, was urged by the king to claim the imperial crown. Theodoric supported him with a large contingent of warriors.

In 456 a Gothic army went to Spain on the emperor's behalf. Theodoric attacked Rechiar, king of the Suebi, to punish his raids on Roman territory, and defeated him at the Battle of Órbigo near Astorga. Rechiar was wounded, escaped, and was hunted down and killed. The Goths took Bracara Augusta (Braga), the Suebi's capital, and by tradition plundered several cities of Gallaecia. Afterwards they controlled Hispania Baetica, most of Tarraconensis and southern Lusitania.

Avitus was unpopular in Italy, where he was seen as a puppet of Theodoric. Ricimer and Majorian defeated him near Piacenza in 456, and he was deposed. Theodoric then began to act against Roman authority, leaving soldier colonies in Spain. Majorian marched against him and defeated the Goths at Arles; Theodoric narrowly escaped, and the Goths gave up their settlements in Spain.

After Majorian's fall in 461 Theodoric gave troops to Ricimer in return for Narbonne and its surroundings, and took the land south of the Loire when Aegidius withdrew northwards. In 463 he sent his younger brother Frederic against Aegidius; Frederic was killed at the Battle of Orleans. Theodoric was himself murdered in 466 by his younger brother Euric, who succeeded him.

The Gallo-Roman Sidonius Apollinaris described Theodoric and his court in a letter to his brother-in-law Agricola. He portrays a king of above average height who heard envoys in the morning, hunted, kept a plain table and enjoyed board games, and he doubts that the king's piety was more than habit. The letter was later largely copied by the chronicler Rahewin for Frederick Barbarossa.
theodoric-the-great: Theodoric, also called the Amal, was born around 454, at about the time the Ostrogoths defeated the Huns after Attila's death. His father Theodemir belonged to the Amal dynasty and his mother Ereleuva was the king's concubine. The Ostrogoths were settled in Pannonia, south of the Danube. In 461, when Theodoric was seven or eight, he was taken as a hostage to Constantinople to secure compliance with a treaty Theodemir had made with the emperor Leo I, which also provided for a yearly payment of gold. There he was well educated.

He returned to Pannonia around 470 and was recognised as king in 471. The emperor Zeno made him commander of the Eastern Roman forces in 483 and consul in 484, but Theodoric remained in constant hostilities with the emperor and often raided East Roman territory.

In 487 Theodoric blockaded Constantinople, occupying suburbs and cutting off its water, though he seems never to have intended to take the city. Zeno was also in difficulty with Odoacer, the king of Italy, and in 488 or 489 ordered Theodoric to overthrow him. Theodoric moved towards Italy in the autumn of 488 and won the battles of Isonzo and Verona in 489. He won the Battle of the Adda River on 11 August 490 and besieged Odoacer in Ravenna until 2 February 493, when a treaty made them joint rulers. Theodoric entered Ravenna on 5 March; at a banquet on 15 March he killed Odoacer and had his most loyal followers slaughtered.

As ruler of Italy he upheld Roman legal administration and learning and promoted a major building programme. He repaired Ravenna's aqueduct, built himself a palace there, and restored the walls of Rome, for which the Senate erected a gilded statue of him. He was an Arian, and in his last years his relations with his Catholic Roman subjects and the emperor Justin I worsened. The philosopher Boethius, his magister officiorum from 522, was put to death in 524, and Pope John I died in 526.

Theodoric died in Ravenna on 30 August 526 and was succeeded by his grandson Athalaric, with Athalaric's mother Amalasuintha as regent. The union of the Gothic realms collapsed after his death, and the later campaigns of the emperor Justinian ended his kingdom. Historians differ on the nature of his rule. Traditionalists call him a Germanic king who imitated Roman customs, while others, citing his use of the title princeps, regard him as a Western Roman emperor in all but name. In medieval German legend he lives on as Dietrich von Bern.
theodoros-kolokotronis: Theodoros Kolokotronis was born on 3 April 1770 at Ramavouni, a mountain in Messenia, into a family of klephts. His father, Konstantinos, a former captain of the Armatoloi in Corinth, took part in the Orlov Revolt, which was encouraged by Catherine the Great of Russia, and Theodoros was named in honour of Fyodor Orlov. His father was killed in 1780 in a fight with Ottoman troops. At 15 he was taken in by Mitros Petrovas, who taught him his first lessons in fighting. Before the revolution he worked as a klepht, an armatolos and a kápos for Peloponnesian notables.

Ottoman attacks on the klephts drove him to Zakynthos in 1806. There, under British occupation, he served under the philhellene Richard Church in the 1st Regiment Greek Light Infantry, became a major in 1810 and took the red helmet he later wore. In the Heptanese he met the revolutionary ideas of the age, which he later credited with opening the eyes of the world.

He returned to the mainland just before the war began in March 1821 and formed a confederation of klepht bands in the Peloponnese. In May 1821 he was named commander-in-chief, and his age of 50 helped win him the name O Geros tou Morea, the Elder of Morea. He led the Greek forces in the siege of Tripolitsa. In 1822 an Ottoman army under Mahmud Dramali Pasha took Corinth and entered the plain of Argos, but the Greek fleet under Andreas Miaoulis cut it off from its supply ships. When Dramali retreated through the Dervenaki Pass, Kolokotronis's quicker forces trapped the Ottomans there in August 1822 and annihilated them in the Battle of Dervenakia.

He then took part in the civil wars among the Greek factions, and when his party was defeated he was jailed on Hydra in March 1825. His eldest son, Panos, was killed in the second civil war. He was released when an Egyptian army under Ibrahim Pasha invaded the Peloponnese, and in 1825 he was appointed commander-in-chief of the Greek forces there. Using guerrilla tactics and scorched earth, he could not prevent the destruction Ibrahim left behind.

After the war Kolokotronis supported Ioannis Kapodistrias, and after Kapodistrias was assassinated on 8 October 1831 he backed Prince Otto of Bavaria for the throne. He later opposed the Bavarian regency and, accused with Dimitrios Plapoutas of conspiracy, was sentenced to death for treason in 1834, then pardoned in 1835. He died in Athens in 1843, a day after his son's wedding. In his last years he learned to write in order to complete memoirs, a leading account of the war. In 1930 Eleftherios Venizelos had his bones moved to Tripoli, and his helmet and arms are in the National Historical Museum in Athens.
theodoros-negris: Negris was born in Constantinople into an old noble family that traced its descent from Genoa. His father was George Negris, and his cousins Alexander Negris and Konstantinos Negris also took part in the Greek War of Independence and later became prominent university professors. The family's wealth gave Theodoros a good education. In 1818 he was initiated into the Filiki Eteria, the Society of Friends, and became one of its most active members. He served as secretary to Scarlat Callimachi, hospodar of Moldavia.

In early 1821 the Ottoman government appointed him its envoy to Paris, but on the way he heard that the Greek War of Independence had broken out and went secretly to Greece. In the massacre of the Greek population of Constantinople that followed, his father was beheaded by the Ottomans. Negris landed on the island of Spetses still in Ottoman dress and was nearly lynched by the crowd until Neofytos Vamvas saved him; his cousin Konstantinos became his student there. He joined his fellow Phanariotes Alexandros Mavrokordatos and Kostakis Karatzas, and on 19 November 1821 he took part in founding the Areopagus of Eastern Continental Greece and became its first president.

Negris sat in the First National Assembly at Epidaurus and the Second National Assembly at Astros. After Astros he changed sides and allied with Theodoros Kolokotronis and Odysseas Androutsos against Mavrokordatos. As the Areopagus he had headed lost power to the central provisional government, Negris too was pushed aside and lost his influence. He died of typhus at Nafplio on 22 November 1824.
theodoros-pangalos: Pangalos was born on the island of Salamis, the son of a family from Kea on his father's side, and graduated from the Hellenic Army Academy on 29 July 1900 as an infantry second lieutenant. He continued his studies in Paris. A staff officer in the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913, he joined Eleftherios Venizelos's Provisional Government of National Defence in 1916 against King Constantine I, and served on the Macedonian front.

He was dismissed from the army in November 1920 after the electoral victory of the pro-royalist United Opposition. In 1922 he supported the revolution of 11 September led by Nikolaos Plastiras, which abolished the monarchy and led to the Second Hellenic Republic, and he prosecuted prominent royalist leaders in the Trial of the Six.

As Minister for Military Affairs from November 1922 he commanded the Army of the Evros, whose reorganisation helped the Turks back down in the Lausanne talks. He opposed the terms of the Treaty of Lausanne, and his stance won him popularity. On 24 June 1925 officers loyal to him overthrew the government and forced President Pavlos Kountouriotis to appoint him prime minister, and he abolished the young republic's parliamentary practice and prosecuted rivals, including Plastiras.

The press was no longer free, and a law limited women's skirts to no shorter than 30 centimetres above the ground. He declared a state of emergency on 3 January 1926, had himself elected president in a rigged election in April, and tried to devalue the currency by ordering banknotes cut in half. He conceded too many rights to Yugoslav commerce at Thessaloniki, and the War of the Stray Dog with Bulgaria harmed Greece's international standing.

On 22 August 1926 a counter-coup led by General Georgios Kondylis deposed him. He was captured the next day and imprisoned for two years in the Izzeddin Fortress. He was imprisoned again from 1930 to 1932 over a building scandal. During the occupation after 1941 he and other Venizelist officers supported the collaborationist regime and had a part, from behind the scenes, in the creation of the Security Battalions.

In 1944 he was arrested after liberation, and in September 1945 he was cleared of all charges. He ran unsuccessfully for parliament in 1950 and died at Kifissia in 1952. His grandson of the same name later served as Deputy Prime Minister of Greece.
theodorus-of-cyrene: The only first-hand accounts of Theodorus that survive are in three of Plato's dialogues, the Theaetetus, the Sophist and the Statesman, and little of his biography can be inferred beyond them. He was born in the North African colony of Cyrene and apparently taught both there and in Athens. In the Theaetetus he complains of old age, and the dramatic date of that dialogue, 399 BCE, suggests that he flourished in the middle of the 5th century BCE.

The dialogue also associates him with the sophist Protagoras, with whom he claims to have studied before turning to geometry. A doubtful tradition repeated by ancient biographers such as Diogenes Laërtius held that Plato later studied with him in Cyrene. According to Plutarch, he was also among Socrates' companions accused of divulging the mysteries at a symposium.

His work is known through a single theorem, reported in the Theaetetus and argued by some to be historically accurate and by others fictional. His student Theaetetus says that Theodorus drew figures to show that squares of three and of five square feet are not commensurable in length with the foot, and so on for each square in turn up to the square of seventeen square feet, at which he stopped. The square of two is not mentioned, perhaps because its incommensurability was already known.

His method of proof is unknown, and it is not even known whether 'up to' includes seventeen. If seventeen is excluded, the proof may have rested only on whether numbers are even or odd. Zeuthen suggested that he applied the Euclidean algorithm as a test for incommensurability. The Spiral of Theodorus, a series of contiguous right triangles whose hypotenuses are the square roots of 2 to 17, is often thought to be the construction in question. The dialogue also suggests that Theaetetus established a more general theory, that the square roots of all non-square numbers are irrational.
theodosius-i: Theodosius was born in Hispania on 11 January, probably in 347. His father, also named Theodosius, was a successful general under the western emperor Valentinian I, and the family appear to have been minor landed aristocrats. He accompanied his father to Britain in 368–369 to suppress the Great Conspiracy, an invasion by Celtic and Germanic peoples.

By 374 he held his first independent command, in the province of Moesia Prima on the Danube, where he repulsed a Sarmatian incursion. Soon afterwards, under mysterious circumstances, his father fell from imperial favour and was executed, and Theodosius retired to his estates in Hispania.

After the eastern emperor Valens was killed at Adrianople, Gratian appointed Theodosius in 379 to take charge of the war against the Goths. He conscripted farmers and miners and enrolled many non-Roman auxiliaries. In 382 the Goths were allowed to settle south of the Danube as autonomous allies, and in 386 a treaty with the Sasanian Empire, the Peace of Acilisene, divided the Kingdom of Armenia between the two powers.

He fought two civil wars. In 388 he defeated the usurper Magnus Maximus, who had killed Gratian. After Valentinian II died in 392 and Arbogast had Eugenius proclaimed emperor in the west, Theodosius defeated him in September 394 and ruled the whole empire. Around April 390 Roman troops massacred civilians at Thessalonica after a riot in which the general Butheric was killed.

He convened the First Council of Constantinople in 381, which confirmed Nicene doctrine and rejected Arianism. He repeated bans on animal sacrifice but let temples stay open, and modern scholars find little evidence of a sustained policy against traditional cults.

Theodosius died in Milan on 17 January 395 and was buried at Constantinople in the Church of the Holy Apostles. His sons Arcadius and Honorius succeeded him in the east and the west, and the east–west division lasted until the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the late 5th century.

Later Christian writers saw him as a champion who stamped out paganism, but modern scholars tend to regard this as the writers' interpretation. He is criticised for fighting two civil wars to defend his dynasty, and he is venerated in the Eastern and Oriental Orthodox Churches.
theodosius-ii: Theodosius II was born on 10 April 401, the only son of Emperor Arcadius and Aelia Eudoxia. His father proclaimed him co-augustus on 10 January 402, at nine months, the youngest to bear the imperial title up to then. On 1 May 408, when Arcadius died, the seven-year-old boy became sole emperor of the Eastern half of the empire. The praetorian prefect Anthemius governed at first, and the Theodosian walls of Constantinople were built under his supervision. In 414 his older sister Pulcheria, who had vowed perpetual virginity, was proclaimed augusta and acted as his guardian, and in June 421 he married Aelia Eudocia, a woman of Athenian origin.

When the Western emperor Honorius died in 423 and Joannes was proclaimed in his place, Theodosius made war on him in 424 and installed Valentinian III in the West on 23 October 425. In 425 he founded the University of Constantinople, with 31 chairs, 15 in Latin and 16 in Greek. In 429 he appointed a commission to collect the laws since Constantine I; a second commission completed the Codex Theodosianus, published in 438 and later a basis for Justinian I's Corpus Juris Civilis.

Against the Huns he paid 350 pounds of gold a year from 424, doubled to 700 pounds in 439 with the rise of Attila and Bleda. After the Huns sacked the middle Danube cities in 441 and defeated Roman armies in 447, a peace brought an annual tribute of 2,100 pounds of gold. Theodosius also made war on the Sasanian Empire in 421 to 422, which ended in stalemate.

He frequently tried to settle disputes about the nature of Christ. He appointed Nestorius archbishop of Constantinople in 428 and called the First Council of Ephesus in 431, which condemned Nestorius. The Second Council of Ephesus in 449 restored Eutyches and deposed Flavian, and Pope Leo I called it the robber synod; the Council of Chalcedon reversed it after the emperor's death.

Theodosius died on 28 July 450 after falling from his horse, and was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles. Pulcheria married Marcian, who became emperor. Ancient and modern historians often see Theodosius as pushed around by his sister, his wife and the eunuch Chrysaphius, whose influence on foreign policy towards the Huns and on the pro-Monophysite line was resented by Pulcheria.
theodulf-of-orleans: Theodulf was born in Spain, probably at Zaragoza, and was of Visigothic descent. He fled Spain because of the Moorish invasion and travelled to Aquitaine, where he was educated, then joined the monastery near Maguelonne led by the abbot Benedict of Aniane. During a visit to Rome in 786 he was inspired by the centres of learning there and wrote to many abbots and bishops of the Frankish empire encouraging them to found public schools. He often called himself a poor traveller or stranger, a reference to his birth in Spain, and held that the door should never be closed to pilgrims, travellers or the poor.

Charlemagne named him Bishop of Orléans around 798 and made him abbot of several monasteries, most notably the Benedictine abbey of Fleury-sur-Loire. He founded public schools outside the monastic areas he oversaw, edited translated texts that Charlemagne thought inaccurate and translated sacred texts directly from Greek and Hebrew. He was one of Charlemagne's favoured theologians and witnessed the emperor's will in 811.

After Charlemagne died in 814, Theodulf was among many at the court of Louis the Pious accused of conspiring with King Bernard of Italy, who had revolted and died after being blinded. He was forced to give up his bishopric in 817 and was exiled to a monastery at Angers in 818. Released in 820, he tried to reclaim Orléans but is believed to have died before reaching it, and he was buried at Angers.

Theodulf is almost certainly the author of the Libri Carolini, a response to a faulty translation of the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea of 787 that seemed to approve the "adoration" of images. It held that images may serve as ornaments, for instruction and in memory of past events, but may not be adored, and that casting them out and destroying them would be wrong.

He also wrote two capitularies for his clergy, and 80 of his hymns and poems survive, the best known being Gloria, laus et honor. The oratory he built in 806 at his villa at Germigny-des-Prés keeps a mosaic of the Ark of the Covenant, virtually the only Carolingian mosaic to survive, though heavily over-restored in the 1860s.
theognis-of-megara: Almost nothing is known about Theognis the man. Ancient sources record little, and modern scholars question the authorship of most of the poems preserved under his name. Eusebius dates him to the 58th Olympiad, the Suda to the 59th and the Chronicon Paschale to the 57th, though the Suda may mean something other than his birth. Chronological hints in the poems point to different periods. Some scholars place his birth on or just before 600 BCE, others around 550 BCE.

His birthplace is also uncertain. Plato took Megara to be Megara Hyblaea in Sicily, while another ancient theory favoured a Megara in Attica. Modern scholars generally prefer the Megara of mainland Greece, and some suppose that he later migrated to the Sicilian one. Lines 783–88 speak of journeys to Sicily, Euboea and Sparta, and lines 1197 to 1201 of dispossession and exile.

About 1,400 lines of verse are attributed to him, more than half of the surviving elegiac poetry of Greece before the Alexandrian period, though several poems come from others, such as Solon and Euenus. The collection survives in more than forty manuscripts, the best from the early 10th century. It ends with a section called Book 2, or Musa Paedica, of about a hundred more couplets on boy love, which some scholars, among them Friedrich Nietzsche, rejected as a later addition.

The poems deal with themes of the aristocratic symposium, the drinking party: wine, politics, friendship, war, the brevity of life, wealth and love. They are addressed to Cyrnus and to others, and distinguish constantly between the good, the aristocrats, and the bad, everyone else. They voice an aristocrat's dismay at social and political upheaval and at newcomers who have displaced the old elite. In lines 19 to 23 the poet says he has placed a seal on his verses so that no one can steal them, and what the seal was is much disputed. Lines 425–8, which say it is best never to have been born, have been called the classic formulation of Greek pessimism.

Scholars divide over the collection. Friedrich Gottlieb Welcker edited it in 1826 to separate genuine verses from spurious ones, while Ernest Harrison defended its authenticity in 1902. In 1978 Martin Litchfield West identified 306 lines as a core that can reliably be attributed to Theognis, since they mention Cyrnus and are attested by Plato and Aristotle. Isocrates counted Theognis among the best advisers for human life, while in the Meno Plato's Socrates dismisses him as a confused and self-contradictory sophist.
theogony: The Theogony is written in the epic dialect of Ancient Greek and contains 1,022 lines. It is a large-scale synthesis of many local Greek traditions about the gods, arranged as a narrative of how they came to be and how they secured permanent control of the cosmos. It is the first known Greek mythical cosmogony. In form it is a hymn invoking Zeus and the Muses, and it developed from the hymnic preludes with which a rhapsode began a performance at poetic competitions. Its written form was established in the 6th century BCE.

The universe begins as Chaos, a dark void. Gaia (Earth), Tartarus and Eros (Desire) then arise, and from Chaos come Erebus (Darkness) and Nyx (Night). Gaia bears Uranus (Sky), the mountains and Pontus (Sea). Uranus and Gaia produce the twelve Titans, the three Cyclopes and the three Hundred-Handers, whom Uranus hides away inside Gaia. At her urging the youngest Titan, Cronus, castrates his father with an adamantine sickle and takes supreme command.

Cronus is told that one of his children will overthrow him, so he swallows each child Rhea bears. Rhea hides Zeus on Crete and gives Cronus a stone wrapped in baby's clothes. Grown, Zeus forces Cronus to disgorge the others, and the Titanomachy follows. In its tenth year Zeus frees the Hundred-Handers, who help him win, and the Titans are thrown into Tartarus. Zeus then defeats the monster Typhon, is elected king of the gods and swallows his first wife, Metis, so that no son of hers can overthrow him.

The poem also gives long genealogies of the gods and their descendants, and tells how Prometheus tricked Zeus over the division of a sacrificial ox, stole fire in a fennel stalk and was chained to a cliff, where an eagle fed on his liver until Heracles freed him.

The decipherment of Hittite texts, notably the Kingship in Heaven text first presented in 1946, showed in Kumarbi an Anatolian parallel to the conflict of Uranus and Cronus. Some scholars hold that Near Eastern traditions such as the Babylonian Dynasty of Dunnum reached Hesiod as lingering traces from the Mycenaean period rather than through contacts in his own time.

Its account of Chaos as the origin influenced the first Greek philosophers, who sought a first principle (arche) of all things. John Milton regarded the poem as inspired by Satan, in line with early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr. The earliest surviving manuscripts date from the end of the 13th century, and about 64 are known from 1600 or earlier.
theophanes-the-confessor: Theophanes was born in Constantinople of wealthy and noble parents who venerated icons: Isaac, governor of the islands of the Aegean Sea, and Theodora. His father died when he was three, and Emperor Constantine V saw to his education at the imperial court. He held several offices under Emperor Leo IV the Khazar.

Married at eighteen, he persuaded his wife to live in virginity, and in 779, after the death of his father-in-law, they separated by mutual consent to take up the religious life. She chose a convent, and he entered the Polychronius Monastery near Cyzicus, then built a monastery on his own lands on the island of Calonymus, where he became skilled at copying manuscripts.

At the urgent request of his friend George Syncellus, Theophanes continued Syncellus's Chronicle during the years 810 to 815. His part runs from the accession of Diocletian in 284, where Syncellus stopped, to the fall of Michael I Rhangabe in 813. It consists of a year-by-year history and chronological tables, which are full of inaccuracies and may have been filled in by someone else.

The history reckons by the years of the world and the Christian era and sets out the regnal years of emperors, Persian kings, caliphs and patriarchs. It is lacking in critical insight, but it surpasses most Byzantine chronicles and preserves accounts of lost authorities for the 7th and 8th centuries, especially from the reign of Justin II onward. Theophanes was the first to claim that Muhammad had epilepsy.

Cyril Mango has argued that Theophanes contributed little and that most of the contents are the work of Syncellus. The chronicle was much used by later writers, and in 873 to 875 the papal librarian Anastasius made a Latin compilation from it that made it known in Western Europe.

Returning to Sigriano, Theophanes founded an abbey and governed it as abbot, and he attended the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, signing its decrees in defence of the veneration of icons. When Emperor Leo V the Armenian resumed the campaign against icons, he had Theophanes brought to Constantinople and tried in vain to make him condemn the veneration. Theophanes was imprisoned and treated cruelly for two years, then banished to Samothrace, where he lived only seventeen days. Miracles were credited to him after his death, and he is venerated on 12 March in both the Catholic and the Eastern Orthodox churches.
theophanes-the-greek: Theophanes came from Constantinople. According to a letter by Epiphanius the Wise, he painted churches in Constantinople, Chalcedon, Galata and Kaffa before moving to Russia, and he settled in Novgorod in 1370. The same letter places him in Nizhny Novgorod, and in the early 1390s he moved to Moscow. His secular frescoes there included a view of Moscow in the palace of Vladimir the Bold, prince of Serpukhov, and an unidentified image in the palace of Vasily I of Moscow. Muscovites described him as learned in philosophy.

Early records mention several fresco cycles, among them the Nativity Church in the Kremlin in 1395, done together with Semyon Chyorny, the Archangel Cathedral of the Moscow Kremlin in 1399, in which he is said to have painted a city with all its particulars, and the Cathedral of the Annunciation in 1405. A series of nine large icons in the Annunciation Cathedral is associated with him and was painted around 1405; the iconostasis is preserved in the cathedral that now stands.

Only part of one fresco cycle survives, in the Church of the Transfiguration in Novgorod of 1378, and it is one of the finest examples of medieval Russian art. His style is noted for the expression it achieves with almost mono-coloured painting. Some contemporaries observed that he seemed to be painting with a broom, a reference to bold, broad brushwork found in some of his finest frescoes, which is unusual in the larger Byzantine tradition. His figures are strongly characterised and his brushwork energetic.

Works attributed to him as panel icons, among them Our Lady of the Don, the Dormition of the Virgin and the Transfiguration, are now the subject of intense academic debate. A contemporary source also describes him as a manuscript illuminator, but no signed or documented works are known, and several illuminations have been attributed to him on grounds of style. He influenced painting in Novgorod and Moscow in the 15th century and is known as the teacher and mentor of Andrei Rublev.
theophanu-abbess-of-essen: Theophanu was born around 997 to Ezzo, Count Palatine of Lotharingia, and his wife Matilda of Germany. Through her mother she was a granddaughter of the Holy Roman Emperor Otto II and of the Byzantine princess Theophanu, and so belonged to both the Ezzonid and the Ottonian dynasties. Nothing is known of where she spent her childhood, and she first appears in a document of 1037. Since she succeeded her aunt Sophia as abbess of Essen in 1039, she may already have lived in the convent before then. She also served as abbess of Gerresheim, though the dates of that office are unclear.

As abbess she was responsible for a number of artistic and architectural commissions. She had the west end of the Münster church at Essen rebuilt after the design of the octagonal chapel at Aachen, and she helped the town obtain from Emperor Henry III the right to hold markets. She died on 5 March 1058.

Among her gifts to the abbey was a Gospel book, now Hs. 3 of the Essen Cathedral Treasury, made to almost the same size as a Carolingian Gospel book kept there, which it may have been meant to replace. It has 157 parchment folios in 21 gatherings, measuring 35.5 by 25 cm, written by a single scribe in Carolingian minuscule, probably at Essen, in one column of at most 27 lines. Initials and portraits of the Evangelists decorate it, likely modelled on earlier examples from what is now northern France and Belgium.

Its link to Theophanu is shown by the inscription THEOPHANU ABBA[tissa] on its ornate cover, which is now kept separately in the Essen Cathedral Treasury. She also gave the abbey the Cross of Theophanu, and her donations of lavish illuminated manuscripts and other objects enriched its treasury during her abbacy.
theophilos-emperor: Theophilos was born in late 812 or early 813, the son of Emperor Michael II and Thekla and the godson of Emperor Leo V the Armenian. Michael crowned him co-emperor in 821. Unlike his father, he received an extensive education, from the grammarian John Hylilas, and was a great admirer of music and art. On 5 June 830, aged seventeen, he married Theodora, and the couple had seven children, among them the future Emperor Michael III.

Theophilos became sole emperor on 2 October 829 and issued an edict against the veneration of icons in 832. He saw himself as a champion of justice. At his accession he faced war with the Arabs on two fronts: Palermo fell to them in 831 after a year-long siege, and the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun invaded Cappadocia. After destroying an Abbasid raiding army at Charsianon in 831, Theophilos held a triumph, but the retaliation cost the Byzantines the fortress of Loulon and the city of Tyana.

In 837 he led an army of 70,000 men into Mesopotamia, but in 838 Caliph al-Mu'tasim invaded Anatolia. Theophilos was defeated on 21 July 838 at the Battle of Anzen, and Amorion, the ancestral home of his dynasty, fell on 12 or 15 August 838 after holding out for fifty-five days. Around 839 or 840 he sought allies against the Abbasids and sent an embassy to the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba. He also gave refuge to Khurramite refugees under the Persian Theophobos, a convert who became one of his generals.

Theophilos was a keen builder. With John the Grammarian he built the palace of Bryas in imitation of Arab palaces, and he decorated the Magnaura hall in Constantinople with a throne and mechanical lions and birds, according to Liudprand of Cremona. He repaired the Walls of Constantinople, and his name appears in their inscriptions more often than any other emperor's.

Theophilos died on 20 January 842. In his last illness he suspected that Theophobos would attempt a coup, and after the emperor's death his leading officers executed Theophobos. His widow Theodora ruled until 856 and defended his reputation, which softened the condemnation of his memory, although later sources that favoured icons remained critical. He was remembered as a just ruler, and the Timarion shows him as one of the judges in the Netherworld.
theophilus-eaton: Eaton was born at Stony Stratford in Buckinghamshire, the son of Rev. Richard Eaton, later Vicar of Great Budworth in Cheshire. His first wife, Grace Hiller, died in 1626, and in 1627 he married the widow Anne Yale, whose children by her first husband, Thomas Yale, grew up in his household. In London he lived between Coleman Street and Lothbury, sat on the Court of Common Council and became Deputy Governor of the Eastland Company, which traded with the Baltic and Scandinavia. His brother Nathaniel Eaton became the first head of Harvard College.

In 1628 he was among the shareholders, with Sir Richard Saltonstall and Sir Henry Rosewell, who bought the right to settle Massachusetts Bay, and he signed the charter of the Massachusetts Bay Company, serving for a time as one of the members who governed it from England. He sailed in the Hector with John Davenport's company and reached Boston on 26 June 1637. Wanting a settlement of their own, they moved south the next spring. On 14 November 1638 Eaton and Davenport signed an agreement with the Quinnipiack sachem Momauquin, who gave up his rights to the land in return for protection against the Mohawk and the Pequot, land to plant and a payment of coats, hatchets, hoes, knives and other goods.

Chosen governor on 4 June 1639, he was re-elected every year. The colony bought land at Greenwich from the Siwanoy in 1640 and eastern Long Island in 1641, where he was among the founders of Southold and East Hampton. Around 1642 he set up the Delaware Company of New Haven to trade furs on the Delaware River, which brought disputes with the Dutch governor Willem Kieft and with Lord Baltimore. In 1643 he became a founding commissioner of the United Colonies of New England, and in 1655 he gave the colony a written legal code.

In 1656 the colony declined Oliver Cromwell's invitation to move its settlers to Jamaica. Eaton died on 7 January 1657/8 by the Julian calendar and was buried on the green in New Haven; his remains were later moved to Grove Street Cemetery. Francis Newman, who had served as his secretary, succeeded him as governor. Eaton's Neck on Long Island, which he acquired from the Matinecock in 1646, bears his name.
theophilus-i-of-alexandria: Little is known of Theophilus's early life, though he was probably born in Egypt in the mid-4th century. He rose to the patriarchate in a time of change in the Roman Empire. Christianity had recently gained imperial support through the policies of Constantine and Theodosius I, displacing long-dominant pagan cults, and Alexandria, a centre of learning and philosophical traditions, became a focus of religious and political tension. He succeeded Pope Timothy I as Patriarch of Alexandria in 385, the twenty-third Pope of Alexandria, and mentored his nephew Cyril of Alexandria, who later succeeded him.

In 391, after imperial edicts of Theodosius I banned pagan worship and closed temples across the empire, Theophilus led efforts to repurpose or dismantle pagan religious structures in Alexandria. According to the church historian Socrates Scholasticus, he publicly mocked pagan artefacts, which provoked violent clashes between pagan and Christian factions. The Serapeum of Alexandria, one of the most prominent temples of the city, was destroyed. Christian sources described it as a victory over idolatry, while modern scholars note that it reflected wider political, religious and social tensions and was part of a campaign to consolidate Christian authority and imperial control.

Theophilus at first supported the allegorical theology of Origen but in 399 changed his position and sided with the Anthropomorphite monks, who read divine imagery literally. At a synod in Alexandria he condemned Origen's writings and expelled Origenist monks, among them the Four Tall Brothers, who took refuge with John Chrysostom in Constantinople. In 403 Theophilus presided over the Synod of the Oak in Constantinople, which deposed Chrysostom, whom he accused of insubordination and heresy, partly for sheltering the exiled Origenists.

Theophilus died on 15 October 412 and was buried in Alexandria. He was a prolific author, but most of his writings survive only in fragments or translations: festal letters announcing Easter, homilies including one on the Crucifixion and the Good Thief, and letters exchanged with Jerome, Pope Anastasius I and Pope Innocent I. His paschal table, dedicated to Theodosius I, is lost. Some of his prayers were translated into Geʽez. He is venerated as a saint in the Coptic Orthodox, Eastern Orthodox Church and the Syriac Orthodox Church, with a feast day on 18 Paopi in the Coptic calendar, 28 October.
theophilus-shepstone: Theophilus Shepstone was born on 8 January 1817 at Westbury-on-Trym near Bristol. When he was three his father, the Rev. William Theophilus Shepstone, emigrated to the Cape Colony, and the boy grew up at the mission stations where his father worked, becoming fluent in the African languages that would shape his career. In the Xhosa War of 1835 he served as headquarters interpreter to the governor, Sir Benjamin d'Urban. In 1838 he joined the party sent from the Cape to occupy Port Natal for Britain, and from 1839 he was British resident among the amaMfengu and other communities in Kaffraria.

For over thirty years Shepstone directed native policy in Natal, holding seats on the executive and legislative councils from 1856. His policy kept customary tribal law where it judged this compatible with humanity and did not try to force the civilisation of the colonisers on them. The Zulus called him Somtseu. Only one serious revolt occurred in his time, that of Langalibalele in 1873 against a demand to register guns. In 1861 he obtained from King Mpande public recognition of Cetshwayo as heir, and he attended Cetshwayo's coronation twelve years later.

In London in 1876 the 4th Earl of Carnarvon, colonial secretary, gave him a commission to discuss federation with the Transvaal government and power to annex the country if he thought it necessary. He reached Pretoria in January 1877 and on 12 April proclaimed British authority, with only twenty-five men of the Natal Mounted Police and no open resistance. Critics called the act premature. He governed as administrator until January 1879, and Sir Bartle Frere described him as a singular type of an Africander Talleyrand.

He retired in 1880 but in 1883 was commissioned to restore Cetshwayo as king in Zululand. Once a close friend of Bishop Colenso, he became estranged from him as Colenso came to see his influence on Zulu affairs as malign. He died at Pietermaritzburg on 23 June 1893. The historian Jeff Guy implicates him in a conspiracy to bring about the invasion and dismemberment of the Zulu kingdom, to supply labour to Natal and regain the Transvaal's friendship. His son George was killed at Isandlwana.
theophylact-i-count-of-tusculum: Theophylact was born before 864, and his origins are unknown and debated. He may have descended from an earlier Theophylact, son of Gregory, the nomenclator of Pope John VIII, who first sided with Pope Formosus and later with his opponents. He held Tusculum, a small hill town near Rome, as its hereditary count, and he first appears in a document of 901 as palatine iudex, a palace judge or leader of the militia, of the Emperor Louis the Blind.

When the emperor returned to Provence in 902, Theophylact stayed in Rome at the head of a body of soldiers. He took a leading part in the overthrow of Antipope Christopher in January 904 and very likely ordered his killing in prison later that year. Allied with Duke Alberic I of Spoleto, he secured the election of Pope Sergius III, under whom he became sacri palatii vestararius and magister militum and effectively took control of the city. Sometime between the end of Sergius's pontificate and the start of John X's, the nobility elected him Roman consul, and from then on every pope was chosen after he had picked him.

He shared his rule to a large degree with his wife Theodora, styled senatrix and serenissima vestaratrix.
