At her suggestion he chose Anastasius III and Lando, and in 914 he backed John X, whom chroniclers called her lover. Theophylact worked closely with John X, supported Berengar I of Italy and fought beside the pope against the Saracens at the Battle of Garigliano in 915.

Theophylact remained the pope's chief political support until his death. His daughter Marozia married Alberic I, and their son Alberic II of Spoleto ruled Rome from 932 to 954; his heirs, the Tusculani, rivalled the Crescentii for control of the city and were the ancestors of the Colonna family. Modern historians believe that Liutprand of Cremona, an opponent of the family, exaggerated Theodora's influence. Later writers, following his moral tone, called the period the pornocracy or Rule of the Harlots, a time modern historians name the saeculum obscurum.
theopompus: Theopompus was born on the Aegean island of Chios. In his early youth he spent time at Athens with his father Damasistratus, who had been exiled for his Laconian sympathies, and there he became a pupil of Isocrates and made rapid progress in rhetoric. In 352–351 BCE he won the prize of oratory given by Artemisia II of Caria in honour of her husband, with Isocrates himself among the competitors. The advice of his teacher is said to have decided his career as a historian. Through the influence of Alexander III he was permitted to return to Chios around 333 BCE, but after Alexander's death he was expelled again and took refuge with Ptolemy in Egypt, where he seems to have met a cold reception.

His works were chiefly historical and are much quoted by later writers. The Hellenica, in twelve books, began where Thucydides ended, in 411 BCE, and ran to 394 BCE, the date of the Battle of Cnidus. His most significant work, the Philippica, filled fifty-eight books on the reign of Philip II of Macedon (360–336 BCE), with digressions on the customs of the many peoples he met. It is also moral commentary on the corruption of Philip's court: he censured Philip for drunkenness and immorality while praising Demosthenes. One digression, On the Athenian Demagogues, was a bitter attack on Athenian statesmen that Plutarch used in several Lives. He also wrote an Epitome of Herodotus, whose authorship is disputed, panegyrics and a Letter to Alexander.

Philip V of Macedon cut the Philippica from 58 books to 16 by removing what had no connection with Macedonia, yet fifty-three books were still extant in the time of Photius in the 9th century. Antiquity blamed Theopompus for censoriousness and for a fondness for marvellous stories. Only fragments of his works survive, and a papyrus published in 1908 that Eduard Meyer and others recognised as part of the Hellenica is attributed by Friedrich Blass, J. B. Bury and others to Cratippus. Modern scholars such as Gordon Shrimpton and W. Robert Connor have re-evaluated him, Connor stressing his disillusionment with the moral state of Greece.
theory-of-relativity: Albert Einstein published special relativity in 1905, building on results of Albert A. Michelson, Hendrik Lorentz, Henri Poincaré and others. Later work came from Max Planck, Hermann Minkowski and others. He developed general relativity between 1907 and 1915, with contributions from many others after 1915, and its final form was published in 1916. The name comes from the expression 'relative theory' used by Planck in 1906, who stressed how the theory uses the principle of relativity. Much of the background lay in attempts to detect the luminiferous aether, the hypothetical medium thought to carry light waves, and the Michelson-Morley experiment, performed in 1881 and again in 1887, found no aether wind.

Special relativity is a theory of the structure of spacetime, introduced in Einstein's 1905 paper on the electrodynamics of moving bodies. It rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same for all observers in any inertial frame, and the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers regardless of the motion of the source. Its consequences include the relativity of simultaneity, time dilation, in which moving clocks tick more slowly, length contraction, a finite maximum speed, and the equivalence of mass and energy, E = mc2.

General relativity is a theory of gravitation. It began with the equivalence principle, under which accelerated motion and rest in a gravitational field are physically identical, so that free fall is inertial motion. Einstein proposed that spacetime is curved, and after discussion with the mathematician Marcel Grossmann he formulated the theory in Riemannian geometry. In 1915 he devised the Einstein field equations, which relate the curvature of spacetime to the mass, energy and momentum within it. Its consequences include gravitational time dilation, the precession of orbits, as observed in the orbit of Mercury, and the bending of light.

By the 1920s the physics community understood and accepted special relativity, and it became a necessary tool in atomic physics, nuclear physics and quantum mechanics. General relativity at first seemed less useful, since its assertions were mostly on an astronomical scale and its mathematics was difficult. Around 1960 it became central to physics and astronomy, as discoveries such as quasars (1963), the microwave background radiation (1965), pulsars (1967) and the first black hole candidates (1981) were explained by it. The theory superseded a 200-year-old mechanics created chiefly by Isaac Newton, and predicted neutron stars, black holes and gravitational waves.
thepphiphit: A Chinese source puts his age at about fifty when he died, so he was probably born around 1718. Known at birth as Prince Khaek, he was a son of Prince Phon by a secondary consort whom the same source calls Baitou, suggesting Northern Thai or Lao origin. Prince Phon won the succession war of 1733 and became King Borommakot, who gave his sons manpower regiments and ranks by their mothers' standing: Khaek became Kromma Muen Thepphiphit, a lower rank than his half-brothers Ekkathat and Uthumphon. In 1757 Thepphiphit and senior ministers persuaded Borommakot to make Uthumphon heir in place of Ekkathat.

Ekkathat nonetheless took the throne. In December 1758 ministers plotting to replace him with Uthumphon approached Thepphiphit, then a monk at Wat Krachom. Uthumphon betrayed the plan to Ekkathat in return for the plotters' lives, and Thepphiphit, deserted by his followers, fled west and was caught in what is now Kanchanaburi province. Spared at Uthumphon's request, he was sent with his family on a Dutch ship to Sri Lanka in early 1759. There Sinhalese monks and nobles plotted in 1760 to put him on the throne of Kandy in place of King Kirti Sri Rajasinha; the plan failed and he had to leave.

He landed at Mergui in Tenasserim in 1762, where Ekkathat kept him confined. When the Burmese took Mergui in January 1765 he was moved to Chanthaburi. In mid-1766, with Ayutthaya under Burmese siege, he gathered 2,000 men of eastern Siam at Paknam Yothaka near Prachinburi, but his force was defeated. He fled to Nakhon Ratchasima, where his son Prince Prayong killed the hostile governor on 18 September 1766 and seized the city, and he was later held at Phimai. After Ayutthaya fell in April 1767, local officials proclaimed him Chao Phimai, Lord of Phimai, one of several regional regimes.

In 1768 King Taksin of Thonburi marched against Phimai, and Thepphiphit and his family were captured and taken to Thonburi. According to the Thai chronicles he refused to bow before Taksin, who reportedly told him that wherever he went his supporters died, and he was executed late in 1768. His daughter, Princess Ubon, became one of Taksin's consorts and was executed on 20 June 1769 after being accused of adultery; his two surviving young sons, Prince Mongkhon and Prince Lamduan, were spared.
therapne: Therapne was a town of ancient Laconia within the territory of Sparta, and its site lies near the modern village of Varika. Greek myth derived its name from a daughter of Lelex. Besides the Menelaion, the town had two fountains, one called Meseida and the other Polideucea. Nearby, at a place called Phoebeon, stood a temple of the Dioscuri, close to a sanctuary of Poseidon. Other places in the neighbourhood were Alesia, where tradition said the mill had been invented, and a heroon, a hero shrine, in honour of Lacedaemon. The place thus gathered several of the hero and god cults of Sparta within a short distance of one another.

The town was known above all as the place where the bodies of Helen of Troy and Menelaus were believed to lie, in the temple to Menelaus called the Menelaion. The lyric poet Alcman, writing in the 7th century BCE, already mentions a temple at Therapne, which shows how old the cult was. A festival called the Meneleaeia was held there in honour of Menelaus and Helen, and the poet Pindar names Therapne among the places where the Dioscuri resided.

Herodotus records a sanctuary of Helen at Therapne and tells a story connected with it. A nurse carried an ugly girl there every day and prayed that she be freed of her ugliness. One day a woman appeared, stroked the child's hair and said that she would become the most beautiful girl in Sparta, and from that day the girl's looks changed. The site of the Menelaion has been excavated many times since the 19th century.
theravada-buddhism: Theravada, Pali for the Doctrine of the Elders, is the oldest existing school of Buddhism. It descends from the Vibhajjavada, a division within the Sthavira nikaya, one of the two major orders that arose after the first schism in the Indian Buddhist community. Theravada sources trace the tradition to the Third Buddhist council, where the elder Moggaliputta-Tissa is said to have compiled the Kathavatthu, which sets out the Vibhajjavada position.

With the patronage of Mauryan kings such as Ashoka, the school spread through India and reached Sri Lanka through missionary monks such as Mahinda. In Sri Lanka it was known as the Tambapaṇṇiya and later as the Mahaviharavasins, based at the Great Vihara in Anuradhapura.

Theravada adherents have preserved their version of the Buddha's teaching, the Dhamma, in the Pali Canon, which Theravada holds to be the highest authority on the Dhamma and on the organisation of the Sangha, the community of monks and nuns. Pali is its sacred language.

The school tends to be conservative about doctrine and monastic discipline, and it rejects the authenticity of the Mahayana sutras, so it does not generally recognise Mahayana Buddhas and bodhisattvas such as Amitabha. Its teachings include karma, which rests on intention, and rebirth in a cycle of birth and death. Release from suffering, nibbana, is reached through four stages of awakening, the last being that of the arahant.

Traditionally the practice of lay people and of monks is distinguished. Lay followers look after the needs of monks and nuns, who may not hold an occupation, and monastic life is hailed as a superior way to reach nibbana, though that view has been disputed. Monks follow 227 rules and nuns 311, and monks belong to ordination lineages called nikayas.

From India and from Sri Lanka, its principal centre of development, Theravada spread to Southeast Asia, where it became the dominant form of Buddhism. It is the official religion of Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Cambodia and the main Buddhism of Laos and Thailand. According to Kate Crosby, in the twelfth century the Mahavihara monastic tradition came to dominate the Buddhism of Sri Lanka and, through it, Southeast Asia.

In the 19th and 20th centuries Theravada Buddhists met Western ideas, religions and science, a response called Buddhist modernism. In Ceylon and Burma, Buddhist institutions lost their role as the main providers of education, and organisations were founded to preserve Buddhist scholarship, with figures such as Anagarika Dhammapala and Henry Steel Olcott in the Sri Lankan revival.
therese-of-saxe-hildburghausen: Therese Charlotte Luise was born on 8 July 1792, a daughter of Frederick, Duke of Saxe-Altenburg, and Duchess Charlotte Georgine of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. Her maternal grandfather, Charles II of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, was the brother of Queen Charlotte, wife of George III, so that Therese was related to Queen Victoria. In 1809 she was on the list of possible brides for Napoleon, but on 12 October 1810 she married the Bavarian crown prince Ludwig in the court chapel in Munich, the first royal wedding there since 1722. Her father told the court on 26 June 1811 that he could not pay for the wedding and dowry from the current budget.

The Kingdom of Bavaria was four years old at the time of the wedding, and it displayed its splendour in five days of celebration with an illuminated city, a folk festival, a free opera, a ball and a music academy. On 17 October the National Guard Cavalry held a horse race on the square before the Sendlinger Tor, where nine farm couples in traditional dress greeted the newlyweds. The area was named Theresienwiese in honour of the crown princess, and because of her popularity the celebrations were repeated the next year and became the Oktoberfest.

Therese became queen in 1825. She took an interest in state affairs and acted as a political companion to Ludwig, informing him of events at court and in the country when he travelled. In March 1830 she collected French and German newspaper articles to draw his attention to the July Revolution. When her son Otto was elected King of Greece in 1832 she urged Ludwig to consult him. Her letters to Ludwig survive in the Wittelsbach house archives. She founded the Theresienorden in 1827, an order for Bavarian women that aimed to provide for the poor, and worked with associations for widows, orphans and day nurseries. She tolerated her husband's love affairs but showed her disapproval discreetly, leaving town in 1831 during one of them.

Ludwig's affair with Lola Montez was one of the factors that made him unpopular, and he abdicated in 1848, while Therese was regarded as an ideal queen, wife and mother. She died on 26 October 1854. She and Ludwig had nine children, among them Maximilian, King of Bavaria as Maximilian II from 1848 to 1864, Otto, King of Greece from 1832 to 1862, and Luitpold, Prince Regent of Bavaria from 1886 to 1912. The Oktoberfest is still held every year on the Theresienwiese.
theresienstadt-ghetto: The fortress town of Theresienstadt, in Czech Terezín, lies in north-western Bohemia across the river from Leitmeritz (Litoměřice), about 70 kilometres north of Prague. It was founded on 22 September 1784 on the orders of the Habsburg monarch Joseph II and named after his mother, Maria Theresa of Austria. Austria-Hungary and, after 1918, the First Czechoslovak Republic used it as a military base, while the Small Fortress across the river served as a prison. After the German invasion of the Czech lands on 15 March 1939 the Small Fortress became a Gestapo prison, and in 1941 the town held about 3,500 soldiers and 3,700 civilians.

The SS set up the ghetto in Terezín in 1941 by deporting Czech Jews there; the first trainload, of 342 young men sent to prepare the town, arrived on 24 November 1941. German and Austrian Jews followed from June 1942, when the town's non-Jewish Czech residents were expelled and the town was closed off. Dutch and Danish Jews came in 1943.

The first transport left for the Riga Ghetto on 9 January 1942, and others went to Auschwitz and further killing sites, their destinations given only as the East. Conditions were overcrowded, with sixty to eighty people to a room, and food was unequally shared: those who did not work, mostly the elderly, received 60 per cent less than heavy labourers, and 92 per cent of deaths were among people over sixty.

A Jewish self-administration nominally governed the ghetto under a Jewish elder, first Jakob Edelstein, but SS quotas set how many people were deported and its Transport Department chose who went, a role that has drawn significant criticism. About 15,000 children lived in the ghetto, and about 90 per cent of them perished after deportation.

In 1944 the SS prepared a beautification campaign for a Red Cross visit, renaming streets and setting up sham shops, and on 23 June 1944 visitors toured a Potemkin village and noticed nothing amiss. A propaganda film was shot that summer but never distributed. As camps were evacuated in 1945, further prisoners arrived, and the SS fled on 5 May 1945.

About 33,000 people died at Theresienstadt, mostly from malnutrition and disease, and more than 88,000 were deported to extermination camps and other killing sites. Around 23,000 people survived in all. The ghetto was known for a relatively rich cultural life of concerts, lectures and clandestine education for children. The Terezín Ghetto Museum is visited by 250,000 people each year.
theriso-revolt: After the revolt of 1897 the Great Powers made Crete an autonomous state under Ottoman suzerainty, with Prince George of Greece, second son of King George I, as High Commissioner and Venizelos as one of his ministers. The two soon quarrelled: Venizelos, chief author of the constitution, thought it gave the prince too much power, since the assembly met only every two years and only the prince could approve laws. George alone dealt with the Powers, hoping to win union through his family connections, while Venizelos thought union premature. When the Powers refused any change in February 1901, Venizelos offered his resignation; the prince dismissed him for insubordination on 20 March and later had him imprisoned after he answered press attacks in the newspaper Kyrix.

In 1905 Venizelos, now for union at all costs, gathered Cretan leaders at Theriso, a village 14 km from Chania in the foothills of the White Mountains, guarded by narrow gorges full of caves; within twenty days some 7,000 sympathisers had come. On 23 March [O.S. 10 March] 1905 some 1,500 Cretans met there and proclaimed Crete's union with the Kingdom of Greece. The rebels set up a provisional government with its own stamps and newspaper, led by Venizelos, Konstantinos Foumis and Konstantinos Manos, and boycotted the elections; the new assembly at Chania nonetheless voted for union in April.

Prince George, with 1,100 gendarmes, declared martial law, and clashes near Chania left dead on both sides. Russian troops were the most active against the rebels, and in August the gunboat Khrabry shelled insurgents at Kasteli Panormos. The Greek government of Theodoros Deligiannis denounced the rising. With winter, debts and defections, Venizelos offered to lay down arms on honourable terms, and on 25 November 1905 the camp broke up under an amnesty in exchange for 700–800 guns.

The Powers then proposed reforms, among them a gendarmerie under a Greek officer, a Cretan force to allow foreign troops to leave, and equal rights for Christians and Muslims. Prince George opposed them, and he left the island for good on 25 September [O.S. 12 September] 1906. Alexandros Zaimis succeeded him, and a constituent assembly under Antonios Michelidakis gave Crete a new constitution. In 1908 the Cretan authorities proclaimed union with Greece, which became official in 1913 after the First Balkan War. The revolt made Venizelos known across the Greek world; he later served seven times as Prime Minister of Greece between 1910 and 1933.
thermae-himeraeae: The site has been populated since prehistoric times. Its documented history begins after the second Battle of Himera in 409 BCE, when the older neighbouring town of Himera was completely destroyed by the Carthaginian army under Hannibal Mago. Survivors moved to a site then called Thermae, today Termini, which became Himera's successor. The new town took its name from the hot springs for which it was known, whose discovery legend connected with the wanderings of Hercules. It quickly became a considerable town, though it stayed under Carthaginian rule.

In 260 BCE a body of Roman troops encamped nearby was attacked by Hamilcar and defeated with heavy loss. Before the First Punic War ended in 241 BCE the Romans besieged and took Thermae, but treated it with unusual favour: Cicero reports that they allowed the Thermitani to govern their city and territory by their own laws as a reward for steady fidelity. In his time it was a flourishing place with considerable trade, and he praised its citizens' taste for art, noting that Scipio had restored statues to them after the conquest of Carthage.

Thermae seems to have become a colony in the time of Augustus. Few accounts survive of later periods, but its name appears in Ptolemy and the Itineraries, and the aqueduct and other remains suggest that it continued through the Roman Empire. After the fall of the Roman Empire it declined, though it remained a bishopric until the 12th century.

From the Middle Ages to the early 19th century it was a major centre for the collection and shipping of grain, stored and taxed in a government warehouse complex, the caricatore regio. This made it one of the major ports of Sicily, with trade links to Genoa, Pisa and Venice. The closing of the caricatore in the 19th century brought a deep economic crisis that lasted until the end of the 20th century.

Termini Imerese is a town of the Metropolitan City of Palermo, about 33 km from Palermo. Its Roman remains include the largest and best preserved aqueduct bridge on the island and an amphitheatre probably of the Augustan age, built into houses. The Greek ruins of Himera lie within the comune's borders, and hot waters have flowed in the thermal baths in the old town since the Roman age.
thermaic-gulf: The Thermaic Gulf, in Greek Thermaïkós Kólpos, is also called the Gulf of Thessaloniki and the Macedonian Gulf. It forms the northwest corner of the Aegean Sea and is about 100 km long. Thessaloniki lies at its northeastern tip. On the west it is bounded by Pieria, Imathia and Larissa, and on the east by the Chalkidiki peninsula, with Cape Kassandra at the south-eastern corner. Narrower definitions exist: one bounds the gulf on the west by a line from the mouth of the Axios, or Vardar, to Cape Megalo Embolo, which makes it about 15 km long, while the smaller Gulf of Salonica is bounded by a line from the mouth of the Gallikos to Mikro Emvolo.

The gulf is named after the ancient town of Therma. To the Romans it was Thermaicus or Thermaeus sinus, the Gulf of Therma, and also Macedonicus sinus, the Gulf of Macedon. Places on its shores include ancient Potidaea, Methoni, Pydna and Kassandreia. The rivers that empty into it are the Pineios, Aliakmon, Loudias, Gallikos and Axios, along with several streams, one of them near Pydna. The gulf was significantly larger in classical times: extensive silting, mainly in the northern and western parts, which receive the bulk of the alluvial outflow, has left ancient seaside cities such as Pella several kilometres inland.

The Port of Thessaloniki is the gulf's largest and busiest port, and twelve small ports provide sea transport in and around it. The A1/E75 motorway from Athens to Thessaloniki encircles the western part of the gulf, and the A24 motorway from Thessaloniki to Nea Moudania almost encircles the eastern part. The shores hold many beaches, Sani Beach among them, but there are none on the northwest coast, where wetlands stretch from Methone to Kalochori, a western suburb of Thessaloniki.
thermidorian-reaction: Robespierre had dominated the Committee of Public Safety, and the conspiracies against him came together on 9 Thermidor. Jean-Lambert Tallien attacked Louis Antoine de Saint-Just in the National Convention and then denounced the tyranny of Robespierre; Jacques Nicolas Billaud-Varenne took up the attack, and Robespierre's appeal to the deputies of the right failed. Troops of the Paris Commune came to free the prisoners, and the Robespierrists barricaded themselves in the Hôtel de Ville. The Convention declared them outlaws and sent its own troops under Paul Barras, who reached the building around 2 a.m. on 28 July after the Commune's forces had deserted.

Robespierre, his jaw broken by a shot that may have been his own, was executed with 21 associates, among them Georges Couthon, Saint-Just, the mayor of Paris Jean-Baptiste Fleuriot-Lescot and François Hanriot. On 29 July seventy members of the Paris Commune were condemned to death, and the Commune was made subject to the Convention. The Montagnards were excluded from power; Billaud-Varenne and Collot d'Herbois were sentenced to exile in South America, while Tallien, Barras, Joseph Fouché and Louis-Marie Stanislas Fréron rejoined the leadership.

Freedom of worship was extended first to the Vendée and then to all France. On 24 December 1794 the Maximum on prices and wages was abolished, and new issues of assignats fed inflation. Riots in support of the radicals led a mob to invade the Convention on 20 May 1795; two days later troops under Pichegru forced the rebels of the Faubourg St-Antoine to surrender. In May and June the White Terror struck Jacobins and officials of the Terror, causing several hundred executions, far fewer than the more than 40,000 deaths of the Reign of Terror.

French armies meanwhile overran the Netherlands, founding the Batavian Republic, occupied the left bank of the Rhine and forced Spain and Prussia to sue for peace. The Constitution of the Year III, drawn up on 22 August 1795, created an electoral college and a bicameral legislature. A royalist revolt on 13 Vendémiaire, 5 October, was put down by troops under Napoleon Bonaparte. Historians of revolutions use Thermidor for the phase when a radical regime gives way to a more conservative one; Leon Trotsky called the rise of Joseph Stalin a Soviet Thermidor.
thermometer: Records of the early history are sparse and conflicting, which makes it hard to pinpoint the invention of the thermometer to one person or date. Because of the many parallel developments and gradual improvements, it is best viewed as an evolving technology rather than a single invention. Philo of Byzantium described an experiment with a tube dipped in liquid and joined to an air-tight hollow sphere. When the air in the sphere was heated by a candle or the sun, bubbles escaped into the vessel; as it cooled, liquid was drawn up the tube.

Hero of Alexandria gave a more elaborate version of the same principle in his Pneumatics, in which heated and cooled air moved water. Translations of the work reached Italy in the late 16th century, and Galileo Galilei had read it by 1594. Robert Fludd used a translation of Philo's experiment around 1617 as the basis for his air thermometer.

A thermometer has two essential elements: a sensor in which something changes with temperature, such as the bulb of a mercury-in-glass instrument, and a way of turning that change into a number, such as a marked scale or a digital readout. W. E. K. Middleton argued that a meter must have a scale or its equivalent, so that a thermometer is simply a thermoscope with a scale, and that the invention of the thermoscope remains far more obscure.

Readings from two thermometers can be compared only if they follow an agreed scale. Traditionally a scale was put on a liquid-in-glass thermometer in three stages: the instrument was placed in a stirred mixture of pure ice and water and the level marked, then in a steam bath at standard atmospheric pressure and marked again, and the distance between the marks was divided into equal parts. The most recent official scale is the International Temperature Scale of 1990.

Fahrenheit proposed his temperature scale in 1724. René Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur invented an alcohol thermometer and a scale in 1730, which proved less reliable than Fahrenheit's mercury instrument. Celsius's scale of 1742 placed zero at the boiling point of water and 100 at the freezing point, the reverse of the scale that now bears his name.

Herman Boerhaave was the first physician to use thermometer measurements in clinical practice. In 1866 Sir Thomas Clifford Allbutt invented a clinical thermometer that gave a body temperature in five minutes instead of twenty. Traditional thermometers did not keep their reading once moved; registering thermometers hold the highest or lowest temperature reached until reset, and electronic ones increasingly provide a digital display or feed a computer.
thermon: Thermos, also called Thermon or Thermum, was not a city in the sense of a built-up centre such as Athens, Argos or Corinth, and until a late date the Aetolian League itself was a loose association on a tribal basis rather than a group of city-states. A spring just south of the temple may have been the original reason for the site's location. Because the sanctuary slowly lost importance, its early temple of Apollo Thermios was never fully rebuilt, as most of its contemporaries were.

The temple's walls were at first of mud brick, its columns and entablature of wood decorated with painted terracotta, and its roof of terracotta tiles, then a recent innovation for the Greeks. In the Hellenistic period the wooden columns were replaced in stone. Its painted metopes, showing a large gorgon head and mythological scenes, are commonly held to be among the oldest known, and their likeness to Corinthian pottery of about the 630s BCE is the main basis for dating the temple.

The site was already an important regional centre around 1500 BCE, with a long apsidal building, houses and imported Mycenaean pottery, and the settlement went on flourishing after the destruction of the Mycenaean palaces. A large rectangular building beneath the temple was long taken as evidence that the Greek temple grew from the Mycenaean palace, but excavations by I. Papapostolou for the Archaeological Society of Athens showed no architectural continuity.

In the Hellenistic period the precinct was fortified on three sides with walls, gates and towers, three long stoas were built, and the spring was enclosed as a stone-lined pool. The Aetolians filled the sanctuary with bronze statues, of which only fragments and their marble bases survive. After Philip V of Macedon sacked it during the Social War, the Romans sacked it again in 189 BCE, which in effect ended its existence; by the 1st century BCE burials were being made in its public buildings.

The nearby Greek village of Thermo keeps the ancient name. What is left of the terracotta metopes and the other finds from the site is in the museum at Thermos, with a selection of the best pieces in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
theron-of-acragas: Theron, son of Aenesidemus, became tyrant of the Greek city of Acragas in Sicily in 488 BCE. According to Polyaenus, he came to power by using public funds meant to hire contractors for a temple building project to hire a bodyguard of his own, with which he seized the city's government. He soon allied himself with Gelon, who controlled Gela and from 485 BCE Syracuse, and Gelon later became his son-in-law. Theron went to war with Selinunte and with Terillus, the tyrant of Himera, and a numismatic study suggests that his realm covered a large part of western Sicily.

Terillus, expelled from his city, sought an alliance with Carthage through his son-in-law Anaxilas, tyrant of Rhegium. Theron occupied Himera but was then besieged there by a Carthaginian army assisted by Terillus. In 480 BCE, with Gelon's support, he won a great victory outside the walls of Himera over the Carthaginians and their allies. During his rule Acragas, Syracuse and Selinunte formed a kind of triumvirate that dominated Greek Sicily.

Theron was briefly succeeded by his son Thrasydaeus, who was defeated by Gelon's brother and successor Hiero I, after which Acragas came under the control of Syracuse. The Temple of Olympian Zeus at Acragas was probably built during his rule. In 1940 Heinrich Drerup argued that it was a monument to the victory of 480 BCE, a theory Mirko Vonderstein rejects, preferring to see the temple as a means of legitimising Theron's rule. The poet Pindar dedicated his second and third Olympian Odes to Theron for a chariot-race victory at the Olympic Games of 476 BCE, and the poet Simonides of Ceos was active at his court.
therouanne: Before the Roman conquest the town was the capital of the Belgian tribe of the Morini, and the Romans also made it the capital of the Civitas Morinorum district. The origin of its name is uncertain: the historian Malbracq derives it from a founder called Lucius Tauruannus, while others derive it from a phrase meaning the land of oats.

In the 7th century, probably around 639, Saint Audomar (Saint Omer) established the bishopric, whose diocese controlled a large part of the left bank of the Scheldt in the Middle Ages. The town lay in the county of Artois, which belonged to the county of Flanders. Flemish forces burnt it in 1303 during the Franco-Flemish War. Through its control of prosperous cities such as Arras and Ypres, the bishopric was able to build Thérouanne Cathedral, then the largest in France.

The Emperor Maximilian and Henry VIII captured the town from the French in 1513 after the Battle of the Spurs. In 1553 Charles V besieged it, then a French enclave in the Holy Roman Empire, in revenge for a French defeat at the siege of Metz. After he took the city he ordered it razed, the roads broken up, and the area ploughed and salted.

Only a small commune outside the walls, then called Saint-Martin-Outre-Eaux, was left standing, and probably around 1800 it took over the name Thérouanne. Part of the cathedral's portal went to Saint-Omer Cathedral, and a colossal statue of Christ sitting in judgement, le Grand Dieu de Thérouanne, is all that is left of it. The loss of the bishopric led to a reform of sees at the Council of Trent, and the diocese was split between those of Saint-Omer and Ypres.

Thérouanne is a commune in the Pas-de-Calais department, 10 kilometres west of Aire-sur-la-Lys and 13 kilometres south of Saint-Omer, on the river Lys. It lies on the Via Francigena. The ruins of the Abbey of St. Jean-du-Mont contain remnants of the Gothic cathedral, with a seventh-century episcopal group and a Carolingian building, and are a registered historical monument. The town appears in Hilary Mantel's novel Wolf Hall.
theseus: In the myth Aegeus, king of Athens, was childless and consulted the Oracle of Delphi, whose cryptic reply he did not understand. His host Pittheus, king of Troezen, understood it and gave him his daughter Aethra. Following Athena's instructions in a dream, Aethra also waded to the island of Sphairia and was possessed there by Poseidon, so that Theseus had both divine and mortal parentage. Before leaving, Aegeus buried his sandals and sword under a huge rock, to be taken by his son when he was strong enough to move it as proof of his royal birth.

Theseus was raised in Troezen. When he grew up he moved the rock and set out for Athens. He chose the dangerous land route round the Saronic Gulf rather than the sea, and defeated a series of bandits on the way: Periphetes, Sinis, the Crommyonian Sow, Sciron, Cercyon and Procrustes, who was cut to fit his own beds. Scholars believe that Theseus, if he lived, may have lived in the Late Bronze Age, or perhaps as a king in the 8th or 9th century BCE.

In Athens Medea, then Aegeus's consort, recognised Theseus and tried to have him killed by sending him to capture the Marathonian Bull. When he returned, she tried to poison him, but Aegeus recognised the sandals and sword and knocked the cup from his hands. Theseus then defeated the Pallantides, the sons of Pallas, who plotted against him as rivals for the throne. He is credited with the synoikismos, the union of Attica under Athenian rule.

Minos of Crete required Athens to send seven youths and seven maidens as tribute to the Minotaur, which lived in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus. Theseus took the place of one of the youths, promising his father to hoist a white sail if successful. Minos's daughter Ariadne gave him a ball of thread, and he killed the Minotaur and escaped. He abandoned Ariadne on Naxos, where Dionysus found and married her, and forgot the white sail. Aegeus, thinking his son dead, threw himself into the sea. In Euripides's version Theseus cursed his own son Hippolytus after Phaedra's false accusation.

In one account Lycomedes of Skyros threw Theseus off a cliff after Theseus had lost popularity in Athens. In 475 BCE, following an oracle, Cimon of Athens conquered Skyros and identified a coffin holding a large corpse with a bronze spearhead and a sword as Theseus's remains, which were reburied in Athens. The Athenians preserved the thirty-oared ship in which Theseus returned from Crete, replacing its planks as they decayed, and sent it each year to Delos in honour of Apollo; philosophers asked whether it remained the same ship, the Ship of Theseus paradox.
thesmophoria: The name joins the Greek words for divine law and bearer. Because the festival was kept across the Greek world, it is thought to go back before the Greek settlement of Ionia in the eleventh century BCE. The best evidence comes from Athens, but there is also evidence from Arcadia, Sicily and Eretria. In some places, such as Delos and Thebes, it seems to have been held in summer and tied to the harvest, and in Syracuse it lasted ten days. According to Plutarch the Boeotians called it the Festival of Sorrow.

Herodotus compared it with an Egyptian mystery rite, without giving details, and claimed that the daughters of Danaus had brought it to the Pelasgian women, that it was nearly lost when the Dorians drove out the Pelasgians of the Peloponnese, and that the Arcadians preserved it.

Men were forbidden to see or hear the rites. It is uncertain whether all free women or only aristocratic women took part, but non-citizen and unmarried women apparently did not, while all Attic wives were expected to, so that taking part could serve as proof of marriage.

On Delos an inscription shows a ritual butcher was paid for the sacrifices; elsewhere the women may have made them. Women called bailers, who had kept ritual purity for three days, brought up the decayed remains from the pits and laid them on the altars with cakes shaped as snakes and phalluses. Walter Burkert called the practice the clearest example in Greek religion of agrarian magic. How long the remains lay in the pits is unknown: perhaps a year, perhaps a few weeks.

In Athens the first day, the anodos or ascent, is usually explained by the women going up to the shrine called the Thesmophorion; two women were chosen to oversee the festival, and the women set up tents to live in for its duration. Matthew Dillon links the name instead to Persephone's return from the underworld. On the second day the women sat on plants believed to dampen desire, and scholars disagree whether its ritual obscenity belonged to this day or another. On the third, the kalligeneia or beautiful birth, they prayed to the goddess Kalligeneia for their own fertility, though Plutarch notes the women of Eretria did not.
thesprotia: Thesprotia borders Albania to the north, the regional unit of Ioannina to the east and Preveza to the south, with the Ionian Sea to the west. Much of the land is mountainous, and most farmland lies in the valleys of the central, southern and western parts. Two of its rivers figure in Greek mythology: the Thyamis and the Acheron, lined with reedbeds and plane trees. The coast has a Mediterranean climate, while the eastern part and the higher ground have cold winters of a semi-alpine kind.

In antiquity the Thesprotians, an ancient Greek tribe, held the land, bordered by Molossia to the north and Chaonia to the east. The Epic Cycle names Thesprotia as a place where Odysseus sailed and married the local queen Callidice. The region joined the Epirote League before Rome annexed it into the Roman province of Epirus. It then belonged to the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire until the late Middle Ages, apart from a period of Bulgarian rule in the 9th to 11th centuries, and fell to the Ottomans in about 1430.

From the 8th or 9th century until the 15th the region was called Vagenetia, after the Slavic tribe of the Baiounitai, who appear in the early 7th century during the Slavic invasions of the Balkans. In the late Ottoman period it was known as Chameria. Ottoman rule lasted until 1913, when the region passed to Greece after the Ottoman defeat in the First Balkan War. Its districts were first divided between the prefectures of Preveza and Ioannina, and a separate prefecture of Thesprotia was set up only in 1937.
In 1920 there were 20,319 Muslim Albanians in Thesprotia. After their expulsion on the orders of Napoleon Zervas at the end of World War II, the census of 1951 counted only 77.

Thesprotia is a regional unit of the Epirus region, created from the former prefecture in the Kallikratis reform of 2011 and divided into the municipalities of Igoumenitsa, Filiates and Souli. Agriculture and tourism are the main activities, the resort of Syvota and the remains of ancient cities drawing visitors. The port of Igoumenitsa serves ferries to Corfu, Paxoi and Italy, and is the western end of the Egnatia Odos motorway, opened to traffic in 2009.
thesprotians: According to legend the people took their name from the Pelasgian leader Thesprotos, their first governor, who built Cichyrus, later called Ephyra, the capital of Thesprotia. Strabo places Thesprotis between the Ambracian Gulf in the south and the River Thyamis (the modern Kalamas) in the north, and between the Pindus mountains and the Ionian Sea; its towns included Pandosia, Cassope, Photice, Phanote and Boucheta. The Thesprotians originally controlled the Dodona oracle. In the Telegony of the Epic Cycle, Odysseus stays for years in Thesprotia, marries its queen Callidice and leaves their son Polypoetes to rule it.

Strabo counted them, with the Chaonians and Molossians, the best known of the fourteen tribes of Epirus, peoples who had once ruled the whole region, the Chaonians first and the Thesprotians and Molossians afterwards. He also records that the Thesprotians, Molossians and Macedonians called old men pelioi and old women peliai, and Thesprotian senators were called Peligones.

An inscription from Goumani of the second half of the 4th century BCE shows a state organised like those of the other Epirotes, with officials called prostates (protectors), a grammateus (secretary), demiourgoi, hieromnemones and synarchontes (co-rulers). The people were divided into many subtribes, among them the Elopes, Graeci, Kassopaeoi and Dodonians, some of which founded colonies in Ithaca, Lefkada, Acarnania, Thessaly and Italy.

In the 5th century BCE the Thesprotians were allied with Corinth, and from 415 to 404 BCE with Athens and Molossis. About 400 BCE the Molossians occupied Kassopaea, Dodona and eastern Thesprotia. A Thesprotian League existed in the middle of the 4th century BCE, and from 343 to 300 BCE the Thesprotians were allied with Macedonia. From 300 BCE they belonged to the League of Molossis, and from 220 to 167 BCE to the Epirote League with the Chaonians and Molossians. Under Rome Thesprotia was a district of Macedonia from 148 BCE and of Achaea from 27 BCE.
thessalonike-of-macedon: Thessalonike's mother was Nicesipolis, Philip II's Thessalian wife or concubine, who died soon after the birth. Her name, joining Thessaly and nike, the Greek for victory, is agreed to commemorate one of her father's victories in Thessaly, though which one is unclear; one story has Philip naming her on the day the armies of Macedon and the Thessalian league defeated the Phocians at the Battle of Crocus Field. Stephanus of Byzantium says Philip gave the baby to a woman named Nice to raise, and she appears to have been brought up by her stepmother Olympias, by far the youngest child in her care.

Neither Philip nor Alexander arranged a marriage for her, Alexander probably to avoid creating rivals, and after his death Olympias sought a husband for her own daughter Cleopatra but not for Thessalonike.

She returned to Macedon with Olympias in 317 BCE and took refuge in the fortress of Pydna with Olympias, Roxana, the young Alexander IV and Deidameia when Cassander advanced. After Pydna fell and Olympias was executed, Cassander married her, possibly by force, to tie himself to the Argead dynasty; historians disagree whether he preferred her to her sister Cleopatra or took her as a second choice. As queen of Macedon she bore three sons, Philip, Antipater and Alexander. Cassander named the city of Thessaloniki, founded on the site of ancient Therma, after her, probably the first city named for a Macedonian woman.

After Cassander's death she kept much influence over her sons. Philip succeeded his father but died soon after, and Antipater then murdered his mother, by most accounts from jealousy; Justin says she had demanded that he share the rule with Alexander, which may mean she was acting as Alexander's regent. A popular Greek legend makes her a mermaid of the Aegean who asks sailors whether King Alexander lives, calming the sea for those who answer that he lives and reigns and conquers the world, and sinking the ships of those who do not.
thessaloniki: Thessaloniki stands on the Thermaic Gulf, at the northwest corner of the Aegean Sea, bounded on the west by the delta of the Axios and on the southeast by Mount Chortiatis. It lies 502 kilometres north of Athens. Under the Roman Empire the Via Egnatia carried trade between Rome and Byzantium through the city and linked the empire with Asia, notably the Silk Road.

Cassander of Macedon founded the city around 315 BCE, on or near the ancient town of Therma, and named it after his wife Thessalonike, a half-sister of Alexander the Great. Under the kingdom of Macedonia it kept its own autonomy and became the most important city in Macedonia, though Pella remained the capital. In the Byzantine Empire it was the second city after Constantinople in wealth and size, with 150,000 inhabitants in the mid-12th century, until it passed to Venetian control in 1423.

Sultan Murad II captured and sacked the city in 1430; contemporary reports estimated that about one-fifth of its population was enslaved. Under Ottoman rule it was one of the empire's most important trading hubs, and Sephardic Jews arriving from Spain made its Jewish community mostly Sephardic. The city passed to the Kingdom of Greece on 8 November 1912. In 1917 a great fire destroyed much of the centre, and planners including Thomas Mawson and Ernest Hébrard rebuilt it on a plan of axes, diagonal streets and monumental squares.

Thessaloniki is the second-largest city of Greece and the capital of the region of Central Macedonia. The municipality had 319,045 inhabitants in 2021 and the metropolitan area 1,006,112. Its Paleochristian and Byzantine monuments form a World Heritage Site, and the Ano Poli, the old town that escaped the fire, is also heritage-listed. The Roman forum, found by accident in the 1960s, is among its sites. Aristotle University, founded in 1926, is the largest university in Greece.
thessaly: Thessaly lies in northern central Greece, east of the Pindus watershed, and borders Macedonia to the north, Epirus to the west, Central Greece to the south and the Aegean Sea to the east. The Trikala and Larissa lowlands form a central plain ringed by mountains, including Mount Olympus, Óssa and Pelion, and its fertility has earned it the name breadbasket of Greece. The main river is the Pineios. The region is named after the Thessaloi, an ancient Greek tribe whose name has no agreed meaning, and before the Greek Dark Ages it was known as Aeolia.

Thessaly had extensive Neolithic and Chalcolithic cultures, such as those at Sesklo and Dimini, around 6000 to 2500 BCE. In Archaic and Classical times baronial families such as the Aleuadae of Larissa and the Scopads of Crannon held the lowlands. In 480 BCE the Persians invaded and Thessaly surrendered to them. In the 4th century BCE Jason of Pherae made the region a significant military power, and Philip II of Macedon was then appointed Archon of Thessaly. Thessalian cavalry played a crucial part in Alexander the Great's victories at Issus and Gaugamela, and his horse Bucephalus came from Thessaly.

After Roman rule the region remained in the Byzantine Empire, which recovered it from the Slavs in the campaigns of Staurakios in 782 and 783. After the Fourth Crusade it passed to the Kingdom of Thessalonica and then to Epirus, and from 1271 to 1318 it was an independent despotate under the dynasty of John I Doukas. The Serbian Empire of Stefan Dušan occupied it in 1348. The Ottomans took Larissa in 1392 or 1393 and ruled Thessaly through the Sanjak of Tirhala. Ali Pasha of Ioannina took control in 1780, and Greek risings in 1821 were suppressed.

Thessaly became part of the Greek state in 1881 after the Convention of Constantinople, though the area around Elassona remained Ottoman until 1912. Ottoman forces briefly captured it in the Greco-Turkish War of 1897. In 1923 its Muslim population was sent to Turkey in the population exchange. Italy occupied Thessaly from April 1941 to September 1943, and it became a major centre of the Greek Resistance. Since 1987 it has been one of Greece's 13 regions, with Larissa as its capital.
thetford: Thetford lies in the south of Norfolk, close to the Suffolk boundary, on the River Little Ouse, which it crossed at an important ford. One possibility is that the name comes from the Anglo-Saxon Theodford, "people's ford", but its origin is unclear. Thetford Forest, heavily planted with pines, lies on the western side of the town.

A fort stood on the Icknield Way at the site of Thetford Castle in the Iron Age, and the town was a tribal centre of the Iceni in the late Iron Age and early Roman period. In the Saxon period it was the principal centre of the eastern Heptarchy and a regular battle site between locals and Viking invaders. The Domesday Book of 1086 estimated the population at between 4,000 and 4,500, which would have made it the sixth largest town in Britain.

The bishopric moved here from North Elmham in 1071 and went to Norwich in 1096. Thetford Castle was built in 1067–1069 on the Iron Age fort, and Roger Bigod founded the Cluniac Priory of St Mary in 1104, the town's largest religious institution.

Henry VIII's commission found the town in great ruin and decay in 1527, and the Dissolution closed the priory in 1540, a blow to townspeople who lived by pilgrims. In 1574 Elizabeth I granted a charter of incorporation, and she visited on 27 August 1578. Allan Glaisyer Minns became the first black mayor in Britain in 1904. Trial tests of the first tank took place in secret nearby in early 1915. After the Second World War Thetford took Londoners as an overspill town, and its population grew from about 5,000 to around 21,000 by the late 1980s.

Thetford is a market town and civil parish in the Breckland District of Norfolk, with a population of 24,340 in 2011. It has the ruins of the castle and the priory, the Grade II listed Bell Inn first mentioned in 1493, and a railway station of 1845 that is one of the best-preserved sets of 19th-century railway buildings in East Anglia. Thetford Warren Lodge dates from about 1400. The Ancient House Museum holds replicas of the Thetford Hoard, and the exterior scenes of the television series Dad's Army were filmed in the town. Thomas Paine was born in Thetford in 1737, and the last Maharaja of the Punjab, Duleep Singh, lived part of his exile at nearby Elveden.
theuderic-i: Theuderic was a son of Clovis I by one of his earlier wives or concubines, possibly a Franco-Rhenish princess named Evochildis of Cologne. In accordance with Salian tradition, Clovis's kingdom was divided at his death in 511 between his four surviving sons. Theuderic inherited Metz, Childebert I took Paris, Chlodomer Orléans and Chlothar I Soissons. Theuderic's realm is called the kingdom of Metz, of Rheims or of Austrasia, according to the writer.

Early in his reign Theuderic sent his son Theudebert to kill the Scandinavian king Chlochilaich, the Hygelac of Beowulf, who had invaded his realm. He then became involved in the war between the Thuringian king Hermanfrid and his brother Baderic, and was promised half of Thuringia for his help. Baderic was defeated, but the land promised was not handed over. In 531 Theuderic, with his brother Chlothar and his son, attacked Thuringia to avenge himself.

With the help of the Saxons under Duke Hadugato, Thuringia was conquered. Chlothar received Radegund, daughter of King Berthar, who had been Hermanfrid's brother. Hermanfrid was killed in battle at Unstrut and his kingdom was annexed. The four sons of Clovis then fought the Burgundian kings Sigismund and Godomar. Godomar fled and Sigismund was taken prisoner by Chlodomer, while Theuderic married Sigismund's daughter Suavegotha.

Godomar rallied the Burgundian army and won back his kingdom. Chlodomer, aided by Theuderic, defeated Godomar again but died in the fighting at Vézeronce. After making a treaty with his brother Childebert, Theuderic died, and the throne of Metz passed without hindrance, and unexpectedly, to his son Theudebert. His daughter Theodechild, by Suavegotha, founded the Abbey of St-Pierre le Vif at Sens.
theuderic-ii: Theuderic II was the second son of Childebert II. At his father's death in 595 he received the kingdom of Burgundy that had been Guntram's, with its capital at Orléans, along with lordship over the cities of Toulouse, Agen, Nantes, Angers, Saintes, Angoulême, Périgueux, Blois, Chartres and Le Mans. His elder brother Theudebert II received Austrasia, with its capital at Metz. During his minority, and later, he reigned under the guidance of his grandmother Brunhilda, whom Theudebert had evicted from Austrasia in 599. A peasant found her wandering near Arcis in Champagne and brought her to Theuderic, who welcomed her and readily fell under her influence.

Brunhilda's influence inclined Theuderic toward war with Theudebert, and he defeated him at Sens. Their cousin Clotaire II of Neustria then prompted the brothers to ally against him, and in 600 they defeated Clotaire at Dormelles. They divided the land between the Seine and the Oise, Theuderic receiving the territory between the Seine and the Loire, and campaigned together in Gascony, where they installed Genialis as duke. The brothers then fought each other, and Theuderic defeated Theudebert at Étampes.

In 604 Clotaire invaded Theuderic's kingdom. Theuderic won at Étampes on the Louet, though his mayor of the palace, Berthoald, was killed, and the next mayor, Protadius, a partisan of Brunhilda, was assassinated by nobles when he urged war with Austrasia. In 610 Theuderic lost Alsace, the Saintois, the Thurgau and Champagne to his brother, and his men east of the Jura were defeated by the Alemanni. He routed Theudebert at Toul about 611 and at Tolbiac in 612, captured him and gave him over to Brunhilda, who had him put in a monastery and probably had him murdered.

Theuderic married Ermenberga, daughter of the Visigothic king Witteric, at Chalon in 606 but sent her home in disgrace the next year. He had four sons by unnamed mistresses. He died of dysentery at Metz in late 613, while preparing a campaign against Clotaire, who had retaken the duchy of Dentelin under a treaty made during the last war between the brothers. His son Sigebert II succeeded him in both kingdoms under the regency of Brunhilda.
thewa: The name comes from a word of the local Rajasthani language meaning setting. The craft grew up in Pratapgarh district, and its origin is placed in the Rajput era. The glass is treated to give a glittering effect that sets off the gold work. Each piece is made by hand and can take up to a month, and the designs, cut freehand, draw on Hindu mythology, Mughal court scenes, historical events and plants and animals. Pratapgarh also makes Thewa on coloured glass bases embossed with gold miniature work.

Descriptions of the process differ. In one, broken terracotta is ground fine and mixed with chemicals and oil into a thick paste spread on a wooden base; a sheet of 23-carat gold of 40 gauge is set on it and the design etched freehand. Black paint spread over the sheet makes the design stand out for finer work with small tools, and the excess gold is removed. In another, the gold is beaten into a very thin sheet, the Thewa Ki Patti, and inscribed with a fine chisel. It is pressed onto a lac-resin compound warmed on a board, the open pattern is knocked out, and the sheet is peeled away with heat.

The process is credited to Nathu ji Soni in 1767. Its secrets have passed from father to son over the generations, among goldsmiths who call themselves the Raj-Sonis. Fine examples are held in museums in India and abroad, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Victoria & Albert. Ramprasad Rajsoni was the first to be honoured for the craft, in 1966, and Jagdish Lal Raj Soni, Beni Ram Soni and Girish Rajsoni were among those given the Shilp Guru Award. Mahesh Raj Soni received the Padma Shree in 2015, and members of the family have received the UNESCO Seal of Excellence Award.
thiaroye-massacre: In the Battle of France in 1940 German forces captured around 120,000 soldiers from the French colonies, about a fifth of them from French West Africa, and summarily killed between 1,000 and 1,500 black prisoners in May and June. The colonial prisoners were held in Frontstalags in France rather than in Germany. Freed after the Normandy landings of 1944, they were repatriated amid delays and disorder, and had not received their demobilisation benefits: only a 1,500-franc advance was paid before they sailed, and there were disputes over exchange rates, savings made during captivity and demobilisation clothing.

On 5 November 1944, 1,635 former prisoners embarked at Morlaix on the British ship Circassia. They landed at Dakar on 21 November and were sent to the Thiaroye camp. On 25 November a group due to leave for Bamako refused to go until the matter was settled. When Brigadier General Marcel Dagnan visited on 28 November, his car was blocked, and he declared the camp in open mutiny and resolved on a show of force.

At 6:30 on the morning of 1 December, three companies of Senegalese Tirailleurs, backed by gendarmes, colonial artillery and an M3 Stuart light tank, entered the camp. Around 9:30 a burst of fire lasting less than a minute killed and wounded dozens. Accounts differ on how it began: some blame a shot from a barracks, others a warning shot by the troops, while a report from an officer of the Circassia and the testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Jean Le Berre suggest the killing was planned or considered in advance and that the men had just woken when they were surrounded. Declassified documents suggest most or all of the victims were unarmed. Dagnan's report of 5 December counted 70 deaths; some veterans later spoke of 300.

A war ministry circular of 4 December falsely stated that the men had been paid in full. In 1945, 34 supposed instigators received prison sentences of one to ten years; they were pardoned in March 1947 but not exonerated, and the widows of the dead never received veterans' pensions. Ousmane Sembène's film Camp de Thiaroye (1988) was banned in France for over a decade, and Fodéba Keïta and Léopold Sédar Senghor wrote works on the massacre. François Hollande called it a bloody repression in 2014, and Emmanuel Macron called it a massacre in 2024.
thibaw-min: Thibaw was born Maung Yay Set, a son of King Mindon and one of his consorts, Laungshe Mibaya, whom Mindon banished from the palace court. As a boy he studied Buddhist texts at a monastery to win his father's favour and passed the Pahtamabyan religious examinations. Hsinbyumashin, the Queen of the Middle Palace, helped arrange his marriage to her eldest daughter Supayagyi, his half-sister by blood.

Thibaw succeeded his father in 1878 after a bloody massacre. Hsinbyumashin, who had grown dominant at Mandalay in Mindon's last days, had royal relatives of close age who might claim the throne killed by edict, to make sure that Thibaw and her daughter would reign. At the coronation Supayalat pushed in beside her sister to be anointed queen as well, so two queens were anointed together, which had never happened in Burma. The treasury was low, taxes on peasants rose, and a national lottery, begun in 1878 on trial, ruined many families and was ended in 1880. In 1878 the Hluttaw was enlarged from four departments to fourteen, and the kingdom was divided into ten districts under district ministers.

Lower Burma, half the kingdom's former territory, had been under British occupation for thirty years, and the king was believed to intend to regain it. Relations worsened when he seemed to be aligning more closely with the French, and again in the incident called the Great Shoe Question, when British dignitaries refused to remove their shoes in the palace and were banished. A proclamation of 1885 calling on his countrymen to conquer Lower Burma gave the British a pretext to call him a tyrant who broke treaties.

An invasion force of 11,000 men under General Harry Prendergast reached Mandalay with little opposition, and the Burmese forces were defeated on 29 November 1885. The king and his family were taken to a steamer on the Irrawaddy in front of a large crowd.

The British sent Thibaw, Supayalat and their two infant daughters to Ratnagiri in British India. They lived for twenty-four years at Outram Hall in Dharangaon, and in 1906 moved into a new residence built for them by the government, known as Thibaw's Palace. His allowance was raised that year to 100,000 rupees. He was reported to be reclusive but sponsored local festivals, particularly at Diwali. He died in December 1916 aged 57 and was buried at Ratnagiri. The surviving royal family was relocated to Burma in 1919.
thies: Thiès lies 72 km east of Dakar on the N2 road, at the junction of railway lines to Dakar, Bamako and Saint-Louis. It is the capital of Thiès Region. Before colonisation the Thiès Plateau was a wooded frontier between the kingdoms of Cayor and Baol, inhabited by the Serer-Noon, a sub-group of the Serer people, who speak the Noon language and still live in the Thiès-Nones quarter of the city.

The village of Dianxene, belonging to Cayor, was founded on the plateau in the 17th century and had only 75 inhabitants in 1860. The French founded a military post there in 1864, and the Spiritans later set up a mission. In 1885 the Dakar–Saint-Louis railway, the first line in French West Africa, opened with a stop at Thiès. The Dakar–Niger line, built between 1906 and 1923, made it a junction. The French created the commune of Thiès in 1904.

The railways brought commerce and migrant labourers, including Bambara from eastern Senegal and Mali. The rail workers played a key part in the rise of Senegal's labour movement. A railway strike was violently repressed by France, and the city was a centre of the general strikes of 1945–1946 and 1947–1948, which also marked the growth of the independence movement across French West Africa. Léopold Sédar Senghor, later the first president of independent Senegal, was elected mayor in November 1956.

Thiès is the hub of an agricultural area producing rice, peanuts, manioc, millet and fruit, and a centre of livestock trading and meat packing. Phosphate is worked nearby at Palo Dial and Taïba. A tapestry factory was set up in 1966 to produce work designed by Senegalese artists, and the city has the University of Thiès, a museum and a crafts village. It is twinned with Caen, Sousse and Solingen.
thietmar-of-merseburg: Thietmar was born on 25 July 975, the son of the Saxon count Siegfried I the Older of Walbeck and his wife Kunigunde, daughter of Henry I the Bald, Count of Stade. Two of his great-grandfathers, both named Liuthar, were killed fighting the Slavs at the Battle of Lenzen. His father fought alongside Margrave Odo against Duke Mieszko I of Poland at the Battle of Cedynia in 972. His uncle Lothair of Walbeck was margrave of the Northern March from 983 until his death in 1003.

Baptized in Halberstadt, Thietmar prepared for a church career. He was educated at the chapter of St Servatius at Quedlinburg Abbey, from 987 at the Benedictine abbey of Berge near Magdeburg, and from 1 November 990 at the Magdeburg cathedral school, together with his relative Bruno of Querfurt. He knew the works of Augustine of Hippo and of Virgil, Horace, Lucan and Macrobius. In 994 he was for a time a hostage in the hands of the Norsemen.

After the death of his parents Thietmar inherited large parts of the Walbeck estates, and in 1002 he became provost of the family monastery founded by his grandfather Count Lothair II. Archbishop Tagino of Magdeburg ordained him priest on 21 December 1004. In 1009, through Tagino's intercession, he became bishop of Merseburg, a diocese that King Henry II had re-established in 1004. Thietmar worked for its full restitution. A loyal supporter of the German kingship, he rarely interfered in political affairs. He died on 1 December 1018 and was buried in Merseburg Cathedral.

Between 1012 and 1018 Thietmar composed the Chronicon Thietmari in eight books, covering the years 908 to 1018 and the reigns of Henry the Fowler, the three Ottos and Henry II. The first three books rest largely on earlier chronicles, such as Widukind of Corvey's Res gestae Saxonicae and the Annales Quedlinburgenses. The fourth, on Otto III, contains much original matter, and the last four are his own narrative and the main source for Saxon history under Henry II. They also give information found nowhere else about the Slavic tribes east of the Elbe, and about Poles, Hungarians and Bulgarians. It includes a detailed history of the bishopric of Merseburg and of the wars against the Wends and Poles.

The surviving manuscript shows amendments and insertions made by Thietmar after its completion. It was moved to Dresden in 1570 and badly damaged when the city was bombed in World War II; only a few folios remain intact, but a complete facsimile had been published by L. Schmidt in 1905. His statement that the Gero Cross in Cologne Cathedral was commissioned by Archbishop Gero, who died in 976, was long dismissed by art historians and was confirmed by dendrochronology in 1976.
thieu-tri: Thiệu Trị, whose personal name was Nguyễn Phúc Miên Tông or Nguyễn Phúc Tuyền, was born on 6 June 1807 and was the eldest son of Emperor Minh Mạng. His reign name means inheritance of prosperity. He was highly educated in the Confucian tradition. Like his father he was conservative, favoured isolationism and worked to entrench Confucianism. He had some curiosity about the West but was very suspicious of all non-Vietnamese outsiders.

Thiệu Trị reigned from 14 February 1841 until his death. France and Great Britain were then in a colonial race in Southeast Asia, and the French pushed hard for stronger relations with Indochina. As under Minh Mạng, mostly Spanish and French Christian missionaries entered the country in defiance of the ban. When the emperor began to imprison them, France responded at once, and in 1843 its government sent a military expedition to Indochina with orders to protect French interests and free the missionaries, if possible without an international incident.

His determination to remove all Roman Catholic missionaries could not be reconciled with peaceful relations with France. In 1845 it almost led to a clash with the American warship USS Constitution, which tried to force him to free the missionary Dominique Lefèbvre. A French task force reached Tourane, now Da Nang, on 23 March 1847 and demanded that French nationals be kept safe and that the persecution stop. The mandarins put off delivering the emperor's reply, and fighting broke out. Thiệu Trị had fortified the coast, but the French easily defeated the Vietnamese, whose equipment was inferior. They destroyed all the coastal forts and sank three Nguyễn junks before sailing away.

After the battle Thiệu Trị called all missionaries enemy spies and ordered that all Christians be executed on the spot. The mandarins did not carry out the order, and no missionaries were executed during his reign. He was deeply disturbed by the battle at Tourane. According to the Đại Nam thực lục, he said that the Westerners were wolves whom no one could satisfy, and that Christianity was a false religion whose harm had reached the level of foreign relations and opened the door to war.
He died on 4 November 1847, at the age of 41, according to some reports of apoplexy. He was buried in the Xương Lăng tomb at Huế, which his son and successor, Emperor Tự Đức, completed.
thihathu: Thihathu was born in 1265 into a prominent family of Myinsaing, the third of four children of Theinkha Bo, a younger brother of the sawbwa of Binnaka, and the daughter of a wealthy banker of the town; the chronicles disagree on his birth and death dates. Like his elder brothers Athinkhaya and Yazathingyan he entered the service of King Narathihapate. From 1285 the three led the defence of central Burma, and in 1287, after the king's assassination, they stopped a Mongol invasion, which withdrew to Tagaung.

In the anarchy that followed, the brothers held the army and the Kyaukse granary. King Kyawswa appointed them viceroys on 19 February 1293, Thihathu at Pinle, but their own inscription declared them the king's equals. Thihathu, the most ambitious, styled himself Lord of the White Elephant in 1295 and Great Lord in 1296. When Kyawswa sought Mongol protection, the brothers deposed him on 17 December 1297, with the help of the dowager queen Pwa Saw, and installed his son Saw Hnit; they executed Kyawswa in May 1299.

A Mongol army of 12,000 from Yunnan besieged Myinsaing from 25 January 1301. Its main attack failed, and on 6 April it withdrew after a bribe of 800 taels of gold and 2,200 taels of silver. Thihathu proclaimed himself king on 20 October 1309, and after Athinkhaya's death on 13 April 1310 he pushed Yazathingyan aside.

Thihathu first chose the site of the later Ava, at the meeting of the Irrawaddy and Myitnge rivers, but rejected it for bad omens and built Pinya a few miles east, opened as Wizayapura on 7 February 1313. At his coronation that day Pwa Saw gave him the golden belt and tray handed down since King Anawrahta. His chief queen was Mi Saw U, a daughter of Narathihapate, and he named her son by Kyawswa, his adopted son Uzana, heir. Saw Yun, his son by a commoner queen, left for Sagaing on 16 May 1315 and walled it; two expeditions failed to retake it, and Thihathu let him be.

The chronicles say he gave his last years to religion and gave Anawrahta's heirlooms to the Shwezigon Pagoda. He died about February 1325, aged 59, and Uzana succeeded him. He is remembered as Tazishin, Lord of One White Elephant.
thiksey-monastery: The monastery stands at 3,600 metres in the Indus Valley and is the largest in central Ladakh. Its buildings climb the hill in ascending order of importance, from the monks' dwellings at the foot to the temples and the residence of the chief lama at the top, which has given it the name Mini Potala. The main building is twelve storeys high, painted red, ochre and white, and built as a fort monastery in the Central Tibetan pattern, like Likir and Rangdum. From it the gompa at Matho, the palace at Stok and the former royal palace at Shey can all be seen.

In the early 15th century Je Tsongkhapa, founder of the Gelug school, sent his disciple Jangsem Sherap Zangpo to the King of Ladakh with a small statue of Amitayus containing bone powder and a drop of Tsongkhapa's own blood. With the king's help Sherab Zangpo founded a small monastery, Lhakhang Serpo, the Yellow Temple, at Stagmo in 1433. His pupil Palden Zangpo then built the larger house at Thiksey; legend says two crows carried off a ritual torma offering and set it down on the site, which he took as a sign.

Thiksey became second in Ladakh only to Hemis, administering ten monasteries such as Diskit, Spituk, Likir and Stok, and held 1,327 acres of land and some 25 villages. Around 1770 younger princes of the royal house, among them Jigsmet Namgyal, were placed there as lamas.

The Maitreya Temple, built to mark the visit of the 14th Dalai Lama in 1970, holds a 15-metre statue of clay, gold paint and copper made over four years by local artists under Nawang Tsering of the Central Institute of Buddhist Studies, the largest such statue in Ladakh, shown seated in the lotus position. The assembly hall keeps 225 volumes of the Tengyur. The monastery supports the nunnery at Nyerma, on land it gave after the founding of the Ladakh Nuns Association in 1996. Its yearly Gustor festival, with masked Cham dances, falls in the ninth Tibetan month.
thimphu: Thimphu lies in the western central part of Bhutan, in the narrow, linear valley of the Wang Chhu, also called the Thimphu River, which flows out into India as the Raidāk. The city extends north and south along the west bank and stands between 2,248 and 2,648 metres above sea level, making it the highest capital in Asia. The surrounding hills range from 2,000 to 3,800 metres, and the two altitude zones, warm temperate and cold temperate, decide the vegetation of the valley. At its southern end the Lungten Zampa bridge connects the east and west banks of the river. The city has no airport of its own and relies on Paro, about 52 kilometres away by road.

Before 1960 Thimphu was a group of hamlets scattered across the valley, among them Motithang, Changangkha, Changlimithang, Langchupakha and Taba. In 1885 a battle at what is now the Changlimithang sports ground ended in a decisive victory that opened the way for Ugyen Wangchuck, the first King of Bhutan, to control virtually the whole country. Under the Wangchuck dynasty the country enjoyed peace and progress under reformist monarchs. The third king, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, abolished serfdom, redistributed land and reformed taxation and the executive, legislative and judicial systems.

The capital was moved from the ancient capital of Punakha to Thimphu, and in 1961 Thimphu was officially declared the capital of the Kingdom of Bhutan by Jigme Dorji Wangchuck. It was then a hamlet of a few houses built around the Tashichho Dzong. It was only after roads were built in the 1960s, and the country opened to the outside world following the coronation of the fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, that the city grew rapidly. India provided financial and other assistance.

Thimphu is the capital and largest city of Bhutan and the seat of most important political institutions, including the National Assembly and the embassies. Dechencholing Palace, the official residence of the King, lies to the north of the city. Vajrayana Buddhism is the state religion, and the chief abbot, the Je Khenpo, spends six months of the year in the Tashichho Dzong in Thimphu and six months in Punakha. The Tshechu festival, held in September or October, features mask dances in the courtyards of the dzong. Other landmarks include the Memorial Chorten, Changangkha Lhakhang, founded in the 13th century, and the National Institute of Zorig Chusum, which teaches the thirteen traditional arts and crafts of Bhutan.
thing-assembly: The word thing appears as þing in Old Norse and Old English and as ting in the modern Scandinavian languages, and derives from a Germanic word meaning appointed time. The place where a thing was held was called a thingstead. Tacitus suggested that things were annual delegate-based meetings with legal and military functions. The Housesteads pillar was raised by a Frisian auxiliary unit of the Roman army on Hadrian's Wall. The Anglo-Saxon folkmoot was an analogous assembly and the forerunner of the witenagemōt.

In the Viking Age things were the public assemblies of the free men of a country, province or hundred. They met at regular intervals, legislated, elected chieftains and kings, and judged according to the law, which the lawspeaker memorised and recited. Under Norway's Law of the Gulating only free men of full age could take part, though women were present at some things. They settled disputes, marriage alliances and inheritances, and reduced feuding.

In Sweden they met at mounds, often burial mounds, with large runestones. Iceland's Althing at Þingvellir was a yearly assembly where cases were judged and laws discussed. Towards the end of the Viking Age kings centralised power and took control of the assemblies, so that in the later Middle Ages things functioned mainly as courts.

The name survives in the legislatures of the Nordic countries: the Icelandic Alþingi, the Danish Folketing, the Norwegian Storting and the Manx Tynwald, whose name is etymologically the same word as Þingvellir. The Tynwald still holds an annual public assembly on Tynwald Hill each 5 July, where new laws are read out. The Icelandic Althing is considered the oldest surviving parliament in the world. Place names mark thing sites elsewhere, among them Dingwall, Tingwall and Thingwall, and Thynghowe in Sherwood Forest, rediscovered in 2005–06. Scholars debate how far things were forerunners of democratic institutions.
thingvellir: The name Þingvellir comes from the Old Norse Þingvǫllr, from þing, meaning assembly, and vǫllr, meaning field: the assembly fields. A thing was a form of governing assembly found in Germanic societies. The name has the same root as Tynwald on the Isle of Man, Tingwall in Shetland and Tingvoll in Norway.

The site lies in a rift valley that marks the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the boundary between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates, about 40 kilometres northeast of Reykjavík. The plates' drift shows in the cracks and faults crossing the area, the largest being the canyon of Almannagjá. To the south lies Þingvallavatn, the largest natural lake in Iceland, and the river Öxará forms a waterfall at Almannagjá.

According to the Book of Settlements, settlement of Iceland began in 874. As the population grew, district assemblies were no longer enough, and chieftains outside the powerful family descended from Ingólfr Arnarson wanted a general assembly to limit its power. Grímur Geitskör was given the task of finding support and a site. The owner of Bláskógar was found guilty of murder and his land was declared public, to be used for the assembly, temporary dwellings, kindling and the grazing of horses. The place was also reachable from the most populous regions. The first proceedings in the summer of 930 are said to mark the founding of the Icelandic nation.

The Alþingi met for two weeks each year from 930 until 1798. Disputes were settled and laws made there. The Lögberg, or Law Rock, was the focal point, and the Lawspeaker, elected for three years, presided and recited the law from memory before it was written down. The Law Council acted as both parliament and supreme court, and only chieftains who held the office of goði, their Þingmen and later bishops had full rights in it. The Alþingi was the legislative and chief judicial authority of the Commonwealth until 1271. Clashes between chieftain families in its last decades brought Iceland under the Norwegian crown, and in 1662 the King of Denmark became its absolute monarch.

Thousands could gather each year. They lived in temporary dwellings with walls of turf and rock, and the only permanent buildings were a farm and later two churches. Merchants, sword-sharpeners and tanners sold goods and services, entertainers performed, and news was told from distant parts.
