Legislation of 1928 made Þingvellir the first national park in Iceland, and the park was founded in 1930 to mark the thousandth anniversary of the Althing. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004 on cultural criteria. The parliament has sat in Reykjavík since 1881. The park is part of the Golden Circle of Icelandic sights, with Gullfoss and the geysers of Haukadalur.
thinis: Thinis, called Tjenu in Egyptian, has never been found, although ancient writers attest it. Mainstream Egyptological opinion places it near Abydos and modern Girga, or at El-Birba, where an inscribed statue fragment mentioning Thinis is said to have been found. The name comes from Manetho's description of Menes as Thinite. Maspero in 1903 used a corrected passage of Hellanicus, which places the city on the river, to support the Girga theory, held also by Champollion. Other proposals, Kom el-Sultan, El-Kherbeh and El-Tineh near Berdis, have lost favour.

Evidence of population in the Abydos and Thinis region dates from the fourth millennium BCE, and Thinis is cited as the earliest royal burial site in Egypt. Abydos ceded its political rank to Thinis at an early point, though it kept supreme religious importance and its principal necropolis. According to Manetho, Thinis was the centre of the Thinite Confederacy, whose leader Menes, or Narmer, united Egypt as its first pharaoh. Its national role ended soon afterwards, when Memphis became the chief religious and political centre. Thinis remained the capital of the eighth nome of Upper Egypt, and in Dynasty V was probably the seat of the Overseer of Upper Egypt.

In the First Intermediate Period Ankhtifi, nomarch of Hierakonpolis, demanded the submission of the overseer at Thinis but, faced with its walls, seems to have bought its neutrality with grain. Thinis then fell to Intef II of the Theban Dynasty XI, whose advance was halted at a battle at Thinis against Kheti III of the Heracleopolitan Dynasty IX, recorded in the Teaching for King Merykara.

Mentuhotep II brought it firmly under his control after a revolt. Ryholt has proposed that the Abydos dynasty of the Second Intermediate Period should be called the Thinite Dynasty. In the Eighteenth Dynasty it regained prominence for its link with oases of military importance, and its mayors included Satepihu, the herald Intef and Min. By the Roman period Ptolemais had replaced it as capital of the nome.

Thinis remained a religious centre as the temple and burial place of Anhur, called bull of Thinis, and the lion-goddess Mehit was also worshipped there. The chief priest of Anhur was called the first prophet, or chief of seers. In Egyptian cosmology, as in the Book of the Dead, Thinis was also a mythical place in heaven.
think-big: The label was coined by the National cabinet minister Allan Highet in a speech to a National Party conference in 1977, and the economist Brian Easton also used it of economic strategies. In the late 1970s New Zealand's economy was suffering from the aftermath of the 1973 energy crisis, the loss of its largest export market when Britain joined the European Economic Community, and high inflation. Bill Birch, Minister of Energy from 1978, saw the natural gas under Taranaki and off its coast as a way to revive it.

The 1979 oil crisis, when the Iranian Revolution took 5.7 million barrels a day out of world supply, deepened the strain: the government banned weekend petrol sales and from 30 July 1979 imposed carless days, on which each motorist could not drive.

To cut the oil import bill, the government borrowed heavily overseas for eight projects: a methanol plant at Waitara, an ammonia-urea plant at Kapuni, a synthetic petrol plant at Motunui, the expansion of the Marsden Point refinery and the Glenbrook steel plant, electrification of the North Island Main Trunk between Te Rapa and Palmerston North, a third line at the Tiwai Point aluminium smelter and the Clyde Dam on the Clutha River.

Motunui turned gas from the offshore Maui field into methanol and then petrol, but falling oil prices made this uneconomic, and New Zealand stopped making synthetic petrol in February 1997, when the plant turned to methanol. A proposed smelter at Aramoana on Otago Harbour was never built, largely because of opposition over the environmental damage.

The billions borrowed weighed on investment and the wider economy. On 27 September 1982 Robert Muldoon froze wages and prices nationally until 22 June 1983, a measure aimed at inflation that cut exporters' profits. Opinion of the programme long followed party lines, National supporters backing it and Labour supporters opposing it, and the name became linked with inflation and industrial trouble. Of the eight projects only the Marsden Point refinery has closed, in 2022.
third-anglo-afghan-war: For the British in India, Afghanistan was a threat in the Great Game, since they feared a Russian invasion of India through it. They fought the First Anglo-Afghan War of 1839 to 1842 and the Second of 1878 to 1880. After 1880 came almost 40 years of good relations under Abdur Rahman Khan and Habibullah Khan, with the British paying a large subsidy to manage Afghan foreign policy.

In 1919 Afghanistan's regular army had about 50,000 men, with 21 cavalry regiments, 75 infantry battalions and about 280 modern guns, and the command could call on up to 80,000 frontier tribesmen. The army was ill-trained and ill-paid, and its upper officer corps was full of intrigue. Amanullah Khan, the new emir, declared a jihad in the hope of proclaiming full independence and strengthening his own legitimacy.

The war began on 3 May 1919, when Afghan troops crossed the frontier at the western end of the Khyber Pass and captured Bagh, which supplied water to Landi Kotal. The British Indian leadership was taken by surprise, a so-called bolt from the blue, although its intelligence had indicated an imminent attack. British India declared war on 6 May. An attack on Bagh on 9 May failed, but the British carried a position known as Stonehenge Ridge. Elsewhere the British posts in the Kurram Valley were abandoned on 23 May, and Nadir Khan attacked Thal in late May.

British airpower proved a main asset. Aircraft bombed Dacca and Kabul, and a single-plane raid on the palace in Kabul on 24 May produced little damage but greatly affected morale and contributed to Amanullah's request for an armistice. He asked for it on 29 May. On 2 June Brigadier General Reginald Dyer's brigade attacked the Afghan regulars near Thal, and replied to Nadir Khan's request to honour the armistice that his guns would answer at once.

The Anglo-Afghan Treaty of 1919 was signed on 8 August. The Afghans regained de jure control of their foreign affairs, and recognised the Durand Line as the border between India and Afghanistan. Historians disagree on the result: some call it a tactical British victory, others a military stalemate, since both sides held enemy territory and no decisive battle was fought, and some see an Afghan political and diplomatic victory, as Afghanistan secured its independence.

The war incited uprisings in Waziristan that lasted until the end of the British Raj. It also led British India to create the Peshawar Intelligence Bureau, and Sir Hugh Trenchard of the Royal Air Force proposed controlling the frontier by air power alone.
third-anglo-burmese-war: After a succession crisis in 1878 King Thibaw Min forced the withdrawal of the British Resident, ending official relations. In the 1880s the British grew concerned about contacts between Burma and France, whose wars in Indochina had brought it to Burma's borders. In May 1883 a Burmese delegation reached Paris and negotiated with the French Foreign Minister Jules Ferry, who admitted to the British ambassador that the Burmese sought a political alliance and the purchase of military equipment.

In 1885 the French consul M. Hass negotiated a French bank, a railway concession and a role in the government's monopolies, and the British secured his recall. A dispute arose when the Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation was fined by a Burmese court for under-reporting teak extractions. The British demanded an arbitrator and issued an ultimatum on 22 October 1885, which would have ended real Burmese independence.

Major-General Harry Prendergast commanded 3,029 British troops, 6,005 Indian sepoys and 67 guns, carried upriver by more than 55 steamers, barges and launches, many of the Irrawaddy Flotilla Company. By 14 November the expedition was assembled at Thayetmyo, and the Burmese had no time to organise resistance. At Minhla on 17 November the Burmese were defeated with 170 killed and 276 taken prisoner.

Some sources say resistance was weak because Thibaw's minister Kinwun Mingyi U Kaung ordered troops not to attack, and because the British let it be thought that they would enthrone Prince Nyaungyan, who was in fact already dead. On 27 November Thibaw ordered his troops to lay down their arms, and Mandalay fell on 28 November, in less than a fortnight. Thibaw was taken prisoner and exiled to India with the royal family.

Burma was annexed on 1 January 1886 by a proclamation of the Viceroy, Lord Dufferin. Many Burmese soldiers had dispersed with their weapons and formed guerrilla bands, and resistance lasted until 1896 despite a system of military police posts and mobile columns under Sir Frederick Roberts, with brutal repression. The British also extended control into the Kachin Hills and Chin Hills. Valuable property of the Burmese government was shipped to Britain or auctioned by a Prize Committee at Mandalay, and in 1886 an expedition opened the ruby mines at Mogok to British merchants. From 1937 the British governed Burma as a separate colony until independence in 1948.
third-anglo-maratha-war: The Maratha Empire was founded in 1674 by Shivaji, and its senior minister, the Peshwa, was the head of a council of eight. The British East India Company, which held small trading posts at Bombay, Madras and Calcutta, fought the Marathas in earlier wars, the first of which, begun after the Treaty of Surat of March 1775, ended with the Treaty of Salabai in May 1782.

By 1817 the Maratha confederacy lacked unity, its artillery was outdated and imported, and it relied heavily on Arab and Pindari mercenaries. Peshwa Baji Rao II, who had lost power under the Treaty of Bassein, prepared secretly for war after the murder of Gangadhar Shastri, an envoy under British protection, for which his minister Trimbak Dengle was suspected.

The British assembled the largest army they had yet raised in India, about 120,000 men, divided between the Grand Army under the Marquess of Hastings and the Army of the Deccan under General Hislop. Daulatrao Shinde was forced into the Treaty of Gwalior on 5 November 1817, ceding his forces and major forts.

On the same day the Peshwa attacked the British cantonment at Pune, with 20,000 cavalry and 8,000 infantry against 2,000 cavalry and 1,000 infantry, but at Khadki British volleys forced a Maratha retreat in four hours at a cost of 86 British dead against 500 Maratha. The Pindaris, estimated at 33,000, were driven beyond the Narmada and scattered within a single campaign. Mudhoji Bhonsle of Nagpur was defeated on 26 November 1817, and Holkar's army at Mahidpur on 21 December, leading to the Treaty of Mandeswar on 6 January 1818.

By mid-1818 all of the Maratha leaders had surrendered. The Peshwa gave himself up on 3 June 1818 and was settled at Bithur near Kanpur on a pension of about 80,000 pounds, terms some British thought too generous. Most of his territory was annexed to the Bombay Presidency, though the Maharaja of Satara was restored, and his territory was itself annexed in 1848. The Nassak Diamond was seized as part of the spoils. The war left the Company in control of virtually all of present-day India south of the Sutlej River, directly or through princely states, and ended the power of the Marathas as its most dynamic opponent.
third-anglo-mysore-war: Tipu Sultan and his father Hyder Ali had fought the East India Company twice before, and the Treaty of Mangalore of 1784 had restored the status quo, though Tipu refused to free his British prisoners. From 1786 Lord Cornwallis, as Governor-General, quietly sought the support or neutrality of the Marathas and the Nizam of Hyderabad. Travancore angered Tipu by extending fortifications into land he claimed and by buying two forts in the Kingdom of Cochin, his tributary, from the Dutch East India Company, and the Madras president Archibald Campbell warned that an attack on Travancore would mean war.

On 29 December 1789 Tipu led 14,000 troops from Coimbatore against the Nedumkotta, the fortified line of Travancore, but its forces under Kesava Pillai drove him back. He breached the line in late April 1790, until the monsoon halted him at the Periyar River. General William Medows entered Coimbatore unopposed on 21 July, but in September Tipu came down from the highlands with 40,000 men, harried the British and swept through the Carnatic, while British forces took the Malabar Coast late in the year.

Cornwallis took command himself, crossed the Muglee Pass on 21 February 1791 and stormed Bangalore after a siege of six weeks. On 15 May he drove Tipu back behind the walls of Seringapatam at Arakere, but with his army near starvation he destroyed his siege train on 22 May and retreated, only three days before the Maratha army arrived. In Coimbatore, Lieutenant Chalmers held out against the Mysoreans until 6 November and was then taken prisoner in breach of the surrender terms.

Cornwallis advanced again in January 1792 and reached the plains before Seringapatam on 5 February, where Tipu met him with rockets. A night attack drove Tipu into the city, Robert Abercromby arrived with the Bombay army on 12 February, and on 23 February Tipu sought peace.

Tipu delivered two of his young sons to Cornwallis as hostages on 26 February. Half of Mysore's territory was divided among the allies, depriving it of much of its coastline, and Tipu signed the Treaty of Seringapatam on 18 March 1792. Cornwallis was made a Marquess, and his Indian soldiers received the Mysore Medal. Tipu's rocket brigades so impressed the British that they inspired William Congreve to develop his rockets. In a fourth war in 1799 Seringapatam was taken and Tipu was killed defending it.
third-battle-of-panipat: The Marathas gained control of a considerable part of India between 1712 and 1757. In 1758, after an alliance with Adina Beg Khan, they took Lahore and drove out Timur Shah Durrani, the son and viceroy of the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani, extending their empire north of the Sindhu river.

Muslim intellectuals such as Shah Waliullah, alarmed at the Maratha advance, appealed to Ahmad Shah. By the end of 1759 he had reached Lahore and Delhi, and he won to his side the Rohillas under Najib-ud-Daula and the Nawab of Oudh, Shuja-ud-Daula. The Maratha army was led by Sadashivrao Bhau, while the bulk of the Maratha forces stayed in the Deccan with the Peshwa.

Skirmishes around Karnal and Kunjpura preceded the battle. The Marathas stormed Kunjpura and killed or enslaved its Afghan garrison, and Ahmad Shah crossed the Yamuna between 23 and 25 October 1760. After two months of siege and skirmishing, with supplies running out and the Maratha chiefs pressing Bhau to fight, the Marathas left their camp before dawn on 13 January and met the Afghans around 8 a.m. Their line ran some 12 km, with artillery in front, and behind it stood civilians, many on pilgrimage.

On 14 January 1761 the Maratha left under Ibrahim Khan Gardi broke the first Rohilla attack, and by noon Bhau seemed close to victory. Ahmad Shah then brought up 15,000 reserve troops and camel-mounted swivel guns. When Vishwasrao disappeared in the fighting, Bhau came down from his elephant to lead the battle, and Afghan prisoners taken at Kunjpura revolted inside the Maratha lines. Troops in the vanguard, seeing the general gone and chaos behind them, panicked and scattered. Historians believe 60,000 to 70,000 troops were killed in the battle, though losses are disputed.

The fleeing Marathas were hunted down. According to the bakhar of Kashi Raja, about 40,000 Maratha prisoners were killed the day after the battle, and some 22,000 women and children were driven off as slaves. Sikhs led by Jassa Singh Ahluwalia saved about 2,000 captives.

The Peshwa, Balaji Baji Rao, was crossing the Narmada with a relief force when he heard of the defeat; he returned to Pune and never recovered from the shock. The Marathas never fully recovered but remained the largest empire on the subcontinent and retook Delhi ten years later; their claim over all of India ended with the Anglo-Maratha Wars of the early nineteenth century.
third-carlist-war: Carlism took its name from the infante Carlos María Isidro, count of Molina and brother of Ferdinand VII. When Ferdinand's pragmatic sanction of 1830 set aside the Salic Law, his daughter Isabella became heir instead of Carlos, and the disputed succession led to the First Carlist War. In 1868 the revolution known as La Gloriosa overthrew Isabella II, and in 1870 Amadeo I, son of King Victor Emmanuel II of Italy, was proclaimed King of Spain, a choice the Carlists took as an insult.

To win support, the pretender Carlos VII promised to restore regional customs and laws, including the Catalan, Valencian and Aragonese fueros abolished by Philip V in the Nueva Planta decrees. The state was close to bankruptcy: in 1872 half of the Treasury's revenue went on interest on the public debt.

A first rising under General Rada failed in the Basque Provinces and Navarre, and Carlos VII escaped to France. General Dorregaray took command, and a second rising set for 18 December 1872 succeeded; by February 1873 the Carlist army numbered around 50,000 men on all fronts. Its war parties, among them one led by the priest Manuel Santa Cruz, fought by hit-and-run tactics against telegraph posts, railways and outposts. The Carlists held inland towns such as La Seu d'Urgell and Estella and besieged Bilbao and San Sebastián without taking them.

Amadeo abdicated in February 1873 and the First Spanish Republic was declared. On 29 December 1874 the pronunciamiento of General Arsenio Martínez de Campos proclaimed Alfonso XII, and a manifesto by the former Carlist leader Ramón Cabrera in support of the new king weakened the cause. After losing Catalonia, the Carlists made a last stand around Estella and Montejurra, and on 28 February 1876 Carlos VII went into exile in France.

The war left between 7,000 and 50,000 casualties. The Basque charters were abolished, customs moved from the Ebro to the coast, and conscription became compulsory. Prime Minister Antonio Cánovas del Castillo then negotiated the first Basque Economic Agreement of 1878, under which provincial councils collected taxes and remitted a share to the state. The defeat opened Biscay's mines to companies such as the Orconera Iron Ore Company, and the loss of home rule helped give rise to Basque nationalism and the Basque Nationalist Party founded by Sabino Arana in 1895.
third-council-of-lima: Lima was then the capital of the Spanish Viceroyalty of Peru, and the council was the third of three held there in the 16th century and the most important of them, since it gave the Church in the Americas its lasting organisation. Archbishop Toribio de Mogrovejo summoned it in 1581, and it met from 15 August 1582 to 18 October 1583.

Its decrees centred on the evangelisation of the indigenous peoples and on their fair treatment, not like slaves but as free men, together with their education and instruction in European customs. It ordered that the indigenous languages be used, forbidding the use of Latin and the use of Spanish alone. Its trilingual catechism, then known as the Catechism of St. Toribius, served this rule.

The council also encouraged the founding of seminaries and set standards for the ordination of priests, who were required to visit their congregations regularly, and for a liturgy that would draw the natives to the celebrations. Its tone was strongly opposed to idolatry. It singled out obscene books in bishops' possession for destruction and ordered quipu recording non-Christian customs to be destroyed completely, while encouraging the making of quipu for confession and for memorising doctrine.

The catechism was also carried east. Luis de Bolaños translated it into Guaraní, and the First Synod of Asunción adopted it in 1603 for use in the basin of the Upper Paraná River, in what are now eastern Brazil, Paraguay and north-eastern Argentina. The rule that the faith be taught in the peoples' own languages thus reached a fourth language beyond the three of the catechism itself.
third-crusade: After the fall of Edessa in 1144 and the failure of the Second Crusade, Nur al-Din of the Zengid dynasty united Aleppo, Mosul and later Damascus, and reduced the Crusader states. His nephew Saladin became vizier of Egypt in 1169 and, after Nur al-Din's death in 1174, took Syria for himself, defeating the Zengids at the Battle of the Horns of Hama in 1175. Raids by Reynald of Châtillon on caravans gave Saladin a pretext to move against the Franks. News of the loss of Jerusalem reached the West in the autumn of 1187, and within ten days of the death of Pope Urban III, his successor Gregory VIII proclaimed a new crusade.

Emperor Frederick Barbarossa took the cross at Strasbourg and put the Jews of Germany under his protection, since the earlier crusades had brought violence against them in Germany. He set out from Regensburg on 11 May 1189 and led his army through Hungary and the Balkans, where relations with the Byzantine emperor Isaac were strained. In Anatolia the army defeated Turkish forces at Iconium on 18 May 1190, but Frederick drowned while crossing a river on 10 June 1190, and most of his troops returned home.

Henry II of England and Philip II of France ended their war in January 1188 and both took the cross; each imposed a Saladin tithe. Henry died on 6 July 1189 and Richard I took his place. The crusaders besieged Acre, where Saladin's forces in turn besieged them, and disease killed Queen Sibylla of Jerusalem in 1190. Philip left the Holy Land in August 1191. Richard won the Battle of Arsuf on 7 September 1191 and took Jaffa. In the winter he advanced to within 12 miles of Jerusalem but turned back because of bad weather and fear of being trapped. Saladin retook Jaffa in July 1192.

The crusade kept the Crusader states from collapse, and the capture of Cyprus strengthened them, but it failed to retake Jerusalem. Historians have called it a success, a failure or hardly justified by its cost. Neither side was satisfied, though trade flourished along the Mediterranean coast. The failure inspired the Fourth Crusade of 1202 to 1204, and Europeans regained the city only briefly, in the Sixth Crusade in 1229.

On 2 September 1192 Richard and Saladin agreed the Treaty of Jaffa. Muslims kept Jerusalem, but unarmed Christian pilgrims and merchants could visit it. The Christians kept a narrow strip of coast from Tyre to Jaffa, with Ramla and Lydda to be divided, and a three-year truce was agreed. Richard left on 9 October 1192 because of threats to his rule in Europe.
third-dynasty-of-egypt: The Third Dynasty was the first dynasty of the Old Kingdom, whose capital was at Memphis, and it followed the turbulent last years of the Second Dynasty, which may have included civil war. Egyptologists now widely believe that Djoser founded it as the direct successor of Khasekhemwy, the last king of the Second Dynasty. Seals naming Djoser were found at the entrance to Khasekhemwy's tomb at Abydos, which shows that Djoser buried him and finished the tomb. Earlier writers such as Wilkinson in 1999 proposed Nebka, also called Sanakht, as founder. Nebka, Sanakht and Sekhemkhet may have been brothers, sons of Khasekhemwy and his favoured consort Nimaathap.

The sources do not agree on the kings. The Turin King List and the Abydos King List each record five, the Saqqara Tablet four, and Manetho nine, many of whom did not exist or are the same king under several names. The Turin King List gives Nebka, Djoser, Djoserti, Hudjefa I and Huni. The archaeological evidence points to the order Djoser, Sekhemkhet, with the Nebty name Djeserty, and Huni, the last king, who may be the same person as Qahedjet or less likely Khaba. The dynasty is credited with about 75 years, but dating is hard. Shaw gives approximately 2686 to 2613 BCE, Baines and Malek 2650 to 2575 BCE, and Dodson and Hilton 2584 to 2520 BCE.

Djoser is the best-known king, for commissioning his vizier Imhotep to build the Step Pyramid, the earliest surviving pyramid. The scribe of the Turin King List wrote his name in red ink, a sign of his importance to the Egyptians. Some authorities believe Imhotep lived into the reign of Huni. Sekhemkhet's reign is thought to have lasted only six or seven years, and his tomb, the Buried Pyramid, was left unfinished. Khaba possibly built the Layer Pyramid at Zawyet el'Aryan, much smaller than intended; whether erosion or an unfinished building explains this is not known.

Reign lengths for Nebka, eighteen years in both Manetho and the Turin Canon, rest on sources written over 1,400 and 2,300 years after his lifetime, so their accuracy is uncertain. Little archaeological evidence survives for Nebka or Sanakht. Some scholars have proposed a southern origin for the dynasty: Flinders Petrie saw it in Sudan from iconographic evidence, while S.O.Y. Keita thought southern Egypt equally likely.
third-dynasty-of-ur: The Akkadian Empire was destroyed in the middle of the 22nd century BCE in circumstances that are not well known, with the Gutians seeming to be the main actors, and Lower Mesopotamia broke into kingdoms centred on cities such as Uruk and Lagash. Utu-hegal of Uruk defeated the Guti king Tirigan but was dethroned after about eight years by court notables led by Ur-Namma, the governor of Ur, who was probably his brother. Ur-Namma (c. 2112 to 2094 BCE) took the title King of Sumer and Akkad, restored cities, sanctuaries and irrigation canals, and issued a law code that presented him as a just king.

His son Shulgi (c. 2094 to 2047 BCE) reigned for about half the dynasty's duration. His campaigns reached the Upper Tigris, the western Zagros and Elam, and he made marriage alliances with kingdoms on the Iranian plateau and with Mari. He was deified, and a literature glorifying him was written. The fall is poorly understood, but Ibbi-Sin held on for about twenty years while controlling only a small part of the empire, after Ishbi-Erra seceded at Isin amid food shortages and revolts. A coalition of Elamite troops from Anshan and Shimashki dealt the fatal blow around 2004 BCE.

The state was a patrimonial system, a hierarchy of households with the royal household at the top, in which all resources belonged to the king and his family. The king, whose power rested on the support of the god Enlil of Nippur, headed the administration and army and appointed high officials. The administration was centralised and bureaucratic, and the vast majority of surviving documents from the period are administrative.

The economy was redistributive. Dependent workers, men and women, were organised in troops and paid in rations of barley, wool and other goods. Textile workshops were the most important, with some 6,000 workers in the province of Girsu under a single office. About 250 trial reports survive, and the Code of Ur-Nammu, known from fragmentary late copies, is the earliest law collection of its kind. Sumerian was the language of administration and literature, and Shulgi sponsored a scribal school, the e2-dubba.

The fall of Ur was a turning point, and a new era, the Old Babylonian period, began. The dynasties of Isin and Larsa that followed claimed its heritage, took up the titles of its kings and wrote lamentations on the fall of Ur, Uruk, Nippur and Eridu, which presented the fall as a divine decision and legitimised the new rulers. Hymns to Ur-Namma and Shulgi continued to be copied in schools. The dynasty never equalled the prestige of the kings of Akkad in tradition, perhaps because its conquests were less impressive.
third-fitna: Al-Walid II succeeded his uncle Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik in 743. His accession was first welcomed, partly because he raised army pay, but members of the Umayyad family turned against him when he named his two underage sons as heirs and flogged and imprisoned his cousin Sulayman ibn Hisham. He persecuted the Qadariyya sect and was seen as siding with the northern Qaysi tribes against the southern Yamani ones, above all after his governor of Iraq, Yusuf ibn Umar al-Thaqafi, tortured his predecessor Khalid al-Qasri to death.

In April 744 Yazid III's supporters, backed by many Kalbis, seized Damascus and proclaimed him caliph; al-Walid II was killed near Palmyra. Yazid presented himself as chosen by an assembly of the community, which he said could depose him, but he died in September 744 after barely six months. His brother Ibrahim was challenged at once by Marwan II, governor of Upper Mesopotamia, who defeated Sulayman's army on the road from Baalbek and entered Damascus late in 744.

When Marwan moved his capital to Harran, the Kalbis of Palestine rose under Thabit ibn Nu'aym in summer 745, and Sulayman raised northern Syria again. Marwan put down the revolts city by city, took Hims after a siege through the winter of 745–746, and in summer 746 tore down the walls of the chief Syrian towns. Meanwhile a Kharijite revolt under al-Dahhak ibn Qays al-Shaybani took Iraq and Mosul, until al-Dahhak was killed at al-Ghazz in Kafartuta in August or September 746. By summer 747 Yazid ibn Umar ibn Hubayra held Iraq for Marwan, and in Arabia the revolt of Talib al-Haqq, who had taken Mecca and Medina, was suppressed the same year.

In Khurasan the governor Nasr ibn Sayyar had spent these years fighting the Yamani leader Juday al-Kirmani and al-Harith ibn Surayj, with no reinforcements to hope for. In summer 747 Abu Muslim raised the black banners of the Abbasid Revolution at Sikadanj, exploiting that rivalry, and his army occupied Merv on 14 February 748. Marwan II was defeated at the Battle of the Greater Zab in January 750 and executed in Egypt that August, ending the Umayyad Caliphate.
third-indochina-war: The war grew out of the rivalry between the Soviet Union and China. After the death of Joseph Stalin in 1953, Nikita Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin and his policy of peaceful coexistence with the West angered Mao Zedong, and the Sino-Soviet split deepened as both powers competed for influence among the new states and factions of the 1960s. North Vietnam allied with the Soviet Union, while the Khmer communists of Cambodia eventually allied with China.

When American forces withdrew and Saigon and Phnom Penh fell in April 1975, followed by a communist takeover in Laos five months later, the common enemy of the communist powers was gone. Armed clashes soon broke out on the border between Cambodia and Vietnam, as Khmer Rouge forces advanced deep into Vietnamese territory and raided villages, killing hundreds of civilians. Relations between Vietnam and China grew tense after Vietnam chose a pro-Soviet course on unification in 1976.

Vietnamese troops reached Phnom Penh in January 1979 and the Thai border that spring, ending the Cambodian genocide and installing a government of opponents of Pol Pot, most notably Hun Sen, a former Khmer Rouge commander. The remaining Khmer Rouge settled in the Thai-Cambodian border region and received support from Vietnam's enemies, while Thailand tolerated their presence. Vietnamese forces attacked their bases inside Thailand, and Thai and Vietnamese regular troops clashed several times with heavy casualties. An anti-Vietnamese coalition government was formed in 1982.

In February 1979 China launched a punitive attack on Vietnam's northern provinces and captured several cities near the border; on 6 March 1979 it declared its mission a success and withdrew, though both sides claimed victory. Border disputes and naval clashes between the two armies continued until 1990 without lasting gains for either.

Isolated except for the support of the Soviet Union and its allies, Vietnam became bogged down in Cambodia. By the late 1980s the Vietnamese Communist Party had adopted its Doi Moi policy and judged that hostility with China harmed its economic reforms, opening the way to normalisation in 1991. The 1991 Paris Peace Accords led to a transition and the restoration of a multi-party constitutional monarchy in Cambodia in 1993. Related conflicts included the insurgency in Laos, the Thai-Laotian Border War, the Johnson South Reef Skirmish and the FULRO insurgency against Vietnam.
third-italian-war-of-independence: Victor Emmanuel II of Savoy had been proclaimed King of Italy on 17 March 1861, but he controlled neither Venetia nor the much-reduced Papal States. The unredeemed lands, later called the Irredente, were a constant source of tension and central to foreign policy. When discord between Austria and Prussia over the German Question turned to open war in 1866, Italy saw its chance, and on 8 April 1866 it signed a military alliance with Prussia through the mediation of the French emperor Napoleon III.

Prussia attacked Austria's German allies on 16 June 1866, and Italy declared war three days later, opening operations on 23 June. General Alfonso Ferrero La Marmora led one army towards the Austrian fortresses of the Quadrilatero, while Enrico Cialdini led a second south of the Po. La Marmora was defeated at the Battle of Custoza on 24 June and retreated in disorder across the Mincio. The Italian army was hampered by quarrels among officers of the armies of the Kingdom of Sardinia and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

Prussia's victory at Königgrätz on 3 July forced Austria to move one of its three army corps from Italy to Vienna. Cialdini crossed the Po on 8 July and reached Udine on 22 July unopposed. On 20 July the Austrian fleet under Wilhelm von Tegetthoff beat the Italian fleet of Admiral Carlo di Persano at the Battle of Lissa, sinking two Italian ships. Garibaldi's volunteers meanwhile advanced into Trentino and won at Bezzecca on 21 July. Ordered on 9 August to evacuate Trentino, he answered simply: Obbedisco, 'I shall obey'.

After the Armistice of Nikolsburg ended the fighting between Austria and Prussia, France and Prussia pressed Italy to make its own armistice. Prime Minister Bettino Ricasoli at first refused, insisting on natural frontiers. The Armistice of Cormons was signed on 12 August and the Treaty of Vienna on 3 October 1866.

Austria gave Venetia, meaning modern Veneto, parts of Friuli and the city of Mantua, to Napoleon III, who passed it to Italy on 19 October under a secret treaty that repaid Italy's earlier acceptance of the French annexation of Savoy and Nice. The treaty made annexation depend on a plebiscite, held on 21 and 22 October, in which 99.9 per cent of participants voted to join Italy. The unification was completed by the capture of Rome in 1870 and, after the First World War, by the annexation of Trentino, the rest of Friuli and Trieste, sometimes called the Fourth Italian War of Independence.
third-javanese-war-of-succession: Prince Mangkubumi was the younger brother of Pakubuwana II of Surakarta. One cause of the war was his humiliation by the Governor-General of the Dutch East India Company, van Imhoff, who demanded the lease of the north coast of Java for 20,000 reales a year. Van Imhoff and the Patih Pringgalaya then persuaded Pakubuwana II to withdraw the fief of Sukawati, now Sragen, promised to Mangkubumi for defeating Raden Mas Said's rebellion there in 1746. Mangkubumi left Surakarta, rose against the Company and the king, and joined forces with his nephew and former enemy Raden Mas Said.

In 1749, in the midst of the rising, Pakubuwana II fell ill and asked Johan Andries, Baron van Hohendorff, to take control of the kingdom. Van Hohendorff asked for written confirmation, and on 11 December 1749 the king signed an agreement handing the sovereignty of Mataram to the Company, which placed Pakubuwana III on the throne as a powerless ruler. Mangkubumi, who saw himself as the rightful heir, claimed the title of ruler, and the people of Mataram called him Hamengkubuwono.

Years of fighting followed, with battles at Grobogan and Demak. The turning point came when Dutch forces under de Clerck suffered a heavy defeat at the Bogowonto River, after which Governor-General Mossel opened peace talks with Hamengkubuwono.

The Treaty of Giyanti of 1755 took its name from the place east of Surakarta where it was negotiated. The old capital of Kartasura, which years of war between brothers had made to seem doomed, was abandoned. Pakubuwana III kept the eastern part of Mataram and built a new kraton in Surakarta, while Mangkubumi became Sultan Hamengkubuwono I of the western half and built his kraton at Yogyakarta, north of Kartasura. Raden Mas Said ruled the princely state of Mangkunegara as Mangkunegara I from a kraton near Surakarta. Mataram, once a single kingdom, was thus divided into three nominally independent princely states.
third-macedonian-war: King Philip V of Macedon died in 179 BCE and was succeeded by his son Perseus, who was hostile to Rome. Seeking allies, Perseus married Laodice, daughter of the Seleucid king Seleucus IV, and arranged for his daughter to marry Prusias II of Bithynia, an enemy of Eumenes II of Pergamon, who was Rome's ally.

The Thracian king Abrupolis, a Roman ally, attacked Macedon as far as Amphipolis and overran the gold mines of Mount Pangaeus, but Perseus drove him out of his own lands. Rome objected to the expulsion of its ally. In 172 BCE a Roman commission demanded concessions that would have ended Macedonian independence; Perseus refused, and Rome declared war.

The war was fought mostly in Macedon and neighbouring Thessaly. For 171 BCE the consul Publius Licinius Crassus received the command, with two legions of 6,000 men each, and Epirus, Aetolia and Thessaly sided with Rome. The cities of Boeotia were divided, and Rhodes was brought into the Roman alliance. A Roman fleet besieged Haliartus, whose 2,500 defenders in the citadel were sold as slaves when it fell, and the town was razed. After an inconclusive battle at Callinicus, several years of campaigning followed. Livy describes Roman commanders plundering Boeotian cities, and records that Perseus surprised the fleet at Oreum on Euboea, capturing five warships and twenty grain transports.

In 169 BCE the consul Quintus Marcius Philippus advanced towards Macedon but fell back when supplies ran short, and Livy notes allegations that he feared to risk battle. Perseus lost the Illyrian king Gentius as an ally through his reluctance to pay the promised silver talents, and in 168 BCE the praetor Lucius Anicius defeated Gentius, who surrendered and was sent to Rome. The consul Lucius Aemilius Paulus prepared his campaign carefully and met Perseus on the River Elpeus. At Pydna the fighting began by accident or design, accounts differ, over a loose mule or a horse sent across a stream. The Romans won decisively.

Perseus fled with his cavalry and retinue, reached Amphipolis three days after the battle and sent ambassadors to the Romans. Aemilius sent troops against towns that had revolted or killed Roman soldiers, among them Agassae and Aeginium. Epirus, which had gone over to Perseus, was pacified by Anicius, and Illyria was split into three cantons, with cities that had deserted Gentius exempted from tribute.

The victory ended the Antigonid dynasty and effectively ended the independence of Macedon, although formal annexation came some years later. The kingdom was divided into four client republics, called merides, with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia, joined in a federal League of the Macedonians. Roman prestige and authority in Greece greatly increased.
third-mithridatic-war: The Third Mithridatic War was the last and longest of the three wars between Mithridates VI of Pontus and the Roman Republic, and both sides drew in many allies across Asia Minor, Greater Armenia, northern Mesopotamia and the Levant. In 89 BCE Mithridates defeated a Roman-led force, and in 88 BCE he orchestrated the massacre of Roman and Italian settlers in Anatolian cities, known as the Asiatic Vespers, in which 80,000 people are said to have died.

Sulla fought the First Mithridatic War from 88 to 84 BCE and ended it with a lenient treaty that the Senate never ratified, and the Second War followed from 83 to 81 BCE. The immediate cause of the Third was the bequest of the kingdom of Bithynia to Rome by Nicomedes IV on his death in 74 BCE, after which Mithridates, who had been rebuilding his forces, invaded Bithynia.

The Senate sent the consuls Lucius Licinius Lucullus and Marcus Aurelius Cotta, since Pompey was in Hispania against the revolt of Sertorius. Mithridates defeated Cotta at the Battle of Chalcedon, capturing or burning 64 ships and killing three thousand men, then took Nicaea, Lampsacus, Nicomedia and Apameia and besieged Cyzicus, the only city to hold to Rome. Lucullus trapped his army on the Cyzicus peninsula in a counter-siege. Famine, plague and the destruction of his cavalry at the Rhyndacus forced Mithridates to retreat, and Lucullus is said to have killed 20,000 at the Granicus. Of the 300,000 who set out, only 20,000 effective troops remained.

Lucullus then destroyed a Pontic fleet off Tenedos and at the island of Neae, where Dionysios committed suicide, and in 72 BCE marched through Galatia into Pontus. Mithridates assembled 40,000 men near Cabira, but after Roman convoys defeated his cavalry his camp panicked and his army broke. He fled to his son-in-law Tigranes of Armenia. Cotta sacked Heraclea Pontica in 71 BCE, while Lucullus took Amisus and Sinope. In 69 BCE Lucullus crossed the Euphrates into Greater Armenia, and began the siege of Tigranocerta.

Lucullus defeated Tigranes at Tigranocerta in 69 BCE and at the Aratsani River in 68 BCE, but his troops mutinied, and in 67 BCE Mithridates returned to Pontus and defeated the legate Gaius Valerius Triarius near Zela, leaving 7,000 Romans dead. Under the Lex Manilia of 66 BCE Pompey took supreme command, defeated Mithridates at the river Lycus near the end of that year, and received the submission of Tigranes.

The war ended the Pontic kingdom and the Seleucid Empire, by then a rump state, and made the Kingdom of Armenia an allied client state of Rome. Mithridates withdrew to the Cimmerian Bosporus, where his son Pharnaces II led a rebellion against him in 63 BCE.
third-partition-of-poland: After the First Partition of 1772, King Stanisław August Poniatowski tried to strengthen the weakened Commonwealth by reforms that reached their climax in the Constitution of 3 May 1791, which established a constitutional monarchy with three branches of government and abolished many privileges of the nobility. Russia, angered by what it saw as dangerous Jacobin-style reforms, invaded in 1792.

Abandoned by its Prussian allies and betrayed by Polish nobles who wanted their privileges back, Poland was forced to accept the Second Partition in 1793, which gave Dobrzyn, Kujavia and much of Greater Poland to Prussia and the eastern provinces to Russia. On 24 March 1794 Tadeusz Kościuszko took command of the Polish armed forces and declared a national uprising. Catherine II and Frederick William II responded, and the uprising was crushed by November 1794. According to legend, when Kościuszko fell from his horse at the Battle of Maciejowice shortly before his capture, he said Finis Poloniae.

Austrian, Prussian and Russian representatives met on 24 October 1795 to dissolve the Commonwealth, and the three powers signed a treaty dividing the territory on 26 January 1797. 2 million people. Prussia received Podlachia, the rest of Masovia and Warsaw, with 1 million people. 2 million people. Unlike in the earlier partitions, no Polish representative took part in the treaty.

King Stanisław was forced to abdicate and retire to St. Petersburg, where he died in 1798. The powers also agreed never to include the name of the Kingdom of Poland in their titles, so that the name 'shall remain suppressed'.

The partition ended the existence of independent Polish or Lithuanian states for 123 years. Many politicians, intellectuals and revolutionaries were forced to leave, in what was later called the Great Emigration, and many served France in the Polish Legions. Polish poets and artists made the desire for national freedom a mark of the Polish Romanticist movement.

Napoleon created the Duchy of Warsaw in 1807, but the Congress of Vienna in 1815 replaced it with a Kingdom of Poland under Russia, whose autonomy was largely ended after an insurrection in 1831. In 1867 Russia made it an official part of the empire. Full independence returned only at the end of the First World War, and on 29 August 1918 the Council of People's Commissars of the Russian republic denounced the partitions.
third-punic-war: The Second Punic War ended in 201 BCE with a treaty that stripped Carthage of its overseas territories and some African ones, and forbade it to wage war outside Africa or, within Africa, without Rome's express permission. Carthage was thereafter politically subordinate to Rome. Masinissa, King of Numidia and an ally of Rome, repeatedly raided and seized Carthaginian land over the following fifty years, and whenever Carthage appealed to Rome for redress or permission to act, Rome backed Masinissa.

Carthage then sent an army under Hasdrubal against the Numidians, treaty or no treaty, and it ended in disaster at the Battle of Oroscopa. A faction in the Roman Senate had long wanted further action against Carthage, among them Cato, whom later tradition credits with ending every speech with Carthago delenda est. The illicit campaign gave them a pretext.

In 149 BCE a large Roman army landed at Utica under the consuls Manius Manilius and Lucius Marcius Censorinus. The Carthaginians tried to appease them and handed over their weapons, including a recorded 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults. Censorinus then demanded that they abandon the city and settle 16 kilometres from the sea. They refused and prepared to defend Carthage. The Roman siege suffered repeated setbacks through 149 and 148 BCE, relieved only by the conduct of Scipio Aemilianus, then a tribune.

In 147 BCE public support for Scipio was so strong that the age limits were set aside and he was elected consul and sent to Africa. He built a large mole to cut off blockade runners. The Carthaginians cut a new channel to the sea and sortied with a rebuilt fleet, but many of their ships were sunk or captured on the withdrawal. Scipio then overran the Carthaginian field army's camp at Nepheris, and most of the towns still holding out surrendered.

In spring 146 BCE the Romans breached the walls, and over six days they worked through the residential quarter, killing everyone they met and burning the buildings behind them. Only on the last day were prisoners taken, 50,000 of whom were sold into slavery. The notion that the site was sown with salt is likely a 19th-century invention. A curse was laid on anyone who resettled the site, which became public land. Carthage's territory became the Roman province of Africa, with Utica as its capital.

Punic culture, language and religion survived in the surviving cities, and the Punic language was still spoken in North Africa until the 7th century CE. Augustus began rebuilding Carthage as a Roman city in 29 BCE. Polybius, the main source, was with Scipio and so presents him favourably.
third-sacred-war: In 357 BCE the Amphictyonic League, the religious body that governed the Temple of Apollo at Delphi and was then dominated by Thebes, fined the Phocian Confederation for cultivating sacred land on the Kirrhaean plain. The Phocians did not deny the offence, but the fine was far beyond their means, and refusing it would make them outcasts liable to a sacred war. The main ancient account is the Bibliotheca historica of Diodorus Siculus, written in the 1st century BCE, which leaves many gaps and gives little firm chronology.

In about July 356 BCE the Phocian leader Philomelus seized Delphi and its sanctuary, killed the nobles of the Thrakidai family and routed a relief force of Ozolian Locrians, whose captives he had thrown from the Phaidriadai rocks, the traditional punishment for sacrilege. Thebes then persuaded most Greek states to declare a sacred war; Sparta and Athens backed Phocis. To pay ever larger mercenary armies the Phocians plundered the dedications of the temple, spending an estimated 10,000 talents of Apollo's treasure.

That wealth let them absorb heavy defeats, among them the battles of Neon and the Crocus Field, and fight on under Onomarchos and then his brother Phayllos. The war spread into Locris, Doris, Boeotia, Thessaly, the Peloponnese and Euboea. Called into Thessaly by the ruling clan of Larissa against Pherae, an ally of Phocis, Philip II of Macedon won at the Crocus Field in 352 BCE and became ruler of Thessaly. By 347 BCE the Phocians were running out of treasure and the Thebans could not defeat them.

In 346 BCE Athens made the Peace of Philocrates with Macedon, while Philip's troops quietly seized the pass of Thermopylae. By 12 July the Athenians knew he was in the gates and reaffirmed the peace, leaving Phocis without help. The Phocian cities were destroyed and a heavy fine imposed on the confederation, which was readmitted to the Amphictyony only in 279 BCE. The settlement marked a major step in Macedon's rise to pre-eminence in Greece, and many offerings of the sanctuary had been lost for good.
third-taiwan-strait-crisis: In 1994, when Lee Teng-hui's plane stopped to refuel in Honolulu, the administration of President Bill Clinton refused him a visa and he spent the night on his plane, a slight he complained of as treatment for a second-class leader. When he was invited to speak on Taiwan's democratisation at Cornell University, his alma mater, Secretary of State Warren Christopher assured the Chinese foreign minister Qian Qichen that a visa would be inconsistent with the unofficial relationship with Taiwan.

Congress, lobbied by the firm Cassidy & Associates, passed a resolution in May 1995 by 396 votes to 0 in the House and 97 to 1 in the Senate, and the State Department gave way on 22 May. At Cornell on 9–10 June Lee called Taiwan a country with independent sovereignty, which the PRC leadership called an effort to split the motherland.

From 21 to 28 July 1995 the Second Artillery Corps fired missiles into areas north of Taiwan, and naval and amphibious exercises followed through the autumn, while the People's Republic told Washington and Taipei it did not intend to invade. American warships passed through the strait, the USS Nimitz and its battle group on 19 December 1995. In early 1996 China massed 100,000 troops along the strait before Taiwan's first presidential election.

On 8 March it fired missiles into waters off Keelung and Kaohsiung, ports that handled over 70 per cent of commercial shipping, and announced live-fire exercises near Penghu. The United States sent the USS Independence and then the Nimitz group, and from 18 to 25 March 150,000 troops rehearsed landings at Pingtan Island.

Shipping and insurance costs for Taiwan rose sharply, and many in Taiwan feared the seizure of small outlying islands such as Wuqiu. The crisis lifted Lee by 5 per cent in the polls, giving him a majority on 23 March 1996.

PLA commanders such as Zhang Wannian called the exercises a success, but the army judged it lacked leverage against the United States, and Jiang ordered a ten-year modernisation that brought Sovremenny-class destroyers, Kilo class submarines and Su-30 warplanes from Russia. The crisis also strengthened the case for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan and tightened military ties between the United States and Japan. In 1999 Major General Liu Liankun and Senior Colonel Shao Zhengzhong were executed for revealing to Taiwan that the missiles carried unarmed warheads.
third-treaty-of-san-ildefonso: Spain had fought the French Republic after the execution of Louis XVI in 1793, but was defeated in the War of the Pyrenees and made the Peace of Basel in 1795. The Second Treaty of San Ildefonso of 1796 then allied Spain with France against Britain, which cost it Trinidad and Menorca, while the British blockade hurt an economy dependent on colonial trade; the national debt rose eightfold between 1793 and 1798. Louisiana, received from France under the Treaty of Paris of 1763, was costly to defend against American settlers.

France, having lost Saint-Domingue, Martinique and Guadeloupe between 1791 and 1794, sought new colonies. After Napoleon seized power in the Coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799, he and Charles Talleyrand hoped to restore New France, with Louisiana supplying raw materials for French plantations in the Caribbean.

The French general Louis-Alexandre Berthier negotiated with the former Spanish chief minister Mariano Luis de Urquijo. Berthier also asked for East and West Florida and ten warships; Urquijo refused the Floridas but agreed to Louisiana and six ships of the line of seventy-four guns. In return Charles IV wanted a state for his son-in-law Louis, Duke of Parma, whose inheritance France meant to annex. The treaty named it only vaguely, perhaps Tuscany or the three Roman legations, and Urquijo held back Louisiana and the ships until France confirmed the territory. The treaty also reaffirmed the alliance of 1796.

After the Treaty of Lunéville of 9 February 1801, the Treaty of Aranjuez of March 1801 confirmed the terms and created the Kingdom of Etruria. Spain's chief minister Manuel Godoy was attacked for terms seen as favouring France, though modern historians are less critical, since Spain effectively controlled only a small part of the territory. The Saint-Domingue expedition failed, its leader General Charles Leclerc dying of yellow fever with an estimated 29,000 men, and Napoleon sold Louisiana to the U.S. in April 1803 for $15 million. Etruria was absorbed into France in 1807.
thirteen-years-war-1454-1466: Poland and the Teutonic Order had disputed Eastern Pomerania since the Order took Danzig in 1308, and the dispute produced Polish–Teutonic wars throughout the 14th and 15th centuries. After the Order's defeat at Grunwald in 1410 its state suffered internal conflict. The Prussian towns grew rich but had no political influence, and customs duties and the system of grain licences hindered trade. The nobility wanted a larger say and looked enviously at the wider privileges of the Polish nobility, and craftsmen resented the artisans the Knights settled near their castles. The Prussian Confederation, representing the nobility and cities, asked Emperor Frederick III for mediation in 1452, but he banned it and ordered it to obey the Order on 5 December 1453.

The Confederation then turned to Poland, with support from Greater Poland and from the party of Queen Sophia of Halshany, while Bishop Zbigniew Oleśnicki of Kraków opposed war. On 4 February 1454 the Confederation sent the Grand Master a formal act of disobedience and began a rebellion, and almost all of Prussia except Marienburg, Stuhm and Konitz soon freed itself. Casimir IV agreed to incorporate Prussia, and the delegates pledged allegiance to him on 6 March 1454.

Both sides expected a quick war, but Marienburg, defended skilfully under Heinrich Reuß von Plauen the Elder, resisted the Prussian forces. German reinforcements took Konitz in March 1454. Poland's levies of nobles, mostly cavalry, were ill suited to sieges, and Casimir had to borrow from the clergy to pay his mercenaries. In 1455 the Order recovered eastern Prussia, including Königsberg's towns, and the Grand Master's unpaid mercenaries took Marienburg, Dirschau and Eylau and began to negotiate their sale to Poland. Emperor Frederick III forbade trade with the Confederation in March 1455 and Pope Callixtus III threatened excommunication that September.

Poland captured the castle of Schwetz in 1461, and Polish privateers hired by Danzig took ships of the Order and of Lübeck. A first group of Polish regulars, about 2,000 men under Dunin, arrived in Prussia around October 1461 and took Lessen and Stuhm. In the summer of 1462 Dunin captured Frauenburg and burned Fischhausen.

The war ended in the victory of the Confederation and Poland and in the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466. The Order became a Polish fief, and its Grand Masters had to do homage to the Polish king within six months of taking power, which was observed for about two centuries. The Order returned Pomerelia to Poland after nearly 150 years and ceded the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia, and both lands formed Royal Prussia under the Polish king. Tensions soon flared, and the War of the Priests (1467–1479) followed, a dispute over the independence of Warmia in which the Knights sought revision of the peace.
thirteenth-amendment: From its founding in 1776 the United States was divided into states that allowed slavery and states that prohibited it. The original Constitution recognised slavery implicitly, in the Three-fifths Compromise, which counted three-fifths of each state's enslaved population for representation and taxation, and in the Fugitive Slave Clause. Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation, effective on 1 January 1863, declared free the enslaved in Confederate-controlled areas, about three million people, but their postwar status was uncertain, and it did not affect the border states. To put abolition beyond legal challenge, an amendment to the Constitution was drafted.

The text has two sections. The first says that neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party has been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States or any place subject to their jurisdiction. The second gives Congress power to enforce it by appropriate legislation.

The Senate passed the amendment on 8 April 1864 by 38 votes to 6. On 15 June the House failed to pass it, thirteen votes short of two thirds, but after extensive manoeuvring by Lincoln's administration it passed on 31 January 1865. Opponents argued from federalism and states' rights. It went to the states on 1 February 1865, and under President Andrew Johnson the reconstructed Southern states of Alabama, North Carolina and Georgia agreed, bringing the count to the required 27 of the 36 states on 6 December 1865. It was proclaimed on 18 December.

The amendment made the whole system of chattel slavery illegal. In Kentucky, between 65,000 and 100,000 people were still legally enslaved when it took effect, and in Delaware about nine hundred. Slavery continued under Native American tribes until new treaties in 1866. Some black Americans in the South were subjected to other forms of forced labour under the Black Codes, and many abuses were given cover by the penal labour exception.

It has rarely been cited in court, but it has been used to strike down peonage and some race-based discrimination as badges and incidents of slavery, and it was the first amendment to govern private individuals directly. It was the first of the three Reconstruction Amendments.
thirty-comrades: In April 1941 small groups of young Burmese left the country in secret to obtain military training for a struggle against British colonial rule. They were sent by the Dobama Asiayone, the We Burmans Association, under the leadership of Thakin Aung San, and had meant to seek help in Guangzhou. Instead they met the Japanese at Amoy, went on to Japan, and were flown to occupied Sanya to be trained by the Japanese Army. For security they were later moved to Formosa, and they returned towards Burma by way of Vietnam and Thailand.

Their mentor and chief trainer was the Japanese officer Suzuki Keiji, known to the Burmese as Bo Mogyo, Commander Thunderbolt, who headed the Minami Kikan, a special intelligence unit formed to support a national uprising in Burma. Each of the comrades took a nom de guerre.

On 26 December 1941, in a house in Bangkok owned by a Burmese doctor, about 25 of the Thirty Comrades drew blood from their arms into a silver bowl and each drank from it, the thway thauk of Burmese military tradition, pledging eternal loyalty to one another and to Burmese independence. Their average age was 24. The group formed the core of the Burma Independence Army, the beginning of the modern Burmese army, and the British were driven out of Burma to India during World War II.

The historian Gordon H. Luce, who taught at Rangoon University before the war, held that the Thirty Comrades under General Aung San helped found the fourth Burmese state in history, after those of King Anawrahta, King Tabinshwehti and King Alaungpaya. Ba Maw, head of state from August 1943 under the administration established by the Japanese, took a somewhat different view of their role. Bo Ne Win ruled Burma from March 1962 and died on 5 December 2002. The last of the comrades, Bo Ye Htut, died on 28 November 2013 at the age of 92.
thirty-three-orientals: Between 1816 and 1820 forces of the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves occupied the Provincia Oriental and defeated José Gervasio Artigas, who went into exile in Paraguay. In February 1824 newly independent Brazil annexed the territory as Cisplatina Province, after subduing a separatist movement of 1822-1823 led by partisans of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata.

Juan Antonio Lavalleja, who had fought beside Artigas, organised a new expedition from Buenos Aires Province with Manuel Oribe. It was backed by ranchers and beef-curers of Buenos Aires who saw the occupation as a threat to their markets, which suffered from competition with Rio Grande do Sul, supplied with cattle from Cisplatina. Juan Manuel de Rosas became an important financier of the movement.

On 1 April 1825 an advance party under Oribe sailed from San Isidro to the island of Brazo Largo on the Paraná River, where the main body joined it on 15 April after bad weather. On the night of 18 April the men slipped through the Paraná Delta past the Brazilian flotilla, crossed the Uruguay River in two boats and landed at Agraciada Beach, also called Arenal Grande, at dawn on 19 April. There they raised a flag of blue, white and red horizontal bars, colours traditional since the time of Artigas.

Drawing country people to their cause, they reached Montevideo on 20 May 1825 and on 14 June set up a provisional government at La Florida, which held elections to the Florida Assembly. The United Provinces recognised the province's incorporation on 24 October, and Brazil declared war that December. After mediation by the British diplomat Viscount Ponsonby, the Preliminary Peace Convention of 27 August 1828 made the province independent of both.

The number thirty-three is official, but lists of the members published between 1825 and 1832 give different names. Jacinto Carranza, comparing them in his 1946 book on how many there were, found Santiago Gadea on every list. Not all were from the province: the band included Argentines from the Paraná islands, Paraguayans and one man born in Mozambique. In 1877 the painter Juan Manuel Blanes portrayed the landing in El Juramento de los Treinta y Tres Orientales, interviewing survivors for the faces.
thirty-tyrants: After the Athenian navy was destroyed at Aegospotami in 405 BCE, Lysander led the Spartan and Peloponnesian League fleet to Athens. Without a navy to defend them or import food, many Athenians starved, and the city surrendered in March 404 BCE. Theramenes negotiated the final terms at Sparta. Although some members of the Peloponnesian League called for the city's destruction, the Spartans refused, arguing that Athens was one of the great cities of Greece.

The terms required Athens to pull down the long walls of Piraeus, readmit exiles, keep only twelve ships and submit to Sparta in peace and war. The Athenians were also to adopt a government dictated by the Spartans. The Ecclesia split over what that should be, with Theramenes the de facto leader of those wanting a democratic system, and when it deadlocked the Spartans demanded that thirty men be appointed to draft new laws. Theramenes chose ten, the five ephors ten and the Ecclesia ten.

The Thirty, whose names Xenophon lists, re-established the Boule of 501 members, appointed ten men to rule Piraeus and hired 300 whip-bearers as a police force. They tried and executed leaders who had opposed the peace, and two of their number, Aeschines and Aristoteles, asked Lysander for a Spartan garrison, which was sent as a supposedly temporary measure.

They delayed drawing up a constitution, and limited citizenship to 3,000 chosen Athenians. Led by Critias, they executed, murdered and exiled hundreds of Athenians and seized their property. Isocrates and Aristotle report that the Thirty executed 1,500 people without trial. Critias, a former pupil of Socrates, forced Theramenes, who opposed his violence, to drink hemlock after accusing him of treason.

Among those exiled was Thrasybulus, a trierarch and supporter of democracy, who led the uprising of 403 BCE that overthrew the Thirty. Critias was killed in the fighting. Socrates stayed in the city, which led the public to associate him with the Thirty. In Plato's Apology he recounts that when the Thirty ordered him and four others to arrest Leon of Salamis for execution, the others obeyed but he went home.

Pausanias, king of Sparta, went to Attica and made the treaty known as the Amnesty of 403, which restored democratic rule and pardoned everyone but the Thirty, the Eleven and the ten who ruled Piraeus, who were exiled. People who feared democratic rule could move to Eleusis, and Piraeus and Munychia returned to Athenian control. Plato's Seventh Letter, whose authenticity several 20th-century scholars question, recalls the rule of the Thirty as reviled by many, so that the former democracy seemed a golden age by comparison.
thirty-years-war: The Reformation had led to the Schmalkaldic War between Protestants and Catholics within the Holy Roman Empire. The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 tried to prevent a recurrence by designating states as Lutheran or Catholic according to the religion of their ruler. It was undermined by the spread of Protestantism, particularly Calvinism, into Catholic areas, and by the fragmented structure of the empire, which had some 300 imperial estates and an Imperial Diet that met rarely. In 1608 Frederick IV, Elector Palatine formed the Protestant Union, and in 1609 Maximilian of Bavaria established the rival Catholic League.

In May 1618 Protestant nobles led by Count Thurn threw two of the Catholic Ferdinand's representatives and their secretary from the windows of Prague Castle, an episode known as the Third Defenestration of Prague. All three survived. Bohemia became the first battleground, and fighting then expanded into the Palatinate, drawing in the Dutch Republic and Spain, and later Christian IV of Denmark. In 1630 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed in Pomerania with nearly 18,000 troops. His line formations and light artillery defeated the army of Tilly at Breitenfeld in September 1631.

The period from 1618 to 1635 was chiefly a civil war within the empire and largely ended with the Peace of Prague. France then entered the war in alliance with Sweden, and the empire became one theatre in a wider struggle against the Habsburgs of Austria and Spain. Related conflicts included revolts in Portugal and Catalonia in 1640, backed by France. Field armies averaged 13,000 to 20,000 men, and the forces deployed by both sides in Germany peaked at 250,000 in 1632.

The Peace of Westphalia consisted of three agreements: the Peace of Münster between Spain and the Dutch Republic, signed on 30 January 1648, the Treaty of Osnabrück between the empire and Sweden, and the Treaty of Münster between the empire and France. Talks had begun in 1642, with 109 delegations attending at one time or another. The settlement confirmed Dutch independence from Spain and reconfirmed the liberties of the German states, ending Habsburg attempts to turn the empire into a centralised state.

Estimates of the dead range from 4.5 to 8 million, most of them civilians and most after Sweden entered the war in 1630; claims of 12 million are no longer considered realistic. Collapse of local government produced landless peasants and rebellions, and witch-hunts began in Franconia in 1626, with over 900 people executed in the Bishopric of Würzburg by 1631. Historians count the war part of the General Crisis of the mid-17th century, and one lesson drawn was the need for permanent state armies.
thirumalai-nayak-palace: The Nayaks of Madurai ruled from 1545 until the 1740s, and Tirumala Nayaka, king from 1623 to 1659, raised many buildings in and around his capital. He built the palace, 2 km south-east of the Meenakshi Amman Temple, as the focal point of Madurai. What survives is the main palace, the king's living quarters; the original complex was about four times larger, 900 ft long by 660 ft wide. Art historians count it a late example of Vijayanagara architecture in its Tamil Nayaka style, which joined Indo-Islamic and Persian influences to the southern Indian tradition.

The buildings are of foliated brickwork finished with chunam, a stucco of shell lime mixed with egg white that gave the surfaces a smooth, glossy texture. The interior is richly decorated, the exterior plainer. Beyond the gates lies a central courtyard of about 3,700 square metres with a circular garden, ringed by massive round pillars 82 feet high. The palace had two main parts, the Swarga Vilasam and the Ranga Vilasam, holding the royal residence, theatre, shrine, armoury, bandstand, pond and garden. The Swarga Vilasam, the throne room, is an arcaded octagon under a dome 60 to 70 feet high, carried on stone ribs and columns linked by pointed, scalloped arches.

A local legend holds that the king hired an Italian architect, and European traders and missionaries did visit Madurai at the time. Some historians regard theories of European architects or a major Western influence on the design as resting on colonial prejudice.

War damaged much of the palace, and in the 18th century many of its structures were pulled down or built into the houses of the neighbouring streets. British records blamed Tirumala's grandson for stripping it to build his own palace at Tiruchirapalli, though some researchers think local people more probably took the materials. The British used surviving parts as granaries, barracks and a factory, and later as the district court of Madura-Ramnad until 1970. Lord Napier, Governor of Madras, partly restored it between 1866 and 1872. After independence it was declared a national monument, and light and sound shows tell the story of the Silappathikaram there.
thirumangai-alvar: Tradition places him in year 399 of the Kali Yuga, 2702 or 2706 BCE; modern scholars date the Alvars between the 5th and 9th centuries, though their dates remain disputed. He is generally held to have been a contemporary of the Pallava king Nandivarman II, since his hymns refer to the later Pallavas. His life is told in hagiographies of the 11th to 14th centuries. Born Kaliyan in Thirukuraiyalur near Sirkazhi, a son of the Chola general Nilam, he was a skilled archer and served the Chola king as a commander, receiving the title Parakala and the small territory of Ali Nadu, whose capital Thirumangai gave him the name Thirumangai Mannan.

According to tradition he fell in love with Kumudavalli, adopted daughter of a Vaishnava doctor, who required him to become a Vaishnava and feed a thousand people daily for a year. Unable to bear the cost, he turned to highway robbery, and while robbing a wedding party he found that the bridegroom was Vishnu himself, who taught him the eight-syllable mantra. The first ten verses of his Periya Tirumoli tell of this change. Giving up his chieftainship, he visited 88 of the 108 Divya Desams, spread the poems of earlier Alvars and preached devotion rather than penance; a later account tells of a meeting with the Shaiva saint Thirugnana Sambandhar at Sirkazhi.

His six Tamil works, 1,361 verses in all, form the largest share of any Alvar in the Divya Prabandham, and Tamil Vaishnavas regard them as the six Angas to the four poems of Nammalvar, held as Vedas. The chief work, the Periya Tirumoli of 1,084 hymns, praises over 40 forms of Vishnu from Badrinath to Thirukkurungudi. In Tirunetuntantakam he speaks as a woman parted from her divine beloved, and in the two Tirumatal poems, as a gopika, he threatens Krishna with the matal, the rejected lover's ancient Tamil custom.

He holds the titles Narkavi Perumal, the excellent poet, and Parakala, and Vaishnavas consider him an incarnation of Sharanga, Vishnu's bow. A temple was dedicated to him in the Vitthala complex at Hampi. Each year in the month of Thai his image is carried to the eleven Thirunaangur temples, where his verses for each are chanted. K. C. Varadachari called him a rebel, a social reformer, even a kind of Robin Hood, and above all an exquisite lyricist.
thiruvananthapuram: The city is built on seven hills by the seashore on the west coast, near the southern tip of mainland India. The Laccadive Sea bounds it on the west and the Western Ghats on the east, and it lies on the shores of the Karamana and Killi rivers. Its name comes from the Malayalam thiru-anantha-puram, the city of Lord Anantha, the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple. It was officially Trivandrum, the anglicised form, until 1991, when the government reinstated the original name; many Malayalees still use the older one.

The earliest known rulers of the region were the Ays, who were more closely related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai than to the rest of Kerala. Vizhinjam, now part of the city, was their capital and an important port from the second century BCE, and the Cholas and Pandyas fought over it. After the death of Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 almost all Ay territory passed to the Chera dynasty. In the tenth century the Cholas sacked Vizhinjam and destroyed its port and the education centre of Kanthalloor Sala. A branch of the Ay family that controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.

Marthanda Varma inherited Venad and expanded it by conquering Kayamkulam, Kottarakkara, Kottayam and other kingdoms, founding the princely state of Travancore in 1729. Travancore defeated the Zamorin of Calicut at Purakkad in 1755, and in 1795 the capital moved to Thiruvananthapuram from Padmanabhapuram. The Sree Moolam Popular Assembly, set up in 1904, was the first elected legislative council in any Indian state. After Travancore joined the Indian union in 1947, Pattom Thanu Pillai headed its first popularly elected ministry from 24 March 1948. The city was capital of Travancore-Cochin from 1949, and of Kerala from 1 November 1956.

The Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple remains the city's best-known landmark, alongside the Sreevaraham and Attukal Bhagavathy temples. The 2011 census counted 957,730 people in the municipal corporation. The University of Kerala and the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre of the Indian Space Research Organisation are based there, and India's space programme began in the city. It is associated with the musician Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma, the painter Raja Ravi Varma and writers such as Kumaran Asan and C. V. Raman Pillai.
this-land-is-your-land: Guthrie set his words to a melody very close to that of Oh, My Loving Brother, a Baptist gospel hymn that the Carter Family had recorded as When the World's On Fire, using the same tune for verses and chorus. The refrain line This land was made for you and me is not written at the end of each verse in the original manuscript, though Guthrie wrote the words at the top of the page and sang them. According to his biographer Joe Klein, Guthrie then forgot the song and did nothing with it for another five years.

The original text held two verses critical of the United States: one about a wall with a sign reading private property, the other about hungry people standing in a relief line. In 1944, during the Second World War, Guthrie prepared a version without them, by which time he supported American involvement in Europe. The earliest known recording, made in April 1944 and kept by the Smithsonian, still has the private property verse. These verses are often read as a protest against inequality and the suffering of the Great Depression, and they are rarely sung in schools or at official functions.

The short version was first released in 1951 on the Folkways album This Land Is My Land: American Work Songs, but the song was already known from songbooks from the mid-1940s. The Canadian group the Travellers had the first popular hit with a Canadian rewording, and in the 1960s Bob Dylan, the Kingston Trio, Peter, Paul and Mary and others recorded it. A 1947 recording was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1989, and in 2002 the Library of Congress added the song to the National Recording Registry.

Bruce Springsteen and Pete Seeger sang it with the restored verses at the Lincoln Memorial on 18 January 2009. In a dispute over a 2004 parody by the website JibJab, the Electronic Frontier Foundation found that Guthrie had first published the song in 1945 and that its copyright had not been renewed in time, so that the published version had been in the public domain since 1973.
thohanbwa: Thohanbwa, Hso Harn Hpa in Shan, was born in 1505, the eldest son of Sawlon of Mohnyin, who had rebelled successfully against Ava in the 1480s. Father and son raided Ava's lands from the north, and in the early 1520s a confederation of Shan States under Mohnyin joined them, stripping Ava of its northernmost territories and sacking the city in 1524. When the confederation besieged Ava again in 1527, King Shwenankyawshin was killed in battle in April and the city fell. Sawlon made his son king of Ava, in effect a viceroy for himself and the confederation.

Unused to governing so large a kingdom, the two raiders kept ministers of the old court and made Mingyi Yan Naung chief minister, while many of Ava's people fled south to Toungoo. In 1533 they attacked Prome, their former ally, and carried off its ruler Bayin Htwe, but Sawlon was assassinated by his own ministers on the march home. Thohanbwa became chief of Mohnyin as well as king of Ava, yet the other saophas did not accept him as first among equals, and the confederation did nothing while Tabinshwehti of Toungoo made war on Hanthawaddy from 1534 to 1539.

Burmese history remembers him for his attacks on Buddhist pagodas and monks. He held that pagodas were treasure chambers with nothing to do with religion and plundered those within reach. In 1540 he had 360 monks of Ava, Sagaing and Pinya killed, 30 of them noted for their learning, and burned the manuscripts of the monasteries. The historian G. E. Harvey called him a full-blooded savage, and Burmans and Shans alike hated him.

Only when Toungoo turned on Prome, Ava's vassal, did Thohanbwa lead the confederation's states, Mohnyin, Mogaung, Bhamo, Momeik, Hsipaw and Yawnghwe, to its defence. General Bayinnaung of Toungoo defeated them outside Prome.
