With his allies at court gone, Yan Naung staged a coup at the summer palace outside Ava: asked to bring the late king's sword, he bowed as if to present it and ran the king through. Yan Naung declined the throne, which passed to Hkonmaing, ruler of Hsipaw, a steadfast ally of Shwenankyawshin.
tholing-monastery: Tholing is the oldest monastery in the Ngari Prefecture of western Tibet. It stands in the remote badlands of Zanda County, near the border with India, on an escarpment above the canyon of the Langchen Tsangpo, the Sutlej River, at an elevation of about 3,800 m. Its name is said to mean hovering in the sky forever. The monastery lies 19 km east of Tsaparang. It is a walled complex of rectangular mud-brick buildings facing east, a style that became the model for later temples of the kingdom of Guge.

Tholing was among the first temples of the second diffusion of Buddhism in Tibet, built when it was the capital of Guge. King Yeshe-Ö sponsored young men as novices and sent Rinchen Zangpo, one of 21 young monks, to study at Vikramshila Mahavihara in India; only he and Lekpai Sherap survived the climate, snake bites and disease to return, and Rinchen Zangpo built three of the major temples. The king invited the Indian master Atiśa to Guge in 1042, and Atiśa spent three years at Tholing and founded the Kadampa school there. The monastery became a gateway for Indian scholars into Tibet, and its fame and that of Guge reached India from Kashmir to Assam.

Giuseppe Tucci, who visited in 1933, called it one of the oldest, richest and finest monasteries of Tibet and saw rain washing away its frescoes. Lama Govinda photographed its paintings and statues in 1948 and made it known abroad. During the Cultural Revolution its temples were destroyed or left to the weather, and of its six chapels only some survive.

The monastery is now mostly in ruins but keeps many well-preserved murals in the west Tibetan style. The Yeshe-Ö Temple, a mandala-shaped temple with red towers, was rebuilt after its demolition, and two of its chapels kept their murals because they were used to store grain. The Dukhang, or assembly hall, and the Lhakhang Karpo, the White Chapel, hold murals of the 15th and 16th centuries.
thomas-aquinas: Thomas Aquinas was most likely born around 1225 in the family castle of Roccasecca, near Aquino, then controlled by the Kingdom of Sicily. His father, Landulf VI of Aquino, was a knight in the service of Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, and his mother was Theodora Galluccio, Countess of Teano. He was the youngest of nine children, and the family intended him to follow his uncle Sinibald into the abbacy of Monte Cassino, where he began his education at five.

In 1239 his parents enrolled him at the studium generale in Naples, where he was presumably introduced to Aristotle, Averroes and Maimonides. At nineteen he resolved to join the Dominican Order, which did not please his family: on his way to Rome his brothers seized him and brought him back to his parents.

Although he wrote actively for only about two decades, Thomas wrote over eight million words. His best-known work is the unfinished Summa Theologiae (1265 to 1274), alongside the Disputed Questions on Truth (1256 to 1259), the Summa contra Gentiles (1259 to 1265) and commentaries on Scripture and on Aristotle.

Thomas treated theology as a science whose data are Scripture and the tradition of the Church, and held that faith and reason, distinct but related, are both necessary for true knowledge of God. He held that rational thinking and the study of nature, like revelation, are valid ways to understand truths about God. His central thought was that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it. He never considered himself a philosopher, and he often cites Aristotle simply as the Philosopher.

Thomas died on 7 March 1274. Dante asserts that he died by poisoning, on the order of Charles of Anjou, but the account of one of his friends gives no hint of foul play. In 1277 Étienne Tempier, bishop of Paris, issued a condemnation listing 219 propositions, twenty of them Thomistic, which severely damaged Thomas's reputation for many years. On 18 July 1323 Pope John XXII, seated in Avignon, pronounced him a saint, and his remains were moved to the Church of the Jacobins in Toulouse on 28 January 1369.
thomas-arne: Thomas Augustine Arne was born on 12 March 1710 in Covent Garden and baptised a Roman Catholic, from a long line of Catholic recusants. His father and grandfather were upholsterers. His grandfather died in the debtors' prison of Marshalsea, and his father, who could afford to send him to Eton College, later lost most of his money and worked as a ticket-counter at the Drury Lane Theatre.

Arne smuggled a spinet into his room and practised at night, damping the sound with a handkerchief, and dressed as a liveryman to reach the gallery of the Italian Opera. There he met Michael Festing, who taught him the violin. His father had articled him to a solicitor, but after discovering him leading musicians at a gathering he allowed him to turn to music.

Between 1733 and 1776 Arne wrote music for about 90 stage works, among them plays, masques, pantomimes and operas, though many scores were probably lost in the fire at the Royal Opera House in 1808. His sister, the contralto Susannah Maria Arne, known as Mrs Cibber, sang in some of them, beginning with his first opera, Rosamund. On 15 March 1737 he married the singer Cecilia Young.

In 1742 he went to Dublin for two years, where he produced the oratorio The Death of Abel, of which only the Hymn of Eve survives. Returning in 1744, he led the band at Drury Lane and the following year became composer at Vauxhall Gardens. After a quarrel between his sister and David Garrick, he moved with her to Covent Garden in 1750.

Thomas and Sally of 1760 was the first English comic opera sung throughout, with no spoken dialogue. Artaxerxes of 1762 was one of the most successful English operas of the century, performed in London into the 1830s. Mozart almost certainly saw it in 1764 and said it influenced his operas, and Haydn was impressed by it in 1791. In 1769 Arne wrote Soft Flowing Avon, with words by Garrick, for the Shakespeare Jubilee at Stratford-upon-Avon.

In Judith in 1773 he introduced women's voices into choruses for the first time. He is also known for A-Hunting We Will Go, written for a 1777 production of The Beggar's Opera. He died on 5 March 1778 and is buried at St Paul's, Covent Garden.
thomas-becket: Becket was born at Cheapside in London, on 21 December, the feast day of Thomas the Apostle. His parents were Gilbert and Matilda Beket, both of Norman descent. Gilbert began as a merchant and later lived on the rents of London properties and served as the city's sheriff. At the age of ten Becket was sent to Merton Priory in Surrey, and he later attended a grammar school in London. When his father suffered financial reverses he worked as a clerk, and later he entered the household of Archbishop Theobald of Bec.

Theobald sent him on missions to Rome and to Bologna and Auxerre to study canon law, and in 1154 made him Archdeacon of Canterbury. As chancellor he enforced the king's traditional revenues, including those owed by churches. After Theobald's death Becket was confirmed as archbishop on 23 May 1162, ordained priest on 2 June and consecrated the next day. He resigned the chancellorship and sought to recover and extend the rights of the archbishopric, to the king's displeasure.

At Clarendon Palace on 30 January 1164 Henry presented sixteen constitutions to limit clerical independence and weaken connections with Rome. All the clergy agreed except Becket, who still refused to sign. Summoned to Northampton Castle on 8 October 1164 to answer charges of contempt of royal authority and malfeasance as chancellor, he was convicted and fled to the Continent. Louis VII of France protected him. He spent nearly two years at the Cistercian abbey of Pontigny, until Henry's threats against the order sent him to Sens. Pope Alexander III favoured diplomacy, and in 1170 Henry offered a compromise that allowed Becket to return.

In 1170 the Archbishop of York crowned the heir, Henry the Young King, which breached Canterbury's privilege, and Becket excommunicated those involved. Henry II is said to have spoken words that his men took as a wish to have Becket killed, and the exact wording is in doubt. Four knights, Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy and Richard le Breton, came to Canterbury on 29 December 1170 and killed Becket in the cathedral. The eyewitness Edward Grim, who was wounded, left an account.

Veneration began across Europe at once, and Alexander III canonised him on 21 February 1173. On 12 July 1174 Henry did public penance at his tomb. In 1220 his bones were moved to a gold-plated shrine in the Trinity Chapel, which Henry VIII destroyed in 1538. Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales is set among pilgrims travelling to it.
thomas-bowdich: Thomas Edward Bowdich was born in Bristol on 20 June 1791 and educated at Bristol Grammar School. In 1813 he married Sarah Wallis, who shared his later travels and work. In 1814, through his uncle John Hope Smith, governor of the British settlements on the Gold Coast, he gained a writership with the African Company of Merchants and was posted to Cape Coast.

In 1817 he was sent with two companions, William Hutchison and Henry Tedlie, to Kumasi on a mission to Osei Bonsu, King of Asante. The mission achieved its aim of securing British control over the coastal peoples, chiefly through his diplomacy. He returned to England in 1818 and in 1819 published Mission from Cape Coast Castle to Ashantee, an account of the mission and of his study of the court. He gave his Asante collection to the British Museum, though its trustees paid it little attention until after his death; it remains the earliest documented collection of Asante material and includes the oldest known surviving adinkra cloth.

Bowdich publicly attacked the African committee that managed the company, and his criticism helped lead the British government to dissolve the company and take direct control of the Gold Coast. From 1820 to 1822 he lived in Paris, studying mathematics and natural science and moving among scholars such as Georges Cuvier and Alexander von Humboldt. There he edited works on Africa and wrote scientific books, among them Elements of Conchology in 1822. In Lisbon he studied historic manuscripts for an account of Portuguese discoveries in Angola and Mozambique, published in 1824.

In 1823 Bowdich and his wife, after months in Madeira and the Cape Verde Islands, reached Bathurst, now Banjul, at the mouth of the Gambia, intending to go on to Sierra Leone and explore the interior. He died there of malaria on 10 January 1824, leaving his widow with three children. Sarah Bowdich Lee published a narrative of the journey in 1825, and their daughter republished his Mission in 1873.
thomas-butler-10th-earl-of-ormond: Thomas Butler was born about February 1531 in southern Ireland, the eldest son of James Butler, later 9th Earl of Ormond, and Joan FitzGerald, daughter of James FitzGerald, 10th Earl of Desmond. His father's family, the Butler dynasty, descended from Theobald Walter, appointed Chief Butler of Ireland by King Henry II in 1177. In May 1544, aged about 13, he was sent to London to be brought up at court, where he took on English speech, dress and manners and the Protestant religion. There he met the young Elizabeth, his distant cousin through her mother Anne Boleyn; she later called him her black husband.

His father died in London on 28 October 1546 after being poisoned at a banquet at Ely House, probably at the instigation of the Lord Deputy Anthony St Leger, and Thomas succeeded as 10th Earl of Ormond and 3rd Earl of Ossory.

Knighted at Edward VI's coronation in 1547, he fought at the Battle of Pinkie that September and helped put down Wyatt's rebellion in 1554. Elizabeth made him Lord Treasurer of Ireland on 26 August 1559, an office he held for life. His long feud with the neighbouring Earls of Desmond, both families more or less Gaelicized Old English and much intermarried, led to the private Battle of Affane on 8 February 1565, where Gerald FitzGerald, 14th Earl of Desmond, was shot in the hip by Ormond's brother Edmund and captured.

In the first Desmond Rebellion some of his own brothers joined the rebels, and three were attainted in 1570. When the second rising began in 1579 he was made governor of Munster and led the royal army that suppressed it, moved, it is held, as much by rivalry with the Desmonds as by religion. Both rebellions left Munster desolate for many years.

He was made a Knight of the Garter in 1588 and carried the sword of state before the Queen at Tilbury. In 1600, during Tyrone's Rebellion, he was held captive from April to June by Owny MacRory O'More. In the 1560s he had built the Tudor manor house at Ormonde Castle, meant to receive the Queen, who planned visits in 1602 and 1603 that never took place. He married three times; his sons by Elizabeth Sheffield died young, and he died at Carrick on 22 November 1614 and was buried in St Canice's Cathedral, Kilkenny. The earldom passed to his nephew Walter of the Kilcash branch.
thomas-carleton: Carleton was born in Strabane, County Tyrone, in Ulster, the son of Catherine Ball and the younger brother of Guy Carleton, later 1st Baron Dorchester. From a military family, he joined the British Army young and was an ensign in the 20th Regiment of Foot by 1753. He served with it in the Seven Years' War and afterwards watched the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774 as an observer.

In 1776, during the American Revolutionary War, he arrived at Quebec City as a lieutenant colonel with forces to relieve his brother, then Governor General of Canada, whom Continental Army troops were besieging there. After Lieutenant Colonel Patrick Gordon died on 25 July 1776 he was given command of the 29th Regiment of Foot. He quarrelled with Frederick Haldimand, who replaced his brother as governor general in 1778, and in 1782 refused Haldimand's demand that he resign as quartermaster general. He returned to England and lodged with Lord Shelburne, then First Lord of the Treasury.

In the summer of 1784 he took charge of the new province of New Brunswick and helped resettle the many Loyalists leaving the United States. He became a major-general on 12 October 1793. In the last years of the century he survived a censure motion and an attempt to remove him led by the assemblyman James Glenie, whom a court-martial including Carleton had convicted in 1780 of conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman.

After he sailed for England in 1803 he never returned. When the Chesapeake–Leopard affair of 1807 raised tension with the United States, he was ordered back to his post, but refused because the new governor general, Sir James Henry Craig, was a lieutenant-general while he was a full general, and his duties fell to a succession of local officers. He died on 2 February 1817. He and his wife Hannah Foy had a son, William, and daughters Emma and Anne. Mount Carleton, the highest mountain in New Brunswick, is named after him.
thomas-chittenden: Thomas Chittenden was born in East Guilford in the Connecticut Colony on 6 January 1730. He lost an eye, and his opponents called him one eye Tom. On 4 October 1749 he married Elizabeth Meigs in Salisbury, Connecticut, and they had four sons and six daughters, all of whom survived to adulthood. He was a justice of the peace, sat in the Connecticut Colonial Assembly from 1765 to 1769 and served in Connecticut's 14th Regiment of Militia from 1767 to 1773, rising to colonel.

With other residents of Salisbury he bought land from the Onion River Land Company of Ethan Allen, Ira Allen, Heman Allen and Remember Baker, and in 1774 he moved to the New Hampshire Grants, now Vermont, as the first settler of the town of Williston. He was a delegate to the convention of 1777 that drew up Vermont's constitution and its Declaration of Independence, and on 12 March 1778 the legislature chose him as governor, with Joseph Marsh as lieutenant governor.

During the American Revolution he sat on a committee empowered to negotiate Vermont's entry into the Union with the Continental Congress, which put the matter off so as not to antagonise New York and New Hampshire, both of which claimed the territory. He also took part in delicate talks with British authorities in Quebec about making Vermont a British province. Vermont was admitted in 1791 as the 14th state, and he remained governor until his death.

Chittenden died at Williston on 25 August 1797 and was buried in the cemetery there that bears his name. His epitaph reads: Out of storm and manifold perils rose an enduring state, the home of freedom and unity. A monument at the cemetery was begun in 1894 and dedicated in 1896. Frank Gaylord made bronze statues of him for the grounds of the State House at Montpelier and for Williston Central School, and Chittenden County and the town of Chittenden are named for him.
thomas-clarkson: Clarkson was the elder son of the Reverend John Clarkson, a Church of England priest and headmaster of Wisbech Grammar School, where he was educated before St Paul's School in London. He entered St John's College, Cambridge, in 1779, took his degree in 1783 and was ordained a deacon, but never went on to priest's orders. The essay competition of 1785, set by the vice-chancellor Peter Peckard on whether it is lawful to make slaves of others against their will, led him to read Anthony Benezet and Francis Moore and to interview people who knew the trade. Riding back to London that summer, he sat down by the road near Wades Mill and resolved that someone must bring these calamities to an end.

Clarkson published the essay in English in 1786, which brought him into contact with James Ramsay, Granville Sharp and the Quakers who had petitioned Parliament in 1783. He approached the young William Wilberforce, gave the committee its public profile and collected evidence in a wooden chest that appeared repeatedly in Parliament. In Liverpool in 1787 a gang of sailors paid to kill him nearly did. He rode some 35,000 miles, interviewed 20,000 sailors, enlisted the ship's surgeons Alexander Falconbridge and James Arnold, gathered handcuffs, shackles and branding irons, and in 1791 published the plan of the slave ship Brooks. He also showed fine African goods to argue for a trade in goods rather than people.

Exhausted, he withdrew in 1794 to Eusemere by Ullswater, where he befriended William and Dorothy Wordsworth, and in 1796 married Catherine Buck. He returned to the campaign in 1804, and after the act of 1807 worked for enforcement and for international agreement, travelling to Paris in 1814 and Aix-la-Chapelle in 1818.

For the Anti-Slavery Society, formed in 1823, he covered 10,000 miles and helped bring 777 petitions to Parliament, and in 1840 he opened the first World Anti-Slavery Convention in London. He hosted Frederick Douglass in 1846 and died at Playford, Suffolk, on 26 September 1846. His chest and collection are in the Wisbech & Fenland Museum, the Clarkson Memorial in Wisbech was unveiled in 1881, a tablet in Westminster Abbey followed in 1996, and the Church of England honours him with Equiano and Wilberforce on 30 July.
thomas-cochrane-10th-earl-of-dundonald: Thomas Cochrane was born at Annsfield, near Hamilton in South Lanarkshire, Scotland, on 14 December 1775, the son of Archibald, Lord Cochrane, who became the 9th Earl of Dundonald in 1778. Through his uncle Alexander Cochrane he was listed on the books of four Royal Navy ships from the age of five, a common though unlawful practice known as false muster. His father got him an army commission, but he preferred the navy, which he joined on 23 July 1793 as a midshipman, just as his family lost its wealth and lands.

A court martial reprimanded him for flippancy toward a superior, the first sign of a pattern of conflict with superiors, colleagues and employers, which led to a long enmity with Admiral John Jervis, Earl of St Vincent. In 1803 he took command of HMS Arab, and in December 1804 of the frigate HMS Pallas, whose cruise near the Azores took three Spanish merchant ships and a privateer. His successes led Napoleon to call him le Loup des Mers, "the Sea Wolf".

He entered Parliament for Honiton in 1806 on a platform of reform, and in 1807 for Westminster, allied with the Radicals William Cobbett, Sir Francis Burdett and Henry Hunt. His criticism of corruption in the navy and of Admiral Gambier's conduct at the Basque Roads made him powerful enemies.

In February 1814 a false report of Napoleon's death raised share prices, and Cochrane, who had sold his entire holding of Omnium stock, was named as one of six conspirators. After a controversial conviction for fraud he was dismissed from the Royal Navy in 1814. In 1818 he agreed to serve the cause of Spanish American independence and reached Valparaíso on 28 November, where he helped organise the Chilean navy. He went on to lead the navy of Brazil in its war of independence against Portugal and, from August 1825, served Greece against the Ottoman Empire, where he met with limited success.

He succeeded to his father's earldom on 1 July 1831 and was restored to the Royal Navy list as Rear-Admiral of the Blue on 2 May 1832, rising to Admiral of the Red in 1857. He refused any command until his knighthood was restored, which took fifteen years. He died on 31 October 1860 and is buried in Westminster Abbey; the Brazilian minister laid flowers in the name of the navy he had created. His career inspired the nautical fiction of Frederick Marryat, C. S. Forester's Horatio Hornblower and Patrick O'Brian's Jack Aubrey.
thomas-cranmer: Thomas Cranmer was born at Aslockton in Nottinghamshire on 2 July 1489, a younger son of a family of established gentry of modest wealth. At 14, two years after his father's death, he was sent to the newly created Jesus College, Cambridge. He took his Master of Arts in 1515 after studying the humanists Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples and Erasmus, was ordained by 1520 and received his Doctor of Divinity degree in 1526.

From 1527 he assisted with the annulment of Henry VIII's marriage while remaining a Cambridge don. In 1529, staying at Waltham Holy Cross to avoid the plague, he suggested putting aside the legal case in Rome in favour of canvassing opinions of university theologians across Europe. Henry took an interest, and Cranmer joined the royal team that gathered them.

A royal letter dated 1 October 1532 informed him that he had been appointed Archbishop of Canterbury, a post secured by the family of Anne Boleyn. Cranmer was consecrated as a bishop on 30 March 1533. He was not at once accepted by the bishops of his province, and Thomas Cromwell, as vicegerent, eclipsed him in the king's spiritual jurisdiction. Under Henry he made few radical changes, because conservatives and reformers struggled for power, and the Act of the Six Articles of 1539 affirmed conservative doctrines such as clerical celibacy. He published the first officially authorised English service, the Exhortation and Litany.

When Edward VI came to the throne in 1547, Cranmer promoted faster change. He wrote four of the twelve Homilies and gave refuge to continental reformers such as Martin Bucer, Peter Martyr and Bernardino Ochino. In the House of Lords in December 1548 he revealed that he had abandoned the doctrine of the corporeal real presence. The Act of Uniformity 1549 backed the first Book of Common Prayer, and a second edition followed. He produced the Edwardine Ordinal in 1550 and, in the same year, the Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament.

Cranmer supported Lady Jane Grey's succession in 1553. After the accession of the Catholic Mary I he was put on trial for treason and heresy and imprisoned for over two years. Under pressure he made several recantations and reconciled himself with the Catholic Church, but Mary wanted him executed on the treason charge. He was burned at the stake on 21 March 1556 and publicly withdrew his recantations on the day.

His death was immortalised in John Foxe's Acts and Monuments, first printed in 1563. The Book of Common Prayer and the Thirty-nine Articles, a statement of faith derived from his work, remain part of his legacy in the Church of England, which honours him as a martyr. His children died without issue, and his line became extinct.
thomas-cromwell: Cromwell is thought to have been born around 1485 in Putney, then a village in Surrey. His father, Walter, was an ambitious yeoman landowner who worked as a sheep farmer and fuller, and also ran a tavern and a brewery.

Around the start of the 16th century Cromwell left his family and crossed to continental Europe, allegedly after time in prison, and later admitted to Archbishop Thomas Cranmer that he had been a ruffian in his youth. Accounts of his years in France, Italy and the Low Countries are problematic. By 1520 he was established in London mercantile and legal circles, and in 1523 he obtained a seat in the House of Commons.

Cromwell secured a seat for Taunton in November 1529 and was reported to be in favour with the King. He joined the Privy Council late in 1530. By the autumn of 1531 he had taken control of the supervision of Henry VIII's legal and parliamentary affairs. In April 1534 Henry confirmed him as principal secretary and chief minister, a position he had held for some time in all but name. He enforced the Act of Succession, and when Sir Thomas More and John Fisher refused the oath, both were imprisoned and within a month executed.

In July 1536 he became Lord Privy Seal and Baron Cromwell of Wimbledon. He orchestrated the Dissolution of the Monasteries. He also secured the licence for the Matthew's Bible and obliged every church to own a Bible by 1538, and the Great Bible followed in 1539. Scholars generally agree that he was a Protestant with a Lutheran mindset. His injunctions for the Ten Articles of 1536 provoked the Pilgrimage of Grace.

Cromwell arranged the King's marriage to Anne of Cleves, which took place on 6 January 1540 and was not consummated. Henry made him Earl of Essex on 18 April 1540, but his conservative opponents, notably the Duke of Norfolk, used the King's anger as their opportunity. Cromwell was arraigned under an act of attainder and executed for treason and heresy on Tower Hill on 28 July 1540.

Until the 1950s historians discounted his role. Geoffrey Elton then presented him as the central figure of a Tudor revolution in government, and later historians agree on his importance if not on that term. Diarmaid MacCulloch credits him with guiding the early careers of William Cecil and Nicholas Bacon.
thomas-douglas-5th-earl-of-selkirk: Thomas Douglas was born on 20 June 1771 at St Mary's Isle, Kirkcudbrightshire, the seventh son of Dunbar Douglas, 4th Earl of Selkirk, and Helen Hamilton. In 1778, when he was seven, a party from John Paul Jones's sloop Ranger came to the house to seize his father as a hostage; a governess hid the boy, and the sailors left with the family silver. Not expecting to inherit, he studied law at the University of Edinburgh, where he took notice of crofters being displaced by their landlords. His six brothers all died before him, and on his father's death in 1799 he became the 5th Earl.

He used his fortune and connections to settle poor Scottish farmers at Belfast, Prince Edward Island, in 1803 and at Baldoon, Upper Canada, in 1804, and in 1805 published Observations on the present state of the Highlands of Scotland. Refused a government grant on the Red River, he and Sir Alexander Mackenzie bought enough shares in the Hudson's Bay Company to control it, and, helped by his wife Jean's brother Andrew Wedderburn on the company's committee, he obtained the grant of Assiniboia, promising the company 200 men a year and keeping the settlers out of the fur trade.

The colony lay across the routes of the rival North West Company, and the Métis, long tied to that company, rejected his authority. The first settlers under Miles Macdonell arrived too late to plant and depended on Métis help. In 1814 Macdonell's Pemmican Proclamation banned the export of food; the Métis arrested him and burned the settlement. In 1816 the Battle of Seven Oaks killed 21 of Selkirk's men, among them Governor Robert Semple, and one Métis.

Selkirk answered by seizing the North West Company's post at Fort William and was charged in Montreal with four offences over its occupation; the men he accused were acquitted and counter-sued him. Suffering from tuberculosis, he wintered at Pau and died there on 8 April 1820, and the two companies merged in 1821. The City of Selkirk and the Selkirk Mountains bear his name, and the Métis date the shaping of their identity as a people, with a flag and an anthem, to their armed resistance in this period.
thomas-edison: Edison was the seventh and last child of Samuel Ogden Edison Jr. and Nancy Matthews Elliott, and the family moved to Port Huron, Michigan, in 1854. He became deaf as a child and learned through books and tinkering. From 1863 to 1869 he held a series of night-shift telegraph jobs across Ontario, Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio and Massachusetts, working the Associated Press news wire as a Western Union employee. His tinkering sometimes interfered with his work.

The laboratory at Menlo Park, built in 1876, was paid for by the sale of his quadruplex telegraph. That year he set out to improve the telephone with a carbon microphone, financed by Western Union, which wanted to compete with Alexander Graham Bell. In 1877 his phonograph, first recording on tinfoil wrapped round a grooved cylinder, made him widely known. As he aged he resented titles that made him a genius and stressed one per cent inspiration and 99 per cent perspiration.

Many incandescent lamps existed before his, but they burnt out quickly and needed high current. After trying carbonised cardboard, then grasses and canes, he settled on bamboo as the best filament and devised a commercially viable bulb on 21 October 1879. He founded the Edison Illuminating Company on 17 December 1880. His direct current system could not serve customers more than 1.6 kilometres from a plant, whereas alternating current could be sent long distances on thinner wires. With William Kennedy Laurie Dickson he also worked on a motion picture camera, first tested publicly on 20 May 1891; much of the credit for it belongs to Dickson.

In January 1916 a hydrogen explosion in the submarine USS E-2, during maintenance with one of his batteries, killed five men; he and Miller Hutchinson blamed operator error, while many naval officials blamed them for overselling the battery. From 1914 to 1924 he made motor camping trips with Henry Ford, Harvey Firestone and John Burroughs, and in 1926 he gave the presidency of Thomas A. Edison, Inc. to his son Charles. His diabetes worsened in his last years, and he died on 18 October 1931 at Glenmont and was buried on the property. A test tube labelled as his last breath is on display at the Henry Ford Museum.
thomas-fitzgerald-10th-earl-of-kildare: Thomas was born in London, the son of Gerald FitzGerald, 9th Earl of Kildare, and his first wife Elizabeth Zouche, a distant cousin of Henry VII. After his mother's death he was raised by Janet Eustace, the wife of his father's steward. He spent several years at the English court and married Frances, the youngest daughter of Sir Adrian Fortescue. In February 1534 his father was summoned to London and left the 21-year-old Thomas, by then Lord Offaly, as deputy governor of Ireland in his absence.

On 11 June 1534 he rode to the council at St Mary's Abbey, Dublin, with 140 armoured gallowglasses whose helmets bore silk fringes, the source of his nickname, and publicly renounced his allegiance to his cousin Henry VIII. When Archbishop Alen urged restraint, his harper recited a poem on the deeds of his ancestors, and Thomas threw down the sword of state and left the hall. Holding most of the Pale's fortresses, he sent lords who refused to swear fidelity to him as prisoners to Maynooth Castle and offered to divide the kingdom with Lord Butler, son of the Earl of Ormond, who refused.

His attack on Dublin Castle in July was routed. Tradition holds that Alen's killers, John Teeling and Nicholas Wafer, took his order in Irish to take the man away as an order to kill, and the killing cost him the clergy's support. His father had meanwhile died in London, so Thomas became 10th earl in name, though the Crown never confirmed the title. In March 1535 Sir William Skeffington took Maynooth Castle by bribing a guard and put the surrendered garrison to death, an act known as the Maynooth Pardon.

When Lord Leonard Grey arrived as Lord Deputy, Thomas, his army melting away, submitted on Grey's guarantee of his personal safety and was sent to the Tower of London in October 1535. The Attainder of the Earl of Kildare Act 1536 allowed his execution and the confiscation of his property. Despite Grey's guarantee he was put to death; his uncles were hanged, beheaded and quartered, while he was hanged and beheaded and his body buried. The revolt turned Henry's attention to Ireland and was a factor in the creation of the Kingdom of Ireland in 1542; the powers of the lords deputy were curbed and surrender and regrant introduced.
thomas-francois-burgers: Burgers was born on 15 April 1834 on the farm Langefontein in the Camdeboo district of Graaff-Reinet, the youngest child of Barend and Elizabeth Burger. He studied theology at the University of Utrecht in the Netherlands, where Professor C. W. Opzoomer drew him to rationalist and liberal ideas, and in 1859 he became parson of Hanover in the Cape Colony.

His views soon embroiled him with the Dutch Reformed synod, which charged him with liberalism and with doubting the literal truth of the Bible. Accused of heresy in 1862, he was found guilty and suspended in 1864, but the Supreme Court overturned the decision and he was readmitted to the ministry in 1865. He also wrote sketches of daily life in Hanover that show some of his unorthodox ideas.

Urged by the burghers of the South African Republic to stand for the presidency, Burgers was elected in 1872 by 2,964 votes to the 388 of William Robinson, becoming its fourth president. In 1874 he introduced the republic's first coins, the Burgerspond, answering a demand for coinage that went back to 1853. They were struck at Heaton's Mint in Birmingham from a portrait he sent to his consul-general, and some citizens objected that putting the president's head on coins likened him to a dictator.

Inspired by the railway programme of the Cape Prime Minister John Molteno, he planned a line linking the Transvaal to the sea and travelled to Europe in 1875 to raise funds. The 1905 New International Encyclopedia called his policies brilliant but impracticable schemes aimed chiefly at territorial expansion. By 1877 he was deeply unpopular and his government insolvent when Britain annexed the Transvaal.

Burgers withdrew from politics, settled again in the Cape Colony and died on 9 December 1881, leaving his family destitute. His former private secretary, Th. M. Tromp, published the Hanover sketches in the Netherlands to help them. Burgers had married Mary Bryson, and he was a Freemason. In 1895 his body was moved to the Pretoria cemetery now known as Heroes' Acre.
thomas-gage: Thomas Gage was born at Firle in Sussex, the second of three children of Thomas Gage, 1st Viscount Gage, whose family had been seated at Firle Place since the 15th century. The family was long Catholic, but his father had adopted the Anglican Church in 1715, and Gage became firmly attached to it, developing a dislike of the Roman Catholic Church. He attended Westminster School from 1728, where he met John Burgoyne, Richard Howe and George Germain.

In 1755 his regiment went to North America with General Edward Braddock, and at the Battle of the Monongahela, where Braddock was mortally wounded and George Washington distinguished himself, Gage was slightly wounded. In December 1757 he proposed a light infantry regiment suited to woodland warfare, and recruited the 80th Regiment of Light-Armed Foot. He married Margaret Kemble on 8 December 1758.

After the French surrender in 1760, Jeffery Amherst named him military governor of Montreal, where he proved a fair administrator. He took over as commander-in-chief in New York on 17 November 1763 and inherited Pontiac's War, which he sought to end by diplomacy through Sir William Johnson as well as by expeditions under Colonel John Bradstreet and Colonel Henry Bouquet.

As colonial tension rose he withdrew troops from the frontier to cities, and in 1768 he recommended sending two regiments to occupy Boston, which further inflamed the city. In 1772 he wrote that democracy was too prevalent in America. He returned to Britain in June 1773, and after the Boston Tea Party he was thought the best man to enforce the Intolerable Acts as governor of Massachusetts Bay.

Orders from London on 14 April 1775 led him to send troops to seize militia stores at Concord on the night of 18 April; the Battles of Lexington and Concord cost the British 273 casualties and the colonists 93. After the Battle of Bunker Hill on 17 June, ministers recalled him, replaced him with William Howe, and he sailed for England on 11 October 1775.

He retained the governorship of Massachusetts, but some writers about him were vicious, while New Hampshire Governor Benning Wentworth called him a good and wise man surrounded by difficulties. He died at Portland Place in London on 2 April 1787 and was buried at Firle. Gagetown in New Brunswick is named after him.
thomas-hardy: Hardy's mother, Jemima Hand, was well read and taught him herself until he entered his first school at Bockhampton at the age of eight. He later attended Mr Last's Academy for Young Gentlemen in Dorchester, where he learned Latin. His family could not afford a university education, so his formal schooling ended at sixteen, when he was apprenticed to the local architect James Hicks.

In 1870, while restoring the parish church of St Juliot in Cornwall, he met Emma Gifford, whom he married on 17 September 1874. In 1885 they moved to Max Gate in Dorchester, a house Hardy designed and his brother built. Emma's death in 1912 affected him deeply, and the Poems of 1912–13 reflect on it. In 1914 he married his secretary Florence Emily Dugdale, 39 years younger.

Hardy's first novel, The Poor Man and the Lady, was finished by 1867 but found no publisher. The poet and novelist George Meredith thought it too politically controversial and likely to harm his prospects. Hardy took the advice, destroyed the manuscript and reused some of its ideas later. He described it as socialistic, not to say revolutionary, though not argumentatively so.

His first volume of verse, Wessex Poems, appeared in 1898 and gathered poems written over thirty years. In the twentieth century he published only poetry, including Poems of the Past and the Present (1901), which contains The Darkling Thrush, and the three-part verse drama The Dynasts (1904–08). From 1908 he also worked with a local amateur group that became the Hardy Players, and wrote a one-act play for them in 1923.

Hardy examined the social constraints on Victorian lives and criticised beliefs about marriage, education and religion that limited people and caused unhappiness. Philip Larkin saw suffering as the centre of his work. His family was Anglican but not especially devout, and he came to question the traditional Christian God, speaking instead of an unconscious will of the Universe.

From the 1880s he campaigned to save ancient buildings from destruction and became an early member of the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings. Younger poets, particularly the Georgians, regarded him as a mentor, and composers including Gerald Finzi, Benjamin Britten and Gustav Holst set his poems to music.
thomas-henry-huxley: Thomas Henry Huxley was born in Ealing, then a village in Middlesex, the second youngest of eight children of George Huxley and Rachel Withers. His father was a mathematics schoolmaster at Great Ealing School until it closed, which put the family into financial difficulty, and Thomas left school at the age of ten after two years of formal schooling. Aged 20, too young to apply for a licence to practise from the Royal College of Surgeons and deep in debt, he applied at a friend's suggestion for an appointment in the Royal Navy.

After a lecture of 30 April 1852 he wrote that science in England did everything but pay. He effectively resigned from the navy by refusing to return to active service and in July 1854 became professor of natural history at the Royal School of Mines. He was president of the Geological Society from 1868 to 1870 and of the Royal Society from 1883 to 1885. For nearly a decade he studied the relationship of man to the apes, which brought him into clash with Richard Owen, and in 1858 his Croonian Lecture rejected Owen's theory that the bones of the skull and the spine were homologous.

Huxley was at first not persuaded by development theory, as evolution was called, and he never quite said that Darwin was right about natural selection, being an empiricist who trusted what he could see. At the British Association meeting at the Oxford University Museum on Saturday 30 June 1860 he answered the Bishop of Oxford, Samuel Wilberforce, in the debate that followed a paper by John William Draper. Robert FitzRoy, captain of HMS Beagle, spoke against Darwin. In November 1864 Huxley launched the X Club, a dining club of nine like-minded men including John Tyndall, J. D. Hooker and Herbert Spencer.

Huxley was a pallbearer at the funeral of Charles Darwin on 26 April 1882. In November 1870 he was elected to the London School Board, and his 1868 lecture On a Piece of Chalk presented science as organised common sense. When Huxley retired most universities had chairs in biological disciplines, where in his youth there were virtually no degrees in the biological sciences, and he was the single most influential person in that transformation. His Romanes Lecture of 1893 was Evolution and Ethics.
thomas-hobbes: Thomas Hobbes was born in Westport, now part of Malmesbury in Wiltshire. He later reported that his mother, hearing of the coming invasion of the Spanish Armada, gave birth prematurely: "my mother gave birth to twins: myself and fear." His father, also Thomas, was vicar of Charlton and Westport; according to the biographer John Aubrey he was uneducated and disesteemed learning. After a fight with local clergy outside his church he was forced to leave, and the family was left in the care of his older brother Francis, a wealthy glove manufacturer. Hobbes graduated from the University of Cambridge in 1608.

Hobbes became a tutor to the Cavendish family, and in 1636 he visited Galileo Galilei in Florence, then under house arrest. He later joined the philosophical groups in Paris gathered by Marin Mersenne. Back in England in 1637, he had written The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic by the end of the Short Parliament in 1640; it circulated only in manuscript until a pirated edition about ten years later.

When the English Civil War began in August 1642 and the royalist cause declined from mid-1644, many royalists came to Paris, and their company renewed his political interests. From 1647 until 1648 he was mathematical instructor to Charles, Prince of Wales. The exiled royalists led him to write Leviathan, which compares the state to a monster composed of men, created under pressure of human needs and dissolved by civil strife arising from human passions.

In Leviathan Hobbes begins from a mechanistic understanding of human beings and asks what life would be like without government, a state of nature in which each person has a right to everything. This, he argues, would lead to a war of all against all, with life "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." In 1658 he published De Homine, completing the system he had planned more than nineteen years before. After the Restoration, his former pupil Charles II granted him a pension of £100. Hobbes died on 4 December 1679 at Hardwick Hall, aged 91, and was interred at Ault Hucknall in Derbyshire.
thomas-hooker: Hooker was probably born in Leicestershire, at Marefield or Birstall, and attended Dixie Grammar School at Market Bosworth; the loss of the Marefield parish records from before 1610 leaves his origins uncertain. He entered Queens' College, Cambridge, as a sizar in March 1604, moved to Emmanuel College, took his degrees in 1608 and 1611, and held a Dixie fellowship at Emmanuel from 1609 to 1619. At St George's Church, Esher, from 1620 he gained a reputation as a preacher, and on 3 April 1621 he married Susannah Garbrand at Amersham.

Around 1626 he became lecturer at St Mary's parish church, Chelmsford, until Archbishop William Laud suppressed church lecturers in 1629; he then kept a school at Little Baddow. Summoned before the Court of High Commission, he forfeited his bond, fled to Rotterdam and then sailed to the Massachusetts Bay Colony aboard the Griffin, becoming pastor of the church at Newtown, later Cambridge. Voting there was limited to freemen admitted to church membership, a restriction he opposed, which set him against his old friend John Cotton. With the Rev. Samuel Stone he led about 100 settlers to Hartford, named after Stone's birthplace of Hertford.

When the General Court of Wethersfield, Windsor and Hartford met in May 1638 to frame a written constitution, Hooker preached the opening sermon on 31 May. The freemen of the three towns ratified the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut on 14 January 1639. He defended Congregationalism in A Survey of the Summe of Church-Discipline and taught preparationism, the doctrine that a person seeking conversion might dispose himself toward receiving grace.

Hooker died in the North American influenza epidemic on 7 July 1647, aged 61. The site of his grave is unknown, though he is believed to lie in Hartford's Ancient Burying Ground. With no portrait to work from, Frances Laughlin Wadsworth modelled the statue erected in 1938 before Hartford's Old State House on the likenesses of his descendants. John Fiske held that Hooker deserved more than any other man to be called the father of American democracy. His son Samuel became minister of Farmington, and his descendants included William Howard Taft and Aaron Burr.
thomas-hutchinson-governor: Hutchinson was born on 9 September 1711 in the North End of Boston, the fourth of twelve children of a wealthy merchant family descended from Anne Hutchinson. He entered Harvard College at twelve, graduated in 1727 and by his own account turned a gift of five quintals of fish into between £400 and £500 by the age of 21. In 1734 he married Margaret Sanford, his third cousin.

Elected a Boston selectman and to the General Court in 1737, he opposed the province's inflationary paper bills of credit, lost his seat in 1739 and later served as speaker from 1746 to 1749. In 1749 he used the British refund of about £180,000 in specie for the Louisbourg expedition to retire the paper money, a reform whose smooth success made him popular. Appointed lieutenant governor in 1758, he was also made chief justice by Governor Francis Bernard in place of James Otis Sr., which turned the Otises and the young John Adams against him; his writs of assistance of 1761 deepened their hostility.

Although he warned London against the Stamp Act, a crowd ransacked his Boston mansion on the night of 26 August 1765, destroying its finishings and scattering his historical manuscripts. He became acting governor when Bernard left in 1769, and after the Boston Massacre of 5 March 1770 he had the soldiers arrested and asked for the troops to withdraw to Castle William. His commission as governor arrived in March 1771.

As governor he moved the assembly to Cambridge and had his salary paid by the crown, measures his opponents denounced as arbitrary. In 1772 he told the assembly the colony was either wholly subject to Parliament or effectively independent. Letters he had written in the late 1760s, sent from London by Benjamin Franklin, were published by Samuel Adams in June 1773, and he was burned in effigy as far away as Philadelphia. In exile in England he advised ministers and in 1776 anonymously published Strictures Upon the Declaration, a rebuttal of the Declaration of Independence. He died on 3 June 1780; the last volume of his History of the Province of Massachusetts Bay appeared in 1828.
thomas-iii-of-saluzzo: Thomas was born in Saluzzo in north-western Italy, the son of Frederick II del Vasto and Beatrice of Geneva; his maternal grandfather was Hugh of Geneva, Lord of Gex, Anthon and Varey. He spent much of his youth in Provence and travelled there in 1375, 1389, 1401, 1403 and 1405. That French upbringing shaped his politics, and his wife Marguerite was French, a daughter of Hugo II, Count of Roucy and Braine.

Thomas kept to his father's French policy, chiefly to meet the threat of Duke Amadeus VIII of Savoy, who aimed to conquer the whole of Piedmont. He had signed the treaty of nominal submission to France well before his father's death. In 1394 Savoyard troops captured him while he was leading a raid on Monasterolo; he was held first at Savigliano and then at Turin, and released two years later on payment of a ransom of 20,000 golden florins.

In his last years he left the succession to his young son Ludovico, under the regency of Marguerite and Valerano. Ludovico married Isabella Palaiologina, a daughter of John Jacob, Marquess of Montferrat, and his sister Ricciardia married Niccolò III d'Este. Thomas also had at least three children with his mistress, Olmeta de Soglio, among them Giovanna, Abbess of Santa Maria di Staffarda.

Thomas was a man of wide learning and the author of Le Chevalier errant, one of the most important chivalric texts of the Middle Ages, probably written while he was a prisoner in Piedmont. Written in French, it is an allegory of the ideals of knighthood, and it inspired the frescoes of the Castello della Manta.
thomas-jefferson: Thomas Jefferson was born on 13 April 1743 (2 April, Old Style) at the family's Shadwell Plantation in the Colony of Virginia, the third of ten children. His father, Peter Jefferson, was a planter and surveyor, and his mother was Jane Randolph. He was born into a slave-owning family and remained a slave owner all his life. He was admitted to the Virginia bar in 1767.

Between 1769 and 1775 Jefferson represented Albemarle County in the Virginia House of Burgesses. In 1769 he wrote and sponsored legislation giving masters of slaves discretion to emancipate them; it met strong opposition. Elected to the Second Continental Congress in 1775, he was named to the Committee of Five with John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Robert R. Livingston and Roger Sherman. Adams persuaded the committee to choose Jefferson to write the Declaration of Independence, which Congress passed in 1776. Jefferson drafted it largely alone.

In 1784 he joined Franklin and Adams in Paris and then succeeded Franklin as Minister to France, serving five years. President George Washington appointed him the first Secretary of State, and he clashed with Alexander Hamilton over the national debt and the site of the capital, settled by the Compromise of 1790 in favour of the Potomac River. With James Madison he founded the Democratic-Republican Party in 1792. He lost to John Adams in 1796, by 71 votes to 68, and became vice president, then won the presidency in 1800 and was sworn in on 4 March 1801.

As president he defended American shipping against the Barbary pirates and British trade policies, acquired the Louisiana Territory, which doubled the nation's size, and reduced military forces and spending. His second term brought the trial of Aaron Burr and, in 1807, the Embargo Act. In 1819 he founded the University of Virginia, designed its buildings and was its first rector from 1825.

Jefferson followed the ideals of John Locke, Francis Bacon and Isaac Newton. He regarded the independent yeoman as the ideal of republican virtue, distrusted cities and financiers, and favoured decentralised government. He wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom and pressed for a wall of separation between church and state. His views became known as Jeffersonian democracy. From 1768 he built Monticello in the Palladian style, with the help of local masons and carpenters and of his slaves. Historians acknowledge his lifelong ownership of large numbers of slaves but differ on his views of slavery.
thomas-jones-missionary: Thomas Jones was born on 24 January 1810, the son of a carpenter, at Berriew (Aberriw) in Montgomeryshire, Wales. He became a Calvinistic Methodist minister in 1840 and soon afterwards set out for India with his wife Anne. In Calcutta Anne gave birth to a child who did not survive, and the couple went on into the Khasi Hills with the aim of converting the Khasi people to Christianity.

Jones succeeded better than the missionaries William Carey had sent to the hills in the 1830s. The Khasi valued his skill in carpentry and other crafts, and he learned their language by living among them, preaching in it with a fluency that astonished his hearers. In 1842 he produced a Khasi Reader and translated the Welsh work Rhodd Mam into Khasi, the first books written in the language, and he also compiled a Khasi alphabet and dictionary.

Anne Jones died in childbirth in 1846. Jones then married Emma Cattell, which brought him into trouble with the Missionary Society because she was only fifteen. A failed attempt to set up a mission of his own at Pomreng led to further difficulties, and the authorities abandoned him in 1847.

After he criticised a local industrialist, Harry Inglis, Jones was forced to leave the area. He caught malaria and died of it on 16 September 1849, and was buried in the Scottish Cemetery at Calcutta. His son, Thomas Cattell Jones, was born after his death. His gravestone calls him the founding father of the Khasi alphabet and literature, and in 2018 the government of Meghalaya declared that 22 June, the day of his arrival at Sohra, would be kept every year as Thomas Jones Day.
thomas-langley: Langley was born around 1363 at Middleton in Lancashire, the third son of William and Alice Langley. In 1375 he was sent to St Mary's Abbey, Thetford, which fed students to Corpus Christi in Cambridge, and he studied at the college until rioters against the poll tax ransacked it on 15 June 1381. Back at Middleton, he became rector of Radcliffe in 1385 and Archdeacon of Norfolk in 1399.

In 1401 he was named Dean of York, but Pope Boniface IX blocked the appointment because of Langley's part in the deposition of Richard II; the same year he received the privy seal, which he kept until 1405. Pope Innocent VII refused to let him take up the see of London, to which he was elected in October 1404, and on 2 March 1405 he became Chancellor. After Archbishop Richard Scrope of York rebelled and was executed, Langley was elected to York in August 1405, but the pope excommunicated him and Henry IV and the election was quashed in May 1406. He was installed as Bishop of Durham at St Paul's Cathedral in 1406 and resigned the chancellorship in 1407.

In 1411 Antipope John XXIII named him a pseudocardinal, an honour he refused. He was at Henry IV's side, as executor, when the king died in 1413, and under Henry V he spent three-quarters of his time in royal service. As Chancellor, on 28 September 1422 at Windsor, he handed the gold seal of England in a purse of white leather to the infant Henry VI. Until his semi-retirement in 1430 he spent 5,670 days in the crown's service, and he later carried out diplomatic work when the government asked.

From 1430 he gave his attention to his diocese, which by his own admission he had neglected. At Durham Cathedral he blocked the great west door with an altar and his own tomb, so that two side doors and great buttresses on the west walls had to be built. At Middleton he rebuilt the parish church in 1412, rededicating it to St Leonard, and founded a school that became Middleton Grammar School; he also founded Durham School. He died on 20 November 1437.
thomas-mann: Thomas Mann was born in Lübeck on 6 June 1875, the second son of Thomas Johann Heinrich Mann, a senator and grain merchant, and Júlia da Silva Bruhns, a Brazilian of German, Portuguese and Native Brazilian ancestry who had come to Germany at the age of seven. His mother was Roman Catholic, but he was baptised into his father's Lutheran religion. After his father died in 1891 the family firm was liquidated and the family moved to Munich. He attended the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität and the Technische Hochschule there, studying history, economics, art history and literature in preparation for a journalism career. His older brother Heinrich was also a novelist, and three of his own six children, Erika, Klaus and Golo, became significant writers.

Mann received the 1929 Nobel Prize in Literature on the nomination of Anders Österling, mainly for Buddenbrooks, which follows the decline of a Lübeck merchant family over four generations. The Magic Mountain grew from a visit to his wife Katia in a sanatorium at Davos in 1912, and the tetralogy Joseph and His Brothers was written over sixteen years. Doctor Faustus tells of the fictitious composer Adrian Leverkühn and the corruption of German culture before and during the Second World War. His style combined a grave surface with a mild irony that he took from Theodor Fontane, and he drew on Goethe, Schopenhauer and the Russian novelists.

During the First World War he supported the war effort, and his Reflections of a Nonpolitical Man (1918) set out a conservative philosophy of spiritual tradition and German patriotism. After Hitler came to power in 1933 he went into exile. From October 1940 he recorded monthly eight-minute addresses in the United States, flown to London and broadcast to Germany by the BBC. During the Cold War he was required to testify to the House Un-American Activities Committee, resigned a post at the Library of Congress and in 1952 returned to Europe, settling at Kilchberg near Zürich.

After his 80th birthday Mann went on holiday to Noordwijk in the Netherlands, where on 18 July 1955 he developed pain and swelling in his left leg. Thrombophlebitis was diagnosed, but a post-mortem found that he had suffered a perforated aneurysm of the iliac artery. He died in Zürich on 12 August 1955 and was buried on 16 August in the village cemetery at Kilchberg. His work influenced later authors such as Yukio Mishima, and in 2017 five institutions associated with his life, in Lübeck, Munich, Zürich, Los Angeles and Nida, founded the network Thomas Mann International.
thomas-more: Thomas More was born in the City of London on 7 February 1478, the second of six children of Sir John More, a successful lawyer and later a judge, and his wife Agnes. He was educated at St. Anthony's School and from 1490 to 1492 served John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury and Lord Chancellor, as a household page. According to his friend Desiderius Erasmus, he once seriously considered becoming a monk, and between 1503 and 1504 he lived near the Carthusian monastery outside the walls of London. He chose to remain a layman, was elected to Parliament in 1504 and married Joanna Colt the following year.

In 1504 More was elected to Parliament for Great Yarmouth, and from 1510 he represented London. Between 1512 and 1519 he worked on a History of King Richard III, which he never finished. Utopia, a frame narrative in Latin, was published by Erasmus at Leuven in 1516; More is a character in it, discussing modern ills in Antwerp with the traveller Raphael Hythlodaeus, who describes the island of Utopia. After the fall of Wolsey, More became Lord Chancellor in 1529. Heresy was the most time-consuming issue of his chancellorship. He saw the Reformation as a threat to the unity of church and society, and he denied stories of torture of Protestants in his Apologia of 1533. Modern commentators remain divided over his campaign against Protestantism.

In 1533 More refused to attend the coronation of Anne Boleyn, and he was later imprisoned in the Tower of London, where he wrote A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation. At his trial on 1 July 1535 he argued that his silence on the new statutes could be taken as consent. He was executed on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535, declaring that he died the king's good servant, and God's first. He was beatified in 1886 and canonised in 1935, and in 1980 the Church of England added him to its calendar of Reformation martyrs.
thomas-munro: Munro was born in Glasgow on 27 May 1761, the son of the merchant Alexander Munro, whose family tobacco business was ruined when the trade collapsed during the American Revolutionary War. He was educated at the University of Glasgow, where he was known for his strength and as a boxer. He was meant to join his father's business, but in 1779 he took up an infantry cadetship in Madras. A claimed descent from George Munro, 10th Baron of Foulis, chief of Clan Munro, has been contested by the clan historian R. W. Munro.

He served in the war against Hyder Ali from 1780 to 1783 and in the first campaign against Tipu Sultan from 1790 to 1792. He was then one of four officers chosen to administer territory taken from Tipu, where he spent seven years learning revenue survey and assessment. After Tipu's final defeat in 1799 he restored order in Kanara, and from 1800 to 1807 he ran the Ceded Districts given up by the Nizam of Hyderabad, where he introduced the ryotwari system.

On a long furlough in Britain he gave evidence on the renewal of the East India Company's charter, and in 1813 he told questioners that if agriculture, manufactures, schools, hospitality and respect towards women denote a civilised people, "then the Hindoos are not inferior in civilization to the people of Europe." He returned to Madras in 1814 to reform the judicial and police systems. In the Pindari War of 1817 he commanded the reserve division against the Peshwa's southern lands, where nine forts surrendered or were taken, and he was made a Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath in 1819.

As governor he founded systems of revenue assessment and administration that largely lasted into the twentieth century, and his official minutes, published by Sir A. Arbuthnot, served later officials as a manual. He was created a baronet in 1825, and a committee of public instruction formed at his request in 1826 led in time to Presidency College. He died on tour in the Ceded Districts, where memorials keep his name, and Francis Chantrey's equestrian statue of him, riding without stirrups, stands in Chennai.
thomas-muntzer: Thomas Müntzer was born in late 1489, or possibly early 1490, in the small town of Stolberg in the Harz Mountains of central Germany. The legend that his father was executed by the feudal authorities is untrue. His background appears to have been relatively comfortable, as his lengthy education suggests. In May 1514 he took up a post as priest in Brunswick, where he began to question the practices of the Catholic Church and to criticise, for example, the selling of indulgences.

In May 1520, using a recommendation Martin Luther had made a year earlier, Müntzer stood in for the reformist preacher Johann Sylvanus Egranus at St Mary's Church in Zwickau. He reached Prague in late June 1521, where he wrote a summary of his beliefs known as the Prague Manifesto, which was never published. In April 1523 he became preacher at St John's Church in Allstedt, where he held services in German and drew people from the surrounding country. Luther asked him to come to Wittenberg, and Müntzer refused.

In 1524 Müntzer went to Mühlhausen, where he worked with the lay preacher Heinrich Pfeiffer. A civic coup in late September 1524 was short-lived, and he had to leave the city. He returned in February 1525 and took over the pulpit at St Mary's Church. He then founded the Eternal League of God, an armed militia that met under a white banner painted with a rainbow. After the Battle of Frankenhausen he was captured, tortured and executed.

Müntzer was deeply read in the early Christian fathers, the late medieval mystics Suso and Tauler, humanist ideas and the Bible. He taught that true belief was dictated by spiritual experience, not by written testimony. The Bible was for him evidence of past spiritual experiences, and its words still had to be validated by the working of the Spirit in the believer's heart. He valued dreams and visions, and held that real suffering was essential to Christian belief.

He believed that the whole cosmos stood at a tipping point: God would set right the wrongs of the world, largely by destruction, with the active help of true Christians. In a confession under torture in May 1525 he named omnia sunt communia, all things held in common, as an aim, though this statement stands alone in his writings. Modern researchers agree that his theology, and not any social doctrine, drove his stand against feudal authority.
thomas-newcomen: Thomas Newcomen was born in Dartmouth into a merchant family and baptised at St Saviour's Church on 28 February 1664. His ironmonger's business specialised in tools for the mining industry. He was a lay preacher and teaching elder in the local Baptist church, and after 1710 he became pastor of a local group of Baptists. His Baptist connections helped to spread his engine: the engineers Jonathan Hornblower Sr. and his son belonged to the Baptist church at Bromsgrove with which he was linked, and a London business contact, Edward Wallin, was a Baptist minister.

Newcomen developed his engine around 1712 to lift water out of a tin mine, combining ideas from Thomas Savery and Denis Papin. Savery had devised a fire engine in which steam was admitted to an empty container and condensed, and the vacuum sucked water up from the sump; it could not work beyond a depth of about thirty feet. Newcomen replaced the receiving vessel with a cylinder and piston after Papin's design, so that the vacuum drew down the piston instead. The piston worked a beam engine, a wooden beam rocking on a central fulcrum, with a chain on the far side attached to a pump at the bottom of the mine.

After 1715 the engine business was run through an unincorporated company, the Proprietors of the Invention for Raising Water by Fire, whose committee included Wallin. Little is known of Newcomen's later life. He died at Wallin's house in 1729 and was buried at Bunhill Fields, though the exact site of his grave is unknown.

Newcomen's engines were installed under Savery's patent, which was extended by statute until 1733. By then about 125 had been installed in most of the important mining districts of Britain and the Continent, draining coal mines in the Black Country, Warwickshire and near Newcastle upon Tyne, tin and copper mines in Cornwall, and lead mines in Flintshire and Derbyshire. The engine held its place without material change for about 75 years, and John Smeaton improved its mechanical details in the early 1770s.

It was far from efficient, since much heat was lost when the steam was condensed in the cylinder, which mattered little at collieries with unsaleable small coal but raised costs in Cornwall. After 1775 James Watt's separate condenser replaced it where coal was dear. Even so, of over 2,200 engines built in the 18th century only about 450 were Watt's.
thomas-paine: Thomas Paine was the son of Joseph Pain, a tenant farmer and stay-maker, and Frances Pain, born Cocke. His father was a Quaker and his mother an Anglican. He attended Thetford Grammar School from 1744 to 1749 and at 13 was apprenticed to his father. At 19 he served as a privateer aboard the King of Prussia, and in 1759 he became a master staymaker in Sandwich, Kent. He married Mary Lambert that year, but his business collapsed, and she and their child died in early labour at Margate. He was using the spelling Paine by 1769, while living in Lewes, Sussex.

Paine barely survived the voyage to Philadelphia, where typhoid fever killed five passengers, and in March 1775 he became editor of the Pennsylvania Magazine. Common Sense appeared on 10 January 1776, signed by an Englishman. He estimated that it sold 100,000 copies in three months, though some historians dispute such figures. Benjamin Rush suggested the title, since Paine had called it Plain Truth.

Rights of Man, a tract of some 90,000 words answering Edmund Burke, appeared on 13 March 1791. Its second part proposed state support for the poor, public education and pensions for workers from the age of 50. Agrarian Justice argued that landed property had robbed most people of a natural inheritance, and proposed a national fund paying fifteen pounds to each person at the age of twenty-one. In The Age of Reason he wrote that he believed in one God and in no church. He was also an abolitionist, and Rush later credited him with a Pennsylvania Magazine article against slavery.

Paine stayed in France until 1802 and returned to the United States at Thomas Jefferson's invitation, to find himself disliked by the devout and by the Federalists. He died on 8 June 1809 at 59 Grove Street in Greenwich Village, aged 72. The Quakers refused to bury him in their graveyard, so he was buried on his farm at New Rochelle. In 1819 William Cobbett dug up the bones to give him a reburial in England that never took place, and they were later lost. His writings gave radical societies in England and Wales in the early 1790s a boost to their confidence. A marble column raised in New Rochelle in 1839 is the oldest memorial to him.
thomas-palaiologos: Thomas Palaiologos was born in 1409, the youngest of the six sons of Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos who survived infancy. As the Byzantine Empire fragmented in the 14th century, its emperors granted remaining lands to their sons as appanages, with the title of despot. John, the eldest, was raised to co-emperor and Theodore became Despot of the Morea. The younger sons, Constantine, Demetrios and Thomas, stayed in Constantinople because there was not enough land left to grant them.

In 1428 John VIII, now emperor, appointed Constantine Despot of the Morea. Theodore refused to step down, so two members of the imperial family governed the despotate for the first time since its creation in 1349. Thomas, aged 19, was soon appointed too, and the nominally undivided despotate split into three smaller principalities. Thomas received lands in the north and based himself in the castle of Kalavryta.

Thomas ended the Principality of Achaea, the crusader state established in 1204 that had once governed almost the entire peninsula, by marrying Catherine Zaccaria, daughter and heir of its last prince, Centurione II Zaccaria. With Centurione's death in 1432 Thomas could claim all his remaining territories. By the 1430s nearly the whole Peloponnese was Byzantine again for the first time since 1204, apart from a few port towns held by Venice.

After Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453, Mehmed II let Thomas and Demetrios keep their lands, demanding an annual tribute of 10,000 ducats. Thomas hoped to make the Morea a rallying point for restoring the empire with support from the Papacy and the West. He and Demetrios could not cooperate, and Mehmed invaded and conquered the Morea in 1460.

Thomas first took refuge at Mantineia and then fled with his family and companions to Methoni, and from there to Corfu on Venetian ships, arriving on 22 July 1460. His wife Catherine and the children stayed on Corfu. He sailed for Italy on 16 November 1460, landing at Ancona, and reached Rome in March 1461, where he hoped to persuade Pope Pius II to call a crusade. He never retook the Morea and died in Rome on 12 May 1465. His claims passed to his eldest son Andreas.
His daughter Zoe, called Sophia in Russia, married Ivan III, Grand Prince of Moscow, in 1472, which strengthened Moscow's claim to be a third Rome. Ivan the Terrible was her grandson.
thomas-picton: Picton was born in Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, probably on 24 August 1758, the seventh of 12 children of Thomas Picton of Poyston Hall. Commissioned ensign in the 12th Regiment of Foot in 1771, he served at Gibraltar and became a captain in the 75th Regiment of Foot in 1778. When that regiment was disbanded he quelled a mutiny but did not receive the promised majority, and he lived for nearly 12 years on his father's estate before going to the West Indies in 1794 as aide-de-camp to Sir John Vaughan.

Under Sir Ralph Abercromby he was present at the capture of Saint Lucia, and after the invasion of Trinidad in 1797 Abercromby made him its governor. He kept order by methods seen as rough justice or as arbitrary brutality; he was accused of the execution of a dozen slaves, and speculation in land and slaves built his fortune. In 1802 William Fullarton was named senior member of a commission to govern the island, with Picton as junior. Fullarton opened enquiries into his past acts, and Picton resigned on 31 May 1803.

Arrested by order of the Privy Council in December 1803 and released on bail of £40,000, he was tried before Lord Ellenborough in 1806 for causing the torture of Luisa Calderón, a 14-year-old girl, in 1801 by picketing, and found guilty. At a retrial in 1808 the jury found that torture had been allowed by the law of the island at its cession, and no judgment was ever delivered.

From 1810 he commanded a division in Spain at Wellington's request, the Fighting 3rd. He fought at Busaco and Fuentes de Onoro, stormed a breach of Ciudad Rodrigo in 1812 and turned the attack on the castle of Badajoz into a real one, where he was wounded. He led his division at Vitoria and in the Pyrenees and entered Parliament for Pembroke Boroughs in 1813.

At Waterloo on 18 June 1815 he commanded the 5th Infantry Division and led a bayonet charge against d'Erlon's corps; he was shot through the temple, the most senior officer to die in the battle. In 1859 his body was reburied in St Paul's Cathedral. In 2020 Cardiff Council voted to remove his statue from City Hall because of his links to slavery.
thomas-preljubovic: Thomas was the son of the caesar Gregorios Preljub, Serbian governor of Thessaly, who died in late 1355 or early 1356, and of Irene Nemanjić, a daughter of Dušan the Mighty, Emperor of Serbia. Driven out of Thessaly by Nikephoros II Orsini in 1356, mother and son fled to Serbia, where Irene married Radoslav Hlapen, ruler of Vodena. Hlapen invaded Thessaly in 1359–1360 on his stepson's behalf, and Simeon Uroš ceded Kastoria to Thomas and married him to his daughter Maria.

In 1366 the citizens of Ioannina, Simeon Uroš's last major fortress in Epirus, asked for a governor to protect them from Albanian raids. Thomas arrived from Edessa in 1367 with a large army and was at first applauded.

The Chronicle of Ioannina, the main source for his rule, calls him wicked, greedy and a murderer; the historian Donald Nicol judged it deeply prejudiced against him. He was said to impose heavy taxes and monopolies on fish, cheese, vegetables and fruit, to seize church property for his Serbian retainers and to force the widows of Greek noblemen to marry Serbs. In 1382 the new archbishop Matthew invested him as despotes on behalf of Emperor John V Palaiologos, but Thomas later exiled him. Some of his measures paid for walls and soldiers in his almost constant wars.

The Albanians under Peter Losha, despot of Arta, attacked Ioannina in his first three years, until Thomas betrothed his daughter to Losha's son in 1370; he made peace with Gjin Bua Shpata in 1375 by betrothing his sister Helena to him. He defeated the Malakasioi in 1377 and 1379, selling captives into slavery and mutilating others, and styled himself Albanian-Slayer after Basil II, the Bulgar-Slayer. With Ottoman help he took a number of fortresses in 1381–1384.

At dawn on 23 December 1384 he was stabbed to death in his bed by his bodyguards Nikephorakes, Rainakes, Artabastos and Anton the Frank, in a conspiracy that included his wife Maria. The people gathered in the cathedral and acclaimed Maria Angelina as despoina, her brother John Uroš Doukas Palaiologos was called in to advise her, and Thomas's collaborators were punished.
thomas-preston-1st-viscount-tara: Preston was the second son of Christopher, 4th Viscount Gormanstown, of a family descended from Robert Preston, 1st Baron Gormanston, who bought the lands of Gormanston in County Meath in 1363. His mother, Catherine FitzWilliam, was a daughter of the Dublin landowner Sir Richard FitzWilliam of Baggotrath Castle. With his elder brother heir to the title, and Catholics barred from state posts in Ireland, he entered the Spanish service and fought in the Thirty Years' War.

In the same Irish regiment as Owen Roe O'Neill, with whom he was bitterly jealous from the first, Preston distinguished himself in the defence of Leuven against the French and Dutch in 1635. After the Irish Rebellion of 1641 he came home and was made general of Leinster, the largest and best equipped of the Confederate Catholic forces. He won praise for the siege of Duncannon in 1645 but lost a string of field battles, among them New Ross in 1643. He was skilled in siegecraft but never had a good grasp of mobile warfare.

In the Confederates' quarrels he first sided with the radicals against the first Ormonde peace, then with the moderates who made the treaty of 1648 with Ormonde and the Royalists. His Royalism was rooted in his Old English origins and his dislike of O'Neill, who led the opposing faction. In 1646 the physician Owen O'Shiel left his command over his drinking and Royalist leanings. During the Cromwellian conquest he held Waterford until hunger and disease forced him to give it up, then marched to Galway, the last Irish-held city, which he surrendered late in 1652 on condition that he and his troops could leave for service in France.

He joined the exiled Royalist court in Paris and offered his services to Charles II, who had created him Viscount Tara in 1650. He died there in October 1655. His wife was a Flemish noblewoman, Claire van der Eycken. His son Anthony succeeded him, and the title became extinct when the 3rd Viscount was murdered by Sir Francis Blundell and his brothers in 1674.
thomas-robert-bugeaud: Thomas Robert Bugeaud was born at Limoges on 15 October 1784, the youngest of thirteen children of a noble family of Périgord. He ran away from home and for some years worked as an agricultural labourer. At twenty he became a private soldier in the Vélites of the Imperial Guard, took part in the Austerlitz campaign, and was commissioned in 1806.

He served in the Jena, Eylau and Pultusk campaigns and in the Peninsular War, including the second siege of Zaragossa, and rose to command a regiment under Suchet. He rejoined Napoleon during the Hundred Days. After the fall of Napoleon he spent fifteen years without employment, farming and developing Périgord. The July Revolution of 1830 reopened his career, and in 1831 he was made a brigadier general and elected to the Chamber of Deputies.

Although he first disapproved of the conquest of Algeria, Bugeaud was sent there and won a victory over Abd al-Qadir at Sikkak on 6 July 1836.
