He signed the Treaty of Tafna on 30 May 1837; the historian James McDougall argues that its French and Arabic texts differed in a way that shows duplicity on Bugeaud's part.

Named governor-general in 1840, he put his "flying columns" into effect in 1841, a tactic of raids known as the razzia, built roads, and was made marshal of France in 1843. At Isly on 14 August 1844 he defeated a Moroccan army and won the title of duke. During his time the number of French colonists grew from 17,000 to 100,000 and French forces from about 60,000 to 109,000 by 1847.

The razzias targeted the agrarian economy and caused widespread famine; one raid on the Beni Zeroual in 1843 killed 150 and took 712 prisoners. In late 1842 about 800 members of the Ouled Riah died in a cave where fires were lit at the entrance, a massacre War Minister Soult tried to cover up but which was leaked to the press and widely condemned. Some historians see Bugeaud as an early practitioner of counter-insurgency. In 1848 he refused to stand for the presidency against Louis Napoleon, and he died in Paris on 10 June 1849. In 2024 the Paris city council voted to rename the avenue Bugeaud.
thomas-robert-malthus: Thomas Robert Malthus was the sixth of seven children of Daniel Malthus and Henrietta Catherine, daughter of the royal apothecary Daniel Graham. He was born at The Rookery at Westcott, near Dorking in Surrey. He had a cleft lip and palate that affected his speech. His father, a friend of David Hume and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, was a gentleman of independent means. Malthus entered Jesus College, Cambridge, in 1784, graduated as Ninth Wrangler in mathematics and was elected a Fellow two years after his MA. In 1789 he took orders in the Church of England and became a curate at Oakwood Chapel in Surrey.

Malthus wrote the first Essay on the Principle of Population in 1798 in reaction to the optimism of his father and his father's circle about the future improvement of society, and as an answer to William Godwin and the Marquis de Condorcet. It appeared anonymously, and a much enlarged second edition of 1803 acknowledged his authorship. In 1799 he toured Germany, Scandinavia and Russia to gather population data, and in 1805 he became professor at the East India Company College in Hertfordshire, where students called him Pop.

In the 1820s he debated political economy with David Ricardo, disagreeing about rent and about the possibility of a general glut, which Malthus held against Say's law. His Definitions in Political Economy of 1827 drew a damaging review from John Ramsay McCulloch.

Malthus argued that population grows whenever food is plentiful until the numbers press on resources and cause distress. Two kinds of check keep it within limits: positive checks that raise the death rate, namely hunger, disease and war, and preventive checks that lower the birth rate, among them later marriage. In later editions he gave more weight to moral restraint.

John Maynard Keynes later extended his idea of demand falling short of supply, and Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace read the Essay. Malthus died suddenly of heart disease on 29 December 1834 and was buried in Bath Abbey.
thomas-scott-orangeman: Little is known of Scott's early years. He was born in 1842 in the Clandeboye area of County Down, was raised a Presbyterian and emigrated to Ontario in 1863. At Red River he worked as a labourer on the Dawson Road, which was to link the settlement with Lake Superior, until a strike in 1869 got him dismissed and convicted of aggravated assault. In Winnipeg he met John Christian Schultz, joined the Canadian Party and backed the annexation of the Red River Settlement to Canada.

In December 1869 Riel's men arrested him at Upper Fort Garry with the party of 45 who had fortified Schultz's store against the Métis National Committee. He escaped in January 1870, as did Schultz and Charles Mair. In February he was among several hundred armed volunteers who gathered at Kildonan Presbyterian Church to free the remaining prisoners; Riel released them and the volunteers dispersed, but Scott's group passed too close to Fort Garry on the way to Portage la Prairie and he was taken again. In captivity he was ill, abusive and refused to recognise his captors' authority, and after a fight with guards he was moved to a stronger cell.

A small Métis court, sitting in private without outside observers, found him guilty of defying the provisional government, fighting the guards and slandering Riel; an eyewitness, Nolin, later testified that Scott was absent when the charges and evidence were heard. Others were sentenced with him but only he was shot. Accounts of his last moments disagree, and two witnesses, John Bruce and Major George Robinson, claimed he survived the volley in a makeshift coffin. His body was never found.

The English-speaking, Protestant population of Ontario hailed him as a martyr, and the Toronto Globe wrote that he had been murdered by enemies of the Queen, country and religion. The historian Lyle Dick has said his death gave expansionists a rallying symbol that sped the dispatch of the Wolseley Expedition, which drove Riel from the settlement. For a century English-speaking historians tended to depict him as an innocent victim and French Canadians to stress his behaviour; J. M. Bumsted finds agreement only that the execution was a political mistake by Riel and the Métis.
thomas-the-apostle: The name Thomas comes from the Aramaic Tʾōmā, meaning the twin, and the Greek equivalent Didymos is also used in the New Testament. Early Syrian traditions give his full name as Judas Thomas. In the Gospel of John he speaks twice: when Lazarus has died he says, Let us also go, that we may die with him, and later he asks how the disciples can know the way. He is best known as doubting Thomas, because he doubted the resurrection of Jesus until he saw the places where the wounds still appeared fresh, and then confessed his faith with the words My Lord and my God.

The earliest tradition about his mission is that his allotted field was Parthia, a statement of Origen preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea. Churches of the Middle East and southern Asia also name Thomas as their first evangelist. According to the traditional accounts of the Saint Thomas Christians of India, he landed at Muziris on the coast of the Chera kingdom, in present-day Kerala, in 52 CE, and founded seven communities there; historians still dispute the visit. Frykenberg, a historian of religion, notes that whatever the doubtful historicity of such traditions, there can be little doubt as to their great antiquity.

The main source is the apocryphal Acts of Thomas, written about 180–230, which most Christian churches regard as apocryphal or even heretical. The two centuries between the apostle's life and the work cast doubt on its authenticity. It tells that a king was angered when Thomas converted a queen and others of his household.

According to Syrian Christian tradition, Thomas was killed with a spear at St. Thomas Mount in Chennai on 21 December 72 and buried at Mylapore. Ephrem the Syrian, whose hymns are the earliest known record of his death, states that he was killed in India and that his relics were taken to Edessa; tradition says the greater part of them was sent there in 232. In 1258 some relics were brought to Ortona in Italy.

The San Thome Church at Mylapore, said to stand at his tomb, was built in 1523 by Portuguese missionaries. The feast of Saint Thomas was entered in the Roman calendar in the 9th century on 21 December and moved to 3 July in 1969, which is also observed by Indian Christians as Indian Christians' Day. The name Thomas remains popular among the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala.
thomas-upington: Upington was born at Rathnee, near Mallow in County Cork, on 28 October 1844. He was educated at Cloyne Diocesan School in Mallow and at Trinity College Dublin, where he took Mathematical Honours in 1863. Called to the Irish Bar in 1867, he became secretary in 1868 to Thomas O'Hagan, 1st Baron O'Hagan, the Lord Chancellor of Ireland. His health was fragile all his life, and for that reason he emigrated to the Cape Colony in 1874.

Elected to the Cape Legislature in 1878, he sat in turn for Colesberg, Caledon and Swellendam, and was a close ally of John Gordon Sprigg, in whose governments he regularly served as Attorney General. In the war of 1877-79 he raised a small unit of 30 men known as Upington's Foot. Sprigg's government was unusually aggressive towards the Cape's indigenous peoples, and in the Koegas affair of 1879-80, when farmers accused of murdering San people were acquitted, a campaign led by Saul Solomon blamed Upington for letting the trial be held in a hostile town.

He became the fourth Prime Minister of the Cape in 1884, called to form a government by the Afrikaner Bond after it forced out Thomas Charles Scanlen. His short ministry was dominated by the Boer states of Stellaland and Goshen in Bechuanaland: the Bond backed them and the British authorities demanded action. His sympathy for the Boers kept his majority but led British politicians in Cape Town to denounce him as a Fenian, and he was known as the Afrikaner from Cork. In 1885 he opened the railway from Cape Town to Kimberley. Under attack over his Basutoland policy, he resigned in 1886, citing ill health, and handed over to Sprigg.

He was made a Knight Commander of the Order of St Michael and St George in 1887. Known for a quick, ornate and witty style of debate, he was often compared with his liberal opponent John X. Merriman. His health worsened, and he died at Wynberg, Cape Town, on 10 December 1898, aged 54. The town of Upington in the Northern Cape bears his name.
thomasites: The Philippines already had a public school system under the Educational Decree of 1863 issued by Queen Isabella II, with compulsory instruction in Spanish. After Admiral George Dewey's victory at the Battle of Manila Bay on 1 May 1898, American soldiers began teaching English and opened the first public school on Corregidor Island. The Taft Commission, headed by William Howard Taft, passed Education Act No. 74 on 21 January 1901, creating the Department of Public Instruction and authorising the deployment of 1,000 more teachers from the United States.

The teachers left Pier 12 in San Francisco on 23 July 1901, at a cost to the government of about $105,000, and reached Manila on 21 August. They came from 43 states and from Harvard, Yale, Cornell, the University of Michigan, the University of California and many smaller colleges and normal schools. A group of 48 teachers had come a few weeks earlier aboard the USAT Sheridan, but the name Thomasite spread to all the pioneer American teachers because the Thomas carried the largest contingent.

After two days of quarantine the teachers stayed in Intramuros before being sent to provinces from Albay, Samar and Cebu to Jolo, Pangasinan and Tarlac. They were offered $125 a month, though their pay was often late and usually made in devalued Mexican pesos. Besides English they taught reading, grammar, geography, mathematics, agriculture, trades, household arts, drawing and sports such as baseball and basketball. More teachers followed in 1902, bringing the total to about 1,074.

The Thomasites built on the Spanish system and the army's efforts, founding or reorganising the Philippine Normal School, the Philippine School of Arts and Trades, Tarlac High School and Tayabas High School, and reopening the Philippine Nautical School of 1839. About a hundred settled in the Philippines for good. Among them were Edwin Copeland, first dean of the College of Agriculture of the University of the Philippines, Horace Brinsmade Silliman, founder of Silliman University, and the historian Carter G. Woodson. They are counted precursors of the Peace Corps.
thomism: Aquinas held that truth is to be accepted wherever it is found, and he was a realist, believing that the world can be known as it is. He wrote commentaries on Aristotle, whom he called simply the Philosopher. A being, in Thomist philosophy, is an essence that exists: its quiddity, or whatness, together with its esse, or existence. He defined the good as what all things strive for, so that evil is a lack of good.

Aquinas held that the existence of God can be demonstrated by reason, and the Summa Theologica gives five ways of doing so: from motion, from efficient cause, from contingency, from degree and from the end of things. God is the sole being whose existence is the same as His essence, for which Aquinas used the term actus purus. Thomists define the soul as the substantial form of living beings, and human beings alone have rational and immortal souls.

The first period of Thomism runs from Aquinas's teaching, beginning at Paris in 1256, until his canonisation in 1325. In 1277 Étienne Tempier, the bishop of Paris, condemned 219 propositions, twenty of them Thomistic; the condemnation was withdrawn after Aquinas was canonised. Thomism declined in the modern period that Descartes opened with his Discourse on the Method in 1637. Salvatore Roselli published a six-volume Summa philosophica in 1777 and is considered to have laid the foundation of Neothomism.

The revival of the mid-19th century drew on Tommaso Maria Zigliara, Josef Kleutgen and Gaetano Sanseverino, and Pope Leo XIII's Aeterni Patris of 1879 gave it impetus. In 1914 Pope Pius X's decree Postquam sanctissimus presented 24 theses as containing the principles of Aquinas.

Aquinas shifted Scholasticism away from neoplatonism and towards Aristotle, and the school that followed is counted among the most influential in philosophy. Several schools of interpretation arose in the 20th century. Existential Thomism, whose chief proponent was Étienne Gilson, stresses Aquinas's doctrine of being as existence, and Jacques Maritain sought to harmonise Thomism with personalism and democracy. Transcendental Thomism, associated with Joseph Maréchal, Karl Rahner and Bernard Lonergan, seeks to reconcile Aquinas with Kant. Lublin Thomism, whose best-known proponent was Karol Wojtyla, later Pope John Paul II, draws on phenomenology.
thondaiman-dynasty: In 1686 the Pudukkottai region was held by a chief called Pallavarayan under Raghunatha Kilavan Setupati, the Raja of Ramnad. Suspecting that the chief would shift his allegiance to the ruler of Thanjavur, the Raja ousted him and gave the region to his brother-in-law, Raghunatha Raya Thondaiman, the brother of his queen Kathayi Nachiar. The new ruler, a son of Avadai Raghunatha Thondaiman, had earlier ruled Thirumayam.

Though nominally feudatories of Ramnad, the Thondaiman rulers soon pursued an independent foreign policy. Raghunatha Raya Thondaiman fought the Nayaks of Tanjore in support of the Nayaks of Madurai, took the important place of Thirukkattupalli and, in a direct clash with Tanjore, conquered the land west of it.

Later rulers helped the Nawab of Arcot against Hyder Ali of Mysore and stayed loyal to the British. When Hyder Ali's army tried to invade Pudukkottai it was defeated and driven away, and the Thondaimans captured Kilanilai and Aranthangi; they also helped the British against Tipu Sultan. Menaced by a resurgent Mysore, which sought French support against the British, Pudukkottai came under formal British protection.

The dynasty kept a special Valari regiment. Its later long reigns included those of Ramachandra Thondaiman, from 13 July 1839 to 15 April 1886, and Marthanda Bhairava Thondaiman, from 1886 to 28 May 1928. The last ruler, Rajagopala Thondaiman, came to the throne on 28 October 1928 and ruled until 4 March 1948, so that the Pudukkottai Samasthanam remained under the dynasty for a year after Indian independence. He kept the title as a titular ruler until 16 January 1997.
thonmi-sambhota: Thonmi is a clan name, and Sambhota means scholar from Tibet. According to Tibetan tradition, Songtsen Gampo sent him to India with 16 other Tibetan students to study Buddhism, Sanskrit and the art of writing; some sources say he went to the monastery of Nalanda. He is said to have been the only one of the students to return, and he became the fourth of the king's seven wise ministers. Tradition also credits him with escorting two princesses, from Nepal and from China, to Tibet to become Songtsen Gampo's queens.

The scholar R. A. Stein summarises the tradition: the young man, Sambhoṭa son of Anu, was sent to India in 632 with other youths to learn the alphabet, and the pattern chosen was the script of Kashmir. Other accounts base the script on the Brahmi and Gupta scripts.

The script is said to have been devised in retreat after his return and prepared at Kukarmaru Palace in Lhasa. The king is said to have spent four years mastering it and its grammar, and then made translations of Buddhist texts, among them the twenty-one Avalokitesvara texts. Thonmi is also credited with six treatises on Tibetan grammar, two of which are included in the Tengyur. These may have been re-edited later, and the two attributed to him might date from after the 13th century.

Stein notes that the ancient annals of Tun-huang record under the year 655 that the text of the laws was written, so that within a couple of decades the alphabet had been adapted to Tibetan with a complex spelling and used for documents. The Chronicle of Ba, the royal records of the Ba clan, also began around 650.

Little is known of the exact origins of the Tibetan script, which appears to have developed over a long period. The earliest sources on Tibet, such as the Old Tibetan Chronicle, do not mention Thonmi Sambhota, and his existence is difficult, if not impossible, to verify. The treatises credited to him by later Buddhist tradition were probably compiled in the decades after Songtsen Gampo's reign. The first Tibetan dictionary, the Drajor Bampo Nyipa, followed in the 8th century and served the translators of the Kangyur and Tengyur.
thopia-family: The Thopia were part of the nobility of the Angevin Kingdom of Albania. They first appear in an Angevin document of 1274 recording a pact between Albanian nobles and Charles I of Anjou, in which a certain Theopia mīles is named. In 1329 Tanusio Thopia was listed among the counts of Albania, and in 1338 he was called Count of Matia. The family converted from Eastern Orthodoxy to Catholicism, and by 1340 it held much of the land between the rivers Mati and Shkumbin. A story told by Gjon Muzaka, who flourished around 1510, has Andrea Thopia abducting and marrying a daughter of King Robert of Naples, who later had the couple executed.

The family reached its height under Karl Thopia. After the death of Emperor Stefan Dušan in 1355 he took much of central Albania from the Serbian Empire, attacked Durrës in 1362 and forced its Angevin holders to pay tribute. Around 1370 he seized the lands between the Shkumbin and Seman rivers from the Muzaka family, so that his domain reached from the Mat to the Seman. Louis of Évreux, Duke of Durazzo, took Durrës in 1376, but Karl regained it in 1383. When Balsha II, allied with the Muzaka, captured the city early in 1385, Karl called on the Ottomans, whose victory at the Battle of Savra let him recover it the same year.

On Karl's death his lands were divided: his son Gjergj kept Durrës, and his daughter Helena, wife of the Venetian nobleman Marco Barbarigo, kept Krujë. Gjergj's half-brother Niketa Thopia ruled south of Durrës and took Krujë from Helena in 1403. Defeated and captured by Teodor III Muzaka in 1411, Niketa was freed through the Republic of Ragusa at the cost of lands near the Shkumbin, and on his death in 1415 the castle of Krujë fell to the Ottomans.

The family's later members include Tanush Thopia, a commander in the army of Skanderbeg who led the garrison of Krujë during its second siege. Through marriage the Thopia were linked to many of the leading houses of the region, among them the Balšić, Branković, Dukagjini, Muzaka, Kastrioti and Crnojević families.
thor: Thor's name descends from the Proto-Germanic *Þun(a)raz, meaning thunder, and its forms include Old English Thunor, Old Saxon Thunar and Old High German Donar. He closely resembles other Indo-European thunder gods, among them the Celtic Taranis, the Baltic Perkūnas, the Slavic Perun and the Hindu Indra, and scholars compare Indra's slaying of Vritra with Thor's battle with the serpent Jörmungandr. For this reason he is generally accepted as ultimately derived from a Proto-Indo-European deity. Roman writers identified him with Jupiter or Hercules, and the weekday name Thursday is a calque of the Latin Iovis dies.

In Norse mythology Thor is a god associated with thunder, storms, strength, protection, fertility and farmers. He is the son of Odin and Jörð and the husband of the golden-haired Sif. He rides in a cart pulled by two goats, Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjóstr, which he eats and brings back to life, and he wields the hammer Mjölnir, wears the belt Megingjörð and the iron gloves Járngreipr. He is foretold to kill Jörmungandr at Ragnarök and then to take only nine steps before dying of its venom.

The earliest record of the name is on the Nordendorf fibulae from Bavaria, which bear the name Þonar in Elder Futhark. A 9th-century codex from Mainz, the Old Saxon Baptismal Vow, lists Thunaer among three gods to be renounced. According to a near-contemporary account, Saint Boniface felled an oak dedicated to Jove, known as Donar's Oak, in Hesse in the 8th century.

In the 11th century Adam of Bremen wrote that a statue of Thor stood at the centre of a triple throne in the temple at Uppsala, and that sacrifices were offered to him when plague or famine threatened. Around 1000 hammer pendants have been found in the Nordic countries, England, northern Germany, the Baltic countries and Russia, and Personal names containing his name are recorded with great frequency only from the Viking Age.

Thor was still invoked in the 12th century, a century after Norway was officially Christianized, as a runic stick from Bergen shows. His name survives in place names such as Þórslundr in Denmark and in Thundersley in England. Scandinavian folklore kept words such as tordön for thunder, and a belief that lightning frightens away trolls. In the modern period he has been the subject of poems by writers including Adam Gottlob Oehlenschläger and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, and veneration of him has been revived in Heathenry.
thorfinn-the-mighty: Thorfinn was the youngest of the five known sons of Earl Sigurd Hlodvirsson and the only son of Sigurd's marriage to a daughter of King Malcolm II. Before Sigurd set out for Ireland, where he was killed at the Battle of Clontarf on 23 April 1014, he sent the five-year-old boy to be fostered by his grandfather. When news of the death came, Thorfinn's elder half-brothers Einar, Brusi and Sumarlidi divided Orkney and Shetland between them, while the king set Thorfinn up as ruler of Caithness and Sutherland with Scots advisors to govern for him.

Joint earldoms were common in Orkney. After Sumarlidi's death Thorfinn claimed his third of the islands; Einar refused until Brusi raised his own men to stand between the two armies and persuaded him to give way. When Einar died the dispute began again, and Brusi took it to King Olaf of Norway, who granted a third to each brother and kept a third for himself. On the advice of his foster-father Thorkel Amundason, Thorfinn accepted the settlement. These events have been dated to 1021.

A large part of the Orkneyinga saga concerns Thorfinn's war with a king of Scots named Karl Hundason, whose identity is uncertain. Thorfinn defeated him in a sea-battle off Deerness, Thorkel killed Karl's nephew Muddan in Caithness, and a battle at Torfness, probably Tarbat Ness, ended with Karl killed or put to flight. Around 1034 Thorfinn is said to have conquered the Hebrides. After Rögnvald Brusason returned in about 1037 the two raided widely around the Irish Sea, before their partnership broke down and Thorkel killed Rögnvald on Thorfinn's behalf.

Unlike his brothers, Thorfinn had been raised a Christian. Probably from 1048 he made a pilgrimage to Rome, travelling through Saxony and meeting Emperor Henry III. The saga suggests that at his request Thorulf was appointed the first Bishop of Orkney, with his seat at the Christchurch that Thorfinn had built at Birsay near his residence. Thorfinn was buried there. The saga places his death towards the end of the reign of King Harald Hardrada, who died in 1066. His sons Paul and Erlend followed him as earls, and his widow Ingibiorg later married Malcolm Canmore, King of Scots.
thoros-ii-prince-of-armenia: Thoros was the second son of Leo I, lord of Armenian Cilicia. In 1137 the Byzantine Emperor John II Comnenus, campaigning against Cilicia and the Principality of Antioch, seized Leo together with Thoros and his younger brother Roupen and carried them to Constantinople. Leo died in prison there in 1141, and Roupen was blinded and later killed. Cilicia remained under Byzantine rule for eight years. According to the Rhymed Chronicle of Vahram of Edessa, the emperor took pity on Thoros after his father's death, freed him and enrolled him in the imperial guard.

Accounts of his return differ. One tradition has him sail alone from Antioch and take Amouda first; another, which Vahram attributes to the emperor's party, says he fled to the mountains with money from a lady, revealed himself to a priest and, hiding as a shepherd, was proclaimed baron by Armenians who resented Greek rule, taking Vahka and then other places. He found the country held by many Greek garrisons.

In 1151, according to the chronicle of Smbat Sparapet, Thoros took Mamistra and Tel Hamdoun and captured Duke Thomas. When Duke Andronicus came against him with 12,000 cavalry, Thoros breached the walls of Mamistra by night and routed the Byzantine force, capturing Oshin of Lampron and other lords who had sided with the emperor. In 1154 Emperor Manuel paid Sultan Masud to attack the Armenians, but the sultan achieved nothing at Anazarbus, and his army fell apart after the Knights Templar destroyed a detachment and disease struck its horses. Thoros kept friendly relations with Sultan Kilij Arslan, even surrendering Berdus to him after his brother Stephen took it without his consent in 1157.

His brother Mleh plotted to kill him during a deer hunt between Mamistra and Adana, but Thoros was forewarned, shamed him before the army and banished him; Mleh entered the service of Nur ed-Din of Aleppo. Thoros later abdicated and became a monk. He died on 6 February 1169 and was buried in the monastery of Drazark. His young son Roupen II died in 1170. Vahram remembered him as tall, compassionate and learned in scripture.
thoros-of-edessa: Thoros, a short Armenian form of Theodoros, had served the Byzantine Empire as a curopalates and as a lieutenant of Philaretos Brachamios. Although Armenian, he practised the Greek Orthodox faith. The Chronicle of Matthew of Edessa calls him the son of Hethum, and the historian Steven Runciman describes him as the son-in-law of Gabriel of Melitene.

Around 1094 the Seljuk emir of Damascus, Tutush I, captured Edessa after defeating and killing the emir Bouzan, and installed Thoros as governor. Thoros at once set out to take the city for himself. He fortified Edessa and cut off its citadel, which held a garrison of Turkish and Armenian troops. The Turks and the Ortoqids besieged the city for two months but could not take it even after breaking through the walls, and when they withdrew Thoros was recognised as lord of Edessa.

As a Greek Orthodox Christian he was not well loved by his Armenian subjects. He held off further Seljuk attacks, but in 1098 he had to seek help from the crusaders, then occupied with the siege of Antioch. Baldwin of Boulogne, who had turned aside from the siege, probably to win land of his own, and had taken Turbessel, made an alliance with Thoros in February 1098.

Once adopted as son and heir, Baldwin attacked Thoros's officers and besieged him in the citadel. Thoros agreed to give up the city and planned to flee with his family to Melitene, but on 9 March 1098 he was killed by the Armenian inhabitants of Edessa, possibly at Baldwin's command, and Baldwin became the first count of Edessa.
thotagamuwe-sri-rahula-thera: He was born in 1408 at Dematana, a village near Dambadeniya in Kurunegala District, with the lay name Jayabahu. His parentage is uncertain; by some accounts his mother, Princess Seelawathi, was the elder sister of Queen Keerawelle Kumari, chief consort of King Parakramabahu VI of Kotte, and after she died in his infancy he was brought up under the guardianship of the king and queen. His first teachers, Uthurumula Rahula Thera and Wilgammula Thera, were relatives who ordained him as a novice with the name Vachissara Rahula Thera.

He moved to the Vijayaba Pirivena at Thotagamuwa, near Hikkaduwa in Galle District, the leading centre of learning of the Kotte era, founded by King Vijayabahu I of Polonnaruwa. There he quickly mastered literature, languages and the Buddhist scriptures, reportedly reciting the whole Tripiṭaka by heart, and he spent most of his life there, in time succeeding as its chief prelate. Parakramabahu VI made him Sangharaja, the first Sri Lankan monk to hold that post. Besides Sinhala he knew Sanskrit, Prakrit, Magadhi, Apabhramsa, Shauraseni and Paisachi, which earned him the title Shad Bhasha Parameshwara, master of six languages. He was also known as an astrologer and an ayurvedic physician.

His works include the Buddhagajjaya (1430), the Uruthamala Sandesaya (1435), the Paravi Sandeshaya (1445), the Selalihini Sandeshaya (1447), the Kavyasekharaya (1449), the Panchika Pradeepaya (1457) and the Buddhipasadiniya (1480), as well as the Gira Sandeshaya, the Parakumba Siritha and the Mawula Sandesaya.

Many stories surround his life. One holds that as a boy he drank a whole bottle of Saraswathi oil, meant to be taken a drop at a time, and so gained his memory. Two traditions tell of his end. In one he died around 1491 at Vijayaba Pirivena and, through a drug he had taken, his body did not decay, so villagers hid it in the Indurugiri cave at Ambana near Elpitiya when the Portuguese arrived in 1505. In the other he retired to Obbegoda temple and Dickwella before settling in that cave, where he died in 1491.
thoth: The Egyptian name of Thoth, written ḏḥwty, may derive from ḏḥw, said to be the oldest known name for the ibis, with an ending marking him as having the ibis's attributes, so that it would mean he who is like the ibis. The Greek form Thoth is more common than the Egyptological rendering Djehuti. Thoth was a moon god. The moon allowed time to be measured at night without the sun, and its phases organised much of the rituals and events of Egyptian society, civil and religious. He therefore came to be seen as a god of wisdom, magic and the measurement and regulation of events and time, and as the secretary and counsellor of Ra.

Thoth was most often shown as a man with the head of an ibis, sometimes wearing a lunar disk on a crescent moon, or as a baboon, or as the ibis itself. Scholars suggest the curve of the ibis's beak was seen as the crescent moon. As Aani, an ape in the underworld, he reported when the scales weighing the heart of the dead against the feather of Maat were exactly even. His feminine counterpart is Seshat, and his wife is Ma'at; with Ma'at he stood beside Ra on the solar barque. He was regarded as the scribe of the gods and the inventor of writing and hieroglyphs, and Egyptian scribes worshipped him, keeping a picture of him in their offices.

In myth Plutarch credits him with the 365-day calendar. When the year had only 360 days and the goddess Nut could bear no children, Thoth gambled with the moon for one seventy-second of its light and won five days, on which Osiris, Set, Isis, Horus and Nephthys were born. In the central Osiris myth he gives Isis the words to restore her husband, and after the battle between Horus and Set he offers counsel.

His chief temple was at Hermopolis, called Khemenu in Egyptian, and in the Late Period his cult gained prominence as Khmun also became the capital. Millions of dead ibis were mummified and buried in his honour. The temple was mostly destroyed before the Christian era, and its large pronaos, standing in 1826, was demolished by the mid-19th century and used as fill for the foundation of a sugar factory. The Greeks identified him with Hermes, and his title Thrice Great, trismégistos in Greek, gave the combined figure Hermes Trismegistus.
thousand-days-war: Colombia was politically unstable throughout the 19th century. Conservatives and liberals pushed for a unitary state on one side and a federal state on the other. After the Civil War of 1885, in which radical Liberals rebelled against the administration of Rafael Núñez, the federal Constitution of Rionegro of 1863 was replaced by the Constitution of 1886. This began a centralist process known as the Regeneración, which brought relative peace but did not settle the disputes between the departments. Tensions rose after the presidential election of 1898, and President Manuel Antonio Sanclemente was unable to lead because of illness.

On 17 October 1899 members of the Liberal Party in the Department of Santander announced an insurrection against the national government. Many Liberals hesitated, believing they lacked numbers and organisation, and hostilities began in earnest on 11 November with the Battle of Bucaramanga. The Conservatives split into Historical and National factions, dismissed Sanclemente and replaced him with José Manuel Marroquín, and the Liberals nominated Gabriel Vargas Santos. Rafael Uribe Uribe won a Liberal victory at Peralonso, and at Palonegro on 26 May 1900 the Conservatives halted the Liberals in a very bloody encounter.

The war extended into Ecuador and Venezuela, where President Cipriano Castro supported the Liberals, and in September 1901 he sent 1,200 Venezuelan troops into Colombia. Fighting centred increasingly on the province of Panama and the Caribbean coast. The first peace treaty was signed on the plantation of Neerlandia on 24 October 1902. The United States, under Theodore Roosevelt, sent its navy to protect its future interest in a Panama canal, and the Liberals under General Benjamín Herrera were forced to surrender. The definitive treaty was signed aboard the American battleship Wisconsin on 21 November 1902.

Estimates of the dead range from 100,000 to 180,000, about 2.5 to 3.8 per cent of the population, which makes the war the deadliest civil war in Colombian history. It brought a partial collapse of the economy and continued governmental instability. The Conservatives won and kept their dominance in Colombian politics for another 28 years. The assassination of Victoriano Lorenzo is understood among indigenous Panamanians as the loss of their struggle for land rights. The department of Panama was lost to Colombia in 1903.
thrace: Thrace is bounded by the Balkan Mountains to the north, the Aegean Sea to the south and the Black Sea to the east. It comprises present-day south-eastern Bulgaria, north-eastern Greece and the European part of Turkey, known as Northern, Western and Eastern Thrace. Its historical boundaries varied, and the ancient Greeks used the name for all the land north of Thessaly that the Thracians inhabited. The name comes from the Greek Thrake, which at first referred to the Thracians themselves.

The Thracians recorded no collective name for themselves, and the Greeks assigned the name. They were divided into numerous tribes, and the first Greek colonies on the coast were founded in the 8th century BCE. In the late 6th century BCE the Achaemenid Persians took control after Darius the Great's Scythian campaign and made the region the Satrapy of Skudra.

The Thracian tribes formed no lasting political organisation until the Odrysian state, of the 4th century BCE. Most of Thrace was conquered in the 4th century BCE by Philip II of Macedon and his son Alexander the Great, and after Alexander's death it passed to Lysimachus, who was defeated by Seleucus I Nicator at Corupedium in 281 BCE.

After the Third Macedonian War of 171 to 168 BCE, Thrace became a tributary to Rome. Augustus tried indirect rule through a Hellenized client kingdom under the Sapaean family, with Bizye as its first centre, until the Romans turned Thrace into a province in 46 CE. By the mid-5th century Thrace had fallen from Roman authority and for much of the next thousand years it was a battleground.

The Byzantine Empire kept it until the 7th century, when the northern half joined the First Bulgarian Empire. The Bulgarian and Byzantine Empires held it in turns through the 13th and early 14th centuries. The Ottoman Turks first made an incursion in 1352, took Gallipoli in 1354 and made Edirne their capital before taking Constantinople in 1453.

The Congress of Berlin in 1878 made Northern Thrace part of the semi-autonomous Ottoman province of Eastern Rumelia, which united with Bulgaria in 1885. After the First World War and the Greco-Turkish War, Southern Thrace was divided between Turkey in the east and Greece in the west. Thracian is now a geographical term used in Bulgaria, Turkey and Greece. Notable people from the region include the philosophers Protagoras and Democritus, both of Abdera, and Spartacus, who led the slave uprising of 73 to 71 BCE.
thracia: Thracia, or Thrace, is the ancient name of the southeastern Balkan region inhabited by the Thracians. From the standpoint of classical Greece it included the land north of Thessaly with no definite boundaries, sometimes taking in Macedonia and Scythia Minor. Later, Thracia proper was understood as the territory bounded by the Danube on the north, the Black Sea on the east, Macedonia on the south and Illyria on the west, roughly the Thracian kingdom as it stood from the 5th to the 1st century BCE.

Thrace was ruled by the Odrysian kingdom in the Classical and Hellenistic eras and briefly by the Greek Diadochi ruler Lysimachus. About 20 BCE the Odrysian kingdom became a Roman client kingdom, while the Greek cities on the Black Sea coast came under Roman control as allied cities with internal autonomy. After the death of King Rhoemetalces III in 46 CE and an unsuccessful anti-Roman revolt, Claudius annexed it as a province. It took in the former kingdom, the north-eastern part of Macedonia and the islands of Thasos, Samothrace and Imbros. Its first capital was Heraclea Perinthus, and its governor was at first a procurator and, after about 107 to 109, a legatus Augusti pro praetore.

The new administration kept the old tribal districts, the strategiai, which numbered fifty in the mid-1st century, fourteen by the early 2nd century, and none after about 136, as cities grew. Septimius Severus travelled through Thrace on campaign from 193 to 198, and Perinthus, which backed him, was twice granted the title of neokoros. As an interior province with the Via Egnatia running through it, Thrace remained peaceful and prosperous until the Crisis of the Third Century, when Goths raided it. Emperor Decius fell at the Battle of Abritus in 251, and Thracia suffered heavily in the Gothic seaborne raids of 268–270, before Aurelian secured the Balkan provinces in 271.

The provincial and urban policy of the emperors, with the foundation of several cities of Greek type, contributed more to the progress of Hellenization than to Romanization, and by the end of antiquity the land south of the Haemus mountains had been almost completely Hellenized. Inscriptions show Thracians, mostly soldiers, serving across the Empire from Syria and Arabia to Britain. Diocletian divided the province into four: Thracia, Haemimontus, Rhodope and Europa, with Philippopolis as the capital of the new Thracia. These were grouped with two provinces of Moesia Inferior into the diocese of Thraciae. The later Byzantine theme of Thracia contained only what is now Eastern Thrace.
thracian-tomb-of-sveshtari: The Getae, a Thracian people, had been federated in the Odrysian kingdom in the fifth century BCE. Philip II of Macedon's Balkan campaigns between 352 and 340 BCE shattered Odrysian authority, and the Getae profited. By the second half of the fourth century they held sites on both banks of the lower Danube. The tomb was built in the first quarter of the third century BCE. It is probably the grave of Dromichaetes, king of the Getae around 300 BCE, and of his wife, a daughter of King Lysimachus, a general and successor of Alexander the Great.

The tomb lies 2.5 kilometres south-west of the village of Sveshtari in Razgrad Province, north-eastern Bulgaria. Its construction follows the basic principles of Thracian cult buildings, but its decoration is considered unique: polychrome caryatids, half human and half plant, and painted murals. The ten female figures carved in high relief on the walls of the central chamber, with the decoration of the lunette in its vault, are the only examples of this type found so far in the Thracian lands.

The tomb was discovered and excavated in 1982, during work on Mound No 7 of the East Mound Necropolis of Sboryanovo, a tumulus of the early Hellenistic period. Near it were found the remains of a large ancient city and dozens of Getic mound tombs, and the tomb is supposed to lie close to the Getic city of Helis. The settlement stood on a plateau among the ravines of the Krapinets River, with a stone wall up to 4 metres thick; amphora stamps and coins show it existed between about 335 and 250 BCE. The tomb is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
thracians: The exact origin of the Thracians is uncertain. It is believed that, like other Indo-European-speaking groups in Europe, they descended from a mixture of Proto-Indo-Europeans and Early European Farmers. During the 5th and 4th millennia BCE the inhabitants of the eastern Balkans formed different groups of indigenous people that the ancient Greeks later named under the single ethnonym Thracians. Their culture emerged during the early Bronze Age, which began about 3500 BCE, and the Getae and Dacians developed from it.

The first record of the name is in the Iliad, where Thracians appear as allies of the Trojans. Only four Thracian inscriptions have been found, among them a gold ring from Ezerovo in Bulgaria, whose text of eight lines in Greek script has not been deciphered.

Greek colonies were founded along the Thracian coasts from the 8th century BCE, and Thracians and Greeks lived side by side. According to Greek and Roman writers the Thracians remained largely disunited until the Odrysian kingdom was established in the early 5th century BCE by King Teres I, after the failure of the Persian invasion of Greece. Teres and his son Sitalces expanded the kingdom, which allied with Athens and joined the Peloponnesian War on its side.

The kingdom showed signs of fatigue by 400 BCE, and Cotys I brought a brief revival that lasted until his murder in 360 BCE. Around 340 BCE it lost independence to Macedon, and around 330 BCE Seuthes III revived a much smaller state with a new capital, Seuthopolis. From the mid-2nd century BCE the Thracians faced gradual conquest by the Romans. The Odrysian heartland became the client Sapaean kingdom, which was finally converted into the Roman province of Thracia.

Greeks and Romans described the Thracians as warlike and barbarian, yet favoured them as mercenaries. They were skilled horsemen and lightly armed skirmishers with javelins, and Thracian peltasts had a notable influence in ancient Greece. In 188 BCE near Cypsela they defeated the troops of the Roman consul Manlius Vulzon. Tattooing was a custom among both men and women.

Their religion was polytheistic. One cult was that of the Thracian horseman, a god of the underworld shown on funeral statues slaying a beast with a spear. Zalmoxis, worshipped by the Getae and Dacians, is the subject of debate over whether his cult was monotheistic.

Later invasions by Romans, Celts, Huns, Goths, Scythians, Sarmatians and Slavs, with hellenization, romanisation and later slavicisation, remade the ethnicity, language and culture of Thrace. Writers spoke of a separate Thracian nationality until the early Middle Ages, and the last reported use of a Thracian language was by monks in the 6th century CE. Late in the 4th century Nicetas of Remesiana brought Christianity to the Bessi.
thrall: The word comes from the Old Norse þræll, a person in bondage, which passed into late Old English as þræl and into Irish as thráill. It goes back to a Common Germanic þragilaz, a runner, and Old High German had the cognate dregil, servant or runner. The older Old English word for a slave was þeow. The same three orders of noblemen, freemen and slaves appear across the Germanic peoples, as eorl, ceorl and þēow in Old English and etheling, friling and lēt in Old Frisian, and the Norse poem Rígsþula tells of them.

Under the Germanic law codes a slave was property and could be bought and sold, yet had some protection: the killing of a freeman was compensated by a weregild, often 200 solidi, while the killing of a slave was paid to the owner by the worker's value. A freeborn person who gave himself into bondage through poverty or debt underwent a process called Flatföring. Most households owned one or two thralls, though some estimates run as high as thirty.

A bryte was a thrall appointed to run a farm for an absent owner. A fostre or fostra, a privileged thrall raised among the owner's children, could be sold only before witnesses and could marry free people, whose children were then born free. Erling Skjalgsson set his thralls a fixed amount of work, let them keep what they earned beyond it, and allowed them to buy their freedom within a year or two. A freed thrall became a leysingi, still bound to vote as his former master wished; it took at least two generations for a family to become fully free.

As Christian opposition to holding Christians as slaves grew and landowners found it more profitable to rent land to free farmers, slavery faded. In Iceland it was last mentioned in a law text of 1122-1133. In Denmark Bishop Absalom's will of 1201 freed a few slaves, and the Jyske lov of 1241 knows none. In Norway the Magnus Lagabøtes landslov of 1274 no longer recognised slavery.
thrasymachus: Thrasymachus was a citizen of Chalcedon on the Bosphorus, and his career appears to have been spent as a sophist at Athens, though the exact nature of his work and thought is unclear. He is credited with increasing the rhythmic character of Greek oratory, especially the use of the paeonic rhythm in prose, and with a greater appeal to the emotions through gesture. The most precisely datable reference is a joke by Aristophanes in a lost play of 427 BCE, from which Nils Rauhut concludes that he had been teaching in Athens for several years by then.

Aristotle names him in the Sophistical Refutations among the successive developers of rhetorical theory, after Tisias and before Theodorus, and in the Rhetoric attributes to him a witty simile about Niceratus. Plato mentions him in the Phaedrus as a successful rhetorician. The Byzantine Suda calls him the first to discover period and colon and credits him with deliberative speeches, an Art of Rhetoric and Rhetorical Resources. Dionysius of Halicarnassus found him pure, subtle and inventive, but a second-rate orator beside Lysias, since he left handbooks and display speeches but no forensic speeches.

The longest surviving fragment of his writing is preserved by Dionysius of Halicarnassus in On the Style of Demosthenes as an example of the middle style. It seems to be the beginning of a political speech, apparently composed for a young upper-class Athenian of conservative sympathies, probably in the early 420s. The speaker regrets that the young must now speak because of the failures of those who administer the state, laments the exchange of peace for war, and says the ancestral constitution is a cause of dissension between the parties.

Thrasymachus is important today chiefly as a character in Plato's Republic. In Book I he disagrees violently with Socrates' discussion with Polemarchus, demands payment before speaking, and claims that justice is the advantage of the stronger and that injustice on a large enough scale is stronger, freer and more masterly than justice. Socrates forces him to admit a standard of wise rule and argues from it to a standard of justice beyond the stronger's advantage. Thrasymachus blushes at the end of the book, and the meaning of the blush is disputed.

His name means fierce fighter, which may have influenced his role. Interpreters differ on whether his statements form a coherent philosophy or are Plato's straw man, and Angie Hobbs suggests his aim may be to expose hypocrisies rather than applaud their manipulation.
three-bishoprics: The government of the Three Bishoprics joined the dioceses of Metz, Verdun and Toul within Lorraine, each before 1552 a prince-bishopric of the Holy Roman Empire. Its territory grew when the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees added the parts of the Duchy of Luxembourg around Thionville, and when several Lorraine villages were annexed in 1661. The Diocese of Saint-Dié, created in 1777 and sometimes called the fourth bishopric of Lorraine, has no historical tie to the three.

Protestant princes angered by the Interim of the 1548 Diet of Augsburg met at Lochau Castle in May 1551, where Maurice of Saxony allied with John Albert I of Mecklenburg, William IV of Hesse, Albert Alcibiades of Brandenburg-Kulmbach and Albert of Prussia. By the Treaty of Chambord of 15 January 1552 they recognised Henry II's lordship as Vicar of the Empire over Metz, Toul, Verdun and Cambrai in return for French money and troops.

Backed by Duke Francis of Guise and Cardinal Charles of Lorraine, Henry launched his Voyage d'Allemagne: troops under Anne de Montmorency entered Metz by surprise on Palm Sunday, Toul fell on 13 April, the young Duke Charles III of Lorraine was taken from Nancy to Paris, and Verdun was occupied on 12 June.

Charles V, holding that the princes had no right to give away imperial territory, besieged Metz from 19 October 1552 to 2 January 1553 without success, and after his abdication in 1556 Ferdinand I gave up the attempt.

Henry II kept a garrison in each city and gradually subjected the citizens to royal authority, while the petitions of Metz to the Imperial Diet went unheeded. At Cardinal Richelieu's initiative a provincial parlement, dominated by the Metz patriciate, was set up in Metz in 1633, and the cities prospered under French rule, though the salt tax caused unrest in Metz. Louis XIV confirmed the citizens' privileges on his accession in 1643.
three-departments-and-six-ministries: The system was the main administrative structure of imperial China from the Sui dynasty to the Yuan dynasty, replacing the Three Lords and Nine Ministers of the Qin and Han. Its offices grew out of older posts. The Department of State Affairs began as the chief steward for writing, one of six stewards of the Qin palace, and Emperor Guangwu of Han made it the head of six sections of government, which later became the Six Ministries. Emperor Wen of Wei formally created the Central Secretariat to draft edicts and balance the Department of State Affairs, and the Chancellery grew from the Han Court of Attendants.

Under the Tang the post of director of the Department of State Affairs was mostly left vacant, and its vice directors, split into left and right to weaken them, ran it; by the mid-Tang it had become a purely executive body. Each ministry was headed by a minister assisted by two vice-ministers and was divided into four bureaus, and the six divisions were repeated at prefectural level. The department also oversaw the Nine Courts and the Three Directorates and was one of the largest employers in the government.

The Central Secretariat read incoming material to the throne and drafted edicts, while the Chancellery reviewed them and advised the emperor. From the mid-Tang the Chancellery lost ground to the Secretariat, and by the 9th century it kept only the imperial seals, court ceremonies and altars. Later in the dynasty the academicians of the Hanlin Academy took over much of the drafting.

Under the Song the Secretariat and Chancellery were joined as the Secretariat-Chancellery. The Yuan made the Central Secretariat the heart of government, in control of the Six Ministries. In the early Ming the Hongwu Emperor executed the chancellor Hu Weiyong in 1380 and abolished the Central Secretariat, placing the Six Ministries directly under the emperor. The ministries continued under the Ming and Qing until new ministries added in 1901 and 1906 made the term obsolete. The system was also used by Balhae and Goryeo and by other states in Manchuria, Korea and Vietnam.
three-field-system: The three-field system is a regime of crop rotation in which a field is planted with one set of crops in one year, a different set in the second year, and left fallow in the third, with the sets rotating from field to field. The arable land of an estate or village was divided into three large fields.

One was planted in the autumn with winter wheat or rye, the second with crops such as peas, lentils or beans, and the third was left unplanted. Cereals deplete the ground of nitrogen, but legumes fix nitrogen and so fertilise the soil. Weeds grew on the fallow field and were used for grazing, and the animals' dung restored its nutrients. Each field was planted in two years out of every three.

The technique was first used in China in the Eastern Zhou period and arose independently in Europe in the medieval period. In Europe it replaced a two-field system under which half the land was left fallow, and the change took place between the 9th and 11th centuries. With more crops to sell in an economy dominated by agriculture, the new system created a significant surplus and increased economic prosperity.

The system needed more ploughing, and its introduction coincided with the adoption of the moldboard plough, two developments that complemented each other and raised productivity. The legume crop needed summer rain, so the system worked less well around the Mediterranean. Oats for horse feed could also be sown in spring, which, with the adoption of horse collars and horseshoes, led to horses replacing oxen for many farming tasks, again raising productivity and the nutrition available to the population. In 1769 Johann Friedrich Mayer was one of the first Germans to advocate new ways of farming beyond the medieval three-field system.
three-gorges: The Three Gorges lie on the section of the Yangtze known as the Chuanjiang, or river of Sichuan, which runs from Jiangjin in Chongqing to Yichang in Hubei. The gorges span 311 km, from Baidicheng in the west to Nanjin Pass at Yichang in the east, with the Fengjie and Wushan counties of Chongqing and the Badong and Zigui counties of Hubei between them. In the past this stretch was the only waterway linking Sichuan and Guizhou with eastern China.

Geologists generally hold that the mountain folding of eastern Sichuan and western Hubei, including the Wu Mountains, came from the Yanshanian movement around 70 million years ago. As the crust kept rising the river cut deeper. The valleys are narrow where hard limestone resists erosion and broad where softer sandstone and shale give way. Among the named sights are Kuimen at the western entrance and the twelve peaks of the Wu Mountains.

The scenery was written about early. In the Northern Wei period Li Daoyuan described the gorges in his Commentary on the Water Classic, and Yuan Shansong of the Eastern Jin wrote a Record of Yichuan's Landscape. The poet Li Bai wrote of them in Setting out from Baidicheng, with monkeys howling on both banks as the boat sped past the mountains.

Advances in shipbuilding and navigation under the Tang and Song dynasties allowed regular traffic, but volumes stayed low until Sichuan was resettled in the 1600s. By the late 1700s about 210,000,000 kg of grain went downstream each year, while boats were hauled upstream by hand. Passage was dangerous, and government and private projects of the 1700s and 1800s carved towpaths, removed rocks and set up pilot and lifeboat stations. Manual towing lasted in part until the 1970s.

Sun Yat-sen proposed damming the gorges in 1919, but work on the Three Gorges project began only in 1994, after the National People's Congress approved it on 3 April 1992 by 1767 votes of 2633. The dam stands at Sandouping in the middle of Xiling Gorge. Its reservoir relocated towns and villages and submerged many archaeological sites, hanging coffins and inscriptions; the Zhang Fei Temple was moved whole, Shibaozhai was ringed by a protective dam, and the Baiheliang hydrographic inscriptions are now seen in an underwater museum.
three-huan: The three houses were cadet branches of the ducal house of Lu, itself a branch of the royal house of the Zhou dynasty. Duke Huan of Lu, who reigned from 711 to 694 BCE, had four sons. The eldest by his main wife Wen Jiang succeeded him as Duke Zhuang of Lu, while the other three, Qingfu, Shuya and Jiyou, became powerful officials under their brother.

Their family names came from the ordinals used in courtesy names to mark a person's place among brothers: Meng for an eldest son born to a secondary wife, Shu for a middle son and Ji for the youngest. As the power of these lines became hereditary, the descendants of Duke Zhuang's brothers took the ordinals as surnames to tell their branches of the House of Ji apart, giving the Mengsun, Shusun and Jisun.

Their hold over Lu began with a succession crisis. The dying Duke Zhuang wanted his son Ziban to succeed; Shuya backed Qingfu and was poisoned by Jiyou, who supported Ziban. Ziban was soon murdered by Qingfu with the help of Duke Zhuang's wife, and Jiyou went into exile. In 660 BCE Qingfu also murdered Duke Min and tried to rule himself, but public outcry drove him to the state of Ju. Jiyou returned from Qi with Duke Min's younger brother, who became Duke Xi, Qingfu was forced to take his own life, and Jiyou served as chief minister for 16 years with the backing of Qi.

Rivalry among the three families shaped the politics of Confucius's time. His disciples Ran Yong, Ran Qiu and Zilu served the Jisun as ministers, and Confucius himself was a subordinate of Ji Huanzi, chancellor to Duke Ding of Lu. He is said to have taken part in efforts to weaken the families and strengthen the ruler, but he was ousted from Lu in 497 BCE and remained in exile until 484 BCE.

At the end of the Spring and Autumn period Duke Ai of Lu, who had no control of his own army, secretly asked the powerful state of Yue to invade, depose the Three Huan and restore the duke's power. The plot was discovered and Duke Ai fled abroad. His son and successor, Duke Dao, remained a puppet of the three houses.
three-kingdoms-of-korea: The Three Kingdoms were founded after the fall of Wiman Joseon and gradually conquered and absorbed many small states and confederacies. After Gojoseon fell, the Han dynasty set up four commanderies in the north-west of the peninsula and in present Liaoning, and three fell quickly to the Samhan while Goguryeo destroyed the last in 313. The three polities made the transition from walled-town states to full state-level societies between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE. The main sources are the Korean histories Samguk sagi and Samguk yusa and the Eastern Barbarians section of the Book of Wei. The Book of Sui records that the customs, laws and clothes of the three kingdoms were generally identical.

Goguryeo arose on the Yalu River and was the largest of the three, holding the north of the peninsula, the Liaodong Peninsula and Manchuria. It was at its height in the 5th century under King Gwanggaeto the Great and his son King Jangsu. Paekche, founded as a member of the Mahan confederacy, controlled most of the western peninsula at its peak in the 4th century and was a maritime power that passed Chinese characters, metallurgy, ceramics, architecture and Buddhism to ancient Japan. Under pressure from Goguryeo it moved its capital south to Ungjin in the late 5th century and later to Sabi.

According to Korean records Silla, in the south-east, began in 57 BCE as a unification of the Jinhan city-states, though other evidence suggests it was the last of the three to build a centralised government. It was the smallest and weakest, but it made pacts with stronger neighbours, took the name Silla in 503 and annexed the Kaya confederacy in the first half of the 6th century. Buddhism became its official religion in 528, after Goguryeo adopted it in 372.
Silla allied with Tang China. Paekche was conquered in 660 and Goguryeo in 668. Silla then drove the Tang forces out of the peninsula and occupied the lands south of Pyongyang.

Silla's unification of the peninsula in the 7th century was the first in Korean history. It was later divided into the Later Three Kingdoms and annexed by Goryeo, a state that revived Goguryeo. The name Samhan, used since the 7th century for the three kingdoms, came to mean Korea as a whole, and the Han in the names Daehan Jeguk and Daehan Minguk refers to it. The Samguk sagi and Samguk yusa, whose titles use the name Three Kingdoms, should not be confused with the Three Kingdoms of China.
three-kingdoms-period: Han power had declined steadily after the death of Emperor He in 105 CE. Boy emperors, imperial relatives and eunuchs struggled for control, and the reigns of Emperor Huan and Emperor Ling were recorded as particularly dark periods. The Yellow Turban Rebellion of 184 began the period of chaotic infighting among warlords. In 189 the eunuchs killed the regent He Jin, Yuan Shao's troops stormed the palace and killed the Ten Attendants, and the warlord Dong Zhuo, invited to Luoyang, took control. After 192 the coalition against him fell apart, and the empire divided among regional warlords.

The majority view dates the period from 220 to 280. On 11 December 220 Emperor Xian abdicated and Cao Pi proclaimed himself emperor of Wei. Liu Bei declared himself Emperor of Han on 15 May 221, in the state known as Shu Han, and Sun Quan, who had recognised Wei, became king of Wu. Strictly, independent states existed only from Sun Quan's proclamation as emperor in 229 until the fall of Shu Han in 263. Zhuge Liang conquered the south of Shu territory up to Lake Dian in Yunnan in 224 to 225.

Wei conquered Shu in 263. In 266 Sima Yan overthrew the Wei emperor and proclaimed the Jin dynasty, and in 280 Jin forces took Jianye and Sun Hao of Wu surrendered. The period was one of the most dangerous in Chinese history, with plagues, famines and civil war. The census of 280 counted 2,459,840 households and 16,163,863 people, against 10,677,960 households and 56,486,856 people in the Han era, though it may not have been accurate. Cao Wei declared silk cloth and grain the main currencies in 221. Technology advanced, and the Wei engineer Ma Jun designed the south-pointing chariot.

The standard history is Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, compiled in the 3rd century, which Pei Songzhi expanded with annotations in 429, nearly doubling its size. All three states claimed the Mandate of Heaven, and later historians disagreed over which, chiefly Wei or Shu, was the legitimate successor to the Han. The period has been romanticised in folklore, opera, novels, film and games, and its best-known fictional treatment is Romance of the Three Kingdoms, a novel by Luo Guanzhong written under the Ming dynasty.
three-principles-of-the-people: Sun Yat-sen founded the anti-Qing Revive China Society in 1894. After a failed uprising in 1895 he went into exile, part of it in England, and later dated the conception of his principles to this period of study. Between 1903 and 1905 he toured overseas Chinese communities to compete for support with the reformists Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao. In a speech in Brussels in 1905 he set out the ideas for the first time.

From 1905 to 1907 Sun and collaborators such as Wang Jingwei, Hu Hanmin and Song Jiaoren wrote on the principles in the Tongmenghui's newspaper Minbao. They answered Liang Qichao, who thought China unready for a republic, by arguing that republicanism was the best form of government and had roots in Chinese culture.

The principles are nationalism (Mínzú), democracy (Mínquán) and people's livelihood (Mínshēng). Sun gave a series of weekly lectures on them in 1924, published as The Three Principles of the People, sixteen in all: six on nationalism, six on democracy and four on livelihood. Two more on shelter and transport were planned but never given. Sun died of liver cancer on 12 March 1925.

On democracy Sun proposed a Five Power Constitution, adding to the legislative, executive and judicial branches a control branch derived from the censorate and an examination branch derived from the civil service examinations. He also distinguished the sovereignty of the people (quan) from the ability of the government (neng), which was to be entrusted to experts. Livelihood covered clothing, food, housing and mobility, and called for state enterprises beside private industry and for land equalisation, in line with the thought of Henry George.

After the Kuomintang's Northern Expedition the lectures became the canonical statement of Sun's thought. From 1928 the government was organised in the five branches (the Executive, Legislative, Judicial, Control and Examination Yuan), and the principles were treated as dogma with rituals such as bowing to Sun's portrait. His Whampoa address was chosen as the party anthem in 1930 and the national anthem in 1937.

The Chinese Communist Party cooperated with the Kuomintang on this basis in the Second United Front. In On New Democracy (1940) Mao reinterpreted them as New Three Principles. Under Deng Xiaoping, Sun was praised for plans of development linked to the Four Modernizations. The principles also inspired the Vietnamese Quốc Dân Đảng and the Tibetan reformer Pandatsang Rapga, who translated them into Tibetan.
three-principles-of-the-people-song: The text was a collaboration between several Kuomintang members: Hu Hanmin, Tai Chi-tao, Liao Zhongkai and Shao Yuanchong. It was first heard on 16 June 1924, as the opening of a speech by Sun Yat-sen at the opening ceremony of the Whampoa Military Academy. After the success of the Northern Expedition, the Kuomintang chose the text as its party anthem and publicly asked for music to go with it. Cheng Maoyun won a contest of 139 participants.

On 24 March 1930 numerous party members proposed that Sun's speech serve as the words of the national anthem. At the time the anthem of the republic was the Song to the Auspicious Cloud. Because many objected to a political party's symbol representing the whole nation, the National Anthem Editing and Research Committee was set up, and it endorsed the party song. The Central Standing Committee approved the proposal on 3 June 1937, and the song became the official national anthem in the 1940s.

The lyrics are in classical literary Chinese and follow classical poetic conventions. They keep to the ancient Fu style of four-character lines, in which the last character of each line rhymes in -ong or -eng. Several words are archaic: ěr is a literary form of you, here plural, fěi is a classical word for not, and zī is an old interjection no longer used in this sense in the modern language. The words relate to how the vision and hopes of a new nation and its people can be achieved and maintained.

In this respect the anthem differs from the March of the Volunteers, the anthem of the People's Republic of China, which was written a few years later entirely in modern vernacular Chinese. The song is sometimes called San Min Chu-i, after its opening line, which refers to the Three Principles of the People, but the name is never used on formal or official occasions. An official English translation by Theodore B. Tu appears in English-language guides to the Republic of China published by the government.

The anthem became the national anthem in Taiwan on 25 October 1945, after Taiwan returned to Chinese rule following the surrender of Japan. When the government of the Republic of China retreated to Taiwan and the People's Republic was established, the song was discontinued as a national anthem on the mainland and replaced there by the March of the Volunteers. At flag-raising ceremonies it is played first, followed by the National Flag Anthem during the raising itself. For many Taiwanese the anthem carries a number of meanings, often conflicting. Some reject it outright as an anachronistic symbol of the defeated Kuomintang dictatorship.
three-qins: In late 208 BCE King Huai II of Chu promised that whoever first entered Guanzhong would rule it. Liu Bang did so in late 207 BCE, taking the Qin capital Xianyang and the surrender of Ziying, the last king of Qin, and winning local support by abolishing the harsh Qin laws. Xiang Yu ignored the promise and in January 206 BCE sent Liu Bang to the remote lands of Hanzhong, Ba and Shu as king of Han, with only 30,000 soldiers.

Wishing to rule his own Chu homeland, Xiang Yu divided Guanzhong among three Qin generals who had surrendered to him after the Battle of Yushui River in July 207 BCE. Zhang Han, the former Qin general-in-chief, received Yong in central Shaanxi and the task of guarding the Qinling passes; Sima Xin received Sai in the northeast and Dong Yi received Di in the north.

Liu Bang's army suffered from shortages and desertions in Hanzhong, but he made Han Xin his general-in-chief, and Han Xin urged a quick invasion while the three kings were new and disliked for having gone over to Xiang Yu. In August 206 BCE he repaired the Ziwu Road as a feint while the main army took the little-used Chencang Road, seized the Sanguan Pass and defeated Zhang Han outside Chencang. Zhang Han fell back to his capital Feiqiu, and the Han forces took Yong, Tai and Haozhi, beat the combined armies of the three kingdoms east of Rang, and occupied Xianyang, which Liu Bang renamed Xincheng.

A Sai and Yong attack on the Han garrison at Jingling failed after twenty days. Sima Xin then surrendered at his capital Yueyang, where Liu Bang moved his headquarters, and Dong Yi surrendered without a fight at Gaonu, the capital of Di. By September Guanzhong was the administrative centre of Liu Bang's dominion.

Feiqiu held out while Liu Bang expanded into the Central Plain and, from April 205 BCE, waged open war on Xiang Yu. By June Han Xin had taken over the siege and had Fan Kuai dig a channel from the Wei River to soak the mudbrick walls, which collapsed after a few days; Zhang Han killed himself as the Han troops entered. The three kingdoms became three prefectures, and after the Han victory Guanzhong became the crown land of the Han dynasty, with its capital at Chang'an near the old Qin capital.
three-seals-law: King Rama I took pains to preserve the Thai texts that had survived the fall of Ayutthaya, among them the royal chronicles and religious works, and in 1804 he completed a revision of the Tipiṭaka, the Buddhist canon. He then turned to the laws. A court had granted a divorce to a woman, Amdaeng Pom, although she had committed adultery, and her husband Bunsi petitioned that the judge had been biased. Every copy of the marriage law upheld her right, which led the king to suspect that the texts had been tampered with.

His preface ordered learned men to cleanse the royal decrees and laws in the palace library from the Thammasat onwards, make them agree with the Pali, arrange them in chapters and correct any departures from justice. The commission was made up of three judges, four royal scribes and four officials of the Department of Royal Teachers.

The laws were written in the folding books known as samut thai khao. Some of the 27 texts hold several laws, 41 in all, and the prefaces date each law in the Chula Sakarat era, though many of these dates were plainly corrupted in copying. Three working copies were kept, in the Royal Bedchamber, the court of justice and the Palace Library, with a fourth made soon after as a backup. Through neglect the volumes were scattered, and a search in 1980 found 80 volumes of the original copies and 17 of the backup. A Penal Code of 1908 and a Civil and Commercial Code issued between 1923 and 1935 replaced much of it; the surviving parts include the Lak Inthaphat, the Tenets of Indra.

In 1849 Mot Amatyakun and the American missionary Dan Beach Bradley printed an edition, but King Rama III had the books destroyed; one copy of the first volume survives in the National Library of Thailand. With King Mongkut's permission Bradley printed it in two volumes in 1862–3. The French legal scholar Robert Lingat prepared the edition of 1938–9 for Thammasat University from which all modern editions stem, and the Royal Institute published a facsimile edition in 2007 for the bicentenary. Yoneo Ishii published an English summary in 1986, Michael Vickery questioned the dates in the prefaces, and Tamara Loos traced the code's replacement by modern law.
three-sovereigns-and-five-emperors: Taoist beliefs consist of parables involving shamanistic themes, and these are the origin of most ancient stories about the Sovereigns Fuxi, Nüwa and Shennong. The idea of five emperors appeared in the 5th century BCE. Scholars believe the tradition of succession by abdication appeared in the early Warring States period to support the political agenda of ministers who frequently overthrew their rulers. In the received account, this system was used until Qi of Xia violently seized power and established a hereditary monarchy. The Five Emperors are described as exemplary sages from a golden age when communication between the human order and the divine was central to all life.

There are six to seven known variations on who made up the Three Sovereigns and the Five Emperors, and many of the sources were written in much later dynasties. The Sovereigns are drawn from Fuxi, Nüwa, Shennong, Suiren, Zhu Rong, Gonggong, the Heavenly, Earthly and Human Sovereigns and the Yellow Emperor. The Emperors are drawn from the Yellow Emperor, Zhuanxu, Emperor Ku, Emperor Yao, Emperor Shun, Shaohao, Taihao and the Yan Emperor. The Sovereigns were said to use magical powers, or harmony with the Tao, to improve their people's lives, and to live to a great age over a period of great peace. The Yellow Emperor was said to have become a xian on his death.

The Sovereigns and Emperors are said to have introduced fire, taught people to build houses and invented farming. The Yellow Emperor's wife is credited with silk culture, and the discovery of medicine and the invention of the calendar and Chinese script are also credited to them. After their era, Yu the Great founded the Xia dynasty, traditionally the first dynasty in Chinese historiography. The Yellow Emperor is supposedly the ancestor of the Huaxia people, and his mausoleum was established in Shaanxi to commemorate the legend.
thrissur: Thrissur is the headquarters of Thrissur district in central Kerala, 284 km north-west of the state capital, Thiruvananthapuram. The city is built around a hillock of 65 acres, Thekkinkadu Maidanam, which holds the Vadakkumnathan temple. From the hillock the land flattens into the Thrissur-Ponnani Kole Wetlands, which act as a natural drainage for the city. The name is a shortened form of the Malayalam Thirusshivaperoor, the city of the sacred Lord Shiva, after the temple's presiding deity. The English form Trichur was the official name until 1990. In ancient times it was also called Vrishabhadripuram.

Numerous prehistoric megaliths and dolmens show that the area was inhabited from at least 1000 BCE to 500 CE. It was once a point of contact for Assyrians, Greeks, Persians, Arabs, Romans, Portuguese, Dutch and English, and Christianity, Islam and Judaism are believed to have entered the subcontinent through Thrissur and its surroundings. In the 16th century the Portuguese had naval influence in much of Kerala, and in the early 17th century the Dutch took their place as the main naval power. With Dutch help the royal family of Cochin recaptured Thrissur from the Zamorin of Calicut in 1710.

Thrissur rose to importance when Maharaja Sakthan Thampuran ascended the throne of Cochin and made it his capital. He invited Syrian Christian families and Brahmins from neighbouring areas, and the city became a financial and commercial hub of South India. Hyder Ali, the Sultan of Mysore, conquered it in 1750–60 and made it a tributary of Mysore.

Sakthan Thampuran's successor, Rama Varma X, signed a treaty with the East India Company that made Cochin a British protectorate. Mahatma Gandhi visited the city in 1927 and 1934 to promote civil disobedience. R. K. Shanmukham Chetty, Diwan of Cochin from 1935 to 1941, built the Thrissur Town Hall and other civic buildings. Thrissur district was formed on 1 July 1949, with its headquarters in the city.

Thrissur is known as the cultural capital of Kerala. Its Thrissur Pooram, held at the Vadakkumnathan temple in April or May, is one of the largest temple festivals in the state, with a large gathering of people and elephants lasting thirty-six hours. The city is a centre of banking, gold jewellery and Ayurvedic drugs, and it holds the Kerala Sangeetha Nadaka Academy, Kerala Lalithakala Akademi and Kerala Sahitya Academy. The Our Lady of Dolours Basilica is the largest church in India.
thuan-hoa: The region began as two Cham prefectures, O, Vuyar in Cham, and Ly, Ulik in Cham, which King Che Man of Champa offered in 1306 in exchange for marriage to the Vietnamese princess Huyen Tran. Emperor Tran Anh Tong accepted and renamed them Thuan prefecture and Hoa prefecture, and the two soon came to be called together Thuan Hoa. For long afterwards Vietnamese, Chams and Lao fought one another there. In 1466, under Emperor Le Thanh Tong, it became one of the twelve prefectures of the country and later a province. Portuguese and later French writers knew it as Sinoa, Singoa, Senna or Sinuua, forms that seem to echo the Chinese reading of its name, Shunhua, perhaps heard from Chinese traders.

Later the Mac dynasty seized the throne of the Le, and Nguyen Kim, leader of the Le loyalists, set up a descendant of the Le emperors as a rival southern court. After Kim was poisoned by a Mac general, his son-in-law Trinh Kiem took the lead and had Kim's eldest son, Nguyen Uong, killed. Fearing the same fate, Kim's younger son Nguyen Hoang feigned illness and asked his sister Ngoc Bao, a wife of Trinh Kiem, to win him the governorship of Thuan Hoa, the southernmost region, where Mac loyalists still held out.

Nguyen Hoang pacified the region, and he and his successor Nguyen Phuc Nguyen quietly made it loyal to their family before rising against the Trinh lords. In the civil war that followed, the Nguyen lords built Thuan Hoa, which then stretched from Quang Binh to Thua Thien–Hue, into the base for their war with the Trinh and their expansion southwards.

By the eighteenth century Thuan Hoa and Quang Nam no longer grew much of their own rice and depended on cheaper rice shipped from the Mekong Delta. Under the Nguyen dynasty, Emperor Gia Long made the region part of the capital territory, one of the three divisions of the country. Prime Minister Tran Trong Kim revived the name in mid-1945, but it was dropped again when his Empire of Vietnam fell.
