thubten-gyatso: Thubten Gyatso was born in 1876 in the village of Thakpo Langdun, near Samye Monastery, to a peasant couple, Kunga Rinchen and Lobsang Dolma. In 1878 he was recognised as the reincarnation of the Dalai Lama and escorted to Lhasa, where the Panchen Lama, Tenpai Wangchuk, gave him his novice vows. He was enthroned at the Potala Palace in 1879 but assumed political power only in 1895, from the monasteries that had wielded great influence through the Regent. His tutor and debating partner, the Buryat Mongol Agvan Dorzhiev, later served as his envoy to Russia.

After the British expedition of Sir Francis Younghusband in 1904, Dorzhiev persuaded the Dalai Lama to flee to Urga in Mongolia, a journey of four months. The Treaty of Lhasa was signed by Britain and Tibet on 7 September 1904. The Dalai Lama later stayed at Kumbum Monastery and at Wutai Shan, where he received envoys including Gustaf Mannerheim, and in September 1908 he was received in Beijing by the Guangxu Emperor and Empress Dowager Cixi but refused to kowtow. When a Qing military expedition reached Tibet in 1910 he fled to India, staying in Sikkim and Darjeeling.

After the revolution of 1911 Chinese forces were expelled, and Tibet was proclaimed independent on 4 April 1912. He returned to Lhasa in January 1913 and declared independence on 13 February. He standardised the Tibetan flag, issued Tibet's first stamps and banknotes, built a medical college, set up a taxation system and a police force, and abolished capital punishment. Secular education was added and four students were sent to England. Electricity, the telephone and the first motor cars reached Tibet, and in 1931 a modern army regiment was created. Tibetan forces fought the Sino-Tibetan War of 1930 to 1933, ending in truces in 1933.

The 13th Dalai Lama died on 17 December 1933 and is remembered as the Great Thirteenth. Shortly before his death he predicted that deceptive acts might occur from without and within, and warned that if Tibet did not protect its territory, its spiritual leaders and political system could vanish. He saw at the end of his life that Tibet was about to retreat from outside influences.
thuburbo-maius: The ruins of Thuburbo Maius stand in open countryside in northern Tunisia, with no town close to them. The site lay on a major thoroughfare that ran from Carthage towards the Sahara, passing other towns such as Sbiba, Sufes and Sufetula, and parts of the old Roman road survive. Its position on these trade routes made it an important settlement, and the land around it produced grain, olives and fruit.

Its Roman name was Colonia Julia Aurelia Commoda. Most of the town was built between about 150 and 200, and it received a capitolium in 168. Its promotion to a municipium under Hadrian helped it grow in wealth. After the Crisis of the Third Century the town was restored in the 4th century. The early 3rd-century Christian martyr Perpetua was born there.

A bishopric was founded under the Roman Empire and survived Vandal and Byzantine rule, ceasing only with the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb. Its known bishops include Sedatus, present at the Council of Carthage in 256, and Faustus, at the Council of Arles in 314. At the Council of Carthage of 411 the town was represented by both a Catholic bishop, Cyprianus, and a Donatist, Rufinus. Bishop Benenatus was exiled by the Vandal king Huneric in 484. The see was refounded in name in the 20th century.

An excavation in 1916 uncovered a tetrastyle temple decorated with statues of Apollo, Venus, Silvanus, Bacchus, the Dioscuri and a satyr, together with three perfume vases showing dogs chasing rabbits. An inscription found in 1920 in honour of C. Vettius Sabinianus showed that several other inscriptions bearing that name referred to the same man. In 1925 the House of Bacchus and Ariadne, dating from the early 5th century, was excavated, and evidence of food preparation in its garden has been used to study daily life.

The town's mosaics, of the late 4th century, show a still life of foods, a sea full of fish with young people fishing from boats, and a nude Venus riding a chariot among plants standing for well-being and fertility; the archaeologist Aïcha Ben Abed has studied them. None of the buildings has been fully restored, but the remains include a forum, an amphitheatre, temples, baths and houses.
thucydides: Little is known of Thucydides's life, and the most reliable information comes from his own History. He identifies himself as an Athenian, gives his father's name as Olorus and names his deme as Halimous. He fought in the war, survived the Plague of Athens, which killed Pericles and many other Athenians, and records that he owned gold mines at Scapte Hyle in Thrace, opposite the island of Thasos. A story that as a boy he heard Herodotus lecture and wept with joy is disputed and most likely comes from a later account.

Because of his influence in the Thracian region, Thucydides was sent as a general to Thasos in 424 BCE. In the winter of 424 to 423 BCE the Spartan general Brasidas attacked Amphipolis, half a day's sail to the west, and the Athenian commander there, Eucles, sent to Thucydides for help. Brasidas, aware of Thucydides's influence with the people of Amphipolis, offered moderate terms, and the city surrendered before Thucydides arrived. Its fall caused consternation in Athens and was blamed on him, although he claimed he had been unable to reach it in time. He was exiled.

Later sources on his life are less reliable. Pausanias says a law passed by Oenobius allowed him to return to Athens after the war ended in 404 BCE and that he was murdered on the way, while Plutarch preserves a tradition that he was murdered at Scapte Hyle and that his remains were brought to Athens. Many doubt the first account, and the evidence suggests he may have lived as late as 397 BCE or slightly later.

Thucydides began to write the History of the Peloponnesian War at the outbreak of the war in 431 BCE, believing it of unmatched importance, and intended it as a possession for all time. It breaks off in the middle of 411 BCE, after the Athenian defeat at Syracuse, so it does not cover the last seven years of the war. The division into eight books was probably made after his death by scholars of Alexandria. He values eyewitness testimony, consulted written documents and interviewed participants, and unlike Herodotus he does not acknowledge divine intervention in human affairs.

He admired Pericles and disliked the demagogues who followed him, such as Cleon and Hyperbolus, but his account is generally even-handed, and he does not minimise the effect of his own failure at Amphipolis. Scholars have seen in him the influence of the Sophists and of Hippocratic medical writing, and the Melian dialogue and his version of Pericles's Funeral Oration are widely studied. Historians such as Jacqueline de Romilly have stressed his concern with Athenian imperialism, and others have read him as a tragedian in the tradition of Homer.
thuin: Thuin is a city and municipality of Wallonia in the province of Hainaut, Belgium. The area was already used as a burial place in Gallo-Roman times, around the 2nd and 3rd century. The earliest name of the settlement, Thudinium Castellum, refers to a Roman fortification and appears on a 9th-century offering in Lobbes Abbey, which lists neighbouring towns and their tithe duties.

The village was a possession of the abbey of Lobbes and, together with the abbey, became part of the Bishopric of Liège in 888. A century later Prince-Bishop Notger had a defensive wall built in Thuin, which became the westernmost of the 23 bonnes villes of the bishopric. In 1048 Adalbert, Duke of Lorraine, was killed at the Battle of Thuin by Godfrey III, Duke of Lower Lorraine, and many more battles followed between the County of Hainaut and the Bishopric of Liège.

In 1654 the Spanish army under the Prince of Condé tried in vain to take the town, a result attributed to the intercession of Saint Roch. Troops of Louis XIV took it in 1675 and occupied it until 1678. On 10 May 1794 General Marceau expelled the Austrians and Thuin became part of France.

The 17th-century belfry is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Other sights include the ruins of the 7th-century Aulne Abbey, burned to the ground in 1794, the 14th- and 15th-century Château du Fosteau, the hanging gardens on the southern flank of the hill, and a museum of the Belgian Vicinal tramway system with a museum tramway. Every third Sunday of May the town commemorates Saint Roch's help in 1654 with a procession that was banned in the 18th century and reinstated in 1866 after a cholera epidemic.
thukela-river: The Thukela, called the Tugela for most of the 20th century, is the largest river in KwaZulu-Natal and one of the most important rivers of South Africa. It rises in the Drakensberg range at Mont-aux-Sources, the source also of the Orange and Caledon rivers, and flows through the KwaZulu-Natal midlands to the Indian Ocean. It drops 1 370 metres in its lower 480 kilometres, and its catchment covers about 29,100 square kilometres, where land use is mainly rural subsistence farming and commercial forestry.

The largest of its tributaries is the Mzinyathi, or Buffalo, River, which joins about 19 kilometres east of Tugela Ferry. The others include the Little Tugela, Klip, Mooi, Blood, Sundays, Ingagani and Bushman rivers. The Blood River was named by the Boers, led by Andries Pretorius, after they defeated the Zulu king Dingane on 16 December 1838, when the river is said to have run red with the blood of Zulu warriors. Below it lies Rorke's Drift, a crossing point and the site of a battle in the Anglo-Zulu War.

The scaly yellowfish, Labeobarbus natalensis, a common fish found only in KwaZulu-Natal, lives in the Tugela system. The spelling Tugela, an Anglicised form of the Zulu name Thukela, was used for most of the 20th century. Earlier writers used many other spellings: Isaacs in 1836 wrote Ootergale and Ootoogale, C. R. Maclean in 1853 wrote Zootagoola, and the artist George French Angas wrote Tugala. Some of the variation arose because early European writers did not know that Zulu grammar uses prefixes such as i- or u- to mark the class of a noun.
thun: Thun lies in the canton of Bern, 30 kilometres south-east of Bern, where the Aare flows out of Lake Thun. The centre stands on both banks of the river and on an island between them, at about 560 metres above sea level, and the municipality covers 21.6 square kilometres. From the town there are views of the Bernese Alps, including the Niesen, the Stockhorn and the peaks of the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.

The area was inhabited from the Neolithic age. A site at Renzenbühl held a grave with one of the richest collections of early Bronze Age artifacts in Europe, including the Thun-Renzenbühl axe, from about 1800 BCE, one of the earliest examples of damascening in the world.

The name derives from the Celtic Dunum, meaning fortified town. Thun fell to Rome in 58 BCE, when Roman legions conquered almost all of Switzerland, and it soon became one of the main centres of Roman administration in the region. Around 400 CE the Burgundians drove the Romans out, and the Aare became the frontier between the Christian Burgundians and the pagan, German-speaking Alemanni to the north. The town is first mentioned in 1133 as Tuno.

The region became part of the Holy Roman Empire in 1033, when Conrad II gained the title of King of Burgundy. The emperors entrusted the Zähringen family with subduing the unruly nobles of central Switzerland, and Duke Bertold V of Zähringen built Thun castle and expanded the town. After his death in 1218 his territories went to Ulrich III von Kyburg. Thun received town rights in 1264, and in 1384 the canton of Bern bought the town. It was the capital of the Canton of Oberland of the Helvetic Republic from 1798 to 1803.
A military school founded in 1819 later became the main military school in Switzerland. Thun was connected to the Swiss railway network in 1859, and telephone access arrived in 1888.

Thun has about 45,000 inhabitants and around 80,000 live in its agglomeration. Most speak German. Its economy rests on tourism, machine and precision instrument engineering, the food industry, armaments and publishing, and it has the largest garrison in the country. Thun Castle, with a history museum, and the 16th-century town hall are its main sights. The Wocher Panorama is the oldest remaining panorama drawing in the world, and the paddle steamer Blüemlisalp is listed among the Swiss heritage sites of national significance. The railway station is the main node for buses and for the passenger ships on Lake Thun.
thurgau: Thurgau is one of the 26 cantons of the Swiss Confederation, in Eastern Switzerland, with its capital at Frauenfeld. It is named after the river Thur and is bounded to the north by Lake Constance, with the High Rhine forming part of the border in the northwest. The name Thurgovia was historically used for a larger area that took in much of the modern canton of St. Gallen, the Appenzell lands and the eastern parts of the canton of Zurich.

In the Neolithic period the land was inhabited by the Pfyn culture, named after Pfyn on Lake Constance. In Roman times it belonged to the province of Raetia until 450, when the Alemanni settled; Roman settlements included Ad Fines (Pfyn), Arbor Felix and Tasgetium. In the sixth century Thurgovia became a Gau of Francia as part of Alamannia, and it passed to the Duchy of Swabia in the early 10th century. Its most important early medieval cities were Konstanz, seat of the bishop, and St. Gallen, home of the Abbey of Saint Gall.

The dukes of Zähringen and the counts of Kyburg took over much of the land in the High Middle Ages. Zurich left Thurgau in 1218, and when the Kyburg dynasty became extinct in 1264 the House of Habsburg took over its lands. In 1460 the Old Swiss Confederacy, allied with ten freed bailiwicks of the former Toggenburg, seized the territory from the Habsburgs, and it became a subject territory of seven cantons: Zurich, Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug and Glarus.

In 1524 local peasants occupied the cloister of Ittingen, driving out the monks. Between 1526 and 1531 most of the population adopted the Reformed faith from Zurich, but Zurich's defeat in the Second War of Kappel in 1531 ended Reformed predominance, and the First Peace of Kappel protected both faiths. Zurich briefly occupied the region in the First War of Villmergen in 1656. Thurgau became a canton in 1798 under the Helvetic Republic and a member of the Confederation in 1803 under the Act of Mediation.

The canton has five districts and 282,909 inhabitants in December 2020, and is mostly German speaking. Its current constitution dates from 1987. Thurgau is known for apples and pears, many of them grown for cider, and for wine from the Thur valley.
thurgood-marshall: Thurgood Marshall was born on 2 July 1908 in Baltimore, Maryland, the son of Norma and William Canfield Marshall. His father worked as a waiter and his mother was an elementary school teacher. His father followed legal cases as a hobby, and Thurgood often went to court with him. Marshall later said that his father never told him to become a lawyer but turned him into one by making him prove every statement. He attended Lincoln University and the Howard University School of Law, where Charles Hamilton Houston taught students to be social engineers willing to use the law against discrimination.

Marshall opened a law practice in Baltimore and volunteered with the local NAACP. In 1935 he and Houston won Murray v. Pearson, forcing the University of Maryland's law school to admit a black applicant. He then joined Houston at the NAACP in New York and became director-counsel of the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund. He took part in landmark cases including Smith v. Allwright, Shelley v. Kraemer and Sweatt v. Painter, and argued Brown v. Board of Education, decided in 1954, using sociological data to show that segregation was inherently unequal. He won 29 of the 32 civil rights cases he argued before the Supreme Court.

President John F. Kennedy named him to the Second Circuit Court of Appeals in 1961, and President Lyndon B. Johnson made him solicitor general in 1965. In 1967 Johnson nominated him to replace Tom C. Clark on the Supreme Court, and the Senate confirmed him by 69 votes to 11. After Richard Nixon's appointments he was often in dissent. He and William J. Brennan Jr. dissented in more than 1,400 cases in which the Court refused to review a death sentence, since he held that capital punishment was cruel and unusual.

Marshall announced his retirement on 27 June 1991, and it took effect on 1 October. He died of heart failure on 24 January 1993, aged 84. He lay in repose in the Great Hall of the Supreme Court, and more than four thousand people attended his funeral at the Washington National Cathedral.
thuringia: Thuringia is a landlocked state in the middle of Germany, bordered by Bavaria, Hesse, Lower Saxony, Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt. It has been called the green heart of Germany since the late 19th century because of its broad, dense forest, and most of it lies in the drainage basin of the Saale, a left-bank tributary of the Elbe. The Thuringian Basin is the driest part of Germany, with only 400 to 500 mm of rain a year. The natural vegetation is beech forest, though centuries of settlement mean that most plains are cleared for farming and most forests are planted with spruce and pine.

The name derives from the Germanic tribe of the Thuringii, who emerged during the Migration Period. Their origin is largely unknown: an older theory made them successors of the Hermunduri, which later research rejected, and other historians argue that they were allies of the Huns. They were first mentioned around 400, when they were known for their excellent horses. The first documented duke of Thuringia was a local noble, Radulf I, appointed by King Dagobert I in the early 630s. He secured the borders on the Saale against Slavic incursions, but in 641 or 642 rebelled against Dagobert's successor Sigebert III and declared himself king of Thuringia.

In the Middle Ages the Saale marked the border between Germanic and Slavic territories, and the movement of eastward settlement assimilated the Slavic population between the 11th and 13th centuries. Thuringia generally accepted the Protestant Reformation, and Roman Catholicism was suppressed as early as 1520. The German Peasants' War of 1525 destroyed many churches and monasteries, and Thomas Müntzer was active among the Anabaptists of Mühlhausen. Catholicism survived within the modern borders only in the Eichsfeld, ruled by the Archbishop of Mainz, and in and near Erfurt.

The modern state was established in 1920 under the Weimar Republic by merging the Ernestine duchies; only Saxe-Coburg voted to join Bavaria instead, and Weimar became the capital. After the Second World War Thuringia lay in the Soviet occupation zone, became part of the German Democratic Republic in 1949, and was dissolved in 1952 into the districts of Erfurt, Suhl and Gera. It was re-established in 1990 after reunification. The Free State of Thuringia has about 2.1 million inhabitants, and its capital and largest city is Erfurt. The Wartburg castle, Classical Weimar and Bauhaus Weimar are UNESCO World Heritage Site listings, and the University of Jena was founded in 1558.
thuringian-forest: The Thuringian Forest runs north-west to south-east through the southern part of Thuringia. The Werra valley skirts it on the south-west, and beyond its north-eastern side lies the Thuringian Basin, which includes the city of Erfurt. Eisenach, Gotha and Arnstadt stand among the foothills at its northern foot, and Ilmenau and Suhl sit in dips on the range itself. It is a continuous chain of ancient rounded mountains with steep slopes on both sides, and it can be crossed easily only through a few passes.

Geologically the range is an uplifted fault block of sandstones, conglomerates, granites, gneisses and volcanic rock. Its uplift, understood as a long-range effect of the Alpine orogeny, began in the upper Cretaceous and ended in the late Tertiary after about 40 million years. Humid air arrives mainly from the west, so the western slopes and the crest receive the most rain, while the Thuringian Basin on the leeward side is one of the driest regions in Germany.

Ore deposits associated with the uplift have been of historical importance to the region, notably in the metalworking tradition of Suhl and the mining history of Ilmenau. The name of the Großer Eisenberg bears witness to past ore mining. Mining for fluorite, baryte and limonite was tried several times in the Little Thuringian Forest, a narrow ridge south of Suhl, but was given up as unprofitable because of difficult drainage.

The Rennsteig, an ancient path, follows the main ridge and connects the summits. It marks the traditional boundary between the hilly terrain of central Germany and the more rugged terrain of southern Germany, and also the boundary between the cultural regions of Thuringia and Franconia, with different dialects, customs and costumes on either side. The slopes were once divided among small states: at the Großer Dreiherrnstein the territories of Schwarzburg-Arnstadt, Saxe-Eisenach and Henneberg met at a tripoint. Wartburg Castle, near Eisenach, is where Martin Luther lived in exile.

The forest is an important year-round tourist destination, with winter sports facilities of international significance around Oberhof. The Rennsteig is the most popular long-distance hiking trail in Germany, and the Rennsteiglied, written about it, is the unofficial hymn of Thuringia. Sights include the Marienglashöhle, a selenite cave in a former mine near Friedrichroda, the firearms museum in Suhl, and the historic town centres of Eisenach and Ilmenau.
thuringian-highlands: The Thuringian Highland, in German the Thüringer Schiefergebirge or Thuringian Slate Hills, is a low range bordering the Thuringian Forest to the south-west. It forms a plateau about 20 km wide that slopes south-east towards the Saale valley. Together with the slate hills of the Vogtland it stretches from the Thuringian Forest to the Ore Mountains, about 75 km from east to west and 50 km from north to south, and forms part of the backbone of the Central Uplands. Its four smaller regions are the upper Saale valley, the Plothen Lake District, the high slate mountains and the Sormitz-Schwarza region.

The rocks date from the Palaeozoic era, from the Ordovician to the Lower Carboniferous: shale, limestone, sandstone, greywacke and volcanic rocks among them. Unlike the Harz, which formed in a similar way, the region lacks sharp fault lines and passes gradually into the land around it. Cave-forming limestone occurs only in a few small patches, so there are very few caves. Typical of the landscape are wooded dolerite peaks such as the Pöhlde and the Hübel, which stand out because this hard volcanic rock weathers more slowly than the rock around it.

The rolling hills mostly lie between about 300 m and 500 m, but around the steep valleys of the Schwarza and Saale the drop from hilltop to valley floor often reaches 300 m or more. The highest summits, in the Sonneberg and Hildburghausen districts, include the Großer Farmdenkopf at 869 m, the Kieferle at 867 m and the Bleßberg at 865 m.

The largest towns are Saalfeld and Bad Blankenburg on the northern edge, Neuhaus am Rennweg in the highest part and Bad Lobenstein in the east, where the hills pass into the Franconian Forest. Two of the largest dams in Germany hold back the Hohenwarte and Bleiloch Reservoirs on the Saale, and the Goldisthal Pumped Storage Station in the Schwarza valley, opened in 2003, is one of the largest of its kind in Europe. Parts of the area lie in the Thuringian Forest and Thuringian Highland and Upper Saale Nature Park.
thurisind: Nothing is known of Thurisind's early life. The Gepids, an East Germanic people, held the eastern part of the Pannonian Basin, and their kingdom, Gepidia, had its centre at Sirmium on the Sava River, today Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia. Around 548, after the death of King Elemund, Thurisind seized the throne in a coup d'état and forced Elemund's son Ostrogotha into exile among the Lombards. The scholar István Boná sees his rise as typical of the struggles among leading families that made the Gepid succession unstable. Thurisind made his eldest son Turismod commander at Sirmium, and so heir apparent.

Emperor Justinian resented the Gepid takeover of Sirmium in 537 and had encouraged the Lombards under Audoin to move into Pannonia to contain them. When Thurisind and Audoin both sent embassies to Constantinople, Justinian sided with the Lombards. In the first war, dated to 547 or 549, Thurisind offered a truce before a Byzantine army of 10,000 horsemen under John, magister militum of Illyricum, arrived. In 549 or 550 both armies panicked and no battle was fought, perhaps, Boná suggests, because of a lunar eclipse. Thurisind then ferried Kutrigur and Sclaveni raiders across the Danube into Byzantine territory.

In 551 or 552 Audoin crushed the Gepids at the Battle of Asfeld west of Sirmium, which Jordanes counted among the bloodiest fought in the region, with no fewer than 60,000 killed. Paul the Deacon writes that the duel in which Alboin killed Turismod decided the war. Justinian imposed an eternal peace that preserved the Gepid kingdom, and Thurisind had to return Dacia ripensis and Singidunum.

To settle the peace, Thurisind and Audoin each secretly had his royal guest murdered, the Lombard pretender Ildigis and Ostrogotha. Paul the Deacon tells how Alboin came with 40 companions to Thurisind's court to be armed by a foreign king, and how Thurisind kept the peace and gave him Turismod's arms; the tale probably comes from a heroic poem. Thurisind died around 560. His son Cunimund was killed by Alboin in 567, when the Lombards and Avars destroyed the Gepid kingdom.
thutmose-i: Thutmose I was the third pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty and came to the throne after the death of Amenhotep I. He never called himself Son of the King, so he is believed to have been born outside the royal family, to a woman named Senseneb and an unknown father. His wife, Queen Ahmose, was probably a daughter of Ahmose I and a sister of Amenhotep I, though she was never called king's daughter and some historians think she was Thutmose's sister. His children included Hatshepsut and Nefrubity, by Ahmose, and a son by Mutnofret who became Thutmose II.

Nubia rebelled when Thutmose was crowned. According to the tomb autobiography of Ahmose, son of Ebana, the king sailed up the Nile and personally killed the Nubian king, and hung his body from the prow of his ship. In his third year he ordered the canal at the first cataract, dug under Sesostris III, to be cleared so ships could pass upstream. A stela at Tombos records a fortress near the third cataract, and an inscription of his reign at Kurgus is the farthest south that Egyptian presence is attested. He appointed a viceroy of Kush, Turi.

In the Levant he campaigned as far as the Euphrates, which he made Egypt's northern border. Texts of his time mention Retenu, Naharin and the land of Mitanni, thought to be the first historical reference to that kingdom. As many as 20 sites in the Levant were destroyed in this period, though Egypt set up no permanent presence there. His largest building works were at the Temple of Karnak, under the architect Ineni: a fourth and a fifth pylon, a hypostyle hall with cedar columns, and two obelisks.

Thutmose I is the first king definitely buried in the Valley of the Kings, and Ineni dug his tomb. He was originally buried and then reburied in KV20, jointly with his daughter Hatshepsut, and later moved by his grandson Thutmose III to KV38, which was plundered late in the 20th Dynasty. He was succeeded by his son Thutmose II, and then by Hatshepsut. A mummy found in the Deir el-Bahri cache was long thought to be his, but in 2007 it was announced to be that of a man of about thirty who died of an arrow wound, probably not Thutmose I.
thutmose-iii: Thutmose III was the son of Thutmose II by a secondary wife, Iset. His father's Great Royal Wife was Hatshepsut. When his father died he was too young to rule, and estimates of his age range from two to 13 years. Hatshepsut became his regent and eventually declared herself pharaoh, though she never denied kingship to Thutmose III. For the first 22 years of his reign he was therefore a junior co-regent while she held the senior place. When he was old enough and had shown his capacity, Hatshepsut appointed him to head her armies, and he became sole ruler after her death around 1458 BCE.

The dating of the reign depends on the chronology used. The Low Chronology gives 1479 to 1425 BCE, the convention in academic circles since the 1960s, while some scholars prefer 1504 to 1450 BCE. The length of the reign is known to the day from the tomb of the commander Amenemheb, who records his death in the 54th regnal year, corresponding to 11 March 1425 BCE.

Thutmose III conducted at least 16 campaigns in 20 years, recorded in the Annals inscribed on the walls of the temple of Amun at Karnak. The first led to the Battle of Megiddo. In his eighth campaign, in Year 33, he carried boats overland, crossed the Euphrates and attacked Mitanni, setting up a stele beside the one his grandfather Thutmose I had raised. To prevent rebellion in Syria he took hostages from the noble families of its cities. His last campaign, in Year 50, reached the fourth cataract of the Nile in Nubia. The Egyptologist James Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt.

He built more than 50 temples and gave Karnak more attention than any other site, adding Pylon VI, a wall around the central sanctuary and a jubilee hall in an early basilica style. Some of Hatshepsut's monuments were defaced after her death. Earlier scholars read this as vengeance and an erasure of her memory by Thutmose III, an interpretation presented as a theory.

Two years before his death, after the death of his firstborn son Amenemhat, Thutmose III appointed Amenhotep II as junior co-regent and successor. His tomb, KV34, was found in the Valley of the Kings by Victor Loret in 1898. His mummy was discovered in the Deir el-Bahari Cache in 1881, along with those of other pharaohs of the 18th and 19th Dynasty.
thutmose-iv: Thutmose IV, whose name means Born of Thoth, was the eighth pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty. He was the son of Amenhotep II and Tiaa and the grandfather of Akhenaten. His throne name, Menkheperure, means Established in forms is Re. He was not the crown prince or Amenhotep II's chosen successor, and some scholars speculate that he ousted an older brother to take power.

His best-known act was the restoration of the Great Sphinx of Giza. According to the Dream Stele, which he set between the Sphinx's paws, the young prince fell asleep while hunting in its shadow, the statue being buried up to the neck in sand. The Sphinx spoke to him in the dream and promised that if he cleared away the sand he would become the next pharaoh. Scholars regard the stele, and an inscription about a falcon-shaped stone he found as a child, as propaganda meant to give legitimacy to his unexpected kingship.

Little is known of his rule. He suppressed a minor uprising in Nubia in his eighth year, attested on his Konosso stela, and a stela calls him Conqueror of Syria. Betsy Bryan, his biographer, reads the Konosso stela as referring to a minor desert patrol to protect gold-mine routes in the Eastern Desert against occasional Nubian attacks.

His rule is significant for peaceful relations with Mitanni, which he sealed by marrying a Mitannian princess, possibly Henutempet. The Amarna letter EA 29, written decades later by the Mitanni king Tushratta, says that Thutmose wrote to Tushratta's grandfather Artatama five or six times for his daughter, and that only after a seventh request was she given. His reign is usually put at nine or ten years, with Manetho crediting him with nine years and eight months; no date later than his year 8 is firmly his.

He completed the eastern obelisk at the Temple of Karnak begun by Thutmose III, at 32 metres the tallest obelisk ever erected in Egypt. Constantius II took it to Rome in 357, and Pope Sixtus V re-erected it in 1588 as the Lateran Obelisk.

Thutmose IV was buried in tomb KV43 in the Valley of the Kings, which appears to have been unfinished at his death, and his body was later moved to the mummy cache in KV35, where Victor Loret found it in 1898. Examination showed him extremely emaciated at death, with an age estimated at 25 to 28 or possibly more. His son Amenhotep III succeeded him.
thyra: Thyra is one of the first queens of Denmark whom scholars regard as historical, but no contemporary source beyond runic inscriptions survives, and her story rests on 12th- and 13th-century accounts that disagree with one another. Saxo Grammaticus made her a daughter of King Æthelred the Unready, a claim that supported Danish kings' rights to the English throne in his own day. Sven Aggesen made her a German whose marriage was arranged by the German emperor, to whom Gorm owed tribute, and who then refused to pay it.

Gorm became king around 936, but it is unknown whether he was already married to Thyra or when she became queen. Because of her prominence on the runestones, some historians have proposed that she belonged to an older royal line and that Gorm became king by marrying her. Besides Harald Bluetooth, she and Gorm were probably the parents of a son, Canute; the Historia Norwegiæ adds a daughter, Gunnhild, Mother of Kings, which no other evidence supports.

The northern mound at Jelling is traditionally called Thyras Høj, though no body was found in it when it was excavated; wood from it has been dated by tree rings to 959-960, the latest date for her death if it is her grave. Saxo has her outlive Gorm, who died around 963, but she is generally believed to have died first, since he raised a stone to her. A minority view holds that the words Danmarkar bót on that stone refer to Gorm, not to her.

Saxo and Aggesen describe her as a wise queen who ordered the building of the Danevirke; Aggesen says she persuaded the emperor that the works were meant to protect Germany from Gorm. The first phase of the fortifications in fact predates her, with timbers felled in 737. Her name appears on five more Danish runestones. Analysis of the carving suggests that at least four, among them the Læborg and Bække 1 stones, commemorate the same woman, which would make her the person named on the most runestones of Viking Age Denmark.
tian: Shang dynasty inscriptions name the highest deity Di or Shangdi and do not mention Tian, which appears mainly in Zhou texts. The sinologist Herrlee Creel concluded that Tian was originally a Zhou deity, identified with the Shang god Di after the Zhou conquest, much as the Romans identified Zeus with Jupiter. Some oracle bone and bronze forms of the character show a human figure with an enlarged head, a great person, and Creel proposed that the word first meant king or kings before coming to mean ancestral kings, a single supreme deity, the realm of the gods and the visible sky.

Tian could mean a supreme power over gods and humans, a force bringing order or catastrophe, destiny, a deity, or a holy world. In Confucianism and Taoism it was paired with Di, Earth, the two poles of reality, with humanity belonging to Earth. Confucius trusted Heaven as overruling human effort; in the Analects he says that at fifty he knew the decrees of Heaven and that, though no one knew him, Heaven did. For Mozi, Heaven was the divine ruler as the Son of Heaven was the earthly one, and because Heaven loves all people equally, people should love one another impartially.

Mount Tai was traditionally the chief place where emperors offered sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, and before the 20th century the worship of Tian was considered an orthodox cosmic principle in China. Three schools described its structure: a canopy over the earth, a rotating sphere around it, and infinite space in which the heavenly bodies float, moved by qi. These views shaped ideas of the universe until the 17th century, when cosmological theories introduced from Europe gradually replaced them. Taoist traditions counted many heavens, often 36 arranged on six levels, and in Buddhist cosmology the word names the heavenly realms and pure lands.
tian-han: Tian Han was born Tian Shouchang on 12 March 1898 in Maoping Village, Changsha County, Hunan, into a poor family. His father died when he was nine, and his mother raised three sons alone, telling them stories from operas. Inspired by the Xinhai Revolution, he changed his name to Han in 1911, and at 13 he wrote a short opera, Xin jiaozi, which was published in the Changsha Daily.

In Japan he developed a lasting interest in modern drama and film and set himself the goal of becoming China's Ibsen. There he helped to organise the Young China Association in 1919, co-founded the Creation Society with Guo Moruo and translated Oscar Wilde's Salomé in 1921.

Back in Shanghai, Tian founded the Southern Film Society in 1926, which became the Southern Society. In 1927 he coined the term huaju, spoken drama, to stress the medium's use of dialogue rather than music. His one-act plays of the late 1920s, among them Tragedy on the Lakeshore, blended melodrama with critical realism.

In April 1930 he published "Our Self-Criticism", announcing his turn to left-wing literature; the Nationalist government closed the Southern Society that September. He effectively led the League of Left-Wing Dramatists and joined the Chinese Communist Party in the spring of 1932. His plays then grew more political, with The Rainy Season (1931) showing factory workers' class struggle.

In late 1934 he wrote the film story Sons and Daughters in a Time of Storm and the poem that became its theme song, March of the Volunteers, set to music by Nie Er. He was arrested in Shanghai in 1935 and released in July. During the Second Sino-Japanese War he organised troupes and singing campaigns in Wuhan and Guilin. After 1949 he directed the Ministry of Culture's Opera Reform Bureau and in 1953 became chairman of the Chinese Dramatists Association; his Xie Yaohuan (1961) is often considered his finest drama.

By 1964 Xie Yaohuan was attacked as a veiled criticism of Mao Zedong, and on 1 February 1966 the People's Daily denounced it as a poisonous weed. Rebels seized Tian on the night of 4 December 1966, and he was held without his medicines for two years.

He died on 10 December 1968, recorded in hospital under the name Li Wu, and his family was not told. His ashes were scattered. He was posthumously rehabilitated in 1979, and his words for the anthem, banned in the meantime, were restored on 4 December 1982. He wrote more than 60 spoken dramas and operas and more than 2,000 poems.
tian-heng: Tian Heng followed his elder brother Tian Rong through the late Qin rebellions and the Chu–Han Contention. The brothers served several claimants to the throne of Qi before Tian Rong rose and took it himself. Xiang Yu, who saw him as a threat to the order he had set up after Qin, attacked Qi and defeated Tian Rong, who was killed, and installed Tian Jia, younger brother of King Tian Jian. Tian Heng's forces drove Tian Jia out, and in 205 BCE he made Tian Rong's son Tian Guang king.

In 203 BCE Liu Bang, King of Han, sent his adviser Li Yiji to persuade Qi to submit, and the king agreed. The Han general Han Xin, on the advice of Kuai Che, attacked anyway. Tian Guang and Tian Heng, enraged by what seemed a ruse, had Li Yiji boiled alive. Han Xin quickly defeated the surprised Qi army and took the capital Linzi; Tian Guang was captured and killed despite help from Chu. Tian Heng proclaimed himself King of Qi and fled to Peng Yue, King of Liang.

After Xiang Yu's defeat at Gaixia, Liu Bang made himself emperor, and Tian Heng took his followers to an island. Fearing his influence in Qi, Liu Bang offered a pardon. Tian Heng said he feared the revenge of Li Shang, Li Yiji's brother and now a Han general; Liu Bang forbade Li Shang on pain of the execution of his family to harm him, while threatening force if Tian Heng did not come at once.

Tian Heng set out for Luoyang with two retainers. At the carriage station of Shixiang, some thirty li from the city, he told them he could not bear to face north and serve the man who had once been his equal, beside the brother of the man he had boiled, and bade them carry his head to the emperor. He then cut his own throat. Liu Bang wept and had him buried with royal honours; the two retainers killed themselves beside the grave, and the followers on the island did the same when they heard. Tian Heng Island, off Jimo in the Yellow Sea, is said to be their refuge, though no archaeological evidence confirms it.
tian-mi-mi: The Taiwanese singer Teresa Teng recorded an Indonesian-language cover of Dayung Sampan while touring Southeast Asia in 1978. On 14 February 1979 she was arrested in Japan and deported to Hong Kong for travelling on an Indonesian passport that Japan found had been obtained from the Indonesian embassy in Hong Kong under suspicious circumstances. Barred from Japan for a year, unable to stay permanently in Hong Kong and fearing punishment in Taiwan, she went to the United States and enrolled at the University of Southern California. There, to meet her contract, she made a Mandarin version of the song.

The new Chinese words, by the lyricist Zhuang Nu, turned the fishers' banter into a playful, sweet love song about someone captivated by a familiar smile. Zhuang, who went on to write many of Teng's later songs, is said to have written them in about five minutes once he heard who would sing them. The singer asks where she has seen the face before and remembers that it was in her dreams; the critic Hua Hsu of The New Yorker wrote that despite this bewitched yearning she sounds calm, curious, almost teasing.

The song first appeared on Teng's album An Unforgettable Day, released in Taiwan by Kolin Records, and then on an album of the same name issued by PolyGram Records on 15 November 1979. A Cantonese version, The Day I Met You, with words by Lo Kwak-chan, followed on her first Cantonese album, Irreconcilable, on 18 December 1980.

Tian Mi Mi became widely popular across the Sinophone world and one of Teng's signature works, and young couples use it to declare their feelings. Faye Wong, Stephen Chow, Leon Lai, Yu Quan and Jane Zhang are among those who have covered it. After Teng's death in 1995, Peter Chan's Hong Kong film Comrades: Almost a Love Story, starring Maggie Cheung and Leon Lai, took its Chinese title from the song in 1996 and used her music throughout. When the film was at last approved for release in mainland China in 2015, Luhan recorded a new version for its soundtrack.
tian-shan: The Tian Shan, also known as the Tengri Tagh or Tengir-Too, is a large system of mountain ranges in Central Asia. It lies north and west of the Taklamakan Desert and directly north of the Tarim Basin, and straddles the border regions of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Xinjiang in northwest China. In the south it connects with the Pamir Mountains, and to the north and east it meets the Altai Mountains of Mongolia. It forms part of the Himalayan orogenic belt, produced by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates in the Cenozoic era. Its highest peak, Jengish Chokusu, rises to 7,439 metres, and its lowest point is the Turpan Depression, 154 metres below sea level.

One of the earliest references to the mountains may be the Xiongnu word Qilian, which the Tang commentator Yan Shigu said meant sky or heaven. Sima Qian mentioned Qilian in the Records of the Grand Historian in connection with the homeland of the Yuezhi, and the term is believed to refer to the Tian Shan rather than the Qilian Mountains about 1,500 km further east. The lower, forested Alatau ranges in the northern Tian Shan are home to Turkic-speaking pastoral tribes. In Tengrism the mountains are sacred, and Khan Tengri, the second-highest peak, means Lord of the Spirits.

Around 950 CE Satuq Bughra Khan converted to Islam, which marked a major turning point in the spread of Islam among the Turkic peoples of the region. The tulip is said to have originated in the Tian Shan and to have reached Turkey along the Silk Road, and the strain of Y. pestis that caused the Black Death may have originated there too. The Russian explorer Peter Semenov documented the range extensively in the 1850s and later changed his family name to refer to the mountains.

During the last ice age a plateau glacier covered the plateau between the Kokshaal-Tau and the Terskey Alatau, and glaciers flowed north into Lake Issyk Kul. The glaciation occupied about 118,000 square kilometres. The mountains hold forests of Schrenk's spruce above 2,000 metres, and the lower slopes have natural forests of wild walnuts and apples. The eastern portion in Xinjiang was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2013 and the western portion in Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in 2016.
tian-yu: Tian Yu, courtesy name Guorang, was born around 171 in Yongnu County of Yuyang Commandery, in present-day Wuqing District, Tianjin. As a young man he placed himself in the care of Liu Bei while Liu Bei was staying with the warlord Gongsun Zan, and Liu Bei thought highly of him. When Liu Bei became Inspector of Yu Province, Tian Yu left to look after his ageing mother, and Liu Bei is said to have wept at losing him.

Tian Yu then served Gongsun Zan as Prefect of Dongzhou County. When Wang Men, one of Gongsun Zan's generals, went over to Yuan Shao and attacked with more than 10,000 troops, Tian Yu went to him in person and shamed him into retreating. After Gongsun Zan's defeat, his friend Xianyu Fu made him an adjutant, and on his advice Xianyu Fu joined Cao Cao, who gave Tian Yu official posts as well.

Early in the reign of Cao Pi, who founded the Cao Wei state in 220, Tian Yu was made Colonel Who Protects the Wuhuan and held the post with distinction for about nine years, until followers of Wang Xiong, Inspector of You Province, slandered him as a cause of trouble on the border. He was moved to be Administrator of Ru'nan. In 232 he ambushed and killed Zhou He and Pei Qian, envoys whom Sun Quan had sent to buy horses from Gongsun Yuan, at Chengshan. Early in the Zhengshi era of Cao Fang he became Inspector of Bing Province, and the frontier peoples, in awe of him, brought tribute one by one.

In his seventies Tian Yu asked again and again to retire, but the Grand Tutor Sima Yi refused. Tian replied that holding office past seventy was like travelling on at night after the bells had rung and the water clocks had run out, and pleaded serious illness, after which he was made Palace Counsellor on a salary. He died at the age of 82 by East Asian reckoning, around 252, and his son Tian Pengzu inherited his peerage.
tiananmen: The Chinese name, Tiananmen, is made of the characters for heaven, peace and gate, which is why it is conventionally translated as the Gate of Heavenly Peace. That rendering is somewhat misleading, since the name derives from a much longer phrase meaning "receiving the mandate from heaven, and pacifying the dynasty". The Manchu name, Abkai elhe obure duka, lies closer to it and can be rendered the Gate of Heavenly Peacemaking.

In the Ming dynasty the gate was called Chengtianmen, the Gate of Accepting Heavenly Mandate, and was modelled on a gate of the same name at an imperial building in Nanjing. Lightning burned it down in July 1457. In 1465 the Chenghua Emperor ordered the Minister of Works, Zigui, to rebuild it, and the design changed from a free-standing paifang to the gatehouse seen today.

The building is 66 metres long, 37 metres wide and 32 metres high, and carries roof decorations reserved for imperial buildings. Two lions stand in front of the gate and two more guard the bridges, since lions are believed in Chinese culture to protect people from evil spirits. Two stone columns called huabiao, each topped by an animal, also stand before it. Such columns were first designed for commoners to post petitions, but those in front of the Imperial City were purely decorative and signified the majesty of the imperial government. The reviewing stands in the foreground are used on International Workers' Day (1 May) and National Day (1 October).

The gate was burned again in 1644 by rebels led by Li Zicheng. After the Manchu conquest it was rebuilt from 1645 and received its present name on completion in 1651. Between 1969 and 1970 it was reconstructed once more, because it had deteriorated partly through heavy use in the 1950s and 1960s. Zhou Enlai ordered the work kept secret, and it was officially called a renovation.

Its position at the front of the Imperial City gave it political weight. A portrait of Sun Yat-sen hung there in 1925 and one of Chiang Kai-shek in 1945. On 7 July 1949 portraits of Zhu De and Mao Zedong were hung, and from 1 October 1949 a single portrait of Mao has been displayed, replaced each year before National Day. Only once, on 9 March 1953, was it temporarily replaced, by a portrait of Joseph Stalin on the occasion of his death.
tianjin: Tianjin lies on the west coast of the Bohai Gulf, surrounded by Hebei Province on every side except the sea, with Beijing about 120 kilometres to the northwest. Its main urban area stands along the Hai River, which connects to the Yellow and Yangtze rivers by the Grand Canal. The land was formed between 900 and 1300 CE by sediments from rivers entering the sea at the Bohai Gulf. The name, written 天津, means the ford of the emperor, and its origin is disputed; the most common theory holds that the Yongle Emperor of the Ming bestowed it after crossing the Gu River on his way south to overthrow his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor.

The Grand Canal, running from Hangzhou to the Beijing and Tianjin region by 609 CE, carried southern grain north and helped the area's development. Tianjin appears increasingly in records under the Song dynasty and gained importance under the Yuan as a storage place for goods and grain. Under the Ming it was a garrison town and shipping station, and the walled city was built in 1404. By the 17th century it was a centre of commerce.

In the Second Opium War the British and French captured the Taku forts near Tianjin in May 1858, and the Treaty of Tientsin signed that June opened the city to foreign trade; the Xianfeng Emperor ratified the treaties in 1860. Between 1895 and 1900 Japan, Germany, Russia and other powers joined Britain and France in establishing self-contained concessions, each with its own prisons, schools, barracks and hospitals, which left churches and thousands of villas. During the Boxer Rebellion the city was the seat of the Tianjin Provisional Government.

Tianjin fell to Japan on 30 July 1937, though the Japanese generally respected the foreign concessions until 1941. In June 1939 the Japanese army blockaded the British concession in the Tientsin Incident. In the Pingjin Campaign of the Chinese Civil War the city was taken after 29 hours of fighting, and the Chinese Communist Party held it from 15 January 1949.

Tianjin is a provincial-level municipality of China with 13,866,009 people at the 2020 census, and the largest coastal city of northern China. Its seaport remains the gateway to Beijing, and some European-style buildings of the concessions are preserved.
tianshui: Tianshui is a prefecture-level city in Gansu province and the second largest in the province after the capital, Lanzhou. It lies in the valley of the Jie River, a major tributary of the Wei River, on the boundary between the Loess Plateau and the Qinling Mountains. The climate is cool and semi-arid, with four seasons of comparatively equal length, cold dry winters and warm, somewhat humid summers; most rain falls from June to September. According to a legend, the name Tianshui, meaning heavenly water, comes from a lake formed from heaven that stayed the same size all year round.

The House of Ying, the ruling family of Qin, the founding dynasty of imperial China, developed from Quanqiu, present-day Lixian, to the south. After the invasions of the Rong that unseated the Western Zhou, Qin recovered the territory of Tianshui from the nomads, and it became an important region of their duchy and, later, kingdom. Characteristic Qin tombs have been excavated at nearby Fangmatan, including a 2,200-year-old map of Qin's Gui County.

Under the Qin Empire the area belonged to Longxi Commandery. Emperor Wu of the Han separated it as the Tianshui Commandery in 114 BCE, as part of his expansion towards the Tarim Basin, and the general Li Guang came from the city. Han conquests and exploration led to the development of the Northern Silk Road, on which Tianshui formed a junction with the Wei River before the road passed Mount Long to Chang'an, present-day Xi'an. Monks travelling along the road and local Buddhists carved the Maijishan Grottoes nearby, which hold thousands of Buddhist sculptures made between the Wei and Song dynasties.

The city was called Hanyang under the Northern Wei, when it was the centre of the Hanyang Commandery, and under the Western Wei the name was changed to Hanyang County. During the Tang and the Five Dynasties it was known as Shanggui and alternated with Chengji, present-day Qin'an, as the capital of Qinzhou province. In 1473, under the Ming dynasty, Li County was separated from its jurisdiction.

The 2020 census counted 2,984,659 inhabitants in the prefecture, of whom 1,212,791 lived in the built-up area formed by the two urban districts of Qinzhou and Maiji. The mild climate makes Tianshui a large producer of fruit, in particular apples, and it is also a major industrial centre of Gansu, especially in electronics. Its best-known dish is guagua, a boiled buckwheat flour dish eaten at breakfast, which legend links to the Han dynasty general Wei Xiao. Besides the Maijishan Grottoes, visitors go to the Fuxi Temple and the Dadiwan Site.
tiaret: Tiaret, called Tahert in Arabic and Tyart in Tamazight, is a major city in north-western Algeria that gives its name to the surrounding farming region of Tiaret Province. It lies in the Tell Atlas, in the western part of the Hautes Plaines, south-west of Algiers and about 150 kilometres from the Mediterranean coast. The name means lioness in the Berber language, a reference to the Barbary lions that lived in the region, as the names Oran and Souk Ahras also refer to lions.

The town occupies a strategic mountain pass at about 1,083 metres, which made it a key to dominating the central Maghreb. From the start of the eighth century it was the northern end of the West African branch of the slave trade, and taxes on that trade made it a desirable prize.

The area has been inhabited since antiquity and has many megalithic monuments. It served as a Roman station and fort, Tingartia. Berber tribes who could build in stone lived there in Late Antiquity. The Rustamid dynasty ruled from Tiaret between 761 and 909, though the capital may have stood about 10 kilometres west of the present town. It was founded by Abd al-Rahman ibn Rustam, an Ibadi theologian from Greater Iran.

Tahert was said to be relatively free-thinking and democratic, a centre of scholarship that permitted a wide range of sects and movements, notably the Mu'tazila. Many Jews lived there until at least the tenth century, among them the scholar and doctor Judah ibn Kuraish. The Rustamid state, called the Ibadite Empire, extended over most of modern Algeria until the Fatimid general Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i overthrew it in 909, and Tiaret ceased to be the capital of a separate state. Most of the population was banished to Ouargla and then escaped to the M'zab.

Later it was administered as part of the Kingdom of Tlemcen and in the sixteenth century fell to the Ottoman Empire. The French took it in 1843 after defeating Emir Abdelkader. The modern town grew around a French redoubt of 1845, and a narrow-gauge railway linked it to Mostaganem in 1889.

The town had a population of 178,915 in 2008. The region is predominantly agricultural, and Ibn Khaldun University has been in Tiaret since 1980. Some thirty kilometres south-south-west stand the Jedars, sepulchral monuments on hill-tops, each a square or rectangular podium surmounted by a pyramid. The tombs date from the fifth to the seventh century and lie in two groups between Tiaret and Frenda.
tiber-river: The Tiber is the third-longest river in Italy and the longest in central Italy. It rises at Mount Fumaiolo in the Apennine Mountains in Emilia-Romagna and flows 406 km through Tuscany, Umbria and Lazio, where the River Aniene joins it, to the Tyrrhenian Sea between Ostia and Fiumicino. Its mouth has advanced by about 3 km since Roman times, which left the ancient port of Ostia Antica 6 km inland. The name is probably pre-Latin and may be Italic in origin; the same root appears in the Latin name Tiberius.

According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BCE on the banks of the Tiber, about 25 km from the sea. Tiber Island was the site of an important ford and was later bridged. Legend says the twins Romulus and Remus were abandoned on the river's waters and rescued by the she-wolf Lupa. The river marked the boundary between the Etruscans to the west, the Sabines to the east and the Latins to the south.

The Tiber was critically important to Roman trade, since ships could reach as far as 100 km upriver. During the Punic Wars of the third century BCE the harbour at Ostia became a key naval base, and it later became Rome's most important port, receiving wheat, olive oil and wine from around the Mediterranean. The Romans linked the river to a sewer system, the Cloaca Maxima. Heavy sedimentation made Ostia difficult to maintain, so Claudius and Trajan established a new port at Fiumicino in the first century CE; both ports were eventually abandoned because of silting.

The Tiber was long known for floods; the Campus Martius, a flood plain, regularly flooded to a depth of about 2 m, and on 15 September 1557 the river rose 19 m above sea level and more than 1,000 people died. High stone embankments, begun in 1876, now confine it within the city. Ancient bridges survive in part, such as the Ponte Milvio and the Ponte Sant'Angelo, and in whole, as the Pons Fabricius. Because the river is identified with Rome, the phrase crossing the Tiber has become shorthand for converting to Roman Catholicism.
tiberias: Tiberias lies on a narrow strip of rolling terrain along the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, also called Lake Tiberias, at between 200 metres below and 200 metres above sea level. The hill country west of the old city rises steeply to about 300 metres above the lake. The city was built close to a spa that had developed around seventeen natural mineral hot springs, Hammat Tiberias, which has been known for its hot springs for some two thousand years. It lies above the Dead Sea Transform, and earthquakes have damaged it repeatedly, among them those of 363, 1033, 1202 and 1837.

Herod Antipas, a Roman client king and son of Herod the Great, founded Tiberias as the capital of his realm in Galilee and named it after the emperor Tiberius. It was at first a strictly pagan city but later became mainly Jewish. After the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish–Roman wars it became a major political and religious hub of the Jews in the Land of Israel. From the second to the tenth centuries it was the largest Jewish city in Galilee, and much of the Mishna and the Jerusalem Talmud were compiled there. A structure of the 3rd century uncovered in 2004 may have been the seat of the Sanhedrin.

Tiberias capitulated to the Arab commander Shurahbil ibn Hasana in about 636 and became the capital of Jund al-Urdunn, flourishing as a multi-cultural trading centre. In the First Crusade the Franks gave it in fief to Tancred, who made it the capital of the Principality of Galilee. In 1099 settlement shifted north to its present site. In 1325 Ibn Batuta described it as a ruin. The Ottoman Empire conquered it in 1516, when it was a small village. After the Galilee earthquake of 1837 it was rebuilt, and it grew after the First Jewish Aliyah of the 1880s.

Tiberias has been considered since the 18th century one of Judaism's Four Holy Cities, with Jerusalem, Hebron and Safed. After the fighting of 1947 and 1948 its Palestinian Arab population was evacuated, and since 1948 the population has been almost entirely Jewish. The Old City was largely demolished in 1949. Preserved buildings include St. Peter's Church, originally built by the Crusaders, two Ottoman-era mosques, several ancient synagogues and the Ottoman citadel. It remains a tourist centre because of the Sea of Galilee and its holiness to Judaism and Christianity.
tiberius: Tiberius was born in Rome on 16 November 42 BCE to Tiberius Claudius Nero and Livia Drusilla, both of the patrician gens Claudia. In 39 BCE Livia divorced Nero and married Octavian, later Augustus. At the age of nine Tiberius delivered the eulogy for his biological father, and in 29 BCE he rode beside Octavian's triumphal chariot after the victory over Antony and Cleopatra at Actium. He entered politics at eighteen as quaestor, with the right to stand for praetor and consul five years before the legal age.

In 20 BCE Tiberius went east to join Augustus, and either Augustus or Tiberius, or both, recovered the standards that Parthia had taken from Roman armies. He then led a force into Armenia. His conquests of Pannonia, Dalmatia, Raetia and, for a time, parts of Germania helped lay the foundations of the empire's northern frontier. In 6 BCE he was granted tribunician power and control in the East, then withdrew from politics and retired to Rhodes, for reasons that are unclear.

The deaths of Lucius Caesar in 2 CE and Gaius Caesar in 4 CE left Augustus no other choice. Tiberius was adopted as full son and heir on 26 June 4 CE, and had to adopt his nephew Germanicus. At Augustus's death in 14 CE he became princeps at 55.

Tiberius refused the title Pater Patriae and the Civic Crown, which the Senate took as insult rather than modesty, and his relations with it were difficult. He was nevertheless an effective administrator. Germanicus died in 19 CE and Tiberius's son Drusus in 23 CE, after which Tiberius grew reclusive. When he withdrew from Rome in 26 CE the praetorian prefect Sejanus was left in charge of the state, and Tiberius had him executed for treason in 31 CE. Tiberius died at Misenum on 16 March 37 CE, and his grand-nephew Caligula succeeded him. The treasury held nearly 3 billion sesterces at his death.
tiberius-coruncanius: Coruncanius was of plebeian descent and is believed to have come from Tusculum. He was first elected consul in 280 BCE, with Publius Valerius Laevinus as his colleague, when the Roman Republic's war with Pyrrhus of Epirus was just beginning.

While Laevinus was sent to southern Italy, where Pyrrhus defeated him at the Battle of Heraclea, Coruncanius led an expedition into Etruria, continuing the conflicts Rome had been fighting there before the Pyrrhic War began. After his northern campaign succeeded and he had held his triumph over the Etruscans of Volsinii and Vulci, he and his forces were sent south to join the effort against Pyrrhus.

Long after his consulship, some time between 255 and 252 BCE, he was elected pontifex maximus, the first plebeian to hold the office. In 246 BCE, during the First Punic War against Carthage, he was made dictator for the purpose of holding elections, since both consuls were away on campaign, and he appointed Marcus Fulvius Flaccus as his master of the horse. He was succeeded as pontifex maximus by Lucius Caecilius Metellus, another plebeian.

According to excerpts of the jurist Sextus Pomponius preserved in the Digest of Justinian, no one had publicly professed law before Coruncanius. Earlier pontiffs had kept their fellow citizens ignorant of the law or shared their knowledge only privately, among friends or within the pontifical college; Coruncanius discussed cases and procedure in public with anyone who showed interest. None of his writings survived even to Pomponius's time, though Pomponius notes that his legal opinions were numerous and influential. He may thus have been the first teacher of Roman law to offer public instruction.
tiberius-gracchus: Tiberius belonged to the Roman aristocracy from birth. His father, also named Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, was consul in 177 and 163 BCE and censor in 169 BCE. His mother, Cornelia, was a daughter of the general Scipio Africanus, and his sister Sempronia married Scipio Aemilianus. Cornelia brought up the children after her husband's death. Tiberius served under Scipio Aemilianus in the Third Punic War from 147 BCE and, according to Plutarch, was among the first to scale the walls of Carthage.

In 137 BCE Tiberius was quaestor to the consul Gaius Hostilius Mancinus in Hispania Citerior during the Numantine War. Mancinus's army was surrounded, and Tiberius negotiated a treaty with the Numantines, helped by the influence his father had gained in the region. The senate rejected it as humiliating and sent Mancinus back to the Numantines stripped and bound. A proposal to send Tiberius in chains as well was defeated, but his political future was damaged.

Elected plebeian tribune for 133 BCE, he proposed the Lex Sempronia agraria. He believed an earlier law had limited the public land any person could hold to about 120 hectares, a limit largely ignored, and he proposed enforcing it and passing the surplus to poor citizens. The reform drew strong support from the rural plebs and from some senators, including his father-in-law Appius Claudius Pulcher, but wealthy holders of public land opposed it. When the tribune Marcus Octavius vetoed the bill, Tiberius had him removed from office, an unconstitutional step. He then proposed using the bequest of Attalus III of Pergamum to fund the land commission, which broke the senate's prerogatives over finance and foreign policy, and his enemies accused him of seeking royal power.

Tiberius then sought a second consecutive tribunate, which broke Roman constitutional norms. At the elections his followers occupied the Capitoline hill. The pontifex maximus Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Serapio asked the consul Publius Mucius Scaevola to use force, and when Scaevola refused, Nasica called on all who wanted the community safe to follow him and led a mob to the assembly. Tiberius and his supporters did not fight back; they were killed with stones, chairs and other blunt weapons, and their bodies were thrown into the Tiber.

The land law was not repealed. Its commission, which included his brother Gaius Gracchus, went on working, and the surviving boundary stones show distributions across southern Italy of some 1.3 million jugera. Historians see the killing as the start of a cycle of violence: before it, domestic strife in the middle republic had basically never ended in violent death. Modern scholars treat 133 BCE as the traditional beginning of the Republic's crisis, while noting that the idea of earlier calm between rich and poor is at best a nostalgic fiction.
tiberius-sempronius-gracchus-consul-177-: Gracchus was a plebeian of the well-connected gens Sempronia; his grandfather, or possibly his father, was the Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus who was consul in 215 and 213 BCE. Little is known of his youth. He may be the same man as the augur of that name who served from 204 to 174 BCE. He served with the Scipios in Asia, where he was sent as an envoy to Philip V of Macedon to negotiate safe passage to the Hellespont.

As tribune of the plebs in 184 BCE, or possibly 187 BCE, he used his veto to save Scipio Africanus from prosecution and Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiagenes from prison, though he was no political ally of theirs. As curule aedile in 182 BCE he staged games so lavish that the senate capped such expenses to spare Rome's Italian allies and provinces.

After his command in Spain, where he claimed to have destroyed three hundred cities, almost certainly an exaggeration, he and his colleague Lucius Postumius Albinus triumphed and presented some 60 thousand pounds of silver. As consul in 177 BCE with Gaius Claudius Pulcher he was sent to Sardinia, where he waged two campaigns against the Ilienses and the Balari. Returning in 175 BCE, he claimed some 80 thousand Sardinians killed or captured and triumphed for the second time.

As censor from 169 BCE, again with Claudius, he was strict enough to provoke a prosecution of his colleague, registered all freedmen in a single urban tribe and built the Basilica Sempronia in the Forum. In his second consulship, in 163 BCE, he made an error in the auspices at the elections for 162 BCE; when he reported it, the new consuls, among them his brother-in-law Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum, had to resign. He also led embassies to the eastern kingdoms.

He married Cornelia, the daughter of Scipio Africanus, a match that Plutarch, following Polybius, places after Africanus's death. She bore him twelve children, of whom three reached adulthood: Sempronia, Tiberius Gracchus and Gaius Gracchus. Plutarch tells that soothsayers warned him over two snakes found in his bedchamber, and that he killed the male, choosing his own death over hers, and died soon after. Cornelia refused further marriages, among them an offer from Ptolemy VIII, and raised their sons, whose fame has since overshadowed his own.
tibes-indigenous-ceremonial-center: The site lies in Sector La Vega de Taní, Barrio Tibes, on the northern outskirts of Ponce, and is the largest ceremonial site in Puerto Rico. Its stone constructions include ball courts of two kinds: rectangular courts formed by two parallel lines of flat stones and open at both ends, and U-shaped courts bounded by walks paved with river cobbles and boulders. There is also a series of triangular stone arrangements around a flat excavated area.

The main feature is a nearly quadrangular plaza bounded by paved walks and flat slabs, many of them bearing petroglyphs; the ground of the courts and plaza was artificially modified. Shell middens lie scattered across the site, and in places the courts cut into them, a sign that the site was occupied for a long time and grew gradually into a ceremonial centre. Its cemetery, with 186 skeletons, is the largest Indigenous burial ground found in the region, and most of the remains belong to the Igneri culture.

Archaeologists attribute the ball courts and plazas to the Igneri, the earliest farming immigrants into the Greater Antilles, and the Taínos were presumably the site's last inhabitants. The archaeologist Osvaldo Garcia Goyco has found that some plazas are aligned with the equinoxes and solstices, and the site is held to be the oldest astronomical observatory in the Caribbean. The evidence suggests that possible influences from Mesoamerica, such as the ball game, reached Puerto Rico as early as 700.

The site was found in 1975, after Hurricane Eloise, by archaeologists of the Guaynia Society of Archaeology and History at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Puerto Rico, in a survey sponsored by the Puerto Rico Institute of Culture. Clearing the high brush revealed the shell middens and the stone constructions.

Tibes was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on 14 April 1978 and in the Puerto Rico Register of Historic Sites and Zones on 16 May 2001. It opened to the public on 30 April 1982, and finds from the site are shown in its museum and at the Ponce Museum of Art. Much of the site has yet to be explored.
tibet: Tibet covers much of the Tibetan Plateau and is the homeland of the Tibetans. It is the highest region on Earth, with an average elevation of 4,380 m, and its southern edge in the Himalayas includes Mount Everest at 8,848 m. Several major rivers rise on the plateau, among them the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Indus, the Mekong, the Ganges and the Salween. Cultural Tibet is divided into Amdo in the northeast, Kham in the southeast, and Ü-Tsang with Ngari in the centre and west.

In the 7th century the Yarlung dynasty of central Tibet expanded into neighbouring regions such as Zhangzhung and Amdo, and by the 9th century the Tibetan Empire stretched from the Tarim Basin and the Pamirs in the west to Yunnan and Bengal in the southeast. After the empire dissolved, the region divided among principalities and tribal groups. Under the Mongol Yuan dynasty the Sakya lama kept a degree of autonomy as political authority, while an appointed administrator, the dpon-chen, held administrative and military power.

Between 1346 and 1354 Tai Situ Changchub Gyaltsen overthrew the Sakya and founded the Phagmodrupa dynasty, and the disciples of Je Tsongkhapa founded the Gelug school and the monasteries of Ganden, Drepung and Sera near Lhasa. In 1578 Altan Khan of the Tümed Mongols gave the Gelug lama Sonam Gyatso the title Dalai Lama. The 5th Dalai Lama (1617–1682), helped by Güshi Khan of the Khoshut Khanate, defeated the Kagyu and Jonang sects and the Tsangpa prince, and his government, the Ganden Phodrang, ruled the heartland.

Qing rule began with an expedition in 1720 that expelled the invading Dzungars. Amdo came under Qing control in 1724 and eastern Kham was joined to neighbouring Chinese provinces in 1728. The Qing sent resident commissioners called Ambans to Lhasa, and after a riot in 1750 in which the Ambans and many Han Chinese and Manchus were killed, they restored the Dalai Lama as ruler while giving the Ambans a larger part in Tibetan affairs.

Lhasa is the traditional capital, and the Potala Palace and Norbulingka, former residences of the Dalai Lama, are World Heritage Sites there. China governs most of the historical area as the Tibet Autonomous Region and as autonomous prefectures within Gansu, Sichuan, Qinghai and Yunnan. Tibetan Buddhism is the main religion and shapes the region's art, music and festivals; Bön is the indigenous religion.
tibet-ladakh-mughal-war: In the late 17th century the Namgyal dynasty of Ladakh sided with Bhutan in its dispute with Tibet. The Tibetans resolved to punish Ladakh for meddling in their relations with Bhutan and for the oppression of Gelug monasteries within its borders. Central Tibet's Ganden Phodrang government had the support of the Oirat Mongol Khoshut Khanate. In 1679 the Fifth Dalai Lama named the Khoshut lama of the Tashilhunpo Monastery, Galdan Tsewang, to lead the expedition, reportedly against the advice of his prime minister.

Galdan Tsewang first secured his flank by a treaty with Raja Kehri Singh of Bashahr, granting him trade rights with Tibet. His first campaign defeated the Ladakhi army under Shakya Gyatso at Khan-dMar, and the next year he beat the Ladakhis again at Chang La and occupied the country. Only the fortresses of Basgo and Tingmosgang held out, and they resisted Tibetan attacks for three years.

Kashmir was then a Mughal province and counted Ladakh within its sphere of influence. In 1683 an army under Fidai Khan, son of Ibrahim Khan, the governor of Kashmir, defeated the Tibeto-Khoshut force, lifted the siege of Basgo and pursued it as far as Lake Pangong, until the Tibetans withdrew into Tashigang.

The Kashmiris helped restore Ladakhi rule on condition that a mosque be built in Leh and that the king convert to Islam. Kashmiri historians assert that he did convert, but the Ladakhi chronicles do not mention it and Ladakhis reject the claim. The king agreed to pay tribute to the Mughals for their help, and the Mughal army withdrew after a treaty with Ladakh.

In 1684 the Tibetan regent Desi Sangye Gyatso and King Delek Namgyal of Ladakh signed the Treaty of Tingmosgang. According to the Ladakh Chronicles it fixed the border at the Lhari stream near Demchok and regulated trade and tribute missions between Ladakh and Tibet. The settlement left Ladakh independent but a tributary of the Mughal Empire.
tibetan-buddhism: Tibetan Buddhism is a branch of the Vajrayana tradition that developed in Tibet. It evolved as a form of Mahayana Buddhism from the latest stages of Indian Buddhism and preserves many Indian tantric practices of the early medieval period, along with native Tibetan developments. The predominant spiritual tradition in Tibet before Buddhism was Bon. Buddhism began to spread into the Tibetan region in the 3rd century CE, and it was formally introduced during the Tibetan Empire of the 7th to 9th centuries.

Buddhist influence went into reverse under King Langdarma (r. 836–842), and his death was followed by the Era of Fragmentation, when the empire's centralisation collapsed and civil wars ensued. In 1042 the Bengali teacher Atiśa (982–1054) arrived in Tibet at the invitation of a west Tibetan king.

Tibetan Buddhism exerted a strong influence on the Mongols from the 11th century. The Mongols invaded Tibet in 1240 and 1244, and in 1249 they appointed the scholar and abbot Sakya Pandita (1182–1251) as Viceroy of Central Tibet.

The Qing dynasty established Chinese rule over Tibet after a Qing force defeated the Dzungars in 1720. The Manchu rulers supported Tibetan Buddhism, especially the Gelug school, and the reign of the Qianlong Emperor was the high mark of this promotion, with temples built in the Tibetan style such as Putuo Zongcheng Temple, modelled on the Potala Palace. From 1959 the Tibetan diaspora carried the tradition beyond Asia, and monasteries, including the three major Gelug monasteries, were rebuilt in India.

Tibetan Buddhism has four major schools: Nyingma, from the 8th century, Kagyu, from the 11th, Sakya, from 1073, and Gelug, from 1409. Its main goal is Buddhahood, and its teachings include the classical Mahayana practices, tantric practices such as deity yoga, and Dzogchen. The dominant philosophy is Madhyamaka, which holds that all phenomena are empty of inherent existence.

Study of major Indian texts is central to the monastic curriculum in all four schools, along with memorisation and formal debate. The canon was mostly finalised in the 13th century and divides into the Kangyur, containing sutras and tantras, and the Tengyur, containing shastras and commentaries. Lamrim, the stages of the path, elaborates Atiśa's 11th-century text A Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment.
tibetans: Tibetan tradition holds that the Tibetan people descend from the monkey Pha Trelgen Changchup Sempa and the rock ogress Ma Drag Sinmo. Genetic studies trace their roots to a deep East Asian lineage representing the indigenous population of the Tibetan plateau from about 40,000 to 30,000 years ago, joined within the last 10,000 years by Neolithic farmers from the Yellow River, who are associated with the spread of the Sino-Tibetan languages. Modern Tibetans are thought to derive up to 20 per cent of their ancestry from the Paleolithic plateau population and most of the rest from Yellow River farmers. Most Tibeto-Burman speakers of south-west China are thought to descend from the ancient Qiang people.

Tibetans carry more than 30 genetic factors suited to high altitude, among them a variant of the EPAS1 gene, which regulates the body's production of haemoglobin. Researchers describe its spread over the past 5,000 years as possibly one of the fastest genetic changes observed in humans.
