Most Tibetans practise Tibetan Buddhism, and a significant minority follow the indigenous Bon religion. According to legend the 28th king, Thothori Nyantsen, dreamed of a sacred treasure falling from heaven, holding a Buddhist sutra, but Buddhism did not take root until the reign of Songtsen Gampo, who married two Buddhist princesses, Bhrikuti of Nepal and Wencheng of China. It gained popularity when Padmasambhāva visited Tibet at the invitation of the 38th king, Trisong Deutson. Tibetan Buddhists walk clockwise around stupas and mani stones and chant Om mani padme hum, while followers of Bon walk in the opposite direction.

Tibetan art is deeply religious. Thangka paintings, a blend of Indian scroll painting with Nepalese and Kashmiri painting, appeared around the 8th century. Lhamo, the folk opera of dances, chants and songs, is traditionally said to have been founded in the 14th century by Thang Tong Gyalpo, a lama and bridge-builder. Traditional medicine draws on up to two thousand plants, and the physician Yuthog Yontan Gonpo of the 8th century is credited with the Four Medical Tantras. The Potala Palace, once the residence of the Dalai Lama, is regarded as the most important example of Tibetan architecture.

The 2010 Chinese census counted 6,282,187 Tibetans, of whom 2,716,388 lived in the Tibet Autonomous Region, with large numbers in Sichuan, Qinghai, Gansu and Yunnan. Communities live also in India, Nepal and Bhutan, and nearly 100,000 Tibetans have lived in exile in India since 1959, many of them at Dharamshala and Bylakuppe.
tibeto-burman-languages: The Tibeto-Burman languages are the non-Sinitic members of the Sino-Tibetan family. More than 400 are spoken across the Southeast Asian Massif and parts of East and South Asia, by around 60 million people. The family takes its name from its two most widely spoken members, Burmese and the Tibetic languages, whose literary traditions date from the 12th and 7th centuries respectively. Most of the other languages are spoken by much smaller communities, many of them in remote mountain areas, and many have not been described in detail or lack a written standard.

In the south the Karen languages are spoken by three million people on both sides of the Burma–Thailand border. Burmese, the national language of Myanmar, has over 32 million speakers and belongs to the Lolo-Burmese group of about 100 languages. More than eight million people on the Tibetan Plateau and in neighbouring areas speak Tibetic languages, and Classical Tibetan has an extensive literature dating from the 8th century. The Newar language of central Nepal has a literature dating from the 12th century, and Meithei is the main language of Manipur. The widest variety lies in the highlands from northern Myanmar to northeast India. Two historical languages, Pyu and Tangut, are believed to be Tibeto-Burman, though their exact affiliation is uncertain.

In the 18th century scholars noticed parallels between Tibetan and Burmese. In the next century Brian Houghton Hodgson collected data on the non-literary languages of the Himalayas and northeast India and noted that many were related to them. James Logan first applied the name Tibeto-Burman in 1856 and added Karen in 1858. Julius Klaproth had noted in 1823 that Burmese, Tibetan and Chinese share basic vocabulary, and Jean Przyluski introduced the term Sino-Tibetan in 1924. The link between Tibeto-Burman and Chinese is now accepted by most linguists.

The classification remains disputed. Paul Benedict, in a work of 1972 written around 1941, saw Chinese as the first branch to split off, and James Matisoff later modified his scheme. Shafer's classification of 1955 did not recognise Tibeto-Burman at all. Some historical linguists criticise the split into Sinitic and Tibeto-Burman because the non-Sinitic languages share no innovations in phonology or morphology that would show them to form a branch. George van Driem rejects it and makes Tibeto-Burman a synonym of Sino-Tibetan. New languages continue to be recognised, some not closely related to others, among them languages described only in the 2010s.
tibnin: The town spreads over several hills between 700 and 800 metres above sea level, about 25 km east of Tyre, in Jabal Amel, the plateau on either side of the Litani river long associated with its Twelver Shia community. Acheulean hand axes of the Lower Palaeolithic and Stone Age megaliths have been found nearby, and scholars have identified the place with Tafnis, named in the Jerusalem Talmud as a northern border of the kingdom of Judah.

The castle took its name, Toron, from an old French word for a peaked hill. After its builder's death Izz al-Mulk, governor of Tyre, raided the village in 1107 and massacred its people. King Baldwin I of Jerusalem gave the lordship to Humphrey I of Toron, whose family held it for generations. The fertile land made it a granary of the kingdom, and under Humphrey III the lordship minted its own copper coins. In 1185 the traveller Ibn Jubair found that the Muslims between Tibnin and the coast largely ran their own affairs.

Crusaders besieged the castle from 28 November 1197 and refused two offers of surrender, then withdrew in February 1198 as an Ayyubid army approached. Sultan Al-Kamil returned the lordship to the Franks in 1229 during the Sixth Crusade, and Alice of Armenia, heiress of the Toron family, held it until about 1239, when it passed to Philip of Montfort. The Mamluk sultan Baibars took it in 1266. Under the Ottomans the castle became a jail and, in the 19th century, the residence of the local governor.

The population is mostly Shia Muslim with a small Greek Catholic minority; no count has been made since the census of 1932, and estimates put it at about 5,000. From 1978 the Irish battalion of the UNIFIL force had its base, Camp Shamrock, in the town. The castle is one of the Lebanese heritage sites UNESCO placed under enhanced protection in November 2024, and one of its medieval walls collapsed in the fighting of that year.
tibor-szamuely: Szamuely was born in Nyíregyháza, in north-eastern Hungary, the eldest of five children of a Jewish family. After university he became a journalist and began his political life in the Hungarian Social Democratic Party. Drafted as a soldier in World War I, he was captured by Russia in 1915 and released after the October Revolution of 1917, by which time he had turned to communism.

In Moscow he and Béla Kun organised a communist group among Hungarian prisoners of war, and many of them, Szamuely and Kun included, fought in the Red Army in the Russian Civil War. From 3 April 1918 the two published the newspaper Socialist Revolution. Many Hungarian prisoners refused to join the Red Guard, and several Hungarian officers were executed in Russia as a result. In December 1918 he took part in Germany in the founding of the Spartacist League with Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg.

He returned to Budapest on 3 January 1919, joined the Central Committee of the Hungarian Communist Party and helped edit its paper. In February 1919 he wrote in Vörös Újság of counter-revolutionaries: "Before they stifle the revolution, suffocate them in their own blood!" After the communist coup of 21 March 1919 set up the Hungarian Soviet Republic, he became one of its leading figures and a face of its Red Terror. His guards, nicknamed the Lenin Boys, worked at times with the Red Guard of József Cserny, travelling the country by armoured train. The revolutionary tribunals executed between 370 and 590 people in custody.

Kun grew uneasy at his power, and Vilmos Böhm ordered the paramilitaries and tribunals dissolved, but Szamuely kept the tribunals at work in Szolnok and then Abony. In late May he flew to Moscow to campaign for world revolution with Vladimir Lenin.

The republic fell after the Hungarian–Romanian War, and Kun went into exile on 1 August 1919. Szamuely left for Austria by car the next day and was arrested after crossing the border illegally. Hungarian and Austrian authorities reported that he shot himself while his guide was being searched; Kun's wife wrote that he had told her he would kill himself if captured, but some believe border guards shot him. A Soviet barge carrier was named after him.
tiburcio-carias-andino: Tiburcio Carías Andino, born in 1876 to Calixto Carías Galindo and Sara Francisca Andino Rivera, studied criminal law at the Central University of Honduras. In 1907 he fought alongside liberal forces and was promoted to general after the Battle of Lizapa; President Miguel R. Dávila Cuéllar then made him governor of the Copán Department. He became prominent in the civil wars of 1919 and 1924 and in March and April 1924 served briefly as chief of the revolution. He lost the 1928 election to Vicente Mejía Colindres of the Liberal Party and accepted the result in a rare peaceful transfer of power between the two main parties.

Carías won the 1932 election by about 20,000 votes, as Mejía Colindres resisted pressure from his own party to manipulate the result. His rule became the longest by one individual in Honduran history. He crushed a Liberal revolt, improved the military, gained the support of the banana companies by opposing strikes, and kept up payments on the national debt through the Great Depression.

Because the constitution barred immediate re-election, he called a handpicked constituent assembly in 1936. Its constitution allowed immediate re-election, lengthened the presidential term from four to six years, restored the death penalty, reduced the legislature's powers and denied women citizenship and the vote. In 1939 the legislature extended his term to 1949. The Communist Party was outlawed in 1935, the opposition press was cracked down on, and by the end of the decade the National Party was the only organised party; opposition leaders were imprisoned or exiled. Sources name the Tela massacre of 1937 against the Garífuna people and the killing of more than 70 protesters at San Pedro Sula on 6 July 1944.

Honduras declared war on the Axis after Pearl Harbor in 1941. Under United States pressure Carías stood aside in 1948 and his choice, Juan Manuel Gálvez, took office in January 1949 after the Liberals boycotted the election.

Carías gave Honduras a long period of relative peace and order. Its finances improved steadily, education improved slightly, the road network grew and the armed forces were modernised, but democratic institutions withered and opposition and labour activity were suppressed. When he sought a return to the presidency in 1954, his candidacy split the National Party; the Liberal Ramón Villeda Morales won a plurality, and Vice President Julio Lozano Díaz seized power in a coup. Carías died in 1969.
ticino: Ticino is a canton unlike the others, since it lies almost entirely south of the Alps and has no natural access to the Swiss Plateau. It borders Valais, Uri and the Grisons along the crest of the Gotthard Massif and adjacent ranges, and shares international borders with Italy. Apart from small areas in the north and south, it lies in the basin of the Ticino, a tributary of the Po, from which it takes its name. It is traditionally divided into the Sopraceneri and the Sottoceneri, north and south of Monte Ceneri. The climate, influenced by the Mediterranean and sheltered by the Alps, is warmer and wetter than in the rest of Switzerland, and German-speaking Swiss call the canton the Sonnenstube, the sun porch.

During the Bronze and Iron Ages the land was settled by the Lepontii, a Celtic tribe. Probably around the time of Augustus it became part of the Roman Empire. After the fall of the Western Empire it was ruled by the Ostrogoths, the Lombards and the Franks. Around 1100 it was the centre of a struggle between the free communes of Milan and Como, and in the 14th century it was acquired by the Visconti, Dukes of Milan. The Swiss Confederates then conquered the valleys south of the Alps in three separate conquests, in the last transalpine campaigns of the Old Swiss Confederacy.

Leventina was a subject of Uri until 1798. In that year the Helvetic Republic joined it with the condominiums of Bellinzona, Riviera and Blenio as the canton of Bellinzona, while Locarno, Lugano, Mendrisio and Vallemaggia formed the canton of Lugano. The Act of Mediation of 1803 combined the two into the canton of Ticino, which joined the restored Swiss Confederation. The former condominiums and Leventina became its eight districts, which still exist. The current constitution derives from a draft approved on 18 August 1801 and was itself approved on 14 December 1997.

Cantonal identity was forged in the 19th century, partly through intellectuals such as Stefano Franscini and Carlo Cattaneo. Because of its position the canton has depended on routes over the Gotthard, a strategic pass since the 13th century. The Gotthard Rail Tunnel, 15 kilometres long, opened in 1882, the Gotthard Road Tunnel in 1980 and the Gotthard Base Tunnel on 1 June 2016.

Ticino is the only canton in which Italian is the sole official language, and its capital is Bellinzona; Lugano is the largest city, and Locarno another notable centre. Its official name is the Republic and Canton of Ticino, a style it shares with Geneva, Neuchâtel and Jura. Four World Heritage Sites lie in it, among them the Three Castles of Bellinzona and Monte San Giorgio. It was the birthplace of the architect Francesco Borromini.
ticino-river: The Ticino is the most important perennial left-bank tributary of the Po, about 248 km long, and it gave its name to the Swiss canton through which its upper part flows. It is one of the four major rivers that rise in the Gotthard region, with the Rhône, Reuss and Rhine. It begins in the Val Bedretto, on the border between the cantons of Valais and Ticino just below the Nufenen Pass, where glaciers and many torrents feed it. Its name may have meant the runner, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to run or flow.

From Val Bedretto it flows north-east to Airolo, where the southern portals of the Gotthard Railway Tunnel and Gotthard Road Tunnel lie, then south-east through the Valle Leventina, with two narrow gorges. At Biasca it receives the Brenno, and near Bellinzona the Moesa. It crosses the flat Piano di Magadino, built from its own sediments over ten thousand years, and enters Lake Maggiore at 193 metres, the lowest point of Switzerland. It leaves the lake at Sesto Calende, passes about 20 km east of Milan and joins the Po a few kilometres below Pavia.

The Gallic leader Bellovesus, known only from tradition, was said to have defeated the Etruscans by the Ticino in about 600 BCE. The river gave its name to the Battle of Ticinus, fought in November 218 BCE between the Carthaginian forces of Hannibal and the Romans under Publius Cornelius Scipio; it was the first battle of the Second Punic War.

In the Middle Ages Pavia, first capital of the Kingdom of the Lombards and then of the kingdom of Italy, was a hub of communications and trade between Venice and the Po valley thanks to the Ticino. Its covered bridge, the ponte Coperto, was until the 19th century the only brick bridge across the river between Lake Maggiore and the Po.

The Visconti built a wooden bridge at Vigevano in the early 14th century, which the Pavia fleet burned in 1315 and again in 1356, after Luchino Visconti had rebuilt it; it was never rebuilt. For much of the later Middle Ages and the early modern period the river lay in the Duchy of Milan, but the upper part as far as Bellinzona fell to the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1500, and as far as the shores of Lake Maggiore in 1513, as a result of the Swiss campaigns in the Italian Wars.

The stretch between Lake Maggiore and the confluence with the Po is the Parco naturale lombardo della Valle del Ticino, a nature reserve included by UNESCO in its World Network of Biosphere Reserves. Towns on the river or its lake include Bellinzona and Locarno in Switzerland and Stresa, Vigevano and Pavia in Italy.
tidung-people: The Tidung originate in Tana Tidung, now part of North Kalimantan. They were once subjects of the Kingdom of Tidung, and the rise of that Muslim kingdom shaped their emergence as a single people. Like other Muslim peoples of the eastern coast of Borneo, such as the Bulungan, Berau, Kutai, Banjar and Paser, they are known as a Malayised Dayak people.

In the Tarakan language of the Tidung the word tidung means hill or hill people. Like many names in the Malay Archipelago it is a collective term for several closely related groups, who all call themselves Tidung and whom modern ethnology treats as one people because of their shared cultural and religious traditions.

Their traditional lands run along the Sembakung River and the Sibuku River, from its headwaters to the estuary north of Tarakan Island, and from there along the coast south to the mouth of the Bulungan River and north to Tawau in Sabah, including Cowie Harbour, with an enclave on the Labuk River. Their numbers were estimated at about 27,000 in Indonesia in 2007, and the census of 2010 counted 28,515 Tidung in the state of Sabah, Malaysia.

The Tidung are traditionally farmers who practise slash-and-burn agriculture, growing sweet potatoes, cassava, lentils, fruits and vegetables, and some are ocean fishermen. They speak the Tidung language, a North Bornean language of the Murutic group, in dialects such as Nunukan, Penchangan, Sedalir, Tikal, Malinau, Sesayap, Sibuku and Tarakan, the last two also spoken in Sabah.

Before the present Roman alphabet the Tidung wrote in the Jawi script. Their folktales include the story of the origin of the Tidung Tenggara people, the tale of Ibenayuk, the tale of the Four-eyed king and the story of Aki Balak.
tien-quan-ca: Văn Cao wrote and composed the march in 1944, basing its words and title on his earlier work Thăng Long, a former name of Hanoi. The text changed repeatedly from the early 1940s. The first line, Đoàn quân Việt Nam đi, meaning The Vietnamese army marches, was originally Đoàn quân Việt Minh đi, The Viet Minh army marches. The sixth part was first a vow to tear apart the enemy and drink their blood, expressing his anger at the colonialists for letting two million Vietnamese people perish in the famine of 1945. After many suggestions he changed it to a line about fighting for the people until the end. The closing line was published as Nước non Việt Nam ta vững bền.

The anthem has two verses, but usually only the first is sung. After the composer had let Vũ Quý try it, it was published in the papers in November 1944, with lithographs by Văn Cao. On 17 August 1945 it was sung for the first time at a rally in Hanoi. The poet and musician Nguyễn Đình Thi, moved by hearing Văn Cao sing it, wrote Diệt Phát Xít, while Văn Cao wrote Chiến Sĩ Việt Nam; both are still sung.

Hồ Chí Minh approved the song as the anthem of the new Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 17 August 1945, and a Liberation Army band played it at Ba Đình Square on 2 September 1945, the day independence was declared. The first National Assembly recognised it officially in 1946, and the first constitution of the republic named it in its third article. In 1955 the Assembly invited authors to edit it again; Văn Cao regretted that the heroic spirit of the song had been lost in the editing. After reunification in 1976 it became the anthem of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. A contest for a new anthem opened in 1981 but no result was ever announced.

In 2015 the composer's family registered the song for royalties, drawing protest from veteran musicians, and the Ministry of Culture told the copyright agency to stop collecting. In July 2016 the family donated the song to the nation at a ceremony in Hanoi.
tienen: Tienen, called Tirlemont in French, is a city and municipality in the province of Flemish Brabant in Flanders, Belgium. The municipality includes the town itself and Bost, Goetsenhoven, Hakendover, Kumtich, Oorbeek, Oplinter, Sint-Margriete-Houtem and Vissenaken. It covers 71.77 square kilometres. Tienen was a Roman settlement and trade centre with roads to other important places. In the early Middle Ages the town was probably ruled by an old German family, Thienen.

During the Franco-Spanish War of 1635 to 1659 Tienen belonged to the Spanish Netherlands, and a combined Franco-Dutch army captured it in May 1635. The town was sacked in one of the most serious atrocities of the Dutch Revolt. Over 200 civilians were killed and many buildings, including Catholic churches and monasteries, were damaged. The episode ended Dutch hopes of winning over the largely Catholic population of the Southern Netherlands. After the Treaty of Utrecht of 1714 the town was incorporated into the Austrian Netherlands.

German forces occupied Tienen in the First World War after breaking through the Belgian defensive lines. Sixty houses were destroyed and 152 damaged, and about 100 soldiers and civilians from the town died.

In the later world war the town was an important railway junction. The Allies bombed it in April 1944, and on 25 May 1944 a larger raid killed 13 civilians and injured 40. The bombs largely missed their intended targets, the bridges and the railway, and hit over 200 houses. The Dean of Rochette died in the confession booth after refusing to leave. The Allies liberated the town on 7 September 1944. The war cost the lives of 80 inhabitants, and 549 houses were destroyed.

Tienen is the centre of Belgian sugar production, and its large sugar refinery stands on the eastern edge of the town. A summer rock festival, Suikerrock, takes place there. The Sint-Germanus Church dates from the 12th century, and its belfry is part of the UNESCO listing of the Belfries of Belgium and France. The principal church, Onze-Lieve-Vrouw-ten-Poel, was begun in the 12th century and enlarged in the 15th, and remains unfinished. Tienen railway station is the oldest in Belgium still in use. The mystic Beatrijs of Nazareth (1200 to 1268) was born in the town.
tierra-de-campos: The Tierra de Campos, the Land of Fields, lies on a fertile plateau averaging about 720 metres in height, a vast plain broken only by wide undulations. Its ground is mostly compact clay, and its climate continental, with long cold winters and short hot summers. Few rivers water it, so the land has traditionally been used for dryland farming, and little natural forest is left.

Since it is a natural and traditional region, its limits have never been fixed officially. One widely accepted line runs along the foothills of the Cantabrian Mountains between Sahagún and Carrión de los Condes in the north, the basins of the Carrión and Pisuerga in the east, the hills of Montes Torozos and the Sequillo basin in the south, and the Salinas de Villalpando and the Cea River in the west.

The region was first known as the Gothic Plains, Campi Gothici or Campi Gothorum, after Visigoths who had fled Aquitaine when the Franks conquered it and settled there. The name first appears in the Codex Vigilanus, also called the Codex Albeldensis, which describes the plains as reaching from the river Douro to the Christian kingdom. Among its towns are Sahagún, Medina de Rioseco, Carrión de los Condes, Frómista and Villalpando. The Channel of Castile, built across it for transport, later became an irrigation system.

Despite the strong identity of its people, the region has no legal standing of its own, and its municipalities manage shared services through a mancomunidad. Palencia is widely considered its capital. Wetlands such as the Laguna de la Nava de Fuentes and the Lagunas de Villafáfila matter for its ecology, and it has the highest concentration of bustards in the Iberian Peninsula, possibly in the world.
tierra-del-fuego: The archipelago consists of a main island, the Isla Grande de Tierra del Fuego, and numerous smaller islands, among them Cape Horn and the Diego Ramírez Islands. The Beagle Channel runs east and west just south of the main island, and the largest islands south of it are Hoste and Navarino. The climate is subpolar and oceanic, with short, cool summers and long, wet winters. About 30 per cent of the islands are forested, with southern beech and the southernmost conifer in the world, while the north-east is steppe and cool semi-desert.

The earliest human settlement dates to about 8,000 BCE, and the Yahgan were among the earliest known inhabitants. Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese sailing for the Spanish Crown, was the first European to visit, in 1520. The name, Spanish for land of fire, comes from the many fires the inhabitants lit along the coast, which he believed were signals of an ambush. Francis Drake in 1578 and a Dutch East India Company expedition in 1616 learned more of its geography, and the latter named Cape Horn.

Salesian Catholic and Anglican missions were set up in the second half of the 19th century. The missionary Thomas Bridges compiled a Yaghan grammar and dictionary of 30,000 words at Ushuaia. After a Chilean expedition reported placer gold in 1879, large numbers of Argentines, Chileans and Croatians immigrated between 1883 and 1909, increasing conflict with the Selkʼnam. Julius Popper, who held Argentine rights to any gold he found, has been identified as a central figure in the Selkʼnam genocide.

The Selkʼnam and Yaghan were greatly reduced by persecution, by diseases to which they had no immunity and by mass transfer to the Salesian mission on Dawson Island. The Boundary Treaty of 1881 divided the archipelago between Argentina and Chile, which had each claimed all of it. Oil was discovered in the north in 1945, and the Argentine part became a new province on 26 April 1990.

About two thirds of the archipelago, including most of its islands, belongs to Chile, and the eastern part to Argentina. Ushuaia, in Argentina, and Río Grande, the largest town of the archipelago, are the main Argentine towns, and Porvenir and Puerto Williams the main Chilean ones. Few Selkʼnam remain, and some of the Yaghan live at Villa Ukika on Navarino Island. Fishing, oil and gas, sheep farming and tourism are the main activities.
tigernan-ua-ruairc: Tigernán Mór Ua Ruairc, anglicised as Tiernan O'Rourke, belonged to the Ua Ruairc dynasty of Breifne, a branch of the Uí Briúin, and through his mother was a half-brother of Donnchad Ua Cerbaill. Mac Carthaigh's Book and the Annals of the Four Masters suggest he ruled as early as 1124, allied with the kings of Meath and Leinster against Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair. The Annals of Ulster and the Annals of Tigernach first name him in 1128, when he robbed and killed members of the Archbishop of Armagh's company, a deed the Annals of Ulster condemned.

He enlarged his kingdom through shifting alliances, the most lasting with Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair, King of Connacht and High King of Ireland, and later with his son Ruaidhrí Ua Conchobair, who married Tigernán's daughter Dubhchoblaigh. In 1143 he helped Toirdelbach capture Ruaidhrí, and in 1144 the High King gave him half of East Meath, the other half going to Diarmait Mac Murchada. Both joined the High King's raid into Munster in 1151.

The Annals of the Four Masters say Derbforgaill returned to him the year after her abduction, and several sources trace his part in Diarmait's expulsion in 1166 to revenge. When Diarmait came back in 1167 with a few Norman knights, Ruaidhrí, Tigernán and the King of Meath defeated him, and he had to pay Tigernán one hundred ounces of gold for the abduction. With Strongbow, Diarmait plundered Tigernán's lands in Meath in 1170. In 1171 Tigernán joined Ruaidhrí's failed siege of Dublin, and his son Aodh was killed in a raid on the Normans around the city.

Giraldus Cambrensis wrote that Ua Ruairc submitted to Henry II in 1171, and that he was killed at a parley on the Hill of Tlachtga by the Cambro-Norman knight Griffin FitzWilliam, acting in defence of Hugh de Lacy and Maurice FitzGerald. The Annals of Tigernach tell instead of betrayal by others, including a son of Strongbow. The Annals of the Four Masters called him a man of great power for a long time. Henry II had granted the Lordship of Meath to de Lacy in 1172.
tiglath-pileser-i: Tiglath-Pileser I, in Akkadian Tukultī-apil-Ešarra, meaning my trust is in the son of Ešarra, was the son of Ashur-resh-ishi I. Under him Assyria confirmed its position as the leading power of the Ancient Near East, which it largely kept for the next five hundred years. According to Georges Roux he was one of the two or three great Assyrian monarchs since the days of Shamshi-Adad I. His first campaign, in 1112 BCE, was against the Mushku, whom the sources call Phrygians, who had occupied districts held by Assyria on the Upper Euphrates. He then overran Commagene and Cappadocia and drove the Hittites from the Hurrian province of Subartu.

Later campaigns reached the mountains south of Lake Van and received the submission of Malatia. In his fifth year he attacked Comana in Cappadocia and placed an account of his victories, engraved on copper plates, in a fortress he built to secure his conquests in Cilicia. He campaigned against the Arameans in the Levant and secured the high road to the Mediterranean by taking the Hittite town of Pitru. At Arvad he sailed out and killed a nāhiru, a sea-horse, which A. Leo Oppenheim translates as a narwhal.

Tiglath-Pileser called himself the unrivalled king of the universe and king of the four quarters. He stressed the brutality of his conquests and was the first Assyrian king to take hostages, sometimes children, as a political instrument against conquered peoples. He restored the temple of the gods Ashur and Adad in the capital Assur and is believed to have been one of the first kings to commission parks and botanical gardens with foreign trees and plants from across his lands.

His inscriptions were written on eight-sided prisms and on tablets. One prism lays out his campaigns year by year and is considered one of the first preserved annals in the world. It states: Altogether I conquered 42 lands and their rulers, from the other side of the Lower Zab to the other side of the Euphrates, to the people of Hatti and the Upper Sea in the west, from my accession year to my fifth regnal year. Returning from campaigns, he set up statues of animals he had met or hunted at the gates of Ashur.

The latter part of his reign appears to have been a time of retrenchment, as Aramaean tribesmen pressed on his realm. He died in 1076 BCE and was succeeded by his son Asharid-apal-Ekur. His sons Ashur-bel-kala and Shamshi-Adad IV later ruled as well.
tiglath-pileser-iii: Tiglath-Pileser III took his name, Tukultī-apil-Ešarra, meaning my trust belongs to the son of Ešarra, probably as a regnal name on accession. Ešarra was a temple of the god Ninurta, who was viewed as the son of Ashur. Later sources call him Pul or Pulu. How he came to the throne is unclear and disputed. The Assyrian King List names his predecessor Ashur-nirari V as his father, while his own inscriptions call him a son of Adad-nirari III and so Ashur-nirari's brother. There was a revolt in Nimrud around 746 or 745, and many historians conclude he was a usurper. Karen Radner thinks that his claims of royal descent were probably true and that he won an intra-dynastic civil war.

Tiglath-Pileser curbed the magnates, the officials and generals whose influence had grown. He split the large provinces they governed into smaller ones under royally appointed governors, restricted the right to commission inscriptions to the king, and had the name of the official Shamshi-ilu erased from records. He turned the seasonal army of conscripts into a professional one, with new weapons and siege engines. The central standing army was called the kiṣir šarri, the king's unit, and was enlarged with troops from conquered lands and mercenaries.

His campaigns began in 744 against Babylonian lands east of the Tigris. In 743 he created two new provinces in the Zagros and defeated the Urartian king Sarduri II in battle near Arpad, reversing the Assyrian defeat there eleven years earlier. He then conquered most of the Levant, ending the kingdom of Aram-Damascus, and in 729 conquered Babylonia, becoming the first king to rule as sovereign of both Assyria and Babylonia. The Hebrew Bible records his actions in the Levant. He used very brutal methods, including impaling and mass dislocation of populations, to keep control.

He is believed to have died peacefully of old age, and was succeeded by his son Shalmaneser V, who was replaced after a few years by Sargon II. By the time of his death he had more than doubled the lands under Assyrian rule. He made conquered lands Assyrian provinces rather than vassal kingdoms, so that Assyria came to depend on taxes collected by governors rather than on tribute. Several Assyriologists see his reign as the point at which Assyria truly became an empire, and later Middle Eastern empires, notably the Achaemenid, took the Assyrian empire as a model.
tigranes-the-great: Tigranes belonged to the Artaxiad dynasty and was either the son or the nephew of King Artavasdes I. Around 120 BCE the Parthian king Mithridates II invaded Armenia, and Tigranes was given to the Parthians as a hostage. He lived at Ctesiphon, where he was schooled in Parthian culture and language, until about 96 or 95 BCE, when Mithridates released him and appointed him king. Babylonian astronomical diaries for 95 BCE mention him as crown prince of Armenia. He ceded an area called the seventy valleys to Mithridates II and remained a Parthian vassal until the late 80s BCE.

Tigranes set out to build a centralised empire and first consolidated his power in Armenia, where the nakharars held great influence. He deposed Artanes, the last king of Sophene, and allied with Mithridates VI of Pontus by marrying his daughter Cleopatra. Between 88 and 85 BCE he retook Adiabene, Gordyene and Media Atropatene.

In 83 BCE, after strife over the Syrian throne, the Syrians chose him as protector of their kingdom and offered him the crown. He then conquered Phoenicia and Cilicia and ended the last remnants of the Seleucid kingdom. His empire stretched from the Pontic Alps to Mesopotamia and from the Caspian Sea to the Mediterranean, and he took the title King of Kings. Many inhabitants of conquered cities were moved to his new capital, Tigranocerta, which was noted for its Hellenistic architecture.

Mithridates VI took refuge at his court after confronting Rome, and Tigranes refused the demand of the Roman commander Lucullus to expel him. Lucullus defeated Tigranes at the Battle of Tigranocerta on 6 October 69 BCE and again at Artaxata in 68 BCE. When Pompey was sent in 66 BCE, helped by Tigranes' son Tigranes the Younger, Tigranes surrendered. Pompey let him keep the heartland of Armenia as a buffer state, removed his conquests and took 6,000 talents of silver.

Tigranes ruled Armenia as a client king of Rome until his death around 55 BCE, aged 85. His successor was his youngest son, Artavasdes II. His court blended Iranian and Hellenistic influences, he took the title Philhellene, and his silver coinage minted at Antioch has been called the finest struck by an Armenian monarch. Armenian tradition ranks him first among its kings, and Movses Khorenatsi called him the most powerful, intelligent and valiant of them. Roman sources marginalised him, and modern historians differ: René Grousset praised him, while Robert H. Hewsen found his short-lived empire not especially significant and noted the forced deportations of his subjects.
tigranocerta: Tigranocerta, also called Cholimma or Chlomaron in late antiquity, bore the name of Tigranes the Great, who founded it as the capital of the Armenian Kingdom. His conquests stretched from the Caspian Sea to southern Syria, and the former capital, Artashat, had become isolated from the main trade routes in the eastern corner of the empire. The new city lay on routes connecting Mesopotamia, the East and the West. It was built in Hellenistic style, with walls 50 cubits high, a citadel and eight gates, and the Nikephorios river ran through part of its fortifications. Estimates of its population run from 100,000 to 500,000.

To populate his capital Tigranes forcibly relocated people from conquered countries: Appian reports 300,000 from Cappadocia and about 100,000 from 12 cities of Cilicia, figures Thomas Sinclair found exaggerated. In the summer of 69 BCE the Roman general Lucius Licinius Lucullus invaded Armenia while Tigranes was in Palestine. Lucullus besieged the city and defeated Tigranes' army, about 80,000 strong according to Plutarch, near the Nikephoria River. On 6 October 69 BCE captive Cappadocians opened the gates. The Romans plundered the city, sent many inhabitants home, destroyed statues, temples and its theatre, and set it on fire, and the city never recovered.

After Tigranes, Tigranocerta never regained its status as capital. The Romans under Corbulo took it again in the war of 58–63 CE, and when Armenia was divided between Rome and Persia in 387 CE it lay on the border on the Roman side as a garrison fortress. Under Arab rule from the 7th to the 9th century, as Muafarkin, it partly revived as a regional administrative centre, but by the 12th century it was an insignificant settlement. Its site is still debated: candidates are near present-day Silvan, east of Diyarbakır, Arzan, or the valley of the Garzan river, as T. A. Sinclair proposed. No systematic excavations have been carried out at the ruins.
tigray-peoples-liberation-front: The front grew out of student politics and a regional memory of revolt. Tigrayan students at Haile Selassie I University formed the Political Association of Tigrayans in 1972, and the Tigrayan University Students' Association had existed since the early 1960s. The name Woyane recalled the armed revolt of 1942–43, the First Woyane, against the restoration of imperial rule after the Italian occupation. A Marxist current in the students' association argued for national self-determination for Tigray within a democratic Ethiopia.

On 14 September 1974, two days after the Derg took power, seven of its leaders founded the Association of Progressives of the Tigray Nation, also known as the Tigrayan National Organization. The Eritrean People's Liberation Front agreed to train its members in November 1974. On the night of 18 February 1975 eleven men left Enda Selassie for Dedebit, where they founded the front. After trainees arrived from Eritrea in June 1975 it had about 50 fighters.

In 1979 its First Organisational Congress declared the struggle the Second Woyane and adopted a programme of self-determination within a democratic Ethiopia, with independence an option only if unity proved impossible. The front relied on the local population for food, shelter and information, and fighters caught mistreating civilians were punished or even executed. Its strength grew to 20,000 fighters in its early years. In February 1991 the EPRDF began an offensive with the support of a large Eritrean contingent, and on 28 May 1991 it captured Addis Ababa.

Once in government the front dropped its Marxist language and adopted multi-party politics, ethno-linguistic federalism and a mixed economy. Meles Zenawi became the first prime minister, and the front came to dominate the federal administration and the army's officer corps. Its ethnic federal system has been blamed for contributing to later civil conflicts. After Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018 he reduced its influence, and in November 2019 the EPRDF's member parties merged into the Prosperity Party, which the front refused to join.

The conflict that followed began in November 2020, after the front attacked the Northern Command of the Ethiopian National Defense Force, which its spokesman called a preemptive strike. The African Union brokered the Pretoria Peace Agreement of 2 November 2022, and the front began disarming in January 2023. Afterwards a hardline faction under Debretsion Gebremichael and a conciliatory one under Getachew Reda contested the leadership. In March 2025 The Guardian reported that Debretsion's faction had taken over several offices in Mekelle. Fighting resumed in September 2026, when the front began an offensive against the Ethiopian government.
tigrinya-language: Tigrinya is an Ethio-Semitic language, a subgroup of the Semitic branch of the Afroasiatic languages. It is spoken mainly by the Tigrinya and Tigrayan peoples of Eritrea and the Tigray Region of Ethiopia, and by diaspora communities. It differs markedly from Geʽez, the classical Ethiopic language, for instance in having phrasal verbs and in placing the main verb last in the sentence. Even so, Geʽez strongly influenced Tigrinya literature, especially in terms relating to Christian life and in Biblical names, and its lexical similarity to Geʽez is 68 per cent, slightly higher than Amharic's 62 per cent.

Tigrinya has a rich oral tradition but historically lacked a written literary tradition, which Carlo Conti Rossini attributed to the use of Geʽez in church texts and learned circles and to Amharic's status as the language of the ruling authorities. The earliest known example of Tigrinya literature is a text of local laws from the Loggo Sarda district of present-day Eritrea, believed to date from the 19th century and inserted into a Geʽez manuscript of the Gospels from about the late 15th or early 16th century.

Its sounds include ejective consonants and a seven-vowel system, and unlike many related languages it kept the two pharyngeal consonants that were apparently part of Geʽez. Verbs are built on consonantal roots, usually of three consonants, and the usual word order is subject, object, verb. Unusually among Ethiopian Semitic languages, it has a definite article. Dialects differ, and none is accepted as a standard, though the Asmara dialect is the most widely used in books, films and news.

Tigrinya is written in the Geʽez script, an abugida in which each symbol stands for a consonant and a vowel. The orthography does not mark gemination. Under British administration in Eritrea, the Ministry of Information issued a weekly Tigrinya newspaper that sold 5,000 copies. Tigrinya and Arabic were official languages of Eritrea during its federation with Ethiopia, until Amharic replaced Tigrinya in 1958. After independence in 1991 Tigrinya kept the status of a working language. It is the most widely spoken language in Eritrea and the fourth most spoken in Ethiopia, after Amharic, Oromo and Somali. Ethiopia recognised it at national level in 2020.
tigris: The Tigris is about 1,750 kilometres long. It rises in the Taurus Mountains of eastern Turkey and flows for 400 kilometres through south-eastern Turkey before forming part of the border between Syria and Turkey. Its tributaries include the Great and Little Zab. Near its confluence with the Euphrates it splits into several channels that feed the marshes, and the main channel joins the Euphrates near al-Qurnah to form the Shatt al-Arab.

Ancient writers such as Pliny held that the two rivers once had separate outlets to the sea. The Tigris has long been a transport route in a largely desert country: shallow-draft vessels can reach Baghdad, while rafts were needed downstream from Mosul. It has also been prone to floods after the April melting of snow in the Turkish mountains.

The name comes through Latin Tigris and Greek Tígris from Old Persian Tigrā, which came from Akkadian Idiglat and Sumerian Idigna. The Sumerian name can be read as the swift river, in contrast to the Euphrates, which flowed more slowly and deposited more silt. In ancient times many of the great cities of Mesopotamia stood on or near the Tigris and drew water from it to irrigate the civilisation of the Sumerians; the city of Lagash was irrigated from the river by a canal dug around 2900 BCE.

In Sumerian mythology the god Enki created the Tigris by filling it with flowing water. In the Book of Genesis it is the third of the four rivers branching from the river that issues out of Eden. The Mandaeans use the river for baptism, and the river appeared on the coat of arms of Iraq from 1932 to 1959.
tigurini: The name has often been derived from the Celtic word for lord, *tigerno-, as in Old Irish tigern and Welsh teyrn, though Peter Schrijver found this doubtful and Xavier Delamarre proposed instead the Celtic tigu-, last or final. Ancient writers name the Tigurini only in connection with the Cimbrian War and Caesar's campaign in Gaul. Caesar's statement that they formed one of four pagi of the Helvetii is the usual basis for placing them among that people, but Appian and Plutarch keep the two apart, and Michel Tarpin has argued that Caesar thereby extended to all the Helvetii a grievance that concerned the Tigurini alone.

According to Posidonius, quoted by Strabo, the plunder of the passing Cimbri drew the Tigurini and the otherwise unknown Tougeni away to join them. The Tigurini seem to have shared in the defeat of the consul Marcus Junius Silanus in 109 BCE, and in 108 BCE they supported the revolt of the Tectosages of Toulouse. At Agen the legate Lucius Piso fell with Cassius, and the survivors were sent under the yoke; Rome remembered the defeat as the clades Cassiana. After the Cimbri and Teutoni were destroyed at Aquae Sextiae and Vercellae, the Tigurini, posted as a reserve in the Noric Alps according to Florus, scattered and escaped.

Nothing is heard of them for four decades; a team led by Thierry Luginbühl has proposed that they moved from the Neckar valley to the western Swiss Plateau. Caesar presented his blow of 58 BCE as late revenge for the clades Cassiana, Piso being the grandfather of his father-in-law, and named the Helvetian envoy Divico as the victor of 107 BCE, though Gerold Walser doubts they were one man. Under the Empire an inscription at Avenches records a pagus Tigurinus.

In the 19th century Divico and the victory of 107 BCE were credited to the Helvetii as a whole, ancestors for the federal state founded in 1848, as in Charles Gleyre's painting The Romans passing under the yoke of 1858. In the early 16th century humanists gave Zurich the Neo-Latin name Tigurum, used by Huldrych Zwingli and the Froschauer press; a Roman tombstone found on the Lindenhof in 1747 showed the Roman name to have been Turicum, and Tigurum was abandoned by the end of the 18th century.
tihama: The name is related to the Proto-Semitic word tihāmat, meaning sea. The same root gave Tiamat, the ancient Mesopotamian god of the sea and of chaos, and the Hebrew təhōm of Genesis 1:2, meaning the primordial ocean or abyss. In Arabic the word is also taken to mean severe heat and lack of wind, and the temperatures of the plain are probably among the hottest on earth.

The region is sometimes divided into Tihāmat al-Ḥijāz in the north and Tihāmat ʿAsīr in the south, with the Yemeni part, Tihāmat al-Yaman, as an extension of the latter. The plain is constricted, reaching a width of 60 to 80 kilometres south of Medina and Mecca. Yanbu, Jeddah and Al Qunfudhah lie in the Hijazi part, and Jizan and Hodeidah in the Asiri-Yemeni part. Most of the sandy plain north of Zabid in Yemen has no trees. In a few places a dense shrub of Vachellia flava grows, and it may be assumed that this was originally the dominant natural vegetation. There are also thickets of Salvadora persica, wild doum palms and planted date palms.

Excavations near the village of Al-Mutaynah, led by Edward Keall of the Royal Ontario Museum's Canadian Archaeological Mission, found more than sixteen megalithic menhirs of granite, weighing up to 20 tonnes. Three of the upright stones stood around 2.4 metres tall, and one fallen stone was over 20 metres long. Copper tools thought to belong to the same era were dated to around 2400 to 1800 BCE, and an older stone tool industry with pottery sherds was dated between 1200 and 800 BCE.

In the time of the prophet Muhammad many military expeditions took place in Tihamah, among them the Battle of Hamra al-Asad and raids on caravans. From January 623 some of the Muslims raided the Meccan caravans that travelled along the eastern coast of the Red Sea from Mecca towards Syria. At Ḥamra' al-Asad Muhammad made an agreement with Mabad al-Khuzaah of Tihamah. Mabad went to Mecca and exaggerated the force Muhammad had gathered, and Abu Sufyan ibn Harb gave up a planned attack on Medina.
tikamgarh: Tikamgarh, also spelled Tikamgadh, is a town and tehsil in Tikamgarh district in Madhya Pradesh. Its earlier name was Tehri, meaning a triangle, because it consisted of three hamlets forming a rough triangle. A locality called Purani Tehri, Old Tehri, still exists in the town. The town eventually took the name of the fort of Tikamgarh, and Tikam is a name of Krishna. The district is known for the old fort of Kundar, Garh Kundar, which the Khangars built and which was the capital of Khangar rulers from 1180 to 1347.

Until Indian independence in 1947 the area was part of the kingdom of Orchha, founded in 1501 by the Bundela chief Rudra Pratap Singh, who became its first king and built the Fort of Orchha. Under Vir Singh Deo, an ally of the Mughal emperor Jahangir who reigned from 1605 to 1627, Orchha reached its height, and palaces such as the Jahangir Mahal remain from that time. In the early 17th century Jhujhar Singh rebelled against the emperor Shah Jahan, whose armies devastated the state and occupied Orchha from 1635 to 1641. Orchha and Datia were the only Bundela states the Marathas did not subjugate in the 18th century.

In the later 18th century the capital moved from Orchha to Tehri, to the south, where the fort of Tikamgarh stood. Hamir Singh, who ruled from 1848 to 1874, was raised to the style of Maharaja in 1865. His successor Pratap Singh, who reigned from 1874 and died in 1930, devoted himself to the development of the state and designed most of the engineering and irrigation works built in his reign. It was the oldest and highest in rank of the Bundela states. Pratap Singh's successor Vir Singh merged the state with India on 1 January 1950. The district became part of Vindhya Pradesh, which merged into Madhya Pradesh in 1956.

Tikamgarh is the headquarters of its district and is governed as a municipality divided into 27 wards. At the 2011 census its population was 79,106. It has become a centre for brass statues. The tradition of casting bronze statues was established in the 1950s by Bhainalal Soni, whose family made silver ornaments, and the President of India awarded Harish Soni and Dhaniran Soni for their craftsmanship. A railway line from Lalitpur reached the town in 2013. Within about 10 kilometres are Kundeshwar, a temple of Shiva, and Paporaji, a Jain site with many temples dedicated to Mahavira.
tikar-people: The Tikar have also been known as Tikari, Tigar, Tigari and Tigre, and in the time of Sultan Njoya of Bamum the missionary Henri Martin recorded that the Bamum took the name to mean those who wander. Some oral traditions trace them to the Nile valley in present-day Sudan, and some sources to the Kingdom of Kush; researchers disagree whether any evidence supports this. The historian Eldridge Mohammadou proposed that the Tikar kingdoms were founded in the 18th century by Bare-Chamba invaders who overthrew Mbum rulers, but the anthropologist David Zeitlyn found that argument short of concrete evidence.

Mbum oral tradition tells of a Princess Wou-Ten, also called Betaka, who left the Kingdom of Nganha for the Adamawa Region and founded Tinkala, held to be the first Tikar fondom. In the late 14th century the brothers Tinki and Guié founded the kingdoms of Bankim, at Rifum, and Ngambé-Tikar. In one account their descendants then founded Bamum, Nso and Nditam, and later Ngoumé, Gâ and Kong; in another, Tinki's son Nchare Yen fled a succession struggle and founded Bamum at Foumban in the late 14th or early 15th century, while his sister Ngonnso founded Nso at Kumbo.

Anthropologists and historians accept Tikar lineage claims only for the Kom, Nso, Bamum, Ndop-Bamunka and Bafut, and E. M. Chilver and Phyllis Mary Kaberry thought smaller groups' claims often political.

In the 18th and 19th centuries Chamba and Fulani slavers, drawn by Tikar iron-working, preyed on the Tikar. Many captives from Cameroon left from the Bight of Biafra, but numbers of Tikar and Duala were sold on to Sierra Leone and to Angola and shipped from there to the Americas, where they formed a large share of the enslaved Cameroonians. The losses brought a steep decline in the Tikar population, though those who remained kept their heritage alive through oral tradition.

Six adjoining Tikar kingdoms remain: Bankim, Ngambé-Tikar, Kong, Nditam, Ngoumé and Gâ, within boundaries unchanged since German colonisation. The Tikar language has four dialects, among them Túmú, spoken in Bankim and Nditam, and lacks the classical Bantu noun-class system. Most Tikar practise Christianity today, with smaller numbers following traditional religion or Islam. They call God the Creator Nyuy and revere their lineage ancestors, whose spirits were traditionally held to dwell in their preserved skulls. The Tikar are known for masks with strongly defined noses and large eyes, decorated brass pipes and carved horns and trumpets, and Toghu and Ndop cloth mark them and other Grassfields peoples.
til-barsip: Til Barsip, also written Til Barsib, lies at Tell Ahmar in the Aleppo Governorate of Syria, beside the Euphrates about 20 kilometres downstream from ancient Carchemish. The site was inhabited as early as the Neolithic. An important city arose there in the Early Bronze Age III period and was completely destroyed in Early Bronze Age IV, but the most important settlement on the mound is the Iron Age city.

In the early Iron Age the city was the Neo-Hittite capital of Masuwari. A well-preserved stele inscribed in Luwian, known as the Ahmar/Qubbah stele, commemorates a campaign by its king Hamiyatas around 900 BCE, records the cult of Tarhunzas of the Army and names the first king of Masuwari as Hapatila, perhaps an old Hurrian name. Hamiyatas set up further Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions, and the scholar Woudhuizen has suggested Semitic readings of both kings' names.

Til Barsip later became the capital of the Aramean state of Bît Adini. The Assyrians captured it from its king Ahuni and renamed it after Shalmaneser III, though the old name stayed in use, as did the Luwian language. Its position at a crossing of the Euphrates made it a leading centre of Assyrian rule in the region, while nearby Carchemish kept its own kings until Sargon II conquered it in 717 BCE. Inscribed steles record how the 8th-century BCE Aramean king Bar Ga'yah, who may be the same man as the Assyrian governor Shamshi-ilu, made a treaty with the city of Arpad.

David George Hogarth first examined the mound and proposed its identification as Til Barsip, and Gertrude Bell visited and photographed inscriptions there in 1909. The French archaeologist François Thureau-Dangin excavated from 1929 to 1931, uncovering the Iron Age city and an Early Bronze Age burial chamber rich in pottery. Guy Bunnens of the University of Melbourne led excavations from the late 1980s until 2010, finding ivory carvings of high quality published in 1997; later work has been under the University of Liège.
tilaurakot: Tilaurakot lies on the bank of the Banaganga river, west of Lumbini and 4.5 kilometres southeast of Nigali Sagar in Nigalihawa. It is one of the best-preserved early historic city sites in South Asia. Its fortified citadel covers about 500 by 400 metres and was laid out on a regular grid of streets running north to south and east to west, with open areas that may have been town squares. An earthen wall, later rebuilt in brick and doubled on the south and east, enclosed it, and an inner walled complex of over 100 by 100 metres stood at its centre.

The walls rose over an earlier wooden palisade of the 6th century BCE, built on a regular plan and perhaps meant to hold back the floods of the Banaganga. Radiocarbon dates place early farming at about 620 BCE, the first urban occupation at about 570 BCE and the earthen wall at about 450 BCE, each with a wide margin of error. Outside the walls lie a brick stupa, a probable Buddhist vihara and Lohasariya, where excavations in 2012 found 9 tons of iron slag from a period beginning around 400 BCE.

Alois Anton Führer noted the site in 1896, and P. C. Mukherji of the Archaeological Survey of India excavated it in 1899, following the accounts of the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang. He identified it with Kapilavastu, and most scholars have agreed, though others favour Piprahwa or Ganwaria. Later work included Debala Mitra's trench of 1962, Nepalese and Japanese excavations from 1967, UNESCO campaigns in 1997 and 1999 that produced the first radiocarbon dates, and joint work with Durham University in 2012 and 2013.

Tilaurakot is now a neighbourhood of Kapilvastu Municipality in Lumbini Province. The Nepalese government placed the site on UNESCO's tentative list in 1996, and objects from the excavations are shown in the Kapilvastu Museum nearby.
tillya-tepe: The name means Golden Hill or Golden Mound. The site lies near Sheberghan, half a kilometre from the heavily fortified town of Yemshi Tepe, which stands five kilometres north-east of modern Sheberghan on the road to Akcha. It was excavated by a Soviet-Afghan team. The six burial mounds held five women and one man, buried with necklaces set with semi-precious stones, belts, medallions and a crown, and with objects of silver and ivory as well as gold.

The coins suggest that the burials were made in the 1st century CE, since none is dated later than its early years. They include a silver coin of the Parthian king Mithridates II held in the hand of the woman in tomb III, a gold imitation of a coin of Gotarzes I in tomb VI, a gold coin of the Roman emperor Tiberius minted at Lugdunum between 16 and 21 CE, and an Indian gold coin in the man's tomb IV whose figure turning a wheel may be an early representation of the Buddha.

The graves most likely belonged to the Yuezhi, the future Kushans, or else to the Sakas or Eastern Parthians; the crown, the daggers and the skull deformation of several bodies point to nomads of Central Asia. Greek influence, from amorini to rings showing Athena with her name in Greek, reflects the Greco-Bactrian and Indo-Greek kingdoms, while Chinese bronze mirrors and Indian ivory plates came from farther away.

In 1989 President Mohammad Najibullah had the hoard moved to an underground vault of the Central Bank of Afghanistan in Kabul, locked with keys held by five trusted people. In 2003 the five keyholders were assembled and the vault opened in the presence of Sarianidi and Fredrik Hiebert, and the National Geographic Society found the collection apparently complete. From 2006 it toured museums in Paris, Washington, London, Melbourne, Tokyo, Beijing and elsewhere, earning over 350 million afghanis by 2020. After the Taliban took Kabul in August 2021 the treasure was apparently missing again.
tilokarat: According to the Chiang Mai Chronicle, Tilokarat was born as Thao Lok, a name meaning sixth, the sixth child of King Samfangkaen of Lan Na. His father first gave him Mueang Phrao Wang Hin, the present-day Phrao district of Chiang Mai province, to rule, but after he disobeyed his father's command he was banished to Yuam Tai, today the Mae Sariang district of Mae Hong Son province.

A royal official named Samdekyoi then plotted to give him the throne. While Samfangkaen was staying at Wiang Chet Lin, Samdekyoi secretly gathered forces, brought Thao Lok from Yuam Tai into Chiang Mai and set fire to the palace at Wiang Chet Lin so that the king would leave. When Samfangkaen returned to Chiang Mai he found that his son had seized the royal palace, and he abdicated in his favour.

The ministers crowned Thao Lok under the regnal name Maha Sri Suthammatilokaraja, and he allowed his father to live at Mueang Sat, in present-day Shan State in Burma. Samdekyoi, rewarded with the title of Saen Khan, soon plotted another rebellion. The king had him arrested by his uncle Muen Lok Nakhon, ruler of Lampang, and imprisoned without harm; on his release he was demoted and sent to govern Chiang Saen.

A younger brother, Thao Soi, ruler of Mueang Fang, invited the deposed Samfangkaen to Fang and rose in revolt. Muen Lok Nakhon captured the old king, who was brought to live in Chiang Mai, while Thao Soi fled to Mueang Thoeng and was killed there. The ruler of Thoeng, Muen Soengsamkaiharn, appealed to King Borommatrailokkanat of Ayutthaya, which began the Ayutthaya–Lan Na War. Tilokarat repelled the attack and executed Muen Soengsamkaiharn.

He went on to conquer Nan and Phrae, and attacked Chiang Hung and the Shan region several times without imposing his control. He faced several revolts, and had his favourite son, Bunruang, executed on suspicion of disloyalty.

Alongside his wars, Tilokarat was a vigorous patron of Buddhism in the Sri Lankan tradition. He built several monasteries, among them Wat Chet Yot and Wat Pa Daeng, and enlarged Wat Chedi Luang in Chiang Mai to house the Emerald Buddha. His ashes have rested since 1491 in the main chedi of Wat Chet Yot.
timar: The nature of the early Ottoman records makes it very difficult to give the timar system a concrete date. Elements of it can be traced to pre-Islamic antiquity, including the ancient Middle Eastern empires, Rome, Byzantium and pre-Islamic Iran, and the pronoia of the late Byzantine era was perhaps its immediate predecessor. Before the empire's collapse under Timur in 1402, Bayezid had granted quasi-timar holdings to his own servants.

A tenure system that was distinctly timar developed only with the re-emergence of the empire under Mehmed I in 1413, and over the next fifty years it was largely expanded and standardised. After the conquest of Constantinople in 1453, the Ottomans moved towards annexing and assimilating provinces, replacing local dynasties with the timar system and other provincial administration.

A timar was a land grant by the sultans between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries with an annual tax revenue of less than 20,000 akçes; grants of 20,000 to 100,000 akçes were called zeamets, and those above 100,000 hass. The projected revenue of a conquered territory was divided among sipahis and other members of the military class, including Janissaries, as compensation for annual military service, for which they received no pay.

The holder did not own the land, which belonged to the state, and a timar could not be inherited, although it was not uncommon for it to be reassigned to a son who performed service. A sipahi who failed to serve for seven years lost his grant. Holders employed agents called kethüda, vekil or voyvoda to collect revenue, and they had police authority but could enforce penalties only after a verdict from a local judge. Conquered territory was first surveyed in registers called tapu-tahrirs, prefaced by a law code called a kanunname.

Under Mehmed II, who ruled from 1451 to 1481, more candidates wanted grants than there were timars, so timars were split into shares or held by more than one sipahi, and sultans waged further wars to create new ones through new surveys. The arpalik, a large estate entrusted temporarily to senior officials, was introduced to compensate them and caused tensions with the provinces.

In 1528 timar holders were still the largest single division of the Ottoman army. Firearms made sipahis obsolete, and long wars against the Habsburgs and the Iranians demanded a standing professional army paid in cash, because the gun was cheaper than a horse. By the early seventeenth century much timar revenue went to the central treasury as bedel, payment for exemption from service, and the vacated holdings became tax farms, muqata'ah.
timbuktu: Timbuktu stands on the southern edge of the Sahara, about 15 to 20 kilometres north of the main channel of the Niger. It is surrounded by sand dunes, and its streets are covered in sand. The port of Kabara lies 8 kilometres to the south. The town's wealth and very existence depended on its place as the southern end of a trans-Saharan trade route.

The one good now routinely carried across the desert is rock salt, cut in slabs at Taoudenni, 664 kilometres to the north. Until the second half of the 20th century large caravans of several thousand camels took three weeks each way. The climate is a hot desert one, with most rain between June and September.

Timbuktu began as a seasonal settlement and became permanent early in the 12th century. After the visit by Mansa Musa around 1325 it flourished on the trade in salt, gold and ivory, and Mansa Musa recruited scholars from across the Islamic world. In the first half of the 15th century the Tuareg held the city for a short period, until the Songhai Empire absorbed it in 1468. A Moroccan army defeated the Songhai in 1591 and made Timbuktu its capital; the invaders formed a ruling class, the Arma, who after 1612 were virtually independent of Morocco.

The French took over Mali in 1893, and colonial rule lasted until 1960. Leo Africanus, born in Granada in 1485 and educated in Fes, visited the city and wrote an account in Italian that gave Europeans most of what they knew of Africa for centuries.

Timbuktu is the capital of the Tombouctou Region of Mali. It has three notable mosques: Djinguereber, built in 1327 under Mansa Musa, Sankoré, built in the 14th or 15th century, and Sidi Yahya, founded in 1400 and completed in 1440. In December 1988 the World Heritage Committee inscribed parts of its historic centre. The city was a world centre of Islamic learning from the 13th to the 17th century, and hundreds of thousands of manuscripts were gathered there, hidden in cellars or buried to survive the decline; libraries in Timbuktu held up to 700,000 in 2003.
time-of-troubles: Tsar Feodor I, a pious and weak ruler who took little interest in politics, governed through his brother-in-law Boris Godunov. His younger half-brother Dmitry died in May 1591; an investigative commission concluded that the boy had accidentally cut his own throat during an epileptic seizure. When Feodor died in January 1598 without an heir, the main line of the Rurik dynasty ended. Godunov was crowned in September 1598 after a sham Zemsky Sobor had elected him. The famine of 1601 to 1603, possibly caused by the eruption of the volcano Huaynaputina in Peru, ruined harvests, killed a large share of the population and damaged Godunov's reputation.

In 1603 a man claiming to be Dmitry appeared in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and in October 1604 he crossed into Russia. After Godunov died in 1605, False Dmitry I entered Moscow and was crowned on 21 July. He was killed in a Moscow uprising on 17 May 1606, and Prince Vasily Shuisky was proclaimed tsar. A second pretender, False Dmitry II, appeared in 1607 and besieged Moscow from Tushino. In 1609 King Sigismund III of Poland besieged Smolensk, and at the Battle of Klushino in 1610 the Poles routed Shuisky's army.

Shuisky was forced to become a monk in July 1610, and a council of Seven Boyars invited Sigismund's son Wladyslaw to rule. Polish troops occupied Moscow, and Sweden occupied Novgorod in 1611. Polish and German troops put down a Moscow uprising in March 1611, killing about 7,000. A second national militia, raised by Kuzma Minin and led by Prince Dmitry Pozharsky, reached Moscow in July 1612, and on 27 October 1612 the Polish garrison surrendered.

The Zemsky Sobor elected the sixteen-year-old Mikhail Romanov tsar on 21 February 1613, and he was crowned on 21 July. The Romanov dynasty ruled Russia until the February Revolution of 1917. The historian Chester Dunning calls it a tragic irony that Mikhail ended the Troubles partly by crushing the Cossacks who had brought him to power. The Ingrian War ended with the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, and the Truce of Deulino of 1619 ended fighting with Poland. Russia kept its independence but made substantial territorial concessions, ceding Ingria to Sweden, though most of the losses were recovered in the following century.
timgad: Timgad lies in the Aurès Mountains of Algeria, about 35 km east of Batna, at roughly 1,000 metres above sea level. Its full name was Colonia Marciana Ulpia Traiana Thamugadi. Trajan named it for his mother Marcia, his eldest sister Ulpia Marciana and his father Marcus Ulpius Traianus, while Thamugadi is the Berber name of the site, the plural of Tamgut, meaning peak or summit. It has been nicknamed the Pompeii of North Africa.

Trajan founded the city as a colony in about 100 CE, intended chiefly as a Roman bastion against the Berbers of the nearby Aurès Mountains, and it was populated largely by Roman veterans and colonists. After a peaceful early existence it became a centre of Christian activity from the 3rd century and a Donatist centre in the 4th, when its bishop Optatus became spokesman for the Donatist movement.

The Vandals sacked the city in the 5th century, and Berber tribes from the Aurès destroyed it at the end of that century. In 539 the Byzantine general Solomon retook and rebuilt it during the Moorish wars. It was no longer inhabited by the 8th century. The Scottish explorer James Bruce reached the ruins on 12 December 1765, probably the first European to see them in centuries. French colonists took control of the site in 1881 and excavated it systematically until 1960.

The ruins are one of the best surviving examples of the Roman grid plan. The decumanus maximus, running east to west, and the cardo, running north to south, were lined with a Corinthian colonnade. Built to hold about 15,000 people, the city outgrew its plan and spread beyond the grid. The Arch of Trajan, a 12-metre triumphal arch of sandstone, stands at the west end of the decumanus.

A theatre of 3,500 seats is in good condition and is used for contemporary productions. Other buildings include four baths, a basilica and a Capitoline temple dedicated to Jupiter, of about the same dimensions as the Pantheon in Rome. The library, a gift of Julius Quintianus Flavius Rogatianus, probably dates from the late 3rd or the 4th century and could have held about 3,000 scrolls. UNESCO inscribed Timgad as a World Heritage Site in 1982.
timisoara: Timișoara lies on the Bega River, the southernmost tributary of the Tisza, in the south-eastern part of the Pannonian Basin. Archaeological remains show farmers, hunters and artisans living in the fertile lands between the Mureș, the Tisza and the Danube by 4000 BCE. The Bega was canalised, and a navigable canal was built along it between 1728 and 1760. The Hungarian name Temesvár was first recorded as Temeswar in 1315 and refers to a castle on the Timiș River; the Romanian and German forms derive from it.

The city is first officially mentioned in 1212 as a royal fortress, though some historians date its first documentary mention to 1266, when the heir apparent Stephen V of Hungary donated part of a fortress built by his father, Béla IV. After Tatar destruction in the 13th century it was rebuilt under Charles I of Hungary, who ordered stone walls and a royal palace in 1307 and moved the royal seat there from Buda between 1316 and 1323.

After the defeat at Mohács in 1526 the Banat was contested between the Habsburgs and the Ottomans. On 22 July 1552 an army led by Kara Ahmed Pasha took the city and made it the capital of the Temeşvar Eyalet; the local commander István Losonczy and other Christians were massacred on 27 July as they tried to escape. In 1716 Prince Eugene of Savoy besieged it for 48 days, and bombardment destroyed much of the city. By the Treaty of Passarowitz (1718) the Banat of Temeswar became a possession of the Habsburg crown under military rule until 1751. From 1848 to 1860 the city was the capital of the Serbian Vojvodina.

Under Austria-Hungary the city grew quickly and its industries included breweries, an iron foundry and a match factory. On 1 November 1918 the Banat Republic was proclaimed briefly. Serbian forces held the city until 1919, and the Treaty of Trianon of 4 June 1920 ceded it to Romania, whose King Ferdinand I made it a university centre that year.

Timișoara is the capital of Timiș County and the main economic and cultural centre of western Romania, with 250,849 inhabitants at the 2021 census. Romanian is the official language; German, Hungarian and Serbian communities remain, and the city has the largest German population in Romania. It was the first city in the Habsburg monarchy with street lighting, in 1760, and the first in Europe lit by electric street lamps, in 1884. It is nicknamed Little Vienna and the City of Roses.
timok: The Timok, also called the Great Timok or Veliki Timok, is a right tributary of the Danube in eastern Serbia. It is a branching system of many shorter rivers, many of them also called Timok with a qualifying word. From the farthest source, that of the Svrljiški Timok, to the confluence it is 202 kilometres long, and its basin covers 4,626 square kilometres. The average discharge at the mouth is 31 cubic metres per second. The Timok Valley holds the most important Vlach population of eastern Serbia. The name comes from antiquity, when the river was Timacus in Latin and Timachos in Greek.

The river gave its name to two tribes on its banks: the Thracian or Thraco-Celtic Timachi, in the 1st to 3rd centuries CE, and the Slavonic Timočani, in the 6th to 9th centuries. It also named the Timok Rebellion of 1883 against King Milan Obrenović. At Čokonjar the Sokolovica power plant was built between 1947 and 1951.

The Timok forms at Zaječar from the confluence of the Beli Timok and the Crni Timok, and the Beli Timok is itself formed at Knjaževac by the Svrljiški Timok and the Trgoviški Timok. It turns north-west, leaves the Timok Valley between the villages of Trnavac and Brusnik, and enters the Negotin Valley. In its lower course it has no major settlement on the Serbian side. For its last 15 kilometres it forms the border between eastern Serbia and western Bulgaria, passing the Bulgarian town of Bregovo.

Its mouth is the northernmost point of Bulgaria and, at 28 metres above sea level, the lowest point of Serbia. The river belongs to the Black Sea basin. Its valley is a natural route for the road and railway between Niš and Prahovo, and mining and heavy-metal industry at Bor and Krivelj have polluted it with lead, copper and cadmium.
timoleon: Timoleon, son of Timodemus, belonged to the Corinthian oligarchy. In the mid 360s BCE his brother Timophanes seized the acropolis of Corinth and made himself tyrant. Timoleon, who had once saved his brother's life in battle, pleaded with him repeatedly to desist and then became involved in his assassination. Most Corinthians approved the act as patriotic, but the killing, his mother's curses and the anger of some fellow citizens drove him to withdraw from public life for twenty years.

In 344 BCE Syracusans appealed to their mother city Corinth for help against the tyranny of Dionysius I and his son and the repeated attacks of Carthage. Corinth's chief citizens declined the task, and Timoleon was chosen by a unanimous vote after an unknown voice named him in the assembly.

He sailed with seven ships and about 700 mercenaries, slipped past a Carthaginian squadron and landed at Tauromenium. He defeated Hicetas, the tyrant of Leontini, at Adranum, and in 343 BCE Dionysius II surrendered Ortygia in return for safe conduct to Corinth. Hicetas received 60,000 Carthaginian troops, but mutual suspicion led Carthage to abandon him, and he surrendered at Leontini.

Timoleon then destroyed the tyrants' citadel and put a courthouse in its place. He brought settlers from across Greece to the depopulated island and restored popular government on the laws of Diocles. When Hicetas persuaded Carthage to send an army of 70,000 men to Lilybaeum, Timoleon marched west with about 12,000, most of them mercenaries, and won a decisive victory at the Crimissus, helped by the unfinished river crossing and a storm blowing in the faces of the Carthaginians.
Hicetas was later captured and put to death. A treaty in 338 BCE confined Carthage to the west of the Halycus river and bound it to give no further help to Sicilian tyrants.

Timoleon retired to private life soon after his aims were met. By then blind, he was carried to the assembly to give his opinion on important matters, and it was usually accepted. The Syracusans buried him at public cost and built a monument in their market-place, later surrounded with porticoes, and a gymnasium called the Timoleonteum.

The historian Timaeus praised him; Polybius thought Timaeus biased, and many modern historians agree. Peter Green sees him as no more than a benevolent tyrant like Pisistratus who posed as a democrat, while George Grote agreed with a Syracusan eulogy that he restored the constitution and laws of the Sicilian Greeks.
timor: Timor lies in the north of the Timor Sea, at the eastern end of the Lesser Sunda Islands, and its name is a variant of timur, Malay for east. Mainland Australia is less than 500 km away. The island covers 30,777 square kilometres, and its mountains reach nearly 3,000 metres. Mutis is the highest in West Timor and Ramelau the highest in Timor-Leste.

The climate has a long dry season from April to November, with hot winds blowing from Australia. Anthropologists identify eleven ethno-linguistic groups on the island, the largest being the Atoni of the west and the Tetun of the centre and east. Most indigenous languages belong to the Timor-Babar branch of the Austronesian family.

The earliest historical record of Timor is the Chinese Zhu Fan Zhi of the 13th century, which calls it Ti-wu and notes its sandalwood. The Javanese Nagarakretagama of the 14th century names it as an island within the realm of Majapahit. By then Timor was part of Javanese, Chinese and Indian trading networks, exporting sandalwood, slaves, honey and wax.

The Portuguese and the Dutch later settled there, the Dutch from Kupang in the mid-17th century, and they fought for control until a treaty of 1859 divided it, though the boundary was not formally settled until 1912. West Timor was Dutch Timor until 1949, when it joined Indonesia, and East Timor was a Portuguese colony until 1975.

In 1789 William Bligh and the seamen loyal to him reached Timor after the mutiny on the Bounty. In December 1941 Australian and Dutch forces occupied Portuguese Timor, and after the Japanese landed in February 1942 a 400-strong Dutch-Australian force and many Timorese volunteers fought a year-long guerrilla campaign. The Japanese occupation killed between 40,000 and 70,000 Timorese.

After the Carnation Revolution of 1974 the Portuguese withdrew, and in 1975 Indonesia invaded and annexed East Timor, an annexation the United Nations and Portugal never recognised. Falintil resisted in a prolonged guerrilla war until a UN-sponsored referendum in 1999 rejected autonomy within Indonesia. The UN governed the territory until it became independent as Timor-Leste in 2002.

The island is divided between Timor-Leste in the east, with its capital at Dili, and West Timor, part of the Indonesian province of East Nusa Tenggara, whose provincial capital is Kupang. Timor-Leste also holds the exclave of Oecusse within West Timor. The official languages of Timor-Leste are Tetun and Portuguese, and in West Timor Indonesian. Christianity is the dominant religion across the island.
