timotheus-general: From 378 to 356 BCE Timotheus often held command as strategos in the wars of Athens, allied with Thebes, against Sparta, when Athens hoped to revive the Delian League and regain command of the sea. In 375 BCE, during the Boeotian War, he sailed round the Peloponnesus, won Cephallenia over to Athens and secured the friendship of the Acarnanians and Molossians.

In 373 BCE he was given a fleet to relieve Corcyra, besieged by the Spartans, but spent time cruising the Aegean to man his ships. Brought to trial for the delay, he was acquitted after Jason, tyrant of Pherae, and Alcetas I of Epirus came to Athens to plead for him. He then took Corcyra and beat the Spartans at sea off Alyzia, but having spent his own money on the fleet he left to serve the king of Persia as a mercenary.

Sent in 366 BCE to support Ariobarzanes, satrap of Phrygia, he found him in revolt against Persia and, following his orders, turned instead on Samos. He went on to take Sestus, Crithote, Torone, Potidaea, Methone, Pydna and other cities, though two attempts on Amphipolis failed.

In the Social War Timotheus was sent with Iphicrates, his son Menestheus and Chares against the rebel allies. In the Hellespont, with a gale blowing, Iphicrates and Timotheus declined battle, while Chares engaged and lost many ships, then blamed his colleagues. Iphicrates was acquitted, but Timotheus, long disliked for his perceived arrogance, was fined too heavily to pay and withdrew to Chalcis. The Athenians later forgave most of the fine, which had passed to his son Conon, buried him in the Ceramicus and set up statues of him in the Agora and on the Acropolis.

Rivals mocked him as merely lucky: Aelian records that painters showed him asleep while Tyche, Fortune, pulled cities into her net. Isocrates, by contrast, described a skilled and cautious general, a generous victor and a quiet diplomat.
timur: Timur was born in Transoxiana near the city of Kesh, now Shahrisabz in Uzbekistan, about 80 kilometres south of Samarkand, then part of the Chagatai Khanate. He belonged to the Barlas, a Turkicized Mongol confederation. His name, Temur, means iron in Chagatai, his mother tongue. Timurid histories trace his descent in the male line from Tumbinai Khan, an ancestor of Genghis Khan, but no written evidence from his own lifetime links him directly to Genghis Khan. By about 1360 he had become a military leader whose troops were mostly Turkic tribesmen, and he campaigned in Transoxiana with the Khan of the Chagatai Khanate.

Timur reduced the Chagatai khans to figureheads and ruled in their name. Because he was not a descendant of Genghis Khan, Mongol tradition denied him the title of khan, so he used the title of amir and set up a puppet khan, Suyurghatmish. His first campaigns took Khwarazm and Urgench, and in 1383 he began his conquest of Persia. When Herat did not surrender he reduced it to rubble and massacred most of its citizens.

In 1398 Timur invaded the Indian subcontinent, where the Tughlaq dynasty's Delhi Sultanate had declined and most provincial governors had asserted their independence. He crossed the Indus on 30 September 1398 with a force of 90,000 and sacked Tulamba, massacring its inhabitants. Before the battle for Delhi on 17 December 1398 he slaughtered some 100,000 captives, fearing that they might revolt. In the following years he fought the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I and the Mamluk sultan of Egypt, Nasir-ad-Din Faraj, and had Ming envoys detained. Scholars estimate that his campaigns caused the deaths of millions.

In December 1404 Timur began a winter campaign against Ming China. He fell ill beyond the Syr Daria and died at Farab on 17 or 18 February 1405. He had outlived two chosen heirs, his son Jahangir and his grandson Muhammad Sultan, and on his deathbed named Muhammad Sultan's brother Pir Muhammad. A civil war among his descendants followed, and his youngest son Shah Rukh took the throne only in 1409.

His legacy is mixed. Central Asia flourished under him, while Baghdad, Damascus, Delhi and other cities were sacked and their people massacred. He keeps a positive image in Muslim Central Asia and is vilified in Arabia, Iraq, Persia and India. Two Zafarnamas written under Timurid patronage present him favourably, while the Arabic chronicle of Ahmad ibn Arabshah is far less so.
timurid-empire: Timur belonged to the Barlas tribe, a Mongol group of the Chagatai ulus that had become Turkified in language and culture. He saw himself as the restorer of the Mongol Empire of Genghis Khan. Because he could not claim descent from Genghis, he married a Genghisid princess, Saray Mulk Khanum, and took the title Gurkani, meaning son-in-law. He took Samarkand in 1366 and Balkh in 1369, and was recognised as ruler of the region in 1370. He acted officially in the name of the Chagatai khan, but in practice Timur chose the khans, who became puppet rulers.

From 1380 Timur campaigned westwards against the successor states of the Ilkhanate. He removed the Kartids from Herat, captured Isfahan in 1387, drove the Muzaffarids from Shiraz and expelled the Jalayirids from Baghdad. In 1394–1395 he defeated Tokhtamysh, khan of the Golden Horde, after a campaign in Georgia, and enforced his sovereignty in the Caucasus. The costs of his conquests included the deaths of possibly 17 million people.

Timur gave the main governorships to his sons and grandsons. After his death in 1405 the dynasty fell into disputes and civil wars, and many governors became independent. Samarkand and Herat became the centres of the Timurid Renaissance under Shahrukh Mirza (1405–1447) and his son Ulugh Beg (1447–1449), and Herat flowered again under Husayn Bayqara (1469–1506). Meanwhile the Timurid habit of partitioning the realm weakened it. The Aq Qoyunlu took most of Iran, and the Safavid Empire under Shah Ismail I soon took Persia, the Caucasus and Mesopotamia. The Uzbeks under Shaybani Khan overran the central Asian principalities and founded the Khanate of Bukhara.

Babur, a Timurid prince exiled from Fergana, set up a base at Kabul in 1504 and invaded the Delhi Sultanate in 1526. The Mughal dynasty he founded was directly inherited from the Timurids, and the last nominal Mughal rule was abolished by the British after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

The Timurid era combined Turco-Mongol origins with Persian high culture. The military was at first almost wholly Turco-Mongolian, while the administration was Persian, and Persian became the official language, with Chaghatay as the family's home language. The golden age of Persian painting began under the Timurids, with Chinese influence. Their architecture favoured large buildings, double-shelled domes and rich tile decoration, as at the Gur-i Amir Mausoleum and the Bibi-Khanym Mosque in Samarkand. Gawhar Shad was its most important patron in the 15th century. Its style passed to the Safavids, the Mughals and early Ottoman builders.
tin: Tin is a chemical element with the symbol Sn, from the Latin stannum, and atomic number 50. It is a soft, silvery-white, malleable metal that can be cut with little force, and a bent bar of tin makes a crackling sound known as the tin cry, caused by the twinning of its crystals. It resists corrosion from water. It does not occur as the native element but is extracted from ores, chiefly cassiterite, the only commercially important source, which is almost always associated with granite.

The word tin is shared among the Germanic languages and traces back to a reconstructed Proto-Germanic form; cognates include German Zinn, Swedish tenn and Dutch tin. The Latin name stannum or stagnum originally meant an alloy of silver and lead, and came to mean tin in the fourth century. The earlier Latin word was plumbum candidum, or white lead. The origin of stannum is unknown and may be pre-Indo-European.

Tin extraction and use can be dated to the beginnings of the Bronze Age around 3000 BCE. The earliest bronze objects had a tin or arsenic content of under 2 per cent and are believed to be the result of unintentional alloying. Adding a second metal to copper increases its hardness, lowers its melting temperature and gives a more fluid melt, which allowed the more complex shapes cast in closed moulds of the Bronze Age.

Arsenical bronze appears first in the Near East, where arsenic is commonly found with copper ore, but its health risks were quickly realised, and the quest for sources of the much less hazardous tin began early in the Bronze Age. This created a demand for rare tin and a trade network linking distant sources of tin to the markets of Bronze Age cultures. The first tin alloy used on a large scale was bronze, of one eighth tin and seven eighths copper; after 600 BCE pure metallic tin was produced. Pewter, an alloy of 85 to 90 per cent tin, has been used for flatware since the Bronze Age.
tincomarus: The name Tincomarus is of a form typical of Celtic names, probably made of tinco-, perhaps a kind of fish, and maro-, big. It was once reconstructed as Tincommius from abbreviated coin legends and a damaged passage of the Res Gestae of Augustus, but coins found since 1996 give the full name. Tincomarus was the son and heir of Commius, king of the Atrebates, an Iron Age Belgic tribe of southern central Britain. The historian John Creighton argues from the imagery of his coins that he may have been brought up as a diplomatic hostage in Rome early in the reign of Augustus, comparing them with the coins of Juba II of Numidia.

Tincomarus succeeded his father around 25 to 20 BCE, and the spread of the coins suggests he may have ruled with Commius in his father's last years. Little is known of the reign, but his coins resemble Roman types far more closely than his father's, and may have been made by Roman die-cutters. George C. Boon has suggested that this reflects wider technical help from the Roman Empire, beyond coinage. His successors called themselves rex on their coins, which indicates that Tincomarus had begun the process of becoming a Roman client king.

By 16 BCE Roman pottery and other imports reached his capital, Calleva Atrebatum, the modern Silchester, in considerable quantities, and he had probably established trading and diplomatic links with Augustus. Around 8 CE his subjects expelled him for unknown reasons, and he fled to Rome as a refugee and suppliant. Augustus chose to recognise his brother Eppillus as king rather than restore him. Augustus may have thought of using the expulsion of his ally as a pretext to invade Britain, but more pressing affairs probably led him to put the plan off.
tinian: Tinian is one of the three principal islands of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. It lies about 9.3 kilometres south-west of Saipan, across the Saipan Channel, and with the uninhabited island of Aguijan forms Tinian Municipality. The island has a land area of about 100 square kilometres and is much flatter than Saipan, with limestone cliffs and caves and a highest point of 187 metres on the Kastiyu plateau. Its main village, San Jose, is on the south-west coast, and the Tinian monarch is the island's only endemic bird.

The Mariana Islands were the first islands settled by humans in Remote Oceania, around 1500 to 1400 BCE, by migrants from the Philippines. A people who built stone structures called taga lived on Tinian thousands of years ago. The Spanish formally occupied the island in 1669 with the missionary expedition of Diego Luis de San Vitores, who named it Buenavista Mariana.

The native population, estimated at 40,000 when the Spanish arrived, fell to under 1,400 through introduced diseases and conflicts over land, and the survivors were forcibly moved to Guam in 1720. Spain sold the island to the German Empire in 1899. Japan captured it in 1914 and was given formal control in 1918 under the South Seas Mandate, and settlers from Japan, Korea and Okinawa built large sugar plantations; by June 1944 about 15,700 Japanese civilians lived there.

The Japanese did not garrison Tinian until the late stages of the Second World War, when its value as a base for American B-29 bombers became clear. Allied forces took the island in the Battle of Tinian, from 24 July to 1 August 1944, in which only 313 of the 8,500-man Japanese garrison survived and many hundreds of civilians were killed or took their own lives. The Americans then built the largest airbase of the war, with a naval base for 40,000 personnel. From North Field the B-29s Enola Gay and Bockscar took off carrying the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The loading pits for the atomic bombs and the remains of the bomber base and Japanese fortifications can still be seen at North Field, where a memorial stands over the pits. After the war Tinian became part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands and has been a municipality of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands since 1978. The House of Taga, a site of latte stones quarried from limestone, is one of the most significant structures in the Marianas, although only one of its twelve large structures still stands.
tintagel: Tintagel, also called Trevena, from the Cornish Tre war Venydh, meaning village on a mountain, is a civil parish and village on the Atlantic coast of Cornwall. The origin of the name is uncertain. It may be Norman French, or Cornish, and Oliver Padel proposes din, a fort, with tagell, meaning neck or narrow place. It first appears as Tintagol in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae, written about 1136. The coastline is of old Devonian slate, and the Tintagel slate quarries, worked from the fifteenth until the early twentieth century, are largely responsible for the jagged coast to the south.

The largest Bronze Age barrow in the parish stands at Condolden, and there were probably Iron Age fortifications at Willapark and Barras Head. A Roman milestone found in the churchyard wall in 1889 refers to the Emperor Licinius. Major excavations beginning with C. A. Ralegh Radford in the 1930s showed that the headland was, in the 5th and 6th centuries, either a high-status Celtic monastery, as Radford held, or, according to later excavators, a princely fortress and trading settlement. Finds of Mediterranean oil and wine jars show that Sub-Roman Britain was not as isolated as once thought. The Ravenna Cosmography, of around 700, mentions Purocoronavis, a fort of the Cornovii, which may have stood at Tintagel or at Carn Brea.

A small cliff castle was founded at Bossiney in Norman times, probably before the Domesday Survey of 1086. In 1253 Richard, 1st Earl of Cornwall, established Bossiney and Trevena as a borough, and Tintagel was one of the seventeen ancient manors of the Duchy of Cornwall. From 1552 to 1832 the borough of Bossiney sent two members to the House of Commons.

In Geoffrey's account, Gorlois, Duke of Cornwall, placed his wife Igraine in Tintagol while he was at war. Merlin disguised Uther Pendragon as Gorlois so that Uther could enter and father a child, who was Arthur. This became the standard origin story of Arthur in later chronicles and romances, and Alfred, Lord Tennyson's Idylls of the King popularised the link in the modern era. Parts of the Tristan and Iseult legend are also set there. The Artognou stone, found in 1998, is not thought by historians to refer to Arthur.

The parish had 1,725 inhabitants at the 2021 census. Tintagel Old Post Office dates from the 14th century and is a Grade I listed building owned by the National Trust. The Church of St Materiana, also Grade I, stands on the cliffs between Trevena and the castle, and its first church was probably of the 6th century. Tintagel has inspired composers, among them Arnold Bax, who wrote the symphonic poem Tintagel after a visit.
tintoretto: Jacopo Robusti was born in Venice, the son of Battista, a dyer, which gave him the nickname Tintoretto, little dyer. According to his early biographers Carlo Ridolfi and Marco Boschini, his only formal apprenticeship was in the studio of Titian, who dismissed him after a few days. Tintoretto then studied on his own, drawing from models and casts, including models of Michelangelo's figures, and often worked by night. Above his studio he placed the inscription Michelangelo's drawing and Titian's colour.

He often worked for little or nothing to win commissions. The first work to bring him notice on a large scale was the Miracle of the Slave, commissioned in 1548 for the Scuola di S. Marco, which was a success despite some detractors.

After Paolo Veronese arrived in Venice in 1551, Tintoretto offered the church of the Madonna dell'Orto two colossal canvases on a cost-only basis, the Worship of the Golden Calf and the Last Judgment, each 14.5 metres tall and painted about 1559 to 1560. In 1564 he won the commission for the Scuola Grande di San Rocco by installing a full-sized painting on the ceiling and offering it as a gift. Between 1565 and 1567, and again from 1575 to 1588, he painted its walls and ceilings, and the scuola and its church hold fifty-two paintings by him.

His quick technique, called prestezza, and his use of assistants let him produce more paintings for the Venetian state than any competitor. He also worked in the Doge's Palace, where a fire in 1577 destroyed earlier pictures. His Paradise there, 9.1 by 22.6 metres, was reputed to be the largest painting ever done on canvas. The commission passed to him after Veronese died in 1588, and his son Domenico helped to finish it.

Tintoretto's style uses bold brushwork, long strokes, extreme foreshortening and emphatic perspective, and conveys narrative through the gestures of figures rather than their faces. His Saint George, Saint Louis, and the Princess of 1553 shows the princess sitting astride the dragon with a whip. He was Venice's most prolific portrait painter, and painted two self-portraits, one about 1546 to 1547 and one about 1588.

He married Faustina de Vescovi about 1560, and had a daughter, Marietta Robusti, before the marriage. She trained with him as a painter and died in 1590 at thirty. Tintoretto died on 31 May 1594 and was buried in the Madonna dell'Orto beside Marietta. El Greco is thought to have studied his work, which was influential on his painting style.
tioman-island: Tioman Island, in Malay Pulau Tioman, lies 39 kilometres off the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia, off the Rompin District of Pahang. It is 20 kilometres long and 12 kilometres wide and has seven villages, of which Kampung Tekek, on the central western coast, is the largest and most populous. The island is densely forested and sparsely inhabited, and is surrounded by numerous coral reefs. Ferries reach it from the coastal towns of Mersing and Teluk Gading.

Austronesian fishermen have used Tioman for thousands of years as a navigation point and a source of fresh water and wood. During the past thousand years Chinese, Arab and European trading ships bound for Champa called at the island, and shards of Chinese porcelain can often be found on its beaches. In the Second World War Tioman hosted both the British and the Japanese navies, and the waters around it are littered with war remains, among them HMS Repulse and HMS Prince of Wales.

Local tradition explains the island's shape in two ways. One legend makes it the resting place of a dragon princess who was flying to visit her prince in Singapore, stopped in the clear waters of the South China Sea, and took the form of an island to shelter passing travellers. Another says it is the dragon Sri Gumom, who was on his way to visit his sister Gunung Linga, the Lingin Peak, when Sri Rama forbade the meeting and turned him to stone.

The inland rainforest was protected in 1972 as the Pulau Tioman Wildlife Reserve, although much of the original reserve was given up in 1984 for agricultural and tourist development, leaving about 8,296 hectares. The island has 45 species of mammals and 138 species of birds, and some species found nowhere else, including the Tioman walking catfish and the Kajang slender litter frog, which is known only from Mount Kajang.

The surrounding waters, with eight other nearby islands, are declared marine parks and reserves, and contain coral reefs, seagrass beds and mangrove forest. Corals were hit by a mass bleaching event in 2010. A proposal to build an international airport on reclaimed land on the west coast was rejected by the authorities in 2018 because of its environmental effects, but an environmental impact assessment for it was later submitted.
tippecanoe-river: The Tippecanoe is a gentle river of 182 miles (293 km) in the Central Corn Belt Plains ecoregion. It rises in kettle lakes left by ancient glaciers in Noble County, flowing from Crooked Lake through Wilmot Pond, Backwaters Lake and Tippecanoe Lake in Kosciusko County. It then runs south and west through Marshall County, north-west through Fulton and Pulaski Counties, where it crosses Tippecanoe River State Park, and on through White and Carroll Counties into Tippecanoe County, where it joins the Wabash River near Battle Ground.

Eighty-eight natural lakes feed the river, and its drainage area of about 5,100 square kilometres spans 14 counties. Its name comes from a word of the Miami–Illinois language for the buffalo fish. Besides Tippecanoe County, five townships along the river, in Carroll, Kosciusko, Marshall, Pulaski and Tippecanoe Counties, carry its name.

The Battle of Tippecanoe, in which Governor William Henry Harrison defeated the confederacy led by Tecumseh, was fought near the south bank of the river, and modern Lafayette grew up near the site. Numerous dams were built along its course to create lakes and ponds for water power. In 1925 two hydroelectric plants were added: the Oakdale plant created Lake Freeman, reaching 7 miles north through Monticello, and the Norway plant created Lake Shafer, reaching 6 miles north from Norway.

The river supports more imperilled species and a greater diversity of species than most streams of the upper Midwest, and the Nature Conservancy has named it one of the ten rivers of the United States most worth preserving. Surveys since 1903 have recorded 57 species of freshwater mussels, among them the northern riffleshell, the kidneyshell and the clubshell, which is federally endangered. Silt from dredging and changes in land use threaten them. Fish surveys of the early 21st century found 54 species in 14 families, nearly 80 per cent of them game fish, with bluegill the most common.
tippu-tip: Tippu Tip, whose full name was Ḥamad ibn Muḥammad ibn Jumʿah al Murjabī, was probably born in Zanzibar in the 1830s, though sources differ on the year. According to Heinrich Brode, who drew largely on Tippu Tip's own recollections, his mother came from a respected and prosperous Muscat family of the Wardi clan, and his paternal ancestors were Arab traders connected with the Swahili Coast and the interior caravan trade.

A paternal great-grandmother was an African woman from Mbwa Maji, south of Dar es Salaam. One translator rendered his nickname as the gatherer together of wealth, but by his own account it came from the sound of gunfire on expeditions in Central Africa. While still young he led about 100 men from Zanzibar into Central Africa in search of slaves and ivory.

He worked for a succession of sultans of Zanzibar and traded in slaves for the island's clove plantations. He led many expeditions into Central Africa and built profitable trading posts deep in the Congo Basin. By 1895 he had acquired seven plantations and 10,000 slaves. He met and helped explorers such as David Livingstone and Henry Morton Stanley. Between 1884 and 1887 he claimed the eastern Congo for himself and for Sultan Bargash bin Said of Zanzibar, ruling a large territory centred on Kasongo.

When fighting broke out in August 1886 between the Swahili and the representatives of King Leopold II at Stanley Falls, he assured the Belgian consul at Zanzibar of his good intentions, since he could see that power in the region was shifting. In early 1887 Stanley proposed that he become governor of the Stanley Falls District of the Congo Free State. Leopold and the Sultan agreed, and on 24 February 1887 he accepted. He also agreed to supply men for Stanley's expedition to relieve Emin Pasha, governor of Equatoria.

Tippu Tip retired in 1891 and returned to Zanzibar, where he became a close adviser to Sultan Hamoud bin Mohammed and made no more journeys into the interior. After he left the Congo, power in its eastern parts still lay largely with Arab and Swahili strongmen, among them his son Sefu bin Hamid. In 1892 Sefu attacked Belgian ivory traders, and the Free State sent a force under Francis Dhanis, which defeated its opponents in several fights, until Sefu died on 20 October 1893.

He wrote an account of his life, the first autobiography in the Bantu Swahili language. Brode transcribed it into Roman script and translated it into German, and it was published in English in Britain in 1907. Tippu Tip died of malaria, according to Brode, at his home in Stone Town, Zanzibar.
tipu-sultan: Tipu Sultan was born on 1 December 1751 in Devanahalli, about 33 kilometres north of Bangalore, and was named after the saint Tipu Mastan Aulia of Arcot. His father, Hyder Ali, was illiterate and took care to give his eldest son a religious education and an early exposure to military and political affairs. French officers in his father's employment instructed him in military tactics. At 15 he accompanied his father against the British in the First Anglo-Mysore War in 1766, and at 16 he commanded a corps of cavalry in the invasion of the Carnatic.

In September 1780, during the Second Anglo-Mysore War, Hyder Ali sent him with 10,000 men and 18 guns to intercept Colonel William Baillie. At the Battle of Pollilur Tipu defeated Baillie. Of 360 Europeans about 200 were captured alive, and the sepoys, about 3,800 men, suffered very high casualties.

He became ruler of Mysore on his father's death from cancer in 1782, during the Second Anglo-Mysore War, and on 29 December 1782 he crowned himself Badshah with the title Nawab Tipu Sultan Bahadur. The Treaty of Mangalore of 1784 ended the war with the position as it had stood before. He also fought the Marathas, and he began a navy in 1786. He introduced a new calendar, new coinage and seven new government departments, and he expanded the use of iron-cased rockets.

In December 1789 he attacked the lines of Travancore, an ally of the East India Company, after a dispute over two Dutch-held fortresses in Cochin. Lord Cornwallis then mobilised Company forces and formed alliances with the Marathas and the Nizam of Hyderabad. In the Third Anglo-Mysore War Tipu was forced into the Treaty of Seringapatam and lost a number of territories, including Malabar and Mangalore. A report that he founded a Jacobin Club in 1794 is doubted: the historian Jean Boutier argued in 2005 that the Company fabricated it to justify intervention.

In 1799, in the Fourth Mysore War, three armies marched into Mysore and besieged the capital, Srirangapatna. More than 60,000 Company soldiers faced about 30,000 men of Tipu's forces. He was killed on 4 May 1799 defending Seringapatam, and General Harris is said to have exclaimed 'Now India is ours.'

Tipu endowed about 156 Hindu temples, including the Ranganathaswami Temple at Srirangapatna, and appointed Hindu officers. His coinage and administrative reforms, and the silk industry that grew under his land revenue system, outlasted him. Assessments of him have often been divided. Two of his rockets, captured at Srirangapatna, were displayed in the Royal Artillery Museum in London.
tipus-tiger: Tipu Sultan used the tiger systematically as his emblem, placing tiger motifs on his weapons, on his soldiers' uniforms and in his palaces. He had inherited power from his father Hyder Ali, who had become an enemy of the British, and he grew up with strongly anti-British feelings.

The automaton belonged to a group of large images he commissioned showing European figures attacked by tigers or elephants, executed or humiliated; many were painted on house walls in his capital, Seringapatam. French craftsmen at his court probably contributed to its internal works. A proposal that the design came from the death of Hector Sutherland Munro, killed by a tiger in December 1792, is weakened by a similar scene on a gun mount dated 1787–88.

The painted wooden shell is 71.2 centimetres high and 172 centimetres long, and the man in European dress is close to life-size. A crank handle powers several mechanisms. Bellows send air through a pipe in the man's throat to produce a wail, while a link makes his left arm rise and fall. A pipe in the tiger's head gives a grunt of two tones.

Behind a flap in the tiger's flank is a small ivory keyboard of a two-stop pipe organ with 18 notes. The style of the shell and the metal of the original pipes indicate local manufacture. A study of 1987 by Arthur Ord-Hume concluded that the instrument had been heavily reworked since it reached Britain.

British troops found the tiger in a room for musical instruments when Seringapatam fell on 4 May 1799, and an aide-de-camp of Richard Wellesley wrote that it might deserve a place in the Tower of London. The East India Company kept it instead and showed it at East India House from July 1808. It was popular with the public, who could turn the crank, and was moved to the Victoria and Albert Museum in 1880.

A German bomb broke its casing into several hundred pieces during the Second World War, and it was back on display by 1947. British viewers took it as a trophy and justification of colonial rule. John Keats mentioned it in The Cap and Bells (1819), and it is now kept in a glass case, so visitors can no longer operate it.
tir-eoghain: The kingdom grew from the lands of Eoghan mac Néill, a son of Niall of the Nine Hostages, which lay first in Inishowen and spread outwards under his descendants. From its foundation in the 5th century the Cenél nEógain formed a sub-kingdom of Ailech, the northern power base of the Uí Néill, which they shared with their Cenél Conaill cousins and usually ruled. Leaders of the Cenél nEógain gave Ireland thirteen High Kings from the 6th to the 10th centuries, from Muirchertach mac Muiredaig to Domnall ua Néill, and later claimants included Domnall Ua Lochlainn and Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn. When Ailech divided, Cenél nEógain became Tír Eoghain, ruled first by the Meic Lochlainn and then by the Ó Néill, and Cenél Conaill became Tír Conaill.

After the Norman invasion of Ulster in 1177 Tír Eoghain became the leading power of the north, a position it regained when the Norman Earldom of Ulster collapsed in the 14th century. Pushing east, it then established Clandeboye, which a branch of the O'Neills soon ruled in its own right. Under the Tudors its kings joined the rebellion of Silken Thomas and the Geraldine League, and after defeat Conn Bacagh O'Neill went to London in 1542, swore allegiance to Henry VIII and was made Earl of Tyrone.

His choice of an illegitimate son, Feardorcha (Matthew), as heir set off a long feud. Shane O'Neill destroyed much of the Earl of Sussex's army at the Battle of the Red Sagums in July 1561 and had himself inaugurated as The Ó Néill, but after defeat by Tyrconnell at Farsetmore in May 1567 he was killed at Cushendun by a warband from Clan MacDonald of Dunnyveg, who had made a deal with the English garrison at Carrickfergus. Turlough Luineach O'Neill ruled after him and in 1593 stood aside for Hugh O'Neill, Baron of Dungannon. Under James I the barony of Loughinsholin was moved into the new county of Londonderry, and in 1607 Hugh fled Ireland in the Flight of the Earls.

The chief seat was Dungannon, and kings were inaugurated at Tullyhogue Fort, where other clans played set parts. The second clan of the kingdom, the Ó Catháin (O'Cahan), also of the Cenél nEógain, ruled a sub-kingdom around Coleraine and held the honour of holding a shoe over the king's head at his inauguration. Most people were Gaels of the Northern Uí Néill, with other Irish clans and, later, Highland Scots mercenaries.
tiradentes: Joaquim José da Silva Xavier was born on 12 November 1746 at the Fazenda do Pombal, near Santa Rita do Rio Abaixo in the Captaincy of Minas Gerais. He was the fourth of seven children of Domingos da Silva Santos, born in Portugal, and Antônia da Encarnação Xavier, born in Brazil. An inventory of his mother's estate listed 35 enslaved people on the family's large farm, where they also worked as miners.

His mother died in 1755 and his father two years later, when he was 11, and the family lost its property to debt. Without regular education, he came under the care of his uncle and godfather, the dentist Sebastião Ferreira Leitão. He worked as a peddler and a miner, became a partner in a pharmacy in Vila Rica, and practised dentistry, which earned him the nickname Tiradentes, "tooth puller", a derogatory name adopted during his trial.

He worked as a surveyor and then joined the Minas Gerais Dragoon Regiment, commanding a detachment on the Caminho Novo, the road along which gold travelled to the coast for shipment to Portugal. He came to see this export of wealth as exploitation, and was dissatisfied that he never rose above alferes, the lowest officer rank, and was eventually dismissed from his command.

In 1788 he met José Álvares Maciel, recently returned from England, and with Cláudio Manuel da Costa, Tomás Antônio Gonzaga and Alvarenga Peixoto a group formed that was influenced by Rousseau and the American Revolution. Its members envisaged an independent republic with São João del Rei as capital and a flag bearing the motto "Libertas Quae Sera Tamen". The plan was to proclaim the republic in Vila Rica on the day the derrama, a heavy tax, fell due, in February 1789.

Joaquim Silvério dos Reis, one of the conspirators, exposed the plot in exchange for a tax waiver, the governor cancelled the derrama, and the rebels were imprisoned. The trial lasted almost three years. Tiradentes and ten others were sentenced to death, but Queen Maria I of Portugal commuted the sentences to perpetual banishment for all except those with aggravating circumstances, and Tiradentes, who took full responsibility for the movement, was among them.

He was hanged in Rio de Janeiro on 21 April 1792, his body was quartered and the pieces were displayed along the road to Vila Rica. Republicans made him a national hero in the late 19th century, and after the republic was established in 1889 the anniversary of his death became a national holiday.
tirailleurs: The word means skirmisher. In the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars it named light infantry trained to fight ahead of the main columns, and the first regiments so called belonged to Napoleon's Imperial Guard, where some 16 had been raised by the fall of the Empire. A metropolitan battalion, the tirailleurs de Vincennes, landed at Algiers in 1840, and the next year the title passed to new battalions of indigenous infantry recruited from the Arab and Berber communities of Algeria. A decree of 10 October 1855 formed them into three regiments of Algerian Tirailleurs.

Algerian tirailleurs fought in the Crimean War, where they gained the nickname Turcos, in the Second Italian War of Independence, in Mexico and in the Franco-Prussian War, and in colonial campaigns from Tunisia to Indochina. Tunisian regiments followed in 1884 and Moroccan ones in 1914. The tirailleurs sénégalais were recruited across French West and Central Africa, and others in Madagascar and in Annam, Tonkin and Cambodia. North African enlistment was mostly voluntary, for three years, though Algeria introduced conscription by ballot in 1913.

In the First World War tirailleurs served on the Western Front, at Salonika and in the Levant with heavy losses, and the Great Mosque of Paris was later built in honour of the Muslim soldiers. In the Second World War they fought notably in the Italian campaign, then in Indochina until Dien Bien Phu and in the Algerian War of Independence.

In December 1944 repatriated Senegalese former prisoners of war at Camp Thiaroye near Dakar protested over unpaid arrears, and French guards opened fire, killing between thirty-five and seventy of them. The provisional government of Charles de Gaulle, concerned at the effect on serving tirailleurs, moved quickly to settle the claims for back pay.

Most regiments were disbanded as the colonies became independent between 1956 and 1962, many of their men passing into the new national armies. The pensions of veterans who became citizens of the new states were frozen, while those of French comrades rose with inflation, until President Jacques Chirac ordered increases in 2006. One regiment survives, the 1st Tirailleur Regiment, descended from the Algerian tirailleurs, which wears items of the old North African uniform on ceremonial occasions. North African tirailleur regiments were among the most decorated units of the French Army.
tiramakhan-traore: Tiramakhan Traore came from the village of Balansan, south-west of Kangaba. Tradition makes him the son of a mighty hunter, Daamansa Wulading, who defeated a cannibal witch, a story that may reflect how Mali's rule in the region overcame disorder caused by endemic raiding and a changing climate. He was an important commander at the Battle of Kirina, which was fought within his lands.

Oral histories hold that around 1235 Sundiata Keita sent a party to the Jolof Empire to buy horses, and that all but one of its members were killed, the survivor being sent back with an insulting message. Traore had already planned to move west into the fertile, thinly peopled lands of the Bainuk, so Sundiata sent him to avenge the insult, with his own son Mansa Wali to learn from him. The column is said to have numbered 75,000 people, 40,000 of them free and 35,000 enslaved, with many artisans, and to have taken a year to reach Wuli, at the eastern end of present-day Gambia, growing crops on the way.

Traore killed the Jolof buurba in battle on the north bank of the Gambia River, crossed at what is now Basse Santa Su, where he founded the village of Kabakama, and fought the Bainuk in the region of Sedhiou in present-day Senegal. Some years later he marched on Mampatim and defeated Kikikor, king of the Bainuk, and founded many new Mandinka towns.

He died at Mampatim or perhaps at Basse, and was buried at Basse, where a tree said to mark his tomb survived into the 19th century. Several royal lines claimed descent from him, among them the Guelowar of Sine and Saloum and the Nyancho aristocracy of Kaabu. Another tradition, held by the Traore kings of Kala and Bendougou in what is now central Mali, says that he came down the river in Mali's early expansion, settled at Tla, moved to Kamiamba and died there. His descendants there ruled small kingdoms including Sibila, Kokry, Farakou Massa and N'Goa.
tirana: Tirana lies on the Plain of Tirana in the centre of Albania, between Mount Dajti to the east, hills to the south and a valley to the north that overlooks the Adriatic Sea. Its average altitude is about 110 metres. The Tiranë and Lanë rivers flow through the city. Dajti National Park lies on the mountain above it, with forests of pine, oak and beech, and the city's mountains are a popular retreat in winter, when snow often covers them although the city itself rarely receives it.

The area has been inhabited since prehistoric times, with the earliest recognised reference at the Cave of Pëllumbas, of the Palaeolithic period. Illyrians were its first population and most likely formed the core of the Illyrian kingdom of the Taulantii. After the Illyrian Wars the Romans integrated the area into their empire. The oldest surviving find from that period is a Roman house of the 3rd century, later turned into a church with a mosaic floor. A castle, possibly known as Tirkan, was built by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian I and was restored by Ahmed Pasha Toptani in the 18th century.

Tirana appears in Venetian documents of the 1350s and in 1418. The first Ottoman land registrations of 1431–32 record 60 inhabited areas with nearly 2,028 houses and 7,300 inhabitants. In 1510 Marin Barleti, in his biography of Skanderbeg, called it a small village, distinguishing Little Tirana from Great Tirana. The town was founded in 1614 by the Ottoman Albanian nobleman Sylejman Pasha Bargjini, who built the Old Mosque, a small commercial centre and a hammam. Some sources describe a bazaar with watermills already existing before 1614. In the 16th century craftsmen made silk and cotton fabrics, leather, ceramics and metal artefacts. The Et'hem Bey Mosque was completed in 1821.

The city was fairly unimportant until the 20th century, when the Congress of Lushnjë proclaimed it the capital of Albania following the Albanian Declaration of Independence of 1912. Its present appearance was shaped by two totalitarian regimes: Mussolini's, whose architects Florestano Di Fausto and Armando Brasini designed the ministry buildings, and Enver Hoxha's afterwards. The population tenfolded between 1820 and 1955, and it grew faster after the fall of communism.

Tirana is the capital and largest city of Albania and seat of its government, parliament and highest courts. The centre from the University of Tirana's Mother Teresa Square to Skanderbeg Square was declared a protected cultural area in 2000. The 2023 census counted 598,176 residents in the municipality. The airport is named after Mother Teresa.
tirant-lo-blanc: The romance was written, according to the usual account, between 1460 and 1464 by the Valencian knight Joanot Martorell. Where he wrote it is unclear, since his whereabouts in his last years are unknown. One hypothesis has him return to Valencia after the death of Alphonse the Magnanimous; another places him in Barcelona at the court of Charles, Prince of Viana, which would suit the dedication to Prince Ferdinand of Portugal; a third identifies him with a knight named Joan Martorell living in Dénia.

The book was printed posthumously in Valencia in 1490 by Nicholas Spiendeler. Martorell had pawned the manuscript to Martí Joan de Galba as a pledge for his debts, and Galba claimed co-authorship in the colophon. Scholars still debate his part. The vocabulary of the first three parts is more archaic than that of the last two and the colophon, which has been used to argue for double authorship.

Tirant is a knight from Brittany who adventures across Europe, joining knightly competitions in England and France. The Byzantine emperor then asks him to help in the war against the Ottoman Turks, who threaten Constantinople. Tirant is made Megaduke of the Byzantine Empire and captain of an army, defeats the invaders and saves the empire. He goes on to fight the Turks in the eastern Mediterranean and North Africa, but dies just before he can marry the heiress of the empire.

Unlike other chivalric works of its time, it lacks the platonic, contemplative love of the usual heroes. Its hero is full of life, sensuous love and sarcasm, and the book is filled with prosaic, even bitter descriptions of daily life. It mixes rhetorical and colloquial registers, perhaps because it was meant to be read aloud, and uses many Catalan proverbs. Parts of the story parallel the career of Roger de Flor, leader of the Almogàvers, a mercenary company.

In Chapter 6 of the first part of Don Quixote, Cervantes praises it as a treasure of enjoyment and a gold mine of recreation, because its knights eat, sleep and die in their beds having made a will. Mario Vargas Llosa called it the first example of a total novel, one meant to create its own reality. Because Martorell perhaps rewrote history after the Fall of Constantinople in 1453 to fit what he wished, it has been called a precursor of alternate history. It has been translated into many languages. The first English versions, abridged, appeared only in the late twentieth century.
tirich-mir: Tirich Mir, also spelled Terich Mir, rises to 7,708 metres in the Chitral District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It overlooks the town of Chitral and can be seen from the main bazaar, and the usual approach is up the Tirich valley, which has the Tirich Glacier at its head. The glacier is encircled by three of the 7,000-metre peaks of the Hindu Kush: Tirich Mir, Noshaq and Istor-o-Nal. Their meltwaters flow down the valley to join the Torkhow River and form a major tributary of the Chitral River. The highest permanent settlement is Shagrom, with summer pastures and shepherd huts above it.

The mountain consists mainly of the mid-Cretaceous granitic Tirich Mir pluton, cut by many dykes. The name combines terich, the valley, with mir, which means mountain in the Khowar language. The linguist Georg Morgenstierne derived it from two Sanskrit words, and several scholars have identified Tirich Mir with the sacred Mount Meru of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain literature.

The first recorded ascent was made on 21 July 1950 by an expedition of Arne Næss, Per Kvernberg, Henry Berg and Tony Streather. They approached from the South Barum glacier and climbed the south ridge. A 1952 documentary film, Tirich Mir til topps, depicts the expedition. In 1967 a Czechoslovak expedition established a route by the Upper Tirich Glacier and the northwest ridge, which is now regarded as the normal route.

Local peoples tell different stories about the mountain. According to the polytheist Kalash, who live nearby, it is the domain of the goddess Krumai, who appears as a wild goat and is associated with childbirth. In one legend she disturbed the other gods and was chased by Imra, who threw her into a fast river. She leapt up the river and ran up the cliff, shaping it with her hooves, then revealed her true form and prepared a feast for the gods, who accepted her into their company. The Muslim Chitrali people believe the mountain is the home and fortress of fairies known as Bohtan Doyak, the stone throwers, and hold that anyone who climbs it will die.
tiridates-i-of-armenia: Tiridates was the youngest son of Vonones II, king of Media Atropatene and later of the Parthian Empire, and had two elder brothers, Pacorus and Vologases. His name means given by Tir, a Zoroastrian divinity equated with Apollo. He was also a Zoroastrian priest. When Vonones II died, Vologases I succeeded him, gave Media Atropatene to Pacorus and invaded Armenia, where the Iberian prince Rhadamistus had seized the throne after killing his uncle Mithridates, the legitimate king.

Vologases took Artaxata and proclaimed Tiridates king. A winter epidemic and a revolt by his son Vardanes forced him to withdraw, but the Armenians, punished by the returning Rhadamistus, revolted and replaced him with Tiridates. Nero sent the general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo east, and in the spring of 58 Corbulo entered Greater Armenia, burned Artaxata and took Tigranocerta. Tiridates fled, and Nero gave the crown to a prince who took the name Tigranes. After the Roman commander Lucius Caesennius Paetus suffered a defeat at Rhandeia in 62, Corbulo and Tiridates met there to agree peace. Tiridates laid his diadem near a statue of Nero, agreeing to receive it back only from the emperor in Rome.

He travelled to Rome in 66 with his wife, children, brothers, 3,000 Parthian horsemen and many Romans. The journey took nine months and went overland, since he did not wish to pollute water, one of the seven Zoroastrian holy elements. In the Forum he knelt and told Nero he would be whatever the emperor ordered, and Nero set the diadem on his head. Nero gave him fifty million sesterces. Back in Armenia he brought artisans to rebuild Artaxata, renamed Neronia, and embellished the royal residence at Garni. In 72 Alans raided northern Armenia, and he narrowly escaped capture when he was lassoed and cut the rope with his sword.

Under the settlement the king of Armenia was to be a Parthian prince, but his appointment required Roman approval; some Roman sources thought Nero had in effect ceded Armenia to Parthia. The peace between the two empires lasted 50 years, until Trajan invaded Armenia in 114. Tiridates began reforming Armenia's administration, bringing in many Iranian customs and offices. The date of his death is unknown, and various sources name Sanatruk as his successor. It has been suggested that his visit to Rome lies behind the Christian story of the Three Magi.
tiridates-iii-of-armenia: Tiridates III was the son of Khosrov II of Armenia, who was assassinated in 252 by a Parthian agent named Anak acting under orders from Ardashir I. Anak and most of his family were executed, while his son Gregory the Illuminator was sheltered in Caesaria, in Cappadocia. As the only surviving heir, Tiridates was taken to Rome as an infant. He was educated there, skilled in languages and military tactics, and understood Roman law. His sister was Khosrovidukht. The name Tiridates means created by Tir, a Zoroastrian divinity.

After the Roman emperor Aurelian pushed the Sassanids back in 270, Tiridates came to Armenia as heir to the Persian-occupied throne, raised an army and drove the enemy out in 298. He then carried his arms into Assyria, but when Narses won a civil war in Persia, Tiridates took refuge with the Romans again. With the help of Diocletian he drove the Persians out of Armenia, and in 299 Diocletian left Armenia in a quasi-independent protectorate, possibly as a buffer. In 297 Tiridates married an Alanian princess, Ashkhen; their children included Khosrov III and Salome.

The traditional story of his conversion rests mainly on the fifth-century history attributed to Agathangelos. Gregory, the son of Anak, was brought up a Christian and served the king as secretary. When he refused to place a wreath before the statue of the goddess Anahit, and was revealed as Anak's son, Tiridates had him thrown into the dungeon of Khor Virap. Later, after the king had tortured and killed a group of nuns led by Gayane who had fled Roman persecution, he fell ill. Gregory, found alive after 13 years, cured him, and Tiridates proclaimed Christianity the state religion and appointed Gregory Catholicos. Mary Boyce considers that the Christianisation was partly in defiance of the Sassanids.

Zoroastrianism was deeply rooted, and Tiridates often used force to impose the new faith. Armed conflicts followed, including a battle between his forces and the Zoroastrian camp, and he spent the rest of his life trying to eliminate the old beliefs, destroying many statues, temples and written documents; as a result little is known from local sources about ancient Armenian culture. He died in 330, and Movses Khorenatsi says that nakharar families conspired against him and poisoned him. Tiridates, Ashkhen and Khosrovidukht are saints of the Armenian Apostolic Church, with a feast day around 30 June, and Tiridates is also venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church.
tirigan: According to the Sumerian King List, Tirigan succeeded Si'um and was the nineteenth and last Gutian ruler in Sumer. The list gives him a rule of 40 days and sums up the whole Gutian line as 21 kings who ruled for 124 years and 40 days, after which the army of Gutium was defeated and the kingship was taken to Uruk. His name is written in cuneiform as ti-ri₂-ga-a-an.

Most of what is known of him comes from the victory stele of his opponent and successor, Utu-hengal of Uruk. It describes the Gutian troops established everywhere: Tirigan held both banks of the Tigris, blocked the water from the fields in the south, in Sumer, and closed off the roads in the uplands, so that grass grew high on the highways of the land.

The stele then tells of Utu-hengal's campaign. After leaving the temple of Iškur he camped at Naĝsu on the Surungal canal and at the shrine at Ili-tappê, and he captured two of Tirigan's generals, Ur-Ninazu and Nabi-Enlil, who had been sent as envoys to Sumer, and put them in handcuffs.

Tirigan, the stele says, ran away alone on foot. The people of the town where he sought refuge knew that Utu-hengal was a king endowed with power by the god Enlil and would not let him go, and an envoy of Utu-hengal arrested him there together with his wife and children. He was handcuffed and blindfolded, and before the god Utu, Utu-hengal made him lie at his feet and placed his foot on his neck.

The inscription calls Gutium the snake of the mountains and ends by saying that Utu-hengal brought back the kingship of Sumer. Both accounts of Tirigan come from the side that defeated him: the king list records only the brevity of his rule, and the stele is the victor's own record of the campaign.
tirot-sing: Tirot Sing, also known as U Tirot Sing Syiem, belonged to the Syiemlieh clan and was Syiem, or king, of Nongkhlaw in the Khasi Hills. He was a constitutional head who shared authority with his council, made up of representatives of the leading clans of his territory. After the Treaty of Yandabo of 1826 gave the British control of the Brahmaputra valley, the Khasi Hills lay between their possessions in Sylhet and their new lands in Lower Assam.

The British wanted a road through the hills to link Guwahati with Sylhet, sparing weeks of travel through malarial country. David Scott, the Governor-General's agent for the Northern Territory, learned that Tirot Sing hoped to regain the duars, the passes into Assam, and after a two-day session of the durbar the assembly agreed to the road, and work began. When Balaram Singh, Raja of Ranee, disputed his claim to the duars, Tirot Sing went with armed men in December 1828 to assert it, expecting British support, but was met by sepoys who barred his way.

Hearing that the British were reinforcing their troops in Assam, he called the durbar again and ordered them to leave Nongkhlaw. They ignored the order, and on 4 April 1829 the Khasis attacked the British garrison there; on his orders his men killed two British officers, Richard Gurdon Bedingfield and Philip Bowles Burlton. The British then opened operations against him and other Khasi chiefs. Armed only with swords, shields, bows and arrows and unable to meet firearms in open battle, the Khasis turned to guerrilla warfare.

Tirot Sing was shot and wounded and hid in a cave to tend his wound. A chief of his, bribed by the British with gold coins, gave away his hiding place, and he was captured in January 1833 and sent to Dhaka. He died on 17 July 1835. The anniversary is kept every year in Meghalaya as U Tirot Sing Day, a state holiday.
tirthankara: A tirtha is a fordable passage across saṃsāra, the sea of interminable births and deaths, and the Tirthaṅkara is its founder. Tirthaṅkaras are variously called Teaching Gods, Ford-Makers, Crossing Makers and Makers of the River-Crossing. Jains hold that they conquered saṃsāra on their own and established a path for others, and that their grace is available to all living beings regardless of religion.

A Tirthaṅkara is an arihant, also called a Jina, or victor, one who has conquered inner enemies such as anger, attachment, pride and greed. After kevala jñāna a Tirthaṅkara preaches the dharma and organises the sangha of monks, nuns, śrāvakas and śrāvikās. In Jain cosmology the wheel of time has an ascending half, Utsarpiṇī, and a descending half, Avasarpiṇī, the present one; in each half 24 Tirthaṅkaras appear, and there have been infinitely many in the past.

Academic and historical consensus broadly accepts Parshvanatha, the 23rd, and Mahavira as historical figures. Parshvanatha is understood as a predecessor who preached the fourfold restraint, the chaturyama dharma. Mahavira is seen as a restorer and reformer and the final systematiser of Jain thought, who re-established the monastic and lay community on Parshvanatha's teachings and added celibacy as the fifth great vow.

The lives of the other 22 are considered part of a sacred cosmological history set in vast non-historical timeframes. Texts such as the Kalpa Sutra give them a formulaic pattern: birth into a royal family, worldly life, renunciation, asceticism leading to omniscience, and liberation. Rishabhanatha, or Adinatha, the first, is said by tradition to have founded human civilisation and taught agriculture, law and social order. Some scholars have speculated about a link with the nude standing figures and the bull motif on seals of the Indus Valley Civilization, as possible but unproven evidence of a proto-Jain cult.

Jain texts hold that a special karma, the tīrthaṅkara nama-karma, raises a soul to this status; the Tattvartha Sutra lists 16 observances that bind it, among them purity of right faith, charity and the propagation of the teachings of the omniscient. Five auspicious events, the pañca kalyāṇaka, mark every Tirthaṅkara's life: conception, birth, renunciation, omniscience and liberation.

After omniscience the Tirthaṅkara preaches in the samavasarana, a three-level pavilion that, according to Jain texts, devas erect. Humans and animals hear the speech in their own language. In tradition twenty Tirthaṅkaras reached liberation on Mount Shikharji in the present Indian state of Jharkhand, while Rishabhanatha did so on Mount Ashtāpada and Mahavira at Pawapuri, near modern Patna.
tiruchirappalli: Tiruchirappalli lies almost at the geographic centre of Tamil Nadu, 322 kilometres south of Chennai. About 16 kilometres west of the city the Kaveri divides into two streams, the Kaveri and the Kollidam, and the Cauvery Delta begins; the island of Srirangam between them now belongs to the city. The ground is nearly flat, with an average elevation of 81 metres, and a few isolated hillocks rise above it. The highest is the Rockfort, whose rock is estimated to be 3,800 million years old.

Tiruchirappalli is one of the oldest inhabited cities in Tamil Nadu, with settlements dating to the Sangam period. Uraiyur, which is now a neighbourhood, was the capital of the Early Cholas for 600 years from the 3rd century BCE, and Ptolemy called it Orthoura. The Kallanai dam, about 18 kilometres from Uraiyur, was built across the Kaveri by Karikala Chola in the 2nd century CE.

In the 6th century the Pallava king Mahendravarman I had the rock-cut cave temples of the Rockfort made. After the Pallavas fell in the 8th century the Medieval Cholas held the city until the 13th century. The Carnatic kingdom was annexed by the British in July 1801, after the discovery of collusion between Tipu Sultan and the son of the Nawab during the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

Trichinopoly joined the Madras Presidency and became the capital of its own district. The 1871 census counted 76,530 people, making it the second largest city of the presidency after Madras. It was known across the British Empire for the Trichinopoly cigar, of which more than 12 million were made and exported each year at the peak, and the South Indian Railway Company had its first headquarters there in 1874. In 1930 the city was the base for the Vedaranyam salt march begun by C. Rajagopalachari.

The city is predominantly Hindu, with a large Muslim minority and a considerable Christian population. Its best-known monuments are the Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangam, dedicated to the reclining form of Vishnu, and the Jambukeswarar Temple at Thiruvanaikaval, dedicated to Shiva. Both are built in the Dravidian style and are often counted among its best examples.

The Archaeological Survey of India lists the rock-cut cave temples of the Rockfort, with the gateway and the Erumbeeswarar Temple, as monuments of national importance. Tiruchirappalli has been an educational centre since British rule: St. Joseph's College moved there from Nagapattinam in 1883, and the commissioning of Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited in the 1960s began its growth as an engineering centre.
tirukkural: The Tirukkural, "sacred couplets", is a classic Tamil text on commoner's morality, made of 1,330 short couplets of seven words each. The word kural means something short and concise, and the couplets are in the kural venba metre. Traditional accounts describe the work as the last of the third Sangam, put to a divine test that it passed, but linguistic analysis suggests a later date of 450 to 500 CE, after the Sangam period. Proposed dates range from 300 BCE to the 5th century CE. Kamil Zvelebil finds the earliest dates unacceptable, because nothing in the text supports them.

The author is traditionally Valluvar, or Thiruvalluvar, who is known by many other names. Almost nothing authentic is known about him, and the text names neither its author nor its original title. The name Thiruvalluvar first appears in a later Shaivite text, the Tiruvalluva Maalai, of unclear date, which says nothing of his birth, family or caste. The many legends about his life date from the early 19th century and are inconsistent.

The work has 133 chapters of ten couplets each. Book I, Aram, on virtue, covers chapters 1 to 38 and the moral values of an individual. Porul, Book II, on polity, covers chapters 39 to 108 and treats society and administration, with chapters on kings, ministers, taxes, justice, forts, war, agriculture, education and abstinence from alcohol. Inbam, Book III, on love, covers chapters 109 to 133 and deals with friendship, love, sexual union and domestic life. It stresses ahimsa, non-violence and moral vegetarianism, along with truthfulness, self-restraint, gratitude, hospitality and kindness.

Zvelebil holds that a single author wrote it, since its language, form and structure are consistent, and that it is not an anthology. The division into three books is probably the author's, while the subdivisions found in manuscripts are likely later. He describes its approach as pragmatic idealism, concerned with man in the totality of his relationships, and finds true poetry mainly in the third book. The text opens with an invocation of God and a praise of rain.

The work is called the "Tamil Veda" and the "Divine Book". It has influenced writers and leaders including Ilango Adigal, Kambar, Leo Tolstoy, Mahatma Gandhi and Albert Schweitzer. It has been translated into at least 57 Indian and other languages and has not been out of print since it was first printed in 1812. The Tamil people and the government of Tamil Nadu have long upheld it with reverence.
tiruppavai: In the hymns Andal takes the guise of a cowherd girl intent on a vow to marry Vishnu and remain in his company forever, and she invites her friends to join her in serving him. The first five stanzas set out the theme: luxuries should be given up in this season, sincere prayer brings abundant rain and prosperity, and fresh flowers offered to Krishna wipe away sins past and future. The next ten describe her village, with birdsong, blossoms, the sound of butter-churning, cattle with tinkling bells and the conch from the temple, as she wakes her friends to bathe in a pond.

Five stanzas follow the group to the temple, where they appease the guards, pray to Krishna's parents to wake Krishna and Balarama, and approach Niladevi, the deity's consort. The last nine praise the deity. Andal lists what she asks for, from milk for the vow to a white conch, lamps, ghee and butter, and the final stanza names her as the daughter of Vishnucitthar (Periyalvar) and promises Krishna's blessings to those who recite it with devotion.

The hymns belong to the pāvai genre, songs tied to the Tamil custom of unmarried girls keeping a vow (vrata) through the month of Margaḻi, a practice already mentioned in the late Sangam anthology Paripatal. Each day of Margaḻi takes its name from one of the thirty verses. Three taniyans, standalone verses by later authors, introduce the work: one in Sanskrit by Parashara Bhattar and two by Sri Uyyakondar.

In Thailand a Giant Swing ceremony called Triyampavai-Tripavai was held every year in major cities until 1935. Its name came from the Thiruvempavai of Manikkavacakar and the Tiruppavai, and T. P. Meenakshisundaram suggests that the Tiruppavai too may have been recited there.

In the Vaishnava tradition the hymns are held to contain the essence of the three basic mantras, the Tirumantram, Dvayam and Charama Sloka. The work is called Vedam Anaithukkum Vithagum, the seed of all the Vedas, whose hidden meaning only an acharya well versed in the scriptures can reveal. It was translated into Telugu by Mullapudi Venkataramana as Melupalukula Melukolupu.
tiruvannamalai: Tiruvannamalai is the administrative headquarters of Tiruvannamalai district, about 196 kilometres from Chennai and 210 kilometres from Bangalore. The Annamalai hill, about 814 metres high, rises behind the Annamalaiyar temple and is held sacred as a lingam, a form of Shiva in itself.

In legend Shiva appeared here as a column of fire to restore light to the world after Parvati playfully closed his eyes, and again as a flame whose top and base Brahma and Vishnu could not find; Brahma lied that he had, and was punished by Shiva's decree that he would never have temples on earth. The names Arunachalam and Annamalai are linked with this fire. The first mention of Annamalai is in the Tevaram, the seventh-century Tamil Saiva canon of Appar and Tirugnanasambandar.

The history of the town revolves around its temple. Its recorded history goes back to the ninth century through Chola inscriptions in the temple, with earlier inscriptions pointing to Pallava rule from Kanchipuram. The Chola kings ruled the region from 850 to 1280 and were patrons of the temple, recording gifts of land, sheep, cows and oil.

The Hoysala kings used Tiruvannamalai as their capital from 1328, as their kingdom in Karnataka was annexed by the Delhi Sultanate, and held out against invaders from Madurai and the Deccan until 1346. Under the Vijayanagara Empire the temple received 48 inscriptions of the Sangama dynasty, two of the Saluva dynasty and 55 of the Tuluva dynasty, including some of Krishnadeva Raya, mostly gifts of land and written in Tamil. The town stood at a crossroads of pilgrimage and military routes.

In the 18th century Tiruvannamalai came under the Nawab of the Carnatic, and after 1753 the temple was besieged in turn by several rival commanders. The French occupied the city in 1757 and the British took it in 1760. Tipu Sultan captured it in 1790, and it came under British rule in the first half of the 19th century.

The Annamalaiyar temple covers 10 hectares and is one of the largest in India, with four gateway towers, the tallest of which, on the east, has eleven storeys and stands 66 metres high. It has a thousand-pillared hall of the Vijayanagara period and is one of the Pancha Bhoota Stalas, the five Shiva temples associated with the elements, here fire.

The festival of Karthikai Deepam, in November or December, lights a lamp holding three tons of ghee on the hill, and on every full moon pilgrims walk barefoot around it in the 14-kilometre Girivalam. The city had a population of 145,278 at the 2011 census, and Tamil is its official language.
tiryns: Tiryns lies in the Argolis in the Peloponnese, 20 km south of Mycenae, on a hill about 300 metres long and no more than 18 metres high. The area has been inhabited since prehistory, and a small Neolithic settlement thrived there. In the middle of the 3rd millennium BCE it was a flourishing early settlement. From this period survives a circular structure 28 metres across, built of two concentric stone walls, which seems to have been a refuge for the inhabitants in war or a residence of a king. The first Greek inhabitants settled there at the start of the Middle Helladic period, from 2000 to 1600 BCE.

The city grew most in the Late Helladic, the Mycenaean period. The acropolis was built in three phases: at the end of Late Helladic II, then in Late Helladic III, and at the end of Late Helladic III B, in 1300 to 1200 BCE, to which the surviving ruins belong. Around 1300 BCE the citadel and lower town held about 10,000 people. The palace was destroyed around 1200 BCE, yet the population kept growing and reached about 15,000 by 1150 BCE. Around 1180 BCE a hoard of gold and silver objects was placed in a cauldron in the lower town. The palace area stayed inhabited until the middle of the 8th century BCE, and a temple was later built among its ruins.

In the Classical period Tiryns, like Mycenae, became insignificant. According to Herodotus, it sent 400 hoplites to the Battle of Plataea in 480 BCE. In 468 BCE Argos destroyed both Mycenae and Tiryns. Pausanias says the residents were moved to Argos, but Strabo says many Tirynthians went to found Halieis. Greek tradition held that the Cyclopes built the walls for Proetus, who fled to Lycia and returned with Lycian help. Heinrich Schliemann tested the site in 1876 and returned in 1884, and after him Wilhelm Dörpfeld, a director of the German Archaeological Institute, studied the ruins properly.

The walls, usually 6 metres thick and up to 17 metres where the tunnels pass through, survive to a height of up to 7 metres; the original height is estimated at 9 to 10 metres. A transverse wall divides the acropolis, with the palace in the southern part. The palace's megaron has a throne place against the wall and a central hearth ringed by four wooden columns. Tiryns and Mycenae were designated a World Heritage Site in 1999.
tisha-bav: Tisha B'Av, Hebrew for the Ninth of Av, is an annual fast day in Rabbinic Judaism. It falls in July or August in the Gregorian calendar and ends the Three Weeks, a period of communal sorrow that begins on the Seventeenth of Tammuz. It is regarded as the saddest day in the Jewish calendar.

According to the Mishnah, Taanit 4:6, five events on the ninth of Av warrant fasting: the return of the Twelve Spies sent by Moses, whose discouraging report left the Israelites in despair; the destruction of the First Temple built by King Solomon; the destruction of the Second Temple by the Romans in 70 CE; the crushing of the Bar Kokhba revolt and the fall of Betar in 135 CE; and the ploughing of the Temple site by the Roman commander Quintus Tineius Rufus.

The fast lasts just over 25 hours, from sunset on the preceding evening until nightfall. Five prohibitions apply: no eating or drinking, no washing or bathing, no creams or oils, no leather shoes, and no marital relations. They are waived for health reasons on a rabbi's ruling. Torah study is forbidden, as an enjoyable activity, except for distressing texts such as Lamentations, Job and parts of Jeremiah.

The Book of Lamentations is read in synagogue in the evening, and much of the morning is spent reciting kinnot, liturgical dirges composed by poets such as Eleazar beRabbi Qallir and Judah Halevi. Over time the day came to recall later calamities as well: the Rhineland massacres of the First Crusade in 1096, the expulsion of the Jews from England on 18 July 1290, from France in 1306 and from Spanish-ruled territories under the Alhambra Decree in 1492, and the Holocaust.

After the Bar Kokhba revolt the Romans barred Jews from Jerusalem, which was rebuilt as Aelia Capitolina. The Bordeaux Pilgrim, in a travelogue of 333, and Jerome, in the late 4th century, both describe Jews coming to lament on the Temple Mount once a year. The ban ended in 637 with the early Muslim conquest. Mourning customs grew stricter after late antiquity, especially from the 15th to the 18th centuries.

Observance differs among modern movements. Conservative Judaism keeps it as a traditional fast, while Classical Reform discouraged it. In Israel restaurants and places of entertainment are closed by law on the eve of the fast and the following day. Iranian Jews call it Noi.
tishomingo-oklahoma: Tishomingo is the largest city and county seat of Johnston County, in south-central Oklahoma, with a total area of 4.5 square miles. U.S. Route 377 runs through the centre of the city, leading south to Madill and north to Ada, and Oklahoma State Highway 22 also passes through it. Pennington Creek flows through the west side of the city and south to the Washita River, where it becomes an arm of Lake Texoma, and the Tishomingo National Wildlife Refuge borders the city to the south. Ardmore lies 31 miles west and Oklahoma City 116 miles to the north-west.

The city was named for Tishomingo, who died of smallpox on the Trail of Tears near Little Rock, Arkansas, after the Chickasaw had been removed in the 1830s from their homelands in and around Tishomingo, Mississippi. Before the founding of the town in 1852 the area was known as Good Springs, and its several springs made it an attractive campsite along the road between Fort Washita and Fort Arbuckle. A small town with permanent buildings replaced the campsites and was renamed Tishomingo by 1856, when it was designated the Chickasaw capital. A post office opened in 1857.

The Chickasaw Capitol Building was built in 1897 of local red granite and dedicated in 1898. It housed the tribal governor, the legislature of two chambers and other officials and clerks, and the territorial court met there from time to time. The territorial government was dissolved at Oklahoma statehood in 1907, and in 1910 the building was sold to the newly organised Johnston County and used as its courthouse. The Western Oklahoma Railroad was built through the town in 1902, was bought by the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railway in the same year, and was abandoned in 1938.

Tishomingo had a population of 3,101 at the 2020 census. It is home to Murray State College, a community college. Tishomingo Cemetery dates back to at least 1832, and those buried there include the Oklahoma governors William H. Murray and Johnston Murray and the Chickasaw Nation governors Douglas H. Johnston and Robert M. Harris.
tisquantum: Almost nothing is known of Tisquantum's life before his first contact with Europeans. The Patuxets, his people, lived on the coast west of Cape Cod Bay and spoke a dialect of Eastern Algonquian; he told an English trader that they had once numbered 2,000.

One scholar has suggested that he was in his twenties or thirties when he was taken to Spain in 1614, which would put his birth around 1585, give or take ten years. Fishermen from Bristol, Normandy and Brittany had visited the coast every spring from as early as 1581, and Europeans very probably introduced diseases to which the Indian population had no resistance.

In 1614 the English captain Thomas Hunt, left in command of a ship after John Smith's voyage along the coast, lured 20 Indians aboard at Patuxet under promise of trade, among them Tisquantum, and seized seven more from the Nausets. He then sailed for Málaga. Tisquantum was later in Newfoundland, where he spoke with Thomas Dermer about New England, and he reached his native village in 1619 to find that his people had been wiped out by epidemic. He went to live with the Pokanokets.

When the Mayflower settlers made their home on the site of his former summer village, Tisquantum worked to bring about peaceful relations with the Pokanokets, and he was decisive at the early meetings of March 1621, partly because he spoke English. He lived with the Pilgrims for 20 months as interpreter, guide and adviser, and the settlers relied on him because he was the only means of speaking with the surrounding Indians. According to William Bradford, he showed them how to set their corn, where to take fish and how to reach unknown places.

Tisquantum fell sick with what Bradford called Indian fever while piloting the settlers' ship around Cape Cod. He died within a few days, on 30 November 1622 in the old-style calendar, asking the governor to pray that he might go to the Englishmen's God. He left some of his belongings to English friends, and Bradford called his death a great loss.

Almost all the records of him were written by English Separatists to attract settlers or to justify themselves, so they treat him as their assistant, and Bradford also wrote that he played his own game to enrich himself. Recent historians give a more nuanced view. A peninsula, Squantum in Quincy, may have been named after him.
tisquesusa: The earliest sources call him Bogotá the Elder, and the Spanish pronunciation of his name gave the Colombian capital its name. The form Tisquesusa first appears in the Elegías de varones ilustres de Indias, written by the poet Juan de Castellanos decades after the conquest; its origin is unknown, and the historian Jorge Gamboa Mendoza, among others, holds that the ruler's name was originally Bogotá. Before his accession Tisquesusa was cacique of Chía, and as the nephew of the previous ruler Nemequene he succeeded his uncle in 1514, as Muisca rules of inheritance required.

Early in his reign Tisquesusa fought the Panche to the west of the Muisca Confederation, and went to war with the northern Muisca ruled by Quemuenchatocha. Forty thousand guecha warriors of the south faced fifty thousand from the north. The iraca Sugamuxi of the Iraca Valley, who had earlier supported the northern troops, this time helped to settle a truce, which lasted until the Spanish arrived in 1537. His brother Sagipa commanded the southern Muisca army.

According to the chronicles, the mohan Popón of Ubaque foretold the coming of foreigners and warned that Tisquesusa would die bathing in his own blood. When the Spanish advanced, Tisquesusa sent a spy to Suesca to learn their strength and weapons, then left his capital for Nemocón; on the way there the Spanish were attacked by more than 600 Muisca warriors. At his fortified place at Cajicá he is said to have told his men that he could not fight an army with weapons of thunder and lightning, and he had Bacatá evacuated before the Spanish reached it.

The conquistadors found him near Facatativá and attacked at night. Alonso Domínguez, one of Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada's soldiers, struck him with his sword but, not knowing who he was, let him go after taking his costly mantle. Tisquesusa fled wounded into the mountains and died there; his body was found a year later, when black vultures were seen circling over it. Against Muisca custom, which gave the succession to the eldest son of the ruler's oldest sister, his brother Sagipa took power and became the last ruler of the southern Muisca.
tisza: The Tisza begins near Rakhiv in Ukraine, at the meeting of the White Tisza, which springs in the Chornohora mountains, and the Black Tisza, from the Gorgany range. It flows west, roughly following Ukraine's borders with Romania and Hungary, briefly forms the border between Slovakia and Hungary, then enters Hungary at Tiszabecs and crosses it from north to south. A few kilometres south of Szeged it enters Serbia and joins the Danube near the village of Stari Slankamen in Vojvodina.

The river has a length of 966 kilometres and drains about 156,087 square kilometres, contributing about 13 percent of the Danube's runoff. It is the Danube's tributary with the largest catchment area, shared by Ukraine, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania and Serbia, of which Romania holds 46 percent and Hungary 29 percent. In antiquity it was known as the Tisia, and another ancient name was Pathissus. Attila the Hun is said to have been buried under a diverted section of it.

The length of the Tisza in Hungary used to be 1,419 kilometres. It crossed the Great Hungarian Plain, one of the largest flat areas in central Europe, in many curves and turns, which led to large floods. After several small-scale attempts, István Széchenyi organised the regulation of the Tisza, which began on 27 August 1846 and was substantially finished in 1880. The river's length in Hungary fell to 966 kilometres, with 589 kilometres of dead channels and 136 kilometres of new riverbed.
