Until the Treaty of Trianon in 1920 the Tisza was commonly called the most Hungarian river, because unlike the Danube it flowed entirely within the borders of historical Hungary. In early 2000 a series of pollution incidents from mining in Romania released sludge containing cyanide and heavy metals into the river, killing 2,000 tons of fish; examination of the sediments shows that mine pollution had occurred for over a century.

The Tisza is navigable over much of its course. It was opened to international navigation only after Hungary joined the European Union, having previously distinguished national rivers, closed to foreign vessels, from international ones. In the 1970s the Tisza Dam at Kisköre was begun to control floods and store water, and the resulting Lake Tisza became one of the most popular tourist destinations in Hungary. The bird reserve at Tiszafüred shelters over 200 species, and the yearly flowering of the Tisza, when swarms of mayflies appear, is considered a local natural wonder. The river holds a special place in Hungarian folk songs and poems, which describe it as wild and winding.
titelberg: The Titelberg lies about three kilometres south-west of Pétange and three kilometres north-west of Differdange, on a bare plateau some 390 metres above sea level. Steep wooded slopes fall about 100 metres to the river Chiers below. The oval plateau is about one kilometre long from north-west to south-east and 500 metres wide. Its position helps to explain its size: it stood close to two of the main Celtic roads, one from the Rhône to the upper Moselle and the north, the other towards Reims and the west, with iron ore and fertile land close by.

There are traces of scattered settlement perhaps as early as 2000 BCE, but a town took shape in the 2nd century BCE, when bronze workshops stood on the site. Around 100 BCE the Treveri entered a period of prosperity and built several oppida near the Moselle valley, of which the Titelberg was by far the largest; in the 1st century BCE it was probably their capital. Ramparts of the murus gallicus type enclosed it, with fortified gates at either end of the main road.

A ditch four metres wide divided the town. In the residential part, where the Treveri nobles appear to have lived, stood rectangular houses of light masonry about 14 by 8 metres, with fireplaces, sometimes ovens, and drains for rainwater. The public part held no dwellings, only the remains of a hall 14 metres square, perhaps a meeting place for political, economic or religious purposes. Large numbers of coins of the Treveri and of other Celtic peoples, minting facilities and many bronze fibulae point to a centre of trade.

About 20 years after the Roman conquest the settlement was rebuilt, with at least two new streets crossing the main road and Roman houses with stone foundations and cellars. No longer a capital, it became a prosperous vicus where metal working went on; minting and smelting continued until at least around 337, as a coin of Constantine II found at the smelter shows. In the former public area a monumental building was later turned into a fanum, a square temple with a roofed porch on every side, while the unmaintained ramparts slowly collapsed.

Some interest was shown in the site in 1928, but systematic excavation began only in 1968, coordinated by Luxembourg's National Museum of History and Art with specialists from the University of Missouri. Celtic graves nearby, at Clemency, Goeblange and Nospelt, held wine flagons, spurs, knives, lances and oil lanterns.
tithe: Tithing was a widespread practice in the ancient Near East, though none of the surviving extrabiblical laws deal with it and the evidence is scant. Mesopotamian texts record a ten percent tax levied on garments by the local ruler, tithes owed to gods such as Shamash and Ninurta, and officials in charge of the tithe. According to Diodorus Siculus, the Carthaginians, originally Tyrian colonists, customarily sent a tenth of all public revenue to Melqart.

The Torah commands several agricultural tithes, though not all had the proportion of one tenth. The first tithe, a tenth of the crop, went to the Levites, who owned no territorial inheritance and lived by it. Genesis tells that Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of what he had taken in battle, and Jacob promised God a tenth of his possessions.

Many Christian churches practised tithing. It was taught by the Council of Tours in 567, and the Third Council of Mâcon in 585 prescribed excommunication for those who did not pay. In England the right to receive tithes was granted to the churches by King Ethelwulf in 855, and the Saladin tithe of 1188 was a royal tax assessed by ecclesiastical boundaries. The Statute of Westminster of 1285 affirmed the legal validity of the tithe system. William Blackstone divided tithes into predial, from the land, mixed, from stock such as wool and milk, and personal, from trades and fisheries.

The Dissolution of the Monasteries transferred many rights to tithe to secular landowners and the Crown. In the 17th century dissenting groups, among them the Quakers, objected to paying tithes to the Church of England as forced payments for the maintenance of a professional ministry. Adam Smith criticised the system in The Wealth of Nations in 1776.

A tithe is a tenth part of something, paid to a religious organisation or as a compulsory tax; historically it was paid in kind, as farm produce, while modern tithes are normally voluntary and paid in money. Many Christian denominations still teach tithing. In Judaism the agricultural tithes apply only within the Land of Israel, and outside it a customary practice of giving about a tenth of income to charity has developed. Zakat, one of the Five Pillars of Islam, is a share of assets given to the poor, and in Sikhism daswandh is a tenth of income donated in the name of God.
titian: Titian, in Italian Tiziano Vecellio, was born in Pieve di Cadore, near Belluno, in territory ruled by Venice. His birth date is uncertain. In old age he claimed in a letter to Philip II of Spain to have been born in 1474, but most modern scholars think this very unlikely and place his birth between 1488 and 1490.

Giorgione died in 1510 and Giovanni Bellini in 1516, while Sebastiano del Piombo had gone to Rome, which left Titian without a rival in Venice. In 1516 he completed the Assumption of the Virgin for the high altar of the Basilica di Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari, where it still stands. It is his largest single panel, and its composition joins the apostles on earth, the Madonna rising and God the Father in heaven into one whole. Bacchus and Ariadne, painted in 1520 to 1523, belonged to a series for the Camerino d'Alabastro in the Ducal Palace at Ferrara, commissioned by Alfonso I d'Este from Bellini, Titian and Dosso Dossi.

After meeting Charles V at the imperial court at Augsburg, Titian built a relationship of mutual trust with the emperor. Commissions from Charles and then from his son Philip II dominated his output from the 1550s. The portrait model he developed for the Habsburgs became a standard for princes, nobles and churchmen, and he reorganised his workshop to meet the demand, producing variants and replicas with the help of assistants whose work he retouched. From the mid-1540s most of his work was done for patrons outside Venice, and he lost influence in the city during his long absences.

Titian painted with open, visible brushwork, a technique that was revolutionary and gave his figures a sensuous effect not seen before. He revised his compositions repeatedly, treated underdrawings as suggestions, and sometimes returned to a background decades after first laying it in. He never engraved, but designed woodcuts in 1515 to 1520, among them a large Drowning of Pharaoh's Army in the Red Sea in twelve blocks, and later supplied drawings to the engraver Cornelis Cort.

Titian died on 27 August 1576 while plague raged in Venice. He was buried beneath the Frari's Altar of the Crucifix, without the Pietà he had designed for his tomb, which the friars had returned to him. His son and heir Orazio died of plague soon afterwards, leaving no will, which complicated the settlement of the estate.
titlis: Titlis is the highest summit of the Uri Alps north of the Susten Pass, between the Bernese Oberland and Central Switzerland. It straddles the border between Obwalden and Bern, and its main summit, sometimes called Gross Titlis, and Klein Titlis both lie between the municipalities of Engelberg on the north and Gadmen on the south. It is the highest point in Obwalden and in the valley of Engelberg. Part of the massif lies in Nidwalden, where the Rotstöckli, 2,901 metres, is the canton's highest point. The geographical centre of Switzerland lies about 15 kilometres to the west.

The range here lies between the valleys of the Hasli on the west and the Reuss on the east, so it divides the waters feeding the Aare and the Reuss. The valley of Engelberg is drained by the Engelberger Aa, a tributary of Lake Lucerne. The northern side of the massif is covered by the Titlis Glacier, the south face rises above the Wenden Glacier, and the east side overlooks the Firnalpeligletscher.

The mountain was formerly known as Wendenstock or Nollen. A document of 1435 calls it Tuttelsberg, after a man named Tutilos, probably a local farmer, and the name developed through Titlisberg to Titlis. The first ascent was probably made in 1739 by Ignaz Hess, J. E. Waser and two other men from Engelberg. The first written evidence of an ascent is a party of four men who reached the summit in 1744, recorded in the Engelberger Dokumente. The first ski ascent was made on 21 January 1904 by Joseph Kuster and Willi Amrhein.

Titlis is reached mainly from Engelberg, which stands at 996 metres. A cable car runs in stages by Gerschnialp, Trübsee and Stand to Klein Titlis, and it is known as the site of the first rotating cable car. The cable car to Klein Titlis was inaugurated in March 1967, and in 2016 a direct route to Trübsee bypassed Gerschnialp. Inside the top station an illuminated glacier cave can be visited. The Titlis Cliff Walk, a suspension bridge, opened in December 2012 to mark the 110th anniversary of the Engelberg-Gerschnialp cableway. Klein Titlis also carries a telecommunications tower, and an observation tower was opened there in May 2026.
tito-okello: Tito Lutwa Okello was born into an Acholi family, around 1914, in Namokora in Kitgum District. He joined the King's African Rifles in 1940 and served in the East African Campaign. He then followed a career as an army officer, holding a variety of assignments, and became a follower of President Milton Obote.

After the 1971 coup that made Idi Amin Uganda's ruler, Okello went into exile. In 1972 rebels invaded Uganda to restore Obote, and Okello was one of the leaders of an insurgent group that targeted Masaka. Loyalist Uganda Army troops defeated the invasion. He later took part in the Uganda–Tanzania War as one of the commanders in the coalition of the Tanzania People's Defence Force and the Uganda National Liberation Army that removed Amin from power in 1979.

Obote returned to the presidency in 1980, and Okello was selected as commander of the Uganda National Liberation Army, a post he held until 1985. In July 1985, together with Bazilio Olara-Okello, he carried out the coup that toppled Obote. He ruled as president from 29 July 1985 until 26 January 1986, and then had to transfer power to the National Resistance Army under Yoweri Museveni.

Okello went into exile in Kenya after his tenure ended. In 1993 President Museveni granted him amnesty and he returned to Kampala. He died on 3 June 1996 at the age of 81 and was buried at his ancestral home in Namokora subcounty, Kitgum District. In January 2010 he was posthumously awarded the Kagera National Medal of Honour for fighting against the Idi Amin dictatorship in the 1970s.
titterstone-clee-hill: Titterstone Clee is the third-highest hill in Shropshire, after Brown Clee Hill and the Stiperstones, and belongs to the Clee Hills within the Shropshire Hills National Landscape. The nearest town is Ludlow. The hill stands above the country around it because a thick sill of dolerite and a band of hornfels cap the softer Devonian Old Red Sandstone, Carboniferous limestones and Coal Measures beneath. The dark dolerite, an olivine basalt, takes its local name from the Welsh du, black. Near the summit lies the Giant's Chair, a pile of boulders formed in cold phases of the Devensian glaciation.

Near the summit are the remains of a Bronze Age cairn about 4,000 years old, which suggests a ceremonial use of the hilltop. The Iron Age hillfort, though partly damaged by quarrying, has survived better than the fort on Brown Clee, and its walls are unusually built of stone blocks rather than earth banks. Clee Hill is one of the few hills marked on the 13th-century Hereford Mappa Mundi. Ironstone was mined in the Middle Ages and coal later, often from small bell pits.

Dhustone was cut into setts for roads and docks, among them the new docks at Newport in South Wales, and later crushed for concrete and road surfaces. Before the Second World War the quarries employed more than 2,000 people, many coming from Bridgnorth and Ludlow, and the villages of Bedlam and Dhustone were built to house them. A narrow-gauge incline, a standard-gauge incline used until the early 1960s and an aerial ropeway from the Magpie Quarry to the railway at Detton Ford carried the stone away. Some disused quarry buildings include some of the earliest known uses of reinforced concrete in Britain. A radar station, RAF Clee Hill, opened in September 1941 and closed in September 1957.

Radar domes on the summit, one nicknamed the golf ball, serve the national air traffic network and a Met Office weather radar. Quarrying for road stone resumed on Clee Hill in the late 1980s. The upper hill is common land grazed by sheep and open to walkers, and the Shropshire Way crosses it.
titu-cusi-yupanqui: Titu Cusi, whose Spanish name was Diego de Castro Titu Kusi Yupanqui and whose Quechua name was Titu Kusi Yupanki, was born in 1529, a son of Manco Inca Yupanqui, and became the penultimate leader of the Neo-Inca State. He was crowned in 1563 after the death of his half brother Sayri Túpac, and ruled from Vilcabamba until his death. His eldest son was Quispe Titu, born in 1550.

During his rule the provisional governor-general Lope García de Castro sought to negotiate with him over his leaving Vilcabamba and accepting a pension from the Crown. As the talks grew tense, about 1568 Titu Cusi was baptised into the Catholic Church as Diego de Castro. He made his brother Túpac Amaru a priest and custodian of the body of Manco Inca at Vilcabamba.

He died in 1571, probably of pneumonia, after catching a chill while fencing with his close companion Martín de Pando, who had worked as a scribe for the Inca for over ten years. Pando and the Augustinian friar Diego Ortiz were blamed for poisoning him, and both were afterwards killed. Túpac Amaru succeeded him as Inca ruler.

In 1570 Titu Cusi narrated to the Spanish missionary Fray Marcos García his Relación de la conquista del Perú, the source of An Inca Account of the Conquest of Peru, which Martín de Pando, his mestizo assistant, transcribed. The hybrid document is a rare firsthand account of the Spanish invasion from the vantage point of an Inca elite, and it describes the confusion and misunderstandings of first contact, including the belief that the Spaniards were gods.

In one passage Manco Inca, the author's father and the brother of Atahualpa, receives the first news of the Spaniards from coastal tribesmen. The messengers tell him that the newcomers are bearded, white people who claim to have come by the wind, eat from silver plates, ride llamas shod in silver, throw "yllapas like the sky" and talk to white cloths, and that they can only be Viracochas.
titus: Titus was born in Rome in the year 39, probably on 30 December, the eldest son of Vespasian and Domitilla the Elder. His brother Domitian was born in 51. The Flavian family had risen from obscurity to prominence in four generations under the Julio-Claudian emperors. Suetonius records that Titus was brought up at the imperial court with Britannicus, the son of Emperor Claudius. He served as a military tribune in Germania from about 57 to 59, and also in Britannia, and returned to Rome about 63 to practise law and become a quaestor.

When the Jews of Judaea revolted in 66, Nero sent Vespasian to put down the rebellion, and Titus joined him at Ptolemais with the Fifteenth Legion. By 68 the coast and north of Judaea had been subdued, with victories at Taricheae and Gamala, where Titus distinguished himself. The campaign stopped when news came of Nero's death, and after Vespasian was declared emperor in 69, Titus was left to end the rebellion.

In 70 he besieged and captured Jerusalem, destroying the city and the Second Temple. He returned to Rome in 71 and rode in a triumph with Vespasian and Domitian, in which treasures taken from the Temple were paraded, and the Arch of Titus at the Forum commemorates the victory. The historian Josephus, who wrote the main account of the war, joined his entourage and took the name Flavius, and the neutrality of his work has been questioned.

Titus succeeded Vespasian on his death in the summer of 79, the first Roman emperor to follow his own father. He ended the treason trials that had long troubled the principate. A few months into his reign Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii and Herculaneum. He appointed two ex-consuls to organise relief and gave large sums from the imperial treasury.

A fire in Rome in 80 burned for three days and three nights and destroyed many public buildings, and he again paid for repairs. The Colosseum, begun in 70 under Vespasian, was completed in 80, and its inaugural games lasted a hundred days. Titus died of a fever on 13 September 81 after about two years in office, and Domitian succeeded him and deified him. Suetonius and Cassius Dio say he died naturally, though Philostratus reports a poisoning. Ancient historians judged him a good emperor.
titus-didius: Titus Didius, also spelled Deidius in ancient times, belonged to the plebeian gens Didia, a family relatively new to Roman politics. His father of the same name passed a sumptuary law, the lex Didia, as tribune of the plebs in 143 BCE, and the Fasti Capitolini name his grandfather Sextus. He first appears as triumvir monetalis, one of the three men in charge of minting coins, probably in 113 or 112 BCE. His denarii show two gladiators fighting, which the historian Michael Crawford reads as a promise of gladiatorial shows should he become curule aedile.

As tribune of the plebs in 103 BCE he tried to veto his colleague Gaius Norbanus's prosecution of Quintus Servilius Caepio after the Battle of Arausio and was driven from the proceedings by force. As praetor in 101 BCE he defeated the Scordisci in Macedon and earned his first triumph on his return in 100 BCE. In his consulship of 98 BCE, the first in his family, shared with Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos, he restored the Villa Publica and passed a law forbidding the joining of two unrelated proposals in one bill.

As proconsul of Hispania Citerior from 97 to 93 BCE he spent nearly all his term at war with the Celtiberi. He is said to have killed 20,000 Arevaci, and he besieged Colenda for nine months, after which its women and children were sold into slavery. He also lured a band of poor people living by banditry into a Roman camp with promises of land and had the families killed. Appian writes that this cruelty provoked a larger rising, which his successor Gaius Valerius Flaccus put down. Quintus Sertorius served under him as a military tribune and won the Grass Crown at Castulo.

During the Social War Didius served as a legate under Lucius Julius Caesar in 90 BCE and then under Lucius Porcius Cato and Sulla in 89 BCE. Shortly after taking Herculaneum, he died in battle on 11 June 89 BCE. He held two triumphs, over the Scordisci and for his victories in Spain.
titus-labienus: Titus Labienus was probably born around 100 BCE, since his praetorship fell in 60 or 59 BCE, and many sources suggest that he came from Cingulum in Picenum. His family was of equestrian status, and he had early ties with Pompey. His first service, about 78 to 75 BCE, was in Cilicia under Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus, fighting pirates and the Isaurian hill tribes. As tribune of the plebs in 63 BCE he cooperated with Gaius Julius Caesar and at his instigation accused Gaius Rabirius of high treason for the killing of the tribune Lucius Appuleius Saturninus in 100 BCE.

The aim was to discredit the senate's emergency decree. Rabirius was ultimately sentenced to exile. In the same year Labienus carried a plebiscite returning the election of the pontifices to the people.

As Caesar's senior legate in Gaul, Labienus was the only legate Caesar names in his account of his first campaign, and he was a skilled cavalry commander. He held the winter quarters at Vesontio in 58 BCE and commanded the legions in Gaul when Caesar was away. In 57 BCE, in the battle near the Sabis against the Atrebates and Nervii, he defeated the Atrebates and sent the 10th Legion against the rear of the Nervii, turning the battle.

He defeated the Treviri under Indutiomarus by sending his cavalry out through two gates to kill the leader first. Later, at Lutetia, he feigned a divided army to draw the Parisii under Camulogene into a trap and annihilated their reinforcements with his cavalry. In September 51 BCE Caesar made him governor of Cisalpine Gaul.

After Caesar crossed the Rubicon, Labienus left his post and joined Pompey, who made him commander of the cavalry. He urged Pompey to face Caesar in Italy. After defeat at Pharsalus, he fled to Corcyra and then to Africa, where he inflicted a slight check on Caesar at the Battle of Ruspina in 46 BCE. After the defeat at Thapsus he joined the younger Gnaeus Pompeius in Hispania. At the Battle of Munda, King Bogud, an ally of Caesar, approached the Pompeians from the rear, and Labienus, commanding their cavalry, took it from the front lines to meet him.

The Pompeian legions took this for a retreat and broke, and Labienus was killed in the rout, on 17 March 45 BCE. According to Appian, his head was brought to Caesar, who had the body sought out and buried with full honours. His son was Quintus Labienus.
titus-quinctius-flamininus: Flamininus belonged to the minor patrician gens Quinctia, which had lost much political influence by the middle of the 4th century BCE. His grandfather Lucius Quinctius was flamen Dialis, the priest of Jupiter, and the cognomen Flamininus derives from that priesthood. The Quinctii were long allied to the Fabii, and Polybius says that a Fabius Buteo was the nephew of Flamininus's wife. His career began unusually during the Second Punic War, when several men skipped steps of the cursus honorum.

In 208 BCE Flamininus served as military tribune under Marcus Claudius Marcellus, who died in an ambush near Crotone. He was probably quaestor in 206 and was sent to Tarentum, a Greek city that had defected to Hannibal and held a Roman garrison. After his uncle died he took command there as propraetor before the age of 25, an achievement explained by the shortage of experienced commanders, and he became familiar with Greek language and culture. In 201 and 200 he sat on commissions settling the veterans of Scipio Africanus.

He stood for the consulship before he was 30. Two tribunes of the plebs vetoed his candidacy because he was too young and had held no curule office, but the Senate compelled them to withdraw. By lot he received the command of the Second Macedonian War, drove Philip V of Macedon out of most of southern Greece and defeated him at the Battle of the Aous. As proconsul he defeated Philip at Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE. Philip had to surrender the Greek cities he held and pay 1,000 talents, but his kingdom was left as a buffer, which displeased the Achaean League. At the Isthmian Games in Corinth in 196 BCE Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of the Greek states.

In 192 BCE Flamininus warned Antiochus III not to interfere with the Greek states, and he was present at the Battle of Thermopylae in 191 BCE. He was elected censor in 189 BCE, defeating Cato the Elder. In 183 BCE he was sent to Prusias I of Bithynia to seek the capture of Hannibal, who killed himself to avoid being taken; according to Plutarch, many senators reproached Flamininus for causing the death of an enemy who had become harmless. He seems to have died around 174 BCE. The Greeks hailed him as a liberator, minted coins with his portrait, and in some cities deified him.
titus-tatius: In the Roman foundation myth Titus Tatius, also called Tatius Sabinus, was king of the Sabines of Cures. Tradition gives him one daughter, Tatia, who married Numa Pompilius, the successor of Romulus, and one son, ancestor of the patrician Tatii. During the reign of Romulus, the first king of Rome, Tatius declared war on Rome after the rape of the Sabine women. He took the stronghold on the Capitoline Hill through the treachery of Tarpeia.

Dionysius of Halicarnassus reports that after a year of preparation the two sides fought several skirmishes and then two major battles. The second took place two days after the first, between the two Roman hills they occupied, and was an epic contest in which each army gained and lost the upper hand. The Sabines retreated to the citadel at the end of the day. Before fighting resumed, the Sabine women, some in funeral dress and some carrying their children, persuaded Tatius and Romulus to stop. A treaty made one kingdom under both kings, still called Rome, though its people were also to be called Quirites.

The kings oversaw the growth of the city, the building of several landmarks and the conquest of Cameria. Their first disagreement came in the sixth year, when friends of Tatius wronged some Laurentii. Dionysius says that Tatius would not let Romulus hand over the culprits, that Sabines ambushed the ambassadors as they slept, and that Tatius freed by force the men Romulus had surrendered. He was later killed at a sacrifice in Lavinium, in retribution. In the account of Licinius Macer he went alone to Lavinium to seek forgiveness and was stoned by an angry mob. Tatius is not counted among the traditional seven kings of Rome.

Theodor Mommsen held that the story of his death is a legend explaining the abolition of blood revenge and that Tatius is the eponymous hero of the priestly college of the Sodales Titii, whose members made a yearly sacrifice at his grave; Augustus revived it, and Augustus and Claudius belonged to it. Tacitus gives two accounts of its origin. Gary Forsythe suggests that Tatius may have been the first real king of Rome.
tiye: Tiye's father, Yuya, was a non-royal, wealthy landowner from the Upper Egyptian town of Akhmim, where he served as a priest and as superintendent of oxen or commander of the chariotry. Her mother, Thuya, held many titles in religious cults. Some Egyptologists have suggested that Yuya was of foreign origin, but a growing number of more recent scholars argue that Tiye and her parents were of indigenous Egyptian origin, since Yuya's name shows no phonological features characteristic of a foreign language. Her brother Anen was Second Prophet of Amun.

Tiye was married to Amenhotep III by the second year of his reign. Commemorative scarabs announced her as Great Royal Wife and gave the names of her parents. Because the king was crowned as a child, scholars have proposed that a regency council formed around him, with Tiye's parents among its members. The couple had six confirmed children, among them Thutmose, crown prince and High Priest of Ptah, and Amenhotep IV, who succeeded his father.

Amenhotep III devoted several shrines to her and built a temple for her at Sedeinga in Nubia, where she was worshipped as a form of Hathor-Tefnut. The American Egyptologists David O'Connor and Eric Cline note that no earlier queen figured so prominently in her husband's lifetime: she appears beside him in statuary, tomb and temple reliefs and stelae, and her name is paired with his on small objects and commemorative scarabs. She was even shown as a sphinx, an image formerly reserved for the king.

Tiye became her husband's trusted adviser and was known for her intelligence and strong personality. Foreign kings such as Tushratta of Mitanni were willing to deal with her directly, and she is regarded as the first Egyptian queen to have her name recorded on official acts. In Amarna letter EA 26, Tushratta wrote to her to recall his good relations with her late husband and to ask for friendship with her son. She had a house at Akhetaten, her son's new capital.

In an inscription dated to the twelfth year of Akhenaten's reign, about 1338 BCE, Tiye is mentioned for the last time, and she is thought to have died soon afterwards. She was probably first buried at Amarna and later moved to the Valley of the Kings.

In 1898 Victor Loret found three mummies in a side chamber of the tomb of Amenhotep II, KV35. The older woman was called the Elder Lady, and several researchers argued that she was Tiye. In 2010, DNA analysis confirmed the identification.
tlacaelel: Tlacaelel, whose Nahuatl name means Man of Strong Emotions, was the son of the ruler Huitzilihuitl and Queen Cacamacihuatl. He was a nephew of Itzcoatl, a brother of the rulers Chimalpopoca and Moctezuma I, and the father of the poet Macuilxochitzin. He is regarded as the principal architect of the Aztec Triple Alliance and so of the Mexica empire.

Under his uncle Itzcoatl he held the office of Tlacochcalcatl, and during the war against the Tepanecs in the late 1420s he was raised to Cihuacoatl, first adviser to the ruler. He kept that office under four successive rulers until his death. He raised the tribal god and hero Huitzilopochtli to the head of the pantheon and increased the militarism of the state. According to the chronicler Diego Durán, he increased human sacrifice, above all during a period of natural disasters that began in 1446, and the flower wars against Tlaxcala and other Nahua city-states were his invention in the reign of Moctezuma I.

To strengthen the nobility he helped create and enforce sumptuary laws that forbade commoners to wear lip plugs, gold armbands and cotton cloaks. He is also credited with a policy of burning the books of conquered peoples, so as to erase the memory of a past before the Aztecs.

In 1484 Tlacaelel dedicated the seventh reconstruction of the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan with the sacrifice of many war captives, at a time when Mexica power stood at its height. After his death in 1487 the empire went on expanding north into the Gran Chichimeca and south towards the Maya lands. The Mexican writer Antonio Velasco Piña made him the hero of the novel Tlacaelel, El Azteca entre los Aztecas in 1979, and Amado Zumaya played him in Juan Mora Catlett's 1990 film Return to Aztlán.
tlacochcalcatl: The title tlacochcalcatl means the man from the house of darts, and the rank is roughly comparable to that of a modern field marshal. In Aztec warfare its holder was second in command only to the tlatoani, the ruler, and usually led the army into battle when the ruler was occupied elsewhere. Once the tlatoani had decided to undertake a campaign, the tlacochcalcatl and the tlacateccatl, or general, took all the military decisions and did the planning.

The tlacochcalcatl was also in charge of the tlacochcalco, the house of darts: four armouries at the four entrances to the ceremonial precinct of Tenochtitlan. They were stocked with new weapons every year during the festival of Quecholli, and the Spanish conquistador Andrés de Tapia estimated the weapons in each armoury at 500 cartloads. The holder of the office was always a member of the military order of the cuachicqueh, the shorn ones.

The office was often the last step towards becoming tlatoani. The first tlacochcalcatl was appointed by Huitzilihuitl, who gave the post to his brother Itzcoatl, and Itzcoatl probably also held it under Chimalpopoca. On becoming ruler, Itzcoatl named Tlacaelel tlacochcalcatl and Moctezuma Ilhuicamina tlacateccatl; when Tlacaelel was appointed cihuacoatl, Moctezuma Ilhuicamina was promoted in his place.

It is not known who held the office during the reign of Moctezuma I, and Tlacaelel may have held two offices at once in this period. Under Axayacatl, Moctezuma Ilhuicamina's son and successor, the tlacochcalcatl was Tizoc, who became ruler at Axayacatl's death. Tizoc was seen as a weak ruler and was removed, and his own tlacochcalcatl, Ahuitzotl, became ruler in turn. Ahuitzotl's tlacochcalcatl was the next ruler, Moctezuma II, whose tlacochcalcatl at the arrival of the Spaniards was Quappiatl.
tlacopan: Tlacopan, also called Tacuba, was an altepetl, a city-state, on the western shore of Lake Texcoco. Its name in Classical Nahuatl, Tlacōpan, comes from tlacōtl, stem or rod, and -pan, place in or on, and means roughly place on the rods; its Otomian name, Abotto, means in the forest of trees. According to Francisco Cervantes de Salazar, six languages were spoken there: Nahuatl, Otomi, Mazahua, a language he called Guata, probably Matlatzinca, one called Chuchumé, probably a Popolocan language, and Chichimec.

Tlacopan was a Tepanec city-state, at first subordinate to nearby Azcapotzalco. Aculnahuacatl Tzaqualcatl, a son of the Tepanec ruler Tezozomoc, was installed as its tlatoani. Totoquihuaztli I is often considered the first tlatoani of Tlacopan and was a co-founder of the Triple Alliance with Tenochtitlan and Texcoco, from which the Aztec Empire grew. Throughout its existence Tlacopan remained a minor partner.

Its later rulers included Chimalpopoca and Totoquihuatzin, who died in 1519, and his son Tetlepanquetzal, who ruled from 1519 to 1525. The Aztec Empire collapsed in 1521 in the Spanish conquest of Mexico, led by Hernán Cortés with his Tlaxcallan allies. From 1526 to 1550 Tlacopan was mostly without a ruler: the city was part of the encomienda of Isabel Moctezuma, its de facto ruler, and its business was handled by appointed governors and nobles unrelated to the old dynasty. After her death Don Antonio Cortés Totoquihuaztli the Elder, a descendant of the pre-colonial tlatoani, was made tlatoani, from about 1550 to 1574.

Over the following centuries Tlacopan was absorbed into Mexico City. Its site is now the neighbourhood of Tacuba, where the archaeological site of Tlacopan lies within the municipality of Miguel Hidalgo.
tlalmanalco: The name comes from Nahuatl and means flat area; the municipality's seal shows flat land with a pyramid, ringed by small mountains, as Aztec codices drew the area. Much of the municipality borders the Iztaccihuatl-Popocatepetl National Park, and pine forest covers about 65% of its land. Its main river, La Compañía, draws much of its water from the Ayolotepito glacier, and the peak of Tlatlachelo, at 3,175 metres, has Toltec-era shrines at its summit.

Archaeological finds just north-west of the main plaza show a fortified village from about 3,100 to 600 BCE. Between the 10th and 13th centuries the area was held by the Xochteca, Cocolca, Olmec-Xicallanca and Quiyahuizteca, who were driven out by Toltecs and Chichimecas. The Nonohualcas, a group of these newcomers, founded a city-state here in 1336 and allied with Amaquemecan, Chimalhuacan and Tenango Tepopollan; after 100 years of fighting the alliance fell to the Aztecs in 1465.

Friar Juan de Rivas founded the Spanish town in 1525, the year Friar Martin de Valencia began the conversion of the people and, according to the Annals of Chimalpain, the native shrine was destroyed. The native population was held in forced indentured servitude from 1550 until 1633. A copper smelter, textile mills and a railway arrived from 1858, and the San Rafael paper mill was among the most important industries in Mexico from 1930 to 1970.

The Franciscan Temple of San Luis Obispo, first opened in 1532 and enlarged between 1585 and 1591, has a cedar altarpiece with paintings by Baltasar de Echave, and Martin de Valencia is buried there. Its open chapel, one of the few intact in Mexico, is an example of tequitqui art, Christian work by indigenous craftsmen, and was left incomplete. The Nonohualca Museum shows stone sculpture of the area. The municipality covers 158.76 square kilometres and had 43,930 inhabitants.
tlaloc: Tlaloc was the god of rain in Aztec religion, and also a deity of the fertility of the earth and of water, worshipped as a giver of life and sustenance. He was feared for his power over hail, thunder, lightning and rain, though not as a malicious figure.

Worship of a storm god tied to mountaintop shrines and life-giving rain is at least as old as Teotihuacan, where an underground shrine of Tlaloc has been found, and archaeological evidence shows he was worshipped in Mesoamerica at least 800 years before the Aztecs. Goggle-eyed rain gods of other peoples, such as the Maya Chaac and the Zapotec Cocijo, are often called Tlaloc generally. His name is thought to derive from the Nahuatl word tlalli, earth.

Representations of Tlaloc are marked by fangs and ringed eyes, with lips shaped like a moustache, and he often carries a vessel of water. In Aztec cosmology four Tlalocs mark the corners of the universe, holding up the sky, and he was lord of the third sun, which was destroyed by fire.

In the Codex Borgia the Five Tlaloque water maize fields with different rains, only one of them beneficial. He ruled Tlalocan, a paradise of unending springtime and green plants, where went those who died by lightning, drowning or water-borne diseases; they were buried with seeds planted in their faces. His sister or older relative was sometimes Chalchiuhtlicue, goddess of ground water.

In Tenochtitlan one of the two shrines on top of the Great Temple, the northern one, was dedicated to Tlaloc, beside that of Huitzilopochtli. The most important site of his worship was the peak of Cerro Tlaloc, a mountain of 4,100 metres on the eastern rim of the Valley of Mexico, where the Aztec ruler came each year and pilgrims left offerings of precious stones and figures.

During the festival of Atlcahualo, from 12 February to 3 March, children were taken to mountaintops such as Cerro Tlaloc and sacrificed; their tears were taken as a sign of coming rain. The Book of Gods and Rites reports a child sacrificed in another pilgrimage, though this may be colonial sensationalism.

The colossal statue found at Coatlinchan, weighing 168 tons and long thought to be Tlaloc, was moved to the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City in 1964, although one scholar thinks it may represent a female deity. Stones depicting Tlaloc were set inside the church of Santiago Tlatelolco in the 16th century.
tlapanec-people: Their language is closely related to the now extinct Subtiaba language of Nicaragua. Before the Spanish conquest the Tlapanecs lived in an isolated mountain area along the Costa Chica region of Guerrero, just east of present-day Acapulco. Their main city was Tlapan, and the name Tlapanec is Nahuatl for "inhabitant of Tlapan". On the eve of Spanish contact, around 1520, their population has been estimated at roughly 54,000, about 7% of the people of what is now Guerrero.

The Tlapanecs explain natural phenomena through myth. In one, the sun (Akha'), the moon (Gon') and the fire god (Akuun mbatsuun') were all born on the bank of a river and raised by Akuun ñee, goddess of the temazcal sweat bath and patron of the duality of hot and cold.

Nagualism is another important part of their culture. When a baby is born, an animal is said to be born at the same moment, and that animal is the child's nahual. No one but the child knows which animal it is, for the nahual shows itself to the child only in dreams.

The Yopi, whose territory near Acapulco was called Yopitzinco, were strong warriors and were never conquered by the Aztec Empire. They remained an independent enclave surrounded by Aztec lands, yet were invited to the coronations of Mexica rulers in Tenochtitlan and given gifts there. Their culture may have differed from that of the Tlapanec proper, with a greater stress on hunting with the bow, which children learned from the age of seven.

Writers such as Sahagún described the Yopi as poorer and less civilised than other Mesoamerican peoples, a reputation that Mexica propaganda explaining their continued independence may have helped to shape. The Yopi were skilled workers of gold and precious stones and worshipped Xipe Totec, whose cult they may have brought to Tenochtitlan. The archaeological site of Tehuacalco was inhabited by the Yopi.
tlaxcalans: The Tlaxcaltecs are a Nahua people who formed in the Puebla-Tlaxcala Valley during the Postclassic period, between about 1200 and 1521. The chronicles place their origin among the teochichimecs, one of seven Nahuatlaca lineages that emerged, according to tradition, from Chicomoztoc, the place of the seven caves. Around 1290 they reached the Valley of Mexico and founded Poyauhtlan on Lake Texcoco, but conflicts with other groups drove them out. The Olmec-Xicallanca granted them land near the hill of Cuatlapanga, where they settled. They became a conglomeration of speakers of Nahuatl, Otomi and Pinome, and formed the confederation of Tlaxcallan from four altepetl: Tepeticpac, Ocotelulco, Tizatlán and Quiahuiztlán.

Unlike the hereditary monarchies of the Mexica and many neighbours, Tlaxcallan was governed by shared power among several noble houses, with no single supreme ruler, and scholars sometimes call it a republic. Its council and rotating military leadership gave continuity under constant war. The economy rested on maize, beans, squash, tomatoes and maguey, which yielded a sweetener, the fermented drink pulque and fibre. Ethnohistorical sources describe a trade embargo of more than sixty years imposed by the Mexica Triple Alliance, though research on obsidian trade questions how effective it was. The Tlaxcaltecs were never conquered, and their wars with the Mexica were called xochiyaoyatl, flower wars.

When Hernán Cortés arrived in September 1519, the Tlaxcaltec senate resolved to fight. Under the general Xicohténcatl Axayacatzin, tens of thousands of warriors fought the Spanish near Tecoac and Tzompantepec. Lords such as Maxixcatzin and Xicohténcatl the Elder then argued for an alliance, and the Tlaxcaltecs became the most numerous indigenous allies of the Spanish.

The Crown gave Tlaxcala the status of an "Indian republic", with its own cabildo, perpetual exemption from tribute and recognition of its nobles as hidalgos. Under the Capitulations of 1591, 400 Tlaxcaltec families settled the northern frontier. After independence, Mexican national narratives often called the Tlaxcaltecs traitors, a view historians such as Federico Navarrete have challenged since the late 20th century.
tlemcen: The area around Tlemcen was inhabited in the Neolithic period. It became a military outpost of Rome in the 2nd century CE under the name Pomaria and was the centre of a diocese, whose bishop Victor represented it at the Council of Carthage in 411. A large Christian population remained for many centuries after the Arab conquest in 708. In the later 8th and the 9th century it was a kingdom of Banu Ifran with a Sufri Kharijite orientation, and these Berber Kharijis developed Saharan oases and linked them into trans-Saharan caravan routes ending at Tlemcen. Idris I founded a congregational mosque at the settlement of Agadir around 790.

In 1081 or 1082 the Almoravid leader Yusuf ibn Tashfin founded Tagrart just west of Agadir, with its congregational mosque, the Great Mosque of Tlemcen. The two settlements fused over time into Tlemcen. The Almohad ruler 'Abd al-Mu'min surrounded the city with a wall in 1145, and under the Almohads it rose to prominence as a major trading and administrative centre.

After the end of Almohad rule in the 1230s, Tlemcen became the capital of one of the three successor states, the Zayyanid Kingdom of Tlemcen. Yaghmurasen Ibn Zyan merged Agadir and Tagrart into one city and gave it its name. He moved the seat of power from the Qasr al-Qadim to a new citadel, the Mechouar. Tlemcen was among the most important economic and cultural centres of the region, alongside Fez, Tunis and Granada. It connected the coastal route across the Maghreb with the trans-Saharan caravans, and it housed a funduk, a European trading centre, so that African gold entered European hands.

In the first half of the 14th century it had perhaps 40,000 inhabitants and several well-known madrasas, among them the Tashfiniya Madrasa founded by Abu Tashfin I. The Marinid sultan Abu al-Hasan Ali and his son Abu 'Inan twice ruled the city but could not hold the region against local resistance. Zayyanid Tlemcen was intermittently a vassal of Ifriqiya, the Marinid dynasty or Aragon. The Spanish took Oran in 1509 and a campaign against Tlemcen in 1543 ended in the capture of the city. In 1551 it came under Ottoman rule.

Tlemcen is the second-largest city in north-western Algeria after Oran and the capital of Tlemcen Province. Its mix of Arab, Berber, Andalusi, Ottoman and Western influences has earned it the title of capital of Andalusian art in Algeria, and it is also called the Pearl of the Maghreb. The Great Mosque is said to be the finest remaining example of Almoravid architecture. The tomb of Sidi Boumédiène adjoins a mosque. Its textiles and handcrafts and its cool climate in the mountains have made it a centre of tourism.
tlingit: The Tlingit, or Lingít, speak the Tlingit language, an independent branch of the Na-Dené family, and their name for themselves means People of the Tides. Their culture developed in the temperate rainforest of the south-east Alaskan coast and the Alexander Archipelago. Culture with elements related to the Tlingit originated around 10,000 years ago near the mouths of the Skeena and Nass Rivers.

The largest territory they historically occupied ran from the Portland Canal along the present border between Alaska and British Columbia north to the coast just south-east of the Copper River delta, and included almost all of the Alexander Archipelago. The Coastal Tlingit controlled one of the mountain passes into the Yukon interior. Inland Tlingit live along the Alsek, Tatshenshini, Chilkat, Taku and Stikine rivers and around Atlin, Teslin and Tagish Lakes, where they built trade networks with Athabascan peoples and often intermarried with them.

Tlingit society is divided into two moieties, the Raven and the Eagle, which are divided into clans and then into lineages or house groups. Kinship is matrilineal, so that children are born into their mother's clan, and property and hereditary roles pass through the mother's line. Each group has heraldic crests, shown on totem poles, canoes, feast dishes, house posts and weavings. Rank rests on wealth and economic power but also on generosity and proper behaviour, and a long tradition of oratory is valued.

Hereditary slavery was practised extensively until the United States outlawed it. The Tlingit built cedar plank houses, now called clan houses, and rely on a diet in which salmon receives the most emphasis, with seal and game close behind, along with halibut, herring, eulachon, shellfish and berries. Traditionally they were animists, and shamans cured disease and aided hunting; a central belief was the reincarnation of humans and animals.

The Tlingit had their first contact with Europeans in 1741, with Russian explorers, and Spanish explorers followed in 1775. They kept their independence but suffered epidemics of smallpox and other diseases brought by Europeans, and the smallpox epidemic of 1862 killed about 60 percent of the Mainland Tlingit and 37 percent of the Island Tlingit. Between 1886 and 1895, when shamans could not treat Old World diseases, many converted to Orthodox Christianity, whose missionaries had translated their liturgy into Tlingit.

Alaska Tlingit have no reservations, since the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act set up regional corporations, among them Sealaska. In Canada the Tlingit belong to First Nations in British Columbia and Yukon. The language has an estimated 200 to 400 native speakers in the United States and 100 in Canada, and several institutions run revival programmes.
tlos: Tlos stands near the modern town of Seydikemer in Muğla Province, some 4 kilometres north-west of Saklıkent Gorge. The city lies on the east side of the Xanthos valley on a rocky outcrop that rises from a plateau and ends in almost sheer cliffs on the west, north and north-east. Its Greek name comes from the Lycian Tlawa. Remains in the city centre and in the nearby caves of Girmeler and Tavabaşı suggest that settlement began more than 4,000 years ago.

Tlos probably lost its independence when the Persians under Harpagus invaded Lycia in 540 BCE, and it prospered under Persian rule from the 5th to the late 4th century BCE. In 168 BCE Rome granted the Lycian League autonomy from Rhodes. Its citizens were divided into demes, three of which were named after the Lycian heroes Bellerophon, Iobates and Sarpedon, and a Jewish community had its own magistrates. Under Rome the city was styled the very brilliant metropolis of the Lycian nation. Earthquakes in 141 and 240 CE caused great damage, and the benefactor Opramoas of Rhodiapolis paid for much rebuilding.

Tlos became a bishopric under the metropolitan see of Mira. Its bishop Andreas attended the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and later bishops sat at councils down to the Photian Council of Constantinople in 879. The Catholic Church now lists it as a titular see. Stephanus of Byzantium recorded a tradition that the city was named after a son of the nymph Praxidike and Tremilus.

Charles Fellows rediscovered the site in 1838, and an interdisciplinary team has excavated it since 2005. On the acropolis an early Classical palace complex and Lycian and Roman walls lie beneath the Ottoman fort of the local governor Kanlı Ali Ağa, beside a sanctuary thought to belong to the Lycian deity Trggas. Below are a Hellenistic stadium for 2,500 spectators with a long pool, a two-storey market, two baths, a Byzantine church and a well-preserved theatre with a three-storey stage.
toamasina: Toamasina is the capital of the Atsinanana region, on the east coast of Madagascar on the Indian Ocean, 215 kilometres northeast of Antananarivo. Its name means like salt or salty. In French it is called Tamatave, and in the past it was also known as Port aux prunes. Its importance comes from a coral reef that forms a spacious harbour, entered by two openings. The city centre is built on a sandy peninsula that projects at right angles from the general coastline, and the mouth of the Ivondro River lies to the south. The climate is a trade-wind tropical rainforest one, with no true dry season. September to November is the driest period and February to April the wettest.

Under French rule Toamasina was the seat of several foreign consuls and of many French officials, and it was the chief port for the capital and the interior. Imports were mainly piece-goods, flour-based foods and iron and steel goods, and the main exports were gold dust, raffia, hides, natural rubber and live animals. Steamers of the Messageries Maritimes and the Havraise companies kept up communication with Europe, and the British Union-Castle Line linked the port with Mauritius and, from there, Sri Lanka.

In the colonial period the soil and a formerly crowded population left the town often plagued by epidemics. Plague broke out in 1898 and again in 1900. The draining of the neighbouring marshes brought some improvement, though malaria and other diseases have continued. The botanist and explorer André Michaux died in Tamatave in 1802.

Toamasina is the chief seaport of Madagascar and the country's main gateway to the Indian Ocean and the world. The railway line to the capital ends here, and National Road 2 runs west to Antananarivo. The town is also the northern end of the Canal des Pangalanes. The University of Toamasina was founded in 1977. Its places of worship are mostly Christian churches, with the Roman Catholic cathedral of St Joseph, and there are also mosques.
tobago: Tobago lies 35 kilometres northeast of Trinidad and about 160 kilometres off the northeastern coast of Venezuela. It has a land area of 300 square kilometres, about 40 kilometres long and 10 wide. The island is hilly and of volcanic origin, with a mountainous spine called the Main Ridge, while the southwest is flat and largely coralline limestone. The Tobago Forest Reserve on the Main Ridge was designated a protected Crown reserve on 17 April 1776 and is the oldest protected rain forest in the Western hemisphere. Christopher Columbus named the island Belaforme, 'because from a distance it seemed beautiful'.

Tobago was settled by people of the Ortoiroid tradition between 3500 and 1000 BCE, followed by Saladoid people in the first century CE, who brought pottery and agriculture. The island linked the Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles with their Kalina allies in the Guianas and Venezuela. Columbus sighted it on 14 August 1498 but did not land. A royal order of 1511 authorised the Spanish of Hispaniola to raid it for slaves, and the raids, continuing until at least the 1620s, decimated its population.

The Dutch founded the first European settlement, Nieuw Walcheren, in 1628 at Great Courland Bay. It was abandoned in 1630 after Indigenous attacks, re-established in 1633 and destroyed by the Spanish in Trinidad. English attempts in the 1630s and 1640s also failed. The Curonians, Dutch, English, French, Spanish and Swedish all tried to colonise the island, which changed hands 33 times, the most in Caribbean history, before the Treaty of Paris ceded it to the British in 1814. From about 1672 plantations of sugar, cotton and indigo grew up, worked by enslaved Africans, and France gave up the island to Britain in 1763. The French retook it in 1781.

After 1814 sugar production flourished again, but a hurricane in 1847, the end of slavery in 1834 and European competition ended the sugar trade. Tobago became a ward of Trinidad in 1889, and Hurricane Flora in 1963 devastated the plantations, turning the economy toward tourism.

Trinidad and Tobago became independent in August 1962 and a republic on 31 August 1976. Tobago is a ward of the republic, governed locally by the Tobago House of Assembly, revived in 1980 after local government ended in 1889. Its capital is Scarborough, and the population was 60,874 at the 2011 census, mostly of African descent. The island has coral reefs, including Buccoo Reef, and nesting beaches for the leatherback turtle.
tobolsk: Tobolsk stands in Tyumen Oblast where the Tobol meets the Irtysh, at the point where the Irtysh turns from flowing westward to flowing northward. The town was founded on the site of the Siberian Tatar town of Sibir-Tura, near the ruins of Qashliq, the capital of the Khanate of Sibir. Yermak Timofeyevich's Cossacks took Qashliq on 26 October 1582, and Kuchum, the khan, retreated. Kuchum regrouped and killed Yermak in a surprise attack on 6 August 1584, and Qashliq passed between Tatar and Cossack hands before it was abandoned in 1588.

Cossacks under Daniil Chulkov founded Tobolsk in 1587, the second Russian town in Siberia after Tyumen. It became the centre of the conquest of Siberia: Beryozovo and Mangazeya were built to bring the Nenets under tribute, and Surgut and Tara to protect Tobolsk. The Cossacks finally defeated Kuchum at the Battle of Urmin in 1598, ending the Khanate of Sibir. Tobolsk grew quickly on the Siberian river routes and prospered on trade with China to the east and Bukhara to the south.

In 1708 it became the capital of the new Siberia Governorate, and the first school, theatre and newspaper in Siberia were founded there. After the Battle of Poltava in 1709, many Swedish prisoners of war were sent to the town, where they numbered about a quarter of the population. Its political importance fell as the governorate was divided, and in the 1890s the Trans-Siberian Railway passed to the south. After the Decembrist Revolt of 1825 some exiled Decembrists settled there. In August 1917 the Provisional Government sent the family of Nicholas II to the former Governor-General's house, and in spring 1918 the Bolsheviks moved them to Yekaterinburg. In 1920 Tobolsk Governorate was abolished, ending 218 years as a provincial capital.

Tobolsk is the only town in Siberia with a standing stone kremlin, a city-fortress of the turn of the 17th and 18th centuries. Its monuments include the Cathedral of St. Sophia, built 1683 to 1686, and the Swedish Chamber of 1713 to 1716. Tobolsk is the seat of the first Orthodox diocese in Siberia. The town had 100,352 inhabitants at the 2021 census, and its economy rests on an oil refinery and the petrochemical industry.
tobruk: Tobruk lies on Libya's eastern Mediterranean coast, near the border with Egypt, and has a strong, naturally protected deep harbour, probably the best natural port in northern Africa. Escarpments run south of the town, as across Cyrenaica, and form a substantial barrier between the north and south of Libya in this area. The city is surrounded by desert lightly populated by nomadic herdsmen who travel from oasis to oasis.

An ancient Greek agricultural colony, Antipyrgus, stood on the site, its name roughly meaning across from Pyrgos, a place in Crete. In the Roman era the town became a fortress guarding the Cyrenaican frontier. With the spread of Christianity it became an episcopal see; only one ancient bishop is known by name, Aemilianus, who took part in the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. Later the site became a way station on the caravan route along the coast, and by 1911 it was an Italian military post.

Tobruk's strategic value in the Second World War rested on its harbour, which could never be wholly rendered useless by bombing, its Italian fortifications, its position on a peninsula that a few troops could defend, and the largest airfield in eastern Libya 24 kilometres away. British, Australian and Indian forces captured it on 22 January 1941. After Erwin Rommel's forces drove the Allies back to the Egyptian border, Tobruk was isolated and besieged. Its defenders included the Australian 9th Division and later the British 70th Infantry Division, the Polish Independent Carpathian Rifle Brigade and a Czechoslovak battalion.

Operation Crusader lifted the siege in late 1941. Rommel took the town on 21 June 1942 in an outflanking attack, capturing the largest number of Commonwealth troops since Singapore. A British raid on 13–14 September 1942 failed with almost 800 casualties. The Allies recaptured Tobruk on 11 November 1942, after the Second Battle of El Alamein.

Rebuilt after the war, Tobruk was expanded in the 1960s with a port terminal linked by an oil pipeline to the Sarir oil field. It is the capital of the Butnan District. King Idris of Libya had his palace at Bab Zaytun, and the city was traditionally a stronghold of the Senussi dynasty.
tocco-family: The family came from Benevento, and its earliest known member is Ugolino Tocco, Grand Seneschal of the Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI. Later genealogies claimed descent from the Ostrogothic kings Theodoric the Great and Totila and from Pyrrhus of Epirus, links historians regard as invented. The Tocchi served the Hohenstaufen rulers of southern Italy and then the Angevins. Guglielmo Tocco, founder of the branch that later ruled in Greece, was a knight and councillor of Philip of Anjou, Prince of Taranto, and governor of Corfu in 1330 and 1331.

Guglielmo's son Leonardo I Tocco, a close confidant of Robert of Taranto, married Maddalena de' Buondelmonti, niece of the Grand Seneschal Niccolò Acciaioli. Called in by locals discontented with the Venetian Zorzi family, he took Lefkada and the mainland fortress of Vonitsa. His son Carlo I Tocco began his reign as an infant under Maddalena's regency, and by the late 1380s was, in the historian William Miller's view, the most powerful remaining Latin ruler in the eastern Mediterranean.

In 1411 the people of Ioannina deposed the widow of Esau de' Buondelmonti and invited Carlo I to rule them; Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos recognised him as Despot in 1415, and in October 1416 he entered Arta, uniting Epirus. Defeated in the Battle of the Echinades in 1427, he gave up his conquests in the Morea, and his niece Creusa, renamed Theodora, married the future emperor Constantine. After Carlo I died in 1429, Ioannina fell to the Ottoman Empire within a year, and Arta followed in March 1449.

In exile in Naples, Leonardo III Tocco sought help to regain his lands, remarking in 1480 that "we may have lost our rings but we still did not lose our fingers". His brother Antonio briefly retook Cephalonia in 1481 but was murdered in 1483. Through Leonardo's wife Milica Branković, a granddaughter of Thomas Palaiologos, the family claimed the senior line of Byzantine imperial heirs. In 1642 Antonio Tocco exchanged the claim to Epirus for the Neapolitan title Prince of Achaea; the heads of the family were later known as Princes of Montemiletto, and the line ended on 24 March 1884.
toda-of-pamplona: Toda was the daughter of Aznar Sánchez of Larraun, a paternal grandson of King García Íñiguez of Pamplona, and of Onneca Fortúnez, a daughter of King Fortún Garcés, so she descended from the earlier royal dynasty of Íñigo Arista. She married King Sancho I of Pamplona. When he died while their son García was still a child, he was succeeded by his brother Jimeno Garcés, the husband of Toda's sister Sancha.

On King Jimeno's death in 931 Toda became regent and guardian of García Sánchez I. In 934 she signed a treaty pledging allegiance to her nephew Abd-ar-Rahman III and released hostages of the Banu Di n-Nun clan, while the caliph confirmed García's rule, a step sometimes read as the caliph's way of freeing García from his mother's control. A count Fortún Garcés rebelled at Falces and was put down with Cordoban arms. Toda broke the treaty in 937, bringing a punitive campaign.

She remained powerful long after the regency. She appears in royal charters to the exclusion of her daughter-in-law the queen from 947 to 955, and in 958 she ruled a subkingdom of her own around Deio and Lizarrara. She arranged political marriages for her daughters across Christian Iberia: Urraca and Onneca became queens of León, and Sancha married Count Fernán González of Castile.

In 958 Toda sought help for her grandson Sancho I of León, whose obesity was largely responsible for his loss of the throne. Abd-ar-Rahman III sent his Jewish physician Hasdai ibn Shaprut, who promised a cure if Toda came to Córdoba. She arrived with García, Sancho, nobles and clergy and was received with full honours. The visit of a Christian queen to the caliphal capital raised the caliph's prestige among his subjects and is considered a landmark of medieval diplomacy, and Sancho's treatment succeeded.
todai-ji: Japan suffered disasters and epidemics in the Tenpyō era, among them a major smallpox outbreak around 735 to 737 and a rebellion led by Fujiwara no Hirotsugu in 740. In 741 Emperor Shōmu issued an edict promoting provincial temples throughout the country, and in 743 he commissioned the Great Buddha. Kinshōsen-ji, the forerunner of Tōdai-ji, was made the provincial temple of Yamato Province and head of all the provincial temples.

According to the temple's records, more than 2,600,000 people contributed rice, wood, metal, cloth or labour, and 350,000 worked directly on the statue. It was cast in eight pours over three years, begun at Shigaraki and resumed in Nara in 745, and finished in 751. The eye-opening ceremony of 752 was attended by 10,000 monks and 4,000 dancers.

The Great Buddha Hall houses the Buddha Vairocana, known in Japanese as Daibutsu, said to be the world's largest bronze statue of him. The original complex also had two pagodas of about 100 metres, which an earthquake destroyed.

The hall has been rebuilt twice after fire. The present building, finished in 1709, is 57 metres long, 50 metres wide and 49 metres high, about 30 per cent smaller than its predecessor, which had eleven bays to its seven. It was the world's largest wooden building until 1998.

In the Nara period the state regulated Buddhism closely, and Tōdai-ji served as the central administrative temple for the provincial temples and for the six Buddhist schools of the time, each of which had an office there. All officially licensed monks had to take Vinaya ordination at the temple. In 754 Ganjin, who had reached Japan after twelve years and six attempts to cross the sea from China, ordained Empress Kōken, the former Emperor Shōmu and others.

The temple's authority declined when the centre of Japanese Buddhism moved to Mount Hiei and political power moved to the shōgun's base at Kamakura after the Genpei war. By the 19th century the Great Buddha Hall was in danger of collapse under its heavy roof. A restoration from 1904 to 1913 propped it up, and a second, from 1974 to 1980, fixed the roof with steel frames and gave the hall its present appearance.
todar-mal: Todar Mal was born in 1523 or the following year in the town of Laharpur in Awadh, in what is now the Sitapur district of Uttar Pradesh, to a Hindu family from Punjab of the Khatri or Kayastha caste. His father died when he was very young and left him without means. He began as a writer, a humble clerical post, and rose when the Sur emperor Sher Shah Suri put him in charge of building the new fort of Rohtas in Punjab, meant to stop Gakhar raids and to bar the Mughals in the north-west.

After the Mughals overthrew the Sur dynasty, Todar Mal entered the service of Akbar, who placed him in charge of Agra and later made him governor of Gujarat; at times he also ran the imperial mint in Bengal and served in Punjab. He was among the 30 officers whom Abu'l-Fazl names as present at Akbar's victory over the rebel governor of Malwa, Abdullah Khan Uzbeg, in August 1564. A mansabdar of 4000, he counted among the Navaratnas of the court and also served as joint Wazir.

As finance minister he introduced standard weights and measures, a land survey and settlement, and revenue districts and officers. Under the zabt system and the dahsala taxation, crop yields and prices were surveyed over the ten years from 1570 to 1580, and a cash tax was fixed for each crop. The empire was divided into 15 subahs, 187 sarkars and 3367 mahals or parganas; land was measured in bighas of 3600 Ilahi gaz, using a measuring rope of bamboo joined by iron rings so that its length would not change with the seasons. This settlement became known as Todar Mal's Bandobast.

Between 1582 and 1584 he decreed that the Mughal administration be written in Persian, and scholars agree that Persian then became the dominant language of Mughal government until the British replaced it with English in the 1830s. He rebuilt the Kashi Vishwanath Temple in 1585, translated the Bhagavata Purana into Persian and commissioned the Todarnanda, a work on law and ethics. According to Beveridge, he was travelling to Haridwar on leave when a letter from Akbar urged work over pilgrimage, and he returned to Lahore, where he died on 8 November 1589 and was cremated by Hindu rites.
todi: Todi stands on a high two-crested hill at an elevation of 447 metres on the left bank of the Tiber, about 40 kilometres from Perugia and 18 kilometres from Spoleto, in the province of Perugia. The town lies between the streams Rivo and Naia, which flow into the Tiber. Its position, commanding distant views in every direction, made it a strong place. Piazza del Popolo occupies the highest point, on the summit of Colle Nidoli, in the area of the Roman forum.

Todi was founded by the Umbri in the 8th or 7th century BCE under the name Tutere, a name that means border, because the city lay on the frontier with the Etruscan lands. Ancient Tuder was one of the most important Umbrian cities and minted its own coinage with the name Tutere. It had strong Etruscan cultural influence before the Roman conquest, which is placed in the 3rd century BCE, and after it Roman customs replaced the earlier Umbrian-Etruscan culture.

The emperor Trajan's family, the gens Ulpia, came from Todi. A legend places the foundation as early as 2707 BCE and says that the first furrow was traced under the guidance of an eagle. Its elevated position made Todi a strong place during the Gothic War and after the fall of the Western Roman Empire, and chronicles say that Saint Fortunatus, bishop of the city, spared it from slaughter and fire.

In the 11th century it set up a free commune with two consuls responsible for administration and justice. Orvieto, helped by Perugia, entered and devastated it by fire and sword after a territorial dispute. In 1311 it fixed its militia at 10,000 cavalry and 3,000 infantry and built fortifications. A plague in the 16th century killed more than two thirds of the population. A period of prosperity is placed between 1566 and 1606 under Bishop Angelo Cesi, and the 17th century brought decline through plagues, wars and famines.

The cathedral, begun in the 12th century and completed in the 14th, stands at the highest point of the city. Around Piazza del Popolo stand the Palazzo del Popolo, built at the beginning of the 13th century and reportedly one of the oldest public palaces in Italy, the Palazzo del Capitano and the Palazzo dei Priori. Roman cisterns beneath the square supported the forum.

Remains of Umbrian-Etruscan walls of large travertine blocks survive at the summit, and an amphitheatre was built outside the walls in the Augustan period. The Mars of Todi, a bronze statue found in the area, is now in the Gregorian Etruscan Museum. The poet Fra Jacopone da Todi, associated with the hymn Stabat Mater, and Pope Martin I were born there.
todo-takatora: Tōdō Takatora was born in Tōdō village, in Inukami district of Ōmi Province, east of Lake Biwa. His branch of the Tōdō clan descended from a samurai, Kagemori Todo, who had served a noble of the imperial court in the 14th century, and he began as an ashigaru, a light foot soldier. At 15 he entered the service of Azai Nagamasa and fought his first battle at Anegawa in 1570 beside his father, Torataka, winning a letter of commendation and a wakizashi for his part in the attack on Usayama Castle.

After the fall of the Azai he served Isono Kazumasa and then, from 1576, Hashiba Hidenaga, the younger brother of Hideyoshi. In Hidenaga's campaigns he took Takeda Castle in Tajima by surprise in 1577, killed the commander of Bessho Nagaharu's horsemen at the Siege of Miki in 1580 and fought in the conquest of Kishu and the invasion of Shikoku in 1585, when he was made commissioner for the building of Wakayama Castle. In 1589 he suppressed the Kitayama Uprising, beheading many farmers at Tahirako Pass.

Under Hideyoshi he commanded ships in the invasions of Korea, was wounded at the Battle of Myeongnyang in 1597 and helped destroy the Korean fleet of Wŏn Kyun at Chilcheollyang. Before Sekigahara he sent his family to Edo as a pledge to Tokugawa Ieyasu, and in the battle his troops engaged those of Ōtani Yoshitsugu. In 1604 he and Date Masamune advised the shogunate to require every lord to keep a residence in Edo, and in 1615 he crushed the army of Chōsokabe Morichika at the Battle of Yao.

By 1617 his holdings came to 323,000 koku, the ninth largest in Japan outside the Tokugawa and Matsudaira domains. In Iga he employed Iga-ryū ninja and local men as musokunin, part-time samurai without land who farmed in peace and took up arms in war. He changed his lord seven times in all. He died at his residence in Edo in 1630, aged 74; records describe him as a large man of about 190 cm whose body was covered with battle scars. He is said to have worked on as many as twenty castles, among them Wakayama, Uwajima, Imabari, Iga Ueno and Sasayama.
todor-zhivkov: Todor Hristov Zhivkov was born in the village of Pravets into a peasant family. The exact date of his birth was disputed within the family: his mother insisted on 20 September 1911, but in his memoirs he said that a drunken Orthodox priest had recorded only the day of baptism, and calculated from local custom that the real day was 7 September.

During the Second World War he took part in the resistance and in 1943 helped organise the Chavdar Partisan Brigade around his birthplace. After the uprising of 9 September 1944 he became head of the Sofia police, restyled the People's Militia, and he rose in the Bulgarian Communist Party, joining its Politburo in 1951 and helping counter rural resistance to forced collectivisation.

Zhivkov became First Secretary in 1954, replacing the hardline Valko Chervenkov, who kept most of his powers as prime minister. After Nikita Khrushchev's secret speech against Stalin, the April plenum of 1956 saw Zhivkov criticise Chervenkov, who was demoted, and he became the de facto leader. He served as prime minister from 1962 to 1971 and then as Chairman of the State Council. His government carried out a relative liberalisation and de-Stalinization, removed monuments of personality cults, allowed some market reforms and ended the persecution of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church. In 1965 a plot by officers who wanted a pro-Chinese Stalinist-Maoist leadership was exposed.

He followed the Soviet Union closely, supporting the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, though he also drew advantage from the relationship, notably in Soviet crude oil refined at Burgas and resold. The economy grew from the mid-1960s to the late 1970s, with new industrial plants and the Kozloduy nuclear power station. Dissidents could still be punished, and exit visas were needed to travel abroad.

In December 1984 the government began the Revival Process, a campaign to replace Turkish with Bulgarian names that many Bulgarian Turks resisted and that led to a large-scale expulsion of Turks and Muslims in 1989. A stagnating economy, a worsening international image and corruption in the party weakened him, and under pressure from senior party members he resigned on 10 November 1989. Communist rule effectively ended within a month.

He was tried on five indictments, including the Revival Process and labour camps, was later released, and wrote memoirs. He died on 5 August 1998. Popularly nicknamed bai Tosho, he remains the longest-serving non-royal ruler in Bulgarian history.
toera: Toera, also called Itoera, was the son of the preceding king of Menabe and a princess, according to the British missionary George Herbert Smith, writing in 1896. His half-brother Ingereza challenged his rule: Ingereza's mother was not royal, but he had been born inside the royal enclosure, while Toera, of royal blood, had been born outside it. At one point Ingereza cut the kingdom's river trade routes and caused starvation that nearly forced Toera to submit, but by 1896 most of his subjects supported Toera.

The Franco-Hova Wars of 1883–1895 brought a French protectorate over Madagascar, and continued resistance led France to place it under a military governor, Joseph Gallieni, who deposed Queen Ranavalona III early in 1897. Toera first sought talks with the French, though some of his subordinates wanted war. The French abolition of slavery threatened his subjects' part in the slave trade, and he drew close to Rainibetsimisaraka, a leader of the Menalamba rebellion. After the Menalamba were defeated by July 1897 he was perhaps the strongest rebel leader left.

Gallieni sent Augustin Gérard against the Sakalava. French accounts accuse Toera of talking peace while his general Mahatanty gathered troops; Menabe accounts say Gérard did the same while he advanced on the capital, Ambiky. Gérard defeated Mahatanty at Anosymena on 14 August and stormed Ambiky on 30 August 1897, killing Toera, his chief minister and the chief Vongovongo and taking 500 Sakalava prisoner. The Menabe rose again, and Gallieni reprimanded Gérard; seven years of campaigning followed before a pro-French ruler was established.

Toera's head was taken to Paris and kept in the collection of the National Museum of Natural History. Under pressure from his descendants and the government of Madagascar, France agreed to return it. DNA tests could not prove the skull was his, but Madagascar accepted it after a Sakalava spirit medium declared it the king's. It was handed over with two other Sakalava skulls on 26 August 2025 and received at a ceremony in Antananarivo on 2 September, attended by President Andry Rajoelina.
tofangchi: Guns and cannon had reached Iran around 1470, before the Safavids came to power. In 1514 the Ottoman Empire defeated the Qizilbash forces of the Safavids at the Battle of Chaldiran, largely through its effective use of firearms. In 1516 Shah Ismail I ordered his vakil, Mirza Shah Hossein, to create a musketeer contingent, and he had 50 cannons and 2,000 arquebuses made. Portuguese soldiers, some assigned and some deserters, trained the new troops, and Ottoman janissaries who went over to the Safavids, 700 in 1518 and 1,500 in 1519, added to their number.

The tofangchis numbered 8,000 in 1517 and between 15,000 and 20,000 in 1521, and the non-tribal part of the army grew from a minor to a significant force. Around 1600 the Qizilbash looked down on them, but Shah Abbas I valued them highly, above all those from Mazandaran; 10,000 marched on his Balkh campaign of 1603, and in the Ottoman–Safavid War of 1623 to 1639 the Safavids relied mostly on them. Estimates of their strength under Abbas I range from 20,000 to 60,000, and under Shah Abbas II they numbered about 40,000 to 50,000.

Nader Shah also recruited them from the peasantry, and the Zand ruler Karim Khan drew them from western and central Iran and from Dashtestan by the Persian Gulf. The Qajar shah Agha Mohammad Khan called his Mazandarani musketeers the Shah's bodyshirt and slept among them in times of danger; at his death in 1797 they made up 10,000 of his 60,000 men.

Most tofangchis were Iranian-speaking peasants recruited across the country and served as a local militia, often posted in fortresses, and worked as farmers in peacetime, though some came from Qizilbash tribes such as the Rumlu and from others such as the Mamasani. They usually fought on foot; the traveller Jean Chardin wrote that they rode only to travel. Their commander, the tofangchi-aghasi, was served by officers of a thousand, a hundred, fifty and ten men, and by a vizier and an accountant who kept the troop list. In 1665 their pay was reported as 5 to 7 tomans a year.
togashi-masachika: Masachika belonged to the Togashi family, which held Kaga Province as shugo in the Muromachi period. Kaga's warriors resisted his rule, and low-level rural violence was probably common there. When the struggle between Hosokawa Katsumoto and Yamana Sōzen grew into the Ōnin War in 1467, the unrest in Kaga became a civil war within the clan over the post of shugo: Masachika sided with the Hosokawa, and his younger brother Kochiyo with the Yamana.

Kochiyo drove Masachika out of Kaga in 1473. Kochiyo patronised the Takada school of Jōdo Shinshū and persecuted followers of its rival, the Hongan-ji, so Masachika turned to Asakura Toshikaga, lord of Echizen, and to the priests of Yoshizaki who followed Rennyo, head of the Hongan-ji.
