He promised the ikki that he would relieve their poverty. With Toshikaga's troops and the Ikkō-ikki rising across Kaga, he quickly overthrew his brother.

The alliance soon broke down. In 1474 the Ikkō-ikki, saying he had not kept his promises, rebelled without Rennyo's approval and were defeated, many fleeing to Etchū Province. In 1475 Shimotsuma Rensu falsely claimed Rennyo's backing for a new rising, which was also put down, and Rennyo excommunicated him. Unrest continued, and the believers refused taxes and seized revenue and land. In 1487 Masachika marched to help Shogun Ashikaga Yoshihisa against Rokkaku Tokoyori in Ōmi Province.

In his absence three of Rennyo's sons, Rengo, Renkō and Rensei, raised a revolt joined by between one hundred thousand and two hundred thousand people. Masachika hurried back and at first defeated the ikki armies, but vassal families including the Motoori and Yamagawa joined the rebels, who cut him off from allies in Echizen, Etchū and Noto. Besieged in his burning castle, he committed seppuku. The rebel vassals put forward his uncle and former shugo, Yasutaka, as a figurehead. The historian David L. Davis suggests the revolt arose because Masachika was trying to end the general anarchy of Kaga and impose discipline on the province.
toggenburg-war: The County of Toggenburg had belonged to the Imperial Abbey of St Gall since 1460, and about two thirds of its people were Protestant after the Reformation. The abbots pressed the Counter-Reformation there, and in 1699 Schwyz proposed a road over the Ricken Pass, which would let Catholic troops reach the Toggenburg quickly. When Wattwil refused to build it by forced labour, Prince-Abbot Leodegar Bürgisser imprisoned the chief Toggenburg magistrate, Josef Germann, and in 1702 concluded a treaty of protection with Emperor Leopold I, which threatened to draw the abbey out of the Confederacy and into the Habsburg sphere.

In March 1707 a Landsgemeinde at Wattwil adopted a constitution giving the Toggenburg self-government and religious freedom. Schwyz went over to the abbot, and by 1710 the Toggenburgers, armed with Zürich's help, held the abbey's fortresses.

Bern and Zürich declared for the Toggenburgers in a manifesto of 13 April 1712, and the five inner cantons of Lucerne, Schwyz, Uri, Zug and Unterwalden armed in reply. Protestant forces took Wil on 22 May and occupied the Abbey of Saint Gall, whose abbot fled to Neuravensburg. In the Aargau the Bernese under Jean de Sacconay won near Mellingen and at Fischbach, and Baden surrendered on 1 June; its fortress, the Stein, was razed.

A first treaty signed at Aarau on 18 July was rejected by the Landsgemeinden of Schwyz, Zug and Unterwalden under the influence of the papal nuncio Giacomo Caracciolo, and fighting resumed. At Villmergen some 8,000 Bernese met 12,000 Central Swiss, and fresh troops and the superior Bernese artillery decided the long battle, in which 2,000 Catholics were killed.

At the Peace of Aarau of 11 August 1712, the Fourth Landfrieden, Zürich, Bern and Glarus kept the County of Baden and the lower Freie Ämter, linking Zürich with the Bernese Aargau, and took Rapperswil, while Bern gained a share in every common lordship. The Second Landfrieden of 1531 lapsed, and Protestants received equal standing before the law. Zürich and Bern governed the abbey's lands and carried off much of its library. The Peace of Baden of 1718 restored the abbey under Abbot Joseph von Rudolphi, but some treasures, among them the globe of St. Gallen, stayed in Zürich until a settlement in 2006.
togha-temur: Togha Temür, also written Ṭaghāytīmūr, a name meaning bowl or pot iron in Middle Mongol, came of a line descended from Genghis Khan's younger brother Qasar that came to lead a nomadic tribe, the Chete. His grandfather Baba Bahadur had moved the Chete into the land between Astarabad and Kalbush on the east bank of the Gorgan, and they were still there when Togha Temür became their leader. Of the many claimants to the Ilkhanate after Abu Sa'id, he was the only one from eastern Iran and the last major candidate of the house of Genghis Khan.

The governor of Khurasan, Shaykh ʿAli b. ʿAli Qushji, proposed him as Ilkhan, and most princes of eastern Iran accepted him. In 1337 his army took the old capital Soltaniyeh with the former Ilkhan Musa Khan, but in June the Jalayirid Ḥasan Buzurg defeated them. Shaykh ʿAli was then executed by Arghun Shah of the Jauni Qurban, who became Togha Temür's chief supporter. Ḥasan Buzurg recognised him as Ilkhan in 1339 to gain his help against the Chobanid Ḥasan Kuchak, but Ḥasan Kuchak broke the alliance by offering Togha Temür the princess Sati Beg and then showing his acceptance to Ḥasan Buzurg. After his brother Shaykh-ʿAli Ke'ün's army was beaten in 1340, Togha Temür gave up the west.

The Sarbadars of Khurasan rose against his subordinate ʿAlaʾ-ad-Din Muḥammad over harsh taxes, defeated his forces and in May 1343 killed his brother. He fled to the Jajrud valley south of Amol, under his vassal the Bavandid Ḥasan II, whose men trapped a Sarbadar army in 1344 and killed its leader Masʿud, letting him regain much of his land.

Arghun Shah's death in 1345 or 1346 cost him the Jauni Qurban, and by 1347/1348 the Sarbadars were minting coins naming no Ilkhan. Their leader Yaḥya Karawi submitted to him and paid tribute, but in his camp Yaḥya and his men struck him down, beheaded him and slaughtered his family and army. Much of his land fell to the Sarbadars; Amir Vali seized Astarabad, and only in 1384 did Timur install Togha Temür's son Luqman-Padishah there as his vassal. His daughter Sulṭān-Khātūn married the Kart ruler of Herat, Muʿizz-ad-Dīn Pīr-Ḥusayn-Muḥammad.
toghon-temur: Toghon Temür was born on 25 May 1320 to Kusala, then in exile in Central Asia. His mother, Mailaiti, was a descendant of Arslan Khan, a chief of the Karluks. After the War of the Two Capitals, which followed the death of Yesün Temür in 1328, Kusala died under suspicious circumstances and his younger brother was restored to the throne as Emperor Wenzong. Toghon Temür was removed from court and exiled, first to Goryeo and later to Guangxi. When Wenzong died in 1332, the succession took months to settle, and Toghon Temür was enthroned only in 1333.

The early reign was dominated by powerful ministers, first El Temür and then Bayan, who carried out political purges and suspended the imperial examination system. In 1340 the emperor allied with Bayan's nephew Toqto'a and removed Bayan in a coup. Under Toqto'a the purges were reversed, the examinations restored and many Chinese literati recalled. The official histories of the Liao, Jin and Song dynasties were completed in 1345.

From the mid-1340s droughts, floods and famines struck the countryside, while the government faced currency depreciation and falling tax revenues. In 1348 illicit salt dealers rebelled against the state salt monopoly, setting off further revolts. When the Red Turban Rebellion erupted in 1351, Toqto'a raised a large army against it, but Toghon Temür dismissed him in 1354. The emperor gradually withdrew from active governance, and in 1364 the warlord Bolad Temür occupied Khanbaliq and expelled the crown prince Ayushiridara. The fighting further weakened central authority.

Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming dynasty and sent his armies north. In 1368 Toghon Temür abandoned Khanbaliq for his summer capital at Shangdu, which the Ming took in 1369. He retreated to Yingchang, in present-day Inner Mongolia, and died there on 23 May 1370. His son Ayushiridara succeeded him and withdrew the court to Karakorum. The remnant court, called the Northern Yuan, continued to claim the title of Emperor of China.

The Ming held that the Yuan had forfeited the Mandate of Heaven and gave him the posthumous name Emperor Shun, meaning compliant. The Northern Yuan's temple name for him was Huizong. He reigned for 35 years, the longest of any Yuan emperor after Kublai Khan, and patronised the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism. Historians debate how far the dynasty fell from structural problems and how far from his withdrawal from government.
togo: Togo is a small tropical country of 56,785 square kilometres, less than 115 kilometres wide between Ghana and Benin. It extends north from the Gulf of Guinea, where its coast is 56 kilometres long and consists of lagoons with sandy beaches, to the border with Burkina Faso. The south has a savannah and woodland plateau reaching a coastal plain with lagoons and marshes, the centre is hilly, and the north is rolling savannah. The highest mountain is Mont Agou at 986 metres, and the longest river is the Mono, at 400 kilometres.

The name Togo means 'by the water' or 'behind the sea', from the Ewe words to, 'water', and go, 'shore'. It originally referred only to the town of Togo, now Togoville, and the Germans later extended it to the whole country.

Archaeological finds indicate that societies in the area could produce pottery and process iron. Between the 11th and 16th centuries the Ewe entered the area from the west, and the Mina and Gun from the east, and most settled on the coast. The Atlantic slave trade began in the 16th century. For the next two hundred years the coastal region was a trading centre for Europeans in search of slaves, which earned Togo and the surrounding region the name the Slave Coast.

In 1884 a paper was forcibly signed at Togoville with King Mlapa III, whereby Germany claimed a protectorate over a stretch of coast and gradually extended its control inland. In 1905 this became the German colony of Togoland. The local population was forced to work, to cultivate cotton, coffee and cocoa, and to pay taxes, and a railway and the port of Lomé were built for export.

Britain and France invaded in August 1914, and German forces surrendered on 26 August. The territory was partitioned into British and French zones, which on 20 July 1922 became League of Nations mandates. French Togoland became an autonomous republic in 1956, and British Togoland voted to join the Gold Coast, as part of Ghana, in 1957. Togo became independent from France in 1960.

Togo is the Togolese Republic, with its capital, Lomé, on the Gulf of Guinea. French is the official language, and Kabiye and Ewe are national languages. The population is about 8 million, with some 40 ethnic groups, of which the Ewe in the south are the most numerous. Culture draws on Ewe and Mina traditions in the south, including the creator god Mawu and the vodun, and on Kabye and Tem traditions in the north, including the Evala wrestling initiation rite.
togodumnus: Togodumnus is known only from Cassius Dio's Roman History. He probably succeeded his father as king of the Catuvellauni, whose capital was at St Albans and who were then the dominant kingdom of south-eastern Britain, holding the lands of their neighbours the Trinovantes and possibly of the Dobunni further west. He can probably be identified with Guiderius, a British king of legend.

Late in Cunobelinus's reign another brother, Adminius, gained control of the Cantiaci in Kent, but he was driven from Britain in 40 CE and took refuge with the emperor Caligula, who planned an invasion in response and called it off at the last minute. Coin finds suggest that Caratacus, following his uncle Epaticcus, completed the conquest of the Atrebates, the Catuvellauni's main rivals, in the early 40s. Their king, Verica, fled to Rome and gave the emperor Claudius a pretext to conquer Britain in 43.

According to Dio, Togodumnus led the first resistance to the invasion beside Caratacus and was killed after the battle on the Thames. The Roman commander Aulus Plautius then dug in at the river and sent for Claudius to join him for the final march on the Catuvellaunian capital, Camulodunum (Colchester). Dio explains the halt by fiercer resistance as the Britons sought to avenge Togodumnus; but since Claudius was no soldier and spent only sixteen days in Britain, the Britons were probably already as good as beaten. Leadership passed to Caratacus, who carried the fight outside Roman-controlled territory and remained at large until 51.
togoville: Togoville, known locally as Togo-Bè, is both a town and a canton. It was originally called Togo, and like the country it takes its name from Lake Togo, on whose northern shore it stands. Near the town, on the shore of the lake, lies a sacred forest where the priests of the old kingdom held their Nyiglin fetish ceremonies.

Before 1884 the town was the seat of the kings of the Mlapa dynasty, who controlled a territory around Lake Togo. They had the right to collect tolls from boats, part of which went to the kingdom and part to the palace, and they led their own troops on the battlefield. The kingdom was divided into five large villages, each with its own congregation of priests of the sacred forest.

Agomegan was king before colonisation, and his son Mlapa III reigned when colonists arrived on the kingdom's coast. Their arrival divided the five villages: Agbodrafo fell under the influence of the French and British, already established in Benin and the Gold Coast, while Mlapa signed the treaty that gave the Germans authority. The line of kings continued afterwards. Sebastien Djossou Mlapa IV reigned from around 1950 until at least 1964, Mlapa V Moyennant became king in 1985, and after 17 years of regency Fiogan Joel Kwassi Mensah Mlapa VI was installed on 7 July 2018.

Togoville Cathedral, built in 1910, includes a shrine to the Virgin Mary marking where she is said to have appeared on 7 November in the early 1970s, and the town is also a centre of voodoo practice, with shrines near the former royal palace. West of the church, the Maison Royale is a small museum holding Mlapa's throne, historic relics and photographs, and a monument to the treaty's centenary was put up in June 1984. Three high schools, among them the College Notre Dame Du Lac, draw students from across Togo and Africa.
togs-ochiryn-namnansuren: Namnansüren was born in 1878 in what is now Uyanga district of Övörkhangai Province. He descended from Onokhui Üizen Noyan, third son of Gersenji Khongtaiji of the Jalayir, who was a son of Dayan Khan and so a descendant of Genghis Khan. In 1896 he became prince of Sain Noyon Khan Province, one of the four Khalkha provinces set up by the Qing dynasty, as the 13th holder of a hereditary title traced to Tumenkhen Sain Noyon in the early 17th century. The Qing court had raised his ancestor Tsering to the rank of khan in 1728, separating the domain from the Tusheet Khanate. He married in 1900.

In 1911 Namnansüren persuaded the Bogd Khan, Mongolia's religious leader, to call a congress of princes and high lamas in Khüree to begin the break from China, and in July 1911 he went to Saint Petersburg with a delegation seeking Russian and Western European support. The Bogd Khan named him prime minister in July 1912, replacing Da Lam Tserenchimed, who as Minister of Internal Affairs had acted as head of government since December 1911.

From November 1913 to January 1914 he led a second delegation to Saint Petersburg during the Russian and Chinese negotiations that produced the tripartite Kyakhta treaty. The agreement reconfirmed Mongolia's status as an autonomous region within China, ending hopes of recognised independence and of union with Inner Mongolia. Russian officials stopped his attempts to contact the ambassadors of the United States, Great Britain, France and Germany and to travel to Western Europe, and his influence had waned when he came home in 1914.

In June 1918, with China demanding that Mongolia give up its Pan-Mongolia ambitions and renounce its autonomy, he travelled to Irkutsk. There he met two Bolshevik representatives, in what is believed to be the first meeting between Soviet and Outer Mongolian officials, but the Bolsheviks, absorbed by the revolution and the civil war, offered little help.

Namnansüren fell seriously ill soon after his return and died in April 1919. Many suspected that he had been poisoned, as several other figures of the revival of Mongolian independence also died early. Shortly afterwards the Chinese warlord Xu Shuzheng occupied Niislel Khüree and installed Gonchigjalzangiin Badamdorj as prime minister. In 1914 Namnansüren had brought films from Russia to show at the Bogd Khan's residence, the first known film showings in Mongolia.
tohoku-region: Tōhoku, like most of Japan, is hilly or mountainous, with the Ōu Mountains running north to south. Many of the region's lowlands lie inland, and much of the population is concentrated there. Because the coastlines do not favour seaport development, settlement came to depend far more than usual on land and rail transport. Low points in the central range make communication between the lowlands on either side moderately easy.

The climate is colder than elsewhere on Honshu because of the stronger effect of the Siberian High, and it permits only one crop a year on paddy fields. The Pacific coast is generally much less snowy than the region's popular image. Tōhoku was traditionally considered the granary of Japan, supplying Sendai and the Tokyo-Yokohama market with rice and other farm goods, and it provided 20 percent of the national rice crop.

The area was held by the Emishi, the indigenous peoples of Honshu, and later by the Ainu. Historically it was the Dewa and Mutsu or Michinoku regions, a name first recorded in the Hitachi no kuni Fudoki of 654. Yamato settlement took place between the seventh and ninth centuries, long after Yamato culture was established in central and south-western Japan. As the last stronghold of the Emishi and the site of many battles, the region at times kept a degree of autonomy from Kyoto.

In the 12th century the Northern Fujiwara ruled Tōhoku as their own realm, independent of the imperial court through the strength of their warrior bands. Their first ruler, Fujiwara no Kiyohira, of mixed Yamato and Emishi parentage, ruled from Hiraizumi in what is now Iwate Prefecture from about 1100. Minamoto no Yoritomo, founder of the Kamakura shogunate, defeated them in 1189.

Date Masamune (1567–1636) of the Date clan expanded trade and ruled one of the largest fiefdoms of the later Tokugawa shogunate. He sheltered Christian missionaries and funded an envoy to the Pope, probably in part out of a wish for foreign technology, but reversed course once Tokugawa Ieyasu outlawed Christianity. The haiku poet Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694) wrote Oku no Hosomichi, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, on his travels through the region.

The region consists of six prefectures: Akita, Aomori, Fukushima, Iwate, Miyagi and Yamagata, and it is often divided into North Tōhoku (Aomori, Akita and Iwate) and South Tōhoku (Yamagata, Miyagi and Fukushima). Sendai is its largest city, with 1,098,000 people, and Miyagi is now the most populated prefecture. Heavy industry began to develop in the 1960s, and tourism became a major industry in the 20th century. Chūson-ji, Hirosaki Castle and the islands of Matsushima Bay are among its historic and scenic sites. A magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami on 11 March 2011 caused 19,759 deaths along the east coast.
toirdelbach-ua-conchobair: Toirdelbach was the youngest son of Ruaidrí na Saide Buide, King of Connacht, and of Mór, daughter of Toirdelbach Ua Briain, so that through his mother he was a great-great-grandson of Brian Boru. According to the Annals of Tigernach his mother died in the year of his birth. In 1092 his father was blinded by Flaithbertaigh Ua Flaithbertaigh, and Connacht came under the domination of the Dál gCais of Munster, led by his uncle Muirchertach Ua Briain, High King of Ireland, who may have raised him in his household. In 1106, with that uncle's support, the eighteen-year-old Toirdelbach deprived his brother Domnall of the kingship.

Divide and rule was his constant method. When Muirchertach fell gravely ill in 1114, Toirdelbach intrigued with his enemies, attacked Munster, ravaged Thomond and destroyed the Ua Briain palace at Kincora. By 1121, after the death of his northern rival Domnall Mac Lochlainn, he was the most powerful man in Ireland, having ended the Ua Briain hold on the high kingship that had lasted since 1002. He placed his sons and loyal nobles over subject lands, making his son Conchobar king of Leinster and Dublin in 1126.

He built Dún Gaillimhe in 1124 as a fort and naval base, the settlement from which Galway city grew, and in 1129 reputedly built the first stone castle in Ireland, at Athlone on the Shannon, followed by others at Dún Mór and Ballinasloe. A canal of six miles diverted the River Suck. He refounded Cong Abbey around 1135. In 1150 he gave hostages to Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn and ceased to be King of Ireland, but in 1151 he and his allies crushed Toirdelbach Ó Briain of Thomond at Móin Mór, where 7,000 of the enemy were said to have been killed.

His sons Ruadhrí and Aedh rebelled in 1136, and Aedh was captured and blinded, while Ruadhrí was twice shielded from punishment by an archbishop. After Conchobar was assassinated in Meath in 1144, Toirdelbach divided that kingdom among three loyal kings. In 1156, when he was almost seventy, his fleet defeated the Norse-Gaels under Mac Scelling off Inishowen at heavy cost. He died that year and was succeeded in Connacht by Ruadhrí, his Tánaiste, who in 1166 became High King. He was first buried at Cong Abbey, which he had rebuilt, and later reburied among other members of his dynasty.
tok-pisin: Tok Pisin is the result of contact among Pacific Islanders. Colonial authorities forced people speaking many different languages to work on plantations in Queensland and on various islands during the period of blackbirding, and the labourers developed a pidgin whose vocabulary came mainly from English but also from German, Malay, Portuguese and their own Austronesian languages, perhaps especially Kuanua, the language of the Tolai.

This pidgin evolved into Tok Pisin in German New Guinea, where it became a widely used lingua franca between the colonial authorities and the indigenous population, although the metropolitan language was German. Bislama in Vanuatu and Pijin in the Solomon Islands developed in parallel and have traditionally been treated as varieties of a single Melanesian Pidgin English.

Tok comes from English talk, with a wider sense of word, speech or language, and Pisin from pidgin. Despite the name, Tok Pisin is a creole in linguistic terms, because many people now learn it as a first language. Tense is marked by separate words: bai for the future, from by and by, and bin for the past, from been. The suffix -im marks transitive verbs, as in luk, look, and lukim, see, and adjectives take -pela, from fellow.

A small vocabulary leads speakers to metaphor: gras bilong het, grass of the head, means hair. The current alphabet has 21 letters and four digraphs; the colonial Department of Education created it in 1955 to increase literacy, replacing earlier spellings that followed each word's source language.

Tok Pisin is one of Papua New Guinea's three official languages, with English and Hiri Motu, and is the most widely used language in the country. Between five and six million people use it to some degree, and perhaps one million as a primary language. It is frequently the language of debate in the national parliament, and some schools teach in it for the first three years of elementary education.

Many children learn it as a first language, especially in urban families whose parents speak different local languages. It has increasingly overtaken Hiri Motu among town-dwellers and is slowly crowding out other languages of Papua New Guinea.
tokat: The city was established in the Hittite era. In the time of King Mithradates VI of Pontus it was one of his many strongholds in Asia Minor. It was known as Evdokia or Eudoxia and was later incorporated ecclesiastically into the western part of the Byzantine Greek Empire of Trebizond. Scholars have debated whether Tokat is the ancient and medieval Dazimon, which Guillaume de Jerphanion and William Mitchell Ramsay held, or the town of Dokeia named in a 10th-century text, as Henri Grégoire argued. Grégoire thought the name Dokeia had no Greek etymology, and that its derivation from Eudokia was a later folk etymology.

After the Battle of Manzikert the town came under the Seljuk Turks, like most of Asia Minor. After the death of Sultan Suleiman ibn Qutulmish in 1086, the emir Danishmend Gazi took control of the area from his base at Sivas. The Seljuks retook the region only many decades later, in the reign of Kilij Arslan II. After the Battle of Köse Dağ they lost their hold, and local emirs such as the Eretna took power until the Ottomans captured Tokat in 1392 under Sultan Bayazid I.

Tokat is the seat of Tokat Province, in the mid-Black Sea region of Anatolia, at the confluence of the Tokat River with the Yeşilırmak. It was historically a centre of copper working and textiles, with copper manufacturing that relied on the Kempan Maden mine. Its main landmark is Tokat Castle, an Ottoman citadel with 28 towers on a rocky hill, in whose dungeon Vlad the Impaler is said to have been imprisoned. Other monuments include the 12th-century Garipler Mosque, the 16th-century Ali Paşa Mosque and Hatuniye Külliyesi, and the Gök Medrese, built in 1270 as a school of theology and later a museum. Its distinctive foods include Tokat kebabı and Zile pekmezi, a grape-molasses confection.
tokelau: Tokelau consists of three tropical coral atolls, Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo, with a combined land area of about 10 square kilometres, between latitudes 8 and 10 degrees south, about midway between Hawaii and New Zealand and some 500 kilometres north of Samoa. The highest point is just 5 metres above sea level, and the islands lie in the Pacific tropical cyclone belt. Swains Island (Olohega), culturally and geographically part of the same archipelago, has been under United States control since about 1900 and is administered as part of American Samoa. The name is a Tokelauan word meaning north wind; European explorers called the group the Union Islands, and it was shortened to Tokelau on 9 December 1976.

Archaeological evidence indicates that the atolls were settled about 1,000 years ago from Samoa. The three atolls functioned separately in politics while keeping social and linguistic cohesion, governed by chiefly clans, with occasional wars between atolls as well as intermarriage; Fakaofo held some dominion over Atafu and Nukunonu. Life was subsistence-based, relying mainly on fish and coconut.

Commodore John Byron sighted Atafu on 24 June 1765, and Captain Edward Edwards visited it in June 1791 in search of the Bounty mutineers. In 1877 an Order in Council placed the islands under United Kingdom protection, and in June 1889 Commander C. F. Oldham of HMS Egeria raised the Union Flag on each atoll. They were annexed on 29 February 1916 and included in the Gilbert Islands. They were placed under the Governor-General of New Zealand in 1925, and New Zealand took over administration on 11 February 1926, though sovereignty remained with the United Kingdom.

Tokelau is a dependent territory of New Zealand, whose King is its head of state, and both governments call it a nation. About 2,500 people live there, and some 94 per cent speak Tokelauan as their first language. Since 1993 the territory has elected its own head of government, the Ulu-o-Tokelau, a post that rotates among the faipule of the three atolls, and the basis of its system is the Tokelau Islands Act 1948. Tokelauans have twice narrowly failed to reach the two-thirds majority needed for further self-determination.
tokharistan: The name means land of the Tochari. Before Islam it appears in Bactrian as Toxoarastano on the 2nd-century silver dish of Nukunzuk and in two 5th-century documents, probably at first for the eastern parts of Bactria only. The region lay in the upper Oxus valley between the Hindu Kush and the Pamir-Alay, reaching east to the Badakshan mountains and south to Bamiyan; Arab writers put Kabul on its southern border and Shaganiyan on its northern. Its people used the East Iranian Bactrian language, current from the 2nd to the 9th century, and Balkh, its chief city, stood on the trade between Sasanian Iran and India.

For three centuries before the Muslim conquest of Persia, Tokharistan lay outside Sasanian control under dynasties of Hunnish or Turkic origin, the Kidarites, the Alchon Huns and the Hephthalites, who led its embassies to the Liang court in the early 6th century. In the 7th and 8th centuries it was incorporated into the Tang dynasty under the Protectorate General to Pacify the West. Buddhist art drew on Gandhara, and a Tokharistan school of painting flourished, possibly under the patronage and tolerance of the Tokhara Yabghus.

Arab raids began as early as 643, under the caliph Umar, but most were brief. In 705 Qutayba ibn Muslim, made governor of Khorasan by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, began the systematic conquest of western Tokharistan and took Balkh, peacefully in one version of al-Tabari and after a revolt in another. Nizak Tarkhan organised a rising of the Hephthalite principalities for the spring of 710 and drew in the weak Jabghu of Tokharistan, but Qutayba forestalled it, crucifying the two sons of Bādām, dihqan of Balkh and Marw al-Rudh.

With Arab governors installed in all the towns of Tokharistan, Nizak fled to a mountain refuge in what is now Baghlan Province and, after a two-month siege, surrendered on a promise of pardon; on al-Hajjaj's orders he was executed with 700 of his followers, and the Jabghu was sent to Damascus as a hostage. Islamic art developed there under the Samanids and Ghaznavids, and the region is now divided between Afghanistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
tokhta: Tokhta was a son of Mengu-Timur and a great-grandson of Batu Khan, the founder of the Golden Horde. His name, Tokhtokh, means to hold in Mongolian, and within his family he was also known as Külüg. His genealogy runs from Genghis Khan through Jochi, Batu and Toqoqan to Mengu-Timur. He became khan in 1291, after the general Nogai Khan arranged a palace coup that ended with the ousting and execution of Talabuga.

At first Tokhta was subordinate to Nogai. In 1293 he sent his brother Tudan to support Andrei against Dmitry, who had backed Nogai, and Tudan's army devastated fourteen towns. Tokhta himself went to Tver and forced Dmitry Alexandrovich to abdicate; Russian chroniclers described the events as the harsh time of Batu returning. A rivalry with Nogai grew, fed by complaints from Tokhta's father-in-law Saljiday and by disputes over the trading rights of Venetian and Genoese merchants.

He lost the first battle against Nogai in 1296 to 1297, and the Ilkhan Ghazan refused to help him. In 1299 or 1300, at the battle of the Kagamlyk River, he defeated Nogai and united the lands from the Volga to the Don. He divided Nogai's lands among his brother Sareibugha and his own sons.

Tokhta later demanded Azerbaijan and Arran back from Ghazan, who refused, and he restored the alliance with the Mamluks of Egypt. In 1304 envoys from the Chagatai Khanate and the Yuan dynasty arrived at Sarai with a plan for peace. Tokhta accepted the nominal supremacy of the Yuan emperor and sent two tumens, 20,000 men, to support the Yuan frontier. He arrested the Italian residents of Sarai and besieged Caffa in 1307, apparently angered by the Italian trade in Turkic slaves sold as soldiers to the Mamluk Sultanate. The Genoese resisted for a year, then set fire to their city and abandoned it in 1308.

Tokhta died in 1312 while preparing a new campaign against the Russian lands. Some sources claim he left no male heir, but the Yuan shi and some Muslim sources say he had at least three sons, one of whom was murdered by supporters of Khan Ozbeg. Though a Shamanist, he took an interest in Buddhism, and he was the last non-Muslim khan of the Golden Horde. In 1297 he married Maria Palaiologina, an illegitimate daughter of the Byzantine Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos.
tokhtamysh: Tokhtamysh belonged to the House of Borjigin. Genealogies trace his descent from Tuqa-Timur, the thirteenth son of Jochi, the eldest son of Genghis Khan. His father, Tuy Khwāja, ruled the Mangyshlak peninsula and refused to join his cousin and suzerain Urus Khan in a campaign against Sarai, so Urus had him executed. Tokhtamysh fled, submitted to his father's killer and was forgiven. In 1373 he tried to make himself khan in Sighnaq but was driven out and was forgiven a second time. When Urus took Sarai in 1375 he fled again and in 1376 reached the court of Timur.

Tokhtamysh was defeated once more by a son of Urus, Tīmūr Malik, and again returned to Timur, whose forces took Sawran and Otrar, then won at Qara-Tal and executed Tīmūr Malik in 1379. Installed as khan in Sighnaq, Tokhtamysh advanced on Sarai in 1380 and defeated the commander Mamai on the Kalka river, becoming the first khan in over two decades to rule both wings of the Golden Horde. He restored peace with the Genoese of the Crimea and confirmed the privileges of the emirs and chieftains.

He then turned to the Russian principalities. Dmitry Donskoy, the Grand Prince of Vladimir-Suzdal, acknowledged him as suzerain but withheld tribute. In 1382 Tokhtamysh crossed the Volga, with the princes of Rjazan' and Nižnij Novgorod serving him as guides, and besieged and sacked Moscow, whose prince had left it under a garrison. Dmitry then submitted, gave his eldest son as a hostage and sent tribute in 1383. In the winter of 1384 to 1385 Tokhtamysh stormed Tabriz and took some 200,000 slaves.

His quarrels with Timur then grew. Timur struck into the Golden Horde and forced a battle at the Kondurcha river in June 1391. A second invasion in 1395 ended in a hard-fought battle on the Terek on 15 and 16 April, where dissension among Tokhtamysh's emirs gave Timur the victory.

Tokhtamysh found refuge in Lithuania, and in 1399 he and Grand Duke Vytautas marched against Tīmūr Qutluq and Edigu. He then went to Siberia, where he held parts of the area from 1400. Edigu is said to have fought him sixteen times, and he was killed late in 1406 near Tyumen. He was the last khan of the Golden Horde to mint coins with Mongolian script.

His sack of Moscow undid the setback that Kulikovo had dealt to Mongol domination two years before. But his conflict with Timur set a course for the undoing of his achievements, and his reliance on Moscow and Lithuania strengthened both.
tokhtamysh-timur-war: The war grew out of the succession crises among the Jochid rulers of the Golden Horde. In the late 1370s and early 1380s Timur helped Tokhtamysh take power in the White Horde from his uncle Urus Khan. Tokhtamysh then seized the Blue Horde from Mamai, weakened by the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380, and united the two hordes. He restored Tatar power over the Russian principalities with a punitive campaign in 1381 and 1382, in which Moscow was besieged and sacked, but his ambitions in Persia and Central Asia set him against Timur.

Timur began his conquest of Persia in 1383 and in 1385 took Herat and Khorasan. In the same year Tokhtamysh raided Azerbaijan and north-western Iran, and in 1386 he plundered Tabriz and withdrew with rich booty. Between 1389 and 1391 the two sides fought hard, and Timur won the first phase at the Battle of the Kondurcha River. Vasily I of Moscow used the war to his advantage: visiting the weakened khan's court in 1392, he was allowed to take the throne of Nizhny Novgorod.

Tokhtamysh recovered, and in the spring of 1395 he raided the Timurid territory of Shirvan. Timur answered with a final assault and routed him at the Battle of the Terek River on 15 April 1395. He then destroyed the major cities of the khanate, Sarai, Ukek, Majar, Azaq, Tana and Astrakhan, and with them the Italian trading colonies of Sarai, Tana and Astrakhan, his first Western European victims. The Genoese city of Caffa in Crimea was spared.

Tokhtamysh was deposed in favour of Edigu and fled to the Ukrainian steppes, seeking help from Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania. Timur turned towards Moscow but withdrew from Russian territory, which chroniclers explained by a vision of the Virgin defending the city. Tokhtamysh and Vytautas were crushed by Temür Qutlugh and Edigu at the Battle of the Vorskla River in 1399, and around 1406 Tokhtamysh was killed in Siberia by Edigu's men.

The Golden Horde never recovered, and in the middle of the 15th century it broke up into the Kazan, Crimean, Astrakhan, Qasim, Uzbek and Kazakh khanates and the Nogai Horde. Its weakness allowed Moscow to continue the gathering of the Russian lands, although an invasion by Edigu in 1408 led Vasily I to recognise the khan as his suzerain again in 1412. Tatar overlordship was finally shaken off at the Great Stand on the Ugra River in 1480.
tokugawa-hidetada: Hidetada was born on 2 May 1579, the third son of Tokugawa Ieyasu by Lady Saigō. In 1590 Toyotomi Hideyoshi took the eleven-year-old Hidetada as a hostage to keep Ieyasu from defecting to the Hōjō in the Siege of Odawara, and in 1592 presided over his coming-of-age ceremony, when he took the name Hidetada. As the eldest surviving son and Ieyasu's favourite, he was named heir, and he returned to his father in 1593. In 1595 he married Oeyo, daughter of Azai Nagamasa and adopted daughter of Hideyoshi, after the death of his first wife O-Hime in 1591. They had two sons, Tokugawa Iemitsu and Tokugawa Tadanaga, and several daughters.

Hidetada led 16,000 of his father's men against the Uesugi in Shinano in 1600 and was ordered to march to Sekigahara, but the Sanada clan tied his force down and he arrived too late for his father's victory. Ieyasu was furious and was dissuaded by advisers from punishing him. Emperor Go-Yōzei made Ieyasu shōgun in 1603, and in 1605 Ieyasu abdicated in favour of Hidetada to set a dynastic pattern, though he kept significant power until his death in 1616.

In 1612 Hidetada arranged the marriage of his daughter Sen to Toyotomi Hideyori, to Ieyasu's dismay, and when this failed to end Hideyori's intrigues father and son brought an army to Osaka. At the Siege of Osaka in 1614–1615 they disagreed on tactics. Hideyori and his mother killed themselves, and Hideyori's infant son was killed; only Sen was spared.

After 1616 Hidetada took control of the bakufu. He improved relations with the imperial court by marrying his daughter Kazuko to Emperor Go-Mizunoo, and their daughter eventually became Empress Meishō. Edo was heavily developed in his time. In 1623 he resigned in favour of Iemitsu and, as Ōgosho, kept effective power.

As Ōgosho Hidetada enacted anti-Christian measures that Ieyasu had only considered. He banned Christian books, forced Christian daimyō to commit suicide, ordered other Christians to apostatise on pain of death, and in 1628 had fifty-five Christians, Japanese and foreign, burned with their children at Nagasaki for refusing to renounce their faith. He died on 14 March 1632, and was buried in the Taitoku-in Mausoleum in Edo. The historian Michifumi Isoda held that the policy of total isolation under Hidetada weakened the military of Japan under the Tokugawa shogunate in the long run.
tokugawa-iemitsu: Iemitsu was born prematurely on 12 August 1604, the eldest son of Tokugawa Hidetada and Lady Oeyo and a grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu. His childhood name was Takechiyo, and he is said to have been sickly from birth. His wet nurse, Lady Kasuga, acted as his political adviser and later led shogunate negotiations with the imperial court. His younger brother Tokugawa Tadanaga, their parents' favourite, became a rival, but Ieyasu made clear that Iemitsu would follow Hidetada. Iemitsu came of age in 1617 and was installed as heir.

Hidetada gave up the post of shogun in 1623, when Iemitsu was nineteen, but ruled as retired shogun until his death in 1632. Relations with Emperor Go-Mizunoo worsened after the Purple Robe Incident, in which the shogunate invalidated purple garments the emperor had bestowed on priests; Go-Mizunoo abdicated and his daughter Meishō became empress, which made the shogun the uncle of the sitting monarch. Once Hidetada was dead Iemitsu ruled carefully until Tadanaga died by seppuku in 1633, then dismissed his father's advisers, appointed childhood friends and built a strong centralised administration.

In 1635 he issued a second version of the buke shohatto, the edicts on the daimyo, raising them from thirteen to twenty-one. They barred the daimyo from building ships larger than 500 koku and established the sankin-kōtai system, under which daimyo lived in Edo in alternating sequence, leaving their wives and heirs there as in effect hostages; it applied at first to the tozama daimyo and to all by 1642.

In the 1630s he ordered nearly every European expelled, and the Sakoku Edict of 1635 forbade Japanese ships and people to travel abroad or return, on pain of death. A revolt at Shimabara in 1637, driven partly by high taxes and cruelty to peasants as well as opposition to anti-Christian policy, killed thousands, with countless more executed afterwards. The shogunate used it as a pretext to expel the Portuguese and confine the Dutch East India Company to Dejima in Nagasaki.

Iemitsu died of a stroke on 8 June 1651, aged 47, the first Tokugawa shogun whose reign ended with death and not abdication. Japan stayed connected to the outside world through four channels: Nagasaki, where the Dutch and Chinese traded, Satsuma and the Ryūkyū Kingdom, Tsushima and Korea, and Matsumae and the Ainu. Since the 1980s scholars have preferred terms such as maritime restrictions to the older description of Japan as closed. The measures lasted until the 1850s.
tokugawa-iemochi: Tokugawa Iemochi was born on 17 July 1846 in the Edo residence of the Wakayama domain, the eldest son of the domain lord Tokugawa Nariyuki and his concubine Jitsujoin. Nariyuki was a younger son of the 11th shogun, Tokugawa Ienari. In 1847 the boy was adopted as heir to the 12th lord of the domain, Tokugawa Narikatsu, and succeeded him in 1850. At his coming of age in 1851 he took the name Tokugawa Yoshitomi. In 1858 he was adopted as the son of the shogun Iesada and named successor, a choice contested by factions that supported Tokugawa Yoshinobu or Matsudaira Naritami, who were adults.

After taking office as shogun in 1858 he changed his name to Iemochi. His years were marked by turmoil caused by the reopening of Japan to Western nations, and the shogunate grew weaker. As part of the movement for union of court and shogunate, on 11 February 1862 he married Princess Kazu, who refused the title of the shogun's wife and used only the title Miya. On 22 April 1863 he travelled to Kyoto in a great procession with 3,000 retainers, summoned by the emperor. It was the first visit by a shogun in 230 years, since Tokugawa Iemitsu.

Iemochi died on 29 August 1866, aged 20, at the time widely reported as heart failure from beriberi, and was buried at Zōjō-ji. Before his death he adopted Tayasu Kamenosuke, later Tokugawa Iesato, who was only three. Because the shogunate was at war with Chōshū, the adult Tokugawa Yoshinobu was made the fifteenth shogun instead. Yoshinobu was the last Tokugawa shogun, and the shogunate gave way to the Meiji Restoration.
tokugawa-ieyasu: Tokugawa Ieyasu was born Matsudaira Takechiyo at Okazaki Castle on 31 January 1543, the son of Matsudaira Hirotada, daimyo of Mikawa, and Odai no Kata. When he was five, Oda Nobuhide abducted him on his way to Sunpu as a hostage of Imagawa Yoshimoto, and held him at the Honshōji Temple in Nagoya for three years. In 1556 he came of age at a ceremony presided over by Imagawa Yoshimoto. After Yoshimoto was killed at Okehazama, he formed the Kiyosu Alliance with Oda Nobunaga, and in 1567 he took the family name Tokugawa.

Ieyasu served Oda Nobunaga as ally and general, fighting Takeda Shingen's invasion of his lands from 1571. In 1579 Nobunaga accused Ieyasu's wife and heir of plotting with Takeda Katsuyori, and Ieyasu had his wife executed and his son Matsudaira Nobuyasu forced to commit seppuku. Nobunaga died at Honnō-ji in 1582. Ieyasu fought Toyotomi Hideyoshi at the Battle of Komaki and Nagakute, then submitted. After the campaign against the Hōjō in 1590 he was moved to the Kantō plains and built his castle at Edo.

Hideyoshi named Ieyasu the most powerful of five regents for his young son Toyotomi Hideyori before dying on 18 September 1598. Opposition gathered around Ishida Mitsunari, and the Battle of Sekigahara began on 21 October 1600, with Ieyasu's Eastern Army initially numbering 75,000 against 120,000 in the Western Army. Afterwards Ieyasu redistributed the domains of the daimyo. Those who had joined him earlier became known as fudai daimyō, and those who joined after the battle as tozama daimyō.

Emperor Go-Yōzei gave Ieyasu the title of shōgun on 24 March 1603. He resigned in 1605 but remained the effective ruler as retired shōgun, or ōgosho, at Sunpu Castle until his death. He supervised the building of Edo Castle, whose cost the other daimyo bore. He distanced Japan from European influence from 1609, though the Dutch East India Company kept preferential trading rights. In 1614 he besieged Osaka Castle, where samurai had gathered around Hideyori, and he then issued the Buke shohatto code, which allowed each daimyo one castle.
Ieyasu devoted himself to the Jōdo-shū school of Buddhism. He died on 1 June 1616. His successors moved the government to Edo in 1638 and enacted the sakoku policy of isolation in 1639.
tokugawa-mitsukuni: Mitsukuni was born on 11 July 1628 in the Mito Domain of Hitachi Province, the third son of Tokugawa Yorifusa, the domain's first daimyo and the eleventh son of Tokugawa Ieyasu. His childhood name Chomaru was later changed to Chiyomatsu, a name granted by his cousin, the shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu. When his elder brother Yorishige fell into poor health, Mitsukuni was chosen as heir, and he underwent the genpuku coming-of-age ceremony at nine. In 1657 he married a daughter of the kampaku Konoe Nobuhiro.

He became daimyo of Mito in 1661. Anticipating the separation of kami and Buddhas ordered in 1868, he had a thousand Buddhist temples in the domain destroyed and ordered at least one shrine for every village. He gathered the Mitogaku scholars to compile the Dai Nihonshi, which portrayed Japan as a nation under the emperor on the model of the Chinese dynasties, and which helped the growth of nationalism in the late shogunate. He also directed at Zuisen-ji the first guide to Kamakura, the Shinpen Kamakurashi, whose names such as Kamakura's Seven Mouths and Ten Bridges are still used.

He received the court office of gon-chūnagon, provisional middle counsellor, and retired in 1691 to his villa Seizan-sō. Known as a gourmet, he is said to have been among the first Japanese to eat ramen and to have enjoyed wine and yogurt. His heir was Tokugawa Tsunaeda, the son of an elder brother, whom he adopted.

Mitsukuni died at Seizan-sō on 14 January 1701. He was given posthumous court ranks in 1869 and 1900 and is regarded as a kami. In the later Edo and Meiji periods a narrative tale, Mito Mitsukuni Man'yūki, invented journeys for him, and in 1951 television first showed him as a wanderer disguised as a commoner; the TBS series Mito Kōmon ran from 1969 to 2011. The city of Mito holds a Mito Komon festival each summer.
tokugawa-muneharu: Muneharu was born on 20 November 1696, the 20th son of Tokugawa Tsunanari by a concubine later known as Senyoin, and a great-great-grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu. His childhood name was Bangoro. As lord of Owari he would be one of the gosanke, and two of his brothers, Tokugawa Yoshimichi and Tokugawa Tsugutomo, were its fourth and sixth lords; another, Matsudaira Yoshitaka, was second lord of the Mino Takasu Domain. A sister, Matsuhime, married Maeda Yoshinori, lord of the Kaga Domain.

As lord of Owari he promoted deregulation and turned Nagoya into one of Japan's major cities. At court he rose to the junior third rank and held the titular office of Gon-Chunagon, acting middle councillor. Given to personal luxury himself, in 1731 he published a book, Onchiseiyo, which criticised the shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune for his policy of excessive frugality. After a long dispute with Yoshimune he was forced to retire in 1739 and confined within the grounds of Nagoya Castle, and a relative succeeded him as lord of Owari under the name Tokugawa Munekatsu. He never married, but had numerous concubines, and most of his children died young; his daughter Katsuhime married the kampaku Konoe Uchisaki.

After Yoshimune's death Muneharu was allowed to move outside the palace grounds. He died on 1 November 1764 without being forgiven, and a metal net was placed over his grave to mark his disgrace. He was posthumously given the junior second rank and the office of Gon-Dainagon. Only when a later shogun installed his own son as lord of Owari, 75 years after Muneharu's death, was the net removed as a sign of pardon. In the television series Abarenbo Shogun he was often shown as a villain plotting to kill Yoshimune and seize the shogunate, acts that are fictional.
tokugawa-nariaki: Nariaki was the third son of Tokugawa Harutoshi, the seventh-generation daimyō of Mito, and of Toyama-dono. His childhood name was Torasaburo, later changed to Keisaburo. The headship of the family passed first to Harutoshi's eldest son, Narinobu, and came to Nariaki only in 1829. He married Arisugawa Yoshiko and had a very large family by his wife and several concubines, with more than twenty sons, several of whom went on to head other domains, such as Tottori, Okayama and Hamada.

As leader of the Jōi party, whose cry was to expel the barbarian, Nariaki was made an adviser to the bakufu on national defence. He held that the shogunate should strengthen its forces and fight the foreigners, which set him against Ii Naosuke. In 1853 he wrote a document entitled Japan, Reject the Westerners, giving ten reasons why Japan should stay isolated and arguing that the Japanese should choose war rather than let Westerners intrude into their affairs.

He favoured the emperor and an imperial restoration and greatly expanded the Mitogaku school founded by Tokugawa Mitsukuni. He was also influenced by the Kokugaku school: Ōkuni Takamasa, a student of Hirata Atsutane, urged him to combine ritual with technology and to revive a national spirit, and the two are credited with laying some foundations for the Meiji Restoration and for State Shinto. In the dispute over the succession to the shōgun Iesada, Nariaki championed his son Yoshinobu, while Naosuke, who prevailed, backed Tokugawa Yoshitomi of the Wakayama Domain.

In 1841 Nariaki laid out Kairaku-en, a garden still well known. He was placed under house arrest twice, in 1844 and again in 1858, when his son Yoshiatsu took his place, and he died of a heart attack in 1860, at the age of 60. Three of his sons were leading figures of the 1860s: Yoshinobu, who became the 15th and last shōgun in 1866; Tokugawa Yoshiatsu of Mito; and Ikeda Yoshinori of Inaba. His writings, among them the Kōdōkan ki, were published after his death, and in 1903 he was posthumously given the Senior First Rank.
tokugawa-yorinobu: Yorinobu was born on 28 April 1602 with the name Nagatomimaru, the son of Tokugawa Ieyasu by his concubine Kageyama-dono, later known as Yoju-in. On 8 December 1603, still an infant, he received the fief of Mito, then rated at 200,000 koku, which had belonged to his older brother Takeda Nobuyoshi. His stipend rose to 250,000 koku in October 1604, and on 12 September 1606 he came of age, taking the name Yorimasa, the court rank of junior fourth, lower grade, and the title Hitachi no Suke.

On 6 January 1610 he was moved to a fief of 500,000 koku in Suruga and Tōtōmi provinces, founding the Sunpu Domain centred on Sunpu Castle, and took the name Yorinobu. After a little under ten years there, he was transferred on 27 August 1619 to the Wakayama Domain, rated at 550,000 koku, when its former rulers, the Asano clan, were moved to Hiroshima in Aki Province. By the end of his life he had reached junior second court rank and held the title of dainagon, or major counsellor.

Yorinobu married Yasohime, a daughter of Katō Kiyomasa, who became known as Yorin-in and lived from 1601 to 1666. His children included his successor Tokugawa Mitsusada; Matsudaira Yorizumi, founder of the Iyo-Saijo Domain; Inaba-hime, who married Ikeda Mitsunaka of the Tottori Domain; and Matsuhime, who married Matsudaira Nobuhira of the Yoshii Domain. He died on 19 February 1671 and was afterwards known by the title Nanryū-in. In 1915 he was posthumously raised to senior second court rank.
tokugawa-yoshikatsu: Yoshikatsu, whose childhood name was Hidenosuke, was born at the Takasu Domain residence in the Yotsuya district of Edo, the son of Matsudaira Yoshitatsu and Norihime, a daughter of Tokugawa Harutoshi. Tokugawa Nariaki was his maternal uncle, the future shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu his cousin and Matsudaira Katamori his brother. Owari's four previous lords had been adopted from lines close to the shogun and ruled from afar, and low-ranking samurai of the Gold and Iron Party twice pressed for Yoshikatsu, in 1839 and 1845, before he was chosen in 1849.

With weaker ties to the shogun than his predecessors, he needed the consent of the senior retainers to govern, and his first measures cut costs. Like Nariaki, Shimazu Nariakira of Satsuma and Date Munenari of Uwajima, he was troubled by the shogunate's concessions after the Perry Expedition. When the Treaty of Amity and Commerce with the United States was signed in 1858, he joined Nariaki, Matsudaira Yoshinaga of Fukui and others in an unbidden visit to Edo Castle to oppose the Tairō Ii Naosuke. He was placed under house arrest and replaced by his younger brother Mochinaga.

After Ii Naosuke's assassination in the Sakuradamon Incident of 1860, a general pardon followed in 1862, and Yoshikatsu went to Kyoto as an assistant to the shogun Tokugawa Iemochi. In 1863 his young son was made the 16th lord as Tokugawa Yoshinori, and Yoshikatsu again wielded power, though the domain split between his supporters and Mochinaga's. He declined a seat on the emperor's council of daimyo, commanded the First Chōshū expedition of September to November 1864 with Saigō Takamori as second-in-command, and refused to take part in the second, which cost the shogunate prestige.

During his house arrest Yoshikatsu took up Western photography and learned to take and develop pictures himself. Almost 1,000 of his photographs survive, among them the Ninomaru Palace of Nagoya Castle, taken in 1870, Hiroshima Castle and the Owari Domain's suburban residence in Edo. They are valued as a historical record of the last years of the shogunate and the first years after it.
tokugawa-yoshimune: Yoshimune was born on 27 November 1684 in Kii Province, ruled by his father Tokugawa Mitsusada, and was a great-grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu. He was not the son of any shōgun. Ieyasu had been aware that his direct line might die out and selected three sons to found the gosanke, the Owari, Kii and Mito houses, which would supply a shōgun if there were no male heir. Yoshimune belonged to the Kii house, founded by Ieyasu's son Tokugawa Yorinobu.

His childhood name was Genroku, and in 1697 he took the name Shinnosuke. In 1705 his father and two older brothers died, and the shōgun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi appointed him daimyō of Kii, when he was 21. He took the name Yorikata. Kii was rich, with over 500,000 koku, but owed large debts to the shogunate, and a tsunami in 1707 destroyed coastal areas and killed many people. He did not trust conservative Confucian advisers such as Arai Hakuseki and worked to stabilise the domain. The boy-shōgun Tokugawa Ietsugu died in early 1716 aged seven and without an heir, and the bakufu chose the next shōgun from a cadet line.

Yoshimune became shōgun in 1716 and served for thirty years. He dismissed Arai Hakuseki and began the Kyōhō Reforms, known above all for their financial measures. He established the gosankyō, three houses that did not rule domains and were founded by two of his sons and a son of his successor Ieshige. Some later shōguns came from the Hitotsubashi line. He also tried to revive swordsmithing, and in 1721 held a contest of smiths from the daimyō fiefs, and he ordered the compilation of the Kyōhō Meibutsu Chō, a list of the best swords in Japan.

Foreign books had been strictly banned since 1640, but in 1720 Yoshimune relaxed the rule. This began an influx of foreign books and translations and the development of Western studies, rangaku. The change may have been influenced by lectures given before him by the astronomer and philosopher Nishikawa Joken.

In 1745 Yoshimune retired, took the title Ōgosho, as Ieyasu and Hidetada had done on retirement, and handed his public post to his eldest son. He died on 12 July 1751 and was buried at Kan'ei-ji. He is considered among the best of the Tokugawa shōguns. He is known for repealing the ban on Western literature.
tokugawa-yoshinao: Yoshinao was born on 2 January 1601, the son of Tokugawa Ieyasu by his concubine Okame no Kata, later known as Sōōin, and was given the childhood name Gorōtamaru. While still a young child he was made lord first of the fief of Kofu in Kai Province and then of the fief of Kiyosu in Owari Province. In 1610 he was appointed to the Owari Domain, centred on present-day Nagoya and one of the most important regions of the country, and so founded the Owari-Tokugawa house.

He rose to junior second court rank and held the title of dainagon, or major counsellor. He began to study the Shinkage-ryū school of swordsmanship under Yagyū Hyōgonosuke at the age of sixteen and was named its fourth sōke, or head, at twenty-one. During the Kan'ei era, which began in 1624, he had a kiln built at the corner of the Ofuke enceinte of Nagoya Castle and invited potters from Seto to work there; their pottery became known as Ofuke ware.

His principal wife was Haruhime, a daughter of Asano Yoshinaga of Kii, whose family was later moved to Hiroshima; she lived from 1593 to 1637 and was afterwards known as Kōgen-in. By his concubines Ojō no Kata and Osai no Kata he had two children: Tokugawa Mitsutomo, who succeeded him as daimyō of Owari, and Kyōhime, who married the court noble Hirohata Tadayuki. Yoshinao died on 5 June 1650. His remains were cremated and laid to rest in his mausoleum at Jōkō-ji in Seto.
tokugawa-yoshinobu: Tokugawa Yoshinobu was born in Edo on 28 October 1837, the seventh son of Tokugawa Nariaki, daimyō of Mito of the Tokugawa branch family of Mito. He was raised in Mito from the age of seven months and educated in the literary and martial arts and in government. At his father's urging he was adopted by the Hitotsubashi-Tokugawa family to improve his chances of the succession, became family head in 1847 and took the name Yoshinobu.

When the thirteenth shōgun, Iesada, died in 1858, Yoshinobu was nominated as a possible successor, but the opposing faction led by Ii Naosuke prevailed, and Tokugawa Yoshitomi became the fourteenth shōgun, Iemochi. Yoshinobu was placed under house arrest in the Ansei Purge, but after Ii's assassination in 1860 he was reinstated and in 1862 became the shōgun's guardian. In 1864, commanding the defence of the imperial palace, he defeated Chōshū forces who tried to seize the Hamaguri Gate in the Kinmon Incident.

Iemochi died without issue in August 1866. Shogunal officials nominated Yoshinobu, who became head of the Tokugawa main family in October but refused the title of shōgun until January 1867. He was the only Tokugawa shōgun to spend his entire tenure outside Edo, and never set foot in Edo Castle as shōgun. He began a government overhaul, with a French military mission.

Samurai of Satsuma, Chōshū and Tosa allied against him, fearing a renewed Tokugawa shogunate. On 9 November 1867 Yoshinobu tendered his resignation to the Emperor, stepping down formally ten days later, and withdrew to Osaka. Satsuma and Chōshū, however, secured an imperial edict later shown to be a forgery, and at a court meeting he was stripped of all titles and land.

When Tokugawa troops marched towards Kyoto to deliver a protest they were attacked, which began the Battle of Toba–Fushimi, the first clash of the Boshin War. Yoshinobu left his army when the Satsuma and Chōshū forces raised the imperial banner, and escaped to Edo. On 11 April 1868 Edo Castle was handed over to the imperial army and the city was spared all-out war. He then moved to Shizuoka and lived in quiet retirement.

On 3 June 1902 the Emperor Meiji allowed him to found his own branch house with the rank of prince. He sat in the House of Peers until 1910 and died in November 1913, and he is buried in Yanaka Cemetery, Tokyo.
tokushima-prefecture: Tokushima Prefecture lies on the island of Shikoku and has an area of 4,146 square kilometres. It borders Kagawa Prefecture to the north, Ehime Prefecture to the west and Kōchi Prefecture to the south-west. It faces the Kii Peninsula of Honshu across the Kii Channel, which connects the Pacific Ocean with the Seto Inland Sea. The Sanuki Mountains run along its northern border, and the Yoshino River flows through the prefecture, with rice fields in its lower valley and along the narrow coastal plains.

The capital and largest city is Tokushima, and other major cities include Anan, Naruto and Yoshinogawa. The Ōnaruto Bridge carries a road across the Naruto Strait to Awaji Island, joining the prefecture to Kobe and the San'yō Expressway on Honshu. Until the Meiji Restoration the area was known as Awa Province.

In ancient times Tokushima City belonged to a district known as Myōdō-gun. In the first wave of consolidation after the abolition of the fiefdoms in 1871 it became Myōdō Prefecture, which included the Awa region and Awaji Island. In 1873 it also took in the area of present-day Kagawa Prefecture. In the second wave of consolidation the Sanuki region separated in 1875 to form Kagawa; in 1876 Awaji Island passed to Hyōgo Prefecture and the Awa region became part of Kōchi Prefecture. On 2 March 1880 the prefecture separated from Kōchi and was inaugurated as Tokushima Prefecture.

In August 1945 the Washi no Mon gate of Tokushima Castle was destroyed by fire at the end of the Second World War. The Nankai earthquake of December 1946 caused vast damage throughout the prefecture. Tokushima University was created in 1949, and Naruto, Komatsushima and Anan were inaugurated as cities between 1947 and 1958. Takeo Miki, who was born in Tokushima, was elected Prime Minister of Japan in October 1974. The Ōnaruto Bridge to Hyōgo was completed in 1985, and the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge in 1998 connected Tokushima with the mainland by road.

The prefecture had a population of 682,439 in February 2025. It depends on agriculture, forestry and fisheries, and Japanese indigo is produced only here. Its produce, including Naruto sweet potatoes, sudachi citrus, lotus roots and strawberries, goes mainly to the Kansai region around Kobe, Osaka and Kyoto. Among its cultural sites are Tokushima Castle, the Iya Valley, the Oboke Koboke Gorge, the Naruto whirlpools, the Otsuka Museum of Art and the Awa Marionette Jōruri tradition of puppet theatre. Its sports teams include the football club Tokushima Vortis.
tole-bi: Töle Bi was born at Jaysan, in what is now Shu District of Jambyl Region, into the Zhanys subtribe of the Dulat, a Kazakh tribe. His father was Alibek Biy, and his grandfather Qudaiberdy Biy had been an adviser to Esim Khan and fought in the battle remembered as Qataghan Qyrghyny, the Massacre of the Qataghan, in 1627 and 1628 against the rebellious Khan Tursyn, then ruler of Tashkent. Besides his work as a biy, a judge and leader, he was an author, orator and poet.

In his poem Sabalaq the poet Bukhar-zhirau tells of the childhood of Ablai Khan, who looked after Töle's sheep, and of their conversations. Töle gave the boy the nickname Sabalaq for his overgrown hair and dishevelled look, which the poem presents as a sign that he saw early the boy's future. Töle's learning and judgement were praised by the zhyraus Synyr-Zhyrau and Zhirenshi, and some believed that the spirit of the earlier wise man Maiky Biy lived on in him.

In 1740, fleeing the Dzungar invasion, he took all his relatives to Abd al-Karim Biy of the Kokand Khanate. The Dzungar leader Galdan Tseren demanded that he be handed over, but Abd al-Karim Biy drove the Dzungar ambassadors away. After the death of Zholbarys, Khan of the Senior Juz, Töle ruled Tashkent for six years, from 1743 to 1749. He took an active part in building public buildings in Shymkent, Turkistan and Tashkent.

Töle Bi was buried in the Shaikhantaur Cemetery in Tashkent, near the mausoleum of Yunus Khan, the maternal grandfather of Babur, and a mausoleum was raised over his grave. Among the people he is known as Karlygash Äulie, the Swallow Saint. His sayings and proverbs are still widespread. Folklorists and historians, among them Shoqan Walikhanov, Grigory Potanin and Baltabai Adambayev, collected material on his life, and Kazakh writers including Shäkärim Qudayberdiuly, Saken Seifullin and Mukhtar Auezov wrote about him. A settlement in Jambyl Region and a district in Turkistan Region bear his name, and monuments to him stand in both regions and in Astana.
toledan-tables: The tables were completed around 1080, shortly before Toledo came under Christian Spanish rule in the mid-1080s. They began as existing Arabic tables made elsewhere, numerically adjusted to be centred on Toledo, and owed much to the tables of Ptolemy and the work of al-Battānī. Apart from al-Zarqali, the mathematician, astronomer and instrument-maker of Toledo, the members of the team that produced them are largely unknown. The original Arabic version is lost.

The collection covered the chronology of eras, trigonometry and spherical astronomy, the mean motions of the Sun, Moon and planets, planetary latitudes, eclipses and astrology. What it did not take from earlier texts were its parameters for mean motion, which used sidereal coordinates, where Ptolemy's had been tropical. Some of the tables gave the arguments of planetary positions in half-degrees, which made them twice as long as tables in whole degrees; this was done for Saturn, Venus and Mercury. Since the tables are almost entirely copies of other tables, their many errors and discrepancies are thought to be mostly copying errors.

At Toledo the translator Gerard of Cremona put them into Latin, and they were then the most accurate compilation in Europe. More than a hundred versions of the Latin text survive. In the mid-13th century Campanus of Novara drew tables for the meridian of Novara from them, and a Greek translation was made in Cyprus in the 1330s, probably by the scholar George Lapithes. Isaac ben Joseph Israeli of Toledo used them for his work on eclipses.

The Alfonsine Tables, made at Toledo in Spanish and Latin in the 1270s, updated them, and their corrected descendants were the most widely used astronomical tables of late medieval Latin astronomy. Their compilers assumed a stationary Earth at the centre of the universe, yet Copernicus used their data in developing his model with a stationary Sun. Modern ephemerides, updated each year by NASA, serve the same purpose.
tolfa: Tolfa is a town of medieval origin in the orbit of Viterbo. It was taken into the Papal States and granted first to the Capocci family and then to the Roman nobles Ludovico and Pietro Frangipani, who walled the community. The discovery of large deposits of alunite, the source of alum, in 1461 gave it sudden importance, and after some confrontations with the Frangipani the Camera Apostolica assumed direct control. Alum was an essential mordant in the textile industry. Previously the only supplies had come from the East, from sources controlled by the Ottoman Turks, through Venice.

Pope Pius II placed the distribution of alum solely in the hands of the Medici, with the explicit thought that the income should serve Christendom against the Turks. Later the monopoly in extraction passed as a papal gift to Agostino Chigi. In 1530 Pope Clement VII granted Tolfa the status of comune, as it had outgrown its medieval walls. The workmen's village of Allumiere was built near the mine and became an autonomous comune in 1826. The Frangipani castle, the Rocca di Tolfa, was destroyed by French troops in 1799 after the town had rebelled against the Roman Republic.

Tolfa is the main centre of the Monti della Tolfa, an extinct volcanic group between Civitavecchia and the Lake of Bracciano, in the Metropolitan City of Rome in Lazio. Its town hall houses a collection of Etruscan and Roman antiquities found nearby. Other sights include the Church of Sant'Egidio Abate, the Augustinian convent of the early 16th century, now a library and civic museum, the Capuchin convent of 1621 and Castle Rota.
tolistobogii: The name appears in two forms: Tolistobogioi, used by Strabo and Livy, and Tolistoagioi, found chiefly in inscriptions; both occur in Polybius and are generally taken to denote one people. The second element is usually read as Celtic, perhaps bogio-, breakers, or agio-, fighters, while the first, tolisto-, has no accepted etymology, and Alexander Falileyev observes that it may not be Celtic at all.

The Tolistobogii reached Anatolia in the migration of Celtic peoples from the middle Danube into the Balkans and Asia Minor in the early 3rd century BCE. After the attacks on Macedonia and Greece, the Galatians crossed the Hellespont through an alliance with Nicomedes I of Bithynia and were settled in north-central Anatolia by the end of the 260s BCE.

In 189 BCE, during the campaign of the Roman commander Gnaeus Manlius Vulso, the Tolistobogii under Ortiagon, joined by the fighting men of the Trocmi, gathered their whole people on Mount Olympus and fortified it with ditches and ramparts. The Romans stormed the position, inflicting heavy losses and taking as many as 40,000 captive. Ortiagon afterwards made himself sole ruler of the region for a time but was defeated by Eumenes II of Pergamon.

In the later 2nd century BCE the chieftain Sinorix was a dominant figure, and his authority passed to his son Deiotarus, whom Rome rewarded with territory and the title of king. After the last Galatian king, Amyntas, was killed in about 25 BCE, Galatia became a Roman province, with Pessinus one of its three centres beside Ancyra and Tavium.

The westernmost of the three Galatian peoples, the Tolistobogii held northern and western Galatia, reaching west across the Sangarius on both sides of the Tembris, the modern Porsuk, as far as Phrygia Epictetus. The temple-state of Pessinus, sanctuary of the mother goddess, was their chief market. Three of their tetrarchies are known by name, the Ambitouti, the Tosiopes and the Voturi, and Deiotarus kept his residence at Blucium and his treasury at Peium.

Their territory holds the most impressive Galatian remains: stone chambered tombs under earthen tumuli, of a type also found in Bithynia and Pontus, with the finest at Karalar, where an inscription names the burial of Deiotarus the Younger, son and co-regent of Deiotarus, who died between 43 and 41 BCE.
tolpuddle-martyrs: The Combination Acts of 1799 and 1800 had outlawed organising for better working conditions, and the Combinations of Workmen Act 1825 that replaced them legalised trade unions but severely restricted their activity. Dorset was by then known for poorly paid farm labour: in 1815, 13% of its people received poor relief, and in 1830 more than forty disturbances of the Swing Riots broke out in the county. The wage gains won then were soon reversed. By 1833 wages at Tolpuddle had fallen to seven shillings a week and were due to fall to six, and the labourers refused to work for less than 10 shillings.

The society met in the house of Thomas Standfield. Groups of its kind often used an initiation in which a blindfolded newcomer swore a secret oath and was then shown a painting of a skeleton, a warning of mortality and of what befalls those who break their promises.

In 1834 James Frampton, a magistrate and landowner of Tolpuddle, complained to the Home Secretary, Lord Melbourne, who advised him to use the Unlawful Oaths Act 1797, passed after the Spithead and Nore mutinies. James Brine, James Hammett, George Loveless, his brother James Loveless, his brother-in-law Thomas Standfield and Thomas's son John Standfield were tried before Sir John Williams. On being sentenced, George Loveless wrote out lines of the union hymn The Gathering of the Unions.

Five of the men reached Sydney on 17 August 1834 and were assigned to farms in New South Wales, while George Loveless reached Hobart on 4 September and worked on the farm of Lieutenant Governor Sir George Arthur. Their supporters organised one of the first successful political marches in the United Kingdom, and Lord John Russell, newly Home Secretary, supported their pardon. George Loveless landed in England on 13 June 1837 and four others at Plymouth on 17 March 1838; Hammett, held in Windsor on a charge of assault, arrived in August 1839.

Five of the men later emigrated to London, Upper Canada, where a monument honours them, while Hammett returned to Tolpuddle and died in the Dorchester workhouse in 1891. A monument was put up in Tolpuddle in 1934, the Shire Hall in Dorchester where they were tried is now a museum, and the Trades Union Congress holds an annual festival in the village in July. Their significance has been debated since Sidney and Beatrice Webb wrote the History of Trade Unionism in 1894.
toluca-valley: The valley, once called Matlatzinco, runs north to south for about 35 km and is about 20 km wide, covering some 700 square kilometres at an average height of 2,570 metres, one of the highest valleys in Mexico. It lies in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, ringed by the Sierra de Las Cruces to the east, the Tenango and Zempoala volcanoes to the south and, to the south-west, the Nevado de Toluca, also called Xinantécatl, whose peak carries snow most of the year. The altitude gives a cool climate, with rains from mid-May to mid-October.

Records of the valley before the Aztecs are scarce, since the Aztecs destroyed many documents of the earlier Tepanec Empire. Teotenango in the south was founded near the end of the Teotihuacan period and later conquered and enlarged by the Matlazinca; Calixtlahuaca in the north was by the late 15th century a powerful city-state. In the Post Classic period, from 900 to 1519, speakers of Matlatzinca, Mazahua, Otomi and Nahuatl lived side by side.

The Aztecs largely left the valley alone until the Purépecha Empire pressed on it in the mid-15th century. The Mazahua north fell in 1473 and Matlazinco and Tollocan in 1475. In 1476 or 1477 the Purépecha decisively defeated an Aztec army on the valley's western edge, a rebellion followed, and Axayacatl returned to reconquer it. Tenochtitlan then ruled the valley more directly than most provinces, with Toluca as its centre. After the Spanish conquest Gonzalo de Sandoval took most of it with Otomi allies, and Franciscan missionaries founded missions and a first school, San Antonio de Padua.

When the Federal District was separated in the 19th century, the State of Mexico's capital moved to Toluca, the valley's main city. More than 1,350,000 people live in the valley, 60 per cent of them in the Toluca metropolitan area. Industry, begun in the 1940s, has cost it much forest and water. Colonial haciendas, churches and former monasteries survive, and plant pathologists hold the valley to be the centre of origin of Phytophthora infestans, the potato blight behind the Great Irish Famine.
toluid-civil-war: The family of Tolui had placed Möngke on the throne at the kurultais of 1250 and 1251, and after a failed plot by the Ögedeid candidate Shiremun and his cousin Nakhu, Möngke purged members of the Chagatai and Ögedei lines. Hulagu of the Ilkhanate then took the Caucasus from the Golden Horde, and his sack of Baghdad in 1258 angered Berke, its khan and a convert to Islam. Möngke died in 1259 without naming a successor; he probably favoured Ariq Böke, whom he had made commander of Karakorum in 1258.

Kublai was campaigning against the Southern Song in 1260 when Ariq Böke challenged him. A kurultai at Kaiping elected Kublai, the first to proclaim a Great Khan outside the Mongol homeland or Central Asia, and a month later a kurultai at Karakorum proclaimed Ariq Böke. Most of Möngke's family and the Golden Horde and Chagatai Khanate backed Ariq Böke; Hulagu alone backed Kublai, but he and Berke were soon fighting each other. Kublai, drawing on the supplies of China, cut taxes, adopted Chinese institutions and the era name Zhongtong, moderate rule, while his allies Kadan and Lian Xixian closed Ariq Böke's supply lines.

Ariq Böke lost the battle of Shimultai in 1261 and fought a stalemate near the Khingan Mountains ten days later. His ally Alghu, whom he had made khan of Chagatai, refused him tax revenues and executed his envoys, and Ariq Böke turned on him, taking Almalikh. His supporters deserted, and Möngke's son Ürüng Tash gave his father's tamga seal to Kublai. Ariq Böke travelled to Shangdu alone and surrendered in 1264.

Kublai imprisoned his brother and purged his sympathisers, executing the official Bolghai and others. Ariq Böke died mysteriously in prison in 1266, and some suspected Kublai of poisoning him. None of the other three khans attended the kurultai that confirmed Kublai, and from 1269 Kaidu of the Ögedei line fought him for decades. The four khanates became functionally independent; the Ilkhanate and the Yuan dynasty kept close ties, but the khanates never again fought together.
tomas-bata: Tomáš Baťa was born on 3 April 1876 into a family with a long history of shoemaking, spanning eight generations and more than three hundred years. He founded the firm in Zlín on 24 August 1894 with 800 Austrian gulden inherited from his mother. His brother Antonín and sister Anna were partners in the new T. & A. Bata Shoe Company. Tomáš obtained sole control in 1908, after Antonín died of tuberculosis, and brought his younger brothers Jan and Bohuš into the business.

In 1904 Baťa travelled to Lynn, Massachusetts, then the centre of world footwear production, worked on an assembly line and learned about its machinery. On his return he began to mechanise production, and he introduced an assembly line at Zlín in 1927. In the interwar period he visited Henry Ford's River Rouge Plant in Dearborn, Michigan, and on his return directed the company to decentralise. With his customers' buying power much reduced after the war, he made low-cost shoes for the general public. He established factories and companies in several countries, among them Poland, France, the United States and India. Each was allowed to be self-sufficient in design, production and distribution. By the early 1930s the firm had made Czechoslovakia the world's leading footwear exporter.

He modernised his hometown through employment and housing, and was elected mayor of Zlín. He is cited as an early pioneer of employee welfare and profit sharing, and the firm used four kinds of wage: a fixed rate for technical and administrative staff, individual rates for some specialists, collective task rates for factory labour and a profit contribution rate for operational managers.
