It was also known for prices ending in nine. The company used air transport to send skilled workers quickly to places where they were needed.

Baťa died on 12 July 1932 when his Junkers F.13 crashed near Zlín airport in dense fog, as he tried to fly to Möhlin in Switzerland on business. His half-brother Jan Antonín Baťa took over the companies and expanded them through the Great Depression, and founded the Zlín aircraft works two years after Tomáš's death. In 1939, after the Nazi invasion of Czechoslovakia, Jan tried to negotiate to keep the company before emigrating, and in 1941 settled in Brazil. The war destroyed many Baťa businesses, and the Communist governments nationalised those that remained. Tomáš's son Thomas J. Bata moved to Canada in 1939 with more than 100 families, founded the factory town of Batawa, Ontario, and rebuilt the Bata Shoe Organization.
tomas-cipriano-de-mosquera: Mosquera was born in Popayán on 26 September 1798 into a wealthy landowning family; one brother, Joaquín, became President of Gran Colombia and another, Manuel José, Archbishop of Bogotá. He was a slaveholder and a self-taught mathematician, historian and writer. By 1814 he served in the independence movement under Simón Bolívar. In 1824, fighting the royalist Agustín Agualongo at Barbacoas, he was shot through the lower jaw and needed a metal prosthesis that left his speech marked by whistling sounds, earning him the mocking nickname Mascachochas. He became a general in 1829.

After diplomatic posts and service as Secretary of War, in which he won the War of the Supremes in 1840, he was elected president of the Republic of New Granada in 1845 with the support of the faction that later formed the Conservative Party. His government signed the Mallarino-Bidlack Treaty with the United States in 1846, abolished remnant colonial taxes, revived the tobacco industry, held the country's first census and began separating Church and State. Drawn ever closer to the liberals, he helped defeat the dictatorship of José María Melo in 1854.

As president of the Cauca State he opposed President Mariano Ospina Rodríguez, and in 1860 declared Cauca's secession and made war on the Granadine Confederation, taking power in 1861. In 1863 he personally led the Colombian army to victory over Ecuador. Elected again in 1866 against the opposition of radical liberals, he clashed with the Church, which brought a strong intervention by Pope Pius IX, and he closed the ordinary sessions of Congress in 1867. A coup removed him on 23 May 1867.

Mosquera spent three years in exile in Lima, where he wrote his Cosmogonía, a study of theories of the creation of the universe. Back in Colombia by 1871, he failed to win the presidency but led the Cauca State until 1873 and was a senator again in 1876. He died on 7 October 1878 at his farm of Coconuco, near Popayán, and was buried in the Panteón de los Próceres there. For the liberal reforms carried out under him he is counted among the most important figures of 19th-century Colombia.
tomas-de-torquemada: Torquemada was born on 14 October 1420, either in Valladolid or in the nearby village of Torquemada. The chronicler Hernando del Pulgar, himself a converso, recorded that Tomás's uncle Juan de Torquemada, a theologian and cardinal, was of converso descent. Pulgar is considered to have made the claim out of hatred for the nephew, and a 2020 study of Juan's ancestors found no Jewish converts. Tomás entered the San Pablo Dominican monastery very young and earned a reputation for learning, piety and austerity. He met the young Princess Isabella, and the two established a religious and ideological rapport. He was present at her coronation in 1474.

The Crown of Aragon had Dominican inquisitors almost continuously through much of the 14th and 15th centuries. Ferdinand and Isabella petitioned Pope Sixtus IV for a Holy Office to administer an inquisition in Spain, and he established it in late 1478. The bull gave the sovereigns full powers to name inquisitors, while Rome kept the right to appoint the nominees formally.

In 1484 Torquemada gave up his role as royal confessor to Diego Deza, who later succeeded him as Grand Inquisitor. The next year, at a general assembly in Seville, he promulgated twenty-eight articles of faith to guide the inquisitors. Under the Alhambra Decree of 31 March 1492 about 40,000 Jews were expelled from Spain, and about 50,000 others received baptism to remain. Many kept some Jewish traditions in secret and were among the chief targets of the Inquisition. So many clemency petitions reached Rome that the Pope called the Inquisition's representatives to Rome three times.

On 23 June 1494 Pope Alexander VI appointed four assistant inquisitors, officially because of Torquemada's failing health, though many historians believe that complaints about his zeal were the real cause. He retired to the monastery of St. Thomas Aquinas in Ávila, where in 1498 he held his last general assembly, setting rules to curb some administrative abuses. He died there on 16 September 1498. His tomb was ransacked in 1832, two years before the Inquisition was disbanded, and his bones were allegedly stolen and burned in the manner of an auto-da-fé.
tomas-estrada-palma: Estrada Palma was born in Bayamo, Cuba, the son of Dr Andrés María Estrada y Oduardo and María Candelaria Palma Tamayo. His birth records were lost in a fire in Bayamo Town Hall on 19 January 1869, so the exact date is not known. From 1857 to 1868 he lived in Bayamo as an administrator and local teacher, and later taught in Honduras and Orange County, New York. He married Genoveva Guardiola Arbizú, daughter of General José Santos Guardiola, President of Honduras, on 15 May 1881.

He was president of the Cuban Republic in Arms during the Ten Years' War, was captured by Spanish troops and went into exile. In New York he worked with José Martí, and after Martí's death became leader of the Cuban Junta and its chief representative. He got the US Congress to pass a joint resolution on 19 April 1898 that disavowed Spanish colonisation of Cuba and said the United States had no intention of occupying or annexing it. He dissolved the largely black and rural Liberation Army and gave more power to the Assembly of Representatives.

General Bartolomé Masó withdrew as a candidate in protest against favouritism by the occupation government, and Estrada Palma was elected president on 31 December 1901 without campaigning. He served from 20 May 1902. American troops left after Cuba lowered tariffs on American goods and wrote the Platt Amendment into its constitution. On 16 February 1903 he signed a treaty leasing Guantánamo Bay to the United States, which had wanted five naval bases. His administration built over 328 kilometres of roads; immigration rose from 10,000 in 1902 to 40,000 in 1905, and the Treasury held a few million dollars when he left office.

His second term was to begin on 20 May 1906. The Liberals opposed it violently, and each side alleged electoral fraud. Estrada Palma and the moderate camp appealed to the United States, which began a second occupation under Charles Magoon, lasting from 1906 to 1909. On 28 September 1906 he resigned, at 71, with the rest of the executive branch.

Estrada Palma died of pneumonia in Santiago de Cuba on 4 November 1908. A statue of him was put up in 1903 on the Avenida de los Presidentes in Havana. Fidel Castro's revolutionaries pulled it down, reportedly because they blamed him for beginning US interventions, and the plinth with a pair of shoes remains. He is known less for his achievements in education, revolution and infrastructure than for his part in the annexationist agenda and his subservience to the United States.
tomas-garrigue-masaryk: Masaryk was born on 7 March 1850 in Hodonín, Moravia, then part of the Austrian Empire, to a poor, working-class family. His father, Jozef Masárik, was a Slovak carter who became steward and coachman at the imperial estate; his mother, Teresie Kropáčková, was a Moravian cook who had received a German education. He grew up in Čejkovice and attended grammar school in Brno and Vienna from 1865 to 1872.

He studied under Franz Brentano at the University of Vienna and took his doctorate there in 1876 with a thesis on Plato. In Leipzig he met Charlotte Garrigue, an American from Brooklyn, whom he married on 15 March 1878; he took her family name as his middle name. He became professor of philosophy at the Czech Charles-Ferdinand University in Prague in 1882, where his students included Edvard Beneš. He challenged the supposedly medieval Czech epic manuscripts and spoke against the blood libel in the 1899 Hilsner trial.

Masaryk sat in the Austrian Reichsrat from 1891 to 1893 with the Young Czech Party and from 1907 to 1914 for the Czech Progressive Party, which he had founded in 1900. At first he favoured restructuring Austria-Hungary as a federal state. When the First World War broke out he concluded that Czechs and Slovaks should seek independence, and in December 1914 he went into exile with his daughter Olga.

He lectured in London and Paris, wrote memoranda, and in January 1917 sent President Woodrow Wilson a first memorandum on an independent Czechoslovak state. He helped organise the Czechoslovak Legion in Russia, which grew to about 40,000 men by 1918 after its performance at the Battle of Zborov in July 1917. In 1918 he travelled to the United States, where he had lectured at the University of Chicago in 1902 and 1907; on 18 October 1918 he submitted the Washington Declaration of Czechoslovak independence to Wilson.

The Allies recognised Masaryk as head of the provisional government, and on 14 November 1918 the National Assembly elected him president while he was in New York. He was re-elected in 1920, 1927 and 1934; the 1920 constitution limited presidents to two terms, but a one-time provision exempted the first holder. The constitution gave the president a limited role, but with ten or more parties in the Assembly and frequent changes of government, his prestige gave the office more influence than its framers intended. He built an informal political network known as the Hrad, the Castle.

He resigned on 14 December 1935 because of old age and poor health and was succeeded by Beneš. He died at Lány on 14 September 1937, at 87, and was buried beside his wife. Masaryk University in Brno bears his name.
tomas-mejia: José Tomás de la Luz Mejía Camacho was born on 17 September 1820, probably in Pinal de Amoles, and went to school in Jalpan, where his father Cristóbal Mejía was prefect from 1840 to 1842. The rebel general José de Urrea, sheltered in the family's house, told him war stories, and when government troops under Juan Cano arrived he enlisted. Cano recommended him to President Anastasio Bustamante for the Military Academy. He fought the Apache from Chihuahua from 1842 to 1845 and saw action at the Battle of Buena Vista in the Mexican-American War.

From 1850 he was military commander of the Sierra Gorda. After the Lerdo law of 1856 stripped the Catholic Church and Indigenous communities of their communal lands, he seized Querétaro in October, promising to defend the church and the communities' lands, and then waged guerrilla war from the Sierra. In the Reform War he joined Miguel Miramón to take San Luis Potosí in September 1858. After the liberals took Mexico City in January 1861 he fought on, capturing Río Verde and its commander Mariano Escobedo, whom he released. President Benito Juárez put a price of 10,000 pesos on his head.

Mejía at first waited on the French intervention, then backed the Second Mexican Empire with Maximilian of Habsburg as its monarch. He took San Luis Potosí on 25 December 1863 and in 1864 defeated Manuel Doblado at Matehuala, for which Napoleon III gave him the Legion of Honour. As American supplies reached the republicans after 1865, he withdrew from Matamoros in June 1866 and joined Maximilian at Querétaro.

Escobedo's republican army appeared before Querétaro on 12 March 1867, and Mejía helped to repulse its assaults until the imperial leaders were captured on 15 May. Escobedo offered him a way to escape, but Mejía refused it unless Maximilian and Miramón could go with him. A court martial presided over by Rafael Platón Sánchez heard that he had spared Escobedo and Jerónimo Treviño, yet sentenced him to death.
tomasi-kulimoetoke-ii: Tomasi Kulimoetoke was born on 26 July 1918 at Ha'afuasia, in the Hahake District of Wallis island. He became the 50th Lavelua of Uvea, one of the three traditional kingdoms of Wallis and Futuna. He was elected king on 12 March 1959, after six months in which the kingdom had been governed by a Council of Ministers.

In his early years on the throne he supported closer links with France, recognising that Wallis depended on French subsidies. After a referendum, he signed the treaty that made Wallis a French overseas territory in 1961. In 2002 he angered many islanders, and France, by shutting down the island's only newspaper after it carried an editorial criticising him for sheltering a family friend who had been sentenced to jail for embezzling public funds. Reformists also mocked his insistence that Wallisians dismount from their bicycles when passing his palace.

In 2005 he nearly lost his throne. His grandson Tomasi Tuugahala had been sentenced to 18 months in prison for the involuntary manslaughter of a pedestrian killed in a drunk-driving incident on New Year's Eve. The king let him take refuge in the royal palace, where he hid for four months before surrendering to the French gendarmes. The king's prime minister, the Kalae Kivalu, urged the French administrator Xavier de Fürst to leave the territory, and the king argued that the case had been settled by customary law and that French penal law should be abolished in Uvea.

Reformists sought to depose him and install Sosefo Mautamakia Ahau Halagahu in his place. Riots broke out, several hundred of the king's supporters marched and built roadblocks, and the coronation of the rival did not take place. The king kept his throne and was again recognised by France.

In his last years, when his health was poor, his daughter Etua took over his ceremonial duties. He had six children. He died at Mata-Utu on 7 May 2007. A six-month period of mourning followed, during which it was taboo to mention a possible successor.
tomasz-dabal: Tomasz Jan Dąbal was born on 29 December 1890 in Sobów. From 1909 to 1914 he studied law in Vienna and medicine in Kraków, and in 1911 he joined the Polish People's Party. During World War I he served in the 87th Infantry Regiment of the Austro-Hungarian Army on the Russian, Balkan and Italian fronts, was wounded three times and reached the rank of captain. In January 1917 he became a machine-gun instructor in the 3rd Legion Infantry Regiment, and near the end of the war he was held for two months in a camp in Udine for political activity in the army.

In early November 1918, as a special representative of the Polish Liquidation Commission in Kraków, he took command of the gendarmerie in the counties of Tarnobrzeg, Mielec, Nisko and Kolbuszowa and turned it into a People's Militia. With Eugeniusz Okoń he founded the Republic of Tarnobrzeg on 6 November 1918. He belonged to the Polish People's Party "Left", then to the Radical Peasant Party, which he founded with Okoń, and sat in the Sejm from 1918 to 1921.

Dąbal joined the Communist Party of Poland in 1920. A few days before the Battle of Warsaw he told the Sejm: "I do not consider the Red Army an enemy. On the contrary, I welcome it as a friend of the Polish Nation." In July 1921 he and Stanisław Łańcucki formed the Sejm Faction of Communist Deputies. Stripped of his immunity in November 1921 and tried for attempting to overthrow the state, he was sentenced on 7 July 1922 to six years of hard labour.

In 1923 he left for the Soviet Union in an exchange of political prisoners. He worked in the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Byelorussia, was deputy secretary general of the Peasant International from 1923 to 1928 and held posts in the International Red Aid and the Comintern. He studied at the Institute of Red Professors from 1930 to 1932, took a doctorate in economics in 1934 and became vice-president of the Belarusian Academy of Sciences in Minsk.

Like most Polish communists in the Soviet Union, he was arrested and executed in the Great Purge, after a confession was extracted from him that he had directed the Polish Military Organization throughout the Soviet Union. The Military Collegium of the Supreme Court of the USSR rehabilitated him on 21 December 1955.
tomb-of-the-diver: The grave was found by the archaeologist Mario Napoli on 3 June 1968 in a small necropolis about 1.5 km south of Paestum. Five slabs of local limestone, bonded with plaster, form its walls and roof around a chamber about 215 by 100 by 80 cm, the floor being cut into the bedrock, and all five were painted on their inner faces in true fresco. Near the badly decayed skeleton, widely supposed to be a young man's, lay a turtle shell, two aryballoi and an Attic black-figure lekythos of about 480 BCE, which helped scholars date the tomb.

On the north and south walls three couches hold five reclining, crowned symposiasts; on the north wall one plays kottabos, tossing wine at a target, and on the rightmost couch a young man resists an older guest's advances. The west wall shows three figures arriving or leaving, an older man with a stick, an undressed man and a woman playing the flute, and on the east wall a nude servant boy holds an oenochoe beside a krater. Two painters have been distinguished, the south wall's the less skilled. Some scholars read the diver as the passage to the otherworld, others as an acrobat at a diving event, a reading Holloway questioned.

Scholars debate whether the tomb was made for a Greek of Poseidonia or for a member of an Italic people living south of the city. The symposium suggests a Greek, while the vessel on the east wall resembles a krater-kantharos, a funerary type of the Italic tombs of the area. The painting was presumably inspired by Etruscan painted tombs, as Paestum lay a few kilometres from the border of Greek and Etruscan influence at the River Sele. Egyptian blue pigment points to a wealthy burial, and analysis of the pigments suggests an artisanal style local to Paestum. Of the thousands of Greek tombs known from about 700 to 400 BCE, this is the only one found with frescoes of human subjects.
tome-de-sousa: Tomé de Sousa was born in Rates, Póvoa de Varzim, the illegitimate son of Dom João de Sousa, a prior descended from King Afonso III. With the support of his cousin Antônio de Ataíde, count of Castenheira, he served the royal court from a young age. He fought the Moors in Morocco and North Africa and commanded the nau Conceição to Portuguese India in the armada of Fernão de Andrade. The government recognised his service in 1536, and he was knighted three years later. He was also the first knight commander of the Monastery of Rates.

The Crown had largely neglected Brazil while it concentrated on the spice trade of India, but the decline of that trade and threats from the neighbouring Spanish colonies led it to act. Sousa sailed with six ships and about 1,000 soldiers, settlers and missionaries, among them four hundred degredados, men banished from Portugal for minor crimes, and the six Jesuits who were the first in Brazil. His aims were to fend off French pirates, convert the Indigenous peoples and strengthen royal power. He bought the site of Salvador from Francisco Pereira Coutinho, the donatário of Bahia, and fortified it.

He sent officials to the other captaincies to regulate their administration, made land grants, set market days for trade between settlers and natives, and introduced livestock and sugarcane. Working with the Jesuit Manuel da Nóbrega, he reduced attacks on the colonists partly by diplomacy but mainly through cruel and often extreme punishment, and drove out hostile peoples. The first bishopric of Brazil, under Dom Pero Fernandes Sardinha, was set up in his time.

In 1553 he strengthened the economy and defences of São Vicente and founded the village of Itanhaém, then left Salvador to Duarte da Costa and returned to Portugal, where he advised the king on Brazilian affairs; he had suggested Rio de Janeiro for settlement in 1552. The de Souza family of West Africa holds by tradition that its founder, the slave trader Francisco Félix de Sousa, was his descendant.
tome-pires: Little is known of Pires's life before he reached India. He was possibly born in Leiria, though the evidence is tenuous, and had at least a brother, João Fernandes, and a sister, Isabel Fernandes. His father was apothecary to King João II of Portugal, and Pires himself served Prince Afonso, the heir apparent, until the prince's death in 1491. In 1510 the court commissioned him as factor of drugs in India, and he arrived at Cannanore in 1511.

In 1512 he was sent to Malacca, recently captured by the Portuguese, as chief accountant of the royal factory. From there and from Cochin he gathered information on the Malay-Indonesian region and visited Java, Sumatra and Maluku himself. The Suma Oriental, couched as a report to Manuel of Portugal and finished before the death of Afonso de Albuquerque in December 1515, was the first comprehensive and reliable account of Asia east of India, with the first European descriptions of the Malay Archipelago and the Spice Islands.

Its history of Malacca is the earliest known, and Pires was the first to use the name Japan, spelt Jampon. He checked what merchants and sailors told him, and his descriptions of Sumatra and Java were not surpassed for a couple of centuries, though his modern editor found his style far from clear. Its only contemporary rival was Duarte Barbosa's book. The work stayed unpublished and was presumed lost until a manuscript copy was found in a Paris archive in 1944; four of his letters also survive.

Pires went to Canton in the fleet of Fernão Pires de Andrade, leading the embassy of King Manuel I to the Zhengde Emperor, the first official European embassy to China since the papal legate Giovanni de' Marignolli, in Beijing from 1342 to 1345. The emperor never received him, because of Chinese suspicion, the hostile conduct of Portuguese traders and the plotting of Mahmud Shah, the sultan deposed at Malacca in 1511. Some members of the embassy were killed. Pires never left China, and accounts of his end differ.
tomebamba: The city's Kichwa name, Tumipampa, means Knife Field; Tumebamba and Tomebamba are Spanish forms of it. Before the Inca conquest the area was called Guapondelig, and the Cañari people had lived there for at least 500 years. The Inca emperor Topa Inca Yupanqui, who ruled from 1471 to 1493, brought it into the empire after long and hard campaigns against the Cañari.

His son and successor Huayna Capac, who ruled from 1493 to 1525, was responsible for most of the Inca building in the city. He modelled it on Cuzco, the Inca capital, and had a royal palace there. Spanish accounts that he had building stones carried from Cuzco to Inca centres in present-day Ecuador were confirmed in 2004, when archaeologists identified 450 stones, weighing up to 700 kilograms each, from a quarry near Cuzco. They had been moved more than 1,600 kilometres along Inca roads by human labour alone, possibly by workers conscripted from peoples who had opposed Inca rule.

Huayna Capac and many other Incas died in an epidemic, probably of a European-introduced disease, about 1525, and his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa fought over the succession. Several battles of the civil war took place near the city, which was largely destroyed. The Cañari had taken Huáscar's side and were treated severely by Atahualpa. When the Spanish chronicler Pedro Cieza de León visited in 1547, he wrote that everything had crumbled and lay in ruins, but that its former grandeur could still be seen.

The Spanish city of Cuenca stands on the Inca city, whose remains are largely buried. Two parts survive, the ruins of Todos Santos and Pumapunku, about 300 metres apart near the Tomebamba River; spinning tools found at Pumapunku suggest that it may have housed aclla, the women set apart by the Incas. The Manuel Agustín Landivar Museum stands beside Todos Santos, and the Pumapungo Museum and Archaeological Park at Pumapunku.
tomioka-silk-mill: After the Meiji Restoration the new government needed export goods to pay for industrialisation. Japanese silk was in high demand, partly because of the silkworm disease pébrine in France and Italy and the turmoil of the Taiping Rebellion in China. The government had earlier refused foreign offers to fund a mill, considering silk a strategic industry, but lacked the technology to build one.

A small model mill at Maebashi, built in 1870 with equipment from Italy and a Swiss engineer, employed only 12 people. Later that year Ōkuma Shigenobu, Itō Hirobumi and Shibusawa Eiichi approached the French embassy and were introduced to Paul Brunat, an engineer working as a raw silk inspector in Yokohama. Edmond Auguste Bastan drew the plans, and construction began in March 1871, with bricks fired in a purpose-built kiln.

The mill, in Tomioka, Gunma Prefecture, started work on 4 November 1872. 4 metres long, held 300 reels, while the largest plants in France and Italy had up to 150. Brunat added a re-rolling process to imitate by machine what Japanese craftsmen had done by hand and to stop the silk threads sticking in the humid climate, and he ordered equipment suited to the smaller stature of Japanese women.

Workers had eight-hour days, Sunday holidays, uniforms and an elementary school. Rumours that the foreigners, seen drinking red wine, lived on workers' blood frightened off recruits, and Odaka Atsutada hired his own daughter to dispel them. By April 1873 there were 556 workers, mainly daughters of former samurai. Turnover was high, and silk from the mill won second place at the 1873 Vienna World's Fair.

Brunat and the foreign engineers left at the end of 1875. Mitsui & Co. bought the mill from the government in 1893, and Hara Tomitarō bought it in 1902. In 1938 it passed to a company managed by Katakura, which shifted production to military materials during the Pacific War.

Production peaked at 373,401 kilograms in 1974, and the mill stopped work on 26 February 1987. Katakura sold the site to Tomioka city in 2005, and it became a National Historic Site. Three buildings were designated National Treasure in 2014: the reeling hall and the east and west cocoon warehouses. The site was registered as a World Heritage Site on 21 June 2014.
tomislav-of-croatia: Tomislav's ancestry is unknown, though he may have belonged to the Trpimirović dynasty, and he is generally assumed to have been a son of Muncimir. He succeeded Muncimir as Duke of Croatia c. 910, the most widely accepted view, and in any case between 910 and 914; the Historia Salonitana of Thomas the Archdeacon of Split, a chronicle of the thirteenth century, names him as duke in 914. Because information on him is scarce, the exact years of his accession and death are unknown.

The Hungarians, after conquering the Carpathian Basin, raided and expanded, killing Braslav, the last Pannonian duke. The Chronicle of the Priest of Duklja credits Tomislav with a victory over them at the Drava, though other chroniclers record Hungarian victories in the same years. Croatia kept its northern borders and expanded into part of the collapsed Pannonian Duchy, including its former capital Sisak. The realm covered most of southern and central Croatia and the Dalmatian coast, excluding the Byzantine Theme of Dalmatia, with parts of western Herzegovina and northern and western Bosnia. Its exact extent is disputed among historians.

By 925 Tomislav was king; the papal chancellery called him the first Croatian ruler it styled king, and a letter of Pope John X names him King of the Croats. It is not known when, where or by whom he was crowned. In 925 he attended the Council of Split, convened to decide which bishop held jurisdiction in Dalmatia and to discuss Slavic liturgy.

The council gave jurisdiction to the Archbishop of Split rather than Bishop Gregory of Nin, and allowed Croatian and the Glagolitic script for local priests and monks. Croatia was also an ally of Byzantium, and Byzantium gave Tomislav the honorary title of proconsul. After Simeon I of Bulgaria destroyed Serbia in 924, he sent Duke Alogobotur against Croatia, and Tomislav destroyed his army in the battle of 926, probably in eastern Bosnia.

After Simeon's death in 927, Pope John X sent legates who restored peace between Croatia and Bulgaria. How Tomislav died is unknown. He disappeared from the political scene after 928 and was succeeded by Trpimir II. Tomislav is honoured as the first Croatian king and founder of the first Croatian state. The Bosnian city of Duvno was renamed Tomislavgrad in 1925 for the thousandth anniversary of his coronation, and a monument to him by Robert Frangeš-Mihanović was erected in Zagreb in 1927.
tomislavgrad: Tomislavgrad is the seat of its municipality in Canton 10 of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It lies 38 kilometres from the canton seat Livno, 88 kilometres from Mostar and 162 kilometres from Sarajevo. The area was inhabited from about 4000 BCE to 2400 BCE, before the Illyrians arrived, and only polished stone axes remain from that time. In the Roman period the town was known as Delminium, from which the name Duvno derives. Its inhabitants are still often called Duvnjaci.

Delminium was a town of the Illyrian tribe of the Dalmatae, whose union was the last bastion of Illyrian freedom against Rome. The first conflict with Rome began in 156 BCE, when the consuls Gaius Marcius Figulus and then Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum conquered and destroyed the town, which the Romans burned with lighted arrows. The Dalmatae were conquered for good in 9 CE. Roads from Salona and Narona crossed at Delminium, and the Romans rebuilt it under Tiberius, building a forum. In 1896 Fra Anđeo Nuć found sculptures of Roman and Illyrian deities, including altars to Diana and to the Illyrian god Armatus.

In the middle of the 16th century the Ottomans founded a qasaba here called Županj-Potok, which became a captaincy on 8 May 1711. Ottoman rule lasted until 1878, when Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina. Under the Kingdom of Yugoslavia the Franciscan Mijo Čuić laid the foundation of the Catholic basilica on 8 July 1924, and it was consecrated on 29 September 1940. In the Independent State of Croatia, established in April 1941, the area fell in the Italian zone; the Ustaše organised the persecution of local Serbs, and Partisan units formed. In 1990 a referendum on restoring the name Tomislavgrad passed with 98.91 percent in favour.

Tomislavgrad had 5,587 inhabitants in 2013. Many people emigrated in the 1960s and 1970s and above all during the war of the 1990s, mostly to Croatia, Western Europe and Australia. The Nikola Tavelić basilica stands on the site of the Roman forum. A large monument to King Tomislav by the sculptor Vinko Bagarić was installed in the 1990s, and the town has the football club HNK Tomislav.
tommaso-campanella: Campanella was born into poverty in Stignano in Calabria, the son of an illiterate cobbler, and was a child prodigy. He entered the Dominican Order before the age of fourteen, taking the name fra' Tommaso in honour of Thomas Aquinas. He became disenchanted with Aristotelian orthodoxy and was drawn to the empiricism of Bernardino Telesio, whom he defended in his first work, Philosophia sensibus demonstrata, published in 1592. His heterodox views brought him into conflict with the ecclesiastical authorities, and he was arrested in Padua in 1594 and confined to a convent until 1597.

On returning to Calabria he was accused of leading a conspiracy against Spanish rule in his hometown of Stilo. He expected the Age of the Spirit to begin in 1600, on the basis of the prophecies of Joachim of Fiore and his own astrological observations. Betrayed by two fellow conspirators, he was captured in 1599 and tortured on the rack in Naples, seven times in all, and sentenced to life imprisonment. In prison he wrote The Monarchy of Spain in 1600, a long letter advising Philip II on founding a universal monarchy. The City of the Sun was written in Italian in 1602 and published in Latin at Frankfurt in 1623.

Pope Urban VIII secured his release in 1626, and he was fully free in 1629. In Rome he advised the pope on astrology for five years. A new conspiracy in Calabria in 1634 led by one of his followers threatened fresh trouble, and he fled to France, where Louis XIII received him with favour and Cardinal Richelieu protected him. He lived in the convent of Saint-Honoré in Paris until his death on 21 May 1639.
tomochichi: Little is known of Tomochichi's early life. He was presumably Creek and was exiled from the Creek nation for reasons that are unclear. In about 1730 he formed the Yamacraw from an assortment of Creek and Yamasee people after the two nations disagreed over relations with the British and the Spanish. His group of about two hundred settled on the bluffs of the Savannah River, a burial place of his ancestors close to British traders. He had dealt with British colonists before and was cautious but unafraid of them.

When General James Oglethorpe and his settlers arrived in February 1733, Mary Musgrove, daughter of a Creek mother and an English father, and her husband John interpreted between the two men. Tomochichi chose to let them found Savannah on Yamacraw Bluff for the sake of trade and diplomatic ties. Oglethorpe later recalled his first speech: he presented a buffalo skin painted with an eagle's head and feathers, the eagle signifying speed and love and the buffalo strength and protection, and asked the English to love and protect their little families.

In England in 1734 he gave King George II eagle feathers as a token of peace at Kensington Palace on 1 August, attended the ratification of the Articles of Friendship and Commerce, and pressed for education and fair trade. On his return he persuaded other Lower Creek chiefs to ally with the colony. He asked John Wesley for Christian teaching for his people without success, but Benjamin Ingham helped open an Indian school at Irene in September 1736. That year he joined Oglethorpe on an expedition to settle Georgia's southern boundary and helped in dealings with the Spanish, and in February 1739 he met a Choctaw delegation at Savannah.

Illness kept him from Oglethorpe's journey to Coweta in the summer of 1739, and he died on 5 October 1739, most accounts say at 95. He asked to be buried among the whites and was given a public military funeral with Oglethorpe as a pallbearer; his wife Senauki and nephew Toonahowi were left in charge of the tribe. The stone pyramid over his grave was last mentioned in 1759. A granite boulder was set up in his memory in 1899, and the Tomochichi Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse in Savannah bears his name.
tomoyuki-yamashita: Tomoyuki Yamashita was born on 8 November 1885, the second son of a local physician in a village in what is now Kōchi Prefecture on Shikoku. He graduated from the Imperial Japanese Army Academy in 1905 and fought against Germany in Shandong in 1914. He became an expert on Germany and served as assistant military attaché at Bern and Berlin from 1919 to 1922. A leading member of the Imperial Way group, he became a rival of Hideki Tojo. After the February 26 Incident of 1936 he lost the trust of Emperor Hirohito by appealing for leniency for the rebel officers, and he was posted to Korea.

On 6 November 1941 Yamashita took command of the Twenty-Fifth Army. He invaded Malaya on 8 December with a force about one third the size of the British forces, relying on speed, and the campaign ended with the fall of Singapore on 15 February 1942, when 30,000 front-line soldiers took 80,000 British, Indian and Australian prisoners. The occupation of Singapore saw atrocities, among them the Alexandra Hospital and Sook Ching massacres. His responsibility is debated: the order to execute Chinese came, according to postwar testimony, from senior officers on his operations staff.

In July 1942 Yamashita was sent to Manchukuo, probably through Tojo's doing. On 10 October 1944 he took command of the Fourteenth Area Army in the Philippines. US forces landed on Leyte ten days later and on Luzon on 6 January 1945. He did not declare Manila an open city, and Rear Admiral Sanji Iwabuchi, against Yamashita's order, defended it; the fighting and Japanese atrocities killed more than 100,000 Filipino civilians. Yamashita surrendered on 2 September 1945.

An American military tribunal in Manila tried him from 29 October to 7 December 1945 for atrocities against civilians and prisoners of war in the Philippines, charging that he had failed to prevent them. He denied ordering or knowing of the crimes and said he was in effect charged with losing the war.

He was found guilty and sentenced to death. General Douglas MacArthur upheld the sentence, the supreme courts of the Philippines and the United States declined to review it, and Justices Frank Murphy and W. B. Rutledge dissented, criticising the haste of the trial. He was executed on 23 February 1946. The principle that a commander is responsible for crimes of his troops that he did not try to stop is known as the Yamashita standard.
tomsk: Tomsk stands on the Tom River, from which the city takes its name. The river's name may derive from the Ket word toom, meaning river, from the Russian tyomny, meaning dark, or from the Turco-Mongol tom, meaning great. The climate is humid continental, barely escaping a subarctic classification, with severe and lengthy winters; the lowest recorded temperature was −55 °C in January 1931.

The fortress of 1604 followed a request from Toian, the Tatar duke of the Eushta Tatars, for the tsar's protection against the Yenisei Kyrgyz and the Oirats. Boris Godunov sent 200 Cossacks under Vasily Fomich Tyrkov and Gavriil Ivanovich Pisemsky, and Toian ceded the land. In 1804 Tomsk became the seat of the Tomsk Governorate, and gold was found in 1830. In the mid-19th century one fifth of its residents were exiles. When the Trans-Siberian Railway of the 1890s bypassed the city, growth shifted south and Novosibirsk in time surpassed it.

Tomsk then built its name on education. Tomsk Polytechnic University was founded in 1896 and opened in 1900, and by World War II every twelfth resident was a student. After 1917 Tomsk became a notable centre of the White movement, led among others by Anatoly Pepelyayev and Maria Bochkareva. Factories moved there from 1941, which led to the creation of Tomsk Oblast. In the Cold War it was a closed city, and in 1949 the secret settlement of Tomsk-7, home to the Soviet Union's first industrial-scale nuclear power station, was founded nearby; it was renamed Seversk in 1992.

Tomsk is the administrative centre of Tomsk Oblast in Russia, with 556,478 inhabitants at the 2021 census. It has six universities with over 100,000 students, among them Tomsk State University, the oldest university in Siberia. The city is known for the elaborate gingerbread decoration of its traditional wooden houses, though their number is falling through redevelopment and fire.
tomyris: Tomyris was the widow of the king of the Massagetae and succeeded him as ruler of the tribe after his death. She is known only from the writings of the Greek historian Herodotus. The few other early sources that cover the period, above all Ctesias, do not mention her. Her name is the Latin form of the Greek Tomuris, itself a Hellenisation of the Saka name *Taumuriyah, which is taken to mean "of family" and is related to Avestan and Old Persian words for seed, germ and kinship.

In the account of Herodotus, Cyrus the Great, the founder of the Achaemenid Empire, asked for her hand in order to gain her kingdom through marriage. Tomyris understood his aim and refused. On the advice of the Lydian Croesus, Cyrus then decided to invade the Massagetae. While he built a bridge over the Araxes river, Tomyris told him to be content with ruling his own kingdom and to let her rule hers.

Cyrus's first assault was routed by the Massagetae. He then left a banquet with large amounts of wine in the tents of his camp as an ambush and withdrew. The Massagetae, led by Tomyris's son Spargapises, who commanded their army, were used to fermented mare's milk and cannabis rather than wine. They became drunk and were slaughtered, which destroyed a third of their army. Spargapises was captured and, once sober, asked Cyrus to free him. Cyrus agreed, and Spargapises killed himself.

Tomyris sent Cyrus an angry message calling the wine a drug that made men speak evil words, and demanded that he leave her land or she would give him more blood than he could drink. In the battle that followed she defeated the Persians and destroyed most of their army. Cyrus was killed, and she is said to have cut off his head and put it in a bag filled with blood, telling him to drink his fill.

Ctesias recorded another version, in which Cyrus died fighting the Derbices, who were either the Massagetae or one of their sub-tribes. About 520 BCE, and possibly earlier, the tribe was ruled by a king named Skuⁿxa, who rebelled against Persia until Darius I campaigned against the Sakas from 520 to 518 BCE and conquered the Massagetae.

Tomyris became a popular subject in European art and literature from the Renaissance, usually shown receiving the head of Cyrus or placing it in a vessel of blood, within the tradition of the Power of Women. Rubens, Mattia Preti and Gustave Moreau are among the artists who portrayed her. Eustache Deschamps included her among the nine Female Worthies in the late 14th century, and an opera, Thomyris, Queen of Scythia, was staged in London in 1707.
ton-duc-thang: Tôn Đức Thắng was born on 20 August 1888 on Ông Hổ Island in the Mekong, about four kilometres from Long Xuyên, to Tôn Văn Đề and Nguyễn Thị Di. From 1897 to 1901 a private tutor taught him Nôm script, history and Confucian philosophy, and the tutor's anti-colonial views influenced his early politics. He learned French at an elementary school in Long Xuyên and lived with his parents until 1906, when he moved to Saigon. He later claimed to have taken part, as a sailor in the French navy, in the 1919 Black Sea mutiny, but the author Christoph Giebel says he apparently did not and calls the story a fabrication that linked Vietnamese communism to the October Revolution.

Tôn joined the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League in 1927. In 1929 he was imprisoned in Saigon and deported to the Côn Sơn Prison, where he stayed until 1945. After the Viet Minh came to power in August 1945 he joined the Cochinchina Party Committee, and in 1946 he presided over the National Assembly. He led the Lien Viet from 1946 to 1954 and then the Vietnamese Fatherland Front, and received the Stalin Peace Award in 1955. He was vice president under Hồ Chí Minh from 1960 and succeeded him as president on 2 September 1969. The post was ceremonial, he was never a member of the Politburo, and most real power lay with the party chief Lê Duẩn.

He became the first president of the reunified Socialist Republic of Vietnam, formalised on 2 July 1976, after the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975. Vietnamese forces invaded Cambodia on 25 December 1978 and took Phnom Penh by 7 January 1979, and China invaded northern Vietnam from 17 February 1979 and began to withdraw on 16 March.

Tôn died in Hanoi on 30 March 1980, aged 91, of heart seizure and respiratory failure, and was succeeded by Nguyễn Hữu Thọ. He is buried in Mai Dịch Cemetery. Known in Vietnam as Uncle Tôn, he gave his name to Tôn Đức Thắng University in Ho Chi Minh City, and a museum devoted to him opened there in 1988, the centenary of his birth.
tonawanda-band-of-seneca: The Seneca are one of the original Five Nations, later six, of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, and speak the Seneca language, an Iroquoian language. On 15 January 1838 the United States made the Treaty of Buffalo Creek with nine Indian nations of New York, including the Seneca, as part of its Indian Removal programme: the Ogden Land Company was to buy the four remaining Seneca reservations in New York, and the proceeds were to fund the nation's removal to Kansas Territory.

The Treaty with the Seneca of 1842 recorded that the company had bought only two reservations, Tonawanda among them, while the Seneca kept Cattaraugus and Allegany. The Seneca of the Tonawanda Reservation protested that they had not been consulted on either treaty and that their chiefs had signed neither, and they refused to leave. When the Seneca of Cattaraugus and Allegany adopted a constitution with chiefs elected by popular vote in 1848, the Tonawanda Band, partly because of the bitterness left by the Buffalo Creek sale, stayed out.

In 1857, by the Treaty with the Seneca, Tonawanda Band, it secured federal recognition as a nation independent of the Seneca Nation of Indians, and with its share of the proceeds of the earlier sale it bought back most of the Tonawanda Reservation from the Ogden Land Company. It also retrieved the horns of authority and other artifacts from the other Seneca communities.

The Nation governs the 7,500-acre Tonawanda Reservation near Akron. Its government is a council of hoyaneh, hereditary chiefs, one for each of its eight clans: the Snipe, Heron, Hawk, Deer, Wolf, Beaver, Bear and Turtle. Each clan mother appoints her clan's chief from hereditary maternal lines, can remove him, and after consulting the clan advises him on tribal government. Chiefs usually serve for life and govern by consensus of the clans. As among all the Haudenosaunee, descent and property pass through the mother, and children belong to their mother's clan.
tondaimandalam: The region's borders were never fixed and probably changed over time. In general it took in the basins of three river systems: the Arani in the north, the Kosasthalaiyar in the middle and the Palar-Cheyyar-Veghavati in the south. Its northern edge lay roughly at Pulicat Lake and its southern somewhere north of the Pennai river. It included the Perumbanappadi chieftaincy in the northwest and part of Pangalanadu, and bordered the Vanakoppadi chieftaincy to the southwest and Naduvilnadu to the south.

Later records divide it into 24 kottams, districts subdivided into nadus, groups of agricultural villages, though only 22 kottams are attested in contemporary sources and the figure of 24 may be conventional. Eyilkottam contained Kanchipuram.

Burial urns, cairn circles and jar burials from about the start of the common era have been found near Mamallapuram. In the early historical period the region was largely pastoral, broken by hills and forest into small pockets of farmland. The Sangam poem Perumpanarruppatai, written about 190-200 CE, describes large tracts of unsettled land with few settlements, and Pallava inscriptions often mention cattle given to temples or taken in raids. In the 3rd century CE it was ruled by Ilandiraiyan, the first king with the title Tondaiman, whom P. T. Srinivasa Iyengar identifies with a Pallava prince.

Under the Pallavas intensive farming and towns spread. From the 7th to the 9th centuries brahmadeya villages, tax-free grants to Brahmins, came with irrigation works kept up by Brahmin assemblies, and in the 9th and 10th centuries grants to temples drove further expansion. The number of nadus grew steadily from the 7th to the 12th century. Trade served the royal court and was conducted mostly at Kanchipuram and its port of Mamallapuram.

The Chola king Aditya I took the region from the Pallava ruler Aparajitavarman. Under Uttama Chola most of it was recovered from the Rashtrakutas, and Raja Raja Chola I gave it its Chola name. Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan I conquered it as far as Nellore in 1258, and after the fall of the Pandyan Empire it came under the Madurai Sultanate in 1323. Kumara Kampana defeated the sultanate in 1361, and the region became part of the Vijayanagara Empire, later passing to the Nawabdom of the Carnatic and, under the British, to the Madras Presidency.
tong-yabghu-khagan: Tong Yabghu was a member of the Ashina clan and the brother of Shikui Khagan, who ruled the western Göktürks from 611 to 618. His name is written in Chinese with a character meaning to unite or to govern. In the 11th century the Karakhanid scholar Mahmud al-Kashgari glossed the Turkic toŋa as meaning tiger, while the modern scholar Gerard Clauson argued that it means hero or outstanding warrior.

He kept close relations with the Tang dynasty of China and may have married into its imperial family. The Old Book of Tang praises him as brave, astute and skilled in war: he controlled the Tiele tribes to the north, confronted Persia to the west, reached Kashmir to the south and moved his tent to Qianquan, north of Tashkent. He set governors, called tuduns, over the peoples under his rule, and he supported the spread of Buddhism, patronising scholars of the monastery of Nalanda such as the translator Prabhakāramitra.

From about 625 he subjugated the Hephthalite principalities, among them Tokharistan, Gandhara, Ferghana and Bactria, and after reaching the Indus valley replaced their dynasties with Turkic rulers. In the early 620s his nephew Böri Shad raided across the Caucasus into Persian territory. Many scholars identified Tong Yabghu with Ziebel, the khagan of the Khazars who campaigned with the Byzantine emperor Heraclius against Persia in 627 and 628, but recent research identifies Ziebel instead with his uncle Sipi, who ruled the western part of the realm.

He was murdered by Külüg Sibir, his uncle and a partisan of the Dulu faction. After his death the power of the Western Göktürks largely collapsed. The khaganate lingered for a few decades before falling to the Chinese Empire, but many client tribes broke away, and successor states such as the Khazar Khaganate and Great Bulgaria became independent. His reign is generally regarded as the high point of the Western Turkic Khaganate; his sons included Sy Yabghu Qaghan and Tardush Shad, Yabgu of Tokharistan.
tonga: Tonga has 171 islands, 45 of them inhabited, in three main groups, Vava'u, Ha'apai and Tongatapu, along an 800-kilometre north–south line directly south of Samoa. The largest island, Tongatapu, covers 257 square kilometres and holds the capital, Nukuʻalofa. Most of the islands have a limestone base formed from uplifted coral, and others have limestone over a volcanic base. In Tongan legend flying bats are sacred and the property of the monarchy, so they are protected. The name comes from fakatonga, southwards, since the group is the southernmost of western Polynesia.

In Tongan mythology the demigod Maui drew up the islands from the ocean. Archaeologists link the first settlers to the Lapita culture, which spread from Island Melanesia to Samoa and then to Tonga, sometime between 1500 and 1000 BCE. Scholars debate exactly when, but thorium dating confirms that settlers had reached the earliest known inhabited town, Nukuleka, by 888 BCE. The precontact history was handed down by oral tradition. From the rule of the first Tongan king, ʻAhoʻeitu, Tonga grew into a regional power whose influence is said to have reached Fiji, Samoa and Niue.

Tonga became known in the West as the Friendly Islands because of the welcome given to Captain James Cook on his first visit in 1773. He arrived at the time of the annual ʻinasi festival, at which first fruits were presented to the Tuʻi Tonga, and so was invited to the festivities. According to the writer William Mariner, the political leaders actually wanted to kill Cook but could not agree on a plan. In 1928 Queen Salote Tupou III, a member of the Free Wesleyan Church of Tonga, made that church the state church, and the Church of Tonga separated from it in opposition.

Tonga is a constitutional monarchy and the only extant indigenous monarchy in the Pacific islands. It has five administrative divisions: ʻEua, Haʻapai, the Niuas, Tongatapu and Vavaʻu. Tongan and English are the official languages, and about 70 per cent of the people live on Tongatapu. Roughly half the population lives abroad, mainly in Australia, New Zealand and the United States. Fahu, a form of social organisation, gives the father's sister the highest rank in a family, and rugby union is the national sport.
tongatapu: Tongatapu covers about 260 square kilometres and lies in Tonga's southern island group, to which it gives its name. It is built of coral limestone and is rather flat, covered with fertile soil made of volcanic ash from neighbouring volcanoes. On the steep southern coast the land rises to an average of 35 metres and at most 70 metres, then falls gradually towards the north.

To the north lie many small islands and coral reefs, reaching up to 7 kilometres from the shore. The almost closed Fanga'uta and Fangakakau lagoons, fringed with mangroves, are breeding grounds for birds and fish, and were declared a natural reserve in 1974. As the southernmost island group of the country, it has a cooler climate than the north, so fruit production is lower there.

Tongatapu holds one of the densest concentrations of archaeological remains in the Pacific. The earliest Lapita pottery found in Tonga dates from about 900 to 850 BCE, around 300 years after the first settlements. The archaeologist David Burley found it near the Fanga'uta Lagoon, some 2,000 kilometres from the Lapita pottery of Santa Cruz in the Solomon Islands. Nukuleka is possibly the site of the first Lapita settlement.

The island was the seat of the Tuʻi Tonga, whose rule over distances of up to 1,000 kilometres was often only symbolic. Their first capital was at Toloa, about 1,000 years ago, and the second at Heketā, where the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui trilithon stands. The third, at Muʻa, was a capital from 1220 to 1851 and has more than 20 royal grave mounds.

Abel Tasman, commanding the Heemskerck and the Zeehaen for the Dutch East India Company, sighted the island on 20 January 1643 and named it Amsterdam Island for its abundant supplies. James Cook visited later and wrote the name as Tongataboo in 1777. British and American whalers called regularly for provisions, water and wood between 1807 and 1899.

Tongatapu is the most populous island of Tonga, with 74,611 residents in 2016, roughly 70.5% of the national total. It holds the capital, Nukuʻalofa, and has become the country's business, trade and labour centre. Its sites include the royal tombs at Muʻa, the blowholes at Mapu ʻa Vaea, the natural land bridge at Hūfangalupe and Tupou College, the first educational establishment in the kingdom.
tongeren: Tongeren lies in the southeastern corner of the Flemish region of Belgium, in the province of Limburg. It is called the oldest town in Belgium, as the only Roman administrative capital within the country's borders. Before the Roman conquest the area was inhabited by Belgic tribes known as the Germani cisrhenani, of which the Eburones were the largest. Caesar's Aduatuca, the fort of the Eburones, is widely equated with Tongeren, though others argue that Aduatuca was a general word for a fort and that Tongeren shows no sign of pre-Roman occupation.

As Atuatuca Tungrorum the town was the capital of the Civitas Tungrorum. Located on the road linking Cologne to Bavay and surrounded by fertile land, it quickly became one of the largest Gallo-Roman administrative and military towns. It suffered a fire during the Batavian siege in 70 CE and in the second century built a defensive wall, parts of which survive. In 358 the future emperor Julian met a delegation of Salian Franks there. In the 4th century it became the centre of a Christian diocese under Saint Servatius, who died in 384, but the seat later moved to Maastricht and then Liège. The town may have been destroyed by the Huns in 451.

In Carolingian times a church and a chapter of canons were founded where the old bishops' houses stood, and the present basilica was begun at the start of the 13th century. A medieval wall, new churches and the beguinage were built, and the town became one of the good cities of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. Louis XIV's troops burned it almost entirely in 1677. It became part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1815 and of Belgium in 1830.

The Béguinage, founded in 1257, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998, and the bell tower of the Basilica of Our Lady is inscribed with the Belfries of Belgium and France. The Gallo-Roman Museum holds Celtic gold, Roman glassware and a Roman dodecahedron, and more than 1,500 metres of the second-century Roman wall can still be seen. A statue of Ambiorix, leader of the Eburones, was erected in 1866. Every seven years the Kroningsfeesten, a religious procession, commemorates the crowning of the statue of Our Lady in 1890.
tongmenghui: The Tongmenghui of China, a secret society and underground resistance movement, was founded in Tokyo by Sun Yat-sen, Song Jiaoren and others on 20 August 1905. Its goal was to overthrow China's Qing dynasty. It was formed by the unification of Sun's Xingzhonghui (Revive China Society), the Guangfuhui (Restoration Society) and many other late-Qing revolutionary groups. Its members included Huang Xing, Li Zongren, Zhang Binglin, Chen Tianhua, Wang Jingwei, Hu Hanmin, Tao Chengzhang, Cai Yuanpei, Li Shizeng, Zhang Renjie and Qiu Jin. In 1904 the movement had joined republican, nationalist and socialist objectives in a political goal: to expel the Manchu rulers, revive Zhonghua, establish a republic and distribute land equally among the people.

In 1906 a branch was formed in Singapore after Sun's visit. Called the Nanyang branch, it served as the headquarters for Southeast Asia. Its members included Tan Chor Lam, Teo Eng Hock and Chan Po-yin, who started the Chong Shing Chinese Daily Newspaper, with a first issue on 20 August 1907 and a daily distribution of 1,000 copies. Chan Po-yin raised over 30,000 yuan to buy military equipment and ship it to China. From December 1906 to April 1908 the Qing government defeated seven Tongmenghui-led uprisings. Numerous members fled to Southeast Asia, and discontent with the leadership grew among the membership.

In 1909 the headquarters of the Nanyang branch moved to Penang, where Sun was based from July to December 1910. The 1910 Penang Conference there planned the Second Guangzhou Uprising. A meeting of Sun's supporters at Ipoh, at the villa of Teh Lay Seng, raised funds, and a drive across the Malay Peninsula collected 47,683 Straits Settlement dollars. After revolutionaries occupied Shanghai in November 1911 the Tongmenghui moved its headquarters there, and then to Nanjing once the Provisional Government was established.

At a general meeting in Nanjing on 20 January 1912, attended by thousands of members, Hu Hanmin moved on behalf of Sun that the oath be changed to overthrow the Manchu government, consolidate the Republic of China and implement the Min Sheng Chu I. After the Republic was established the Tongmenghui became a political party on 3 March 1912 and elected Sun Yat-sen chairman, with Huang Xing and Li Yuanhung as vice-chairmen. It issued a provisional constitution of 34 articles. In May 1912 it moved to Beijing, where it was the largest party in China, with branches in Guangdong, Sichuan, Wuhan, Shanghai and other cities, and about 550,000 members. In August 1912 it formed the nucleus of the Kuomintang.
tongwan: Tongwancheng, the city ruling ten thousand, stands at the southern edge of the Maowusu Sands of the Ordos Desert, on what was once a strategic site in the centre of the Ordos Plateau, on the fertile upper reaches of the Wuding River. It is the largest urban centre of the Southern Xiongnu yet found. The city was built largely of wood, inside very thick outer walls coloured white with white clay and powdered rice, and had a lake at its centre. From a distance it was said to look like a giant ship, and it is also known as Bai Cheng, the White City.

The city was raised by around 100,000 Xiongnu under Helian Bobo, also known as Liu Bobo, a descendant of the Xiongnu chanyu. He wanted it impenetrable and made his general Chigan Ali the architect. The soil of the walls was steamed to harden it, and if an iron wedge could be driven an inch into a section, the workmen responsible were executed. White cities were generally ceremonial and status centres built after conquest, white being a holy colour for the Xiongnu, but the walls were needed in a time of constant war. At its height the city had about 10,000 inhabitants.

Helian Bobo died in 425 and was succeeded by his son Helian Chang. In 426 Emperor Taiwu of Northern Wei made a surprise attack: a brief incursion burned only the main temple, but the hinterland was devastated. The river and lake later dried up, possibly through deforestation, and the sands gradually buried the city. Tibetan forces besieged it in 786, and in 994 Emperor Taizong ordered it destroyed and its people moved, partly because the desert was spreading. Jurchen soldiers invaded it in 1206, and by the early Ming dynasty it was abandoned.

The ruins were rediscovered in 1845 and formally identified in 1956, and in 1996 they were listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level. They lie in Jingbian County, Shaanxi, near the border with Inner Mongolia, and are well preserved. The site was properly surveyed only in the 2000s and has not been fully excavated; its Yong'an Platform, where dignitaries inspected troops, has been restored.
tongwen-guan: Small government schools of foreign languages had existed in China since the Ming dynasty. From 1407 the Office for the Languages of Nations of Four Directions, under the Hanlin Academy, trained students chosen from the Guozijian to translate documents of tribute-bearing peoples such as the Mongols, Jurchens, Hui and Burmese; its graduates became translation officials, re-examined every three years. In 1708 the Qing Lifan Yuan set up a Russian College for students of the Eight Banners, since Russia threatened the empire's north-west border. That college was merged into the Tongwen Guan in 1863.

The new school grew out of defeat. In 1860 Britain and France won the Second Opium War, occupied Beijing and burned the Summer Palace and Old Summer Palace, while the Xianfeng Emperor fled to Chengde, where he died. Reformers called for learning from the West, and after the Convention of Peking the court created the Zongli Yamen in 1861 and the school a year later to supply its language skills.

The first teacher was the British missionary John Shaw Burdon, head instructor until 1869, when the American missionary W. A. P. Martin took over and remained until 1900. Other teachers included John Fryer and Hosea Ballou Morse in English, Anatole Billequin in chemistry and the mathematician Li Shanlan, who began teaching in 1869. Besides English, the school came to teach French, German, Russian and Japanese, along with medicine, machine-making and geography. Similar colleges were founded at Canton and Shanghai, and the school published several influential works that introduced Western knowledge into China. War interrupted its work in 1900.

After 1902 the Tongwen Guan became one of the founding parts of the Imperial University of Peking, now Peking University. Its language courses were the direct forerunners of that university's language programmes, and it is counted among the institutions of the Self-Strengthening Movement, the Qing effort to adopt Western techniques after the wars of the mid-19th century.
tonkin-campaign: Nine years after the French government cut short Francis Garnier's unsanctioned attempt to conquer Tonkin in 1873, Commandant Henri Rivière seized the citadel of Hanoi on 25 April 1882 with a small force of marine infantry, and on 27 March 1883 he captured Nam Định. His defeat and death at the hands of Liu Yongfu's Black Flag Army at the Battle of Paper Bridge on 19 May 1883 led the French government to send reinforcements, organised as the Tonkin Expeditionary Corps under General Alexandre-Eugène Bouët and supported by the gunboats of the Tonkin Flotilla.

On 20 August 1883 French troops stormed the Thuận An forts guarding the river to Huế, part of a plan, urged by the civil commissioner François-Jules Harmand, to coerce the Vietnamese court into accepting a French protectorate over Tonkin. Bouët's attacks on the Black Flags at Phủ Hoài and Palan had little success, but Hải Dương fell on 13 August amid atrocities on both sides. In December Admiral Amédée Courbet led 9,000 men against Sơn Tây, which fell on 16 December at a cost of 83 French dead and 320 wounded; some observers held that the fighting broke the Black Flags as a serious force.

General Charles-Théodore Millot then routed China's Guangxi Army at Bắc Ninh in March 1884 with just over 11,000 French, Algerian and Vietnamese soldiers, and took Hưng Hóa on 11 April. The outbreak of the Sino-French War in August 1884 put the French on the defensive. By then more than 20,000 French soldiers were serving in Tonkin, and Millot's final order of the day warned them against the contempt many showed for the local people.

The Treaty of Tientsin of 9 June 1885 made China abandon its claim to suzerainty over Vietnam, but the French still had to conquer the country they had been granted. By the summer of 1885 they had 35,000 soldiers in Tonkin. The Huế Ambush of 2 July 1885 began the Cần Vương uprising in Annam, and a cholera epidemic, worsened by General de Courcy's neglect of quarantine, killed more French soldiers than nine months of war with China. The campaign officially ended in April 1886, when the corps became a division of occupation, but Tonkin was not effectively pacified until 1896.
tonle-sap: Tonle Sap, whose Khmer name means Fresh River or, commonly, Great Lake, lies in the northwest of the lower Mekong plain in central Cambodia. It is the largest freshwater lake in Southeast Asia. Its basin covers about 86,000 square kilometres. The Tonle Sap River, about 120 kilometres long, joins the lake to the Mekong.

The lake changes enormously with the seasons. In the dry season it covers about 2,500 to 3,000 square kilometres and is about a metre deep. In the rainy season, from May to October, the Mekong's rising water reverses the flow of the Tonle Sap River, so that it runs into the lake for about six months and out again for the other six. The lake then reaches up to 16,000 square kilometres and a depth of 9 to 14 metres, and acts as a natural flood reservoir for the Mekong system.

The lake has long been a vital area for fishing and farming in Cambodia, and it largely sustained Angkor, described as the largest pre-industrial settlement complex in history. Fish came into the flooded forests to spawn, and the Mekong floods brought large numbers of fry. Historical research indicates that the people of Angkor dug large reservoirs to hold water in the wet season and released it in the dry season through an irrigation system, which doubled and sometimes tripled the rice crops each year. That network no longer exists, and farmers now take one crop a year.

Henri Mouhot described the lake in 1864 as covering an immense space for more than five months of the year, swollen by the current of the Mekong. Its most productive fishing grounds were leased by the government for more than a century. Many people of Vietnamese origin live in floating villages on the lake, as do Cham communities.

About 1.2 million people live around the lake and fish its waters, and the catch supplies much of Cambodia's freshwater fish. UNESCO designated the area a Biosphere Reserve in 1997, and a royal decree of 2001 made the lake and nine surrounding provinces the Tonle Sap Biosphere Reserve, with core, buffer and transition zones. The lake supports at least 149 fish species, including the Mekong giant catfish.
tonton-macoute: After the July 1958 coup attempt against President François Duvalier, he purged the Haitian Army and the law enforcement agencies and executed numerous officers he saw as a threat. To counter such plots he created a force that bore several names: the Cagoulards (Hooded Men) in 1959, then the Milice Civile, and later the Volontaires de la Sécurité Nationale. People began to call it the Tonton Macoute when others disappeared or were found dead for no apparent reason. The name comes from a Haitian bogeyman, Uncle Gunnysack, who snares unruly children in a sack and carries them off. The force answered to Duvalier alone.

Duvalier authorised the force to use systematic violence, terrorism and human rights abuses against political opposition. Opponents often disappeared overnight or were attacked in daylight, and corpses were sometimes hung in trees as warnings. Family members who tried to remove the bodies for burial often disappeared themselves. The leadership also practised corruption and extortion, taking money from businessmen as supposed donations for public works. The Tontons Macoutes are credited with the murder of between 30,000 and 60,000 Haitians.

Luckner Cambronne led the force through the 1960s and the early 1970s. He earned the nickname Vampire of the Caribbean by selling blood plasma and cadavers. After Duvalier died in 1971, his widow Simone and his son Jean-Claude Duvalier ordered Cambronne into exile in Miami. The force took on Vodou imagery. Members wore blue denim shirts, straw hats and dark glasses, carried machetes in reference to Ogun, and included some Vodou leaders, which gave them an unearthly authority in the eyes of the public. They were ubiquitous at the polls in 1961, when the official count of a referendum was 1,320,748 to 0, and again in 1964, when a constitutional referendum made Duvalier president for life.

On 29 July 1985, Tonton Macoute day, members were given new uniforms and honoured by Jean-Claude Duvalier's cabinet, and in the exuberance they shot 27 people in the streets. The force was formally disbanded in 1986, at the height of the anti-Duvalier protests, but its members continued to terrorise the country. Paramilitary groups that grew out of it carried out massacres during the following decade. The Front for the Advancement and Progress of Haïti, led by Emmanuel Constant, was described by the journalist Linda Diebel as a modern Tonton Macoute, and it was disbanded in 1994.
tonyukuk: Tonyukuk, Bilgä Tuňuquq in Old Turkic, was born around 646. His name is read in many ways, among them Tunuquq, Tonuquq and Toɲ Yuguq; according to Sertkaya it means the owner of a deep and pure idea, while René M. Giraud read it as whose dress is blessed with oil. His title Bilge means wise. In his own inscription he says he was born when the whole Turk people was under Chinese rule. He fled the Tang dynasty in 679 and joined Ilterish Qaghan in 681.

As baga-tarkhan, supreme commander, he advised four successive khagans: Ilterish, Qapaghan, Inel and Bilge. He lost early wars against Xue Rengui but was a leading force in founding the Second Turkic Khaganate, and he campaigned against the Tölis, Xueyantuo, Toquz Oguz, Yenisei Kyrgyz, Kurykans, Khitan and Tatabi as well as the Tang. In 703 Qapaghan Qaghan sent him to propose a marriage to the Wu Zhou dynasty; Wu Zetian accepted, but the accession of a new emperor changed the political climate and the marriage was cancelled. In 712 he commanded the Turkic army at the Battle of Bolchu, a disaster for the Turgesh.

He kept out of politics under Inel Qaghan, who spared him, perhaps for his authority and age or because he was the father-in-law of Bilge Qaghan. In 716 Bilge named him master strategist. Chinese sources say he talked Bilge out of turning to Buddhism and building cities and temples, arguing that a nomadic life made the Turks stronger than the Tang. When the Tang chancellor Wang Jun planned an attack in 720, Tonyukuk crushed the Baximi in the autumn of 721.

His life, deeds and advice on government were carved in Old Turkic script on two steles set up around 716, before his death, at Bayn Tsokto in the Nalaikh district of Ulaanbaatar. He was remembered in Uyghur Manichaean texts at Qocho, and the Yuan official Xie Wenzhi and the Gyeongju Seol clan of Korea claimed descent from him. Friedrich Hirth proposed that he was the same man as the general Ashide Yuanzhen; Chen Hao rejects the idea as anachronistic.
toompea: Toompea, from the German Domberg or Cathedral Hill, is a limestone hill of about 7 hectares in the centre of Tallinn, rising 20 to 30 metres above its surroundings. It emerged as an island from the Baltic Ice Lake about 10,000 years ago and later joined the mainland. Its upper layer is Ordovician limestone, and cliffs of up to 25 metres border it on three sides. In Estonian mythology, as told in the national epic Kalevipoeg, it is the burial mound that Linda heaped over the grave of her husband Kalev.

A stronghold was built on the hill in the 10th or 11th century by residents of the county of Revala, and Henry of Livonia's chronicle calls it Lindanise. In the summer of 1219 King Valdemar II of Denmark took the deserted stronghold and began a castle there. In 1227 the Brothers of the Sword took it and built the first stone castle, but it returned to Denmark by the Treaty of Stensby in 1238, and the cathedral was completed in 1240 where it now stands. Toompea became the centre of provincial authority, clergy and nobility, while the Lower Town gained its own administration, and King Eric IV granted it Lübeck city rights in 1248.

After the St. George's Night Uprising Denmark sold northern Estonia in 1346, and Toompea passed to the Livonian Order, which made its castle a strong centre and completed the first part of the tower Pikk Hermann by 1371. Sweden took the region in 1561 and Russia conquered Tallinn in 1710. A fire in 1684 destroyed most of the buildings of the Great Castle, including the cathedral. Under Catherine II the east wing became an administrative building in 1767 to 1773. Toompea was joined with the Lower Town in 1878, and the Russian Orthodox Alexander Nevsky Cathedral was built in 1894 to 1900.

Toompea is part of Tallinn's Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Toompea Castle houses the Riigikogu, the Estonian parliament, in an expressionist building of 1922 beside the governor's palace and the medieval walls. The Lutheran Cathedral has best kept its medieval look, the Government of Estonia sits in the Stenbock House, and the Estonian Academy of Sciences is in the Ungern-Sternberg palace.
topasses: The origin of the name is obscure. It may come from the Tamil word tuppasi, meaning bilingual or interpreter, or from the Hindi topi, the hat worn by the men of the community as a sign of their attachment to the European community; Portuguese accounts call them gente de chapeo and French ones gens à chapeau. The group partly overlapped with the mardijkers of the Dutch, who also had a Portuguese cultural background but served the Dutch colonial authorities, while the Topasses of Timor were firmly opposed to the Dutch.

The community arose from the 1560s around the Portuguese settlement on the island of Solor, a stepping-stone to the sandalwood trade of Timor. When the Dutch East India Company took Solor in 1613, the Portuguese community moved to Larantuka on Flores. In time it became a mix of Portuguese, Florenese, Timorese, Indians and Dutch deserters.

In 1641 their leader Francisco Fernandes led an expedition against the Muslim Makassarese, who had made inroads in Timor, and his musketeers settled on the island. After the Dutch set up a post at Kupang in 1653, part of the population of Larantuka moved to West Timor, and with Timorese allies the Topasses defeated Dutch expeditions in 1653, 1655, 1656 and 1657. The peace of 1663 between Portugal and the Dutch Republic lifted the immediate threat. From 1664 the Hornay and da Costa families governed them as captain-major or lieutenant general, pressing Timorese princes to bring sandalwood to the coast for sale to merchants from Macau or to the Dutch.

They had little contact with the viceroy of Portuguese India and resisted Portuguese officials: they drove out the governor António Coelho Guerreiro in 1705, and after further attacks the Portuguese base moved from Lifau to Dili in 1769. In 1749 Gaspar da Costa marched on Kupang and was routed and killed at the Battle of Penfui, after which many Timorese princedoms went over to the Dutch. The Topasses held on in Oecussi and killed the Dutch commander Hans Albrecht von Plüskow in 1761.

The name Topasses disappears from the records in the 19th century. Descendants of the Hornay and da Costa families continued to govern locally as rajas, or liurais, of Oecussi into modern times; in the early 1900s the enclave was ruled by Dom Hugo da Costa and Rainha Elena Hornay.
topiltzin-quetzalcoatl: The full name, Cē Ācatl Topiltzin Quetzalcōātl, means Our Prince One-Reed Precious Serpent. He appears in 16th-century accounts of Nahua historical traditions, and the Aztecs, who saw the Toltecs as their predecessors in the region, placed him in the 10th century, though the dates given for his life vary between accounts. One version has him born in what is now Tepoztlán. Sources name four possible fathers, most often Mixcōatl, the god of war, fire and the hunt and presumably also an earlier Toltec king; his mother is usually given as Chimalman.

Few accounts tell of his childhood, but all agree that he proved himself first as a warrior and then as a priest of Tōllan. As lord of the Toltecs he is said to have reigned in peace and prosperity and to have been held a god on earth by his followers. The tradition credits him with ending human sacrifice, so that the Toltecs offered snakes, birds and other animals instead, and with founding a cult of the serpent in which worshippers drew their own blood, priests remained celibate and intoxication was forbidden. Later rulers claimed descent from him to legitimise their rule.

In one version he went in a year 1 Acatl, aged 53, to Tlapallan on the Gulf coast, where he took a canoe and burned himself. Other tales have him travel across Mesoamerica founding communities and naming places, then cross the sea to the east, vowing to return and reclaim Cholula, as Chimalpahin, Motolinia and Ixtlilxochitl tell it; Las Casas, Mendieta and Veytia instead wrote that he would send representatives. In El Salvador, legend makes him the founder of Cuzcatlán, and Maarten Jansen identifies him with the ruler Four Jaguar of the Mixtec codices.

He was often conflated with the deity Quetzalcoatl. The Florentine Codex, compiled under Bernardino de Sahagún, records that Moctezuma II mistook Hernán Cortés for the returning Quetzalcoatl, but most modern scholars regard this as one of the myths of the conquest that arose in the early post-conquest period. He is usually shown with a plumed headpiece, a curved baton and a feather-rimmed shield bearing the wind jewel.
topkapi-palace: Mehmed the Conqueror ordered the palace built in 1459, six years after the conquest of Constantinople. It was first called the New Palace, Yeni Saray, to distinguish it from the Old Palace in Beyazıt Square, and received the name Topkapı, Cannon Gate, only later: during the reign of Mahmud I the name of a destroyed seaside palace was transferred to it.
