The complex expanded over the centuries, with major renovations after the earthquake of 1509 and the fire of 1665. The Conqueror's Pavilion, built about 1460, is among its oldest buildings.

The palace stands on Seraglio Point, a promontory where the Golden Horn, the Bosphorus and the Sea of Marmara meet. It has four main courtyards and many smaller buildings. The First Courtyard, the largest, was an outer precinct known as the Court of the Janissaries, and held the church of Hagia Irene, which the Ottomans used as a storehouse and armoury.

The Second Courtyard, or Divan Square, was probably completed around 1465 and took its final form around 1525 to 1529 under Suleiman I; the Imperial Council building stands there, where the Grand Vizier and other ministers met, with the kitchens, remodelled by the court architect Mimar Sinan after the fire of 1574. Beyond the Gate of Felicity lies the Third Courtyard, the private and residential part, which holds the Audience Chamber and the library of Ahmed III. The Fourth Courtyard has pavilions, gardens and terraces, including the Baghdad Kiosk, built after the Baghdad campaign of Murad IV.

The palace served as the administrative centre of the Ottoman Empire and the main residence of its sultans. The Imperial Harem, with more than 400 rooms, housed the sultan's mother, his consorts and concubines, his children and their servants, under the guard of eunuchs. The Sultan received audiences in the Second Courtyard, seated on the gold-plated Bayram throne.

After the 17th century the palace gradually lost importance, as sultans preferred their new palaces along the Bosphorus, but it kept functions such as the imperial treasury, library and mint. A government decree of 3 April 1924 made it a museum. Its collections include Ottoman clothing, weapons, miniatures, religious relics and illuminated manuscripts, and the palace forms part of the Historic Areas of Istanbul, recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1985.
toprak-kala: Toprak-Kala is part of the Fifty fortresses oasis of modern Uzbekistan. Its founding probably followed the abandonment of Akchakhan-Kala, 14 km to the south-west. The small fortress of Kyzyl-Kala, the Red fortress, stands 1 km to the west and was also built in the 1st to 4th centuries CE, possibly to defend the city. Koi Krylgan Kala, another major site of the oasis, lies 30 km to the south-east.

The city appears to have been built by Artav (Artabanos), ruler of Khwarezm, in the 1st or 2nd century CE. Coins of the Kushan rulers Vima Kadphises and Kanishka found there interrupt a series of coins of Chorasmian kings, which suggests to some scholars that Chorasmia was under Kushan control for a time in the 2nd century CE; others read the coinage as showing that the Kushan did not control Khwarezm. Sometime after 305 CE, under the Afrighid dynasty, the Chorasmian capital moved to Kyat, modern Beruniy.

Sergey Tolstov's Chorasmian Expedition explored the ruins in 1938, and the palace was dated by the coins of Vima Kadphises, Kanishka and Artav. Its wall paintings represent Zoroastrian deities. High-reliefs of standing figures in robes of Hellenistic style are thought to derive from the Greco-Buddhist art of Gandhara, reflecting Kushan influence, though they may also be the work of artisans from nearby Bactria, where a Hellenistic tradition had lasted since the Greco-Bactrian kingdom.

The ruins lie in Karakalpakstan, in Uzbekistan, and Sergey Tolstov drew a reconstruction of the ancient city. The statues found there are now in the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg. Kyzyl-Kala, once restored in the 12th century CE, has been renovated in modern times to show how such a fortress originally looked.
torah: The Hebrew word tōrā derives from a root meaning to guide or to teach, so "teaching" or "instruction" fits it better than "law". The Alexandrian Jews who made the Septuagint used the Greek word nomos, and Greek and Latin Bibles then began calling the five books The Law. Scholars usually call them the Pentateuch, from a Greek word meaning five scrolls, first used in the Hellenistic Judaism of Alexandria. The Talmud states that Moses wrote the Torah, except for its last eight verses, which it assigns to Joshua. Most scholars see the final Torah as a product of the Persian period (539–332 BCE, probably 450–350 BCE), resting on earlier sources.

The Torah opens with the creation of the world and ends with the death of Moses on Mount Nebo, just before the Israelites cross into Canaan. Genesis divides into a primeval history (chapters 1–11), including the flood, and an ancestral history (chapters 12–50) of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. Exodus tells of the departure from slavery in Egypt and the giving of laws at Mount Sinai. Leviticus gives rules for the Tabernacle, clean and unclean foods, the Day of Atonement and a Holiness Code. Numbers takes its name from two censuses. Deuteronomy consists of three speeches by Moses on the plains of Moab, followed by the Song of Moses and the Blessing of Moses.

In Rabbinic Judaism the Written Torah is paired with the Oral Torah, interpretations that tradition says were handed down from Moses and are now embodied in the Talmud and Midrash. A scribe copies the text by hand on a scroll, and an error in a single letter of its 304,805 letters makes a scroll unfit for use. A portion is read in synagogues on Monday and Thursday mornings and on Saturdays. The Greek Septuagint dates from the 3rd century BCE. The Samaritans keep their own Pentateuch in the Samaritan script, with some 6,000 differences from the Masoretic Text. Muslims hold that a Tawrāh was given to the Children of Israel but was later corrupted.
toramana: Toramana, also called Toramana Shahi Jauvla, was king of the Alchon Huns from about 493. He consolidated Alchon power in Punjab and conquered parts of northern and central India, including Eran in Madhya Pradesh. The Sanjeli inscription speaks of his control of Malwa and Gujarat, and his territory also took in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Kashmir. Seals in the names of Toramana and Hunaraja found at Kausambi suggest that the Alchon Huns sacked the city around 497-500.

His inscriptions show him adopting Indian ways of rule. The Khura inscription from the Salt Range, now in Lahore, gives him the Indian titles Rajadhiraja Maharaja beside Central Asian ones; written in hybrid Sanskrit, it records the gift of a Buddhist monastery to the Mahisasaka school by Rotta Siddhavriddhi, who wished to share its merit with the king and his family. The Eran Boar inscription, cut in eight lines of Brahmi on the neck of a statue of Vishnu as the boar Varaha, records a temple built by Dhanyaviṣṇu in the first year of the reign of the King of Kings Toramana.
A few of his silver coins closely follow Gupta silver coins, with the king's head turned to the left, the fantailed peacock on the reverse and the name Toramana Deva.

The Risthal inscription, found in 1983, records that the Aulikara king Prakashadharma of Malwa defeated him around 515. The historian Thaplyal argues that Toramana then ruled as a vassal, probably continuing under Yasodharman, and his inscriptions trace his change from an independent Maharajadhiraja to a subordinate king. He may also have been defeated by the Gupta emperor Bhanugupta in 510, though the inscription does not name the opponent in the great battle it mentions.

Toramana is known from the Rajatarangini, his coins and his inscriptions. The Gwalior inscription of his son and successor Mihirakula praises him as a ruler by whom the earth was governed with justice, and the 8th-century Jaina work Kuvalayamala says he lived at Pavvaiya on the bank of the Chandrabhaga and enjoyed the sovereignty of the world.
torc: The word comes from Latin torquis, from torqueo, to twist, after the twisted shape of many of the rings. Rigid gold and sometimes bronze necklaces and collars appear in the later European Bronze Age, from around 1200 BCE, among them the three specimens of the 12th or 11th century BCE from Tiers Cross in Pembrokeshire. Many are too small for an adult's neck and were bracelets or armlets, or were worn by children or statues. In Scythian art torcs appear from the Early Iron Age, and thin torcs with animal-head terminals are found in the art of the Achaemenid Empire.

A torc is a large rigid neck ring, made in one piece or from twisted strands, nearly always open at the front. Rings that open at the back are usually called collars. Most surviving examples are gold or bronze, less often silver or iron, since gold, bronze and silver survive burial better. Elaborate examples, sometimes hollow, were cast and then worked, and the Ipswich Hoard includes unfinished torcs that show the stages of work. The Vix torc has two finely made winged horses standing beside its terminals. The Snettisham Torc, a multi-stranded electrum piece of the 1st century BCE found in Norfolk, and the hollow torc of the Broighter Gold hoard in Ireland are among the finest insular examples.

Among the Celts the earliest torcs are mostly found in women's graves, such as the princess's chariot burial at Waldalgesheim and graves at Vix and Reinheim. Some authors think the torc was mostly a woman's ornament until the late 3rd century BCE, when it became a warrior's. Gods such as Cernunnos on the Gundestrup cauldron wear or hold torcs. Some may have been placed on cult statues, and many hoards are deliberate deposits, whether ritual or hidden for safety in war.

According to the Roman tradition, Titus Manlius took a torc from a Gaul he killed in single combat in 361 BCE and received the name Torquatus, and the Romans later adopted the torc as a decoration for distinguished soldiers. Gerald of Wales described a torc called Saint Kynauc's Collar in 1188, a relic on which men swore oaths. Celtic torcs disappeared in the Migration Period, but silver torc-style necklaces returned in the Viking Age.
tore-hund: Thorir Hund, Thorir the Hound, was born around 990, early in the Christian era in Norway, and was both strongly independent and a devout pagan. In Hålogaland, Christianity was also a political tool for subjecting the old chiefs to a king from the south. He belonged to the Bjarkøy clan, one of the more powerful families of northern Norway in the Viking Age, and led expeditions towards Russia, trading in Bjarmaland, today the area of Arkhangelsk.

His family was allied with the most powerful chiefs of Norway. His sister Sigrid Toresdatter married Olve Grjotgardsson of Egge, and his brother Sigurd Toresson, a chief at Trondenes, married Sigrid Skjalgsdatter, sister of Erling Skjalgsson of Sola. With his wife Ranveig he had a son, also called Sigurd Toresson, who later served as a sheriff under Harald Hardrada.

Thorir opposed King Olaf's efforts to unify Norway and convert it to Christianity, and held a personal grudge after the king's reeve Asmundr Grànkelsson murdered his nephew Asbjørn Selsbane; Thorir avenged him and was fined heavily by the king. In 1026 he joined the forces of Canute the Great that drove Olaf out, and he was named Canute's representative in Norway with Hårek of Tjøtta. After Erling Skjalgsson was killed in 1028 he led the faction against Olaf with Einar Thambarskelfir and Kalv Arnesson.

When Olaf returned in the summer of 1030, Thorir and his men led the line against him at Stiklestad, a farm in the valley of Verdal. Earlier reports do not name the man who killed the king, but Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla says Thorir thrust a spear, tipped with the point that had killed his nephew, up under the king's mail shirt.

When Olaf's son Magnus took power, backed by some of Thorir's former allies, Thorir was pushed aside, and he never returned to Bjarkøy. A monument to him and the Bjarkøy clan by the artist Svein Haavardsholm was raised beside the road to the church on Bjarkøy in 1980.
torf-einarr: Einarr Rognvaldarson was the youngest of the natural sons of Rognvald Eysteinsson, Jarl of Møre, by a concubine. The Orkneyinga saga names five brothers: Hallad and Hrollaug, also born out of wedlock, and Ivar, Hrólfr, whom the saga writers identify with Rollo of Normandy, and Thorir the Silent. Rognvald's family had conquered Orkney and Shetland in the late 9th century, and Hallad was sent to govern them but gave up the earldom, unable to hold it against Danish pirates. The sagas describe Einarr as tall, ugly and blind in one eye.

When Einarr offered to go to the islands, the saga has his father scorn him for his slave-born mother but give him a ship and crew. On arrival he defeated two Danish warlords, Thorir Treebeard and Kalf the Scurvy, and made himself earl of Orkney and Shetland. After two sons of King Harald Finehair, Hálfdan Longlegs and Gudrod the Gleaming, burned Rognvald in his house, Hálfdan sailed west and displaced Einarr, who fought back from Caithness and killed him on North Ronaldsay. The sagas claim Hálfdan was sacrificed to Odin as a blood eagle, but the earlier verses suggest he died under a volley of spears.

Harald then campaigned against Einarr but could not dislodge him, and agreed to end the feud for a fine of 60 gold marks. Einarr paid all of it in return for the allodial lands of the islanders, a step later commentators took as the moment the earls came to hold the whole island group from the King of Norway.

Einarr is said to have died of sickness in his bed, leaving three sons, Arnkel, Erlend and Thorfinn, who became earls after him; his dynasty ruled Orkney until 1470. Several sources date his death to about 910, while the historian Crawford suggests he lived into the 930s. Five verses attributed to him survive in the Landnámabók, and the Háttatal names a metre after him, Torf-Einarsháttr. Historians note that much of his saga may derive from those verses, and that his single eye and the sacrifice of Hálfdan give him traits of the god Odin. The true reason for his byname is unknown.
torghut: The Torghut are one of the four major subgroups of the Four Oirats. Their nobles traced their descent to the Keraite ruler Toghrul, and many Torghuts descended from the Keraites. They may once have served as kheshigs, guards of the Great Khans before Kublai Khan, and the Torghut clan first appeared as an Oirat group in the mid-16th century.

After the collapse of the Four Oirat Alliance, most of the Torghuts under Kho Orluk moved west to the Volga region in 1630 and formed the core of the Kalmyks. A few nobles followed Toro Baikhu Gushi Khan to Qinghai Lake and joined the Upper Mongols. In 1698, 500 Torghuts on pilgrimage to Tibet could not return home and were resettled on the Ejin River by the Kangxi Emperor, and in 1699 some 15,000 households went back from the Volga to Dzungaria.

Harsh treatment by Russian governors drove most of the Volga Torghuts to leave en masse on 5 January 1771. Estimates of the group range from 150,000 to 400,000 people, with perhaps six million animals. Beset by raids, thirst and starvation, about 85,000 survivors reached Dzungaria and settled with the Qing emperor's permission, but the Qing coerced them into giving up nomadic life for farming as a deliberate policy to weaken them. Around 70,000 who stayed behind, according to legend because the Volga had not frozen, became known as the Kalmyks.

Kalmyk archers under the Russian general Mikhail Kutuzov fought Napoleon's army in 1812. In 1906 the Qing placed the New Torghuts of western Mongolia under the Altai district; after Mongolian independence in 1911–12 one prince fled to Xinjiang, while the rest were joined to Khovd Province.

Thomas De Quincey wrote a narrative of the flight from the Volga in 1837, and an exhibition in memory of the exodus stands at the Potala Palace in Chengde. Torghut communities live today in Xinjiang in China, Kalmykia in Russia and Khovd in Mongolia.
torgils-knutsson: Torgils, also called Torkel or Tyrgils, came from an old noble family of West Geatish ancestry related to the House of Bjälbo. He is first mentioned in 1282, and documents of 1288 name him as a knight and a member of the Privy Council. Before his death in 1290, King Magnus Ladulås appointed his kinsman, then Constable of the Realm, guardian of his son Birger, and on the king's death Torgils became regent for the underage Birger Magnusson.

After the Republic of Novgorod attacked Tavastland in 1292, he led the campaign of 1293 that conquered parts of Karelia. In 1299 and 1300 he attacked the Novgorodians again and founded the Landskrona fortress on the Okhta river where it meets the Neva. The old trade treaties with Lübeck were renewed on condition that the town supplied Novgorod with neither weapons nor provisions. At home the law of Uppland was established during his regency, and like Birger Jarl before him he sought to end the clergy's exemption from tax, which brought the church's discontent into the open in 1303.

In the quarrels between the king and his brothers, Erik Magnusson, Duke of Svealand, and Valdemar Magnusson, Duke of Finland, he stood by the king. At his castle of Aranäs in 1304 the dukes promised not to work against the king, but they fled abroad and, with the support of King Haakon V of Norway, attacked Västergötland. Torgils helped the king take Duke Erik's castle of Nyköping, and at Kolsäter in 1305 forced the dukes to promise him no harm.

As the dukes' power grew again he made peace with the church, renewing its old rights by a charter of 1305. The dukes won the king's trust and turned him against Torgils, and in December 1305 the king and the dukes arrested him at his estate of Lena in Västergötland. He was beheaded in February 1306 and later reburied in the Franciscan church in Stockholm. His daughter Kristina had married Duke Valdemar, who seems to have repudiated her after the execution. His fall is the subject of Beskow's tragedy Torkel Knutsson, and a statue by Ville Vallgren was raised in Vyborg in 1908.
toribio-montes: Toribio Montes was baptised on 7 May 1749 in the Cantabrian village of San Mamés, into a military family of rural hidalgos; his father, Pedro Montes-Caloca, was a councillor and trustee for the Polaciones valley. He joined the Prince's Infantry Regiment as a captain in 1766, served more than four years at Oran and was wounded in the Invasion of Algiers of 1775. With the America Regiment he took part in the siege of Gibraltar in 1779 and the reconquest of Menorca.

In the War of the Pyrenees he fought at Peyrestortes and Truillas, and as a brigadier commanding the Murcia Regiment he was wounded in 1794 and lost the use of three fingers. He was later governor of the castle of Montjuic, became a field marshal in 1802 after the War of the Oranges, and from 1804 governed Puerto Rico as captain general for almost five years.

Appointed in November 1811 to preside over the Royal Audience of Quito and command the Spanish army there, he and Brigadier Juan de Sámano defeated the patriots of the independent State of Quito and restored the Crown's authority there; he was promoted lieutenant general in 1812. He then turned north against the patriots of New Granada.

After Antonio Nariño's campaign was defeated before Pasto in 1814 and Nariño captured, Montes, who had ordered the execution of other captured patriot officers, commuted his sentence and sent him to prison in Spain. A royalist offensive took Popayán on 29 December 1814 but was beaten at the Battle of the Palo River on 5 July 1815, and Montes recalled Sámano, who defeated the insurgents at Cuchilla del Tambo in 1816.

Montes left Quito on 26 July 1817 and reached Cádiz on 29 April 1819. He was made a member of the orders of Isabella I of Castile and San Fernando and of the Military Junta of the Indies. After sixty-three years in the army he asked to retire to Murcia; when absolutism was restored after the invasion of the Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis, he was given command of the province until he was replaced on 31 December 1827.
torna-a-surriento: Tradition dates the song to 1902, when Guglielmo Tramontano, mayor of Sorrento, asked his friend Giambattista De Curtis to write a song for the prime minister Giuseppe Zanardelli, then on holiday at Tramontano's seaside Imperial Hotel Tramontano. The piece was said to celebrate Zanardelli's stay, and some hold that it was also a plea to him to keep his promise to help the poor town, which badly needed a sewage system. Later research found that the brothers had deposited a copy with the Italian Society of Authors and Editors in 1894, so the song may only have been reworked for the occasion.

The Neapolitan words praise the beauty of the sea and the scent of the orange gardens of Sorrento, and ask a departing lover how anyone could have the heart not to return to this land of love. The second verse says that even someone who has travelled the whole world has never seen a sea like this, and pictures the mermaids gazing at the beloved, wanting to kiss them. Each verse ends with the refrain asking the lover not to leave, not to give this torment, but to come back to Sorrento and let the singer live.

The song was copyrighted officially in 1905 and became one of the best-known Neapolitan songs, beside 'O sole mio, Funiculì funiculà and Santa Lucia. Claude Aveling wrote English words for it under the title Come Back to Sorrento. It runs through the 1954 film Seagulls Over Sorrento, played on the concertina by the actor David Orr, and in an episode of The Honeymooners Ralph Kramden misnames it as Take Me Back to Sorrento by Ernesto Dequisto.
torna-fort: Torna Fort, also known as Prachandagad, stands in Pune district of Maharashtra, about 50 kilometres south-west of Pune by way of the Pabe ghat, above the base village of Velhe. At 1,403 metres above sea level it is the highest hill-fort in the district. The name Prachandagad joins the Marathi words prachanda, huge or massive, and gad, fort. From the fort the forts of Raigad, Lingana, Rajgad, Purandar and Sinhagad can be seen, along with Budhla Machi, Zungar Machi and gates such as the Kothi Darwaja, the Konkan Darwaja and the Bini Darwaja.

Torna is a destination for trekkers, above all after the south-west monsoon, from September to December, and private vehicles run from Pune and Nasrapur to Velhe at the foot of the hill. By order of the District Collector visitors may not stay overnight and must leave the fort by 5 in the evening.

The fort is believed to have been built by the Shiva Panth in the 13th century. A temple of the goddess Menghai Devi, also called the Tornaji temple, stands near its entrance, and a temple of the goddess Toranji is also on the hill.

Shivaji took the fort in 1646, at the age of sixteen, making it one of the first of the forts that would belong to the Maratha state. He built several monuments and towers inside it. While the fort was being repaired and its ruins dug, a large quantity of gold buried at some unknown time was found, and Shivaji used it to build Rajgad and other forts.

After the killing of Shivaji's son Sambhaji, the Mughal Empire briefly held Torna. The emperor Aurangzeb renamed it Futulgaib, in recognition of how hard the defence had been for the Mughals to overcome before they could take it. The fort later returned to the Maratha confederacy.
torontal-county: From 1779 until 1920 the county bordered the Hungarian counties of Bács-Bodrog, Csongrád, Csanád, Arad and Temes. The Tisza formed its western border and the Maros (Mureș) its northern one, and the rivers Aranca, Bega, Timiș and Bârzava flowed through it. The Banat Military Frontier lay along its southern edge until it was abolished in 1873; after that the Danube was its southern border, shared with the Principality of Serbia. Around 1910 it covered 10,042 square kilometres.

A medieval Torontál county existed before the 15th century, with its seat at Aracs, now part of Novi Bečej, until the Ottoman Empire took the area in 1552 and placed it in the Temeşvar Eyalet. In 1594 local Christians, mainly Serbs and Romanians, rose in the Banat uprising. The Habsburg monarchy captured the region in the war of 1716 to 1718, and under the Treaty of Passarowitz it became part of the Banat of Temeswar. The restored county of 1779 had very different borders from the medieval one, and after a great fire in Nagybecskerek its seat moved to Nagyszentmiklós from 1807 to 1820.

In 1848 and 1849 the self-proclaimed Serbian Vojvodina claimed the area, and from 1849 to 1860 it belonged to the Voivodeship of Serbia and Temes Banat, an Austrian crownland. The county was recreated in January 1861 and enlarged in 1876 with the District of Velika Kikinda, having earlier taken in parts of the former Military Frontier, including Pancsova. In late 1918 the Banat Republic claimed it, and on 25 November an assembly in Novi Sad proclaimed the region's union with the Kingdom of Serbia.

Under the Treaty of Trianon of 1920 most of the county went to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and is now part of Serbia, mostly in Vojvodina. The north-eastern part went to Romania and lies in Timiș county, while Kiszombor and eight nearby villages south of Szeged remained in Hungary and are now in Csongrád County.
toronto: Toronto stands on a harbour on the north-western shore of Lake Ontario, on a broad sloping plateau interspersed with rivers, deep ravines and urban forest. The city covers 631 square kilometres and has a 46-kilometre waterfront. The Toronto Islands and Port Lands extend into the lake and shelter the harbour south of downtown. The name was recorded in many spellings. The early form Taronto referred to the Narrows between Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching, which the Mohawk called tkaronto, meaning where there are trees standing in the water, a name recorded as early as 1615 by Samuel de Champlain.

Indigenous peoples have inhabited the area for more than 10,000 years. The Wendat, an Iroquoian-speaking agricultural people, farmed it for centuries before European contact, until the Haudenosaunee invaded and massacred them between 1648 and 1650. By the 1660s the Haudenosaunee had two villages in what is now Toronto, Ganatsekwyagon on the Rouge River and Teiaiagon on the Humber River. By 1701 the Mississaugas, an Anishinaabe-speaking people from northern Ontario, had displaced them at the end of the Beaver Wars. A portage route from Lake Ontario to Lake Huron, the Toronto Carrying-Place Trail, led to the wide use of the name.

French traders founded Fort Rouillé in 1750 but abandoned it in 1759 during the Seven Years' War. The British defeated the French and their Indigenous allies, and in 1763 the area became part of the colony of Quebec. After the broadly disputed Toronto Purchase, in which the Mississaugas surrendered the area to the British Crown, the British established the town of York in 1793 and later made it the capital of Upper Canada.

During the War of 1812 York was the site of the Battle of York, which caused heavy damage and a two-week occupation by American troops. It was renamed and incorporated as the City of Toronto in 1834. In 1867, at Canadian Confederation, it became the capital of the province of Ontario. The city grew beyond its original limits by annexation and amalgamation, reaching its present area in 1998. The completion of the St. Lawrence Seaway in 1959 gave ships access to the Great Lakes from the Atlantic.

Toronto is the capital of Ontario and the most populous city in Canada, with 2,794,356 people at the 2021 census. About half of its residents were born outside Canada, over 200 ethnic origins are represented, and more than 160 languages are spoken. It is governed by a mayor and a unicameral city council of 25 councillors. It is Canada's largest financial centre and the home of the Toronto Stock Exchange, and of institutions such as the National Ballet of Canada, the Canadian Opera Company and the Toronto Symphony Orchestra.
toroodbe: The Torodbe came from Futa Toro, an agricultural strip along the Senegal River and once part of the state of Takrur, and spread from there among the Fulbe. They may have been a distinct group by the fifteenth century, when the Denianke conquered Takrur. In 1644 the Zawaya Berber reformer Nasr ad-Din launched a jihad to restore purity of observance in the Senegal valley and gained the support of the Torodbe clerical clan against the region's traditional leaders. He was killed in 1674 and the movement was defeated by 1677, after which some Torodbe migrated south to Bundu and the Fouta Djallon.

The Torodbe first recruited from all levels of society, especially the poor, and included people of Fula, Wolof, Mande, Hausa and Berber origin, but they spoke Fula, married into Fulbe families and became the Fulbe scholarly caste. Warrior groups looked down on them. They lived at first on charity, and the name is derived from tooraade, to ask for alms. They kept schools teaching in Arabic and built mosques that served as administrative centres, and they levied tithes on harvests and inheritances. Some made the pilgrimage to Mecca and stayed for years in countries such as Egypt.

They aimed to purify Islam and to make Islamic law the law of the land. In practice, particularly in Futa Toro and Bundu, they became a closed society of a few families, and the divisions between slaves and free people and between hereditary occupations did not change.

Malick Sy founded the state of Bundu in the 1690s. A jihad began in Futa Jallon around 1726 or 1727, under Karamokho Alfa, who took the title almami. In Futa Toro Sulayman Baal led a jihad between 1769 and 1776, and in 1776 the Torodbe threw out the Denianke dynasty. His successor Abdul Kader became first Almamy of the theocratic Almamyate of Futa Toro. By his death in 1806 a few elite Torodbe families dominated the state.

In the nineteenth century Usman dan Fodio, born into a Torodbe clan in 1754, led the largest of the Fulani jihads and established the Sokoto Caliphate in 1808. El Hadj Umar Tall created the Toucouleur Empire. By the mid-nineteenth century the Torodbe almamis in present-day Senegal had become hereditary oligarchies, and the French gave them political and economic support in return for permission to build fortified posts along the Senegal valley.
toros-roslin: Little is known of Roslin's life beyond what the colophons of his manuscripts record, in which he appears as a chronicler of his time. In the earliest, the Zeytun Gospel of 1256, he signed himself Toros surnamed Roslin. Only noble Armenians bore surnames, yet Roslin is not among the noble families, and he may have descended from one of the marriages between Armenians and Franks. Levon Chookaszian traced the name to Henry Sinclair, baron of Roslin, who accompanied Godfrey of Bouillon on the crusade of 1096.

His colophons name his brother Anton and ask readers to remember his teachers in their prayers. In 1260 he mentions a son, which suggests that he was a priest rather than a monk, and by 1265 he had apprentices of his own.

He worked in the scriptorium of Hromkla, the patriarchal see since 1151. His patrons were Catholicos Constantine I, King Hethum I, his wife Isabella, their children and above all Prince Levon, whom he portrayed in 1250 and again in 1262 with his bride Keran of Lampron. Four of his signed manuscripts belong to the Armenian Patriarchate of Jerusalem; the Sebastia Gospel of 1262, the most richly decorated, is in the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore, and the Zeytun and Malatia Gospels are at the Mashtots Institute of Ancient Manuscripts in Yerevan. In a colophon of the Malatia Gospel he described the capture of Antioch by the Mamluk sultan Baibars.

He brought new themes into Armenian painting, such as the Incredulity of Thomas and the Passage of the Red Sea, and revived the royal portrait. He added bust portraits and prophets to the canon tables, along with dog- and goat-headed men among the beasts. In his Nativity of 1260 the bodyguards of the Magi are shown as Mongols, the eastern people best known to him and, as Sirarpie Der-Nersessian notes, the allies of King Hethum I.

Neither his contemporaries nor his pupils mention him, and later centuries name him only once, when the scribe Mikayel at Sebastea in the late 17th century found and copied a gospel book that Roslin had illustrated in 1262. Der-Nersessian gave him the longest chapter of her Miniature Painting in the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia. A basalt statue of him 3.4 metres high has stood before the Matenadaran since 1967.
torpedo: The word torpedo first named electric rays, from the Latin torpēdō, meaning lethargy or sluggishness. In naval usage the American inventor David Bushnell was reported to have used it for his submarine, and this probably inspired Robert Fulton, who used it for his stationary mines. Historically the term covered primitive naval mines and spar torpedoes, used ad hoc until the late 19th century, and from about 1900 it has been used strictly for self-propelled underwater explosive devices. Around 1280 the engineer Hasan al-Rammah, who worked for the Mamluk Sultanate, described a rocket-propelled surface craft carrying an explosive payload, which historians classify as a surface-skimming rocket rather than an underwater missile.

The first prototype of a self-propelled torpedo came from a commission by Giovanni Luppis, an Austro-Hungarian naval officer from Fiume, and Robert Whitehead, an English engineer who managed a factory there. In 1864 Luppis gave Whitehead the plans of the Salvacoste, a floating weapon steered from the land by ropes, which the naval authorities had dismissed because its steering and propulsion were impractical.

The Whitehead torpedo of 1866, the first successful self-propelled torpedo, used compressed air stored at pressures of up to 2.55 MPa to drive a piston engine turning a single propeller. It travelled about 180 metres at an average speed of 6.5 knots. The Austrian government invested in it, and by 1870 improved devices could run about 900 metres at up to 6 knots. In 1871 the British Admiralty paid Whitehead £15,000 for certain developments. In 1906 his torpedoes covered nearly 1,000 metres at an average of 35 knots. Rivals included the wire-driven Brennan torpedo, the flywheel-driven Howell torpedo and John Ericsson's electric torpedo of 1873.

The Royal Navy frigate HMS Shah first fired a self-propelled torpedo in anger at the Battle of Pacocha on 29 May 1877, against the Peruvian ironclad Huáscar, which outran it. On 16 January 1878 the Turkish steamer Intibah became the first vessel sunk by self-propelled torpedoes, launched from torpedo boats under Stepan Osipovich Makarov during the Russo-Turkish War. Torpedoes allowed small boats to destroy large ships without big guns. In the First World War German submarine torpedoes disrupted supply lines to Britain, and in May 1915 a torpedo from SM U-20 sank the Lusitania off Ireland in eighteen minutes, killing nearly 1,200 civilian passengers.
torquato-tasso: Tasso was born in Sorrento, the son of Bernardo Tasso, a nobleman of Bergamo and a well-known poet, and Porzia de' Rossi, a noblewoman born in Naples. His father served Ferrante Sanseverino, Prince of Salerno, and when the prince was outlawed by the Spanish government of Naples, Bernardo shared his fate and was proclaimed a rebel along with his son. In 1552 Torquato was in Naples, educated by the Jesuits, and at eight he was already known for his precocity.

He later joined his father in exile in Rome. His mother died suddenly in 1556, and his father believed she had been poisoned by her brother. From 1565 Tasso's life centred on the castle at Ferrara, where he wrote love poems for Lucrezia Bendidio and Laura Peverara and was protected by the princesses Lucrezia and Eleonora d'Este.

Gerusalemme liberata, Jerusalem Delivered, takes the First Crusade as its subject and aims to ennoble the Italian epic with a strict unity of plot, with Virgil as model. Its nominal hero is Godfrey of Bouillon, but readers have been drawn more to its romantic episodes: Armida, the witch converted by her love for a crusader, Clorinda, the female warrior baptised as she dies, and Erminia, in love with Tancredi.

His other works include the Rime, nearly two thousand lyrics written between 1567 and 1593 under Petrarch's influence, the tragedy Re Torrismondo, 28 Dialogues, and the Discorsi del poema eroico, published in 1594, his main statement of poetics. In 1592 he published a revised poem, Gerusalemme Conquistata, from which the romantic episodes were removed.

In the 1570s Tasso developed a persecution mania, fearing denunciation to the Inquisition and poison. After quarrels at the Ferrara court he was sent in March 1579 to the madhouse of St. Anna, where he remained until July 1586. His illness is now believed to have been bipolar disorder. He spent his last years moving between Rome, Naples, Florence and Mantua, and died on 25 April 1595, a few days before he was to be crowned on the Capitoline Hill by Pope Clement VIII.

Spenser and Milton were greatly influenced by him, Monteverdi set his verse, and Goethe wrote a play, Torquato Tasso, in 1790. Edward Fairfax's complete English translation, Godfrey of Bouillon, appeared in 1600. Until the early 20th century he remained one of the most widely read poets in Europe.
torrazzo-of-cremona: Popular tradition holds that work on the tower began in 754. In fact it was built in four phases: the first in the 1230s, up to the third dripstone; the second between 1250 and 1267, up to the dripstone below the quadriphore; the third around 1284; and the last, the marble spire, completed in 1309. Excavations in the 1980s found older structures beneath it, thought to be the remains of an earlier churchyard or its cemetery, or of Roman buildings.

The tower measures 112.54 metres. A plaque in the wall at its base gives its height as 250 arms and 2 ounces, about 111 metres in the old measures of the Lombard towns. It is counted the third tallest brick bell tower in the world, after the tower of St. Martin's Church in Landshut, completed in 1500, and that of the Church of Our Lady in Bruges, completed in 1465, but it is older than both and is the oldest standing brick structure taller than 100 metres.

On the fourth storey is the largest astronomical clock in the world, with a dial 8.20 metres across. Its mechanism was built by Francesco and Giovan Battista Divizioli, father and son, between 1583 and 1588. The face shows the sky with the zodiac constellations and the Sun and Moon moving through them, and has been repainted many times, among others by Giovanni Battista Dordoni. Its hands, four in number with one of them double, show the phases of the Moon, the solstices, the equinoxes and eclipses. The tower holds seven bells, all tuned in the scale of A major, and a further bell that strikes the hour.
torrens-title: Under the common law a seller proved ownership by tracing the chain of title deeds back to the Crown's first grant, perhaps centuries earlier, and even a full search gave a buyer no complete security, since no one can give what he does not have. Deeds registration gave registered documents priority, but its register could be challenged in court at any time, so transfers stayed slow and costly.

Sir Robert Richard Torrens, Registrar-General and Treasurer of South Australia and later a member of its House of Assembly, lobbied for years for change and steered his private member's bill through Parliament as the Real Property Act 1858. He drew on the British registration of merchant ships, which he knew from his years as a customs official, and on the ideas of Ulrich Hübbe, a German lawyer in South Australia who knew the Hanseatic registry of Hamburg. The first sale under the system went to the pastoralist William Ransom Mortlock on 25 August 1858.

The system rests on title by registration: the register itself is conclusive evidence of ownership, termed indefeasibility, and land changes hands by an entry on it rather than by deed. Three principles describe it. The mirror principle holds that the register shows every dealing affecting a lot; the curtain principle that a buyer need not look behind it; the indemnity principle that the state compensates loss caused by fraud or by the Registrar's error. Each parcel receives a volume-folio number tied to a registered plan, and once registered land cannot leave the system. Indefeasibility has limits, such as fraud by the registered holder, which differ between jurisdictions.

All the Australian colonies adopted the system between 1858 and 1875. The colony of Vancouver Island followed in 1861, New Zealand in 1870 and Ireland in 1892; Thailand took it up in 1901, the Philippines in 1902, the Dominican Republic in 1920 and Turkey in 1926, and the British brought it to Mandatory Palestine. In the United States the title insurance industry strenuously opposed it, and several states that tried it, among them Illinois after the Great Chicago Fire and California from 1914 to 1955, later gave it up.
torres-strait-islanders: The Torres Strait Islanders are predominantly of Melanesian descent and share some genetic and cultural traits with the people of New Guinea. Archaeological, linguistic and folk-history evidence suggests that the core of Island culture is Papuo-Austronesian. Before colonisation the Islanders were not a homogeneous group and did not regard themselves as a single people.

Sources agree on five geographical or cultural divisions, though they name them differently; one Queensland government publication lists the Top Western, Mid-Western, Lower Western, Central and Eastern Islanders. Oral history tells of four brothers, Malo, Sagai, Kulka and Siu, who paddled from Cape York to the central and eastern islands. Malo settled on Mer and set out rules for living that combined religion and law, which Eddie Mabo presented in the Mabo native title case in 1992.

Christianity reached the islands in 1871, when the London Missionary Society party led by Samuel Macfarlane and Archibald Wright Murray arrived on Erub (Darnley Island) on 1 July. The elder Dabad received the Bible Macfarlane offered, an event Islanders call the Coming of the Light and celebrate every year on 1 July. In June 1875 a measles epidemic killed about a quarter of the population, and up to 80 per cent on some islands, because Islanders had no immunity to European diseases.

Missionaries sometimes banned traditional sacred objects. In 1898 and 1899 the British anthropologist Alfred Cort Haddon collected about 2,000 objects, now the Haddon Collection at Cambridge. Interest in old ways revived from the 1960s and 1970s, helped by Margaret Lawrie's recorded stories. Until the late twentieth century the Islanders were administered through elected councils, and since 1994 the Torres Strait Regional Authority, with 20 elected representatives, has overseen the islands.

Of the 133 islands, only 38 are inhabited, and the 2021 census counted 4,124 people living on them; many more Torres Strait Islander people live on the Australian mainland. Two Indigenous languages are spoken, Kalaw Lagaw Ya in the west and centre and Meriam Mir in the east, along with the English-based Torres Strait Creole. Islanders have long farmed as well as hunted and gathered, and dugong, turtle and fishing remain central to a seafaring tradition.

Song and dance carry oral history, and each island group has its own performances, with headdresses called dhari. Islanders are the only people known to make turtleshell masks. Their spiritual system includes the stories of the Tagai, and most Islanders are Christian, combining the faith with the customs known as Ailan Kastom. The five-pointed star on their flag represents the five cultural groups.
torrijos-carter-treaties: Panama had sought to renegotiate the Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty almost since it was signed in November 1903, weeks after independence from Colombia. Pressure grew after the Suez Crisis. On 9 January 1964 students raising the Panamanian flag in the Canal Zone were harassed and the flag was torn; in the rioting that followed over 20 Panamanians were killed and about 500 injured, mostly by fire from United States troops. The day is now Martyrs' Day in Panama, and Panama broke off relations until talks on a new treaty were agreed.

A treaty negotiated in 1967 was never ratified in Panama. After the 1968 military coup the government of Omar Torrijos rejected it, held a United Nations Security Council session in Panama City in March 1973 and won the 1974 Tack-Kissinger agreement, which framed later negotiations.

The Carter administration made the canal a priority, guided by a commission under Ambassador Sol Linowitz. Talks resumed on 15 February 1977 and ended on 10 August. Ellsworth Bunker and Linowitz negotiated for the United States, Rómulo Escobar Bethancourt for Panama. The Neutrality Treaty gave the United States a permanent right to defend the canal's neutral service, and the Panama Canal Treaty set the handover of operations and primary defence.

In Panama, where press and party restrictions were lifted for the campaign, the treaties won 67.4% in a referendum on 23 October 1977, with a turnout of 96%. The Senate gave its consent by 68 votes to 32 on 16 March and 18 April 1978, after an amendment sponsored by Senator Dennis DeConcini.

Conservatives led by Ronald Reagan, Strom Thurmond and Jesse Helms called the treaties the surrender of a strategic asset, while supporters ranged from the Joint Chiefs of Staff and Howard Baker to William F. Buckley Jr., who debated Reagan on Firing Line. Under the treaty some 7,000 buildings and nearly 370,000 acres passed to Panama by 2000, many areas in stages as enclaves within Panamanian territory. In December 2024 President-elect Donald Trump raised the idea of the United States taking the canal back, which Panama's president José Raúl Mulino rejected.
torshavn: The Viking settlers of the 9th century held their parliaments, called tings, at neutral and uninhabited places so that no location favoured anyone. The main ting met on the flat rocks of Tinganes, the peninsula that divides the harbour in two, which was the most central place in the islands although no settlement stood there. The Færeyinga Saga says the ting of the Faroese was on Streymoy at the harbour called Tórshavn. A market grew beside the ting and gradually became a permanent trading area, and Tórshavn was never a distinct farming community like other Faroese villages.

In 1271 the Norwegian Crown set up a royal trade monopoly at Tórshavn, with two ships sailing regularly from Bergen with salt, timber and cereal. Officials of the Norwegian and then Danish administration made their home there. Around 1580 Magnus Heinason built the small fort of Skansin at the north end of the harbour, and in 1584 the town had 101 inhabitants. From 1655 to 1709 the von Gabel family held the islands and the monopoly, a period known as Gablatíðin, when islanders complained of unjust treatment and fixed prices. A gunpowder explosion burned Tinganes in 1673, and smallpox in 1709 killed about 250 of some 300 inhabitants.

The town began to develop in the later 18th century, while Niels Ryberg ran the trade monopoly. From 1768 he carried on an entrepot trade, mostly smuggling to England, and he was the first to think of profiting from fishing, with salted cod and herring. Tórshavn Cathedral was first built in 1788 and partly rebuilt in 1865.

On 30 March 1808, during the Anglo-Danish Gunboat War, HMS Clio entered the harbour and the fort at Skansin surrendered without firing a shot. The trade monopoly was abolished in 1856, opening the islands to free trade and putting Tórshavn at the centre of a changed economy. Its town council was founded in 1866, and in 1909 it became a market town with the same charter as Danish ones.

Tórshavn is the capital and largest town of the Faroe Islands, on the east coast of Streymoy, with 14,223 inhabitants in 2024 and 22,444 in the greater urban area. Mountains rise to the northwest and southwest, separated by the Sandá River. It is the seat of the Faroese self-rule government, part of which still sits on Tinganes, and of the Løgting. Since 1990 it has been the seat of the Bishop of the Faroe Islands.
torstenson-war: Denmark–Norway had withdrawn from the Thirty Years' War in the Treaty of Lübeck of 1629. Sweden, successful in Germany under Gustavus Adolphus and then under the Lord High Chancellor Count Axel Oxenstierna, was continually threatened by Denmark–Norway, which almost completely encircled it from the south, west and north-west, through Blekinge, Scania, Halland, Bohuslän, Jämtland and Härjedalen. The Danish Sound Dues were a continuing source of irritation. In the spring of 1643 the Swedish Privy Council concluded that its military strength made territorial gains at the expense of Denmark–Norway feasible, drew up a plan for war, and directed a surprise multi-front attack in May.

Field Marshal Lennart Torstensson, marching from Moravia on Oxenstierna's order, entered Holstein on 12 December 1643, and by the end of January 1644 the Jutland peninsula was in his possession. In February 1644 Field Marshal Gustav Horn, with 10,600 men, occupied most of Scania, Halland and Blekinge except the fortress towns of Malmø and Kristianstad.

King Christian IV placed his confidence in the fleet and just won the Battle of Colberger Heide on 1 July 1644, but on 13 October the Danish fleet suffered a decisive defeat at Fehmarn against the Swedish fleet, which included leased Dutch ships under Mårten Anckarhielm. Norway, governed by Hannibal Sehested, was a reluctant participant, and the war was lampooned there as the Hannibal War. Jacob Ulfeldt drove the Swedes out of Jämtland in May 1644, and in 1645 Sehested destroyed the new Swedish town of Vänersborg.

Exhausted, Christian accepted the mediation of France and the United Provinces, and the Peace of Brömsebro was signed on 13 August 1645. Swedish ships were exempted from the Sound Dues, and Denmark–Norway ceded Jämtland, Härjedalen, Idre and Särna, and the islands of Gotland and Øsel. Sweden held Halland as a guarantee for thirty years.

The defeat reversed the balance of power in the Baltic, giving Sweden domination of it and ending its encirclement, while Denmark–Norway looked for a chance to recover its losses, setting the stage for conflict over the next century. With Denmark–Norway out, Torstensson pursued the Imperial army under Gallas south to Bohemia and defeated it at the Battle of Jankau.
tortola: Tortola is a mountainous island of volcanic origin, 19 kilometres long and 5 kilometres wide, with an area of 55.7 square kilometres. Its highest peak is Mount Sage, at 530 metres, and it lies near an earthquake fault, so minor earthquakes are common. Road Town, on its south coast, is the capital of the British Virgin Islands. The name may be an anglicisation of the island's original Dutch name Ter-Tholen, after the Dutch island of Tholen; some sources say that Christopher Columbus named it Tortola, Spanish for turtle dove, while others say he called it Santa Ana.

On his second voyage Columbus sighted the Virgin Islands and named the archipelago after the 11,000 virgins of the martyr Saint Ursula. The Spanish made a few attempts to settle there, but pirates such as Blackbeard and Captain Kidd were the first permanent residents.

The English then established a plantation colony on Tortola and the surrounding islands, and large sugarcane plantations depended on the labour of enslaved Africans. Most early settlers came in the late 18th century, when Loyalists from the Thirteen Colonies received land grants from the Crown after the American Revolutionary War, bringing enslaved people who outnumbered the colonists. Sugar dominated the island's economy for more than a century.

After Britain abolished the international slave trade, the Royal Navy settled Africans freed from illegal slave ships at Kingstown on Tortola, where St Phillip's Church was built as one of the earliest free black churches in the Americas. After slavery was abolished in the British colonies in 1834, planters found it hard to make a profit from free labour, and competition from beet sugar added to the downturn. Many white landowners left, and an earthquake and tsunami struck in 1867.

Tortola is the largest and most populous of the British Virgin Islands, which are under the British flag but use the United States dollar as their official currency because of their trade with the neighbouring American islands. Financial services are a major part of the economy, and the International Business Companies Act of the early 1980s encouraged offshore companies.

In the late 1970s the activist Noel Lloyd led a protest that stopped a plan to lease a large part of the neighbouring island of Anegada for 199 years, and a park on Tortola is named for him. Hurricane Irma caused extensive damage across the islands in September 2017, most severely on Tortola.
tortona: Tortona stands on the right bank of the Scrivia, between the plain of Marengo and the foothills of the Ligurian Apennines, in the Province of Alessandria. It is the capital of the Colli Tortonesi, an area that stretches to the border with Liguria and is known for intensive wine production, including Barbera, Dolcetto, Moscato and Timorasso, the last tracing its origin to the 14th century. It is also the only place in Piedmont with three varieties of truffle.

The Romans knew the city as Dertona, probably their oldest colony in the westernmost section of the valley of the Po. It was founded about 123 to 118 BCE at the junction of the Via Postumia and the Via Aemilia Scauri, which merged to become the Via Julia Augusta, and so became an important military station on the road from Genua to Placentia. It seems to have been recolonised under Augustus, and some inscriptions give it the title Julia Dertona. Brutus encamped there while pursuing Mark Antony after the Battle of Mutina.

A bishopric was founded early. Until the 9th century the city was under the rule of its bishop, and in 1090 it became a free commune. In the Middle Ages it was a faithful ally of the Guelphs and was destroyed several times, notably by Frederick Barbarossa, who took it after a siege in 1155 and razed all its buildings. From 1260 to 1347 a series of Italian noble families and adventurers dominated the city, and in 1347 it was incorporated into the Duchy of Milan.

One of its lords, Facino Cane, left his lordships and wealth to his wife Beatrice, who married Filippo Maria Visconti. After the War of the Polish Succession the King of Sardinia occupied the city and count of Tortona was added to the titles of the House of Savoy.

The cathedral dates from the mid-16th century with a neoclassical façade added in the 19th, and the Bishops' Palace from 1584 has a Renaissance portal. The Romanesque Abbey of Santa Maria di Rivalta, in a hamlet nearby, was founded before 1151. Roman remains in the town are traditionally identified as the Mausoleum of the Emperor Maiorianus. Lorenzo Perosi, composer of church music and Perpetual Director of the Sistine Choir, and the cyclist Fausto Coppi were born in Tortona.
tortosa: Tortosa is the capital of the comarca of Baix Ebre in Catalonia, Spain, standing 12 metres above sea level beside the Ebro river. It is protected on its northern side by the mountains of the Cardó Massif, and across the river rise the Ports de Tortosa-Beseit, a limestone massif that has been inhabited since prehistoric times.

Tortosa, from Latin Dertosa and Arabic Ṭurṭūshah, is probably the ancient Hibera, capital of Ilercavonia, whose settlement may lie on the hill of the Castillo de la Zuda. In Roman times it lay on the Via Augusta. It was occupied about 714 in the Arab conquest of the Visigothic Kingdom and remained under Muslim rule for more than 400 years. King Louis the Pious besieged it in 808–809 and, although the city submitted, did not occupy it.

In 1148 Count Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona conquered the city as part of the Second Crusade. Following the appeal of Pope Eugene III, crusaders of many origins, among them Anglo-Normans, Occitans, Germans, Flemish and Dutch, aided the siege on their way to the Holy Land, and the chronicler Caffaro narrated it. The city and its territory were then divided among the victors, with lands granted to foreign crusaders and to the military and religious orders.

Tortosa had a sizable Jewish community in the 14th and 15th centuries. In 1413 and 1414, as an attempt to force conversion, Jews were made to defend their religion in the two-week Disputation of Tortosa, held in the cathedral.

The Castle of Sant Joan, or Suda, commands the city from a hill 59 metres high; the Romans first fortified the place, and the present structure dates to the caliph Abd ar-Rahman III. After 1148 it became a residence of the Montcada and the Knights Templar, and from the 13th century a royal mansion. The cathedral was begun in 1347 and consecrated in 1597. The Royal Schools, founded by Charles V for the education of the Moors, are a leading example of Renaissance civil architecture in Catalonia.
torun: Toruń stands on the Vistula in north-central Poland. Archaeologists date the first settlement near it to 1100 BCE, in the Lusatian culture, and there are few traces from the 5th century BCE to the 8th century CE. In the Roman period two settlements and a cemetery have been found, and a river crossing is visible near the village of Stary Toruń. It was first mentioned in 1226 as Thorun, and from the 15th century the form Thorn came into use.

From the 7th to the 13th century an old Slavonic settlement stood at a ford of the Vistula, on the site where the Teutonic Castle was later built. In the 10th century it became part of the emerging Polish state of the Piast dynasty and grew into a fortified stronghold, which was destroyed around the turn of the 12th and 13th centuries, most likely in a Prussian raid. The Teutonic Knights expanded the town in 1233. From 1264 until 1411 it belonged to the Hanseatic League, and by the 17th century it was a leading trading point, which shaped its architecture from Brick Gothic to Mannerist and Baroque.

Nicolaus Copernicus was born there in 1473. John I Albert, king of Poland, died there in 1501 and his heart was buried in St. John's Cathedral. Toruń became a royal city of Poland in 1506, and a royal mint began work in 1528. After the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 it was annexed by Prussia, was part of the Duchy of Warsaw from 1807 to 1815, serving as temporary capital in April and May 1809, and then returned to Prussia.

Under German rule it was a strong centre of Polish resistance to Germanisation, and the Toruń Scientific Society was founded in 1875. It became Polish again after the First World War, and German forces occupied it from 7 September 1939 to 1 February 1945, arresting, deporting and murdering many Poles, especially the Polish elites.

The city was spared bombing in the Second World War, and its Old Town and central marketplace are entirely preserved. The medieval part was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997. It has the largest number of preserved Gothic houses in Poland, as well as the 14th-century cathedral, which holds the Tuba Dei, the largest medieval church bell in Poland. Nicolaus Copernicus University, founded in 1945, is the largest institution of higher education in the city.
tosa-province: Tosa Province lay in the south of Shikoku, bordering Awa to the northeast and Iyo to the northwest. Its abbreviated name was Doshū. In the Gokishichidō system it belonged to the Nankaidō circuit, and under the Engishiki classification it ranked as a middle country in importance and a far country in distance from the capital. The provincial capital stood in what is now the city of Nankoku, and the ichinomiya, the province's chief shrine, is the Tosa shrine in the city of Kōchi.

The Ritsuryo reforms formed the province by combining the territories of the Tosa kuni no miyatsuko in the east and the Hata kuni no miyatsuko in the west. The name appears in the Nihon Shoki in an entry dated March 675, usually in connection with natural disasters, among them the Hakuhō earthquake of 684, in which a tsunami reportedly swept away a ship carrying the provincial governor. From the Asuka period the province seems to have served as a place of exile. At the end of the Heian period the Heike clan exiled there Minamoto no Mareyoshi, younger brother of Minamoto no Yoritomo, and other exiles included Fujiwara no Moronaga, Emperor Tsuchimikado and Prince Takanaga.

In the Kamakura period the Ichijō family of court nobles established a huge shōen estate in western Tosa and held it into the Sengoku period. In the Muromachi period the Hosokawa clan were shugo but preferred to rule through the Ohira clan from Kyoto. When income from the estate faltered because of the Onin War, Kanpaku Ichijo Norifusa moved to Tosa with the help of the Ohira and became a local power in the west. The rest of the province was held by clans including the Motoyama, Aki, Kira, Tsuno, Chōsokabe and Kosokabe. Chōsokabe Motochika brought all of Tosa under the Chōsokabe and went on to expand across Shikoku, until Toyotomi Hideyoshi confined him to Tosa.

His son Chōsokabe Morichika was dispossessed for siding with the losing Western army at Sekigahara in 1600, and the Tokugawa shogunate gave the province to Yamauchi Kazutoyo, whose clan ruled it as daimyō of the Tosa Domain until the Meiji Restoration. Under the Yamauchi, Kōchi Castle was built and Kōchi became the capital. In the Bakumatsu period Sakamoto Ryōma, Nakaoka Shintarō, Itagaki Taisuke and Gotō Shōjirō, among others, were active in overthrowing the shogunate and founding the early Meiji government.

An early Meiji government survey recorded 348 villages in the province, with a total kokudaka of 494,087 koku. After the abolition of the han system in 1871 Tosa Province became Kōchi Prefecture. The Imperial Japanese Navy battleship Tosa, lead ship of its class, was named after the province.
totila: Totila was the name used by the Byzantine historian Procopius, who accompanied Belisarius during the Gothic War and is the main source for his life. His real name was Baduila, as his coinage shows. Marco Cristini has argued that the consistent use of Totila by Eastern Roman authors may have served a propagandistic purpose, encouraged by Justinian I to delegitimise him as a usurper. He was born in Treviso, a grandnephew of Theudis, king of the Visigoths, and a sword-bearer.

The Ostrogothic nobles elected him king in the autumn of 541, after the killing of Ildibad and then of Eraric, both slain by the Gothic nobility for attempting to surrender to the Romans. The official Byzantine position, adopted by Procopius and by the Romanized Goth Jordanes, was that he was a usurper, but according to Peter Heather he came from a prominent Gothic family.

In 542 Totila defended Verona and defeated a Roman army at the Battle of Faventia, then won at Mucellium, captured Naples in the spring of 543 on generous terms, and by 543 had retaken most of southern Italy. He won support from the lower classes by liberating slaves and distributing land to the peasants, though Cristini holds that Procopius exaggerated the slaves' part in his army. His strategy was to move fast and take the countryside, leaving Byzantine forces in well-defended cities and ports, and he collected rent and taxes instead of plundering. Procopius also records cruelties, including the beheading of Herculanus, bishop of Perugia, and the maiming of the captive general Demetrius.

Totila besieged Rome from December 545 and entered the practically empty city a year later, praying at St. Peter's Basilica. Belisarius dissuaded him from razing it, and retook it by April 546. After Belisarius retreated to Constantinople in 549, Totila recaptured Rome and went on to conquer Sicily, Corsica and Sardinia. A Byzantine fleet defeated his own in 551.

In 552 the eunuch Narses led a force including Lombards, Gepids and Heruls against him at the Battle of Taginae. Ordered to charge with spears alone, the Gothic cavalry rode into the crossfire of Narses's archers and broke. Procopius reports that a Gepid officer, Asbados, speared the fleeing king in the back, and that Totila died at a village called Caprae. A second account says a stray arrow struck him as he fled.

His successor Teia died at the Battle of Mons Lactarius. The Pragmatic Sanction of 554 voided Totila's edicts and called him a most abominable tyrant. Italy was so ravaged by the war that normal life could not return, and in 568 most of the country was conquered by Alboin of the Lombards.
totomi-province: Tōtōmi Province was a province of Japan in the area of what is today western Shizuoka Prefecture. It bordered on Mikawa, Suruga and Shinano Provinces, and its abbreviated name was Enshū. Its name derives from the old name of Lake Hamana. It was one of the original provinces established in the Nara period under the Taihō Code, and its first capital stood in what is now Iwata, at a place called Mitsuke, a name that survived as Mitsuke-juku, a post station on the Tōkaidō. Under the Engishiki it was ranked a "superior country" in importance and a "middle country" in distance from the capital.

In the early Muromachi period the Imagawa clan ruled it nominally before it passed under the Shiba clan, but in the Sengoku period the Imagawa recovered it and effectively annexed it to Suruga Province. After the Imagawa were defeated at the Battle of Okehazama, Tōtōmi was divided between the warlords Takeda Shingen of Kai and Tokugawa Ieyasu of Mikawa. Ieyasu built Hamamatsu Castle, which became the capital of the province in practice, and parts of Tōtōmi stayed contested between Tokugawa and Takeda until Shingen's death.

After the Battle of Odawara and the rise of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Ieyasu was forced to exchange his domains in the Tōkai region for the Kantō. Hamamatsu went to the Horii clan and Kakegawa Castle to Yamauchi Kazutoyo. Once the Tokugawa shogunate was established the Tokugawa recovered their lost lands and assigned Tōtōmi to various fudai daimyōs. The Tōkaidō road from Edo to Kyoto passed through the province, and for defence the shogunate forbade bridges over the major rivers such as the Tenryū, which led to towns growing up at the river crossings. At the end of the shogunate the province was divided among several domains.

After the Boshin War the last shōgun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, returned to Suruga in 1868 to rule the short-lived Shizuoka Domain, and the daimyōs of Tōtōmi were reassigned. After the han system was abolished in 1871 the province's prefectures were merged into Hamamatsu Prefecture, which became part of Shizuoka Prefecture on 21 August 1876. Many unemployed former samurai settled in the Makinohara region and developed the green tea industry. With the Tōkaidō Main Line railway Hamamatsu grew into a major commercial and industrial centre, especially through the cotton and silk-spinning industries.
tottori-prefecture: Tottori Prefecture lies in the Chūgoku region of Honshu and has an area of 3,507.13 square kilometres. It borders Shimane Prefecture to the west, Hiroshima to the south-west, Okayama to the south and Hyōgo to the east. Its capital and largest city is Tottori, and other major cities include Yonago, Kurayoshi and Sakaiminato.

The prefecture holds the Tottori Sand Dunes, the largest dune system in Japan, and Mount Daisen, at 1,729 metres the highest peak of the Chūgoku Mountains. The name combines the characters for bird and to get: early residents lived by catching the region's plentiful waterfowl. It first appears in the Nihon shoki, in an account of a swan given to a mute imperial prince.

People settled the area early, as remains from the Jōmon period show. The Mukibanda Yayoi remains, in the foothills of Mount Daisen, are the largest known Yayoi settlement in Japan, and many kofun tumuli date from the Kofun period. Under the Taika reforms of 645 the area became two provinces, Hōki and Inaba.

During the Genpei War of 1180–1185 Tottori was a base for forces opposed to the Taira, notably at the temples of Daisen-ji and Sanbutsu-ji. Successive clans, above all the Yamana, held the region in the Sengoku period. After the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 the Tokugawa shogunate installed the Ikeda clan at Tottori Castle, and the clan kept control through the Edo period.

The two provinces remained until the Meiji Restoration of 1868. In the 20th century Tottori's harbours on the Sea of Japan served as a transit point for goods to Japan's colonial territories. The 1943 Tottori earthquake, of magnitude 7.2, destroyed 80 percent of the city of Tottori. Postwar land reform greatly increased agricultural output.

Tottori is the least populous prefecture of Japan, with about half a million people. It is heavily agricultural, producing nashi pears, nagaimo yams, Japanese scallions, watermelon and rice. Natural parks cover part of its area, including the Daisen-Oki and Sanin Kaigan National Parks. Sanbutsu-ji at Misasa, a Heian period temple, and the Ishitani Residence at Chizu, an Edo period family residence, are each designated a National Treasure of Japan. Sakaiminato Port offers a ferry route to Oki Island, and Sakaiminato's Kitarō Road honours the manga character created by Shigeru Mizuki.
touba: Touba began as a simple hamlet of Baol. Cheikh Amadou Bamba (1853 to 1927), the Sufi founder of the Mouride order, is said to have raised it to prominence when under a large tree there he experienced a cosmic vision of light. He founded Touba in 1887, and the holy site remained a small isolated place in the wilderness until his death and burial, 40 years later, at the site of the Great Mosque. The origin of the name is uncertain. The Encyclopaedia of Islam concludes that it most likely stems from a reference to tuba, blessing, and the name also matches that of a tree in Paradise in Islamic tradition.

Touba is a city in central Senegal, in Diourbel Region, forming an urban agglomeration with Mbacké. It had 1,120,824 inhabitants in 2023. It is the holy city of Mouridism, which Bamba conceived as having a social mission to return society to the Straight Path of Islam. Alcohol and tobacco are forbidden. The Grand Magal pilgrimage attracts around two million people each year, mostly Mourides.

The city is a sacred area with a quasi-extraterritorial status in Senegal, under the control of a general caliph and his helpers. The Great Mosque, completed in 1963 and enlarged since, has five minarets and three large domes; its central minaret, 87 metres high, is called Lamp Fall after Sheikh Ibrahima Fall, one of Bamba's disciples. Bamba is buried there, and nearby are the mausolea of his sons, the caliphs of the order.
toubou-people: The name Toubou or Tubu is explained in the Kanuri language as meaning man who lives in Tibesti, or alternatively from Old Tebu as rock people. The Toubou are native to the Tibesti Mountains and live in the central Sahara in northern Chad, southern Libya, north-eastern Niger and north-western Sudan.

They are generally divided into two closely related groups, the Teda in the north and the Daza to the south, who are believed to share a common origin and speak the Tebu languages, Tedaga and Dazaga, of the Saharan branch of the Nilo-Saharan family. The Daza are the more numerous. Their ancient history is unclear. They may be the Ethiopians whom Herodotus describes as hunted by the Garamantes, though Jean Chapelle calls that connection speculative.

The earliest known mention of the Toubou in Islamic literature, together with the Zaghawa, is in a ninth-century text by the scholar Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Khwarizmi in the same century mentioned the Daza. During the era of trans-Saharan trade they lived on lands that merchant caravans often crossed, along the Kufra oasis routes, though it is not known whether they took part in the caravan trade. In the eighteenth century the Toubou of Kaouar formed an independent city until 1870, when the Kerdusian tribe of the Fezzan ended their rule, according to a manuscript.

In 1936 the French colonial administration in Chad gave legal standing to Toubou regional groupings by dividing the Daza and Teda regions into cantons, which continued after independence in 1960. In 1953 Kelleï Chahaïmi, chief of the Kamaya canton, decreed with the French the emancipation of all slaves in the Borkou region. In the First Chadian Civil War the derde Oueddei Kichidemi went into exile in Libya after protesting abuses by the Chadian garrison at Bardaï, and his son Goukouni Oueddei became a leader in FROLINAT and later a head of state. Hissène Habré replaced him in 1982.

Toubou life centres on herding or on farming oases, where dates, grain and legumes are grown. Herds include dromedaries, goats, cattle, donkeys and sheep, which also serve as dowry. In a few places the Toubou mine salt and natron. Many remain semi-nomadic, and others live in palm-thatched or mud houses. Society is patrilineal and clan-based, each clan having certain oases, pastures and wells, and the clan holds the strongest sense of identity. Because nomads are scattered, belonging to a clan means finding hospitality in most settlements. Customary law draws on Islamic law, and a killing is settled between the families, ending in payment of blood money.

According to Chapelle, Toubou society was historically stratified into freemen, artisanal castes such as the Azza, who were segregated by others, and slaves. Slaves entered Teda and Daza society through raids on peoples to the south.
toul: Toul was known to the Romans as Tullum Leucorum and was the capital of the Gaulish tribe of the Leuci. The diocese of Toul was founded around 365 and lasted until 1807, so the town was the seat of the bishops of Toul. In 550 King Theudebald convoked a synod here, and in 612 King Theudebert II of Austrasia was defeated near the town by King Theuderic II of Burgundy.

By the Treaty of Meerssen of 870 Toul became part of East Francia, the later Holy Roman Empire. In the High Middle Ages it became a Free Imperial City. King Henry II of France annexed it in 1552, and the Holy Roman Empire recognised this in the Peace of Westphalia of 1648. It then formed part of the French province of the Three Bishoprics.

In the siege of 1870 during the Franco-Prussian War, the last time Toul's defences were used as a classic fortress, 64 guns opened fire at 6:00 a.m. on 23 September. The fortress surrendered at 3:00 p.m. after 2,433 shells had been fired. In the First World War the town was the primary base of the Air Service of the United States Army, and the St. Mihiel Offensive and the Meuse-Argonne Offensive of September 1918 were launched from the Toul Sector.

Toul is a commune in the Meurthe-et-Moselle department and a sub-prefecture of it, between Commercy and Nancy, where the Moselle meets the Canal de la Marne au Rhin. The stone ramparts that encircle the old town are the work of Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban, Louis XIV's military engineer, who designed a new enclosure in 1698, with work beginning in 1699 to 1700. They are not on the UNESCO list of Vauban's fortifications. The old town has a major Gothic cathedral and many houses built as canonical residences in the Late Middle Ages. The surrounding countryside is a wine-growing region, known for the AOC Côtes de Toul and especially the Gris de Toul.
toulon: Toulon lies on the French Riviera at the eastern end of the Gulf of Lion, in the historical region of Provence. Greek colonists from Phocaea founded trading depots along this coast from about the 7th century BCE, and the Ligurians settled the area from the 4th century BCE. After the Romans defeated the Ligurians, a settlement named Telo Martius arose on the site of the city. It became one of the two principal Roman centres for the purple dye used in imperial robes, made from the murex sea snail.

Toulon was Christianized in the 5th century, and its first cathedral was built then. Pirates and Saracens attacked the town often as Roman power crumbled. Provence became part of France in 1486, and in 1494 Charles VIII of France began a military port at the harbour to make France a Mediterranean sea power. In 1524 Francis I completed the Tour Royale at the harbour entrance, but its commander sold it to an imperial commander and Toulon surrendered. In the winter of 1543 the fleet of the Ottoman admiral Barbarossa occupied the town, whose residents were made to leave, under the Franco-Ottoman alliance.

Toulon resisted a siege by the Imperial Army under Duke Victor Amadeus II of Savoy and Prince Eugene in 1707. In 1720 plague from Marseille killed about 13,000 people, half the population. In 1793 the city joined the Federalist revolts against the First Republic and handed itself and its fleet to the British; Republican forces forced them out, and the town was briefly renamed Port-la-Montagne. From 1803 to 1805 a fleet under Horatio Nelson blockaded the port. In 1849 Georges Eugène Haussmann, then prefect of the Var, laid out the street plan of the city centre. On 27 November 1942 French naval officers scuttled the fleet based there, after German forces occupied southern France, and Allied bombing the following November destroyed much of the port.

Toulon is the prefecture of the Var department and has 179,116 inhabitants in 2023, with a metropolitan area of 591,135. It is the third most populous French city on the Mediterranean, after Marseille and Nice. Its military port is the chief naval centre of France's Mediterranean coast, and the city also has shipbuilding, fishing, winemaking and several manufacturing industries. The University of Toulon opened in 1979.
toulouse: Toulouse lies on the banks of the Garonne, 150 kilometres from the Mediterranean Sea, 230 kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean and 680 kilometres from Paris, on the axis of communication between the two seas. The Garonne valley has been a central point for trade between the Pyrenees, the Mediterranean and the Atlantic since at least the Iron Age. The historical name of the city, Tolosa, and that of its inhabitants, the Tolosates, first recorded in the 2nd century BCE, is of unknown meaning or origin, and has been connected with the Gaulish Volcae Tectosages and, by others, with a root meaning little hill.

Charlemagne created the county of Toulouse in 778 to guard the border of Muslim Spain. The disintegration of the kingdom of Aquitaine and the weakness of royal power in the following centuries led to the de facto independence of the county. The treaty of 1229 made Toulouse subordinate to the kingdom of France, and when Joan of Toulouse and her husband Alphonse of Poitiers died without heirs in 1271 the city had no count and was annexed to the royal domain. Royal officers settled in the city, trade and crafts grew, and in 1298 King Philip the Fair eased the ennobling of the capitouls, whose annually renewed council was increasingly made up of rich merchants.

The University of Toulouse was founded in 1229. In the 16th century the woad trade brought merchants of international stature to the city, and the Parlement of Toulouse made it the judicial capital of much of the south of France.

On 10 April 1814 Wellington's Hispanic-British troops fought the French under Marshal Soult at the Battle of Toulouse, four days after Napoleon's surrender, though neither army yet knew of it; it was the last Franco-British battle on French territory. In the First World War the city, sheltered from attack, gained chemical industries and aviation workshops, which began its aeronautical tradition and gave rise to the airmail company Aéropostale.
