Toulouse is the prefecture of the Haute-Garonne department and of the Occitania region, with 514,819 inhabitants within its municipal boundaries in 2023. Its architecture of pinkish terracotta brick has earned it the name La Ville rose. The Basilica of Saint-Sernin, the largest remaining Romanesque building in Europe, and the former hospital Hôtel-Dieu Saint-Jacques are World Heritage Sites for their place on the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, as is the Canal du Midi, which begins in the city. Toulouse is the centre of the European aerospace industry, with the headquarters of Airbus, and its rugby club, Stade Toulousain, is among the most successful in Europe.
toungoo-dynasty: King Mingyi Nyo founded the First Toungoo Empire at Taungoo, far up the Sittaung River south of Inwa, towards the end of the Ava Kingdom. After Shan sawbwas led by Mohnyin conquered Inwa in 1527, many Burmese speakers migrated to Taungoo, which became a new centre. Mingyi Nyo's son Tabinshwehti unified most of Burma, overran the Irrawaddy Delta and crushed the Hanthawaddy capital of Bago, and in 1544 was crowned king of all Burma at the ancient capital of Bagan. The Portuguese had by then conquered Malacca, and the arrival of European traders made Burma an important trading centre again, so Tabinshwehti moved his capital to Bago.

Tabinshwehti was defeated at Arakan and again in the Burmese–Siamese War of 1547–49, and he was assassinated in 1550. His brother-in-law Bayinnaung reigned for thirty years and invaded Manipur in 1560 and Ayutthaya in 1564, making Taungoo the most powerful state in Southeast Asia. He died in 1581 as he was about to attack Arakan, which was never conquered. His son Nanda Bayin and his successors had to put down rebellions, and the empire collapsed in the 18 years after Bayinnaung's death.

Faced with rebellion and renewed Portuguese incursions, the kings withdrew from southern Burma and founded a second dynasty at Ava. Anaukpetlun reunited Burma in 1613 and defeated Portuguese attempts to take over. His successor Thalun rebuilt the war-torn country, and his revenue inquest of 1635 put the Irrawaddy valley's population at about 2 million. From the 1720s the kingdom was beset by raids by the Meitei people of the Chindwin River. The Mon rebellion of 1740 founded the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom, whose armies captured Inwa in 1752 and ended the 266-year-old dynasty.

Restored Toungoo kings created a legal and political system whose basic features continued under the Konbaung dynasty well into the 19th century. The crown replaced hereditary chieftainships with appointed governorships throughout the Irrawaddy valley and reduced the hereditary rights of Shan chiefs. Senior princes of lowland principalities had to live at the capital under supervision, and from 1635 the crown held regular censuses to consolidate its access to manpower and taxes. At its peak the empire has been described as probably the largest in the history of Southeast Asia.
tournai: Tournai lies on the river Scheldt in the Province of Hainaut, 89 kilometres by road south-west of Brussels. In Roman times it was a place of minor importance, a stopping place where the road from Cologne to Boulogne crossed the Scheldt. It was fortified under Emperor Maximian in the 3rd century CE, when the Roman limes was withdrawn to a string of outposts along the road. The Salian Franks took it in 432, and under King Childeric I it was the capital of the Frankish realm. In 486 Clovis moved the centre of power to Paris.

After the partition of the Frankish Empire, Tournai stayed in the western part, which became France in 987. It joined the 11th-century rise of towns in the Low Countries on a woollen cloth industry, and the rebuilding of its cathedral began in 1030. The commune won independence from the local counts in 1187 and was thereafter directly subject to the French Crown. In 1340 Edward III of England besieged it for a month without success, which bankrupted him and forced the Truce of Espléchin. In the 15th century it was a major supplier of tapestry, and the painters Jacques Daret, Robert Campin and Rogier van der Weyden came from Tournai.

Henry VIII of England captured the city in 1513, making it the only Belgian city ever ruled by England, and it returned to France in 1519 after the Treaty of London. In 1521 Charles V added it to his Low Countries possessions. Tournai became a bulwark of Calvinism in the 16th century, until the Duke of Parma conquered it after a long siege in 1581. The Spanish Netherlands, including Tournai, passed to the Austrian Habsburgs in 1713, and France annexed the region in 1794. From 1815 the city formed part of the United Netherlands and after 1830 of Belgium. It was badly damaged in 1940 and has since been restored.

The mixed Romanesque and Gothic Cathedral of Our Lady and the Belfry, considered the oldest in Belgium, are World Heritage Sites. The cathedral holds the Châsse de Notre-Dame flamande, a 12th-century reliquary. The Bishopric of Tournai was the religious capital of Flanders from 496 to 1559. The Grande Procession, begun by Bishop Radbot II during a plague, has been held every year since 1092 except 1566. French is the dominant language, and the municipality had an estimated 68,518 people in 2022.
touro-synagogue: Fifteen Spanish and Portuguese Jewish families reached Newport in 1658, probably from the Dutch or British West Indies, by way of communities such as Curaçao and Suriname. They followed the Spanish and Portuguese liturgy and for more than a century worshipped in rooms of private homes, though they bought and dedicated a cemetery in 1677. The synagogue was built between 1759 and 1763 under the leadership of the cantor Isaac Touro, a Dutch-born rabbi, and dedicated on 2 December 1763. Aaron Lopez, a Portuguese-born merchant and the wealthiest man in Newport, whose trade included candles, whale oil, rum and enslaved people, laid the cornerstone.

The building is held to be the most notable work of the British architect Peter Harrison, an immigrant to British America who lived in Rhode Island. It faces east toward Jerusalem, with the ark of the Torah on the east wall. Twelve Ionic columns, each carved from a single tree and standing for the twelve tribes of Israel, carry the balconies. Above the ark a mural of the Ten Commandments in Hebrew was painted by Benjamin Howland, Newport's city clerk from 1825 to 1875. It stands at 72 Touro Street and remains an active Orthodox synagogue.

In the late 18th century the community sent its Torah scrolls and the deed to Congregation Shearith Israel in New York for safekeeping, and the keys passed to the Goulds, a Quaker family. The building opened only now and then from the 1850s, until Ashkenazi immigrants from eastern Europe revived Jewish life and regular worship resumed in 1883. Judah Touro, son of Isaac, left $10,000 for the synagogue and cemetery.

The congregation reads Washington's letter every year with invited speakers. The site became a National Historic Site in 1946. A dispute over the building began in 2012 when the Newport congregation offered its silver rimonim to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; in 2017 a federal appeals court awarded ownership to Shearith Israel, and in 2019 the Supreme Court declined the case.
tours: In Gallic times Tours was an important crossing of the Loire. It became part of the Roman Empire in the 1st century and was named Caesarodunum, meaning hill of Caesar; by the 4th century the name had changed from Turones to Civitas Turonum and then Tours, and the Tours Amphitheatre was built. Around 380 to 388 it became a metropolis of the Roman province of Lugdunum, dominating Maine, Brittany and the Loire Valley. Its bishop Saint Martin, who shared his coat with a naked beggar at Amiens, made the city a major centre of the medieval West on the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela.

In the 6th century Gregory of Tours, author of the Ten Books of History, restored a cathedral destroyed by fire in 561, and Saint Martin's monastery received patronage from the Frankish king Clovis I. In the 9th century Alcuin of York, a book collector and abbot of Marmoutier Abbey, made the city a heart of the Carolingian Renaissance. In 732 Abdul Rahman Al Ghafiqi's army from Al-Andalus, having advanced 500 km into France, was stopped by Charles Martel at the Battle of Tours. Tours repelled a Viking attack by Haesten in 845, but the Vikings sacked it in 852.

Medieval Tours had two competing centres: the City in the east, with the cathedral and the castle of the Counts of Tours, and in the west Châteauneuf around the Abbey of Saint Martin, which became the economic centre after its enclosure around 918. The two were joined in the 14th century. Touraine was disputed between the counts of Blois and Anjou, and Anjou won in the 11th century.

Under Louis XI, who lived at the castle of Montils, Tours was the capital of France, and he introduced the silk industry, which still survives. The kings and court stayed in Touraine until the 16th century, and the Renaissance left the private mansions and châteaux of the Loire. Protestants were imprisoned by the aldermen in the Wars of Religion, which prevented their massacre.

Tours is the largest city of Centre-Val de Loire and the prefecture of Indre-et-Loire, with 138,668 inhabitants in 2022. From 10 to 13 June 1940 it was the temporary seat of the French government, and German incendiary bombs then burned part of the city centre from 20 to 22 June. Its historical centre is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
toussaint-louverture: Louverture was born into slavery in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the eldest son of Hyppolite, a slave from Allada on the slave coast of West Africa, and his second wife Pauline, who was of the Aja ethnic group. He was a devout Catholic and gained some education from his godfather Pierre-Baptiste on the Bréda plantation. Until 1938 historians believed he had been enslaved until the revolution began. A marriage certificate and baptismal record of 1776 to 1777 then showed that he had been freed between 1772 and 1776.

As a free man he worked as a salaried overseer on his former master's plantation and became a slave owner himself, with several coffee plantations. In 1782 he married his second wife, Suzanne Simone-Baptiste. He later told General Caffarelli that he had fathered at least sixteen children.

When the revolution began he was nearly 50, and he started as a lieutenant to Georges Biassou, a leader of the 1791 slave revolt. He allied first with the Spanish of neighbouring Santo Domingo. He then switched to the French when the Republican government moved to abolish slavery in its colonies. Historians debate the timing and his motives: C. L. R. James held that he joined the French on learning of the emancipation decree, while Thomas Ott sees him as both a power-seeker and a sincere abolitionist.

The third commission's Sonthonax promoted him to general. Toussaint negotiated the British withdrawal and trade agreements with the United Kingdom and the United States, and in 1799 he fought a civil war against the southern general André Rigaud. That War of the South lasted more than a year, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who led much of the campaign, became infamous for massacring mulatto captives and civilians. Estimates of the dead range from a few hundred to 10,000.

On 7 July 1801 he promulgated a constitution that made him governor-general for life with near absolute powers, which challenged Napoleon Bonaparte's authority. He restored the plantation system using paid labour.

Napoleon sent troops under his brother-in-law General Charles Emmanuel Leclerc to take the island. In 1802 Louverture was invited to a parley by General Jean-Baptiste Brunet and arrested on arrival. He was deported to France and jailed at the Fort de Joux, where he died. His wife Suzanne was deported to Jamaica and died there in 1816.

Dessalines led the revolution to its end. The final major battle was fought at Vertières on 18 November 1803, and independence was declared on 1 January 1804 under the name Haiti, from the Taíno Ayiti. Louverture is known with Dessalines as one of the Fathers of Haiti, and in the 19th century African Americans cited him as an example of how to reach freedom. John Brown claimed to be influenced by him.
tovsta-mohyla: Tovsta Mohyla, whose name means fat barrow, is a kurgan in southern Ukraine near the city of Pokrov. It was raised by the Scythians, a semi-nomadic, Iranian-speaking people who lived around the north of the Black Sea and dominated the Pontic steppe from about the 7th to the 3rd century BCE, trading with the Greeks, Persians and Chinese. The land of present-day Ukraine, which Herodotus described in his account of the Scythians, holds perhaps the largest and most significant burials of that era.

When Borys Mozolevsky excavated the mound in 1971 he found two burial vaults of Scythian nobles. The central vault, which held the remains of a nobleman, had been looted, but the side vault, from a later period, was intact. It contained five skeletons, the main ones those of a noblewoman and a child, generously covered with gold. Four slain servants accompanied the noble dead to the afterlife. At the entrances lay wheels from dismantled hearses, and a separate niche held a bronze cauldron and a frying pan.

Above one entrance pit lay a large set of bronze ornaments from a funeral procession, among them six openwork bronze finials decorated with stylised deer and griffins. East of the central tomb were two horse graves with six horses, whose gear was richly decorated with gold, silver and bronze, and three slain servants buried to attend them. Among the weapons, ornaments and clothing the outstanding find was the Golden Pectoral, a neckpiece of solid 24-carat gold 30.6 cm across and weighing about 1,150 grams. Its style is Greek, though its imagery reflects Scythian interests.
tower-of-belem: In the late 15th century King John II planned a defence system for the mouth of the Tagus, but he died before any plans were drawn for a strong fort. King Manuel I revisited the proposal twenty years later and ordered a military fortification on the northern bank at Belém. The architect Francisco de Arruda was named master of the works, and in 1516 he began to receive blocks of stone, partly from those collected for the Monastery of Santa Maria de Belém.

The tower was built of lioz limestone on a basalt outcrop on a small island near the shore, and was finished in 1519. Gaspar de Paiva was appointed its first Captain-General in 1521, and the fortress was named the Castle of St Vincent, after the patron saint of Lisbon.

The tower served as a point of embarkation and disembarkation for Portuguese explorers and as a ceremonial gateway to Lisbon. In 1580 its garrison surrendered to Spanish forces under the Duke of Alba after a few hours of battle, and its dungeons served as a prison until 1830. In 1655 an inscription records its function as a customs control point, where ships paid a tax on entering the harbour. French troops were quartered in it from 1808 to 1814, and King Miguel I imprisoned his liberal opponents there. In 1845–46 renovations demolished the Philippine barracks built over the bastion in the late 16th century.

The tower is a principal work of the Manueline style, with elaborate rib vaulting, crosses of the Order of Christ, armillary spheres and twisted rope, while its minarets reflect Moorish influence. It consists of a hexagonal bastion with spaces for 17 cannons and a four-storey tower about 30 metres high. A carved rhinoceros recalls the animal sent to Manuel by an Indian ruler.

It has often been stated that the tower once stood in the middle of the Tagus and was left near the shore when the 1755 earthquake redirected the river, but it was built on a small island near the bank. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 together with the Jerónimos Monastery, and was added to the Seven Wonders of Portugal in 2007.
tower-of-hercules: The tower is known to have existed by the 1st century CE. It was built, or perhaps rebuilt, by Emperor Trajan, possibly on foundations following a design of Phoenician origin and based on the plans of the Lighthouse of Alexandria. A cornerstone at its base is inscribed to Mars and names the architect Gaius Sevius Lupus, from Aeminium (present-day Coimbra, Portugal) in the province of Lusitania, who made it as an offering to the god.

Until the 20th century the tower was known as the Farum Brigantium, and farum derives from the Greek Pharos. The earliest known reference to the lighthouse at Brigantium is by Paulus Orosius, in his Historiae adversum Paganos written around 415 to 417, who calls it a very tall lighthouse set up to look towards Britannia.

The lighthouse stands on a peninsula about 2.4 kilometres from the centre of A Coruña, overlooking the Atlantic coast. It is 55 metres tall: 34 metres of surviving Roman masonry and 21 metres added in the restoration. The original tower was shorter and wider, since its core was surrounded by a spiral ramp, whose outline is still visible in the restored exterior. The final storey was probably topped with a dome.

In the 18th century the naval engineer Eustaquio Giannini restored the surviving core and built a new fourth storey. UNESCO has called the restoration exemplary, praising the protection of the central core of the Roman monument alongside its return to working condition. Within, the much-repaired Roman and medieval masonry remains visible. The Romans who conquered this region believed it to be the end of the Earth, hence the name Finisterra, and the coast is notorious for shipwrecks, earning it the name Costa da Morte.

Many myths of the lighthouse's origin have been told. In one, mixing Celtic and Greco-Roman elements, Hercules slew the giant Geryon after three days and three nights of battle, buried his head with his weapons and ordered a city built on the site. A skull and crossbones beneath the lighthouse appear in the coat of arms of A Coruña. Another legend, from the Irish Lebor Gabála Érenn, has King Breogán build a tower so high that his sons saw a green shore from it and sailed north to Ireland.

In the Middle Ages crusader fleets bound for the Holy Land stopped there, often landing to walk to the shrine of James the Greater at Santiago de Compostela. Some texts spread the belief that Julius Caesar built it, perhaps from a misreading of the ancient inscription. The tower is a National Monument of Spain and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 27 June 2009. A sculpture garden on its grounds has works by Pablo Serrano and Francisco Leiro.
town-musicians-of-bremen: The Brothers Grimm first published the tale in the second edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen in 1819, where it is number 27, basing it on the account of the German storyteller Dorothea Viehmann, who lived from 1755 to 1815. Contrary to the title, the characters never arrive in Bremen. The tale is classified in the Aarne-Thompson-Uther Index as type ATU 130, The Animals in Night Quarters, and the folklorists Stith Thompson and Barre Toelken see a deep relation between it and type ATU 210, which concerns a cock, hen, duck, pin and needle on a journey.

Four ageing domestic animals, a donkey, a dog, a cat and a rooster, are neglected, mistreated or marked for death by their masters. They set out together for Bremen, a city known for its freedom, to live without owners and become musicians. On the way they see a cottage with light in the windows, where three robbers are enjoying their ill-gotten gains. Standing on each other's backs, the animals perform their first song, and the robbers run away in fright. The animals eat a meal in the house and settle down for the night, the donkey outside, the dog by the door, the cat on the mantle and the rooster in the loft.

The robbers return, and one goes back to check. He mistakes the cat's shining eyes for coals, and the cat scratches him, the dog bites his leg, the donkey kicks him and the rooster crows in his ear. He tells the others that he was attacked by a witch, a monster with a knife, a giant with a club and a judge calling from the rooftop. The robbers abandon the cottage, and the animals live there happily for the rest of their days.

Several variants exist. In a version said to date from the 12th century the robbers are a brown bear, a lion and a grey wolf, all animals of heraldry, and the townsfolk of Bremen applaud the donkey and his friends for ridding the district of them. In another variant the animals return the stolen wealth to their master so that he can rebuild. The folklorist Antti Aarne proposed an Asian origin for the tale type, and Paul Delarue distinguished a Western form, in which the animals are domestic, from an Eastern one with inferior animals, popular in Japan, China, Korea, Melanesia and Indonesia.
townshend-acts: After the Seven Years' War the British government was deep in debt, and Parliament sought to raise revenue in the colonies, first with the Sugar Act 1764 and then the Stamp Act 1765, which was repealed the following year together with the Declaratory Act's claim that Parliament could legislate for the colonies in all cases whatsoever. The Chatham ministry concluded that colonists who had objected to a direct, internal tax would accept indirect, external duties on imports, and Townshend's program rested on that belief. Historian John Phillip Reid called it a mistaken belief of vital importance in the events leading to the Revolution.

Five acts are usually counted. The Revenue Act and the Commissioners of Customs Act passed on 29 June 1767; the first laid the duties and allowed colonial supreme courts to issue writs of assistance to search private property, the second created an American Board of Customs Commissioners of five members based in Boston. The New York Restraining Act and the Indemnity Act followed on 2 July 1767, the one barring New York's assembly from passing bills until it complied with the Quartering Act 1765, the other cutting duties on East India Company tea. The Vice Admiralty Court Act of 8 March 1768 added courts at Boston, Philadelphia and Charleston that judged smuggling cases without a jury.

The revenue was meant to pay the salaries of colonial governors and judges, so that they would remain loyal to Great Britain, and the acts were also to establish the precedent that Parliament had the right to tax the colonies. Townshend himself died suddenly on 4 September 1767, before the last act was introduced.

John Dickinson's twelve Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, appearing from December 1767, argued that any tax laid by Parliament for revenue was unconstitutional. Boston merchants agreed to stop importing certain British goods from 1 January 1768, and George Washington and George Mason organised a boycott in Virginia; British exports to the colonies fell by 38 percent in 1769, but the movement faded by 1771. In Boston the seizure of John Hancock's sloop Liberty on 10 June 1768 set off riots, and troops were sent to the city. Lord North's partial repeal received royal assent on 12 April 1770, but historian Robert Chaffin judged that scarcely anything had changed.
toxandria: Texandria, later written Toxandria or Taxandria, lay in what is now the southern Netherlands and northern Belgium, the area known today as the Campine, Kempen in Dutch. The tribal name Texandri, which may be related to it, appears as Texand(ri) on an inscription dated 100 to 225 CE and as Texuandri in the work of Pliny in the 1st century CE. The form Toxiandria occurs only once, in a 9th-century manuscript of the Res Gestae of Ammianus Marcellinus, while Taxandria appears five times in 9th-century sources and in later documents. Copyists' errors, or the older form falling out of use, may explain the spellings.
The name is generally thought to come from the Proto-Germanic stem *tehswō(n)-, meaning right hand or south, with a contrasting suffix, so that Texandria may be read as the land of the southerners.

Ammianus Marcellinus, writing around 390 CE, is the first to mention the region: after their defeat by Julian, the Salian Franks were allowed to settle at a place in Toxiandria. The name returns in sources of the early Middle Ages. Between 709 and 795 the pagus of Texandria centred on the basin of the river Dommel and its tributaries, with one cluster of settlement between Alphen and Waalre and another around Overpelt.

Through a growing network of alliances among the elite, the region expanded between 815 and 914 to cover modern North Brabant and neighbouring parts of the provinces of Antwerp and Limburg, possibly between Oosterhout, Laakdal and Reppel. In the mid-11th century Stepelinus, a monk of Saint-Trond, placed a region called Campania within Texandria, the first record of that name. From about 1225 Campania, the modern Campine, replaced Texandria as the name of the region. Texandria survived for a time as the name of a large archdeaconry in the diocese of Liège, until Campania replaced it there too by the end of the 14th century.
toyo-queen: Toyo, whose name is written 臺與 or 台与 and who is also known as Iyo (壹與 or 壱与), appears in few historical records, and her origin is unknown. Her birth is given as 235. The Records of Wei and other traditional sources call her a close relative of Queen Himiko, and from Chinese sources and archaeological and ethnological finds Japanese scholars have concluded that she was Himiko's niece. Like Himiko she is described as a female shaman, so that her sovereignty had both a political and a religious character.

When Himiko died, according to the Records of Wei, a great mound more than a hundred paces across was raised over her, and over a hundred male and female attendants followed her to the grave. The man then placed on the throne was not obeyed, and in the killing that followed more than a thousand people died. The ruling council chose another woman, and Iyo, a girl of only thirteen, was made queen. Zhang Zheng, an ambassador from Wei, issued a proclamation that she was the ruler, and order was restored as she followed the political line Himiko had taken.

Iyo continued or restored the tributary relations between Wa and the Chinese state of Wei, and Wei officials were among her advisers. She sent an embassy of twenty people, led by her grand steward Isako, to accompany some of these officials back to China. As tribute it presented 30 Japanese male and female slaves, five thousand white pearls, two large green hooked beads and twenty pieces of brocade with unusual patterns.

Some historians believe that she was the mother of Emperor Sujin. In modern times she has appeared in novels, manga and video games, among them Junji Hasegawa's novel series Matsura Iyohime of 1991, Kentaro Yabuki's manga Yamato Gensōki and Ryoko Yamagishi's manga Ao no Jidai.
toyotomi-hideyoshi: According to tradition, Hideyoshi was born on 17 March 1537 in Nakamura in Owari Province. He had no traceable samurai lineage, and his father Kinoshita Yaemon was an ashigaru, a peasant employed by samurai as a foot soldier, who died in 1543. His childhood name was Hiyoshimaru. Contemporary writings confirm his poor background, and one notes that he had begged in the streets. In 1558 he became an ashigaru of the Oda clan under Oda Nobunaga and soon his sandal-bearer, a position of relatively high status. In 1561 he married Nene, the adopted daughter of Asano Nagakatsu.

Nobunaga and his eldest son were killed in the Honnō-ji incident on 21 June 1582. Hideyoshi made peace with the Mōri clan and defeated the assassin Akechi Mitsuhide at the Battle of Yamazaki on 2 July. He then destroyed Shibata Katsuie's forces at the Battle of Shizugatake and fought Tokugawa Ieyasu to a stalemate at Komaki and Nagakute in 1584. He never took the title of shōgun. Instead he was adopted by Konoe Sakihisa of the Fujiwara and became kampaku, imperial regent, in 1585 and daijō-daijin, chancellor, in 1586, when the court gave him the clan name Toyotomi.

He took Shikoku in 1585 and Kyūshū in 1587, where 200,000 soldiers faced about 30,000 Shimazu. The unification was completed at the Siege of Odawara in 1590, during which Ieyasu accepted the eight Hōjō provinces of the Kantō in exchange for his own five. Osaka Castle was begun in 1583. He disarmed the peasants, required samurai to live in castle towns, and ordered surveys of land and production. In July 1587 the Bateren Edict ordered Christian missionaries out of Japan.

His only son Tsurumatsu died in September 1591, and in January 1592 Hideyoshi adopted his nephew Hidetsugu and made him kampaku, taking the title of taikō himself. In April 1592 he sent an army to Korea, aiming at the conquest of Ming China. Konishi Yukinaga took Seoul on 19 June, but the war settled into stalemate.

Peace talks collapsed in 1596 when a forged memorial came to light, and a second invasion in 1597 had less success. Hideyoshi died at Fushimi Castle on 18 September 1598, and the Council of Five Elders kept his death secret and ordered the troops home. His young son Hideyori was displaced by Tokugawa Ieyasu at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, which led to the Tokugawa shogunate.
traben-trarbach: Traben-Trarbach lies on the Middle Moselle in the Bernkastel-Wittlich district of Rhineland-Palatinate, some 40 kilometres north-east of Trier and 60 kilometres south-west of Koblenz. Traben stands on the left bank at the foot of the former fort of Mont Royal and stretches in a broad strip along the river. Trarbach lies on the right bank, on the Hunsrück side, and reaches inland between steep mountains up the Kautenbach valley. The municipal area of 31.35 square kilometres, largely wooded, makes it the biggest town by land area on the Middle Moselle. The name Traben comes from a Celtic word, Traven, meaning a small settlement.

The Aachener Hof, an estate at Traben, was mentioned as early as 830, when Emperor Louis the Pious donated Traben with its rights to the minster at Aachen. Trarbach was the main centre of the Hintere, or Rear, County of Sponheim, and after the comital family died out the inheriting landholders made it a Palatine-Badish condominium; Trarbach was also the seat of a Palatine Oberamt. The Grevenburg, built about 1350, was destroyed in 1734 after many sieges. Because the county belonged to the Reformation, the town remained mainly Evangelical.

France seized the area in the War of the Reunions of 1683 to 1684, and at Traben Vauban built the fortress of Mont-Royal. Its main ramparts were 30 metres high and 3 kilometres long, with room for 12,000 troops. It was demolished when the French withdrew after the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697, and only its lower foundations remain. The area around Trarbach was annexed to Prussia in 1816, although Zell, not Trarbach, was made the district seat. The two towns were among the first municipalities in Germany to install electric street lighting from the Edison Company, and in 1904 Traben and Trarbach merged into the town of Traben-Trarbach.

The bridge built between the two centres to plans by Bruno Möhring was the first road bridge between Bernkastel and Koblenz and was blown up in 1945, and Möhring also designed the Brückentor and several houses in the town. The Mittelmoselmuseum covers the history of the Moselle valley, the County of Sponheim, Mont Royal and the Grevenburg. Traben-Trarbach is a state-recognized climatic spa, seat of the Verbandsgemeinde of the same name, and home to many wineries.
trabzon: The city stands on the Black Sea coast of north-eastern Turkey, on a table-like central hill between the Zağnos (İskeleboz) and Kuzgun streams. The Greek name Trapezous refers to this hill, since the word τράπεζα meant table in Ancient Greek. Before the Greek colony was founded the area was dominated by Colchian and Chaldian tribes, and Greek authors later mentioned the Macrones and the Chalybes as native peoples. The Pontic Mountains rise behind the coast, and the province's total area is 4,685 square kilometres.

The city was founded in 756 BCE as Trapezous by Greeks from Miletus. It was added to the Achaemenid Empire by Cyrus the Great, later belonged to the Kingdom of Pontus, which challenged Rome until 68 BCE, and then passed to the Roman and Byzantine empires. In the time of Justinian I it served as an important base in his Persian Wars, and an inscription above its eastern gate recorded the rebuilding of the walls at his expense after an earthquake. Its university, the Pandidakterion, was re-established before the 7th century and drew students from Armenia as well.

The Empire of Trebizond formed after a Georgian expedition into Chaldia, commanded by Alexios Komnenos a few weeks before the sack of Constantinople in 1204. It was the longest surviving of the Byzantine successor states. Byzantine writers connected with the Lascaris and later the Palaiologos regarded its rulers as not true emperors. The last emperor, David, surrendered the city to Sultan Mehmed II in 1461, and Mehmed sent many Turkish settlers into the area, though the Greek, Laz and Armenian communities remained.

Under the Ottomans the city was a sanjak centre and then part of several provinces. Ottoman tax books of 1523 show that about 85 percent of the population was Christian, mostly Greek, with an Armenian community making up thirteen percent of adult men. In July 1915, during the Armenian genocide, most adult male Armenians of the city were marched south in five convoys and never seen again.

Trabzon is the capital of Trabzon Province and the second largest city and port on the Black Sea coast of Turkey. Its Byzantine Hagia Sophia, now a mosque, is probably its most important sight. From 1683 to 1921 the Phrontisterion of Trapezous, a teachers' college, operated here and helped spread Greek education across the region; its 1902 building survives. Karadeniz Technical University is in the city, and the horon is the dance of the area.
trachonitis: The Lajat is the largest lava field in southern Syria, covering some 900 square kilometres about 50 kilometres from Damascus, between the Hauran plain to the west and the foothills of Jabal al-Druze to the south. It lies 600 to 700 metres above sea level, and its highest volcanic cone, just west of Shahba, reaches 1,159 metres. Jagged basalt boulders cover most of it, with patches of arable land in shallow depressions. Springs are scarce, and its villages store rainwater in cisterns. The Greek name means the land of the rugged stony tract; the Hebrew Bible calls the region Argob.

For much of the 1st and 2nd millennia BCE the region was influenced by the Arameans of Damascus and the Israelites, and in the 2nd century BCE the Seleucid Empire annexed it. To deal with the brigands, Herod the Great settled 3,000 Idumaeans there, and around 7 BCE he invited Zamaris, a Jew from Babylonia, with 500 mounted archers to settle Bathyra in Batanea. Under Trajan the region passed to the province of Arabia. The Romans built a road through its centre, and towns such as Shahba and Zorava, today Izra', grew up between the 1st and 4th centuries.

Under Byzantine rule building flourished, and Zorava, where the martyrium of Saint George replaced a pagan temple in 515, became a bishopric in 542; by the mid-6th century most of its Arab inhabitants were Christians. The region was later abandoned, then resettled by refugees during the Mongol invasions of the 13th century, which gave it the Arabic name al-Laja, the refuge.

Druze migrants from Wadi al-Taym and Mount Lebanon settled the Lajat from the late 18th century, above all after the 1860 Mount Lebanon civil war, and clashed with the Bedouin Sulut in 1868. Druze live in its central and eastern parts, and Muslims and Melkite Christians in villages along its western edge. UNESCO made the Lajat a World Biosphere Reserve in 2009.
tractor: The word tractor comes from the Latin trahere, to pull, and the earliest recorded use for an engine or vehicle that pulls wagons or ploughs dates from 1896, from the earlier term traction motor of 1859. The first powered farm machines of the early 19th century were portable steam engines on wheels that drove other machinery through a flexible belt. Richard Trevithick designed a semi-portable barn engine in 1812 to drive a corn threshing machine, and William Tuxford of Boston, Lincolnshire, invented a truly portable engine in 1839.

The first gasoline tractors were built in Illinois by John Charter in 1889, combining single-cylinder Otto engines with a Rumely steam engine chassis. John Froelich built another in Clayton County, Iowa, in 1892 and started the Waterloo Gasoline Engine Company, but the venture failed and he was out of business by 1895.

A tractor is designed to deliver high tractive effort at slow speeds, for hauling a trailer or machinery. The earliest, called standard tractors, were meant almost only for ploughing and harrowing, which were difficult tasks for people and draft animals. Implements were first attached by a drawbar, a steel bar to which the implement's hitch was pinned, so the tractor could be used for other tasks daily. Harry Ferguson later developed the three-point hitch, which lets hydraulics raise and lower the equipment. From the 1910s to the 1950s farm mechanics in the United States often converted automobiles, especially Ford Model Ts, into tractors, and dozens of firms sold conversion kits.

Economic historians have called the farm tractor one of the most revolutionary technological innovations in the history of modern agriculture, which vastly increased farm power, raised productivity and reshaped the rural landscape. Adoption met resistance. There were 500 gas tractors in the United States in 1910 and nearly 5,000 in 1920, when 3.6 per cent of American farms had one. The share reached 13.5 per cent by the end of the 1920s and rose to 40 per cent during the Great Depression. By 1935 nearly a million tractors were in use in the United States, against 15,000 in Germany. In the 1910s and 1920s the Nebraska tests, run by the University of Nebraska, helped farmers see through marketing claims.
traidenis: His ancestry is unknown, but Traidenis came from Aukštaitija and was Duke of Kernavė before he took the throne. After King Mindaugas was assassinated in 1263, his son Vaišelga, an Orthodox monk who had set aside his vows, ruled with the support of the princes of Halych-Volhynia and shared power with Vasylko Romanovych and Shvarn of Halych. Traidenis saw a ruler leaning on Ruthenian Orthodox arms as a threat to Lithuania's polytheistic traditions and pressed his own claim.

Vaišelga abdicated in favour of Shvarn and returned to monastic life, and in late 1267 he was murdered by Leo, Shvarn's brother. Whether Traidenis conspired with Leo is uncertain. Vasylko fought on alone through 1268 and was defeated; Traidenis lost three brothers, Barza, Liesis and Svalkenis, in the war.

Tension with Galicia–Volhynia led to the war of 1274–1276, which Traidenis won despite Mongol support for his enemies, bringing Black Ruthenia, with Novogrudok, Grodno and Slonim, firmly into Lithuania. He raided Poland around Lublin and Łęczyca but spared Masovia, allying with its Piast dukes by marriage: in 1279 Bolesław II of Masovia married his daughter Gaudemunda.

Against the Livonian Order he won the Battle of Karuse on the ice near Saaremaa in 1270, killing the master Otto von Lutterberg, and later killed his successor Andreas von Westfalen. The Order built Dinaburg Castle on his lands in 1273, which he failed to take. In 1279 the Order's army was defeated at the Battle of Aizkraukle and its master Ernst von Rassburg killed, and the Semigallians under Nameisis rose and sought his help. In 1281 he took Jersika Castle and exchanged it for Dinaburg.

Traidenis died soon afterwards, the first known Lithuanian monarch to die a natural death, and aid to the exhausted Semigallians dwindled. He left a state more unified than under Mindaugas, with firm royal authority over a core of ethnic Lithuanian lands, and he sheltered Prussian and Skalvian refugees from the Teutonic Order. The alliance with Masovia began over a century of cooperation, and the strengthened state passed to the House of Gediminas.
trail-of-tears: In 1830 the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee and Seminole nations, later grouped as the Five Civilized Tribes, were living autonomously in what would become the American Deep South. Many of their people had become integrated into the regional economy, including the plantation economy and the holding of slaves, who were also forcibly relocated during the removal. American settlers pressed the federal government to remove them, some encroaching on their lands and others wanting more land made available.

President Andrew Jackson, who made removal his top legislative priority, won passage of the Indian Removal Act of 1830, which authorised the government to extinguish Indian title to land claims in the Southeast. In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) the Supreme Court held that the Cherokee were not a sovereign and independent nation. In Worcester v. Georgia (1832) it ruled that the Cherokee Nation was subject only to federal law, not to the laws of Georgia.

The Choctaw were the first to sign a removal treaty, the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, ratified in early 1831. The Seminole were called to Payne's Landing in 1832; most of their chiefs later renounced the agreement, and in December 1835 Seminoles and Black allies ambushed a US Army company, killing all but three of 110 soldiers. The Muscogee had already lost most of their Georgia lands by the Treaty of Indian Springs of 1825. The Chickasaw were paid for their lands and moved from 1837, merging with the Choctaw nation in Indian Territory.

By 1838 about 2,000 Cherokee had gone voluntarily. Forcible removal began in May 1838, when General Winfield Scott received the order to relocate the remaining Cherokee, enforcing the Treaty of New Echota, which the elected tribal leadership and a majority of the Cherokee never accepted. The people were gathered into camps in groups often over 700, where disease spread quickly. The marchers faced extortion, violence, exposure and starvation, and approximately 4,000 Cherokee died.

In all, about 60,000 people were displaced between 1830 and 1850. Exposure, disease and insufficient rations killed up to one-third of the Choctaw and other nations on the march. Historians and the affected nations debate whether the name should cover the whole history of removals or the Cherokee removal alone, and historians classify the events variously as ethnic cleansing or as genocide.

In the Cherokee language the event is called the place where they cried. In 1987 federal law authorised about 3,500 km of trails, the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail, to mark the removal of 17 detachments of the Cherokee. In 1905 the Court of Claims ruled in favour of the Eastern Cherokee Nation's claim, and 1 million dollars was appropriated for eligible individuals and families.
trajan: Trajan was born Marcus Ulpius Traianus at Italica, a Roman colony in Hispania Baetica, near present-day Seville, to a family that came from Tuder in Umbria. His father, of the same name, was a general and distinguished senator who governed Syria in 76 and 77, when Trajan served there as a tribune. In 89 Trajan, commanding a legion in Hispania Tarraconensis, supported Domitian against a revolt on the Rhine led by Antonius Saturninus. He then governed Germania and Pannonia. The elderly and childless Nerva was unpopular with the army, and in the summer of 97 he named Trajan his adoptive son and successor. Some contemporary sources hint that the adoption was imposed on him.

Trajan's entry into Rome in 99 was understated. He gave the people a gift of money but halved the donative to the troops. By showing reluctance to hold power he built a consensus in the Senate, and Pliny the Younger praised him as a ruler who governed by example rather than fear. The Senate gave him the title optimus princeps. He rebuilt the Circus Maximus in stone by 103 and, with the architect Apollodorus of Damascus, built a great bridge over the Danube. He also formalised the alimenta, which supported orphans and poor children in Italy from Dacian war booty, estate taxes and gifts.

In letters to Pliny about the Christians of Pontus he ruled that anonymous denunciations were not to be accepted, though those who admitted the faith and refused to recant were to be executed. He overcame the Dacian king Decebalus, annexed the Nabataean kingdom after Rabbel II's death in 106, and from 113 fought Parthia over Armenia. A Jewish uprising in the eastern provinces in 116 and 117 forced him to withdraw his army.

Trajan fell ill early in 117, sailed for Italy and died at Selinus shortly before 11 August. Tradition places his ashes in the small chamber at the base of Trajan's Column. Dio reports that his wife Pompeia Plotina secured Hadrian's succession by hiding his death until a document of adoption was signed, a story that may rest on rumour. Ancient sources on Trajan are unanimously positive, and in the fourth century emperors were hailed as more fortunate than Augustus and better than Trajan.
trajans-column: Trajan's Column stands in Trajan's Forum, north of the Roman Forum, and commemorates the emperor's victory in the Dacian Wars. It was probably built under the supervision of the architect Apollodorus of Damascus at the order of the Roman Senate, and was completed and dedicated on 12 May 113. It was placed at the northern end of the forum, between two libraries, one for Greek and one for Latin scrolls, and beside the Basilica Ulpia. The Latin library probably held Trajan's own lost account of the Dacian Wars, the Dacica, which many scholars think the sculpted spiral was meant to echo.

The shaft rises from a large pedestal and is hollow: a spiral staircase of 185 steps, lit by 43 window slits, leads to a viewing platform. The frieze winds 23 times round the shaft from base to capital and was an architectural innovation. Its lower half shows the first Dacian war, of 101 to 102, and its upper half the second, of 105 to 106. A personification of Victory writing on a shield separates the two. Repeated scenes show the emperor addressing the army, sacrificing, and the army setting out, while battle scenes are a minority.

Key episodes include the crossing of the Danube, Trajan's voyage up the river, the Dacian surrender at the end of the first war, the assault on the Dacian capital and the death of the Dacian king Decebalus. The relief shows Roman and Dacian arms, forts, ships and costume in detail, and Trajan himself appears 58 times. Some scholars suggest the emphasis on orderly soldiers and construction was meant to reassure the people of Rome, its main audience, about the army.

After Trajan's death in 117 the Senate voted to place his ashes in a chamber in the base, which is decorated with captured Dacian arms; the ashes of his wife Plotina were set there too, in golden urns that later disappeared. His statue on top vanished in the Middle Ages, and on 4 December 1587 Pope Sixtus V crowned the column with a bronze figure of Saint Peter, which remains.

The design inspired later victory columns, among them those of Marcus Aurelius, Arcadius in Constantinople and the Colonne Vendôme in Paris. Its inscription, among the best-known examples of Roman square capitals, is the basis of the typeface Trajan, designed in 1989. Plaster casts of the relief made in the 19th and 20th centuries, now shown in museums in Rome, Bucharest and London, are in some details more legible than the original.
trajans-dacian-wars: Dacia had been on the Roman agenda since before Julius Caesar, when the Dacians defeated a Roman army at the Battle of Histria. Domitian's Dacian War ended in a peace in 89 CE, but King Decebalus used the Roman annual subsidy of 8 million sesterces and the craftsmen and war machines Rome had supplied to fortify his own defences. Rome was in economic difficulty, and rumours of Dacian gold inflamed the conflict. Dacia had rich iron and copper and prolific metalworkers, so many Dacians owned swords, which reduced Rome's military advantage, and it could field about 250,000 potential combatants. It was allied to several neighbours of Rome. Trajan, an experienced soldier, withdrew troops from other borders to prepare for war.

After obtaining the Senate's approval Trajan advanced in 101 with two legionary columns, burning towns and villages on the way, and defeated a Dacian army at the Third Battle of Tapae. In the winter of 101–102 the army gathered near the later city of Nicopolis ad Istrum to meet an attack by the Sarmatian Roxolani, allies of the Dacians, and defeated it. In 102 Decebalus sought peace once the Roman advance on his capital, Sarmizegetusa, seemed unstoppable. The terms obliged him to give up territory and the engineers provided by Domitian, return equipment and accept Roman garrisons. Apollodorus of Damascus designed the great stone bridge across the Danube at Drobeta, probably the largest of its time.

Decebalus soon broke the agreement, rebuilt his forces, stirred up neighbouring tribes and plundered Roman colonies across the Danube. In 105 Trajan gathered his forces at the Danube, probably at Drobeta. Like the first, the second war involved costly skirmishes, and the legions struggled against the numerous allies of the Dacians. The Romans gradually took the mountain fortresses round Sarmizegetusa in 106. A traitor among the Dacians helped them find and cut the city's water pipes, and when it ran out of water and food it fell and was razed. Decebalus fled and killed himself rather than submit. A confidant, Bicilis, betrayed the king's treasure, which Carcopino estimated at 165,500 kilograms of gold and 330,000 of silver.

The southern half of Dacia became a province, secured by the permanent legions XIII Gemina and V Macedonica, and settled with colonists from across the empire. The gold mines were secured, and the remains of the mining are still visible at Roșia Montană. A hundred thousand male slaves are said to have been sent to Rome. Trajan announced 123 days of celebration, and Trajan's Column in Rome shows the wars in detail. The province's population changed greatly: of 3,000 personal names identified there only 60 were Dacian and 2,200 Roman. The northern part of Dacia stayed free.
trakai: Trakai lies 28 kilometres west of Vilnius. About 200 lakes lie in the region, the deepest being Galvė with its 21 islands. Trakai Historical National Park was founded on 23 April 1991 to preserve Trakai as a centre of Lithuanian statehood as well as the park's authentic nature. The name was first recorded in 1337, in the chronicles of the Teutonic Knights, and is derived from the Lithuanian word trakai, meaning glades. In Polish the town is called Troki, and the surname Trotsky, adopted by Leon Trotsky as a pseudonym, comes from the name.

According to a legend, Grand Duke Gediminas found a beautiful lake-surrounded place after a hunting party and built a castle at Senieji Trakai, Old Trakai. The year 1337 is considered the official date of the city's foundation. When Gediminas settled in Vilnius, Senieji Trakai passed to his son Kęstutis, who moved the town to its present site. There he built the Peninsula Castle and the Island Castle, and a village grew around them. Both wooden castles were raided several times by the Teutonic Knights.

In 1382 Jogaila tricked Kęstutis and imprisoned him in Kreva, where he died, and the castles went to Jogaila's brother Skirgaila. Vytautas and the Teutonic Knights captured the town in 1383. After the Astrava Agreement of 1392 Vytautas became Grand Duke and regained his father's lands. Although his official capital was Vilnius, Vytautas spent more time in Trakai, and in the early 15th century he replaced the wooden fortress with a stone castle.

In 1409 the town received Magdeburg Rights, and Vytautas made it the capital of Lithuania and moved the State Treasury and the Lithuanian Metrica there. In 1413 it became the seat of the Trakai Voivodeship. After the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was formed in 1569 its importance declined. Sigismund I the Old made the castle a summer residence, but after his death in 1548 it fell into disrepair. Russian forces plundered the town and demolished both castles during the war of 1654 to 1667.

Karaims, a small Turkic-speaking people, were resettled in Trakai by Vytautas in 1397 and 1398 from Crimea, after a campaign against the Golden Horde, and the town remained a centre of Karaim cultural and religious life. Their wooden kenesa, with an interior dome, survives, and the pastry kibinai has become a local speciality.

Historically Lithuanians, Poles, Russians, Jews, Tatars and Karaims lived there together. The Island Castle was reconstructed in stages: the Polish authorities ordered restoration in 1929, work halted in the early 1960s, and it was completed in the early 1990s. A history museum was established in the castle in 1962, and concerts and festivals take place there in summer.
trakai-voivodeship: The voivodeship, known in Latin as Palatinatus Trocensis and in Polish as Województwo trockie, was divided into four powiats or districts: Grodno, Kaunas, Upytė and Trakai, the last ruled directly by the voivode. Its largest cities were Kaunas, Grodno and Trakai. The voivodes lived in the town of Trakai, near Lake Galvė and north of the Trakai Peninsula Castle.

Grand Duke Vytautas the Great created the Trakai Voivodeship together with the Vilnius Voivodeship in 1413, under the Union of Horodło. He copied the Polish system of administrative division in order to centralise and strengthen his government. The new province replaced the Duchy of Trakai, which had been ruled directly by the grand duke or a close relative such as a brother or son, and the Duke of Trakai gave way to appointed officials: a voivode and his deputy, the castellan.

The Voivode of Trakai held one of the most important offices of the Grand Duchy. Chosen from prominent magnate families, the voivodes rivalled only the Voivode of Vilnius and the grand chancellors in power and prestige, and they sat ex officio in the Lithuanian Council of Lords. Holders of the office included Jonas Goštautas, Radvila Astikas, Konstanty Ostrogski, Mikołaj Krzysztof Radziwiłł, known as the Orphan, and members of the Pac, Ogiński and Tyszkiewicz families.

In 1513 Sigismund I the Old split off the western part of the voivodeship, which was organised as the Podlaskie Voivodeship. After the Union of Lublin the province, with the whole Grand Duchy, belonged to the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth until the partitions. When the Commonwealth was partitioned in 1795, most of its territory passed to the Russian Empire, while the lands west of the Neman River became part of the Province of East Prussia.
tralee: Tralee, in Irish Trá Lí, formerly Tráigh Lí, meaning strand of the River Lee, is the county town of County Kerry and the largest town in the county. It stands on the northern side of the neck of the Dingle Peninsula, at the confluence of some small rivers and next to marshy ground at the head of Tralee Bay. It lies at the foot of an ancient roadway that heads south over the Slieve Mish Mountains. On this old track stands a large boulder known as Scotia's Grave, reputedly the burial place of an ancient queen.

Anglo-Normans founded the town in the 13th century, and it became a stronghold of the Earls of Desmond, who built Tralee Castle. John Fitz-Thomas FitzGerald founded a Dominican monastery and was buried there in 1260. The medieval town was burnt in 1580 in retribution for the Desmond Rebellions against Elizabeth I. In 1587 she granted Tralee to Edward Denny, and it received a royal charter in 1613 under James I, with the right to elect two members of parliament. The Dennys occupied the Desmond castle only from 1627.

The modern layout dates from the 19th century. Denny Street, a wide Georgian street, was completed in 1826 on the site of the old castle, and the courthouse was built in 1834. The Tralee Ship Canal was built to replace the silting quay at Blennerville, and it opened in 1846 but soon silted itself. Fenit Harbour was built as a deepwater port in the 1880s. The Tralee and Dingle Light Railway opened in 1891 and closed in 1953.

Tralee saw much violence in 1919–1923. In November 1920 the Black and Tans besieged the town in revenge for the killing of two Royal Irish Constabulary men, and near-famine conditions were reported by the end of the week. In August 1922 Free State troops landed at Fenit and took Tralee from the anti-Treaty garrison. In March 1923 nine prisoners were killed by a land mine at nearby Ballyseedy.

Tralee is known for the Rose of Tralee International Festival, held annually in August since 1959 and inspired by a 19th-century ballad about a woman named Mary. The Kerry County Museum, in the Ashe Memorial Hall built in 1928, includes a reconstruction of medieval Geraldine Tralee in 1450. Ratass Church, a tenth-century medieval church with a sixth-century ogham stone, lies in the eastern suburbs. The Dingle Way, a trail of 162 kilometres, begins and ends in Tralee.
tran-nghe-tong: Born Trần Phủ in 1321, he was the third son of Emperor Minh Tông and the concubine Lê, younger sister of Empress Hiến Từ. Under his brothers Hiến Tông and Dụ Tông he held the title Prince Cung Định. When Dương Nhật Lễ took the throne in 1369 he married the prince's daughter, but his attempts to change his family name back to Dương, which would have ended the Trần dynasty, provoked several plots. One was led by Prince Cung Định with his brother Trần Kính and his sister Trần Ngọc Tha; Nhật Lễ surrendered the throne and was later beaten to death on the new emperor's orders.

Crowned in 1370 at the age of 49, Nghệ Tông tried slowly to restore order at court but lacked able officials, and the chronicle Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư judged that he lacked decisiveness. In March 1371 Chế Bồng Nga, king of Champa, attacked Thăng Long, and the court fled while the capital was looted. Two months later the emperor raised Hồ Quý Ly, a relative by marriage, to one of the highest offices. In 1372 he gave the throne to his brother, who became Duệ Tông, and as retired emperor oversaw him and his two successors, as Trần tradition allowed.

Duệ Tông was killed in the disastrous Đồ Bàn campaign against Champa that began in December 1376; Hồ Quý Ly and the commander Đỗ Tử Bình fled, and only Đỗ Tử Bình was punished. Nghệ Tông then enthroned Duệ Tông's son, Phế Đế, whose weakness Hồ Quý Ly exploited. In 1383 Nghệ Tông abandoned Thăng Long against his court's advice, for which the historian Ngô Sĩ Liên criticised him. In 1387 he made Hồ Quý Ly co-prime minister, and when Phế Đế plotted against Quý Ly he deposed him and forced him to commit suicide, giving the throne to his own youngest son, Thuận Tông.

Trần Khát Chân, whom Nghệ Tông placed over the war with Champa in 1389, won a decisive victory on 23 January 1390 in which Chế Bồng Nga was killed. Yet the Trần government kept weakening: with the retired emperor's passive approval Hồ Quý Ly had the prime minister Trần Ngạc beaten to death in 1391. Nghệ Tông died at the age of 73, leaving the court in Hồ Quý Ly's hands. Most cities of Vietnam have major streets named after him.
tran-nhan-tong: Trần Nhân Tông was born Trần Khâm on 7 December 1258, the first son of Emperor Trần Thánh Tông and Empress Thiên Cảm Trần Thị Thiều. Made crown prince in December 1274, he married that month Princess Khâm Từ, eldest daughter of Trần Quốc Tuấn, and was taught by the mandarin and general Lê Phụ Trần. His father ceded him the throne on 8 November 1278 but, as Emperor Emeritus, went on ruling beside him until his death in 1290.

After the Yuan dynasty crushed the Song at the Battle of Yamen in 1279, the two emperors prepared for war, calling the royal family and court to Bình Than in October 1282 and naming Trần Quốc Tuấn commander-in-chief in 1283. In December 1284 Prince Toghan invaded from the north while General Sogetu's fleet advanced through Champa. The emperors retreated, several of the royal family defected, and Trần Bình Trọng was killed defending them. Victories at Hàm Tử in April 1285 and Chương Dương on 10 May turned the war, and the emperors returned to Thăng Long on 6 June 1285.

A third Yuan invasion, begun in March 1287, ended with the destruction of the Yuan navy at the Battle of Bạch Đằng on 8 March 1288. Defectors of the Trần clan were made to take the family name Mai. Ruling alone after 1290, Nhân Tông relaxed taxes, relieved the poor and put off a campaign against Ai Lao so the country could recover from war, famine and natural disaster. He passed the throne to his son Trần Thuyên on 3 March 1293.

Ordained as a Buddhist monk in 1295, he settled in 1299 on the mountain of Yên Tử, took up the ten ascetic practices and founded a monastery; he is thought to have founded Trúc Lâm, the only indigenous Thiền sect in Vietnam. In 1301 he spent nine months at the court of Jaya Sinhavarman III of Champa, and in 1306 he gave his daughter Princess Huyền Trân to that king in marriage in return for two Cham provinces. He died on 16 December 1308, and most Vietnamese cities have major streets named after him.
tran-quoc-pagoda: The temple is said to have been built during the reign of Emperor Lý Nam Đế, from 544 to 548, and its first name, Khai Quốc, means National Founding. It stood on the shore of the Red River, outside the Yên Phụ Dyke, and was moved because the river was encroaching on it. Its new site was Kim Ngư, or Golden Fish, islet near the south-eastern shore of West Lake (Hồ Tây), linked to the mainland by a small causeway. Over the years the temple was also called An Quốc, Pacification of the Realm, and Trấn Bắc, Guardian of the North.

The last major repair took place in 1815, when the main sanctuary, the reception hall and the rear hall of the dead were renovated, and the historic relics include statues dating to 1639. The pagoda holds the ashes of important monks. Lotus flowers, symbols of purity and enlightenment, appear in statues and in carvings on a stone wall beside the pagoda. A Bodhi tree on the grounds was grown from a cutting of the tree at Bodh Gaya, given in 1959 to mark the visit of the Indian president Rajendra Prasad.

Monks have lived at the pagoda for centuries, teaching Buddhism to the public and praying at the shrines around the grounds; they are vegetarian, so offerings are made without meat. Visitors burn incense at the main shrine in odd numbers, held to be lucky, and leave food or small sums of money. Shrines at the front of the courtyard honour the Mẫu, or Mothers: the green Mother of mountains and forests, the white Mother of the water and the red Mother of the sky, among the oldest deities worshipped in Vietnam, there before the Buddha. Worshippers come especially in the first month of the Vietnamese calendar.
tran-thai-tong: Trần Cảnh, also called Trần Nhật Cảnh, was born on 17 July 1218 in what is now Nam Định province, in the last years of the Lý dynasty. The ancestors of the Trần clan had come from Fujian under Trần Kính, and the Chinese writer Zhou Mi claimed that his real name was Hsieh Sheng-ch'ing, a man from Fujian. His father, Trần Thừa, was a senior official of the Lý court, and his rise to the throne was mostly the work of his uncle Trần Thủ Độ, then commander of the Lý capital.

He reigned for 33 years under the era names Kiến Trung, Thiên Ứng Chính Bình and Nguyên Phong. In 1237, with no son after the early death of Crown Prince Trần Trịnh, he followed the advice of Trần Thủ Độ and made Princess Thuận Thiên, the wife of his elder brother Trần Liễu, then three months pregnant, his empress, demoting Chiêu Hoàng. Trần Liễu rose in revolt at the Cai River, and the emperor, ashamed, withdrew to Yên Tử Mountain until the monk Đạo Viên and Trần Thủ Độ persuaded him to return. When Trần Liễu surrendered two weeks later, the emperor shielded him with his body from execution and granted him lands.

In the autumn of 1257 the Mongol general Uriyangkhadai sent three letters demanding passage to attack the Song dynasty, and when the envoys were imprisoned in Thang Long he invaded. The emperor led his army from an elephant, but Aju ordered his troops to shoot at the animals' feet, the elephants panicked and the army was beaten at No Nguyen and again at the Phu Lo bridge, so the court evacuated the capital. After the Mongol departure from Thang Long, he agreed to send tribute to the court of the Mongol Empire every three years. In 1258 he abdicated in favour of his son, Crown Prince Trần Hoảng.

He lived 19 more years as retired emperor and died on 5 May 1277. Learned in Confucianism and Buddhism, he wrote many works on Mahayana Buddhism, few of which survive; the best known, the Khóa Hư Lục or Instructions on Emptiness, a collection of sermons and essays, still influences Vietnamese Buddhism. One of his daughters, Princess An Tư, married Prince Toghan, ninth son of Kublai Khan.
tran-trong-kim: Kim was born in 1883 in Nghi Xuân, Hà Tĩnh Province, in the French protectorate of Annam, a region that soon afterwards saw the guerrilla movement of Phan Đình Phùng. He studied in Hanoi at schools for the elite and began as an interpreter for the French administration in Ninh Bình. In 1905 he went to France as an employee of a private company, and in 1908 a scholarship of the École Coloniale took him to the École Normale of Melun. From September 1911 he taught in Annam, and by 1942 he was an inspector of elementary public instruction in Tonkin.

Kim was known for textbooks written in the Vietnamese alphabet, chữ Quốc Ngữ, on Confucianism, Buddhism and Vietnamese history. His two best-known works were Việt Nam sử lược (A Brief History of Vietnam, 1920), which stressed Chinese influence on Vietnamese society, and Nho giáo (Confucianism, 1929-1933). The second strongly praised Confucianism, provoked wide debate on its place in Vietnamese life and was seen as a bridge between scholars raised under the old examination system and those of the French schools. He led Buddhist and Confucian associations and in 1939 joined the Chamber of People's Representatives in Tonkin.

Contacts with Japanese scholars made him suspect to the Vichy administration of Admiral Jean Decoux, and on 28 October 1943 Japanese agents took him under the protection of the Kenpeitai in Hanoi. He was moved to Saigon, Singapore and Bangkok, then recalled to Saigon on 30 March 1945, after Japan had deposed the French.

On 7 April he at first refused the post of prime minister, saying he was too old and had no party, but on 16 April he agreed and the next day proposed a cabinet of ten ministers. The government was hampered by its short time, Japanese wartime control and Allied bombing. After it fell he returned to scholarship. Milton Sacks and John T. McAlister regarded him as a Japanese puppet; Trương Bửu Lâm saw his cabinet as apolitical technocrats.
tranquebar-mission: Tranquebar had been acquired for the Danish Crown in 1620 by Admiral Ove Gjedde, through an agreement with Raghunatha Nayak of the Tanjore Nayak Kingdom. King Frederick IV of Denmark wished to spread Christianity among his non-European subjects, but his call for royal missionaries found little response among his Danish subjects, so his court chaplain Franz J. Lütkens searched the German universities. Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau, both from Halle, were ordained in Copenhagen and sailed on the Sophia Hedewig on 29 November 1705, reaching Tranquebar on 9 July 1706.

About 15,000 people then lived in and around Tranquebar: Hindus, Muslims, Indian Catholics and Europeans of the East India Company. The Danish authorities opposed the mission despite its royal charter, fearing that conversion would bring disorder, and Ziegenbalg was once held for four months. The first convert was baptised ten months after the mission began. Ziegenbalg learnt Tamil by sitting with the village children at the local school, opened a school for girls in 1707 and persuaded the University of Halle in 1711 to take up the scholarly study of Tamil. In a letter of 1713 he counted 47 pupils in the Tamil school, 20 in the Portuguese and 15 in the Danish, the first two given free tuition, board and food.

Between 1717 and 1718 the mission built the New Jerusalem Church for the local people, with services in Tamil. When Ziegenbalg died on 23 February 1719, aged 37, he had translated the New Testament and the Old Testament from Genesis to Ruth, and the mission had two churches, a seminary and a congregation of 250. Christian Friedrich Schwarz later served the mission for 48 years.

On 14 January 1919 the Tamil congregations of the German, Danish and Swedish Lutheran missions joined to form the Tamil Evangelical Lutheran Church, whose bishop holds the title Bishop of Tranquebar; the first, the Swedish missionary Ernst Heuman, was ordained in 1921. The New Jerusalem Church, damaged with other mission buildings in the tsunami of 2004, was re-consecrated on 9 July 2006 for the mission's 300th anniversary before nearly 10,000 people, and India Post issued a stamp of Ziegenbalg.
trans-amazonian-highway: The Trans-Amazonian Highway, officially BR-230 and named Rodovia Transamazônica, was inaugurated in 1972. The military dictatorship that governed Brazil from 1964 to 1985 began the project out of a perceived need to secure control over remote regions while encouraging economic use of their natural resources. The road was meant to link those regions with the rest of the country and with Colombia, Peru and Ecuador. Another main goal was to ease the effects of drought in the Northeast by giving access to largely empty land in the rainforest, which could be settled. It was originally planned as a fully paved highway, but the plans were modified after its inauguration.

The road runs from the port city of Cabedelo in Paraíba to Lábrea in Amazonas and crosses the states of Paraíba, Ceará, Piauí, Maranhão, Tocantins, Pará and Amazonas. It is the third longest highway in Brazil. It also connects with ports on the north-east coast, such as Suape, and in Paraíba it is the main axis of movement of people and goods between municipalities.

Because of high construction costs and Brazil's financial crisis in the late 1970s, only part of it was paved, from the start to 200 km beyond Marabá. In the wet season, from October to March, travel on the unpaved stretches is extremely difficult and cars often get stuck, while in the dry season potholes in the dry mud damage vehicles. Building it was hard because of the remoteness: workers were frequently isolated, and sites were reached mostly by small aircraft on temporary airstrips and by boat.

Paving continued in later decades. In 2009 work was under way between Ruropolis and Itaituba and north to Santarém, a route meant to link soy plantations with trucking routes to the south. West of Itaituba stretches were left untouched, at times narrowing to about two metres. In 2019 the Brazilian government announced that it would seek to privatise major sections of the road in order to pave more of it, and in September 2022 it finished restoring a paved section of 33.3 km in northern Tocantins, between Aguiarnópolis and Trevo de Nazaré. Many stretches in the Amazon remained entirely unpaved.
trans-caspian-railway: The railway was built by the Russian army during the expansion of the Russian Empire into Central Asia, at first as a narrow-gauge line to Gyzylarbat for the conquest of Transcaspia under General Mikhail Skobelev. It was quickly changed to the standard Russian gauge of 1,524 millimetres. Its first purpose was military, to help the army against local resistance. Under General Annenkoff the line was completed through Ashgabat to Merv in 1886. It first began at Uzun-Ada on the Caspian Sea, but the terminus was later moved north to Krasnovodsk. It reached Samarkand by way of Bukhara in 1888 and halted for ten years before being extended to Tashkent and Andijan in 1898.

The railway greatly increased the cotton exported from the region, from 873,092 pudy in 1888 to 3,588,025 in 1893, while sugar, kerosene, wood, iron and building materials were brought in. Governor-General Nikolai Rozenbakh used these figures to argue for the extension to Tashkent, and the merchant N. I. Reshetnikov offered private funds. A permanent bridge over the Oxus was completed only in 1901, and a train ferry crossed the Caspian from Krasnovodsk to Baku by 1905. The Tashkent Railway of 1906 linked the line to the rest of the Russian and European network.

Lord Curzon visited the line and remarked that its significance went beyond local military control and threatened British interests in Asia. Railway workers became key activists in the revolution: thirty-five of them founded the Tashkent Soviet on 2 March 1917, and the western part of the line broke away to set up the Ashkhabad Executive Committee on 14 July 1918. Troops of the British Indian Army fought in some of the battles along the line during the Civil War. In the Soviet period it was administered from Tashkent. Today it runs from Turkmenbashi along the Karakum Desert through Ashgabat, Mary, Turkmenabat and Bukhara to Samarkand and Tashkent.
trans-indochinese-railway: In 1895 the outgoing Governor-General of French Indochina, Jean Marie de Lanessan, urged his successors to give priority to a line between Hanoi and Saigon, which he called the backbone of Indochina. Paul Doumer, appointed in 1897, proposed a railway programme that included this line and what became the Yunnan–Vietnam Railway, and the French government approved a loan of 200 million francs. The Hanoi–Vinh section was built from 1899 to 1905 and the Nha Trang–Saigon section from 1905 to 1913, with lines around Huế opened in 1906 and 1908. Vinh–Huế followed between 1913 and 1927 and Huế–Nha Trang between 1930 and 1936.

The first through journeys on the Transindochinois took about 60 hours, cut to about 40 by the late 1930s, behind French Pacific or Mikado locomotives with dining and sleeping cars. Japanese forces used the line heavily in World War II, drawing sabotage by the Viet Minh and American bombing. In the First Indochina War the French ran the armoured train La Rafale from February 1951, but the Viet Minh kept lifting rails and built a network of 300 km of their own between Ninh Hoa and Da Nang.

After the Geneva Accords of 1954 the line was cut at the Hiền Lương Bridge over the Bến Hải River. South Vietnam, with American support, rebuilt the track between Saigon and Huế in the late 1950s, but 795 attacks between 1961 and 1964 forced it to abandon long sections. In the North, American raids struck railway bridges, among them the Thanh Hóa Bridge, which withstood repeated attacks from April 1965 until laser-guided bombs destroyed it in April and May 1972.

After the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 the line was restored and reopened on 31 December 1976 as a symbol of Vietnamese unity; 1,334 bridges, 27 tunnels and 158 stations were repaired, and other lines such as the Da Lat–Thap Cham Railway were dismantled for materials. It remains a single-track line operated by Vietnam Railways, the main railway of the country, and its trains are sometimes called the Reunification Express, though no train carries that name officially.
trans-iranian-railway: Proposals for a railway across Iran date from before the First World War. Russian promoters suggested a line linking the Russian Empire and British India in 1889, 1900 and 1905, and in 1910 twelve Russian banks formed a Trans-Iranian Railway Consortium. Britain and Russia disagreed over the route, with Russia concerned chiefly with the northern section and Britain with the south, and in 1914 Russia repudiated its obligation to build the Tehran–Khanaqin line a few days after the outbreak of war.

After the war Reza Shah revived the project as part of his modernisation of Iran. In 1924 the American company Ulen negotiated with Reza Khan, later Reza Shah, a feasibility study. Legislation then secured internal funding from taxes on sugar and other goods, which excluded the foreign debts that had burdened earlier rulers. The railway cost Iran 2,195,180,700 rials through 1938–1939, and some Iranians and foreign observers argued the money would have been better spent on roads.

The line was built to standard gauge. From 1927 an international syndicate of the American Ulen and Company and German firms began two test lines, one from Bandar Shahpur and one from Bandar Shah. The Americans ended their contract in 1930 after delayed payments, and in April 1933 Iran signed with the Danish firm Kampsax, which divided the work into 43 lots. It finished under budget and ahead of schedule, and the whole line opened on 26 August 1938.

The route climbs through daunting mountains, with gradients of up to 1 in 36 and spirals such as the Three Golden Lines on the Mazandaran branch. Its highest point is at Arak, 2,220 m above sea level. Engineers abandoned tunnels through a salt dome, powdery gypsum and pumice, and Veresk Bridge carries the line across the Alborz. The line is 1,394 km long. It was extended from Bandar Shah to Gorgan in 1961, and UNESCO designated the original 1938 route a World Heritage Site in July 2021.

The railway's place in the Persian Corridor was one of the reasons for the Anglo-Soviet invasion of August 1941. In September 1941 the Allies took over its operation, with British and Empire Royal Engineers running the southern division and the Soviet Army the northern. When the British took over the south the line moved one freight train a day. By September 1943 it was moving 5,400 tons a day. In December 1942 the US Army Transportation Corps replaced the British, and in 1944 it averaged 6,489 tons per day. Aid to Russia traffic ceased by May 1945, and the line returned to Iranian State Railways.
trans-siberian-railway: In the late 19th century Siberia's development was hampered by poor transport. Apart from the Great Siberian Route, roads suitable for wheeled traffic were rare, and for about five months of the year rivers were the main means of travel, with horse-drawn sledges over frozen winter roads. Steamboats appeared on the Ob in 1844, but the river systems ran mostly north to south, making west to east transport difficult.

The first Siberian railway projects emerged after the Saint Petersburg–Moscow Railway opened in 1851, among them a proposal by the American entrepreneur Perry Collins. The central government largely ignored them before 1880, and the design of the line then took ten years. On 9 March 1891 the government issued an imperial rescript announcing a railway across Siberia, and Tsarevich Nicholas, later Nicholas II, inaugurated construction at Vladivostok on 19 May that year.

The line was divided into seven sections worked on at once by 62,000 workers, with an estimated cost of £35 million. To save money and avoid disputes with landowners it was laid outside existing cities: the railway crossed the Ob at Novonikolaevsk, later Novosibirsk, 70 kilometres south of Tomsk, which got only a dead-end branch. Lake Baikal was crossed by the ice-breaking train ferry SS Baikal, built in 1897 at Newcastle upon Tyne, until the Circum-Baikal Railway was completed in 1904. The Amur River line, finished in 1916, made the railway continuous from Petrograd to Vladivostok.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905 exposed the limits of a single-track line, where trains waited in sidings to pass one another; this limited capacity and contributed to Russia's defeat.
