After 1917 the railway was the main line of communication for the Czechoslovak Legion and the Allied forces in the Siberian Intervention. The whole length was double-tracked by 1939.

Siberian grain began moving west on the railway, and from 1896 to 1913 Siberia exported on average about 501,932 metric tons of grain and flour a year. Between 1906 and 1914 about four million peasants migrated to Siberia from western Russia and Ukraine. The historian Christian Wolmar judges the railway a failure, built for narrow political reasons and to a deficient standard, with flimsy rails and rotting ties; others stress the commercial and political importance of its Manchurian section, the Chinese Eastern Railway.

In the Second World War the railway carried Soviet industry eastward from 1941 and, after Germany invaded the Soviet Union, served as a route for Lend-Lease supplies. Electrification began in 1929 and was completed in 2002. The main line runs 9,289 kilometres from Moscow to Vladivostok across eight time zones, with branches known as the Trans-Manchurian and Trans-Mongolian routes.
transamund-ii-of-spoleto: Transamund came to power in Spoleto by deposing his own father, Duke Faroald II, and having him tonsured and confined in a monastery. In 737 or 738 he captured Gallese, cutting communication between Rome and Ravenna. Pope Gregory III offered to pay for its return in exchange for a peace treaty, which also included Duke Gregory of Benevento. The Lombard king Liutprand rejected the treaty as contrary to his interests and attacked Transamund as a traitor.

By 16 June 739 the king had taken Spoleto and installed Hilderic as duke. Transamund fled to Rome, where Liutprand besieged him and took the towns of Amelia, Orte, Bomarzo and Bieda, but the pope still refused to give up his refugee and wrote to Charles Martel, Duke of the Franks, asking for help. Charles refused.

In December 740, with help from the pope and Benevento, Transamund recovered his duchy and killed Hilderic. He did not, however, return the papal towns that had been seized, and his alliance with the pope broke down. Liutprand had never recognised the reconquest and set out to remove him again; in 742 he met Gregory's successor, Pope Zachary, and by promising to restore the four towns won the Romans to his side. Transamund was forced to flee and was caught and placed in a monastery. Liutprand's nephew Agiprand became duke. The king then turned against Godescalc, the new Duke of Benevento, who had taken office without royal assent and had continued to support Transamund.
transatlantic-telegraph-cable: As early as 1840 Samuel F. B. Morse expressed faith in a submarine line across the Atlantic, and by 1850 a cable ran between England and France. In 1854 the financier Cyrus West Field discussed a Newfoundland line with the telegraph engineer Frederic Newton Gisborne and began to think of extending it across the ocean.

Field knew little of the deep sea, so he consulted Morse and the oceanographer Lieutenant Matthew Maury, whose charts from ships' soundings showed a feasible route that Maury named the Telegraph Plateau. Field's New York, Newfoundland and London Telegraph Company first completed the link from Cape Ray, Newfoundland, to Aspy Bay, Nova Scotia, in 1856, after a failed attempt in 1855.

The main ocean section of the first cable had a seven-strand copper core covered by four layers of gutta-percha, wrapped in tarred hemp and protected by ten steel wires. It weighed nearly 550 kilograms per kilometre. William Thomson analysed the cable as a long conductor and derived his law of squares, which predicted slow signalling.

He quarrelled with the electrician Wildman Whitehouse, a former physician without formal training in physics, who wanted to drive the cable with a high-voltage induction coil. Thomson found variations of up to a factor of two in the resistance of sample copper cores and developed a sensitive mirror galvanometer. Field chose the thinner and cheaper cable that Whitehouse favoured.

Messages passed in August 1858, and Queen Victoria's telegram to President James Buchanan set off celebrations in New York, with a salute of 100 guns. The line was slow, at about 0.1 words a minute, and Whitehouse's attempts to drive up to 2,000 volts through it damaged the insulation. He also passed off a message received on Thomson's galvanometer as one received on his own printing telegraph.

Public confidence fell, and Field raised new capital only in 1864. A heavier cable laid from the SS Great Eastern reached Heart's Content, Newfoundland, on 27 July 1866 and carried about 8 words a minute, 80 times faster than the 1858 cable. A 2018 study in the American Economic Review estimated that the telegraph raised efficiency by about 8 percent of export value.
transcaspian-oblast: The Transcaspian Oblast, or Transcaspia, was an oblast of the Russian Empire and early Soviet Russia east of the Caspian Sea. It was bounded to the south by Iran's Khorasan Province and Afghanistan, to the north by the former Ural Oblast, and to the northeast by the Russian protectorates of Khiva and Bukhara. It formed part of Russian Turkestan. The name means Beyond the Caspian. Until the Trans-Aral Railway was built in the early 20th century, the easiest way to reach it from central Russia or Transcaucasia was across the Caspian by boat from Astrakhan or Baku. Its population in 1897 was 382,487, mostly Turkmens, with significant Kazakh and Russian minorities. The Turkic-speaking population totalled 328,059, or 85.8 per cent.

Russia conquered Transcaspia in a series of campaigns led by Generals Nikolai Lomakin, Mikhail Skobelev and Mikhail Annenkov. Construction of the Transcaspian Railway began from the Caspian shore in 1879, to secure Russian control and provide a fast military route to the Afghan border. In 1885 the Russian annexation of the Panjdeh oasis, south of Merv, nearly led to war with Britain, since the Russians were thought to be planning to march on Herat. Until 1898 Transcaspia belonged to the Governor-Generalship of the Caucasus Viceroyalty, administered from Tiflis. In that year it became an oblast of Russian Turkestan, governed from Tashkent.

General Kuropatkin was probably the best-known military governor to rule the region from Ashkhabad. His authoritarian methods made the province hard for his successors to control, and its administration became a byword within Russian Turkestan for corruption and brutality. Russian administrators turned their districts into petty fiefdoms and extorted money from the local population. The Pahlen Report of 1908–1910 exposed these abuses.

In July 1918 anti-Bolshevik railway workers set up a provisional Transcaspian government at Ashkhabad, dominated by members of the Socialist Revolutionary Party with Menshevik participation. British forces of the Malleson Mission entered from Persia the following month and supported it in fighting along the railway until the last British troops left on 14 April 1919. Bolshevik forces took Merv in May 1919, and the anti-Bolshevik government and troops left Ashkhabad on 15 July and retreated westwards. The capture of Krasnovodsk by Bolshevik forces in February 1920 completed the reconquest of Transcaspia.
transfer-of-the-portuguese-court-to-braz: On 19 November 1807 French and Spanish forces invaded Portugal, one of Britain's last allies on the Continent. Prince Regent John, ruling since 1799 for his mentally ill mother, Queen Maria I, ordered the court to Brazil before he could be deposed. Secret negotiations in London by the ambassador Domingos António de Sousa Coutinho had secured British protection in exchange for access to Brazil's ports and Madeira. The court embarked on 27 November on an Anglo-Portuguese fleet led by the 90-gun Príncipe Real and sailed on 29 November, escorted most of the way by Commodore Graham Moore's ships of the line.

The court reached Salvador on 22 January 1808, where John opened Brazil's ports to friendly nations, ending the colonial pact that had tied its trade to Portugal. On 1 April 1808 he lifted the ban on manufacturing. In Rio de Janeiro the crown founded the royal printing press, two medical schools, military academies, the Banco do Brasil, a botanical garden, an art academy and an opera house, and built roads between the scattered cities. Between 1808 and 1821 John granted 145 titles of nobility, only six of them to Brazilians, and nearly every official was Portuguese.

The changes rested on slavery. About 328,000 enslaved people arrived during the court's stay and the decade after, and the enslaved came to make up more than half of Rio's population at its height. Fearing revolt after the slave revolution in Haiti, the court created the Royal Police Guard. On 16 December 1815 John raised Brazil to a kingdom equal to Portugal within the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves, and after Maria's death in 1816 he became king, acclaimed in Rio in 1818.

Portugal's political crisis after the Liberal Revolution of 1820 forced John VI to return in April 1821, leaving his heir Pedro in Rio. When the Cortes demanded that Brazil return to colonial status, Pedro refused to leave on the Dia do Fico, 9 January 1822. Brazil declared independence on 7 September 1822, and Pedro was crowned emperor on 12 October. Raised in Rio from the age of nine, he identified as Brazilian, and his position as heir helped him prevent serious Portuguese efforts to retake the country.
transhumance: Transhumance is a type of mobile pastoralism in which livestock are driven in herds between several fixed pastures with the seasons. It differs from sedentary pastoralism, where animals stay on one fenced area all year, and from nomadic pastoralism, where animals are moved irregularly in search of pasture. In mountain regions it means moving between high summer pastures and lowland valleys in winter, called vertical transhumance. Movement across the same plains or plateaus is horizontal transhumance.

Usually only the animals and a small number of herders travel, living in camps or huts at the grazing sites, while most of the community lives in permanent settlements. Nomadic pastoralists, by contrast, move whole communities with their herds in portable shelters such as tents and yurts. The milk, butter, yogurt and cheese of the herds may form much of the diet of such societies.

The word comes from French and derives from the Latin trans, across, and humus, ground. Transhumance developed on every inhabited continent and was practised before recorded history; in Europe, isotope studies of livestock bones suggest that certain animals were moved seasonally. Many languages have words for the high summer pastures, often used as place names, such as hafod in Wales, shieling in Scotland, and Alm or Alp in German-speaking regions.

In Wales farm workers spent the summer at a hillside hafod and returned in late autumn to the main house, the hendref. In Ireland the practice was called booleying, after the buaile, the summer pasture; it is mentioned in the Brehon Laws and was widespread in the west until the Second World War. In southern Italy drovers' roads called tratturi, up to 100 metres wide and more than 100 kilometres long, were regulated by law, with a mounted police force as far back as the 17th century. Spanish transhumance is the origin of the cowboys of the United States and the gauchos of South America.

In the Pyrenees herds went to the high mountains from late May or early June to early October, a system that evolved in the Middle Ages and lasted into the 20th century. In the Balkans, Albanians, Sarakatsani, Romanians, Aromanians and Yörük spent summers in the mountains and winters on lowland plains. The Bhotiya of Uttarakhand practised it until the closure of the Sino-Indian border after the war of 1962. Colonists began summer grazing in the Australian Alps in the 1830s.
transition-from-sui-to-tang: By 611 the Sui dynasty had known more than two decades of peace since ending the Chen dynasty in 589, and both the Eastern Göktürks and Goguryeo were its vassals. When King Yeongyang of Goguryeo refused to pay homage in 610, Emperor Yang planned its conquest. Building a fleet and shipping supplies to Zhuo Commandery, near modern Beijing, disrupted farming and killed many conscripts, and from 611 men who refused service rose as agrarian rebels under leaders such as Wang Bo and Liu Badao.

The campaign of 612 failed before Liaodong and at the hands of the Goguryeo general Ŭlchi Mundŏk, with the loss of about 300,000 men. During the second campaign, in 613, the general Yang Xuangan rebelled near Luoyang; he was defeated, but the emperor's heavy-handed reprisals did not stop further revolts.

In 616 Emperor Yang went to Jiangdu, and the rebels near Luoyang gathered under Li Mi, while Dou Jiande grew strong north of the Yellow River. Several leaders, Li Yuan among them, submitted to the Eastern Göktürk ruler Ashina Duojishi and received military aid. In winter 617 Li Yuan took Chang'an and made Yang You emperor. In spring 618 officers of the Xiaoguo Army led by Yuwen Huaji killed Emperor Yang; Li Yuan then executed Yang You and founded the Tang, while at Luoyang Wang Shichong made himself regent and in 619 took the throne, ending the Sui.

Li Shimin, the Prince of Qin, did much of the fighting. He destroyed Xue Rengao's Qin state, drove out Liu Wuzhou by summer 620 and besieged Luoyang. In spring 621 he defeated and captured Dou Jiande at the Hulao Pass, after which Wang Shichong surrendered; the same year Li Xiaogong received the surrender of Xiao Xian's Liang state at Jiangling. Liu Heita, who rose in the former Xia lands, was executed in 623, and Fu Gongshi's Song and Gao Kaidao's Yan were absorbed in 624.

Liang Shidu, protected by the Eastern Göktürks, held out longest. In 626 Li Shimin ambushed and killed his brothers Li Jiancheng, the Crown Prince, and Li Yuanji, and forced his father to yield the throne to him. By 628 the Eastern Göktürks were divided by disagreements between the Jiali Khan Ashina Duobi and the Tuli Khan Ashina Shibobi and could no longer shield Liang Shidu, whose cousin Liang Luoren killed him and surrendered. Most of China was again under a single power.
transitional-federal-government: The government of the Somali Democratic Republic collapsed in early 1991, and between 1991 and 2000 no central government existed in Somalia. A Transitional National Government formed in Djibouti in 2000 was opposed from the start by Ethiopia, which feared that an independent Somali state would renew its claims on the Ogaden region and sponsored opposition alliances against it. Its successor, set up in Nairobi under the Transitional Federal Charter, was the 14th attempt to establish a central government since the civil war began.

In October 2004 Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed was elected president with strong Ethiopian backing, and he appointed Ali Mohammed Gedi as prime minister. In March 2005 a parliamentary vote rejecting the deployment of foreign troops, Ethiopian forces among them, ended in a brawl and was declared invalid. The government moved to Somalia in 2005 and in February 2006 made Baidoa its seat after a deal with the warlord who held the city. It was installed in Mogadishu after Ethiopia's 2006 invasion overthrew the Islamic Courts Union, which set off an insurgency led by Al-Shabaab.

By 2008 most of the country was under insurgent control and more than 80% of the police and army had deserted. Talks in Djibouti between 31 May and 9 June 2008, brokered by the United Nations envoy Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah, produced an agreement with the Alliance for the Re-liberation of Somalia for the withdrawal of Ethiopian troops. Yusuf resigned when parliament began impeachment proceedings, parliament was enlarged to 550 seats, and the former Islamic Courts chairman Sharif Sheikh Ahmed was elected president. With the help of the African Union Mission in Somalia the government took control of Mogadishu in 2011, and its mandate ended on 20 August 2012.

The Transitional Federal Parliament elected the president and prime minister and could pass and veto laws. Each of the four major clans held 61 seats and an alliance of minority clans 31; after the alliance with the Islamic Courts Union and other Islamist groups these were given 200 seats, while citizens' groups and the Somali diaspora held 75. At least 12% of members had to be women. The Council of Ministers began with 42 offices and was cut to 18 posts in 2010. Clan-based militias dominated the security forces, and human rights organisations documented serious violations of humanitarian law, widespread corruption and the looting and blockading of aid.
transitional-national-government: The government took shape at the Somalia National Peace Conference, held at Arta in Djibouti from 20 April to 5 May 2000, where its name was chosen and clan representatives elected Abdiqasim Salad Hassan president. The Transitional National Charter behind it recognised de facto regional autonomy and the new entities in the north of the former Somalia. The Islamic Courts, whose militias had united into one force that year, backed the new government: they protected the president on his return to the capital in August 2000, handed over their heavy weapons, and were absorbed during 2001.

Ethiopia opposed the government from the start, fearing renewed claims on the Ogaden, and sponsored opposition alliances, above all the Somalia Reconciliation and Restoration Council, a warlord coalition founded in Ethiopia in mid-2001. Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed, leader of Puntland, asked the United Nations in January 2001 to review its recognition and joined the coalition. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 the Ethiopian government accused the government's leaders of Islamic extremism, and the council called for international intervention.

According to the scholar Le Sage, by 2002 the government had all the organs of a state, including a parliament, a police force and a standing army, which in March 2002 numbered 2,010 men and 90 women. Its institutions remained weak, lacking office equipment, territorial control and tax revenue, and it could not provide basic services; ministers complained of being shut out of decisions and of irregular pay. It had four prime ministers, beginning with Ali Khalif Galaydh, and was reported bankrupt in December 2003.

Ethiopia backed the formation of the Transitional Federal Government in 2004 and the presidency of Abdullahi Yusuf, expecting him to give up Somalia's claim to the Ogaden. On 10 October 2004 the new parliament elected Yusuf with 189 votes against 79 for Abdullahi Ahmed Addou in the third round, and Abdiqasim Salad Hassan withdrew peacefully. The academics Ashley Elliot and Georg-Sebastian Holzer concluded that Ethiopia's success in undermining the interim government showed that Addis Ababa held an effective veto over its neighbour's political direction.
transkei: The South African government set up the area as one of two homelands for Xhosa-speaking people in Cape Province, the other being Ciskei, and Prime Minister Hendrik Verwoerd gave it nominal autonomy in 1963. The first election was won by the Democratic Party, whose founder, Chief Victor Poto, opposed independence for the Bantustans, but the government was formed by the Transkei National Independence Party. Of the 109 members of the regional parliament, 45 were elected and 64 were chiefs holding seats ex officio. The name means the area beyond the Kei river.

Transkei became nominally independent in 1976 under Chief Kaiser Daliwonga Matanzima, prime minister until 1979 and then president until 1986. South Africa's prime minister, B. J. Vorster, defended the step by invoking the right of every people to control its own affairs. The United Nations General Assembly declared the independence invalid, and the African National Congress condemned it as designed to consolidate apartheid. The economy stayed dependent on South Africa, where much of the population was recruited to work in the Rand mines.

In April 1978, over a territorial dispute about East Griqualand, Matanzima announced a break in diplomatic ties with South Africa, but backed down because of Transkei's dependence on economic aid. In 1984 a student protest at the University of Transkei was stormed by riot police and a student, Patricia Cele, died; a state of emergency followed that lasted over three years. Matanzima retired on 20 February 1986 and his brother George succeeded him. In 1987 General Bantu Holomisa forced George Matanzima out and then overthrew Stella Sigcau in a coup. Transkei was reincorporated into South Africa on 27 April 1994 and became part of the Eastern Cape.

Transkei had three disconnected sections covering 45,000 square kilometres, the main one lying between the Umtamvuna and Great Kei rivers, with the Indian Ocean and the Drakensberg on its eastern and western sides. Xhosa was the sole official language by its constitution, although Sotho and English were used for laws. An estimate of 1982 gave the population as about 2.3 million, with roughly 400,000 citizens living permanently outside its borders. The Transkei Defence Force, formed in October 1976 with about 2,000 men, was incorporated into South Africa's forces in 1994.
transnistria: Transnistria is a narrow valley stretching north to south along the bank of the Dniester river, which forms the natural boundary along most of its de facto border with Moldova. It borders Bessarabia, the region on which the Republic of Moldova is based, for 411 kilometres to the west and Ukraine for 405 kilometres to the east. Its capital and largest city is Tiraspol. It also controls the city of Bender on the western bank, which the Moldovan authorities do not count as part of the territorial unit.

The name is the Romanian colloquial name of the region, meaning "beyond the Dniester". It was first used for eastern Moldova in 1989, in an election slogan of Leonida Lari, a member of the Popular Front of Moldova.

The Moldavian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was proclaimed in 1924 within the Ukrainian SSR. It included present-day Transnistria and an area around Balta, but nothing from Bessarabia, then part of the Kingdom of Romania; one reason for its creation was the Soviet wish to incorporate Bessarabia eventually. On 28 June 1940 the USSR annexed Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina under the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, and on 2 August 1940 the Supreme Soviet created the Moldavian SSR from part of the annexed territory and part of the former autonomous republic roughly equivalent to Transnistria.

Armed clashes began at Dubăsari in November 1990, with volunteers including Cossacks coming from Russia to help the separatists. Concerted fighting began on 2 March 1992, and the Soviet 14th Guards Army entered at the final stage; about 700 people were killed. A ceasefire was signed on 21 July 1992 and created a Joint Control Commission with Moldova, Russia and Transnistria and a trilateral peacekeeping force.

Transnistria is a semi-presidential republic with its own government, parliament, military, police, postal system and currency, the Transnistrian ruble, and its authorities have adopted a constitution, flag, national anthem and coat of arms. All UN member states treat it as part of Moldova; only Abkhazia and South Ossetia have recognised it. A census held by its authorities in 2015 counted 475,373 people, among them Russians (29.1 per cent), Moldovans (28.6) and Ukrainians (22.9), and the schools mainly use the Russian curriculum. In March 2022 the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe adopted a resolution that defined the territory as under military occupation by Russia.
transoxiana: Transoxiana, the Latin name meaning land beyond the Oxus, lies in lower Central Asia between the Amu Darya to the south and the Syr Darya to the north. It corresponds roughly to eastern Uzbekistan, western Tajikistan, southern Kyrgyzstan and parts of southern Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan. The name was coined in the 4th century BCE, when Alexander the Great's troops conquered the region. Khwarazm, Sogdiana, Chaghaniyan and Khuttal lay in its southern part; Chach, Osrushana and Farghana in the north.

Persian writers called it Farā-rūd, 'beyond the river', and ancient Iranians knew the area as Turan, a term used in the Shahnameh. Early Arab writers used Mā Warāʾ an-Nahr, 'what is beyond the river', and Chinese sources called it Hezhong.

Under the Achaemenid Empire the region was a satrapy named Sogdia. Alexander's successors founded the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, whose Greek presence lasted over two hundred years. The region was ruled in turn by the Seleucids, the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, the Parthian Empire and the Kushan Empire before Sasanian rule, under which it became a major cultural centre through the wealth of the Northern Silk Road. Hephthalite invaders interrupted Sasanian rule at the end of the 5th century, and it returned only in 565.

Arab conquest came between 705 and 715, under Qutayba ibn Muslim, after rule by the Göktürks; the Abbasid Caliphate replaced the Umayyads in 750. The people spoke Sogdian, and the conquest spread Arabic elite culture and New Persian. Samarkand and Bukhara remained centres of Persian culture and helped revive it through the Samanid Empire. Before Islam the principal religion was Zoroastrianism, with Buddhism, Nestorian Christianity and Manichaeism also present, and this diversity was gradually eroded.

Genghis Khan invaded in 1219 while conquering Khwarezm, and before his death in 1227 assigned the lands of Western Central Asia to his second son, Chagatai Khan, so that the region became the Chagatai Khanate. In 1369 Timur, of the Barlas tribe, became its effective ruler and made Samarkand the capital of his future empire. Transoxiana was flourishing in the mid-14th century and became a great centre of Muslim civilisation.
transvaal-province: The Transvaal took its name from the Latin prefix trans, meaning across, and referred to its position north of the Vaal River. The province lay between the Vaal in the south and the Limpopo River in the north. To its south were the Orange Free State and Natal, to its west the Cape Province and the Bechuanaland Protectorate, to its north Rhodesia, and to its east Portuguese East Africa and Swaziland. Except on the southwest, the borders were mostly defined by natural features. The Waterberg Massif, an ancient geological feature, lies within it. Pretoria was its capital and also the executive capital of the country.

The area has been inhabited since at least the 8th century by the Venda and Sesotho people. From 1817 several Nguni groups, such as the Matabele, who had been expelled from Natal by the Zulus, invaded the region in the Mfecane. At the end of the 1830s the Boers left on the Great Trek into the interior, where the South African Republic was founded. It was an independent country ruled by the Dutch-speaking Boers from 1852 to 1902, and the borders of the later province coincided with it. Pretoria and Johannesburg emerged as major cities in this period. In 1902 the republic was conquered by the United Kingdom and became the Transvaal Colony.

In 1910 four British colonies united to form the Union of South Africa, and the Transvaal Colony became the Transvaal Province. In 1961 the union left the Commonwealth of Nations and became the Republic of South Africa. The conurbation centred on Pretoria and Johannesburg, called the PWV, became the country's economic centre. Several Bantustans lay wholly within the province, among them Venda, KwaNdebele, Gazankulu, KaNgwane and Lebowa, and parts of Bophuthatswana lay there too. The province was a stronghold of the National Party.

In 1994, after the fall of apartheid, a new constitution abolished the former provinces and the Transvaal ceased to exist. Its south-central portion, including the PWV, became Gauteng, its northern portion became Limpopo and its southeastern portion became Mpumalanga. Most of North West came from its southwestern portion, and a small segment joined KwaZulu-Natal. The old regional names Northern, Eastern, Western and Southern Transvaal survive in the names of sporting teams: the Blue Bulls were formerly Northern Transvaal, and the Golden Lions, formed in 1889, were formerly Transvaal.
transylvania: Transylvania is a historical region in Central Europe, bounded on the east and south by the Carpathian Mountains and on the west by the Apuseni Mountains. Its core is the Transylvanian Plateau, 300 to 500 metres high, drained by the Mureș, Someș, Criș and Olt rivers. The name first appears in a Medieval Latin document of the Kingdom of Hungary in 1078 as ultra silvam, meaning beyond the forest. The German name Siebenbürgen refers to the seven cities of the Transylvanian Saxons.

The first known people of the territory were the Agathyrsi, followed by the Celtic La Tène culture from the 4th century BCE and the Dacian tribes, who were united under King Burebista. Trajan's wars created Roman Dacia in 106, and Emperor Aurelian withdrew the legions south of the Lower Danube in 275. The Goths, Huns, Gepids and Avars then held the region in turn, and the First Bulgarian Empire expanded into its south in the 9th century. Hungarian tribes conquered it in the late 9th century, and King Stephen I of Hungary brought it into the Kingdom of Hungary in 1002. Saxon colonists settled in the 12th and 13th centuries.

Historians disagree about the early population. The theory of Daco-Roman continuity holds that Romanians lived there without interruption, while its opponents point to the lack of written, archaeological and linguistic evidence. After the Battle of Mohács in 1526 the region belonged to the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom, from which the Principality of Transylvania emerged in 1570 under the Treaty of Speyer. For most of the 16th and 17th centuries it was a vassal of the Ottoman Empire, with dual Ottoman and Habsburg suzerainty. In 1848 the Hungarian government proclaimed union with Transylvania, but the Compromise of 1867 reincorporated it into the Kingdom of Hungary within the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

The National Assembly of Romanians from Transylvania proclaimed union with Romania on 1 December 1918, and the Treaty of Trianon confirmed new borders in 1920. Over a million Hungarians remained on the Romanian side, mainly in the Székely Land. Northern Transylvania returned to Hungary in 1940 under the Second Vienna Award and to Romania after the Second World War. Its fortified churches, the old town of Sighișoara, the Dacian fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains and Roșia Montană are World Heritage Sites. Bram Stoker's 1897 novel Dracula made the region a byword for vampires in popular culture.
transylvanian-saxons: The Transylvanian Saxons are a Germanic people who settled in Transylvania in several waves, from the twelfth-century Ostsiedlung to the middle of the nineteenth century. Most of the first settlers came from the Low Countries, Luxembourg and Alsace, as well as other parts of present-day Germany, though the name Saxon was used loosely for Germanic peoples generally.

In medieval Transylvania the term could also denote a nobleman's title and not necessarily a German speaker. Colonisation began under King Géza II of Hungary (1141 to 1162). For centuries the settlers defended the southern, south-eastern and north-eastern borders of the kingdom against Cumans, Pechenegs, Mongols and Tatars, and later Ottomans, and developed agriculture; those in the north-east also worked in mining.

The Diploma Andreanum, issued by King Andrew II of Hungary in 1224, gave the Germans of the territory between Drăușeni and Orăștie administrative and religious autonomy and fixed their duties: a yearly tax to the king and military contributions in case of attack. Their land of about 30,000 square kilometres was called the Royal Land, in German Königsboden, and even Hungarians could not settle on it.

The Mongol invasion of 1241–42 destroyed many Saxon settlements, after which many towns were fortified with stone castles. In 1438 the Saxons, the Hungarian nobility and the Szeklers joined in the Unio Trium Nationum, a charter that kept their political rights and excluded the largely Hungarian and Romanian peasantry.

Under the influence of Johannes Honterus, most Saxons turned to Lutheranism in the Reformation, and Paul Wiener became the first superintendent of their Lutheran Church after a synod on 6 February 1553. Wars between the Habsburgs and the Ottomans from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries reduced their numbers, and a smaller third phase of settlement followed when Transylvania came under Habsburg control. In the late eighteenth century Emperor Joseph II tried to revoke the Union of the Three Nations; his actions were rescinded, but many Saxons came to see themselves as a small minority.

The earliest religious organisation of the Saxons was the Provostship of Hermannstadt, now Sibiu, founded on 20 December 1191. In the Middle Ages about 300 villages were defended by Kirchenburgen, fortified churches with massive walls and watch towers. The Saxons also founded or helped found towns outside the Carpathian arch, such as Câmpulung and Târgoviște in Wallachia and Baia in Moldavia. Their dialect, Transylvanian Saxon, is a conservative form of German close to Luxembourgish, and its earliest text was written by Johannes Tröster in 1666.
traprain-law: Traprain Law rises about 220 metres above sea level, 6 km east of Haddington. Like nearby Berwick Law and the Bass Rock it is made of phonolite, an unusual rock intruded about 350 million years ago into the sandstones and limestones of the Carboniferous Ballagan Formation. The name Traprain Law dates only from the late 18th century, after a local hamlet; earlier maps call the hill Dunpendyrlaw, and fishermen who use it as a landmark still call it Dunpelder, perhaps the Cumbric for fort of the spear shafts. In 1547 a beacon was placed on it to warn of an English invasion.

The hill was a place of burial by about 1500 BCE and shows signs of occupation and ramparts after 1000 BCE; the ramparts were rebuilt and realigned many times, and at its maximum extent the fort covered about 16 hectares. Excavations show occupation in the Late Iron Age from about 40 CE until the last quarter of the 2nd century. The Romans recorded the Votadini here in the 1st century, and the site is generally identified with Curia, named by Ptolemy. It is thought to have been the capital of the kingdom of Gododdin before the seat moved to Din Eidyn, the Castle Rock of Edinburgh.

A team led by Curle and Cree excavated from 1914 to 1923, and in 1919 Alexander Ormiston Curle recovered the treasure from a pit: over 24 kg of hacked Roman silver, mostly table ware but also early Christian items and parts of an officer's uniform, some perhaps from Rome, Ravenna, Antioch or Constantinople. Coins of Valens, Arcadius and Honorius date it after the Roman departure from Britain. Scholars have proposed raiding plunder or payment for mercenary service as its origin.

The treasure is in the care of the National Museum of Scotland. A quarry for road stone, leased to the district council in 1938, has scarred part of the hill. In legend it was the cliff from which Thenaw, mother of Saint Mungo, was thrown by her father, King Lot.
traprain-law-treasure: The hoard was found during excavations on 12 May 1919 on land then owned by the former prime minister A. J. Balfour. It seems to have been buried in a pit within a cluster of houses on the uppermost levels of the hill's western shoulder. In the Roman Iron Age Traprain Law was a major political centre beyond Hadrian's Wall, and its many Roman finds point to long contact with the Roman world. It is the largest hoard of Roman hacksilver now known.

The Edinburgh silversmiths Brook & Son restored the silver, heating it to make it malleable so that pieces could be shaped back to their original form. They also made replicas for sale, some faithful copies and others adapted to contemporary taste, as when a spoon was turned into a tea strainer.

Most of the pieces began as high-status tableware: large platters, small bowls and spoons for feasting, and jugs for wine and water. Another group is toilet silver, such as cosmetic containers, fluted water basins and pieces of mirrors. A near-complete jug bears scenes from the Old and the New Testament, and a fluted wash basin shows a Nereid riding a sea-panther, so both Christian and pagan imagery appear. There are a few belt fittings and a brooch, and clipped silver siliquae of Valens, Arcadius and Honorius. Ownership graffiti show the silver came from many different sets and owners.

When it was found the hoard was read as barbarian loot hacked up after raids on the Roman empire. Later study showed that many pieces had been cut carefully to standard Roman weights, which suggests the silver was turned into bullion in times of economic crisis and then used for diplomatic gifts or payment for military service. Many pieces were cut more than once, so they probably passed through several hands. Crucibles from the hill show that silver was worked there, and a massive silver chain found on the site was probably made from reused Roman silver.
trausnitz-castle: The castle stands on a hill above Landshut, which it guarded together with the land around it. Until the 16th century it bore the same name as the town, Landshut, protector of the land. Its size has changed little since its foundation. The Knights' Hall, of about 245 square metres in two naves, was already standing around 1260 and is built in the style known in German as Zisterziensergotik. Above it, in the Dürnitz wing, is the White Hall, probably of the 15th century and apparently never finished, since it bears no trace of the paintings usual in the castle at the time.

The castle was complete by the time Emperor Frederick II visited in 1235. In the first half of the 13th century it was a centre of imperial politics and of Staufer culture, and minstrels such as Walter von der Vogelweide and Tannhäuser came to Landshut. In the 15th century the dukes of Landshut repeatedly enlarged it, building the Dürnitz and raising the outer walls. Duke Louis X furnished it in the south German Renaissance style in 1516, and Friedrich Sustris built the courtyard arcades between 1568 and 1578 for Crown Prince William, adding paintings in the Florentine style that fires later destroyed.

Prince Ferdinand Maria had burned paintings restored between 1675 and 1679. In the 18th century the castle served as a barracks and a prison for noble prisoners, and early in the 19th century as a hospital. King Ludwig II of Bavaria had a private apartment decorated on the second floor of the prince's wing between 1869 and 1873, but a fire on 21 October 1961 destroyed much of the interior, including the king's rooms.

The Knights' Hall, the White Hall and the loggia known as the Söller are used for banquets, concerts, lectures and exhibitions. The Chamber of Art and Curiosities, arranged by Prince Wilhelm in 1579 and later taken to Munich, reopened in the castle in September 2004 as part of the Bavarian National Museum, with some 750 objects in four themes: works of art, natural wonders, exotic crafts and scientific instruments.
travancore-dutch-war: In the early 18th century the Malabar Coast was divided among small chiefdoms from which the Dutch East India Company bought its spices. In 1733–1734 Marthanda Varma of Travancore conquered Peritally, Eledattu Svarupam and Maruthurkulangara, states bound to the Company by monopoly contracts, and their supplies stopped. Julius Valentyn Stein van Gollenesse, the Dutch commander at Kochi, asked in vain for the contracts to be honoured, while Travancore sold the pepper to the Company's rivals.

In 1739 Gustaaf Willem van Imhoff, the Dutch Governor of Ceylon, reported that the Company's business in the region was in complete ruin and would have to be saved by violent redress. The Dutch formed an alliance with the rulers of Kochi, Thekkumkur, Vadakkumkur, Purakkad, Kollam and Kayamkulam. When van Imhoff threatened an invasion, Marthanda Varma replied that he had been thinking of invading Europe some day.

Without waiting for permission from Batavia, the Dutch command declared war. On 12 November 1739 the Dutch and their allies routed the Travancore army near Kollam after a grenade blew up its powder store, and took 16 cannon at Tangasseri. They restored the princess of Eledattu Svarupam but were driven back at Attingal, and on 20 February 1740 won a costly victory at the Attingal ferry.

Reinforced from Ceylon, a Dutch force under De Lennoy landed at Colachel and took the country up to Kottar. Marthanda Varma saved Kalkulam, pursued the Dutch to Colachel and defeated them on 10 August 1741, capturing 24 officers including De Lennoy. In 1742 Travancore took the fort of Kilimanoor, held by the Dutch, and Kottarakkara, but failed to capture Kollam and withdrew after losing 6,000 soldiers.

Short of money and troops, the Dutch reopened talks, which failed at Mavelikkara, Paravur and Pulikkara as Marthanda Varma hardened his terms on learning that van Imhoff's forces would not come. On 22 May 1743 van Gollenesse's successor, Reinicus Siersma, concluded a peace accepting most of Travancore's terms.

Travancore went on to take Kayamkulam and Ambalapuzha and to annex Thekkumkur and Vadakkumkur in 1749 and 1750. In the Treaty of Mavelikkara of 1753 the Dutch adopted a strict policy of non-intervention and gave up their alliances with other Kerala powers. De Lennoy later commanded Travancore forces with Prince Rama Varma at the Battle of Anadeswaram in 1754, and a pillar near the coast at Colachel still records the victory.
trave: The Trave is a river in Schleswig-Holstein, about 124 kilometres long, running from its source near the village of Gießelrade in Ostholstein to Travemünde, where it flows into the Baltic Sea. It rises and flows south-west through the Wardersee to Bad Segeberg, then south to Bad Oldesloe, where it bends eastward and passes Moisling, a district of Lübeck, before reaching Lübeck.

Its tributaries include the Wakenitz and the Stepenitz. Sea-going vessels can navigate it from the Baltic to the Lübeck ports. The lower course arose in the last ice age, the Weichselian glaciation, when glacier flows carved deep fjords into what is now the Baltic coast; its lower end is called the Traveförde.

In the early Middle Ages the upper Trave, together with the Schwentine, formed part of the Limes Saxoniae and the western boundary of Wagria. In medieval Lübeck the river was reshaped for shipping and for the town's defence, turning the Old Town into an island. South of Lübeck Cathedral the channel forks, the original channel being the Town Trave, while the town moat branches off to the west and the Canal Trave runs in the former bed of the Wakenitz. The river forms part of the medieval fortifications. North of Lübeck, on the peninsula between the Schwartau and the Trave, lies the site of the Slavic castle of Liubice.

North of the Old Town the seaports begin, and Lübeck's commercial port lies between the Old Town and Teerhof Island. The Elbe–Lübeck Canal joins the river from the south shortly before Lübeck. The Herren Tunnel and numerous bridges cross the Trave, and a ferry connects Travemünde with Priwall. The lower reaches form the border between Schleswig-Holstein and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. The surrounding area is a protected habitat under the European Union Habitats Directive, with several nature preserves, and the German Friends of Nature named the Trave its German Riverscape of the Year for 2016/17.
trdat-the-architect: Trdat was the chief architect of the Bagratid kings of Armenia and worked in the country both before and after his time in Constantinople. In 961 King Ashot III moved his capital from Kars to Ani, where he built new palaces and rebuilt the walls. The Catholicosate was moved to the Argina district in the suburbs of Ani, and there Trdat completed the Catholicosal palace and the Mother Cathedral of Ani, an example of a cruciform domed church set within a rectangular plan. He is also believed to have designed or supervised Surb Nshan, the Holy Sign, completed in 991, the oldest building of Haghpat Monastery.

After the great earthquake of 989 partly brought down the dome of Hagia Sophia, Byzantine officials summoned Trdat to organise its repair, and the rebuilt dome was finished by 994. The Armenian historian Stepanos Taronetsi, called Asoghik, wrote at the time that many skilled Greek workers had tried and failed to rebuild the church, and that Trdat, who happened to be there, presented a plan, prepared a model and began the work, so that the church was rebuilt more handsomely than before.

How Trdat came to be asked to repair the dome is unknown. The art historian Sirarpie Der Nersessian held that the fact alone was a sufficient sign of his renown, while Richard Krautheimer was more dismissive, suggesting that he might have been summoned only as a technician. Garbis Armen suggested that Trdat brought to Hagia Sophia ways of protecting a dome against earthquakes found at the seventh-century Saint Hripsime Church in Vagharshapat, among them ribs, narrow windows and short buttresses that steady the dome against lateral thrust.
treasury-of-atreus: The Treasury of Atreus is the largest and most elaborate tholos tomb known from the Aegean Bronze Age, and one of the last built in the Argolid. It stands about 500 metres south-southwest of the Lion Gate at Mycenae, alone on the eastern slope of the Panagia ridge, on a spot where an earlier building was demolished. Nothing is known of who was buried in it, though the immense labour involved and its likeness to the architecture of the citadel have suggested a ruler of Mycenae or someone close to the rulers.

The name is modern. When Pausanias visited in the 2nd century CE he placed the graves of Atreus and Agamemnon within the walls of Mycenae, and Edward Daniel Clarke reported the name Treasury of Atreus as a local tradition in the early nineteenth century.

Like other Mycenaean tholoi, it has a narrow passage, the dromos, a deep doorway, the stomion, and a circular burial chamber, the thalamos, under a corbelled dome. The doorway is topped by two lintel blocks, the inner one about 120 tons, the heaviest single piece of masonry known from Greek architecture. Above it a relieving triangle channelled the weight of the dome away from the lintel.

The chamber is built of 33 courses of cut limestone, 14.5 metres across and 13.2 metres high. The dome was the largest in the world until the Roman period and remains the world's largest corbelled dome. A doorway leads to a six-metre square side chamber, which most scholars think held any burials. The façade bore green and red marble columns and a frieze with rosettes and spirals. Building it took at least 20,000 worker-days.

The tomb was open and partly filled with debris by 1801. In 1802 Lord Elgin had it cleared and took away pieces of the columns and gypsum reliefs of bulls. In 1810 Veli Pasha, the Ottoman Pasha of the Morea, excavated it and reportedly found bones covered with gold, and removed four large column fragments, some of which reached Ireland and later the British Museum.

Its date was controversial in the early twentieth century. Arthur Evans, who saw Mycenaean civilisation as a Cretan offshoot, wanted an early date, while Alan Wace argued for a later one and for the continuity of mainland culture; John Percival Droop called the quarrel the Helladic Heresy. Wace's excavations of 1920 to 1921 and 1939 for the British School at Athens helped settle the question, and scholars still differ on the tomb's place in the sequence of Mycenae's fortifications.
treaties-of-nijmegen: The Franco-Dutch War of 1672–78 was the source of all the other wars that were ended formally at Nijmegen. Separate conflicts such as the Third Anglo-Dutch War and the Scanian War had been directly caused by it and formed part of it. England took the French side at first but withdrew in 1674 after the Treaty of Westminster, then allied with the Dutch in 1677. The Electorate of Cologne left the war in 1674, the Prince-Bishopric of Münster switched sides that year, and Denmark–Norway joined the anti-French side in 1675, fighting mainly against Sweden. Peace negotiations began as early as 1676, but nothing was signed before 1678.

The treaties were signed in the Dutch city of Nijmegen between August 1678 and October 1679, and they ended wars among France, the Dutch Republic, Spain, Brandenburg, Sweden, Denmark–Norway, the Prince-Bishopric of Münster and the Holy Roman Empire. The most significant was the first, between France and the Dutch Republic, which placed the northern border of France very near its modern position. Some peaces were signed elsewhere: the Treaty of Celle, between Sweden and Lüneburg (Celle); the Treaty of Saint-Germain, between France and Sweden and Brandenburg; and the Treaty of Fontainebleau, in which France dictated peace between Sweden and Denmark–Norway.

The treaty with Spain gave France the Franche-Comté and more of the Spanish Netherlands, adding to what it had annexed in 1659 and 1668. These included Saint-Omer with the rest of the northwestern part of Artois, the lands of Cassel, Aire and Ypres, the Bishopric of Cambrai, and the towns of Valenciennes and Maubeuge. Louis XIV in turn ceded Maastricht and the Principality of Orange to the Dutch stadtholder William III, and French forces withdrew from several occupied territories in northern Flanders and Hainaut.

Emperor Leopold I kept the fortress of Philippsburg but had to accept French occupation of Freiburg, until 1697, and of Kehl, until 1698, on the right bank of the Rhine. The treaties did not result in a lasting peace. Marc-Antoine Charpentier wrote a Te Deum for the occasion, whose prelude is also known as the Eurovision theme.
treaties-of-rome-1941: After the Yugoslav coup d'état of March 1941, Adolf Hitler resolved to dismember the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and Benito Mussolini hoped to gain territory along the eastern Adriatic. When Vladko Maček of the Croatian Peasant Party refused to lead a Croatian state, the post went to Ante Pavelić and the Italian-based Ustaše. The Independent State of Croatia was declared on 10 April 1941, and on 14 April at Karlovac Mussolini's envoy Filippo Anfuso obtained Pavelić's written promise to recognise Italian claims in Dalmatia. Foreign ministers Joachim von Ribbentrop and Galeazzo Ciano then split the new state into German and Italian zones along the Vienna Line.

Talks between Pavelić and Ciano in Ljubljana on 25 April, in Zagreb and at Monfalcone on 7 May settled the terms, signed in Rome on 18 May with no ratification foreseen. The Treaty on Frontiers gave Italy 5,380 square kilometres with 380,000 inhabitants, including Šibenik, the hinterland of Zadar, a strip in north-west Croatia and the Bay of Kotor, largely organised as the Governorate of Dalmatia. A military agreement barred Croatian troops from a coastal Zone II, and a 25-year Treaty of Guarantee and Collaboration bound the state to Italy in defence and foreign policy. Victor Emmanuel III named Prince Aimone, Duke of Spoleto, as king of Croatia.

The treaties made the state an Italian quasi-protectorate and were received very badly by Croats, above all on the coast, becoming a natural base for recruitment by the Yugoslav Partisans in Dalmatia. Italy reoccupied Zones II and III from 22 August 1941; when it later withdrew many battalions and leaned on Chetnik auxiliaries, the Partisans retook Bihać in November 1942 and founded the Bihać Republic.

After the Armistice of Cassibile, Pavelić declared the treaties void on 10 September 1943 and claimed Zadar, Rijeka and Istria, but Hitler blocked the claim by creating the Operational Zone of the Adriatic Littoral. Italy has treated the treaties as null since 1943, and the peace treaty of 1947 does not mention them.
treaties-of-tilsit: Two treaties were signed by Napoleon at Tilsit, today Sovetsk in Russia, in the aftermath of his victory at Friedland, at the end of the War of the Fourth Coalition. The first was concluded on 7 July with Alexander I when the two emperors met on a raft in the middle of the Neman river. The second, with Prussia, followed on 9 July. King Frederick William III of Prussia had already agreed to a truce on 25 June after the Grande Armée had captured Berlin and pursued him to the easternmost frontier of his realm.

The raft was meant to express the perfect equality of the two emperors. Tilsit was declared neutral, with one part held by a Russian Guard battalion and the other by a French one. Napoleon gave his Guard the password Alexander, Russia, Greatness, and the Russian Guard was given Napoleon, France, Prowess.

The Franco-Russian treaty ended the war and began an alliance between the two empires. Russia agreed to join the Continental System against the British Empire, and Napoleon persuaded Alexander to enter the Anglo-Russian War and to instigate the Finnish War against Sweden. The tsar was to evacuate Wallachia and Moldavia, and the Ionian Islands and Cattaro, taken by Russian admirals, were to be handed to the French. Napoleon guaranteed the sovereignty of the Duchy of Oldenburg and several small states ruled by the tsar's German relatives.

Prussia lost about half its territory, falling from 5,700 square miles to 2,800 and from 9.75 million inhabitants to no more than 4.5 million. The Kingdom of Westphalia, the Duchy of Warsaw and the Free City of Danzig were formalised, Cottbus went to Saxony and Białystok to Russia. Prussia was to reduce its army to 43,000, and in 1808 France fixed its tribute at 154,500,000 francs, later lowered to 120 million.

Talleyrand had advised milder terms, and the treaties marked an important stage in his estrangement from Napoleon. Many observers in Prussia and Russia viewed them as unequal and a national humiliation. Napoleon's plan to marry the tsar's sister was stymied by Russian royalty, and cooperation broke down in 1810 when the tsar began to admit neutral ships to Russian ports. Napoleon crossed the Neman to invade Russia in June 1812.

The treaties freed French forces for the Peninsular War, which began on 19 November 1807, and Central Europe became a battlefield again in 1809 with the War of the Fifth Coalition. The Congress of Vienna restored many Prussian territories after 1815. By signing, France also left Persia and the Ottomans, which had hoped for its help, in the face of Russian aggression.
treaties-of-tirana: An earlier treaty of Tirana, signed on 2 August 1920, had ended fighting between Italian troops and Albanian nationalists after the First World War: Italy recognised Albania's independence and gave up Vlorë, which it had held since 1914, while keeping the island of Saseno. Italy saw Albania as its gateway to the Balkans, Greece and the Near East. Ahmet Zogu, elected president in 1925, sought to develop the economy, secure his power and win recognition from his neighbours, and knew he could not do so without outside support.

In May 1925 Albania accepted an Italian proposal to found the Albanian National Bank, which acted as the treasury though it was controlled by Italian banks, and came with a five-year loan of about 2 million pounds and mineral concessions. Mussolini weighed two courses: economic penetration until a de facto protectorate was reached, or permanent occupation.

The first treaty, the Treaty of Peace and Security, was signed on 27 November 1926 for five years. Its five articles treated anyone who challenged the Albanian status quo as an enemy of both states, barred either party from agreements harmful to the other and provided for conciliation in disputes; it was to be registered with the League of Nations. Albania accepted Italian officers to oversee and train its army and police, and the treaty came with payments to Zogu, who feared unrest might cost him power. Yugoslavia, backed by France, answered with military action on Albania's northern border.

The second treaty, signed on 22 November 1927, was a defensive alliance for twenty years, meant to stay secret. Under its seven articles each party was to help the other if attacked, with armed force and money, and neither could make peace alone. Italy was to protect Albania's territory, and Albania placed its whole military arsenal at Italy's disposal.

The alliance let Italy send two hundred and eighty officers to train the Albanian army and gave its navy access to the port of Vlorë, and a ministry in Rome was set up to handle Albanian affairs. In 1937 the Italian Foreign Minister, Ciano, secured a further 60 million gold francs for Albania. On 7 April 1939 Italy occupied the country and Zog fled; the crown passed to Victor Emmanuel III on 12 April.
treaty-of-aberconwy: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd sought to strengthen his links to royalty by marrying Eleanor de Montfort, daughter of Simon de Montfort and cousin of Edward I. They were married by proxy in 1275, but when Eleanor sailed from France, Edward had pirates seize her ship and held her at Windsor Castle. Edward, newly king, saw Llywelyn as a threat and disliked a match with the house of de Montfort, who had been the chief threat to his predecessor's reign. Llywelyn refused repeated summonses to appear before him, saying he would not be safe at court.

In 1276 Edward declared Llywelyn a rebel and raised a very large army. By the summer of 1277 his forces had reached the heart of Gwynedd, and the seizure of the harvest on Anglesey left the Welsh without food and forced Llywelyn to surrender.

The treaty was signed on 10 November 1277. Eastern Gwynedd was divided between Edward and Llywelyn's brother Dafydd ap Gruffydd, who had gone over to the English, and the other lands once tributary to Llywelyn passed effectively under Edward's control. Deheubarth, Powys and mid-Wales became a mixture of royal land and compliant English protectorates, giving Edward a degree of direct control in the native Welsh areas that no earlier English king had achieved. The treaty completed the first stage of Edward's conquest of Wales and made it all but certain that Welsh self-rule would end with Llywelyn's death.

Llywelyn paid homage and tribute, and Edward allowed the marriage to go ahead: in 1278 Llywelyn and Eleanor were married in Worcester Cathedral with the king present. Dafydd, however, was dissatisfied with his reward and rebelled in 1282. His rising took on the character of a national struggle, which Llywelyn and the other Welsh leaders joined, and Edward came to treat it as a war of conquest. Llywelyn was killed at the Battle of Orewin Bridge in December 1282, and the conquest was completed with Dafydd's capture in June 1283.
treaty-of-accession-1972: Denmark, Norway and the United Kingdom were already linked economically in the European Free Trade Association, while Ireland, which sent nearly 75 per cent of its exports to the United Kingdom, sought to reduce that dependence. The United Kingdom, Ireland and Denmark applied to join the European Communities on 31 July 1961. In 1963, after long negotiations, France vetoed the British application: Charles de Gaulle regarded the United Kingdom as a Trojan horse for the United States. Under de Gaulle's successor Georges Pompidou, France lifted its opposition after the Hague summit of 1969, opening the way to enlargement.

The treaty provided for the accession of Denmark, Ireland, Norway and the United Kingdom to the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community. In the accompanying Act concerning the Conditions of Accession, the new members undertook to observe the principles and guidelines deriving from the existing members' declarations and resolutions, and to adjust their international agreements to the rights and obligations of membership.

France approved enlargement by referendum in April 1972 with 68 per cent of the vote. Ireland ratified the treaty by referendum on 10 May 1972 with 81.3 per cent, Denmark by referendum with 63.3 per cent, as its constitution requires for any change in national sovereignty, and the United Kingdom through Parliament. In Norway's referendum of September 1972, 53.5 per cent voted against, and Prime Minister Trygve Bratteli resigned. The other three joined on 1 January 1973, when the treaty entered into force.

The British public was first asked after accession, in a referendum held by Harold Wilson's Labour government on 5 June 1975, the first national referendum in the country; 67.23 per cent voted to stay. After a referendum in 2016 in which 51.9 per cent voted to leave, the United Kingdom left the European Union on 31 January 2020, after 47 years of membership, and ceased to be bound by the treaty.
treaty-of-addis-ababa: The First Italo-Ethiopian War grew out of the Treaty of Wuchale of 1889. Its Italian text obliged Ethiopia to conduct all foreign affairs through Italy, in effect making it an Italian protectorate, while the Amharic version only gave Ethiopia the option of dealing with other powers through the Italian government. Emperor Menelik II believed he had been deceived, and the Italians had meanwhile been encroaching on Ethiopian territory until fighting began in 1895.

After the Battle of Adwa in March 1896, Menelik held 3,000 Italian prisoners and faced the demoralised remnants of the Italian army in Eritrea, and news of the defeat forced Prime Minister Francesco Crispi to resign. A secret agreement was negotiated days after the battle, and the final treaty superseded it.

The first Italian offer, presented by Major Tomasso Salsa on 11 March, was to abrogate Wuchale in exchange for a new treaty of peace and friendship, but it asked that Menelik accept the protection of no other power. According to the historian Harold G. Marcus, Menelik was so angered that he demanded the return of their secret truce and said he would hold Salsa hostage until then. Only on 23 August did Italy agree to the unconditional abrogation of Wuchale and recognition of Ethiopia's sovereign independence, after which talks moved quickly to the signing on 26 October 1896.

The prisoners of war, whose captivity Marcus calls reasonably benign, were to be repatriated, and Italy was to pay an indemnity of 10,000,000 lire for their upkeep. Italy kept most, if not all, of the land it had taken beyond the Mareb-Belessa and May/Muni rivers, and Ethiopian monarchists hold that Menelik gave away a sizable part of Tigray. The border with Eritrea was defined in agreements of 1900, 1902 and 1908. France signed a treaty treating Ethiopia as an equal in late January 1897 and the United Kingdom on 14 May 1897.
treaty-of-adrianople-1829: The treaty was signed in Adrianople on 14 September 1829 by Count Alexey Fyodorovich Orlov for Russia and Abdülkadir Bey for the Ottoman Empire, and its terms favoured Russia. The Ottoman Empire gave Russia access to the mouths of the Danube and the fortresses of Akhaltsikhe and Akhalkalaki in Georgia. The Sultan recognised Russia's possession of Georgia, with Imeretia, Mingrelia and Guria, and of the Khanates of Erivan and Nakhichevan, which Persia had ceded to the tsar in the Treaty of Turkmenchay a year earlier. Russia also took control of the towns of Anape and Poti in the Caucasus, and Russian traders in Turkey were placed under the jurisdiction of the Russian ambassador.

The treaty opened the Dardanelles to all commercial vessels, which freed the trade in grain, livestock and lumber. The Sultan renewed his earlier guarantee of autonomy to Serbia and promised autonomy for Greece. In recognition of the Treaty of London, the independence of Greece, or autonomy under Ottoman suzerainty, was accepted.

Russia was allowed to occupy Moldavia and Wallachia until the Ottoman Empire had paid a large indemnity. The Ottoman Empire kept nominal suzerainty over the Danube states of Moldavia and Wallachia, which for practical purposes were independent. The treaty also fixed the border between the Ottoman Empire and Wallachia on the thalweg of the Danube, transferring to Wallachia the rule of the districts of Turnu, Giurgiu and Brăila. The indemnities were sharply reduced by the later Treaty of Hünkâr İskelesi of 1833, which was also needed finally to settle the Straits Question between the two states.

The annexed territory had a mostly Georgian population, with Azerbaijanis, called Tatars at the time, Turks, Armenians and Kurds. Soon after the fighting ended, the Turks and Kurds left for the Ottoman Empire, and about 30 thousand Ottoman Armenians from the pashaliks of Erzurum and Kars settled in their places. They were settled in the regions of Akhaltsikhe and Akhalkalaki and also in Tbilissi, Erevan and Nakhchivan.
treaty-of-aix-la-chapelle-1748: Britain and France opened talks at Breda in 1746. The Duke of Newcastle, who controlled British foreign policy, delayed them in hopes of a better position, but the Dutch army collapsed and British hopes of recovering the Austrian Netherlands failed. France, though victorious in Flanders, was hard pressed by the British naval blockade, and after the Second Battle of Cape Finisterre in October 1747 could no longer protect its merchant convoys. Austria had made peace with Bavaria and Prussia and was kept in the war only by British subsidies. A congress assembled at Aachen on 24 April 1748, and a draft was agreed on 30 April.

The final treaty was signed on 18 October 1748 by Britain, France and the Dutch Republic; Austria, Sardinia, Spain, Modena and Genoa acceded in documents of 4 December 1748 and 21 January 1749. All accepted the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713, and Austria recognised the Prussian acquisition of Silesia. Austria ceded Parma, Piacenza and Guastalla to Philip of Spain and minor territories, including Vigevano, to Sardinia, and withdrew from Modena and Genoa.

France withdrew from the Austrian Netherlands and returned the Dutch Barrier forts, Maastricht and Bergen op Zoom. Britain and France exchanged Louisbourg on Île-Royale for Madras. Spain renewed the Asiento de Negros, the monopoly contract to supply slaves to Spanish America, which Britain had held since 1713; Britain renounced it in the Treaty of Madrid in 1750 for £100,000. France agreed to expel Charles Edward Stuart.

The treaty largely failed to settle the issues that had caused the war. Prussia, which doubled in size and wealth with Silesia, gained most. Maria Theresa resented her exclusion from the talks and the pressure from Britain to cede territory, while many in Britain questioned the value of the subsidies paid to her. These tensions led to the Diplomatic Revolution and the Seven Years' War, which began in 1756. In the Treaty of Aranjuez of 1752 Austria, Spain and Sardinia agreed to respect each other's boundaries in Italy.

In France the return of conquests, forced by the state of its finances, gave rise to the phrase as stupid as the Peace. The treaty ended the First Carnatic War between the British and French in India. Celebrations in London featured George Frideric Handel's Music for the Royal Fireworks.
treaty-of-alcacovas: After Henry IV of Castile died in 1474, his half-sister Isabella, married to Ferdinand II of Aragon, and his daughter Juana de Trastámara disputed the crown. Juana was called la Beltraneja because her father was alleged to be Beltrán de la Cueva. Afonso V of Portugal married her and invaded Castile in May 1475. The indecisive Battle of Toro on 1 March 1476 became a strategic victory for the Catholic Monarchs on land.

At sea the two kingdoms fought for Guinea, whose gold and slaves were the heart of Portuguese power. According to the historian Stephen R. Bown, Castile renewed its claim to the Canaries and the Guinea coast, and in 1478 a Castilian fleet of thirty-five caravels was intercepted and most of it taken to Lisbon. The war thus ended with Castile victorious on land and Portugal at sea.

The treaty was in fact four treaties. Besides the renunciations of both thrones, Portugal kept Guinea and its gold mines and won the exclusive right to conquer the Kingdom of Fez and to navigate, conquer and trade in the Atlantic south of the Canaries, covering lands yet to be found. Castilians could not sail to Portuguese possessions without licence. Portugal received 106,676 dobles of gold as a war compensation in the form of a dowry.

Under the arrangement called the Tercerias de Moura, Isabella, eldest daughter of the Catholic Monarchs, was to marry Afonso, heir of Prince John of Portugal; both children lived at Moura at Castilian cost. Juana chose a religious life in Portugal over marriage to Prince Juan, and her Castilian supporters were pardoned.

The papal bull Aeterni regis ratified the treaty in 1481. Shut out of Africa, the Castilian rulers funded Christopher Columbus in 1492 in the hope of reaching Asia westward. The treaty was the first to define fields reserved for future discoveries, and it is seen as a landmark of colonialism: European powers dividing the world into spheres of influence without the consent of its peoples, a principle carried on by the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 and the Conference of Berlin of 1884.
treaty-of-alcaraz: The Hudid Emirate of Murcia had been unstable since the assassination of Ibn Hud in 1238. By early 1243 its emir, Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Hud Baha al-Dawla, was threatened by the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada among others, and he offered to become a vassal of Castile, sending his son as an emissary to Burgos. The infante Alfonso negotiated on behalf of his father, King Ferdinand III of Castile, with representatives of Murcia's Muslim noble families.

The treaty was signed around 2 April 1243 at the Shrine of Our Lady of Cortes in the Castilian town of Alcaraz and made Murcia a Castilian protectorate. Its rulers accepted vassalage to the Castilian king, Castilian troops were to hold the fortresses of the region, and Castile was to collect a share of its taxes. In return the religious practice and property of the Muslim population were to be respected, and Muslim governors were to go on ruling under Castilian oversight. The settlement thus left local government in Muslim hands while placing the fortresses and part of the revenue with Castile.

Not every town accepted the settlement. Lorca, Mula and Cartagena refused the treaty; Lorca and Mula were conquered in 1244, and Cartagena fell to Alfonso in the spring of 1245 with the help of a fleet from the Cantabrian coast. Settlers came to the city of Murcia from all parts of Iberia until Christians were the majority there, and the Muslims were confined to the suburb of Arrixaca. The Mudéjar revolt of 1264–1266 in the Kingdom of Murcia in effect released Alfonso X from any obligation to honour the treaty's terms.
treaty-of-almizra: The Treaty of Almizra, also written Almiçra, was the third of a series of agreements between the Crown of Aragon and the Crown of Castile meant to fix the limits of their expansion into al-Andalus and so prevent quarrels between the Christian princes. It followed the treaties of Tudilén and Cazorla, which had been constantly breached. Their central clause, that neither crown should reduce the share assigned to the other or obstruct the other in winning it, was the one neither side kept: James I of Aragon took Caudete, Villena and Sax in Castile's zone, while the infante Alfonso held Xàtiva in the zone reserved for Aragon.

The treaty defined the borders of the Kingdom of Valencia. All lands south of a line running from Biar to Villajoyosa by way of Busot were reserved for Castile. James I signed it on 26 March 1244 at Campo de Mirra, but Alfonso, the future Alfonso X of Castile, did not confirm it until much later. The line ended most further Aragonese expansion on the Iberian peninsula.

The treaty is first mentioned in the second chapter of the Llibre dels fets, but its text was published only in 1905. A monument raised at Campo de Mirra in 1977 commemorates it. The frontier it drew did not last unchanged. In 1296, during a pause in the war between the two crowns, James II of Aragon conquered the Kingdom of Murcia. That kingdom was then divided, and the districts of Medio Vinalopó, Bajo Vinalopó, L'Alacantí and Vega Baja del Segura were joined to Valencia by the treaties of Torrellas in 1304 and Elche in 1305.
treaty-of-altranstadt-1706: Charles XII of Sweden had occupied much of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, and on his behalf Stanisław Leszczyński was crowned king of Poland on 4 October 1705. A faction of the Commonwealth, organised in the Sandomierz Confederation, stayed loyal to Augustus the Strong, elector of Saxony and Polish king since 1697, who was allied with Tsar Peter the Great of Russia. The civil war in Poland of 1704 to 1706 went badly for Augustus.

Early in 1706 his attempt to regain control was thwarted by Charles XII at the Battle of Grodno and by Carl Gustav Rehnskiöld at the Battle of Fraustadt. Fraustadt left the Saxon electorate virtually undefended, and when Charles joined his forces with Rehnskiöld's and moved through Silesia to occupy it, he met no resistance.

The treaty was concluded in secrecy. Augustus made peace with the Swedish Empire, accepted Stanisław Leszczyński as king of Poland and had to congratulate him. His alliance with Russia, formalised in the Treaty of Preobrazhenskoye and the Treaty of Narva, was declared void, and all Russians under his command were to be handed over to the Swedish as prisoners. The diplomat and politician Johann Patkul was declared a criminal and likewise taken into Swedish custody.

Patkul was executed. Peter the Great, who regarded Augustus as a close friend as well as an ally, was disappointed when the treaty was revealed to him. His diplomats had known that a separate peace between Saxony and Sweden was possible, and had themselves been negotiating one for Russia since 1703, but they could not intervene. Peter then offered the Polish crown, not yet conquered, to Francis II Rákóczi, to John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough, to Jakub Sobieski, to Eugene of Savoy and to others, without success.

In the Commonwealth the treaty strengthened Stanisław Leszczyński, who won the loyalty of part of the lesser gentry. The settlement did not last. After Peter's victory over Charles XII at the Battle of Poltava on 27 June 1709, the Treaty of Thorn of 1709 restored Augustus as Polish king and renewed his alliance with Russia.
treaty-of-amiens: The War of the Second Coalition began well for the coalition, but after French victories at Marengo and Hohenlinden Austria eventually signed the Treaty of Lunéville in 1801, leaving Britain the only major power still at war with France. Horatio Nelson's victory at Copenhagen on 2 April 1801 halted the League of Armed Neutrality. Napoleon Bonaparte had made truce proposals as early as 1799, but the foreign secretary Lord Grenville and Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger rejected them. When Pitt resigned in February 1801 over domestic issues, the more accommodating Henry Addington replaced him.

Addington's foreign secretary, Lord Hawkesbury, opened talks with the French commissary Louis Guillaume Otto, and preliminaries were signed in London on 1 October 1801. Lord Cornwallis went to France in November to negotiate the final text against Joseph Bonaparte and Talleyrand, who kept shifting their positions. Pressure on Cornwallis was great, since the British public expected peace and Parliament was discussing the budget. The chief difficulty was Malta.

The treaty called for the restoration of prisoners and hostages. Britain was to return the Cape Colony and most of Dutch Guiana to the Batavian Republic and withdraw its forces from Egypt, while the Batavian Republic ceded Ceylon. Spain accepted British rule of Trinidad, and Menorca went back to Spain. France was to withdraw from the Papal States and the Kingdom of Naples, and the Septinsular Republic was recognised. Malta, Gozo and Comino were to be restored to the Knights Hospitaller and declared neutral, and the House of Orange-Nassau was to be compensated for its losses in the Netherlands.

News of the peace was greeted with celebration in Britain and France, and upper-class British visitors flocked to Paris in the second half of 1802. Among them were Charles James Fox, J. M. W. Turner and William Hazlitt, who spent much of three months copying Italian masters in the Louvre. Napoleon used the interlude for reforms, among them the Napoleonic Code and the Concordat with the Vatican, and for a constitution that gave him lifetime control.

The peace did not last. The British objected to Napoleon's exclusion of their trade from France and its client states, and to his reordering of Switzerland, Germany, Italy and the Netherlands, while Napoleon objected to Britain's refusal to evacuate Malta. Addington kept a large peacetime army of 180,000 and used the interlude to rebuild British strength. Britain declared war on France on 18 May 1803, and the Napoleonic Wars began.
treaty-of-amritsar-1809: Ranjit Singh had made Lahore his capital in 1799, proclaimed himself maharaja of the Punjab in 1801 and by 1808 controlled the land between the Jhelum and Sutlej rivers. The Sikh chiefs of Malwa, between the Sutlej and the Yamuna, feared he would absorb them and asked the British for protection. The East India Company at first declined, since after the Treaty of Tilsit of 1807 it feared an invasion by Napoleon and Russia and wanted Ranjit Singh's kingdom as a buffer.

Ranjit Singh met the Company's envoy Charles Metcalfe, and during months of talks crossed into Malwa to show his hold over it and to claim the Yamuna as his border. The Company sent troops to the Sutlej, and on 9 February 1809 General David Ochterlony declared that further incursions south of the river would be met with force. When Napoleon's attack on Spain made an invasion of India unlikely, the Company offered a new treaty, and Ranjit Singh, aware of his relative military weakness, agreed to sign it at Amritsar in April 1809.

The treaty declared perpetual friendship between the British Government and the State of Lahore, and the British undertook to have no concern with the Raja's territories and subjects north of the Sutlej. On the left bank he was to keep no more troops than internal duties required and was not to encroach on the neighbouring chiefs. The chiefs of Malwa and Sirhind came under British protection, free of tribute, but bound to supply British armies and join them against an enemy. On 12 June Ochterlony sent Ranjit Singh the ratified treaty.

Ranjit Singh kept the cis-Sutlej lands he had held before his third expedition there, but gave up Faridkot and Ambala and could make no alliance with the chiefs south of the river. The boundary of British India moved from the Yamuna to the Sutlej. Free to act to the north, he turned to the Gurkha occupation of the Punjab Hills and to Afghanistan, and took Peshawar, Multan and Kashmir from the Durrani Empire. The Sikh Empire lasted until the British conquest of 1849.
treaty-of-amritsar-1846: After the East India Company's decisive victory at the Battle of Sobraon, Raja Gulab Singh, acting as Wazir of the Sikh Empire, negotiated peace terms that included the cession of the land between the Sutlej and Beas, an indemnity of 1.5 crore rupees and a drastic reduction of the Sikh army. The regent Rani Jindan then replaced him with Lal Singh, who said the Lahore court could pay only half a crore in cash and offered territory for the rest. The British asked for the whole hill country between the Beas and the Indus, including the Kashmir Valley.
