Gulab Singh had built strong relations with the British, and the Governor-General offered to recognise him as independent sovereign of the ceded lands if he paid the indemnity. Article XII of the Treaty of Lahore bound the Sikh state to accept his sovereignty over whatever territory the British granted him by a separate treaty. The British kept the land between the Beas and the Ravi, with the Kullu Valley and the forts of Kangra and Noorpur.

The treaty was signed at Amritsar on 16 March 1846 by Frederick Currie and Brevet-Major Henry Montgomery Lawrence for the Governor-General, Sir Henry Hardinge, and by Gulab Singh in person. It gave him and his male heirs the hill country east of the Indus and west of the Ravi, including Chamba and excluding Lahul, for 75 lakhs of Nanak Shahi rupees. He was to refer disputes with his neighbours to British arbitration, join British troops in the hills with all his forces, and employ no European or American without consent. In token of British supremacy he was to send each year one horse, twelve shawl goats and three pairs of Kashmir shawls.

The treaty began Dogra rule in Kashmir. When Gulab Singh's officials began collecting revenue in Hazara in May 1846, Pashtun and other groups resisted, and in early 1847 he returned Hazara to the Lahore court in exchange for land nearer Jammu. Henry Lawrence settled a dispute over Chamba the same year, leaving it independent of Kashmir under British suzerainty. Gulab Singh's descendants ruled the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir as maharajas until its accession to India in 1947.
treaty-of-ancon: During the War of the Pacific and the Chilean occupation of Peru several rival Peruvian governments arose. The Chilean administration set up a collaborationist government at La Magdalena under Francisco García Calderón to represent the occupied country in negotiations, while Nicolás de Piérola's constitutional government moved to Ayacucho and a third, under Lizardo Montero, sat at Arequipa. In 1883 Chile recognised a fourth government, under Miguel Iglesias, who wanted peace at any cost, including the loss of territory. Andrés Avelino Cáceres, who opposed him, was defeated at the Battle of Huamachuco on 10 July 1883. The treaty was signed at Ancón, near Lima.

Article 2 ceded Tarapacá to Chile unconditionally, and Article 13 required recognition of the Chilean administrative and judicial acts of the occupation. Article 3, the most controversial, left Tacna and Arica under Chilean administration for ten years, after which a plebiscite would decide their fate and the country chosen would pay $10,000,000 to the other. Chilean historians hold that it was a covert transfer of both provinces, which Peruvian historians such as Jorge Basadre dispute.

Articles 4 to 10 dealt with the guano and saltpetre deposits: half the profits from guano in deposits already known were to go to paying Peru's debt, and the Lobos de Afuera Islands were to stay under Chilean exploitation while their guano lasted, with half the profits for Peru. Article 12 set up tribunals to compensate Chilean citizens expelled from Peru at the start of the war.

Discontent with the treaty led to the Peruvian Civil War of 1884–1885, which overthrew Iglesias. The Castellón-Elías protocol of 8 January 1890 gave Peru practically all the guano exploitation of Tarapacá on condition that it pass it to the creditors. The Tacna–Arica question was settled by the Treaty of Lima in 1929, through the mediation of the United States under President Herbert Hoover: Arica went to Chile, while Peru regained Tacna and received USD 6 million. A clause barring Chile from ceding former Peruvian territory to another nation without asking Peru was invoked in 1975, when Peru rejected a Chilean offer of minor ports to Bolivia.
treaty-of-ankara-1921: The agreement, also called the Accord of Ankara or the Franco-Turkish Agreement of Ankara, was signed at Ankara, then also known as Angora, and ended the Franco-Turkish War. It was signed for France by the diplomat Henry Franklin-Bouillon and for the Grand National Assembly of Turkey by its foreign minister, Yusuf Kemal Bey. In return for economic concessions from Turkey, France ceded large areas, and the Turkish government acknowledged French sovereignty over the French Mandate of Syria.

The treaty moved the Syria–Turkey border set by the Treaty of Sèvres of 1920 to Turkey's benefit, giving it large parts of the Aleppo and Adana vilayets. From west to east Adana, Osmaniye, Marash, Aintab, Kilis, Urfa, Mardin, Nusaybin and Jazirat ibn Umar (Cizre) passed to Turkey. The line ran from the Mediterranean just south of Payas to Meidan Ekbis, which stayed in Syria, and joined the Baghdad Railway at Al-Rai.

From there it followed the railway to Nusaybin, with the track itself in Turkish territory, and then the old road to Jazirat ibn Umar, which both countries could use. The sanjak of Alexandretta was given a special administrative status, with official recognition of the Turkish language and provision for the culture of its Turkish inhabitants, the largest single group there. Article 9 kept the Tomb of Suleyman Shah, grandfather of Osman I, in Syria as Turkish property under the Turkish flag.

The end of French claims over Turkish land was later recognised in the Armistice of Mudanya, and the new border in the Treaty of Lausanne of 1923. The treaty was registered in the League of Nations Treaty Series on 30 August 1926.
treaty-of-apamea: The Treaty of Apamea was the peace treaty made in 188 BCE between the Roman Republic and Antiochus III, ruler of the Seleucid Empire. It ended the Roman–Seleucid War. It followed Roman victories at the Battle of Thermopylae in 191 BCE and the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BCE, and Roman and Rhodian naval victories over the Seleucid fleet. It was formalised at Apamea in Phrygia.

According to Appian, the treaty obliged Antiochus to give up Europe altogether and all of Asia west of the Taurus Mountains. He had to surrender all his war elephants and keep none in future. His navy was limited to twelve warships for keeping his subjects under control, although he could build more if attacked. He could not recruit mercenaries north of the Taurus, which was territory just ceded to the Roman allies Pergamon and Rhodes, nor receive fugitives from it. He had to give twenty hostages chosen by the Roman consul, changed every third year except for the son of Antiochus.

The Seleucids were to pay an indemnity of 15,000 talents of silver: 500 Euboic talents at once, 2,500 more when the Roman Senate ratified the treaty, and instalments of 1,000 talents each year for twelve years. They also owed 540,000 modii of corn. Antiochus had to give up all prisoners and deserters to his enemies, and to Eumenes II of Pergamon whatever remained of the possessions Antiochus had gained by his agreement with Attalus I, the father of Eumenes.

Rome gave control of a large part of Asia Minor to Eumenes. Antiochus kept Cilicia, while most of Lycia and Caria became part of the Rhodian Peraia. The treaty let the Romans extend their political hegemony to the Eastern Mediterranean, although their power was still indirect and relied on allies of the second rank such as Pergamon and Rhodes. The harsh reparations weakened the Seleucid Empire by causing a shortage of money. The naval conditions appear to have fallen into abeyance, but the other conditions held.

Rome used the threat of renewed war to check Seleucid power. In the Sixth Syrian War it insisted that the Seleucids leave the Ptolemaic Empire alone after they had occupied much of Egypt and Cyprus in 168 BCE, and Antiochus IV grudgingly accepted. As late as 162 BCE, according to Polybius, a Roman delegation under Gnaeus Octavius used the treaty to hamstring Seleucid war elephants and destroy ships. Leptines of Laodicea killed Octavius, and the Senate seems to have disavowed Octavius's actions and let the killer go.
treaty-of-aranjuez-1801: After the Coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799, First Consul Napoleon and his foreign minister Talleyrand made colonial expansion a key policy. Napoleon wanted Louisiana as the hub of a new French empire in North America, to replace the one lost in 1763, and as a source of food and slaves for French plantations in the West Indies. Spain's alliance with France had brought on the Anglo-Spanish War of 1798 to 1802 and a British blockade that hurt its economy, while American settlers pressing west made Louisiana costly to hold.

The Spanish chief minister Manuel Godoy was willing to give up the territory, but asked for six French ships of the line and compensation in Italy to make the deal acceptable to Charles IV. Charles's wife, Maria Luisa of Parma, was the sister of Ferdinand of Parma, whose duchy France had occupied since 1796, so Talleyrand proposed a kingdom for Ferdinand's younger son Louis. The terms were fixed in the secret Third Treaty of San Ildefonso of October 1800, kept quiet while France negotiated the Convention of 1800 with the United States.

The terms were vague: the second clause said the new state might be the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, the three Roman legations or other provinces of Italy forming a rounded state. The Treaty of Lunéville with Austria in February 1801 made Ferdinand III, Grand Duke of Tuscany, exchange his duchy for Salzburg and Berchtesgaden, and in the Treaty of Florence of 28 March 1801 Naples handed Piombino and the State of the Presidi to France. Talleyrand kept the Presidi and joined Piombino to Tuscany to form the Kingdom of Etruria.

Spain confirmed the transfer of Louisiana after 30,000 French troops landed on Saint-Domingue in December 1801. That expedition failed, and its leader, General Charles Leclerc, died of yellow fever with an estimated 22,000 of his men. Without Saint-Domingue, Napoleon judged Louisiana irrelevant and in April 1803 sold it to the United States for $15 million. Etruria was dissolved and joined to France in 1807, and the Congress of Vienna restored Tuscany and Parma in 1815.
treaty-of-arras-1482: The dukes of the House of Valois-Burgundy, a cadet branch of the French royal house, held lands on both sides of the border between the Kingdom of France and the Holy Roman Empire. When the last duke, Charles the Bold, died at the Battle of Nancy on 5 January 1477 without sons, his daughter Mary of Burgundy claimed all his lands. Louis XI instead took the domains held from the French crown as reverted fiefs, among them the Duchy of Burgundy and the counties of Vermandois, Boulogne and Artois; only Flanders escaped him.

To secure her inheritance Mary married Archduke Maximilian of Austria on 19 August 1477, as her father and Emperor Frederick III had agreed in 1476. Maximilian defended her lands and defeated Louis's army at the Battle of Guinegate in 1479. After Mary died on 27 March 1482, Maximilian struggled to be accepted as regent for their young son Philip, and the treaty ended the first phase of the War of the Burgundian Succession.

Acting for Philip, Maximilian agreed to betroth his daughter Margaret, not yet three years old, to the Dauphin, so the marriage was settled in principle and left for the future. The contested lands were defined as her dowry: the counties of Artois, Auxerre, Burgundy, Charolais and Mâcon and the lordships of Bar-sur-Seine, Château-Chinon, Chaussin, Laperrière, Noyers and Salins. France had held all of them since 1477, so the dowry acknowledged that fact. Flanders and the other north-eastern lands of the Burgundian Netherlands went to Philip, while the treaty left the Duchy of Burgundy and several Picard counties in French hands without naming them.

The betrothal was formalised in 1483, and Margaret came to live at the French court; that year Charles succeeded his father as king. In 1491 the French side renounced the engagement when Charles decided to marry Duchess Anne of Brittany. The question of Margaret's dowry lands was reopened and settled in 1493 by the Treaty of Senlis.
treaty-of-athis-sur-orge: The treaty was signed at Athis-sur-Orge on 23 June 1305 between King Philip IV of France and Robert III of Flanders, and concluded the Franco-Flemish War, which had lasted from 1297 to 1305. It followed the Battle of Mons-en-Pévèle. Although Philip had won that battle, his kingdom was too drained financially and militarily to take advantage of the victory, and he sought instead to make Flanders pay a heavy price for peace.

Flanders kept its count but was to be held as a fief of France. The Flemish were to pay reparations of 400,000 pounds and a yearly penalty of 20,000, to furnish Philip with 600 knights, and to tear down the fortresses around their large cities. As an act of penance Bruges had to send 3,000 people on pilgrimage, 1,000 of whom were to travel overseas. Robert III, who had signed for the county, faced the impossible task of satisfying the French monarchy while keeping the Flemish cities from revolt, and it was only after 1309 that some of the reparations were actually paid.

Because its financial terms were so severe, the treaty met wide disapproval in Flanders. In June 1310 Pope Clement V, under pressure from Philip, declared that those who failed to fulfil its terms would be excommunicated. Tax collection brought riots in Aardenburg and Ghent in 1311. The burden fell hardest on the Flemish farmers and the middle class, and in 1323 the Peasant Revolt in Flanders broke out. It grew into a popular uprising that dominated Flemish politics for five years until it was crushed at the Battle of Cassel in 1328.
treaty-of-basel-1499: The treaty was concluded as an armistice after the Battle of Dornach, the last engagement of the Swabian War between the Swabian League and the Old Swiss Confederacy. Although the Swiss had won a series of victories, both sides were exhausted and their leaders wanted peace, and they met at Basel to agree its terms.

The treaty restored the territorial status quo ante. Eight of the ten members of the League of the Ten Jurisdictions were confirmed as nominally subject to the Habsburgs, but their membership of the league and its alliance with the Swiss Confederacy remained in place. The Swiss were not made to join an Imperial Circle, and the Habsburgs gave up their dynastic claims in Switzerland.

Jurisdiction over Thurgau, until then an imperial loan to the city of Constance, passed to the Swiss Confederacy. The imperial ban and all embargoes imposed on the Swiss cantons during the war were to be lifted.

Nineteenth-century Swiss historians presented the treaty as an important step towards the Confederacy's separation from the Holy Roman Empire; Wilhelm Oechsli in 1890 called it the recognition of Swiss independence by Germany. Twentieth-century scholars such as Sigrist (1949) and Mommsen (1958) found no sign that the leaders of the Confederacy at the time wished to distance themselves from the Empire.

Whatever its meaning for the Empire, the treaty substantially strengthened the Confederacy as a polity. One immediate consequence was the accession of Basel and Schaffhausen as cantons in 1501, part of the expansion between 1481 and 1513 that turned the late medieval Eight Cantons into the early modern Thirteen Cantons.
treaty-of-batum: On 5 December 1917 the armistice of Erzincan ended the fighting between Russia and the Ottoman Empire in the Caucasus Campaign, and Russia left the First World War on 3 March 1918 under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. From 14 March to April 1918 the Ottoman Empire and a delegation of the Transcaucasian Sejm, the ruling body of Transcaucasia, held the Trabzon peace conference. Enver Pasha offered to give up all Ottoman ambitions in the Caucasus in return for recognition of the Ottoman reacquisition of the east Anatolian provinces.

On 5 April the head of the Transcaucasian delegation, Akaki Chkhenkeli, accepted the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk as a basis for negotiation. In Tiflis the mood was very different, and Armenians pressed the Commissariat to refuse. Hostilities resumed, and Ottoman troops overran new lands to the east and reached the prewar borders. About 40,000 civilians died during the retreat of Armenian and Georgian volunteers and the Ottoman advance.

A new conference opened at Batum on 11 May. The Ottomans widened their demands to include Tiflis, Alexandropol and Echmiadzin, and wanted a railway built to connect Kars and Julfa with Baku, with free right of passage through the new Armenian state. The Armenian and Georgian delegates began to stall. From 21 May the Ottoman army advanced again into Russian Armenia, which led to the battles of Sardarapat, Karakilisa and Bash Abaran.

The treaty, with 14 articles, was signed in Batumi on 4 June 1918 by the Ottoman Empire and the First Republic of Armenia, the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic and the Democratic Republic of Georgia. It was the first treaty of the Armenian and Azerbaijani republics. The Ottoman signatories included Halil Menteshe and Wehib Pasha, the Armenian Avetis Aharonian and Alexander Khatisian, the Azerbaijani Mammad Amin Rasulzade and the Georgian Noe Ramishvili.

The Ottoman Third Army held positions 7 km from Yerevan and 10 km from Echmiadzin when the treaty was signed. The majority of the 1,250,000 prewar inhabitants of the surrendered territories had been Armenians, with more than 400,000 in the ceded sector of Yerevan province alone. The treaty left the Armenians with less than one ninth of Eastern Armenia. The German diplomat Bernstorff remarked that Turkey had left the Armenians only Lake Sevan, where they could swim but had no place to come out and dry off.
treaty-of-belgrade: In the last stage of the war between the Habsburg Monarchy and the Ottoman Empire, the main Habsburg army under Field Marshal Wallis suffered a strategic defeat at the Battle of Grocka on 21 and 22 July 1739. It retreated into the Belgrade Fortress, which Ottoman forces soon besieged. On 31 July the government in Vienna took Wallis's powers to negotiate from him and gave them to Count Neipperg, who reached the Grand Vizier's camp on 18 August with instructions approved by Emperor Charles VI. There he found himself increasingly isolated and dependent on the French mediator, Marquis Louis Sauveur de Villeneuve.

On 1 September Neipperg agreed to a preliminary peace with the Ottomans. His report reached Vienna on 7 September and provoked outrage, because he had signed without knowing that the Emperor had sent him new instructions on 31 August and that his powers had been revoked on 3 September. Only on returning to Belgrade did he learn this, and it was too late to reverse. Further negotiations led to the final treaty, concluded on 18 September in the Grand Vizier's camp near Belgrade.

By the treaty the Habsburgs ceded three regions to the Ottomans: the Banat of Craiova, in modern Oltenia, the Kingdom of Serbia with Belgrade, and the Bosnian part of Posavina. All of them had come to the Habsburg Monarchy by the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 and had remained under its rule until 1739. The new border was set along the rivers Sava and Danube. The territorial changes were substantial and favoured the Ottoman side. The treaty is also noted as one of the last international treaties written in Latin.

The treaty ended the existence of the Habsburg-held Kingdom of Serbia, which had lasted since 1718. The withdrawal of Habsburg forces was followed by a large Serbian migration out of the ceded lands. They stayed under Ottoman rule until the next Habsburg-Ottoman war of 1788 to 1791, when Habsburg forces, supported by Serbian rebels, occupied them temporarily in 1788 and 1789.

The Habsburg decision to negotiate in August 1739 forced its ally Russia to accept talks as well, through French mediation. A separate preliminary treaty was signed in Belgrade on 18 September and finalised by the Treaty of Niš on 3 October, ending the Russo-Turkish war. After ratification, the instruments were exchanged and a final convention was signed in Constantinople on 28 December 1739, again through French mediation. Meanwhile Neipperg and Wallis were arrested and accused over the unfavourable outcome; both were pardoned only after the Emperor's death in 1740.
treaty-of-benavente: Sancha and Dulce were the daughters of Alfonso IX of León by Theresa of Portugal; Ferdinand was his son by Berenguela of Castile, a marriage annulled in 1204. The Treaty of Cabreros of 1206 confirmed Ferdinand's right to the Leonese throne, but after Berenguela inherited Castile in 1217 and at once abdicated in his favour, a peace of 26 November 1217 excluded him from León in favour of Alfonso's brother Sancho Fernández, or failing him the two princesses. By 1221, Sancho having died, they were generally recognised as co-heiresses, though one faction preferred Ferdinand.

Alfonso IX died on 24 September 1230. The princesses reached León first but, in the words of the Chronica latina regum Castellae, were not received as they wished. Ferdinand lifted the siege of Jaén, was acclaimed in León, and by early November styled himself king of Castile and León. Seeing her daughters' weak position, Theresa offered to negotiate in Berenguela's own town of Valencia. Archbishop Rodrigo Jiménez de Rada wrote that Berenguela kept the king in León for fear of the kingdom being ravaged, and settled terms with Theresa herself. The treaty was sealed at Benavente on 11 December 1230 in the presence of both queens.

Ferdinand was to pay the princesses 30,000 maravedíes a year for life, drawn partly from the income of Avilés with its port and saltworks, A Coruña with its port, and the storerooms of 19 towns, mostly in Asturias, among them Gijón, Grado, Cangas and Navia. The king kept the coinage, garrison and justice in these places, and any shortfall was to be met from the martiniega tax owed by Mayorga, Toro, Zamora, Salamanca, Alba and Ledesma.

As a guarantee twelve castles in León and Galicia, among them Castrogonzalo and Allariz, were placed under castellans who were vassals of both the king and the princesses. If one princess died or married, her half of the annuity returned to the crown and the other kept six castles; all reverted to the crown once both had died or married. Ferdinand promised to obtain papal protection for them, and the princesses gave up their castles and any claim to the throne.
treaty-of-berlin-1742: The treaty was concluded between Maria Theresa, Habsburg archduchess and Queen of Bohemia, and the Prussian king Frederick the Great. It turned into a formal peace the preliminary agreement reached with English mediation at Breslau on 11 June 1742. Frederick had invaded Silesia in the First Silesian War, using as one pretext a claim to the former Duchy of Jägerndorf.

Under article 5, the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia ceded Lower and Upper Silesia from the Lands of the Bohemian Crown to the King of Prussia for all eternity and with full sovereignty, except for the Principality of Teschen and the city of Troppau. Austria kept the districts of the Duchy of Troppau south of the Opava river, including the southern part of Jägerndorf, and the whole Duchy of Teschen, ruled by Maria Theresa's husband, Francis Stephen of Lorraine. The Duchy of Neisse, held by the bishops of Breslau, was divided, the fortress-city of Nysa and the larger northern part going to Prussia. The lands Austria kept became the crown land of Austrian Silesia.

Prussia in turn left the anti-Habsburg coalition that it had formed with France, Spain, Sweden, Naples and the electorates of Bavaria, Saxony and Cologne, and took over debts of about 1.7 million florins that Austria owed to Great Britain. King George II of Great Britain acted as guarantor.

The gain enlarged Prussian territory by a third, raised Prussia to the rank of a European great power and opened a hundred-year rivalry with Austria. King Louis XV of France resented a peace that left Austrian, British and Hanoverian forces free to drive out the French at the Battle of Dettingen in 1743, an alienation that ultimately led to the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756. Emperor Charles VII, Maria Theresa's Wittelsbach rival, was left in exile at Frankfurt while Austria occupied his Bavarian electorate. The peace did not last: both sides prepared for the Second Silesian War, which Frederick opened by marching on Prague in August 1744.
treaty-of-berlin-1889: The treaty, also known as the Samoan Treaty, was the concluding document of a conference on Samoa held at Berlin in 1889. The conference was proposed by the German foreign minister, Count Herbert von Bismarck, son of Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, to reconvene the Washington conference on Samoa of 1887, which had been adjourned. In April 1889 he invited delegations of the United States and the British Empire to Berlin.

The treaty set up a condominium in Samoa under the United States, Germany and Great Britain. It was designed to preserve the rights the three powers had secured in separate treaties with the Samoan government in 1878 and 1879. It guaranteed the independence and neutrality of the Samoan government, reorganised its public finances and restored the king who had been elected in 1881.

To strengthen the judiciary, the treaty created a court and the office of Chief Justice of Samoa, an American or European appointed by all three powers; if they could not agree on the appointment, the King of Sweden would make it. The municipality of Apia was re-established, chaired by a council president.

The treaty was signed at Berlin by the three powers on 14 June 1889. The United States Senate ratified it on 3 February 1890, ratifications were exchanged on 12 April 1890, and the Samoan government gave its assent on 19 April 1890, so that in effect four governments were party to the Berlin Act.

The condominium lasted ten years and ended in political disorder, with the ratification of the Tripartite Convention of 1899 and the partition of the Samoan archipelago between the powers that followed from it.
treaty-of-big-tree: In the Phelps and Gorham Purchase of 1788 the Haudenosaunee had already sold their rights to the land between Seneca Lake and the Genesee River. The talks of 1797 concerned what lay west of the river. They took their name from Big Tree, a Seneca village just across the Genesee in present-day Leicester, probably named after a chief known by that title, Ga-on-dah-go-waah or Karontowanen; local lore later confused it with the great Wadsworth Oak at Geneseo.

The delegates met from 20 August to 16 September 1797 near the log cabin of James and William Wadsworth, where the delegates of the United States lodged, in a council house the Seneca built nearby. Nearly 3000 Seneca and other members of the Six Nations attended, represented by chiefs including Cornplanter, Red Jacket, Young King, Farmer's Brother, Handsome Lake and Little Beard, by the clan mothers and by Mary Jemison, a captive who had married her Seneca captor and helped win better terms.

Colonel Jeremiah Wadsworth represented the United States as commissioner, with Robert Morris, his son Thomas Morris, and agents of the Holland Land Company such as the surveyor Joseph Ellicott. The treaty was signed on 16 September after nearly a month of often heated negotiation.

The Seneca gave up nearly 3.5 million acres. The money was not paid to them directly but invested in shares of the Bank of the United States, to yield them up to six percent, or 6,000 dollars, a year. Morris asked that the principal pass to his heirs if the Seneca nation ever became extinct, which the secretaries of the Treasury and State refused.

Twelve reservations were kept, among them land at Cattaraugus, forty-two square miles that became the Allegany Reservation and two hundred square miles at Buffalo and Tonawanda creeks, with hunting and fishing rights. A survey of 1798 fixed the Buffalo Creek Reservation at 83,557 acres, bending its corner to leave out the mouth of the creek. The Oil Spring Reservation was omitted, and in 1861 the Seneca won a lawsuit that granted them sovereignty over it.
treaty-of-breda-1667: The Second Anglo-Dutch War grew out of commercial tension. Charles II and his brother James founded the Royal African Company in 1660, challenging the Dutch in West Africa, and the Dutch East India Company enforced a monopoly on spices, leaving only the nutmeg plantations on Run, which the English reoccupied in late 1664 and the Dutch expelled them from again.

In August 1664 the English occupied New Netherland, later renamed New York. By late 1666 Charles was short of money, while the Dutch economy had largely recovered. Negotiations were slow until Louis XIV's invasion of the Spanish Netherlands in late May 1667, which the Dutch saw as a graver threat, and the Dutch Medway Raid of June, which deepened English war-weariness.

The Peace of Breda was signed on 31 July 1667 and consisted of three treaties between England and the Dutch Republic, France and Denmark-Norway, along with an Anglo-Dutch commercial agreement. Its principle was uti possidetis, "what you have, you hold". The Dutch kept Surinam, Fort Cormantin and Run, while the English kept New Netherland, later divided into New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut and Delaware.

A separate treaty amended the Navigation Acts, and England accepted that free ships make free goods. By the French treaty England returned Cayenne and Acadia, though the handover was delayed until 1670, and regained Montserrat and Antigua, with the Anglo-French division of Saint Kitts restored.

By exchanging New Netherland and Run, the treaty removed two major disputes and cleared the way for the Triple Alliance of 1668 between the Dutch Republic, Sweden and England. In the longer term the English and Dutch came to see France as a greater threat than each other.

On 5 August 1667 the States of Holland passed the Perpetual Edict, which abolished the position of stadtholder of Holland, disappointing the Orangists. Sweden, which had acted as mediator, gained improved terms and a place in the Triple Alliance, and the Dutch considered the treaty a diplomatic triumph in a period often seen as the high point of the Dutch Golden Age.
treaty-of-brest-litovsk: By 1917 the Eastern Front was stalemated and the Russian economy had nearly collapsed. The February Revolution forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate, but the Provisional Government continued the war. After the Red Guards seized the Winter Palace on 7 November in the October Revolution, the new government at once issued a Decree on Peace. An armistice with the Central Powers was concluded on 15 December 1917, and negotiations opened at Brest-Litovsk on 22 December.

The Soviet delegation was led first by Adolph Joffe, with Max Hoffmann, Richard von Kühlmann, Ottokar Czernin and Talaat Pasha among the Central Powers' negotiators. The Soviet side demanded peace with no annexations or indemnities; the Central Powers accepted this only if all belligerents did, and Hoffmann then made clear that Poland, Lithuania and Courland, already occupied, would separate from Russia.

Leon Trotsky replaced Joffe, since the Soviets hoped to prolong the talks until revolutions broke out in Central Europe. The Central Powers signed a treaty with Ukraine on 8–9 February 1918. Trotsky's formula of 'no war, no peace' was announced on 10 February, but on 18 February 53 German divisions advanced against near-empty Soviet trenches. Lenin argued that the Soviets must sign or face an even more ruinous treaty, telling the Central Committee that they must concede space to win time.

After Hoffmann presented harsher terms on 23 February, the Central Committee backed signing, and the All-Russian Central Executive Committee passed it by 116 to 85, with the Left Socialist-Revolutionaries jeering Lenin as a traitor. Grigori Sokolnikov signed on 3 March 1918.

Russia renounced territorial claims in Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, most of Belarus and Ukraine, and the districts of Ardahan, Kars and Batum were to be cleared of Russian troops. It lost 89% of its coalfields and 26% of its railways, and Kotkin writes that no Russian government had ever surrendered so much territory or sovereignty. A supplementary agreement of 27 August 1918 obliged Russia to pay six billion marks.

The occupation proved costly for Germany, with over one million troops staying in the east. The treaty split the Bolsheviks from the Left SRs, who assassinated the German ambassador in July 1918. The Armistice of 11 November 1918 abrogated the treaty. Poland and the Baltic states re-emerged, and at Rapallo in 1922 Germany and Russia renounced all wartime claims.
treaty-of-bretigny: King John II of France was taken prisoner at the Battle of Poitiers on 19 September 1356. He worked with King Edward III of England on a Treaty of London, which the French Estates-General condemned, advising the Dauphin Charles to reject it. Edward, who wished to yield few of the advantages that treaty had claimed, besieged Rheims. The siege lasted until January, and with supplies running low he withdrew to Burgundy. After a futile siege of Paris the English army marched to Chartres, and discussion of terms began in early April 1360.

The treaty was drafted in May 1360 by the Dauphin Charles and six English knights at the Hôtel de Sens. On 14 June John, a prisoner in England, ratified it at a banquet attended by Edward III, his son the Prince of Wales and the other French prisoners from Poitiers. It was finalised at Calais on 24 October 1360, hence its other name, the Treaty of Calais.

Edward III obtained Guyenne, Gascony, Poitou, Saintonge and Aunis, Agenais, Périgord, Limousin, Quercy, Bigorre, Angoumois, Rouergue, Ponthieu, Calais and other lands, to hold free and clear without homage. The title duke of Aquitaine gave way to lord of Aquitaine. The English king renounced all claims to the French throne, and the terms were meant to untangle the feudal obligations that had caused so much conflict. John had to pay three million écus for his ransom and would be released after paying one million. The occasion saw the first minting of the franc, equal to one livre tournois. He gave as hostages two of his sons, Louis I of Anjou and John of Berry, with princes, nobles and townsmen.

John returned to France to raise the ransom. In 1362 his son Louis of Anjou, a hostage at Calais, escaped, and John felt honour-bound to return to captivity in England, where he died in 1364. His son Charles V succeeded him, and in 1369, on the pretext that Edward had failed to observe the treaty, the French king declared war again. By the deaths of the Black Prince in 1376 and Edward III in 1377 the English had been pushed back into the southwest around Bordeaux. The treaty gave nine years' respite from the Hundred Years' War, during which Bertrand du Guesclin won at Cocherel on 16 May 1364.
treaty-of-bromsebro-1645: The Torstenson War between Sweden and Denmark–Norway began in 1643 as a local conflict within the larger Thirty Years' War. Negotiations for peace opened in February 1645 and ended with the signing on 13 August. The talks were held at the creek of Brömsebäck, which formed the eastern border between the Danish province of Blekinge and the Swedish province of Småland. An islet in the creek, joined to both banks by bridges, held a stone marking the exact border, and there the delegates met to exchange greetings and the signed documents.

The Danish delegation lodged in Kristianopel and the Swedish one in Söderåkra. Sweden was led by its Lord High Chancellor, Axel Oxenstierna, with Johan Skytte, who died during the negotiations and was replaced by Ture Sparre. Corfitz Ulfeldt and Chancellor Christen Thomesen Sehested led for Denmark. The French diplomat Gaspard Coignet de la Thuillerie was chief mediator, and observers from the Hanseatic League, Portugal, Stralsund and Mecklenburg followed the talks. In the end Sweden's military strength forced Denmark–Norway to accept its demands.

Besides the islands, provinces and toll exemption, the Imperial Prince-Bishopric of Verden and Bremen passed from Danish to Swedish control, and Hamburg was freed from tolls Bremen had levied. The Norwegian regions of Idre and Särna, taken by Dalecarlian peasants at the Swedish government's suggestion, were not formally conceded until 1751. Halland was held by Sweden as a guarantee that these terms would be kept.
treaty-of-bucharest-1812: The Russo-Turkish War of 1806 to 1812 began while the Napoleonic Wars were spreading across Europe. A French move into the Balkans led Russia to send troops into Moldavia and Wallachia, and the sultan declared war. An Ottoman offensive against Bucharest failed, and Russia destroyed the Ottoman fleet at the Battle of Athos. In 1811 Grand Vizier Ahmed Pasha gathered 60,000 soldiers in Ottoman Bulgaria, but the Russians led his army into an ambush and surrounded it. Soon afterwards Russia chose to make peace.

Negotiations opened in Bucharest on 11 January 1812. Russia at first wanted more land in the Balkans and the Caucasus, and the British plenipotentiary Stratford Canning advised it to moderate its demands, since the Ottomans might otherwise turn to France. The treaty was signed in Manuc's Inn on 28 May 1812 and ratified on 5 July 1812. The Ottoman Empire, to which Moldavia was a vassal, ceded to Russia the Budjak and the eastern half of the Principality of Moldavia between the Prut and Dniester rivers, an area of 45,630 square kilometres that became Bessarabia. Russia also obtained trading rights on the Danube.

In Transcaucasia the Ottomans gave up their claims to most of western Georgia by accepting the Russian annexation of the Kingdom of Imereti in 1810, and kept Akhalkalaki, Poti and Anapa. Article 8 provided a truce with the rebelling Serbs and gave autonomy to Serbia. The treaty was signed for Russia by Mikhail Kutuzov.

The Ottomans had extricated themselves from a potentially disastrous war with a slight loss of territory, while the Russians were free for the coming war with France, and the treaty became the basis for later Russo-Ottoman relations. In 1914 a statue of Tsar Alexander I was inaugurated in Kishinev, to mark a hundred years since Russia's annexation of Bessarabia, and it was demolished in 1918 after Bessarabia's union with Romania.
treaty-of-campo-formio: France had been at war with Austria since 20 April 1792, when the French Legislative Assembly voted to declare war and began the War of the First Coalition. After several years of stalemate along the Franco-Italian border, the French Revolutionary Army under Napoleon Bonaparte went on the offensive on 10 April 1796 against Austria and its Italian ally Sardinia. Sardinia signed a peace treaty with France on 15 May. After several major defeats in Italy and Germany, Austria signed the Peace of Leoben with Bonaparte on 18 April 1797.

The treaty was composed and signed after five months of negotiations, and its terms largely reflected those of Leoben. Campo Formio, now called Campoformido, is a village west of Udine in Friuli, midway between the Austrian headquarters at Udine and Bonaparte's residence at Villa Manin, the mansion of Ludovico Manin, the last Doge of Venice. The treaty was signed in an old house in the main square, owned by a local merchant.

Bonaparte signed for France and Philipp von Cobenzl for Austria on 17 October 1797. The city of Venice with the Terraferma, Venetian Istria, Venetian Dalmatia and the Bay of Kotor were turned over to the Habsburg emperor, while Corfu and other Venetian possessions in the Ionian Sea passed to France. Austria recognised the Cisalpine Republic and the newly created Ligurian Republic as independent powers. The Italian states ceased to owe fealty to the Holy Roman Emperor, ending the formal existence of the Kingdom of Italy.

The public articles concerned only France and Austria and called for a Second Congress of Rastatt to negotiate a final peace between France and the Holy Roman Empire. Secret clauses divided other territories and agreed to extend the borders of France up to the Rhine, the Nette and the Roer, with free French navigation on the Rhine, the Meuse and the Moselle. Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, a prisoner since the Revolution, was released from Austrian captivity.

Austrian troops entered Venice on 18 January 1798. Napoleon's biographer Felix Markham wrote that the partition of Venice was a moral blot on the settlement and left Austria a foothold in Italy that could only lead to further war. The treaty reshaped the map of Europe, yet it proved only a respite: Franco-Austrian tensions led France to declare war on Austria on 12 March 1799, in the War of the Second Coalition.

In the Southern Netherlands the introduction of French conscription helped provoke the Peasants' War of 1798. The passing of the Ionian Islands to French rule also affected later Greek history in ways neither intended nor expected at the time.
treaty-of-canandaigua: After the American Revolutionary War Britain gave up its claims east of the Mississippi to the United States, angering the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, whose land it had been. Some western peoples stayed loyal to Britain, and the United States, fearing renewed frontier war, needed Haudenosaunee neutrality. The treaties of Fort Stanwix and Fort Harmar had raised tensions rather than easing them. The Secretary of War, Henry Knox, opened a frontier campaign in September 1790 and named Timothy Pickering commissioner to hear Haudenosaunee grievances; by 1793 the Ohio Valley was at open war, and in June 1794 the confederacy rejected both earlier treaties at Buffalo Creek.

The formal conference opened on 18 October 1794 with more than 1,500 Haudenosaunee present. The two sides understood treaties differently: according to the scholar Granville Ganter, the Haudenosaunee saw them as needing constant renewal, which they called brightening the chain of friendship. The Seneca leader Red Jacket helped bridge the gap, reminding Pickering that peace needs a language of peace, not blame. Haudenosaunee women, who held a large place in their governance, took part; the historian Joan M. Jensen records that Seneca women spoke during the talks. Among the signers were Corn Planter, Handsome Lake, Little Beard and Farmer's Brother.

In seven articles the treaty promised perpetual peace and friendship, acknowledged the lands of the Oneida, Onondaga and Cayuga, defined the bounds of Seneca territory and bound the United States never to claim or disturb Haudenosaunee lands. It confirmed the road from Fort Schlosser to Lake Erie as Seneca, promised $4,500 a year, and provided for any breach of the peace to be settled through a third party.

The United States did not keep Article Two. In the early 19th century federal agents failed to stop New York buying Oneida treaty lands and encouraged the Oneida to move west, and by 1920 the nation kept only 32 acres of the six million it had held before the Revolution. The historian Robert W. Venables calls the treaty the legal keystone of relations between the United States and the Six Nations, central to their land claims and self-government.
treaty-of-chambord: In the Schmalkaldic War Emperor Charles V defeated a number of rebellious Protestant princes, and in 1548 he issued the sharply worded Augsburg Interim to bring the Lutheran movement back into the Catholic Church and prevent a split of the Empire. To defend their autonomy, several Protestant Imperial States formed the Alliance of Torgau in 1551. Chief among them was Maurice of Saxony, who had strongly supported the emperor in the Schmalkaldic War, together with William IV of Hesse-Kassel, Margrave Albert Alcibiades of Brandenburg-Kulmbach and his cousin Albert, Duke of Prussia.

The treaty was signed on 15 January 1552 at the Château de Chambord. Maurice ceded to France the vicariate over the Three Bishoprics of Toul, Verdun and Metz, and Henry II promised military and economic aid against the emperor. The German princes had neither the right nor any authority to give away imperial territory, so by legal standards the accord had no force. Its text described the bishoprics as not of German language, implying that the transfer was limited to non-German lands.

Maurice, then charged by the emperor with subduing Magdeburg, made peace with the city and changed sides, while French troops marched to occupy the bishoprics. The princes' forces campaigned in the Tyrol and forced Charles V to flee towards Villach in Carinthia, and in August 1552 his brother Archduke Ferdinand I of Austria concluded the Peace of Passau, accepting the Lutheran Augsburg Confession, which the emperor confirmed in the Peace of Augsburg of 1555.

During the Italian War of 1551–59 Charles V tried to regain the bishoprics by force, but his troops were defeated by Duke Francis of Guise at the Battle of Renty in 1554. Ferdinand I made no further attempt, and the Empire acknowledged their incorporation into France in the Peace of Westphalia of 1648. The treaty set a pattern for French policy in the following decades, which used conflicts between the emperor and the German princes to France's own advantage.
treaty-of-coche: By 1863 the Federal War had lasted four years, and the military victory of the Liberal Federalist forces was close. The country lay in ruins: more than 150,000 people had died, and many towns had been destroyed or deserted. The estate of Coche, which gave the agreement its name, then lay very close to Caracas and is now part of the city's Parish of Coche. There representatives of Falcón and Páez met to agree on a definitive peace.

The agreement was first reached on 23 April 1863, behind closed doors, between Pedro José Rojas, secretary general to José Antonio Páez as Supreme Chief of the Republic, for the Conservatives, and Antonio Guzmán Blanco, secretary general to Juan Crisóstomo Falcón as Provisional President of the Federation, for the Liberals. Páez and Falcón confirmed it on 25 May 1863. It provided for a lasting peace and for the calling of a National Assembly or Congress of 80 members, and it laid down that Páez should resign the presidency to ease the transition.

The treaty brought the Liberals and the Liberal Party back to power and gave the country the peace it badly needed. New recruitment into the armed forces was stopped and then forbidden, the central government's army was reduced, and public order brigades were formed to head off fresh outbreaks of violence. Even so, a large part of the population left the countryside for fear of further fighting, and the government took on more debt with a new loan from the English firm Matheson & Company.
treaty-of-concordia: The Spanish had occupied Saint Martin from 1633 to 1648. A shared aversion to the Spanish, together with economic, strategic and geographical reasons, led the French and Dutch on the island to come to terms once the Spanish had gone.

The treaty, also known as the Partition Treaty of 1648, was signed on Mount Concordia by the island's two governors, Robert de Longvilliers for the Kingdom of France and Martin Thomas for the States General of the Netherlands. The French kept the area they occupied and the coast facing Anguilla, and the Dutch the area of the fort and the land around it on the south coast. The inhabitants were to live together peaceably and share the island's natural resources.

France and the Netherlands went on disputing ownership of the island until 1817, when its borders were finally set. Several zones whose boundary the treaty left unclear, above all the lagoon at Oyster Pond, were settled only in 2023. It has been suggested that the freedom of movement the treaty allowed helped the inhabitants of both halves of the island to develop a common identity.

At the time, agreements signed by the monarch's representatives had to be registered at the King's Council, and this was never done for the treaty, so its validity has been questioned several times. French civil law has nevertheless recognised it on many occasions, and the treaty has been applied in practice and cited in later texts: the Franco-Dutch Convention of 28 November 1839, an order of the French side's governor of 11 February 1850 allowing its inhabitants to consume and export salt harvested on the Dutch side under the treaty, and a decree of 30 July 1935 giving Dutch citizens from the Dutch part freedom of establishment in the French part.
treaty-of-constantinople-1700: As a member of the anti-Ottoman Holy League, the Tsardom of Russia had fought the Ottoman Empire in the eastern theatre of the Great Turkish War. When the other members, the Holy Roman Empire, the Republic of Venice and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, had reached their war aims, they made peace with Sultan Mustafa II at Karlowitz in 1699, a settlement that ignored Russian interests.

Tsar Peter the Great joined the negotiations in person and agreed a two-year truce with the Ottoman Empire at Karlowitz. A final settlement was prevented by the gap between his demands, which included protection of the Christians in the Ottoman Balkan provinces, and Russia’s military position, and by the lack of support from the other Holy League members.

In the autumn of 1699 Peter sent Yemelyan Ignatievich Ukraintsev to the sultan’s court at Constantinople. The Russian aims were Ottoman recognition of the gains around Azov and free passage for Russian merchant ships into the Black Sea. The talks moved slowly, and as Peter came under pressure to attack the Swedish Empire he urged Ukraintsev to settle, and the demand for Black Sea access was dropped.

Concluded on 13 July 1700, the treaty set a truce of thirty years and recognised Russian possession of the Azov area, including the new fortresses of Taganrog, Pavlovsk and Mius. Russia gave up its claims to the Kerch Strait but was relieved of the annual payment to the Crimean Khanate. The Dnieper fortresses razed by Russian forces went back to the Ottoman Empire, and the lower Dnieper area became a demilitarised zone. Russian pilgrims gained free passage to the Holy Land, and Russia gained a diplomatic representative in Constantinople.

Peter had arranged a three-front attack on Sweden with August the Strong of Saxony and Poland–Lithuania and Frederik IV of Denmark-Norway, but his own part was to begin only once peace with the Ottoman Empire was made. The delay meant that Denmark-Norway was already defeated when his army left Moscow, and Sweden was able to repulse the Russian attack on Ingria.

The Ottoman Empire entered the Great Northern War nine years later, after Charles XII of Sweden, beaten by Peter at the Battle of Poltava, camped the remnants of his army at Bender. The sultan declared war, and the treaty was superseded by the Treaty of the Pruth, which returned Azov to the sultan, and then by the Treaty of Adrianople of 1713, which restored a peace intended to last twenty-five years.
treaty-of-constantinople-1832: The settlement was delayed when Leopold of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha refused the Greek throne, dissatisfied with the Aspropotamos–Spercheios line, which had replaced the more favourable Arta–Volos line the Great Powers had considered earlier. His withdrawal and the July Revolution in France put off a final decision on the frontiers until a new government was formed in London, where Lord Palmerston, the new British foreign secretary, agreed to the Arta–Volos line. The London Conference, attended by Britain, France and Russia on one side and the Ottoman Empire on the other, opened in February 1832, and the treaty was its product.

The Treaty of London of 7 May 1832, between Bavaria and the protecting Powers, had already defined Greece as an independent kingdom with the Arta–Volos line as its northern frontier, arranged the regency until Otto came of age and concluded a second Greek loan of £2,400,000. At Constantinople on 21 July 1832 the British ambassador Sir Stratford Canning and the other representatives concluded the treaty setting the boundary along that line. The Ottoman Empire received 40,000,000 piastres in compensation for the territory it lost.

The Great Powers ratified the treaty's terms on the border in the London Protocol of 30 August 1832, which marked the end of the Greek War of Independence and established modern Greece as an independent state free of the Ottoman Empire. The protocol reiterated the borders of the Kingdom of Greece as they had been agreed at Constantinople. A secret note on Crete, which the Bavarian plenipotentiary had sent to the courts of Britain, France and Russia, bore no fruit.
treaty-of-copenhagen-1660: The treaty concluded the Second Northern War between the Swedish Empire and an alliance of Denmark-Norway and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. It was a smaller follow-up to the Treaty of Roskilde, which had set the boundaries of Denmark, Sweden and Norway. Charles X of Sweden would accept nothing less than Akershus county in exchange for returning Trøndelag and Bornholm, while Frederick III of Denmark wanted to return to the terms of the Second Treaty of Brömsebro of 1645.

Both kings were stubborn, and mediating powers had to broker the treaty: France and England on the Swedish side, the Dutch Republic on the Danish side. Frederick argued that Swedish control of Scania would be a lasting threat to Copenhagen, but the Dutch had agreed with England that no single country should hold both shores of the Øresund, to prevent a rise in the Sound toll.

When Charles died in February 1660, Frederick proclaimed the Treaty of Roskilde void. France and England assured the Swedes that they would secure a treaty on Roskilde's terms if Sweden gave up its claim to Trøndelag. On 8 March 1660 the Dutch admiral Michiel de Ruyter was ordered to leave the harbour of Landskrona, where he had blockaded the Swedish fleet, and Frederick yielded.

Talks began on 24 March. The hardest point was Bornholm, where the islanders had risen against their Swedish occupiers and killed the commander, Johan Printzensköld, and now feared reprisals. Frederick had promised to protect them and demanded the island back. As the mediators' representatives became involved in intrigues, Hannibal Sehested proposed direct talks between Denmark and Sweden, and in a few days the terms were agreed.

The treaty was signed on 27 May 1660 in tents halfway between Copenhagen and the Swedish camp of Carlstad. Sweden kept the territories east of the Sound: Ven, Scania, Halland, Blekinge and Bohuslän. Trøndelag, then including Nordmøre and Romsdal, went back to Norway and Bornholm to Denmark, with Sweden receiving several nobles' estates in Scania as indemnity. Sweden was exempted from the Sound Dues, Denmark was to pay 3,500 riksdaler a year for the beacons between Skagen and Falsterbo, and prisoners of war were released. The boundaries it confirmed are almost exactly the same today.
treaty-of-corbeil-1258: The treaty was signed on 11 May 1258 at Corbeil, today Corbeil-Essonnes in the Île-de-France. It settled overlapping claims inherited from earlier centuries. The French king claimed, as heir of Charlemagne, feudal overlordship over the counties known to historians as the Hispanic March, the part of the March of Gothia that lay within what was called Catalonia from the 12th century onwards. The counts of Barcelona, for their part, held or claimed rights over a wide arc of lordships in what is now southern France, some going back to enfeoffments of 1112 and 1179 and to the inheritance of Douce I of Provence.

Louis IX renounced his claim to overlordship of the counties of Catalonia. James I gave up his claims to Fenouillet-du-Razès and Peyrepertuse, with the castles of Puilaurens, Fenouillet, Castellfisel, Peyrepertuse and Quéribus, and his feudal overlordship over Toulouse, Saint Gilles, Quercy, Narbonne, Albi, Carcassonne, Razès, Béziers, Lauragais, Termes and Ménerbes, Agde and Nîmes, and Rouergue, Millau and Gévaudan. He kept the viscounty of Carlat and the lordship of Montpellier with the barony of Aumelas. The treaty also arranged the marriage of James's daughter Isabella to Philip, son of Louis IX.

When he ratified the document on 16 July 1258, James refused to give up his feudal rights over the County of Foix, which the text had at first included, arguing that Foix was not under the overlordship of the king of France. On 17 July he also renounced his hereditary rights to the County of Provence, then an imperial fief, in favour of Margaret, daughter of his uncle Ramon Berenguer IV, Count of Provence, and wife of the French king.

The direct result was to separate the House of Barcelona for good from the politics of what is now southern France. The close cultural and economic ties between the lands that became Catalonia and Languedoc faded gradually after it. A further effect was that Provence could pass to the Capetian House of Anjou and, once that house died out, be incorporated into France.
treaty-of-cordoba: The treaty has 17 articles, which developed the proposals of the Plan of Iguala. It recognised New Spain as an independent empire, defined as monarchical, constitutional and moderate. The crown was to be offered first to Ferdinand VII of Spain. If he did not come to Mexico to take the oath within the time set by the Mexican Cortes, it would pass in turn to his brothers, the Infantes Carlos and Francisco, and to their nephew Duke Charles Louis, or to another member of a royal house chosen by the Cortes.

If none accepted, the Cortes could name a new king, without any requirement that he belong to a European royal house. This last clause was not in the Plan of Iguala: Agustín de Iturbide added it to leave open the possibility of taking the crown himself. Juan O'Donojú, as captain general and jefe político superior, had no authority to sign such a treaty. He wished to keep Mexico for the Spanish royal family and probably signed without considering that Iturbide might seek the throne.

The Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City on 27 September 1821, and the next day the Declaration of Independence of the Mexican Empire became widely known. Offers of the throne to the House of Bourbon failed, and the Spanish government published its rejection of the treaty in Madrid on 13 and 14 February 1822. The Mexican Congress then chose a Mexican monarch, and Iturbide was proclaimed emperor on 18 May 1822. After the republican revolution of Casa Mata, Congress no longer treated the Plan of Iguala or the treaty as in force. The treaty was the first document in which Spanish and Mexican officials accepted Mexico's independence, though the founding moment is usually placed at the Grito de Dolores of 16 September 1810.
treaty-of-daan: Relations between the Ottomans and the Zaydi imams had long been hostile. The Ottoman authorities treated the imams merely as local religious leaders and denied them any right to temporal rule, while the imams looked back to their historical claim over greater Yemen. The Zaydi political doctrine, which encouraged an imam to rise against an unjust ruler as a religious duty, lay behind the periodic uprisings. Imam Yahya had led such risings in the highlands since 1905, though his revolt of 1911 had almost collapsed by the end of April for lack of support from tribesmen of several farming districts.

As chief of the Ottoman general staff, Ahmed Izzet Pasha had proposed ending the costly military stalemate by leaving the mountainous Zaydi regions in the imam's effective control, while the empire kept the coastal Tihamah and only a token garrison in Sanaa.

Izzet Pasha, now the Ottoman wali and commander-in-chief of Yemen, opened secret talks with Imam Yahya in June 1911 on that basis, and a compromise was reached in September. Both parties signed the treaty on 18 October 1911 at Daan, north of Amran. The outbreak of the Italo-Turkish War, when the Italians attacked Tripoli in September 1911, pressed the Ottomans to settle, since they could not send troops to Yemen and Tripoli at once. The cabinet in Constantinople apparently accepted the terms in principle, and the treaty was ratified in 1913.

The Ottomans undertook to support Yahya against any future rival to the imamate, to let him reside in Kawkaban and to pay him an annual subsidy of 25,000 Turkish pounds from the province's revenues; leading Zaydi sheikhs also received subsidies. Ottoman civil law was abolished in the seven highland districts of Amran, Kawkaban, Dhamar, Yarim, Ibb, Hajjah and Hajjur and replaced by Islamic law administered under the imam, whose nominations of qadis needed the central government's approval.

Yahya in turn gave up his claim to the caliphate and the title Commander of the Faithful used by his predecessors and himself, styling himself simply Imam of the Zaydis, and renounced the collection of zakat in the areas left under Ottoman jurisdiction. The settlement removed the main causes of friction between the imam and the Ottomans and marked a turning point in the Yemeni uprisings that had followed the Ottoman occupation of Sanaa in 1872.
treaty-of-dancing-rabbit-creek: The Choctaw chiefs were to have met President Andrew Jackson at Franklin, Tennessee, on 25 August 1830, but Greenwood LeFlore told Secretary of War John H. Eaton that they were fiercely opposed to attending. Jackson instead sent Eaton and General John Coffee as commissioners to meet them in their own country. On 15 September 1830 the commissioners met the chiefs and headmen at Dancing Rabbit Creek, known to the Choctaw as Bok Chukfi Ahilha, and explained the policy of removal through interpreters to some 6,000 people. The Choctaw faced a choice between moving west of the Mississippi and living under United States and state law as citizens.

In exchange for their remaining homeland the Choctaw were to receive about 15 million acres in the Indian Territory, in what became Oklahoma, with removal to run from 1831 to 1833. The Choctaw Nation's autonomy there was to be secured forever from the laws of states and territories, and the United States would provide wagons, steamboats and food during removal and for twelve months after. Article 14 allowed a Choctaw head of family who wished to stay and become a citizen to claim 640 acres, with more for children. The chief negotiators, LeFlore, Mosholatubbee and Nittucachee, received land and annuities, and the treaty promised a Choctaw delegate in the House of Representatives. The Senate ratified it in February 1831.

It was the last major land cession signed by the Choctaw and one of the largest land transfers made between the United States and American Indians in peacetime. Nearly 15,000 Choctaws, with 1,000 slaves, moved west in stages, and about 2,500 died along the Trail of Tears, through journeys that met a cholera epidemic in 1832. The chief George W. Harkins wrote in a farewell letter that the Choctaw chose to suffer and be free rather than live under laws in whose making they had no voice.

Between 5,000 and 6,000 Choctaws remained in Mississippi in 1831 and faced years of harassment; in 1849 they described homes burned, fences destroyed and people beaten. The promised delegate was never seated. In Oklahoma the Choctaw Nation's government was later dismantled under the Curtis Act and its lands allotted under the Dawes Act, and those in Mississippi reorganised in 1945 as the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians.
treaty-of-edinburgh-northampton: The war arose from the uncertain succession to the Scottish crown after the death of Alexander III in 1286 and began with the English invasion of Scotland in 1296. Robert the Bruce was crowned in 1306 and defeated the English under Edward II at Bannockburn in 1314. Peace talks between 1321 and 1324 made little progress, since the English refused to recognise him as King of Scots, although a truce was agreed in 1323 to last thirteen years.

English privateers went on attacking Flemish ships trading with Scotland, and Robert renewed the Auld Alliance with France by the Treaty of Corbeil of 26 April 1326. In 1327 the Scots invaded northern England and won the Battle of Stanhope Park in Weardale. The Dowager Queen Isabella and Mortimer, Earl of March, governing for the underage Edward III, then turned to peace and sent envoys to Scotland in October 1327.

On 1 March 1328, at a parliament at York, Edward III issued letters patent setting out the core of the agreement, and on 17 March the treaty was signed in the King's Chamber of the Abbey of Holyrood. Scotland was to keep its border as in the reign of Alexander III, separate from England and free of any subjection. In return the Scots would pay £20,000 sterling, with a possible further £100,000 if the marriage of the four-year-old David and the six-year-old Joan failed; they married on 17 July 1328. The surviving document, in French, was made as a chirograph cut along a wavy line, and its lower copy is held by the National Archives of Scotland.

A concurrent agreement may have provided for the return of the Stone of Destiny, and a royal writ of 1 July ordered it taken to Edward's mother, but it was not sent; the historian Colm McNamee doubts that its return was agreed at all. The stone reached Edinburgh Castle only on 30 November 1996. Many English nobles called the treaty the Shameful Peace. It lasted only five years: in 1333 Edward III, ruling in his own right, overturned it, and the Second War of Scottish Independence continued until a lasting peace in 1357.
treaty-of-falaise: The quarrel went back to Northumbria. In 1139, by the second Treaty of Durham, David I of Scotland had won from King Stephen of England control of Northumbria, Cumberland and other border lands, including the earldom of Northumbria for his son Henry, the father of Malcolm IV and William. In July 1157 Henry II took these lands back from Malcolm. William, king from 1164, pressed his claim to them in 1166 and again at Windsor in April 1170, and was rebuffed each time.

When three of Henry's sons, Queen Eleanor of Aquitaine and Louis VII of France rose against Henry in 1173, William saw another chance. Louis promised him the land north of the Tyne and the counties of Westmoreland and Cumberland. William offered Henry 1,000 knights and 30,000 soldiers in return for Northumberland, was refused, and invaded. On 13 July 1174, raiding with only a small retinue, he was surprised at Alnwick and surrendered to Ranulph de Glanvill. He was later brought before Henry at Northampton with his feet tied beneath a horse's belly.

For the first time the relationship between the two kings was set down in writing. William became Henry's liegeman for Scotland and all his other lands, where earlier homage by Scottish kings had been given for their English holdings, as earl of Huntingdon, and had been left deliberately vague. Scottish nobles and clergy were to do fealty to Henry and his heirs against all men, and the Scottish Church was to submit to the English Church, a move to establish the Archbishop of York's supremacy over Scotland.

William had to seek Henry's leave before acting in Galloway, faced challengers such as Donald MacWilliam in Moray and Ross, and visited Henry's court about eight times in ten years. Henry also chose his bride: in 1186 William married Ermengarde, daughter of Richard, viscount of Beaumont, and received Edinburgh castle back as a gift.

The Church clauses had the opposite effect to the one intended. A dispute between Canterbury and York over which should be Scotland's metropolitan allowed time for an appeal to Rome, and in the bull Super anxietatibus of 30 July 1176 Pope Alexander III placed the Scottish bishops directly under the pope; the bull Cum universi made this official in 1192. After Richard I's Quitclaim of Canterbury of 5 December 1189 the original treaty was handed back to William.
treaty-of-fez: Morocco had been weakened by defeat in the Franco-Moroccan War and by later treaties. The Anglo-Moroccan Treaty of 1856 broke the state's monopoly on customs revenue, a vital income for the makhzen, and the Treaty of Wad Ras after the Hispano-Moroccan War of 1859–60 forced it to take a British loan larger than its national reserves to pay an indemnity to Spain. After the Madrid Conference of 1880, European advisers, doctors, businessmen and missionaries became far more numerous. Loans from French banks followed from December 1901, and Morocco suffered famine from 1903 to 1907 and insurrections led by El-Rogui and Mulai Ahmed er Raisuni.

The agreements of 1904 between the United Kingdom and France, known as the Entente Cordiale, gave Morocco to France as a sphere of influence, and the Treaty of Algeciras of 1906 confirmed French pre-eminence. After the Agadir Crisis of 1911 Germany recognised the French position and received territory in the French Congo in return.

Sultan Abd al-Hafid, signing under duress, and the French diplomat Eugène Regnault concluded the treaty on 30 March 1912, after talks at the Royal Palace in Fes that lasted six hours on 29 March while French troops surrounded the city. Abdelqader Benghabrit interpreted. The treaty gave France the right to occupy parts of the country on the pretext of protecting the sultan from internal opposition. The French Resident-General held absolute powers in external and internal affairs and alone could represent Morocco abroad, while the sultan kept the right to sign the decrees, called dahirs, that the Resident-General submitted. Makhzen officials had expected something like British Egypt, but the text followed the Treaty of Bardo of 1881 for Tunisia.

The treaty was kept secret until 17 April, when the people of Fes learned of it and riots broke out. Abd al-Hafid had already left for Rabat. French artillery bombarded the Mellah, the Jewish quarter, which tribesmen then sacked. Resident-General Hubert Lyautey afterwards made Rabat the capital instead of Fes. Abd al-Hafid abdicated in favour of his brother Yusef.

The treaty between France and Spain of 27 November 1912 established the Spanish protectorate, with a zone in the Rif and the Cape Juby area under a Spanish high commission. Moroccan nationalists dispute that the sultan's government kept control of its own citizens, since France influenced Moroccan affairs through the treaty. Resistance continued in the Zaian War and the Rif War. The treaty stayed in effect until the Franco-Moroccan Joint Declaration of 2 March 1956.
treaty-of-fomena: Through the 19th century the Ashanti made a series of invasions of the Gold Coast and extended their influence there. In answer the British sent the Wolseley expedition under General Garnet Wolseley. After the Battle of Amoaful and the Battle of Ordashu the Ashanti forces fell back, and the British took Kumasi and the country around it on 4 February 1874. A few days later the Ashanti ruler Kofi Karikari called for peace and asked for a meeting with the British, and the agreement reached there became known as the Treaty of Fomena.

The treaty itself gives 13 February 1874 as the day of signing, though some have placed it in March. The Ashanti promised to pay 50,000 ounces of gold, gave up their claims to Assin, Akim, Adanse and Denkyira, and renounced their claims to Elmina and other allies and to all payments from the British government for the use of the forts. They were to withdraw their troops from the south-west and other places and to end human sacrifice. The king also guaranteed that the road from Kumasi to the River Pra would always be kept open, so that trade could pass between the two powers.

The terms fell hard on an empire already passing through a time of instability. The British victory and the settlement that sealed it ended the Ashanti hope of extending their power to the coastal states and helped bring about the kingdom's later collapse. The defeat also led to the independence of the states of Brong, Gonja and Dagomba.
treaty-of-fontainebleau-1762: The treaty followed the Battle of Signal Hill in September 1762, the last battle of the French and Indian War in North America, which confirmed British control of Canada, while in Europe the Seven Years' War went on. Having lost New France, King Louis XV of France proposed to King Charles III of Spain that France give Spain the country known as Louisiana, as well as New Orleans and the island on which the city stands.

Charles ratified the agreement on 13 November 1762 and Louis ten days later. It was kept secret even while France negotiated and signed the Treaty of Paris with Britain in February 1763, which ended the war. That treaty divided Louisiana at the Mississippi, giving the eastern half to Britain and leaving the western half and New Orleans nominally with France. Spain, which knew it would rule western Louisiana and had ceded Florida to Britain under the same peace, did not contest Britain's hold on the east. The Treaty of Paris also allowed French colonists 18 months to leave British territory, and many moved to Louisiana without knowing it had already been given to Spain.

The cession was finally made public in 1764. In a letter of 21 April 1764 Louis informed the governor, Jean-Jacques Blaise d'Abbadie, expressing the hope that the Spanish king would give his new subjects the protection and goodwill that the misfortunes of war had kept France from offering. The colonists of western Louisiana refused the change and expelled the first Spanish governor, Antonio de Ulloa, in the Louisiana Rebellion of 1768. Alejandro O'Reilly, an Irish émigré, put down the rebellion and took formal possession for Spain in 1769. When Britain returned Florida to Spain in 1783, Spanish territory encircled the Gulf of Mexico.
treaty-of-fort-laramie-1868: The first Treaty of Fort Laramie, signed in 1851, defined the territories of the Sioux, Arapaho and Cheyenne, Crow and other peoples and promised an annuity of $50,000 a year, which the Senate cut from 50 years to 10. The United States violated it almost at once, as miners and settlers moved onto Indian land, and an army invasion led to the Grattan massacre of 1854 and the first Sioux War. The government-appointed Indian Peace Commission, whose members included William Tecumseh Sherman and William S. Harney, negotiated the new treaty to replace it.

The treaty's 17 articles set aside the Great Sioux Reservation, west of the Missouri River in present-day South Dakota, for the absolute and undisturbed use of the tribes, about 25% of the Dakota Territory of the time. Land north of the North Platte River and east of the Big Horn Mountains became unceded Indian territory. The tribes were to hand offenders over to the government, accept railroads and roads, and send children aged six to 16 to school, while allotments, farm buildings and prizes for crops were meant to turn them to farming. Hunting rights north and west of the Black Hills lasted so long as the buffalo ranged there in numbers, and any later cession needed the consent of three-fourths of the adult men.

Under Article II the negotiators also sold the whole Ponca Reservation to the Lakota, breaking a separate treaty with the Ponca, who were not a party. In 1876 President Ulysses S. Grant ordered the Ponca removed to the Indian Territory, and the Ponca Trail of Tears of the following year caused over 200 deaths.

Over 192 days ending on 6 November 1868 the treaty was signed by 156 Sioux and 25 Arapaho, Red Cloud among the last; later arrivals had it read to them and were asked only for their marks. Many never signed or recognised it, and war broke out again in 1876. On 30 June 1980, in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, the Supreme Court upheld an award of $15.5 million for the land's value in 1877 plus interest. The Lakota have refused the payment and demand the land's return.
treaty-of-fort-stanwix-1784: In the Treaty of Paris that ended the Revolutionary War, the British ceded their claims in North America to the American government against the wishes of their Native American allies, and the status of Indian lands was ignored. Many Haudenosaunee fled to Canada to go on receiving British support; some later returned to the Ohio region, where they often came into violent conflict with colonists trying to settle the area.

The treaty was meant both as a peace between the Americans and the Haudenosaunee and as a way to secure lands farther west, which the Haudenosaunee had gained by conquest during the Beaver Wars of the previous century. It was the first of several treaties between Native Americans and the United States after the American victory.

Joseph Brant led the Haudenosaunee at the start of the negotiations. He told the commissioners that his delegation had been sent to make peace and was not authorised to agree to any particular cession of lands. Brant had to leave early for a planned journey to England, and the leading Native representatives who signed were Cornplanter and Captain Aaron Hill. Under the treaty the confederacy gave up all claims to the Ohio territory, a strip of land along the Niagara River and all land west of the mouth of Buffalo Creek. In Pennsylvania the land gained is known as the Last Purchase.

The Six Nations council at Buffalo Creek refused to ratify the treaty, denying that its delegates had the power to give away such large tracts, asking for the return of the deeds and offering to repay any presents received. The wider Indian confederacy also disavowed it, since most of the Six Nations did not live in the Ohio territory, and the Ohio Country peoples, among them the Shawnee, the Seneca-Cayuga and the Lenape, rejected it.

A run of treaties and land sales followed: Fort McIntosh in 1785, Fort Finney in 1786, the Phelps and Gorham Purchase in 1788, Fort Harmar in 1789, Canandaigua in 1794 and Big Tree in 1797. The war had already weakened the confederacy, and the negotiations at Fort Stanwix divided it further; it never regained its former influence.
treaty-of-fort-wayne-1809: In 1809 William Henry Harrison began to press for a treaty that would open more land to white American settlement. The Miami, Wea and Kickapoo were strongly opposed to selling more land around the Wabash River, so Harrison decided, against the wishes of President James Madison, first to make a treaty with the peoples willing to sell and use it to influence those who held out. In September 1809 he invited the Potawatomi, Lenape, Eel River people and Miami to Fort Wayne. The Shawnee, minor inhabitants of the area whom the Miami war chief Little Turtle had earlier asked to leave, were excluded.

Harrison promised large subsidies and direct payments. Only the Miami objected: they produced a copy of the Treaty of Greenville guaranteeing their possession of the Wabash lands, protested that the Wea, the main inhabitants of the land being sold, were absent, and asked to be paid by the acre. Harrison made the treaty depend on the Wea's approval but refused to buy by the acre. After two weeks the Potawatomi persuaded the Miami to accept. The land lay mostly along the Wabash north of Vincennes.

With the help of the Miami chief Pacanne, Harrison won the Wea's acceptance that winter with a large subsidy, and the Wea in turn pressed the Kickapoo to agree; by the spring of 1810 the treaty was complete. Although Harrison had forbidden the distribution of alcohol to Indians near Vincennes on 23 August 1809, he had whiskey handed out to the negotiators on a large scale: the historian Robert M. Owens states that the 1390 Indians at Fort Wayne consumed 218 gallons in September and October 1809.

Tecumseh, leader of a breakaway Shawnee group living just north of the treaty lands, held it illegitimate.
