In August 1810 he came down the Wabash to Vincennes with 400 armed warriors of several peoples, asked Harrison to annul it, admitted he had threatened to kill the signing chiefs if they carried out its terms, and said he would seek a British alliance otherwise. Harrison replied that the Miami owned the land. Hostilities followed, leading to the Battle of Tippecanoe in what is sometimes called Tecumseh's War, an episode that later helped Harrison win the presidency in 1840.
treaty-of-frankfurt-1871: Several considerations shaped the new frontier. The German military wanted Alsace up to the Vosges and the route between Thionville and Metz as protection against a future war with France. Politically, without a shift westward the new empire's frontier with France would have lain largely along the states of Baden and Bavaria, whose governments did not welcome a vengeful France on their doorstep and which kept considerable autonomy under the unification treaty.

The new border largely, though not entirely, followed the linguistic border. Most people in the annexed territory spoke Germanic dialects, and the area had once belonged to the Holy Roman Empire, which let Berlin justify the annexation on nationalist grounds. The taking of French-speaking areas such as Metz caused outrage in France.

The treaty was signed in Frankfurt on 10 May 1871 by the German Empire and the French Third Republic. It ceded 1,694 French villages and cities: in Alsace the departments of Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin except Belfort and its territory, and in Lorraine most of Moselle, a third of Meurthe including Château-Salins and Sarrebourg, and the cantons of Saales and Schirmeck in Vosges. Residents had the right of option until 1 October 1872 to keep French nationality and emigrate or to stay and become German citizens.

France was to pay five billion francs within five years, with German occupation of parts of France until payment; it paid sooner, and German troops withdrew in September 1873. The treaty also recognised Wilhelm I of Prussia as German Emperor and gave Germany most-favoured-nation terms in trade.

France lost 1,447,000 hectares, 1,597,000 inhabitants and about 20 percent of its mining and steel potential. The treaty shaped French policy towards Germany for some forty years, and recovery of the lost provinces became a revanchist aim, one of the strongest motives for France's part in World War I. In 1918 Woodrow Wilson called for the return of Alsace-Lorraine as the eighth of his Fourteen Points, and it was restored to France by the Treaty of Versailles in 1919.
treaty-of-fredrikshamn: The treaty, also called the Treaty of Hamina, was concluded on 17 September 1809 between Sweden and Imperial Russia and ended the Finnish War. It was signed in the Finnish town of Fredrikshamn. Russia was represented by Nikolay Rumyantsev and David Alopaeus, its ambassador to Stockholm, and Sweden by Infantry General Kurt von Stedingk, a former Swedish ambassador to Saint Petersburg, and Colonel Anders Fredrik Skjöldebrand.

Sweden ceded parts of the provinces of Lappland and Västerbotten east of the Tornio and Muonio rivers, Åland, and all provinces east of them. The ceded territories became the Grand Duchy of Finland, to which Russia's eighteenth-century conquests of parts of Karelia and Savonia, later called Old Finland, were joined in 1812 as Viborg County. The treaty referred to Emperor Alexander's promise to keep Finland's old laws and privileges, but it gave no formal guarantee of the legal position of the inhabitants: the Russians refused, and the Swedes were in no position to insist.

Together with the Diet of Porvoo of 1809 and the Oath of the Sovereign, the treaty is regarded as the basis of the autonomous grand duchy, with its own administration and institutions, and thus a start of the development that led to the revival of Finnish culture, the equal position of the Finnish language and, in 1917, Finland's independence. Similar clauses had been common in peace treaties and were regularly circumvented. During the period of Russification of Finland about ninety years later, the Russian government argued that the treaty had not been violated and that the matter was solely one for the Emperor who had granted the original promise.

During the negotiations the Swedish representatives tried to avoid losing the Åland islands, which Napoleon called the fore-posts of Stockholm; they were culturally, ethnically and linguistically purely Swedish. In the nineteenth century the islands proved to be a British interest, and after the Crimean War the Åland Convention in the Treaty of Paris of 1856 demilitarised them. On 5 April 1812 Russia and Sweden concluded an alliance against France, planning a landing in Swedish Pomerania and promising that Russia would press Denmark to cede Norway to Sweden, but Napoleon's invasion of Russia frustrated the plans.
treaty-of-ganghwa: In January 1864 King Gojong came to the throne at the age of 12, and his father Yi Ha-ŭng, the Daewongun, ruled in his name and set out to continue Korea's isolation. Western ships had appeared in Korean waters since the early 19th century, and in August 1866 the American merchant ship General Sherman steamed up the Taedong River to Pyongyang, where its crew fired on Koreans onshore, killing seven, and the ship was burned and its crew killed.

The French launched an unsuccessful expedition in 1866 and the Americans a victorious one in 1871, yet Korea stayed closed. After the Meiji restoration, an envoy arrived in 1869 with a letter using a character for the Japanese emperor that Koreans reserved for the Chinese emperor, and Korea, still within the Sinocentric order, refused to receive him. The Daewongun was later forced into retirement by Gojong and his wife, and officials who favoured trade took power.

On the morning of 20 September 1875 the Japanese gunboat Un'yō began surveying the west coast of Korea and reached Ganghwa Island, where earlier clashes with foreign forces were fresh in memory. Commander Inoue sent a boat ashore to ask for water and provisions, and the Korean forts opened fire.

The Un'yō silenced their guns, a landing party burned several houses, and the Japanese, with modern rifles, routed Koreans who carried matchlocks; thirty-five Korean soldiers were killed. The ship then attacked a fort on Yeongjong Island and withdrew. News reached the Japanese government on 28 September, and it sent warships to Pusan to protect Japanese residents. The treaty followed on 26 February 1876 and was negotiated chiefly by Kuroda Kiyotaka and Shin Heon.

Japan used gunboat diplomacy to press Korea to sign what was an unequal treaty. Article 1 declared Korea an independent state with the same sovereign rights as Japan, which ended Joseon's status as a tributary state of the Qing dynasty. Article 2 provided for an exchange of envoys within fifteen months, and Article 4 ended the centuries-old role of Tsushima as intermediary.

Besides Pusan, Article 5 provided for two more ports to be found and opened in October 1877. Article 7 allowed Japanese mariners to survey Korea's coasts, Article 8 allowed Japanese merchants to reside and trade, and Article 10 gave Japan extraterritoriality, the feature of earlier Western treaties most widely resented in Asia. It was the first of many unequal treaties Korea signed, and it left Korea open to the influence of imperial powers.
treaty-of-georgievsk: Under the treaty Russia's empress became the sole suzerain of the rulers of Kartli-Kakheti, guaranteeing the Georgians' internal sovereignty and territorial integrity and promising to regard their enemies as hers. Each Georgian king was to swear allegiance to the Russian emperors, support Russia in war and hold no diplomatic communications with other nations without Russia's consent. The preamble and article VIII acknowledged the bond of Orthodox Christianity, and Georgia's Catholicos became Russia's eighth permanent archbishop and a member of its Holy Synod. Article VI left internal administration, law and the collection of taxes to the Georgian king and forbade Russian authorities to intervene.

Given Georgia's history of invasions from the south, an alliance with Russia may have been seen as the only way to resist Persian and Ottoman aggression. Pavel Potemkin negotiated for Russia, with Prince Grigori Potemkin as plenipotentiary. The Georgian delegates, Ioane of Mukhrani and Garsevan Chavchavadze, signed at the fortress of Georgievsk in the North Caucasus, and Erekle II and Catherine the Great ratified it in 1784.

The results proved disappointing. Erekle's adherence prompted Persia's new ruler, Agha Mohammad Khan, to invade, and Russia did nothing to help at the Battle of Krtsanisi in 1795, which left Tbilisi sacked. Catherine belatedly declared war on Persia, but her death in November 1796 ended Russia's Persian Expedition. Erekle was succeeded in January 1798 by George XII. Strife broke out among the sons of George and of Erekle over the throne, and George secretly invited Paul I to govern the kingdom from St. Petersburg while he and his descendants reigned nominally.

Paul tentatively accepted, but on 18 December 1800 he issued a decree annexing Kartli-Kakheti and deposing the Bagratids. George died on 28 December 1800, before he knew he had lost his throne. On 12 September 1801 Alexander I confirmed the annexation, and Russian troops took over the administration. By the Treaty of Gulistan of 1813 Persia ceded eastern Georgia to Russia. Soviet historians later called the treaty an act of brotherhood justifying annexation, though no amendment had altered article VI. In 1983 the Soviet authorities marked its bicentennial. This provoked protests from Georgian dissidents, several of whom were arrested.
treaty-of-ghent: In late 1813 Emperor Alexander I of Russia offered to mediate, but Britain rejected Russian mediation. After the abdication of Napoleon in April 1814, British public opinion demanded major gains against the United States. Lord Liverpool, the prime minister, was aware of growing opposition to wartime taxation and of merchants who wanted to reopen trade with America. With Napoleon beaten, the aims of stopping American trade with France and impressing sailors lost their point, and President James Madison told Congress that the United States could no longer demand an end to impressment.

The treaty released all prisoners and restored captured lands and ships. The United States kept Mobile and the part of Spanish West Florida west of the Perdido River, which it had occupied in 1813, and returned only Pensacola. It made no change to the prewar boundary on the border between the United States and Canada. Article IX committed both governments to make peace with their Indigenous foes and to restore Indigenous nations to the possessions, rights and privileges they had enjoyed in 1811. Britain promised to return enslaved people it had freed during the war, and paid compensation to slaveholders in 1826 instead.

Talks moved to Ghent in late June 1814. The five American commissioners were John Quincy Adams, Henry Clay, James A. Bayard, Jonathan Russell and Albert Gallatin; the British sent minor officials who kept in close touch with London. The British demanded an Indigenous state under their sponsorship in the territory from present-day Ohio to Wisconsin. Adams argued that bringing allied Indigenous nations into a bilateral treaty would mean abandoning American sovereign claims, and the British government backed down. The Duke of Wellington wrote that Britain had no right to demand territory, and Liverpool told his negotiators to offer the status quo.

The commissioners signed on 24 December 1814 in the former Carthusian charterhouse where the British delegation was lodged. The Senate approved the treaty unanimously on 16 February 1815, and Madison exchanged ratifications with a British diplomat the next day.
treaty-of-ghilajharighat: The Treaty of Asurar Ali of 1639 fixed the limit between Ahom and Mughal interests at the Barnadi river on the north bank of the Brahmaputra and the Asurar Ali on the south. During the Mughal war of succession of 1658–1659 Pran Narayan, king of Koch Bihar, attacked the Mughal faujdar at Guwahati. The Ahoms refused a Koch offer to partition Kamrup, drove the Koches out and took the whole valley up to the Sankosh River.

Aurangzeb made Mir Jumla II subahdar of Bengal. He annexed Koch Bihar in December 1661, recovered Guwahati on 5 February 1662 and occupied Garhgaon on 17 March. The rains from April turned the country to marsh and brought food shortage and cholera to the camps, while the Ahoms waged the guerrilla warfare devised by Atan Burhagohain. When the rains ended the Mughals recovered and the king withdrew to Namrup. The Ahom commander-in-chief, Baduli Phukan, defected at the end of November, and Mir Jumla, by then ill, reached Tipam by 18 December with a worn-out army eager to go home.

Atan Burhagohain persuaded the king that further fighting was futile and sent four emissaries offering tribute if the Mughals left Assam. Mir Jumla, who had refused everything short of unconditional surrender, took the opening and left the bargaining to Dilir Khan. The terms are pieced together from Persian and Assamese sources that do not fully agree.

The king accepted Mughal vassalage; his daughter Ramani Gabharu went to the imperial harem with a dowry of 20,000 tolas of gold and 120,000 of silver. The indemnity was 300,000 tolas of silver within a year and 90 elephants in instalments, the annual tribute 20 elephants. Four sons of leading nobles were to be hostages. The ceded land ran from Guwahati to the Bharali River on the north bank and to the Kolong River on the south.

The princess left on 5 January 1663 with the gold, silver and part of the elephants, and Mir Jumla ordered the retreat from Tipam on 10 January. He died on board on 31 March 1663. Jayadhwaj Singha founded a new capital at Bakata and died in November 1663; his cousin succeeded as Chakradhar Singha. Neither king could accept tributary status, and the terms were only partly fulfilled. The treaty was the root of the later conflicts, which ended with the Mughal defeat at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671 and, after the Battle of Itakhuli in 1682, the end of Mughal interests in the Brahmaputra valley.
treaty-of-giyanti: Pakubuwono II of Mataram had backed a Chinese rebellion against the Dutch, and in 1743, in return for his restoration, ceded the north coast of Java and Madura to the Dutch East India Company; before his death in 1749 he ceded the rest of the kingdom. The company placed his son on the throne as Pakubuwono III. The new king faced his father's rival Raden Mas Said, who held the region of Sukowati, and in 1749 Prince Mangkubumi, brother of the late king, dissatisfied with his lowly position, joined Raden Mas Said. Company troops could not put the rising down.

According to the daily register of Nicolaas Hartingh, the company's Governor for North Java, he left Semarang on 10 September 1754 and met Mangkubumi on 22 September. In closed talks Hartingh doubted that one realm could have two rulers; Mangkubumi answered that Cirebon had more than one sultan. Mangkubumi refused at first to give up the title of Sunan, by which his people had hailed him five years before.

On 23 September they agreed that he would take the title of sultan and half the realm, half the palace heirlooms and half the company's payment for the coast. Pakubuwono III gave his consent in a letter of 4 November 1754 to the Governor-General, Jacob Mossel, and the treaty was signed at Giyanti, near present-day Karanganyar in Central Java.

The eastern half of Mataram went to Pakubuwono III with Surakarta as its capital, the western half to Mangkubumi, who set up his court at Yogyakarta near Kotagede, where Senopati, founder of Mataram, is buried. The sultan's chief minister and regents were to swear allegiance to the company and could not be appointed or dismissed without its approval. He gave up all claim to Madura and the coast in return for 10,000 a year, promised to help Pakubuwono III and to sell the company goods at fixed prices, and accepted the treaties of earlier rulers. Raden Mas Said made his own treaty with the company in 1757 and became Mangkunegara I. The division is told in the Javanese texts known as the Babad Giyanti.
treaty-of-granada-1491: The treaty, also known as the Surrender of Granada or the Capitulations, ended the Granada War, which had begun in 1482. The Nasrid Kingdom, the last part of Al-Andalus, had been weakened by a civil war between Boabdil and his father and uncle, and Ferdinand and Isabella used this to take key cities such as Malaga and Baza. When the siege of Granada began in the spring of 1491, the city was crowded with refugees and facing starvation. The terms were negotiated in secret over several months, to avoid a riot among townspeople not yet ready to give in.

The capitulation ran to sixty-seven articles. Mosques and their religious endowments were to remain as before, muezzins were not to be interrupted, and Muslims were to be judged only by their own laws. No badge or distinctive mark was to be imposed on them, no Christian soldiers were to be billeted in their houses, and Muslims were exempted from taxation for a number of years. Captives taken during the siege were to be freed, and those who chose to cross to Africa were to be carried there in the king's ships. A request that the Pope sign the treaty himself was not carried out.

At first the terms were kept. A joint municipal council was set up, and Muslims elected their own representatives. Ferdinand resisted pressure from the clergy, and Hernando de Talavera, a friar known for his moderation, became archbishop of Granada, preferring preaching to punishment. When Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros arrived, he began imprisoning Muslims who would not convert, especially noblemen, and his own church council warned that his methods might breach the treaty.

In December 1499 the Albayzín, the Muslim quarter of Granada, rose in armed revolt after the authorities tried to reconvert a Muslim woman who had left Christianity. Cisneros persuaded the monarchs to pardon the rebels on condition that they became Christians, and the whole city nominally converted. The treaty's guarantees were undone, and the end of the war freed the Crown's money and attention for wider ventures, including the voyage of Christopher Columbus.
treaty-of-greenville: After the Battle of Fallen Timbers and the scorched-earth tactics that followed, General Anthony Wayne courted leaders of the Western Confederacy with food and materials for crops. Blue Jacket, the Shawnee war chief who had led the Native force at Fallen Timbers, urged others to accept his terms, and the Wyandot chief Tarhe held that the defeat showed the Great Spirit favoured the Americans. Little Turtle of the Miami led the opposition, arguing that the earlier treaties of Fort McIntosh, Fort Finney and Fort Harmar were invalid. Wayne told the chiefs that the Senate had ratified the Jay Treaty, ending British supplies, and Little Turtle at last signed reluctantly.

The treaty had ten articles. In exchange for goods worth $20,000, such as blankets, utensils and domestic animals, the tribes ceded large parts of modern Ohio, and the treaty began the annuity system of yearly payments in money and supplies, which gave outsiders considerable control over tribal life. The Greenville Treaty Line ran from the mouth of the Cuyahoga River at present-day Cleveland to Fort Laurens, then west to Fort Recovery and south-southwest to the Ohio River opposite the mouth of the Kentucky River; Rufus Putnam surveyed it.

The United States kept reserved tracts within Indian Country, among them the future site of Fort Dearborn, now Chicago, and the tribes recognised it as sole sovereign of the territory. The Senate ratified the treaty on 22 December 1795.

The peace proved temporary. Wayne died in December 1796, and his second-in-command James Wilkinson, later found to be a spy for Spain, never enforced the treaty. The Shawnee chief Tecumseh, who had not signed, condemned the peace chiefs for giving away land they did not own, and as settlers kept encroaching he rebuilt the confederacy at Prophetstown; the unrest culminated in the Battle of Tippecanoe in 1811. Purchases of land by treaty and removals by law followed, and by 1840 the Old Northwest was essentially clear of its Indigenous peoples. A painting of the treaty by Howard Chandler Christy hangs in the Ohio Statehouse.
treaty-of-grimnitz: The House of Pomerania and the Hohenzollern electors of Brandenburg had long disputed whether the Pomeranian dukes held their duchy as a fief of Brandenburg or directly from the Holy Roman Emperor. The Treaties of Prenzlau of 1472 and 1479 had ruled for Brandenburg, but the Treaty of Pyritz of 1493 between John Cicero and Bogislaw X released the dukes from that obligation while giving the Hohenzollern the succession should the Pomeranian line die out.

When children were born to Bogislaw, John Cicero worked to keep him from gaining imperial immediacy, and Emperor Charles V invested both houses with the duchy and collected the tax from both. Bogislaw's sons Barnim IX and George I carried on the dispute with Joachim I Nestor after 1523, until the dukes of Brunswick, Eric I and Henry IV, mediated a settlement at the electors' hunting seat in the Uckermark.

Besides the exchange of immediacy for the right of succession, Brandenburg was to be told before any investiture of Pomeranian dukes, could touch the flags they received from the emperor, could send an envoy when the Pomeranian nobility swore allegiance, and was itself to be invested with the expectancy by the emperor. The treaty was to be announced and renewed at every new investiture, and the electors could bear the Pomeranian title and arms wherever the dukes were not present.

At the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 Barnim and George received their duchy as a fief for the first time. Joachim protested, seconded by George, Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach, and as the dukes took the flags of Pomerania, Stettin, Kashubia, Rügen and other lands from the emperor he laid his hands on each; the ceremony was repeated at every investiture.

When Bogislaw XIV died in 1637, during the Thirty Years' War, George William, Elector of Brandenburg, claimed the duchy under the treaty. Bogislaw had allied with Sweden in the Treaty of Stettin of 1630 and named Sweden to govern after his death, and Sweden refused to give it up. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 divided Pomerania between Sweden and Brandenburg, a partition carried out by the Treaty of Stettin in 1653.
treaty-of-guadalupe-hidalgo: Mexico had claimed the northern lands since winning its independence from the Spanish Empire in 1821. The Spanish had conquered part of the area from Indigenous peoples over three centuries, but powerful independent Indigenous nations remained there. Most of the land was dry and mountainous, and about 80,000 Mexicans lived in California, New Mexico, Arizona and Texas between 1845 and 1850. The United States annexed the Republic of Texas, which Mexico had never recognised, with effect from 29 December 1845, and Mexico had warned that annexation would be treated as an act of war.

U.S. forces moved quickly beyond Texas to conquer Alta California and New Mexico, and fighting there ended on 13 January 1847. By the middle of September 1847 they had occupied Mexico City. Nicholas Trist, chief clerk of the State Department, accompanied General Winfield Scott as President James K. Polk's representative and negotiated with a commission of José Bernardo Couto, Miguel de Atristain and Luis Gonzaga Cuevas.

Article V set the new border: the Rio Grande to the southern boundary of New Mexico, due west to the 110th meridian, north to the Gila River, and from the mouth of the Gila a straight line to a point one marine league south of the southernmost part of San Diego Bay, so that the United States received San Diego and its harbour. Mexicans in the annexed areas could relocate within Mexico or take U.S. citizenship and full civil rights.

The U.S. Senate ratified the treaty by 38 votes to 16, but removed Article X, which guaranteed land grants, and changed Article IX. A protocol signed at Querétaro on 30 May 1848 explained the amendments. The United States later ignored it, on the grounds that its representatives had over-reached their authority.

The ceded land became all or part of several U.S. states between 1850 and 1912. Disputes over whether to make the new territory slave or free states contributed to the tensions that led to the American Civil War. Surveying the boundary took over seven years, and the border commission contended with difficult terrain, extreme weather and Indigenous Americans who had not been considered in the negotiations. In 1889 the International Boundary and Water Commission was established to maintain the border. Writing many years later, Nicholas Trist called the treaty "a thing for every right-minded American to be ashamed of".
treaty-of-gulistan: Alexander I became tsar in 1801, eager to expand Russia's control over its neighbours. In Iran Fath Ali Shah Qajar had become shah after the assassination of his uncle Agha Mohammad Khan in 1797. Agha Mohammad Khan had re-subordinated the vassals and subjects in what are now eastern Georgia, Armenia, southern Dagestan and Azerbaijan. After his death and that of Heraclius II of Georgia, Russia, seeking territory and trade, took the chance to annex eastern Georgia.

Persia's primary motive in entering the war was to reassert control over Georgia and protect its north-western borders. Its army was as much as five times larger than the Russian force in the Caucasus but lagged behind technologically and was poorly trained. The Persian court declared a jihad against Russia and asked Napoleon for aid, but after the Treaty of Tilsit in 1807 France left Persia unassisted. The turning point was the Battle of Aslanduz on 31 October 1812, a decisive Persian defeat.

The treaty was concluded on 24 October 1813 in the village of Gulistan. The negotiations had been precipitated by General Pyotr Kotlyarevsky's storming of Lankaran on 1 January 1813. The text was prepared by the British diplomat Sir Gore Ouseley, who acted as mediator, and signed by Nikolai Rtischev for Russia and Mirza Abolhassan Khan Ilchi for Persia.

Russia was confirmed in possession of the khanates of Karabakh, Ganja, Shaki, Shirvan, Derbent, Quba and Baku, with part of Talysh and the fortress of Lankaran. Persia abandoned its claims to Dagestan, Georgia, Mingrelia, Imeretia and Abkhazia. Iran lost the right to navigate the Caspian Sea, and Russia received exclusive rights to station a military fleet there. Free trade was agreed, with a 5% duty on imports on both sides, and Russia promised to support Abbas Mirza as heir to the Persian throne.

The treaty did not settle whether the Persian army would be disarmed or allowed to regroup, and both sides saw that Persia might try to reclaim the territories. The costs of the war nevertheless led to relative peace from 1813 to 1826, and permanent diplomatic missions were set up in both countries to keep trade open. The treaty contributed directly to the Russo-Persian War of 1826 to 1828, which ended in the Treaty of Turkmenchay, by which Iran lost its last Caucasian territories.

Iranians regard Gulistan and Turkmenchay as among the most humiliating treaties ever signed, and Fath Ali Shah is judged for it as one of the most incompetent rulers in memory. Imperial Russian historians argued that Russia's absorption of Transcaucasia shielded local populations from Iranian and Ottoman invasions. The ceded territories came under Russian, and later Soviet, control for about 180 years.
treaty-of-hartford-1638: The Pequot War of 1636 and 1637 had all but eliminated the Pequot people. The victors, English colonists living along the Connecticut River and their Mohegan and Narragansett allies, met at Hartford to divide the fruits of their victory. The English party was made up of the three settlements in New England that would form the Connecticut River Colony in 1639.

The treaty was signed on 21 September 1638. The surviving Pequot prisoners were shared out: the Mohegan and the Narragansett received 80 captives each, 20 went to Ninigret, a sachem of the Eastern Niantic, who were allies of the Narragansett, and the English kept an unspecified number. The Pequot lands passed to the Connecticut River towns.

The treaty sought to erase Pequot identity altogether. Pequots were forbidden to return to their lands or to speak their language, no Pequot town or settlement was to be allowed, and any survivors were in future to be called Mohegans or Narragansetts rather than Pequots.

The Massachusetts Bay Colony, which had also taken part in the alliance against the Pequot, was not a party to the treaty. It insisted that the treaty usurped the rights over Pequot lands it held under earlier agreements with the Narragansetts and the Mohegans, which led to a dispute between Massachusetts and Connecticut.

The treaty was debated again in 2025, when the Connecticut state senator Cathy Osten proposed a resolution condemning it, supported by testimony from Latoya Cluff, vice chair of the Mashantucket Pequots Tribal Council. In March 2025 the Government Administration and Elections Committee approved the measure by 14 votes to 5 and sent it to the state Senate. Four years earlier an effort to remove John Mason's sculpture from the State Capitol building had failed.
treaty-of-hubertusburg: Austria's resolve to recover the province of Silesia from Prussia was the major conflict leading to the Seven Years' War. Maria Theresa, Archduchess of Austria and Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, won the support of Russia, Sweden, Saxony, Spain and France against Prussia and its ally Great Britain. It was King Frederick II of Prussia who opened hostilities in 1756 with his attack on and capture of Saxony.

In the first half of the war the Prussians were mostly victorious, defeating the French and imperial troops at Rossbach on 5 November 1757, the Austrians at Leuthen later that year and the Russians at Zorndorf in 1758. By 1759 the Russians held eastern Prussia, Berlin was occupied for some weeks, and Frederick was running short of soldiers. The tide turned after Empress Elizabeth of Russia died and her successor Peter III, an admirer of Frederick, made peace in the Treaty of Saint Petersburg. Sweden also made peace in 1762. The turn in fortune was called the Miracle of the House of Brandenburg.

Fighting alone in the east, the Austrians were defeated at the Battle of Burkersdorf in July 1762. After protracted negotiations between the war-weary powers, Prussia, Austria and Saxony made peace at Hubertusburg Castle on 15 February 1763, five days after Great Britain, France and Spain signed the Treaty of Paris. The treaty ended the continental war with no significant change in prewar borders. Austria and Saxony renounced all claims to the Silesian territories that had been ceded to Prussia.

The treaty restored the prewar situation but marked the ascendancy of Prussia as a leading European power, and it sharpened the rivalry with Austria. Through the Treaty of Paris, Great Britain emerged as the world's chief colonial empire and France lost most of its overseas possessions. The phrase Hubertusburg Peace is sometimes used for any treaty that restores the situation that existed before a conflict broke out.
treaty-of-hudaybiyyah: Muhammad had migrated to Medina in 622, and armed conflict followed with the Quraysh of Mecca, who kept him and his followers from the Kaaba. In March 628 he set out for the lesser pilgrimage with about 1,500 Muslims, reportedly after a dream in which he circled the Kaaba. The Meccans presumed an attack and sent cavalry to stop them, but Muhammad took an unconventional route and camped at Hudaybiya, on the edge of the sacred territory.

He told the Quraysh he wished to perform the pilgrimage rather than fight, but they refused to let him enter that year. A rumour that Uthman, sent to negotiate, had been killed led the Muslims to swear the Pledge of the Tree to fight, and when it proved false the Quraysh sent Suhayl ibn Amr to settle terms.

The treaty set a truce of ten years. A man of the Quraysh who fled to Muhammad without his guardian's permission would be returned, while a Muslim who went to the Quraysh would not. Any tribe could enter a covenant with either side.

The Muslims would go back to Medina that year but could make the pilgrimage the next, staying three days while the Quraysh left the city, carrying no weapons except sheathed swords. Ali wrote the document. Suhayl objected to the opening Basmala and to the words Messenger of God, and Muhammad accepted the wording Muhammad, son of Abdullah to preserve the agreement; according to tradition, he erased the phrase himself when Ali was reluctant to.

Some followers, Umar among them, reportedly objected to the terms. Abu Jandal, Suhayl's son, converted and was returned to his father under the return clause, but Muhammad did not return believing women who emigrated, citing Quran 60:10. Abu Basir, who was also returned, escaped and with other converts raided Meccan caravans until the Meccans asked Muhammad to take them in.

The treaty held for about two years, until the Banu Bakr, allies of the Quraysh, attacked the Banu Khuza'ah, allies of Muhammad, with help from some Quraysh. The Quraysh would not meet Muhammad's demands, and in 630 he took Mecca. Historians regard the treaty as an important stage in his consolidation of power, since the Quraysh implicitly treated him as an equal.
treaty-of-hue-1883: The French took the Thuận An forts at the mouth of the Huế River on 20 August 1883, leaving the capital open to attack. Nguyễn Trọng Hợp, the Vietnamese minister of personnel, accompanied by Monsignor Gaspar, the French bishop of Huế, agreed a 48-hour armistice, and the court gave up twelve inland forts on the river. Jules Harmand, the French civil commissioner-general for Tonkin, then went upriver and gave the court an ultimatum: it had forty-eight hours to accept his terms whole and without discussion, or the name of Vietnam would be erased from history. The court gave way at once.

In twenty-seven articles Vietnam again recognised French rule in Cochinchina and accepted that France would conduct all its relations with foreign powers, China included. Its troops were to leave Tonkin, and a permanent French garrison would hold the Thuận An forts and the Đèo Ngang mountains on the border between Annam and Tonkin. A resident at Huế gained the right to a private audience with the king, a concession the court had never made before. The provinces of Nghệ An, Thanh Hóa and Hà Tĩnh were transferred to Tonkin, under direct French oversight, and Bình Thuận was ceded in return for the cancellation of Vietnam's debts to France.

French residents would control the police in the towns, dispense justice between Europeans and natives, oversee taxes and replace hostile mandarins; customs passed wholly to French administrators. Tourane and Xuan Day were opened to trade with Qui Nhơn. France undertook to drive the Black Flag Army out of Tonkin and keep the Red River open, which it meant to do in any case.

The French foreign ministry, which preferred to govern Vietnam indirectly, thought the territorial terms too harsh, and the treaty was never ratified in France. The court paid it only lip service until Admiral Courbet defeated Liu Yung-fu and Hoàng Kế Viêm at Sơn Tây in December 1883. In January 1884 the diplomat Arthur Tricou obtained the court's full adhesion, with its hope that some clauses would later be softened. After the Tientsin Accord of 11 May 1884, in which China implicitly gave up its suzerainty, Jules Patenôtre negotiated the new treaty of 6 June 1884, which remained the basis of French rule until the Élysée Accords of 1949.
treaty-of-hue-1884: The treaty followed the Tientsin Accord with China, concluded three weeks earlier, by which China implicitly gave up its historic suzerainty over Vietnam. It replaced the vague Philastre treaty of 15 March 1874, the Treaty of Saigon, which had given France limited commercial privileges in Tonkin, and restated in milder language the Harmand Treaty of 25 August 1883, which the French parliament had never ratified. In January 1884 the diplomat Arthur Tricou hinted at Huế that harsher clauses might be revised, and the Vietnamese court declared its full adherence while trusting that the terms would later be softened.

In nineteen articles, Annam accepted the French protectorate, France took charge of its foreign relations, a French force was to occupy Thuận An permanently and the forts on the Huế River were to be razed. A Resident General was to live in the citadel of Huế and Residents in the chief towns of Tonkin, where native officials would govern under their control and be removed at French request. France also took over the customs, jurisdiction over foreigners and a telegraph line from Saigon to Hanoi, and undertook to defend the king against attack and rebellion.

The French foreign ministry preferred indirect rule to the outright conquest that Harmand had favoured, so the provinces of Nghệ An, Thanh Hóa, Hà Tĩnh and Bình Thuận, taken a year earlier, returned to Vietnamese jurisdiction. To spare China's dignity, Patenôtre dropped the phrase including China from Article I. At the signing, however, the seal that the Chinese emperor had given the Vietnamese king Gia Long decades before, a gilded silver plaque carved with a sitting camel, was melted down before the plenipotentiaries.

Signed for Vietnam by Phạm Thận Duật and Tôn Thất Phan, the treaty formed the basis of French colonial rule over central and northern Vietnam for the next seven decades. The Nguyễn government cancelled it with Japanese help in 1945, but France recognised the end of the protectorates only with the Élysée Accords of 8 March 1949, which transferred sovereignty to the former emperor Bảo Đại and led to the establishment of the State of Vietnam.
treaty-of-jaffa-1192: The Kingdom of Jerusalem had lost almost all of its territory after the Battle of Hattin in 1187, and the crusade that followed had not won back the holy city. The truce between Richard the Lionheart, King of England, and Saladin, Sultan of Egypt, was agreed shortly after the Battle of Jaffa of July and August 1192.

Neither ruler was pleased with the accord, but neither had much choice. Saladin had been weakened by the trials and expense of the war, while Richard had too few men and provisions to conquer Jerusalem. Each also had to deal with threats to his own kingdom at home.

The treaty, also called the Treaty of Ramla, was signed on 1 or 2 September 1192, the 20th of Sha'ban 588 in the Islamic calendar. It was negotiated with the help of Balian of Ibelin and guaranteed a truce of three years between the two armies. It dealt with two main questions: the status of Jerusalem and the rights of Christian pilgrims, and the extent of the kingdom's lands in the Holy Land.

Christians and Muslims were guaranteed safe passage through Palestine. Jerusalem stayed under Islamic rule but was opened to Christian pilgrimage. The Christians were to hold the coast from Tyre to Jaffa, so that the kingdom was restored as essentially a coastal strip between the two cities. The fortifications of Ascalon were to be demolished and the town returned to Saladin.

The treaty brought the Third Crusade to an end, and Richard left Acre on 9 October 1192. A similar double settlement followed in 1229, when treaties signed at Tell el-Ajjul and at Jaffa ended the Sixth Crusade. They settled the territorial disputes between the competing Ayyubid rulers of Egypt, Syria and several smaller principalities, which allowed Sultan al-Kamil of Egypt to reach a diplomatic agreement with the leader of that crusade, Emperor Frederick II.
treaty-of-jaffa-1229: Frederick II and al-Kāmil had exchanged embassies in 1227, when, according to the Arabic chronicles, the sultan sought Frederick's help against his brother al-Muʿaẓẓam of Damascus and offered land in return. Al-Muʿaẓẓam died soon after, and when Frederick reached Acre on 7 September 1228 the family dispute was unresolved. The two rulers never met: envoys passed between their camps, first Acre and Nablus, later Jaffa and Tall al-ʿAjūl. Al-Kāmil's chief negotiator was Fakhr al-Dīn, with whom Frederick could talk directly in Arabic, and the largely secret talks came with gifts and questions on philosophy and mathematics.

Frederick's position was weak: he was excommunicate, Pope Gregory IX invaded Sicily during the talks, and his army could not take and hold Jerusalem. Al-Kāmil meanwhile agreed with his brother al-Ashraf on dividing the Ayyubid lands in Asia, and according to al-Maqrīzī he settled with Frederick because otherwise he could not enforce that bargain, which required a siege of Damascus. A draft was reached on 11 February 1229 and accepted by the sovereigns on 18 February.

No complete copy survives, and the terms are reconstructed from Christian and Muslim writers who do not always agree. Jerusalem passed to the emperor with a corridor to the coast, including the diocese of Lydda, while the Ḥaram al-Sharīf stayed in Muslim hands with a Muslim garrison and judge, open to pilgrims of both faiths; other Muslims, and the Jews, were to leave the city. Christian possession of Acre, Jaffa, Nazareth, Sidon and Toron was recognised, and a truce of ten years, five months and forty days was agreed. The sources differ on whether Frederick could rebuild the walls.

Frederick entered Jerusalem on 17 March and was crowned in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre the next day, after which the city was placed under interdict because an excommunicate had negotiated the treaty. In besieged Damascus, al-Nāṣir Dāʾūd had Sibṭ ibn al-Jawzī denounce the treaty in the Umayyad Mosque, while al-Kāmil argued that he had conceded only some churches and ruined houses. Frederick's poets Freidank and Guillem Figueira praised the recovery, but the church hierarchy and the Templars and Hospitallers, who had not been consulted, were angered. Jerusalem was not refortified during the truce.
treaty-of-jeddah-2000: The dispute grew out of the Treaty of Taif of 1934 between Yemen and the newly formed Saudi Arabia, and from the marking of the boundary three years later. The line was placed ambiguously, and for the rest of the twentieth century both states made competing claims, complicated by traditional pre-colonial claims, crude border markers and uncertainty over which mountain peak the treaty text named. Wars were fought over the border in 1934 and 1969.

By the mid-1990s both governments accepted the need for a clear, agreed border. A Memorandum of Understanding followed in February 1995, and a meeting at Lake Como in Italy drew the provisional Como Line in the summer of 1997. Progress then stalled for three years, partly over where the maritime boundary should meet the Red Sea, and there were clashes, among them a confrontation between Yemeni and Saudi forces over Duwaimah Island, south of the Farasan Islands, in July 1998.

In May 2000 Crown Prince Abdullah of Saudi Arabia visited Yemen for the first time, for the tenth anniversary of Yemeni unification. Intensive talks followed, and the treaty was signed at Jeddah, to take effect the next month. It was signed by the foreign ministers of both states and by the Yemeni deputy prime minister, Abd al-Rahman Bagammal. The treaty gave exact coordinates for the land and sea border and set rules for the grazing rights of shepherds, the placing of armed forces and the future extraction of natural wealth along the line.

In 2003 Saudi Arabia began building a border wall, citing organised smuggling and security. Under international pressure, and amid accusations that the wall breached the 20-kilometre buffer zone the treaty reserved for grazing, Saudi Arabia agreed in February 2004 to halt construction, and both sides undertook to uphold the treaty. The wall was nevertheless completed in 2009 and 2010. Patrols increased and crossings were restricted after the Yemeni Revolution of 2011 and Saudi Arabia's involvement in the Yemeni Civil War.
treaty-of-kadesh: The Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty, also called the Eternal Treaty or the Silver Treaty, was concluded between Ramesses II of Egypt and Ḫattušili III of the Hittite Empire. It is sometimes called the Treaty of Kadesh, although its text does not mention the Battle of Kadesh and it was signed long after that battle. It ended a long war between two empires that had fought for over two centuries for mastery of the eastern Mediterranean. In about 1274 BCE the Hittites stopped an Egyptian invasion at Kadesh on the Orontes River. Both sides lost heavily, and the conflict went on for about fifteen more years.

Egypt faced a growing threat from the Sea Peoples, and the Hittites were concerned about the rising power of Assyria. The treaty is thought to have been negotiated by intermediaries without the two kings ever meeting. It was ratified in the 21st year of Ramesses II and stayed in force until the Hittite Empire collapsed eighty years later.

Each side pledged brotherhood and peace. Both powers guaranteed not to invade the other's land and renounced further hostilities over Syria. A second clause promised aid, most likely military, if either party was attacked by a third party or by rebels from within. Each country swore to send political refugees back, and in the Hittite version Ramesses II agreed to support the successors of Ḫattušili III against any who disputed the Hittite throne. Both rulers called on the gods of Hatti and Egypt to witness the agreement, and the treaty bound the children and grandchildren of the parties.

It is nearly symmetrical. The Hittite preamble is somewhat evasive, saying that the god had not permitted hostility between Egypt and Hatti since eternity, while the Egyptian version states plainly that the two states had been at war.

The treaty is the oldest known surviving peace treaty, and the only one from the ancient Near East for which the versions of both parties have survived. It did not bring an enduring peace: an atmosphere of enmity lasted many years, until a treaty of alliance was signed. The Egyptian version was engraved on the walls of the Ramesseum and Karnak. The Hittite version, in Akkadian on baked clay tablets, was found in 1906 by the German archaeologist Hugo Winckler at Hattusa, in a royal archive of some 10,000 tablets. Both texts were translated from silver tablets that were given to each side and are now lost.
treaty-of-kalisz-1343: The treaty closed the Polish-Teutonic War, which had begun in 1326 or 1327, and long disputes over Pomerelia, including Gdańsk, which the Order had held since 1308 and claimed through the Treaty of Soldin of 1309 with the margraves of Brandenburg. In the Warsaw Process of 1339, envoys of Pope Benedict XII ruled that the disputed lands belonged to Poland and awarded compensation of 194,500 grzywna, but the pope did not uphold the verdict and ordered the claims re-examined. His successor, Pope Clement VI, sided with the Order.

With the Order at the height of its power and a war likely to go badly, King Casimir III chose peace and turned to expansion south-eastward in Galicia-Volhynia. The treaty was drafted at Kalisz on 8 July 1343 and sworn on 23 July in a ceremony on a meadow near Wierzbiczany between the king and Grand Master Ludolf König von Wattzau.

Casimir relinquished his rights to the disputed lands but did not confirm them as the Order's property, leaving their status in legal limbo. The treaty dropped the formula agreed at the Congress of Visegrád in 1335, which had described Pomerelia as the king's perpetual alms to the Order, and recognised his earlier overlordship there, so that he and his successors kept the title of Duke of Pomerania. The peace was also confirmed by seven cities: Poznań, Kalisz, Włocławek, Brześć Kujawski, Kraków, Sandomierz and Nowy Sącz.

Although it delayed the recovery of Pomerelia, the settlement helped to consolidate the idea of a united Polish kingdom. The peace held for 66 years, while Pomerelia remained in dispute, until the Polish-Lithuanian-Teutonic War broke out in 1409. By the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 the Kingdom of Poland regained the Pomerelian lands, which were incorporated into Royal Prussia.
treaty-of-karlowitz: The treaty was signed on 26 January 1699 at Karlowitz, now Sremski Karlovci in Serbia, in the Military Frontier of the Habsburg monarchy, after a two-month congress. On the principle of uti possidetis, each power kept what it held. The Habsburgs received the Eğri and Varat eyalets, much of the Budin Eyalet, the northern part of the Temeşvar Eyalet and parts of the Bosnia Eyalet, which amounted to much of Hungary, Croatia and Slavonia. The Principality of Transylvania remained nominally independent but was subject to the direct rule of Austrian governors.

The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth recovered Podolia with the fortress of Kamianets-Podilskyi, undoing the loss of the Treaty of Buchach of 1672, and gave back captured fortresses in Moldavia. Venice obtained most of Dalmatia and the Morea, though the Peloponnese was restored to the Ottomans within 20 years by the Treaty of Passarowitz. The Ottomans kept Belgrade and the Banat of Temesvár, as well as suzerainty over Wallachia and Moldavia.

Negotiations with the Tsardom of Russia went on for a further year under a truce agreed at Karlowitz, and ended in the Treaty of Constantinople of 1700, in which the sultan ceded the Azov region to Peter the Great. Russia returned it eleven years later after the Pruth River Campaign. Commissions marked the new borders between the Austrians and the Ottomans, with some parts disputed until 1703, and the work of the Habsburg commissioner Luigi Ferdinando Marsili produced a border marked by physical landmarks for the first time.

The Habsburg gain of about 160,000 square kilometres of Hungarian territory, and of the Banat of Temesvár 18 years later at Passarowitz, made the monarchy the dominant power of Central Europe. For the Ottoman Empire it was a watershed: after three and a half centuries of expansion in Europe it lost substantial territory for the first time. Its borders in the region shifted over the next century, but it never again gained land on the scale of the 15th and 16th centuries.

In the Commonwealth the Sejm judged the Cossack regiments of the Right Bank unneeded, and in 1699 voted to abolish them. This was a primary cause of the Paliy uprising against the nobility in Right-bank Ukraine from about 1700.
treaty-of-kepno: Poland had been divided among rival dukes since the death of Bolesław III Wrymouth in 1138. Przemysł II, High Duke of Poland and ruler of Wielkopolska, held the provinces of Poznań, Wielkopolska and Kraków, and the addition of Gdańsk Pomerania to them was an important step towards reuniting the country. Under the agreement suzerainty over Gdańsk Pomerania passed to Przemysł, who took the title dux Polonie et Pomeranie, Duke of Poland and Pomerania.

Mestwin II kept de facto control of the province for the rest of his life, while Przemysł became its ruler de jure. Some sources suggest that Mestwin kept full control and that the agreement only laid down that whichever of the two outlived the other would take over his lands. As custom required, an assembly of nobles of both Pomerania and Wielkopolska affirmed and approved the treaty.

The first effect of the treaty was that the two dukes pursued a single foreign policy, above all towards Brandenburg and Western Pomerania. Przemysł also placed several trusted men from Wielkopolska in offices in Gdańsk and the surrounding area. As part of the settlement Przemysł also granted the town of Kępno municipal rights based on those of Kalisz.

Further meetings followed at Nakło in 1284, Rzepka in 1288 and Nakło again in 1291, and another at Słupsk was attended by Bogusław IV, Duke of Szczecin-Pomerania, of the Griffin dynasty. There the three rulers concluded a mutual-defence alliance against the expansion of Brandenburg and agreed that Bogusław would inherit Pomerania if both Przemysł and Mestwin died without heirs. The alliance was reaffirmed at Nakło in 1291.

In 1296 Przemysł was assassinated by agents of the Margrave of Brandenburg and members of the Nałęcz family, both of whom opposed a strong central power in Poland. His realm, Pomerania included, then became the object of a civil war between Wenceslaus II of Bohemia and Władysław I the Elbow-high, each of whom at some point had himself crowned king of Poland. Although Bogusław outlived both Mestwin and Przemysł, the Nakło provisions were never carried out and he never gained Gdańsk Pomerania.
treaty-of-kiel: Denmark-Norway and Sweden tried at first to stay neutral in the Napoleonic Wars but joined opposite camps. After a British fleet bombarded Copenhagen in 1807 and seized or destroyed the Dano-Norwegian ships, Denmark-Norway aligned with France. In 1810 the French Marshal Jean Baptiste Bernadotte was elected heir to the Swedish throne. Sweden allied with Russia in 1812 and with the United Kingdom and Prussia in 1813, and Bernadotte made the gain of Norway his condition for joining the anti-Napoleonic alliance, which the United Kingdom and Russia accepted in May 1813.

Denmark, which had kept to its alliance with Napoleon because of the Swedish claim, was isolated and bankrupt after the war. After Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig in October 1813, Bernadotte took a combined Swedish and Russian army, defeated the outnumbered Danish army and occupied Holstein and Schleswig in late December. Frederick VI agreed to peace once it was clear that Bernadotte would occupy Jutland and Zealand, if necessary with British naval help, to force the cession of Norway.

The Danish treaty with Britain was negotiated by the Danish diplomat Edmund Bourke and the British envoy Edward Thornton. Britain returned occupied Danish possessions except Heligoland, which George III received in full sovereignty, and the Danish king joined the alliance and undertook to keep 10,000 men with the Allied forces in northern Germany, with British subsidies of 400,000 pounds a year.

In the treaty with Sweden, Frederick VI renounced Norway "irrevocably and forever" and Swedish Pomerania was to pass to Denmark. Greenland, Iceland and the Faroe Islands were excepted from the cession, through an insertion written by Bourke. Sweden took over Norway's debts, and the king promised to maintain the University of Christiania and the University of Greifswald.

The Swedish crown prince intended to invade Norway to enforce the treaty, but the Norwegian elite in Christiania supported resistance. Norway declared its independence, adopted a constitution and elected Crown Prince Christian Frederik as king. After a short war with Sweden, Norway accepted a personal union at the Convention of Moss. The Storting elected Charles XIII as king of Norway on 4 November 1814.

Because Norway refused to submit, Sweden did not hand over Swedish Pomerania. The Congress of Vienna settled the matter in 1815 on a plan of Karl August von Hardenberg: Pomerania passed to Prussia, and Denmark received the Duchy of Lauenburg with a payment of 3.5 million thalers. The Danish claim to all of Greenland was contested by Norway in the Eastern Greenland case of 1931 to 1933, which the Permanent Court of International Justice decided in Denmark's favour on the basis of the Treaty of Kiel and later treaties.
treaty-of-kucuk-kaynarca: The treaty was signed on 21 July 1774 at Küçük Kaynarca, today Kaynardzha in Bulgaria, after the Ottoman defeat at the Battle of Kozludzha. Russia was represented by Field-Marshal Count Pyotr Rumyantsev and the Ottoman Empire by Muhsinzade Mehmed Pasha. After the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 the Ottoman Empire had ceased to be an aggressive power, and by the middle of the 18th century the tsars had taken over the Habsburgs' fight against the Turks. The Russians sought the Black Sea, the bulwark of Constantinople.

Russia returned Wallachia and Moldavia to Ottoman control but gained the right to intervene there in case of Ottoman misrule. It kept Kabardia, the port of Azov, the ports of Kerch and Enikale on the Kerch peninsula, and part of the Yedisan region between the Bug and the Dnieper, including the port of Kherson. Russian merchant ships were allowed through the Dardanelles, giving Russia two outlets to the Black Sea.

The Ottomans recognised the Tatars of Crimea as politically independent, although the sultan remained their religious leader as caliph. Article 14 allowed Russia to build a church in Constantinople, under the protection of the Russian minister. The Ottomans also had to pay a large indemnity. Original copies were written in Russian, Italian and Turkish, and the Italian text was to prevail in a divergence.

Russia later read the treaty as giving it the right to protect Orthodox Christians in the Ottoman Empire, and used this claim in the Danubian Principalities. Historians dispute whether the articles gave such a right, since some consider it granted and others think the wording too vague. A French translation made at St Petersburg in 1775 left out the church's Russian character, which helped later Russian claims. The church was most likely never built.

The Crimean Khanate kept nominal independence, while depending on Russia, until Catherine the Great annexed it in 1783. In 1787 Abdul Hamid I declared war on Russia again. The treaty is regarded as a milestone in the decline of the Ottoman Empire, since a foreign power now had a say in the fate of its Orthodox subjects, and it opened the era of the Eastern Question. The Crimean War of 1853 broke out over the Russian claim.
treaty-of-lahore: Maharaja Ranjit Singh had made Lahore the capital of the Sikh Empire of the Punjab, which he built up between 1799 and his death in 1839. After his death factions and assassinations broke the state's unity, which alarmed the British because it weakened a buffer against feared invasion from the north. Provocations on both sides raised tension, and on 13 December 1845 the Governor-General, Sir Henry Hardinge, declared war. The British came close to defeat at the Battle of Ferozeshah but won at the Battle of Sobraon and marched unopposed into Lahore on 20 February 1846.

The treaty was signed on 9 March 1846 by Hardinge and two officers of the East India Company and, for the Sikhs, by the seven-year-old Maharaja Duleep Singh and members of his court. It was drafted by Frederick Currie, helped on military matters by Brevet-Major Henry Lawrence. The Lahore state gave up the territory south of the Sutlej and the forts and lands of the Jalandhar Doab between the Sutlej and the Beas, its army was limited in size and thirty-six field guns were taken. Control of the Sutlej, the Beas and part of the Indus passed to the British.

The British demanded 15 million rupees for the cost of the war. Unable to pay it all, the Lahore government ceded lands including Hazara and Kashmir in place of 10 million rupees and was to pay 6 million at once. A supplement of 11 March, signed at the Durbar's request, kept a British force in Lahore until the end of the year to protect the Maharaja and the city during the reorganisation of the Sikh army.

On 16 March 1846, by the Treaty of Amritsar, the British sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh, Raja of Jammu, for 7.5 million rupees, making him the founder and first Maharaja of the princely state of Kashmir and Jammu. As the end of the year neared, the Durbar asked the troops to stay until the Maharaja turned 16, and the Treaty of Bhairowal of 26 December 1846 placed a British Resident in Lahore with full authority over every department of the state. The regent, Maharani Jindan Kaur, was pensioned off and replaced by a Council of Regency under the Resident, which in effect gave the British control of the government.
treaty-of-lausanne: The treaty was negotiated at the Lausanne Conference of 1922 to 1923 and signed in the Palais de Rumine in Lausanne on 24 July 1923. It was a second attempt at peace after the Treaty of Sèvres of 1920, which had sought to partition Ottoman territories but was never ratified. The Turkish National Movement rejected its terms.

After the Greek defeat in the Greco-Turkish War, Turkish forces recaptured İzmir, and the Armistice of Mudanya of October 1922 provided for an exchange of Greek and Turkish populations and for civilian passage through the Turkish Straits. The conference opened on 20 November 1922 and took eight months of negotiation, with several Turkish withdrawals. İsmet İnönü was chief negotiator for Turkey, Lord Curzon for the Allies and Eleftherios Venizelos for Greece.

The treaty had 143 articles and was written in English and French. It provided for the independence of the Republic of Turkey, and for the protection of the Greek Orthodox minority in Turkey and the Muslim minority in Greece. Most of both populations had already been moved under the earlier convention on the exchange of populations; only the Greek Orthodox of Constantinople, Imbros and Tenedos, about 270,000 people, and the Muslim population of Western Thrace, about 129,120 in 1923, were excluded.

Islands in the Aegean beyond three miles from the Turkish shore went to Greece, except Imbros, Tenedos and Rabbit Island. Turkey renounced its claims to the Dodecanese, Cyprus, Egypt and Sudan, Syria and Iraq, and left the fate of the province of Mosul to the League of Nations. Greece gave up reparations in exchange for ceding Karaağaç. Annex VIII, the Declaration of Amnesty, granted legal immunity for acts committed between 1914 and 1922 on account of military or political action, which ended efforts to prosecute Ottoman war criminals.

Turkey ratified the treaty on 23 August 1923 and all other signatories had done so by 16 July 1924. It took effect on 6 August 1924. It brought international recognition of the sovereignty of the Republic of Turkey as successor to the Ottoman Empire, and the Ottoman public debt was divided between Turkey and the states that emerged from the empire.

The convention on the Straits lasted thirteen years until the Montreux Convention of 1936. For Greece, the treaty ended the impetus behind the Megali Idea. David Lloyd George called it an abject, cowardly and infamous surrender. Historians such as Norman Naimark describe it as a decisive precedent for transferring populations against their will in the 20th century.
treaty-of-le-goulet: The death of Richard I of England left a disputed succession, and John's claim to the Angevin lands was challenged by Arthur of Brittany, the son of John's late brother Geoffrey, whom Philip II of France supported. The treaty ended this first war of succession. It was signed at Le Goulet, an island in the middle of the Seine near Vernon in Normandy, and temporarily settled the territorial quarrels over Normandy.

Philip dropped his support for Arthur and accepted John's claim to the English throne. In return John acknowledged Philip as his overlord for his French lands and recognised the French king's supremacy over the territories in France that had belonged to the Angevin Empire. He paid Philip 20,000 marks as relief, in exchange for formal recognition of his rule over Brittany, and accepted that the counts of Boulogne and Flanders were vassals of the French king, promising not to support any rebellion against them.

John also gave up land. The Vexin passed to France, except for Les Andelys, where the fortress of Château Gaillard stood, together with Évreux, Issoudun, Graçay and other lands in Berry. One side effect was that the Channel Islands were cut off from mainland Normandy. The Duchy of Aquitaine stayed with John, since it still legally belonged to his mother, Eleanor of Aquitaine. To seal the peace a marriage was arranged between John's niece, Blanche of Castile, and Philip's son, the future Louis VIII of France.

The marriage was meant to bind the Angevin and Capetian dynasties together, but the treaty gave only a short pause in the fighting. In 1202 Philip declared that John had forfeited his French lands by failing to appear at his court, and war broke out again. Philip's forces quickly took Normandy, which was formally annexed to the crown lands of France, strengthening the French crown and ending Plantagenet rule in the duchy.
treaty-of-lima-1929: In the War of the Pacific Chile defeated Peru and Bolivia and conquered the Peruvian territories of Tarapacá, Tacna and Arica. Under the Treaty of Ancón of 1883 Tarapacá was annexed to Chile, while Tacna and Arica stayed under Chilean administration until a plebiscite due in 1893. The plebiscite never took place, as the two countries could not agree on its terms. Chile began a campaign of Chilenization in 1909, and in 1911 Peru recalled its ambassador and broke off diplomatic relations.

On 20 July 1922 the two countries agreed to submit the dispute to the arbitration of the President of the United States. President Calvin Coolidge appointed General John J. Pershing as arbitrator in 1925, and General William Lassiter took over in 1926 after Pershing resigned on 18 January, but neither could break the deadlock. In 1928 the Secretary of State, Frank B. Kellogg, suggested direct negotiations in Washington, D.C., which led to the treaty.

The treaty was signed in Lima by the Peruvian representative Pedro José Rada y Gamio and the Chilean representative Emiliano Figueroa Larrain. It divided Tacna Province, the administrative division Chile had established, in two: Tacna went to Peru and Chile kept Arica. It fixed the border between the two states, Chile agreed to pay Peru up to US$6 million in compensation, and Peru received the administration of the Tacna–Arica railway and a Peruvian-administered wharf in the port of Arica.

Bolivia's ruling elite, which had hoped to gain access to the sea, saw the compromise as a setback, although the United States had promoted an option giving Bolivia such access. The treaty stiffened Bolivian positions on the Chaco and contributed to the outbreak of the Chaco War with Paraguay in 1932. Only in 1999 did Chile and Peru agree to implement the treaty fully, providing Peru with its port facilities in Arica.
treaty-of-limerick: The victory of William III at the Battle of the Boyne in July 1690 proved less decisive than it seemed, the Jacobites losing about 2,000 of 25,000 men. The Declaration of Finglas, largely dictated by Irish Protestants, offered amnesty to the rank and file but excluded senior officers, so the war went on. The Jacobites held a line along the Shannon and repulsed attempts on Limerick and Athlone, but Connacht and County Kerry could not feed the army and its refugees, and by the spring of 1691 soldiers and civilians were starving.

The Irish Jacobites were split between a pro-war faction under Sarsfield and those led by Tyrconnell, who wanted to negotiate while they still had an army. William, who saw Ireland as secondary to the war in Europe, authorised De Ginkell to offer whatever terms were needed for peace.

The military treaty of twenty-nine articles was agreed between Ginkell and the French lieutenant-generals D'Usson and de Tessé, and signed also by Patrick Sarsfield, Earl of Lucan, and other Jacobite officers. Some 14,000 Jacobites marched to Cork and embarked for France, many with their wives and children; about 1,000 joined the Williamite army and some 2,000 went home. The civil treaty of thirteen articles, drafted by Sir Toby Butler, protected the property of Jacobite gentry and merchants who swore allegiance to William III and Mary II, and allowed Catholic noblemen to bear arms.

The civil articles were not honoured by the victorious Williamite government. The few Catholic landowners who took the oath in 1691–93 kept their protection, while the non-jurors were treated as suspect. After the Papacy again recognised James II as lawful king of Ireland in 1693, the Parliament of Ireland enacted harsh penal laws from 1695, and reforms did not begin until the 1770s. In December 1699 the Commissioners of Forfeitures reported that 3,921 persons had been outlawed, owning 1,060,792 acres, about a twentieth of Ireland's land, and that 491 had been pardoned under the treaties of Cavan and Limerick.
treaty-of-lisbon-1668: By 1640 King Philip IV of Spain had lost the trust of most Portuguese nobles; the country was overtaxed and its colonies left unprotected. On 1 December 1640 conspirators in Lisbon proclaimed the Duke of Braganza king as John IV, taking advantage of the revolt in Catalonia and Spain's war with France. Portugal at first lost colonies to the Dutch, but regained Angola, São Tomé and Brazil by 1654. Spain made peace with France in 1659, yet Portugal could draw on the wealth of Brazil and the help of France and then England, while Spanish finances stayed in crisis.

With the help of a British brigade the Portuguese won at the Battle of Ameixial on 8 June 1663, where the count of Vila Flor and Marshal Frederick Schomberg defeated John of Austria the Younger, at Ciudad Rodrigo in 1664, and at the Battle of Montes Claros on 17 June 1665. Spain, desperate to reduce its commitments, signed a treaty with England at Madrid in 1667, and England then mediated the peace.

Queen Mariana of Austria negotiated as regent for the young Charles II of Spain, and Prince Pedro, the future Peter II, for his incapacitated brother Afonso VI. Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich, mediated for Charles II of England. Spain recognised the Braganza dynasty, and Infanta Catarina, Duchess of Braganza, grandmother of John IV, was acknowledged after her death as a legitimate heir to the throne. Portugal's colonies were confirmed, except Ceuta, which had not accepted the new dynasty. The parties agreed on prisoners, reparations and renewed trade, and by custom the title King of Spain was avoided in letters between Madrid and Lisbon.

Spain was relieved to end a ruinous war, and Portugal was free to pursue its overseas possessions. Afterwards Portugal looked to France and England for ideas and skills, consolidating its independence from Spain in what historians call a gradual de-Iberianization. Its economy rested in the 17th century on the entrepôt trade in tobacco and sugar and the export of salt, and in the 18th century more on slaves, gold, leather and wine, centred on the port of Lisbon and the colonial economy of Brazil.
treaty-of-london-1839: Since 1815 Belgium had been a reluctant part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. In 1830 Belgians broke away and set up an independent Kingdom of Belgium. The largely Catholic population objected to King William I's favouritism towards Protestantism, French-speakers disliked his disdain for their language, and the middle classes resented the Dutch monopoly of public office. There was also unemployment and industrial unrest. About 600 volunteers died in the small-scale fighting and are commemorated in the Place des Martyrs in Brussels. An international settlement of 1831, the Treaty of the XVIII Articles, was rejected by the Dutch, who invaded in the autumn of 1831, and it took a French army recapturing Antwerp in 1832 before an armistice was agreed.

The treaty was signed on 19 April 1839 at the end of the London Conference of 1838 to 1839. The powers recognised the southern provinces of the Netherlands, independent in fact since 1830, as the Kingdom of Belgium, and the Province of Limburg was split into Belgian and Dutch parts. The Grand Duchy of Luxemburg, in personal union with the Netherlands and a member of the German Confederation, lost two thirds of its territory to Belgium's new Province of Luxembourg. The remaining third stayed in personal union with the Netherlands under William I, a settlement confirmed by the Treaty of London of 1867 and lasting until the death of William III on 23 November 1890.

Article VII required Belgium to remain perpetually neutral, and the five great powers, Austria, France, Prussia, Russia and the United Kingdom, pledged to guarantee its neutrality. The treaty also guaranteed Belgium a right of transit by rail or canal across Dutch territory to the German Ruhr, the basis of the later Iron Rhine dispute.

The treaty became central to European international law. On 31 July 1914 the Belgian king pointed out that Germany, Britain and France were legally bound to respect his country's neutrality. When Germany invaded Belgium in August 1914 after an unanswered ultimatum, Britain declared war on 4 August. The German chancellor Theobald von Bethmann Hollweg said he could not believe the two countries would go to war over a scrap of paper. Christopher Clark notes that the British cabinet had agreed on 29 July that the treaty did not oblige Britain to use force, and that fears of German dominance in Western Europe weighed heavily in its decision. Few historians now hold that Belgium's fate was the real motive for the declaration of war.
treaty-of-london-1867: The Luxembourg Crisis erupted after the French Emperor Napoleon III tried to buy Luxembourg from the Dutch King William III. The Austro-Prussian War had led to the collapse of the German Confederation, of which both the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg and the Duchy of Limburg had been members, with the Dutch king as head of state of each. For Prussia, keeping Luxembourg under Dutch dominance and free from French interference was of paramount importance.

Article I reaffirmed the personal union between the Netherlands and Luxembourg under the House of Orange-Nassau. The neutrality of Luxembourg, set out in the First Treaty of London of 1839, was also reaffirmed, and the parties that had not signed the earlier treaty became guarantors of it. Belgium was an exception, being itself bound to neutrality.

To secure that neutrality, the western fortifications of Luxembourg City, known as the Gibraltar of the North, were to be demolished and never rebuilt. The Prussian garrison, stationed there since 1815 under the decisions of the Congress of Vienna, was to be withdrawn. The treaty also affirmed the end of the German Confederation and declared Limburg an integral part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

The treaty was signed on 11 May 1867 by representatives of Austria-Hungary, Belgium, the French Empire, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Prussia, Russia and the United Kingdom. Italy was not at first invited; King Victor Emmanuel II persuaded the others to include it, and it was the first time Italy took part in an international conference as a Great Power.

Dismantling the western and underground fortifications took sixteen years and cost 1.5 million gold francs. It required the destruction of over 24 km of underground defences and 4 hectares of casemates, batteries and barracks. The large residual fortifications of Luxembourg City are now on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

The personal union with the Netherlands lasted until 1890. When Wilhelmina ascended the Dutch throne, agnatic succession under the Nassau Family Pact of 1783 barred her from Luxembourg, which passed to the older branch of the House of Nassau, giving the grand duchy its own dynasty. Luxembourg rejoined the German customs union, the Zollverein, and remained in it until 1 January 1919.
treaty-of-london-1915: Soon after the outbreak of the First World War the Triple Entente powers, the United Kingdom, France and Russia, sought more allies. The first attempt to bring in Italy came in August and September 1914, on Russian initiative. On 4 August, a day after Italy declared neutrality, its ambassador to Russia said Italy might join the Entente in return for Trentino-Alto Adige, Vlorë and a dominant position in the Adriatic. The British Foreign Secretary, Edward Grey, would consider nothing further until Italy committed itself, and the Italian prime minister, Antonio Salandra, said that was impossible at the time.

Talks were taken up again by Salandra's foreign minister Sidney Sonnino, who on 4 March 1915 presented Grey with sixteen conditions. The Entente was at the same time courting Bulgaria, and the Italian claim to Dalmatia clashed with the Adriatic outlet offered to Serbia as compensation. Grey judged the Italian claims excessive but not against British interests. Russia's foreign minister, Sergey Sazonov, objected to Italian claims in Dalmatia, and negotiations ran on for six weeks.

Article 1 provided for a military agreement guaranteeing the number of troops Russia would commit against Austria-Hungary. Article 2 required Italy to enter the war against all the enemies of the three Entente powers, and the French and British navies were obliged by Article 3 to support it by destroying the Austro-Hungarian fleet. Under Article 4 Italy received Trentino and the southern part of Tyrol, with a new frontier between the Piz Umbrail and Toblach and an eastern frontier from Tarvisio to the Kvarner Gulf that left Rijeka outside Italy.

Article 5 awarded Italy the part of Dalmatia north of a line running northeast from Cape Planka, with Zadar and Šibenik, and all the Austro-Hungarian Adriatic islands except a list of twelve. The remaining coast between Rijeka and the Drin River went to Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro.

Although it was meant to be secret, an outline became known in late April 1915 to the Yugoslav Committee, which with Serbia protested strongly. Italy declared war on Austria-Hungary in May 1915 but waited a year before declaring war on Germany, which France and the United Kingdom resented. At the Paris Peace Conference the United States pressed to void the treaty as contrary to self-determination. Italy received Trentino-Alto Adige and the Julian March, and under the Treaty of Rapallo Istria and Zadar, but the Entente did not provide the promised colonies or part of Asia Minor.

The result turned wartime fervour into nationalist resentment. Gabriele D'Annunzio called the outcome a mutilated victory and led veterans and soldiers to seize Rijeka in the Impresa di Fiume. His short-lived Italian Regency of Carnaro influenced the development of Italian fascism.
treaty-of-lubeck: The Lower Saxon or Emperor's War, the Danish phase of the Thirty Years' War, began in 1625. After early Danish successes under Christian IV and Ernst von Mansfeld, the tide turned in 1626 at the battles of Dessau Bridge and Lutter am Barenberge. Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, and Albrecht von Wallenstein joined their armies in the summer of 1627, invaded Holstein in September and advanced through Jutland as far as the Limfjord.

Christian still held the western Baltic and the Danish isles. In 1628 his fleet raided the occupied coasts and destroyed Wallenstein's naval facilities in Ålborg, Wismar and Greifswald, and in April he allied with Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, with whom he supported Stralsund's successful resistance. His defeat at the Battle of Wolgast in August, the last battle of the war, left him ready to negotiate, and Wallenstein, alarmed by the Scandinavian alliance, was ready too.

A proposal drafted by Tilly and Wallenstein in September 1627 would have had Christian buy back Holstein, Schleswig and Jutland for two million Reichstaler each; the Danish council of the realm accepted it as a basis, but Christian rejected it. Envoys met at Lübeck in January 1629, and the real bargain was struck in secret talks at Güstrow in Mecklenburg.
