Concluded on 22 May 1629 and ratified by Emperor Ferdinand II on 7 June, with the Catholic League added as a party, the treaty restored Christian's pre-war possessions. He gave up his claims to the Lower Saxon bishoprics and his alliances with the North German states, and Tilly failed to make him pay the imperial war costs.

The treaty marked the decline of Denmark–Norway from a major European power to a politically insignificant state. Sweden took its place as the Nordic power, landing in Pomerania in 1630 and later, from the Torstenson War onwards, taking Denmark's provinces across the Kattegat and Norway's Jämtland and Härjedalen. Ferdinand was disappointed with the terms Wallenstein had obtained, and the treaty deepened the rift between Christian and his council. Without Danish protection the North German states faced the Edict of Restitution, issued during the negotiations, which sought the return of church lands secularised in the Reformation.
treaty-of-luneville: The Austrian army had been defeated by Napoleon Bonaparte at the Battle of Marengo on 14 June 1800 and by Jean Victor Moreau at the Battle of Hohenlinden on 3 December. Two armistices, the Convention of Alessandria on 15 June in Italy and the Armistice of Parsdorf on 15 July in Germany, preceded the talks. A first preliminary peace, signed in Paris on 28 July by Count Joseph von Saint-Julien, largely copied the Treaty of Campo Formio, but the emperor rejected it and Saint-Julien was imprisoned for signing without authority. Austria was also bound to Britain by an alliance, which complicated the negotiations.

Talks opened at Lunéville on 9 November 1800 between Joseph Bonaparte and the Austrian foreign minister, Count Ludwig von Cobenzl, but began in deadlock because Cobenzl could not treat separately from Britain. The French victory at Hohenlinden and Britain's suspension of its subsidy changed the position. On 31 December Cobenzl told the French that he would negotiate without Britain.

The discussion then centred on boundaries and indemnities in Italy, and Cobenzl had to move his demands eastward as the French advanced there, from the Oglio to the Adige. The last week concerned the left bank of the Rhine. The treaty was signed at five in the evening on 9 February 1801.

The treaty required Austria to enforce the conditions of Campo Formio and recognised the independence of the Cisalpine, Ligurian, Batavian and Helvetic republics. The entire left bank of the Rhine, including the Austrian Netherlands, was ceded to France. Unlike Campo Formio, it also gave the Grand Duchy of Tuscany to France. Princes who lost territory, including the Grand Duke of Tuscany and the Duke of Modena, were to be compensated east of the Rhine by secularising ecclesiastical principalities, under French supervision. Austria's acquisition of the Venetian Terraferma, Venetian Dalmatia and all of Istria was confirmed.

The Imperial Diet accepted the treaty on 7 March. An Imperial deputation, influenced by France and Russia, settled the compensation, and the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss of 25 February 1803 secularised all ecclesiastical states except the Electorate of Mainz and removed the sovereignty of almost all free imperial cities. It was the last major law of the Holy Roman Empire before its dissolution in 1806. Britain stayed at war with France for another year.
treaty-of-madrid-1670: The Anglo-Spanish War had begun in late 1654, and although the conflict in Europe ended with the Treaty of the Pyrenees and the restoration of Charles II in 1660, England and Spain signed no peace. In the Caribbean, after a failed attempt on Hispaniola and the conquest of Jamaica, buccaneers such as Christopher Myngs and Henry Morgan raided the Spanish Main for the Jamaican governor Thomas Modyford. A Treaty of Madrid of 1667 favoured England in trade but said nothing of the colonies, and Morgan went on to sack Portobello and Lake Maracaibo.

In 1669 the Queen Regent Mariana ordered attacks on English shipping, and Charles had Modyford issue letters of marque in return. Seeing Spain weakened by years of war and infighting, Charles judged the moment right to negotiate, and talks began that autumn between Gaspar de Bracamonte, Count of Peñaranda, and the English envoy William Godolphin.

In Article VII the two crowns agreed that all past offences in America should be buried in oblivion, and Spain accepted that the King of Great Britain should hold for ever all the lands, islands and colonies in America that he and his subjects then possessed, in effect the doctrine of adverse possession. Spain revoked all letters of reprisal, ships in distress were to be aided and allowed to repair in each other's ports, English ships gained freedom of movement, and each side promised not to trade in the other's Caribbean territory. The treaty, written in Latin, was ratified on 28 September.

Many in Spain and its colonies saw the treaty as a humiliating surrender, and the crown compensated Spanish merchants with special tax cédulas. It fixed no boundaries, only the principle of actual possession, which in North America legalised English ownership as far south as Charleston, to the consternation of the Spanish in Florida. News came too late to stop Morgan's raid on Panama City on 28 January 1671; he and Modyford were recalled and arrested but released unpunished, and Morgan was knighted and made Lieutenant Governor of Jamaica. Spain and England then stayed at peace until 1702.
treaty-of-mangalore: Hyder Ali had taken power in Mysore in 1761, displacing the Wodeyar dynasty. His first war with the British, from 1766, ended with the Treaty of Madras in April 1769, which restored all conquests and promised mutual aid in a defensive war. Hyder held that the British had broken it by giving no help when the Marathas attacked Mysore, and in 1780 he led 80,000 to 90,000 men into the Carnatic, laying waste the country around Vellore and Madras.

His son Tipu Sultan crushed a British force at Pollilur, where the Company lost about 4,000 men, its worst defeat in India to that date, and in 1782 he destroyed Colonel Braithwaite's force of about 2,000 men at Tanjore. The British won at Porto Novo, the second Pollilur, Sholinghur and Negapatam. Hyder died suddenly in 1782 and Tipu became ruler; the British took Coimbatore in 1783, and by January 1784 Tipu had retaken Mangalore. With neither side able to win, the war ended in stalemate.

The Company was represented by Anthony Sadlier, George Leonard Staunton and John Hudleston. Tipu was to evacuate the Carnatic within thirty days, except the forts of Amboorgur and Satgur, which were to follow, and to release all prisoners. The British were to give up Onore, Carwar and Sadasewgude, Caroor and other districts, and then Dindigul, while Cannanore went back to its queen, Ali Rajah Biby. Tipu renounced any future claim on the Carnatic, confirmed the trade privileges granted by Hyder in a treaty of 8 August 1770 and restored the English factory at Callicut.

The Company's commissioner from Madras had to travel to Mangalore, Tipu's recent reconquest on the opposite coast, to sign. The humiliation, coming soon after the loss of the Thirteen Colonies in America, made the British determined to defeat Tipu. Many in Britain saw the treaty as the beginning of the end of the Company; its stock fell, and because its trade made up a sixth of British national income the government intervened with what is now called Pitt's India Act, which gave the Governor-General new powers.
treaty-of-meerssen: The treaty was the third of the partitions of Francia between August 843 and August 870, after the Treaty of Verdun and the Treaty of Prüm. Verdun had divided the empire of Louis the Pious among his sons: Lothair I received the imperial crown and Middle Francia, Louis the German East Francia, and Charles the Bald West Francia. When Lothair I died in 855, Prüm split Middle Francia among his sons: Louis II of Italy took Italy, Charles of Provence became king of Provence, and Lothair II received Austrasia, Frisia and Upper Burgundy, a realm that came to be called Lotharingia.

Lothair II died in 869 without legitimate children. His heir was his brother Emperor Louis II of Italy, who was then campaigning against the Emirate of Bari, so their uncles Louis the German and Charles the Bald took the inheritance. Charles had himself crowned at Metz that year, but his brother forced him to share, as they had agreed at Metz in 868.

The treaty, concluded on 8 August 870, divided the northern half of Middle Francia, stretching from the Rhone valley to the North Sea, into two larger eastern and western divisions. The border ran roughly along the Meuse, the Ourthe, the Moselle, the Saône and the Rhone. In the north Louis received most of Lothair's Austrasia, including Aachen and Metz, and most of Frisia, though large parts of the Frisian coast were under Viking control and were divided only on paper.

In the south Louis received most of the Upper Burgundy left to Lothair, while Charles received Lothair's inheritance in Lower Burgundy, including Lyon and Vienne, and a small western part of Upper Burgundy, including Besançon, which opened his way to Italy. Louis joined the newly acquired parts of central Austrasia to the subkingdom of his son Louis the Younger, and Lothair II's illegitimate son Hugh was granted the Duchy of Alsace.

The arrangement did not last ten years. After Louis the German died in 876, Charles the Bald, by then king of Italy and emperor, attacked eastern Lotharingia but was defeated by Louis the Younger at the Battle of Andernach in 876. In 879 Louis the Younger campaigned in western Lotharingia, and Charles's grandsons were forced to cede the whole of it to him, as sealed by the Treaty of Ribemont in 880, by which it finally became part of East Francia.
treaty-of-mellifont: After the English victory at the Battle of Kinsale, Lord Deputy Charles Blount, 8th Baron Mountjoy, knew that Hugh O'Neill, though in hiding, was still a threat: Rory O'Donnell, Brian Oge O'Rourke, Cuchonnacht Maguire and Donal Cam O'Sullivan Beare remained loyal to him. In the spring of 1603 Mountjoy campaigned in the northern counties and Leinster, ordering the land scorched, and famine followed. The war was costing three quarters of the Exchequer's annual revenue and an army of 20,000 men, and Queen Elizabeth I dropped her demand for unconditional surrender.

Mountjoy's agents were Sir William Godolphin and Sir Garrett Moore, a friend of O'Neill, who found him near Lough Neagh in early March and persuaded him to negotiate under a safe conduct. The talks were held at Mellifont, Moore's seat, bought by his family after the dissolution of the Cistercian abbey. On 27 March Mountjoy learnt that the Queen had died three days earlier, but he kept the news from the others until 5 April. O'Neill submitted on 30 March.

The terms were thought very generous. In return for giving up the Gaelic title of The O'Neill, his attainder was reversed, restoring him as Earl of Tyrone with a seat in the Irish House of Lords, and he kept his core territory, apart from Church lands, in freehold under English law. He swore loyalty, promised to seek no foreign help and was pardoned. English law was to replace Brehon law on his lands, English was to be the official language, the earls could no longer support the Gaelic bards, and no Catholic colleges could be built on his property. Unlike earlier surrender and regrant agreements, he was not required to join the Church of Ireland.

The Treaty of London between England and Spain in 1603 ended any hope of Spanish aid. O'Neill went to London with Mountjoy in June 1603, and an Act of Oblivion in 1604 pardoned offences committed before King James's accession. Sir Arthur Chichester, Lord Deputy from February 1605, worked to undermine O'Neill's authority and wealth, and after the Flight of the Earls in 1607 seized their lands, opening the way to the Plantation of Ulster.
treaty-of-melno: The First Peace of Thorn of 1411 had given Samogitia to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania only for the lifetimes of King Jogaila of Poland and Grand Duke Vytautas, both elderly men. Vytautas then claimed the whole northern bank of the Neman River, including the port of Memel (Klaipėda). When Sigismund, Holy Roman Emperor, ruled against the Lithuanians, Jogaila and Vytautas invaded the Teutonic state in July 1422. Grand Master Paul von Rusdorf could mount no adequate defence, but Poland-Lithuania sought to end the war before reinforcements arrived from the Empire. A truce followed on 17 September, and eight envoys from each side met at the Polish camp near the lake.

For the first time the Knights renounced all territorial, political and missionary claims against Lithuania. The border ran from the wilderness of Suvalkija to Nemirseta on the Baltic, leaving the Knights the lower Neman and Memel. Lithuania kept about 15 kilometres of coast between Palanga and Šventoji, though it never developed a real harbour there; for the Knights the strip cut Prussia off from their branch in Livonia. Poland received Nieszawa and half of the Vistula channel from the mouth of the Drwęca and gave up claims to Pomerelia, Culmerland and the Michelauer Land, results described as a disappointment for Poland.

Rusdorf tried to renegotiate, but at Käsmark Sigismund and Jogaila agreed on 30 March 1423 that the emperor would drop his support for the Knights and Poland-Lithuania would stop aiding the Hussites. The treaty was ratified at Veliuona in May 1423, with some 120 seals, and approved by Pope Martin V on 10 July. It ended warfare between the Knights and Lithuania that had gone on since the 13th century, though Polish-Teutonic disputes continued. The border was redrawn more precisely in 1532 and 1545 and survived until the First World War; its southern part still divides Lithuania from Kaliningrad Oblast.
treaty-of-mignano: The treaty ended more than a decade of constant war in the Italian Mezzogiorno that followed the union of the mainland duchy of Apulia and Calabria with the County of Sicily in 1127. When Antipope Anacletus II crowned Roger II king in 1130, Pope Innocent II refused to recognise the title, and many of Roger's vassals on the peninsula objected to his royal authority over them.

Through the 1130s Roger defeated his vassals one by one, until in 1137 Emperor Lothair II came south with the pope and conquered most of the region. Lothair's death left the southern barons without support, and Roger quickly won back his lands. In 1139 Ranulf of Alife, the duke of Apulia set up by pope and emperor, died.

Innocent and the dispossessed Prince Robert II of Capua then marched to restore their authority, but at Galluccio Roger's son, with only a thousand knights, ambushed the papal army and captured the pope and his entourage. Three days later, at Mignano, Innocent invested Roger with his titles as king of Sicily, duke of Apulia and prince of Capua. He also invested Roger's son as duke of Apulia and another son, Alfonso, as prince of Capua. Roger agreed to pay the pope a tribute of 600 schifati.

In 1143 Innocent refused to recognise the treaty, but after Roger sent Robert of Selby to march on the papal city of Benevento, the settlement of Mignano was reaffirmed. In 1156 the Treaty of Benevento confirmed the tribute agreed in 1139 and added another 400 schifati for lands Roger had since conquered.
treaty-of-montgomery: Rulers of Gwynedd had claimed primacy in Wales before. Llywelyn's grandfather, Llywelyn the Great, styled himself "Prince of Aberffraw, Lord of Snowdon" in the 1230s after subduing the other Welsh dynasties, and his uncle Dafydd ap Llywelyn claimed the title Prince of Wales during his rule from 1240 to 1246. Many of the terms of 1267 had been anticipated in the Treaty of Pipton of 1265 between Llywelyn and Simon de Montfort. By the late 1260s Llywelyn's supremacy forced an English Crown weakened by internal division to recognise his authority.

The treaty, signed in Montgomeryshire, gave Llywelyn Builth, Brecon and Gwerthrynion in mid-Wales and the four cantrefs of Perfeddwlad, as well as Whittington Castle, which his grandfather had held in the 1220s. The disputed castle of Cefnllys, taken from Roger Mortimer in 1262, went back to Roger on condition that he held it from Llywelyn if Llywelyn could prove his right. Robert of Moltant was to build no castle at Hawarden for thirty years, and Llywelyn's brother Dafydd ap Gruffudd, who had defected to England, was to be restored.

The largest English concession was the title of Prince of Wales, with overlordship of every other Welsh lord except Maredudd ap Rhys, who stayed a direct vassal of the king. In return Llywelyn and his successors owed the king fealty, homage and service. It was the only time an English ruler recognised the right of a ruler of Gwynedd over Wales.

Although the treaty required homage, it was in effect an acknowledgement of Llywelyn's power. After Edward I came to the throne in 1272 relations worsened, Edward declared war on Llywelyn in 1276, and the Treaty of Aberconwy of 1277 replaced the settlement of Montgomery and sharply reduced Llywelyn's power. In December 1282, fifteen years after the treaty, the army of Montgomery marched from Montgomery Castle to Builth Wells to surprise and kill Llywelyn.
treaty-of-nanjing: In the late 18th and early 19th centuries Britain ran a growing trade deficit with China, since it had nothing to offer that matched its imports of tea and porcelain. Opium grown in British India was auctioned to merchants who sold it to Chinese smugglers, although Chinese law forbade its import and sale. When Lin Zexu seized the opium and ordered its destruction at Humen, Britain demanded reparations and then declared what became known as the First Opium War. British military technology brought a major victory.

With British warships poised to attack Nanjing, the officials negotiated on board HMS Cornwallis in the Yangtze. On 29 August 1842 Sir Henry Pottinger for Britain and Keying, Yilibu and Niu Jian for the Qing signed the treaty of thirteen articles.

The treaty's fundamental purpose was to change the Canton system of foreign trade, in force since 1760. Article V abolished the monopoly of the Cohong merchants and their Thirteen Factories, and the ports of Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai opened alongside Canton, where foreign merchants could trade with anyone. Britain could send consuls to the ports, and trade there was to be subject to fixed tariffs agreed between the two governments.

The Qing government was to pay 27 million silver dollars in instalments over three years: 6 million for the opium Lin Zexu had confiscated, 6 million for the Ransom of Canton, 3 million for the debts of Canton merchants to British merchants and 12 million for the cost of the war. Hong Kong Island was ceded to Queen Victoria as a crown colony, in perpetuity, to give British traders a harbour. The treaty did not mention the opium trade, and the British asked the Chinese to legalise it themselves, which they refused.

The Daoguang Emperor ratified the treaty on 27 October and Queen Victoria on 28 December, and the exchange took place in Hong Kong on 26 June 1843. Because the treaty was brief, a supplementary Treaty of the Bogue followed in 1843, giving Britain extraterritorial rights and making its citizens in the treaty ports exempt from Chinese law. Together with the treaties of 1843, 1858 and 1860 it ended the Canton system and set a framework for China's foreign trade that lasted almost a hundred years.

Chinese nationalists later called it an unequal treaty, since its terms were all concessions from China, among them extraterritoriality and fixed tariffs, and counted it the start of a century of humiliation. Joanna Waley-Cohen writes that the Qing did not at the time regard it as very important, since it resembled an earlier treaty with Kokand. Extraterritoriality was not formally abolished until 1943.
treaty-of-nerchinsk: From about 1640 Russians entered the Amur basin from the north, into land the Qing dynasty claimed. By the 1680s the Qing had completed the conquest of China proper, and by 1685 most of the Russians had been driven from the area; the Qing twice overran the outpost at Albazin, in 1685 and 1686.

The Russian government knew the Amur could not be defended and sent Fyodor Golovin east as plenipotentiary. Fighting between the Oirats and the eastern Mongols delayed the talks, and Golovin moved to Nerchinsk. Both sides had reasons to settle: Russia was beginning a war with the Ottoman Empire, and the Kangxi Emperor wished to turn to the Dzungar Mongols and wanted a fixed frontier.

Qing troops under Songgotu arrived in July 1689, and talks went on from 22 August to 6 September. Latin was the language used. The Russian translator was a Pole, Andrei Bielobocki, and the Qing side relied on the Jesuits Jean-François Gerbillon and Thomas Pereira.

Tents were set up side by side so that neither side would seem to visit the other. The treaty was signed on 27 August 1689 by Songgotu for the Kangxi Emperor and Golovin for the tsars Peter I and Ivan V. The authoritative text was in Latin, with translations into Russian and Manchu, and no official Chinese text existed for another two centuries.

The border ran along the Argun River to the Shilka, up the Shilka and the Gorbitsa, along the watershed of the Stanovoy Mountains and down the Uda to the Sea of Okhotsk. Albazin was to be abandoned and destroyed. Fugitives who had settled before the treaty stayed, those arriving later were returned, and travel and trade across the frontier were allowed with proper documents. Russia yielded the land north of the Amur up to the Stanovoy Range but kept the region between the Argun and Lake Baikal and gained access to Chinese markets for its furs.

The border west of the Argun was not defined. The arrangement lasted until the mid-nineteenth century, when the Treaty of Aigun in 1858 and the Convention of Peking in 1860 gave Russia the Amur lands and the Pacific coast.
treaty-of-neuberg: Albert and Leopold were the younger brothers of Duke Rudolf IV of Austria, who on the death of their father, Duke Albert II, in 1358 took the rule of Austria, of the Duchy of Styria, held in personal union with it under the Georgenberg Pact of 1186, and of the Duchy of Carinthia with the March of Carniola. Rudolf raised himself to archduke through the Privilegium Maius and acquired the County of Tyrol from the last Meinhardiner countess Margaret in 1363. On his early death in 1365 he left his brothers lands stretching from Vienna to the dynasty's original Further Austrian possessions in the west. His house law of 1364, the Rudolfinische Hausordnung, had decreed their joint rule, but they soon fell out.

Albert and his heirs kept Austria proper, the later Upper and Lower Austria, with the Traungau and the Salzkammergut. Leopold became sole ruler of Styria, which then included Pitten and the town of Wiener Neustadt, of Carinthia, of Carniola, enlarged since 1374 by the Windic March and territory in the March of Istria, of Tyrol and Further Austria, and of Trieste and acquisitions in Friuli. Whatever their lands, all Habsburg rulers were to keep the Austrian archducal title.

Under Leopold's sons his lands were divided again, into Inner Austria (Styria, Carinthia, Carniola and the Littoral) and an Upper Austria of Tyrol and the Further Austrian lands, ruled from 1406 by his youngest son, Duke Frederick IV. The split weakened the dynasty. Albert V of Austria, of the Albertinian line, was elected King of the Romans in 1438 but died a year later, and his line ended with the death of his son Ladislaus the Posthumous in 1457. Its lands passed to Frederick V of Inner Austria, of the Leopoldian line, Albert's successor as King of the Romans and from 1452 Holy Roman Emperor, and in 1490 Archduke Sigismund handed Tyrol and Further Austria to Frederick's son Maximilian I.
treaty-of-neuilly-sur-seine: The Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine was made between the victorious Allies of World War I and Bulgaria, one of the defeated Central Powers. It was signed on 27 November 1919 in the town hall of Neuilly-sur-Seine, just west of Paris. It belonged to the series of treaties after the war, with those of Versailles, Saint-Germain, Trianon and Sevres, that were meant to reduce the military and political strength of the defeated Central Powers. Like the others, it contained the Covenant of the League of Nations, and for that reason the United States did not ratify it.

Bulgaria had to cede Western Thrace to the Entente, which awarded it to Greece at the San Remo conference, cutting Bulgaria off from the Aegean Sea, and to sign a convention on population exchange with Greece. It also had to give up territory on its western border to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and to return Dobruja to Romania, restoring the border set by the Treaty of Bucharest of 1913. It was to return or pay for property taken from occupied territory, to reduce its army to 20,000 men, to pay reparations of 100 million pounds and to recognise the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

The four small regions ceded to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, called the Western Outlands in Bulgarian writing, had been part of Bulgaria since it became a principality in 1878, except the region around Strumitsa, which joined in 1912. The cession was partly compensation for the Bulgarian occupation of southern and eastern Serbia from 1915 to 1918 and partly strategic: the old boundary followed high mountain ridges, while the new one exposed the Bulgarian capital, Sofia.

In Bulgaria the results of the treaty are popularly known as the Second National Catastrophe. Bulgarian sources claim that Bulgarians made up 98 per cent of the population of Bosilegrad and 95 per cent of Tzaribrod at the time. Bulgaria regained Southern Dobruja permanently through the Treaty of Craiova in 1940. During the Second World War, together with Nazi Germany, it temporarily reoccupied most of the other territories that the treaty had taken from it.
treaty-of-new-echota: By the late 1820s the Cherokee Nation, with an estimated 16,000 people, lay mostly in north-western Georgia, with smaller parts in Tennessee, Alabama and North Carolina. After Andrew Jackson, a supporter of Native removal, was elected president in 1828, Georgia passed laws abolishing the Cherokee government and extending state law over its territory. After gold was found in 1829, the state surveyed Cherokee lands and gave them out by lottery in 1832. That year the Supreme Court struck down Georgia's laws in Worcester v. Georgia, but the state ignored the ruling, and Jackson told John Ridge he would not use federal force against it.

John Ridge, his father Major Ridge and Major Ridge's nephews Elias Boudinot and Stand Watie came to believe that removal was inevitable and formed the Treaty Party, while the National Party of Principal Chief John Ross held out. Tensions grew until several Treaty advocates, most notably John Walker Jr., were assassinated.

In October 1835 the General Council rejected a proposed treaty, and John F. Schermerhorn, Jackson's envoy, urged a meeting at New Echota. Between 100 and 500 men came in December 1835, almost all from the Upper and Lower Towns, since heavy snow kept those of the Hill and Valley Towns from travelling; Ross and his supporters did not attend. Besides the payment for the land, the terms offered $500,000 for education, title in perpetuity to land in Indian Territory equal to that given up, and compensation for property left behind. A clause letting Cherokee stay as citizens of their states on allotments of 160 acres was later struck out by Jackson.

The National Party, representing the large majority, declared the treaty invalid, but the Senate approved it by a single vote. A petition with almost 16,000 signatures, which Ross delivered to Congress in the spring of 1838, was ignored by President Martin Van Buren, who directed General Winfield Scott to remove those who had not yet gone west.

On 22 June 1839 teams of Ross's partisans killed Major Ridge, John Ridge and Elias Boudinot, enforcing the Cherokee law that made it a capital crime to cede national land; there is no evidence that Ross knew of their plans. The killings began a Cherokee civil war that lasted until after the American Civil War.
treaty-of-nonsuch: The treaty was a response to the Treaty of Joinville of 1584, under which Philip II of Spain undertook to finance the Catholic League. It was the first international treaty signed by the rebel provinces that would become the Dutch Republic, and the troops it promised were at first meant to help lift the siege of Antwerp.

Elizabeth I agreed to send 6,400 foot soldiers and 1,000 cavalry under Robert Dudley, 1st Earl of Leicester, with an annual subsidy of 600,000 florins, about a quarter of the yearly cost of the revolt. As security the Dutch were to hand over Brill and Flushing, known as the Cautionary Towns, which England would garrison at its own expense; Zeeland, which stood to lose most, objected. Elizabeth gained the right to appoint two councillors to the Council of State of the United Provinces but refused the title of General of the Provinces offered to her.

Philip II treated the treaty as a declaration of war, and the Anglo-Spanish War is conventionally dated from it. Three years later he sent the Spanish Armada against England, spending 10 million ducats that were diverted from the struggle with the Dutch, a campaign that cost Spain around 110 million ducats.

Leicester's time as governor was a failure: Habsburg forces kept advancing and he clashed with the States of Holland and Zeeland over their powers. In October 1587 the States of Holland published the Deduction of the lawyer François Vranck, arguing that sovereignty had always lain with the States, and Johan van Oldenbarnevelt had Leicester's command revoked at the end of 1587. Leicester resigned in early April 1588, and the instruction of 12 April 1588 transferred his powers to the Council of State. The alliance held, and the treaty was renewed by the Treaty of Westminster of 1598.
treaty-of-noteborg: In the mid-thirteenth century Sweden consolidated its rule over Tavastia and expanded into western Karelia to control the waterways between Lake Ladoga and the Gulf of Finland, on which the Novgorod Republic relied for its trade with Western Europe. After Sweden gained full control of the western outlet of the Vuoksi River in 1293, it founded the fortress of Viborg.

Swedish attempts to seize Kexholm and to hold the fortress of Landskrone, at the mouth of the Okhta, were repulsed in 1294 and 1300, and the Novgorodians demolished Landskrone in 1301. In 1322 the Swedes again tried to control Kexholm, while the Novgorodians unsuccessfully tried to drive them out of Viborg. The next year the Novgorodians built the fortress of Oreshek, where the two sides agreed to end hostilities.

The treaty was signed at Oreshek, called Nöteborg in Swedish, on 12 August 1323. The Russian text names Yury of Moscow, then prince of Novgorod, the mayor Varfolomey Yuryevich and the chiliarch Avram. The seven-year-old Swedish king Magnus Eriksson was represented by the lords Erik Turesson and Hemming Ødgislason, the castellan of Viborg Peter Jonsson and the priest Waemundus, and two merchants from Gotland represented the Hanseatic League.

The border was defined by a list of 18 points. The southern part near Viborg, the most important, was set by twelve points and divided the Karelian Isthmus in half, running north along the Sestra and Volchya rivers to the Vuoksi and on to Särkilahti on Lake Saimaa. Novgorod ceded the parishes of Savilahti, Jääski and Äyräpää to Sweden.

The northern six points crossed sparsely populated country and were defined vaguely; historians have debated them for generations. Nineteenth-century historians took the border to run north through Kainuu, while Jalmari Jaakkola argued in 1925 for a line towards the Gulf of Bothnia. John Lind proposed in the 1990s that the treaty set two borders with common land between them.

The Finnic peoples on both sides had no say in the treaty. The northern border later became a centre of contention, and within five years Swedish colonists were moving into northern Ostrobothnia. Because the line cut through the Karelian heartland, Novgorod relied on Lithuanian service princes, whose reliance on local contributions did not make its rule popular.

By 1337 a local uprising at Korelsky Gorodok called for Swedish intervention and led to the killing of Russian merchants and other Christians. After two years of fighting the treaty was renewed in 1339 with an added clause on fugitive Karelians. In 1348 Magnus launched another crusade to the Neva region and captured Oreshek, but the Swedes could not hold it. The border did not change until the Treaty of Teusina in 1595.
treaty-of-nymphaeum-1261: After the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204, the Empire of Nicaea emerged as one of the Byzantine successor states. Following the Treaty of Nymphaeum of 1214 it slowly won back much former Byzantine territory, and by the late 1230s the Latin Empire held little more than Constantinople itself. But the city had never been taken without control of the sea around it, and Venice, allied with the Latins, kept a patrol of thirty ships in the Bosporus.

The Nicaean fleet had recovered several Aegean islands but was no match for the Venetian fleet. In the joint Nicaean-Bulgarian siege of Constantinople in 1235 a blockading fleet of allegedly 100 ships was beaten by a Venetian force a quarter its size, and the failed Nicaean siege of 1260 showed again that a fleet was needed.

Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos therefore turned to Genoa, Venice's commercial and naval rival, already at war with it. The agreement signed at Nymphaion on 13 March 1261 bound Genoa to ally with Nicaea in war and to provide up to fifty ships for the planned siege of Constantinople, sixteen of them at once. Nicaea might buy horses and weapons in Genoese territory and take Genoese subjects into its service. In return Genoa received tax and customs concessions throughout the empire, with a trading quarter of its own at Pera, across the Golden Horn, and in other ports. The terms resembled those Venice had gained in the Byzantine-Venetian Treaty of 1082.

On 28 April Michael added an annex, carried to Genoa by three ambassadors, Theodore Kriviziotes, Leo, archdeacon of Hagia Sophia, and Isaac Doukas Mourtzouphlos, who died there and was buried in Genoa Cathedral. Genoa's popular assembly ratified the treaty on 10 July.

Alexios Strategopoulos retook Constantinople unexpectedly on 25 July 1261, and Michael VIII began building a navy of his own. Because Venice and other Catholic powers still threatened invasion, the treaty stayed in force with minor changes. For Genoa it laid the foundations of a commercial empire in the Near East, centred on Galata, which became the main trading hub of the region. In the long run, especially after Michael's death, the Byzantine Empire became dependent on both Genoa and Venice, which took over the commercial and naval supremacy it had once held.
treaty-of-nystad: The Treaty of Nystad, also called the Treaty of Uusikaupunki, was the last peace treaty of the Great Northern War of 1700 to 1721. It was concluded between the Tsardom of Russia and the Swedish Empire on 10 September 1721 (30 August in the old calendar) in the then Swedish town of Nystad, in the south-west of present-day Finland. Sweden had already settled with the other parties to the war in Stockholm in 1719 and 1720 and at Frederiksborg in 1720.

During the war Peter I of Russia had occupied all Swedish possessions on the eastern Baltic coast: Swedish Ingria, where in 1703 he began to build the future Russian capital of St Petersburg, Swedish Estonia and Swedish Livonia, which had capitulated in 1710, and Finland.

King Frederick I of Sweden formally recognised the transfer of Estonia, Livonia and Ingria to Russia, while Russia granted toll-free export of grain from Livonia up to a value of 50 000 rubel a year. South-eastern Finland, the county of Kexholm and part of the Karelian Isthmus, passed to Russia in exchange for two million silver riksdaler. Russia returned the bulk of Finland to Swedish rule, which took place within four weeks of ratification.

The treaty also confirmed the rights of the ceded territories to keep their financial system, their customs border, their self-government and their Lutheran religion. For the German Baltic nobility of Estonia and Livonia it protected the German language. This special position within the Russian Empire was reconfirmed by every tsar from Peter the Great to Alexander II. Russia gained the right to mediate in conflicts between Sweden and Poland, while promising not to interfere with the Swedish crown and succession, and prisoners of war on both sides, civilians included, were to be released.
Nystad marked a decisive shift in the European balance of power. The Swedish imperial era ended and Sweden entered the Age of Liberty, while Russia emerged as a new empire.

Before 1917, a thoroughfare in the Vyborgsky district of St Petersburg, the district nearest the Russo-Finnish border, was named Nystadt Street after the treaty. The district also holds St Sampsonius' Cathedral, a church commemorating the first Russian victory of the Great Northern War, at the Battle of Poltava.
treaty-of-paris-1259: The Norman Conquest of England in 1066 left the kings of England sovereign over some of their territory but bound by homage to the kings of France for land on the continent. King John's refusal to answer Philip II of France over the apparent murder of his nephew Arthur gave Philip a pretext for recovering Normandy in 1204. The English kept the Channel Islands and Aquitaine, and despite the Treaty of Lambeth of 1217 both kings continued to fight wars of conquest and reconquest over Normandy and the borderlands.

The treaty, also called the Treaty of Abbeville, was signed on 4 December 1259 by Louis IX of France and Henry III of England. Henry acknowledged the loss of Normandy and renounced Maine, Anjou, Touraine and Poitou, but remained Duke of Aquitaine as a vassal of Louis. In exchange Louis withdrew support from English rebels and gave Henry the bishoprics and cities of Limoges, Cahors and Périgueux, along with other lands including Saintonge and Quercy.

As liege homage was due, Henry could give no aid to enemies of the French king, and the French king could exercise legal jurisdiction in the duchy, so that its people could take disputes to the Paris Parlement. Many in Aquitaine opposed the settlement for this reason. Islands the English king held were retained by him as peer of France and Duke of Aquitaine, the basis of the special status of the Channel Islands.

Doubts about the treaty's interpretation began almost as soon as it was signed, since it kept English kings subject to French kings in disputes over their continental lands. The French historian Édouard Perroy considered that it lay at the very root of the Hundred Years' War. The alliance it created also affected English politics: in 1264 Louis IX gave the Mise of Amiens in favour of Henry against the barons over the Provisions of Oxford, which led to the Second Barons' War. Simon de Montfort was killed at the Battle of Evesham, and in 1265 Henry III issued the Dictum of Kenilworth.
treaty-of-paris-1763: The treaty was signed on 10 February 1763 by the kingdoms of Great Britain, France and Spain, with Portugal in agreement. Prussia and Austria were not party to it and signed a separate agreement, the Treaty of Hubertusburg, five days later. Most conquered territories went back to their former owners. France and Spain restored all their conquests to Britain and Portugal, and Britain returned Manila and Havana to Spain, and Guadeloupe, Martinique, Saint Lucia, Gorée and the Indian trading posts to France.

In return France recognised British sovereignty over Canada, Dominica, Grenada, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Tobago. France ceded the eastern half of French Louisiana, the area from the Mississippi River to the Appalachian Mountains, and Spain ceded Florida. France kept fishing rights off Newfoundland and regained the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon. In India France regained its factories but recognised British clients as rulers of key native states and pledged not to send troops to Bengal. Britain agreed to demolish its fortifications in British Honduras but kept a logwood-cutting colony there.

Britain had conquered a great deal during the Seven Years' War, from Canada and Guadeloupe to Manila and Havana. The British debated the relative merits of Guadeloupe, which produced £6 million a year in sugar, and Canada, which was expensive to keep. They chose Canada for strategic reasons. The prime minister, Lord Bute, wanted a peace that would not push France toward a second war.

The French Foreign Minister, the Duke of Choiseul, expected war to return but needed peace to rebuild. France preferred its profitable sugar islands to the vast Canadian lands, which had been a financial burden. French diplomats believed that without France to keep them in check the American colonists might attempt to revolt. France also asked for toleration of Roman Catholics in North America.

France lost all its mainland North American territory except Louisiana west of the Mississippi. It had already secretly given that land to Spain in the Treaty of Fontainebleau three months earlier, though Spain did not take possession until 1769 and the transfer was not publicly announced until 1764. Article IV allowed the French inhabitants of Canada eighteen months to emigrate and sold their estates to British subjects, and Britain agreed to grant liberty of the Catholic religion as far as the laws of Great Britain permit.

The treaty ended the conflict between France and Britain over North America and began an era of British dominance outside Europe. The Mississippi corridor in what is now Louisiana was later reunited under the United States after the Louisiana Purchase in 1803 and the Adams–Onís Treaty in 1819.
treaty-of-paris-1783: Peace negotiations began in Paris in April 1782, after the fall of Frederick North's government on 20 March following the British defeat at Yorktown. The United States was represented by Benjamin Franklin, John Jay, Henry Laurens and John Adams, and Britain by David Hartley and Richard Oswald. In September 1782 the French foreign minister Vergennes proposed a settlement that would confine independence to the area east of the Appalachian Mountains, which the American delegation rejected.

John Jay told the British he was willing to negotiate directly with them and bypass France and Spain, and Prime Minister Lord Shelburne agreed. He saw a chance to split the United States from France and to make the new nation a valuable economic partner. The treaty was drafted on 30 November 1782.

The treaty was signed on 3 September 1783 at the Hôtel d'York in Paris by Adams, Franklin, Jay and Hartley. Britain acknowledged the thirteen former colonies, listed by name, as free, sovereign and independent states. The United States gained all the land east of the Mississippi River, north of present-day Florida and south of present-day Canada, and fishing rights on the Grand Banks and in the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Creditors on either side were to meet no lawful impediment to recovering debts, Congress was to recommend that the states restore confiscated Loyalist property, and prisoners of war were to be released.

Britain signed separate agreements with France, Spain and, provisionally, the Netherlands. East and West Florida went to Spain without a clear northern boundary, and Spain also received Menorca. The Congress of the Confederation ratified the treaty at Annapolis on 14 January 1784, and the ratified copies were exchanged in Paris on 12 May 1784.

Historians have often called the treaty very generous to the United States, and some argue that the British aimed at close economic ties and profitable trade. Much of it did not work as written. The states ignored the recommendation to restore Loyalist property, and Virginia kept laws against paying debts to British creditors. Spain used its control of Florida to block American use of the Mississippi, and a dispute over the Florida boundary lasted until the Treaty of Madrid in 1795.

Britain kept eight forts on what was technically American soil, citing American failure to compensate Loyalists. They were given up peacefully under the Jay Treaty of 1794. Only Article 1, acknowledging the United States as free, sovereign and independent, remains in force.
treaty-of-paris-1814: The treaty was signed on 30 May 1814 and ended the war between France and the Sixth Coalition. It followed an armistice of 23 April between Charles of Bourbon, Count of Artois, acting as Lieutenant General of the Realm, and the allies. Napoleon had abdicated as Emperor on 6 April after negotiations at Fontainebleau. Peace talks began on 9 May, with Talleyrand negotiating on behalf of the exiled Bourbon king Louis XVIII. The allies had defined their common war aim at Chaumont in March.

The signatories were Talleyrand for France, Lords Castlereagh, Aberdeen and Cathcart for Great Britain, Counts Razumovsky and Nesselrode for Russia, Prince Metternich and Count Stadion for Austria, and Baron Hardenberg and Wilhelm von Humboldt for Prussia. Portugal and Sweden also signed, and Spain ratified in July. The allies concluded separate treaties with France rather than a common document.

The allies wished to establish a lasting peace and did not think harsh terms necessary now that France had a monarchy again. France kept the borders of 1792 and was allowed to retain Saarbrücken, Saarlouis, Landau, the County of Montbéliard, part of Savoy with Annecy and Chambéry, and Avignon with the Comtat Venaissin. It also kept the artworks acquired during the war. Britain kept Malta, and the treaty recognised the independence of Switzerland and returned Santo Domingo to Spain.

Article 32 called for a congress of all the belligerents within two months, which became the Congress of Vienna, held from September 1814 to June 1815. The treaty also aimed to end the French slave trade over five years, though not slavery itself, and it left French territories outside this aim. Several powers still feared a revival of French power. The Netherlands, now freed from French rule, accepted William I of the House of Orange as its prince, with the secret support of the great powers.
After Napoleon's brief return to power and his defeat, a second Treaty of Paris was signed on 20 November 1815. For this reason the treaty of 30 May 1814 is sometimes called the First Peace of Paris.
treaty-of-paris-1815: Napoleon Bonaparte escaped from exile on Elba in February 1815, entered Paris on 20 March and began the Hundred Days of his restored rule. After the defeat of France by the Seventh Coalition at the Battle of Waterloo he abdicated again on 22 June. King Louis XVIII, who had fled when Napoleon arrived, took the throne for a second time on 8 July.

The first Treaty of Paris, of 30 May 1814, had been negotiated after two months. The second took five months of heated and bitter discussion, dominated by the British and the Prussians, the victors of Waterloo. The Prussians, led by the general staff and supported by Marshal Blücher, demanded Alsace, Lorraine, the Saarland, Luxembourg and Savoy and a far larger indemnity.

Four identical treaties were signed on 20 November 1815, between France and each of Austria, Great Britain, Prussia and Russia, written in French. Castlereagh, whose concern was not to alienate the French from the restored Bourbons, helped keep them only moderately harsher than that of 1814.

France lost the gains of the Revolutionary armies of 1790 to 1792 and was reduced to its 1790 boundaries, keeping the Comtat Venaissin, the County of Montbéliard and the Republic of Mulhouse but losing the former duchy of Bouillon, Landau and Saarlouis. Six communes of the Pays de Gex went to the Canton of Geneva. France was to pay 700 million francs in five yearly instalments and to maintain a Coalition army of 150,000 men on its eastern frontier for up to five years.

Further conventions covered the indemnity, the military line, private claims and the claims of British subjects. An additional article reaffirmed the condemnation of the slave trade, and an act confirmed the perpetual neutrality of Switzerland. The treaty also required that artworks looted by French armies since 1793 be returned, one of the first treaties to require the return of war booty on a large scale. The Quadruple Alliance was renewed in a separate treaty.

The treaty was signed for Britain by Viscount Castlereagh and the Duke of Wellington and for France by the Duc de Richelieu. Wellington commanded the occupation, which was judged necessary for only three years, and the foreign troops left France in 1818 after the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle. With interest and the upkeep of the army, the burden on France approached 1.7 billion francs. The renewed alliance introduced the idea of a peacetime congress to maintain peace in Europe, on the pattern of the Congress of Vienna.
treaty-of-paris-1856: The Crimean War began on 23 October 1853, when the Ottoman Empire formally declared war on Russia after Russian troops occupied the Danubian Principalities. By its end all sides wanted a lasting settlement after the casualties and attrition they had suffered, though competing ideas of resolution complicated the drafting. Russia had lost over 500,000 troops. Alexander II, who took the crown in 1855, sought peace to keep some imperial possessions, to stop the deaths of thousands of army reserves and to prevent an economic crisis.

Britain and France wanted a stable balance of power, preventing Russia and Austria from growing stronger at the Ottoman Empire's expense. Public opinion mattered: the war was one of the first to receive relatively prompt press coverage, and Lord Aberdeen lost a parliamentary vote and resigned in favour of Lord Palmerston.

The treaty was signed on 30 March 1856 by representatives of France, Austria, the United Kingdom, Prussia, Russia, Sardinia and the Ottoman Empire. It admitted the Ottoman Empire to the European concert, and the powers promised to respect its independence and territorial integrity. Russia gave up its claim to a protectorate over Christians in the Ottoman domains, and a European commission was set up to guarantee freedom of commerce and navigation on the Danube. Sevastopol and other towns in southern Crimea went back to Russia.

Moldavia and Wallachia stayed under nominal Ottoman rule but were to have independent constitutions and national assemblies monitored by the powers. Moldavia recovered part of Bessarabia, creating a buffer between the Ottoman Empire and Russia. The treaty also demilitarised the Åland Islands, part of the Russian Grand Duchy of Finland, where British and French forces had destroyed the fortress of Bomarsund in 1854. The Declaration of Paris set new rules of wartime commerce, including that privateering was illegal.

The Black Sea prohibitions were renounced in the Treaty of London in 1871, and Moldavia and Wallachia were united in 1859. The war and its settlement did little to create lasting stability in the Concert of Europe, and the Ottoman Empire faced a number of patriotic uprisings in its provinces in the following decades. By 1877 Russia and the Ottoman Empire were again at war.

Austria, which had mobilised troops against its former ally and sent an ultimatum asking for the withdrawal of Russian armies from the Balkans, saw relations with Russia remain strained. Russia's resentment contributed to its non-intervention in the Franco-Austrian War of 1859, the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 and the Ausgleich with Hungary of 1867.
treaty-of-paris-1857: The negotiations were conducted on the Persian side by the ambassador Farrokh Khan. Besides giving up Herat, which Dost Mohammad Khan of Afghanistan was later allowed to occupy, the Persians undertook to apologise to the British envoy on his return to the country and to sign a commercial treaty with Britain.

Britain made concessions in turn. It agreed not to shelter opponents of the Shah in its embassy, and it abandoned two demands it had pressed during the dispute: that the grand vizier Mirza Aqa Khan Nuri be replaced, and that Persia make territorial concessions to the Imam of Oman, a British ally.

The settlement grew out of British strategic interests in Afghanistan, an early consequence of the Great Game. It ended Qajar hopes of keeping Herat as a frontier vassal state after more than fifty years of Iranian engagement there, and with it three and a half centuries in which Herat had been, almost continuously though often chaotically, part of Iran.

The treaty marked a turning point in relations between Iran and Britain, as the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828 had done in relations between Iran and Russia. The conflict over Herat showed the Qajar government the serious consequences of confronting a European colonial power by force, and Iran's rulers came to accept that in an age of empires they would have to lose territory on the outskirts in order to protect the centre. Like the earlier loss of the Caucasian provinces, the loss of Herat showed that lands bound to Iran by history and culture, and long counted as part of Greater Iran, could no longer be held as provinces within the Guarded Domains of Iran.
treaty-of-paris-1898: The Spanish–American War began on 25 April 1898, after escalating disputes between the two nations. Cubans had attempted revolution in 1868 to 1878 and again in the 1890s under José Martí, and in the Philippines a first call to revolt on 26 August 1896, led by Andrés Bonifacio, was followed by the leadership of Emilio Aguinaldo. The war had overwhelming public support in the United States, owing to enthusiasm for Cuban freedom. A protocol signed at Washington on 12 August 1898 provided for each side to appoint up to five commissioners to meet in Paris, and for the United States to occupy Manila until a treaty settled the Philippines.

The American commission was headed by William R. Day, who had resigned as Secretary of State to lead it, and included three senators, which newspapers noted meant they would later vote on their own work. Spain's commission was led by Eugenio Montero Ríos. At the first session, on 1 October, the Spanish demanded the return of Manila, which the Americans refused. Felipe Agoncillo, a Filipino lawyer representing the First Philippine Republic, was denied participation.

For almost a month the talks concerned Cuba. The Teller Amendment made it impractical to annex the island, so it was agreed that Cuba would be independent and that Spain would assume the Cuban debt, and that Spain would cede Guam and Puerto Rico. On the Philippines the Spanish hoped to cede only Mindanao and perhaps Sulu, while some Americans had favoured keeping only Manila or Luzon. President William McKinley cabled that the cession must be of the whole archipelago. The Americans offered 20 million dollars on 21 November, and Queen-Regent Maria Christina accepted. The treaty was signed on 10 December 1898.

The Cortes in Madrid rejected the treaty, but Maria Christina signed it under a clause of the Spanish constitution. In the American Senate, opponents of expansion included George Frisbie Hoar, who said it would make the country an empire controlling subject races. After fighting broke out between Filipino and American forces in Manila on 4 February 1899, the Senate approved the treaty on 6 February by 57 votes to 27, just over the two-thirds required. It came into effect on 11 April 1899. It became a major issue in the election of 1900, in which McKinley was re-elected.

The treaty marked the end of the Spanish Empire apart from small holdings, and its loss produced the cultural movement known as the Generation of '98 in Spain. The Philippine-American War, which began on 4 and 5 February 1899, ended in an American victory in 1902. Philippine revolutionaries had declared independence on 12 June 1898 and continued to resist American sovereignty.
treaty-of-passarowitz: Between 1714 and 1718 the Ottomans had been successful against Venice in Ottoman Greece and Crete, but they were defeated at Petrovaradin in 1716 by the Habsburg troops of Prince Eugene of Savoy. Peace was arranged with the intervention of Great Britain and the Dutch Republic, and the treaty was signed by Sir Robert Sutton and Jacob Colyer on behalf of their governments. The other signatories were Damian Hugo, Count of Virmont, and Michael von Talmann for the Habsburg monarchy, Vendramino Bianchi and Carlo Ruzzini for Venice, and Silindar Ibrahim-aga and Mehmed-efendija for the Ottoman Empire.

The Ottoman Empire lost the Banat of Temeswar, western Wallachia, northern Serbia including the fortress town of Belgrade, and the northern part of Bosnia, the region of Posavina, to the Habsburgs. The Habsburgs also received assurances that their merchants could operate in the Ottoman domain and that Catholic priests would regain revoked privileges. This allowed the Habsburg emperor to interfere in Ottoman affairs through connections with the church community and by championing the Catholic faith.

Venice ceded the Morea, its last outposts in Crete, and the islands of Aegina and Tinos. It retained the Ionian Islands, with Ottoman-occupied Kythira added to them, and the cities of Preveza and Arta on the Epirote mainland. In Dalmatia Venice made small gains by taking the areas of Imotski and Vrgorac.

The treaty gave the Habsburgs control over the northern part of present-day Serbia, which they had temporarily occupied during the Great Turkish War between 1688 and 1690. They established the Kingdom of Serbia as a crown land and formed the Banat into another. In its time the treaty was regarded in Vienna as an exceptional success and a source of pride, and it marked the end of Ottoman occupation within the Kingdom of Hungary.

Habsburg control lasted 21 years, until the Turks won the Austro-Russian–Turkish War of 1735 to 1739. In the Treaty of Belgrade of 1739 the Ottoman Empire regained northern Bosnia, Habsburg Serbia including Belgrade, and the southern parts of the Banat of Temeswar, and Oltenia was returned to Wallachia.
treaty-of-perth: The Hebrides and the Isle of Man had become Norwegian territory over centuries in which both Scotland and Norway were still forming themselves as coherent states. Norwegian control had been formalised in 1098, when Edgar of Scotland signed the islands over to Magnus III of Norway. In Norwegian terms the islands were the Sudreys, the Southern Isles, and the long contest over them came to a head in the reign of Alexander III of Scotland.

The decisive clash was the Battle of Largs in 1263. Largs is often claimed as a great Scottish victory, but the Norwegians held that their forces, led by King Haakon IV of Norway, had not been fully committed to battle and that the result was inconclusive. Haakon planned to renew the campaign the following summer, but he died in Orkney during the winter. His successor, Magnus the Lawmender, sued for peace, and the treaty was agreed after negotiations held in Perth during 1265 and 1266.

Under the treaty Scotland confirmed Norwegian sovereignty over Shetland and Orkney, while Norway recognised Scottish sovereignty over the disputed islands to the west. The annual payment of 100 marks was made through the decades that followed. It was cancelled only in 1469, as part of the agreement for the marriage of James III of Scotland and Margaret of Denmark, who became Queen of Scotland.

The historian Michael Lynch has compared the importance of the treaty with that of the Treaty of York of 1237. That earlier agreement defined a border between Scotland and England almost identical to the modern one, while the settlement made at Perth three years after Largs fixed the western limits of the Scottish kingdom and left only the northern isles under the Norwegian crown.
treaty-of-petropolis: The treaty was signed in the Brazilian city of Petrópolis and ended the Acre War, fought over a territory on the border of Bolivia and Brazil that the rubber boom of the time had made desirable. It was drafted by the Brazilian foreign minister José Maria da Silva Paranhos. Brazil received Acre, about 191,000 km2, which is today the state of Acre.

In exchange Bolivia received over 3,000 km2 of Brazilian land between the Abuna River and the Madeira River and two million British pounds, paid in two installments. Brazil also pledged a rail link between the Bolivian city of Riberalta and the Brazilian city of Porto Velho, a line that would bypass the rapids on the Madeira.

The line became the Madeira-Mamoré Railway. It was the third attempt at such a route: in the 1870s, during the rubber boom, the American George Church had twice been defeated by the heat, the difficulty of the terrain and the loss of life from fever. Another American, Percival Farquhar, won the contract the treaty required. Construction began in August 1907 and was completed on 15 July 1912, at a cost of US$33 million, and at least 3,600 men died building its 367 km of track.

The railway was meant to reach Riberalta, on the Beni River above its rapids, but stopped short at Guajará-Mirim. It had about a year of full operation before the collapse of rubber prices, the opening of a railway from Bolivia to the Pacific through Chile and the Panama Canal made it uneconomical. It was kept running until 1972, and the BR-364 road later took over its route and railway bridges.
treaty-of-pilar: The treaty was a pact among the rulers of the provinces of Santa Fe, Entre Ríos and Buenos Aires, signed in the town of Pilar, in Buenos Aires Province, after the Battle of Cepeda had brought down the national government. Its signatories were Estanislao López, governor of Santa Fe, the caudillo Francisco Ramírez for Entre Ríos and the provisional governor Manuel de Sarratea for Buenos Aires. José Gervasio Artigas, leader of the Free Peoples' League, who had fought alongside Santa Fe and Entre Ríos against the centralist government in Buenos Aires, had shortly before been defeated by the Brazilian-Portuguese Empire at the Battle of Tacuarembó, on the Eastern Bank.

The treaty proclaimed national unity and an end to hostilities between the provinces. Military forces were to withdraw from Buenos Aires, a general amnesty was granted to those persecuted for politics, and the signatories were to have free navigation of the Paraná and Uruguay rivers. Each was to send deputies to a congress at San Lorenzo, in Santa Fe, sixty days later to decide on a federal form of government.

Artigas, left out of the agreement, denounced it as treason by his allies; López answered that it served the common good. The Treaty of Benegas soon followed, binding Santa Fe and Buenos Aires to defend each other against an expanding Entre Ríos, and two years later came the Quadrilateral Treaty, which joined Corrientes Province to the three signatories of Pilar. The treaty is regarded as the foundation of the federal organisation of the country. The preamble of the Argentine Constitution of 1853 refers to it as one of the pre-existing pacts that the constitution fulfilled.
treaty-of-pontotoc-creek: The treaty belonged to the Indian Removal policy, under which the Muscogee, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Cherokee nations signed removal treaties in the 1830s. Earlier Chickasaw cessions in 1805, 1816 and 1818 had given up land along the Tennessee River and everything north of Mississippi's border with Tennessee, much of it to the profit of the land speculators Andrew Jackson, John Coffee and James Jackson.

After the Indian Removal Act of May 1830, Chickasaw leaders met President Andrew Jackson at Franklin, Tennessee, hoping for federal protection from Mississippi, which had forbidden tribal government and extended state law over the nation. On 27 August 1830 they agreed to cede their land if a delegation found comparable land in the west. The delegation judged the land unacceptable, and the Senate never ratified the Franklin treaty.

Squatters and Mississippi laws challenging Chickasaw self-government wore down resistance, and in 1832 the National Council agreed to negotiate with John Coffee. The preamble written by the Chickasaw minkos said the nation felt oppressed by being made subject to state laws and preferred to seek a home in the west where it could be governed by its own laws. The historian Arrell M. Gibson calls the treaty the basic Chickasaw removal document.

Landholders were to be paid for their improvements, and the Chickasaw, unlike other nations, were to pay for their own migration from the sale proceeds. Until they left, families were allotted the land they lived on as temporary homesteads, protected by the federal government from squatters, a benefit later denied to the Cherokee.

White settlers occupied unallotted land at once, although the treaty barred them until the Chickasaw had gone. The Treaty of Washington of 1834 confirmed Pontotoc. Under the Treaty of Doaksville of 1837 the Chickasaw agreed to live in a Chickasaw District of the Choctaw Nation, with representation in its government, paying the Choctaw $530,000. From 1837, 4,914 Chickasaws and the 1,156 people they held in slavery emigrated there. The nation received over $3 million from the Mississippi allotments, and agents and contractors worked to defraud it. Chickasaw Removal was the least traumatic removal of any of the Five Tribes, yet it damaged tribal culture and structure for decades.
treaty-of-portsmouth: The Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905 pitted the Russian Empire, with one of the largest armies in the world, against a Japan only recently industrialised. Russian armies had been driven from southern Manchuria and the Battle of Tsushima was a disaster for the Russian navy. The war was unpopular in Russia, whose government faced growing threat of revolution, while Japan's economy was strained, its foreign debts were mounting and its supply lines in Manchuria were lengthening. As early as July 1904 the Japanese government sought intermediaries.

It approached US President Theodore Roosevelt, who had been pro-Japanese at first but later worried about Japan's growing power. Tsar Nicholas II was at first adamant that Russia would win. After the costly Battle of Mukden the Japanese Foreign Minister, Komura Jutarō, judged that a settlement was critical. Russia replied favourably only after Tsushima, on 8 June 1905. Roosevelt chose Portsmouth, New Hampshire, partly for its cooler summer climate.

The delegations arrived on 8 August. Komura led the Japanese side and the former finance minister Sergei Witte the Russian. They stayed at a hotel in New Castle and were ferried each day to the naval base at Kittery, Maine. Tsar Nicholas had forbidden any territorial concessions or reparations. Twelve sessions were held between 9 and 30 August. In the first eight the delegates agreed on a ceasefire, recognition of Japan's claims to Korea, Russian withdrawal from Manchuria and the transfer to Japan of the leases in southern Manchuria and the South Manchuria Railway. Russia kept the Chinese Eastern Railway.

The last sessions dealt with reparations and territory. Witte offered that Japan keep Sakhalin and drop its claim to reparations, warned that the war would resume, and had his delegation pack its bags. He pressed his case through the American media. Outmanoeuvred, Komura yielded: in exchange for the southern half of Sakhalin, Japan dropped its claim to reparations. The treaty was signed on 5 September, and ratified in Japan on 10 October and in Russia on 14 October 1905.

The treaty brought three decades of peace between the two nations and confirmed Japan as the leading power of East Asia. Its second article acknowledged Japan's paramount interests in Korea, and Korea was annexed in 1910. The Japanese public, unaware how far its country's power was overextended, received the terms badly, and the frustration led to the Hibiya riots and the fall of the First Katsura Cabinet on 7 January 1906. Roosevelt received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906, though he never went to Portsmouth.
treaty-of-prum: From 830 Lothair and his brothers Pepin I of Aquitaine and Louis the German fought a series of dynastic struggles with their father, Emperor Louis the Pious. After the emperor's death in 840, Lothair, co-emperor since 817, claimed supremacy over his surviving brothers Louis the German and Charles the Bald, but they defeated him at the Battle of Fontenoy in 841 and confirmed their pact by the Oaths of Strasbourg.

By the Treaty of Verdun of August 843 Louis the German received the lands east of the Rhine and Aare, Charles the Bald those west of the Scheldt, Meuse, Saône and Rhône, and Lothair the lands between, from Frisia to Italy, with Aachen, Rome and the imperial title. This Middle Francia combined long, exposed borders with poor internal communications, and it suffered both Viking raids in the north and Muslim incursions in the south.

The settlement of 19 September 855 was the second of the main partition treaties of the Carolingian Empire. The eldest son, Louis II, received the imperial crown and the Kingdom of Italy, which then covered only the northern half of the peninsula. Lothair II took Frisia and the parts of Austrasia his father had kept at Verdun, including Aachen, a kingdom later called Lotharingia after him. The youngest, Charles, became King of Provence, with Provence and most of the former Frankish Kingdom of Burgundy except the lands west of the Saône.

The division did not last. Charles died in 863 and Lothair II in 869, and by the Treaty of Meerssen of 870 Burgundy and Lotharingia were shared out between East Francia, West Francia and the Kingdom of Italy. Lotharingia, the shortest-lived of the three kingdoms, was succeeded about a century later by the duchies of Upper and Lower Lorraine, while Charles's lands later grew into the Kingdom of Burgundy, also called the Kingdom of Arles. The last effects of the treaty ended when Otto I of Germany conquered Italy in 951, and he was crowned emperor in 962. Historians regard the treaty as one of the last major results of partible inheritance before feudalism became the main cause of the breaking up of European states.
treaty-of-punakha: Between 1864 and 1865 Bhutan fought and lost the five-month Duar War with British India. Under the Treaty of Sinchula, signed on 11 November 1865, it ceded territory in the Assam Duars and Bengal Duars and the eighty-three square kilometre district of Dewangiri in the south-east, in return for an annual subsidy of 50,000 rupees. By the turn of the century, changing circumstances in the region raised the question of a new agreement, and in December 1907 Ugyen Wangchuck, who had consolidated power as Penlop of Trongsa, was unanimously elected monarch.

The treaty was signed at Punakha Dzong on 8 January 1910 by Charles Alfred Bell, Political Officer in Sikkim, and Ugyen Wangchuck, the first Druk Gyalpo, and ratified by the Viceroy and Governor-General of India in Council at Fort William on 24 March 1910. It was not a stand-alone document but an amendment of Articles IV and VIII of the Treaty of Sinchula, whose other terms it kept.

Britain raised the annual allowance from 50,000 to 100,000 rupees with effect from 10 January 1910 and undertook not to interfere in Bhutan's internal administration, while Bhutan agreed to be guided by British advice in its external relations. Disputes with the Maharajas of Sikkim and Cooch Behar were to be referred to British arbitration.

Agreements made at the same time shared the profits of elephant hunting in Britain's favour, assigned land at Motithang and a hill station between Chukha and Thimphu to the British, and gave Bhutan part of British Kalimpong, which later became Bhutan House, owned by the Dorji family. The treaty set a precedent for foreign conduct of Bhutan's external relations and for foreign subsidy to its government.

Once India was independent, Sonam Topgay Dorji led a Bhutanese delegation that met Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru on 23 April 1948, and the talks ended in the Indo-Bhutan Treaty of 8 August 1949, under which India returned the land around Deothang. In February 2007 King Jigme Khesar Namgyal Wangchuck signed a new treaty of friendship with India, replacing that of 1949.
treaty-of-pyritz: The Electorate of Brandenburg, ruled by the House of Hohenzollern, claimed the Duchy of Pomerania as a fief, while the House of Pomerania, the Griffins, claimed imperial immediacy; the frontier was also disputed and often fought over. The conflict sharpened in 1464, when Otto III, Duke of Pomerania, died without issue and left Pomerania-Stettin vacant. The Treaty of Soldin of 1466, under which the Griffins would hold Pomerania-Stettin as a Brandenburg fief, never came into effect, and war resumed.

The Treaty of Prenzlau of 1472 forced the Griffins to accept Brandenburg overlordship and succession and to give up territory. After renewed war from 1477, Bogislaw X, by then sole duke, renewed those terms in 1479. He pledged allegiance to Albrecht III, Elector of Brandenburg, but refused it to his son John Cicero. Bogislaw's first marriage, to Margarethe of Brandenburg, was childless; in 1490 he married Anna Jagiellon of Poland, who was pregnant when the treaty was made.

John Cicero accepted that the dukes of Pomerania were not obliged to take their duchy as a fief from the Hohenzollern or to pledge allegiance to the electors. In return Bogislaw assured the Hohenzollern of the succession should his house die out. John Cicero gave his assurance at Pyritz on 26 March, and Bogislaw answered at Königsberg on 28 March. 150 Pomeranian prelates and landlords confirmed the Brandenburg right of succession by oath. The treaty is regarded as the chief achievement of Bogislaw's foreign policy.

The birth of Georg I, Duke of Pomerania, on 11 April 1493, followed by four more children, ended Brandenburg's hope of an early succession. In 1495 John Cicero had Bogislaw's invitation to the Imperial Diet at Worms intercepted and arranged for his brother to receive Pomerania there as a fief. In 1521 Emperor Charles V enfeoffed both the Hohenzollern and Bogislaw. The Treaty of Grimnitz of 1529 confirmed Pomerania as an immediate imperial fief while letting the electors attend every investiture and style themselves dukes of Pomerania.
treaty-of-raciaz: In 1401 Poland, with the support of the papacy, strengthened its ties with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania through the Union of Vilnius and Radom. In the same year the Samogitians rebelled against the Teutonic Knights and burnt several of their castles, and the Knights retaliated with raids on Kaunas and Grodno. In 1402 the Order allied with the Lithuanian duke Švitrigaila, brother of King Władysław II Jagiełło, who promised to honour the Treaty of Salynas of 1398 and cede Samogitia to the Knights.

Negotiations began in the summer of 1403, when neither side had achieved a decisive victory and Vytautas the Great wished to turn his attention to a war against Yury of Smolensk. The treaty, signed on 22 May 1404, addressed only some of the territories disputed between Poland, Lithuania and the Order. Poland in essence confirmed its earlier Treaty of Kalisz with the Order, and Lithuania the Treaty of Salynas: Dobrzyń Land was to return to Poland for a fee, and Samogitia was to remain with the Order. Talks on the Gdańsk region were inconclusive, and Švitrigaila was allowed to return to Podolia.

The settlement did not prove stable. Once Vytautas had concluded his wars in the east with the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1408, he could again concentrate on the Teutonic Knights, and in 1409 the Samogitians rebelled a second time. The revolt led to a new war between Poland-Lithuania and the Knights, who were decisively defeated at the Battle of Grunwald in 1410, and the Peace of Thorn of 1411 changed the borders that the treaty had set.
treaty-of-rapallo-1920: The treaty was meant to settle the Adriatic question, Italy's claim to territories on the eastern Adriatic that the Treaty of London of 1915 had promised it in return for entering the war against Austria-Hungary. After the Armistice of Villa Giusti of 3 November 1918, Italian troops occupied Istria, Rijeka and part of the Dalmatian coast, including the area between Zadar and Šibenik and several islands. At the Paris Peace Conference Woodrow Wilson rejected the Treaty of London and favoured self-determination, and the British and French did not support enforcing it. In 1919 Gabriele d'Annunzio and a group of Italian veterans seized Rijeka and set up the Italian Regency of Carnaro.

By late 1919 the delegation of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, led by Nikola Pašić and Ante Trumbić, could not agree with Italy, and both sides were told to negotiate directly. Talks between Italian foreign minister Carlo Sforza and the Yugoslav delegation under Milenko Vesnić took place on 9 to 11 November 1920, and the treaty was signed on 12 November in the Villa Spinola at Rapallo.

Italy received Istria and the lands to its north, running from Tarvisio by way of Triglav and Snežnik to the Kvarner Gulf, which brought Trieste, Pula and Gorizia into Italy. It also received Zadar as a semi-enclave and the islands of Cres, Lošinj, Lastovo and Palagruža. The articles on Dalmatia were otherwise largely ignored.

Article 4 created the independent Free State of Fiume within the borders of the former Austro-Hungarian Corpus separatum, with a strip of coast joining it to Italy in Istria; the suburb of Sušak went to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Other articles provided for a commission to mark the border, a conference on economic cooperation, and the rights of Italians in the Kingdom, who could opt for Italian citizenship within a year. The Italian text was to prevail in a dispute.

The treaty brought about half a million Slovenes and Croats into Italy and was unpopular among them in the Kingdom. In Italy, the relinquished claim to Dalmatia fed the myth of the mutilated victory, the view that Italy had won the war but lost the peace. D'Annunzio condemned the treaty on 17 November, and the Italian Navy drove him from Rijeka in the clash known as Bloody Christmas, after which the Free State could be established. Italy annexed it four years later under the Treaty of Rome.

Rijeka's port declined with the loss of its hinterland. Zadar's growth was limited by its position as a semi-enclave, and Split overtook it as the regional capital of Dalmatia. Italian support for Montenegrin resistance and for the Croatian Committee ended after the treaty. Most of Italy's territorial gains were reversed after World War II.
treaty-of-rastatt: The Treaty of Rastatt followed the Treaty of Utrecht of 11 April 1713, which ended hostilities between France and Spain on one side and Great Britain and the Dutch Republic on the other. Austria began to negotiate with France after its allies, particularly Great Britain, had abandoned it during the Utrecht talks. Great Britain feared a personal union of Austria and Spain under Emperor Charles VI, who took the imperial throne in 1711 and claimed the Spanish throne, since that would shift the European balance of power toward the House of Habsburg.
