By 1713 all parties were militarily depleted. In June 1713 France launched a Rhine campaign against the Holy Roman Empire and took Kaiserslautern, Landau and Breisgau. After these defeats Charles VI accepted an offer from Louis XIV to reopen negotiations.

The First Congress of Rastatt opened in November 1713 between France and Austria. Marshal Claude Louis Hector de Villars negotiated for France and Prince Eugene of Savoy for Austria. The treaty was concluded on 7 March 1714 in the Baden city of Rastatt.

Austria received the Spanish territories in Italy, Naples, Milan and Sardinia, as well as the Spanish Netherlands. It also gained Freiburg and several small areas on its eastern borders from France, while France retained Landau. Austria obtained much more than it had been offered at Utrecht, where it had originally taken part in the talks as a negotiating party.

A third treaty, at Baden in Switzerland, was needed to end hostilities between France and the Holy Roman Empire. As a result of Rastatt, the Habsburg Empire reached its largest territorial extent since the division of Charles V's possessions in 1556. Emperor Charles VI was nevertheless outraged at the loss of Spain and thought the outcome of the war an unacceptable failure.

For France, the treaties of Utrecht and Rastatt confirmed that the Spanish throne would belong to the House of Bourbon, but denied it the additional territory it had sought, and they affirmed that the thrones of France and Spain could not be united. The settlement is associated with a change in European politics that stressed the balance of power.
treaty-of-ribe: For centuries Danish kings and the Holstein nobility had fought over Schleswig, the Danish duchy on the border with the Holy Roman Empire. After the bankruptcy of the Danish state in the early fourteenth century, Holsatian nobles took control of much of the kingdom, and in 1326 King Valdemar III of Denmark was forced to sign the Constitutio Valdemaria, promising that Schleswig and the Kingdom of Denmark would never be united under one ruler. Schleswig passed as a fief to Count Gerhard III of Holstein-Rendsburg of the Schauenburg dynasty.

In 1439 King Christopher III granted the whole Duchy of Schleswig as a hereditary fief under the Danish crown to Count Adolf VIII of Holstein-Rendsburg. Adolf died without an heir in 1459, and no other count could claim both lands. Christian I held a claim to Schleswig, and a separation of the two would have ruined many nobles who held estates in both. Summoned to Ribe, the nobles agreed on 2 March 1460 to elect him.

Holstein was the simpler case: Christian added the title of count to his own, but he was forbidden to annex Holstein to Denmark, which kept its place within the Empire. In Schleswig the Danish king became duke of a Danish fief, in effect his own vassal, an arrangement meant to guard against excessive Danish domination of the union. A further clause gave the nobility the right to revolt if the king broke the agreement, a feature of several medieval coronation charters.

In 1474 Emperor Frederick III raised Christian from count to Duke of Holstein, making him an immediate vassal of the Empire; the smaller Holstein-Pinneberg stayed with the House of Schauenburg until 1640. Schleswig was left out of later Danish laws, though it kept the Code of Jutland, and the gradual arrival of German-speaking administrators led to a lasting Germanisation of its southern part, a process quickened by the Lutheran Reformation. In the nineteenth century German nationalists cited the treaty to claim both duchies, while Danes sought to bind Schleswig to the kingdom. The dispute led to the First War of Schleswig in 1848–1851 and the Second War of Schleswig in 1864.
treaty-of-rome: In 1951 the Treaty of Paris created the European Coal and Steel Community, an idea conceived by Jean Monnet and announced by Robert Schuman, the French Foreign Minister, on 9 May 1950. Its aim was to pool Franco-West German coal and steel production and to strengthen Franco-German cooperation so as to banish the possibility of war. Two further communities proposed by the French, a European Defence Community and a European Political Community, failed when the French Parliament rejected the first.

Monnet resigned from the High Authority in protest and began work on communities based on economic integration. The Benelux states and West Germany wanted a general common market, which France opposed because of its protectionist policy, so Monnet proposed a common market and a separate nuclear community. The Messina Conference of 1955 appointed Paul-Henri Spaak to chair a preparatory committee, and its report was accepted at the Venice Conference on 29 and 30 May 1956.

The treaty was signed on 25 March 1957 at the Palazzo dei Conservatori on Capitoline Hill in Rome, together with the Euratom Treaty. It proposed the progressive reduction of customs duties and a customs union, and a common market for goods, labour, services and capital across the member states. It also proposed a Common Agriculture Policy, a Common Transport Policy and a European Social Fund, and established the European Commission.

The new communities shared the Common Assembly and the European Court of Justice with the Coal and Steel Community, but not its Council or High Authority. France was reluctant to accept more supranational powers, so the new bodies were called Commissions, with only basic powers, and important decisions had to be approved by the Council of national ministers, which now adopted majority voting.

The treaty came into force on 1 January 1958. In 1965 President Charles de Gaulle recalled French representatives from the Council of Ministers in the Empty Chair Crisis, which was resolved by the Luxembourg Compromise giving members a veto. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 removed the word economic from the title, and in 2009 the Treaty of Lisbon renamed it the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

The historian Tony Judt argued that it did not represent a fundamental turning point, being largely a declaration of future good intentions, with one significant innovation, the European Court of Justice under Article 177, whose importance was unnoticed at the time.
treaty-of-roskilde: During the Second Northern War, Charles X Gustav of Sweden crossed the frozen straits from Jutland and occupied the Danish island of Zealand, beginning the invasion on 11 February 1658. A preliminary treaty, the Treaty of Taastrup, was signed on 18 February, and the final Treaty of Roskilde on 26 February 1658 (OS), or 8 March (NS). It was negotiated at the parsonage of Høje Taastrup Church and concluded in Roskilde between Charles X Gustav and Frederick III of Denmark-Norway.

After a devastating defeat, Denmark-Norway gave up a third of its territory. Scania, Blekinge, Halland and Bornholm passed to Sweden from Denmark, and from Norway Bohuslän, which secured Sweden unrestricted access to western trade, and Trøndelag with Nordmøre and Romsdal. Halland had been leased to Sweden for thirty years under the Peace of Brömsebro of 1645. Denmark also renounced all anti-Swedish alliances, undertook to keep hostile warships from passing the straits into the Baltic, restored the Duke of Holstein-Gottorp to his estates, paid for the Swedish occupation forces and provided troops for Charles X Gustav's wider wars.

At a council at Gottorp on 7 July 1658 the Swedish king resolved to wipe Denmark-Norway from the map, and without warning he attacked again, including Copenhagen. Its residents, helped by a Dutch fleet and army that defeated the Swedish fleet in the Battle of the Sound, held out, and Charles withdrew in 1659.

Norwegian forces expelled the Swedes from Trøndelag, whose men had been conscripted into Swedish armies, and the Treaty of Copenhagen in 1660 restored Trøndelag to Norway and Bornholm to Denmark. The other provinces stayed Swedish. In Scania the ninth article assured inhabitants of their privileges, old laws and customs, but the province was gradually integrated into Sweden; Denmark conquered most of it in 1676 and lost it again, and Swedish law replaced Scanian law in 1683.
treaty-of-ryswick: The Nine Years' War was financially crippling for its participants, partly because armies had grown from an average of 25,000 in 1648 to over 100,000 by 1697. The war absorbed 80% of English state revenue in the period. The 1690s were also the coldest point of the Little Ice Age, and harvests failed across Europe in 1695 and 1696; in Scotland and parts of Northern Europe an estimated 5 to 15% of the population starved. Fighting largely ended in Europe after 1695, but King William's War continued in the Americas, where England occupied Acadia and the French captured York Factory.

Talks were dominated by the Spanish succession. Charles II of Spain was unlikely to leave an heir, and the leading claimants were Louis XIV and Emperor Leopold I. Louis, unable to impose his solution, tried to prevent discussion of it by dividing the Grand Alliance. He made a separate peace with Savoy in the Treaty of Turin of 1696, returned Luxembourg to Spain and agreed to recognise William III rather than the exiled James II.

Formal talks were held at the Huis ter Nieuwburg in Ryswick, mediated by the Swedish diplomat Baron Lilliënrot. Leopold would agree only to a ceasefire, since the terms left the inheritance open. William and Louis sent personal representatives, the Earl of Portland and Marshal Louis-François de Boufflers, who finalised terms near Brussels in June 1697. On 20 September France signed peace treaties with Spain and England and a ceasefire with the Holy Roman Empire, and on 21 September a treaty of peace and commerce with the Dutch Republic. Leopold delayed, then signed on 30 October after William threatened to dissolve the Alliance.

France gave back Freiburg, Breisach, Philippsburg and Lorraine to the Empire and evacuated Catalonia, Luxembourg, Mons and Kortrijk, but kept Strasbourg. Louis withdrew support from the Jacobites and gave up claims to Cologne and the Palatinate. In North America France regained Acadia, though low-level conflict persisted, and the Dutch returned Pondichéry to France.

All sides took the peace as a truce, and the death of Charles II in 1700 led to the War of the Spanish Succession. The Partition Treaties of The Hague in 1698 and London in 1700 failed to prevent it. The war showed that France could not impose its aims without allies. Historians treat Ryswick as a turning point in England's rise as a maritime power, with London replacing Amsterdam as Europe's commercial centre. After James II died in 1701, Louis proclaimed his son rightful king of England.
treaty-of-saint-clair-sur-epte: Vikings had raided Frankish lands since Charlemagne's time, reaching Paris in 845 and 885, and Carolingian kings from Charles the Bald onwards failed to stop them by force or by payment. In time the counts and dukes of West Francia fortified their own lands, and raiding grew harder. Rollo, according to Dudo of Saint-Quentin, had fought a rebellion against the King of Denmark before he became one of the leaders of the Viking Siege of Paris in 885 and 886. By 900 his followers had settled along the Seine around Rouen.

In June 911 Rollo besieged Chartres without success, and on 20 July the Franks under Robert, Count of Paris, later Robert I of France, relieved the town. Charles the Simple, who was with the army, then chose to negotiate.

Rollo refused an offer of Flanders and asked for better farmland. The extent of the grant west of the Epte is debated, but the consensus is that it was broadly Rouen and present-day Upper Normandy, possibly the pagi of the Caux, Évrecin, Roumois and Talou. Rollo pledged vassalage, vowed to guard the Seine estuaries, and took the baptismal name Robert after his godfather. Some authors argue the land was granted outright, with no oath owed. The deal was to be sealed by a marriage to Gisela, daughter of Charles.

The terms are known only through Dudo, writing a century later, and the agreement was probably verbal and likely made in the autumn. A royal diploma of 918 confirms the grant. Dudo's tale of a warrior toppling the king while kissing his foot is likely exaggerated.

Rollo shared the lands between the Epte and the Risle among his chieftains and settled at Rouen. Their descendants adopted the local Gallo-Romance language, married into the native population and took up Christianity, and the Northmen became known as Normans, though the first settlers also brought slaves, mainly from the British Isles. Rollo's successors extended the domain to the Cotentin and the Pays de Caux. Charles himself was deposed in 923, and Rollo's descendant William became king of England after the Battle of Hastings in 1066.
treaty-of-saint-germain-en-laye-1919: On 21 October 1918, 208 German-speaking delegates of the Austrian Imperial Council convened a provisional national assembly of German-Austria, and on 30 October it elected the Social Democrat Karl Renner as state chancellor. The Armistice of Villa Giusti on 3 November sealed the fate of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy, and on 11 November Emperor Charles I declared that he would relinquish every participation in the administration. The next day the assembly declared German-Austria a democratic republic. Meanwhile Czechoslovakia, Poland and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes had been proclaimed on the territory of the former Austrian half of the empire, and Italian forces occupied South Tyrol and Trentino.

Renner reached Saint-Germain in May 1919 and found the Austrian delegation excluded from negotiations led by the French prime minister, Georges Clemenceau. After an Allied ultimatum he signed on 10 September 1919, at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye. The treaty declared the Austro-Hungarian Empire dissolved, and in article 177 Austria accepted, with the other Central Powers, responsibility for starting the war. Austria recognised the independence of Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. It also required reparations, though the sum was never fixed or collected.

Cisleithanian Austria lost over 60 percent of its prewar territory. Bohemia and Moravia formed the core of Czechoslovakia, Galicia went to Poland, Bukovina to Romania, and the southern half of Tyrol up to the Brenner Pass, with Trentino, to Italy. Austria received western parts of the Hungarian counties of Moson, Sopron and Vas, though after an uprising and a plebiscite Sopron and eight villages returned to Hungary. The territory finally gained was organised as the state of Burgenland. Article 88 forbade Austria to compromise its independence, which barred union with Germany without the League of Nations council's consent. The army was limited to 30,000 volunteers.

The name German-Austria had to be changed to Austria. The loss of land and population left the new state much reduced relative to the old empire, and the economy suffered most in Vienna, an imperial capital without an empire to support it. For a time the country's very existence was questioned. Many Austrians found the settlement harsh, and the economic weakness that followed was one reason why union with Nazi Germany later proved popular. The Treaty of Trianon in June 1920 completed the disposition of the former Dual Monarchy. The United States did not ratify the treaty and made a separate peace with Austria in 1921.
treaty-of-san-francisco: The treaty, also called the Treaty of Peace with Japan, was signed on 8 September 1951 at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco. China was not invited because the United States and the United Kingdom disagreed on whether the Republic of China on Taiwan or the People's Republic of China represented the Chinese people; the United States recognised the former, while Britain had recognised the latter in 1950. As a compromise neither was invited. Korea was not invited for a similar disagreement, and Italy and Portugal were not invited either. Afghanistan, Burma, India, Nepal, Yemen and Yugoslavia were invited but did not take part. India considered some provisions to limit Japanese sovereignty, and signed a separate treaty on 9 June 1952.

The treaty ended the legal state of war, brought the Allied occupation to an end and returned full sovereignty to Japan. It came into force on 28 April 1952. Japan renounced its rights to Korea, Formosa and the Pescadores, the Kuril Islands, the Spratly Islands, Antarctica and South Sakhalin. Article 3 left the Bonin, Volcano and Ryukyu Islands under a potential United Nations trusteeship, which was never set up. In Article 11 Japan accepted the judgments of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East and other Allied war crimes courts. Article 14 recognised that Japan should pay reparations but that its resources were insufficient to make complete reparation, so it would negotiate with Allied states whose territories it had occupied.

Under Article 16 Japan transferred assets to the International Committee of the Red Cross for former prisoners of war and paid £4,500,000. The Philippines and South Vietnam received compensation in 1956 and 1959, and the last payment went to the Philippines on 22 July 1976. Burma and Indonesia later signed bilateral treaties instead. The Soviet delegation under Andrei Gromyko opposed the draft and refused to sign, as did Czechoslovakia and Poland. Japan and the Soviet Union ended the war by a Joint Declaration on 19 October 1956.

Together with the Security Treaty signed the same day, the treaty began what is called the San Francisco System, which defines Japan's relationship with the United States. It left some questions open. It did not name a recipient for Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China, which was absent, has never recognised the treaty. The absence of clarity over which islands Japan gave up gave rise to the Kuril Islands dispute. A separate treaty between Japan and the Republic of China was signed at Taipei on 28 April 1952, hours before the San Francisco treaty took effect. Because South Korea did not sign, it was not entitled to the benefits of Article 14, and in 1965 Japan agreed to settlements with its government.
treaty-of-san-stefano: The treaty was signed on 3 March [O.S. 19 February] 1878 at San Stefano, then a village west of Constantinople, at the end of the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878. Count Nicholas Pavlovich Ignatiev and Aleksandr Nelidov signed for the Russian Empire, and Foreign Minister Saffet Pasha and Ambassador to Germany Sadullah Pasha for the Ottoman Empire. According to the official Russian position, Russia never intended it to be more than a temporary rough draft, so as to allow a final settlement with the other Great Powers.

The treaty created an autonomous Principality of Bulgaria with a Christian government and the right to keep an army, after almost 500 years of Ottoman rule in the Bulgarian lands. Though still tributary to the Ottomans, it would have functioned as an independent nation. It would have included the plain between the Danube and the Balkan mountains, the region of Sofia, Northern Thrace, parts of Eastern Thrace and nearly all of Macedonia, giving it direct access to the Mediterranean. Its prince was to be elected, and Russian troops were to remain for two years.

Montenegro more than doubled its territory, gaining Nikšić, Podgorica and Bar, and the Ottoman Empire recognised its independence. Serbia gained Niš and Leskovac and became independent, and Turkey recognised Romanian independence, while Romania gained Northern Dobruja and ceded Southern Bessarabia to Russia. In exchange for war reparations the Ottomans ceded Ardahan, Artvin, Batum, Kars and other territories in the Caucasus to Russia. Bosnia was to become an autonomous province, and the Straits were declared open to all neutral ships.

The enlarged Bulgaria alarmed France and the United Kingdom, since Russian ships might use Bulgarian Mediterranean ports as naval bases, and Serbia feared for its own interests. British Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli was unhappy with the extension of Russian power, and the British Foreign Secretary set out his objections in the Salisbury Circular of 1 April 1878. Three months later the Congress of Berlin replaced the treaty with the Treaty of Berlin, and the enlargement was never implemented. Romania, Austria-Hungary and the Albanians were also disappointed, and the reaction of the Albanians led to the formation of the League of Prizren. Bulgarians celebrate 3 March as Liberation Day.
treaty-of-sapienza: After the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204, the Partitio Romaniae assigned most of the Peloponnese, or Morea, to the Republic of Venice, except Corinthia and Argolis. Venice did not enforce its claim at once, and in 1205 a few hundred crusaders under William of Champlitte and Geoffrey of Villehardouin conquered much of the peninsula on their own account, breaking the main Greek resistance at the Battle of the Olive Grove of Koundouros. A Venetian fleet took the Messenian peninsula with Modon and Coron from Champlitte's men in 1206 or 1207.

Late in 1208 Champlitte left to take up his inheritance in Burgundy, and Villehardouin succeeded him, using feudal law to keep Champlitte's nephew from the title. Negotiations probably began at the Parliament of Ravennika in May 1209, likely through the mediation of the Latin Emperor Henry of Flanders, and the treaty was signed in June.

Venice recognised Geoffrey as master of the whole Peloponnese as far as Corinth, except Modon and Coron. Geoffrey became a vassal of the Republic in a perpetual alliance; he and his heirs were to become Venetian citizens, keep a house in Venice and send each year two silk brocades for St Mark's Basilica and one for the Doge. Venetian merchants were freed from all tariffs and could have a church, a market and a court in every city of the principality.

Venice gained a valuable outpost and protected its trade, while Achaea won the support of the Venetian fleet for a largely theoretical overlordship, and Geoffrey secured Venice's backing against the Champlitte claimants; by 1210 the pope recognised him as princeps Achaiae. The text is also a unique source for the young principality. The French medievalist Antoine Bon noted that the later Chronicle of the Morea presents its feudal order as complete by 1209 or 1210, whereas the treaty shows it still taking shape. Laconia was then still held by the Greeks, Argos and Nauplia held out until 1211/12, and Monemvasia surrendered only in 1248. The treaty also preserves the names of many lords not otherwise recorded.
treaty-of-schonbrunn: During the Peninsular War and Spanish resistance to Napoleon, Austria tried to reverse the Peace of Pressburg of 1805 by sparking national uprisings in French-occupied Central Europe, most notably the Tyrolean Rebellion against Napoleon's Bavarian allies. French forces occupied Vienna in May 1809, and Austrian troops under Archduke Charles repulsed them at the Battle of Aspern on 21 and 22 May. A few weeks later Napoleon crushed Charles's army at the Battle of Wagram on 5 and 6 July, and the archduke signed the Armistice of Znaim on 12 July. In October Foreign Minister Johann Philipp Stadion was replaced by Klemens von Metternich.

France imposed harsh terms. Austria ceded the Duchy of Salzburg to Bavaria and West Galicia to the Duchy of Warsaw, and the Tarnopol district to the Russian Empire. It gave up Gorizia and Gradisca, the Imperial Free City of Trieste, Carniola, the March of Istria, western Carinthia with East Tyrol and the Croatian lands southwest of the Sava to the French Empire, which made them the Illyrian Provinces, so that Austria lost its access to the Adriatic Sea. Austria recognised Napoleon's earlier conquests and his brother Joseph Bonaparte as King of Spain, paid a large indemnity and agreed to reduce its army to 150,000 men, a promise it did not keep. It also had to apply Napoleon's Continental System against Britain.

While the negotiations went on, Napoleon narrowly escaped an attempt on his life. On 12 October 1809 Friedrich Staps, a seventeen-year-old son of a Lutheran pastor from Naumburg, was arrested by General Jean Rapp and found to carry a large kitchen knife. Asked by Napoleon whether he would be grateful if pardoned, Staps replied that he would kill him none the less. He was shot a few days later, reportedly crying Long live freedom! Long live Germany! After 1813 Staps was seen as a martyr of German nationalism.

Austria, though much weakened, remained a European great power. In 1810 Emperor Francis I married his daughter Marie Louise to Napoleon, and under Metternich's changed policy Austrian forces joined the French invasion of Russia in 1812.
treaty-of-seeb: The Imamate had appeared in cycles in Oman for more than 1,200 years. British influence in the coastal Sultanate of Muscat revived its cause in the interior, and Imam Salim ibn Rashid al-Kharusi led a rebellion against Muscat among the Ibadi tribes of the interior from 1913 to 1920. Both states were Ibadi, but the Imamate opposed foreign interference in internal affairs and held that the ruler should be elected. The settlement was reached on 25 September 1920 between Sultan Taimur bin Feisal and Isa bin Salih al-Harthi, the Hinawi leader, who signed for the tribes, with the British Political Agent Ronald Wingate as mediator. It takes its name from the coastal town of Seeb.

The text set out four conditions for each side. The Sultan's government was to take no more than 5 percent on goods brought from the interior to Muscat, Matrah, Sur and the other coast towns, to give all Omanis safety and freedom there and lift restrictions on entry and exit, and not to shelter fugitives from Omani justice or interfere in the interior's internal affairs. The tribes and shaikhs in turn were to keep peace with the Sultan, not attack the coast towns or meddle in his government, let lawful travellers and trade pass freely, expel criminals who fled to them, and hear merchants' claims according to the sharia.

The Imamate made its capital at Nizwa, and relations stayed largely peaceful until 1945, when news of Imam Muhammad bin Abdullah al-Khalili's illness led Sultan Said bin Taimur to tell the British he wished to occupy the interior after the Imam's death. Ghalib Alhinai was elected Imam in 1954.

On 25 October 1954 the Muscat Infantry under Lieutenant Colonel Coriat entered Fahud, which the Imamate held to be a breach of the treaty, and the Jebel Akhdar War followed. The Sultan occupied Nizwa in 1955; Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Iraq backed the Imamate, and Talib bin Ali Alhinai revived the rebellion. After British intervention, including the Royal Air Force and the Special Air Service, the war ended in 1959 with the rebels defeated and their leaders exiled to Saudi Arabia.
treaty-of-seringapatam: The Third Anglo-Mysore War broke out in late 1789, when Tipu Sultan, ruler of the Kingdom of Mysore, attacked Travancore, an ally of the British East India Company. After a little over two years of fighting, the Company's forces under Lord Charles, 2nd Earl Cornwallis, together with allied armies of the Maratha Empire and Hyderabad, laid siege in February 1792 to Seringapatam, the Mysore capital.

Rather than storm the works at great cost to all sides, Cornwallis opened negotiations with Tipu, and the treaty was signed on 18 March 1792. Cornwallis had hoped to make it a wide-ranging settlement that would reduce or remove the threat from Mysore and also prevent conflict between Hyderabad and the Marathas, but the Marathas resisted the inclusion of such terms.

Mysore ceded about half of its territories to the other signatories. The Peshwa gained land up to the Tungabhadra River. The Nizam was awarded the country from the Krishna to the Penner River, together with the forts of Cuddapah and Gandikota on the south bank of the Penner. The East India Company received a large part of Mysore's territories on the Malabar Coast, between the Kingdom of Travancore and the Kali River, as well as the districts of Baramahal and Dindigul.

Mysore also recognised the independence of the rajah of Coorg, although Coorg in effect became a dependency of the Company. The treaty set an indemnity of 330 lakhs of rupees, and Tipu Sultan was required to surrender two of his three sons as hostages of war. Lord Cornwallis signed for the Company, with representatives of the Nizam of Hyderabad and of the Maratha Empire signing alongside Tipu.
treaty-of-sevres: France, Britain and Italy had secretly begun planning the partition of the Ottoman Empire as early as 1915. Open negotiations covered more than 15 months, from the Paris Peace Conference of 1919 through the Conference of London in February 1920, and took definite shape only after the San Remo Conference of April 1920. The delay came from disagreement among the powers, which hinged on the outcome of the Turkish National Movement.

The Allies submitted their draft at San Remo and asked for a response within a month. The former Grand Vizier Tevfik Pasha found it incompatible with independence and even statehood. The Ottoman government sent recommendations on 25 June 1920, but the Allies replied that only minor changes were possible. Sultan Mehmed VI convened a council of 57 delegates, none from the Turkish National Movement, and all but one voted to approve the signature.

The treaty was signed on 10 August 1920 at the Manufacture nationale de Sèvres porcelain factory. Its terms were far more severe than those the Treaty of Versailles imposed on Germany. The Ottoman Army was limited to 50,700 men, and an air force was prohibited. The Allies were to control the empire's finances, and the capitulations abolished in 1914 were restored. Article 230 required the surrender of those responsible for the massacres of the war years, including the Armenian genocide, though the Allied attempt to prosecute them was suspended.

Eastern Thrace and the islands of Imbros and Tenedos went to Greece, and Italy received the Dodecanese. Smyrna was left under Turkish sovereignty but administered by Greece, with a plebiscite after five years. A Zone of the Straits would internationalise the Bosporus and Dardanelles. Armenia was recognised as free and independent, a referendum was planned for Kurdistan, and the mandates for Palestine, Syria and Lebanon, and Iraq were settled.

The Ottoman government accepted the treaty, but it was never ratified, and Greece did not ratify it either. Mustafa Kemal Pasha's Grand National Assembly, set up in Ankara in April 1920, declared on 7 June 1920 invalid all treaties signed by the Istanbul government since 16 March 1920. The Turkish War of Independence followed. The Chanak crisis of September 1922 nearly led to war with Britain over the Straits, but the Armistice of Mudanya was concluded on 11 October. The Allies returned to negotiate at Lausanne, and the Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 replaced Sèvres, restored a large territory in Anatolia and Thrace to the Turks, did not make Constantinople an international city, and led to the Republic of Turkey.
treaty-of-shimonoseki: The peace conference ran from 20 March to 17 April 1895 at the Shunpanrō hotel in Shimonoseki, Japan. Count Itō Hirobumi and Viscount Mutsu Munemitsu negotiated for Japan, and Li Hongzhang and his son Li Jingfang for the Qing dynasty, with the former American secretary of state John W. Foster advising the Qing side. On 24 March Li Hongzhang was shot and wounded by a right-wing Japanese extremist. The public outcry led the Japanese to temper their demands and agree to a temporary armistice, and the conference resumed on 10 April.

Itō and Mutsu wanted to reduce Qing power in Korea and also on Taiwan, whose importance for expansion towards South China and Southeast Asia Mutsu had noticed. Li argued that Taiwan had never been a battlefield in the war and, having been a province since 1885, could not be given away. He finally agreed to the cession of Penghu and part of Liaodong, but under Japan's military advantage he gave up Taiwan too.

The treaty had eleven articles. China recognised the full independence and autonomy of Korea, ending the tribute and ceremonies Korea had performed to China. China ceded the Penghu Islands, Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula, and agreed to pay an indemnity of 200 million Kuping taels, over seven years. It opened Shashi, Chongqing, Suzhou and Hangzhou to Japanese trade and granted Japan most favoured nation status. The Guangxu Emperor ratified the treaty despite vigorous opposition from Chinese scholars and officials.

Russia, France and Germany, which were active in China, intervened and demanded that Japan give up Liaodong, mainly out of concern for Port Arthur. In November 1895 Japan returned the territory in exchange for an additional indemnity of 30 million taels. The cession of Taiwan met strong local resistance, and Japan did not take over the islands until October 1895. Pro-Qing officials and gentry declared a Republic of Formosa that year but gained no international recognition.

In China the treaty was regarded as a national humiliation. It weakened support for the Qing, and the Self-Strengthening Movement was judged a failure, which fed the Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 and the uprisings that ended in the fall of the dynasty in 1911. Many Japanese historians regard the Triple Intervention as a turning point towards outright imperialism. The Treaty of Taipei of 28 April 1952 is held to have formally abrogated the Treaty of Shimonoseki, though the cession provision is disputed by some.
treaty-of-simulambuco: Portugal had held trading ports on the African coast since the early 16th century. When the European colonial powers agreed at Berlin on how to divide Africa, the Portuguese, not wanting to miss out on the Scramble for Africa in lands near their old possessions, began to extend their rule further inland. The Treaty of Simulambuco, signed by emissaries of the Portuguese Crown and the princes and notables of Cabinda, including officials of the Kingdom of N'Goyo, was drawn up in response. In contrast to the violent struggles between the Portuguese and some peoples of Mozambique, the colonisation of Cabinda was peaceful.

The treaty made Cabinda a protectorate of the Portuguese Crown, at the request, in its words, of the princes and governors of Cabinda. Under Article 1 the princes and chiefs and their successors declared that they voluntarily recognised Portuguese sovereignty and placed all the territories they governed under its protection. Article 2 bound Portugal to maintain the integrity of the territories placed under its protection. The agreement gave rise to three territories within the Portuguese protectorate of Cabinda: Cacongo, Loango and Ngoio.

Cabinda lies apart from its larger southern neighbour, Angola, separated from it by the Congo River and a strip of land belonging to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Article 2 of the treaty has often been cited in separatist arguments. In 2005 Cabindans marked the 120th anniversary of the treaty, to the annoyance of Angolan officials, who regard it as running counter to their own position on the territory, and the dispute over the treaty has fed a long separatist conflict.
treaty-of-stensby: From May 1223 to November 1225 Count Henry of Schwerin held King Valdemar II of Denmark and his son Valdemar the Young captive, and Danish power in the Baltic declined. In 1225 Denmark handed authority over Estonia to William of Modena, but the Livonian Brothers of the Sword took possession of the territory and refused to give it up. In 1233 they refused the papal legate Baldwin of Alna's demand to hand over the castle of Reval and defeated his troops, and Valdemar II took his case to the Roman Curia.

In February 1236 Pope Gregory IX ruled that the Sword Brothers must cede Reval, Jerwia, Harria and Vironia to the Danish king. In September 1236 they were heavily defeated by the pagan Lithuanians at the Battle of Saule, and in May 1237 they were reorganised as the Livonian Order, an autonomous branch of the Teutonic Order.

The treaty was signed at Stensby on Zealand on 7 June 1238. The Order returned Revala, with Reval, modern Tallinn, Virumaa, Järva and Harju to Valdemar II, who then gave Järva to the Order on condition that it built no castles there without his consent and that the county stayed in the Diocese of Reval. The king also agreed to support the Order's future campaigns, and lands conquered jointly from the pagans were to be divided, two-thirds to the king and one-third to the Order. Some later historians claimed that the treaty planned an attack on Rus', but it mentions only pagans and forbids Christians to take up arms against one another without papal permission.

The settlement was not carried out smoothly. William of Modena excommunicated all who violated the peace in his legation, and former Sword Brothers rebelled against the new Teutonic Landmeister in Livland, Hermann Balk, who fled to Germany. According to the historian Anti Selart, Valdemar II never led the crusade the treaty envisaged; he died in 1241, and a war of succession between his sons Erik and Abel followed. Pope Innocent IV confirmed the treaty in September 1243.
treaty-of-stettin-1570: The Kalmar Union of Sweden, Denmark and Norway had broken apart in 1523. Frederick II of Denmark tried to restore it under his own rule, showing the union's three crowns in his coat of arms and invading Sweden in 1563, the acts counted as the start of the Northern Seven Years' War. The Danes had the upper hand on land and took Älvsborg, while the Swedes did better at sea and in Livonia, which the surrounding powers were contesting after its secularisation. Denmark's allies, Lübeck and Poland, were divided among themselves.

In July 1570 Emperor Maximilian II called a peace congress at Stettin, now Szczecin. Duke Johann Friedrich of Pomerania-Stettin led the emperor's delegates, the French envoy Charles Dancey and Martin Kromer, bishop of Warmia, were among the mediators, and Augustus of Saxony came in person. Denmark sent Peder Bille, Jørgen Rosenkrantz, Henrik Rantzau, Niels Kaas and Joachim Henke; Sweden sent Jöran Gera, Bengt Gylta and Erik Gyllenstjerna, among others.

John III of Sweden gave up all claims to Gotland and the Norwegian provinces, recognising for the first time Skåne, Blekinge and Halland as Danish. Sweden was to pay 150,000 riksdaler for the return of Älvsborg Castle and 75,000 daler to Lübeck, and handed over its Livonian possessions in return for a payment by the emperor. To raise the ransom, Sweden taxed all movable property, from a tenth for peasants to a twelfth for unburned towns and an eighteenth for burned ones, deepening the poverty of the war-torn population.

The treaty made Denmark the dominant power in Northern Europe for a short time, but it failed to restore the Kalmar Union, left the quarrel over the three crowns unsettled and, being unfavourable to Sweden, led to further wars that ended only in 1720/21. Lübeck gained nothing: John III granted the same privileges to Stralsund, the payments were never made, and Swedish pirates kept seizing its ships. Maximilian II never paid Sweden either, lost his influence in the Baltic, and the Livonian War went on. Denmark did receive its money in the end, as John III sold warships and debased the Swedish currency to keep Älvsborg, his only port on the west coast.
treaty-of-stettin-1653: Sweden occupied the Duchy of Pomerania in 1630, during the Thirty Years' War. When the last duke of the House of Pomerania, Bogislaw XIV, died in 1637, Brandenburg claimed the succession under the Treaty of Grimnitz of 1529, while Sweden based its claim on the Treaty of Stettin of 1630. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 provided for a partition of the duchy between the two, and the Treaty of Nuremberg of 1650 roughly outlined each side's share, leaving the exact line to be settled.

The treaty of 4 May 1653, known in German as the Grenzrezeß von Stettin, drew the border along a line east of the Oder. It ran north from the Brandenburg frontier, leaving the commanderies of Greifenhagen and Wildenbruch, the town of Gollnow and the district round Kammin with Sweden, and reached the Baltic between Raddack and Lüchentin. Western Pomerania, including Stettin, became Swedish Pomerania, and Farther Pomerania passed to Brandenburg. Sweden kept the right to half the customs revenues of the Farther Pomeranian towns even after its troops had gone.

The first diet of Brandenburgian Pomerania met at Stargard on 19 July 1653, and the Swedish withdrawal from Farther Pomerania was complete in 1654. Together with the lower Weser and Elbe, won at Westphalia, the Oder estuary gave Sweden control of the mouths of every major German river except the Rhine, and Swedish Pomerania became its largest foothold in Germany. The line moved slightly west after the Scanian War by the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye in 1679, and far west to the Peene after the Great Northern War by the Treaty of Stockholm in 1720.
treaty-of-stolbovo: The Treaty of Stolbovo ended the Ingrian War, fought between the Swedish Empire and the Russian Tsardom from 1610 to 1617. Representatives of Sweden and Russia met at the village of Stolbovo, south of Lake Ladoga, after nearly two months of negotiations, and the meeting took place on 9 March 1617, which is 27 February by the older calendar. Sweden entered the talks with very high ambitions. It hoped to fulfil an old dream of making all Russian trade pass through Swedish territory, and at first demanded far-reaching gains in western Russia, including the northern port of Arkhangelsk.

King James I of England sent a delegation to mediate, and the United Provinces did the same, mostly to keep Arkhangelsk out of Swedish hands, which would have made the trade between Western Europe and Russia far harder. England was officially credited with brokering the peace through its mediator John Mericke, but the Dutch effort was also important. Arkhangelsk did not change hands, partly because of these efforts and mostly because Russia had united under Tsar Michael I. Russia also became serious about the talks when word came that Sweden's war against Poland might soon end, which would let Sweden renew the war on only one front.

Sweden gained the province of Kexholm in Karelia and the province of Ingria, including the fortress of Nöteborg, now Shlisselburg. Russia renounced all claims to Estonia and Livonia and agreed to pay an indemnity of 20,000 rubles. Novgorod and other Swedish gains of the war were returned to Russia, though Gdov stayed in Swedish hands until the peace was confirmed and the borders fixed.

Sweden recognised Michael Romanov as rightful tsar and ended its claims to the Russian throne. Russia was allowed free trade at normal tariffs, which ensured that Sweden would not cripple it completely, and each side could set up merchant houses: Russians in Stockholm, Reval and Viborg, Swedes in Novgorod, Pskov and Moscow. After the war King Gustavus Adolphus granted the Dutch delegation's leader, Reinoud van Brederode, the title of baron and the barony of Wesenberg (Rakvere) in Estonia.
treaty-of-sugauli: After the unification of Nepal under Prithvi Narayan Shah, the Gorkha state expanded, conquering much of Sikkim in the east and, in the west, the basins of the Gandaki and Karnali and the regions of Garhwal and Kumaon. This brought it into conflict with the British, who controlled the plains of northern India between Delhi and Calcutta. The East India Company also wanted Nepal's trade routes to Tibet and its Gurkha soldiers. In 1815 General David Ochterlony drove the Nepalese out of Garhwal and Kumaon across the Kali River, ending a 12-year occupation remembered for its brutality.

Nepal at first refused Ochterlony's terms, and a further campaign the next year targeted the Kathmandu Valley. According to the historian John Whelpton, the draft initialled at Sagauli in Bihar required Nepal to give up all territory west and east of its present borders, surrender the whole Tarai and accept a permanent British resident; Kathmandu agreed only after Ochterlony occupied the Makwanpur Valley, thirty miles from the capital. Nepal was represented by Guru Gajraj Mishra. Article 5 ceded the lowlands between the Kali and Rapti and all the hill territories west of the Kali, which became the western border. The prime minister, Bhimsen Thapa, judged that a secure frontier was the best guarantee of freedom from interference.

In 1817 the Nepali governor Bam Shah claimed the villages of Changru and Tinkar in Byans, east of the Kali, and the British conceded them; his further claim that the western headwater was the true Kali was rejected by Lord Moira in September 1817. Three decades of peace followed. In June 1840 an army mutiny over pay cuts nearly became an attack on the British residency, and in 1842 a debt case brought friction with the resident Brian Hodgson. After Gurkha troops aided the British in the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the Boundary Treaty of 1860 revised the settlement in Nepal's favour. The question Bam Shah raised lies behind the Kalapani dispute, and Nepal's political map of 2020 claimed Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura.
treaty-of-tafna: In the summer of 1836 French forces under Thomas Robert Bugeaud defeated a mixed army of Emir Abdelkader's regular and tribal warriors at the Sikkak river, and letters passed between the two commanders. That year General Clauzel had been defeated in the east of Algeria, and the French War Ministry charged Bugeaud with making peace with the Emir so that France's limited forces could avenge that defeat. Other accounts stress French dissatisfaction with an earlier treaty that had given Abdelkader much control over trade with the French enclaves, a matter of political weight for the merchants of Marseilles.

In its French text Abdelkader recognised French sovereignty in Africa, and France in exchange recognised his rule over about two-thirds of Algeria. The Arabic text said only that the Emir was aware of the rule of French power in Africa; the historian James McDougall argues from Abdelkader's letters that this cannot have been a translation error and that the difference was duplicity on Bugeaud's part. France kept the major ports, through which all of Algeria's trade was to pass, though traders on both sides ignored the rule.

Bugeaud and Abdelkader also made private agreements. Bugeaud promised modern weapons and the forced removal of the Dawa'ir and Zmala tribes and the exile of their chiefs, for which he received a cash payment that he spent on roadworks in his constituency in France.

The peace allowed the French to concentrate their forces in the east, where they took Constantine on 13 October 1837. Abdelkader consolidated his power over the tribes of the interior, set up a capital at Tagdempt and rebuilt his forces. He claimed under the treaty the Iron Gates, a valley commanding the main route between Algiers and Constantine; when French troops marched through it in late 1839, he declared the treaty broken and renewed the call for jihad. The treaty enhanced Bugeaud's reputation, and the historian Naylor argues that its terms show the French treated Abdelkader's territory as sovereign.
treaty-of-tartu-finland-russia: Finland declared independence in November 1917, after a November election won by the coalition of pro-independence parties. The Bolsheviks, whose ideology formally upheld each people's right to self-determination, supported the declaration, and Lenin saw in it a showpiece of the benevolence of the new Soviet system. The Finnish Civil War followed, in which the Finnish Red Army fought the forces loyal to the legal government. The government's forces, assisted by a division of German regular forces and Swedish volunteers, won within some months, but the border with Russia remained unsettled.

The defeat of the Central Powers ended the government's ties with Germany. Finland now had to deal with the new Bolshevik government, as other countries were doing, for example in the Russian–Estonian Treaty of Tartu. The large moderate social democrats were willing to normalise relations, while some nationalist and rightist members of parliament thought the planned treaty went too far, since it gave up the ideal of a greater national state that included the eastern territories settled by Karelian people.

The treaty was signed on 14 October 1920 at the building of the Estonian Students' Society, after negotiations lasting nearly five months. The border was to follow the old line between the autonomous Grand Duchy of Finland and Imperial Russia. Finland also received Petsamo, with its ice-free harbour on the Arctic Ocean, which it had already annexed. As far back as 1864 Tsar Alexander II had promised to join Petsamo to Finland in exchange for a piece of the Karelian Isthmus.

Finland left Repola and Porajärvi in Russian East Karelia, taken during the Viena and Aunus expeditions, and handed North Ingria to Russia, which ended the short-lived Republic of North Ingria. The Soviet side guaranteed free navigation for Finnish merchant ships from Lake Ladoga to the Gulf of Finland by way of the Neva, and Finland guaranteed land transit through Petsamo to Norway.

Ratifications were exchanged in Moscow on 31 December 1920, and the treaty was registered in the League of Nations Treaty Series on 5 March 1921. It became a matter of controversy during the East Karelian Uprising of 1921 to 1922, when the Finnish government allowed volunteers to take part in the conflict. The Soviet Union broke the treaty in 1939, when it began the Winter War against Finland. In hindsight the settlement was rather favourable to Finland, especially when compared with the treaties made at the end of the Second World War.
treaty-of-tartu-russian-estonian: Estonia had been a province of Imperial Russia since 1721. In 1917, three years into the First World War, the Russian Empire fell into revolution and civil war. As part of this larger conflict the Estonians declared independence from the warring Russian and German empires, and they won their freedom in the Estonian War of Independence of 1918 to 1920.

The treaty established the border between Estonia and Russia, affirmed the right of Estonians to return to Estonia and of Russian people to return to Russia, and required that Estonian movable property evacuated to Russia in the First World War be returned. Russia also agreed to absolve Estonia of Russian Imperial debt and to pay Estonia 15 million gold rubles, a share of the gold reserves of the former Russian Empire.

Russia further agreed to grant concessions to exploit one million hectares of Russian forest land and to build a railway line from the Estonian border to Moscow. Jaan Poska signed for Estonia and Adolf Joffe for Soviet Russia, together with other representatives of both parties. Ratifications were exchanged in Moscow on 30 March 1920, and the treaty was registered in the League of Nations Treaty Series on 12 July 1922.

The treaty has been regarded as the birth certificate of the Republic of Estonia because it was the first de jure recognition of the state. It was also of great importance to diplomatically isolated Soviet Russia, and Lenin expressed satisfaction with it as "an incomparable victory over Western imperialism". Some members of the Entente opposed the treaty, intending to keep Soviet Russia in international isolation.

After the signing, Soviet Russia did not fulfil several points of the treaty. The migration of Estonians was obstructed, and the museum collections of the University of Tartu were not returned from Voronezh. Estonia was occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940 to 1941 and again from 1944 to 1991.
treaty-of-teusina: Sweden and Russia had agreed a truce in 1593 after the death of John III of Sweden. The Swedes sought peace because they had lost their king and feared for their army in Estonia, which lacked funds. Sigismund was named the new king, but Sweden soon fell into a power struggle between Sigismund and his uncle, the future Charles IX. In Russia Tsar Fyodor I Ivanovich reigned, while real power lay with his adviser and later successor Boris Godunov.

Sigismund set as Sweden's minimum demand a return to the pre-war borders with some territorial compensation. The Russian delegation, led by the boyar Afanasiy Pushkin, used the Swedish quarrel to its advantage and threatened to break off the talks, and the final agreement was reached in May 1595 at the village of Tyavzino, Täyssinä in Finnish, in Ingria.

The treaty revised the Truce of Plussa of 1583 and restored the borders that had stood before the Livonian War. Sweden gave up the occupied lands of Kexholm and Ingria, and Russia received Kexholm County with Korela Fortress and most of Ingria, with the towns of Ivangorod, Yama and Koporye. Russia renounced all claims west of the river Narva and accepted Swedish sovereignty over Estonia. Prisoners were exchanged without ransom, and the safety of Russian subjects and their property was guaranteed. The border was traced from the mouth of the Systerbäck on the Gulf of Finland past the lakes Saimaa and Inari and the settlement of Neiden to the Barents Sea.

The peace ended twenty-five years of destructive war, in which tens of thousands of civilians had been killed, at that time a much larger portion of the population of the regions where the war was fought. Its provisions on Russian foreign trade, which was to pass through Swedish ports, favoured Sweden commercially. The borders it set lasted 22 years, until the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617.
treaty-of-the-hague-1661: In 1648–49 the Portuguese defeated the Dutch in the first and second Battles of Guararapes and then gradually removed the Dutch presence from their colonies of Brazil and Angola. When the Dutch in Brazil surrendered in January 1654 they signed the Treaty of Taborda, but only as a provisional truce. The First Anglo-Dutch War had kept the Dutch Republic from properly supporting the GWC, the company that ran the colony in Brazil, and the Republic was not yet ready to accept the loss.

With the war against the English over, the Dutch demanded the return of the colony in May 1654. The Province of Zeeland had the most to gain from getting Brazil back, but Johan de Witt, the Grand Pensionary of Holland, preferred a payment in money: he did not want to reoccupy the colony and gave priority to stronger trading ties with Portugal. To compensate Zeeland and save face he asked Portugal for eight million guilders. The Portuguese refused both to return the colony and to pay.

The Dutch fleet was worn out after the English war, so at first the Republic authorised privateers to attack Portuguese shipping. In 1657 the fleet was again fit for large operations and the war resumed. Until 1661 Dutch squadrons, while also taking part in the Second Northern War, regularly cruised off the Portuguese coast. Portuguese privateers did considerable harm to Dutch West African and American shipping, but the blockades crippled Portugal's maritime trade, and in the same years the Dutch East India Company (VOC) completed its conquest of Ceylon and the Malabar Coast in India.

Under the settlement of 1661 Portugal agreed to pay compensation, to be spread over sixteen years, and also ceded Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) and the Maluku Islands, so that the Dutch gave up Brazil while keeping their gains in Asia. The treaty did not stop the VOC at once: under Rijckloff van Goens the company captured a few more Portuguese settlements in Asia before hostilities finally came to an end.
treaty-of-the-hague-1720: The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713, which ended the War of the Spanish Succession, rested on the principle that neither France nor Austria could be united with Spain. Philip V, grandson of Louis XIV, was confirmed as the first Bourbon king of Spain, but he ceded Naples, Sardinia, Milan and the Southern Netherlands to Austria and Sicily to Savoy, while Britain kept Gibraltar and Menorca. Philip saw the recovery of these lands as vital to his prestige, and it became the main aim of his chief minister, Cardinal Giulio Alberoni.

Elisabeth Farnese, niece of the Duke of Parma, whom Philip married in 1714, supported the policy because she wanted an Italian inheritance for her own children. With Austria fighting the Austro-Turkish War of 1716 to 1718, Spain occupied Sardinia unopposed in 1717 and landed on Sicily in July 1718. Britain and France answered with the Treaty of London on 18 July, which Austria joined on 2 August, and the British fleet under Admiral Byng destroyed the Spanish fleet at the Battle of Cape Passaro on 11 August.

Philip still hoped to keep Sicily by negotiation, counting on divisions within the alliance, but in December 1718 a Spanish-backed conspiracy to replace the Duke of Orléans as Regent of France was uncovered, and France declared war on 2 January 1719. Without control of the sea Spain could not win. An attempt to divert British forces through the Jacobite Rising of 1719 failed, and the Capture of Vigo in October showed how exposed the Spanish coast was to the Royal Navy. Philip dismissed Alberoni in December 1719 and agreed to end the war.

There was little negotiation: by joining the alliance Spain accepted the terms set in 1718, and four-year-old Charles of Spain, Philip's third son, was recognised as heir to Parma, Piacenza and Tuscany. The settlement did not end attempts to alter the Utrecht arrangements. In the Treaty of Madrid of 1721 George I agreed to raise the return of Gibraltar in Parliament at a favourable opportunity, which the Spanish took as a promise, and commercial tensions led to a new Anglo-Spanish War in 1727.
treaty-of-the-pyrenees: France entered the Thirty Years' War after the Spanish Habsburg victories in the Dutch Revolt in the 1620s and at the Battle of Nördlingen in 1634. By 1640 France was aiding the revolt in Catalonia, while Spain responded in 1648 by aiding the Fronde in France. At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 France gained the Sundgau and cut Spanish access to the Netherlands from Austria, which increased hostilities. An Anglo-French alliance won the Battle of the Dunes on 14 June 1658, but the war ground to a halt the next year when the French campaign to take Milan was defeated.

The treaty was negotiated and signed on Pheasant Island, in the Bidasoa River on the border between the two countries, by Louis XIV of France and Philip IV of Spain and their chief ministers, Cardinal Mazarin and Don Luis Méndez de Haro. France gained Roussillon, including Perpignan, and the northern half of Cerdanya, along with Montmédy and other parts of Luxembourg, Artois and towns in Flanders such as Arras, Béthune, Gravelines and Thionville. A new border was fixed at the Pyrenees. Because the treaty spoke only of villages, the town of Llívia was unintentionally left to Spain as an exclave, and the border was not properly settled until the Treaty of Bayonne of 1856.

Spain was forced to recognise the French gains of the Peace of Westphalia. In exchange, the French king pledged to stop supporting Portugal and renounced his claim to the Principality of Catalonia. The treaty also arranged the marriage of Louis XIV to Maria Theresa, daughter of Philip IV, who renounced her claim to the Spanish throne in return for a dowry that was never paid, a factor in the War of Devolution of 1667. England received Dunkirk and sold it to France in 1662.

The historian J. H. Elliott sees the treaty as the decisive admission of defeat in Spain's long struggle to maintain the Pax Hispanica. Paul Kennedy identifies it as the climax of the Habsburg bid for mastery, and attributes Spain's fall to imperial overstretch. It was Cardinal Mazarin's last major diplomatic achievement, and together with the Peace of Westphalia it gave Louis XIV stability and diplomatic advantage. By 1660 most of the European continent was at peace, and the Bourbons had ended the dominance of the Habsburgs. In the Pyrenees the treaty established border customs and restricted the free flow of people and goods.
treaty-of-the-triple-alliance: Brazil and Argentina were traditional enemies, and the region's navigable rivers, above all the Paraná and Paraguay, and vast unmarked borderlands were in dispute. Between 1854 and 1864 Paraguay built up its forces under Francisco Solano López, importing about 200 foreign technicians to build an iron foundry, arsenal, shipyard, telegraph and railway; he became ruler in September 1862. When Brazil intervened in Uruguay in 1864, Paraguay seized the Brazilian ship Marquês de Olinda in November and invaded Mato Grosso and later Rio Grande do Sul. On 13 April 1865 Paraguayan ships seized two Argentine vessels at Corrientes and Paraguay invaded the province, which brought Argentina into the alliance.

Command of the land forces went at first to President Bartolomé Mitre of Argentina, and of the naval forces to the Brazilian admiral Joaquim Marques Lisboa, Viscount of Tamandaré. The allies pledged not to lay down their arms until the López government was gone and not to treat separately with it, while declaring that their enemy was the government and not the country, whose independence they would guarantee for five years. Paraguay was to pay an indemnity, and Article XVI set the new borders, giving Argentina a strip of the Chaco north of the Pilcomayo River. A protocol required the demolition of the Fortress of Humaitá and Paraguay's disarmament.

Under Article XVIII the whole treaty was secret, though its main provisions soon leaked to the Buenos Aires press. In Brazil the Council of State judged the terms negotiated by Francisco Otaviano de Almeida Rosa too generous to Argentina, and the Argentine Congress, which ratified the treaty in secret session on 24 May 1865, quietly left the clause on fortifications unapproved.

The allies invaded Paraguay in April 1866 and, after four years held up largely by Humaitá, overthrew López, who was killed in battle. On a conservative estimate Paraguay lost between a quarter and a half of its population. The indemnities were never paid. Brazil worked against Argentina's Chaco claim, which the Hayes arbitration awarded to Paraguay, and the two allies stood on the brink of war between 1870 and 1876.
treaty-of-tientsin-1885: In December 1884, alarmed by Japanese ambitions in Korea, Empress Dowager Cixi ordered her ministers to bring China out of the undeclared war with France that had broken out on 23 August 1884. French victories in Tonkin and on Formosa in February and early March 1885 strengthened her resolve. A Chinese victory in late March, when General de Négrier's 2nd Brigade was defeated at Bang Bo and Lạng Sơn was reoccupied, was offset by the French capture of the Pescadores Islands.

The fall of Jules Ferry's ministry at the end of March gave China an opening. It agreed to carry out the Tianjin Accord of 11 May 1884, and the French dropped their demand for an indemnity for the Bắc Lệ ambush. Preliminaries of peace signed on 4 April 1885 brought a ceasefire in Tonkin and Formosa. The Yunnan and Guangxi armies and Liu Yongfu's Black Flag Army withdrew from Tonkin, while France kept its rice blockade of the Yangtze River and held Keelung and the Pescadores as a surety.

The treaty of ten articles restated the accord of 1884 in greater detail. France undertook to keep order in the provinces of Annam bordering China and to respect the frontier, and China pledged not to send troops into Tonkin and to respect the treaties France had made or would make with Annam. Commissioners were to mark the border after six months, and two trading posts were to be opened on the Chinese side, above Lào Cai and above Lạng Sơn, with the same advantages for French merchants as in the treaty ports.

France was to build roads in Tonkin, and China, should it build railways, was to turn to French industry, though without granting France an exclusive privilege. French forces were to leave Formosa and the Pescadores within a month. Hardliners at the Qing court, who blamed Li Hongzhang for earlier concessions, had insisted that he negotiate alongside two members of the Zongli Yamen, Xi Zhen and Deng Chengxiu of the Purist party.

The French lifted their blockade on 10 June 1885, left Keelung on 21 June and the Pescadores on 22 July, and ratifications were exchanged at Beijing on 28 November 1885. A Sino-French commission marked the border between late 1885 and 1887; France refused Chinese claims to Đồng Đăng but awarded the Bailong peninsula to China, and an agreement confirming the line, which largely forms today's China-Vietnam border, was signed in Beijing on 26 June 1887. Discredited by the defeat, the Purists soon lost influence at court.
treaty-of-tlatelolco: In 1962 the Brazilian delegate to the United Nations General Assembly spoke of a denuclearised zone in Latin America, and the President of Mexico, Adolfo López Mateos, proposed a treaty after the Cuban Missile Crisis. He invited the presidents of Bolivia, Brazil, Chile and Ecuador, Víctor Paz Estenssoro, João Goulart, Jorge Alessandri and Carlos Julio Arosemena Monroy, to a Joint Declaration of 29 April 1963 announcing a multilateral nuclear agreement. Its presentation at the General Assembly authorised Mexico to lead the drafting, which the diplomats Alfonso García Robles, Ismael Moreno Pino and Jorge Castañeda carried forward.

The Preliminary Meeting on the Denuclearization of Latin America (REUPRAL), held from 23 to 27 November 1964, set up the Preparatory Commission (COPREDAL), which sat in Mexico City in four sets of sessions. One working group studied control systems and technical problems, another legal and political questions, and a drafting group prepared the final texts. The draft was approved on 12 February 1967.

The parties undertake to prohibit and prevent the testing, use, manufacture, production or acquisition of nuclear weapons, and their receipt, storage, installation, deployment or possession. Each must conclude comprehensive safeguards agreements with the International Atomic Energy Agency, and a state may ask for special inspections when it suspects a violation; OPANAL monitors compliance. Protocol I binds the United States, the United Kingdom, France and the Netherlands for their territories in the region, and Protocol II commits the declared nuclear weapons states not to undermine the zone, which stretches from the Rio Grande to Tierra del Fuego.

There were 13 initial signatories. The Latin American countries other than Cuba signed in 1967, with Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago, and all of these had ratified by 1972. Argentina ratified only in 1994 and so was outside the zone during the Falklands War, and Suriname ratified in 1997, 21 years after signing. Cuba was the last to sign, in 1995, and to ratify, on 23 October 2002, with a reservation about United States hostility and the Guantánamo Bay base. All five recognised nuclear weapons states had ratified Protocol II by 1979, and García Robles received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1982.
treaty-of-tolentino: The treaty followed Napoleon Bonaparte's Italian campaign of 1796 and 1797 during the War of the First Coalition. After defeating the Austrians at the Battle of Arcole, the Battle of Rivoli and at Mantua, Bonaparte had no enemies left in northern Italy and could turn against the Papal States. Nine months of negotiations had produced no settlement, and in February 1797 some 9,000 French soldiers invaded the papal region of Romagna, leaving Pope Pius VI no choice but to accept French terms. France was represented by Bonaparte and by François Cacault, the Directory's ambassador to the Holy See, facing four representatives of the papal curia.

The treaty confirmed the harsh terms of the earlier armistice signed at Bologna and added 15 million livres to the 21 million already taken from the Papal States, 36 million in all. The cession of Avignon and the Comtat Venaissin, occupied by French troops early in the Revolution, ended about half a millennium of papal rule there. The legations, already in French hands, were incorporated into the newly created Cispadane Republic.

More than a hundred paintings and other works of art were to go to the Louvre in Paris, and the French commissioners could enter any public, religious or private building to choose what would be taken. In 1798 treaties with other Italian states extended this practice to all of Italy. The pope also had to compensate the family of the French journalist Hugh de Basseville, who had been killed by a crowd in Rome for allegedly insulting the pope.

The removal of the art was criticised by many as theft and plunder. Among its fiercest opponents was Quatremère de Quincy, who had argued in a pamphlet of 1796 that taking a work from the place for which it was made irreparably impaired its meaning. Most of the works were returned after Napoleon's fall. The treaty did not satisfy the Directory, which still sought to end the temporal power of the Holy See: a year later the French army invaded the rest of the Papal States, arrested Pius VI and set up a Roman Republic.
treaty-of-tordesillas: The dispute arose after Christopher Columbus returned in 1493 from his first voyage under the Crown of Castile. He stopped first at Lisbon, and King John II of Portugal then claimed the new lands under the Treaty of Alcáçovas of 1479 and the papal bull Aeterni regis of 1481, which granted Portugal all lands south of the Canary Islands. He wrote a threatening letter to Ferdinand and Isabella and prepared a fleet.

On 4 May 1493 Pope Alexander VI decreed in the bull Inter caetera that lands west of a line 100 leagues west of the Azores or the Cape Verde Islands should belong to Castile. John II felt this gave him too little: by 1493 Portuguese explorers had reached the Cape of Good Hope, and a later bull that named India as Spanish was a major issue for his near-term goal. He therefore negotiated directly with the Catholic Monarchs.

The treaty was signed in Tordesillas on 7 June 1494 and ratified in Setúbal. It placed the line of demarcation 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, with lands to the east for Portugal and to the west for Castile. Portugal had asked for the line to be moved 270 leagues further west than the pope's, to protect its route along the coast of Africa.

The treaty did not define the league or say which Cape Verde island was meant. It provided that these points be settled by a joint voyage, which never took place, and later expert opinions placed the line at roughly 42° to 47° west. It was negotiated without consulting Alexander VI, but Pope Julius II sanctioned it by the bull Ea quae pro bono pacis of 24 January 1506.

Very little of the divided area had been seen by Europeans. In 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral landed on the easternmost part of present-day Brazil on his way to India, and it fell to Portugal. Some historians contend that the Portuguese already knew of the coast. Spain did not resist Portuguese expansion across the meridian in Brazil.

After Portugal reached the Moluccas in 1512, Spain argued that the treaty divided the whole globe in two. The Treaty of Zaragoza of 22 April 1529 set an antimeridian and Spain gave up its claim to the Moluccas for 350,000 ducats of gold. France's Francis I and the Protestant maritime powers, England and the Netherlands, did not recognise a division of the world between two Catholic nations. The Treaty of Madrid of 1750 superseded the Tordesillas line, and UNESCO added the treaty to its Memory of the World register in 2007.
treaty-of-trianon: Hungary had been at war since August 1914 as part of Austria-Hungary. On 31 October 1918, in the Aster Revolution, King Charles IV appointed the liberal Count Mihály Károlyi prime minister, and Hungary declared its independence from Austria. Károlyi had the army, which still numbered more than 1,400,000 soldiers, unilaterally disarmed, and an armistice was signed on 13 November 1918. Serbian, Czechoslovak and Romanian forces crossed the borders in the following days, and Hungary's neighbours blockaded the country.

On 21 March 1919 Béla Kun led a communist coup and proclaimed the Hungarian Soviet Republic. In June the Entente ordered Romania and Czechoslovakia to stop their advance and accept new demarcation lines as future borders. After Kun's fall Admiral Miklós Horthy entered Budapest on 16 November 1919, and Count Albert Apponyi led the Hungarian delegation to the Paris Peace Conference.

The treaty, dictated by the Allies rather than negotiated, was signed in the Grand Trianon at Versailles on 4 June 1920 and came into force on 26 July 1921. It legalised the existing demarcation lines as the new borders. The Allies refused plebiscites, explaining in the Millerand letter that a popular consultation would not produce significantly different results; the letter also suggested that the League of Nations might mediate border corrections, which Hungarian diplomats read as a promise.

Hungary became a landlocked state of 93,073 square kilometres and 7.6 million people, and 3.3 million Hungarians lived in the areas allocated to its neighbours. The army was limited to 35,000 men, heavy artillery, tanks and air force were forbidden, and the Austro-Hungarian Navy ceased to exist. Hungary had to pay reparations and recognise minority rights. The treaty also ended the blockade and ordered the resumption of trade and of coal supplies.

The Hungarian delegation signed under protest, and agitation for revision began at once. Irredentism, the demand for reunification of Hungarian peoples, became a central theme of Hungarian politics and diplomacy. Romanians joined Romania, and Slovaks, Serbs and Croats helped form Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia, but as many as a third of Hungarian speakers found themselves outside the new borders. The economic effects were severe, since the Austro-Hungarian economy had been one unit: mills around Budapest operated at 20% capacity. Hungary's boundaries have remained mostly the same since 1920, apart from the short-lived expansion of 1938–1941. The treaty is known in Hungary as the Peace Dictate of Trianon.
treaty-of-troyes: English kings had claimed the French throne since Edward III assumed the title in 1340. Henry V invaded France in 1415 and again in 1417, helped by the condition of Charles VI, who suffered bouts of mental illness from 1392 and whose intermittent incapacity encouraged rivalry among the royal family.

The murder of the king's brother Louis, Duke of Orléans, on the orders of John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, in 1407 left a lasting division between Burgundians and Armagnacs. After Henry conquered Normandy, talks in 1419 collapsed, and on 10 September 1419 John the Fearless was assassinated at Montereau by one of the Dauphin's attendants. His son Philip the Good then allied with Henry, and Henry now demanded the French crown itself.

The treaty was sealed in Troyes Cathedral on 21 May 1420, in the name of Charles VI, though Henry largely dictated its terms. Charles was to remain king for life, after which the crown would pass to Henry and his heirs, with the two kingdoms keeping their own laws and customs.

Henry was to be styled heir of France, to take over the government, and to marry Charles's daughter Catherine of Valois; the wedding took place on 2 June 1420. The Dauphin was disinherited and referred to only as "Charles, calling himself dauphin of Viennois". The treaty avoided saying whether Henry's right came from the English claim or from Charles's authority.

The Estates General approved the treaty in December 1420, though it represented only those parts of France willing to accept it, and its validity was questioned in France from the outset, since a king could not disinherit his son. Henry V died on 31 August 1422, less than two months before Charles VI, so his infant son Henry VI became king of England and, under the treaty, of France.

The Dauphin claimed the throne as Charles VII and was crowned at Reims on 17 July 1429. Philip the Good broke with the English in 1435 at the Treaty of Arras. The treaty was never formally rescinded, and English and British monarchs styled themselves kings of France until 1801.
treaty-of-tubingen: Württemberg, a county of the Holy Roman Empire since the late 11th century, was raised to a duchy by Emperor Maximilian I at the Diet of Worms in 1495. The count at the time, Eberhard V, who had reunited the county in 1480, died that year and left the duchy, with 300,000 florins of debt, to his cousin, Duke Eberhard II. Maximilian deposed Eberhard II in March 1498, and the Estates formed a four-man regency council for the nine-year-old Ulrich until Maximilian declared him of age in 1503, against the Treaty of Esslingen of 1492, which set the age of majority at 20.

Ulrich opened his reign with a successful campaign in the War of the Succession of Landshut, but his debts grew until by 1514 the duchy owed more than a million florins. A 6% wealth tax was so unpopular that it never became law, and the indirect tax on consumables that followed fell hardest on the lower classes. Peasants of the Remstal rose against it in 1514 in the Poor Conrad revolt, one of the Bundschuh peasant risings in south-western Germany between 1493 and 1517.

The treaty ended the revolt: Ulrich's recent taxes were annulled, and the Estates agreed to pay off his large debts. It turned the Estates into a check on ducal power and served as a kind of written constitution for the duchy until its annulment in 1805. Scholars once called it a Württemberger Magna Carta, a comparison since discredited, and the theologian and historian Hellmut G. Haasis called it a shambles that made no real progress towards a democratic state. For the city's part in ending the revolt, Ulrich granted Tübingen the right, on 18 August 1514, to bear the ducal stag antlers on its coat of arms.
treaty-of-turin-1860: At a secret meeting at Plombières-les-Bains on 21 July 1858, Emperor Napoleon III and Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Sardinia, agreed that France would back Sardinia's unification of Italy, provided the Pope kept Rome, and that Sardinia would cede the Duchy of Savoy and, more contentiously, the predominantly Italian speaking County of Nice. Austria declared war on Sardinia in April 1859 and was beaten at Palestro, Montebello, Magenta and Solferino, but Napoleon III, horrified by the bloodshed, ended the fighting with the armistice of Villafranca on 12 July 1859.

Among the liberal elites in francophone Savoy, many resented what they saw as discrimination against French speakers in government posts, and on 25 July 1859 about 30 leading citizens of Chambéry asked Napoleon III to annex the province. In the north of Savoy opposition mobilised, and some proposed joining Switzerland, an outcome Great Britain favoured.

In the treaty the King of Sardinia consented to the annexation of Savoy and the arrondissement of Nice and renounced his rights to them, on the understanding that it would be carried out without constraint on the wishes of the populations. He could transfer the neutralised parts of Savoy only on the terms on which he held them, and a mixed commission was to fix the frontier. A duty-free zone was confirmed north of a line through Saint-Genix-sur-Guiers, Le Châtelard, Faverges and Ugine, and the neutrality agreed for northern Savoy in 1815 at the Congress of Vienna was restated. Baron de Talleyrand Périgord and Benedetti signed for France, Cavour and Farini for Sardinia.
