The plebiscites were open to adult men only. In northern Savoy the accepted vote was Yes and Zone. France took formal possession of Nice and Savoy on 12 June 1860, ending centuries of Savoyard rule. The vote in Nice has been heavily criticised: many Niçards were left off the electoral lists, French residents were enrolled, and the poll took place under French authorities with French troops in the city. Of 119 Niçard sailors who voted at sea, 114 chose to remain with Italy. About a quarter of the Niçard Italians emigrated to Italy in what became known as the Niçard exodus.
treaty-of-turkmenchay: The treaty was the second of a series of agreements between Qajar Iran and Imperial Russia that forced Iran to cede or recognise Russian influence over territories that had formerly belonged to it. The first was the Treaty of Gulistan of 1813 and the last the Treaty of Akhal of 1881. It was signed on 22 February 1828 in Torkamanchay, a village between Tabriz and Tehran, for Iran by Crown Prince Abbas Mirza and Allah-Yar Khan Asef al-Dowleh, chancellor to Fath-Ali Shah Qajar, and for Russia by General Ivan Paskievich. As with Gulistan, the treaty was imposed after a Russian military victory, and Paskievich threatened to occupy Tehran in five days unless it was signed.

Under Article 4 Iran ceded the Erivan Khanate, the Nakhchivan Khanate and the Talysh Khanate, together with the Ordubad and Mughan regions, and repeated the cessions of Gulistan. The Aras River became the boundary. Iran promised to pay 10 korur in gold or 20 million silver rubles, and Persian ships lost the right to navigate the Caspian Sea, which passed to Russia. Russia promised to support Abbas Mirza as heir to the throne, a clause that became moot when he died before Fath-Ali Shah.

The treaty also recognised capitulation rights for Russian subjects in Iran and allowed Russia to send consular envoys anywhere in the country. Article 15 gave the inhabitants of Iranian Azerbaijan the right to move to Russian districts within one year, and provided for the resettlement of Armenians in the Caucasus.

The historian Alexander Mikaberidze describes the treaty as the definite acknowledgement of the Persian loss of the Caucasus to Russia. The formerly Iranian territories came under Russian, and later Soviet, control for about 180 years. Dagestan remains a constituent republic of the Russian Federation, while Georgia, Azerbaijan and Armenia, which together held most of the territory ceded at Gulistan and Turkmenchay, became independent after the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

Armenians from Iranian Azerbaijan used the freedom to emigrate, and in the years 1828 to 1831 some 45,000 are recorded as moving to Russian Armenia. Anti-Russian feeling was widespread in Persia after the treaty. On 11 February 1829 a mob stormed the Russian embassy in Tehran and killed almost everyone inside, among them the newly appointed ambassador, the playwright Aleksander Griboyedov, who had helped to negotiate the terms. As an apology the shah presented the tsar with the Shah Diamond.
treaty-of-utrecht: The War of the Spanish Succession involved three contenders for the vacant throne of Spain and drew in much of Europe for over a decade. On 2 January 1710 King Louis XIV of France agreed to open peace negotiations at Geertruidenberg in the Netherlands. France and Great Britain came to terms in October 1711, when the preliminaries were signed in London, and these rested on a tacit acceptance of the partition of Spain's European possessions. The Congress of Utrecht opened on 29 January 1712. Little progress came until 10 July 1712, when Philip V signed a renunciation of the French throne.

The peace was a series of treaties signed in Utrecht between April 1713 and February 1715. The main treaties were signed on 11 April 1713, five separate agreements between France and Great Britain, the Dutch Republic, Savoy, Prussia and Portugal. Spain signed treaties with Savoy and Great Britain on 13 July 1713. Philip V, grandson of Louis XIV, remained king of Spain and renounced the French throne for himself and his descendants, with reciprocal renunciations by French Bourbons.

In Article X Spain ceded Gibraltar and Menorca to Britain, which also gained the Asiento de Negros, the monopoly contract to supply slaves to Spain's American colonies, for thirty years. Britain demanded that France level the fortifications of Dunkirk, the main base of French privateers. Savoy received Sicily and parts of the Duchy of Milan, while the former Spanish Netherlands, Naples, Sardinia and most of Milan went to Emperor Charles VI. France ceded Nova Scotia and its claims to Newfoundland and Rupert's Land to Britain, and the French portion of Saint Kitts.

The treaty stipulated that one person should never become king of both France and Spain. Some historians see it as a milestone in the evolution of the balance of power. The Whigs in Britain opposed the peace, but the Tory ministry of Robert Harley and Viscount Bolingbroke persuaded Queen Anne to create twelve new Tory peers to ensure ratification in the House of Lords. Dutch influence was slight, though the talks were held on their territory.

Catalonia received no guarantees of its rights, and the War of the Catalans of 1713 to 1714 followed. The Dutch Republic ended the war effectively bankrupt, and Britain emerged with naval superiority and commercial access to Spain and America. The historian G. M. Trevelyan wrote that the treaty marked the end of danger to Europe from the old French monarchy and the maritime, commercial and financial supremacy of Great Britain.
treaty-of-venlo: The Guelders Wars, which the treaty ended, grew out of an old dispute. At the end of the Second War of the Guelderian Succession (1423–1448), Gerhard VII, Duke of Jülich-Berg, sold his claims to the Duchy of Guelders to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy. Philip's son Charles the Bold exploited a quarrel in the ruling House of Egmont between Duke Arnold and his son Adolf to seize Guelders in 1473. After Charles died in 1477, his daughter Mary married Maximilian of Austria, and the Burgundian lands passed to the Habsburgs.

The States of Guelders used the confusion to declare independence and proclaim Adolf's son Charles II as duke, and the Guelderian War of Independence (1477–1499) ended in a Habsburg defeat. From 1502, with the support of France, Charles II fought Philip the Handsome and then his son Charles V for 36 years, at times holding Oversticht, Nedersticht, the city of Groningen and its Ommelanden and most of Frisia, and raiding Holland and Brabant.

Charles II died without an heir in 1538, and the States of Guelders elected William, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, to succeed him. By 1543 Habsburg troops occupied all of Guelders, Zutphen and Jülich, and France failed to come to William's aid, so he sued for peace. At Venlo he gave up his claims to Guelders and Zutphen in favour of Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain, and committed himself to suppressing Protestantism in his remaining lands of Jülich, Cleves, Berg, Mark and Ravenstein.

The treaty brought the Guelders Wars of 1502–1543 to a close and completed the Habsburg acquisition of the Duchy of Guelders and the adjoining County of Zutphen, which were added to the Habsburg Netherlands.
treaty-of-verdun: After Charlemagne's death Louis I was made ruler of the Frankish Empire, and he divided it so that each of his sons could rule a kingdom under his own greater rule. His eldest son, Lothair I, held the title of emperor, but after several re-divisions and the revolts that followed he became much less powerful. When Louis died in 840, Lothair claimed overlordship over the entire realm. His brother Louis II and his half-brother Charles II refused to accept it and declared war. They defeated Lothair at the Battle of Fontenoy in 841 and sealed their alliance in 842 with the Oaths of Strasbourg, which declared Lothair unfit for the imperial throne. After this he was willing to negotiate.

The treaty was agreed on 10 August 843, after more than a year of negotiations, and ended the civil war. Each brother already held a kingdom: Lothair in Italy, Louis in Bavaria and Charles in Aquitaine. Lothair kept the imperial title, but it now gave only nominal overlordship of his brothers' lands. He received Francia Media, the Middle Frankish kingdom, with the two imperial cities, Aachen and Rome. This domain later covered the Low Countries, Lorraine, Alsace, Burgundy, Provence and the Kingdom of Italy.

Louis received Francia Orientalis, the East Frankish kingdom, all lands east of the Rhine, which became the high medieval Kingdom of Germany. Charles received Francia Occidentalis, all lands west of the Rhône, which eventually became the Kingdom of France.

The division followed the old Frankish custom of partible inheritance among a ruler's sons rather than primogeniture, which both Frankish kingdoms would soon adopt. It was the first of four partition treaties of the Carolingian Empire, followed by those of Prüm in 855, Meerssen in 870 and Ribemont in 880. Only Charles the Fat briefly reassembled Charlemagne's empire.

After Lothair's death in 855 his eldest son Louis II inherited Italy and the imperial claim, and the northern territory was named Lotharingia after Lothair II. With long, vulnerable land borders and poor communications, it was not a viable entity and soon fragmented. Generations of kings of France and Germany failed to establish firm rule there, and Alsace-Lorraine passed between the two powers from the 18th to the 20th century.
treaty-of-vereeniging: On 9 April 1902, under a British guarantee of safe passage, the Boer leaders met at Klerksdorp in the Transvaal: the Free State president Marthinus Steyn, the acting Transvaal president Schalk Burger and the generals Louis Botha, Jan Smuts, Christiaan de Wet and Koos de la Rey. On 12 April a ten-man delegation went to Melrose House in Pretoria and put a seven-point proposal to General Kitchener, asking for a return to the pre-war position with a commercial union, votes for uitlanders, equal languages in schools and an amnesty.

Kitchener forwarded it to London knowing it would be refused, because he wanted the talks to go on. Alfred Milner, who joined on 14 April, was hostile to the Boers and wanted an unconditional surrender. The British government rejected the proposal.

On 15 May thirty delegates elected by the commandos of each republic met at Vereeniging. The Transvaalers, whose civilians lived in desperate conditions, wanted an end to the war, while the Free Staters wished to fight on. Their compromise, brought to Pretoria on 19 May, would have kept the republics independent under British control of foreign relations, and was rejected. Kitchener sought reconciliation and Milner humiliation, and the talks dragged on. Botha asked £3 million for the Boers' war debts and promissory notes against a British offer of £1 million, and Kitchener sided with him.

The Boers received the final terms on 28 May and were given three days to answer. Steyn, who argued against them, resigned through illness after the first day of debate. At about 2 pm on 31 May the delegates voted 54 to 6 in favour, and the treaty was signed that day at Melrose House.

All Boer fighters surrendered and were disarmed and had to swear allegiance to the Crown. In return no death sentences would be passed, a general amnesty applied, Dutch was allowed in schools and law courts, property rights were respected, no land taxes were introduced and registered private guns were permitted. Cape rebels lost the vote for five years. The two colonies received civil government in 1906 and 1907. The Union of South Africa followed on 31 May 1910, and the country became a republic in 1961.
treaty-of-versailles: The armistice of 11 November 1918 ended the fighting but left the peace to be settled. It took six months of Allied negotiations at the Paris Peace Conference to conclude a treaty. Talks between the Allies began on 18 January 1919 at the French Foreign Ministry on the Quai d'Orsay, with 70 delegates from 27 nations.

The victors wanted different things. France had lost 1.3 million soldiers and had its industrial north-east devastated, and Clemenceau sought security by weakening Germany. British opinion favoured a just peace in which Germany paid reparations. President Woodrow Wilson, whose Fourteen Points of 8 January 1918 had called for a League of Nations and self-determination, hoped for a peace of reconciliation. The result was a compromise that satisfied none of them.

The treaty was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Palace of Versailles, five years to the day after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Germany lost 65,000 km2 of territory and 7 million people. Alsace-Lorraine returned to France, the Saar coalfield passed to France with the territory under League of Nations control for 15 years, and Eupen-Malmedy went to Belgium. Germany's colonies became League of Nations mandates, and its concessions in Shandong were given to Japan.

The army was limited to 100,000 men, conscription was abolished and the General Staff was dissolved. Allied troops were to occupy the Rhineland for up to fifteen years. Article 231, the so-called War Guilt clause, made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage of the war, and a Reparation Commission was to fix the sum. The Covenant of the League of Nations formed Part I of the treaty.

Germany protested that it was excluded from the talks. The government of Philipp Scheidemann resigned rather than sign, and Gustav Bauer's government signed after an Allied ultimatum threatening an invasion across the Rhine. The United States Senate never ratified the treaty, and the United States made a separate peace with Germany.

In 1921 the Reparation Commission set Germany's share at 50 billion gold marks, later reduced by the Dawes Plan and the Young Plan. The last Allied troops left the Rhineland on 30 June 1930. Critics such as John Maynard Keynes thought the treaty too harsh, while Marshal Ferdinand Foch thought it too lenient, and historians still disagree about its effects. Resentment of the treaty, together with the stab-in-the-back myth, was exploited by Adolf Hitler, and the treaty has been cited as a cause of the Second World War.
treaty-of-vilnius-1561: In 1513 the Grand Master of the Livonian Order had bought the order out of its union with the Teutonic Knights, and in 1546 the Recess of Wolmar forbade any future secularisation. The Protestant Reformation, begun in Riga in 1517, spread across Livonia. Weakened by internal struggles and a civil war from 1556, the Livonian Confederation turned to Poland–Lithuania for protection in the Treaty of Pozvol of 1557, which prompted Ivan IV of Russia to intervene in what became the Livonian War.

By an earlier Treaty of Vilnius, of 31 August 1559, Gotthard Kettler placed the order's lands under Sigismund's protection, but he was defeated at Ērģeme in 1560 and could not prevent Russian forces from occupying most of Livonia. The confederation then broke apart. In 1560 Magnus, brother of King Frederick II of Denmark, bought the bishoprics of Ösel-Wiek and Courland, in June 1561 part of Estonia submitted to Sweden, and Riga turned to the Holy Roman Empire.

The settlement had two parts. In the Pacta subiectionis, also called the Provisio ducalis, the Livonian estates accepted Polish-Lithuanian overlordship. In the Privilegium Sigismundi Augusti, Sigismund guaranteed their privileges: religious freedom under the Augsburg Confession, the Indigenat and the continuation of traditional German jurisdiction and administration. Courland and Semigallia became a hereditary fief on the Prussian model. North of the Daugava, Livonia was placed directly under Sigismund as the Duchy of Livonia, with Kettler as royal administrator, though without Riga, Swedish Reval or Danish Ösel.

Historians regard the secularisation of the order as the final act in Livonia's passage from the Middle Ages to the early modern era. Ivan IV overran nearly all of the Duchy of Livonia between 1572 and 1577, and only after the Battle of Wenden in 1578 and the end of the war could Sigismund's successor Stephen Báthory take control. He refused to confirm the privileges, replaced them in 1582 with the Constitutiones Livoniae and supported the Counter-Reformation. Swedish rule after the conquest restored privileges like those of 1561, and when Livonia capitulated to Russia in 1710 its terms explicitly cited the Privilegium, confirmed in the Treaty of Nystad of 1721.
treaty-of-wad-ras: Morocco entered the war already weakened. It had been defeated by the French in the Franco-Moroccan War of 1844, and in 1856 it signed the Anglo-Moroccan Treaty, which opened the country to foreign trade, granted rights to British subjects and reduced the control of the Makhzen, the sultan's government, over the economy. The Spanish campaign of 1859 answered skirmishes by local tribes around the Spanish enclaves.

After the Battle of Tetuan and the capture of the city in 1860, the Spanish general Leopoldo O'Donnell turned towards Tangier. The Moroccan army under al-Abass Bin Abderrahman, brother of Sultan Muhammad IV, met him at Wad Ras and suffered a heavy defeat, which forced the sultan to accept peace on Spain's terms.

Morocco was to pay a war indemnity of 20 million duros, far more than its treasury held, and Spain would occupy Tetuan and its surroundings until the sum was paid. The territory of Ceuta was extended to the Bullones Mountains, and a joint committee of engineers was to map the new border. The sultan confirmed an agreement of 24 August 1859 that pushed the limits of Melilla, Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera and the Alhucemas Islands out to a cannon shot, and undertook to guard the Spanish areas against hostile tribes.

Morocco gave up the land around the fort of Santa Cruz de la Mar Pequeña, later Sidi Ifni. Other articles provided for a Spanish mission in Fes, a Catholic church in Tetuan, most favoured nation status for Spain in trade, the right of the Spanish colonies to buy and export timber, and the release of prisoners on both sides.

To pay the indemnity Morocco borrowed from private investors in Britain. The loan amounted to £501,200, of which the sultan actually received £426,000, and it was to be repaid from half of the customs revenue of Moroccan ports under the oversight of European agents, while the other half went to Spain. The repayments took 12% of the customs revenue each year until the loan was cleared in 1882 and the British officials left the country.
treaty-of-waitangi: In nineteenth-century New Zealand the British wanted to formalise their involvement, protect British interests, regulate land speculation and control violence and disordered settlement. They faced a Māori population that was more numerous, with cultivated land and its own government. The New Zealand Company, acting for settlers and would-be settlers, was establishing a colony, and some Māori leaders had petitioned the British for protection against French ambitions.

With no draft from lawyers or Colonial Office officials, William Hobson wrote the treaty himself with his secretary James Freeman and the British Resident James Busby, neither a lawyer. It was prepared in three days and revised many times, and there were doubts even during drafting that the chiefs would grasp the idea of relinquishing sovereignty. It was translated into Māori overnight on 4 and 5 February 1840.

The treaty has a preamble and three articles, in English and Māori texts that differ. In Article One the Māori text grants kawanatanga, translated by Hugh Kāwharu as complete governance, while the English text cedes all the rights and powers of sovereignty. In Article Two the Māori text promises rangatiratanga, full chieftainship, over lands, villages and treasures, and the English text guarantees full, exclusive and undisturbed ownership, with the Crown holding the exclusive right of pre-emption to buy land.

Article Three gave Māori the Queen's protection and the rights of British subjects. At the signing a further statement was added in writing that the faiths of England, of the Wesleyans, of Rome and also Māori custom would be protected alike.

Hobson read the treaty in English and Henry Williams the Māori text to a hui of northern chiefs on 5 February 1840, and signing began on 6 February. Eight further copies were sent around the country for more signatures; around 530 to 540 Māori signed the Māori version and only 39 the English. On 21 May 1840 Hobson proclaimed sovereignty over the whole country, the North Island by treaty and the South Island and Stewart Island by discovery.

In 1877 Chief Justice Prendergast called the treaty a simple nullity in the case of Wi Parata v Bishop of Wellington, which remained legal orthodoxy until at least the 1970s. A Māori protest movement then called for the government to honour the treaty. The Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 marked a paradigm shift in official discourse on Māori rights, 6 February is now the national day, Waitangi Day, and the treaty entered UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 1997.
treaty-of-waitangi-act-1975: The treaty had been a focus of Māori activism for several years when Matiu Rata introduced the Treaty of Waitangi Bill in Parliament on 8 November 1974. Its purpose, he said, was to provide for the observation and confirmation of the principles of the treaty and to determine claims about matters inconsistent with them. The act gave the Treaty of Waitangi recognition in New Zealand law for the first time.

The preamble recalls that a treaty was entered into at Waitangi on 6 February 1840 between Queen Victoria and the Māori people, and that its English and Māori texts differ. The tribunal it set up was to determine the meaning and effect of the treaty and to investigate breaches of its principles by the government or any state-controlled body. It could recommend remedies but not enforce them, and many Māori were disappointed, since the gravest breaches, such as land confiscation in the New Zealand Wars, lay in the nineteenth century.

The 1985 amendment, part of the Fourth Labour government's policy of giving the treaty greater weight, enlarged the tribunal and required a Māori majority, a rule removed in 1988. The scope it opened led to continuing debate over how the Crown should answer the tribunal's findings. In 1988 different panels were allowed to hear claims at once, and after a court found the government ignoring treaty principles in selling state-owned land, covenants allowed such land to be claimed back even from private hands, the only legally binding orders the tribunal can make.

A 1993 amendment, following the Te Roroa Report, barred the tribunal from recommending the return or purchase of other private land. In 2006 a closing date of 1 September 2008 was set for historical claims, those concerning the Crown's acts before 21 September 1992, and settlement acts remove the tribunal's jurisdiction over claims already settled. In 2014, in the Te Paparahi o Te Raki inquiry, the tribunal concluded that Māori never ceded their sovereignty in 1840. In May 2025 the Minister of Māori Development, Tama Potaka, announced a review of the act.
treaty-of-washington-1871: Early in 1871 the government of William Gladstone sent Sir John Rose to the United States to learn whether President Ulysses S. Grant would accept talks on the north-western boundary dispute. Secretary of State Hamilton Fish received him cordially, and on 26 January Sir Edward Thornton, the British minister in Washington, proposed a joint high commission. The United States agreed on condition that the differences arising from the American Civil War were also on the table, and Britain accepted.

Britain named the Earl de Grey and Ripon, Sir Stafford Northcote, Lord Tenterden, Thornton, Mountague Bernard and the Canadian prime minister John A. Macdonald. The American commissioners were Fish, as chairman, Robert Schenck, Ebenezer R. Hoar, George Henry Williams, Samuel Nelson and J. C. Bancroft Davis. Macdonald's presence showed that the new Dominion of Canada would take part in settling foreign matters that touched it directly. On 8 May the commission concluded a treaty, which both governments promptly approved.

Besides the Alabama claims, the treaty set up a mixed commission at Halifax to value the fishing privileges each side granted the other, and in 1877 it directed the United States to pay $5,500,000 to Britain. William I, German Emperor, was made arbitrator over the San Juan Islands, and on 21 October 1872 he awarded the whole archipelago to the United States. At Geneva in 1872 the United States was awarded $15,500,000; Britain apologised for the damage done by the British-built Confederate ships but admitted no guilt.

The treaty brought Canada no compensation, and it was widely condemned in the Canadian press. When it came before the House of Commons, Macdonald revealed that he had secretly obtained an American cash payment for the use of Canadian fishing grounds, in place of any claim over the Fenians, and a British guaranteed loan of £3,600,000 for the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Parliament of Canada then ratified it.

The scholar of international law John Bassett Moore singled it out as a treaty of actual and immediate arbitration without equal. Its rules of Washington on the duties of neutrals influenced the Congress of Berlin of 1878. After it, war between the United States and Britain was never seriously considered again, the United States largely stopped official talk of annexing Canada, and the treaty made possible the Great Rapprochement between the two powers.
treaty-of-westminster-ardtornish: During the minority of James III of Scotland the Scottish crown took the Lancastrian side in the Wars of the Roses by welcoming the fugitive Henry VI of England, who was then in the keeping of James's mother, Mary of Guelders. Edward IV of the House of York sought to reduce the threat of the exiled king by forming alliances with disaffected English and Scottish nobles.

The Earl of Douglas and his brother John Douglas of Balvenie carried Edward's proposals to the west of Scotland. The highland lords gave their assent at Ardtornish Castle on 19 October 1461 and sent Ranald of the Isles and Duncan, Archdeacon of the Isles, to London as their envoys. The articles were finalised and sealed at Westminster Palace on 13 February 1462, and Edward IV signed them on 17 March. John of Islay, Earl of Ross, Donald Balagh and his son and heir John, with all the people of Ross and the Isles, were to become Edward's subjects at Whitsunday.

The agreement was followed by an attack by the Earl of Ross on crown lands near Inverness in 1462 and 1463. The Scottish crown made its own alliance with Edward IV by the treaty of York in 1464. When the English court revealed the agreement in 1475, John was summoned for treason, the charges including leagues and bands with Edward IV and the banished Earl of Douglas, and he calmed matters only by giving up Ross, which then included Skye.

In 1491 his half-nephew tried to recover Ross in the Raid on Ross, which the Scottish king used as grounds for abolishing the Lordship of the Isles. Historians have judged the treaty differently. Andrew Lang described it as an attempt to stab Scotland in the back with a Celtic dirk, while Norman Macdougall thought its significance had been overplayed by such earlier writers. The Douglases were at that time generally the leaders of the pro-English party in Scotland.
treaty-of-windsor-1175: The treaty was made during the Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland, at Windsor in Berkshire, in the octaves of Michaelmas, around 6 October 1175. It was negotiated for Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair by Catholicus, Archbishop of Tuam, the abbot of Clonfert and Master Laurence, chancellor of the king of Connacht. Among its witnesses were Laurence O'Toole, Archbishop of Dublin, William, Earl of Essex, and the justiciar Richard de Luci.

Henry II granted Ruaidrí, as his liegeman, that he would be king under him and hold his land as fully as before Henry entered Ireland, so long as he served him faithfully and paid tribute. Ruaidrí was to keep the rest of Ireland under him and collect its tribute for the king of England: one acceptable hide for every ten animals slaughtered. The other kings and peoples kept their lands while they stayed loyal, and any who rebelled Ruaidrí was to judge and remove, with the help of Henry's constable if needed.

Outside his authority stayed the lands Henry kept for himself and his barons: Dublin, Meath, the whole of Leinster, and Waterford with its territory as far as Dungarvan. Irish who had fled the barons' lands might return in peace, and Ruaidrí was to take hostages from those committed to him and give hostages himself. All Ireland was also bound by the religious provisions of the papal bull Laudabiliter and the Synod of Cashel of 1172.

The two kings understood the treaty differently. Henry saw Ruaidrí as his subordinate in the feudal order, paying him a yearly rent on behalf of all his sub-kings, while Ruaidrí saw himself as the restored High King of Ireland, owing only a modest tribute; the Annals of Tigernach recorded that the kingship of all Ireland had been given to him. The treaty was soon broken as land-hungry Anglo-Norman lords expanded, and in 1177 Henry repudiated it and named his son John Lord of Ireland.
treaty-of-wuchale: The treaty was signed in the small Ethiopian town of Wuchale by Menelik II, King of Shewa acting as Emperor of Ethiopia, and Count Pietro Antonelli for Italy, after the Italian occupation of Eritrea. European colonisation of Africa was expanding fast, and Italy, which already held large territories in Eritrea and Somalia, wished to extend its rule to Ethiopia. Menelik resisted this and agreed to a treaty instead, yielding some territory in return for assurances of Ethiopia's independence and for financial and military help from Italy.

The treaty had twenty articles in Amharic and Italian. It declared peace between the two monarchs and their successors, allowed each to appoint consuls in the other's lands and drew a boundary in the highlands, leaving Segheneiti and other highland places to Italy. The monastery of Debra Bizen stayed under Ethiopian control but could not be used for military purposes. Ethiopia paid an eight per cent duty on goods through Massawa but could move its army through the port free of charge. Other articles allowed trade and travel, guaranteed freedom of religion, dealt with disputes, inheritance, crime and extradition, and gave the emperor the right to act against slavery and the slave trade, which Menelik opposed.

Article 17 differed between the two texts. In Amharic it said the King of Kings of Ethiopia could use the Italian government for all business with other powers, leaving him a choice; the Italian text obliged Ethiopia to conduct its foreign affairs through Italy, in effect making it a protectorate. The Italians attributed the difference to the mistranslation of a verb, permissive in one language and mandatory in the other.

In October 1889 Italy told the European governments that Ethiopia was now its protectorate and that they could not deal with it directly. All accepted the claim except the Ottoman Empire, which still claimed Eritrea, and Russia, which disliked an Orthodox nation being subjected to a Catholic one. Menelik rejected Italian protection and denounced the treaty, and Italy invaded in 1895. The war ended with Ethiopia's victory after a two-day battle at Adwa, which preserved its independence, and with the Treaty of Addis Ababa.
treaty-of-yandabo: The First Anglo-Burmese War had formally broken out on 5 March 1824. After their victory at the Battle of Danubyu in April 1825, which killed the Burmese commander-in-chief Maha Bandula, the British held Lower Burma, Rakhine, the Taninthayi coast, Assam and Manipur. Peace talks opened in September 1825 at Ngagyaungbinzeik, north of Pyay. The British demanded Rakhine, a Resident at the Court of Ava and an indemnity of two million pounds; the Burmese envoy, the lord of Kawlin, offered to give up Assam and Manipur and to cede Taninthayi but not Rakhine.

The talks broke down. In November 1825 Burmese forces under Maha Ne Myo, largely Shan regiments led by their own sawbwas, nearly recaptured Pyay, but by early December British firepower had defeated them. Early in 1826 the British advanced on Ava, taking Pagan on 8 February and the village of Yandabo on 16 February, about four days' march from the capital.

King Bagyidaw sent a delegation of one American, one English and two Burmese ministers to General Sir Archibald Campbell. There was no real negotiation: the Burmese accepted every demand. The treaty was signed by Campbell and by Maha Min Hla Kyaw Htin, Governor of Legaing. The Burmese paid a first installment of 250,000 pounds in gold and silver bullion and released British prisoners of war; the British would stay in Yangon until the second installment was paid.

The war was the longest and most expensive in the history of British India. Some 40,000 British and Indian troops took part, of whom 15,000 died, with an unknown but probably higher number of Burmese dead. Its cost contributed to an economic crisis that by 1833 had bankrupted the Bengal agency houses and cost the East India Company its monopoly of trade with China.

For Burma the indemnity, equal to 10 million kyat when a villager in Upper Burma lived on one kyat a month, left the royal treasury bankrupt for years. The Court of Ava tried without success to recover the lost lands. The British fought two more wars against the weakened kingdom, in 1852 and 1885, and annexed the whole country by 1885.
treaty-of-yazhelbitsy: The war of 1456 closed a long succession struggle in which Grand Prince Vasily II of Moscow and Vladimir prevailed over his cousin, Prince Dmitry Shemyaka. Shemyaka had died by poison in Novgorod in 1453, probably at the hands of the grand prince's agents, though some scholars suggest that Archbishop Evfimy II had him poisoned as a liability to Novgorod. His widow fled to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania with their son, Ivan Dmitriyevich. After their crushing defeat the Novgorodians met in their assembly, the veche, and according to the sources asked the archbishop to go to the grand prince's camp at Yazhelbitsy and learn his terms.

After several days of hard bargaining the treaty was signed in February 1456. It survives in two copies, one signed by Moscow and one by Novgorod, both now in the Russian National Library in Saint Petersburg, and their texts differ. The Novgorodian version has the archbishop blessing the treaty and a chronicle says he led the delegation, but the Muscovite version does not list him among the envoys. Novgorod kept some customary guarantees against the grand prince's meddling in its internal affairs, but it lost the right to pass its own laws, the grand prince became its highest court, and the seals of the veche and of the posadniks were replaced by the princely seal.

Moscow did not yet rule the city directly, but Novgorod's republican system was heavily curtailed. Vasily II was satisfied enough to make small territorial concessions, and the seals were exchanged at once. Other terms were broken again and again, partly because the two versions were worded differently: Novgorod went on admitting Moscow's enemies, while Vasily II and his successor Ivan III upheld Muscovite boyars who seized Novgorodian estates. Fifteen years of mutual accusations led to a new war in 1471, and in 1478 Ivan III took direct control of Novgorod.
treaty-of-zadar: After the Árpád dynasty died out in 1301, the Angevin dynasty came to rule Hungary and Croatia. Its first king, Charles Robert, who ruled from 1312 to 1342, was at first supported by the most powerful Croatian nobleman, Pavao Šubić, Prince of Bribir and Ban of Croatia, who held the coastal cities of Split, Trogir and Šibenik and wielded many of a monarch's powers, from minting coin to taxing towns.

The Croatian nobles revolted against Pavao and turned to King Charles for help, but in return had to swear direct allegiance to the Hungarian crown. This prepared the way for Hungarian attempts to drive Venice from the Dalmatian coast, where the towns were caught in a tug of war between the two powers. Ragusa, then held by Venice, was meanwhile growing rich from its position between the West and the mineral-rich kingdoms of Serbia and Bosnia.

In the 1350s Louis I of Hungary gathered a force of 50,000 men, joined by troops of the Duke of Austria, the Counts of Gorizia, Francesco I da Carrara, Lord of Padua, and the Patriarchate of Aquileia. In 1356 the coalition besieged the Venetians at Asolo, Conegliano, Ceneda and Treviso, while along the coast it attacked Zadar, Trogir, Split, Ragusa and smaller towns, which mostly surrendered quickly. After a series of defeats Venice accepted unfavourable terms, and the treaty was signed in the cloister of the Monastery of St. Francis in Zadar.

Venice kept the Istrian coast and the region of Treviso, and its naval predominance in the Adriatic survived, since Louis agreed not to build a fleet of his own. Louis entered Zadar in triumph in 1358, granted wide privileges to its nobility and made it the capital of Dalmatia. The treaty marked the rise of the Republic of Ragusa as an independent and successful state. Zadar fared differently: it was later sold back to Venice by Ladislaus of Naples.
treaty-of-zamora: After his victory at the Battle of São Mamede, Afonso Henriques held the County of Portugal but avoided the title of count, which implied subordination to León, calling himself infante or prince instead. When Alfonso VII crowned himself Emperor of Spain in 1135 and received the homage of the peninsula's rulers, Afonso stayed away. He allied with King García Ramírez of Navarre, seized Tuy and Turonio in Galicia, and in 1139, at the Battle of Ourique, was raised on a shield and hailed as king by his troops.

A Leonese invasion ended in the Battle of Arcos de Valdevez in 1141, a minor encounter favourable to the Portuguese, in which several high-ranking Leonese nobles were captured. The truce that followed was mediated by João Peculiar, Archbishop of Braga, who brought both kings and the legate of Pope Innocent II to Zamora.

The two cousins met at Zamora on 4 and 5 October 1143 and parted amicably. The text has been lost, so the conditions are known only indirectly. Both kings pledged peace, and Afonso was acknowledged as king, apparently while keeping earlier duties of military aid. He probably agreed not to expand eastwards into León and to turn against al-Andalus instead. Alfonso VII seems to have granted him the lordship of Astorga to bind him as a vassal, keeping a technical superiority.

The treaty eased border tensions until 1157. Afonso styled himself rex Portugallensis without formal protest from León, and later Leonese lists of Alfonso VII's vassals left him out. On 13 December 1143 he wrote to the Pope declaring himself a vassal of Saint Peter and offering four ounces of gold a year. Pope Lucius II accepted the tribute in 1144 but still called him dux Portugalensium.

After Alfonso VII died in 1157, his son Ferdinand II of León tried to reassert overlordship, but by 1166 he had given up the claim. Afonso raised his tribute to two marks, and Pope Alexander III's bull Manifestis Probatum confirmed Portugal's independence. In Portugal 5 October is today a national holiday, as the day the republic was established in 1910.
treaty-of-zaragoza: The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 set a meridian in the Atlantic, with areas to the west exclusive to Spain and those to the east to Portugal, but the precise line was never established and each side interpreted it in the most favourable light. Afonso de Albuquerque conquered Malacca in 1511. Learning the location of the Spice Islands, the Bandas and Ternate and Tidore in the Malukus, then the single source of nutmeg and cloves, he sent an expedition under António de Abreu, which arrived in early 1512. Abreu's lieutenant Francisco Serrão obtained a licence at Ternate to build a Portuguese factory and fortress.

Letters from Serrão helped his friend Ferdinand Magellan persuade the Spanish crown to finance a voyage round the world. On 6 November 1521 Magellan's fleet, now under Juan Sebastián Elcano, reached the Moluccas from the east. Charles V then sent García Jofre de Loaísa to colonise the islands. The Spanish built a fort on Tidore, there was conflict with the Portuguese on Ternate, and nearly a decade of skirmishes followed.

In 1524 both kingdoms organised the Junta de Badajoz–Elvas. Each crown appointed three astronomers and cartographers, three pilots and three mathematicians, to fix the antimeridian of Tordesillas, with the aim of dividing the world into two equal hemispheres. The committee met several times without agreement, since geographic knowledge was inadequate to assign longitude accurately and each group chose maps or globes that put the islands in its own hemisphere.

Marriages eased the way. Charles V's sister Catherine of Austria married John III on 10 February 1525, and on 11 March 1526 Charles married John's sister Isabella of Portugal. It was in the emperor's interest to avoid conflict so as to concentrate on European policy, and the Spaniards did not yet know how to carry spices from the Malukus to Europe by the eastern route.

The treaty fixed the eastern boundary between the two zones at 297½ leagues, or 1,763 kilometres, or 17°, east of the Maluku Islands, leaving them within the Portuguese domain, in exchange for 350,000 gold ducats paid to Charles V. A safeguard clause allowed the emperor to undo the deal by reimbursing the money, but he needed the Portuguese payment to finance the War of the League of Cognac against Francis I of France. The treaty did not clarify the Tordesillas line or validate Spain's claim to equal hemispheres of 180° each, so the two lines divided the Earth into unequal portions: about 191° for Portugal and about 169° for Spain.
treaty-of-zboriv: The treaty was signed on 18 August 1649 after the Battle of Zboriv, where Crown forces of about 35,000 under King John II Casimir clashed with about 50,000 Cossacks and Crimean Tatars led by Hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky and Khan İslâm III Giray of Crimea. It consisted of two separate agreements, one between Ukraine and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and one between Crimea and the Commonwealth. Ivan Vyhovsky signed beside Khmelnytsky, while Adam Kysil, Jerzy Ossoliński, Janusz Radziwiłł and Władysław Dominik Zasławski represented the Polish side.

All freedoms of the Zaporozhian Cossacks were kept, and the hetman was to draw up the register himself, to be completed by the feast of the Intercession of the Theotokos. The territory ran on the Right Bank of the Dnieper through Dymer, Korostyshiv, Vinnytsia and Bratslav to Yampil on the Dniester, and on the Left Bank through Oster, Chernihiv, Nizhyn and Romny to the Muscovite border. Chyhyryn was made the Cossack Host's city forever and given to Khmelnytsky.

Past acts in the rising were to be forgotten, and the nobles who had joined the Cossacks, Orthodox and Catholic alike, were pardoned. Crown troops, Uniates and Jews were barred from the three voivodeships, offices there were reserved for Orthodox nobles, and the Orthodox Church gained privileges. Jesuit fathers were not to be established in Kiev or the other Ukrainian cities, and a large sum was to be paid to the Crimean Khanate.

The Sejm of the Commonwealth ratified the treaty on 22 November 1649, approving the declaration made at Zboriv with the consent of all the Estates. Hostilities resumed when Catholic bishops refused to accept its provisions, notably the admission of the Orthodox metropolitan of Kyiv, Sylvestr Kosiv, to the Senate. In the history of Ukraine the treaty is seen as having turned former rebels against the Commonwealth into citizens of a new political community.
treaty-of-zuhab: The Treaty of Zuhab is also called the Treaty of Qasr-e Shirin. It was signed on 17 May 1639 at Qasr-e Shirin in western Iran and ended the Ottoman-Safavid War of 1623 to 1639. That war was the last conflict in almost 150 years of intermittent wars between the two states over territorial disputes. The treaty can roughly be seen as a confirmation of the earlier Peace of Amasya of 1555, and according to Professor Ernest Tucker it was the culmination of a process of normalisation between the two empires that had begun with that peace.

The treaty confirmed a permanent partition of the Caucasus between the two powers. East Armenia, eastern Georgia, Dagestan and Shirvan stayed under Safavid control, while western Georgia and most of Western Armenia came fully under Ottoman rule. All of Mesopotamia, including Baghdad, was ceded to the Ottomans and became Ottoman Iraq. Eastern Samtskhe (Meskheti), which had been Safavid, passed to the Ottomans too, so that Samtskhe was entirely an Ottoman possession. Eastern Armenia remained for more than eight decades under Safavid rule, which divided it into the Erivan and Karabakh provinces.

The treaty was vague, and that opened the regions it settled to later contestation. Border disputes between Iran and the Ottoman Empire did not end: between 1555 and 1918 the two signed no fewer than 18 treaties that re-addressed their disputed borders.

Efforts to fix the exact line, using this treaty and other sources, began in the 19th century and laid out the rough outline of the frontier between modern Iran and the states of Turkey and Iraq, which was the Ottoman-Iranian border until 1918. Unlike any other Ottoman-Safavid treaty, Zuhab proved resilient and became a point of departure for almost all later diplomatic agreements between the two neighbours.
treaty-on-the-creation-of-the-ussr: The treaty's text was prepared by a commission of the Central Committee of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and was the result of many conflicts within the party and the governments of the republics. The failure of the Polish–Soviet War put plans for world revolution on hold. In spring 1922 Lenin suffered his first stroke, and Joseph Stalin became General Secretary of the Communist Party. Stalin argued that, with the Civil War over, the state should become a single sovereign entity whose legal form matched its de facto condition.

This conflicted with supporters of korenizatsiya and with local governments, notably in Ukraine, where Christian Rakovsky opposed it, and in Georgia, where the dispute gave rise to the Georgian Affair. The treaty can be read as a compromise that also created a centralised federal government with key functions in Moscow. The first talks between the republics began in August 1922.

The treaty and the declaration were approved on 30 December 1922 by a conference of delegations from the Russian SFSR, the Transcaucasian SFSR, the Ukrainian SSR and the Byelorussian SSR, and confirmed by the First All-Union Congress of Soviets. The treaty had a preface and 26 articles. The Union took charge of foreign affairs, war and peace, foreign and domestic trade, the armed forces and a single judiciary, and could overturn republican acts that violated the treaty.

Legislative power lay with the Congress of Soviets and, between congresses, the Central Executive Committee, while the Council of People's Commissars was the executive. The treaty created a single Soviet citizenship, a flag, anthem and coat of arms, and named Moscow the capital. Article 26 affirmed each republic's right to leave the Union.

In January 1924 the Second Congress of Soviets ratified the first Soviet Constitution, which rewrote and expanded the treaty. Some experts argue the original Union ceased to exist when the constitution of 5 December 1936 centralised it. On 8 December 1991 the Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian leaders signed the Belovezha Accords, denouncing the 1922 treaty and establishing the Commonwealth of Independent States. On 26 December 1991 the Council of the Republics of the Supreme Soviet voted the Soviet Union out of existence.
treaty-principles-bill: The Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840 by Māori chiefs and representatives of the British Crown: 39 chiefs signed the English text and over 500 the Māori text, Te Tiriti o Waitangi, which is not an exact translation of it. The Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which set up the Waitangi Tribunal, introduced the phrase the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi without defining them, leaving the Tribunal, the courts and the Crown to interpret them.

In March 2022 David Seymour, leader of the libertarian ACT Party, proposed redefining the principles in law, arguing that the treaty was not a partnership between the Crown and Māori and that co-governance arrangements were not a necessary extension of it. After the 2023 general election ACT's coalition agreement with the National Party committed the government to introduce such a bill, with National and New Zealand First supporting it only as far as the select committee.

Cabinet signed off the bill's outline on 9 September 2024. It set out three principles: that the Government has full power to govern and Parliament full power to make laws; that the Crown recognises and will protect the rights hapū and iwi had when they signed the Treaty, which differ from everyone's rights only where legislation, Treaty settlements or other agreements specify; and that everyone is equal before the law. The Ministry of Justice's regulatory impact statement said this did not reflect Article 2's affirmation of tino rangatiratanga and reduced indigenous rights to ordinary rights.

The bill passed its first reading on 14 November 2024 by 68 votes to 54, after Te Pāti Māori MP Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke tore her copy in two and led a haka that halted the House for half an hour. The Waitangi Tribunal had already recommended that the bill be abandoned, the New Zealand Law Society argued that it diminished Māori rights, and the Hīkoi mō te Tiriti marched on Wellington from Cape Reinga and Bluff. On 10 April 2025 Parliament rejected the bill at its second reading by 112 votes to 11, with only ACT voting in favour; Seymour said his party would never give up on fighting for equal rights.
trebbia: The Trebbia is a river mainly of Liguria and Emilia Romagna in northern Italy, and one of the four main right-bank tributaries of the Po, with the Tanaro, the Secchia and the Panaro. Its drainage basin covers 1,150 square kilometres, divided among Emilia Romagna, Liguria and Lombardy. The spring lies in the Ligurian Apennines, on the south slopes of Monte Prelà in the comune of Torriglia, at about 800 metres.

The river flows north-east past Gorreto, Ottone, Bobbio, Travo and Rivergaro, where the valley widens into the plain of the Po, and joins the Po just west of Piacenza. Its principal tributaries are the torrents Aveto, Perino and Boreca. The highway SS45 follows almost its whole course between Piacenza and Genoa.

Archaeological evidence indicates that the valley has been continuously occupied since the end of the Acheulian in the Paleolithic, about 150,000 years ago. Mesolithic hunters kept summer camps at high altitude, and Neolithic cultures began about 4500 BCE. The Bronze Age population lived in naturally defended settlements, Etruscan elements appeared in the Iron Age, about the fifth century BCE, and Celtic artefacts immediately preceded the Roman presence. The river's name is first known from Polybius, though which people first gave it, and when, is unclear.

Along its eastern banks in 218 BCE Hannibal defeated a Roman consular army in the Battle of the Trebbia, one of the battles of the Second Punic War. In 1799 a major battle was fought there between the French and a Russian and Austrian army under Suvorov.

The braided streams that drain the northern Apennines run through largely undeveloped mountain country known for its wildlife. The valley is covered by a reddish or brown loess soil, on average about four metres deep, laid down in glacial maxima beginning about 400,000 years ago. Beech, oak and chestnut forests grow there, and the valley lies within the range of Moltoni's warbler. Dikes now confine the lower Trebbia and the Po, so that long stretches of stream flow above the level of the surrounding land, in places as high as rooftops.
trebinje: Trebinje is the southernmost city of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the Trebišnjica river in the region of East Herzegovina, at the foot of Leotar and about 30 kilometres by road from Dubrovnik. The river floods in the winter, and after it passes through Popovo Polje it runs underground towards the Adriatic. It is heavily used for hydroelectric power. The municipality covers 904 square kilometres and lies in the south of Republika Srpska, bordering municipalities of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio mentions the region as Travunija. Prince Vlastimir of Serbia married his daughter to Krajina, son of Beloje, and that family became hereditary rulers there. The town commanded the road from Ragusa to Constantinople, which Raymond IV of Toulouse and his crusaders followed in 1096. At the end of the 12th century Stefan Nemanja conquered Trebinje, and it belonged to the Serbian Kingdom and Empire until the Balšić family took it in 1373. In 1377 it was incorporated into the Bosnian state under Tvrtko I and later belonged to the Kosača family's domains.

Ottoman forces first took Trebinje in 1465, it was returned to Vlatko Hercegović Kosača in 1470, and by 1478 it was finally captured. The Ottomans built the Old Town, called Kastel, on the site of the medieval fortress of Ban Vir. The Arslanagić Bridge, built in the 16th century by Mehmed-Paša Sokolović, stands in a village north of the town. From 1596 the Tvrdoš Monastery was the centre of anti-Ottoman activity in Herzegovina, and the region suffered from raids by uskoks and hajduks. Austria-Hungary administered the town from 1878 to 1918, building fortifications on the hills, a garrison and the present main street.

Under Socialist Yugoslavia, between 1945 and 1980, Trebinje grew rapidly as dams, lakes and hydroelectric plants were built. During the Bosnian War the town was controlled by Bosnian Serb forces and served as a command and artillery base for the Yugoslav People's Army troops besieging Dubrovnik; ten of its mosques were destroyed with explosives. After the Dayton Agreement of 1995 the former Trebinje municipality was divided between Republika Srpska and the Federation. The Old Town and the Arslanagić Bridge remain its best-known monuments.
treblinka-extermination-camp: Treblinka lay in a forest about 80 kilometres northeast of Warsaw. Before the war the site held a gravel mining enterprise owned by the Polish industrialist Marian Łopuszyński, linked by rail to the main cities of central Poland. The Germans found it well connected yet isolated, halfway between some of the largest ghettos in occupied Europe, among them the Warsaw Ghetto and the Białystok Ghetto. It consisted of two camps. Treblinka I, opened on 1 September 1941, was a forced-labour camp through which 20,000 people passed, and about half of them died of exhaustion, hunger and disease. Treblinka II, the extermination camp, was built from 10 April 1942.

Treblinka II was part of Operation Reinhard, the programme for the genocide of the Jews outlined after the Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942. It had one function, to murder those sent there, and it was disguised as a transit camp with a false station, a painted clock and a ticket window. Mass deportation from the Warsaw Ghetto began on 22 July 1942, and the gas chambers began operating the next morning. German records give 265,000 Jews carried from the ghetto between 22 July and 12 September 1942. Almost 20,000 foreign Jews arrived between October 1942 and March 1943. Romani people were also killed there.

Irmfried Eberl, the first commandant, was replaced by Franz Stangl on 1 September 1942, after the early gassing machinery broke down and the mass graves overflowed. From early 1943 the bodies were dug up and burned on open pyres. A small group of prisoners was kept alive to work, and in early 1943 they formed a resistance organisation. On 2 August 1943, about 700 prisoners revolted, set buildings ablaze and attacked the gate; most were shot, but about 200 escaped, half of whom were killed in pursuit. Around 70 are known to have survived the war, among them Samuel Willenberg. Gassing ended in October 1943 and the camp was dismantled, with a farmhouse built on the site and the ground ploughed over.

Soviet forces reached the site in August 1944. Treblinka was long looted by local people digging for valuables, and the site was not at first protected. A memorial designed by Franciszek Duszeńko was begun in 1958, and Treblinka was declared a national monument of martyrdom on 10 May 1964. The first German trials of former SS personnel were held at Düsseldorf in 1964 and 1965. An exhibition centre opened in 2006. Estimates of the number of dead differ between scholars and museums.
trebuchet: A trebuchet is a type of catapult that uses a hinged arm with a sling attached to the tip to launch a projectile. It was a common powerful siege engine until the advent of gunpowder. As a compound machine it makes use of the mechanical advantage of a lever. Typical constructions are large, with a beam as much as 15 metres long. The beam is attached by an axle to a stout frame and base, so that it can rotate vertically through an arc typically over 180 degrees. The projectile section of the beam is usually four to six times longer than the section where force is applied.

The traction trebuchet, which uses manpower to swing the arm, first appeared in China by the 4th century BCE. It spread westward, possibly via the Avars, and was adopted by the Byzantines, Persians, Arabs and other neighbouring peoples by the sixth to seventh centuries CE. The counterweight trebuchet appeared in both Christian and Muslim lands around the Mediterranean in the 12th century and was carried back to China by the Mongols in the 13th century.

There is little consensus on where and when the counterweight trebuchet was first developed. The earliest known description and illustration comes from a commentary on the conquests of Saladin by Mardi ibn Ali al-Tarsusi in 1187, though cases have been made for earlier European and Muslim machines. In China the traction trebuchet was called the pào and the counterweight trebuchet the húihúi pào, the Muslim trebuchet.

With the introduction of gunpowder the trebuchet lost its place as the siege engine of choice to the cannon. Trebuchets were still used at the siege of Burgos in 1475 to 1476 and the siege of Rhodes in 1480. One of the last recorded military uses was by Hernán Cortés at the 1521 siege of Tenochtitlán, where limited gunpowder motivated the attempt. It was reportedly unsuccessful: the first projectile landed on the trebuchet itself and destroyed it.

The methods of construction were lost at the beginning of the 16th century. In 1984 the French engineer Renaud Beffeyte made the first modern reconstruction, based on documents from 1324. Most use in recent centuries has been recreational or educational.
treguier: Tréguier, Landreger in Breton, is a port town and the capital of the province of Trégor. It lies 36 miles north-west of Saint-Brieuc by road. The port is about 5 and a half miles from the English Channel, at the confluence of two streams that form the Tréguier River. Its inhabitants are called trécorrois in French. In the past saw-milling, boat-building and flax-stripping were carried on there, together with trade in cereals, cloth and potatoes, and the port had fishing, coasting and a small foreign trade.

Tréguier, called Trecorum, dates from the sixth century and grew up round a monastery founded by Saint Tudwal, who died about 564. In the 9th century it became the seat of a bishopric, which was suppressed on 12 July 1790 under a decree of 14 November 1789. Count Stephen of Tréguier was the second Earl of Richmond, inheriting the peerage that William the Conqueror had created for his second cousin Alan Rufus.
The United States Navy established a naval air station there on 1 November 1918 to operate seaplanes during the First World War, and it closed shortly after the Armistice of Compiègne.

The cathedral, dating from the 14th and 15th centuries, has three towers over the transept, one of them with a fine spire. It holds the mausoleum of Ivo of Kermartin (Saint Yves), who died in 1303, a canon of the cathedral and patron saint of lawyers, to whom its building was largely due. South of the church is a cloister of 1468. The Pardon of Saint Yves draws lawyers and judges from many countries, and the Tro Breizh pilgrimage links Tréguier with the towns of the other founding saints of Brittany.

A statue of Ernest Renan, born in the town in 1823, stands near the cathedral. Renan was a prominent sceptic, and when the statue was unveiled in 1903 with a figure of the goddess Athena, it provoked widespread protests from the Catholic Church. The town has a museum in his birthplace. Others born there include the critic Ernest Hello and the Dominican Hervaeus Natalis, who was Master General of the order.
trekboers: The Trekboers began moving inland from the districts around what is now Cape Town, such as Stellenbosch, founded in 1679, and Paarl and Franschhoek, settled from 1688, in the late 17th century and throughout the 18th. In part they grew out of the Dutch East India Company's loan farm system, under which the company leased grazing rights over large but less fertile farms, which encouraged farmers to move with their flocks in search of seasonal pasture. Others sought to escape the company's rule, which they believed corrupt and indifferent to the free burghers, the class to which most of them belonged.

From 1700 the Trekboers crossed the Berg River into the Tulbagh basin; in the early 1710s they spread into the Olifants River valley and the Bokkeveld, by the 1740s into the Little Karoo and by the 1760s into the Great Karoo. Between 1699 and 1725, when the company lifted its ban on livestock trading, their trade with the Khoikhoi largely meant stripping them of their herds. Many Khoikhoi, having lost their livestock, became servants on Dutch-speaking farms. The San lost water, game and grazing, and San and some Khoi resisted with guerrilla attacks that halted the advance after about 1770.

The company had tried to stop settlers moving beyond the western Cape, but the authorities in Cape Town lacked the means to police the frontier. In 1795 groups of Boers rebelled against company rule and set up republics at Graaff-Reinet and, on 17 June, at Swellendam. The British, who took Cape Town in September 1795, tightened government oversight, and tensions came to a head in the Slachter's Nek Rebellion of 1815, quickly put down with its leaders executed. Dissatisfaction with British rule, constant wars with the Xhosa and shortage of land eventually led many to join the Great Trek.

Some had a loan farm as a base, sometimes shared by several families, but the poorer Trekboers lived in their wagons and seldom stayed long in one place. Their hardy herds of local stock linked the interior with the suppliers of ships at the Cape. Their identity rested on Christian faith, customs of European origin and militia practices. They spoke a variety of Dutch they called die taal, the language, from which Eastern Border Afrikaans developed. Many continued as nomadic pastoralists well into the 19th century.
trelawny-town: Cudjoe's Town lay in the mountains at the southern edge of the parish of St James, close to the border of Westmoreland; despite its later name it was not in the parish of Trelawny, though both were named after the governor. Its people descended from the Akan fighters who in 1690 attacked Sutton's Estate in Clarendon, freed between 300 and 400 enslaved people and founded a free settlement in the Cockpit Country. Maroon oral history makes Naquan the organiser of that rising and his son Cudjoe the first leader of the western Maroons.

Cudjoe signed the treaty of 1739 with Governor Edward Trelawny, reportedly at Petty River Bottom near the present village of Flagstaff, although the Maroons of Accompong hold that it was signed in their town. The population grew from 276 in 1740 to 594 in 1788, and the Maroons of Trelawny Town helped the colonial authorities put down the risings of Tacky and Apongo in the 1760s. Land disputes with neighbouring planters, in which the Assembly took the planters' side, and the dismissal of the superintendents John James and John Montague James built up tension.

The Second Maroon War began in 1795 when the magistrate of Montego Bay had two Maroons flogged by slaves for stealing two pigs. The Maroons under Montague James killed 65 British soldiers in the first two weeks, while recent research puts the Maroons killed by the militias at about 16. Drought, scorched earth and hunting dogs wore them down, and by 22 December Colonel George Walpole had persuaded them to come to terms on the promise that they would not be transported. The governor, Alexander Lindsay, 6th Earl of Balcarres, used a loophole to break it and deported just under 600 to Nova Scotia; most of the town's 1,500 acres were auctioned.

In 1800 the exiles were taken to Sierra Leone, where they helped suppress a rising of the Black Nova Scotians. From 1839 some returned to Jamaica, perhaps a third of the Sierra Leone Maroons in the 1840s, among them Peter Campbell, whose flogging had begun the war. Families such as those of Mary Brown and Mary Ricketts settled near the old town, still calling it Cudjoe's Town, and founded Flagstaff, where their descendants, the Returned Maroons, still live.
trelleborg-slagelse: When it was built, the fortress stood on a peninsula reaching into a swamp between two rivers, the Vårby Å and the Tude Å. The swamp was linked to the Great Belt by a lake that Viking ships could navigate, and the fort may have commanded the sea traffic between Zealand and Funen.

The circular main castle was enclosed by a rampart 5 m high, 17.5 m wide at the base and 137 m across, faced with oak and filled with loam and stones. Two roads crossing at right angles led to four gates, and each quarter held four almost identical longhouses with bulging walls and a central hall of 18 by 8 m.

Unlike the other ring castles, Trelleborg had a bailey with its own rampart and 14 longhouses whose axes pointed to the centre of the main castle. Beside it lay a cemetery of 135 graves, mostly of young men. The fortress may have held some 1,300 people.

Dendrochronology shows that the timber was felled in the autumn of 980 and probably used in the spring of 981; earlier datings had put the castle near the year 1000. The short building time and the lack of any sign of repair suggest the buildings were used for perhaps 10 to 15 years, and the outer eastern rampart was probably never finished.

Excavations from 1934 to 1942 found mostly everyday objects, but 19 arrowheads driven into the ramparts and gates, three mass graves of men with wounds from close combat, and traces of fire point to an attack. Strontium analysis showed that many of the dead came from present-day Norway and Poland, and they are thought to have been foreign mercenaries serving as guards.

Trelleborg is the best preserved of the Viking ring fortresses. Post-glacial rebound has shrunk the swamp to a small bog and the rivers to narrow streams. A longhouse was reconstructed on the site in 1948, though later study has questioned its design, and since 1995 the Trelleborg Museum has run the site as an open-air museum, with other finds kept at the Nationalmuseet in Copenhagen.
trencin: Trenčín lies in the central valley of the Váh River in the Trenčín Basin, near the Czech border and about 95 kilometres from Bratislava, at an altitude of 217 metres. The basin is surrounded by the Strážov Mountains, Považský Inovec and the White Carpathians. It was first mentioned under the Greek name Leukaristos on a world map based on Ptolemy, around 150 CE, and the Roman inscription of 179 CE names the place as Laugaricio. The medieval name probably derives from a personal name, Trnka or Trenka, meaning blackthorn, with a possessive suffix, and the first medieval mentions date from 1111 and 1113.

Trenčín is one of the suggested locations for the capital of Samo's Empire in the 7th century, and Trenčín Castle may have been founded in the Great Moravian era. In 1017 Stephen I of Hungary conquered the region, which stayed part of Hungary until 1918. By the end of the 11th century the castle was the administrative centre of Trencsén county. As one of the few stone castles in the country it resisted the Mongol invasion of 1241. Between 1302 and 1321 it was the seat of the magnate Matthew Csák, who controlled most of present-day Slovakia and challenged King Charles Robert. The Treaty of Trentschin between Bohemia, Hungary and Poland was signed in the city in 1335.

The town gained freedom from tolls in 1324 and free royal town status from King Sigismund in 1412. Imperial troops captured it in 1528 during the conflict between the Habsburgs and the supporters of János Szapolyai. The Ottomans failed to take it in the 17th century. The Battle of Trenčín was fought near the city on 3 August 1708, and a plague killed 1,600 inhabitants two years later. In 1790 the town and castle burned down, and the castle has been a ruin since. The 19th century brought railways and new industries.

Trenčín is the seat of the Trenčín Region and District and has more than 55,000 inhabitants. Trenčín Castle, the third largest in Slovakia, stands on a rock above the city, with its upper castle and central medieval tower. The old town has a large main square, a baroque church and a town tower. The Roman inscription on the rock below the castle, carved in 179 CE during the Marcomannic Wars, is its best-known monument. The historical centre has been largely restored since 1990.
trentino: Trentino, officially the Autonomous Province of Trento, lies in the far north of Italy and covers 6,207 square kilometres. With South Tyrol it forms the autonomous region of Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol. The province is mountainous and contains much of the Dolomites, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, whose highest peak, the Marmolada, rises to 3,343 metres. The Adige River flows through its centre, and its valley, where the principal towns lie, has long connected Italy with Central Europe. The name derives from the capital, Trento, and originally referred only to the city and its surroundings. Under Austrian rule the common German name was Welschtirol, or Foreign Tyrol.

The valleys were inhabited from the mid-Stone Age. In the early Middle Ages the area belonged to the Kingdom of Italy and the March of Verona. In 1027 Emperor Conrad II established the Bishopric of Trent as a state of the Holy Roman Empire, governed by prince-bishops. The Council of Trent, held in three sessions between 1545 and 1563, set out Roman Catholic doctrine in response to the Protestant Reformation.

After the Napoleonic Wars the bishopric was secularised and absorbed into the Austrian County of Tyrol. Trentino lay on the front line between Austria-Hungary and Italy and saw heavy fighting in the First World War. Italy occupied it in November 1918 and it was formally ceded under the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye in 1919. After the Second World War the Gruber-De Gasperi Agreement created the autonomous region, and a second Statute of Autonomy in 1972 devolved most powers to the two provinces.

Trentino has more than half a million people and 166 municipalities. Italian predominates, but three indigenous minorities, speakers of Ladin, Mòcheno and Cimbrian, are protected by law. The province has its own elected government and a council of 35 members, one of whom must by law come from the Ladin minority. Since 1996 it has belonged with South Tyrol and the Austrian state of Tyrol to a Euroregion whose boundaries match the old County of Tyrol. Its castles include Castel del Buonconsiglio in Trento and Castel Thun in the Non Valley.
trento: Trento stands on the Adige river, on the river route to Bolzano and the low Alpine passes of the Brenner and the Reschen Pass. It is the capital of the autonomous province of Trento, or Trentino, in the region of Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol, and has 119,359 inhabitants. The city centre lies just under 200 metres above sea level, while the municipality reaches 2,000 metres at Monte Bondone. Before the river was diverted in the mid-nineteenth century the Adige ran through the centre of the town and was a navigable commercial route in the Alps. Its old course is now covered by Via Torre Vanga, Via Torre Verde and Via Alessandro Manzoni.

The origins of Trento are uncertain. Some scholars hold that it was a Rhaetian settlement, though the Adige area was influenced by neighbours including the Veneti, the Etruscans and the Gauls. Other theories say the Gauls founded the city in the fourth century BCE. A late-Roman basilica lies beneath the later cathedral, which can be seen in an underground crypt. The Castello del Buonconsiglio was the seat of the Prince-Bishops of Trento, and the Council of Trent was held in the city in the sixteenth century. It was part of Austria and then of Austria-Hungary before Italy annexed it in 1919.

The railway station opened in 1859 on the Brenner line from Verona to Innsbruck, the main rail link between Italy and Germany. The Teatro Sociale was built in 1819. The University of Trento was founded in 1962 as a Higher University Institute of Social Sciences.

Much of the Late Medieval and Renaissance centre has been restored to its pastel colours and wooden balconies. Part of the medieval walls and a circular tower can be seen in Piazza Fiera. The Romanesque-Gothic Cathedral of Saint Vigilius dates from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and the Piazza Duomo beside it has frescoed Renaissance buildings and the Late Baroque Fountain of Neptune of 1767 to 1768. The Tridentine Diocesan Museum, in the Palazzo Pretorio, shows the artistic treasures of the diocese and the influence of the council on the city. Since 2011 Trento has belonged to the Euroregion Tyrol-South Tyrol-Trentino.
trepanning: The word trepan comes from Old French, from Medieval Latin trepanum and Greek trúpanon, meaning borer or auger. The operation exposes the dura mater and was mainly performed by priests or healers. Its purposes may have included treating intracranial disease, releasing blood that pooled after an injury, removing splinters of bone and relieving pressure. In some societies it was believed to release the evil spirits blamed for abnormal behaviour. Archaeologists identify a trephined skull by the hole, the shape of its edges and signs of healing.

Early tools were hand-held and made of flint, obsidian or harder stone, and later of bronze and copper. In early Peru the tumi, a ceremonial knife, was used, and in the South Pacific sharpened seashells. Five methods are recorded: rectangular intersecting cuts, scraping, circular grooving, cutting with a circular trephine or crown saw, and boring a ring of holes and chiselling between them. The Greeks and Romans were the first to design instruments for the purpose, such as the terebra serrata.

Among the Andean peoples, including the Paracas culture, the Muisca and the Inca, skulls with trepanation are common, between 11 and 40 per cent in parts of Peru, and many holes avoid the midline of the skull, which suggests a wish to reduce risk. Chinese examples include a skull from Shandong dated to about 5,000 years ago. In Europe, Iron Age populations had success rates of 78 per cent, and seven of eight skulls of the 6th to 8th centuries from south-western Germany show healing.

In the 1870s the French anthropologist Paul Broca found several European and South American children's skulls of the Neolithic that had been perforated surgically. He found no fractures to explain the operation and proposed a ritual or religious purpose, perhaps to remove confined demons or to make talismans from the removed bone. He also suggested it might treat childhood conditions such as febrile seizures. The idea that the holes treated headaches spread in the 19th century, but this belief is a myth.

In modern medicine trepanation is the ancestor of the craniotomy, used for epidural and subdural haematomas. Since the 1960s a few people have drilled holes in their own skulls, among them the Dutch librarian Bart Huges in 1965, who claimed it increased brain blood volume. Research has not supported these claims.
tres-zapotes: The site lies just north of the present village of Tres Zapotes, west of Santiago Tuxtla, on the banks of the Rio Hueyapan in the Papaloapan River plain. Standing where the Los Tuxtlas Mountains meet the river delta, it drew on both the forested uplands and the swamps and streams of the lowland. About 10 km to the east rises Cerro el Vigía, an extinct volcano that supplied basalt, sandstone and clay; most of the site's stonework was carved from the smooth boulders on its summit, and the nearby site of Rancho la Cobata may have served as a workshop for monuments.

Founded in the centuries before 1000 BCE, Tres Zapotes became a regional centre around the time San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán declined. Its two colossal heads, Monument A and Monument Q, are thought to date from the Olmec phase; under 1.5 m high, they are smaller than those of San Lorenzo and, with the cruder head at Rancho la Cobata, show a local style. Unlike La Venta, the site was not abandoned around 400 BCE, and over the following centuries its culture turned gradually into the Epi-Olmec.

Most of its monumental sculpture is Epi-Olmec, from the Late Formative period. Stela D frames a historical scene in the mouth of a monster, as Izapa Stela 2 does at much the same time; recent scholarship sees the two as descendants of a common Olmec tradition. The 1969 discovery of the upper half of Stela C confirmed Marion Stirling's reading of its first digit as 7. In the Classic era, from about 300 CE, building continued but the centres of Classic Veracruz culture outgrew the site.

Over 160 mounds and platforms have been recorded, most of them low house platforms. Four main mound groups stand almost 1 km from one another, a spacing taken to reflect a decentralised political order of separate factions, unlike the centralised plan of La Venta. A museum in the village displays the colossal heads and one half of Stela C; the other half is in Mexico City.
tretyakov-gallery: The Muscovite merchant Pavel Mikhailovich Tretyakov began collecting art in the middle of 1850, and the gallery's founding year is taken to be 1856, when he bought two paintings by Russian artists of his day: Temptation by Nikolay Shilder and Skirmish with Finnish Smugglers by Vasily Khudyakov. Earlier, in 1854 and 1855, he had bought 11 drawings and nine pictures by Dutch Old Masters. His aim was a collection that might one day grow into a museum of national art. In 1867 the Moscow City Gallery of Pavel and Sergei Tretyakov was opened, holding 1,276 paintings, 471 sculptures and 10 drawings by Russian artists as well as 84 paintings by foreign masters.

In August 1892 Tretyakov presented his collection to the city of Moscow.
