It then included 1,287 paintings and 518 graphic works of the Russian school, 75 paintings and eight drawings of European schools, 15 sculptures and a collection of icons. The museum officially opened on 15 August 1893. It was housed in a mansion the Tretyakov family had bought in 1851 and extended several times. The façade, designed by the architect V. Bashkirov from drawings by the painter Viktor Vasnetsov in a Russian fairy-tale style, was built in 1902 to 1904.

On 3 June 1918 the gallery was declared the property of the Russian Federated Soviet Republic and named the State Tretyakov Gallery, with Igor Grabar as its director. In 1932 the former Church of St Nicholas in Tolmachi, closed in 1929, was given to the gallery. In the summer of 1941 the collection was taken to Novosibirsk on a train of 17 wagons, the paintings rolled on wooden shafts and packed in boxes, and the gallery reopened in Moscow on 17 May 1945. The Alexander Ivanov Hall, built for his painting The Appearance of Christ Before the People, was completed in 1956. From 1986 to 1995 the main building in Lavrushinsky Lane was closed for a major renovation.

The State Tretyakov Gallery is considered the foremost depository of Russian fine art in the world. Its collection runs to more than 130,000 exhibits, from the Theotokos of Vladimir to Wassily Kandinsky's Composition VII and Kazimir Malevich's Black Square. In 1977 it kept a significant part of the George Costakis collection. In 1985 it was merged with a gallery of contemporary art in the Central House of the Artists, whose grounds hold Socialist Realism sculpture and statues of the former Soviet Union moved from their original sites. Its organisation also includes branches in Kaliningrad and Vladivostok.
trevoux: The Treaty of Verdun of 843 divided the empire of Charlemagne and made the Saône the frontier between France and the Empire. Trévoux owed its particular political status to this border position. In the 11th century it belonged to the lords of Thoire-Villars, from whom it acquired its freedom. The Bourbons bought it in 1402, and it became the capital of the Dombes and had its own mint. The river toll grew important, and the town built a castle and walls.

On 30 June 1417 the local baron issued a decree allowing the Jewish population to continue to study the Talmud, contrary to a decision taken at Chambéry in January 1417, after which Jewish books had been seized and burned. In 1523 King François I confiscated the Dombes and founded a parliament for the region in Lyon, and in 1560 the Dombes fell to the Bourbons. The town grew rich as capital of the principality and seat of its parliament.

A printing works was established in 1603. In the 18th century the Jesuits printed there the Journal de Trévoux and a universal dictionary, the Dictionnaire de Trévoux, from 1704 to 1771. At the end of the 17th century two sovereign princes, Anne-Marie Louise of Orléans, Duchess of Montpensier, known as la Grande Mademoiselle, and her successor Louis-Auguste of Bourbon, Duke of Maine, raised two monuments that still mark the landscape: the Montpensier hospital and the Palace of the Dombes Parliament. The principality of the Dombes was absorbed definitively into France in 1762.

Trévoux is a commune in the Ain department of eastern France, built on the steeply sloping left bank of the Saône and known for its fort; its inhabitants are called Trévoltiens. It remained a sub-prefecture of Ain until 1926. From the end of the 19th century until the 1950s it was the world capital of the manufacture of synthetic diamonds.
triangular-trade: Triangular trade is trade between three ports or regions. It usually evolves when a region has export commodities that are not required in the region from which its major imports come, and it has been used to offset trade imbalances. The most commonly cited example is the Atlantic slave trade, but others existed. In the seventeenth century manufactured goods went from England to New England and Newfoundland, dried cod went from there to the Mediterranean and the Iberian peninsula, and gold, silver, olive oil, tobacco, dried fruit and sacks of wine came back to England. Maritime carriers called this the sack trade.

In the Atlantic triangle, ships left European ports such as Bristol and Nantes for West Africa loaded with manufactured goods, including copper, cloth, guns and ammunition, which were bartered for enslaved Africans. The second leg, the Middle Passage, carried the enslaved to Brazil, the Caribbean and the American colonies, where they were sold to plantation owners. An estimated 12 to 13 percent died of disease or in rebellions on board, and the average ship carried just over 300 people. The third leg took sugar, rum and molasses, or tobacco and hemp from Virginia, back to Europe.

A classic example is the colonial molasses trade between West Africa, the West Indies and the northern colonies of British North America in the 17th and 18th centuries. Enslaved people grew the sugar used to brew rum, which in turn was traded for more slaves. Great Britain, Portugal and France controlled the transatlantic slave market until the 18th century in terms of the number of enslaved people shipped.

Historians have questioned the neat picture. The triangle route was not generally followed by individual ships: slave ships were built to carry people, not cargo, and often returned with ballast, while cash crops travelled on a separate fleet. No New England trader is known to have completed the full circuit. The idea of a New England triangular trade was first suggested, inconclusively, by George H. Moore in 1866, and developed in a lecture by William B. Weeden in 1887. Even so, the Atlantic slave trade was one of the more complex international trades of the modern period, and an estimated 12.5 million people were transported from Africa.
tribal-hidage: Three versions, or recensions, of the list survive, all apparently copied from one lost manuscript. Recension A, the earliest and most complete, was written by several scribes no later than 1032 in a miscellany of Old English and Latin works that includes Aelfric's Latin Grammar, now in the British Library. Recension B appears in a Latin treatise written by Henry Spelman in 1626, and Recension C survives in six Latin documents, four of 13th-century origin and two a century older.

Historians disagree on when and where the original was compiled. Most hold that it was Mercian, since Mercia heads the list and its kings held power over the peoples south of the Humber from the late 7th to the early 9th century; Wendy Davies and Hayo Vierck placed it at 670-690. Nicholas Brooks argued for a Northumbrian origin, which would explain the inclusion of Elmet and the absence of Deira and Bernicia, and N. J. Higham linked it to Edwin of Northumbria in the 620s, a theory D. P. Kirby says has not been generally accepted.

The list opens with Mercia at 30,000 hides, followed by small peoples to its west and north assessed at no more than 7,000 hides each, among them the Wrekin dwellers, the Lindsey folk and the Western men. Others have between 300 and 1,200 hides; some of these, such as the Herefinna, Noxgaga, Hendrica and Unecungaga, cannot be identified, and others, such as the Hicca, have been located only through place-names.

The list ends with the larger kingdoms: the East Angles at 30,000 hides, the East Saxons at 7,000, Kent at 15,000, the South Saxons at 7,000 and Wessex at 100,000. The round figures make an accurate survey unlikely. Cyril Hart saw it as a tribute list made for Offa of Mercia, P. H. Sawyer as a symbolic expression of each kingdom's status, and Frank Stenton judged the figures for Mercia and Wessex at variance with other information.

Spelman first published the text, but discussion began only with John Mitchell Kemble's The Saxons in England in 1848. Walter de Gray Birch announced the discovery of Recension A in 1884, and Frederic William Maitland gave the list its name in Domesday Book and Beyond in 1897. In 1971 Hart mapped southern England as Mercia's provinces and dependencies. The list is generally agreed to be the earliest fiscal document to survive from medieval England, and it records the kingdom of East Anglia for the first time.
tribhuwana-wijayatunggadewi: Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi was born Dyah Tya, according to the Geneng II inscription, the eldest daughter of Kertarajasa Jayawardhana, the founder of Majapahit, and his principal wife Gayatri. Her half-brother Jayanegara succeeded their father in 1309, and she and her sister Dyah Wiyat received the title Bhre, she as Bhre Kahuripan. According to the Pararaton, Jayanegara wanted his half-sisters as consorts, which Javanese tradition abhorred, and the council of royal elders led by Gayatri opposed him.

He then confined the two princesses in the women's quarters of the palace, denying them contact with the court, until they passed the usual age for marriage. After his death, her husband Cakradhara, later Kertawardhana, won a contest for her hand; their children were Hayam Wuruk, born in 1334, and Dyah Nertaja.

According to the Nagarakretagama, she came to the throne by her mother's order, replacing Jayanegara, who was murdered in 1328, and took the regnal name Tribhuwannottunggadewi Jayawishnuwardhani. She governed with her husband. In 1331 she led the army herself, with her cousin Adityawarman, to crush rebellion at Sadeng and Keta.

In 1334 she appointed Gajah Mada as mahapatih, or prime minister, and he proclaimed his Palapa oath to extend the kingdom's influence across the archipelago; when his rival Ra Kembar mocked him, a duel followed, warranted by Tribhuwana, in which Ra Kembar died. With Gajah Mada's help she pursued a great expansion: in 1343 Majapahit conquered Bali, and in 1347 Adityawarman was sent to conquer the rest of Srivijaya and the Melayu kingdom.

Tribhuwana ruled under the auspices of her mother, and when Gayatri died in 1350 she abdicated in favour of her son Hayam Wuruk. She stayed active in state affairs, serving again as Bhre Kahuripan and sitting on the council of royal elders, the Bhattara Saptaprabhu. After her death a Hindu cremation ceremony was held, and she was posthumously deified as Parvati in the Rimbi temple in East Java. Tradition describes her as a woman of exceptional valour, wisdom and intelligence.
tributary-system: A tribute is wealth, often in kind, that one party gives to another as a sign of submission, allegiance or respect. Various ancient states exacted tribute from the rulers of lands they conquered, and in alliances lesser parties might pay tribute to more powerful ones as a sign of allegiance. Tribute differs from taxes: it is not collected in the same regular, routine manner, and it uniquely requires the payer to recognise political submission to the payee.

Ancient China received tribute from states including Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Cambodia, Borneo, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Myanmar and Central Asia, and the Aztec Empire received tribute from the city-states and provinces it conquered.

The Aztecs used tribute to maintain control over conquered areas. Rather than replacing local rulers or colonising, they collected tribute and ideally did not interfere in local affairs unless it went unpaid. Strategic provinces, regarded as client states, paid consensually in exchange for good relations, while tributary provinces were required to pay regularly whether they wished to or not.

Aztec officials managed the system at several levels. The calpixque collected, transported and received tribute in each province, the huecalpixque managed them, and the petlacalcatl, based in Tenochtitlan, oversaw the whole system. A military official, the cuahtlatoani, was involved only when newly conquered provinces resisted. Tribute took the form of natural resources such as obsidian and salt, of gold, silver and jade, and of goods and rotational labour owed by commoners to their lords, who could also call them for military service and construction.

China received tribute from states under the influence of Confucian civilisation and gave them Chinese products and recognition of their authority in return. The relationship is known as Jimi, Cefeng or Chaogong. According to the Book of Han, the tribes of Japan had entered tributary relationships with China by the first century, though Japan later left the system during the Heian period. Goguryeo sent a diplomatic representative to the Han dynasty in 32 CE, and China's tributary relationship with Korea continued in varying degrees until China's defeat in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894 to 1895.

China ended its suzerainty over Vietnam with the Treaty of Tientsin in 1885, after the Sino-French War. The theoretical justification was the Mandate of Heaven, under which the Chinese emperor ruled with the authority of heaven. The Islamic Caliphate introduced the jizya, a tax on adult men only, unlike Roman tribute, which could be levied on land, landowners and slaveholders. Iberian Christians translated it as tributo, and the Spanish empire later applied it in the New World.
tridu-songtsen: Tridu Songtsen, also known as Dusong Mangban, came to the throne on the death of his father, Mangsong Mangtsen, in 676. Because of his youth he was enthroned with Khri 'bring, the second son of the minister Gar Tongtsen, as regent, and in the early part of the reign power lay with his mother, Khri ma lod, and with his ministers and generals. The firm government of the leaders of the Gar clan brought the western kingdom of Zhangzhung back under Tibetan control after it revolted on the old king's death.

In 676 the Tibetans raided several districts of Gansu, and although the Chinese won at Longzhi, a Chinese army under Li Jingxuan was heavily defeated near Qinghai Lake; by the end of 677 Tibet held the whole of the Tarim Basin. In 678 the Tibetans took the Tang fortress of Anrong on the Min River north of Chengdu, which they kept as a frontier post for more than sixty years. A Chinese invasion under Wei Daijia failed in 689, but in 692 two Tibetan generals went over to the Chinese with their troops, and the Chinese regained the Tarim Basin.

In 694 the Western Turkic leader Ashina Tuizi visited the Tibetan court, and together they defeated the Chinese at Lengjuan. In 696 Gar Trinring Tsendro went to Chang'an to offer peace to Empress Wu Zetian, who refused to negotiate. Seeing that the Gar had become independent warlords, the king in 699 staged a great hunt at which his men turned on the clan and its supporters; Gar Trinring Tsendro surrendered without a fight and, according to the Old Book of Tang, took his own life.

Nepal appears to have stayed tributary to Tibet throughout the reign: a Nepalese stone edict of 695 under the Licchavi king Shivadeva II refers to taxes paid to Tibet, and the Tibetan Annals record the king spending the summers of 690, 697 and 699 in Nepal. Though remembered chiefly as a warrior, he supported Buddhism according to the Testament of Ba and had a temple called Khri rtse built in Gling Khams.

He died in battle in Mywa territory, in present-day Yunnan, in 704, on a campaign that the Tang Annals say was aimed at the tributary kingdoms of Tibet's southern borders. There was a dispute among his sons before Me Agtsom, his son by Chimza Tsenmotok, Princess of Chim, was placed on the throne. He is buried beside his father in the royal burial grounds near Yarlung.
trienio-adeco: President Isaías Medina Angarita furthered the professionalisation of the Venezuelan officer corps, sending among others Capt. Marcos Pérez Jiménez to the Peruvian military academy. A group of conspiring officers formed under Carlos Delgado Chalbaud, son of Román Delgado Chalbaud, who had opposed Juan Vicente Gómez; he had grown up in France, studied at St. Cyr and been commissioned in 1939, and Pérez Jiménez was second in the group. Rómulo Betancourt, who had flirted with communism in exile, now led Acción Democrática, the strongest party in the country.

For the 1945 elections Betancourt accepted Medina's invitation to take part on the tacit understanding that the official candidate, Diógenes Escalante, would win with the party's support and that the next elections would be fully democratic. Escalante, returning from his post as ambassador in Washington, began making incoherent statements and had to abandon politics. Medina chose Ángel Biaggini, his Minister of Agriculture, without consulting the party, and Betancourt made a pact with the conspirators, none of them above the rank of major.

In October 1945 the military rose in Caracas and Betancourt called for a civilian rising. Medina resigned, though most of the army is generally held to have been on his side; he did not want a bloody civil war. A junta headed by Betancourt as provisional president took power, with Delgado Chalbaud as Minister of Defence. The 1946 Constituent Assembly election showed the party had the support of the great majority, while Rafael Caldera founded COPEI and Jóvito Villalba made URD his own. Development minister Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonso decreed a 50-50 sharing of oil profits with the companies, agrarian reform was approved, Catholic schools were closed for a time while a national curriculum was drawn up, and a national education campaign began.

Rómulo Gallegos won the presidential election of 1947 by a huge margin, but the middle class, Caldera's base of support, which gave him 262,000 votes, and the upper class were discontented, and the officers who had brought the party to power were waiting for their chance. No single incident set off the bloodless coup of 1948, led by Delgado Chalbaud, and there was no popular opposition. All prominent adecos were expelled, and the other parties were allowed to exist but silenced.
trier: Trier lies in a hollow midway along the Moselle valley, between low vine-covered hills in the west of Rhineland-Palatinate, near the border with Luxembourg, which is some 15 kilometres away. Most of the city is on the east bank of the river. Wooded and vineyard-covered slopes stretch up to the Hunsrück plateau in the south and the Eifel in the north. The city lies within the Moselle wine region.

The Celtic tribe of the Treveri settled the area in the last pre-Christian centuries. The Romans subdued them in the 1st century BCE and founded Augusta Treverorum around 16 BCE. From 293 to 395 the city was one of the residences of the Western Roman emperor, and in the 4th century it was one of the largest cities of the empire, with some 75,000 people and perhaps as many as 100,000. The Porta Nigra dates from this age. Emperor Constantine the Great exiled Athanasius of Alexandria to Trier in 336, and Saint Ambrose was born there. The Franks seized the city in 459.

In 870 Trier became part of Eastern Francia, which developed into the Holy Roman Empire. Relics of Saint Matthias began widespread pilgrimages, and the archbishops grew powerful. The University of Trier was founded in 1473. The Trier witch trials of 1581 to 1593 reached the city itself in 1587 and led to the deaths of about 368 people. France annexed Trier in 1794 and dissolved the electoral archbishopric, and after 1815 it passed to Prussia. Karl Marx was born there in 1818.

Trier is a city of about 110,000 on the Moselle, and several Roman and medieval monuments are a World Heritage Site. They include the Porta Nigra, the best-preserved Roman city gate north of the Alps, the Aula Palatina, the throne hall of Constantine, now a Protestant church, a Roman bridge of the 2nd century still used by traffic, and the largest Roman baths north of the Alps. Trier Cathedral houses the Holy Tunic, one of a number of garments claimed to be the robe Jesus wore when he died.
trierarchy: The exact origin of the trierarchy is disputed. Its growth followed the Athenian naval buildup of the early 5th century BCE, paid for by a rise in silver from the mines of Laurion in 482 BCE. The great cost of the service probably explains the syntrierarchy, in which two or more men shared a ship and agreed its command between themselves privately; this also widened the pool of possible trierarchs. By the mid-350s BCE too few eligible citizens were willing to give their time and money, which prompted the reforms of Periandros and Demosthenes. Under Periandros's Law the cost still fell equally on members of unequal wealth, and the full register was often not assembled.

Only a wealthy, property-owning citizen could be named, often at the start of an expedition, and he served under the generals, the strategoi. The treasurer gave a Trierarchic Crown to the first trierarch to have his ship ready, and one who failed to appear by the last day of the set month could be arrested. A trireme carried about 200 men: the trierarch, 16 petty officers, 10 to 20 marines and the rowers. The officers included the helmsman, the boatswain, the bow officer, a shipwright and a piper who kept the rowers in time.

Building a trireme cost about one talent, 26 kilograms of silver. Crews were usually conscripted from official lists and paid between two obols and a drachma a day, so a month at sea at a drachma a man cost another talent. A trierarch could add to the pay or hire seasoned men at his own expense, and his successor repaid him for any improvements left on the ship.

After the Lamian War of 323 to 322 BCE the Athenian fleet shrank sharply, and the Macedonians held the Piraeus from 294 to 224 BCE. The historian Christian Ammitzbøll Thomsen believes the number of trierarchs fell while their duties stayed largely the same. Elsewhere the word came to mean a ship's commander. In Lebedos and Teos the trierarchy was a liturgy, as in Athens, while in Ptolemaic Egypt trierarchs were paid directly from the royal treasury in Alexandria.
trieste: Trieste lies at the head of the Gulf of Trieste, on a narrow strip of Italian territory between the sea and Slovenia, which is about 8 km to the east. Most of the city is built on a hillside at the foot of an escarpment that drops from the Karst Plateau towards the sea. The city lies where the Italian region, the Balkan Peninsula and central Europe meet. Its deep-water port is a maritime gateway for northern Italy, Germany, Austria and Central Europe.

The site has been inhabited since the second millennium BCE. The Veneti seem to have given the town its name, Tergeste, from a word for market. It became part of the Roman Republic in 177 BCE during the Second Istrian War. It belonged to the Habsburg monarchy from 1382 until 1918. Venice occupied it in 1508, but the Habsburg Empire recovered it a little over a year later. In 1719 Emperor Charles VI made it a free port, and the reign of Maria Theresa began a very prosperous era.

French troops occupied Trieste in 1797, 1805 and 1809, and from 1809 to 1813 it was part of the Illyrian Provinces, which interrupted its free port status and its autonomy. In the 19th century it was the most important seaport of the Habsburg monarchy and the fourth largest city of Austria-Hungary. James Joyce lived there between 1904 and 1915, working on Dubliners and Ulysses. Italy annexed Trieste at the end of the First World War. In 1947 it was declared the Free Territory of Trieste under United Nations protection, divided into Zones A and B along the Morgan Line; the Free Territory lasted until 1954.

Trieste is the capital and largest city of the autonomous region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Half the city was built in the Austro-Hungarian period, giving it some of the architecture of Vienna. Its sights include Miramare Castle, built between 1856 and 1860 for Archduke Maximilian, the Roman theatre, and the cathedral of St Justus. Piazza Unità d'Italia is the largest seafront square in Europe.
trigonometry: The word comes from the Ancient Greek trigonon, "triangle", and metron, "measure". Sumerian astronomers studied angle measure, dividing the circle into 360 degrees. They and the later Babylonians studied the ratios of the sides of similar triangles and found some of their properties, but did not make a systematic method for finding the sides and angles of triangles. The ancient Nubians used a similar method. In the 3rd century BCE Hellenistic mathematicians such as Euclid and Archimedes studied chords and inscribed angles in circles and proved theorems equivalent to modern trigonometric formulae, though they presented them geometrically rather than algebraically.

Hipparchus of Nicaea gave the first tables of chords in 140 BCE, and in the 2nd century CE Ptolemy constructed detailed tables in Book 1 of his Almagest. Ptolemy's treatise stayed in use for calculations in astronomy for the next 1,200 years in the Byzantine, Islamic and later Western European worlds.

Trigonometry relates the angles of a right triangle to the ratios of its side lengths. The sine is the ratio of the side opposite the angle to the hypotenuse, the cosine the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse, and the tangent the ratio of the opposite to the adjacent side. Their reciprocals are the cosecant, secant and cotangent. With the laws of sines and cosines one can find the remaining sides and angles of any triangle once enough of them are known. Spherical trigonometry applies the same ideas to triangles on a sphere, and was long used to locate the sun, moon and stars and to predict eclipses.

The modern definition of the sine is first attested in the Surya Siddhanta, and Aryabhata documented its properties in the 5th century CE. Medieval Islamic mathematicians translated and expanded Greek and Indian works. Habash al-Hasib al-Marwazi made the first table of cotangents in 830 CE, and by the 10th century Abu al-Wafa al-Buzjani used all six functions, with sine tables in steps of a quarter of a degree.

Nasir al-Din al-Tusi was the first to treat trigonometry as a discipline independent of astronomy, and in the 14th century Madhava of Sangamagrama developed infinite series for sine, cosine and arctangent. Knowledge reached Western Europe through Latin translations of the Almagest and the works of al-Battani and al-Tusi. Regiomontanus wrote De Triangulis in the 15th century, and Copernicus devoted two chapters of De revolutionibus orbium coelestium to the basics. Bartholomaeus Pitiscus first used the word trigonometry in his Trigonometria of 1595, and Gemma Frisius described the method of triangulation still used in surveying.
trikala: The city straddles the Lithaios river, a tributary of the Pineios, and lies close to Meteora and the southern Pindus mountains. Its name comes from the ancient Trikka or Trikke, itself named after a nymph, a daughter of Peneus or, according to others, of the river god Asopus. The region has been inhabited since prehistoric times: the cave of Theopetra holds the first signs of permanent settlement, from about 49,000 BCE, and Neolithic settlements go back to about 6,000 BCE.

Ancient Trikke was founded around the third millennium BCE on a defensible site between a hill and the Lithaios. In the Mycenean period it was the capital of a kingdom, and later the main centre of the Thessalian region of Estaiotis. Homer's Iliad names it among the cities that sent thirty ships to the Trojan War under Asclepius' sons Machaon and Podalirius. It fell to the Achaemenid Persians in 480 BCE, joined Philip II's Macedonia in 352 BCE, and passed to the Roman Republic after 168 BCE.

The present name appears in the 11th century. After 1204 the town was part of the Despotate of Epirus, and in 1259 it passed to the Empire of Nicaea. In 1348 Stefan Dušan's Serbian Empire took Thessaly, and in 1359 his half-brother Symeon Uroš set up his court at Trikala; about 1366 he founded the Meteora monasteries nearby. The Ottoman conquest of Thessaly came about 1393.

Under the Ottomans the city, called Tırhala, was the centre of the Sanjak of Trikala. Turahan Bey and his son Ömer Bey raised mosques, medreses, a hammam and a khan there. The 17th-century traveller Evliya Çelebi counted 2,300 houses and eight mosques; only the Osman Shah Mosque, built by Mimar Sinan, survives. A great fire in 1749 burned much of the city. It passed to Greece on 23 August 1881 under the Treaty of Constantinople, and in 1906 the first agricultural cooperative of Greece was founded there.

Trikala has 62,064 inhabitants, with 78,605 in the municipality (2021 figures). Its old town below the Byzantine castle keeps churches from the 14th to the 19th centuries, and the Asklepieion of Trikke, which Strabo called the most ancient in Greece, lies beside St. Nicholas Cathedral.
trim-county-meath: Trim lies 61 m above sea level on the River Boyne in County Meath. Its Irish name, Áth Truimm or Átha Troim, means the ford of the elder trees, and the crossing at Watergate Street is thought to be the original ford. The town first appears in the record in an account in the Book of Armagh of the foundation of a church there in 432 by Saint Lommán, the town's patron saint. It was historically the county town of Meath until the title passed in 1898 to the larger neighbouring town of Navan.

A monastery was founded early at Trim, within the petty kingdom of the Cenél Lóegairi, and tradition ascribes it to Saint Patrick and Lommán. The church was burned several times in the twelfth century. The English captured the town during the Norman invasion of Ireland and built a castle, but a large Irish army under Ruadhrí Ua Conchobair, King of Ireland, recaptured the town and burned the castle. Trim and the surrounding lands were granted to Hugh de Lacy, Lord of Meath, and the town became one of the most important Hiberno-Norman settlements of the Middle Ages.

Later it was refounded as St. Mary's Abbey under Augustinian rule, and its abbey church sheltered Our Lady of Trim, a wooden statue reported to work miracles. The statue made Trim a major pilgrimage site from at least 1397. It was burned during the Reformation, and Henry VIII dissolved the abbey. The Norman-Irish parliament met in Trim in the 15th century, and sessions of the Irish Parliament were sometimes held there, as in 1542. Elizabeth I proposed Trim as the site of a Protestant university, but Sir Francis Drake argued for Dublin instead. In 1649, after the sacking of Drogheda, the garrison fled and Oliver Cromwell's army occupied the town.

Trim Castle, built in the late twelfth century, is the largest Norman castle in Ireland. The Yellow Steeple, the bell tower of the 14th-century St. Mary's Abbey, is the tallest building in the town, and other remains include the Black Friary, a 13th-century Dominican friary, and St. John's Priory, a medieval hospital. A column to the Duke of Wellington was raised in 1817. The 2022 census gave the town a population of 9,563. Trim won the Irish Tidy Towns Competition in 1972, 1984, 2014 and 2022.
trimurti: The Puranic period, from the 4th to the 12th centuries CE, saw the rise of post-Vedic religion, which R. C. Majumdar calls synthetic Hinduism. It included orthodox Vedic Brahmanism, remnants of older Vedic traditions and the sectarian religions of Shaivism, Vaishnavism and Shaktism, and one of its marks was a spirit of harmony between orthodox and sectarian forms. Majumdar saw its most notable expression in the Trimurti, the manifestation of the supreme God in three forms. He judged the attempt not a great success, because Brahma never rose to the standing of Shiva or Vishnu, and the sects often took the three as forms of their own god.

The word trimurti means three forms: Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer. Brahma, the creator god, is to be told apart from Brahman, Ultimate Reality. The Vishnu Purana (1:2:66) names the three in one verse, describing the one supreme being dividing itself into three forms, and the Kūrma Purāṇa emphasises their unity. The Maitri Upanishad (5:2) calls Brahma, Rudra and Vishnu the supreme forms of God. Arthur Llewellyn Basham doubted that Hindu tradition ever recognised Brahma as the Supreme Deity as it did Vishnu and Shiva. The Tridevi are the goddess consorts of the Trimurti, or sometimes a feminine version of it.

Shaivites hold that Shiva performs five actions, creation, preservation, dissolution, grace and illusion, so that Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra are forms of Shiva, and the Trimurti Sadashiva sculpture in the Elephanta Caves is a prominent example. Vaishnavism generally does not acknowledge the Trimurti and holds that Shiva and Brahma are forms of Vishnu. In Shaktism the three roles belong to the goddesses Mahasarasvati, Mahalaxmi and Mahakali. Smartism, popularised by Śankarācārya in the ninth century, invokes five deities, Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma, Shakti and Surya, as forms of the one Brahman.
trincomalee: Trincomalee is the main city of the Eastern Province of Sri Lanka and the administrative centre of Trincomalee District, overlooking Trincomalee Harbour. It is built on a peninsula of the same name that divides the inner and outer harbours. The temple on Swami Rock, a cliff that drops 120 metres into the sea, gave the city its Tamil name Thirukonamalai, meaning roughly Lord of the Sacred Hill. Its Sanskrit name Gokarna means Cow's Ear. Tamil-speaking culture has had one of its main centres here for nearly a millennium.

The harbour has drawn seafarers, traders and pilgrims since ancient times, and the town has been a seaport since 400 BCE. The earliest inscriptions found in the city are in Tamil, and Chola inscriptions of 900 to 1000 CE concern the Koneswaram temple. The shrine has a recorded history from the 3rd century BCE and drew pilgrims from all parts of India. The Tevaram hymns of Sambandar, composed around 600, praise its deity.

The Portuguese demolished the temple in 1622 and fortified the heights with its stones. A Danish expedition under Ove Giedde had reached the island in May 1620 and occupied the temple. Fort Frederick was built in 1623 by the Portuguese and captured by the Dutch in 1639. In 1782, during the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War, the British took it, after which the French captured it; the French handed it back to the Dutch for a large sum. The British took it again in 1795 and Trincomalee became part of British Ceylon in 1815.

In 1942 the city was attacked by Japan as part of the Indian Ocean raid. After Sri Lanka's independence in 1948, relations between Tamils and Sinhalese worsened, and the city and its district were severely affected by the civil war of thirty years that followed. In 1950 workers digging a well found bronze statues from the 10th century, including Shiva as Somaskanda; they were reinstalled in a restored shrine on 3 March 1963.

The city has a population of 99,135 and holds naval and air force bases at the Trincomalee Garrison. It contains the Hoods Tower Museum and the Dutch fort, and the Koneswaram compound remains a place of pilgrimage sacred to Hindus; some Buddhists also worship at these sites.
trinh-kiem: Trịnh Kiểm, first named Trịnh Phiến, was born on 14 September 1503 in the village of Hổ in Thanh Hoa province, the third of seven children of Trịnh Lâu and Hoàng Thị Ngọc Dốc. His great-grandfather Trịnh Khả had been a close ally of Lê Lợi. His father died when he was six, and the family fell into poverty; he worked as a buffalo herder and was expelled from his village with his mother after killing an injured buffalo to feed his friends.

After Mạc Đăng Dung overthrew the Lê dynasty in 1527, Kiểm and his mother took refuge with the Mạc general Ninh Bang Hầu, who set him to tend livestock; a Cham horse trainer, Vũ Thì An, taught him to judge and train horses. He later fled, and the general had his mother drowned in a bamboo cage.

Kiểm joined Nguyễn Kim, who in 1533 placed Lê Trang Tông on the throne and began the war between the Southern Court of the Lê and the Northern Court of the Mạc. Kim made him commander of the cavalry, gave him his daughter Nguyễn Thị Ngọc Bảo in marriage, and in 1539 the emperor made him Grand General. After Kim was poisoned in 1545, Kiểm took command, defeated a Mạc attack at the Phù Chẩn River and was named supreme commander and Grand Mentor. From then on every important decision was his, and the emperor approved it afterwards.

From his base at Vạn Lại he recruited men of talent, held civil service examinations in Confucian studies and drew defectors such as the Mạc grand chancellor Lê Bá Ly, who came over in 1550 with more than 13,000 troops. In 1554 his armies took Thuận Hóa and Quảng Nam, and in 1558 he proposed that Nguyễn Hoàng govern Thuận Hóa as a frontier stronghold.

In failing health, Kiểm handed power in 1569 to his eldest son, Trịnh Coi, and died in 1570. Coi was defeated by a Mạc army that year and replaced by his younger brother Trịnh Tùng, who declared himself lord and gave his father the title posthumously. Though he never won a decisive victory over the Mạc or took a higher rank than Thái Quốc Công, Kiểm began the line of the Trịnh lords, who ruled Đại Việt in the name of the Lê emperors for two centuries.
trinh-tung: Trịnh Tùng, also called Trịnh Tòng, was born on 19 December 1550, the second son of Trịnh Kiểm, who held the real power of Đại Việt as a duke behind the Lê emperors but never claimed the title of Trịnh lord. Tùng is therefore counted the first official Trịnh lord, although he was so young when his family came to power that in effect he belonged to its second generation. When his father died, command passed to his elder brother, Trịnh Cối, whom Tùng challenged at once; after Cối lost a battle to the Mạc, Tùng took charge.

The Lê loyalist army briefly took the Eastern Capital, Thăng Long, from the Mạc emperor Mạc Mậu Hợp, but was driven out by a counter-offensive. Amid the reverse the nominal Lê emperor, Lê Anh Tông, fled to Nghệ An; Tùng enthroned Lê Thế Tông in his place and had the former emperor killed. The war with the Mạc went on for twenty years, and further campaigns followed in 1593 and 1594 with help from the Nguyễn. In 1599 he was given the title Bình An Vương, Pacifying Prince. From his time the Trịnh lords chose the crown prince and controlled political and military affairs.

In 1619 Emperor Lê Kinh Tông plotted with Tùng's own son, Trịnh Xuân, to recover real power for the throne. The plot was discovered, the emperor was forced to garrotte himself and Lê Thần Tông was set up instead. Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên then formally broke off relations with the court, a break that after seven more years led to the Trịnh–Nguyễn War.

In old age Tùng tried to secure the succession by dividing power between two sons, but his family quarrelled before he died, a brother also reaching for power. Taken ill to his brother's house, he saw his younger son murdered there, while the elder, Trịnh Tráng, fled to Thanh Hóa with the emperor and the royal family. Driven from the house and abandoned by the servants carrying his sedan chair, he died alone on the road on 17 July 1623.
trinidad: Trinidad lies 11 kilometres off the north-eastern coast of Venezuela and sits on the continental shelf of South America. It is the southernmost island in the Caribbean, with an area of 4,768 square kilometres, and the fifth largest in the Caribbean. Its landforms include the Northern, Central and Southern Ranges, the Caroni, Nariva and Oropouche swamps and the Caroni and Naparima plains. The highest point is El Cerro del Aripo, at 940 metres. The island's fauna is overwhelmingly of South American origin, and the Pitch Lake and the oil and gas fields of its south belong to its geology.

Kalinago and Arawakan-speaking peoples lived on Trinidad long before Christopher Columbus reached it on 31 July 1498, on his third voyage. The Arawakan name was Iëre, meaning land of the hummingbird. Columbus named the island for the Trinity, fulfilling a vow, after a sailor sighted three peaks. The island remained Spanish until 1797, but it was settled mostly by French colonists from the French Caribbean, especially Martinique.

In 1889 Trinidad and Tobago became a single British crown colony. It was granted self-governance in 1958 and independence from the United Kingdom in August 1962, and became a republic in September 1976. In the 19th century recruiters from India called the island Chinidat, the land of sugar, to lure workers into indentureship, and the Indian ancestry of much of the population is still marked by holidays such as Divali and Indian Arrival Day.

Trinidad is the largest and most populous island of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago. At the 2011 census its population was 37 per cent Indo-Trinidadian, 32 per cent Afro-Trinidadian and 24 per cent mixed race. The steelpan originated on the island and is the national instrument, and Carnival, J'ouvert and the Panorama steelpan competition are among its festivals. Venezuela's influence appears in the parang music style.
trinidad-and-tobago: The country covers 5,128 square kilometres and consists of two main islands separated by a strait of twenty nautical miles, with smaller islands such as Chacachacare, Monos, Huevos, Gaspar Grande and Little Tobago. Trinidad lies just six nautical miles off the coast of Venezuela across the Columbus Channel, and the islands are a physiographic extension of South America. Because they lie on the continental shelf and were once joined to the mainland, their wildlife has more in common with Venezuela's than with other Caribbean islands. The country lies outside the main hurricane alleys, although Hurricane Flora struck Tobago on 30 September 1963.

Banwari Trace in south-western Trinidad, from about 5000 BCE, is the oldest pre-Columbian archaeological site in the Caribbean and yielded Banwari Man, the oldest human skeleton found in the region. Columbus named Trinidad for the Trinity, fulfilling a vow made before his third voyage. He also reported Tobago on the horizon, calling it Bellaforma, but did not land. Whether the Indigenous name of Trinidad was Cairi, meaning Land of the Humming Bird, is disputed by other authors.

In 1797 a British force under General Sir Ralph Abercromby sailed through the Bocas and anchored off Chaguaramas. Seriously outnumbered, the Spanish governor, José María Chacón, capitulated without fighting. Trinidad became a British crown colony with a largely French-speaking population and Spanish laws, and British rule was formalised under the Treaty of Amiens in 1802. Its first British governor, Thomas Picton, was recalled after a heavy-handed approach that included torture and arbitrary arrest. Independence came on 31 August 1962, but Elizabeth II remained head of state, represented by Governor-General Solomon Hochoy, until the Republican Constitution of 1976.

The capital is Port of Spain, and the most populous municipality is Chaguanas. Tobago is administered by the Tobago House of Assembly. English is the official language, and the two main groups are of Indian-South Asian and sub-Saharan African heritage. The country is known for its Carnival, for the festivals of Diwali and Hosay, and as the birthplace of the steelpan, calypso, soca and the limbo. Indian Arrival Day marks the arrival of indentured Indian workers beginning in 1845, and Emancipation Day commemorates the end of slavery; it was the first country to recognise both as public holidays.
trinidad-and-tobago-carnival: The festival dates to the 1780s, when immigrants from the French West Indies, among them French planters, free people of mixed race and enslaved Africans, came to Trinidad under the Cédula de Población. Barred from the planters' masquerades, the enslaved are said to have staged small carnivals of their own, imitating or mocking their masters' balls, and formed a parallel celebration, Canboulay (from the French cannes brulés, burnt cane), with drums, singing, calinda dancing and stick-fighting. After emancipation the freed Africans began to celebrate their freedom during the Carnival season, carrying burning sugarcane.

Through the mid- and late 1800s the colonial government tried to suppress the festivities, provoking the Canboulay riots of 1881 and 1884. The Peace Preservation Act of 1884 banned the public carrying of torches, drumming, blowing horns and stick-fighting, and fixed the official start of Carnival at 6 a.m. on the Monday before Lent. Bamboo-Tamboo sticks beaten together replaced the banned drums and were banned in turn; in 1937 they reappeared as an orchestra of frying pans, dustbin lids and oil drums, the first steelpans.

Carnival proper opens early on Monday with J'ouvert (from the French for break of day), when revellers in homemade or satirical costumes, doused in oil, mud and powder, dance through the streets in the tradition of Canboulay; more formal costumes follow later that day and on Tuesday. Fetes such as band launches lead up to it, and costume (mas), stick-fighting, limbo and steelpan competitions are central to it. Soca has begun to replace calypso as its most popular music.

Its traditional characters include the Midnight Robber, who boasts of his valour, the Jab Jab devil, the stilt-dancing moko jumbie of African origin, the Dame Lorraine, a parody of 18th-century French aristocratic dress, and the Pierrot Grenade, a jester in scraps of cloth posing as a scholar. The Trinidad carnival has spread to other Caribbean islands and to cities such as Toronto, Miami, Houston, London and New York.
trinitarians: The Trinitarians, formally the Order of the Most Holy Trinity and of the Captives, are a mendicant order of the Catholic Church for men, founded at Cerfroid, outside Paris, in the late twelfth century and approved by Pope Innocent III on 17 December 1198. Papal documents name the founder only as Brother John; tradition identifies him as John of Matha and says the order grew from his vision of Christ with two captives around 1193.

Trinitarian tradition also counts Felix of Valois as co-founder. The founding intention was the ransom of Christians held captive by Muslims, a consequence of crusading and of piracy along the Mediterranean coast. Between the eighth and fifteenth centuries raids by militias, bands and armies from both sides were almost an annual occurrence in Catalonia, Languedoc and other coastal provinces.

The order grew quickly from three first houses, at Cerfroid, Planels and Bourg-la-Reine, into a network of houses. The first mission was undertaken by two English friars, who went to Morocco in 1200 and returned to France with 186 liberated captives. The first generation counted some fifty foundations, and in northern France the friars were called Mathurins from their base at the church of Saint-Mathurin in Paris, held from 1228.

The rule required a third of all income to be set aside for ransom. Louis IX installed a house of the order in the palace at Fontainebleau, chose Trinitarians as his chaplains and was accompanied by them on crusade; the Master of the Trinity was taken captive with him after the Battle of Al Mansurah.

The thirteenth century was a time of vitality, and later centuries brought decline in some areas. Reforms followed the Council of Trent, notably the Spanish Discalced Trinitarians under John Baptist of the Conception, and at the beginning of the eighteenth century the order still had 250 houses. Revolution, suppression and civil war later reduced it sharply, but from the late nineteenth century it began to grow again in Italy and Spain.

The habit was white, bearing a cross of red and blue. The rule approved in 1198 was revised in 1267 and 1631. Each local community served its area through hospitality, care of the sick and poor, churches and education, and the friars later took on evangelisation. The wider Trinitarian family includes priests, brothers, cloistered nuns, several congregations of sisters and lay tertiaries, found across Europe and the Americas and in Africa, India, Korea and the Philippines. Their patroness is Our Lady of Good Remedy.
trinity: The doctrine was formulated as early Christians tried to understand the relationship between Jesus and God in their scriptures and earlier traditions. Scholars cite New Testament passages that present a triadic understanding of God, among them Matthew 28:19, in which disciples are to baptise in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and Paul's blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:13. Larry Hurtado notes that the developed doctrine is not explicit in those books. Towards the end of the first century Clement of Rome asked in his epistle whether Christians did not have one God, one Christ and one Spirit, and the Didache directs baptism in the threefold name.

In the fourth century Arianism, as traditionally understood, taught that the Father existed before the Son, who was a changeable creature granted the dignity of Son of God. In 325 the First Council of Nicaea adopted the Nicene Creed, which used the term homoousios, of one substance, for the relation of Father and Son. After more than fifty years of debate the term was accepted as the hallmark of orthodoxy and developed into the formula of three persons, one being. The First Council of Constantinople in 381 expanded the creed to say that the Holy Spirit is worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son.

Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa and Basil the Great held that the distinctions among the persons lay solely in their inner relations, so that there are not three gods but one divine Being in three persons. Augustine of Hippo used a psychological analogy of memory, intelligence and will, and in De trinitate, written between 399 and 419, he described love as having three aspects: the lover, the beloved and the love. John of Damascus, who died in 749, made perichoresis, the mutual indwelling of the persons, a technical term. The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 declared that the Father begets, the Son is begotten and the Holy Spirit proceeds.

Adoptionism and Arianism existed before the formal definition at the councils of Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus. Adoptionists held that Jesus became divine only at his baptism, resurrection or ascension. Judaism traditionally rejects the doctrine, although the Zohar of 1286 contains a passage some read as a kabbalistic trinity. The doctrine left marks on church building: many churches have three doors, and Gothic cathedrals used trefoils to represent it. In Christian art it is most often shown with the Spirit as a dove with wings outspread, though images with three human figures appear in most periods.
trinity-college-dublin: A medieval University of Dublin was founded in 1320 under a papal brief issued by Pope Clement V in 1311. It kept an intermittent existence at St Patrick's Cathedral but did not flourish and ended during the Reformation. In 1592 a small group of Dublin citizens obtained letters patent from Elizabeth I incorporating Trinity College on the site of the disbanded Augustinian Priory of All Hallows, southeast of the city walls, which the Corporation of Dublin provided.

The college was established to consolidate Tudor rule in Ireland. Provost Adam Loftus named it after Trinity College, Cambridge, and it was founded on the model of Oxford and Cambridge. It was the only college ever established within the University of Dublin.

In the 18th century Trinity was the university of the Protestant Ascendancy. The Parliament of Ireland, meeting across College Green, made generous grants for the neoclassical Parliament Square, whose first building was the Old Library, begun in 1712, followed by the Printing House and the Dining Hall. The library has housed the Book of Kells since 1661. Trinity gained the world's oldest chairs in French and German (1776), Irish (1840) and English literature (1867).

Women were admitted as full members for the first time in 1904. From 1904 to 1907 women from Oxford and Cambridge, who were not granted degrees there, came to Trinity to receive them; known as the Steamboat ladies, they paid fees that helped to fund Trinity Hall.

The college is governed by the Provost, Fellows and Scholars under letters patent that later monarchs amended. Charles I in 1637 raised the number of fellows from seven to 16 and established the Board. The university was linked to parliamentary representation from 1613, when James I granted it two seats in the Irish House of Commons; the vote was first limited to the Provost, Fellows and Scholars, extended in 1832 to holders of an MA and in 1918 to all graduates. After the Acts of Union 1800 it elected members to Westminster, among them W. E. H. Lecky and Edward Carson.

Trinity is a sister college of Oriel College, Oxford, and St John's College, Cambridge, and a graduate of any of the three universities may be incorporated into another. Traditions include Commons, a meal in the Dining Hall begun by the slamming of its doors, and Trinity Week in April. The student society The Hist was founded in 1770, and from 1869 to 1893 the college's literary magazine Kottabos was edited by Robert Yelverton Tyrrell.
trinity-lavra-of-st-sergius: Sergius of Radonezh, one of the most venerated Russian saints, founded the monastery in the 14th century by building a wooden church in honour of the Holy Trinity on Makovets Hill. In 1355 he introduced a charter that required auxiliary buildings such as a refectory, kitchen and bakery. It became a model for his many followers, who founded more than 400 monasteries across Russia, including Solovetsky, Kirillov and Simonov.

Sergius supported Dmitri Donskoi against the Tatars and sent two monks, Peresvet and Oslyabya, to the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380. A Tatar raid devastated the monastery by fire in 1408. In 1422 Sergius was declared patron saint of the Russian state, and in the same year a team of Serbian monks who had found refuge there after the Battle of Kosovo built the first stone cathedral. Andrei Rublev and Daniil Chyorny were summoned to decorate it with frescoes.

The monastery grew into one of the wealthiest landowners in Russia. Woods around it were cleared and a village, or posad, grew up near its walls and gradually became the town of Sergiyev Posad. It was also a notable centre of chronicle-writing and icon painting. The six-pillared Assumption Cathedral, commissioned by Ivan the Terrible in 1559, took 26 years to build and holds the burials of Boris Godunov and his family.

In the 1550s a wooden palisade was replaced by stone walls 1.5 km long with twelve towers. They helped the monastery withstand a Polish-Lithuanian siege of 16 months in 1608 to 1610, and a shell-hole in the cathedral gates recalls a failed siege by Wladyslaw IV in 1618. The young Peter I twice took refuge there. In 1744 Empress Elizabeth gave the cloister the dignity of a lavra, and the metropolitan of Moscow became its archimandrite.

After the Russian Revolution of 1917 the Soviet government closed the lavra in 1920, and its buildings were given to civic institutions or declared museums. In 1930 the monastery bells, including the Tsar-Bell of 65 tons, were destroyed. In 1945 Joseph Stalin's temporary tolerance of the church during World War II allowed the lavra to be returned to the Russian Orthodox Church, and divine service was renewed in the Assumption Cathedral on 16 April 1946.

It was the seat of the Moscow Patriarchate until 1983 and remains a prime centre of religious education, with more than 300 monks. It was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1993. Sergius of Radonezh and Boris Godunov are among those buried there.
tripartite-convention-1899: In the 1870s rival Samoan factions made separate treaties with the foreign powers: the United States concluded a friendship treaty in 1878, Germany a treaty with the same faction in 1879, and Britain an Anglo-Samoan treaty with a rival faction later that year. Quarrels among the foreigners and among the Samoans, sharpened by modern weapons, turned into deadly fighting. A conference in Washington in June 1887 adjourned without results, and open conflict between the powers was checked only when the Apia hurricane of 1889 wrecked their warships.

At Berlin in 1889, at the invitation of the German foreign minister Count Herbert von Bismarck, the three powers set up a joint protectorate, or condominium, with a chief justice, a municipal council for Apia and a free right of the Samoans to elect their king. The arrangement soon broke down: other chiefs rebelled against the king, civil war followed, and by the end of the century the three governments freely admitted its failure.

A joint commission of the three powers arrived in Samoa in May 1899, ended the fighting and decided by July that the islands must be partitioned. Britain, then engaged in the Second Boer War, reached an agreement with Germany signed on 14 November 1899, before Kaiser Wilhelm II's visit to England. The convention that secured American approval was signed at Washington on 2 December 1899 by Secretary of State John Hay, Baron Theodor von Holleben and Sir Julian Pauncefote, and ratifications were exchanged on 16 February 1900. The dividing line was longitude 171 degrees west.

On 19 February 1900 President William McKinley placed Tutuila and the islands east of the line under the Department of the Navy as a naval station; the cession of the Manua Group followed in 1904, and the name American Samoa came into use in 1905. Upolu, Savaii, Apolima and Manono became German Samoa, with a flag raising on 1 March 1900 and Wilhelm Solf as governor. Britain received the German rights in Tonga, the German islands of the Solomon group east and south-east of Bougainville, a boundary in the neutral zone of West Africa and the end of German extraterritoriality in Zanzibar. These arrangements lasted until the outbreak of World War I in 1914.
tripartite-pact: Germany and Japan had technically been allies since the Anti-Comintern Pact of 1936, but the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of 1939 between Germany and the Soviet Union came as a surprise to Japan. In November 1939 the two signed an Agreement for Cultural Cooperation, which restored what has been called their reluctant alliance. The Tripartite Pact, also known as the Berlin Pact, was signed in Berlin by Joachim von Ribbentrop for Germany, Galeazzo Ciano for Italy and Saburō Kurusu for Japan, in the presence of Adolf Hitler.

Under Article 1 Japan recognised the leadership of Germany and Italy in establishing a new order in Europe, and under Article 2 they recognised Japan's leadership in a new order in Greater East Asia. Article 3 bound the three to assist one another with all political, economic and military means if one was attacked by a power not at present involved in the European War or the Japanese-Chinese conflict. Article 5 left unchanged each signatory's existing relations with the Soviet Union. The pact was to last ten years.

It was directed chiefly at the United States, but its practical effects were limited, since the Italo-German and Japanese theatres lay on opposite sides of the world and the partners' strategic interests differed. Its defensive clauses were never invoked. Joint technical commissions were agreed on 20 December 1940, yet the military commission in Berlin met only two or three times by 1943, and there were no trilateral naval talks.

Hungary joined on 20 November 1940, Romania on 23 November, Slovakia on 24 November and Bulgaria on 1 March 1941. Hungary had first sent notice of spiritual adherence, after Ribbentrop's speech seemed to invite new members, though Ciano opposed adding smaller states. Bulgaria signed after Germany needed to move troops through it. Yugoslavia signed on 25 March 1941, and the military coup in Belgrade two days later was followed by invasion by Germany, Italy and Hungary. The Independent State of Croatia, created from conquered Yugoslav territory, signed on 15 June 1941. Finland and Thailand declined to join, and German talks with the Soviet Union about joining went nowhere.

On 11 December 1941, the day Germany and Italy declared war on the United States, the three powers agreed not to make a separate peace with the United States or Britain. The historian Paul W. Schroeder describes the pact as virtually inoperative by December 1941. Its symbolic effect was larger: it persuaded the American public that Japan was acting in concert with Germany, and the charge that it coordinated aggression was part of the case at Nuremberg and at the Tokyo trials.
tripitaka-koreana: Work on a first Tripiṭaka Koreana began in 1011 during the Goryeo–Khitan War and was completed in 1087. It was based primarily on the Kaibao Canon, completed in the 10th century, and the compilers also consulted other texts, such as the Khitan Tripiṭaka, to find items that needed revision. Carving the woodblocks was regarded as a way of changing the country's fortune by invoking the Buddha's help. The original set was destroyed by fire during the Mongol invasions in 1232, although scattered parts of its prints survive.

To implore divine help against the Mongol threat again, King Gojong ordered the canon recreated. The carving was completed in 12 years, with the support of Ch'oe U and his son Ch'oe Hang and the involvement of monks of both the Seon and Gyo schools. This second version is usually what is meant by the name. The scholar Robert Buswell Jr. calls the project an enormous national commitment of money and manpower, perhaps comparable to the 1960s Apollo program Moon landings.

The collection holds 1,496 titles in 6,568 books, with 81,258 pages and a total of 52,330,152 characters. It includes texts beyond the Tripiṭaka proper, such as travelogues, Sanskrit and Chinese dictionaries and biographies of monks and nuns, so Buswell proposed in 2013 that it be called the Korean Buddhist Canon. Each block measures 24 cm by 70 cm and weighs about three to four kilograms, and each side carries 23 lines of 14 characters. Stacked, the blocks would weigh about 280 tons.

The blocks were made of birch wood from the southern islands of Korea. They were soaked in sea water for three years, cut and boiled in salt water, and then dried in the shade and wind for three years before carving. After carving, each was coated in a poisonous lacquer against insects and framed with metal to prevent warping. The consistent style led people to think one man carved the whole set, but an estimate puts the team at 30 men.

The National Preceptor Sugi checked the text against other versions and published 30 volumes of Additional Records listing the errors, redundancies and omissions he found. The popular belief that the text has no error is a misconception, since a survey found missing characters and errors. Japanese Buddhists coveted it from 1388, and 45 complete printings were given to Japan from the Muromachi period; it served as the basis for the modern Taishō Tripiṭaka. It was moved to Haeinsa in 1398, was designated a National Treasure of South Korea in 1962 and was inscribed in the UNESCO Memory of the World register in 2007.
triple-alliance-1668: Under the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees, Louis XIV of France married Maria Theresa of Spain, eldest daughter of Philip IV of Spain, who renounced her inheritance rights in return for a dowry of 500,000 gold écus that was never paid. When Philip died in September 1665, leaving his four-year-old son Charles II of Spain as king, Louis argued that the unpaid dowry made the renunciation invalid and that her rights devolved to him under the Jus Devolutionis. He launched the War of Devolution on 24 May 1667, and by September his troops held much of the Spanish Netherlands.

After the Treaty of Breda ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War on 31 July 1667, England and the Dutch Republic began talks on a common front against France. Charles II of England blamed Louis for the humiliation of Breda, and Parliament and the City of London wanted peace. Sir William Temple persuaded the States General to approve the alliance before consulting the provincial bodies, reversing normal practice, so that the French ambassador, Godefroi, Comte d'Estrades, could not delay it with bribes. Sweden, which controlled the Baltic trade in pitch and timber, signed on 5 May.

The alliance had three parts: a defensive alliance, a guarantee of terms for ending the War of Devolution, and secret clauses. France would withdraw from the Spanish Netherlands but keep Lille, Douai, Tournai, Oudenaarde, Kortrijk, Charleroi and other towns. One secret clause required Spain to end its war with Portugal; another committed the allies to force France back to its 1659 boundaries if it fought on. The English Parliament approved £300,000 if needed, and the States General activated 48 warships and the recruitment of 18,000 more troops. Sweden's demand for 480,000 rixdollars was passed on to Spain.

French troops conquered Franche-Comté in February 1668. With the war costing far more than expected, and a secret partition treaty with Emperor Leopold promising him much of the Spanish inheritance should Charles of Spain die, Louis decided to make peace on terms agreed at Saint Germain in April.

The alliance did not last: commercial disputes led to the Third Anglo-Dutch War, and Sweden and England backed France at the outset of the Franco-Dutch War of 1672-1678. Yet it ended the long Franco-Dutch alliance and was the first step towards the anti-French coalition that lasted until 1714. From 1668 to 1674 Parliament voted large sums for the Royal Navy, and English diplomacy turned to Sweden, Brandenburg and Denmark.
triple-alliance-1882: The man chiefly responsible for the alliance was Otto von Bismarck, the Chancellor of Germany. After unifying Germany in 1871 his main aim was to preserve the status quo in Europe, and he feared that France would find allies to help it regain Alsace-Lorraine. By promising aid to Austria-Hungary and Italy if they were attacked, he sought to make them somewhat dependent on Germany and unsympathetic to French adventures. Germany and Austria-Hungary had been closely allied since October 1879.

Italy had several motives. Its government was then controlled by conservatives who sympathised with the two monarchies, and Catholic Austria was a traditional protector of the Papacy, with which Italy had poor relations. Above all Italy sought allies against the French Third Republic. Italian anger at the French conquest of Tunisia in 1881, called the Slap of Tunis by the Italian press, pushed it towards the two monarchies, even though it had fought three wars against Austria-Hungary in the previous 34 years.

Each member promised mutual support in the event of an attack by another great power. Germany and Austria-Hungary were to assist Italy if France attacked it without provocation, and Italy would assist Germany in the same case. If Austria-Hungary and Russia went to war, Italy promised to remain neutral.

The treaty was renewed periodically. In February 1887 Italy gained a promise of German support for its colonial ambitions in North Africa, which proved empty. Bismarck pressed Austria-Hungary to accept consultation and mutual agreement with Italy on any territorial change in the Balkans or on the coasts and islands of the Adriatic and Aegean. In 1891 attempts to bring Britain into the alliance failed, though Russian diplomats widely believed they had succeeded. Romania, ruled by Carol I, also secretly pledged support on 18 October 1883.

The alliance was never comfortable. Italian opinion was unenthusiastic about an alignment with the former enemy of Italian unification, whose districts in the Trentino and Istria irredentists saw as occupied. Austria-Hungary's general staff kept plans for a war against Italy from at least 1903, and as late as 1911 its chief, Franz Conrad von Hötzendorf, urged a preemptive strike. Shortly after the alliance was renewed in June 1902, Italy secretly gave France a similar guarantee, and on 1 November 1902 the two agreed to stay neutral if the other was attacked. In 1909 Italy and Russia made the Racconigi Bargain.

When Austria-Hungary began a war in August 1914, Italy proclaimed neutrality, regarding Austria-Hungary as the aggressor, and it had not consulted Italy as the 1912 renewal required. After negotiating with both sides, Italy sided with the Triple Entente and declared war on Austria-Hungary. Romania likewise stayed neutral in 1914 and entered the war against the Central Powers on 27 August 1916.
triple-entente: After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 to 1871, Prussia forced France to cede Alsace-Lorraine to the new German Empire, and France built up its army to deter German aggression. Russia had been a member of the League of the Three Emperors of 1873 with Austria-Hungary and Germany, but rivalry in the Balkans prevented its renewal in 1887. Bismarck's secret Reinsurance Treaty with Russia lapsed in 1890, and Russian leaders, alarmed at their isolation, joined the Franco-Russian Alliance in 1894. It was designed as a counter to the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy.

Britain kept to its policy of splendid isolation through the 1890s. By the early 1900s it saw the German threat as having grown sharply, and when overtures to Berlin were not returned it turned to Paris and St. Petersburg. In 1904 Britain and France signed five agreements on spheres of influence in North Africa, mostly settling colonial disputes, which began the Entente cordiale.

The Tangier Crisis encouraged cooperation between Britain and France from their shared fear of German expansion. Russia had lost the Russo-Japanese War, which contributed to the Russian Revolution of 1905. In 1907 the Anglo-Russian Entente tried to settle disputes over Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet and to end the rivalry in Central Asia known as the Great Game, and it eased British fears about the Baghdad Railway. The Franco-Japanese Treaty of 1907 also formed part of the coalition. The Anglo-German naval race left an atmosphere of mutual hostility, and Lord Haldane's mission to Berlin in February 1912 failed.

The Entente was not an alliance of mutual defence, unlike the Triple Alliance and the Franco-Russian Alliance, so Britain was free in 1914 to make its own decisions. The Foreign Office official Eyre Crowe wrote that it was nothing more than a frame of mind. In 1914 all three powers entered the First World War as Allied Powers, and on 4 September 1914 they declared that they would not make a separate peace.

Historians continue to debate how far the alliance system caused the First World War. The alignment of Russia with France and Britain was controversial on both sides, since Russian conservatives distrusted the secular French and British and many French and British politicians disliked the tsarist regime. Mistrust lasted into the war, and British and French politicians expressed relief when Nicholas II abdicated in 1917. The British king withdrew an offer of asylum to the Romanovs, and France never raised the subject. The Triple Entente was the coalition that fought the First World War against the Central Powers.
triple-intervention: The Treaty of Shimonoseki, signed on 17 April 1895, ceded Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula, with the harbour city of Port Arthur, to Japan. As soon as its terms became public, Russia, which had its own designs in China, objected to the Japanese gain and its possible effect on China's stability. Russia had been extending its influence in the Far East since the Treaty of Aigun of 1858, was building the Trans-Siberian Railway, and needed a warm-water port that Japanese control of Port Arthur would deny it.

France joined because of its military alliance of 1893 with Russia and its wish not to be diplomatically isolated, although it had cordial relations with Japan and no ambitions in Manchuria. Germany hoped to turn Russian attention eastward, away from itself, and to win Russian support for German concessions in China.

The three powers advised Japan to renounce the peninsula on the grounds that holding it would cause instability. Britain and the United States would not intercede, and Japan could not resist three European powers at once: they had 38 warships of 95,000 tons already in East Asia, against an Imperial Japanese Navy of 31 warships of 57,000 tons in all. On 5 May 1895 Prime Minister Itō Hirobumi announced the withdrawal in exchange for an additional indemnity of 30 million kuping taels, the renunciation was made by treaty on 8 November, and the last Japanese troops left in December.

Russia moved almost at once to fortify Port Arthur, Germany secured concessions in Shandong Province, and France and Britain took the port cities of Guangzhouwan and Weihaiwei. The Japanese felt cheated of their spoils, and the humiliation fed the Gashin Shōtan movement, a call to persevere through hardship that meant building up heavy industry and the armed forces, above all the navy. Japanese diplomacy afterwards sought to prevent any new combination of European powers against Japan, which led directly to the Anglo-Japanese Alliance of 1902. Resentment of the intervention was one of the causes of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905.
tripoli-greece: Tripoli lies in the centre of the Peloponnese, at the western border of a large basin, a polje about 650 metres above sea level and roughly 30 kilometres long. It has a hot-summer Mediterranean climate with some continental features, and snow or sleet can fall between November and early April. The ground of the basin is karstic: water seeps into the underground through ponors rather than draining over the surface, so heavy winter rains can leave temporary lakes. Because the city is at the centre of the Peloponnese, it is a transport hub.

In the Middle Ages the place was known as Drobolitsa, perhaps from the Greek Hydropolitsa, Water City, or from the South Slavic for Plain of Oaks. It appears in a list of abandoned Byzantine sites of 1467. After the Ottoman conquest of the Morea the cultural and administrative centre of the Tegean plain moved from Mouchli to Drobolitsa, and after 1540 the settlement below the fortress, called Tarabluca, became the political centre.

In spring 1770, during the Greek uprising known as the Orlov Revolt, the revolutionary armies were halted outside Tripolitsa. Albanian mercenaries of the Ottomans killed 3,000 Greeks in a few hours on entering the city, and Osman bey, their leader, intervened to prevent its total destruction.

Before the Greek War of Independence, as Tripoliçe, it was an Ottoman administrative centre in the Peloponnese, the Morea Eyalet, often called the pashalik of Tripolitsa, with large Muslim and Jewish populations. Greek insurgents stormed it after a bloody siege in 1821 and exterminated the Muslim population. Ibrahim Pasha retook the city on 22 June 1825, after the Greeks had abandoned it. Before he evacuated the Peloponnese in early 1828 he destroyed the city and tore down its walls. The siege is the subject of the folk song Forty lads from Livadeia.

After the independent Greek state was established in 1830 the old Ottoman buildings, including the walls, were destroyed or demolished. Tripoli was renamed and rebuilt, and during the 19th and 20th centuries it became the administrative, economic, commercial and transport centre of the central and southern Peloponnese. It is the capital of the Peloponnese region and of the regional unit of Arcadia, and its municipality had 44,165 inhabitants in 2021. Tripoli is the flagship campus of the University of the Peloponnese, founded in 2000. Theodoros Kolokotronis, the pre-eminent general of the Greek War of Independence, is among its notable people.
tripura: Tripura is a landlocked state of about 10,491 square kilometres, bordered by Assam and Mizoram and by Bangladesh, and one of the Seven Sister States of North East India. Five ranges of hills, Baramura, Atharamura, Longtharai, Shakhan and the Jampui Hills, run from north to south with valleys between them, while Agartala stands on a plain in the west. The highest point is Betling Shib, at 939 metres. The climate is tropical savanna, with heavy monsoon rain from May to September, and more than half of the land is forest.

The Mahabharata, the Puranas and the Edicts of Ashoka are said to mention Tripura, and the Mahabharata names the region Kirat Desh, though it is unclear whether that land matched the modern state. The Twipra Kingdom ruled the area for centuries, but when its dynasty began is not documented. The Rajmala, a chronicle first written in the 15th century, lists 179 kings down to Krishna Kishore Manikya, who reigned from 1830 to 1850, but it is not a reliable source. The name is linked to the goddess Tripura Sundari, whose temple at Udaipur is one of the 51 Shakta pithas.

After 1947 Tippera district in the plains became part of East Pakistan, while Hill Tippera stayed under a regency council until 1949. On 9 September 1949 the Maharani Regent signed the Tripura Merger Agreement, making Tripura a Part C state of India. Partition cut it off: the road distance from Kolkata to Agartala grew from under 350 kilometres to 1,700. In 1947–51 an estimated 610,000 Bengali refugees entered, a number almost equal to the state's whole population, and about 1.038 million more came during the war of 1971.

Agartala is the capital and largest city. The official languages are Bengali, Kokborok and English. The 2011 census counted 3,671,032 people, and in 2001 Bengalis were almost 65 per cent of them, with 19 scheduled tribes, of which the Kokborok-speaking Tripuris are the largest. Most of the land belongs to the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council. The sculptures at Unakoti, Pilak and Devtamura show a fusion of organised and indigenous religious art.
trireme: The trireme developed from the penteconter, a single-banked warship with 25 oars on each side, and from the bireme, a two-banked warship of Phoenician origin. Biremes are common on vases and pottery fragments from the 8th century BCE, and the first references to three-banked ships come at the end of that century.

Modern scholars are divided on whether the trireme came from Greece or Phoenicia. Thucydides says the Corinthians introduced it to Greece in the late 8th century BCE, and Pliny and Diodorus took this to mean that it was invented at Corinth. Clement of Alexandria attributes it to the Sidonians. The first definite reference to triremes in battle is of about 525 BCE, when Polycrates of Samos contributed 40 to a Persian invasion of Egypt. By 490 BCE they were the backbone of the Persian fleet.

Excavated ship sheds at Zea in Piraeus, the main war harbour of Athens, were about 40 metres long and 6 metres wide, which with Vitruvius's allowance for each rower suggests a ship just under 37 metres long. Its draught was about 1 metre, and it could be beached easily. The ship had 170 oars, one man to each, two masts with square sails, and two steering oars at the stern.

The complement was about 200: the 170 rowers, a deck crew under the trierarch and a marine detachment. Crews were free men, not galley slaves. An Athenian crew in the Peloponnesian War typically had 80 citizens, 60 metics and 60 foreign hands. In Athens a wealthy trierarch paid to man and maintain the ship, which belonged to the city.

The trireme relied on speed and manoeuvre rather than boarding. Squadrons used the periplous, outflanking the enemy to strike the rear, and the diekplous, a charge to break the enemy line. In 483/2 BCE Themistocles persuaded the Athenian assembly to build 200 triremes with the income of the Laurion silver mines. The Persian fleet was defeated at Salamis, after a first clash at Artemisium.

In the Hellenistic period larger warships, the quinqueremes, replaced it as ramming grew less effective against armoured bows. Between 1985 and 1987 a trireme named Olympias was built at Piraeus on the advice of the historian J. S. Morrison and the naval architect John F. Coates.
