Crewed by 170 volunteers, it could turn through 180 degrees in one minute, and its trials suggest that ancient accounts of its performance were not exaggerated.
trisong-detsen: Trisong Detsen was the 38th king, or Tsenpo, of Tibet and succeeded his father Tridé Tsuktsen in 755, at the traditional young age of 13. He inherited an empire that had declined somewhat from its extent under Songtsen Gampo: in 694 Tibet lost control of several cities in Turkestan, and in 703 kingdoms in Nepal rebelled. By the end of his reign he had extended the empire beyond its previous borders.

In 763 he sent an army of 200,000 men to the Tang frontier, defeated the forces there and took Chang'an, forcing Emperor Daizong of Tang to flee the capital. In 783 a peace treaty gave Tibet all lands in present-day Qinghai. He allied with Nanzhao in 778 to attack Sichuan, though Nanzhao broke away at the Battle of Shenchuan in 794 and restored its alliance with China. Trisong Detsen also pushed west to the Amu Darya and threatened the Abbasid caliph Harun ar-Rashid, who allied with China, and Arab wars occupied him until 797.

Trisong Detsen was one of the three Dharma Kings, with Songtsen Gampo and Ralpachen, honoured for introducing Buddhism to Tibet. His conversion came in 762, at the age of 20. He invited the Indian masters Padmasambhava, Śāntarakṣita and Vimalamitra, and Śāntarakṣita helped build Samye Monastery as the first monastery in Tibet. In 779 Śāntarakṣita initiated seven Tibetans as monks, among them reportedly former soldiers. A large project translated Buddhist scriptures from Pali and Sanskrit into Classical Tibetan.

He also sent parties to Yizhou in about 761 and 763 to receive Chan teachings. From 792 to 794 he hosted a two-year debate at Samye, known in Western scholarship as the Council of Lhasa, between the Chan master Moheyan and Kamalaśīla, a student of Śāntarakṣita. Sources differ on its nature and its victor, and Stein holds that Kamalaśīla won and that the king sided with him.

Trisong Detsen retired in 797 to the palace at Zungkar to write dharma texts and passed the throne to his second son, Muné Tsenpo. The Testament of Ba states that Muné Tsenpo insisted that his father's funeral follow Buddhist rather than traditional rites. Muné Tsenpo reigned a year and a half, and the throne then passed to his brother Mutik Tsenpo, who was on it by 804. Mutik's sons included Ralpachen. Tradition also links Trisong Detsen with the building of the Boudhanath stupa in the Kathmandu Valley.
tristan-de-luna-y-arellano: Tristán de Luna y Arellano was born in Borobia, Spain, to a noble family. He was a cousin of Antonio de Mendoza, viceroy of New Spain, and of Juana de Zúñiga, the wife of Hernán Cortés. In Mexico he served with Francisco Vásquez de Coronado on the expedition to the Seven Cities of Cíbola and put down an Indian rebellion in Oaxaca.

Luís de Velasco, viceroy of New Spain, chose him to found a settlement on the Gulf Coast and to open an overland route to Santa Elena, in present-day South Carolina, where a second outpost was planned. His fleet of eleven ships carried more than 1,500 soldiers and settlers under six captains of cavalry and six of infantry. Passing over Filipina Bay, modern Mobile Bay, it settled on Ochuse Bay, modern Pensacola Bay, and in late August and September 1559 founded Santa María de Ochuse.

On the night of 19 September 1559, before the ships had been unloaded, a hurricane with a storm surge struck the anchorage. Most of the men moved inland to the abandoned village of Nanipacana on the Alabama River, which they renamed Santa Cruz de Nanipacana. Relief ships sent in November carried the colony through the winter, but the supplies promised for the spring did not come, and hunger drove Luna to send a detachment of 200 men up to the Coosa chiefdom in north-west Georgia, where it stayed until November.

Luna proved an ineffective leader, and tension grew between him and his officers and men. The viceroy replaced him with Ángel de Villafañe, who reached Pensacola Bay in April 1561. Luna was allowed to leave by way of Havana for Spain, but he spent the rest of his life in Mexico.

Luna died on 16 September 1573. Europeans did not settle the Pensacola area again until the Spanish founded Presidio Santa Maria de Galve in 1698. Archaeologists of the University of West Florida have identified a site of about 13 to 15 hectares as his settlement, the largest Spanish site of the mid-sixteenth century in the Southeast and the earliest European settlement in the United States to last several years.
tristan-und-isolde: Richard Wagner called the work a music drama in three acts, to a German libretto of his own loosely based on Gottfried von Strassburg's 12th-century romance. He preferred the term Handlung, plot or action, to distinguish its continuous narrative flow, the endless melody, from conventional opera with its recitatives and showpiece arias, which he regarded with disdain. First conceived in 1854, it was inspired in part by the philosophy of Arthur Schopenhauer and by Wagner's relationship with his muse Mathilde Wesendonck.

Wagner had fled to Zurich after a warrant was issued for his arrest for taking part in the May Revolution of 1849, and there in 1852 he met the silk trader Otto Wesendonck, who supported him for several years. According to his autobiography, he decided to dramatise the legend after his friend Karl Ritter tried to do so.

In the first act Isolde, promised in marriage to King Marke, is carried by ship to Cornwall in the care of Marke's nephew Tristan, whom she scorns and blames. In the second, the lovers meet at night when Marke leaves on a hunt. They declare that only in the long night of death can they be eternally united. The knight Melot leads Marke to find them, and Marke is heartbroken that Tristan betrayed him.

In the third act Kurwenal has brought the wounded Tristan to his castle at Kareol in Brittany, where a shepherd's pipe announces whether a ship is in sight. Tristan curses the love potion and, when Isolde's ship is at last piped, tears the bandages from his wounds in his excitement. He dies with her name on his lips as she arrives at his side.

The music was composed between 1857 and 1859, but the opera proved difficult to stage. Proposals for Rio de Janeiro, Strasbourg, Paris and Karlsruhe came to nothing, and a Vienna production was abandoned in 1864 after over seventy rehearsals, which gave it a reputation as unperformable. It was premiered in Munich on 10 June 1865 under Hans von Bülow. The Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung called it an act of indecency.

The Tristan chord of its prelude marks a defining moment in the move away from traditional tonal harmony, and some scholars see in the opera the beginnings of atonality. It directly inspired Anton Bruckner, Gustav Mahler, Richard Strauss, Alban Berg, Arnold Schoenberg and Benjamin Britten, while Claude Debussy, Maurice Ravel and Igor Stravinsky formed their styles in contrast to it.
tristao-da-cunha: Tristão da Cunha was born in Portugal around 1460. He served in the Third Italian War under the Castilian general Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba and took part in the Battle of Cerignola. He was tasked with hosting the funeral of the fallen French general Louis d'Armagnac, Duke of Nemours, and he commanded Roca Guillerma, between Gaeta and Salerno, where he was briefly captured by the French in a betrayal by local nobles before being freed. After he returned to Portugal he was named the first viceroy of Portuguese India in 1504, but temporary blindness kept him from taking up the post.

In 1506 he was appointed commander of the 8th Indian Armada, a fleet of 15 ships bound for the east coast of Africa and India. His cousin Afonso de Albuquerque led a squadron of five vessels that later detached, with the mission of taking Socotra and building a fortress there in the hope of closing the Red Sea trade. On the voyage, Da Cunha sighted a group of remote islands in the South Atlantic, 2,816 km from South Africa. Rough seas prevented a landing, but he named the main island after himself, and it became Tristan da Cunha.

After attacks on Arab cities on the east coast of Africa, he fought at Barawa, in Ajuran Empire territory, where the Portuguese burned and looted the city and he was wounded. In 1507 he and Albuquerque captured the port of Suq on Socotra, where the Forte de São Miguel de Socotorá was begun; famine, sickness and ship losses followed, and the Portuguese abandoned the island in 1511. In India he relieved the garrison at Cannanore on 27 August with 11 ships and 300 men, and he raided northern Madagascar.

In 1514 King Manuel I sent him as ambassador to Pope Leo X with Garcia de Resende as secretary. The embassy of one hundred and forty people entered Rome on 12 March 1514 in a procession of exotic animals, among them an elephant named Hanno, a gift to the pope. Da Cunha later joined the Portuguese Privy Council. His son Nuno da Cunha became the ninth governor of Portuguese India in 1529, and his tomb is at the convent of Nossa Senhora da Encarnação in Olhalvo.
troad: The Troad, also called Troas, is a historical region in northwestern Anatolia. It corresponds with the Biga Peninsula in the Çanakkale Province of modern Turkey. It is bounded by the Dardanelles to the northwest and the Aegean Sea to the west, and separated from the rest of Anatolia by the massif that forms Mount Ida. It is drained by two main rivers, the Scamander (Karamenderes) and the Simoeis, which join in the area containing the ruins of Troy.

The Troad is first mentioned by that name in Hittite records as Taruiša. The identification was first put forward by Emil Forrer but was largely disputed by Hittite experts until 1983, when Houwink ten Cate showed that two fragments came from the same cuneiform tablet and that Taruiša and Wiluša (Troy) were correctly placed in northwestern Anatolia. Greek settlements flourished in the Archaic and Classical ages, as shown by the number of Greek poleis that coined money in their own names.

The region was part of the satrapy of Hellespontine Phrygia of the Achaemenid Empire until its conquest by Alexander the Great. It then fell to the Seleucid Empire and passed to Rome's ally, the kingdom of Pergamon. The Attalid kings ceded Mysia, including the Troad, to the Roman Republic on the death of King Attalus III in 133 BCE. Under the Roman Empire it became part of the province of Asia and later of the smaller Mysian province Hellespontus, and it was important enough to have suffragan bishoprics. Under the later Byzantine Empire it belonged to the thema of the Aegean Islands, and after the Ottoman conquest it formed part of the sanjak of Biga.

In the New Testament the apostles Paul and Silas first visited Troas on their journey from Galatia to Macedonia. Paul also referred to Troas when he asked Timothy to bring the cloak he had left there. The change from "they" to "we" in Acts 16 and Acts 20 implies that Paul was joined by Luke when he went through Troas.
trocmi: Strabo and other Greek writers call them Trokmoi, Livy and Pliny Trogmi and Cicero Trocmi. The name is probably Celtic but its origin is unclear; a link with Old Irish tróg, miserable, has been suggested. They came to Anatolia as the last stage of the movement of Celtic peoples from the middle Danube into the Balkans and Asia Minor. After the Celtic attacks on Macedonia and Greece, the warrior bands were brought across the Hellespont through an alliance with Nicomedes I of Bithynia, who wanted them as allies against the Seleucids. A tradition reported by Strabo from Posidonius that derived them from Gaul is rejected by modern scholars.

By the end of the 260s BCE the Galatian groups were settled, the Trocmi in the easternmost lands, along the right bank of the middle Halys, now the Kızılırmak, beside Pontus and Cappadocia. The local population was neither wiped out nor driven away and probably remained the majority. Their centre, Tavium, had been a place of worship since Hittite times, when it was called Tawinija, and later held a sanctuary of Zeus Tavianos; Posdala was another of their towns.

The twelve tetrarchs of the three peoples met in council at the Drunemeton. In the mid-1st century BCE the Trocmian tetrarch was Brogitarus, husband of Adobogiona, daughter of Deiotarus of the Tolistobogii. In Pompey's settlement of the East in 63 BCE he received Mithridatium, a fortress in Pontus, and land in Armenia Minor, and about 58 BCE Clodius had him made king at Rome, with control of Pessinus. After his death in the late 50s BCE the tetrarchy passed to Deiotarus, apart from a brief recovery by Brogitarus' nephew Mithridates of Pergamon from about 47 to 45 BCE.

Under Augustus, Tavium, until then a fortified place rather than a city, became an autonomous polis and one of the three centres of the provincial league with Ancyra and Pessinus. Its coins of the 1st and 2nd centuries CE name the community the Sebastēnoi Trokmoi Tavianoi. A late Hellenistic cemetery at Boğazköy in their territory has given stone cist graves, jar burials of children, a La Tène fibula and an iron sword with its scabbard.
troia-apulia: According to legend, the ancient town of Aecae on this site was founded by the Greek hero Diomedes, who had destroyed Troy. Polybius and Livy mention Aecae during the operations of Hannibal and Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus in Apulia. Like many Apulian cities it joined the Carthaginians after the Battle of Cannae, but Fabius Maximus recovered it in 214 BCE after a regular siege. Pliny lists its people, the Aecani, among the inland towns of Apulia, and the Roman itineraries place it on the Appian Way between Aequum Tuticum and Herdonia, 29 to 31 kilometres from the latter.

That distance matches the position of modern Troia, and medieval chroniclers state that the present town was founded about the beginning of the 11th century on the ruins of Aecae. It was built as a fortified town by Basil Boioannes. Until it was overshadowed by Foggia it was an important strategic town in southern Italy, and was besieged several times, notably by the emperors Henry II and Frederick II. After Frederick's fall it sided with the Angevines and later, against them, with the Aragonese.

After the unification of southern Italy in 1861, Troia rebelled, and Savoy troops intervened with cannon. Cluverius mistook Aecae for Accadia, a village in the Daunian Mountains south of Bovino, but his error was corrected by Holstenius.

Troia stands on a hill of moderate height above the fertile plain of Apulia, 15 kilometres south of Lucera and 22 kilometres south-west of Foggia, and is a bishop's seat. Its main sights include the cathedral, an example of Apulian Romanesque architecture, and the Basilica of St. Basil from the 11th century. There are also the Baroque church of St. Francis, the Church of San Vincenzo from the 10th century, the Palazzo Principi d'Avalos and the Jesuits' Palace of the 16th century.

The Municipal Museum holds archaeological finds from the area and an art gallery. The Diocesan Museum, in an 18th-century Benedictine nunnery, and the New Museum of the Cathedral's Treasure house the medieval rolls of the Exultet.
trois-rivieres: Trois-Rivières lies on the north shore of the Saint Lawrence River at the mouth of the Saint-Maurice River, in the Mauricie region of Quebec. The name means three rivers and refers to the three channels into which the Saint-Maurice is divided at its mouth by two islands. François Gravé Du Pont, a geographer under Samuel de Champlain, first used the name in 1599, when sailing upriver he took the channels for three separate tributaries.

For thousands of years the area was frequented by Indigenous peoples. The Algonquin and Abenaki used it as a summer stopping place to fish, hunt and gather roots and nuts. Jacques Cartier described the site in 1535 and planted a cross on Saint-Quentin Island. In 1603 Samuel de Champlain recommended a permanent settlement, and the village was formed on 4 July 1634 under its first governor, Sieur de Laviolette. It played an important part in the fur trade with First Nations peoples and became the seat of a regional government in 1665. Ursuline nuns who arrived in 1697 founded its first school.

French rule ended in 1760, when the town was taken in the British conquest of Canada. On 8 June 1776 the Battle of Trois-Rivières was fought here during the American invasion of the province of Quebec. Its first foundry opened in 1738 and supplied iron, much of it shipped to France for the navy, for about 150 years. A fire in 1908 destroyed most of the city, including many buildings from the French colonial years; the Ursuline Monastery and the De Tonnancour Manor survived.

From the late 1920s to the early 1960s the city was known as the pulp and paper capital of the world. Industry declined later, and in the 1960s the city began to diversify its economy. The Old City was declared an historic sector in 1964 and the Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières was founded in 1969.

Trois-Rivières is the economic and cultural hub of the Mauricie region, roughly halfway between Montreal and Quebec City, and French is the mother tongue of the great majority of its people. Its landmarks include the Forges du Saint-Maurice, a foundry dating from the 1730s, and the Notre-Dame-du-Cap Basilica. It has a major ice-free port on the Saint Lawrence.
trojan-war: In the Greek tradition the war arose from a quarrel among the goddesses Hera, Athena and Aphrodite, caused by Eris, the goddess of discord, who threw a golden apple inscribed to the fairest into the wedding of Peleus and Thetis. A shepherd, in fact the Trojan prince Paris, judged between them and chose Aphrodite, who caused Helen, the queen of Sparta, to fall in love with him.

When Helen left with Paris, her former husband Menelaus called on the kings and princes of Greece, who were bound by the oath of Helen's suitors to defend her marriage. Agamemnon sent emissaries to gather them. When the fleet reached Aulis the winds ceased, and in some versions Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to appease Artemis.

The Iliad covers four days and two nights in the tenth year of the siege. Agamemnon refused to return Chryseis, the daughter of Apollo's priest Chryses, and Apollo afflicted the Achaean army with plague. When Agamemnon was forced to give her up, he took Achilles's concubine Briseis. Enraged, Achilles withdrew from the fighting, and Zeus agreed to give the Trojans success in his absence.

Troy fell, according to the tradition, when the Achaeans entered the city and killed its sleeping population. Neoptolemus killed Priam at the altar of Zeus, and Menelaus took Helen back to the ships. Ajax the Lesser raped Cassandra on Athena's altar. The Trojan Horse does not appear in the Iliad; it became familiar through Virgil's account in the second book of the Aeneid.

The gods, angered by the sacrilege, decided that most of the Greeks would not return home. Agamemnon reached Argos safely and was killed there, in the oldest versions by Aegisthus. Ajax the Lesser drowned after a storm sent by Athena, and Nestor alone made a fast and safe return. Odysseus's ten-year journey home is told in the Odyssey, and Aeneas's flight to Italy in the Aeneid, whose hero carries the household gods that Romans claimed to preserve as guarantees of Rome's security.

Most classical Greeks thought the war historical, though Thucydides doubted that 1,186 ships were sent. Ancient authors gave dates for the fall of Troy between 1334 BCE and 1135 BCE. After excavations at Hisarlık, Troy VIIa, destroyed around 1180 BCE, has come to be regarded as the most likely Homeric Troy. Many scholars now accept a historical core in a Greek expedition against the city, but few think the Homeric poems faithfully represent it.
trondheim: Trondheim lies on the south shore of Trondheim Fjord, at the mouth of the river Nidelva, with an excellent and sheltered harbour. In the Middle Ages the river was deep enough for most boats, but in the mid-17th century an avalanche of mud and stones made it less navigable and partly ruined the harbour. Despite its northerly latitude it has a mild climate. Around the summer solstice the nights are light enough that no outdoor lighting is needed between 23 May and 19 July, while at the winter solstice the sun stands only slightly more than 3 degrees above the horizon at midday.

The settlement was founded in 997 as a trading post by the Viking king Olav Tryggvason, who named it Kaupangen, meaning market place. Shortly afterwards it came to be called Nidaros, the outlet of the river Nid. The district around it, Trondheim, meant the home of the Trønder people, and Trøndelag the law area of the Trønder. The city served as the king's seat and was the capital of Norway until 1217. From 1152 to 1537 it was the seat of the Catholic Archdiocese of Nidaros; it then became, and has remained, the seat of the Lutheran Diocese of Nidaros.

Nidaros Cathedral, begun in 1070, is the most important Gothic monument in Norway and was Northern Europe's most important Christian pilgrimage site in the Middle Ages, with routes leading to it from Oslo and from the Jämtland and Värmland regions of Sweden. Sverre Sigurdsson built the fortification Sverresborg in 1182 and 1183; it was burned in 1188 and had been restored by 1197. Kristiansten Fortress, built from 1681 to 1684, repelled invading Swedes in 1718 and was decommissioned in 1816. During the German occupation of Norway in the Second World War the city held a submarine base for the 13th U-boat Flotilla, and Vollan District Jail was used for prisoners of war and political prisoners.

Trondheim is a city and municipality in Trøndelag county, the third most populous municipality in Norway. It was incorporated as a city on 1 January 1838, and its present municipality was formed in 1964 by merger with four neighbouring municipalities, and enlarged again in 2020. The Norwegian University of Science and Technology and the research foundation SINTEF have their headquarters there, and the cathedral stands beside the Archbishop's Palace in the city centre.
trongsa: Trongsa, earlier spelled Tongsa, is the capital of Trongsa District in central Bhutan, and its name means new village in Dzongkha. The valley is also known as Mang-Dey, a name that traces to Mang-Deg. According to the tradition told of it, the Buddhist scholar Kuenkhen Longchen Rabjam visited around 1357 and taught at a place called Sherabling, where the people offered him plentiful grain, and he said the place would be called Mang-Deg, from mang, plenty, and deg, offered.

The first temple was built in 1543 by the Drukpa lama Ngagi Wangchuck, great-grandfather of Ngawang Namgyal, Zhabdrung Rinpoche, the unifier of Bhutan. A local account says that the tutor of Kuenkhen Pema Karpo visited the village of Yoeling to the north of the present dzong in that year. He saw a light shining from a cliff in a forest at night, and found there the marks of the goddess Pelden Lhamo. He built a hermitage and took the place as a prophecy that a great dzong would rise there.

Chökhor Raptentse Dzong was built at Trongsa in 1644. It stands on a mountain spur high above the gorges of the Mangde Chhu and controlled east–west trade for centuries. The only road linking eastern and western Bhutan, the precursor of the modern Lateral Road, passed through its courtyard, and at the command of the penlop, or governor, its massive doors could be shut, dividing the country in two. The dzong was the seat of power of the Wangchuck dynasty before it became ruler of Bhutan in 1907.

Traditionally the King of Bhutan first becomes the Trongsa Penlop, is then named Crown Prince and eventually becomes King. Higher on the mountainside above the dzong stands a watchtower, the Ta Dzong, built to guard the dzong from enemies. It now houses a museum and a chapel dedicated to Jigme Namgyal, who was Trongsa Penlop from 1853 to 1870.
troodos-mountains: The Troodos Mountains are the largest mountain range of Cyprus, lying roughly in the centre of the island and covering a third of its area, across most of its western side. The highest peak is Mount Olympus, also called Hionistra, at 1,952 metres. The range forms a significant rain shadow on the island. The name probably comes from one of two sources: the Greek words for three and road, referring to the three roads that lead to the mountain, or a phrase meaning the mountains of Adonis. The Cyprus cedar and many other plants and animals found nowhere else live there.

The mountains have been known since antiquity for their mines, which for centuries supplied copper to the entire Mediterranean. In the Byzantine period they became a centre of Byzantine art, as churches and monasteries were built in the mountains, away from the threatened coastline. The region is known for Byzantine churches and monasteries richly decorated with murals, of which the Kykkos monastery is the richest. Nine churches and one monastery in Troodos together form a World Heritage Site, first inscribed by UNESCO in 1985; they include Panagia tou Araka, Agios Nikolaos tis Stegis and Agios Ioannis Lampadistis at Kalopanagiotis.

Geologists value the range for an undisturbed ophiolite sequence, the Troodos Ophiolite. It rose slowly from the sea as the African and European plates collided, a process that eventually formed the island. Erosion exposed the former magma chamber beneath the mountains, revealing intact rocks and petrified pillow lava formed millions of years ago. Observations of the Troodos ophiolite by Ian Graham Gass and his colleagues were among the evidence that led to the theory of seafloor spreading.

The mountains hold resorts, villages in the valleys and on terraced hillsides, and many Byzantine monasteries and churches on the peaks. The climate is Mediterranean, with greater daily ranges in temperature than on the coast. Trees include the Turkish pine and golden oak, with Anatolian black pine higher up. The endangered Cyprus mouflon is the chief wild animal.
tropaeum-alpium: The Tropaeum Alpium commemorated the subjection of the Alpine peoples to the imperium of the Roman people under Augustus. The campaigns it recorded probably took place between 25 and 14 BCE: in 25 BCE the Salassi of the Aosta Valley were finally crushed, between 17 and 15 BCE peoples of the central and eastern Alps were subjected and Rome's armies reached the Danube, conquering Raetia, and in 14 BCE the Ligurian Comati were reduced in the western Alps. The Via Julia Augusta, marked out with milestones in 13 and 12 BCE, suggests that the essential operations on the coast were over by then.

The monument stood on a spur above the col of La Turbie, the highest point of the Via Julia Augusta as it crossed the Alps. Sophie Binninger notes that this low southern col was not a strategic point like the other passes, so commemorating the victory there was a symbolic choice. The trophy was novel in being dedicated to Augustus himself rather than to the god who gave victory.

The text of the dedication survives only through Pliny the Elder, who quoted it at the close of the third book of his Natural History. It states that the senate and people of Rome dedicated the monument to Augustus because under his command and auspices all the Alpine peoples from the upper sea to the lower, that is from the Adriatic to the Tyrrhenian, had been brought under Roman rule. It then lists the conquered peoples, among them the Trumpilini, Camunni, Vindelici, Salassi and Veragri. Pliny adds that fifteen Cottian communities which had not been hostile were not included.

The ruins show a mixed quadrangular and cylindrical building: a double square base under a circular colonnade. The architects Jean-Camille and Jules Formigé proposed that the inscription stood on the lower base, with statues of Augustus's legates and of members of his family behind the colonnade and a statue of Augustus above. Binninger stresses that this reconstruction remains largely hypothetical, as the sculpture is extremely fragmentary and there are no close parallels.

The monument was repeatedly fortified and damaged over the centuries, and was partly destroyed by mining in 1705 and afterwards used as a quarry. The site was classed as a monument historique in 1865, and in 1905 to 1908 Philippe Casimir cleared it, uncovering hundreds of dressed blocks. Between 1920 and 1934 Jules Formigé rebuilt the west face to carry the inscription, using about 140 original fragments set into a modern panel, and had thirty-two houses demolished to clear the surroundings. The work was financed by the American patron Edward Tuck and inaugurated in 1934.
trophonius: The name derives from the Greek verb trepho, to nourish, and Strabo and several inscriptions call him Zeus Trephonios, one of several chthonic forms of Zeus known in the Greek world. In the Homeric Hymn to Apollo he is a son of Erginus, king of Minyan Orchomenus, while Pausanias makes Apollo his father. Pindar tells that after the brothers finished the temple at Delphi the oracle bade them do as they wished for six days, and on the seventh they were found dead; Cicero tells the same story with three days.

Pausanias gives another tale. The brothers built a treasure chamber for King Hyrieus of Boeotia with a secret entrance and used it to steal his fortune. When Agamedes was caught in a snare, Trophonius cut off his head so that he could not be recognised, and was then swallowed by the earth and became a subterranean god. His cave was found again only when the Lebadaeans, struck by plague, were told by the Pythia to honour a neglected hero, and a shepherd boy followed a trail of bees into a hole in the ground.

Pausanias describes the rites in his account of Boeotia. A consultant lived for some days in a set house, bathed in the River Herkryna, named after his daughter, and ate sacrificial meat, sacrificing by day to Cronus, Apollo, Zeus the king, Hera the Charioteer and Demeter-Europa. At night he cast a ram into a pit sacred to Agamedes, drank from two rivers called Lethe and Mnemosyne and went down into the cave. Most were frightened out of their wits and forgot the experience. Seated afterwards on a chair of Mnemosyne, they spoke while the priests recorded their ravings and composed an oracle from them.

To go down into the cave of Trophonius became a proverbial way of saying to suffer a great fright, alluded to in Aristophanes' Clouds. Heraclides Ponticus and other ancient philosophers wrote commentaries on the cult that are now lost. Classical scholars compare its rivers of forgetting and memory with the Myth of Er in Plato's Republic, the Orphic gold leaves and passages of Hesiod's Theogony. The Hellfire Club built a Cave of Trophonius for its revels, and both Søren Kierkegaard and Friedrich Nietzsche referred to him.
troupes-de-la-marine: Before the 17th century soldiers serving at sea were seconded from the French Army. In 1622 Cardinal Richelieu created the first French troops for maritime service, the Compagnies Ordinaires de la Mer, intended as marines on the ships of the French Navy, and soon merged them into the Régiment de La Marine, which fought at the Siege of La Rochelle. Further naval regiments followed during the Franco-Spanish War, and Jean-Baptiste Colbert raised two more in 1669, but all were eventually transferred to the Army between 1640 and 1673.

During the Nine Years' War an ordinance of 16 December 1690 created 80 infantry companies under the name Compagnies Franches de la Marine, each commanded by a lieutenant de vaisseau. Their strength rose and fell with war and the budget: 100 companies of 100 men in theory from 1691, 50 men after the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697, 100 again in 1705, and repeated cuts after the Treaty of Utrecht.

The companies guarded arsenals and naval ports, served aboard warships and garrisoned the colonies in Canada, the Antilles and India. Some charged at the Battle of Camaret in 1694; at the Battle of Málaga in 1704 they lost 150 officers and 1,500 soldiers; and 2,500 of their men fought at Rio de Janeiro under René Duguay-Trouin in 1711.

Between 1683 and 1688 Louis XIV sent thirty-five companies to Canada, and they remained the only regular troops in New France until 1755. In 1688 Canada held 1,418 soldiers for a population of almost 10,300. From 1685 Canadian gentlemen obtained commissions, and by 1722 more than half the officers had been born in Canada; a commission was a source of income and prestige, with a waiting list. With the Canadian militias and allied guerrilla units the troops bore the defence of New France, and at the end of the French regime 2,600 of them were in Canada.

After the conquest of 1760 many veterans settled in the new territory, while others were reluctantly repatriated to France. In 1762 the duties of the companies passed to 23 line regiments and three artillery brigades. In 1769 César Gabriel de Choiseul founded the Corps royal d'artillerie et d'infanterie de la marine, and further reorganisations followed under the monarchy, the Republic and the Empire.
trowulan: Trowulan lies in Trowulan Subdistrict, Mojokerto Regency, and covers about 100 square kilometres. As the capital of Majapahit the city was called Majapahit or Wilwatikta. The poet Mpu Prapanca described it in the 14th-century Nagarakretagama: a royal compound within a thick, high wall of red brick, entered by a north gate with doors of decorated iron, courtyards with religious buildings and bathing canals, a great hall, and the king's quarters on decorated brick bases, with the compounds of priests, nobles and the chief minister Gajah Mada beyond. A 15th-century Chinese source describes a clean palace within a brick wall more than 10 metres high.

Excavations have found traces of industry, trade, religion, houses with wells and drains, and canals, evidence of a dense population in the 14th and 15th centuries. Goldsmiths worked imported gold in the hamlet still called Kemasan, from mas, gold, and bronze was cast at Pakis. Chinese bronze coins became Majapahit's official currency around 1300, and clay piggy banks have been found. Islamic tombstones at Troloyo, most dating from between 1350 and 1478, show a Muslim community within the royal capital.

Sir Thomas Stamford Raffles, Lieutenant-Governor of British Java, reported ruins of temples scattered for many miles and called Trowulan this pride of Java, though dense teak forest then prevented a survey. Parts of the old city lie under metres of mud and volcanic debris from Mount Kelud and floods of the Brantas River.

Most finds are shown in the Trowulan Museum beside Segaran Pool, a brick reservoir of 800 by 500 metres uncovered by Henri Maclaine Pont in 1926. The surviving red-brick monuments include Tikus Temple, a ritual bathing pool found in 1914, the paduraksa gate of Bajang Ratu, the split gate of Wringin Lawang and Brahu Temple. In October 2009 Indonesia submitted Trowulan to the UNESCO World Heritage list.
troy: The archaeological site of Troy consists of the hill of Hisarlık and the fields below it to the south. The hill is a tell, formed of strata holding the remains of more than three millennia of occupation. Nine main layers are identified, numbered with Roman numerals from Troy I, the earliest, to Troy IX, the latest, with sublayers marked by letters such as VIIa and VIIb. Relative dates come from comparing artefacts with those from other sites, and precise absolute dates are not always possible because radiocarbon dating has limited accuracy.

Troy I was founded around 3000 BCE beside a shallow lagoon and was notable for massive limestone fortifications. Built around 2550 BCE, Troy II was twice the size, with a lower town and a citadel divided into two precincts; its Megaron IIA is the biggest known building of its kind in the Aegean and Anatolian region. Troy VI–VII was a major Late Bronze Age city with a steep citadel and a sprawling lower town, in contact with Mycenaean Greece. Hittite records name a city of Wilusa, usually identified with it, though not all scholars regard the identification as firmly established. Sublayers VIh and VIIa show possible signs of violent destruction and are candidates for the setting of the later myths.

Troy VIII grew from about 700 BCE, when Greek immigrants began building, and lasted into the Roman era. Herodotus says that Xerxes sacrificed 1,000 cattle at the sanctuary of Athena Ilias on his march towards Greece. Ilion was destroyed in 85 BCE after an eleven-day siege by the Roman general Fimbria, then rebuilt after Sulla bestowed benefactions on it, and its new civic calendar took 85 BCE as its first year. Earthquakes around 500 CE devastated the city, and from the 4th century until the Byzantine era Ilion was the seat of a Christian bishop.

Interest in the site began with travellers who mistook Alexandria Troas for Troy. Charles Maclaren was the first to identify Hisarlık with confidence, in 1822, and Frank Calvert surveyed it in 1865. Heinrich Schliemann secured permission to excavate in 1868 and began his trench in April 1870; Wilhelm Dörpfeld, Carl Blegen and, from 1988 to 2005, Manfred Korfmann continued the work, the last revealing the lower city. Schliemann proposed Troy II as the city of legend, though later research showed it predates the Mycenaean era by several hundred years. The relationship between myth and reality remains unclear. The Turkish government created a Historical National Park at Troy in 1996, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998.
troyes: Troyes lies on the Seine about 140 km south-east of Paris, within the Champagne wine region. Prehistoric evidence suggests that a settlement may have developed there as early as 600 BCE, and Celtic grave-mounds and artifacts have been found in and near the city. In the Roman era the town, called Augustobona Tricassium, stood at the meeting of many roads, above all the Via Agrippa, which led north to Reims and south to Langres and on to Milan.

Troyes was the civitas of the Tricasses, whom Augustus separated from the Senones. Little of the early Gallo-Roman city survives apart from scattered remains and traces of an aqueduct, and by the late Empire the settlement had shrunk. Its later name came from Tricassium or Tricassae. The people had become Christian by the fourth century and the city became the seat of a bishop.

The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains, also called the Battle of Troyes, was fought nearby in 451, when Flavius Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I fought Attila. In 878 Louis the Stammerer received the crown of West Francia from Pope John VIII at Troyes. After Norman raids at the end of the ninth century the counts of Champagne chose it as their capital, and it remained the capital of the Province of Champagne until the Revolution.

In the Middle Ages it was an important international trading town, driven by the Champagne cloth fairs, and the troy weight for gold is named after it. Rashi, the commentator on the Bible and the Talmud, was born there in 1040 and founded an influential school. In 1417 John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, worked to have Troyes made the capital of France.

The Treaty of Troyes was signed there on 21 May 1420, betrothing Henry V of England to Catherine, daughter of Charles VI, and making Henry rather than the Dauphin the heir to the French crown. Joan of Arc and the Dauphin, later Charles VII, restored French control of the town in 1429.

Troyes is the capital of the department of Aube in the Grand Est region. Many half-timbered houses, mostly of the 16th century, survive in the old town, and it is designated a City of Art and History. Its Gothic churches include the cathedral of Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul and the Basilica of Saint-Urbain, begun by Jacques Pantaléon, who became Pope Urban IV in 1261.
trpimir-i: Trpimir succeeded Duke Mislav around 845 and took power at Klis, where he enlarged an early Roman stronghold into Klis Fortress, the seat of his domain. Formally he was a vassal of the Frankish Emperor Lothair I, but he used Frankish-Byzantine conflicts to rule on his own. In 846 he fought successfully against the Byzantine coastal cities under the strategos of Zadar, and in 854 he drove back an army of the Bulgarian Khan Boris I, then made peace with him and exchanged gifts. Bulgarians and Croats lived peacefully side by side after that.

The Saxon theologian Gottschalk of Orbais stayed at his court between 846 and 848, after leaving Venice and before going on to Bulgaria. His work De Trina deitate is an important source for the reign: it describes Trpimir's victory over a Byzantine patricius in 846, which Gottschalk tied to his theory of predestination, and calls him rex Sclavorum, a sign of admiration and of his independent rule.

His Latin charter, issued at Biaći on 4 March 852, confirmed Mislav's gifts to the Archbishopric of Split and calls the realm the Regnum Chroatorum, a word other rulers of the time also used to mark their independence without meaning a kingdom. It survives only in a copy of 1568. The charter records his decision to build a church and the first Benedictine monastery at Rižinice, between Klis and Solin, which brought the Benedictine order into Croatia; a carved gable arch from its altar screen bears his name and title. He probably also built a church at Kapitul near Knin castle, and he made a pilgrimage to Cividale with his son Peter.

Trpimir died in 864, and the order of his successors is unclear. He had three sons, Peter, Zdeslav and probably Muncimir, who in a charter of 892 said he had returned to his father's throne after Branimir had usurped it. Trpimir was followed either by Zdeslav, soon deposed by Domagoj, or by Domagoj directly, who forced the sons to flee to Constantinople. The dynasty named after him ruled Croatia, with interruptions, until 1091.
trpimirovic-dynasty: The house took its name from its founder, Duke Trpimir I, known from other sources as ruling around 845 to 864. Its royal estate, the terra regalis, lay between Trogir and Split, in the area of today's Kaštela, Solin and Klis, from where the family ruled, and between Split and Omiš. The first rulers were vassals of the Franks and fought the Venetian Republic and the Byzantine Empire for control of the coast, gaining greater autonomy at the end of the 9th century.

Their hold was broken more than once. After Trpimir's death power passed for a time to Domagoj of the Domagojević dynasty. Trpimir's son Zdeslav overthrew Domagoj in 878 but was himself overthrown by Branimir, and only around 892 did Zdeslav's brother Muncimir restore the family to power.

In the first half of the 10th century Tomislav united Pannonian and Dalmatian Croatia into a kingdom, kept an alliance with the pope, defended the country against the Hungarians and took part in the Church Councils of Split in 925 and 928. His successors could not keep a stable kingship: in a quarrel between the brothers Miroslav and Michael Krešimir II, the ban Pribina took Michael's side and King Miroslav was murdered in 949. The country recovered under Michael Krešimir II and his son Stephen Držislav, after whose death in 997 his sons Krešimir III and Gojslav rebelled against their brother Svetoslav Suronja and deposed him.

The house gave Croatia four dukes, thirteen kings and a queen, and split into the Svetoslavić branch, descended from Svetoslav, and the Krešimirović branch, which went on ruling. It reached its height under Petar Krešimir IV, who consolidated and enlarged the kingdom. Its chronology remains uncertain. The Croatian Encyclopedia notes that for lack of sources the exact years of most reigns cannot be fixed, and the generally accepted scheme of Franjo Rački and Ferdo Šišić, built on the De Administrando Imperio, includes a Trpimir II whom no source names, which has led historians to propose revised chronologies.
truce-of-altmark: The truce ended the Polish–Swedish War of 1626–1629. It was signed in the village of Altmark (Stary Targ), in Poland, with the help of Richelieu's envoy Charnacé, and it was meant to last six years. Shortly before it was signed, Sweden had been defeated at Trzciana by Polish forces led by Field Crown Hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski, together with Holy Roman imperial troops. The fighting there came close to the capture of King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, who was wounded several times and was once saved by one of his own men.

Sweden kept control of Livonia north of the Daugava River, which became Swedish Livonia, while Latgale, the south-eastern part of the region, stayed under Polish rule. Sweden evacuated most of the Duchy of Prussia but kept the coastal cities, and Poland had the other Swedish gains from the invasion of 1625 returned to it. For the six years of the truce Sweden also received two thirds of the shipping tolls collected at Polish ports such as Gdańsk (Danzig) and Elbląg (Elbing), and in the Duchy of Prussia. These tolls helped to pay for Sweden's later part in the Thirty Years' War.

Poland had little means of carrying on. The Sejm did not vote new taxes to pay the imperial army serving under Hans Georg von Arnim-Boitzenburg, and low morale led some of its soldiers to mutiny or to go over to Sweden. Several other states also intervened diplomatically, and in the end these pressures forced King Sigismund III of Poland to accept the truce.

In 1635 the truce was extended by the Treaty of Stuhmsdorf. Sweden gave up the Prussian ports, and Poland ceded most of Livonia, including Riga, while keeping Latgale. The most important result of the Truce of Altmark was that it confirmed Sweden as the ruler of the northern Baltic coast down to the Daugava, Riga included.
truce-of-andrusovo: The truce was signed on 9 February 1667, which was 30 January by the old-style reckoning in the village of Andrusovo, not far from Smolensk, by Afanasy Ordin-Nashchokin for the Tsardom of Russia and Jerzy Chlebowicz for the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Representatives of the Cossack Hetmanate were not allowed to take part. It set a truce of thirteen and a half years, during which both states were obliged to prepare the conditions for eternal peace.

Russia secured Left-bank Ukraine, the Siever lands and Smolensk. The Commonwealth kept Right-bank Ukraine and Russian-occupied Belarus, with Vitebsk, Polotsk and Dzwinsk. Kiev, though on the right bank of the Dnieper, was handed to Russia for two years, a transfer phrased as temporary but in fact made permanent in 1686 in exchange for 146,000 rubles. The Zaporozhian Sich became a condominium of both states, and both agreed to common defence against the Ottoman Empire and to free trade. Russia was to pay the Commonwealth 1,000,000 złotych, or 200,000 rubles, for Left-bank Ukraine.

The transfer of Kiev had far-reaching consequences. Kiev was the seat of the Orthodox metropolitan, who kept authority over the Orthodox population of the Commonwealth's eastern lands, and it hosted the Mohyla Academy, which opened Orthodoxy to Western influence. It had been an Orthodox counterweight to the Moscow patriarchate, founded in 1589. The transfer came only days after Patriarch Nikon won the upper hand over Avvakum, which led to the schism between the Reformed Orthodoxy and the Old Believers. Kiev now gave the Russian patriarch an academy whose scholars Nikon had already relied on for his reforms.

As the metropolitan's see, Kiev also gave Moscow influence over the Orthodox of Poland-Lithuania, and protection of that population later became an argument for Romanov influence over eastern Poland-Lithuania. In Ukraine the treaty is often seen as leading to the partition of the Hetmanate between its stronger neighbours. Polish opinion considers it a significant mistake that tipped the balance of power and replaced Poland as the dominant state of Eastern Europe with the emerging Russian Empire.
trucial-oman-scouts: The force was founded after consultation between the British Foreign Office and Brigadier John Bagot Glubb, commander of the Jordanian Arab Legion. With a budget of £30,000 it began under Major Hankin Turvin with two Arab officers and 32 other ranks seconded from the Arab Legion. Its duties were to keep the peace in the Trucial States, suppress the traffic in slaves, though not slavery within the states, which the British treated as an internal affair, and escort British political representatives. The Rulers were not consulted; only the Ruler of Sharjah, who leased the base, was informed.

Its soldiers were recruited mostly from Abu Dhabi, with Yemeni soldiers from the Aden Protectorate Levies. In November 1952 three Yemeni soldiers shot dead the commander, Major Otto Thwaites, at Buraimi, where he was investigating sales of ammunition to the Saudis.

In October 1955 two rifle squadrons, with troops of the Sultan of Muscat and Oman, evicted a 15-man Saudi police garrison that had held the Buraimi Oasis since 1952, in a dispute over Saudi claims to land in Abu Dhabi where oil was suspected. Most of the fighting came after the Saudis surrendered, against about 200 Bedouin, and nine men died. Two companies later fought in the Jebel Akhdar War in Oman, a use criticised in the Trucial States as unsuitable for an internal force.

The Scouts numbered 1,000 by 1960, when they began blasting roads through the mountains from Masafi to Fujairah and Dibba. By 1964 they had 1,500 Arab and 100 British personnel in five rifle squadrons, and by 1965 the British Government spent some £2 million a year on them. Freddie De Butts, their commander from March 1964, saw their reporting to the British Political Resident as one cause of Sheikh Shakhbut's founding of the Abu Dhabi Defence Force in 1965.

The handover to the Union Defence Force took place on 22 December 1971, with 2,500 men. In January 1972 its troops helped surround the Sharjah palace after supporters of the former ruler, Sheikh Saqr bin Sultan, had killed Sheikh Khalid bin Mohammed Al Qasimi. In May 1976 the Union Defence Force absorbed the forces of the individual emirates. The former base of the Scouts at Mirgab became the headquarters of the Sharjah Police Special Tasks Department.
trucial-states: The British called the south-eastern coast of the Persian Gulf the Pirate Coast, arguing that raiders based there, particularly the Qawasim or Al Qasimi, the ruling families of Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah, harassed British-flagged shipping. The first of many skirmishes came in 1797, when the snow Bassein was seized and released two days later. British expeditions to protect Indian trade struck Ras Al Khaimah and other harbours in 1809 and again, with far greater destructive force, in 1819.

A peace treaty was signed in January 1820 and adhered to by all the sheikhs of the coast. Sultan bin Saqr Al Qasimi of Sharjah signed on 6 January, and Shakhbut bin Diyab Al Nahyan signed for his son Tahnoon, ruler of Abu Dhabi, on 11 January. The rulers of Ajman and Umm Al Quwain acceded on 15 March aboard the ship of Major-General William Keir Grant.

The treaty was not a conspicuous success: conflicts that the British considered raids continued until 1835, when the sheikhs agreed not to fight at sea. After a ten-year truce in 1843 they signed the Perpetual Treaty of Maritime Peace in 1853, overseen by Captain A. B. Kemball. Treaties of 1847 and 1856 undertook to abolish the slave trade. In 1892, mainly in reaction to the ambitions of France and Russia, six rulers signed the Exclusive Agreement, promising not to dispose of territory except to Britain nor to deal with other foreign governments without its consent. Britain promised protection against attack by sea and help in case of attack by land.

Aeroplanes arrived in the 1920s as Britain sought an air route to India, and an airfield opened at Sharjah in 1932. Kalba was granted trucial status in 1936 as the site of a back-up landing strip and rejoined Sharjah in 1951. Fujairah was recognised in 1952 after pressure from Petroleum Concessions Limited, which wanted a free hand to explore for oil along the east coast. The Trucial States Council, a consultative forum presided over by the British Political Agent, first met in 1952 and received a British grant in 1965.

On 16 January 1968 Harold Wilson announced that British troops would be withdrawn from east of Suez. Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi and Sheikh Rashid of Dubai agreed the principle of a union on 18 February 1968, and after two years of often stormy talks, Bahrain and Qatar dropped out, leaving six emirates to agree on union on 18 July 1971. The Act of Union was signed on 2 December 1971, and Ras Al Khaimah joined on 10 February 1972, after Iran seized the Tunb islands and occupied Abu Musa on 30 November 1971.
true-cross: The term True Cross refers to any relic claimed to be part of the original wooden cross on which Jesus of Nazareth was crucified. The Catholic Church, Eastern Orthodoxy, the Oriental Orthodox churches and some denominations of the Church of the East have all claimed relics of it as objects of veneration. There is no evidence that any particular relic is part of the original cross, and historians generally dispute their authenticity, as do Protestant and other Christian churches, which do not hold them in as high regard.

Some fourth-century historians and Christian legends say that Helena, the mother of the Roman emperor Constantine the Great, recovered the cross at the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem during her travels in the Holy Land in 326 to 328. The Life of Constantine by Eusebius of Caesarea, the earliest main source on the rediscovery of the tomb of Jesus, does not mention the cross.

About forty years after Cyril, a fully developed story existed. Gelasius of Caesarea recorded it in a lost Greek history before his death in 395, and Rufinus of Aquileia adapted it around 402. In it Helena tore down a temple of Aphrodite and found three crosses beneath the rubble. The cross of Jesus was identified, with the help of Bishop Macarius of Jerusalem, when it cured a mortally ill woman. A church was built on the spot and the relic divided, part staying in Jerusalem and part going to Constantine with the nails.

A silver reliquary at the Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre was shown periodically to the faithful. In the 380s the pilgrim Egeria described the veneration of the cross at Jerusalem in a long letter known as her Itinerary.

During the Byzantine-Sasanian war of 602 to 628 the Sasanian shah Khosrow II took the part held in Jerusalem as a trophy after capturing the city in 614. The Byzantine emperor Heraclius defeated Khosrow and regained it in 628, restoring it to Jerusalem on 21 March 630. Constantin Zuckerman has suggested that the Persians had actually lost the cross and that the wood Heraclius brought was a fake.

A Syriac tradition replaced Helena with a fictitious first-century empress named Protonike, and in 1260 Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend gave several accounts of the cross's origin in trees from Adam's grave. By the end of the Middle Ages so many churches claimed relics that John Calvin remarked that there was enough wood in them to fill a ship.
true-whig-party: The party was founded in the township of Clay-Ashland as a reorganised version of the Opposition Party. It began as an alliance of mostly dark-skinned upriver planters and the dark-skinned faction among the coastal merchants, against the lighter-skinned mulatto elite represented by the Republican Party. Its ideology was modelled on that of the United States Whig Party, from which it took its name, and it took its elephant mascot from the American Republican Party.

The party first came to power when Edward James Roye won the election of 1869. As the Republican Party declined, most Americo-Liberians moved their support to the True Whig Party. The settlers and their descendants were a small minority of the population but made up nearly all of the citizens able to vote, and the party chiefly represented them, often working in tandem with the Masonic Order of Liberia.

After Anthony W. Gardner was elected president in 1878, the party held a monopoly on Liberian politics, though opposition parties were never outlawed. In 1930 it was accused of sending contract migrant labourers, under conditions tantamount to slavery, to the Spanish colonists of Fernando Pó; a League of Nations investigation and a five-year American and British boycott followed, and President Charles D. B. King resigned.

Under William Tubman (1944–1971) the party was pro-American and anti-communist and pursued an open door policy to attract foreign investment and modernise the country's infrastructure. His successor, William Tolbert, opened relations with the Soviet Union and other African states and brought more native Liberians into government, which angered some of his cabinet. Tolbert was killed in the coup of 12 April 1980 led by Samuel Doe; leading members such as E. Reginald Townsend and Cecil Dennis were executed, others fled, and the party lost its official status.

The party survived as a rump and in 1985 was banned with all other opposition after a coup attempt against Doe. It was officially reconstituted in 2005 under Peter Vuku and took part in that year's election within the Coalition for the Transformation of Liberia. It stood alone in 2017, winning 0.96% of the vote, and in 2020 joined the Rainbow Alliance.
trujillo-peru: Trujillo lies on the Moche River, near its mouth at the Pacific Ocean, in the Moche Valley, on a coastal plain about 34 metres above sea level. It has a desert climate but is called the City of Everlasting Spring, because the Humboldt Current keeps temperatures moderate. The river has been used for irrigation since the time of the Moche and Chimú.

The area was long a centre of successive pre-European cultures. Huaca Prieta was occupied as early as 4700 BCE, and the Cupisnique, Moche and Chimú all developed here. Chan Chan, the largest adobe city of the ancient world, and the Temples of the Sun and Moon lie close to the modern city.

According to the historian Napoleón Cieza Burga, Diego de Almagro founded the first settlement in November 1534 as Trujillo of New Castile, after Francisco Pizarro's home city. It was placed among four Chimú settlements to create an alliance against the Incas. On 23 November 1537 King Charles I of Spain gave it the rank of city and a coat of arms, the first in Peru granted by the king. By 1544 it had around 300 homes and 1,000 inhabitants, with an economy based on sugar cane and wheat.

Led by the mayor and intendant José Bernardo de Tagle, the Intendancy of Trujillo declared independence from Spain on 29 December 1820. The Department of Trujillo, created in 1821, covered nearly half the country and was until 1825 the only stable area able to organise the new republic. In 1824 Simón Bolívar declared the city the provisional capital of Peru.

Trujillo is the capital of the La Libertad region and the third most populous city of Peru. Its historic centre, bounded by Avenida España where the city wall once stood, holds colonial and republican buildings and ten colonial churches. Chan Chan was designated a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1986. The city is known as the capital of the marinera, a traditional dance, and the poet César Vallejo lived there from 1910 to 1917. Irrigated lands produce sugarcane, rice and asparagus, and the shoe industry is a major employer.
truman-doctrine: At the conclusion of World War II, Turkey was pressured by the Soviet government to allow Soviet shipping free passage through the Turkish Straits, which connect the Black Sea with the Mediterranean. Turkey refused, and a show of naval force took place at the Straits. In Greece, the Dekemvriana clashes of December 1944 were followed by a period of persecution of leftists known as the White Terror, which contributed to the outbreak of the Greek Civil War in 1946, in which Communist Party of Greece guerrillas fought the government.

By late 1946 Britain informed the United States that its declining economy no longer allowed it to support the Greek government. In February 1946 the American diplomat George F. Kennan had sent his Long Telegram from Moscow, recommending a long-term strategy of containment. After Prime Minister Konstantinos Tsaldaris asked for help in Washington in December 1946, the State Department planned aid to both Greece and Turkey. Policy makers feared that if Greece were lost to communism, Turkey would not last long.

Truman needed the support of the Republicans, who controlled both houses of Congress. Senator Arthur Vandenberg backed him and advised him to appear before Congress and scare the hell out of the American people. Dean Acheson compared a communist state to a rotten apple that could infect a whole barrel. Secretary of State George C. Marshall, Kennan and others thought the draft of the address contained too much rhetoric, but Truman answered that the request would pass only if he played up the threat.

On 12 March 1947 Truman spoke to a joint session of Congress for eighteen minutes. He said that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures. He added that help should be primarily through economic and financial aid. Congress approved 400 million dollars in military and economic aid to Greece and Turkey by a large majority in May 1947.

The domestic reaction was broadly positive, though the columnist Walter Lippmann was sceptical of the open-ended pledge, and others pointed out that the Greek monarchy Truman proposed to defend was itself repressive. The doctrine was the first of a series of containment measures, followed by the Marshall Plan and the creation of NATO in 1949. The historian Eric Foner writes that it set a precedent for American assistance to anticommunist regimes throughout the world, however undemocratic.
trunajaya: Trunajaya, also written Tronajâyâ and known by the title Panembahan Maduretno, was a prince and warlord from Arosbaya in Bangkalan, on the island of Madura. From 1674 he led a revolt against two kings of Mataram, Amangkurat I and his son Amangkurat II, with the support of itinerant fighters from Makassar under Karaeng Galesong.

The revolt moved quickly and gathered strength, and by mid-1677 it had captured the Mataram court at Plered. Amangkurat I escaped to the north coast with his eldest son, the future Amangkurat II, leaving his younger son Pangeran Puger in Mataram. Trunajaya, more interested in profit and revenge than in governing a struggling realm, looted the court and withdrew to his stronghold at Kediri in East Java, leaving Puger in control of a weak court.

Amangkurat I died at the village of Tegalarum near Tegal while on his way to Batavia to seek Dutch help, and Amangkurat II became king without an army or a treasury. To regain his kingdom he made large concessions to the Dutch East India Company (VOC), among them a promise to hand over the port of Semarang in return for troops. The company accepted, judging that a stable Mataram deeply in its debt would secure trade on good terms. Its mixed forces of European soldiers and lightly armed troops from Makassar and Ambon defeated Trunajaya at Kediri in November 1678.

Trunajaya was captured in 1679 near Ngantang, west of Malang, and executed by order of Amangkurat II at Payak in Bantul on 2 January 1680. The rebellion is remembered with pride in Madura as a heroic struggle of the Madurese people against the Mataram state and the VOC, and Trunojoyo Airport in Sumenep and Trunojoyo University in Bangkalan are named after him.
trunajaya-rebellion: Amangkurat I took the throne of Mataram in 1646, succeeding Sultan Agung, and his early reign was marked by executions and massacres of his political enemies. In 1659 he had his father-in-law Pangeran Pekik and his relatives killed, which estranged his East Javanese subjects and his own son, the crown prince. Trunajaya, a descendant of the rulers of Madura, had been kept at the Mataram court since Madura's annexation in 1624; after his father was executed in 1656 he married into the Kajoran family of clerics, befriended the crown prince, and in 1671 made himself master of Madura.

After the VOC defeated the Gowa Sultanate in the Makassar War of 1669, bands of Makassarese soldiers turned to piracy along the coasts of Java. Their leader, the Kraeng of Galesong, allied with Trunajaya in 1675 through a marriage agreement.

In September 1676 a rebel army of 9,000 crossed from Madura, and at Gegodog, east of Tuban, it routed a much larger Mataram force under the crown prince. Within months the rebels held nearly every coastal town between Surabaya and Cirebon except Jepara. A VOC fleet under Admiral Cornelis Speelman stormed Surabaya in May 1677, and Trunajaya moved his capital to Kediri, but in June 1677 other rebel forces took Plered and carried the royal treasury away.

The new king, Amangkurat II, had neither army nor treasury. He promised the VOC the income of the northern harbour towns and ceded the Priangan highlands and Semarang. A VOC and Mataram army took Kediri on 25 November 1678 in an assault led by Captain François Tack, and Bugis forces under Arung Palakka joined the war. Trunajaya surrendered to the VOC on 26 December 1679 and was stabbed by the king and his courtiers at Payak; the VOC doubted the king's claim that Trunajaya had tried to kill him but did not call him to account.

Amangkurat II built a new capital at Kartasura, with a VOC fort beside the royal residence, and his brother Pangeran Puger, who had held Plered as a rival king, submitted only in November 1681. The war set the precedent of the VOC backing Javanese kings in exchange for concessions, but the promised payments were not made: by 1682 the king's debt exceeded 1.5 million reals, about five times the royal treasury.
truso: Truso was a port of trade set up by Scandinavians on the banks of the Nogat branch of the Vistula delta, close to a bay that is now Lake Drużno, where the river emptied into the shallow, brackish Vistula Lagoon. It lay on the Amber Road, which drew merchants from central and southern Europe who supplied the markets of the Mediterranean and the Middle East, and on routes leading from Birka through Visby to the southern Baltic coast. Westward routes ran from Truso and its rival Wiskiauten along the Baltic to Jutland and Hedeby.

Wulfstan of Hedeby made his seven-day voyage to Truso at the behest of King Alfred the Great. His account names the lands he passed under sail, with Weonodland, the land of the Wends, on his right as far as the Vistula estuary and lands subject to Denmark and to the Sweons on his left, and places Truso near Estmere, his name for the Vistula Lagoon. Historians still debate the purpose of the voyage. Marija Gimbutas called the name of the town the earliest known historically in the Baltic Sea area.

The goods most sought at Truso were amber, furs and pagan slaves, and its smiths and amber workers made goods for trade. In the second half of the 10th century silting in the Nogat began to cut the town off from the lagoon and the sea, and Gdańsk, on the coast, rose in its place as the local trading centre. Mateusz Bogucki holds that a strong political power, probably of Piast origin, sent warriors to take control and destroyed the town.

Searches for the site began in the early 16th century. Finds of 1897 and excavations from the 1920s placed it at Janów Pomorski near Elbląg, and in the 1980s Marek Jagodziński cleared about 20 hectares, where a series of structures had burnt down around the year 1,000. Finds include scales, weights, silver horseshoe brooches, swords, coins and Scandinavian jewellery, and long houses of about 6 by 21 metres. Scandinavians lived in the central and port area, while Balts and Slavs may have lived on the edges.
trustees-for-the-establishment-of-the-co: In February 1729 Parliament set up a committee to investigate prison conditions, with James Edward Oglethorpe as its chair. Its work led to the release of prisoners onto the streets of London and other cities with no prospect of work, and Oglethorpe conceived a colony as a way to employ such people usefully; the plan soon widened to other philanthropic and strategic aims. Dr. Thomas Bray, a supporter of prison reform, offered his organisation, the Associates of Dr. Bray, as the body to seek a charter, and Oglethorpe added members of the prison committee and other reformers.

After Bray died in February 1730 Oglethorpe became the driving force. Money from the D'Allone Legacy helped finance the trust. The petition for a royal charter was submitted in July 1731, George II signed the charter in April 1732, and it reached the trustees in June 1732.

Oglethorpe led the first colonists himself, leaving England in November 1732 and arriving at the site of present-day Savannah in February 1733. Although he and others had wanted debtors to people the colony, the Crown decided otherwise: Georgia was to be a military buffer for South Carolina against the Spanish and some Creek factions. The settlers were chosen for useful skills, the men trained and enrolled in the militia, and most of the 114 travelled with wives, children and servants. The trustees laid down the Oglethorpe Plan, which set out how towns and districts were to be laid out, how land was to be shared and how the settlers were to defend themselves.

The trustees named in the charter included Thomas Coram, John, Viscount Percival, later Earl of Egmont, and several members of parliament; more were added at annual meetings, beginning in March 1733. In London Benjamin Martyn served as secretary and Harman Verelst as accountant, while in Savannah William Stephens was secretary and later president of the colony. The trustees governed Georgia from its founding until 28 June 1752, the period known as Trustee Georgia. In 2008 the Georgia Historical Society revived the name, admitting two new Georgia Trustees each year for their service to the state.
truth-and-reconciliation-commission-of-c: The commission was set up on 1 June 2008 as one of the requirements of the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement, reached between survivor groups, the Assembly of First Nations, church bodies and the Government of Canada, with a budget of $60 million over five years. Unlike South Africa's commission it was not a state-led body, and it had no power of subpoena, no power to offer amnesty and no power to name individuals. On 11 June 2008 Prime Minister Stephen Harper apologised for the role of past governments in running the schools, about 70 percent of which the Catholic Church had administered with government funds.

Its first chair, Justice Harry S. Laforme of the Ontario Court of Appeal, resigned on 20 October 2008, accusing the other commissioners, Claudette Dumont-Smith and Jane Brewin Morley, of insubordination; both left in January 2009. On 10 June 2009 Murray Sinclair became chair, with Marie Wilson and Wilton Littlechild as commissioners.

Over six years the commission travelled across Canada and heard more than 6,500 witnesses in community hearings, sharing circles and panels, many of whom described being stripped of their language and culture and suffering abuse, sexual assault and malnutrition. Records supplied by Library and Archives Canada in 2014, after a court order of January 2013, led to an extension. The commission held its closing event in Ottawa from 31 May to 3 June 2015 and in June released its summary and 94 calls to action, divided into Legacy and Reconciliation.

The final report of December 2015 estimated that about 150,000 children attended the schools over their 120-year history and that about 3,200 died in them. Its records went to the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation at the University of Manitoba in Winnipeg, which opened in November 2015 and holds more than five million documents. Critics such as Glen Coulthard argued that it treated colonialism as a closed chapter, while others, among them Hymie Rubenstein and Rodney A. Clifton, faulted its use of evidence. Norway in 2018, and Sweden and Finland in 2021, set up commissions on the Saami modelled on it.
truth-and-reconciliation-commission-peru: In December 2000 the interim president Valentín Paniagua approved a truth commission, which President Alejandro Toledo ratified in 2001; it worked from 13 July 2001 to 28 August 2003. Its mandate covered the violations committed between May 1980 and November 2000 by the state, the Shining Path and the Túpac Amaru Revolutionary Movement, under the governments of Fernando Belaúnde, Alan García and Alberto Fujimori: to analyse the causes of the violence, measure its scale, assess responsibility and propose reparations and reforms. It had no judicial powers but full access to state records.

The commission had twelve commissioners, ten men and two women, under its president, the philosopher Salomón Lerner Febres, rector of the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Perú, with Bishop Luis Bambarén Gastelumendi as observer. About five hundred staff worked from regional offices in Lima, Huanuco, Huancayo, Huamanga and Abancay, with local leaders such as the Asháninka activist Luzmila Chiricente Mahuanca as translators. Its budget of about $13 million for two years came nearly half from international donors.

It gathered about seventeen thousand testimonies from 129 provinces and 509 districts, 54% of them given by women, and held 27 public hearings at which 422 people spoke about 318 cases. It took part in exhumations of clandestine graves with the Attorney General's Office and commissioned Yuyanapaq, Quechua for to remember, a photographic record of the conflict drawn from more than 90 archives.

The final report of 28 August 2003 put the dead and disappeared at about 69,280, against an earlier estimate of 24,000, and found both institutional and individual responsibility. It opposed any amnesty and sent 43 cases to the Ombudsman's Office and the Public Prosecutor's Office. It proposed an Integral Reparations Plan, which a High Level Multi-Sectoral Commission was set up to oversee. Critics said it gave too little attention to the forced sterilisation of some two hundred thousand poor Indigenous women under Fujimori, and a 2019 study, whose findings the commission disputed, estimated 48,000 killings, with a larger share by the state.
truth-and-reconciliation-commission-sout: The commission was set up under the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act, No. 34 of 1995, and was based in Cape Town. Authorised by Nelson Mandela, it was a court-like body of restorative justice, charged with bearing witness to and recording human rights violations, granting amnesty in some cases, and offering reparation and rehabilitation to victims. A register of reconciliation let ordinary South Africans express regret for past failures.

Besides Tutu, its members included Alex Boraine as deputy chairman, Sisi Khampepe, Wynand Malan, Klaas de Jonge and Emma Mashinini. Tutu enriched the mandate with the African concept of Ubuntu, which in Xhosa expresses the idea that together people make one another human.

The work was divided among three committees. The Human Rights Violations Committee investigated abuses between 1960 and 1994, the Reparation and Rehabilitation Committee was charged with restoring victims’ dignity and proposing ways to help them, and the Amnesty Committee considered applications from individuals. Public hearings were held at many venues, among them Cape Town, Johannesburg and Randburg. They were at first to be held in camera, but 23 non-governmental organisations won media access, and on 15 April 1996 the national broadcaster televised the opening of the first hearing live.

Amnesty could be granted where crimes were politically motivated, proportionate and fully disclosed. To avoid victor’s justice, no side was exempt from appearing: the commission heard both the apartheid state and the liberation movements, the African National Congress among them. It found 7,000 political deaths under apartheid between 1948 and 1989, 73 of them in detention in the hands of the security police, and more than 19,050 victims of gross human rights violations. Of 7,111 amnesty applications, 849 were granted and 5,392 refused.

South Africa’s first coalition government chose forgiveness over prosecution and reparation over retaliation, in contrast to the Nuremberg trials, and opinions differ on how well this restorative approach worked. A 1998 survey of several hundred victims found that most felt the commission had failed to bring reconciliation between the black and white communities. Critics such as Madeleine Fullard and Mamphela Ramphele argued that its definition of gross violations left out systemic wrongs such as forced removals and pass arrests.

Many black South Africans were angered by amnesty for abuses committed by the apartheid government, and the family of Steve Biko challenged the commission in the highest court as unconstitutional. Urgent interim reparations were made available only in 2003, five years after the commission recommended them. The Institute for Justice and Reconciliation was established in 2000 as its successor.
trzebiatow: Trzebiatów, in German Treptow an der Rega, is a town in the West Pomeranian Voivodeship in north-western Poland. It lies on the Rega River, roughly 9 kilometres south of the Baltic coast, and had 10,119 inhabitants in 2016. Its Old Town is a protected historical monument of Poland, with Gothic churches, defensive walls and towers, a market square and a palace. The area was the site of a West Slavic fortified settlement in the 9th century and became part of the emerging Polish state under Mieszko I around 967.

The town belonged to the Duchy of Pomerania. Its first recorded mention is from 1170, when Duke Casimir I granted a few villages and oversight of a church in the town to settlers from Lund in Sweden. In the early 13th century Duchess Anastasia of Greater Poland made it her seat, and in 1277 the settlement received town privileges under Lübeck Law. In 1416 it joined the Hanseatic League and became an important trade post in Brick Gothic style. Johannes Bugenhagen became rector of the local school in 1504.

On 13 December 1534 a diet assembled in the town, where Dukes Barnim XI and Philip I and the nobility officially introduced Lutheranism to Pomerania, against the vote of Erasmus von Manteuffel-Arnhausen, Prince-Bishop of Cammin. The following month Bugenhagen drafted the new church order.

After the Thirty Years' War the town passed to Brandenburg-Prussia under the Peace of Westphalia of 1648. In 1750 the palace was refurbished in classicist style for General Frederick Eugene of Württemberg, and later the Polish writer Maria Wirtemberska lived there; it now houses a public library named after her. From 1871 to 1945 the town was part of the German Reich. In 1945 it again became part of Poland, its German population was expelled and Poles settled in it, in accordance with the Potsdam Agreement. Each August the town holds the Day of the Buckwheat.
trzebnica: Trzebnica, in German Trebnitz, is a town in the Lower Silesian Voivodeship in south-western Poland, in the Trzebnickie Hills about 6 km north of Wrocław, and part of the Wrocław metropolitan area. It was an early medieval religious and trading centre, possibly more important than Wrocław. It is first mentioned in a deed of 1138, when it was held by the Polish voivode Piotr Włostowic and later seized by the Silesian duke Władysław II the Exile.
