Duke Henry I the Bearded and his wife Hedwig of Andechs founded the first Cistercian convent in Poland at Trzebnica, settled with German nuns from Bamberg. In 1218 Hedwig's daughter Gertrude became abbess, the first of many Piast princesses to hold the office. Henry died in 1238 and was buried in the church; his widow moved to the convent, where she died in October 1243 and was buried too. She was canonised in 1267. The town received town privileges in 1250 and became a Bohemian fief in 1328. The Hussites plundered it in 1430, and fires struck in 1456, 1505, 1511 and 1534. In 1742 Austria ceded Trzebnica with most of Silesia to Prussia, and the monastery was secularised in 1810.

The former convent church is the Sanctuary of St. Jadwiga, a regional pilgrimage site since the 14th century and a listed Historic Monument of Poland. The town was heavily damaged in the Vistula–Oder Offensive of the Red Army in the last days of World War II and came under Polish administration under the Potsdam Agreement, when the remaining German population was expelled. From April to June 1945 it was the first post-war regional capital of the Lower Silesian Voivodeship.
tsakhurs: The Tsakhur, also called Saxur, are a people of northern Azerbaijan and southern Dagestan in Russia, and number around 30,000. They are also called yiqy, but are generally known by the name Tsakhur, which derives from the name of a Dagestani village where they are prominent. They are first mentioned in 7th-century Armenian and Georgian sources, where they are named Tsakhaik.

After the conquest of Caucasian Albania by the Caliphate, the Tsakhurs were governed by a semi-independent state, later a sultanate, of Tsuketi in south-western Dagestan. By the 11th century the Tsakhurs, who had mostly been Christian, converted to Islam. From the 15th century some began moving south across the mountains to what is now the Zaqatala District of Azerbaijan. In the 18th century the capital of the state moved south from Tsakhur in Dagestan to İlisu and came to be called the Elisu Sultanate. West of the sultanate the Tsakhurs formed the Djaro-Belokani free communities. The sultanate lay in the sphere of influence of the Shaki Khanate. The Tsakhurs were conquered by the Russian Empire by the beginning of the 19th century.

Tsakhurs live in Azerbaijan's Zaqatala region, where they make up 14 per cent of the population, and in Gakh, where they make up less than 2 per cent. In Dagestan they live in the mountainous parts of the Rutulsky district. According to Wolfgang Schulze, nine villages in Azerbaijan, all in Zaqatala, have a Tsakhur majority, and 13 more villages in Zaqatala and Gakh have a significant Tsakhur minority. The main traditional occupation is herding sheep, the most important part of their economy, but Tsakhurs are also known as stonemasons, tailors, carpenters and makers of handicrafts, including carpet-weaving and knitting. Most speak Tsakhur as their native language; bilingualism in Tsakhur and Azeri is high, and Russian and Lezgian are also widely used.
tsaparang: Tsaparang lies in the Garuda Valley of the upper Sutlej River in Ngari Prefecture, near the border of Ladakh, 26 km west of the 11th-century monastery of Tholing and not far west of Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar. The fortress is perched on a pyramid-shaped rock about 152 to 183 metres high at the end of a long, narrow spur, and is riddled with tunnels and caves cut into the rock. Nearby is the Bon monastery of Gurugem.

According to some accounts Tsaparang was made the capital of Guge by Namde Wosung, a son of Langdarma, the anti-Buddhist king of Tibet, after Langdarma's assassination; others say Langdarma's grandsons fled to western Tibet around 919. Guge controlled an ancient trade route between India and Tibet and was a regional power by the 10th century. In the 11th century King Yeshe-Ö, with the translator Rinchen Zangpo and the Indian master Atiśa, reintroduced Buddhism to western Tibet.

In the summer of 1624 the Portuguese Jesuits António de Andrade and Manuel Marques, the first known Europeans to cross the Himalayas, reached Tsaparang and gained the king's leave to preach. With three more Jesuits they built a church at the foot of the citadel and another at Rudok. In 1630 Senge Namgyal of Ladakh overthrew Guge and took its pro-Jesuit king, Tri Tashi Drakpa, captive, and the mission fell into disarray. In 1679–80 Tsaparang and Guge were conquered by Central Tibet under the 5th Dalai Lama.

The common people lived in a village at the base of the rock; above it stand two public temples, the Lhakhang Marpo (Red Chapel) and Lhakhang Karpo (White Chapel), with the monks' quarters, and higher still, reached by a twisting stone staircase in a tunnel, the royal quarters and at the very top the summer palace. Despite the damage of 1679–80, and the destruction of most of the statues and murals of both chapels by the Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution, many frescoes survive. The historian Michael Wood has suggested that Tsaparang was the historical origin of the legend of Shangri-La.
tsar: Tsar, also spelled czar, is a Slavic title derived from the Latin caesar. It entered the Slavic languages through the Gothic kaisar and served as the equivalent of the Greek basileus, which referred to Byzantine emperors and the kings of the Bible. It was meant to denote an emperor in the medieval European sense, a ruler of the same rank as a Roman emperor who held it by the approval of another emperor or a supreme ecclesiastical official, but Western Europeans usually took it to mean king.

The first ruler to adopt the title was Simeon I of Bulgaria, after a makeshift imperial coronation performed by the Patriarch of Constantinople in 913. The Byzantine government recognised it in 924 and again in 927, after a decade of intensive warfare. Stefan Dušan of Serbia was crowned emperor at Skopje at Easter 1346, and his son Stefan Uroš V succeeded him in 1355. Bulgaria's Ferdinand I took the title again in 1908, and it lasted until the monarchy ended in 1946.

In Russia, church officials once called Yaroslav the Wise tsar, but other princes of Kievan Rus' did not style themselves so. Ivan III, who asserted independence from the khan in 1476, began using the title regularly in diplomacy with the West. Its growth was tied to Russian ambitions to be a third Rome after the fall of Constantinople in 1453, and Emperor Maximilian I recognised the Moscow monarch as an emperor in 1514. The first Russian ruler formally crowned tsar of all Russia was Ivan IV in 1547.

In 1721 Peter the Great formally adopted the title of Emperor, but tsar stayed in common use and was kept in the full title as the style of rule over states absorbed by the Russian monarchy, such as the Tatar khanates and the Georgian Orthodox kingdom. In the 18th century it was increasingly seen as inferior to emperor.

By 1815 it had come to be read in Russia as the equivalent of the Polish król, king, and the emperor took the title tsar of Poland. Among the indigenous peoples of Siberia and the Muslims of the Volga region, Central Asia and the Caucasus, Russian autocracy became identified with the White Tsar. In English, tsar has been used since 1866 as a metaphor for a person of high authority.
tsarevo: Tsarevo is a town and seaside resort on a cove 70 km south-east of Burgas, on the southern Bulgarian Black Sea coast, at the eastern foot of the Strandzha mountains and a few kilometres from Strandzha Nature Park. It is the seat of the Municipality of Tsarevo in Burgas Province. Until 1950 the settlement was known as Vasiliko, in Greek Βασιλικό, and from 1950 to 1991 it was named Michurin, after the Soviet botanist Ivan Vladimirovich Michurin.

Underwater surveys have found amphoras of the 4th to 6th century and red-polished pottery made in Constantinople, Syria and North Africa, which points to prosperous trade in late antiquity. The southern peninsula has the remains of a medieval fortress. The 12th-century Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi first mentions the town as Vasiliko. In the 15th and 16th centuries it was an Ottoman port, and in 1662 the traveller Evliya Çelebi described a square fortress on a ridge above the sea, surrounded by vineyards. Its cove could hold the largest ships but was avoided by sailors because it gave little shelter from the powerful eastern winds.

In 1787 an Austrian ambassador in Constantinople reported 200 houses and a lively port, and in the first half of the 19th century the town had a fleet of 42 ships, ten windmills and a watermill, and vineyards producing up to 6,000 pails of wine a year. A Greek school there was also attended by many Bulgarians. A fire in 1882 destroyed almost the whole town, and the inhabitants rebuilt it on the peninsula of the northern cove, called Limnos. Between 1878 and 1912 it was the centre of the Ahtabolu kaza in the Kırkkilise sanjak of the Edirne Vilayet.

The town was ceded to Bulgaria in 1913 after the Balkan Wars. Its Greek population moved to Greece and was replaced by Bulgarians from Eastern Thrace. A new wharf was built from 1927 to 1937 with financial aid from Tsar Boris III, and the town was renamed Tsarevo, a literal translation of Vasiliko, meaning royal place, in his honour.
tsetse-fly: Tsetse flies are large biting flies that inhabit much of tropical Africa. They include all the species of the genus Glossina, which has its own family, Glossinidae, and they live by feeding on the blood of vertebrate animals. Adults are 0.5 to 1.5 centimetres long and fold their wings completely over the abdomen when at rest.

They have an unusual life cycle: a female develops one offspring at a time inside her uterus, feeding it with a milky secretion, and the larva leaves the uterus only in its third stage, when it crawls into the ground and forms a hard case. Glossina is almost entirely restricted to wooded grasslands and forested areas, and its species are divided into savannah, forest and riverine flies.

The tsetse is a biological vector of trypanosomes, single-celled parasites that cause trypanosomiasis. In humans this is sleeping sickness, caused by Trypanosoma brucei, which is invariably fatal if untreated. In cattle and horses it is called nagana, and it reduces the growth, milk yield and strength of farm animals and generally leads to their death. Some breeds of cattle are called trypanotolerant because they can survive and grow when infected.

In East Africa C. F. M. Swynnerton did much of the earliest research on tsetse ecology in the first half of the 20th century, and the species Glossina swynnertoni was named for him in 1922. Early control methods included slaughtering the wild animals the flies fed on: Príncipe was cleared of feral pigs in the 1930s, which ended the fly there.

Writers on environmental determinism have linked the tsetse to difficulties in early state formation where the fly is common. A 2012 study built a suitability index from population growth, climate and geospatial data and found that more suitable conditions for the fly were associated with weaker agriculture, urbanisation and institutions.

Its authors concluded that the fly decimated livestock, forcing early states to rely on slave labour to clear land and preventing farmers from using animal fertiliser, which may have kept population density low. In the 19th century the rinderpest epidemic, introduced in 1887 in livestock brought by an Italian expeditionary force to Eritrea, together with the tsetse fly is said to have depopulated much of Africa. Land infested with tsetse is often farmed with hoes rather than draught animals.
tsewang-dorji-namjal: Tsewang Dorji Namjal was born in 1732, a son of Galdan Tseren, ruler of the Dzungar Khanate, which covered most of present-day Xinjiang and parts of eastern Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and southern Siberia. His father left a strong state. A form of peace with the Qing dynasty had held since 1739, and the trade with China that followed widened the khanate's economic base. Galdan Tseren had also brought Turkic Taranchi people into the fertile oases to build irrigation systems, and although tension with Imperial Russia grew in his last years, an influential faction in Russia valued an independent Dzungaria as a counterweight to China.

Galdan Tseren had three sons and a daughter. At his death the eldest son, Lama Dorji, was 17, Tsewang Dorji Namjal 13 and the youngest, Tsewang Dashi, seven. The father's will named Tsewang Dorji Namjal as his successor, and in 1746 the Dzungar nobility proclaimed him their leader.

Little is known of him. The surviving sources describe him in his youth as perverse, cruel and paranoid, a heavy drinker who was more interested in killing dogs than in affairs of state; one says that he liked to roam the villages drinking chang and seducing girls. Several missions to Tibet further weakened his standing among the Dzungar elite.

Lama Dorji conspired with the husband of their sister Ulam Bayar, the Baghatur Sayin Bolek, and with other saisans, the high officials of the khanate, to kill Tsewang Dorji Namjal on a hunting trip. During a failed attack on the plotters he was captured and blinded, and he was sent as a prisoner to Aksu in Xinjiang together with his brother Tsewang Dashi. He died in 1750. The internal struggle for power that had begun after his father's death led to anarchy and, in the end, to the destruction of the khanate.
tsewang-rabtan: Tsewang Rabtan was a Choros prince, the son of Sengge, Galdan's brother and the Khong tayiji of the Dzungar Khanate, who was killed in 1670 by his half-uncles Chechen tayiji and Zotov Batur. Galdan avenged Sengge and went on to invade the Yarkent Khanate, the Kazakh Khanate and the Khalkhas. Tsewang Rabtan revolted against his uncle, went over to the Qing side in 1689 and established himself as Khong tayiji in 1697, after Galdan's death. He was married to the sister of Lha-bzang Khan.

In 1698, after a Kazakh raid had killed Urkudei batur tayiji and 500 civilians, he declared war on the Kazakh Khanate, routing its army on the Chu and Talas rivers and taking about 10,000 prisoners. A Dzungar attack in 1708 drew a Kazakh counterstroke led by Bogembai batyr deep into Dzungaria. In 1714 his son Lobsangtur and Galdan Tseren recaptured lost lands from the Kazakhs, and he regained the city of Hami, lost in 1698. That year he also married his daughter Boitalak to Danjung, Lha-bzang Khan's eldest son.

In 1717 the Dzungars defeated the Kazakhs on the Ayagoz river. The same year he sent 300 men into Amdo to bring the 7th Dalai Lama to Lhasa, and 6,000 under his brother Tseren Dhondup, who took Lhasa from the Khoshut and killed Lha-bzang Khan. The Dzungars defeated a poorly organised Qing force at the Battle of the Salween River in 1718, but a larger Qing expedition took Lhasa in 1720 and established Qing rule in Tibet. In 1719 Galdan Tseren defeated a Russian expedition at Lake Zaysan. Freed from war with the Qing, Tsewang Rabtan opened a fifth war on the Kazakhs, in which Lobsangtur ravaged and occupied the Kazakh Steppe.

Danjung died around 1717, allegedly at Tsewang Rabtan's hands, and Boitalak married a Khoid prince; their son Amursana (1723-1757) later became khan of Dzungaria under the Qianlong Emperor. Tsewang Rabtan's death in 1727 set his sons Galdan Tseren and Lobsangtur at war. Galdan Tseren won, killed Lobsangtur and inherited the khanate.
tsilhqotin-war: The Tsilhqot'in, like many First Nations of the Pacific Northwest, had just been devastated by the 1862 smallpox epidemic, which some colonists saw as a chance to take Indigenous lands; many Indigenous people, the Tsilhqot'in among them, believed it had been spread deliberately to that end. In 1862 Alfred Waddington began lobbying for a wagon road from Bute Inlet up the Homathko valley and across the Chilcotin Plateau to Fort Alexandria, where it would join the Cariboo Road to the goldfields at Barkerville. Tsilhqot'in men worked on the road unpaid, were repeatedly lied to and went near starving.

On 29 April 1864 the ferryman Timothy Smith was killed after refusing a demand for food from Chief Klattasine, Tellot and others, and the next day the road crew's camp was attacked at daylight; three men escaped. The foreman William Brewster and three of his men were killed further up the trail, as were the settler William Manning at Puntzi Lake and three drivers of Alexander McDonald's pack train. In all nineteen men were killed.

Governor Seymour, a month into his term, learnt of the attacks on 14 May. Chartres Brew's party could not get up the Homathko trail, and a second party under Gold Commissioner William Cox was ambushed and withdrew. A larger force with the Governor reached the area from Bentinck Arm in July, and the scout Donald McLean was shot dead. Believing they were coming to peace talks, Klattasine, Tellot and others met Cox and were arrested; they said they had been promised immunity, which Cox denied. Tried before Judge Begbie at Quesnel in September 1864, they were found guilty, Klattasine saying they had waged war, not murder.

The conflict cost the colony about $80,000. Begbie judged that concern over title to the land, not plunder or revenge, was the main cause. In 1993, after a report by Judge Anthony Sarich, British Columbia's Attorney General apologised for the hangings. Premier Christy Clark exonerated the six chiefs in 2014, and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau did so for Canada in Parliament on 26 March 2018, when Tsilhqot'in chiefs were invited onto the floor of the House of Commons, and visited Tsilhqot'in land on 2 November 2018.
tsinghua-bamboo-slips: The strips were donated to Tsinghua University in July 2008 by an alumnus, named in the Guangming Daily as Zhao Weiguo, who had bought them at a foreign auction. Where and when they were dug up is unknown, but the illegal excavation was probably of a tomb in Hubei or Hunan province. Similarities with the manuscripts of the Guodian tomb point to a mid-to-late Warring States tomb in the region culturally dominated by the state of Chu.

When they reached the university the strips were badly affected by mould. After conservation, a Center for Excavated Texts Research and Preservation was set up at Tsinghua on 25 April 2009, with Li Xueqin directing the project. The team published its first volume of photographs, transcriptions and commentary in 2010, in a series planned at 18 volumes, while studies and translations appear in a series edited by Huang Dekuan and Edward Shaughnessy.

Several texts bear on the Shang Shu, the Exalted Writings. The Yin zhi partly overlaps the Tang shi chapter and a manuscript of volume nine largely overlaps the Jin teng, while other texts in the same style are missing from the received book, either never taken into the canon or lost in transmission. Volume two holds a single text, the Xinian, on 138 well-preserved strips, probably composed around 370 BCE: it records key events of Zhou history and traces the origin of Qin to supporters of the Shang dynasty who opposed the Zhou conquest.

Other texts include a gathering of the Zhou elite in the ancestral temple of King Wen of Zhou, with hymns in the style of the Shi Jing; the Baoxun, presented as King Wen's deathbed admonition to his son on the concept of the Middle; the Xin shi wei zhong, which holds that humans are in charge of their destiny; the Wu yin tu, one of the few writings on music older than the empire; and five manuscripts on judging, treating, training and riding horses.

On 7 January 2014 the journal Nature announced that 21 of the strips, put in the right order, form a decimal multiplication table able to multiply whole or half numbers up to 99.5. Joseph Dauben of the City University of New York called it the earliest artefact of its kind in the world, and Guo Shuchun of the Chinese Society of the History of Mathematics said it filled a gap in the mathematical record before the Qin dynasty. Officials are presumed to have used it to calculate land areas, crop yields and taxes.
tsiribihina-river: The Tsiribihina drains a basin of 49,800 square kilometres and, with a mean annual discharge of around 32 cubic kilometres, is the largest river in Madagascar by volume. Its headwaters lie on the Central Highlands. Four main tributaries, the Mahajilo and Manandaza from the north and the Mania and Sakeny from the south, flow down to the Betsiriry Plain, which runs north to south, and join there to form the river. The Mania's basin alone covers 18,565 square kilometres.

Where the rivers meet, the plain has extensive seasonal wetlands and shallow lakes, and its rich alluvial soils make it one of the best farming regions of western Madagascar. The Tsiribihina then cuts a steep, winding gorge westward through the Bemaraha Plateau, a limestone formation along the plain's western edge. Beyond the plateau it widens and meanders past shallow lakes such as Lake Kimanomby near Ambohibary and Lake Masoarivo near Masoarivo, before reaching the Mozambique Channel.

The delta stretches about 35 kilometres from north to south, with beaches and dunes, mudflats, salt flats that often flood in the rainy season, freshwater marshes and mangroves 2 to 4 metres high. Eighty-two species of birds have been recorded on the river and its delta, 22 of them endemic to Madagascar. Bernier's teal breeds in the mangroves, the Madagascar pratincole gathers in large numbers on the banks, and a few pairs of Madagascar fish eagle live along the river.

The Menabe Antimena protected area covers the south bank of the lower river, the delta and the mangroves. The Tsiribihina Delta is a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention, and the river and its delta are an Important Bird Area of Birdlife International.
tsogt-taij: Tümengken Choghtu Khong Tayiji was a noble of northern Khalkha with a base on the Tuul river. Known as an intellectual, he embraced the Karma Kagyu sect of Tibetan Buddhism and built monasteries and castles, among them the White Castle, or White House, which he built in 1601. In 1621 he wrote a poem that was carved on the surface of a rock in 1624 and still exists.

He submitted to Ligdan Khan, the last grand khan of the Mongols, and joined his campaign to Tibet in support of the Karma sect. Ligdan Khan died in 1634 before their forces joined, but Choghtu pursued the campaign, conquered the Tümed around Kokonor, the Qinghai Lake, that year and moved his base there, expanding into Amdo, the present-day Qinghai.

At the request of Shamar Rabjampa he sent an army under his son Arslan to central Tibet in 1635. Arslan instead attacked the allied Tsang army, met the fifth Dalai Lama and paid homage to Gelug monasteries rather than destroying them, and Choghtu had him assassinated.

The Gelug sect turned for help to Törü Bayikhu, known as Güshi Khan, leader of the Khoshut tribe of the Oirat confederation, who in 1636 led the Khoshuts and the Dzungars into Tibet. The next year a decisive war between the two ended in Güshi Khan's victory, and Choghtu was killed.

Descendants of his grandson Sutai Yeldeng held the office of jasagh of a banner in the Sain Noyon Khan Aimag. The Gelug tradition has portrayed him as evil, while the Mongolian film Tsogt taij of 1945 treated him as a national hero.
tsonga-people: The Tsonga, or Vatsonga, are a Bantu ethnic group living mainly in southern Mozambique, in Inhambane, Gaza and Maputo, and in South Africa, in Limpopo and Mpumalanga, with very small numbers in Zimbabwe and northern Eswatini. They speak Xitsonga, which is one of the official languages of South Africa. Historians hold that Xitsonga had already developed in the 1500s from a predecessor called Thonga, and the name Tsonga is related to the older Thonga. The Thonga are said to have left Central Africa between 200 and 500 CE. Historical research indicates that a common language and cultural integration had been developing since the 1200s.
Early Tsonga groups named in Henri Philipe Junod's history of the period 1498 to 1650 include the Mpfumo, who belong to the Rhonga clan, and the Valenga, Vacopi, Vatshwa and Vandzawu.

Tsonga groups held large territories in southern Mozambique and parts of South Africa and took tribute from those who passed through. In the 1800s the Nkuna and Valoyi supplied soldiers to the Modjadji kingdom, and the Nkomati and Mabunda supplied regiments to the army of João Albasini. Leadership was traditionally in the hands of senior chiefs.

In the 1820s Soshangane, a Nguni general of the Ndwandwe, raided Mozambique and built what became the Gaza Empire, whose rule included areas occupied by the Tsonga. The name Shangaan comes from him and properly applies to the tribes he founded or absorbed, though it is often used for all Tsonga in South Africa. The Chopi stayed independent throughout the Gaza kingdom. When its ruler Nghunghunyana tried to subdue them in 1888, a war followed that ended in 1895 with his defeat by the Portuguese under Mouzinho de Albuquerque, allied with Chopi soldiers led by their king Xipenenyana.

Under apartheid the Gazankulu Bantustan was created in the 1960s from part of northern Transvaal and was granted self-government in 1973. About 500,000 people, less than half the Tsonga of South Africa, ever lived there. Sunduza II Mhinga rallied the chiefs from 1957 to resist absorption into the Venda and Lebowa territories, and Hudson Ntsanwisi became Gazankulu's first Chief Minister.

The traditional economy rests on mixed farming and herding. Cassava is the staple, with maize, millet and sorghum; women do much of the farming and men and boys tend the herds. Boys attend an initiation school with circumcision, called Ngoma, and girls attend the Khomba school led by older women. Tsonga belief gives ancestors a considerable influence on the lives of their descendants, and healers called n'anga diagnose illness and train new diviners. In 2011 there were about 7.3 million Tsonga speakers, 3.3 million in South Africa and 4 million in Mozambique.
tsongkhapa: Tsongkhapa, whose name means the man from Tsongkha, was born in 1357 into a nomadic family with a Mongolian father and a Tibetan mother, in the walled city of Tsongkha in Amdo, in present-day Qinghai. His first teacher, the Kadam monk Choje Dondrub Rinchen, taught him Buddhism from an early age, and he became a novice monk at six. At sixteen he travelled to Central Tibet and studied at the scholastic institutions of Sangphu monastery, the Drikung Kagyu and the Sakya tradition, among them with Chenga Chokyi Gyalpo at Drikung Thil Monastery. He also studied Tibetan medicine and all the major Buddhist scholastic subjects.

From 1390 to 1398 Tsongkhapa lived in extended meditation retreats with a small group of attendants, best known in the Wölkha Valley. He formed a close relationship with the hermit Umapa Pawo Dorje, who had frequent visions of black Mañjuśrī, and later had visions of Mañjuśrī himself, in which he asked about the right view of emptiness.

His best-known work is the Great Exposition of the Stages of the Path, the Lam rim chen mo, of about 1402, which outlines the Mahayana path to enlightenment. In 1405 he finished the Great Exposition of Tantra. Other major works include Essence of Eloquence, Ocean of Reasoning, a commentary on Nagarjuna, and Elucidation of the Intent, his last major writing.

His philosophy rests on Indian madhyamaka thinkers such as Nagarjuna, Buddhapalita and Chandrakirti and on the epistemology of Dharmakirti. He held that all phenomena lack inherent existence because they arise in dependence on other things, and that emptiness and dependent arising are inseparable. This does not mean that things do not exist: they exist conventionally, in what he called mere existence. He also argued that meditation must be joined to rigorous reasoning, and he favoured Candrakirti's prasangika reading of madhyamaka.

Tsongkhapa died in 1419 at the age of 62 at Ganden Monastery, by then a well-known figure with a large following. His three principal disciples were Khedrup Gelek Pelzang, the first Panchen Lama, Gyaltsap Darma Rinchen and Dülzin Drakpa Gyaltsen. Jamyang Chöjé and Jamchen Chöjé founded Drepung and Sera monasteries, and the first Dalai Lama, Gendün Drup, was also his student.

His disciples spread the teachings, and the Gelug school, a descendant of the Kadam school, emphasised monastic discipline and rigorous study of the Buddhist classics. According to Thupten Jinpa, by the end of the fifteenth century the tradition had spread across the Tibetan Plateau, from western Tibet to Kham and Amdo in the east.
tsu-mie: Tsu lies in the east-central Kii Peninsula, in central Mie Prefecture. It stretches across the width of the prefecture, from Ise Bay in the east to Nara Prefecture in the west, and it has an area of 711.11 square kilometres, making it the largest city in the prefecture by area. Parts of the city are within the Murō-Akame-Aoyama Quasi-National Park. It has a humid subtropical climate with hot summers and cool winters with little or no snowfall.

Tsu originally developed as a port town called Anotsu in the Nara and Heian periods. In 1498 the port was devastated by the earthquakes and tsunami of the Meiō era, including the 1498 Meiō Nankaidō earthquake, and its residents were forced to relocate.

The town was rebuilt as a castle town and a post station by the Tōdō clan, daimyō of Tsu Domain under the Tokugawa shogunate. During the Edo period it became a popular stopping point for travellers to Ise Grand Shrine, about 40 kilometres to the south-east. Tōjin Odori, a dance from the Wakebe-chō neighbourhood, began around 1636 as part of the festival of Tsu Hachiman Shrine and imitates the Joseon Tongsinsa, the Korean diplomatic missions to Edo-period Japan.

After the Meiji Restoration Tsu became the capital of Mie Prefecture. When the modern municipal system was established on 1 April 1889, Tsu was one of the original 31 cities proclaimed in Japan and the only one in Mie. It grew by annexing neighbouring villages between 1909 and 1943. The first bombs fell on 12 March 1945, and three heavy air raids in June and July destroyed about 73 per cent of the city centre by incendiary bombs. The worst raid, by about 70 B-29 bombers on 24 July 1945, killed an estimated 1,200 to 1,300 people.

On 1 January 2006 Tsu merged with the neighbouring city of Hisai and several towns and villages in the Age and Ichishi districts, forming the new city of Tsu, which became the largest in Mie by area. It is the administrative and educational centre of the prefecture. Mie University, the prefecture's only national university, is here. The ruins of Tsu Castle have been made into a downtown park, and Kitabatake Shrine and Yūki Shrine are notable local Shinto shrines.
tsugaru-clan: Much about the clan's ancestry is uncertain. Later Tsugaru records traced it to the Fujiwara and gave it an ancient claim to the Tsugaru region, while the records of the rival Nanbu clan made Ōura Tamenobu, born in 1550, a member of a minor Nanbu branch driven out after a quarrel with his elder brother. The Ōura served as deputies to the Nanbu magistrate Ishikawa Takanobu, but in 1571 Tamenobu killed Ishikawa and began seizing Nanbu castles in the region. When the Nanbu split into factions after the death of Nanbu Harumasa in 1582, he declared his lands independent, and in 1590 he pledged fealty to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who confirmed his holdings.

The clan sided with Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara in 1600 but remained suspect, since Tamenobu sheltered a son of Ishida Mitsunari and married Mitsunari's daughter to his heir, Tsugaru Nobuhira, and its domain rose only to 47,000 koku. Disputes over the succession broke out in 1607, 1612, 1634 and 1647. Later lords faced eruptions of Mount Iwaki, bad harvests and mounting debt. Under Tsugaru Yasuchika the domain's rating was raised to 100,000 koku to pay for troops sent to guard Ezo, and in 1821 he survived an attempt on his life by Sōma Daisaku, a former Nanbu retainer. Tsugaru Yukitsugu, adopted from outside the family in 1839, restored the finances and modernised the army through Western learning.

In the Boshin War of 1868 to 1869 the last lord, Tsugaru Tsuguakira, first backed the imperial government, briefly signed the pact of the Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei, then returned to the imperial side and joined the attack on the Republic of Ezo at Hakodate.

The clan escaped the punishment dealt to the northern domains and gained 10,000 koku. Its lords of Hirosaki and Kuroishi became imperial governors in 1869 and lost their offices when the domains were abolished two years later. Tsuguakira was made a count in the kazoku peerage. A descendant, Hanako, daughter of Count Tsugaru Yoshitaka, married Prince Hitachi, younger son of Emperor Shōwa. The clan's main temple in Hirosaki is Chōshō-ji.
tsugaru-nobuhira: Tsugaru Nobuhira was born on 9 May 1586, the third son of Ōura Tamenobu, head of the Ōura clan. In 1596 he and his two elder brothers, Nobutake and Nobukata, are known to have converted to Christianity. At the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 he accompanied his father in the Eastern Army of Tokugawa Ieyasu and served in Ieyasu's retinue, while Nobutake was a page to Toyotomi Hideyori at Osaka Castle. As with the Sanada clan, the division ensured that the family would survive whichever side won.

When his father died, Nobuhira became head of the clan over the objections of a faction that supported his nephew Tsugaru Kumachiyo, the young son of Nobutake. The dispute, the first of many internal conflicts of the Tsugaru clan in the Edo period, put the domain at risk of attainder, but the Tokugawa shogunate arbitrated and confirmed Nobuhira as daimyō. To secure his standing with the shogunate he married Mate-hime, a niece of Tokugawa Ieyasu and the widow of Fukushima Masayuki; his first wife, Tatsu-hime, a daughter of Ishida Mitsunari, was reduced to the status of concubine and sent to the clan's small holding in Kōzuke Province.

He built the castle at Takaoka in haste, demolishing other castles of the domain for their materials, and its five-storey donjon was far larger than usual for a lord of 47,000 koku. In 1614 he sent troops to support the Tokugawa in the Osaka Winter Campaign. In 1619 the clan was ordered to move to Echigo Province to make way for Fukushima Masanori, but with the help of the priest Nankōbō Tenkai the order was turned aside. In September 1627 lightning set the donjon on fire and a store of gunpowder exploded; the castle was rebuilt on a smaller scale and renamed Hirosaki Castle in August 1628.

Nobuhira developed the port of Aomori on Mutsu Bay for shipping to Edo and for passage to the northern island of Ezo, and he raised rice production with new paddy fields and irrigation and by bringing in craftsmen from other parts of Japan. He died at the clan residence in Edo in 1631 and was buried at Shinryō-in, a subsidiary temple of Kan'ei-ji in Tokyo. His eldest son, Tsugaru Nobuyoshi, born to Tatsu-hime, succeeded him, while Tsugaru Nobufusa, his son by Mate-hime, received a holding of 5000 koku at Kuroishi and was the ancestor of the later lords of Kuroishi Domain.
tsugaru-tamenobu: Tamenobu was born on 18 January 1550 and was the adopted son and heir of Ōura Tamenori, a retainer of the Nanbu clan, whose seat was Sannohe Castle. He succeeded his father in 1567 or 1568 as castellan of Ōura Castle, in what is now part of the city of Hirosaki. Later Tsugaru clan records traced the family to the noble Fujiwara clan, while the records of their rivals, the Nanbu, held that he came from a minor branch of the Nanbu and had been driven out after discord with his elder brother.

The Ōura were hereditary deputies to the Nanbu clan's local magistrate, Ishikawa Takanobu. In 1571 Tamenobu attacked and killed Ishikawa and went on to take the Nanbu castles of the region one after another, among them Ishikawa, Daikoji and Aburakawa. After the death of Nanbu Harumasa in 1582 the Nanbu split into factions, and Tamenobu declared the territories he held independent. Proclaimed a traitor, he sought the support of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, but his attempts to travel south in 1586, 1587 and 1588 were blocked by hostile forces.

In 1589 he sent horses and falcons for Hideyoshi through Ishida Mitsunari and asked to be recognised as daimyō of the three Tsugaru districts of Hiraga, Hanawa and Inaka, assessed at 45,000 koku. Nanbu Nobunao, backed by Maeda Toshiie, demanded his punishment as a rebellious vassal, but Tamenobu had the support of Ishida Mitsunari, Hashiba Hidetsugu and Oda Nobukatsu and had pledged fealty earlier than Nobunao. He joined the suppression of the Kunohe Rebellion in 1591 and moved his seat to Horikoshi Castle in 1597.

His reward for Sekigahara was only 2000 koku in Kozuke Province, which brought the domain to 47,000 koku. Afterwards he sheltered the orphaned children of Ishida Mitsunari and married his son Nobuhira to Mitsunari's daughter. A rising during his absence briefly held Horikoshi Castle, and he then began a new castle on a large scale at Takaoka, between the Iwaki and Tabuchi rivers, which became Hirosaki Castle.

He died in Kyoto at the age of 58, having set out to visit his eldest son, who had fallen ill there and died before he arrived. He was buried at Kakushū-ji, the Tsugaru clan temple in Hirosaki. As his second son, Nobukata, had died in 1597, the succession went to Nobuhira, which many retainers opposed in favour of the eldest son's son, until the Tokugawa shogunate intervened and confirmed Nobuhira.
tsuruga-castle: The castle stands in the middle of the Aizu basin, at the crossroads of routes to Kōriyama, Yonezawa and Murakami on the Sea of Japan. Its forerunner was Kurokawa Castle, built in 1384 by Ashina Naomori of the Ashina clan, which ruled the area. Date Masamune took it in 1589 at the Siege of Kurokawa Castle, but in 1590 he submitted to Toyotomi Hideyoshi and was moved to Sendai. Hideyoshi's general Gamō Ujisato, set to watch Masamune, rebuilt the castle in 1592 as Tsuruga Castle and in 1593 raised a seven-storey tenshu with black walls and gold roof tiles.

After Uesugi Kagekatsu, who sided with the Toyotomi in the Sekigahara campaign and was moved to Yonezawa, the domain passed to Katō Yoshiaki, who rebuilt the tenshu smaller and white after an earthquake in 1611. From 1643 it was the seat of Hoshina Masayuki, a son of the shogun Tokugawa Hidetada, whose successors took the Matsudaira name and made Aizu one of the strongest Tokugawa domains. In October 1868, in the Battle of Aizu, the forces of the Satchō Alliance shelled the castle with Western artillery from the surrounding hills, and Matsudaira Katamori surrendered it in November. The damaged buildings were pulled down in 1874, though one yagura survived at the temple Amida-ji.

The castle had a pentagonal inner bailey about 200 metres long, with deep moats and tall stone walls, three outer enclosures to the west, north and east, and a river on its south side; the whole covered 600 by 400 metres. An army garrison held the central 23 hectares until 1908. Interest in the Byakkotai story led to its preservation as a public park, and it became a National Historic Site in 1934. The concrete tenshu of 1965 holds a museum and an observation gallery, and the restored tea room Rinkaku is a Fukushima Prefecture Important Cultural Property.
tsuruoka: Tsuruoka lies on the coast of Yamagata Prefecture, bordering the Sea of Japan, and covers 1,311.53 square kilometres, which makes it the largest city in the Tōhoku region by area. Two main rivers run through it, the Akagawa and the Mogami. All three of the Three Mountains of Dewa lie at least partly within its limits: Mount Haguro, the smallest at 436 metres, Mount Gassan, the highest at 1,984 metres, and Mount Yudono at 1,500 metres. The winters bring heavy snowfall, and some neighbourhoods can expect up to 2 metres.

The area was part of ancient Dewa Province. In the Edo period it was the capital of the Shōnai Domain and a minor port for the kitamaebune coastal trade. After the start of the Meiji period it was organised as Tsuruoka Town in 1878. It became a city on 1 October 1924, the 100th city in Japan. It annexed the town of Kamo and nine neighbouring villages in 1955 and the town of Oyama in 1963. On 1 October 2005 the towns of Fujishima, Haguro, Kushibiki and Atsumi and the village of Asahi merged into it.

The Three Mountains are the core of the practice of Shugendō, often seen as a blend of Shinto and Buddhism. The Yamabushi, the men who practise it, believe in the Buddha but also that a god resides in all things in nature. The pilgrimage of the three mountains is understood to represent death and rebirth. Mount Haguro has a five-storied pagoda that is one of Japan's National Treasures, and a cedar more than 1,000 years old. The Yamabushi's vegan temple food is called shōjin ryōri.

In 2014 Tsuruoka was registered as a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy, in part because of more than 50 kinds of ancestral food crops that have remained intact for centuries. They include the minden eggplant and the Atsumi turnip. The city is also known for dadachamame soybeans and for its local rice. Thatch-roofed houses are among its symbols, and the Chidō Museum preserves one.
tsushima-island: Tsushima lies between the Tsushima Strait and the Korea Strait, roughly halfway between Kyushu and the Korean Peninsula. The Korea Strait splits at the archipelago into two channels, and the wider one, closer to the Japanese mainland, is the Tsushima Strait. The main island, once a single island, was divided in two in 1671 by the Ōfunakoshiseto canal and in three in 1900 by the Manzekiseto canal, forming North Tsushima and South Tsushima. The group also includes over 100 smaller islands.
It measures about seventy by fifteen kilometres. Forest covers about 90 per cent of the island, and there are few plains, so the islanders have lived mainly by fishing and trade.

In Japanese mythology Tsushima was one of the eight original islands created by the deities Izanagi and Izanami. Archaeological evidence suggests that settlers from the Japanese archipelago and the Korean Peninsula lived there from the Jōmon period to the Kofun period. The Chinese Records of the Three Kingdoms describes a country called Duì hǎi guó, commonly identified with Tsushima, as one of about 30 that made up the Yamatai union. Its families controlled Iki Island and traded with Yayoi Japan. A mountain castle on Jouyama, built in 667 by Emperor Tenji, housed border guards, and from the early sixth century Tsushima was an official province of Japan.

In the feudal period it was an important trading centre. Private trade between Goryeo, Tsushima, Iki and Kyūshū halted during the Mongol invasions of Japan between 1274 and 1281, and the Goryeosa records that in 1274 Korean troops of the Mongol army led by Kim Bang-gyeong killed a great number of people on the islands. Tsushima became one of the main bases of the Wokou, Japanese pirates, along with Iki and Matsuura. Korea at times placated the pirates with trade agreements and at times used force, and in 1389 General Pak Wi of Goryeo wiped out the Wokou on Tsushima.

In 1861 the Imperial Russian Navy tried to establish a base on the island, in what is known as the Tsushima incident. The plan had been made by Vice Admiral Ivan Likhachev, but the Russians withdrew under pressure from Vice Admiral John Hope, who commanded the British ships in Japanese waters on the orders of Sir Rutherford Alcock.

Tsushima is part of Nagasaki Prefecture, and Tsushima City, formed on 1 March 2004 from six towns, covers the whole island. Izuhara was the castle town of the Tsushima domain until the Edo period, and ancient stone walls still stand in its samurai street. The Ofunaeato ruins, docks created in 1663, served the Korean trade and the alternate attendance system. The sacred Mount Shiratake, 519 metres high, is a national natural monument for its primeval forest.
tsutsujigasaki-castle: Tsutsujigasaki stood in what is now the centre of the city of Kōfu, in Yamanashi Prefecture. The Takeda, a cadet branch of the Minamoto clan, had gained control of Kai Province from the late Heian period from their bases at Hakusan Castle and Yato Castle, and by the Sengoku period they held the office of shugo. Takeda Nobutora chose a gentle slope in the flatlands of the Kōfu Basin for the residence and its castle town. By the standards of the time, which placed fortifications on mountains, the site was indefensible, and Nobutora also built Yōgaiyama Castle nearby as a supporting castle and final redoubt.

The residence had two main enclosures inside a triple ring of two flooded moats and one dry moat. The central enclosure, 200 metres square, held the private residence of the Takeda ruler, and the western enclosure, 100 by 200 metres, was a public area for the administration of the domain, with two-storey fortified gates to the north and south. Two secondary enclosures with their own moats, the Miso-guruwa and Baio-guruwa, flanked them. It was the largest residential complex in eastern Japan in the Sengoku period.

Takeda Shingen, who deposed his father in 1540, kept Tsutsujigasaki as his principal residence. The residence is not called a castle in Japanese, in keeping with the Takeda policy to make men their castle, their walls and their moats. Shingen's son Takeda Katsuyori built Shinpu Castle at Nirasaki, a new and larger castle, and moved there in 1581. In February 1582 the Takeda clan was destroyed by the forces of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu.

The ruins have been protected as a National Historic Site since 1938 and are listed among Japan's Top 100 Castles. Only some of the water-filled moats and minor stonework survive. The Takeda Shrine, a Shinto shrine built in 1919 and dedicated to the deified spirits of the Takeda clan, stands at the centre of the site, with a museum beside it.
tswana-people: Before colonial rule, Tswana-speaking communities were organised into chiefdoms, merafe, often built round clan lineages and governed by dikgosi, chiefs, with advisory councils. In the early nineteenth century the Difaqane, or Mfecane, a period of warfare and displacement from 1815 to 1840, raided or moved many Tswana settlements; it contributed to stronger centralised states such as the Bangwaketse, Bakwena and Bangwato.

In the 1840s and 1850s trade with merchants of the Cape Colony let the chiefdoms rebuild. The Bakwena, Bangwaketse, Bangwato and Batawana worked together to control the ivory trade and used the proceeds to buy horses and guns, which let them dominate what is now Botswana by about 1880, subjugating the Bushmen, Bakalanga, Bakgalagadi and Batswapong.

After the Great Trek, Afrikaners settled on the borders of the Tswana lands in the Transvaal. In 1852 a coalition of chiefdoms led by Sechele I resisted them at the Battle of Dimawe, and the Boer commando retreated; after about eight years of tension a peace agreement at Potchefstroom in 1860 settled the modern border.

In 1884 the Batawana under Kgosi Moremi, supported by Wayeyi allies, defeated Ndebele raiders at Khutiyabasadi. In 1893 and 1894 some 700 Tswana allies under Khama III marched on Bulawayo with the British South Africa Company in the First Matabele War. European missionaries had established stations from the mid-nineteenth century, and Christianity spread as several dikgosi adopted it or allowed it.

The kgotla, a public assembly where disputes are settled and decisions debated, was the central institution of governance, though it largely excluded women from formal debate. Descent was patrilineal. Young people were incorporated into age-regiments called mephato; boys were circumcised and, on completing their training, were brought to the kgotla, given a regimental name and presented with weapons. Girls passed through the initiation called bojale. Traditional belief centred on Modimo, a supreme spiritual force, and Badimo, the ancestral spirits. Marriage was formalised by bogadi, bridewealth usually paid in cattle, and sorghum porridge, bogobe, is the staple food.

The Republic of Botswana, formerly the British protectorate of Bechuanaland, is named for the Tswana, and ethnic Tswana made up about 85 per cent of its population in 2011. The largest number of Tswana live in South Africa, where Setswana is one of eleven official languages. From 1948 to 1994 the apartheid government defined South African Tswana as citizens of Bophuthatswana, one of ten bantustans. It was granted nominal independence on 6 December 1977 and reincorporated into South Africa on 27 April 1994.
tu-duc: Tự Đức, whose personal name was Nguyễn Phúc Hồng Nhậm, was born on 22 September 1829, a son of the emperor Thiệu Trị. He succeeded his father in 1847 as the fourth emperor of the Nguyễn dynasty. Thiệu Trị had passed over his more moderate eldest son Hồng Bảo in favour of Tự Đức, who was known for his staunch Confucianism and his opposition to foreigners and innovation. Dissatisfaction with Nguyễn rule was already widespread because of the repressive policies of the previous emperor, and Hồng Bảo offered a legitimate royal figure around whom opponents could gather.

Hồng Bảo plotted rebellion with Confucians, supporters of the Lê dynasty, corrupt mandarins, Catholic missionaries and converts, and peasants unhappy with taxation. He was arrested in 1854 and killed himself in prison. In 1866 his son Đinh Đạo rebelled, and after the revolt was crushed Tự Đức ordered Đinh Đạo, his brothers and his mother put to death. A cholera epidemic in 1849 killed about 600,000 according to the royal archives, and droughts from 1864 and typhoons in Tonkin in 1880 and 1881 added to the strain.

Tự Đức kept Vietnam closed to the outside world and refused efforts at modernisation. He oppressed foreigners and above all Christians, calling their religion a perverse doctrine. An order of 1848 commanded Catholic converts to renounce their faith or be branded on the face. The Christian mandarin Nguyễn Trường Tộ urged reform forty-three times without success, and a plan for a school of sciences and crafts at Huế was dropped. In the north, Chinese bands such as the White Flags and Yellow Flags invaded Tonkin, and the court hired the Black Flag Army of Liu Yongfu against them.

France and Spain sent an expeditionary force that attacked up from the south in 1858 to 1862, using the execution of a Spanish bishop as justification. Faced with rebellions as the French advanced, Tự Đức preferred a deal with France to the risk of being deposed. He signed away Cochinchina as a colony, which caused uproar, and officials such as Trương Định fought on. In 1876 and 1880 he sent missions to Beijing to affirm Vietnam's tributary status to China.

Tự Đức died on 19 July 1883, the longest-reigning Nguyễn emperor and the last Vietnamese monarch to rule independently. Smallpox had left him unable to father children, and his adopted son Dục Đức, who succeeded him, was deposed by court officials after three days. According to legend, he cursed the French with his dying breath.
tu-scendi-dalle-stelle: Alphonsus Liguori wrote both the melody and the original words, while staying at the Convent of the Consolation, a house of his order at Deliceto in the province of Foggia. The Italian carol, titled "Little song to Child Jesus", followed an earlier song in Neapolitan, "Quanno nascette Ninno", which is sometimes called the "Carol of the Bagpipers". The Italian carol became widely popular in Italy. Though sung in many arrangements, it is traditionally associated with the zampogna, the large Italian bagpipe.

The text addresses the infant Jesus as the King of Heaven who comes down from the stars to a cave, in cold and frost. The first stanza calls him a trembling baby and asks how much it cost him to have loved the singer. The second describes the Creator of the world as lacking clothes and fire, and says that his poverty makes the singer love him the more, since love made him poor. Several English translations exist, some in the style of the King James Bible, as well as a literal English rendering of the Neapolitan song.

The earliest known sound recording was made by the baritone Rodolfo Fornari, a member of the Boston Opera Company, in New York on 21 September 1915 under the title "Novena Di Natale", and was issued in 1916 by Columbia. On 24 September 1917 the tenor Pasquale Feis recorded it for Victor as "Pastorale Di Natale"; the Library of Congress preserves that recording. A version published in 1932 by A. Paolilli's Music Co. of Providence, Rhode Island, credits the music to Tommaso Capocci and the words to Pope Pius IX, without mentioning the earlier work.

Robertino Loretti recorded it in 1961, and Sergio Franchi in 1965. The bilingual song "O Bambino (One Cold and Blessed Winter)", composed by Anthony Velona with words by Remo Capra, takes its melody directly from the carol and was first recorded by the Harry Simeone Chorale in 1964. Domenico Scarlatti used the tune in a sonata, and Ottorino Respighi used it in the second movement of his Trittico botticelliano of 1927.
tuareg: The Tuareg are an Amazigh people who speak the Tuareg languages, known as Tamasheq in Mali, Tamahaq in Algeria and Libya, and Tamajeq in the Azawagh and Aïr regions of Niger. They are descended from indigenous Berber communities of North Africa. Some researchers tie the origin of the Tuareg to the fall of the Garamantes, who lived in the Fezzan from the 1st millennium BCE to the 5th century CE. The Lamtuna, a Sanhaja Berber tribe that formed the core of the Almoravid dynasty, were closely related to their ancestors.

In tradition the Tuareg moved south from the Tafilalt region into the Sahel under their founding queen Tin Hinan, believed to have lived between the 4th and 5th centuries. Her tomb at Abalessa in the Hoggar Mountains of southern Algeria bears traces of an inscription in Tifinagh, the Libyco-Berber script that the Tuareg still use.

The invasion of North Africa from the Middle East in the 7th century triggered migrations of Tuareg groups such as the Lemta and the Zarawa. Later, the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym Arab tribes moved into Tuareg regions in the 11th century and pushed the Tuareg south, into seven clans which oral tradition holds are descended from one mother. Tuareg people are credited with spreading Islam in North Africa and the adjacent Sahel.

At the turn of the 19th century, Tuareg territory was organised into confederations, each ruled by a supreme chief, the amenokal, with a council of elders from each tribe. They were sometimes called drum groups after the amenokal's symbol of authority. There were seven major confederations, including the Kel Ajjer, Kel Ahaggar, Kel Adagh, Kel Ayr and Kel Gres. When African states became independent in the 1960s, Tuareg territory was divided among Niger, Mali, Algeria, Libya and Burkina Faso. A Tuareg uprising in Mali in the 1960s was suppressed by the army.

Tuareg society has traditionally had clan membership, social status and caste hierarchies within each confederation. Its strata included nobles, clerics, craftsmen and unfree people, and slavery was widespread. The nobles carried arms, owned camels and collected tribute from their vassals. Culture is largely matrilineal, and men, not women, traditionally wear the veil, the indigo tagelmust, a combined turban and veil. The Tuareg are a pastoral people with an economy based on livestock, trade and agriculture. They have long organised caravans across the Sahara, such as the salt caravans from Agadez to Fachi and Bilma and from Timbuktu to Taoudenni. They are mostly Muslim, and their population is estimated at 1.2 to 3 million.
tuban: Tuban lies on the north coast of Java about 100 kilometres west of Surabaya, and it is the administrative capital of Tuban Regency, which borders Lamongan Regency to the east, Bojonegoro Regency to the south and Rembang Regency in Central Java to the west. The town covers 21.29 square kilometres. The area is known for its beaches, teak forests and many caves with stalactites and stalagmites, among them Goa Akbar and Goa Maharani, which have earned it the name City of a Thousand Caves. Its climate is tropical savanna, with heavy rain from December to March.

Chinese records mention Tuban from the eleventh century, and an anchor said to come from one of Kublai Khan's ships is kept in its historical museum. The town dates its official history to 12 November 1293, when the king of Majapahit crowned Ronggolawe as head of the Tuban region; its 700th anniversary was marked with a parade of decorated floats in 1993. Local stories derive the name from the Javanese phrase watu tiban, a stone fallen from the sky, dropped by a pair of birds flying from Majapahit to Demak.

Tuban is believed to have been Islamised before Demak conquered it around 1527, yet it remained loyal to Hindu-Buddhist Majapahit in the interior. The spread of Islam there was led by Sunan Bonang, one of the Wali Sanga, and his follower Sunan Kalijaga, and Tuban was a centre of Islamic culture and politics in the 15th century. The Dutch called the town Toeban.

Tuban had an estimated 88,128 people in mid 2025. The grave of Sunan Bonang, a few minutes' walk from the town square, is an important destination for Muslim pilgrims, and the Chinese temple of Kwan Sing Bio by the beach holds a 30-metre statue of Kwan Kong. The town is known for tobacco, teak, the batik called Batik Gedog and the palm wine tuak, and a large cement factory opened there in 1994.
tubingen: Tübingen is a traditional university city in central Baden-Württemberg, 30 kilometres south of Stuttgart. It grew around the base of the fortress Schloss Hohentübingen and of the St. George's Collegiate Church, on both sides of the Neckar and Ammer rivers. The Neckar flows east through the city, just south of the medieval old town. To the north lies the Schönbuch, a densely wooded nature park, while the Swabian Alb rises to the south-east. The Schlossberg and the Österberg stand in the city centre, and large parts of the city are hilly.

The area was probably first settled in the 12th millennium BCE. The Romans left traces in 85 CE, when they built a limes frontier wall at the Neckar in confrontation with the Alamanni. Records of the castle of Hohentübingen go back to 1078, when Henry IV, King of Germany, besieged it. In the middle of the 12th century the Counts of Zollern were raised to Imperial Counts Palatine, with their seat at Tübingen. By 1231 it was a civitas, which meant the Crown recognised its civil liberties, a market and a court system.

In the later 13th century the town gained Augustinian and Franciscan monasteries and a Latin school, today's Uhland-Gymnasium. In 1342 the town and castle passed to the Counts of Württemberg. The clock tower of the Collegiate Church was begun in 1411. The Jewish community, centred on the Judengasse below the Rathaus, was expelled in 1477, the year the university was founded.

The university, Eberhard Karl University, is one of the oldest north of the Alps. In the 19th century it was associated with the German-patriotic student Burschenschaften, whose large fraternity houses remain a feature of the town. It was associated with the rise of National Socialism in the years between the world wars. Among those linked with the town are Philip Melanchthon, the astronomer Johannes Kepler, and Wilhelm Schickard, professor of Hebrew and astronomy and inventor of a mechanical calculator. Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel and Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling studied there, and Friedrich Hölderlin studied, lived and died in the town, as did the theologian Ferdinand Christian Baur.

Tübingen survived the Second World War with its historic fabric almost wholly intact, and its old town, with crooked cobblestone lanes, half-timbered houses and the Rathaus on the central market, is one of the few Altstädte in Germany that is completely intact. Students make up almost a third of its 90,000 residents. After the 1960s the city expanded on the high ground to the north, and later into the Loretto and French Quarter on land that French military bases had left. It is the capital of a district and of an administrative region, and the university is its largest employer.
tudela: Tudela stands in the Ebro valley in Navarre, Spain, and is the second largest city of that chartered community. It is the capital of the agricultural region of Ribera Navarra. Excavations show that the area has been populated since the Lower Paleolithic, and the town has been inhabited continuously since Roman times. The Roman poet Martial recalls the town of Tutela in grateful verse in his Epigrams.

The town was taken by the Arabs during the Umayyad conquest of Hispania and was named Tatīlah. At the beginning of the 9th century its position on the Ebro made it strategically important, and it became the base of the Banu Qasi, a family of local magnates who had converted to Islam. They remained independent of the emirs and kept on-off alliances with the kings of Pamplona for the next century. As their power faded at the start of the 10th century, the town came under the influence of the Caliphate of Córdoba.

Muslims used Tudela as a bridgehead against the expanding Kingdom of Navarre. When Christians under Alfonso the Battler conquered it in 1119, Muslims, Mozarabs and Jews lived there. Relations afterwards appear to have been strained, and the Muslims were made to live in a suburb outside the walls. In 1157 the English scholar Robert of Ketton, the first translator of the Koran into Latin, became a canon of Tudela. The principal mosque was handed to the Catholic Church in 1121, and by the end of the 12th century work had begun on the cathedral.

Jews were banished in 1498, and Muslims and Moriscos were expelled in 1516 and 1610. Tudela was the last Navarrese stronghold of the Agramont party to surrender to Ferdinand II of Aragon's troops in the 1512 invasion. Marshal Lannes won the Battle of Tudela for Napoleon Bonaparte on 23 November 1808, and the railway station was built in 1861.

Tudela has about 35,000 inhabitants. The Cathedral of Our Lady of Solitude, built in the 12th and 13th centuries, includes Romanesque work such as the Door of the Last Judgement, with Gothic influence and Baroque additions. The Romanesque churches of Magdalene and San Nicolás also date from the 12th century, and examples of Mudéjar architecture remain.
tudhaliya-i: Tudḫaliya I is attested as the son of a certain Kantuzzili, who is not known to have reigned or to have descended from an earlier Hittite king. Most scholars assume this Kantuzzili was the Commander of the Golden Squires who, with his apparent brother, the Chief Cupbearer Ḫimuili, murdered the preceding king, Muwatalli I. Jacques Freu opposes that identification because the sources about the two are consistently incompatible, though he allows that the father may have been the general of the same name who fought the Hurrians. Onofrio Carruba and Freu propose that his mother was Walanni, who may have been a daughter of the earlier king Zidanta II.

The numbering of the Hittite kings named Tudḫaliya is disputed. Many scholars see a single king, called Tudḫaliya I or I/II, while others consider two, Tudḫaliya I and Tudḫaliya II. Freu notes that Tudḫaliya I was the son of a non-reigning father, whereas Tudḫaliya II writes that he came to the throne as a youth after his father's death. If there was only one king, his queen would have been Nikal-mati, his daughter Ašmu-Nikkal and his son-in-law and successor Arnuwanda I.

Tudḫaliya came to the throne on the murder of Muwatalli I. He appears to have pardoned and purified the regicides, Ḫimuili and Kantuzzili. Muwatalli's Commander of the Guard, Muwa, may have murdered a queen in retribution and then tried to stage a revolution with the help of Hurrians led by Kartašura. Tudḫaliya and his general Kantuzzili defeated them.

Having secured his eastern flank, Tudḫaliya apparently turned south. By Freu's reconstruction he was responsible for the earlier, equal treaty with Šunaššura I of Kizzuwatna, and probably the Kuruštama Treaty with Egypt, whose king Thutmose III had been active in northern Syria and had reached the Euphrates. Freu believes he also made unequal treaties with the rulers of Alalaḫ, Emar and Nuhašše, and a treaty with Tunip on the Orontes. A much later treaty of Muršili II records a treaty with Aleppo. When Aleppo left the alliance for Mittani, Tudḫaliya defeated Aleppo and its Mittanian allies and destroyed the city.

If Tudḫaliya I and II were one person, the wars in western and northern Anatolia would belong to his reign. A number of modern biblical scholars believe that Tudḫaliya I, or a proto-Hittite Tudḫaliya, was the Tidal, king of Nations, who in the Book of Genesis joined Chedorlaomer in attacking rebels in Canaan.
tudhaliya-iv: Tudḫaliya IV was a king of the Hittite Empire, the younger son of Ḫattušili III and the great queen Puduḫepa. He was probably born at his father's court in Ḫattuša, after his brother Nerikkaili, the crown prince, while their father was still governing on behalf of his own brother Muwatalli II. Tudḫaliya was a good friend of Muwatalli's son Kurunta, and Ḫattušili ordered that the two stay on good terms.

According to the document known as the Apology or Autobiography of Ḫattušili III, the future king named him priest of the goddess Šauška of Samuha. After Ḫattušili, now king, drew up a treaty confirming Kurunta's rule over Tarḫuntašša, he raised Tudḫaliya above his older brother to be crown prince. His sister Maathorneferure served as Great Royal Wife to Pharaoh Ramesses II of Egypt.

The empire covered large parts of Anatolia and Syria. Drier conditions brought a severe drought, and Tudḫaliya IV responded by building at least 13 dams to secure water supplies, one of which still survives at Alacahöyük. To the east he faced the Assyrians and suffered a severe defeat at the hands of Tukulti-Ninurta I in the Battle of Nihriya. In a treaty with his vassal Šaušgamuwa of Amurru he named the kings of Egypt, Karanduniyaš, which is Babylon, and Assyria, and possibly Aḫḫiyawa, as equal to himself, and ordered that Šaušgamuwa treat the Assyrian king as an enemy and bar his own merchants from trade with Assyria.

The wording hints at an alliance or tacit understanding with Babylon. In the south-west the empire had been divided, with parts of the territory under Kurunta of Tarḫuntašša, and Tudḫaliya drew up a treaty, recorded on a bronze tablet, confirming his links with Kurunta. A clay tablet from the reign of Šuppiluliuma II says Tudḫaliya set up a statue to commemorate his conquest of Alasiya, possibly Cyprus. He had two sons, Arnuwanda III and Šuppiluliuma II, who are considered the last two kings of the Hittite Empire.
tufa-wugu: Tufa Wugu's father, Tufa Sifujian, was a great-grandnephew of the Xianbei general Tufa Shujineng, who had troubled the Jin dynasty under Emperor Wu. Sifujian became tribal chief in 356 as a vassal of Former Qin; when he died and was succeeded by his son is not known. Tufa Wugu was described as brave and ambitious and set his sights on Liang Province. On the advice of his general Fen Tuo he encouraged agriculture and tried to rule efficiently and fairly.

In 394 Lü Guang, ruler of Later Liang, offered him a generalship. Most of his advisers thought it humiliating to become a vassal, but the strategist Shizhen Ruoliu argued that he was not yet strong enough to oppose Lü Guang and should submit so as to make him arrogant, and Tufa Wugu accepted. In 395 he forced neighbouring tribes, among them the Yifu and Zhejue, to submit, built Lianchuan Castle as his headquarters and was made Duke of Guangwu by Lü Guang.

When Lü Guang took the title Heavenly King in 396 and offered him further honours, Tufa Wugu refused them, denouncing Lü Guang's sons and nephews as corrupt and cruel, though he kept the musicians and artisans sent with the titles. In 397, after Lü Guang was defeated by Qifu Gangui of Western Qin, he claimed a regal title of his own, changed the era name and took the city of Jincheng, then defeated the Later Liang general Dou Gou.

His aim was to weaken Later Liang and take its capital, Guzang. In 398 the Later Liang generals Yang Gui and Wang Qiji went over to him, and after he defeated the Qiang chief Liang Ji the Qiang and Xiongnu tribes south of the Hongchi Mountain submitted. Late that year he changed his title to Prince of Wuwei, perhaps a sign of his designs on Guzang. In spring 399 he moved his capital to Ledu, and he was remembered for placing Han and other subjects alike according to their talent.

Later in 399 he helped the Northern Liang prince Duan Ye fend off an attack by Lü Guang's sons Lü Shao and Lü Zuan. Soon afterwards he fell from his horse while drunk and suffered a severe chest injury, remarking that he was making Lü Guang and his sons happy. As he grew worse he ordered that an older man should succeed him, and the nobles chose his brother Tufa Lilugu. His posthumous title was Prince Wu of Wuwei.
tughlaq-dynasty: The Tughlaq dynasty was the third to rule the Delhi Sultanate. Tughlaq was the personal name of the founder, Ghazi Malik, rather than an ancestral designation, and historians use it for the whole dynasty as a convenience. His ancestry is debated, but he is usually considered to be of Turko-Mongol or Turkic origin. The Khalji dynasty had ruled before 1320. Its last ruler, Khusro Khan, lacked the support of the Muslim nobles, who invited Ghazi Malik, then governor in Punjab, to lead a coup. In 1320 he killed Khusro Khan and took the throne as Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq.

Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq built Tughlakabad, a city six kilometres east of Delhi with a fort considered more defensible against Mongol attacks. His son Jauna Khan captured Arangal in 1323 and annexed Kakatiya territory. According to many historians, including Ibn Battuta, Ghiyasuddin was killed by Jauna Khan in 1325, and Jauna Khan ruled as Muhammad bin Tughlaq for 26 years. His campaigns between 1330 and 1335 brought the sultanate to its territorial zenith, but they were expensive and the extended empire was hard to retain. Rebellions became routine, and the Deccan, Bengal, Sindh and Multan became independent.

Muhammad bin Tughlaq raised the land tax on non-Muslims tenfold in some districts of the Ganges and Yamuna region and twentyfold in others. Villages left their fields, and famines followed; Ibn Battuta, who arrived in 1334, noted a seven-year famine from 1335 near Delhi. The court historian Ziauddin Barani records bloodshed among Muslims as well. After a short rule by Mahmud Ibn Muhammad, his nephew Firuz Shah Tughlaq reigned for 37 years; Barani calls him the mildest sovereign since Islam came to Delhi. Civil wars broke out in 1384 and 1394.

In 1398 Timur defeated four armies of the Sultanate. Sultan Mahmud Khan fled, and Delhi was plundered for eight days and its population massacred. Khizr Khan, whom Timur is believed to have appointed viceroy at Delhi, entered the city on 6 June 1414 and founded the Sayyid dynasty.

The Tughlaqs managed their expanded empire by appointing family members and Muslim aristocrats as na'ib of iqta' provinces under contract. The na'ib deposited a fixed sum with the Sultan and kept a share of the taxes collected; excess collected from non-Muslims was split between na'ib and Sultan in a 20:80 ratio, which Firuz Shah changed to 80:20. Campaigns yielded loot and slaves, and the sultans patronised a slave market. The sultans, particularly Firuz Shah, also sponsored many construction projects and are credited with developing Indo-Islamic architecture.
tughlugh-timur: Tughlugh Timur was a son of Esen Buqa, a direct descendant of Chagatai Khan and himself a former khan of the Chagatai Khanate. After Qazan Khan was killed in 1346, Turko-Mongol tribes under the Qara'unas amirs took control of Transoxiana in the west and set up puppet khans. The east, most of it known as Moghulistan, was mainly Mongol and largely Buddhist and Shamanist, and its strongest family was the Dughlat amirs, who held Kashgar, Aksu, Yarkand and Khotan. When the Dughlat amir chose him as khan, Tughlugh Timur was little more than an adventurer.

The story of his conversion tells that the Persian cleric Mauláná Arshad al-Din, son of Shaykh Jamal al-Din, strayed onto his hunting grounds; when Tughlugh said a dog was worth more than a Persian, the cleric answered that without the true faith they would indeed be worse than dogs, and so taught him Islam. The amirs of Moghulistan followed, the people more slowly; the Tarikh-i-Rashidi claims 160,000 confessed Islam on one day.

With Transoxiana under the weak amir Buyan Suldus, he invaded in March 1360, and most amirs submitted; Hajji Beg of the Barlas fled and his lands went to his young nephew Timur. Returning in 1361, the khan executed amirs including Bayazid and Buyan Suldus, defeated the Qara'unas Amir Husayn south of the Amu Darya and plundered as far as Kunduz, reuniting the Chagatai Khanate before going back to Moghulistan.

He appears to have been tolerant of other faiths and shared his predecessors' interest in Buddhism: around 1363 he invited the Tibetan lama Rol-pai Dorji, returning from the Yuan court at Dadu, who declined because of the distance and the khan's conversion. In his time the Moghuls kept their Mongol identity and language. He was buried at Almaliq. His conquest of Transoxiana was short-lived, as Amir Husayn and Timur soon took it from Ilyas Khoja. Babur traced his grandfather Yunas Khan's descent through him.
tughril: Tughril was born most likely in the Central Asian steppes, where nomadic Oghuz Turks roamed in search of pasture. His name was the Old Turkic word for a bird of prey, possibly the crested goshawk. After the death of his father Mikail, he and his brother Chaghri were reportedly raised by their grandfather Seljuk, the eponymous founder of the dynasty, in Jand. The family seems to have converted to Islam, at least nominally, in this period. For decades the Seljuks served as mercenaries for warring factions in Transoxiana and Khwarazm in exchange for pasture for their herds.

They then asked Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni for leave to settle in Khorasan, where pastures were scarce for them in their old lands. Mahmud allowed it, and they crossed the Amu Darya and settled around Sarakhs, Farava and Bavard.

Under Mahmud's successor Masʽud I the Seljuks fought near Nasa in 1034, and Tughril took the city. In 1037 the Seljuk notables declared him sultan and a sermon was delivered in his name. His victory over the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040 ended their rule in Greater Khorasan, and he made Nishapur his capital. He and Chaghri Beg, whose names were read together in the sermons and struck on coins, shared rule according to the Turkic custom of a khagan and a yabghu.

With the help of his half-brother Ibrahim Inal, Tughril conquered Jibal and Iraq-i Ajam between 1040 and 1054 and ended Buyid rule in those areas. He took Ray, later making Isfahan his capital, and brought Azerbaijan under his control. From 1048 Turcomans under Ibrahim began systematic campaigns into Byzantine lands. In 1055, at the invitation of the caliph al-Qa'im, he entered Baghdad and ended the Buyid dynasty by arresting its last ruler in Iraq, Malik al-Rahim. He later put down a revolt by Ibrahim Inal and defeated Arslan al-Basasiri, who had Fatimid backing.

Tughril died in Ramadan in 455 AH (1063), without an heir, near Ray, and was buried there in the Tughril Tower. He was known as devout, built many mosques and madrasas, followed the Hanafi school and, with his vizier Amid al-Mulk Kunduri, restricted other Islamic sects. Some sources describe him as a just ruler who avoided bloodshed, while others report oppressive conduct by him and his army.

His legacy was an administrative model that joined Turkic political tradition, regional customs and the religious legitimacy of the Abbasid caliphate. It made the sultanate a form of absolute rule that recognised the caliph's spiritual leadership but overshadowed his worldly power. Before the Seljuks Iran had been divided among warring local powers such as the Buyids, Kakuyids and Ghaznavids, and under Tughril peace and prosperity came to Iran and Mesopotamia.
tughril-iii: Tughril was born in 1168, the son of Sultan Arslan Shah II, whom the atabeg Eldiguz had installed in 1161 as a figurehead while he controlled the army, the treasury and the grants of land. By then the Great Seljuk Empire had broken apart, and atabegs ruled their provinces with only nominal loyalty to the sultan. When Arslan Shah died suddenly at Zinjan, possibly poisoned, while marching against Eldiguz's son Muhammad Jahan Pahlavan, the child Tughril was installed as sultan at Hamadan.

Jahan Pahlavan treated him well and ruled in his name. After Jahan Pahlavan's death in 1186 his brother Qizil Arslan took his place, and Tughril, resenting his harsh treatment, joined rebels backed by Turkmens. In 1188 he defeated a caliphal army of 15,000 at Hamadan and captured its commander, but his losses were heavy, and executions among his own commanders cost him his allies. Qizil Arslan captured him in 1190 and imprisoned him in Kuhran fortress near Tabriz.

Freed in May 1192, Tughril won near Qazvin on 22 June 1192 and retook Hamadan, Isfahan and Jibal. His rival Qutlugh Inanch Muhammad called in the Khwarazmshah Ala ad-Din Tekish, who took Rey; Tughril accepted a truce as his vassal, then in March 1193 retook Rey and killed its Khwarazmian governor Tamghach. At Rey on 19 March 1194 he charged the Khwarazmian army against his commanders' advice, followed by only sixty of his guard. Wounded by an arrow, he fell from his horse and was beheaded by Qutlugh Inanch, and Tekish sent his head to Caliph al-Nasir in Baghdad.

With his death the titles of Seljuk sultan of Iraq and Great Seljuk sultan came to an end, and his lands passed to the Khwarazmian Empire. Judgements of him differ: some see a noble warrior fighting against impossible odds, others a rash, wilful and bloodthirsty ruler. His contemporary Nīshāpūrī praised his perfect judgement and love of the ulama, and the later writer Abū Hamid Muhammad b. Ibrāhīm also described him as just. Two of his sons, held as hostages at Gurganj, were executed in 1220 on the order of Terken Khatun.
tughshada: Tughshada was the son of the Bukhar Khudah Bindu, who was killed by the Umayyad general Salm ibn Ziyad during the Muslim conquest of Transoxiana when Tughshada was a few months old. In his childhood Bukhara was governed by his mother, known only by her title of Khatun, whom local tradition celebrates for her wisdom and capable rule. She is said to have held court daily, attended by two hundred young men of the landowning and princely families girded with gold belts and bearing swords.

In 706 civil war broke out around Bukhara. The ruler of nearby Wardana, the Wardan Khudah, seized most of the principality, while a Sogdian magnate, Khunuk Khudah, rallied the nobles of Bukhara and declared himself Bukhar Khudah. When the new Umayyad governor of Khurasan, Qutayba ibn Muslim, sacked the rebellious city of Paykand, the brutality of the sack drove Khunuk and the Wardan Khudah into alliance, but the Wardan Khudah was killed in the fighting. Qutayba took Bukhara, imposed a tribute of 200,000 dirhams and an Arab garrison, and restored the city to the young Tughshada, executing Khunuk and his faction.

In 712/3 Qutayba built a mosque in the citadel of Bukhara and paid local people to attend prayers, but Islamization proceeded very slowly.
