Tughshada still sought independence from the caliphate: in 718, with Gurak of Samarkand, Narayana of Kumadh and Tish of Chaghaniyan, he sent an embassy to the Tang dynasty of China asking for help against the Arabs. An anti-Arab revolt broke out in Bukhara around 728 and was put down a year later.

Tughshada had ruled as a vassal of the Umayyad Caliphate while seeking help abroad against it. He was assassinated in 739 by two angry dehqan nobles. He was succeeded by his son Qutayba, named in honour of the Umayyad general who had restored his father to Bukhara.
tughtakin-ibn-ayyub: Tughtakin, whose full style was al-Malik al-Aziz Zahir al-Din Sayf al-Islam Tughtakin Ahmad ibn Ayyub, was the youngest son of Najm ad-Din Ayyub; his brothers included Saladin, founder of the Ayyubid Empire, and al-Adil, later sultan of Egypt. After Saladin overthrew the Fatimid Caliphate of Egypt, Tughtakin acquired lands in the Adawiya district near Cairo that had belonged to Christian churches, most likely by force. He built houses and planted gardens there, and the former Fatimid head of the Diwan al-Nazar, the Office of Inspection, entered his service.

His brother Turan-Shah left Yemen in 1182 after rebellions across the country, and Tughtakin, who had written to Saladin asking for the post, was made emir that year. From his base at Zabid he consolidated Ayyubid rule throughout Yemen. He surrounded Zabid with a wall with four gates, Saham, Ghulafiqah, al-Shubariq and al-Qurtub, and had the main parts of the fortress of Ta'izz rebuilt. Under him and his predecessor Aden was the only city in Yemen to mint gold coins, and he founded Dar al-Sa'ada, the main transit area for imported goods there.

Under Turan-Shah a galley tax had been levied for patrols to guard merchant ships, but the warships lay on the beaches most of the time. On the advice of his aides Tughtakin put them to use, sending galleys to protect cargoes from pirates and to watch maritime traffic, as far as India. In Mecca he had dinars and dirhams struck in Saladin's name. According to the chronicler Ibn al-Athir he tried to take control of Mecca, but Saladin stopped him after protests from the Abbasid caliph al-Nasir.

Ibn al-Athir described him as a stern ruler, harsh to his subjects, who bought merchants' goods for himself and sold them at whatever price he wished. Tughtakin died in Zabid in August or September 1197. His son al-Muizz Ismail succeeded him but was killed on 17 January 1202, after which power passed to a mamluk, a slave soldier, of Ismail's younger brother an-Nasir Ayyub.
tughtekin: Tughtekin, a Turkoman, began as a junior officer of Tutush I, Seljuq emir of Damascus and Syria. When civil war broke out after Tutush's death in 1095, he backed Tutush's son Duqaq against Ridwan, the emir of Aleppo. When a Crusader army besieged Antioch, Duqaq sent him to relieve the city, but on 31 December 1097 he was defeated by Bohemund of Taranto and Robert II of Flanders. A second attempt, with Kerbogha, the atabeg of Mosul, was crushed on 28 June 1098.

On Duqaq's death Tughtekin had the junior son Tutush II proclaimed emir, married Duqaq's widow and kept the title of atabeg. He then deposed Tutush II, named Duqaq's brother Irtash emir and soon exiled him; Irtash, backed by Aytekin al-Halabi of Bosra, failed to retake Damascus and fled to King Baldwin I of Jerusalem. In May 1108 Tughtekin defeated a small force under Gervaise of Bazoches, lord of Galilee, who was executed after refusing to give up his lands for his freedom. In April 1110 he captured Baalbek and made his son Buri its governor.

With Fatimid help he forced the Franks to raise their siege of Tyre on 10 April 1112. He joined Mawdud of Mosul in 1113, winning the Battle of al-Sannabra but failing to take Tiberias. When Mawdud was killed by the Assassins in Damascus on 2 October 1113, most contemporary commentators blamed Tughtekin, though there is no clear evidence against him, and the suspicion isolated him from the Seljuks. In 1115 he rebelled against Sultan Muhammad I Tapar and briefly allied with the Crusader states, before seeking the sultan's pardon in Baghdad the following year.

Allied with Ilghazi, emir of Aleppo, he was defeated at the Battle of Hab on 14 August 1119. The Fatimids sold him Tyre in 1122, but his garrison lost it to the Franks on 7 July 1124. Joining al-Bursuqi, he was defeated again at the Battle of Azaz on 11 June 1125, and the following January he repelled an invasion by Baldwin II of Jerusalem.

Tughtekin died in 1128 and was succeeded by his son Buri, whose name the dynasty bears. Throughout his rule he balanced between the Franks and the Seljuk sultans while keeping his own independence. In the Old French chansons de geste of the Crusade cycle he appears as Dodequin.
tugu-inscription: The inscription is carved on a round, egg-shaped stone about 1 metre across, found in the hamlet of Batutumbuh in Tugu village, Koja, North Jakarta. Its five lines run around the surface of the stone in the Pallava script, written as Sanskrit verse in the Anustubh metre. An image of a staff crowned with a trident (trisula) separates the end of each sentence from the beginning of the next.

The edict is issued in the name of Sri Maharaja Purnawarman and records river works. It recalls an earlier canal of the Chandrabhaga river, dug to carry water to the sea, and then the digging of the Gomati, a canal of clear water that ran through the residence of the king's grandfather, ordered in the 22nd year of Purnawarman's reign. The work began in the month of Phalguna and took 21 days, and the canal measured 6,122 bows in length. On its completion Brahmins performed a ceremony and were given 1,000 cows. The straightening and widening of the river was meant to prevent floods in the wet season and to serve irrigation in the dry season.

In 1911, on the initiative of P. de Roo de la Faille, the stone was moved to the museum of the Bataviaasch Genootschap van Kunsten en Wetenschappen, now the National Museum of Indonesia, where it bears the inventory number D.124. Like the other Tarumanagara inscriptions it gives no date, and scholars have placed it in the middle of the 5th century from the forms of its letters. Its script is closely similar to that of the Cidanghyang inscription, which writes citralaikha as citralekha, and this has led to the view that one person wrote both. The Tugu inscription is valued in particular as a record of hydraulic works carried out in the fifth century.
tuhfat-al-nafis: The Tuhfat al-Nafis opens with a summary drawn from the Sulalatus Salatin, the Malay Annals, and then gives a far more detailed history of the Johor-Riau Sultanate. Among the events it records are the founding of the state of Terengganu, the murder of Sultan Mahmud Shah II of Johor, and the relations between the Bugis and the kings of Johor and Sumatra. It also touches, though not in great detail, on the organisation of the Minangkabau invasion of Johor in 1718, the true identity of Raja Kechil, and the war between the Bugis and the Minangkabau in Kedah between 1723 and 1725.

A recurring theme of the first half is conflict between the Minangkabau of Riau and the allied forces of the Bugis and Malays, fought in Riau and in Kedah, Selangor, Siak and Kalimantan. The second half runs from the middle of the 18th century to 1864. It traces the growing hostility between Bugis and Malays in Riau and two Bugis raids against the Dutch, in 1756 and 1784. The last ended when the Sultan of Riau signed a treaty with the Dutch that made his kingdom a fief of the Dutch East India Company.

Raja Ali Haji wrote the work in the Jawi script. As court genealogist and historian he compiled it from court notebooks, histories kept in the court archives and the accounts of people who still remembered the recent past. He also drew on written works as varied as the Karangan Engku Busu, the Hikayat Negeri Johor, the Siak Chronicles and the Sejarah Pihak Terengganu, which is now lost.

Four manuscripts of the Tuhfat al-Nafis are known. One, copied in 1890, was published in 1923 in the Journal of the Malayan Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society in London. Historians agree that the work leans towards the Bugis. Many of the events it covers are also told in the Siak Chronicles, which favour Siak, and the Tuhfat al-Nafis is valued as a counterbalance to that source on the same matters.
tui-haatakalaua: The first holder, Moʻungāmotuʻa, appears around 1470. His elder brother Kauʻulufonua I, the Tuʻi Tonga, stayed in his residence on the high ground of Olotele at Muʻa, while Moʻungāmotuʻa lived on the low land of Fonuamotu, reclaimed from the lagoon, the two separated by the Fonuamoa road. His followers therefore became known as the Kauhalalalo, the low road people, and the chiefs of the Tuʻi Tonga line as the Kauhalaʻuta, the inland road people. Later events suggest that Moʻungāmotuʻa took power from his brother without daring to do away with the Tuʻi Tonga, sending Kauʻulufonua to Samoa and ruling in his name; it took about a century for the new line to eclipse the old.

Around 1550 Vakalahi-Moheʻuli, or his father, allowed the Tuʻi Tonga to return from exile in Samoa. Moʻunga ʻo Tonga appointed several sons as governors, among them Ngata in the Hihifo district, who began the Tuʻi Kanokupolu line, and a daughter married the Tuʻi Tonga Fatafehi, joining the two dynasties by blood. Fotofili met Abel Tasman in 1643. Vaea found that the Tuʻi Kanokupolu had become a serious rival and fought a civil war against Mataelehaʻamea.

After him quick successions point to decline. Tupoulahi, who gave up the Tuʻi Kanokupolu title around 1771 because of old age, may have been offered this title, though it is doubted that he was formally installed. Maealiuaki, also a former Tuʻi Kanokupolu, met Captain Cook in 1777 and died soon after, and with him went the last real holder. Toafunaki, named by missionaries around 1790, died young in 1797, and his reburial in 1799 gave the occasion for the assassination of the Tuʻi Kanokupolu Tukuʻaho.

By the time of Mulikihaʻamea the title had become defunct, but his descendants took a new one, Tungī, still among the highest noble titles in Tonga; Viliami Tungī Mailefihi of this line joined it with the Tuʻi Kanokupolu. Four of Tonga's 33 hereditary noble titles, Tungī, Luani, Fotofili and Fakafānua, trace their authority to the line. Its burial grounds lie on ʻEua and at Lapaha.
tui-kanokupolu: The line began with Ngata, youngest son of Moʻunga ʻo Tonga, the sixth Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua, and of Tohuʻia, a Samoan princess from Upolu. Ngata was sent to the Hihifo district in western Tongatapu to govern it on behalf of the Tuʻi Tonga and the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua, supported by his mother's family, the Fale Haʻakili, who remained the traditional supporters of the title. He married two daughters of Ahomeʻe, a chief of Hihifo, and their children formed the first clan, the Haʻa Ngata. The Kanokupolu chiefs are called Kau Halalalo, the lower side of the road, because at Muʻa they lived on the beach side while the sacred Tuʻi Tonga lived inland.

Mataelehaʻamea, the fourth holder, went to war with the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua Vaea to extend his control into central Tonga, and from then the Tuʻi Kanokupolu gained power over the older line, while their daughters became the principal wives (moheofo) of the Tuʻi Tonga. Captain James Cook visited the retired Maealiuaki in 1777.

Late in the eighteenth century Tupou Moheofo, daughter of Tupoulahi, held the title until her cousin Tukuʻaho defeated her and installed his father Mumui. George Vason, who lived in Tonga from 1797, the year the first missionaries of the London Missionary Society came, described Mumui's funeral, at which two of his wives were strangled, and the chiefs' election of Tukuʻaho, whom none dared oppose. Tukuʻaho was assassinated by Tupouniua and ʻUlukalala, his successor Maʻafu ʻo Limuloa was murdered the same night, and a long interregnum followed until Tupou Malohi was appointed in 1808.

ʻAleamotuʻa became Tuʻi Kanokupolu in 1826, was installed at Hihifo on 7 December 1827 and was baptised by a Methodist missionary on 18 January 1830, taking the name Josiah Tupou. He died in 1845, and his successor Tāufaʻāhau, son of Tupoutoʻa, was installed as King George Tupou I. The title has passed with the crown since: Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV ascended in 1965, George Tupou V reigned from 2006 until his death in 2012, and his younger brother succeeded him as Tupou VI. The Haʻa Maʻafu, descendants of the sixth holder, include the princes of the royal household and live in Nukuʻalofa.
tui-manua-elisala: Elisala was born on the island of Ta'u, the second son of Tuʻi Manuʻa Alaalamua and Sofe, a daughter of Matiu of Ta'u, and his genealogy descended from the Sa Tagaloa. He attended the London Missionary Society seminary at Malua on 'Upolu and returned to serve as the Congregationalist minister of Fitiuta. After his father's death three branches of the family put forward candidates: Elisala himself, who refused because of his religious calling, Taofi, and a young woman named Matelita, whose party won the greater support and who held the title until her death in 1895.

When the Faletolu, the chiefly assembly of Ta'u, first asked him to take the title, Elisala declined on the grounds of his ministry. Once the Manuʻa islands came under the protection of the United States, however, the people petitioned him zealously, and he received the paramount title of Tuʻi Manuʻa on Ta'u on 25 October 1899. Manuʻa was grouped with Tutuila and Aunu'u in the possession now called American Samoa, and the presidency of the United States and the US Navy supplanted his role by arresting his talking chiefs and twice putting him on trial, once off the coast of Ta'u in the so-called Trial of the Ipu.

After ceding Manuʻa to the United States in 1904, Elisala was made Governor of Manuʻa for life, on the understanding that the title would end with him. He died in 1909. After a fifteen-year break the Faletolu and Anoalo named Chris Taliutafa Young, Matelita's brother, Tuʻi Manuʻa in 1924, but Governor Edward Stanley Kellogg, fearing a king who would trouble the administration, refused to recognise him. Holding a monarchy incompatible with the Constitution of the United States and citing Elisala's pledge to be the last holder, he had Young brought to Tutuila and kept from exercising the office.
tuileries-palace: The site lay just outside the walls of Paris, on land occupied by workshops that made tuiles, roof tiles. After the death of Henri II in 1559, his widow Catherine de' Medici planned a new residence close to the Louvre with space for a large garden. Between 1563 and 1568 she bought several plots, and construction began in 1564 with Philibert de l'Orme as chief architect. After he died in 1570 Jean Bullant took his place. The Day of the Barricades in 1588 halted the work.

Henri IV resumed construction in 1594 and built the Grande Galerie, which connected the Tuileries to the Louvre. Between 1659 and 1661, and again from 1664 to 1666, Louis Le Vau enlarged the palace for Louis XIV. The finished façade was 266 metres long.

The court occupied the palace from 1667 to 1672 and then moved to Versailles. Louis XV lived there from 1716 to 1722. On 1 December 1783 the first manned flight in a hydrogen balloon, by Jacques Charles and the Robert brothers, took off from its garden. On 6 October 1789 Louis XVI and his family were forced to leave Versailles for the Tuileries, and the National Constituent Assembly later met in its Salle du Manège. After the failed flight to Varennes in June 1791 the royal family was returned to Paris, and on 10 August 1792 a mob stormed the palace and massacred the Swiss Guards who defended it. The National Convention then met there during the Reign of Terror.

Napoleon Bonaparte moved in on 19 February 1799 and had Charles Percier and Pierre Fontaine redesign the interior. The House of Bourbon returned after his fall, Louis Philippe d'Orléans used the palace until 1848, and Napoleon III took up residence in 1852 and extensively redecorated it.

On 23 May 1871, during the suppression of the Paris Commune, twelve men under Jules Bergeret set the palace on fire with petroleum, tar and turpentine. The fire lasted 48 hours and gutted it, apart from the foundations and the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel. The walls stood for eleven years until the Third Republic had them demolished between February and 30 September 1883. Pieces of the stone were sold as souvenirs. The Tuileries Garden survives, as does the Axe historique running through the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe, which was once centred on the palace façade.
tujibids: The historian Ibn Hazm traced the family, also called the Banu al-Muhajir, to two sons of al-Muhajir ibn Naywa, ʿAmira and ʿAbd Allah, who came from Egypt with Musa ibn Nusayr for the conquest of Iberia in the early 710s and settled in Aragon. In the second half of the 9th century Emir Muhammad I of Córdoba recruited the sons of ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Tujibi against the rebel Banu Qasi, granting them towns including Daroca. In 862/3 he gave the rebuilt Calatayud to ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, whose sons founded the lines of Zaragoza, Calatayud and Almería.

In January 890 ʿAbd al-Rahman's son Muhammad gained the trust of the governor of Zaragoza, Ahmad ibn al-Barraʼ al-Qurashi, murdered him and had himself named governor, founding what was in effect an autonomous hereditary protectorate. He held out against a 17-year siege by the Banu Qasi. His grandson Muhammad ibn Hashim allied with Ramiro II of León against Caliph ʿAbd al-Rahman III, who took Zaragoza in 937 but restored him as a tributary; he was captured at the Battle of Simancas in 939 and ransomed. In 989 Almanzor executed the Tujibid leader ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad for joining a plot by one of Almanzor's sons.

Al-Mundhir ibn Yahya, of the Daroca branch, who had begun as a simple soldier, became governor of the Upper March and in 1018 declared Zaragoza independent. His grandson al-Mundhir II was murdered in 1039 by his cousin, the qadi ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Hakam al-Tujibi, whom the people saw as a usurper. ʿAbd Allah fled to Rueda with the treasury, and Sulayman ibn Hud, lord of Lérida, took Zaragoza as al-Mustaʿin I.

A junior line descended from Sumadih, the Banu Sumadih, fled to the Taifa of Valencia after a quarrel with al-Mundhir I. Its ruler made Maʿn ibn Muhammad governor of Almería in 1038, and in 1042 Maʿn made it an independent taifa. His son al-Muʿtasim, a noted poet, ruled for 41 years; his successor Ahmad Muʿizz al-Dawla abandoned Almería to the Almoravids and died in exile at Dellys in Algeria.
tukaram: Tukaram's name at birth was Tukaram Bolhoba Ambile. He spent most of his later years in devotional worship, community kirtan, which is group prayer with singing, and the composition of abhanga poetry. Mambaji Gosavi, who ran a matha in Dehu, was one of his main opponents. Tukaram had first entrusted him with performing puja at his temple, but Mambaji became jealous of Tukaram's growing popularity among the villagers and attacked him with a thorn stick. He later became one of Tukaram's devotees.

Tukaram composed abhangas, a Marathi genre that is metrical, simple and direct and fuses folk stories with deeper spiritual themes. His verse is informal and written in the vernacular, in contrast to the grace of style of predecessors such as Dnyaneshwar and Namdev. His abhangas name four sants as the main influence on him: Namdev, Dnyaneshwar, Kabir and Eknath. The Tukaram Gatha, a compilation likely composed between 1632 and 1650, covers a wide range of experience, including the conflict between pravritti, passion for life, and nivritti, the wish to renounce everything for liberation.

Scholars disagree whether his thought was monist, in the manner of Adi Shankara, or dualist, in the manner of Madhvacharya and Ramanuja, since some abhangas support one view and some the other. Tukaram denounced mechanical rites, sacrifices and vows and encouraged direct devotion, and he treated kirtan as bhakti itself. He accepted disciples regardless of gender and taught that pride of caste never made anyone holy.

Historians widely accept that Tukaram died in 1650. The first modern compilation of his poems was published in 1869, and it noted that some of its manuscripts had been corrected and rearranged. Over about 200 years after his death the text was reworked, which raises doubts about how faithfully it represents him. About 3,700 poems were translated into English by Fraser and Marathe between 1909 and 1915, and Mahatma Gandhi read and translated Tukaram while imprisoned at Yerawada.

Richard Eaton writes that Tukaram and his predecessors gave voice to a collective identity among Marathi speakers. Places in Dehu associated with him include the temple at his birthplace and the Gatha temple, where about 4,000 abhangas are carved on the walls. Many Indian films have been made about him, among them Sant Tukaram of 1936, which was screened open-air for a year to packed audiences in Mumbai.
tukoji-rao-holkar-iii: Tukoji was born on 26 November 1890, the son of Shivajirao Holkar, Maharaja of Indore, and Maharani Sita Bai. His father abdicated on 31 January 1903, and as the new maharaja was only thirteen a council of regency governed until he came of age. He was educated at the Daly College in Indore and at Dehradun. On 6 November 1911 he was invested with ruling powers, and in the same year he attended the coronation of King George V in London.

As ruler he founded two orders, the Order of Merit of Holkar in February 1914 and the Order of Ahilyabai Holkar on 22 November 1920. In the New Year Honours of 1918 he was made a Knight Grand Commander of the Order of the Star of India.

In January 1925 Mumtaz Begum, a courtesan and one of his mistresses, left his harem after what she described as repressive conditions and the death of her daughter, which she blamed on palace nurses. While performing in Bombay she met Abdul Bawla, a 25-year-old Memon businessman, who was threatened several times and told to send her back, and refused. On 12 January a group of assassins attacked the couple at Malabar Hill. Bawla was shot in the head and killed; Mumtaz Begum survived with a wound to the face after British officers who were nearby intervened.

She testified against nine accused, among them men of the maharaja's household. The court sentenced three men to death and three to life imprisonment. One of the latter, General Anandrao Gangram Phanse of the Indore army, escaped the death penalty after being represented by Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The court did not formally hold Tukoji responsible, but under British pressure he abdicated on 26 February 1926 and left Indore.

After his abdication he lived mainly in France. He had married three times. His senior wife, Chandravati Gawade, whom he married on 16 March 1895 when both were small children, stayed in Indore and brought up their son, the new maharaja. His second wife, Indira Talcherkar, married in 1913, also remained there and became a patron of historical research bodies such as the Rajwade Historical Research Institute.

In 1928 he married Nancy Anne Miller, who before the wedding embraced Hinduism, was received into the Dhangar community and took the name Sharmista Devi Holkar; they had four daughters. The Bawla case inspired a film of 1925, Kulin Kanta, and two books. Tukoji died in Paris on 21 May 1978, leaving one son and six daughters.
tukulti-ninurta-i: Tukulti-Ninurta I succeeded his father, Shalmaneser I. He won a major victory against the Hittite Empire at the Battle of Nihriya in the first half of his reign and took Hittite territory in Asia Minor and the Levant. He kept Assyrian control of Urartu. He is the first king known to use the title King of Kings.

He later defeated Kaštiliašu IV, the Kassite king of Babylonia, and captured Babylon. According to his own account he took Kaštiliašu captive single-handed, trod with his feet upon the king's lordly neck as though it were a footstool, and deported him in chains to Assyria. He demolished the walls of Babylon, massacred many of its inhabitants and carried off the Statue of Marduk from the Esagila temple. He set himself up as king of Babylon and took the ancient title King of Sumer and Akkad, first used by Ur-Nammu.

A letter found at Dūr-Katlimmu, addressed to his grand vizier Ashur-iddin, reports the captive king's journey into exile with his wife and a large retinue. Tukulti-Ninurta also defeated the Elamites, who had coveted Babylon, and an epic poem, the Tukulti-Ninurta Epic, records his wars against Babylon and Elam. After a Babylonian revolt he plundered the temples of Babylon, an act regarded as sacrilege by all Mesopotamians, Assyrians included.

Relations with the priesthood in Aššur deteriorated, and the king built a new capital, Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta. His sons rebelled against him and besieged him there, and he was murdered during the siege. One of them, Ashur-nadin-apli, succeeded him on the throne. After his death the Assyrian Empire passed through a brief period of stagnation.
tula-mesoamerican-site: Tula, in Nahuatl Tollan Xicocotitlan, lies in the Tula River Valley in the southwest of the present Mexican state of Hidalgo, about 75 kilometres north of Mexico City. The name means near the cattails. The Aztecs used the term Tollan to mean an urban centre, and the word Toltec later came to mean an urban person, artisan or skilled worker. The ceremonial centre, Tula Grande, stands on a limestone outcrop with steep banks on three sides, which made it defensible. The city was aligned 17 degrees east of true north, like structures at Teotihuacan.

The earliest well-defined settlements in the area appear around 400 BCE. Tula Chico, the Small Tula, was occupied from 650 to 900. After the decline of Teotihuacan, small city-states dominated their regions, and the pottery and architecture of Tula show influence from the west, north and east, which suggests a multiethnic population. The city reached its height between 900 and 1150. At that time it probably covered 14 square kilometres and held about 60,000 people, with another 20,000 to 25,000 in the surrounding countryside. Its economy rested on irrigated maize and on mining and working obsidian, and ceramics from Guatemala and Costa Rica show long-range contact.

Around 1000, leaching of the soil and a drier climate moved Chichimecas south and caused ethnic strife that eventually brought the city down. Many living quarters appear to have been abandoned by 1150, and the ceremonial centre was burned and its pyramids destroyed. The site was looted but kept some occupation into the colonial period.

The main structure at Tula Grande is Pyramid B, also called the Pyramid of Quetzalcoatl or of the Morning Star, a five-tiered building similar to the Temple of the Warriors at Chichen Itza. Four basalt columns carved as Toltec warriors, each four metres high, once supported the roof of its temple. A serpent wall, the Coatepantli, surrounds it and later inspired a similar wall at Tenochtitlan. The centre also has two main ballcourts and long halls with benches carved with reliefs of warriors in procession. The site became a national park in 1981.

Aztec accounts mythologised Tula. They link the feathered serpent god Quetzalcoatl with a ruler of the city, Ce Acatl Quetzalcoatl, whose fall to the temptation of the god Tezcatlipoca destroyed it. The relation between Tula and Chichén Itzá remains debated.
tulagi: Tulagi is a small island in the Solomon Islands, just off the south coast of Ngella Sule. Its town is the capital of Central Province. The British chose it as their colonial capital because it was better isolated and healthier than the disease-ridden larger islands of the archipelago.

The first recorded European sighting was by the Spanish expedition of Álvaro de Mendaña on 16 April 1568. More exactly, it was made on a local voyage by a small boat, the brigantine Santiago, commanded by Maestre de Campo Pedro Ortega Valencia, with Hernán Gallego as pilot. From 1896 to 1942 the town was the capital of the British Solomon Islands Protectorate.

The Japanese occupied Tulagi on 3 May 1942, intending to establish a seaplane base nearby. Planes from USS Yorktown raided the ships in the harbour the next day, a prelude to the Battle of the Coral Sea. On 7 August Allied forces, mainly the 1st Marine Raiders, landed and captured the island after a day of hard fighting, as part of Operation Watchtower. Under United States control it hosted a squadron of PT boats for a year, among them John F. Kennedy's PT-109, along with other facilities. A small 20-bed dispensary operated until 1946, and the nearby Purvis Bay held many US Navy ships through 1942 and 1943. After the war the capital of the Solomon Islands moved to Honiara on Guadalcanal.

Tulagi has a fishing fleet and is developing a tourism industry based on scuba diving. The wrecks of USS Aaron Ward, USS Kanawha and HMNZS Moa lie close by, all three sunk in a Japanese air raid on 7 April 1943; the Aaron Ward rests upright and intact at 70 metres. In October 2019 the government of Central Province signed a 75-year lease of the whole island to the Chinese company China Sam Enterprise Group. The Solomon Islands parliament declared the deal unconstitutional a week later, and it was cancelled.
tulayha-ibn-khuwaylid: Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid ibn Nawfal al-Asadi was a wealthy clan chief and military commander of the Banu Asad ibn Khuzaymah. He opposed Muhammad for years: in 625 a Muslim force defeated him in the Expedition of Qatan, and in 627 he fought against Muhammad at the Battle of the Trench. In 631 he declared himself a prophet who received divine revelation and rebelled, the third Arab to claim prophethood against Muhammad. Many tribes accepted him, and he led a confederacy of them against the Muslims.

After Muhammad's death in June 632, Tulayha's forces prepared to attack Medina. Abu Bakr raised an army in July 632 under Ali ibn Abi Talib, Talha ibn Ubaidullah and Zubair ibn al-Awam, who held at the Battle of Zhu Qissa until Abu Bakr reinforced them and drove Tulayha back to Zhu Hussa. Khalid ibn al-Walid then defeated him at Buzakha, after which many of the rebel tribes surrendered. Tulayha escaped to Syria and converted to Islam when the Muslims conquered it, and in 634 he paid homage to Umar in person on his accession as caliph.

He then fought against the Sassanid Empire at Jalula, al-Qadisiyyah and Nahavand. The chronicle of al-Tabari records that his Banu Asad played a large part on the first day of al-Qadisiyyah, and that Tulayha slipped into the Sassanid camp by night, killed two soldiers, took two horses and brought a captive back to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Tulayha was killed fighting on the Muslim side at the Battle of Nahavand. When Sa'd asked for reinforcements, Umar is reported to have written that he was sending 2,000 men, Amr ibn Ma'adi Yakrib and Tulayha, each counting as a thousand. Jabir ibn Abdullah named Tulayha among the fighters of al-Qadisiyyah who sought no worldly gain and were pious and trustworthy. The account of al-Ya'qubi, which historians treat as doubtful, has him among those who found the body of the Sassanid commander Rostam Farrokhzād.
tulip-revolution: The revolution, also called the First Kyrgyz Revolution, followed parliamentary elections held on 27 February and 13 March 2005. Opponents accused President Askar Akayev, his family and supporters of corruption and authoritarianism. Pro-Akayev candidates did well, but foreign observers criticised the result, and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe was critical of the government. Akayev himself coined the name Tulip Revolution in a speech in which he warned that no colour revolution should happen in Kyrgyzstan, recalling the Rose Revolution in Georgia and the Orange Revolution in Ukraine. The Georgian politician Givi Targamadze, who had consulted Ukrainian opposition leaders, later advised the Kyrgyz opposition.

Protests began in the western and southern cities, including Jalal-Abad, Osh and Uzgen. A bomb exploded in the apartment of the opposition leader Roza Otunbayeva on 3 March; the government denied responsibility. Kurmanbek Bakiyev joined protesters outside parliament in Bishkek on 10 March. On 19 March three thousand people in Bishkek and fifty thousand in Jalal-Abad joined the protests, and by 20 March protesters had taken control of all the large cities of the south. The opposition leaders formed an interim government on 22 March. Akayev dismissed his interior minister and prosecutor general and, on 23 March, deployed riot police.

On 24 March 2005 Akayev fled with his family, first to Kazakhstan and then to Russia, where President Vladimir Putin offered him exile. Prime Minister Nikolai Tanayev resigned, police melted away or joined the protesters, and imprisoned opposition leaders, including Felix Kulov, were released. Mobs looted stores in Bishkek and three people had died. The Supreme Court declared the election results invalid. Bakiyev became acting prime minister and acting president, and Kulov became acting interior minister. Akayev signed his resignation in Moscow, and the interim parliament ratified it on 11 April.

Presidential elections were held on 10 July 2005. Bakiyev, who had agreed with Kulov that Kulov would be prime minister if he won, took ninety percent of the vote and became president the next day. Western observers praised the conduct of the election but noted irregularities. The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe noted significant shortcomings in the runoff, while observers of the Commonwealth of Independent States called it free and fair. Reports also said that the United States government and American organisations had funded opposition media. The interim government faced land seizures, unrest and violence before the election, and the alliance of Bakiyev and Kulov lasted until January 2007.
tulln: Tulln lies in the centre of the Tulln Basin, which stretches to the Vienna Woods in the south, about 40 kilometres northwest of Vienna. Most of its built-up area is on the southern bank of the Danube. Because of its many parks and gardens the town is often called Blumenstadt, the City of Flowers. The municipality consists of several cadastral communities, among them Langenlebarn, Staasdorf and Mollersdorf, and the town proper has about twelve thousand inhabitants. It is the administrative seat of Tulln District.

The name Tulln is presumably of Celtic origin, and the place was settled before Roman times. It gained importance as the Roman fort of Comagena, also called Comagenis. In the last years of Roman rule Saint Severinus of Noricum is said to have visited the town and saved it from the barbarians. A Roman tower of the 4th century still stands. The town is first mentioned as Tullina in a deed of 859, when the area belonged to the Bavarian marcha orientalis.

Tulln became important as a residence of the House of Babenberg, who ruled as Austrian margraves from 976, and lost its significance after they moved their residence to Vienna. The first public clock tower is recorded here in 1372. On 6 September 1683 the Polish cavalry of King John III Sobieski joined Imperial forces and troops from Saxony, Bavaria and Baden at Tulln before the Battle of Vienna against the invading Ottoman army. In 1986 the town applied to become capital of Lower Austria, but Sankt Pölten was chosen.

Tulln has a large sugar-producing plant, and trade fairs, including camping equipment and boat shows, take place there. The Federal School of Aviation and several state institutions of Lower Austria, such as the fire brigade and the disaster relief service, have their seat in the town. According to the Nibelungenlied it was at Tulln that Attila the Hun saw Kriemhild and proposed to her, and a Nibelungen Fountain was dedicated to the episode in 2005. The painter Egon Schiele was born in Tulln, which has a museum dedicated to him. The Minoritenkloster, a convent, is among the sights.
tullus-hostilius: Tullus Hostilius came from a Roman family of Alban descent. According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, its earliest known member, Hostus Hostilius, had migrated to Rome from Medullia and fell in the front ranks fighting beside Romulus against the Sabines. After the death of Numa Pompilius, the Senate appointed interreges, each serving for five days, and the Curiate Assembly elected Tullus king by acclamation. He still needed the auspices, the sanction of the gods, before entering office.

According to Dionysius, Tullus began by dividing the royal estates among landless Romans. He brought the Caelian Hill within the walls and lived there for a time. Livy records that after the conquest of Alba Longa he added ten squadrons of Albans to the cavalry, raising it from 300 to 600. Ancient sources credit him with the Curia Hostilia, the first senate house, and the Comitium, with the Fetial college, which conducted Rome's treaties and declarations of war, and with the Salii Collini, a second college of priests.

War with Alba Longa began with cattle raids across the border. Rather than fight a full battle, the Alban dictator Mettius Fufetius proposed that three brothers from each city fight for supremacy; Rome's champion, Publius Horatius, won. Later, in a war against Veii and Fidenae, Mettius held the Alban troops back on a hilltop and betrayed both sides. Tullus had him executed, destroyed Alba Longa, and brought its people to Rome as citizens. Leading Alban families, including the Julii, entered the Senate. Sources also record a Sabine war won at the Battle of the Malitiosa.

Livy says Tullus neglected the gods until omens and a pestilence came late in his reign. He fell ill, tried to perform rites from Numa's writings, and did the ceremony for Jupiter Elicius wrongly; lightning struck his house and burned it with his family. Dionysius gives another version, in which Ancus Marcius and his followers killed Tullus and his household on a stormy night.

Modern historians treat the early kings with scepticism, since Livy, Dionysius and Plutarch wrote at least five hundred years later. Most nonetheless accept that Tullus existed, because Tullus is a rare praenomen and the name Hostilius did not belong to a great Republican family. Some see his story as modelled on Romulus. Corneille's tragedy Horace (1640) and Jacques-Louis David's Oath of the Horatii (1784) draw on the legend of the duel.
tullyhogue-fort: The name comes from the Middle Irish Tulach Óc, meaning hill of youth or mound of the young warriors. The site is a large mound with a depressed centre, surrounded by trees, on the outskirts of Tullyhogue village in the townland of Ballymully Glebe. The date of its construction is not known, but it is believed to have held ritual importance long before the O'Neills became associated with it.

The ráth was first associated with the Uí Tuirtri of Airgialla, who were displaced by branches of the Cenél nEógain. The Cenél mBinnig came first, in the 10th century, and were later replaced by the Cenél Feargusa, among them the O'Hagans, who took possession of the site as stewards of the royal household before 1056 and held it down to the 17th century. For a short time before 1084 the local branches, lacking leaders of their own, took kings from outside: Conchobar and his brother Cennétig, grandsons of Donnchadh mac Briain of the royal Munster O'Brien dynasty, who ruled in turn as Kings of Telach Óc.

In the later medieval period, the site became the place where each new lord was given the title The O'Neill. O'Cahan, the principal sub-chief, threw a golden sandal over the new lord's head for good fortune, and O'Hagan, the hereditary guardian, placed the shoe on his foot and handed him a rod of office. The burial place of the O'Hagans was at Donaghrisk at the foot of the hill. The last such inauguration was that of Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, in 1595.

The inauguration stone, a boulder called the Leac na Rí, the flagstone of the kings, stood outside the fort and by the 16th century had been built into a ceremonial chair of three large slabs. It is described as the Ulster counterpart of the Stone of Destiny and was reputedly blessed by St. Patrick. The fort is a State Care Historic Monument, and the inauguration site is a Scheduled Historic Monument.
tulsidas: Tulsidas was born Rambola Dubey, on the seventh day of the bright half of the month of Shraavana. The exact date and year of his birth are disputed among scholars and biographers. Tulsidas himself gives only a few facts about his life, and the early sources are the Bhaktamal of Nabhadas, a contemporary who calls him an incarnation of Valmiki.

Many believe he was a reincarnation of Valmiki. According to the Tulsi Prakash and some other works he married Ratnavali, and after she rebuked him for his attachment to her he left for Prayag and became a sadhu. Most stories about him are apocryphal and have been carried forward by word of mouth, since none was related by Tulsidas himself.

After renunciation he spent most of his time at Varanasi, Prayag, Ayodhya and Chitrakuta, and travelled to many other places. Tradition holds that he began composing poetry in Sanskrit in Varanasi, but that the verses he wrote by day were lost each night.

On the eighth night Shiva is believed to have ordered him in a dream to compose in the vernacular and to go to Ayodhya to write in Awadhi. He is generally believed to have died in 1623 at Assi Ghat in Varanasi, though the exact day and month are disputed.

Twelve works are widely considered to be his, six major and six minor, in Awadhi and Braj. The Ramcharitmanas, composed between 1574 and 1576, is his longest and earliest work, of around 12,800 lines in seven books, about one third the size of Valmiki's Ramayana. His other works include the Dohavali, the Vinaya Patrika, the Gitavali, and the Parvati Mangal and Janaki Mangal, on the marriages of Parvati and of Sita.

The Hanuman Chalisa is popularly attributed to him and bears his signature, though some authors doubt he wrote it. In his teaching Tulsidas holds that the Nirguna Brahman, without qualities, and the Saguna Brahman, with qualities, are one and the same, but he favours the Saguna aspect. Repeating the name of Rama is, in his view, the only means to reach God in the Kali age.

He sees no incompatibility between devotion to Rama and attachment to Shiva, and his writings aim to teach bhakti to Rama as the means of salvation, free and open to men of the lowest caste. The Tulsi Ghat in Varanasi is named after him, and the Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple there is believed to stand where he saw Hanuman.
tulu-nadu: Tulu Nadu lies on the Konkan Coast between the Arabian Sea to the west and the Western Ghats to the east, and covers about 8,441 square kilometres. Historically it stretched from the Gangavalli River in the north to Nileshwar, with the Chandragiri river as a traditional southern border. The climate is tropical: the monsoon begins in June, the heaviest rain falls in the month of Aati, from mid-July to mid-August, and winter lasts from December to early February. The name appears as Tuḷu Nāṭṭu in the Akananuru, one of the Eight Anthologies of Sangam literature.

Sangam literature counts Tulu Nadu among the twelve regions of ancient Tamilakam, and it probably formed part of the Chera realm until it separated sometime between 300 and 500 CE, when the Kadambas invaded the northern Chera lands. The Alupas, its oldest known native dynasty, were feudatories of the Kadambas of Banavasi, then of the Rashtrakutas, the Chalukyas, the Hoysalas and Vijayanagara, though their subordination was largely nominal. The Greco-Roman geographer Ptolemy's Olokhoira is widely taken to be a corruption of Alva Kheda, the land of the Alvas.

Under Vijayanagara the region was governed as Mangaluru Rajya and Barkuru Rajya and grew very prosperous, with local houses such as the Chowtas of Ullal and Moodabidri and the Ajilas of Venur ruling as feudatories. The Keladi Nayakas of Ikkeri followed. Konkanis came by sea from Goa, and Catholics in large numbers in the 16th century. Hyder Ali of Mysore conquered the region in the mid- to late 18th century, and after the British defeated Tipu Sultan in 1799 it became the district of South Canara in the Madras Presidency. In the linguistic reorganisation of 1956 it passed to Mysore state, later Karnataka, while Kasaragod went to Kerala.

Mangaluru, or Kudla, is the largest city, with Udupi and Kasaragod the other main towns. Tulu, a Dravidian language once written in the Tulu–Tigalari script derived from Grantha, had about 1.7 million speakers in 2001, and many communities follow the matrilineal Aliyasantana system of inheritance. The Jains left temples at Moodabidri and monolithic statues of Bahubali at Karkala, Venoor and Dharmasthala. After 1956 Tuluvas began to demand official status for Tulu and a state of their own, a cause taken up by groups such as the Tulu Rajya Horata Samiti.
tulunid-dynasty: The Tulunids were a Mamluk dynasty of Turkic origin who ruled Egypt on behalf of the Abbasid Caliphate and were autonomous from 868 until 905. Their rise came when the Turkic military held growing power within the caliphate and separatist tendencies emerged among governors.

The founder's father, Tulun, was a mamluk sent as a gift by the governor of Bukhara to the caliph al-Ma'mun in 816 and rose to command the guard. In 868 the Turkic commander Baykbak, who had been granted Egypt but preferred to stay near the caliph's court, sent his stepson Ahmad ibn Tulun as deputy. Ahmad entered Egypt on 15 September 868.

Ahmad ibn Tulun first faced revolts, mostly shaped by religious and sectarian tensions, and used them to establish security and consolidate his position. A revolt in Palestine and Jordan gave him a pretext to intervene in the Levant, and he formed a private army. Under him and his successors the domains grew to include the Jordan Rift Valley, the Hejaz, Cyprus and Crete. Ahmad changed the taxation system, aligned himself with the merchant community and established the Tulunid army. He also founded a new capital, al-Qata'i, north of Fustat, around 870, where the Mosque of Ibn Tulun, in the Samarran style, survives.

Ahmad ruled from 868 to 884 and his son Khumarawayh from 884 to 896. Khumarawayh's military and diplomatic achievements made him a major figure in the region, and the Abbasids affirmed their recognition of the Tulunids as legitimate vassal rulers. After his death his successors, Jaysh, Harun and Shayban, were ineffectual and let Turkic and black slave-soldiers run the state. In 905 the Tulunids could not resist an Abbasid invasion, and the Abbasids restored direct caliphal rule in Syria and Egypt.

The Tulunid period saw economic and administrative reforms alongside cultural ones. Ahmad ibn Tulun's relations with the Byzantines were marked by enmity, as he held the position of emir over the frontier regions. Surviving houses of the period have Samarran-style stucco panels, and the mosque built in al-Qata'i is the dynasty's best-known monument.
tum-collegiate-church: The church of St. Mary and St. Alexius stands on an islet once surrounded by wetlands and marshes. A papal bull of Pope Innocent II shows that a wooden monastery of the early Benedictine Brothers stood there at least a century before it. Older studies credited its foundation to Boleslaus I, the first King of Poland, and Saint Adalbert of Prague around 997, but more recent research places it most likely in the Restoration period of the second half of the 11th century. The monastery made way for the church, which Janik, Archbishop of Gniezno, began around 1149; the unfinished building was consecrated on 21 May 1161.

Tum was the site of 21 provincial synods, from 1181 to 1547. The fortified church could also shelter the townsfolk from enemy troops. It held out during the first Mongol invasion of Poland in 1241, but around 1293 the army of Vytenis, the pagan Duke of Lithuania, captured the settlement; some of those who had taken refuge in the church were killed and others enslaved, and the gord to the south-west was burned and abandoned. The Teutonic Knights pillaged the church repeatedly in the 14th century.

The church was built of granite blocks and sandstone in the opus emplectum technique, as an aisled basilica with galleries. Its sculpted main portal, on the north side, dates from the first half of the 12th century. A legend of the townsfolk of Łęczyca held that the dimples in the stonework were made by the hands of the devil Boruta, who tried to destroy the church. Later rebuildings were Gothic in the 15th century and Neoclassical in the 18th.

During the Battle of the Bzura in September 1939 a German soldier used the northern tower as an observation post, the Polish army shelled the church, and bombing by the Luftwaffe left it an empty shell, though the original stone walls survived. Reconstruction from 1947 under Jan Zachwatowicz and Jan Koszczyc Witkiewicz removed the Gothic and Neoclassical elements and returned the church to its Romanesque form, with round turrets added at the east. It was reconsecrated in 1961, and in 2022 it was designated an official Polish Historic Monument.
tuman-bay-ii: Tuman Bay was a Circassian who, like the sultans before him, had been a domestic slave of the palace. He rose to the office of prime minister and held it until Sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri marched north and left him in charge of Cairo. His name joins the Turkic tümen, ten thousand, and bay, chief. By December 1516 Tripoli, Safed, Damascus and Gaza had fallen to the Ottomans, and an army under Emir Janberdi Al-Ghazali was beaten back before it reached Gaza.

Selim I demanded that the sultan acknowledge his supremacy in the coinage and the Friday prayers. Tuman was inclined to agree, but his emirs prevailed and the envoys were put to death, while Khayr Bay and other emirs betrayed him. At the Battle of Ridanieh on 22 January 1517 he fought his way to Selim's tent, but his army was routed. The Ottomans entered Cairo, killed the Circassian garrison of the Citadel and hunted down Mamluks; 800 found in hiding were beheaded.

Tuman retook the lightly held city by night with Bedouin allies, but was driven out and fled to Upper Egypt. From Giza he cut supplies to Cairo and offered to recognise Selim if the invaders withdrew, yet his emirs killed the Ottoman delegation, and Selim executed 57 captive emirs in reply. Towards the end of March the two armies fought for two days beneath the Pyramids of Giza, and Tuman was defeated.

He sought refuge with a Bedouin chief whose life he had once saved, who handed him over. Brought before Selim, he denied any part in killing the envoys and defended his cause so boldly that Selim thought of sparing him, but Khayr Bay and Janberdi Al-Ghazali argued that Ottoman rule would not be safe while he lived. His body hung for three days and was buried in the Sultan al-Ghuri Complex; his general Shadi Bay was also executed. He was the last Sultan of Egypt until Hussein Kamel in 1914, and streets in Egypt bear his name.
tumbuka-language: Tumbuka, or Chitumbuka, is a Bantu language of Central and Southern Africa spoken primarily in Malawi, Zambia, Tanzania and Zimbabwe. It is the native language of more than 13 peoples, among them the Senga, Tumbuka, Yombe, Phoka, Henga, Fungwe, Hewe, Northern Ngoni, Kamanga and Tonga, with 12 known dialects. The prefix chi- means "the language of". In 2024 there were approximately 7.1 million native speakers in Malawi, Zambia and Tanzania, and nearly 1,600,000 people spoke it as a second language in Malawi and Zambia.

As in other Bantu languages, nouns are grouped into noun classes by their singular and plural prefixes, and verbs, adjectives and pronouns agree with the noun through concords. Every verb has a subject prefix, as in ciŵinda ci-ka-koma nkhalamu, "the hunter killed a lion". A negative is made by adding yayi or cha(ra) at or near the end of the clause. Tone plays only a limited part: every word spoken in isolation has the same falling tone on the penultimate syllable.

All Tumbuka dialects have been affected to some extent by the Zulu language, chiNgoni, most of all in Mzimba District. The Ngoni originated from the Ndwandwe people, who were neighbours of the Zulu clan before they were conquered by the Zulu and assimilated into the Zulu identity. The language the Ndwandwe spoke was therefore nearly identical to Zulu. Most words of Zulu or Ndwandwe origin have Tumbuka counterparts that can be used interchangeably, and the Mzimba dialect has click consonants in words such as chitha, "urinate", which do not occur in other dialects.

In 1947 Chitumbuka was made an official language of Malawi for 21 years, along with Chewa and English. In 1968 Hastings Kamuzu Banda removed it under his one-nation, one-language policy, and it was taken out of the school curriculum, the national radio and the print media. With the advent of multi-party democracy in 1994, Chitumbuka programmes were started again on the radio.

Two systems of writing are in use. The traditional spelling writes banthu, "people", and chaka, "year", with b and ch; the new official spelling writes them ŵanthu and caka. There is also uncertainty over where to write r and where l, since [l] and [r] are allophones of the same phoneme.
tumbuka-people: Like several neighbouring peoples, the Tumbuka trace their origins to the Luba Kingdom in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which they are said to have left in the early 1400s. Oral history holds that they travelled with the ancestors of the Hehe and Gogo peoples of Tanzania and the Mwakyusa under an overall leader named Mudala, the Tumbuka themselves being led by Mulonga Mbulalubilo. They probably entered the land between the Luangwa valley and northern Lake Malawi in the fifteenth century. More than fifteen related groups, among them the Senga, Nyika, Henga, Yombe, Phoka and Tonga, speak dialects of Chitumbuka.

By the start of the eighteenth century the Tumbuka lived in small, independent communities without any central organisation. Traders from the Unyamwezi region of present-day Tanzania, who came for ivory and to some extent slaves, allied with groups of Henga, and their leader founded the Chikulamayembe dynasty, which ruled a federation of small chiefdoms; by the 1830s it was in decline. In the 1840s Jumbe Salim bin Abdallah set up a trading centre at Nkhotakota, and his trade in slaves for the clove plantations of Zanzibar brought raids and violence against the Tumbuka.

The Ngoni under Mbelwa, a son of Zwangendaba, settled in what is now Mzimba district around 1855. They treated the Henga as subjects, exacting tribute and taking captives who were kept as unfree agricultural workers or enrolled in Ngoni regiments. Under colonial rule, from the 1880s, Tumbuka and Tonga men left to work as porters and estate labourers in the south of Nyasaland, and mission-educated Tumbuka went on to Southern Rhodesia and South Africa. Levi Mumba, Charles Chinula and many other leaders of the movement that won Malawi's independence in 1964 were Tumbuka-speaking northerners.

Tumbuka society is patrilineal: on marriage a woman moves to her husband's village, a custom generally traced to Mulowoka's settlement and still more to the Ngoni invasion. A child's first name is given by the father and paternal grandfather once the umbilical cord has detached. Traditional religion centres on a supreme creator, Chiuta, associated with the sun, alongside reverence for ancestor spirits. Most Tumbuka today are Christian. Vimbuza, therapeutic drumming, music and dance for illness held to come from possessing spirits, belongs to the wider ngoma complex of central and southern Africa. Malawi's census of September 2018 counted 1,614,955 Tumbuka, 9.2 percent of the population.
tumkur: Tumkur is a city in the southern state of Karnataka, India, at an altitude of around 800 metres above sea level and about 70 kilometres northwest of the state capital, Bengaluru. The surrounding district has elevated terrain cut by river valleys, with hilly and forested areas such as the Devarayanadurga hill range, in the southern part of which the river Shimsha originates. Agriculture is supported by monsoon rainfall and favourable terrain, and major crops include coconut, areca nut, rice, ragi, groundnut and several oilseeds.

The origin of the name is uncertain. It is believed to have changed from Tumbe ooru, after the abundance of thumbe hoovu, a kind of flower, or from thamate ooru, after the folk percussion instrument thamate, which may have been used most here. Another account says that Gulur was the capital during the rule of the Cholas, and that because Tumkur stands high, guards on a hill beat a drum called the tumaki to sound alerts. The area is also called Kalpatharu Nadu, the land of coconut trees.

Tumkur was accorded the status of a city corporation on 28 August 2010. The central government approved the renaming of Tumkur and twelve other cities in October 2014, and it officially became Tumakuru on 1 November 2014.

At the 2011 census Tumkur had approximately 542,000 inhabitants, most of them Hindu, with Muslim and Christian minorities. Kannada, the official language of the state, is the language of the majority, and there are many Urdu speakers and small Telugu, Tamil and Hindi communities. The railway station lies in the centre of the city, on the Bangalore–Hubli main line. The Siddaganga Matha, a Lingayat monastery, provides free education and accommodation for more than 9,000 children; Shivakumara Swami was its president.
tumu-crisis: After the death of the Yongle Emperor in 1424, the defence of the Ming northern frontier declined: officers seized soldiers' farms, training and supply suffered, and the Beijing garrison was used to build palaces and residences. Among the Mongols, the Oirats took control of the Mongolian Plateau, and from 1440 Esen, holding the title of taishi, was their effective ruler. The Mongols wanted free trade, horses for tea and silk, but the Ming limited it to a few border towns. In 1449 the Ming gave only a fifth of the goods requested and refused Esen's request for an imperial princess to marry his son.

In July 1449 Esen invaded in three columns, against Liaodong, Xuanfu and Datong. Emperor Yingzong, encouraged by Wang Zhen, resolved to lead a punitive expedition himself, against the protests of the Minister of War Kuang Ye and his deputy Yu Qian. The army left Beijing on 4 August after only a few days' preparation, with Wang Zhen as its effective commander. It marched through heavy rain to Datong, where reports of danger made Wang Zhen declare the campaign a victory and turn back on 20 August.

On the way back the Mongols destroyed the rearguard. The army camped at the Tumu post station without water on 31 August, Wang Zhen refusing to shelter in the walled city of Huailai. Some 20,000 Mongols routed the hungry and thirsty Ming troops on 1 September, nearly half of whom were lost, together with two dukes, two marquises, five counts and hundreds of officials.

In Beijing Yu Qian opposed moving the capital south and, as Minister of War, brought in grain and troops. When Esen reached the city on 27 October, its 220,000 defenders held off his 70,000 men, and after five days of fighting the Mongols withdrew. Border raids went on, but no territory changed hands. On his return the former emperor was kept under house arrest in the Southern Palace. Esen's failure weakened his authority in Mongolia; he declared himself Khan in 1453 and was murdered two years later.
tun-perak: Tun Perak was the son of Sri Wak Raja Tun Perpatih Besar, the first bendahara of Malacca, and in his early life he served the rulers of Malacca as a soldier-statesman. In 1445 he was appointed Malacca's representative in Klang. A Siamese invasion began that year and lasted until 1446, and another Siamese attack came in 1456, by which time he had become the fifth bendahara, a rank similar to that of a prime minister.

He served under four sultans: Muzzafar Shah, Mansur Shah, Alauddin Riayat Shah and Mahmud Shah. He was instrumental in bringing Pahang, Terengganu, Johor, Riau, Lingga, Bengkalis, Karimon, Rokan, Siak, Kampar, Jambi, Inderagiri and Aru under Malacca, and the rulers of these lands converted to Islam under Malaccan influence.

His loyalty to the sultanate was shown when his son, Tun Besar, was killed through a misunderstanding by Raja Muhammad, a son of Sultan Mahmud Shah. Tun Perak did not seek revenge against the sultan. Instead he asked that Raja Muhammad be crowned somewhere other than Malacca, and the sultan granted the request: Raja Muhammad was made sultan in Pahang.

Tun Perak died in 1498 and was succeeded as bendahara by his younger brother, Tun Perpatih Putih. His death is widely held to mark the beginning of the decline of the Malaccan Empire. Many places are named after him, among them streets called Jalan Tun Perak in Kuala Lumpur, Malacca and Ipoh, the Tun Perak Tower in Kuala Lumpur, formerly the Maybank Tower, residential colleges at Universiti Putra Malaysia and Universiti Teknologi MARA, and secondary schools in Jasin, Padang Rengas and Muar.
tungabhadra-river: The name joins two streams, the Tunga and the Bhadra, from the Sanskrit tunga, high, and bhadra, auspicious. Both rise at Gangamoola in the Varaha Parvatha of the Western Ghats, at an elevation of 1,458 metres, and flow down the eastern slope. The Tunga runs about 147 km and the Bhadra a little more before they meet at Koodli near Shimoga. The joined river then meanders through the plains for about 531 km.

Of that length, 382 km lie in Karnataka, 58 km form the boundary between Karnataka and Telangana, and 91 km run in Andhra Pradesh. The catchment covers 69,552 square kilometres. The river is perennial and is influenced chiefly by the south-west monsoon, though its summer flow dwindles sharply. Near Hampi it has cut a narrow gorge through piles of granite. The wedge of land between the Tungabhadra and the Krishna is known as the Raichur Doab.

Hindu tradition holds that the two source rivers were formed from the sweat of Varaha, the third incarnation of Vishnu, who rested on the peak after killing the demon Hiranyaksha. Many holy places stand along the banks: the Sringeri Sharada Peetham founded by Adi Shankara on the Tunga, the Virupaksha Temple at Hampi, Nava Brindavana, an island with the resting places of nine Madhva saints, and the Sangameswaram Temple where the river meets the Krishna. The ruins of Vijayanagara and Hampi, the seat of the Vijayanagara Empire, overlook the river, and Hampi is listed by UNESCO.

Krishnadevaraya built stone flood-protection walls along the banks between 1525 and 1527, from Sringeri to near Kurnool, using very large boulders; they are still intact. The British engineer Arthur Cotton built the Sunkesula Barrage near Kurnool around 1860, first intended for navigation and later used for irrigation through the K. C. Canal. In the middle of the twentieth century the Tungabhadra Dam was built at Hospet to supply agriculture and industry; its architect was Malur Srinivasa Thirumale Iyengar.

The river still supplies irrigation, power and drinking water, with further dams at Gajanur on the Tunga and Lakkavalli on the Bhadra. The Tungabhadra Dam holds a storage capacity of 135 Tmcft, reduced by siltation by about 30 Tmcft. Industry and mining along its banks produce effluents that have polluted its water and harmed its fisheries.
tunisia: Tunisia lies on the Mediterranean coast of north-west Africa, bordered by Algeria to the west and south-west and Libya to the south-east. It covers 163,610 square kilometres and has a coastline of about 1,300 kilometres. The Dorsal, the eastern extension of the Atlas Mountains, crosses the country north-eastward; north of it lies the Tell, a region of low hills and plains. The Sahel, a coastal plain on the east, is among the world's premier areas of olive cultivation, and much of the south is semi-arid and desert. Tunis, the capital, stands on a hill slope above the lake of Tunis.

Tunisia was inhabited by Berber tribes at the beginning of recorded history. Phoenicians began settling the coast from as early as the 12th century BCE, at Bizerte and Utica. Carthage, founded in the 9th century BCE, became the dominant power in the western Mediterranean after wars with the Greek city-states of Sicily. According to the Greek writer Timaeus of Tauromenium, Dido of Tyre founded it in 814 BCE, though this is regarded as legend. Its people worshipped Baal and Tanit. After the Second Punic War, in which Hannibal invaded Italy, Carthage was a client state of Rome until it was conquered in 146 BCE and made the province of Africa.

Arab Muslims conquered Tunisia in the 7th century CE, and the migration of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym tribes in the 11th and 12th centuries accelerated the process, and by about the 15th century the region was almost completely Arabised. The Ottoman Empire took control in 1546 and held it until the French conquest of 1881. Tunisia became independent as the Tunisian Republic in 1956.

The Tunisian Revolution of 2011 overthrew President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali after 24 years in power and set off the wider Arab Spring. A new constitution was adopted on 26 January 2014, and a constitutional referendum in 2022 made it a unitary presidential republic.

The population is 12.1 million, the vast majority Arab and Muslim. Arabic is the official language, and French serves as an administrative and educational language without official status. The European Union is the first trading partner: Tunisia signed an Association Agreement with it in July 1995, the first Mediterranean country to do so.
tunja: Tunja lies in the Eastern Ranges of the Colombian Andes, in the region known as the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, 130 kilometres northeast of Bogotá. The city centre stands at 2,820 metres above sea level, and the city ranges from about 2,700 to 2,900 metres, making it one of the higher cities of Colombia. It has a subtropical highland climate with little variation in temperature and a dry season from December to February. It is the capital of the department of Boyacá.

Before the Spanish conquest the settlement was called Hunza and was the seat of a Muisca ruler. According to Muisca tradition the prophet Goranchacha moved the capital of the northern Muisca from Ramiriquí to Hunza. Hunzahúa, who came from Ramiriquí, was elected supreme chief and took the title of hoa, great lord. Later the ruler Eucaneme avoided any aggression against the Europeans and sent them gifts, hoping to stop them while he hid his treasures.

Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada's expedition reached Hunza on 20 August 1537 and found Quemuenchatocha, the ruler, seated and dressed in gold; the conquerors took gold, emeralds and fabrics. He was succeeded by his nephew Aquiminzaque, whom the Spaniards accused of planning an insurrection. In 1540 Aquiminzaque was beheaded, which ended the dynasty of the zaques of Hunza. Captain Gonzalo Suárez Rendón founded the Spanish city on 6 August 1539 on the lands of Quemuenchatocha. The main square was laid out first, and in 1550 the outlines of the city were consolidated. The Franciscans arrived in 1550, the Dominicans a year later, the Augustinians in 1585 and the Jesuits in 1611.

Tunja is known for colonial religious architecture, and the Casa del Fundador Gonzalo Suárez Rendón is recognised as its oldest remnant. The city also holds the most surviving Muisca architecture, including the Hunzahúa Well, the Goranchacha Temple and the Cojines del Zaque. The Colegio de Boyacá, founded on 20 October 1822 by Vice President Francisco de Paula Santander, was the first public school in the territories of Venezuela, Ecuador, Panama and Colombia. Tunja has a large student population, and its main university, the Pedagogical and Technological University of Colombia, is a public one.
tunku-abdul-rahman: Tunku Abdul Rahman was born on 8 February 1903 in Alor Setar, Kedah, the seventh son and one of 45 children of Sultan Abdul Hamid Halim Shah. His mother, Cik Menyelara, the sixth consort of the Sultan, was of Thai descent. Kedah was afflicted by cholera and malaria, and several of his siblings died of illness. He studied in Malaya and graduated from St Catharine's College, Cambridge.

In January 1931 he joined the Kedah Civil Service as a cadet and became District Officer of Padang Terap, where he had the swamps drained to rid Kuala Nerang of malaria. He married Violet Coulson, which the regent Tunku Ibrahim had opposed, and a transfer to the isolated post at Langkawi followed. During the Japanese occupation, as District Officer in Kulim, he organised a vigilante corps to prevent looting. After a period of law study in England he qualified as an advocate and solicitor and became a deputy public prosecutor in 1949.

He won the leadership of UMNO in 1951, and in 1952 he formed the Alliance Party with the Malaysian Chinese Association and the Malaysian Indian Congress, holding that each community needed its own party. The Alliance won a landslide in the 1955 general election and he became chief minister. He offered amnesty to the communist revolutionaries of the Malayan Emergency and tried to end it at the Baling Talks, without success.

He led the Merdeka Mission to constitutional talks at Lancaster House in London in January 1956, and the Treaty of London secured independence. He proclaimed Malayan independence on 31 August 1957. As prime minister he was also foreign minister, and he led the Alliance to victories in 1959 and 1964. He oversaw the formation of Malaysia in 1963 with Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak.

Ethnic tensions grew, above all in the relationship with Singapore. After mutual provocations between UMNO and the People's Action Party under Lee Kuan Yew he resolved to expel Singapore, with separation taking effect on 9 August 1965. Violent unrest in the 13 May incident of 1969 followed the Alliance's reduced majority. He stepped down in 1970, succeeded by Abdul Razak Hussein.

In retirement he served as the first secretary-general of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. He had been president of the Asian Football Confederation from 1958 until 1977 and started the Merdeka Tournament in 1957. He died in Kuala Lumpur on 6 December 1990, aged 87, and was buried at the Langgar Royal Mausoleum in Alor Setar. He is recognised as the country's founding father, and places such as Putrajaya and several universities bear his name.
tunnel-of-eupalinos: The tunnel was dug in the mid-6th century BCE by two groups working under Eupalinos of Megara, to bring fresh water to the ancient capital of Samos, today called Pythagoreion. The city had outgrown its wells and cisterns, and its main source of fresh water lay on the other side of Mount Kastro. Running underground, the aqueduct could not easily be found and cut by an enemy. Herodotus describes it in his Histories (3.60) as the work of a Megarian named Eupalinus, son of Naustrophus.

Water came from a spring near the modern village of Ayiades, about 52 metres above sea level, and ran through a buried channel 890 metres long to the northern mouth. The tunnel is generally 1.8 by 1.8 metres, the northern half in places just wide enough for one person. Its floor lies about 3 metres above the water at the source, so a separate channel, 4 to 8.5 metres deep, was dug beneath it, where the water ran in a pipe of some 5,000 terracotta sections.

Only two diggers could work at a face, so it was cut from both ends at once. H. J. Kienast calculated that they could cut 12 to 15 centimetres of stone a day, so the work took at least eight years. About 273 metres from the northern end, water, weak rock and mud forced a diversion to the west. To make sure the two halves met, Eupalinos turned both towards each other, and they join at a dog-leg; at the meeting point their altitudes differed by only a few decimetres.

The aqueduct was used for 1,100 years before it began to silt up. In the 7th century CE the southern section became a refuge, with a cistern built 400 metres from the southern entrance to collect water dripping from the rock.

Prompted by Herodotus, scholars began searching for the tunnel in the 19th century. Victor Guérin identified the spring in 1853, and in 1882 an attempt to clear the tunnel for reuse was abandoned, though it allowed Ernst Fabricius to investigate it for the German Archaeological Institute. Ulf Jantzen cleared its full length from 1971 to 1973, and Kienast made a detailed survey. It is on the UNESCO World Heritage List with Pythagoreion and the Heraion of Samos, and parts are open to the public.
tuoba: The Tuoba were a clan of the Xianbei, whose peoples ranged from present-day north-eastern China to Mongolia. The Tuoba were among the largest western Xianbei clans, living from present-day Shanxi westward and north-westward. According to the Book of Wei, the Xianbei originated from the Donghu and the Tuoba from the Xianbei. Scholars think the Xianbei were probably a multilingual, multi-ethnic confederation. No Tuoba texts survive, only glosses in Chinese sources, and there is no consensus on whether the Tuoba language was Mongolic or Turkic, although Charles Holcombe stated in 2022 that opinion had shifted in favour of Mongolic.

During the Sixteen Kingdoms period the Tuoba established the state of Dai, which ruled from 310 to 376. The dynasty was restored in 386 and renamed Wei, later called the Northern Wei, which gained control of most of northern China, supported Buddhism and became increasingly sinicised.

In the 480s the court began arranging marriages between Chinese elites and Tuoba princesses, and in 496 Emperor Xiaowen changed the imperial clan's surname from Tuoba to Yuan. The empire split into Eastern Wei and Western Wei in 535, and the Western Wei rulers briefly resumed the Tuoba name in 554. A western branch known as the Tufa ruled the Southern Liang dynasty from 397 to 414.

Because of the Northern Wei's contacts with Central Asia, Turkic sources used Tabgach as the name of China or its ruler until the 13th century. The 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions use it for China, and the 11th-century scholar Mahmud al-Kashgari described Tawjach as one of three parts of China. Byzantine writers such as Theophylact Simocatta knew it as Taugas or Taugast. The derivation of the name from Tuoba is widely believed but remains, as Holcombe notes, hypothetical. The Karakhanid rulers adopted the title Tamghaj Khan and minted coins bearing it.
tuoba-yilu: Tuoba Yilu was a son of Tuoba Shamohan, and his brothers included Tuoba Yituo and Tuoba Fu. In 295 the Tuoba chieftain Tuoba Luguan divided the lands under Tuoba control into three parts: a western tract running from White Mountain, north-east of Zhangjiakou, to Dai, the area of modern Datong; a region around Shengle, south of Hohhot, and beyond; and a central area that took in northern Shanxi and the lands to its north. Yilu was made chieftain of the western part, which he held until 307.

As chieftain of the west, Yilu defeated the Xiongnu and the Wuhuan, winning the support of Han Chinese and Wuhuan people as well as his own Xianbei. In 304 he and Tuoba Yituo joined the armies of the Jin and defeated Liu Yuan. Yituo died in 305 and Luguan in 307, after which Yilu became supreme chieftain of all the Tuoba.

The name Dai dates from 310, when the Western Jin made him Duke of Dai and granted him five commanderies as a reward for helping Liu Kun, governor of Bingzhou in modern Shanxi, against the Xiongnu state of Han. In 312 he helped Liu Kun retake Jinyang, in modern Taiyuan, from the Han general Liu Yao. In 315 the Jin court raised his fief from a duchy to a principality, and he became the first ruler of the kingdom of Dai.

Yilu named his youngest son, Tuoba Biyan, as heir apparent in place of his eldest son, Tuoba Liuxiu, and the choice set father and son against each other. In 316 Liuxiu killed him in the dispute over the succession. Leadership of the Tuoba passed to Tuoba Pugen.
tuol-sleng: Tuol Sleng is in Phnom Penh. The site was a secondary school, Tuol Svay Prey High School, named after a royal ancestor of King Norodom Sihanouk. To hold the victims of purges important enough for the attention of the Khmer Rouge, its five buildings were converted into a prison and interrogation centre and renamed Security Prison 21 (S-21). The buildings were enclosed in electrified barbed wire, classrooms became tiny cells and torture chambers, and windows were covered with iron bars and barbed wire to prevent escapes and suicides. It was one of between 150 and 196 torture and execution centres established by the Khmer Rouge.

At any one time the prison held between 1,000 and 1,500 prisoners, who were repeatedly tortured and coerced into naming family members and associates, who were in turn arrested. In the early months most victims came from the previous Lon Nol regime, among them soldiers, officials, academics, doctors, teachers, students, factory workers, monks and engineers. Later purges brought thousands of party activists and their families, including senior figures such as Khoy Thoun, Vorn Vet and Hu Nim, officially arrested for espionage. Confessions ran to thousands of words and are believed to have been mostly false.

Most prisoners were held for two to three months. Killing prisoners outright was discouraged because the Khmer Rouge needed their confessions. Corpses were at first buried near the prison, but by the end of 1976 burial space had run out, and prisoners and family members were taken to the Boeung Choeung Ek extermination centre, fifteen kilometres from Phnom Penh. The prison had a staff of 1,720 under its chief, Khang Khek Ieu, known as Comrade Duch, a former mathematics teacher. Some staff themselves became prisoners.

In 1979 the prison was uncovered by the invading Vietnamese army, and Hồ Văn Tây, a Vietnamese combat photographer, was the first journalist to document it. The government of the People's Republic of Kampuchea reopened it as a historical museum memorialising the actions of the Khmer Rouge regime. The buildings are preserved, some rooms as they were when the Khmer Rouge were driven out, and several rooms are lined with photographs of prisoners. Paintings by Vann Nath, a former inmate spared because he could paint, show people being tortured.

On 26 July 2010 the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia convicted Kang Kek Iew of crimes against humanity; he died in 2020. In 2025 the site was designated a World Heritage Site as part of the Cambodian Memorial Sites.
tupac-amaru: Túpac Amaru was born on 14 April 1545. After the Spanish conquest of Peru in the 1530s, some members of the royal family set up a small independent Neo-Inca State at Vilcabamba, in the Upper Amazon northeast of Cusco. Its founder, Manco Inca Yupanqui, had first allied with the Spanish, then fought an unsuccessful war against them, and settled in Vilcabamba in 1540. After he was killed in a Spanish attack in 1544, his son Sayri Túpac took the title of Sapa Inca, accepted Spanish authority in 1558, moved to Cuzco and died in 1561, perhaps by poison. His brother Titu Cusi succeeded and died in 1571, and Túpac Amaru, another brother, then took the title.

The Spanish did not yet know that Titu Cusi was dead and sent two ambassadors to continue negotiations, but an Inca captain killed both at the border.
