Citing the violation of the law protecting ambassadors, the new viceroy, Francisco de Toledo, declared war on 14 April 1572. The first fighting began in the Vilcabamba valley on 1 June, where the lightly armed Incas repeatedly tried to lift the siege held by the Spanish and their native allies. On 24 June the Spanish entered Vilcabamba and found it deserted and destroyed, and the Neo-Inca State ceased to exist.

Túpac Amaru had left the day before with about 100 people, heading west into the lowland forests. Spanish parties captured his relatives and generals, and forty hand-picked soldiers under Martín García Óñez de Loyola followed him down the Masahuay river. With help from the Manarí they found him and his wife by a campfire, and he surrendered after they assured him no harm would come to him.

The captives were marched into Cuzco on 21 September 1572, and the Spanish destroyed the mummified remains of earlier rulers and a gold statue of Punchao. Túpac Amaru was convicted of murdering the priests in Vilcabamba and sentenced to be beheaded. Clerics reportedly pleaded in vain that he be sent to Spain for trial; Philip II disapproved of the execution. Some argue that Toledo exceeded his authority; others that Túpac Amaru was in rebellion. Beheaded on 24 September before the Cathedral of Santo Domingo in Cuzco, he died before crowds said to number 10,000 to 15,000. In 1780 José Gabriel Condorcanqui, who claimed descent from him, took the name Túpac Amaru II and led an indigenous uprising against Spanish rule.
tupac-amaru-ii: Túpac Amaru II was born José Gabriel Condorcanqui Noguera at Surimana, Tungasuca, in the province of Cusco, to Miguel Condorcanqui, kuraka of three towns in the Tinta district, and María Rosa Noguera. His parents died when he was twelve, and at sixteen he received a Jesuit education at the San Francisco de Borja school, founded for the sons of kurakas. He married Micaela Bastidas and succeeded his father as kuraka, inheriting 350 mules, so that he was both head of several Quechua communities and a regional muleteer.

He petitioned the authorities in Tinta, Cusco and Lima to relieve the tribute and the mining mita, the forced labour at Potosí, and met only refusal or indifference. He adopted the name Túpac Amaru II after his ancestor Túpac Amaru I, the last Sapa Inca of the Neo-Inca State.

The rebellion began on 4 November 1780 with the capture and hanging of Antonio de Arriaga, corregidor of Tinta, accused of repeated abuses. Its immediate cause lay in the Bourbon reforms, which centralised administrative and economic control and laid heavier taxes and labour burdens on Native and Creole populations. It was not at first an independence movement but a protest against colonial abuses, often speaking in the king's name, though some of his followers, mainly poor peasants, artisans and women, hoped for a restored Inca order. On 16 November 1780 he decreed the abolition of slavery for Black people.

At Sangarará on 18 November 1780 his forces killed all 578 Spanish soldiers, but the rebels' killing without orders ended any hope of Creole support. His 40,000 to 60,000 followers were repelled from Cusco, where reinforcements had arrived from Lima. His wife Micaela Bastidas commanded a battalion and is often credited with sharper strategy than his. Betrayed by two of his own officers, he was captured.

On 18 May 1781 he was executed in the Plaza de Armas of Cusco, after being forced to watch the deaths of Micaela Bastidas, his eldest son Hipólito and others. The sentence called for his limbs to be pulled apart by horses; the attempt failed and the body was quartered by hand and beheaded. The authorities ordered his houses demolished, his relatives declared infamous and Inca dress and the identity of Inca outlawed.

The revolt continued under his cousin Diego Cristóbal Túpac Amaru and spread through Upper Peru. Although not an independence movement in the modern sense, the rebellion was the first large-scale revolt in the Spanish colonies, and Túpac Amaru II later became a symbol of social justice and resistance in Peru.
tupac-amaru-revolutionary-movement: The Túpac Amaru Revolutionary Movement, in Spanish Movimiento Revolucionario Túpac Amaru or MRTA, was formed between 1980 and 1982 by the merger of the Revolutionary Socialist Party (Marxist-Leninist) and MIR El Militante, the militant faction of the Revolutionary Left Movement. The first gathered former members of the armed forces who had served under the leftist government of Juan Velasco Alvarado, and the second came from a Castroist guerrilla faction defeated in 1965.

It took its name from Túpac Amaru II, the eighteenth-century rebel who led a revolt against the Spanish from 1780 to 1782 and took his name from the last Inca ruler, executed in 1572. Its declared aims were to show leftist groups the viability of radical revolution and to offer an alternative to the Shining Path. It was led by Víctor Polay Campos until his sentencing to 32 years in prison in 1992, and then by Néstor Cerpa Cartolini.

Its first action was a bank robbery in La Victoria, Lima, on 31 May 1982, in which the committee member Jorge Talledo Feria was killed by friendly fire. On 28 September 1984 members disguised as police fired on the United States Embassy, causing damage but no casualties. The group's attempt to expand into the countryside brought it into conflict with the Shining Path, which was stronger there, and it remained largely urban and middle-class. Counterterrorist measures, infighting, the imprisonment or deaths of senior leaders and the loss of leftist support weakened it further.

Its last major action was the hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima. In December 1996 fourteen members occupied the residence and held 72 hostages for more than four months. In April 1997, on the orders of President Alberto Fujimori, the armed forces stormed the building, rescuing all but one of the remaining hostages and killing all fourteen militants. Later revelations suggested that at least three, and perhaps as many as eight, were executed after surrendering. The episode ended the movement as a threat to the Peruvian state and effectively dissolved it.

Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in its report of 2003 that the movement was responsible for 1.5 per cent of the deaths it investigated. The commission observed that, unlike the Shining Path, the movement claimed its actions, wore uniforms and abstained from attacking the unarmed population, but also that it carried out assassinations, hostage-taking and systematic kidnapping. It argued that the movement's attempt to justify violence helped legitimise the repressive policies of the Fujimori government. In 2006 a Peruvian court found Polay guilty of nearly 30 crimes. The People's Democratic Front, a far-left organisation of former members and sympathisers, has claimed the movement's legacy.
tupac-inca-yupanqui: Topa Inca Yupanqui was the tenth Sapa Inca, fifth of the Hanan dynasty, and belonged to the Qhapaq Panaca, one of the clans of Inca nobles. His father was Pachacuti, and his principal wife, or quya, was his older sister Mama Ocllo. His father made him head of the Inca army and gave him the title of Auqui, or crown prince, at a young age. In that role he launched large expeditions to the north, subduing Hatun Xauxa, the Bombon Plateau and Huaylas and besieging and capturing Curamba, Huaylla-Pucara, Canta and, most importantly, Chan Chan.

He extended the realm along the Andes through modern Ecuador and developed a particular fondness for Quito, which he rebuilt with architects from Cusco. On his father's death in 1471 he became Sapa Inca, and he ruled until his own death in 1493. He conquered Chimor, which held the northern coast of what is now Peru and was the largest remaining rival of the Incas, and he conquered the province of Antisuyu and subdued the Qulla people. In his reign he imposed rules and taxes and created two Suyuyoc Apu, governors general, one at Jauja and one at Tiwanaku. The fortress of Saksaywaman, begun by Pachacuti above Cusco, was built throughout his reign.

Topa Inca died about 1493 at Chincheros, leaving two legitimate sons and 90 illegitimate sons and daughters. His wife Chuqui Ocllo had persuaded him that their son Capac Huari would succeed, but he changed his mind and chose Titu Cusi Hualpa, later the emperor Huayna Capac. Chuqui Ocllo, angered, poisoned him; she and her favourite son were killed soon after.

He is also credited with a voyage of about ten months into the Pacific around 1470, reported by Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, Martín de Murúa and Miguel Cabello de Balboa. In Sarmiento's account merchants arriving at Tumbez spoke of islands called Avachumbi and Ninachumbi, and he sailed on balsas with more than 20,000 men and returned with slaves, gold and other trophies. María Rostworowski and others identify the islands with Mangareva and Easter Island, though some historians doubt that the voyage took place.
tupamaros: The National Liberation Movement, known as MLN-T, was a Marxist-Leninist urban guerrilla group. Uruguay had been one of the most prosperous countries in Latin America after the reforms of the Batlle era, but from the mid-1950s falling demand for agricultural exports brought a severe economic crisis. The Tupamaros arose in this period and drew professionals, workers, trade unionists and students.

One of its leaders, Eleuterio Fernández Huidobro, placed the formal founding in 1965, although its first action was the theft of weapons and ammunition from the Tiro Suizo shooting range in Nueva Helvecia in 1963. The name honoured Túpac Amaru II, who led a large indigenous revolt against the Viceroyalty of Peru in 1780. Its most important leader was Raúl Sendic.

The movement began with robberies of banks, gun clubs and other businesses, and distributed stolen food and money among the poor of Montevideo. Its slogan was "Words divide us; action unites us." In June 1968 President Jorge Pacheco declared a state of emergency and suspended constitutional safeguards; political dissidents were imprisoned and torture was used in interrogations. In 1969 the Tupamaros carried out the largest robbery in Uruguayan history and occupied the town of Pando on 8 October.

They then turned to kidnappings, armed propaganda and assassinations. Dan Mitrione, an official who advised the Uruguayan police, was kidnapped on 31 July 1970 and killed on 10 August; the Tupamaros said he had been advising police in torture. The British ambassador Geoffrey Jackson was kidnapped in January 1971. In September 1971 more than 100 imprisoned Tupamaros escaped from Punta Carretas prison through a tunnel, and the government called in the military.

In 1972 the group was crippled. Its violence had weakened popular support, and its wave of assassinations after the killing of four Tupamaros by illegal parapolice squads concentrated opposition against it. After the movement killed soldiers, the army responded with heavy use of torture and persuaded senior members, among them Héctor Amodio Pérez, to collaborate. The group collapsed in mid-1972. According to its own officials about 300 Tupamaros died, mostly in 1972, and about 3,000 were imprisoned. Nine leaders, including Sendic and José Mujica, were held in harsh conditions until 1985.

After the military completed its coup in June 1973, democracy returned in 1985, and amnesty was granted to the Tupamaros and the military. Former members joined the Broad Front, which the movement had helped to form. In 1989 the group was admitted to it, and many members joined the Movement of Popular Participation. Mujica served as president from 2010 to 2015.
tupelo-mississippi: Tupelo lies in north-eastern Mississippi on Interstate 22 and U.S. Route 78, midway between Memphis, Tennessee, and Birmingham, Alabama. It covers about 51 square miles, and the 2020 census counted 37,923 people. The Tupelo area is also the headquarters of the Natchez Trace Parkway, which follows the route of an ancient trail used by indigenous peoples long before Europeans came and connects Natchez, Mississippi, to Nashville, Tennessee. Nearby are the Pharr Mounds, a complex of nearly 2,000-year-old burial earthworks of the Middle Woodland period.

The Chickasaw and Choctaw occupied the area before European settlement, and the French and British traded with them and sought alliances. On 26 May 1736 the Battle of Ackia was fought near the site of present-day Tupelo, where British and Chickasaw soldiers repelled a French and Choctaw attack on the Chickasaw village of Ackia. The French governor of Louisiana, Jean Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville, had sought to link Louisiana with Acadia and the other northern colonies of New France. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 authorised the relocation of the Southeast Native Americans to territory west of the Mississippi River, completed by the end of the 1830s.

The settlement was founded in 1860 on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and was first called Gum Pond, from the local tupelo trees known as blackgum. Union and Confederate forces fought in the area in 1864 in the Battle of Tupelo and the Battle of Old Town Creek. The town took the name Tupelo in honour of the battle and was incorporated on 20 July 1870.

By the early twentieth century it had cotton textile mills, which under segregation employed only white adults and children. On 7 February 1934 Tupelo became the first city to receive power from the Tennessee Valley Authority, and President Franklin Roosevelt visited this First TVA City in 1935.

On 5 and 6 April 1936 a tornado struck, levelling 48 city blocks and more than 200 homes and killing 216 people in the official count. It destroyed the Gum Pond neighbourhood. Because white newspapers did not report news about Black people until the 1940s and 1950s, historians estimate the real toll was higher. Elvis Presley, then a baby, survived it.

Tupelo is the seat of Lee County and the birthplace of Elvis Presley, and the Elvis Presley Birthplace is among its cultural institutions. The Tupelo National Battlefield and the Brices Cross Roads National Battlefield, about ten miles to the north, commemorate Civil War battles. A statue of the Chickasaw leader Piomingo stands in front of the city hall.
tupua-tamasese-lealofi-iii: Born on 4 May 1901, Tamasese held the Tupua Tamasese dynastic title. In 1924 Administrator George Spafford Richardson banished him to Savai'i for failing to remove a hibiscus hedge from his land; when he came back to ask how long the banishment would last he was imprisoned, deprived of his title and banished again. This treatment was reported as one of the main drivers of the Mau. He joined the movement when Olaf Frederick Nelson founded it and in 1927 argued for Samoan self-government before a commission of inquiry in Apia.

After Nelson's exile Tamasese became the Mau's leader early in 1928. In March 1928 he was arrested with 400 Mau police in an attempt to break a boycott, and he spoke for them at their trial and during their imprisonment at Mulinuʻu. In September 1928 he refused to pay taxes, and after a failed attempt in early November he was arrested later that month, sentenced to six weeks for refusing tax and six months for resisting arrest, and deported to serve the sentence in New Zealand. An application for habeas corpus failed; released in June 1929, he returned to Samoa to a hero's welcome.

The procession of 28 December 1929 welcomed Alfred Smyth home from exile. The administration had armed the police with revolvers and rifles and mounted a Lewis gun on the police station balcony. When police tried to arrest a man in the crowd a brawl broke out and they opened fire; Tamasese, calling for peace at the front, was shot from behind by an officer on the balcony, and those who tried to help him were also shot. A New Zealand coroner found the rifle fire unnecessary, but no one was prosecuted.

His tomb of tiered black stones stands in Lepea village near Apia. His younger brother succeeded to the title as Tupua Tamasese Meaʻole and in 1962 became co-Head of State of independent Western Samoa. His eldest son, Tupua Tamasese Lealofi IV, later served two terms as prime minister.
tuqa-timur: Tuqa-Timur, also written Toqa-Temür and Toghai-Temür, was the thirteenth and youngest or penultimate son of Jochi, and a younger brother of Batu Khan and Berke Khan, rulers of what came to be called the Golden Horde. His mother is identified as Kaghri Khatun, a concubine of Jochi from the Merkit tribe. Perhaps thought too young to attend the qurultai that enthroned the great khan Ögedei in 1229, he stayed in his father's ulus and apparently governed it while his older brothers were away, holding a three-day feast for Batu on his return.

Batu later gave him an ulus of his own, perhaps under the intermediate authority of another brother, Orda. Tuqa-Timur took part in Batu's Western Campaign without a distinguished role, and is credited with a leading part in campaigns against the Bashkirs and Alans. He attended the qurultai that proclaimed Güyük great khan in 1246, which Batu refused to attend. After the assembly of 1250 that chose Möngke, he and Berke escorted the new great khan to Mongolia with an army and were generously rewarded.

Following Berke's example, he converted to Islam some time after Berke's own conversion in 1251-1252. He outlived Batu and died some time after Berke became khan in 1257, presumably before 1267, when his son Urung-Timur received the Crimea from Khan Mengu-Timur. Unlike Batu, Orda and Shiban, he never headed a lasting territorial polity, a point the Shibanids raised against his descendants in the late 14th century.

Rashid ad-Din and the genealogy Muʿizz al-ansab give him four sons. From the 1360s his descendants contested the throne of the Golden Horde with Shiban's, beginning with the probable Tuqa-Timurid Ordu Malik, who overthrew Timur Khwaja in 1361. A Crimean branch supplied the beglerbeg Mamai with three puppet khans between 1361 and 1380, and other lines rose in the east under Qara Noqai, Urus Khan and Tokhtamysh. The khanates of Kasimov, Kazan, Astrakhan and the Crimea, the Kazakh Khanate and, after 1599, the Khanate of Bukhara were all founded by princes of his line.
tura-river: The Tura is a left tributary of the Tobol in the basin of the Irtysh, flowing across the Tura Plain through the Sverdlovsk and Tyumen oblasts of Russia. It is 1,030 kilometres long, with a drainage basin of 80,400 square kilometres, and is navigable for 635 kilometres from its mouth. Near its source it is also called the Dolgaya. It begins at an elevation of 370 metres from the confluence of several streams southwest of the Khrebet-Uralsky railway station. The upper valley is narrow with steep slopes and a rocky bed, and in the lower reaches the flow is smooth. The main tributaries are the Salda, Tagil, Nitsa, Pyshma, Aktay and Is.

In 18th-century sources G. F. Müller explained the name from the Tatar word tura, meaning city, referring to the town of Chimgi-Tura on the river. Modern hypotheses link it to an Ural-Altaic root tur, meaning watercourse or body of water, which passed into several Ugric and Turkic languages. The Babinov Road, also known as the Sovereign's Road, was built along the river. Several cities lie on the Tura, from source to mouth Verkhnyaya Tura, Nizhnyaya Tura, Lesnoy, Verkhoturye, Turinsk and Tyumen.

The river freezes in November and thaws mainly in the first half of April, and ice jams sometimes accompany the break-up. Its flood lasts about two and a half months, and the winter low water lasts on average 140 to 160 days. The Tura is the primary source of water for the water supply of Tyumen. In the upper part of the basin lie deposits of copper, iron ores, gold and platinum, and the industries based on them are one of the main sources of pollution of the river. Three reservoirs, with a total area of 23 square kilometres, include the Verkhoturye Hydroelectric Station, and their construction changed the river's water regime.
turangawaewae: In August 1921 Ngāti Tamaoho hapū, led by Princess Te Puea Hērangi, began clearing swampy land overgrown with scrub and blackberry vines, part of it recently used as a rubbish dump. Te Puea aimed to raise the mana of the Kīngitanga and its Arikinui by improving the health, housing and employment of the people and by creating a national marae at Ngāruawāhia as a centre of Māori culture and politics. With the 1918 flu pandemic still fresh in local memory, she meant the Māhinārangi meeting house, built in 1929, to be a hospital where Māori could be treated in a traditional manner, but the Ministry of Health refused the permits.

The house was named after Māhinārangi, an East Coast ancestress, and her husband Tūrongo, a Tainui chief, at the request of Sir Āpirana Ngata, whose Ngāti Porou had raised thousands of pounds for it and who sent expert carvers and weavers. After a visiting prime minister called Māhinārangi a fine sitting room for King Korokī, Te Puea planned Tūrongo House, the monarch's residence, built in 1938.

Both buildings are of wood, covered in carvings painted burgundy and cream, in a blend of classical Māori and Edwardian architecture. Tūrongo House has a seven-sided corner tower representing the seven initial waka that, according to tradition, brought the Māori to Aotearoa, cladding of untreated ponga logs, and two pātaka on the roof that serve as dormer windows and hold taonga of the Kīngitanga, among them gifts from Polynesian royal houses such as that of Queen Salote of Tonga.

The marae is the administrative headquarters of the Kīngitanga and the setting of the annual Koroneihana festivities, and its visitors have included Nelson Mandela and Queen Elizabeth II. A renovation of both houses designed by the architects Salmon Reid in 2012, which strengthened their structures and added modern utilities, won the New Zealand Institute of Architects' Waikato-Bay of Plenty Regional Award in the Heritage Category.
turar-ryskulov: Turar Ryskulov was born on 26 December 1894 in the East-Talgar volost of Semirechensk Province, now Talgar District of Almaty Region, into the family of a nomadic herder. He took part in the Central Asian revolt of 1916 and then in the Russian Revolution in Turkestan and Kyrgyzstan.

After the Red Army took Tashkent in 1920, Ryskulov became chairman of the Central Executive Committee of the Turkestan Soviet Republic, which then covered all of Russian-ruled Central Asia, until Mukhammedzhan Biserov replaced him. He proposed that Turkestan be an independent republic ruled by a Turkic Communist Party, separate from the All-Russian Communist Party; Vladimir Lenin overruled the plan, summoning him to Moscow in May 1920 and persuading him to give it up.

In 1921–1922 he served as Deputy People's Commissar for Nationalities under Joseph Stalin. In June 1923 Stalin accused him of pan-Turkism and of having supported Mirsaid Sultan-Galiev, the arrested leader of the Tatar communists; Ryskulov answered that Stalin himself had once praised Sultan-Galiev as a devoted communist. From 1922 he chaired the Council of People's Commissars of the Turkestan Republic until it was divided in 1924 into Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. He was then sent by the Communist International to Ulaanbaatar as chief Soviet adviser to the Mongolian People's Party and helped create the Mongolian People's Republic. From 1926 to 1937 he was deputy chairman of the government of the Russian republic.

Ryskulov was arrested in the Great Purge on 21 May 1937, sentenced to death on 8 February 1938 and executed two days later. He was rehabilitated on 8 December 1956, though Soviet sources still charged him with political errors. In Kazakhstan he is regarded as a national hero: a large statue stands at the Turar Ryskulov University in Almaty, a district and the city of Imeni Turara Ryskulova bear his name, and the major cities have streets named after him.
turfan: Turpan, also written Turfan, is a prefecture-level city in the east of the Xinjiang autonomous region, about 150 kilometres south-east of Ürümqi, on the northern side of the Turpan Depression at about 30 metres above sea level. It has an extremely continental desert climate, with very hot summers, very cold winters and annual precipitation of only 15.7 millimetres. The ancient irrigation system and the summer heat allow the countryside to produce great quantities of high-quality fruit, and the region is China's largest raisin-producing area. The historical centre of the area has shifted, from Jiaohe to Qocho, also called Gaochang, and to Turpan itself.

The Jushi Kingdom ruled the area in the 1st millennium BCE until the Chinese Han dynasty conquered it in 107 BCE. Han and Xiongnu contended for it. After the fall of the Han in 220 the region was virtually independent. Tocharian-speaking people lived in Turpan and nearby city-states up to at least the 8th century, and many Han Chinese and Sogdians settled there. In 327 the Former Liang created the Gaochang Commandery here, and from 460 Gaochang was a vassal kingdom of the Rouran Khaganate under a Han Chinese king. Later kings of the Qu dynasty were vassals of the Göktürks.

The Tang dynasty conquered the region in 640 and renamed it Xi Prefecture; Sogdian and Chinese merchants traded extensively, and contracts found in the Astana Cemetery record sales of slaves. The Tibetans took Turfan in 792, and in 803 the Uyghurs seized it from them. After the Kirghiz destroyed the Uyghur Khaganate in Mongolia in 840, many Uyghurs moved here. The Uyghurs set up the Idikut kingdom, also called the Kara-Khoja Kingdom, with its capital at Gaochang, which lasted from 856 to 1389. Its people were first Manichaean and later converted to Buddhism, funding the Bezeklik Caves, and the kingdom became a vassal of the Kara-Khitans and then of the Mongol Empire.

German expeditions between 1902 and 1914 took paintings and other art to the Museum of Asian Art in Berlin, and many of the artefacts of Manichaean and Buddhist origin were later destroyed or looted during the Second World War. The Turfan fragments, over 40,000 manuscripts and fragments in 16 languages, are kept in the Berlin State Library. They hold Buddhist, Christian-Nestorian, Manichaean and secular texts, among them parts of the Gospel of Mani. Many texts survive because the Astana graveyard used discarded paper to make clothing for corpses. The conversion of the Buddhist population to Islam was completed in the second half of the 15th century.
turgut-reis: Turgut Reis, known as Dragut, was born near Bodrum on the Aegean coast of Asia Minor. His father was a farmer named Velî, and the family were either Greek Christians or Turkish Muslims. At the age of 12 an Ottoman army commander noticed his talent with spears and arrows and recruited him; he was trained as a sailor, gunner and master of siege artillery. In 1517 he went to Egypt as a cannoneer in the Ottoman conquest, then joined the fleet of Sinan Pasha at Alexandria, became captain of a brigantine and then of a galiot, and operated against the shipping routes between Venice and its Aegean islands.

In September 1538 at the Battle of Preveza he commanded the centre-rear wing of the Ottoman fleet that defeated the Holy League under Andrea Doria. In 1539 he succeeded Sinan Pasha as governor of Djerba. Surprised at Girolata in Corsica, he was captured by forces of Giannettino Doria and spent nearly four years as a galley slave and in prison at Genoa, until in 1544 Barbarossa appeared before Genoa with 210 ships and secured his release for 3,500 gold ducats. After Barbarossa died in July 1546, Turgut became supreme commander of Ottoman naval forces in the Mediterranean.

In August 1551 he captured Tripoli, held by the Knights of St. John since 1530, and Sultan Suleiman awarded it to him with the title of Sanjak Bey. In 1560 the fleet under Piyale Pasha and Turgut Reis defeated a Christian fleet of 200 ships at the Battle of Djerba.

In March 1556 he was appointed Pasha of Tripoli, where he strengthened the citadel and built a fortress. When Suleiman ordered the Great Siege of Malta in 1565, Dragut joined Piyale Pasha on 31 May with 1,600 men and 15 ships, landing at a cape later named Dragut Point. He advised capturing Cittadella and Mdina first, but the advice was not taken, and he concentrated cannon fire on Fort St. Elmo. He died on 23 June 1565. The town of his birth was renamed Turgutreis in 1972, and Turkish Navy ships bear his name. In Maltese history he is regarded as a nemesis.
turicum: Turicum lay at the lower end of Lake Zurich, in the Roman province of Germania Superior near its border with Raetia. Its core was the Lindenhof, a moraine hill in what is now the Altstadt of Zurich, about 428 metres above sea level and some 25 metres above the Limmat. The settlement was bounded on the west by the line of the present Rennweg and Bahnhofstrasse and on the north by the slope towards the old delta of the Sihl. Its importance came from the waterway running from the Walensee through Lake Zurich and down the Limmat, Aare and Rhine.

Neolithic pile dwellings stood on the marshy shore nearby, and Celts settled on and around the Lindenhof probably in the 1st century BCE or earlier. Finds of the La Tène period include lumps of Potin coins, the largest weighing 59.2 kilograms and made of about 18,000 coins of around 100 BCE, which researchers now take to be cult offerings. The Roman vicus was founded probably around 15 BCE. It belonged first to Gallia Belgica and from 90 CE to Germania Superior.

The name is first attested on the tombstone of Lucius Aelius Urbicus, infant son of the head of the toll station, found on the Lindenhof in 1747 and dated to 185/200 CE. Turicum had no walls; its buildings grouped round the customs post, the Quadragesima Galliarum, which levied a duty of 2.5% where cargoes passed between lake ships and river boats. A harbour district grew at the foot of the Lindenhof in 70/75 CE, and baths of the 2nd to 4th centuries have been excavated near the Weinplatz. In 122 CE, under Emperor Hadrian, a round wooden temple was built on the island of Grosser Hafner.

According to Christian legend, Felix and Regula were executed at the site of the Wasserkirche in 286. Under Emperor Valentinian I (364–375) the army built a fort of 4,500 square metres on the Lindenhof against the Alamanni, with ten towers and walls two metres thick. The Alamanni settled probably from the 5th century, when Roman troops withdrew to Italy, but the fort lasted into the 7th century.

Few remains of Roman Zurich have been excavated systematically, since they lie under the dense centre of the modern city and digs usually come with the renewal of buildings. Some finds are shown in place at the Thermengasse and in the Lindenhofkeller on the Lindenhof hill. The Lindenhof is listed as a Class A site of national importance in the Swiss inventory of cultural property.
turin: Turin lies in north-western Italy, mainly on the western bank of the River Po, surrounded on the west and north by the Alps and on the east by a high hill that continues the hills of Monferrato. Four major rivers pass through it: the Po and its tributaries the Dora Riparia, the Stura di Lanzo and the Sangone.

The Taurini, a Celto-Ligurian Alpine people, occupied the upper valley of the Po. In 218 BCE Hannibal, allied with their enemies the Insubres, took their chief town, Taurasia, after a three-day siege. In the 1st century BCE the Romans founded Augusta Taurinorum, a town of about 5,000 inhabitants within high walls; its Porta Palatina is still preserved. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the town was held by the Heruli, Ostrogoths and Lombards, and passed to the Franks under Charlemagne in 773. The Counts of Savoy gained control after the marriage of Adelaide of Susa to Otto, son of Humbert Biancamano, and when the city was annexed to the Duchy of Savoy at the end of the 13th century it had 20,000 inhabitants.

Emmanuel Philibert, nicknamed Iron Head, made Turin the capital of the Duchy of Savoy in 1563. The French Empire annexed it with the rest of Piedmont in 1802, and in 1814 the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia was restored with Turin as its capital. That kingdom led the struggle for the unification of Italy, and Turin was the political and intellectual centre of the Risorgimento. It became the capital of the new Kingdom of Italy in 1861; the capital moved to Florence in 1865 and to Rome after the conquest of the Papal States in 1870.

Turin is the capital of Piedmont and is sometimes called the cradle of Italian liberty. Its architecture is predominantly Baroque, and part of the historical centre is inscribed in the World Heritage List as the Residences of the Royal House of Savoy. It is the base of Fiat, Lancia and Alfa Romeo, and hosted the 2006 Winter Olympics.
turin-king-list: The Turin King List is a hieratic papyrus thought to date from the reign of Ramesses II, who ruled from 1279 to 1213 BCE. It is the most extensive list of kings compiled by the ancient Egyptians and the basis of most Egyptian chronology before his reign. The list is written on the back of a discarded tax register, which may mean the writer did not treat it as formally important; its main function is thought to have been as an administrative aid.

Its beginning and end are lost, with no introduction and nothing after the 19th Dynasty, so it may have been composed at any time from Ramesses II to as late as the 20th Dynasty. It is a sloppy copy of a more detailed original that rested on much older sources. Only the kings of the First and Second dynasties have both their length of reign and age at death.

The papyrus is divided into eleven columns. The first two hold the gods, spirits and mythical kings; the human kings follow, from the First Dynasty to the 17th, and perhaps once a twelfth column carried the 18th and 19th. It gives the length of each reign in years, with months and days for some, and sometimes groups rulers by family, roughly as Manetho's dynasties do. It includes ephemeral rulers and those of small territories who are unmentioned elsewhere.

It also lists the Hyksos kings of the 15th Dynasty, who ruled Lower Egypt and the Nile delta. They have no cartouches, and a sign marks them as foreigners, although foreign rulers are not usually listed in king lists. Kim Ryholt estimates that the list once held about 250 kings, with about 270 from Narmer or Menes to Ramesses II over some 1,800 years.

The circumstances of discovery are unknown. The Italian traveller Bernardino Drovetti bought the papyrus at Thebes around 1818. It was purchased at Livorno in 1820 and reached Turin in 1824, where the Egyptian Museum acquired it as Papyrus Number 1874. When its box was opened, it had crumbled into small fragments. Jean-François Champollion drew what he could read, and Gustav Seyffarth rebuilt it from the fibres of the papyrus alone, before hieratic could be read.

Giulio Farina published a new placement of fragments with a transcription, translation and commentary in 1938, and Ryholt published a new interpretation in 1997. Donald Redford has noted discrepancies between its names and monuments and other documents. About half the papyrus is still missing; it is now 1.7 m long and 0.41 m wide in over 160 fragments, and unpublished fragments were found in the museum's storage in 2009.
turkey: Turkey, officially the Republic of Türkiye, lies mainly in Anatolia, which makes up 97% of its surface, with a smaller part called East Thrace in Southeast Europe. Together they cover 783,562 square kilometres, and the Turkish straits and the Sea of Marmara run between them. The inland Anatolian Plateau grows more rugged towards the east, where Mount Ararat, the highest point at 5,137 metres, and Lake Van, the largest lake, are found. The Euphrates, the Tigris and the Aras rise in the east, and the country is divided into seven major regions.

The area has been inhabited by modern humans since the late Paleolithic and holds some of the oldest Neolithic sites, among them Göbekli Tepe, close to 12,000 years old, and Çatalhöyük. Written records begin with clay tablets of about 2000 BCE from Kültepe, which belonged to an Assyrian trade colony. The Hittite kingdom, with its capital at Hattusa, lasted approximately between 1700 and 1200 BCE, and Phrygia was established around 750 BCE. Alexander the Great's conquests brought Hellenization, followed by Romanization under the Roman and Byzantine empires.

The Seljuk Turks began migrating into Anatolia in the 11th century, and the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum ruled until the Mongol invasion of 1243, after which Turkish principalities emerged. From 1299 the Ottomans united them, and Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453. The Ottoman state entered World War I in 1914. Its government committed genocides against its Armenian, Greek and Assyrian subjects. After defeat came the Turkish War of Independence, the abolition of the sultanate and the Treaty of Lausanne. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and first president, proclaimed the Republic on 29 October 1923.

Turkey has more than 86 million people. Most are ethnic Turks, and Kurds are the largest minority, with estimates ranging from 12 to 20% of the population because census figures have not recorded ethnicity since 1965. Ankara is the capital and Istanbul the largest city. The country is a presidential republic under the constitution approved by referendum in 1982, with a 600-member Parliament and 81 provinces.
turkification: Turkification, also Turkization or Turkicization, describes a shift in which populations or places take on Turkic culture, language, history or ethnicity. The term is often applied more narrowly to Turkish rather than Turkic change, most often to the policies of the Ottoman Empire or of the Republic of Turkey towards minorities. Before the 20th century, the change in Anatolian, Balkan, Caucasian and Middle Eastern regions was said to be Ottomanization, and the two terms became interchangeable after the rise of Turkish nationalism. Greek has used a word for it, meaning becoming a Turk, since the 1300s.

The earliest instance took place in Central Asia, where by the 6th century migration of Turkic tribes from Inner Asia began a language shift among the Iranian peoples. By 750 the Qarluq Turks, ancestors of the Karakhanids, were turkifying Kashgar and also Islamized its people, and the Iranian language of Khwarezm eventually died out. In Azerbaijan the Turkic settlement that began in the Seljuq period continued through the Mongol period, and the Turkish scholar Faruk Sumer names three periods of Turkification there: Seljuq, Mongol and post-Mongol.

Anatolia had been Hellenized, and by the 5th century its native people were entirely Greek in language and Christian in religion. From the eleventh century war between the Byzantine and Seljuk empires destroyed settlements, and as areas were depopulated Turkoman nomads moved in with their herds. The conquest brought enslavement, flight, plague and famine and left the church impoverished. Even so, Christians were still an overwhelming majority 50 years after the Battle of Manzikert. Turks also intermarried with Greek, Armenian and Georgian natives, and the children, called Mixobarbaroi, were raised as Turks and Muslims.

In the late Ottoman period the government sought a core identity with a single Turkish religion, language, history and culture. The sociologist Ziya Gökalp believed that a modern state must be homogeneous. After the Young Turks took power in 1909 Turkish was imposed in administration, courts and schools in Arabic-speaking areas, and the prevailing view holds that Arab nationalism arose in response, though not all scholars agree. Uğur Üngör writes that the policies of forced assimilation culminated in the Armenian and Assyrian genocides.

In 1916 a campaign began to resettle whole Kurdish tribes where they would be no more than 10% of the local population, and Armenian orphans were given Turkish and Arabic names. Scholars believe that at least two million Turks have an Armenian grandparent.
turkish-war-of-independence: The Armistice of Mudros, signed on 30 October 1918, ended the First World War for the Ottoman Empire. The army was to demobilise, and Article VII gave the Allies the right to occupy the forts of the Straits and, in case of disorder, any territory threatened by insecurity. The Committee of Union and Progress dissolved itself, and its leaders Talât, Enver and Cemal fled, leaving a power vacuum. Sultan Mehmed VI sent Mustafa Kemal Pasha to restore order as inspector of the Ninth Army, but he became the leader of Turkish nationalist resistance.

Most historians date the war's start to the Greek landing at Smyrna on 15 May 1919, when hundreds of Turkish and about a hundred Greek soldiers and civilians were killed or wounded. Kemal landed at Samsun on 19 May and organised mass meetings. The Erzurum Congress drafted the National Pact, based on self-determination, and set up a Committee of Representation with Kemal as chairman.

On 16 March 1920 the Allies occupied Istanbul and arrested nationalist politicians, and the Grand National Assembly then convened in Ankara. Turkish forces defeated the French in the south, and in the east the army partitioned Armenia with the Bolsheviks, resulting in the Treaty of Kars in 1921. On the Western Front, the Greco-Turkish War, the regular army under İsmet Pasha fought the Greeks to a standstill at the First and Second Battles of İnönü. The Greeks won at Kütahya-Eskişehir and advanced on Ankara, but were checked at the Battle of Sakarya, and a Turkish counter-attack, the Great Offensive, expelled them.

The war ended with the recapture of İzmir, the Chanak crisis and an armistice at Mudanya. On 1 November 1922 the Assembly voted to abolish the sultanate, and Mehmed VI left on 17 November 1922, ending the monarchy of over 600 years.

The Treaty of Lausanne, signed on 24 July 1923 and more favourable to Turkey than Sèvres, was followed by the Allied evacuation of Istanbul. The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed on 29 October 1923, with Mustafa Kemal elected its first president, and he went on to introduce sweeping reforms. A population exchange between Greece and Turkey accompanied the end of the Ottoman era.

The war also reshaped Turkey's population. Historians note that the nationalists carried out massacres and deportations of Christian populations, continuing policies of the First World War: over a million Greeks were expelled, and the remaining Armenians of several districts were forced into French-mandate Syria. Greek and Armenian civilians were massacred in the fire of Smyrna. Muslims rose from 80% to 98% of the population. Some historians dispute the name war of independence, given the scale of civilian deaths among Christian minorities.
turkistan-city: Turkistan is the administrative centre of Turkistan Region in Kazakhstan, near the Syr Darya river, 160 kilometres north-west of Shymkent on the Trans-Aral Railway between Kyzylorda to the north and Tashkent to the south. Its name comes from the Turco-Persian phrase Hazrat-i-Turkistan, 'Saint of Turkistan', a reference to Ahmad Yasawi, a prominent 11th-century poet and Sufi who rests in the city. Earlier, and through much of the medieval and early modern era, it was called Iasy or Shavgar.

The city has an archaeological record reaching back to the 4th century. It emerged as a commercial centre after the decline of Otrar, an ancient city near the Syr Darya, and in honour of Ahmad Yasawi it became a hub of spiritual growth and Islamic education for the people of the Kazakh steppes. In the 1390s Timur built a domed mausoleum over Yasawi's resting place, one of the most notable architectural landmarks in Kazakhstan. The city also has a medieval bath-house and four mausoleums, one for Rabiya Sultan Begim, Timur's great-granddaughter, and three for Kazakh khans.

Before the Russian arrival in the 19th century Turkistan stood on the boundary between the Perso-Islamic oasis civilisation of Transoxiana to the south and the Kazakh steppes to the north. From the 16th to the 18th century it was the capital of the Kazakh Khanate and the political centre of the steppe. As Russia expanded and weakened the khanate, smaller southern states fell, and by 1864 the Russian general Veryovkin had captured Turkistan from the Kokand Khanate. It became part of the Syr-Darya Oblast in Russian Turkistan, briefly of the Turkistan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic after 1917–18, and in 1924 of the Kazakh ASSR.

The Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its image appeared on Kazakhstan's banknotes until 2006. According to local tradition, visiting Turkistan three times equals a single hajj to Mecca, and the city has been called the Second Mecca of the East; it draws thousands of pilgrims. In 2018 it became the administrative centre of the renamed Turkistan Region, and the 2019 census counted 165,000 inhabitants, Kazakhs and Uzbeks making up almost all of them.
turkmenbasy: Türkmenbaşy lies on the Türkmenbaşy Gulf of the Caspian Sea at an elevation of 27 metres, on the site where the dry bed of a former mouth of the Amu-Darya River once emptied into the sea. It has a cold desert climate with hot summers and somewhat chilly winters, and average annual precipitation of 125 millimetres. The city has been known by several names: Shagadam, Kyzyl-Su, meaning Red Water, Krasnovodsk, its Russian translation, and Türkmenbaşy.

In 1717 the Russian prince Alexander Bekovich-Cherkassky landed here and set up a secret fortified settlement. He intended to march an army up the dry riverbed and conquer the Khanate of Khiva. The expedition failed, and the Russians abandoned the settlement for over 150 years.

In 1869 the Russians came a second time, captured the settlement and named their fort Krasnovodsk. It served Imperial Russia as a base of operations against Khiva and Bukhara and against the semi-nomadic Turkmen tribes. The Trans-Caspian Railway had begun at Uzun-Ada on the Caspian, and its terminus was shifted north to the harbour at Krasnovodsk. The Russian station building dates from 1895, and the Church of St. Michael the Archangel was moved to the town from Uzun-Ada in the same year. The Armenian Apostolic church was built in 1903.

The town fell to the Red Army in February 1920. Krasnovodsk Oblast was formed on 21 November 1939 and was repeatedly abolished and restored until 1988. In 1942 a large part of the Polish Anders' Army, together with many civilians, was evacuated from the USSR through the port to Iran. On 8 October 1993 President Saparmurat Niyazov renamed the city Türkmenbaşy, meaning Head of all Turkmens, after his own self-proclaimed title.

Türkmenbaşy is a major port in Balkan Province in western Turkmenistan. Its seaport is Turkmenistan's main sea link to the west, with ferries across the Caspian to Baku, about 260 kilometres away, and it is the western terminus of the Trans-Caspian railway, which runs to Ashgabat. The country's largest oil refinery is here. Most of the population are Turkmens, who are Sunni Muslim, with Russian, Armenian and Azerbaijani minorities.
turkmenistan: Turkmenistan is a landlocked country in Central Asia, bordered by Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to the north, Afghanistan to the southeast, Iran to the south and southwest, and the Caspian Sea to the west. Most of the country is covered by the Karakum Desert. Ashgabat is the capital and largest city, and the population is over 7 million, the smallest of the Central Asian republics. The name combines the ethnonym Türkmen with the Persian suffix -stan, meaning place of. Turkmen comes from Turk plus a Sogdian suffix -men, meaning almost Turk. Muslim chroniclers such as Ibn Kathir derived it instead from Türk and the Arabic iman, faith, referring to the conversion to Islam of two hundred thousand households in 971.

The territory was historically inhabited by Indo-Iranians, and its written history begins with its annexation by the Achaemenid Empire. In the 8th century CE Turkic-speaking Oghuz tribes moved from Mongolia into present-day Central Asia, and they formed the ethnic basis of the modern Turkmen. The name Turkmen was first applied in the 10th century to Oghuz groups that accepted Islam and began to occupy what is now Turkmenistan. They came under the Seljuk Empire, which was made up of Oghuz groups living in present-day Iran and Turkmenistan. Merv, among the oldest oasis cities of Central Asia, was once one of the biggest cities in the world and an important stop on the Silk Road.

The Russian Empire annexed Turkmenistan in 1881, and the territory figured prominently in the anti-Bolshevik movement in Central Asia. In 1925 it became the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic, a constituent republic of the Soviet Union, and it remained one for 67 years. Turkmenistan declared its independence on 27 October 1991 after the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Its declaration of permanent neutrality was formally recognised by the United Nations in 1995, and neutrality has a place in its constitution. Saparmurat Niyazov, called Türkmenbaşy, led the country until his death in 2006.

Turkmenistan is a unitary state, divided into five regions called welayatlar and one capital city district. The Assembly, known as the Mejlis, has 125 members elected for five years and has been the unicameral legislature since January 2023. The country is one of six independent Turkic states and a member of the United Nations, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the Economic Cooperation Organization, and it is an observer state in the Organisation of Turkic States.
turku: Turku lies at the mouth of the Aura River in the south-western corner of Finland and covers both banks. The eastern bank, where Turku Cathedral stands, is the older and original centre; the western side, with Turku Castle, is the newer part. South-western Finland stayed below sea level for a long time after the Ice Age, and tectonic uplift turned the region from an outlying archipelago into a shoreline between about 3000 and 2000 BCE. In the Iron Age it was densely populated, and the word Finland once referred only to the area round Turku, which is why the province is called Finland Proper.

The Finnish name Turku is related to the word torg, meaning market. Pope Gregory IX mentioned the town of Aboa in his bull of 1229, and that year is now used as the founding year of the city. By the pope's permission of 23 January 1229 the episcopal seat was moved from Nousiainen to Koroinen, near the present centre. Because no reliable document records the founding, it has also been suggested that the city was founded in the 1280s or 1290s by the joint initiative of the king, the bishop and the Dominican Convent of Saint Olaf. Turku was the most important city in Finland under Swedish rule.

After the Finnish War, Sweden ceded Finland to Russia at the Treaty of Fredrikshamn in 1809, and the Russians entered Turku in October 1809 without resistance. Turku became the capital of the Grand Duchy of Finland but lost the status in 1812, when Emperor Alexander I decided to move the capital to Helsinki. After the last great fire, in 1827, most government institutions were moved to Helsinki together with the Royal Academy of Turku, founded in 1640, which later became the University of Helsinki.

Turku is the oldest city in Finland and the regional capital of Southwest Finland, with about 210,000 inhabitants. It is officially bilingual in Finnish and Swedish. The Swedish-language Åbo Akademi was founded there in 1918 and the Finnish-language University of Turku two years later. Its port runs ferries to Stockholm and Mariehamn.
turku-castle: Turku Castle stands on the banks of the Aura River and, with Turku Cathedral, is one of the oldest buildings still in use in Finland. It is the largest surviving medieval building in the country. The castle was the centre of the historical province of Finland Proper and the administrative centre of all Finland. It consists of the medieval keep, a square fort with two square gateway towers and walls 5 metres thick at the base, and the Renaissance bailey. In the Middle Ages a moat joined it to the river, which made it basically an island.

Swedes stationed in the region began the fort around 1280 as a military fortress and outpost. Over the next two centuries its defences were strengthened and living quarters were built, and it served as a defensive and administrative centre of Österland, the name of the region now called Finland. The keep was finished in the early 15th century, and the bailey was begun in the late 15th century and finished in the 16th. Between 1395 and 1398 the castle may have served as a base for the Victual Brothers, privateers turned pirates, invited by its chief, Knut Bosson Grip. The castle also took part in power struggles within Sweden and the Kalmar Union and stood sieges.

It reached its peak in the mid-16th century under Duke John of Finland and Catherine Jagellon, who built the Renaissance Floor and the King's and Queen's halls. From 1573 to 1577 the deposed Swedish queen Karin Månsdotter was kept prisoner there. A great fire in 1614 destroyed the wooden structures of the old parts almost completely, and the main structure was largely abandoned and used as storage. The castle lost its status as administrative centre in the 17th century, after Per Brahe's period as governor-general ended. It was a prison from the 18th to the end of the 19th century, and the Russian Navy used it during the Finnish War of 1808–1809.

The Turku Historical Museum gained control of the castle in 1881, and the Republic of Finland took ownership after independence in 1917. Renovation began before the Second World War, stopped during the Winter War and the Continuation War, when Soviet incendiary bombardment damaged the castle, and ended with a full restoration in 1987. The City of Turku took responsibility for it on 12 October 1993. It is a historical museum and part of the Turku Provincial Museum, and it is Finland's most visited museum.
turnip-winter: Germany entered the war in the summer of 1914 facing France, Britain and Russia on two fronts. The Schlieffen Plan, meant to defeat France quickly, failed at the First Battle of the Marne in September, and by the end of 1914 the Western Front had settled into trench warfare. Towards the end of that year the Royal Navy blockaded the northern approaches to the North Sea to cut off supplies to the Central Powers. Germany could produce most of the industrial needs of the war but not enough food.

Poor weather reduced the harvest, above all of cereals, and a poor autumn potato harvest left much produce rotting in the fields. The blockade, the army's seizure of horses, the conscription of farm workers and a shortage of fertiliser, as nitrogen went into explosives, all added to the shortfall. The government had founded the War Food Office on 22 May 1916 to run rationing. In the summer of 1917 the ration gave only 1,560 calories a day, falling to 1,000 in winter, against the 3,000 the Imperial Health Office set for a healthy adult man.

The historian Avner Offer suggests that one-fifth to one-third of food could be had only on the black market. Hungry children broke into barns and stripped orchards, and youth crime roughly doubled. The historian G. J. Meyer cites a prominent Berlin physician's report that eighty thousand children had died of starvation in 1916. Food shortages led to strikes, the best known in Düsseldorf in the summer of 1917, where workers complained that food was shared out unevenly. Female mortality rose by 11.5% in 1916 and by 30% in 1917 compared with pre-war rates.

The hardship showed Germans how hard-pressed the country had become and badly affected morale. Potatoes had been the food Germans ate most, and the switch to the Swedish turnip, or rutabaga, normally fed to animals, changed their tastes and deprived them of the vitamins and minerals they were used to. Kriegsbrot, the war bread made with potato flour, became much harder to digest once substitutes replaced the potato flour. Evelyn Blücher, an English woman married to Prince Blücher, wrote that the rounded contours of the German nation had become a legend of the past. There were social consequences too, such as the pillaging of food stores after the war.
turpan-khanate: The khanate, also known as Eastern Moghulistan, the Kingdom of Uyghurstan or the Turfan Khanate, was a Sunni Muslim Turco-Mongol state ruled by descendants of Chagatai Khan. It was the eastern division of Moghulistan, itself an eastern offshoot of the Chagatai Khanate. Its founder, Ahmad Alaq, broke away from his brother Mahmud and ruled the northern part of the Tarim Basin from Turpan, at what is now Gaochang. Under Ahmad Alaq and his eldest son Mansur, Turpan became more Muslim.

Ahmad Alaq made peace with Ming China, with which his father Yunus Khan had contested the Kara Del kingdom of Hami, and exchanged envoys with it. In the early 1500s he was defeated and killed in a battle against Muhammad Shaybani of the Khanate of Bukhara. His successor Mansur took Aksu, drove out his brother Sultan Said Khan, and in 1513 conquered the Kara Del kingdom; the Buddhists of the Hami area then migrated into Ming territory. The historian Mirza Muhammad Haidar Dughlat called Mansur's war with the Ming over Hami a holy war.

Sultan Said Khan, sheltered by his cousin Babur in Kabul, returned to Moghulistan and declared himself khan in 1514. Blocked in the steppe by the Uzbeks and Kazakhs, he took the western Tarim Basin around Kashgar and Yarkand, and his state became known as the Yarkent Khanate. The brothers were later reconciled, and the two khanates existed side by side. From the 16th century leaders of the Khojas gained strong influence, replacing the Dughlat faction.

After Mansur's death the khanate declined rapidly under Shah Khan. In 1570 an army of the Yarkent Khanate led by Abduraim Sultan, governor of Khotan and brother of Abdul Karim Khan, invaded and took the ruler Muhammad Khan ibn Mansur Khan prisoner, and Turpan came under the control of Yarkand. The last that was heard of the khanate were embassies sent from Turpan to Beijing in 1647 and 1657, which the Qing dynasty regarded as coming from a genuine Chagatayid.
tursunzoda: Tursunzoda is a city in western Tajikistan, 60 km west of Dushanbe and 40 km west of Hisor, near the border with Uzbekistan. The Shirkent and Karatag rivers lie immediately west and east of the city, and the Kofarnihon further east. It lies in the western part of the Gissar Valley, where plentiful irrigation supports fruit, vegetables and cotton, and the district is a major rice-growing region that produced 1,400 tons, about 13 per cent of the country's rice harvest, in 2006.

The city began as the village of Regar, meaning a town on sand, and grew into a regional centre for the agricultural district. In the 1960s the Nurek Dam hydroelectric power station on the Vakhsh made it a good location for industry, and besides the aluminium plant it acquired china, brick, cable and cotton-cleaning works.

Construction of the aluminium smelter, TadAZ, began in 1972, and the first aluminium was poured on 31 March 1975. The country has no native aluminium ore, so the raw material is imported. In 1978 the town and its district were renamed for the Tajik national poet Mirzo Tursunzoda, though its railway station is still called Regar. During the Tajikistani Civil War the city came under the control of the warlord Mahmud Khudoyberdiev.

The city proper had an estimated population of 55,700 in 2020, against 40,600 in the 1989 census. The aluminium smelter is Tajikistan's chief industrial asset and consumes 40 per cent of the country's electrical power, and a study of 2002 found it responsible for notable fluorine water pollution and air pollution in the region. The city has two television stations, two newspapers and a football club, Regar-TadAZ Tursunzoda.
turtle-ship: The Korean Joseon Navy used turtle ships from the early 15th century until the 19th century, alongside the panokseon warships, against invading Japanese fleets. The earlier, first-generation ships were called gwiseon. Records of 1413 and 1415 in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty mention a mock battle between a gwiseon and a Japanese warship, but these early ships soon fell out of use during a long period of relative peace and declining naval preparedness.

Turtle ships took part in the war against the Japanese forces of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who tried to conquer Korea from 1592 to 1598. Admiral Yi Sun-sin, who won all his battles against the Japanese navy, is credited with designing the improved version. From their first appearance at the Battle of Sacheon, his turtle ships contributed to 16 victories against fleets led by daimyo, mostly from western Japan. Under Wŏn Kyun the Joseon Navy nevertheless suffered a heavy defeat at the Battle of Chilcheollyang. How many of Yi's turtle ships were built is not known.

Later turtle ships differed from earlier ones. They had higher bulwarks, which allowed more slots for weapons or ventilation. Early illustrations show overlapping planks on the deck structure, while later depictions show flush hexagonal plates of wood or iron. The ship was oar and sail powered and was designed to be fast. Its roof was covered with iron spikes to prevent boarding. According to historical records the spikes were hidden under rice sacks or mats to lure Japanese soldiers into boarding, although modern authors consider this unlikely because it would have invited fire arrows.

Whether the ship was ironclad is disputed. No contemporary Korean source from Yi's time calls it so. A Japanese chronicle describes three turtle ships "covered in iron" in August 1592, which may refer to the spikes. Stephen Turnbull notes that in February 1593 the Japanese government ordered iron plate to be used in building ships, possibly in response. Samuel Hawley suggests the idea of ironclad turtle ships comes from Western writers of the late 19th century.

It carried cannon called cheonja, jija, hyeonja and hwangja, and an arquebus called seungja. The seungja ranged 200 metres, while the light hwangja reached 1,200 metres. A Japanese record of the Battle of Angolpo on 9 July 1592 describes the turtle ships attacking with fire-arrows until about six in the evening, even from 18 to 30 feet, and wrecking almost every part of the Japanese ships. A dragon's head at the bow was meant to frighten Japanese soldiers, and one version carried a projector that released dense toxic smoke to obscure vision. Reconstructions are displayed at Yeosu and Tongyeong, where visitors can go inside.
tuscarora-people: The Tuscarora are an Iroquoian people of the Northeastern Woodlands. Their own name, Skarù·ręˀ, may mean "hemp gatherers" or "shirt-wearing people". Before European contact they lived in the Carolinas along the Roanoke, Neuse, Tar and Pamlico Rivers, as a confederacy of three tribes, the Katenuaka, Akawenteaka and Skaruren. Their members belonged to about seven matrilineal clans: Bear, Beaver, Deer, Eel, Snipe, Turtle and Wolf. Their language, Skarure, belongs to the northern branch of the Iroquoian languages and is closely related to Nottoway and Meherrin.

In early 18th-century North Carolina, colonists reported two main branches of the Tuscarora, a northern group led by Tom Blunt and a southern group led by Hancock. Hancock's people suffered colonists who raided villages and kidnapped people to sell into slavery, as well as epidemic disease. On 22 September 1711 the southern Tuscarora and allied nations attacked settlers, beginning the Tuscarora War.

North Carolina's governor secured South Carolina's help, and in 1713 the southern Tuscarora were defeated at Fort Neoheroka, where 900 were killed or captured. Hancock was captured with Blunt's help and executed. About 1,500 Tuscarora fled north, and in 1722, sponsored by the Oneida, the Tuscarora were accepted as the sixth nation of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Migration north continued over about 90 years.

During the American Revolutionary War, part of the Tuscarora allied with the colonists, while those who supported the British followed Joseph Brant to Ontario, where they helped found the Six Nations of the Grand River reserve. In the War of 1812 Tuscarora warriors fought a delaying action at Lewiston, New York, on 19 December 1813, allowing townspeople to escape.

Today the Tuscarora Nation lives in New York, near Niagara Falls, and the Tuscarora First Nation is part of the Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario. In the mid-20th century New York City commissioner Robert Moses negotiated the purchase of 550 acres of the reservation for the reservoir of a Niagara hydroelectric project, a controversial sale.
tuscarora-war: The Tuscarora, an Iroquoian people believed to have moved from the Great Lakes into the Piedmont centuries before European colonisation, lived at peace with the English settlers of North Carolina for more than 50 years after the first successful settlement in 1653. Trade in weapons and metal goods gave them commercial dominance over neighbouring peoples, a benefit felt more by the Northern Tuscarora than by the Southern, who were cut off by the growing number of settlers.

Settlers pushing west into the fertile uplands competed with the Tuscarora for land and hunting grounds, and their demand for workers fed the Indian slave trade. The Tuscarora held John Lawson to account for the founding of New Bern on their land. The northern group under Chief Tom Blount stayed out of the war at first, but the southern group under Chief Hancock, whose people had suffered raids and kidnappings by slave traders, attacked with the Coree, Neuse, Pamlico, Machapunga and others, killing hundreds of settlers, Lawson among them.

North Carolina, weakened by Cary's Rebellion, turned to South Carolina, which sent Colonel John Barnwell with 30 white officers and about 500 Native Americans, among them Yamasee, Wateree, Congaree and Apalachee. Arriving in January 1712, they attacked the Tuscarora, who withdrew to Fort Neoheroka and agreed a truce. When some South Carolina officers kept Tuscarora to sell as slaves, fighting broke out again amid an outbreak of yellow fever.

A second force under Colonel James Moore, 33 colonists and nearly 1,000 Native Americans, arrived in December 1712. The settlers offered Blount control of the whole Tuscarora people if he helped them; he captured Hancock, whom the settlers executed. At Neoheroka the Tuscarora's defences equalled comparable frontier forts of the time, but they lacked their enemies' artillery and explosives, and about 950 people were killed or captured and sold into slavery in the Caribbean or New England.

Many Tuscarora moved to New York, where the Haudenosaunee accepted them as the Sixth Nation in 1722; the last bands left North Carolina in 1802. Barnwell's and Moore's Native allies, having seen how deeply the colonists were invested in the slave trade, attacked South Carolina in April 1715, beginning the Yamasee War. By 1717 South Carolina had begun to regulate its slave trade, and Native Americans came to be valued more as allies than as slaves. Fort Neoheroka was added to the National Register of Historic Places on 17 July 2009.
tusculan-disputations: The Tusculan Disputations is a series of five books written by Cicero around 45 BCE, attempting to popularise Greek philosophy, Stoicism included, in ancient Rome. It is so called because it was reportedly written at his villa in Tusculum. In 45 BCE, when Cicero was around 61, his daughter Tullia died after childbirth. Her loss affected him so deeply that he withdrew from public business and devoted himself to philosophy.

He addressed the work to his friend Brutus, later an assassin of Julius Caesar, and framed it as the record of five days of discussions with friends. The conversations are one-sided: the anonymous friend of each dialogue only supplies the topic and eases the transitions. Cicero relied heavily on Crantor’s On Grief, which he also used for his Consolatio on Tullia’s death.

Each book takes a theme: contempt of death, bearing pain, grief of mind, other disturbances of the mind, and whether virtue alone is sufficient for a happy life. In the first, Cicero refutes the claim that death is an evil. He offers largely Platonist arguments for the immortality of the soul and dismisses the myths of the Greek underworld, and he argues that even if death ends all feeling it is no evil. In the second he holds that pain is overcome by fortitude and patience rather than by Epicurean maxims.

The third treats the alleviation of sorrow. Cicero observes that grief is often put on or continued only because the world expects it, and that foreseeing misfortunes helps to repel or soften them. The fourth classes the passions as diseases of the soul under four Stoic heads: grief, fear, excessive gladness and immoderate desire, all arising from false opinions about good and evil. The fifth argues, in a view close to the Stoic one, that virtue suffices for happiness in poverty, exile, blindness and even under torture.

The work is the locus classicus of the legend of the Sword of Damocles and the sole mention of cultura animi, the cultivation of the mind, as an agricultural metaphor for human culture. It also draws on ancient fable, Greek and Roman history and the Latin poets.

The theme of contempt of the world was taken up by Boethius and by Bernard of Cluny in the first half of the 12th century. Saint Augustine referred to the work in his Confessions and The City of God, and Thomas Jefferson included the Tusculan questions in a list of books he recommended to Robert Skipwith for a general library.
tusheti: Tusheti lies on the northern slopes of the Greater Caucasus Mountains. Chechnya borders it to the north and Dagestan to the east, and the Georgian historic provinces of Kakheti and Pshav-Khevsureti lie to the south and west. By the convention that follows the watershed of the Greater Caucasus as the boundary of Europe and Asia, it is a European part of Georgia. The Tusheti National Park lies within it.

Historically Tusheti comprised four mountain communities: the Tsova in the Tsova Gorge, the Gometsari along the Tushetis Alazani River, the Pirikiti along the Pirikitis Alazani River, and the Chaghma near the meeting of the two rivers. The population is mainly ethnic Georgians called Tush or Tushetians. They divide into the Chaghma-Tush, who speak the local Georgian dialect, and the Tsova-Tush, better known as Bats or Batsbi, who speak a Nakh language.

Pagan Georgians from Pkhovi are said to have taken refuge in the uninhabited mountains during their rebellion against the Christianization imposed by the Iberian king Mirian III in the 330s. From the 5th century the region belonged to the Kingdom of Iberia. In the 8th century it joined the Khundzakhi community in the duchy of Tsuketi, the period regarded as that of its conversion. After the collapse of the unified Georgian monarchy it came under the Kakhetian kings in the 15th century.

In 1659, during the Kakhetian uprising, the Tush contributed to the battle of Bakhtrioni against invaders, and legend ties the bravery of their leader Zezva Gafrindauli to the grant of the Alvani Valley. The kings Teimuraz II and Erekle I later confirmed the Tush right to its pastures. In the first half of the 19th century many families moved south to Alvan, the first being the Bats after a landslide destroyed one of their main villages around 1830 and plague broke out. A minor anti-Soviet revolt took place in the area in 1942-1943.

Tusheti is administratively part of the Akhmeta district of Kakheti, and its largest village is Omalo. Traditionally the Tush are sheep herders, and Tushetian Guda cheese and wool were exported. Shepherds spend the summer in the highlands and the winter in the lowland villages of Zemo Alvani and Kvemo Alvani. Because of pre-Christian customs, pork is considered bad luck and some families avoid it altogether. The region is also a popular venue for mountain trekking.
tushpa: Tushpa, Turuspa in Akkadian and Tosp in Armenian, takes its name from an Urartian word meaning to destroy, that is, victorious; it was possibly pronounced Tospa, since Akkadian cuneiform had no separate sign for O. It later became known as Van, from Biainili, the native name of Urartu. Settlement in the region goes back at least to 5000 BCE. The ruins lie just west of the modern city of Van, on the steep bluff now called Van Fortress, close to the shore of Lake Van.

The fortress was held by Urartu from the 9th to the 7th centuries BCE and is the largest complex of its kind. Its lower walls are of unmortared basalt and the rest of mud-brick; such fortresses served for regional control rather than defence against foreign armies. The region came under the Orontid dynasty of Armenia in the 7th century BCE and under the Persians in the mid-6th century BCE. Darius cut a niche in the rock face about 20 metres above the ground, and his son Xerxes had a text of 27 lines in Old Persian, Babylonian and Elamite carved in it. Eugène Burnouf's reading of it, published in 1836, advanced the decipherment of Old Persian cuneiform.

Alexander the Great took Tushpa in 331 BCE, and it passed to the Seleucid Empire and, by the early 2nd century BCE, to the Kingdom of Armenia; the History of Armenia attributed to Moses of Chorene calls it Tosp. The Byzantine Empire held the region from 628 to 640, before the Arab conquest. Van was one of the residences of the Artsruni kings of Vaspurakan from 908 until 1021, when John-Senekerim Artsruni ceded the kingdom to the Byzantine Empire. After Manzikert in 1071 it passed to the Seljuqs, later to the Mongols, the Kara Koyunlu and the Timurids, and after Safavid rule from 1502 the Ottomans took final control in 1548.

The fortress has been held over the centuries by Armenians, Romans, Medes, Persians, Arabs, Seljuqs, Ottomans and Russians, and medieval walls stand on its ancient foundations. Several cuneiform inscriptions survive on the site. In 2016 Tushpa was placed on Turkey's tentative list of World Heritage Sites.
tushratta: Tushratta was the son of Shuttarna II and the grandson of Artatama I. He was placed on the throne after the assassination of his brother Artashumara. He was probably quite young and was meant to serve only as a figurehead, but he managed to dispose of the murderer. A tablet found in a Mitanni building at Tell Brak states that it was witnessed in the presence of Tushratta, the king, and bears on its reverse the seal of an earlier king, Shaushtatar, as was common practice. His name is an Akkadianised form of an Indo-Aryan name, Tvaiṣaratha, meaning one with a charging chariot.

Tushratta ruled from the end of the reign of Amenhotep III through the first half of that of Amenhotep IV. His sister Gilukhipa and his daughter Tadukhipa were married to Amenhotep III, and Tadukhipa later married Amenhotep IV. The Amarna letters include tablets from Tushratta about her marriage to Amenhotep IV, explicitly to solidify an alliance with Egypt, as well as letters to Amenhotep III and to Queen Tiye about gifts and missing gold statues.

At the start of his reign the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I reconquered Kizzuwatna and then invaded the western Euphrates valley. He made a treaty with Artatama, a rival who is called king of the Hurrians while Tushratta bears the title King of Mitanni. When Suppiluliuma began to plunder the west bank of the Euphrates, Tushratta threatened to raid beyond the river if even a single lamb or kid was stolen. A Hittite army then crossed into Isuwa and marched on the Mitanni capital, Washshukanni. Suppiluliuma claims Tushratta fled and that he brought back loot and captives, but he failed to capture the capital, and Tushratta kept his throne.

In a second campaign the Hittites subdued Halab, Mukish, Niya, Arahati, Apina and Qatna. Egypt failed to respond in time, perhaps because of the sudden death of Amenhotep IV and the struggle for the throne that followed.

According to a later treaty between Suppiluliuma I and Shattiwaza, a son of Tushratta, a third devastating Hittite raid led to the fall of Carchemish, and Tushratta was assassinated by a group led by one of his sons. Civil war followed, and it ended when Suppiluliuma I placed Shattiwaza on the Mitannian throne.
tuskahoma-oklahoma: Tuskahoma lies four miles east of Clayton, in the Kiamichi River valley among the Kiamichi Mountains. To the north rise the serrated Potato Hills, with peaks of about 1,000 feet, and the white boulders of McKinley Rocks, named after President William McKinley; to the south is a roadless mountain wilderness reaching about 1,600 feet. The name means red warrior in the Choctaw language and was written Tvshka Homma in the 1852 Choctaw-English dictionary of the missionary Cyrus Byington, a spelling the nation's publications have since taken up.

An act of the Choctaw Nation of 20 October 1882 made Tuskahoma the permanent seat of government. The nation's first capital after the Trail of Tears had been at Nanih Waiyah, two miles away, named after the sacred mound in Mississippi; later it had moved to Doaksville, Skullyville, Fort Towson and Boggy Depot, and in the Civil War to Armstrong Academy. The two-storey brick capitol with a French mansard roof, completed in 1884, held rooms for the Senate, the House of Representatives, the Supreme Court and the Principal Chief, and many called it the finest building in the Indian Territory.

A town grew up beside it, but in the mid-1880s the St. Louis and San Francisco Railway laid its tracks two miles to the south, where the trains could take water from the Kiamichi River. Business moved to the station, and the capitol precinct stood empty outside sessions of government. The Tuskahoma Female Academy, the nation's girls' school, opened nearby in 1892 under Peter J. Hudson and burned in 1925. The railway town prospered until commerce shifted to Clayton and elsewhere in the 20th century.

Tuskahoma is an unincorporated community and census-designated place in Pushmataha County; the 2020 census counted 102 inhabitants. The Choctaw Capitol Building is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the festival held on its grounds draws between 50,000 and 100,000 visitors.
tutankhamun: Tutankhamun was born in the reign of Akhenaten, during the Amarna Period. His original name, Tutankhaten or Tutankhuaten, meant living image of Aten, reflecting the shift to Atenism that characterised Akhenaten's reign. When he became king he married Ankhesenpaaten, one of Akhenaten's daughters, who later changed her name to Ankhesenamun. They had two daughters who died at or soon after birth and were buried with him in his tomb.

Tutankhamun became pharaoh between 8 and 9 years of age, after the short reigns of Akhenaten's successors Smenkhkare and Neferneferuaten, and he took the throne name Nebkheperure. At the start of his reign the court was still at Amarna and the Aten was still acknowledged, but his court was trying to reconcile Atenism with the traditional religion. Activity at Amarna decreased during the first four years, and given the king's age the reversals of Akhenaten's policies must have been instigated by his advisors. His restorations of cults were recorded on the Restoration Stela.
