He sought to restore diplomatic relations with other kingdoms, in particular with the Mitanni, and battles with Nubians and Asiatics were recorded in his mortuary temple at Thebes, both as Egyptian victories. He was one of the few pharaohs worshipped as a deity during their lifetime, as temples in Nubia and stelae at Karnak indicate. There are no surviving records of the circumstances of his death. Hawass and his team postulate that it resulted from a leg fracture, perhaps from a fall, combined with a severe malarial infection.

Tutankhamun's two known children were stillborn or died shortly after birth, and his death left no immediate heir. Ay, who performs the opening of the mouth ritual for him on the burial chamber wall, became pharaoh, and Horemheb, commander-in-chief of his armed forces, succeeded Ay. Horemheb completed the restoration of the traditional religion and had his own name inscribed on monuments that Tutankhamun had commissioned.

His tomb was unusually small for his status, and its entrance was lost under debris from later tombs and workers' houses. Howard Carter found it in 1922, with the patronage of George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon. It is the only royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings found in near-intact condition, with 5,398 items, among them a solid gold coffin, a face mask, thrones, bows and trumpets, and Carter took ten years to catalogue them. Rumours of a curse of the pharaohs followed the death of Carnarvon on 5 April 1923. In 1962 the Louvre held an exhibition of the treasures that drew 1.2 million visitors.
tutira-mai-nga-iwi: Huata wrote the song while driving from Wairoa, Hawke's Bay, to Napier with his children: passing Lake Tūtira, he sang the words and the children repeated them, learning it on the way. It spread as he performed it in churches and Bible classes. By the 1960s the Ministry of Education was publishing it for New Zealand schools without his consent and without crediting him, and after fifty years of use in schools his daughter revealed that some of the words had been printed incorrectly.

As with many older folk songs, there is some conjecture about the exact words, but it is generally agreed to be a song of unity, with the repeated refrain tātou tātou e, meaning all of us, all of us. New Zealanders often sing it at times when standing together and supporting one another is fitting; it was used, for example, to show support for the New Zealand Muslim community after the Christchurch mosque shootings.

In 2017 the New Zealand Rugby Union, in a campaign led by the police constable and former All Black Glen Osborne, urged fans to adopt the song as a rallying chant during the British and Irish Lions tour. The attempt was poorly received by All Blacks fans, the Lions supporters changed the chorus to Lions, Lions, and a New Zealand sports writer judged it an inappropriate choice.

On 28 May 2020 a performance by navy, army and air force bands of New Zealand and the United States was published online, with the permission of Huata's whānau. On 12 November 2022, at Eden Park in Auckland, Ruby Tui of the Black Ferns led the crowd in singing it to celebrate the team's 34-31 World Cup final win over England.
tutuila: Tutuila is part of the Samoan Islands and is the third largest island of that chain. It lies roughly 4,000 kilometres northeast of Brisbane and over 1,200 kilometres northeast of Fiji. It is a volcanic island of early Pliocene age, about 33 kilometres long and little more than 4.8 kilometres across at its widest point. The highest point is Matafao Peak at 653 metres.

Pago Pago Harbor, a large natural harbour, divides the island into two parts. The island has six terrestrial and three marine ecosystems, with lowland and montane rain forest. The National Park of American Samoa, established in 1988, protects part of the forest and coast, including two species of flying fox that Samoans regard as guardians of the forest and its people.

Polynesians first reached Samoa around 1000 BCE, and by 600 BCE they had a settlement on Tutuila at Tula. Around 1200 CE, in the reign of Momo, the tenth Tuʻi Tonga, the Tongans invaded and occupied Tutuila and other Samoan islands for nearly two centuries. Under the paramount chief Malietoa the Samoans rose against them, and Fau'au of Pago Pago led the local resistance that expelled the Tongans from Tutuila.

Jacob Roggeveen encountered the Samoan Islands in 1722, and Louis Antoine de Bougainville named them the Navigator Islands in 1768. Whalers and Protestant missionaries arrived in the early 19th century, and traders developed Apia on Upolu rather than Pago Pago as their station.

The US Navy saw Pago Pago as an ideal refuelling station for the new San Francisco-to-Sydney steamship service, and the United States Congress ratified a treaty for it in 1878. Great Britain and Germany also had interests, and in 1879 the three powers formed a tripartite government. Their dispute led in 1899 to a division of the islands: the eastern islands, including Tutuila, became American Samoa and the western ones came under European control. The US flag was raised on Tutuila on 17 April 1900.

Tutuila holds about 95 per cent of the population of American Samoa and some 68 per cent of its land. The capital, Pago Pago, stands on the harbour, and Pago Pago International Airport is on the island. American Samoa is an unincorporated and unorganised territory of the United States, and more than 90 per cent of its land is communally owned. Relics of the Second World War, including guns and bunkers around the harbour, survive on the island.
tutul-xiu: The name Tutul-Xiu was said to be of Mexican, that is Nahuatl, origin, xiu meaning a herbaceous plant. Later accounts credit the Cocom family with founding Mayapan, but earlier accounts make the Xiu its first rulers, dominant for its first century, c. 1180 to 1280. In this period more stelae were dedicated to mark the ends of k'atun periods, perhaps on the model of Uxmal, and Mayapan worked with Uxmal and with Chichen Itza, which was by then in decline.

The Xiu gradually lost Mayapan, which by 1300 was in the hands of the Cocom and their Canul mercenaries, and around 1400 the Cocom expelled many Xiu from the city. In 1441 the Xiu rose against them: a party led by Ah Xiu Xupan, aided by mercenaries from elsewhere in Mexico, killed every member of the Cocom in Mayapan, the only notable survivor being away on a trading mission. Excavations have found burnt buildings, ceremonial deposits and human bones from this time. The leading families left to found new settlements and Yucatán broke into 18 petty kingdoms, the Chel at Tecoh, the surviving Cocom at Tibolon and the Xiu at Mani.

When the Spanish came, the Xiu were among their most willing allies, while the Capul and Cocom were among their fiercest opponents. The Xiu later said they had submitted because prophecies foretold the arrival of the Spanish, but their cooperation seems to have been driven by hope of Spanish help against the Cocom. Their first envoys met Francisco de Montejo the Younger at Tuchi-caan around 1539.

The province took its name from the ruling family, but many other lineages lived in it, among them the Na, Ku, Dzul, Tun, Cime and Uluac. A Spanish mission was set up at Mani, the Xiu capital, in 1547, and the Mani Land Treaty of 1557 settled a border dispute between the Xiu of Mani, the Cocom of Sotuta and the Copul.
tutush-i: Abu Sa’id Taj al-Dawla Tutush was a brother of the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah I. In 1077 Malik-Shah appointed him to take over the governorship of Syria. Later that year Tutush reached Aleppo, then ruled by the Mirdasid emir Sabiq ibn Mahmud, and began a siege of the city that lasted three months.

Malik-Shah later sent Tutush to Damascus to help Atsiz ibn Uvaq, an independent Turkish warlord who had taken the city in 1076 and was besieged by Fatimid forces. Once the siege had ended, Tutush had Atsiz executed and installed himself in Damascus. He went on to annex Sidon, Gibelacar, Tiberias, Ramla, Jaffa and Jerusalem, which he granted to another Seljuk commander, Artuk Bey.

He returned to besiege Aleppo, but reinforcements he had called from Malik-Shah were ambushed and routed at Wadi Butnan by Arab tribesmen led by the Kilabi chief Abu Za’ida, and the Aleppines raided his camp. In 1080 he seized Manbij, Azaz and other towns around Aleppo. In 1086 he defeated Suleiman ibn Qutalmish, a Seljuk who had established himself in Anatolia, at the battle of Ain Salm. Suleiman was killed and his son Kilic Arslan captured. Tutush occupied Aleppo except for its citadel in May 1086, but left for Damascus in October as Malik-Shah’s armies advanced. He also finished the Citadel of Damascus, begun under Atsiz.

Tutush took control of Syria in 1092 after Malik-Shah died, naming himself sultan. He captured Nisbis, Amida, Mayyafariqin and Mosul in Upper Mesopotamia, but returned in December 1093 when Bozan of Edessa and Harran and Aq Sunqur of Aleppo declared for his nephew, Sultan Berkyaruq. He defeated them at Tell Sultan in June or July 1094, where both were killed.

Tutush then marched east with his general Ali ibn Faramurz as far as Hamadan, and was defeated near Ray by Berkyaruq’s forces. He and Ali were killed on 25 February 1095, and his head was displayed in Baghdad. His son Duqaq inherited Damascus and Ridwan received Aleppo, splitting the realm; his youngest son Irtash was briefly ruler of Damascus in 1104.
tuul-river: The Tuul River, also called the Tula River and in older sources the Tola, is a river in central and northern Mongolia. It is 882.8 kilometres long and drains an area of 49,840 square kilometres. It originates in the Khan Khentii Strictly Protected Area in the Khentii Mountains, in the Erdene sum of Töv aimag, and travels southwest until it reaches the territory of Ulaanbaatar. Its water runs through the southern part of the capital and continues westward in large loops.

On meeting the border of Bulgan aimag it turns north and runs along that border. After it enters Selenge aimag it discharges into the Orkhon River near the sum centre of Orkhontuul sum. The Orkhon flows into the Selenge River, which flows into Russia and Lake Baikal. The Tuul also flows along the Khustain Nuruu National Park.

The Tuul is sacred to the Mongols and is generally called the Hatan Tuul, meaning Queen Tuul. In Old Turkic sources it appears as Toɣla ögüz. The Secret History of the Mongols, of 1240, frequently mentions a Black Forest of the Tuul River, where the palace of Ong Khan was located.

The river is typically frozen over from the middle of November through the middle of April. Willow forests grow along its banks, and the river is home to endangered species of sturgeon. In 2014 almost 100 million cubic metres of water were withdrawn from it for domestic, livestock, cropland and industrial use, making it the most used river in Mongolia.
tuva: Tuva lies at the geographical centre of Asia in southern Siberia, and its capital, Kyzyl, stands near the geographic centre of the continent. The republic is a mountain basin about 600 metres above sea level, encircled by the Sayan and Tannu-Ola ranges, and mountains and hills cover over 80 per cent of its territory. Its highest point is Mongun-Tayga, at 3,970 metres. There are over 8,000 rivers, including the upper course of the Yenisei. It borders Mongolia to the south.

The territory was controlled by a succession of powers, among them the Xiongnu, the Rouran Khaganate, the Tang dynasty, the Mongol Empire and the Yuan dynasty. From 1758 to 1911 Tuva was part of China's Qing dynasty, administered through Outer Mongolia. During the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 a separatist movement formed among the Tuvans, and on 17 April 1914 Tuva became a Russian protectorate as Uryankhay Krai. In 1918 and 1919 it was occupied by the White Russian troops of Alexander Kolchak, later by China, until the Bolsheviks expelled the Chinese in 1921.

On 14 August 1921 the Bolsheviks established the Tuvan People's Republic, popularly called Tannu-Tuva, formally independent between the World Wars. Its capital was renamed Kyzyl, meaning red, in 1926. A coup of 1929, carried out by five young Tuvans trained in Moscow, replaced Chairman Donduk Kuular, and Buddhist and Mongol influences were then curtailed. The Soviet Union annexed Tuva in 1944, with the approval of its Little Khural but without a referendum. Tuva signed the treaty creating the Russian Federation on 31 March 1992.

The Republic of Tyva is a republic of the Russian Federation, with 336,651 inhabitants at the 2021 census, more than a third of them in Kyzyl. Tuvans make up most of the population and speak the Tuvan language, a Turkic language. Tuvan and Russian are both official. Tuvan throat singing, in which the singer produces a fundamental tone and an overtone together, is a defining tradition. Tibetan Buddhism, first met in the 13th and 14th centuries, coexists with shamanism, which is preserved as part of traditional culture.
tuvalu: Tuvalu consists of three reef islands, Nanumanga, Niutao and Niulakita, and six true atolls, Funafuti, Nanumea, Nui, Nukufetau, Nukulaelae and Vaitupu, with a land area of only about 26 square kilometres. The islands lie west of the International Date Line and have poor soil. The highest point, on Niulakita, is 4.6 metres above sea level, and the islands are open to flooding in cyclones and storms. Rainwater harvesting is the principal source of fresh water. The name means eight standing together in Tuvaluan, because eight of the nine islands were inhabited.

The first inhabitants were Polynesians, part of a migration into the Pacific that began about 3,000 years ago, and there was frequent canoe voyaging between the nearer islands, including Samoa and Tonga. Álvaro de Mendaña sighted the islands on 16 January 1568, sailing past Nui, which he charted as Isla de Jesús because the previous day was the feast of the Holy Name. He made contact with the islanders but could not land.

Trading companies became active in the mid-19th century. John O'Brien was the first European to settle, as a trader on Funafuti in the 1850s, and he married Salai, the daughter of the paramount chief. British subjects in the islands came under the Western Pacific High Commission in 1877, and Captain Herbert Gibson of HMS Curacoa declared protectorates over each island between 9 and 16 October 1892. The United States Marine Corps landed on Funafuti on 2 October 1942, and the atoll became a base for attacks on the Gilbert Islands, occupied by Japan. Toaripi Lauti became the first prime minister on 1 October 1978, and Tuvalu joined the United Nations on 5 September 2000 as its 189th member.

Funafuti is the capital. The census of 12 December 2022 recorded 10,643 people, and Tuvaluan and English are the national languages. The Congregational Christian Church of Tuvalu is the state church, which in practice gives it the privilege of conducting special services on national occasions. Each island has its own high chief, called ulu-aliki, several sub-chiefs and a community council, the Falekaupule, the traditional assembly of elders. The country is a constitutional monarchy within the Commonwealth with no regular military forces.
tuvan-peoples-revolutionary-party: The party grew out of a conference of Tuvan revolutionaries that met under Soviet sponsorship on 29 October 1921 and formed an organisation bureau. It held single-party control over the government of the Tuvan People's Republic, founded the same year, as a vanguard party. Its first congress met on 28 February 1922, when the Tuvan People's Government was established.

Soviet dissatisfaction soon reshaped it. When the Second Congress convened on 6 July 1923, the existing party was dissolved and a new one organised in its place. The Fourth Congress followed in October 1925 and the Seventh in 1928, and the Central Committee was empowered to set up party cells and branches of the league of revolutionary youth across the country. A leading figure of these early years was Donduk Kuular.

At the Second Plenary Session of the Central Committee in 1929 the right-wing leadership, which had wanted to keep Tibetan Buddhism as a state religion against the proclaimed constitution, was destroyed. Under the watchword of antifeudal revolution, the Eighth Congress opened the way to socialist reconstruction through collectivisation. A rising in April and May 1930, described by the party as a counter-revolution of the Tuvan nobles and Russian kulak colonists, was put down by force.

The Central Committee then resolved to confiscate the property of the exploiter class and to collectivise agriculture, officially on a voluntary basis. Between 1929 and 1932, beginning with the Tuvan coup of 1929, the elements of the party that Stalin regarded as nationalist, Kuular among them, were purged, and Salchak Toka took over the leadership. In 1935 the Seventh Congress of the Comintern admitted the party as a sympathising party.
tuxtla-mountains: The Sierra de los Tuxtlas is a volcanic belt along the southeastern Gulf coast of Veracruz. Its highest peaks, Volcano Santa Marta and Volcano San Martín Tuxtla, both rise above 1,700 metres, and hundreds of smaller cinder cones dot the range. Extinct volcanoes include San Martin Pajapan, at 1,160 metres, and Cerro El Vigia, at 800 metres. The belt stands apart from the rest of Mexico's volcanoes: about 250 km separate it from the nearest volcano of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt to the west, and almost 330 km from the Central American Volcanic Belt to the southeast.

During the Early Formative period, from about 1500 BCE to about 400 BCE, the Olmec culture used the mountains as a source of basalt. The quarried stone was carried by raft along a network of rivers to sites in the Olmec heartland, where it was worked into monuments, the colossal heads among them. San Martín Tuxtla, a broad alkaline shield volcano with a summit one kilometre wide, is the only volcano of the belt active in recent times; it erupted in 1664 and again in May 1793.

The coast and the higher ground of the range lie within the Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve. Tropical rainforest covers the upper flanks of San Martín Tuxtla and Santa Marta, while the lower slopes are pasture and grassland. Species found nowhere else include the Tuxtla quail-dove, the endangered Volcan San Martin rainfrog and a giant scarab beetle, Dynastes moroni, described in 2005.
tvrda: Tvrđa stands on the right bank of the River Drava, where medieval Osijek had grown up as a trade and port settlement from the early 12th century on the road south from Pécs and Buda. Between 1526 and 1687 the town was ruled by the Ottomans, who added mosques but kept its layout; a stretch of their fortress wall, the Turkish Wall, survives beside the access road. Osijek was then known for the Suleiman Bridge, a wooden road on piers about 7 kilometres long to Darda, begun on 16 August 1526, burnt on the orders of Nikola VII Zrinski in 1664 and finally by Habsburg armies in 1686.

After Habsburg armies took Osijek in 1687, Louis William, Margrave of Baden-Baden, urged a new fort on Vauban's principles, and an Ottoman attack in October 1690 showed it could not wait. The first plan was Mathias von Kaiserfeld's of 1691. From August 1712, to designs by Maximilian Gosseau de Henef on the Dutch lowland model, engineers under General Johann Stephan von Beckers built barracks, headquarters, churches and monasteries within moats and bastions. Five bastions and two gates stood by 1715, three northern bastions followed by 1735, and the last gate in 1783. Covering 80 hectares, it was the largest fortress on the Ottoman border.

Churches replaced the mosques: the Franciscans consecrated theirs in 1732, and the Jesuits began St. Michael's in 1725. A Holy Trinity plague column rose on the main square in 1730. In 1786 Joseph II merged Tvrđa with the Upper and Lower Towns. After the Congress of Berlin of 1878 its military role faded, and most of the walls were demolished between 1923 and 1926 to make way for an electric tramway.

Only the northern wall with its water gate and parts of the first and eighth bastions remain, but the interior core is intact and holds churches, schools, faculties of the Josip Juraj Strossmayer University of Osijek and the Museum of Slavonia. About 90 per cent of its buildings were damaged in the war of 1991-95, and it was placed on the 1996 World Monuments Watch list. Tvrđa is on Croatia's tentative list for World Heritage status.
tvrtko-i-of-bosnia: Tvrtko was the elder son of Vladislav Kotromanić and Jelena Šubić, whose marriage was held in 1337. His uncle, the ban Stephen II, was succeeded by Tvrtko directly, although Vladislav was still alive; the reason is unclear. Tvrtko was about fifteen, so his father governed as regent, and after Vladislav's death in 1354 his mother Jelena replaced him. She travelled to Hungary to obtain the consent of Tvrtko's overlord, King Louis I, and held an assembly at Mile confirming the privileges of the nobles. In 1363 a conflict with Louis broke out, and the defence of the Srebrenik fortress marked his first victory over Hungary.

The Serbian Empire broke up into autonomous lordships after the accession of Uroš the Weak in December 1355. In 1373 Tvrtko and Lazar Hrebljanović, both backed by Louis, defeated Nicholas Altomanović, and Tvrtko took the upper Podrinje, Gacko and part of Polimlje with the Mileševa Monastery. A genealogy published in his new Serbian lands stressed his Nemanjić ancestry through his paternal grandmother Elizabeth, daughter of King Dragutin, and he was crowned king of Bosnia and Serbia in the autumn of 1377, probably on 26 October.

After Louis died on 11 September 1382, the unpopularity of the queens Mary and Elizabeth gave Tvrtko his opening. He took Kotor and Drijeva, and between 1385 and 1390 won large parts of Dalmatia and Croatia. In late August 1388 his army under Duke Vlatko Vuković defeated an Ottoman and Zetan force at Bileća. When the Battle of Kosovo was fought on 15 June 1389, he sent troops to help Lazar; after Lazar's successors accepted Ottoman suzerainty, his Serbian claim was only nominal. In May 1390 the Dalmatian cities and islands surrendered.

Tvrtko died on 10 March 1391, while negotiating peace with Sigismund of Hungary, and is buried at Mile beside Stephen II. He left at least one son, Tvrtko II, but a minor was not considered fit to rule, and Dabiša, a relative exiled for his part in a rebellion of 1366, was elected king; under him the realm began to decay.

Tvrtko is considered one of the leading medieval rulers of Bosnia, who left a country larger, stronger and more influential than the one he inherited, with a flourishing economy and new trade centres. The historian Vladimir Ćorović saw him less as an ambitious conqueror than an able statesman, who appeared to Serbians as a legitimate heir and to Croatians as the preferable ruler.
twelve-articles: On 6 March 1525 about 50 representatives of the Upper Swabian peasant bands, the Baltringer Haufen, the Allgäuer Haufen and the Lake Constance Haufen, met in Memmingen to agree a common stance against the Swabian League. A day later, after difficult negotiations, they proclaimed the Christian Association, a confederation of the Upper Swabian peasants. At further meetings on 15 and 20 March they adopted the Twelve Articles together with a Federal Order (Bundesordnung), a model for a federal order built on the village community.

The text is usually traced to Sebastian Lotzer, a journeyman furrier and lay preacher of Memmingen, who is believed to have drafted it between 27 February and 1 March 1525; the town's reformer Christoph Schappeler is generally credited with the preamble and its theological grounding. About twenty-five villages around Memmingen had already presented grievances, and historians also note likenesses to the demands of Joß Fritz in the Bundschuh uprisings of 1513.

The first article asked that each community elect its preacher and dismiss him if he misbehaved, and that he preach the gospel without human additions. Others asked that preachers be paid from the great tithe and the small tithe abolished, and claimed the right to hunt, fowl and fish. They sought compulsory labour limited to what earlier generations had owed, fines judged by the old written law rather than at will, commons returned and the death duty abolished. The twelfth article offered to withdraw any demand shown from what is written to be against the word of God.

The Articles were printed more than 25,000 times within two months, and copies spread throughout Germany. Martin Luther told the lords that some articles were so just that they shamed them before God and the world, but he urged the peasants to keep the peace, and after rebels under Jäcklein Rohrbach killed Count Ludwig Helferich von Helfenstein at Weinsberg he called in May 1525 for the rebels' destruction. Some historians regard the Articles as the first draft of human rights and civil liberties in continental Europe since the Roman Empire, and peasants raised some of the same demands again in the March Revolution of 1848.
twelver-shiism: The term Twelver rests on the belief that twelve male descendants of the family of Muhammad, from Ali ibn Abi Talib to Muhammad al-Mahdi, are Imams with religious and political authority. The division of Islam into Shia and Sunni traces back to the crisis over the succession to Muhammad. According to Tabatabai the word Shia first referred to the partisans of Ali at the time of Muhammad himself. Ali moved the capital of Islam to Kufa and fought Mu'awiyah, who refused him allegiance. The death of Husayn played an important part in the spread of Shi'ism in Iraq, Yemen and Persia.

Twelvers believe that the Twelve Imams are divinely appointed spiritual and political successors to Muhammad, with special knowledge and authority to guide the Muslim community. They hold that Muhammad and the Imams must be free from error and sin, a doctrine called Ismah. Twelvers differ from the Isma'ili and Nizari branches in the number of Imams and the line of succession, and in rejecting the abrogation of Sharia laws. Their theology rests on the Quran and on hadiths from Muhammad and the Imams, especially Jafar al-Sadiq, and has been shaped by events such as the Battle of Karbala and the occultation of the twelfth Imam.

Many Twelvers add Ali is the viceregent of God to the Shahada. Their jurisprudence is called Ja'fari. The Usuli school accepts ijtihad, or rational effort, while the Akhbari school relies on the hadith of the Prophet and the Imams alone.

In the 10th century Baghdad was the centre of Mu'tazila theologians, whose ideas affected Shia thinkers. Abu Sahl al-Nawbakhti fused Mu'tazili theology with Imami thought, while Ibn Babawayh of Qom answered them from the hadiths. Al-Shaykh al-Mufid, Sharif al-Murtaza and Shaykh al-Tusi were the leading figures of the Baghdad school, and al-Muhaqqiq al-Hilli of the school of Hillah brought ijtihad into jurisprudence.

In 1501 Isma'il I took power in Iran, founded the Safavid dynasty and declared Twelverism the official religion of his empire, although most of the larger cities were Sunni. Shia scholars were brought in to set up seminaries, and religious authorities were appointed for all major cities. Twelver Shi'ism is the largest branch of Shia Islam, and Iran is the only country where it is the state religion.
twentieth-dynasty-of-egypt: The Twentieth Dynasty was the third and last dynasty of the Egyptian New Kingdom. With the Nineteenth Dynasty it forms the Ramesside period, so called because so many rulers bore the name Ramesses. After the death of Queen Twosret, last pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty, Egypt entered a period of civil war, as the Elephantine stela of Setnakhte attests. Her fate is uncertain: she may have died peacefully or been overthrown by Setnakhte, who was probably middle-aged. The cause of the war is unknown because historical records are lost.

Setnakhte ended the conflict and founded the dynasty. He stabilised Egypt and may have driven off an attempted invasion by the Sea Peoples. He ruled for about three or four years before his son Ramesses III succeeded him.

Ramesses III defeated a Libyan invasion in his fifth year and, in his eighth, a confederacy of Sea Peoples, including the Denyen, Tjekker, Peleset, Shardana and Weshesh, in the Battle of Djahy and the Battle of the Delta. In his twenty-ninth year the workmen of Set Maat, now Deir el-Medina, held the first labour strike recorded in history when their rations could not be supplied. A harem conspiracy in which Queen Tiye sought to put her son Pentawer on the throne ended in the king's death, and his heir Ramesses IV had about thirty conspirators put to death.

Later reigns were weaker. Ramesses V ruled no more than four years, and workmen at Set Maat had to stop work at times for fear of raiders, presumed Libyan. Under Ramesses IX, tomb robbery trials found many tombs broken into. Three sons of Ramesses III assumed power as Ramesses IV, VI and VIII, and droughts, low Nile floods, famine and corruption limited the capacity of any king.

A consistent theme was the loss of pharaonic power to the High Priests of Amun. The Wilbour Papyrus, thought to date from Ramesses V, shows that most land in Egypt was controlled by the Temple of Amun, which had complete control of finances. Under Ramesses XI, the last king, the High Priests of Amun at Thebes became the de facto rulers of Upper Egypt, while Smendes controlled Lower Egypt even before the king's death.

A period of chaos followed his death, ended by Smendes, who founded the Twenty-First Dynasty at Tanis. The dynasty is generally considered to mark the beginning of the decline of ancient Egypt, coinciding with the Bronze Age Collapse and the onset of the Third Intermediate Period. Although it defended Egypt against the Sea Peoples, its trade routes were damaged as most trading partners had been destroyed.
twenty-fifth-dynasty-of-egypt: The Twenty-fifth Dynasty, also called the Nubian Dynasty and the Napatans after their capital Napata, was the last dynasty of the Third Intermediate Period. It originated in the Kingdom of Kush, in present-day northern Sudan, and most of its kings saw Napata as their spiritual homeland. The dynasty was highly Egyptianized, using the Egyptian language and writing and showing an unusual devotion to Egypt's religious, artistic and literary traditions. Scholars have criticised the term Black Pharaohs, because it suggests that other dynasties did not share southern origins.

Piye, spelled Piankhi in older works, invaded Egypt from Napata and recorded his victory on the Stele of Victory, which names him Pharaoh of all Egypt. Tradition holds that Shabaka brought the Nile Valley under Kushite rule, but recent archaeological evidence shows that he ruled after Shebitku, not before. Shabaka restored monuments and temples and moved the capital to Memphis.

Taharqa's reign was prosperous, with a large Nile flood and abundant crops. He gave gold to the temple of Amun at Kawa, built or restored works at Jebel Barkal, Kawa, Qasr Ibrim and Karnak, and raised the largest pyramid in the Nubian region at Nuri. The imperial ambitions of Assyria made war inevitable. Esarhaddon invaded Egypt in 674 BCE and was defeated, according to Babylonian records, but in 671 BCE he conquered northern Egypt and captured Memphis. Ashurbanipal later advanced as far south as Thebes, and Taharqa retreated to Nubia, where he died in 664 BCE.

His successor Tantamani sailed north from Napata to Thebes, where he was ritually installed as king, and reconquered Egypt as far north as Memphis. Psamtik I returned with Ashurbanipal, Tantamani fled to Nubia, and the Assyrians sacked Thebes in 663 BCE. Psamtik I became the first ruler of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty and in 656 BCE sent a large fleet south to Thebes, peacefully taking control of Upper Egypt.

The dynasty ruled Egypt for less than a century, but it holds an important place in Egyptian history for its restoration of traditional Egyptian values, culture, art and architecture. It revived the building of pyramids for dead rulers, at El-Kurru and Nuri, about 1,000 years after Egyptian burial methods had changed. Its successors continued their kingdom in Nubia at Napata and then at Meroë. Psamtik II destroyed the monuments of the Kushite kings in Egypt, erasing their names, and sent an army to Nubia in 592 BCE. Even so, the memory of Shabaka survived, and Egyptians named a street after him in Late Period Memphis.
twenty-seventh-dynasty-of-egypt: The Twenty-seventh Dynasty, also called the First Egyptian Satrapy, was a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire between 525 and 404 BCE. Cambyses II founded it after defeating the last pharaoh of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, Psamtik III, at the Battle of Pelusium in May 525 BCE, and was crowned pharaoh that summer at the latest. Egypt was joined with Cyprus and Phoenicia to form the sixth satrapy of the empire, with Aryandes as satrap. Under Cambyses the resources of the traditional temples diminished: a decree in demotic script limited the resources of all temples except those of Memphis, Heliopolis and Wenkhem.

After Cambyses died in 522 BCE, Darius I took the throne. Late in 522 or early in 521 BCE a local prince rebelled as Pharaoh Petubastis III; Polyaenus blames oppressive taxation by Aryandes. Darius reportedly codified Egypt's laws, completed a canal from the Bitter Lakes to the Red Sea and supported Egyptian temples, earning a reputation for religious tolerance. Aryandes was executed in 497 BCE, most likely for trying to issue his own coinage. Under Xerxes I, Egypt rebelled again; he installed his brother Achaemenes as satrap, increased supply requirements and stopped funding Egyptian monuments. In 460 BCE the Libyan chief Inaros II, substantially assisted by the Athenians, killed Achaemenes and took Memphis, but the Persian general Megabyzus defeated him in 454 BCE.

Near the end of the reign of Darius II a rebellion led by Amyrtaeus took place. In 405 BCE, with the help of Cretan mercenaries, he expelled the Persians from Memphis and declared himself pharaoh the next year, ending the dynasty. Artaxerxes II planned an expedition to retake Egypt but abandoned it because of trouble with his brother Cyrus the Younger. Three native dynasties, the 28th, 29th and 30th, then ruled until Artaxerxes III reconquered Egypt in 343 BCE, a brief second period known as the Thirty-first Dynasty. A 2019 analysis by H. P. Colburn finds the Achaemenid legacy in Egypt significant.
twinkle-twinkle-little-star: The words of Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star come from an early nineteenth-century English poem, The Star, by Jane Taylor (1783–1824). It is written in couplets and was first published in London in 1806 in Rhymes for the Nursery, a collection of poems by Jane and her sister Ann Taylor (1782–1866).

Where Jane Taylor was when she wrote it is contested, with Colchester and Chipping Ongar each asserting a claim. Ann Taylor, however, wrote in The Autobiography and Other Memorials of Mrs. Gilbert that Jane first saw the village of Ongar in the summer of 1810, when she noticed a signpost during a picnic in Epping Forest, four years after the poem had appeared.

The poem has five stanzas, though only the first is widely known. It addresses a star as a diamond in the sky and describes how its light guides the traveller in the dark, and the speaker wonders what it is. When it is sung, the first two lines of the whole poem are repeated as a refrain after each stanza. The words were first published with the tune in 1838, in The Singing Master: First Class Tune Book. The tune is the French melody Ah! vous dirai-je, maman, first published in 1761 and later arranged by several composers, among them Mozart in his Twelve Variations on Ah vous dirai-je, Maman.

The melody serves other nursery rhymes, including the ABC Song and Baa, Baa, Black Sheep. The text has been varied many times. Frederick Marryat's 1840 novel Poor Jack has a version beginning Pretty little twinkling star, and Mildred J. Hill's Song Stories for the Kindergarten of 1896 adds a stanza about the rising sun that makes the star fade from sight.

Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland has the Mad Hatter recite a parody, Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Bat, and its opening lines begin the traditional murder ballad Duncan and Brady. There is also a version that uses synonyms from Roget's Thesaurus, and the song can be played as a singing game.
two-ewalds: The two priests were companions from Northumbria who bore the same name and were told apart by the colour of their hair and complexion, the Black and the White. Like many of their time they spent several years as students in the schools of Ireland. Hewald the Black was the more learned of the two, though both were known for holiness of life. They seem to have known Saint Willibrord, the Apostle of Friesland, and some sources count them among his eleven companions, but they more probably set out from England after his departure, hoping to convert their own kin in Old Saxony.

Their mission lay in the country of the Old Saxons, later part of Westphalia and covered by the dioceses of Münster, Osnabrück and Paderborn. They lodged with the steward of a Saxon ealdorman, a satrapa in Bede's word; Bede noted that the Old Saxons had no king but several ealdormen who cast lots for leadership in war. The steward promised to take them to his lord, to whom they said they had a message of great importance.

Suspecting that they meant to convert their overlord and destroy their temples, the pagan Saxons seized them. Hewald the White was killed quickly by the sword, while Hewald the Black was tortured and torn limb from limb, and both bodies were thrown into the Rhine. This is understood to have happened on 3 October at Aplerbeck, now a district of Dortmund, where a chapel stands. The ealdorman, angry and fearing reprisals, had the killers put to death and their villages burned.

Christian sources tell of miracles: the bodies carried forty miles against the stream under a heavenly light, and a vision that led the monk Tilmon to find and bury them. Pepin, Duke of Austrasia, had them enshrined in the church of St. Kunibert in Cologne. At the opening of the shrine in 1074 Archbishop Anno of Cologne gave the heads to Frederick, Bishop of Münster; those relics were probably destroyed by the Anabaptists in 1534. Until Saint Boniface was killed in 754 they were the last missionaries martyred in the region, and their feast on 3 October is kept in the dioceses of Cologne and Münster.
two-treatises-of-government: Locke's full title announces that in the former treatise the false principles and foundation of Sir Robert Filmer and his followers are detected and overthrown, while the latter is an essay concerning the true original, extent and end of civil government. Peter Laslett showed that the bulk of the writing belonged to the Exclusion Crisis, when Lord Shaftesbury, Locke's mentor and patron and leader of the Whigs, introduced a bill to bar James, the Catholic-convert brother of Charles II, from the throne.

Locke was driven into Dutch exile in 1683. In the preface Locke says the purpose is to justify the accession of William III, but it is more likely that the Glorious Revolution of 1688 gave him a chance to publish an existing manuscript. He did not acknowledge the work until just before his death.

The book was first published anonymously in December 1689. Locke was dissatisfied with the many errors and corrected the third edition by hand. More than half of his original draft, which lay between the two treatises, was irretrievably lost, and the First Treatise breaks off in mid-sentence.

The First Treatise refutes Filmer's Patriarcha, which held that Adam as father had unlimited power over his children and that this authority passed down through the generations. Locke argues that fatherhood could confer authority only by begetting, which cannot be transmitted because only God creates life.

The Second Treatise begins with a state of nature, a condition of perfect freedom and equality under the law of nature, and holds that civil society was created for the protection of property, by which Locke means life, liberty and estate. Legitimate government rests on the consent of the majority, and a legislature that takes away the property of the people or reduces them to slavery puts itself in a state of war with them, which gives them a right to revolution.

The Two Treatises were somewhat neglected at first. Of about 200 tracts on the legitimacy of the Glorious Revolution published between 1689 and 1694, only three mention Locke. They were not widely read until the 1760s. Mark Goldie names 1701 and the Kentish petition as the moment their ideas entered public debate, notably through Daniel Defoe.

Their influence on the American Revolution is disputed. Phrases in the Declaration of Independence echo them, and Jefferson wrote that Bacon, Locke and Newton had laid the foundation of the physical and moral sciences, but Bernard Bailyn and Gordon S. Wood stress classical republicanism, and Garry Wills Scottish moral philosophy. The book is a key text in the theory of liberalism.
tyana: Tyana lay in Cappadocia, at the foot of the Taurus Mountains near the Cilician Gates, and the district around it was known in Classical Antiquity as Tyanitis. The name came down through several languages: Tūwanuwa in the Hittite Empire, Tuwana in Luwian, Tuḫana in Neo-Assyrian Akkadian and Tyana in Greek and Latin. According to later Hittite sources the city was an important cult centre, whose local gods were the Storm-god Tarḫunzas of Tūwanuwa and his consort Šaḫḫaššara.

Tūwanuwa first appears in Hittite texts. The Telipinu Proclamation lists it among the territories conquered by Labarna I, the 17th-century BCE founder of the Old Kingdom. Under Tudhaliya III it became a border town after Arzawa invaded the Lower Land, and the prince Suppiluliuma recaptured it and used it as a base to reconquer the region. After the collapse of the Hittite Empire it became the centre of the Luwian-speaking kingdom of Tuwana, the largest and most prominent of the southern Tabalian states. Its kings, probably one dynasty, included Warpalawas II, who offered tribute to the Neo-Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III in 738 and 737 BCE. Sargon II later placed Tuwana under an Assyrian governor.

Tyana was an important Persian administrative centre, mentioned by Xenophon in the Anabasis. In the Hellenistic period it was renamed Eusebeia near the Taurus, probably after Ariarathes V Eusebes refounded it, and was, after Mazaca, the second most important city in Cappadocia. Under Roman rule it was among the most Hellenised cities of the region and was the reputed birthplace of the philosopher Apollonius of Tyana. Under Caracalla it became a colony, and the emperor Aurelian took it in 272 after it had sided with Shapur and then with Queen Zenobia of Palmyra. In 372 Valens made it capital of Cappadocia Secunda.

After the Muslim conquests the Byzantine frontier ran along the Taurus, and Tyana was raided in 708, 806 and 831. The Umayyads sacked it in 708 after a long siege. Harun al-Rashid took it in 806 and began to make it a military base, and Al-Abbas ibn al-Ma'mun razed it in 831 and rebuilt it three years later, until the campaign was abandoned after al-Ma'mun's death in 833. It declined after 933. Tyana was a bishopric from 325 and a metropolitan see until the fourteenth century.

The site corresponds to the modern town of Kemerhisar in Niğde Province, Turkey. Ruins of the Byzantine city are still visible, and in 2020 excavations uncovered an octagonal church and coins of the fourth century.
tyburn: Tyburn was a manor of Middlesex, one of two served by the parish of Marylebone, and took its name from the Tyburn Brook, a tributary of the River Westbourne; Teo Bourne means boundary stream. The Domesday Book of 1086 records it with eight households, held before and after the Norman Conquest by the nuns of Barking Abbey. It was bounded by two Roman roads, the modern Edgware Road and Oxford Street, whose junction was marked by Oswulf's Stone, which gave its name to the Ossulstone Hundred. In 1236 the City of London contracted with Gilbert de Sandford to draw water from the Tyburn Springs for its first piped supply.

The first recorded execution took place in 1196, when William Fitz Osbert, leader of a popular revolt in London, was dragged behind a horse to Tyburn and hanged. Executions for London and Middlesex were moved there from Smithfield in the 1400s, and in 1537 Henry VIII hanged leaders of the Pilgrimage of Grace there. The Tyburn Tree, a wooden triangle on three legs, was put up in 1571, and its first victim was the Catholic John Story on 1 June 1571. On 23 June 1649 it hanged 24 prisoners at once, and in January 1661 the bodies of Oliver Cromwell, Henry Ireton and John Bradshaw were hanged on it on the orders of the Cavalier Parliament.

The condemned rode from Newgate in an open cart, about three miles that could take three hours, stopping for a last drink at the Bowl in St Giles. Crowds of thousands watched, the wealthy from paid stands, with traders, pickpockets and surgeons seeking bodies for dissection. A ride to Tyburn meant going to be hanged. Movable gallows replaced the fixed ones in 1759, and the last hanging, of the highwayman John Austin, took place on 3 November 1783; executions then moved to Newgate.

The site of the Tyburn Tree lies near Marble Arch, where three oak trees planted in 2014 on a traffic island at the junction of Edgware Road and Bayswater Road surround a roundel inscribed The site of Tyburn Tree. The Tyburn Convent remembers the Catholic martyrs executed there.
tycho-brahe: Tycho was born Tyge Ottesen Brahe on 14 December 1546 at his family's seat at Knutstorp in Scania, then Danish, the oldest of twelve siblings. He was heir to several of Denmark's most influential noble families, and both his grandfathers and all his great-grandfathers had served on the king's Privy Council. In 1566 he went to study at the University of Rostock. On 29 December of that year he lost part of his nose in a sword duel with his third cousin Manderup Parsberg, after a drunken quarrel over who was the better mathematician, and he wore a prosthetic nose for the rest of his life. His family had expected him to enter politics or law but supported his choice of the sciences.

Tycho devoted himself to more accurate instruments, enlarging the sextant and the quadrant, and mounted them underground on the bedrock once he realised that wind and the movement of buildings affected them. King Frederick II granted him an estate on Hven and money to build Uraniborg, the first large observatory in Christian Europe. In De nova stella of 1573 he refuted the Aristotelian belief in an unchanging celestial realm, and he showed that comets were not atmospheric phenomena. He could not reconcile Copernican heliocentrism with Aristotelian physics, so he devised a system in which the Sun and Moon orbit the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun.

After Frederick's death in 1588 Tycho's influence at court declined, and in 1597 he was forced by the new king to leave Denmark. He was invited to Prague, where he became imperial astronomer and built an observatory at Benátky nad Jizerou.

Tycho fell ill after a banquet in Prague and died eleven days later, on 24 October 1601, aged 54. Before dying he urged Johannes Kepler to finish the Rudolphine Tables using Tycho's own planetary system. Kepler used Tycho's records of the motion of Mars to deduce his laws of planetary motion. Tycho's planetary model was soon discredited, but his observations were an essential contribution to the Scientific Revolution. Danish scholarship often depicted him as a mediocre scholar and a traitor to the nation, but from the second half of the 20th century scholars reassessed his significance.
tydings-mcduffie-act: A first attempt to fix a date for independence, the Hare–Hawes–Cutting Act of 1933, was passed by Congress over President Hoover's veto but needed the consent of the Philippine Senate. Its President, Manuel L. Quezon, persuaded the senators to reject it because it would have let the United States keep military bases in the islands permanently. In 1934 Quezon led a Philippine Independence mission to Washington, which lobbied Congress for a new bill. Written by Senator Millard Tydings of Maryland and Representative John McDuffie of Alabama, it was signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on 24 March 1934.

The act set a procedure for drafting a constitution of the Commonwealth within two years, laid down provisions it had to contain, and required its approval by the US president and by Filipinos. Until independence the United States could keep military forces in the islands and call all Philippine forces into its service, and within two years after independence the president could negotiate over naval reservations and fuelling stations. The act also reclassified all Filipinos, including those living in the United States, as aliens for immigration purposes, with a quota of 50 immigrants a year; until then they had been US nationals, free to migrate but denied naturalisation.

Immigration in fact ran well above the quota, as agricultural lobbies such as the Hawaiian sugar planters won leave to bring in more male Filipino farm workers. The act extended the Asian-exclusion policy of the Immigration Act of 1924 to the islands, so that a Filipino in the United States who went home on a visit might never be allowed back, and it led to the Filipino Repatriation Act. The Luce–Celler Act of 1946 raised the quota to 100 a year and opened naturalisation to Filipinos. President Harry S. Truman's Proclamation 2695 of 4 July 1946 recognised the independence of the Philippines.
tyendinaga-mohawk-territory: The territory, Kenhtè:ke in Mohawk, is the main reserve of the Mohawks of the Bay of Quinte First Nation, east of Belleville and near the site of the former Mohawk village of Ganneious. The official history of the Mohawks of the Bay of Quinte holds that it was the birthplace of the Great Peacemaker, a founder of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. For much of the 18th century the land was home to the Mississauga.

The settlers came from Fort Hunter, New York. Their chief, John Deseronto, a Loyalist captain, chose the site against the wishes of Joseph Brant, who preferred the Grand River, and of the officials Frederick Haldimand and Sir John Johnson. On 22 May 1784 about 20 families, some 100 to 125 people, landed after canoeing from Lachine, an arrival re-enacted each year. On 1 April 1793 Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe granted them a tract of 12 by 13 miles, affirmed in the Simcoe Deed. A feud in which Isaac Hill's followers killed two of Deseronto's relatives was settled at a council in September 1800.

In the early 19th century the government leased Mohawk land for timber without sharing the payments, and from 1820 to 1843 let Loyalist settlers onto the territory despite Mohawk appeals, so that two-thirds of it passed into private ownership. An 800-acre tract sold around 1836 to Deseronto's grandson John Culbertson became the town of Deseronto; the Mohawk have called the sale illegal since the 1830s, and the Culbertson Tract claim was heard by the Federal Court in 2013. The physician Oronhyatekha lived and worked here from the 1860s.

Four Federal Indian Day Schools opened in 1882 and 1883; these and the later Quinte Mohawk Indian Day School are covered by the class action of former students over abuse. In 1974 the community opened its own Quinte Mohawk School, after control of education passed to First Nations. In February 2020 residents blockaded a railway line for nearly a month in solidarity with the Wetʼsuwetʼen hereditary chiefs, until the Ontario Provincial Police made arrests on 24 February.

Christ Church, a Gothic chapel built in 1843, was designated Her Majesty's Chapel Royal of the Mohawk in 2004. The territory is home to the First Nations Technical Institute, founded in 1985, and to Tsi Tyónnheht Onkwawén:na, which works to keep the Mohawk language alive.
tylos: The name Tylos is thought to be a Hellenisation of the Semitic Tilmun, from Dilmun. In the classical era the island was a centre of maritime trade and pearling in the Erythraean Sea, and from the 6th to the 3rd century BCE it was part of the Persian Empire. After the conquest of Persia by Alexander the Great, his admiral Nearchus led an expedition that reached the island, and Androsthenes of Thasos, who served under him, left an extensive account of it in the Periplus of India. Later writers drew on it, among them the botanist Theophrastus, who described the island as a rich source of cotton and timber.

The Greek geographer Strabo named islands in the Persian Gulf Tyre and Arad, the latter now Muharraq, and recorded a local legend that they were the mother cities of the Phoenicians, and Herodotus reports a Tyrian tradition that the Phoenicians came from the Persian Gulf. The paired names have been much discussed as possible signs of colonisation in one direction or the other, but there is little evidence of any occupation of Bahrain at the time such a migration would have taken place.

Whether Bahrain belonged to the Seleucid Empire is not known, though the site of Qalat Al Bahrain has been proposed as a Seleucid base. Tylos was part of the Hellenised world: Aramaic was in everyday use, while the upper classes spoke Greek. Local coins show a seated Zeus, who may have been worshipped as a form of the Arabian sun-god Shams, and the island held Greek athletic contests. As Seleucid power waned it passed to Mesene, the kingdom founded by Hyspaosines in 129 BCE, which ruled it until the 2nd century CE, through a strategos and later, under King Meredates, a satrap.

In the 3rd century CE the Sassanids succeeded the Parthians as overlords of Mesene, and Bahrain was later incorporated into the Sassanid province of Mazon on the southern shore of the Gulf. By the 5th century it was a centre of Nestorian Christianity with an episcopal see at Samahij, and in 410, according to the synodal records of the Syriac church, a bishop named Batai was excommunicated there. A shark deity called Awal was also worshipped, and for many centuries afterwards the islands were known as Awal.
tynwald: Tradition dates Tynwald to 979, and the Manx people marked its millennium in 1979, but the year was picked arbitrarily by officials and no evidence shows that such an assembly met then. The available historical evidence points to the 13th century. The first record of the place-name occurs in the Chronicles of Mann of the 13th and 14th centuries, and the first description of the role and composition of an assembly held on the site dates from the early 15th century. The name derives from the Old Norse þingvǫllr, meeting place of the thing, or assembly, as in Iceland's Þingvellir.

Tynwald originally comprised only the 24 members of the House of Keys, four for each of the six sheadings of the island. The earliest surviving record of the Keys dates from 1417. Membership was for life, the remaining members chose any replacement, and seats generally passed down through leading families. In 1600 the Keys became a permanent body, and the power to make new laws developed from their role of declaring the ancient common law around 1610.

The island fell to Parliamentary forces in October 1651, and Tynwald met only sporadically. After the Restoration the Lords of Mann returned and the Keys lost power. In 1737 Tynwald's agreement became required for all taxation, but in 1765 the Lord of Mann sold his rights to the British Crown, and Tynwald was left with little power and no money. A Royal Commission was appointed in 1791, after the Keys petitioned for a new elected parliament. In 1866 legislation provided for some members to be elected for the first time. Marion Shimmin was the first woman elected, at a by-election in 1933.

Tynwald has two branches, the directly elected House of Keys and the indirectly chosen Legislative Council, which together sit as Tynwald Court. The Keys originate most legislation and the Council acts as a revising chamber. If the Council rejects a bill against the Keys' wishes, the Keys may repass it without the Council's approval.

On Tynwald Day, usually 5 July, the court meets in the open air at Tynwald Hill at St John's, presided over by the Lieutenant Governor unless the monarch as Lord of Mann, or a representative of the Royal Family, is present. All laws are promulgated there in both Manx and English and petitions are received. An Act not promulgated at St John's within 18 months of passage becomes void.
typewriter: The typewriter was invented in small steps by many people working independently or in competition over several decades, as the automobile, the telephone and the telegraph were. Historians have estimated that some form of it was invented 52 times. The Hansen Writing Ball, invented by Rasmus Malling-Hansen of Denmark in 1865, went into commercial production in 1870 and was the first typewriter sold. It printed only capital letters and was still reported in use in European offices in 1909.

Each key of a typewriter causes one character to be printed on paper by striking an inked ribbon against the page with a type element. The first commercially successful machine was patented in 1868 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, by Christopher Latham Sholes, Frank Haven Hall, Carlos Glidden and Samuel W. Soule. The clockmaker and machinist Matthias Schwalbach made the working prototype.

Sholes and James Densmore bought out the others and agreed with E. Remington and Sons, then known for sewing machines, to sell it as the Sholes and Glidden Type-Writer, which gave the machine its name. By about 1910 the manual typewriter had a fairly standard design of typebars striking a ribbon against a cylindrical platen.

Manufacturers at first found it hard to sell. Buyers compared a Remington costing 125 dollars with a pen costing a penny, and some recipients of typed letters felt insulted. Makers trained customers and referred typists to employers, and business colleges began to teach typing. Remington assumed the machine would be used for taking dictation and operated by a woman, and women filled many clerical posts during the First World War. Mark Twain bought a Remington in autumn 1874 and was using it for correspondence by December. The typewriter was also an early accessibility tool for blind people, and Sir Francis Campbell began adapting one with Braille output in 1875.

The Sholes and Glidden machines established the QWERTY layout, which remains the standard for English-language keyboards, and variants such as the French AZERTY and German QWERTZ arose for other languages. Typewriters were a fixture of offices until the 1980s, when personal computers began to replace them, and IBM sold its typewriter division in 1991. Habits such as typing two hyphens for a dash, and terms such as backspace, carriage return and cc for carbon copy, descend from the machine.
typhus: Typhus is a group of infectious diseases that includes epidemic typhus, scrub typhus and murine typhus. Common symptoms are fever, headache and a rash, typically beginning one to two weeks after exposure. Epidemic typhus is caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii and spread by body lice, scrub typhus by Orientia tsutsugamushi and spread by chiggers, and murine typhus by Rickettsia typhi and spread by fleas.

Epidemic typhus, the most severe form, generally occurs in outbreaks where poor sanitation and crowding are present. Without treatment, death may occur in 10 to 60 percent of cases. The antibiotic doxycycline is the treatment. The name comes from the Greek tûphos, meaning hazy or smoky, a word for delusion, and typhus is a different disease from typhoid fever.

Typhus has been described since at least 1528. The first reliable description appears in 1489, during the siege of Baza in the War of Granada, when the Spanish lost 3,000 men to enemy action and a further 17,000 to typhus. Gaol fever, common in English prisons where inmates were crowded into dark, filthy rooms, is believed to have been typhus. In 1750 it killed the Lord Mayor of London and many court officials at the Old Bailey, next to Newgate Prison.

Epidemics occurred routinely across Europe from the 16th to the 19th centuries. Typhus may have killed more than 10 percent of the German population in the Thirty Years' War. In Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812, more French soldiers died of typhus and dysentery than were killed by the Russians.

An epidemic in Ireland between 1816 and 1819 killed an estimated 100,000 people, and typhus with typhoid fever is said to be responsible for 400,000 deaths in the Great Irish Famine of 1846 to 1849. In the First World War typhus ravaged the armies of the Eastern Front, with over 150,000 deaths in Serbia alone. In 1922 the epidemic in Soviet territory peaked at some 20 to 30 million cases in Russia, and during the civil war it killed 2–3 million people.

Rudolf Weigl developed the first typhus vaccine in the interwar period; it did not prevent the disease but reduced mortality. In the Second World War typhus killed prisoners in camps and ghettos, among them Anne Frank and her sister Margot at Bergen-Belsen. Epidemic typhus is now rare.
tyrian-purple: Tyrian purple is a reddish-purple dye secreted by several predatory sea snails of the family Muricidae, among them Bolinus brandaris, Hexaplex trunculus and Stramonita haemastoma. The colouring compound is 6,6'-dibromoindigo. The dye was made from a mucous secretion of the snail's hypobranchial gland, and it was valued because it did not fade but grew brighter with weathering and sunlight. Production for textiles is dated to about 1200 BCE among the Phoenicians, and it may have begun as early as 1570 BCE. Shells found on Crete suggest that the Minoans may have extracted purple centuries before the Tyrians, and Hala Sultan Tekke on Cyprus exported purple-dyed textiles in the Late Bronze Age.

Twelve thousand snails of Murex brandaris yielded no more than 1.4 grams of pure dye, enough to colour only the trim of a single garment, according to an experiment of 1908 cited by David Jacoby. Excavations at Tyre show that the snails were collected in large vats and left to decompose, which produced a stench that ancient authors mention. Pliny the Elder described salting the extracted glands, steeping them for three days, boiling the liquor and testing it with a fleece.

The most prized shade, compared to blackish clotted blood, is believed to have come from dipping cloth twice, in the blue dye of H. trunculus and the purple-red dye of B. brandaris. The Phoenicians also ran a production station on the Iles Purpuraires at Mogador, in Morocco.

The cost made purple cloth a mark of rank, and sumptuary laws restricted it. The most senior Roman magistrates wore a toga praetexta edged in purple, and generals celebrating a triumph wore the toga picta, solid purple with gold-thread edging. By the 4th century CE only the Roman emperor was permitted to wear it, so that donning the purple came to mean becoming emperor. The Byzantine court controlled and subsidised its production, and from the 9th century a child born to a reigning emperor was called porphyrogenitos, born in the purple. Production for the court ended with the sack of Constantinople in 1204, and western Europe turned to the insect dye kermes instead.
tyrol: Tyrol is a historical region in the Alps of northern Italy and western Austria, with an area of 26,673 square kilometres. It consists of the Austrian State of Tyrol and, in Italy, the Province of South Tyrol and the Province of Trento, along with a few municipalities of Veneto and Lombardy. Its largest cities are Innsbruck, Trento and Bolzano. The main chain of the Alps runs across it, along the border between North and South Tyrol, and the Brenner Pass, at 1,370 metres, is the lowest pass across that chain. The Ortler, at 3,905 metres, is the highest mountain. German and Italian are the main languages, with Ladin, Cimbrian and Mócheno as minority languages.

The earliest evidence of settlement is from the Tischofer Cave, about 28,000 years ago. In 15 BCE Roman forces under Drusus and Tiberius conquered Tyrol and organised the provinces of Raetia and Noricum. In the Middle Ages most of the region fell to the Duchy of Bavaria, created about 555, while the south, including Bolzano, remained with the Lombards. Christianity spread through the bishoprics of Brixen and Trento. The County of Tyrol took shape in the 12th century, and Innsbruck became a centre of European politics and culture when Emperor Maximilian I took up residence there.

From the mid-16th century Tyrol was ruled by younger sons of the Habsburg emperors until all Habsburg lands came under Emperor Leopold I in 1665. From the time of Maria Theresa it was governed from Vienna in major matters, and in 1803 the lands of the bishoprics of Trent and Brixen were secularised and added to the county. The Tyrolean Rifles, a militia authorised by Maximilian I in 1511, became known in 1809, when peasants rose against the French-Bavarian occupation under Andreas Hofer in four battles at Bergisel. In 1919 the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye divided Tyrol into the Austrian state and the Italian region of Trentino-Alto Adige.

Tyrol has long been a transit route between northern and southern Europe, and the Brenner Railway, opened in 1867, runs from Innsbruck to Verona. Tourism is the most important economic sector, helped by railways in the 19th century and the Brenner motorway in the 1960s, and agriculture and forestry shape the landscape; apples and wine are grown in the south. The Tyrol-South Tyrol-Trentino Euroregion, a cross-border body, has had its own legal entity since 2011. The arms of Tyrol show a red eagle on a silver field.
tyrol-castle: Tyrol Castle stands in the comune of Tirol near Merano, in the Burggrafenamt district of South Tyrol. Its hill has been inhabited since ancient times: archaeologists have found artefacts and a field of graves from the early Middle Ages, and have excavated a church with three apses from the early Christian period.

The castle grew in several phases. The keep dates to 1139/40, and a further phase of building followed in the second half of the 13th century under Count Meinhard II of Gorizia-Tyrol. In 1347 his granddaughter, Countess Margaret of Tyrol, was besieged here by the forces of the Luxembourg king Charles IV.

The castle remained the seat of Tyrol's sovereigns until 1420, when the Habsburg archduke Frederick IV moved the administrative seat to Innsbruck, north of the Brenner Pass. In modern times parts of the castle fell into the Köstengraben, a steep gorge beside it, and it was even sold to be used as a quarry. It was restored in the 19th century, and the keep was rebuilt in 1904.

The chapel's frescos and two Romanesque portals with marble sculptures of fabulous creatures, religious themes and geometric ornaments are its main works of art. The chapel also holds the oldest known painting of the coat of arms of Tyrol, the Red Eagle. The castle has housed a museum since the early 1980s, and excavations since then have yielded a series of finds from the late Middle Ages. Since 2003 it has been home to the South Tyrolean Museum of History, and a falconry with a nursing ward for birds of prey stands next to it.
tyrrhenian-sea: The Tyrrhenian Sea lies off the western coast of Italy. The islands of Corsica and Sardinia bound it on the west, the Italian Peninsula, in the regions of Tuscany, Lazio, Campania, Basilicata and Calabria, on the north and east, and Sicily on the south. Its maximum depth is 3,785 metres. The International Hydrographic Organization defines its limits by lines across the Strait of Messina, from Sicily to Sardinia, across the Strait of Bonifacio and along the north from Cape Corse in Corsica to the Italian coast. The sea contains smaller islands such as Capri, Elba, Ischia and Ustica, and the eight Aeolian Islands lie in its southern part, north of Sicily.

It lies near the meeting of the African and Eurasian plates, and mountain chains and active volcanoes such as Mount Marsili are found in its depths. It is a back-arc basin that formed during the Neogene as the Calabrian slab rolled back towards the south-east. Episodes of fast and slow retreat formed first the Vavilov basin and then the Marsili basin, which are separated by an undersea ridge, the Issel Bridge. The same process gave rise to submarine volcanoes and to the active volcano Mount Stromboli.

The name derives from the Greek name for the Etruscans. Hesiod, in the 8th century BCE, first mentions them, describing them as living in central Italy alongside the Latins. The Etruscans lived along the coast of modern Tuscany, Latium and Campania, and they called the water the Sea of the Etruscans. In Greek mythology the cliffs above the sea were believed to house the four winds kept by Aeolus: the Mistral from the Rhône valley, the Libeccio from the southwest, and the Sirocco and Ostro from the south.

The main Italian ports on the sea are Naples, Palermo, Civitavecchia, Salerno, Trapani and Gioia Tauro, and Bastia lies on Corsica. The maritime facilities called the port of Rome are at Civitavecchia, about 68 kilometres north-west of the city, since Rome itself has no port. Its islands include Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily, the Tuscan Archipelago, the Pontine Islands, Procida and the Aeolian Islands.
tyrtaeus: Almost everything known about Tyrtaeus comes from two entries of the Suda, a Byzantine encyclopedia compiled in the 10th century CE, and from accounts that were mostly deduced from his poetry or invented. Ancient writers disagreed about his origin. Pausanias told of a lame and stupid Athenian schoolteacher whom the Athenians sent to Sparta in response to an oracle. Modern scholars generally think the story was an Athenian invention, and conclude that he was a native of Laconia, because in one fragment he counts himself among the Heraclidae whom Zeus gave to Sparta and addresses Spartan warriors with authority.

His poems arose from two crises. One was civil unrest that threatened the authority of kings and elders; Aristotle recalls that some Spartans, hard pressed by war, demanded a redistribution of land. The other was the Second Messenian War, which followed the Spartan conquest of Messenia in the 8th century BCE.

Tyrtaeus was chiefly an elegiac poet, and his works were thought to fill five books. About 250 lines or parts of lines survive, through quotations and papyri. The Suda names a Constitution, generally treated as another title for the Eunomia, which stressed the role of divine providence in the state and the cooperation of kings, elders and people. It also names Precepts in elegiac couplets and war songs, and later writers add marching songs in anapaests, whose authenticity is doubtful.

The three longest fragments are complete or nearly complete poems on the ideal warrior and the glory or disgrace that follows his choices. One describes hoplites fighting foot against foot, shield against shield and breast against breast. His language is largely Homeric even though his audience spoke Doric, and a line on dying fighting for the fatherland echoes Hector's speech in the Iliad. He holds that patriotic military valour is the highest form of arete, which can be reached only among comrades, and he names no individual warriors.

In the 4th century BCE, when his poetry was an established classic, Spartan armies on campaign were made to listen to it. Plato quotes his elegy on arete in the Laws. Some modern scholars believe he helped turn Sparta from its arts toward military austerity, though others see no real evidence for this.

During the Renaissance he came to be seen as the prototype of the artist who uses his talent to urge his countrymen to fight for freedom, partly through a story in Plutarch's Life of Cleomenes, in which King Leonidas praises him. A bronze statue of a hoplite raised in the central square of Sparta in 2006 carries one of his poems in modern Greek.
tzachas: Very little is known of his life, and nearly all of it from one source, the Alexiad of the Byzantine princess Anna Komnene, daughter of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos. The 13th-century Danishmendname also names him, as Chavuldur Chaka, but it mixes history with legend and is not a reliable source. In Anna's account he was a raider of Oghuz Turk origin who was taken prisoner during the reign of Nikephoros III Botaneiates, entered Byzantine service and rose quickly, receiving the title of protonobelissimos and rich gifts. When Alexios deposed Botaneiates in 1081, he lost his position and fled.

From Smyrna he waged war on the Byzantines. With Christian craftsmen he built a fleet, took Phocaea and the islands of Lesbos (except the fortress of Methymna), Samos, Chios and Rhodes, and defeated a Byzantine fleet sent against him under Niketas Kastamonites. Some modern scholars have suggested that he acted in concert with two Byzantine rebels of the time, Rhapsomates in Cyprus and Karykes in Crete. He may also have converted to Christianity to fit into Byzantine society.

Constantine Dalassenos recovered Chios in 1090/91, but Tzachas rebuilt his forces, proclaimed himself emperor and sought an alliance with the Pechenegs in Thrace for a joint attack on Constantinople. In 1092 Dalassenos and the megas doux John Doukas besieged the fortress of Mytilene on Lesbos. Tzachas held out for three months before negotiating its surrender, and on his way back to Smyrna his fleet was almost destroyed.

According to the Alexiad, Tzachas attacked the port of Abydos in the spring of 1093. Alexios called on Kilij Arslan I, Sultan of Rum, who was married to Tzachas's daughter Ayşe Hatun, to strike him from the rear; the sultan advanced to Abydos, invited his father-in-law to a banquet and had him murdered. Around 1097, when John Doukas retook Smyrna, a Tzachas, possibly his son, was still reported holding the city. The modern Turkish Naval Forces count his capture of Smyrna as their founding date.
tzanetos-grigorakis: Grigorakis was born in 1742 at Skoutari near Gytheio in Laconia, the son of Demetrios Grigorakis; his name Tzanetos is the Maniot form of Ioannis. He began his military service within his clan, and in the Russo-Turkish War of 1768-1774 he served in the Ionian Islands with the rank of major in the Imperial Russian Army under Emmanouil Papadopoulos. When Hassan Ghazi, the ruler of Tripoli, had the clan leader Exarchos Grigorakis seized and hanged, Tzanetos took command and, in revenge, led about 3,000 Maniots against the Ottomans at the castle of Passavas in Las, where 700 families were slaughtered.

He at first refused the office of bey, until Nikolaos Mavrogenis, dragoman of the Ottoman fleet, seized him at Gytheio, sent his two sons as hostages to Sultan Abdul Hamid I and forced him to accept. As bey he fortified the border, moved his seat to Gytheio, then called Marathonisi, and founded the village of Mavrovouni, where he built the Melissi castle, finished in 1795. He served 16 years, the longest of the beys of Mani.

He sought Russian help against the Ottomans, and in 1792 he warned Lambros Katsonis, who had refused to accept the peace, so that the Ottomans captured only 11 empty ships. In 1798 he offered Napoleon Bonaparte the use of Mani's harbours through Demetrio Stefanopoli, and his son Pierros fought for Napoleon in Italy. When the Ottomans attacked, Grigorakis drove them back with about 1,000 men, but they replaced him with Panagiotis Koumoundouros.

In 1803 a second Ottoman invasion almost destroyed the Melissi castle, and Grigorakis held out in the castle of Cranae against some 2,000 cannonballs. His cousin Antonis Grigorakis was then made bey and ordered to arrest him and Pierros, and Tzanetos fled to Zakynthos while the clan's towers and property were confiscated. When Pierros prepared a campaign under the Russian flag, the Ottomans pardoned them both, and in 1806 they returned to Mani. Tzanetos died in 1813 in his castle at Mavrovouni. He is counted with Petrobey Mavromichalis among the most prominent beys of Mani.
tzitzak: Tzitzak, in Greek Τζιτζάκ, was the daughter of Bihar, khagan of the Khazars. Her name is most widely thought to be a Hellenized form of a Turkic word derived from Proto-Turkic čeček, related to Chuvash and Turkish words meaning flower. Marcel Erdal, however, notes that Constantine VII used tzitzak for the empress's garment and finds the idea that it was her personal name far-fetched. He thinks the word more likely described the colourfulness of the garment, and he compares the Hebrew ṣiṣiṯ, the fringed Jewish ceremonial shawl.

In 732 the Byzantine Empire was threatened with invasion by the Umayyad Caliphate. Seeking allies, Leo III the Isaurian sent an embassy to Bihar, and the alliance was sealed by the marriage of Tzitzak to Constantine V, Leo's son and junior co-ruler. She was escorted to Constantinople. Constantine was about fourteen, and Tzitzak may have been even younger, since she did not give birth for eighteen years. She became a Christian under the baptismal name Irene. Her wedding gown started a fashion in Constantinople for male robes called tzitzakia.

Leo III died on 18 June 741 and Constantine V succeeded him, with Irene as empress. Civil war broke out almost at once, when Artabasdos, Constantine's brother-in-law, claimed the throne. It lasted until 2 November 743, and the chronicle of Theophanes the Confessor does not describe any part Irene played in it. Theophanes records that she learned to read religious texts, and that she lived piously, which he contrasts with the impiety of her father-in-law and husband. Both emperors were iconoclasts, while Theophanes was an iconodule monk, and his praise probably reflects that Irene shared his views.

On 25 January 750 Constantine and Tzitzak had a son, Leo, who succeeded his father as Emperor Leo IV and is better known as Leo the Khazar. His birth is the last mention of Irene in the historical record. By the following year Constantine was already married to his second wife, Maria. Lynda Garland has suggested that Tzitzak died in childbirth, which would fit the death c. 750 given for her.
tzutujil-people: The Tzʼutujil are one of the 22 Maya ethnic groups of Guatemala, and about 100,000 live around Lake Atitlán, on its southern watershed in the Solola region of the highlands. Their ancestors came from Tollan, the ancient capital of the Toltecs. Their capital Chiaa, meaning close to the water, stood on the hill of Chuitinamit. It was ruled by a supreme lord, the Ahtzʼiquinahay or Lord of the House, and a lesser lord called the Tzʼutujil, who gave the people their name. In the 15th century the Ki’che’ ruler Quicab blocked their expansion westward by force.

After the Spanish victory near Panajachel the Tzʼutujil lost part of their lands and control of the lake. Franciscan friars moved the capital to Santiago Atitlán and built a monastery there, and from 1533 the Spanish set up cofradías, brotherhoods devoted to Catholic saints that also collected revenue. Their population is estimated to have fallen from 72,000 in 1520 to 5,300 in 1575, through epidemic disease, gold mining and war.

In the 20th century indigenous land was taken for estates called fincas, and by 1928 80% of the Tzʼutujil worked in debt peonage. On 2 December 1990 soldiers fired on a protesting crowd in Santiago Atitlán, killing 14 people, and the army then had to leave the town.

Many Tzʼutujil keep the Atiteco religion, alongside Catholicism and Evangelical Protestantism. They hold that the Santo Mundo, the Holy World, is a living body with a centre and four corners marked by the solstice sunrises and sunsets, that ancestral spirits called Nawals taught their customs, and that time is cyclical, with children often the reincarnation of grandparents. Women weave on the backstrap loom, the weaving seen as a kind of birth, and songmen sing the sacred songs called bʼix. Many farm coffee and maize, and painters in San Juan La Laguna work in the Arte Naif style.
